After staying there for a few days, Pillaiyar worshipped other shrines, including ThiruPaiṅgīli and Thiru Īṅkōymalai, and then journeyed westward to Koṅgu Nāḍu. On the southern bank of the Kaveri in Koṅgu Nāḍu, at ThiruKoḍimāḍa Cheṅkūṉṟu, devotees welcomed Pillaiyar. He worshipped the Lord, sang hymns, praised Him. Pillaiyar remained in that town.

Later, he departed from there, worshipped all the Shiva shrines in the western direction, went to ThiruNāṉā (Bhavani Temple), worshipped the Lord, and then returned to ThiruKoḍimāḍa Cheṅkuṉṟūr where he had stayed before.

During that time, the cold season arrived, and a chilling wind blew intensely. As Pillaiyar’s attendants had stayed in that region for many days, they developed a fever due to the cold, affecting all the devotees as if to afflict them. They informed Pillaiyar and worshipped him. He prayed for the Lord’s grace and, with the sentiment, “Though this is the nature of this land, it should not befall us,” He sang a hymn to the Lord, beginning with “Avviṉaikku Ivviṉai” (For that deed, this deed) and praising with “Seiviṉai Vanthu Emai Thīṇḍap PeṟāthiruNīlakaṇḍam” (No deed can touch us, O Blue-throated Lord), issuing a divine command. By this command, the disease was removed not only from the people living in that area but also throughout the entire country.

After staying there for some days, he worshipped many other shrines and went to ThiruPāṇḍik Koḍumuḍi, where he worshipped and sang the hymn “Pāṇḍik Koḍumuḍiyārē.” Then he journeyed eastward, worshipped at the holy temple of Selva Karuvūr Thiru Āṇilai, then revered ThiruVeñjamā Kūḍal, worshipped many shrines, and departed from Koṅgu Nāḍu. He arrived at ThiruVāṭpōkki, a shrine on the southern bank of the Kaveri, and worshipped there. He delighted in worshipping many hills and holy places, then worshipped ThiruParāyththuṟai, Thiruchchi. He worshipped shrines such as Senthuṟaidi and Thiruchchirāppaḷḷi, and then arrived at ThiruĀṉaikkā.

There, he worshipped the Lord, who emerged beneath a white Naval tree, and praised Him in his hymn by mentioning the services rendered by Airāvatham and Kōchcheṅgaṇ Chōzhar. He also sang the hymn called “Kūḍa Sathukkam,” which praises ThiruĀṉaikkā, Mahendram, Kailai, and ThiruVārūr, and stayed there for some days.

Afterward, he worshipped ThiruThavaththuṟai, ThiruPāṟṟuṟai, ThiruVerumpiyūr Malai, and then worshipped ThiruNeḍuṅkaḷam. He sang a hymn with the theme of “remove the troubles that prevent devotees from expressing their love.” After worshipping ThiruKāṭṭuppaḷḷi, devotees grandly welcomed him. He went to ThiruPūnthurutthi, worshipped PoiYili Appar, then worshipped ThiruKaṇḍiyūr Veerattam.

There, among the devotees. He sang a devotional hymn inquiring about the Lord’s grace.

After that, he worshipped ThiruSoṟṟuththuṟai, ThiruVēthikuḍi, ThiruVeṇṇi, ThiruChakkaraPpaḷḷi, Thiru Ālandurai, and ThiruPālaisthuṟai, then reached and worshipped ThiruNallūr, where he resided. From there, he worshipped ThiruKarukāvūr, ThiruAvazhivanaḷḷūr, ThiruParuthiniyamam, and ThiruĀvūr Pasupathīchcharam, and then returned to ThiruNallūr. From there, he was welcomed by devotees and affectionately worshipped ThiruValañchozhi. He resided in that holy place, praising daily with great love.

At that time, summer arrived. Due to the sun entering Mithuna hora, its scorching rays caused even the oceans to shrink. The summer intensified, becoming a severely hot season. It transformed into a time of intense heat.

At that time, Pillaiyar, walking from ThiruValañchozhi to reach Pazhaiyāṟai, joined and worshipped at ThiruĀrai Mēṯṟazhi, and then proceeded to worship ThiruPattīchcharam. To alleviate the heat of the sun, Shiva Bhoothas erected a cool pearl canopy over his head and proclaimed, “Pattīsar has blessed us and sent us.” Immediately, his attendants held the jeweled shaft of the canopy. As the Devas showered flowers, those very flowers formed a flower canopy. Pillaiyar, as if under the shade of the Lord’s feet, resided beneath that canopy. He reached ThiruPattīchcharam, where, with great love, he worshipped and praised the Lord. From there, he went to worship Thiru Irumpūzhaí, and sang a hymn that expounded the meaning of the sacred Vedas.

From there, Thiru. He worshipped shrines such as Aṟathai Perumpāzhi, ThiruChērai, ThiruNāḷūr, ThiruKuḍavāyil, ThiruNaṟaiyūr, Thenthiruppūththūr, and ThiruSivapuram, and then arrived at ThiruKuḍamūkku, also known as Kumbakonam. Devotees welcomed him. He worshipped the Lord at ThiruKuḍamūkku, ThiruKīzhkōṭṭam, and ThiruKuḍanthai Kārōṇam, and also reverently worshipped the Mahamaham sacred tank.

Afterward, he worshipped ThiruNāgēswaram and delightedly resided there. Subsequently, seeing ThiruViḍai Maruthūr appear before him, he sang “Iḍaimaruthu Īthō” (Here is ThiruViḍai Maruthūr) and went to worship and immerse himself in song. During his stay there, he journeyed along the Kaveri bank, worshipped ThiruKuṟaṅkāḍu Thuṟai, and reached ThiruĀvuḍuthuṟai. He worshipped the Lord at ThiruĀvuḍuthuṟai and resided there.

At that time, the period for performing the Yaga. Upon its arrival, ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān’s father came to ThiruĀvaḍuthuṟai and informed Pillaiyar, who was residing there. Pillaiyar, firmly believing that “Are not the Lord’s feet the ultimate wealth?”, went to the temple and stood before the Lord. He sang a hymn with the sentiment, “I have nothing else to give to those who ask for wealth; I know nothing but Your feet,” stating, “Is this how You rule us? We have nothing. Is this Your sweet grace?” As he sang this hymn, by the grace of the Lord, Shiva Bhoothas placed a purse containing one thousand gold coins on the pedestal, saying, “This purse of gold will never diminish; the Lord has granted it to you,” to Pillaiyar.

That Bhootha. Pillaiyar, hearing this, worshipped, took the purse, and gave it to his father, saying, “With this, you and the other Brahmins in Sīrkāzhi should perform many good Yagas to worship the Lord.” He further blessed, saying, “This purse of gold will increase without diminishing.” Afterward, ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān’s father went to Sīrkāzhi and conducted good Yagas there.

Then, Pillaiyar worshipped the Lord at ThiruĀvaḍuthuṟai.

Following this, he worshipped ThiruKōzhambam, Vaikal Māḍakkōyil, ThiruNallam, ThiruAzhunthūr Māḍakkōyil, ThiruThurutthi, and Mūvalūr. He then entered ThiruMayilāḍuthuṟai, welcomed by devotees, worshipped, rejoiced, and resided there.

After that, he worshipped ThiruChempanpaḷḷi, ThiruVizhanagar, and ThiruPaṟiyal Vīraṭṭam, and then proceeded towards the seashore, worshipping ThiruVēṭṭa. Pillaiyar worshipped Kuḍi and reached ThiruTharumapuram. This place was the birthplace of ThiruNīlakaṇḍa Yāzhppāṇar’s holy mother.

Therefore, ThiruNīlakaṇḍa Yāzhppāṇar’s relatives welcomed and worshipped both Pillaiyar and ThiruNīlakaṇḍa Yāzhppāṇar. There, ThiruNīlakaṇḍa Yāzhppāṇar informed all his relatives that he had served Pillaiyar by playing and singing his hymns on the Yazh. ThiruNīlakaṇḍa Yāzhppāṇar blessed his relatives. Hearing this, they praised ThiruNīlakaṇḍa Yāzhppāṇar, saying, “The sound of those hymns, arranged and performed by you on the Yazh, has caused that music to resonate and flourish throughout the world.” They praised ThiruNīlakaṇḍa Yāzhppāṇar, stating that the hymns were set to music because of his skill. Hearing this, ThiruNīlakaṇḍa Yāzhppāṇar trembled.

He worshipped Pillaiyar and requested, “You must bless me with a boundless hymn, a hymn whose greatness cannot be confined by musical scales. To let not only these people but everyone in the world know your greatness, please sing a hymn that transcends musical limitations.” Pillaiyar then sang a hymn. He sang it in a way that could not be contained by the vocal chords or instruments of people, nor by the efforts described in musical treatises. He sang the hymn beginning with “Māthar Maḍappiḍi” and worshipped the Lord. He graciously sang that hymn. The minstrel, as before, tried to play that hymn on the Yazh, but he found that the hymn could not be contained within the scope of the Yazh.

Then he prostrated at Pillaiyar’s feet and said, “I began by saying I would play the music of this great one’s hymns on the Yazh, I would set it to the Yazh. Is it not because I have this instrument in my hand?” And he raised it to break it. Seeing this, Pillaiyar stopped him, took the Yazh, and said, “Sir, why are you breaking this Yazh? Can the grace of Ammaiyappar be contained within this instrument? It is customary to play within the limits of the instrument, as much as is suitable for our nature, so that the world may know. Can the greatness of that music, which cannot be measured by thought, be contained in action?

“You shall continue to play this Yazh.” He spoke thus and handed over the Yazh. ThiruNīlakaṇḍa Yāzhppāṇar took it, held it in his hand, and, along with his relatives, worshipped Pillaiyar’s feet. After staying there for some days, Pillaiyar worshipped other shrines and proceeded to the holy place of ThiruNallāṟu. Devotees welcomed him, worshipped him, and surrounded him as he entered the temple. He worshipped according to custom and sang the hymn “Pōgamārtha Pūṇmulaiyāḷ” (She with adorned breasts, full of pleasure), praising the Lord.

“Pillaiyar then graciously asked ThiruNīlakaṇḍa Yāzhppāṇar to play that hymn on the Yazh. ThiruNīlakaṇḍa Yāzhppāṇar played it on the Yazh as requested, and everyone rejoiced.

“We will continue to contemplate the brief history of ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam Part 543, Vambara Varivaṇḍuch Chaṟukkam, authored by Sekkizhar Swamigal, recounts the history of ThiruGnanaSambandha Nāyanār. Departing from the holy place of ThiruNallāṟu and worshipping other shrines, ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān arrived at the holy place of ThiruChāththamaṅgai. ThiruNīlanakka Nāyanār decorated the town and, with auspicious signs, welcomed Pillaiyar. Pillaiyar entered the Ayavanthi Temple, worshipped, and then graced ThiruNīlanakka’s home. He sat there with the devotees as ThiruNīlanakka Nāyanār offered a feast.

That night, according to Pillaiyar’s instructions, ThiruNīlakaṇḍa Yāzhppāṇa Nāyanār and his wife, Mathaṅkachūḷāmaṇi Ammaiyār, were given a place to rest beside the sacrificial fire altar where ThiruNīlanakka Nāyanār maintained his ritual fire in the middle of his house. They slept there. The sacrificial fire blazed brightly.

Afterward, he sang a hymn praising the unique qualities of ThiruNīlanakka Nāyanār, granted him leave, cherished his friendship, and proceeded to worship other shrines. Subsequently, Pillaiyar worshipped holy places such as ThiruNāgai Kārōṇam and Thiru Kīzhvēlūr. Hearing of Pillaiyar’s arrival, Siruthoṇḍa Nāyanār rushed to worship him and requested him to come to his hometown, ThiruCheṅkāṭṭaṅkuḍi. Pillaiyar, delighted, worshipped the Lord at Gaṇapathīchcharam there, sang a hymn praising the greatness of Siruthoṇḍa’s holy service, and then resided in his home.

Later, he went to ThiruMarugal and worshipped. During those days, a merchant, accompanied by a woman, spent the night in a monastery in ThiruMarugal.

At that moment, a snake bit him. The poison spread, and life was about to depart. The woman, weakened and distraught, wept and cried beside him, unable to touch him. Even with all the treatments given by powerful sorcerers skilled in Garuḍa Vidya and Iḍibhāvaṉa, the poison did not recede. As the long night approached dawn, the woman, utterly exhausted, wept bitterly. “I left my parents and came here with you as my refuge.

“If you leave me, what will I do? Is there no one here to relieve this suffering?” she cried out in deep sorrow. She stretched out her hands towards the entrance of the Lord’s temple and worshipped. All the devotees cried out, “May all beings thrive! O Lord Who consumed poison! O Lord Who, at the request of Kama’s consort, revived him after being consumed by fire!

“O Lord Who kicked Yama for Mārkaṇḍeya, who sought refuge in You! Please grant Your grace so that this venom may subside and I may overcome this ocean of suffering.” She cried out, praising the Lord. That sound, at dawn, reached the ears of Pillaiyar, who had risen to worship the temple. Pillaiyar, with compassion in his heart, went with the devotees to where she was. He saw her crying out, praising Lord Shiva’s grace. He asked her, “Do not be afraid.

“Tell me your suffering and worry.” She fell at Pillaiyar’s feet, worshipped, rose, and spoke. He asked her, “Do not be afraid. Tell me your suffering and worry.” She fell at Pillaiyar’s feet, worshipped, rose, and spoke. “In the village of Vaippūr, near this town, lives a merchant named Thāman. He is my father. The man lying here, bitten by a snake, is my father’s son-in-law.

“My father has seven daughters. He promised to give his eldest daughter in marriage to this man, but he did not fulfill that promise. He took a large sum of money and married his eldest daughter to someone else. My father continued to promise each of us to this man, but he married each of us off to others. I was the only one remaining.

“So, with great concern for him, I left my parents and came here with him. As soon as we arrived, he was bitten by a snake. He died from a snakebite. I stand here like a ship capsized in the middle of the ocean. If you would show mercy to relieve my sorrow,” he said, Pillaiyar, to bestow grace upon her, pleaded with the Lord of ThiruMarugal to remove the poison and sang the hymn “Uḍaiyāṉai Ivaḷ Ivvāṟu Uṉ Mezhithal Uṉakku Thakumō” (Is it proper for You, O Lord, to allow her to suffer thus?), which includes the phrase “Saḍaiyāy Eṉumāḷ” (The one who says, “O Lord with matted locks”). Immediately, the merchant revived, free from the poison.

“The crowd of devotees shouted the Lord’s name in jubilation. The woman and the merchant clasped their hands above their heads and prostrated at Pillaiyar’s feet. Pillaiyar blessed them with a good life by arranging their marriage and, granting them leave, departed from there. On that day, Siruthoṇḍa Nāyanār came and requested him to stay. As he was taking leave, the Lord revealed His form at ThiruCheṅkāṭṭaṅkuḍi there.

“Therefore, he sang the hymn “Aṅgamum Vēthamum” (Both the limbs and the Vedas), combining two hymns, and resided with Siruthoṇḍanār in ThiruCheṅkāṭṭaṅkuḍi for some days. Afterward, he returned to ThiruMarugal and, after some days, went to ThiruPukalūr and worshipped. He resided in the monastery of ThiruMuruga Nāyanār.

“At that time, ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān, after worshipping the Lord in ThiruVārūr, arrived there, intending to worship ThiruPukalūr. Upon hearing this good news, Pillaiyar, with great love, along with his devotees, came to the border of ThiruPukalūr to welcome ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān. As Arasu also arrived, both, out of their mutual affection, bowed down and expressed their joy, each offering and receiving good wishes. Since Arasu had come after worshipping ThiruVārūr, Pillaiyar asked him, “How many times have you worshipped ThiruVārūr and been saved?” He asked how many times he had worshipped ThiruVārūr and been saved. He replied by describing the opulent festivities of the ThiruĀthirai festival in the hymn “Muththuvithāṉam.” Hearing this description, Pillaiyar immediately, out of love, said to Arasu, “I will go to ThiruVārūr, worship, and then return to join you.” He obtained Arasu’s consent and immediately proceeded to ThiruVārūr.

“Arasu, with his love following Pillaiyar, went to worship ThiruPukalūr and resided there, praising the Lord. Pillaiyar worshipped at ThiruVīrakkuḍi Veerattam.

“Then, singing “Ārūr Aḍaivōmē” (Let us reach Ārūr), he approached the outskirts of ThiruVārūr. There, the town of ThiruVārūr appeared like a golden world, with abundant groves, tall mansions, and banners touching the solar orb. He sang a hymn proclaiming, “This is Ārūr.” He reached the border of the holy city. The flood of love overflowed boundlessly. He descended from his palanquin, worshipped by showering abundant flowers from his hands, and prostrated, singing “Thiru Irukku Kural.” At that moment, Ārūr shone with great splendor. By the grace of Thyāgathyāgēsa Perumān, devotees and attendants came to the city’s border to welcome Pillaiyar.

“Before them, Pillaiyar sang the hymn “Anthamāy Ulakāthi” (The end and beginning of the world), with the line “ThiruVārūr Enthaithāṉ Eṉa Ēṉṟu Koḷluṅkaḷō” (Will my Father of ThiruVārūr accept me?). He then reached the temple, worshipped at the Thēvāsirya Maṇḍapam, circumambulated the holy precinct, entered, and before the Lord, prostrated many times with great love, rose, sang hymns, immersed himself in devotion, came out, and reached the monastery. He worshipped the path of righteousness of ThiruVārūr and resided there, worshipping the Lord who resides in the anthill at all times. During that time. He remembered having been told to stay in ThiruVārūr. Worshipping ThiruVārūr, he set off towards ThiruPukalūr, with the thought, “O mind, fear not!

“Worship Shiva’s Ārūr. Worship without fail to be saved. It is difficult.” He sang the hymn “Pavaṉamāychchōḍaiyāy” and, worshipping ThiruVārūr, departed from there. Along the way, he worshipped shrines like ThiruPaṉaiyūr and arrived at ThiruPukalūr.

“There, ThiruNāvukkarasu Swamigal, ThiruMuruga Nāyanār, and other devotees came, bowed, and welcomed him. Pillaiyar went with them to the temple, worshipped, and then stayed for some days in ThiruMuruga Nāyanār’s monastery.

“During that time, ThiruNīlanakka Nāyanār and Siruthoṇḍa Nāyanār also arrived there. Pillaiyar, along with the virtuous devotees, stood in worship of the Lord, intently discerning the true essence of noble devotion, and resided there with them as days passed. He resided there, intently discerning the true essence of noble devotion, as days passed. On that day, he sang a hymn of ‘harmonious music’ and praised the greatness of that holy place. From there, he desired to worship other shrines. Siruthoṇḍa Nāyanār and ThiruNīlanakka Nāyanār returned to their respective holy places.

“Muruga Nāyanār remained in ThiruPukalūr. Pillaiyar, after worshipping Pukalūr, began to proceed further. ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān and Pillaiyar journeyed together on their pilgrimage.

“At that time, as Pillaiyar walked close to ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān, ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān said to Pillaiyar, “You should ride in the pearl palanquin that the Lord has given you.” Pillaiyar said to ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān, “If this is the Lord’s grace, then you, with your devotees, go ahead. “I will follow you,” he said. Arasu agreed to do so, and from that day on, their entire pilgrimage together proceeded in this manner.

“Thus, Pillaiyar and ThiruNāvukkarasu Swamigal reached the holy place of ThiruAmpar. ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān sang the hymn “Pulku Poṉṉiṟam” (Embrace the golden hue) and extolled the holy work done by Kōchcheṅgaṇ Chōzhar there. From there, ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān and ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān went to worship ThiruKaḍavūr.

“There, Kuṅkiliya Kalaya Nāyanār welcomed these two great individuals. Upon reaching ThiruKaḍavūr, Pillaiyar sang the hymn “Saḍaiyuḍaiyāṉ” (He with matted locks), praising the Lord who heroically kicked Yama in that holy place, and then resided in the monastery of Kuṅkiliya Kalaya Nāyanār with ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān. Pillaiyar accepted the feast arranged by Kuṅkiliya Kalaya Nāyanār with great pleasure. He gladly accepted the feast and stayed there.

“Afterward, he worshipped shrines like ThiruĀkkūr and ThiruPāmbaram, and then approached ThiruVēḷimizhalaí. ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān went first, followed by Pillaiyar.

“The Brahmins in that town welcomed both of them and decorated the town. They sang the hymn “Arayār Virikōṇa Vāḍai” (The fragrance of broad, conical garments), and after both great persons worshipped the Lord, ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān and the devotees stayed in a monastery outside the temple wall, while Pillaiyar resided in a monastery on the northern side, near the gopuram. During those days, Brahmins from Sīrkāzhi came to ThiruVēḷiMizhalai, desiring to see Pillaiyar, and visited ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān.

“There, they worshipped the Lord and then. They worshipped the feet of ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān and requested him to come to Thōṇipuram (Sīrkāzhi) with them. Pillaiyar replied that they could stay there tonight and, after receiving the grace of the Lord of ThiruVēḷiMizhalai, depart for Sīrkāzhi.

“That night, ThiruThōṇiyappar himself appeared in Pillaiyar’s dream and revealed, “I will show you the celestial vimana of ThiruVēḷiMizhalai as I am in Thōṇi; I will show you the sight from Thōṇipuram. You shall know it.” Pillaiyar, realizing this, arose in wonder and went to the temple. He saw ThiruThōṇiyappar himself in the celestial vimana of the ThiruVēḷiMizhalai temple and began the hymn “Maimaru Pūṅkuzhal” (Dark, fragrant tresses), singing about Pukali and ThiruVēḷiMizhalai. He rejoiced, singing the hymn with the sentiment, “What is this wonder that the form residing in Thōṇi is manifest in the celestial temple of Vēḷi?” He rejoiced, singing and praising. He also conveyed this to the Brahmins who had come from Sīrkāzhi and permitted them to return to Sīrkāzhi.

“Those Brahmins returned to Sīrkāzhi. There, Pillaiyar resided at ThiruVizhimizhalai, worshipping the Lord with ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān.

“We will continue to contemplate the brief history of ThiruGnanaSambandha Nāyanār.”” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam Part 544, Vambara Varivaṇḍuch Chaṟukkam, authored by Sekkizhar Swamigal, recounts the history of ThiruGnanaSambandha Nāyanār. ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān and ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān were residing in ThiruVīḷimizhalai.

At that time, there was a prolonged drought in the world. Rivers dried up, and creatures suffered from lack of food. Even the worship of the Devas was disrupted. A great famine arose in the world. Seeing this, both great individuals wondered if Shiva’s devotees would face sorrow. They worshipped the Lord and retired for the night.

That night, the Lord of ThiruVīḷimizhalai appeared in their dreams. He said, “The hunger and illness caused by these worldly events will not afflict you, yet to alleviate the suffering of those who follow Shiva’s path, you two will be given a coin each at the eastern and western pedestals of the ThiruVīḷimizhalai temple.

“We will continue to provide this until this suffering ends.” He appeared in their dream and stated that the hunger and disease afflicting the world would not reach them, but to alleviate the suffering of those who stand in the path of Shiva, he would provide one coin each at the eastern and western pedestals of the ThiruVīḷimizhalai temple, and this would continue until the suffering ended. Both great individuals, realizing this, praised the Lord’s grace and circumambulated the temple. Pillaiyar found a coin granted by the Lord on the eastern pedestal. He bowed, took it, and revered it.

“Similarly, the Lord gave ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān a coin at the western pedestal.

“The Lord ordered that the devotees be fed daily, and made arrangements for them to have delicious meals twice a day.

“Thus, the feeding of devotees regularly took place at ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān’s monastery and ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān’s monastery. However, at ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān’s monastery, there was a delay in preparing food for the devotees. When Pillaiyar asked why, they explained that the coin ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān received was of lesser value, and it took time to exchange it and purchase food items. They also mentioned that ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān’s coin was of full value.

“Therefore, ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān praised and worshipped the Lord, singing the hymn “Vāsi Thīravē” (May the defect be removed). From that day onwards, the Lord bestowed a full-value coin upon ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān.

“Later, rain fell, the world recovered from its distress, and prosperity returned. After praising the Lord for many days, both great individuals sought permission from the Lord and departed from there to worship other shrines. They visited and worshipped holy places such as ThiruVāñchiyam, ThiruThalaiyālaṅkāḍu, ThiruPeruvēlūr, ThiruChāththaṅkuḍi, ThiruKaravīram, ThiruViḷamar, ThiruVārūr, ThiruKārāyil, ThiruThēvūr, ThiruNellikka, ThiruKaichchinnam, ThiruThēṅkūr, ThiruKoḷḷikkāḍu, ThiruKōṭṭūr, ThiruVeṉthuṟai, ThiruThaṇḍalai Nīzhneṟi, and ThiruKaḷar. They then arrived at the holy place of ThiruMaṟaikkāḍu.

“The devotees of ThiruMaṟaikkāḍu welcomed both of them, worshipped, went to the temple, worshipped according to custom, and entered. In earlier days, the Vedas had worshipped there and sealed the temple doors, making it impossible to open them until today. The temple doors, sealed by the Vedas, remained closed because the devotees, who possessed the ability to chant those Vedas, had not removed the seal. Both great individuals arrived before that holy entrance.

“At that moment, Pillaiyar turned to ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān and said, “Whatever may happen, we must open this main entrance, enter, and worship the Lord. For that, you must sing a hymn.” He replied, “If this is your grace, I shall sing as you wish.” He sang the hymn “Paṉṉiṉēr Mozhiyāḷ” (She of fragrant words), but even after completing all ten verses, the door did not open. ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān, with great sorrow, pleaded with the Lord in the concluding verse of his hymn, and the holy door opened.

“The devotees shouted “Hara Hara” and rejoiced. Both great individuals entered through that path, worshipped the Lord, praised His grace, immersed themselves in the flood of joy, sang hymns, and then came out.

“At that moment, ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān asked Pillaiyar to sing a hymn to close the holy doors. As Pillaiyar began to sing the hymn “Chathuram Maṟaithāṉ” (The Four Vedas), the door immediately became sealed and closed. Seeing this, the devotees rejoiced and praised both the Lord’s grace and the two great individuals.

“From that day on, the custom of devotees entering and worshipping through that holy entrance came into being.

“Thus, contemplating the immense grace bestowed by the Lord, the rarity of his own hymn that opened the door, and the ease with which Pillaiyar closed it, ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān. As ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān was resting in a part of the monastery, the Lord appeared in his dream in the guise of a Shaiva ascetic and said, “I am in Vāymūr; follow me.” Realizing this, he immediately prostrated himself, rose, and followed that ascetic.

“At that moment, ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān asked, “Where has Appar gone?” Learning of Appar Swamigal’s departure, he immediately followed him. Both reached ThiruVāymūr.

“The Lord revealed a wondrous golden temple, entered it, and disappeared.

“At the same time, Pillaiyar arrived beside ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān.

“The Lord then granted Pillaiyar a vision of His Rishabha form in the sky. Pillaiyar sang the hymn “Thaḷirizha Vaḷar” (The tender-leafed growth). He also showed that divine vision to ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān.

“Afterward, both went to ThiruVāymūr, worshipped, and then returned to ThiruMaṟaikkāḍu and resided there.

“At this time, the Samaṇa religion was flourishing in Pāṇḍiya Nāḍu, and the influence of Shaivism had diminished somewhat.

“The King of Pāṇḍiya Nāḍu had also converted to the Samaṇa faith. The good path of Shaivism had deviated and changed there. All the towns of Tamil Nadu were filled with Samaṇa pāḷi and schools. Everywhere, the Samaṇas proliferated. Only two individuals, the Pāṇḍiya Queen Maṅgaiyarkkarasiyār and the Minister Kulachchiraiyār, upheld the Shaiva faith there. They, too, were distressed by the harm that had come to their country and continued to follow the Shaiva tenets without the Pāṇḍiya King knowing of their adherence.

“They practiced Shaivism without the Pāṇḍiya King knowing.

“At that time, they heard the news that Pillaiyar was residing in ThiruMaṟaikkāḍu. They sent their attendants as messengers to Pillaiyar, requesting him to come to Pāṇḍiya Nāḍu to spread the glory of Shaivism.

“Therefore, the messengers of Pāṇḍiya Queen and Kulachchirai Nāyanār arrived at Pillaiyar’s monastery in ThiruMaṟaikkāḍu, approached Pillaiyar, and made their request. Pillaiyar graciously granted them audience and then, accompanied by ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān, went to worship the Lord. From inside the gopuram, he recounted all these events to ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān. Pillaiyar informed ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān of his intention to go to Pāṇḍiya Nāḍu.

“At that moment, Vāgīsa Perumān said, “Child, those Samaṇas are wicked and deceitful. “The planets are not in a favorable position right now, so I do not approve of you going to Pāṇḍiya Nāḍu,” ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān refused. To this, ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān replied, “If we worship the Lord, the planets will not be evil; they will bestow only good. The Lord’s sacred ash will defeat the Buddhists and Samaṇas in argument; this is certain.” With these words, he sang the hymn “Vēyuṟu Thōḻi Paṅkaṉ” (He whose consort has bamboo-like shoulders), which is a hymn to dispel planetary evils. Hearing this, ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān agreed and prepared to accompany him. Pillaiyar stopped ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān, asked him to stay there, worshipped the Lord, took his leave, and departed.

“ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān also took his leave and remained there. Pillaiyar, having bid farewell to ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān, chanted the five-letter mantra, meditated on the Lord’s feet. He adorned himself with the sacred ash and rode in the palanquin. All the devotees chanted the names of Shiva. As people from all four directions praised and devotees welcomed him everywhere with auspicious signs, ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān traveled towards Pāṇḍiya Nāḍu, worshipping the shrines along the way. Pillaiyar continued, worshipping and singing hymns at holy places such as ThiruAgaththiāṉpaḷḷi, ThiruKōḍikkuḷakar, ThiruKaḍikkuḷam, ThiruIḍumpāvaṉam, and ThiruUsāththāṉam.

“He passed through fertile Marutham lands, rich with ponds and flowerbeds, and passed through towns where Brahmins and good devotees resided. Leaving the Chōzha Nāḍu, he crossed the Mullai land and then the land inhabited by warriors, and arrived in the glorious southern Pāṇḍiya Nāḍu. Having crossed the land inhabited by forest dwellers, he arrived in the southern Pāṇḍiya Nāḍu.

“There, he worshipped ThiruKoḍuṅkuṉṟam, also known as Pirāṉmalai, and traversed hills and forests to reach the holy city of Madurai. As Pillaiyar arrived in Madurai, ominous signs appeared for the Samaṇas in Pāṇḍiya Nāḍu. Owls and other ill-omened birds fought above the Samaṇa pāzhi, schools, and refectories, foretelling the impending calamities for them. Their peacock feathers, staffs, and mats fell down. The Samaṇas stumbled, and their left eyes twitched. The Samaṇas abandoned virtues like patience, and evil traits predominated.

“Additionally, the Samaṇas experienced bad dreams. Saying these things to each other, all the Jains surrounding Madurai gathered in Madurai and shared the bad omens that had befallen them. An Ashoka tree fell to its roots on top of the Arhat, and then that Arhat deity – the Jains shared all these bad dreams and evil dreams with each other.

“Therefore, they grieved, lamenting that harm was about to befall the Jains, and this was indeed true, so they did not eat and wailed. As the Jains reached this state there, auspicious omens appeared for Queen Mangaiyarkarasi and the wise minister Kulachiraiyar. Seeing this, both rejoiced. The good news of Pillaiyar’s arrival The arrivals convey to both of them, and great joy arises. Queen Mangaiyarkarasi instructs the minister, “Go before Pillaiyar, welcome him well, and bring him here.” Minister Kulachirai Nayanaar, believing this action will reassure the king, travels a long distance outside Madurai and welcomes Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan at the border of Madurai. He tells the king that he must worship the Lord enshrined in Aalavaai and goes with his retinue to Aalavaaiyudaiyar’s temple to stand there and welcome him himself.

“As the pearl palanquin proceeds like a full moon, the pearl umbrella provides shade, the crowd of ash-clad devotees swells, the Brahmins’ Vedic chants resound, and the sweet Tamil breezes serve from all sides, Jainism like an army of virtue advancing as the great army of sin breaks and flees, like the Ganga coming to wash away the defilement of Jainism, like the lamp of knowledge rising to dispel the darkness of Jainism, showing many good things that foster Saivism, with all the auspicious symbols announcing, “The one who knows the other religions has come!” Pillaiyar proceeds.

“Now, let us reflect on the condensed sacred history of Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan, who continuously came to Madurai, the capital of the Pandya country. Thiru Thiruchitrambalam.”” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Five Hundred Forty-Five, Vampara Varivanda Charukkam, authored by Sekkilar Swamigal. The sacred history of Thiru Gnanasambandha Nayanaar. Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan arrives in Madurai, the capital of the Pandya kingdom. Kulachirai Nayanaar lies prostrate on the ground, bowing towards the crowd of devotees accompanying Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan. Seeing his prostrate state, the attendants inform Pillaiyar, who is in the palanquin.

Hearing this, Pillaiyar descends from the palanquin, approaches Kulachirai Nayanaar, and raises him from his prostrate position. Kulachirai Nayanaar then stands with folded hands. Pillaiyar speaks in a sweet voice, asking, “Are the divine blessings of the Lord abundantly bestowed upon Mangaiyarkarasi, the daughter of the Chola king, and upon you, who possess a rectified mind?” To this, the minister replies, “We suffered no harm in the past, and we shall receive special blessings in the future. This is because of the great fortune of Your Holiness’s arrival today. We are always blessed by His grace.

“This country, steeped in an unrighteous path, and its righteous Tamil king have obtained salvation and achieved the glory of shining in the light of the sacred ash.” He further states, “Our lives have been uplifted by the great news of Your Holiness’s arrival.” Kulachirai Nayanaar then adds, “Queen Mangaiyarkarasi ordered me to go forth and prostrate myself before Your Holiness.” Having said this, he bows again. As Pillaiyar blesses him and proceeds, the city surrounded by walls Madurai appears before them. Pillaiyar asks the devotees, “Where is the Lord’s sacred Aalavaai?” They point with their hands, indicating the towering gopuram reaching the sky is Thiruaalavaai. At that very spot, Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan prostrates himself on the ground and begins singing a Thiru Pathigam (devotional hymn) starting with “Mangaiyarkarasi.” In that hymn, he praises the services of both Queen Mangaiyarkarasi and Kulachirai Nayanaar. Proceeding further with the minister, he approaches Thiruaalavaai, bows at the side of the gopuram, circumambulates the mansion, and enters the sacred temple. He beheld the Lord of Aalavaai, fulfilling the purpose of his eyes, prostrated himself countless times, and sang the Thiru Pathigam “Neelama Midatru” (The Long-Throated One) in praise, then reached the outer court.

“Pillaiyar, upon entering, When he entered, Mangaiyarkarasi, who had stood aside without coming forward, now approached with tears welling up, bowed down, and stood with folded hands. When the minister announced her as the Chola princess, Pillaiyar, filled with great joy, went to meet her. The Queen prostrated herself at Pillaiyar’s feet. Pillaiyar, with great compassion, raised her, and the Queen, overjoyed that her desire was fulfilled, spoke with trembling voice and tearful eyes, saying, “What great penance have I and my land performed!” Pillaiyar then blessed her, saying, “We have come to see you, who live righteously amidst the rival religions.” The minister narrates all the events. Pillaiyar blesses the Queen, bids her farewell, and proceeds with the true devotees.

“The devotees serving at Thiru Aalavaai come forward and say to Pillaiyar, “We have performed immeasurable penance for Your Holiness to come here to dispel the darkness of Jainism.” They prostrate themselves. After bestowing his gracious glance upon them all, Pillaiyar takes a seat with the devotees in the sacred monastery shown by Kulachirai. Kulachirai provides a feast, by the grace of Queen Mangaiyarkarasi, for Pillaiyar who is residing there. As Pillaiyar and his devotees were seen arriving during the day, the Jains, upon hearing the music played in the darkness of the night, became agitated and envious. They decided to plot against the king. They went to the palace, informed the gatekeepers, and then nervously presented themselves before the king.

“When the king asked why they had come, they replied that it was very painful to tell. The king asked, “What trouble has befallen you?” They replied, “Oh King, a Saivite Brahmin has arrived in your Madurai, and because of this, we have been defiled by his presence.” Hearing this, the king said, “I too have been defiled just by hearing this!” He then asked, “Who is this Shiva devotee, and why have they come here?” The Jains replied, “A young Brahmin from Seerkazhi in the Chola country, who has received the grace of Sulapani, has come here with a group of devotees, riding in a pearl palanquin. He has come to defeat us in debate.” When Pillaiyar’s sacred name reached his ears, the king became angry and asked, “If that youth has come here, what should we do?” The Jains replied, We must cause trouble for that Brahmin.

“Therefore, we will use our mantras to create fire in the monastery where he is staying, so he will leave this city without spending the night. If this is what must be done, then do it immediately, the king commands. The king, full of anxiety, goes to sleep.

“At that moment, Queen Mangaiyarkarasi, seeing the king silent and troubled, asks, “My lord, you are not happy. What has happened to you?” The king replies, “Someone from Seerkazhi in the Chola country, who has received the grace of Shiva, has come here to defeat the Jains in debate. Because of this, the Jains feel defiled by sight, and I feel defiled by hearing.” Queen Mangaiyarkarasi says, “Given your situation, it would be appropriate for you to side with those who win the debate, considering their profound divine nature. Do not grieve.” She then rejoices over Pillaiyar’s gracious arrival to claim her and shares this news with the minister. The minister bows and says, “We have been blessed with the arrival of Pillaiyar, so what harm can the deceit of the Jains inflict now?” Queen Mangaiyarkarasi, greatly afraid, replies, “These treacherous wretches will only do evil. If they cause any harm to Thiru Gnanasambandar, then it is our duty to protect him.” She then asks about the Jains’ situation.

“The Jains, having taken leave from the king, proceed to cause fire in Pillaiyar’s monastery through their incantations. The primordial mantra, the sacred five-syllable mantra, will be recited. Will the rules of other mantras operate in the direction they look, or will they not?

“Thus, the Jains realize that their magical incantations have no effect on Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan.

“Therefore, unable to create fire through mantras, they resolve to go directly and set fire themselves. They approach the sacred monastery where Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan is residing and carry out their intended action. Seeing the fire breaking out there, the attendants, panicking, extinguish it and inform Pillaiyar. Pillaiyar, with compassion, says, “Should these sinners commit such harm in this sacred monastery where great ascetics sleep?” Then, he reflects, “Even though this harm was done for my sake, can it truly affect Shiva’s devotees?” Angered, he realized that the king’s justice had weakened here, and that was the reason. He commanded the Thiru Pathigam “Seyyane” (O Red One) and instructed the fire set by the Jains in the monastery where Saivites resided to gently go and affect the Pandya king.

“With the intention of protecting Mangaiyarkarasi’s sacred necklace and anointing the king with sacred ash to save him, he commanded the fire to gently go and affect him. That fire then went and afflicted the Pandya king, manifesting as a fever.

“Let us continue to reflect on the condensed sacred history of Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Five Hundred Forty-Six, Vampara Varivandu Charukkam, authored by Sekkilar Swamigal. The sacred history of Thiru Gnanasambandha Nayanaar. The fire set by the Jains in the monastery where Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan was staying slowly transformed into a burning fever for the Madurai king. In accordance with Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan’s command, that night passed and dawn broke. Hearing about the evil deed committed by the Jains during the night, Queen Mangaiyarkarasi, the queen of that land, and the great minister were deeply distressed, regretting that they had invited Pillaiyar to a country where such evil people lived.

Later, learning that no harm had befallen the monastery where Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan was staying, they were somewhat comforted.

At the same time, the king’s bodyguards arrived and announced that the king had contracted a fever. Queen Mangaiyarkarasi and Kulachirai Nayanaar quickly went to the king’s chambers. The king’s fever burned throughout his body like fire. Even those standing outside the king’s chambers were scorched by the heat.

Therefore, those who came near the king could not approach him and stood at a distance. Even banana plantains and banana leaves brought near the king withered and blackened. Such was the heat in the king’s body. Although doctors applied treatments according to the medical texts, they could not even slightly reduce the fever. The great minister Kulachirai Nayanaar tells the king that the cause of all this is the evil deed committed by the Jains, and its consequence.

Therefore, if one tries to cure this fever, it will not be cured, but will only increase. If a solution is desired for this, then the grace of Pillaiyar is needed. If Thiru Gnanasambandha Moorthy Nayanaar, who has attained divine knowledge, directs his gracious gaze, this fever will be cured, and the suffering of rebirth will also be dispelled.

Thus, the great minister Kulachirai Nayanaar informs the king. For the first time, Kulachirai Nayanaar whispers the name Thiru Gnanasambandar into the king’s ear. As soon as the king heard that sacred name, his suffering slightly diminished. The king looked at the great minister and said, “It would be very good if the Saivite Brahmin youth came here and cured this illness of mine. I will join the side of those who cure this disease and win. If you agree to this, then summon him.” Hearing this, Queen Mangaiyarkarasi and the great minister Kulachirai Nayanaar immediately went to Pillaiyar’s sacred monastery.

There, they informed the guards at the monastery gate. They ask the guards to convey their arrival to Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan. The guards then go to Pillaiyar and relay the message. Pillaiyar instructs the guards to bring Queen Mangaiyarkarasi and Minister Kulachirai Nayanaar inside. Queen Mangaiyarkarasi and Kulachirai Nayanaar enter the sacred monastery.

There, they see his divine form. They behold Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan. They see the support of the Vedas. They see the crescent moon growing on earth, not in the sky. They joyfully behold the seven births of the song that praises Shiva’s glory. They behold the divine form of knowledge, the unique support of the four Vedas, Sekkilar Peruman composes this verse here: ‘The crescent moon that grows on earth, not in the sky, a unique support of the four Vedas, the seven births of the song that praises the glory of the Lord with honey-laden Konrai flowers in his red matted locks, they joyfully beheld.’ As soon as they saw Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan, remembering the cruel deeds committed by the Jains against him, tears streamed down their faces.

With folded hands, they sighed deeply, their voices trembled, their bodies shook, and they fell to the ground, as if knowing nothing. They clasped Pillaiyar’s lotus feet, like someone lost in the sea of worries finding a raft, or someone who finds a boat clinging to it, they clung to Pillaiyar’s lotus feet. Out of love, you relentlessly lay prostrate there. Pillaiyar lovingly lifted and comforted both of them with his sacred hand. He asked them, “O virtuous ones, is there any harm upon you?” They recounted everything that had happened. They pleaded, “If you cure the king’s fever and defeat the Jains, then the king’s life and our lives will be saved.” Pillaiyar reassures them, saying, “All creation and destruction are His deeds.

“I understand the Lord’s will to dispel the evil that may befall the sinful Jains and to defeat them.” The Lord Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan sets out to understand the divine will and enters the Thiru Aalavaai temple in Madurai. Facing Sokkanatha Perumaan, he sings the Thiru Pathigam “Kaattuma” (Will you show?), addressing the Lord who is a form of fire, saying, “I have come seeking your divine will to debate with the Amaras, who have no prescribed path.” He then focuses on the Lord’s grace.

“Following this, with the intention of defeating them in debate, he sings the Thiru Pathigam beginning with “Vedavai Velviyai” (Vedic sacrifice). He supplicates the Lord at Thiru Aalavaai, saying, “O Primordial One, I earnestly desire only your glory, which is knowledge.” Having received the Lord’s grace, he joyfully ascends the palanquin and proceeds. The shouts of “Hara Hara” raised by the devotees The roaring echoes filled everywhere. Like the radiance of the sacred ash, Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan’s pearl umbrella and insignia resounded, and this sacred sight shone in the streets of Madurai city. The people of Madurai city were then followers of other religions, Jains. Nevertheless, they pondered, “What penance have we performed for this holy figure, Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan, to come and enter Madurai for the sake of the Pandya king?” Queen Mangaiyarkarasi’s palanquin followed behind Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan’s palanquin.

“Minister Kulachirai Nayanaar, the great lord, walked among the crowd of holy devotees in front of Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan’s palanquin.

“Thus, Pillaiyar arrives at the palace. The minister goes ahead and informs the king of Pillaiyar’s arrival. Hearing this, the king’s distress further lessens. The king instructs that a jeweled seat be placed beside his head for Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan.

“Thus, the ability to speak also comes to the king as soon as he hears the news of Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan’s arrival. He then orders the minister to bring Pillaiyar. The Jains ask the king, “Is this how you preserve our religion? Why did you invite him?” They further tell the king, “We Jains and Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan will attempt to cure your disease at the same time. Even if the disease is cured by the grace of Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan, you must say that it was cured by us,” the Jains tell the king.

“At that time, it was the period when the fruits of the king’s past penance were coming to fruition.

“Therefore, the king, not agreeing to the evil words of the Jains, tells them, inspired by divinity, “You two should cure it separately.” At the same time, Pillaiyar descends from the palace courtyard and enters the palace. The king sees Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan like the moon descending from the sky to dispel the darkness on earth. Upon seeing him, the king The king salutes with folded hands and indicates the jeweled seat beside his head. Pillaiyar then ascends that jeweled seat. As soon as he beheld Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan’s divine form, the king’s fever further subsided. The king then asks Pillaiyar, with great eagerness, “Which village are you from?” Pillaiyar replies, “Seerkazhi, also known as Thiru Kazhumalam, is our village.” He then recites the Thiru Pathigam called “Thiruchakkaramaatru,” listing the twelve names of Seerkazhi.

“At that moment, the Jains surround Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan, shouting and bickering. Pillaiyar tells them, “Speak the truth of your teachings, expound upon its reality.” Hearing this, many Jains again gather around Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan, agitated and wailing. Queen Mangaiyarkarasi, unable to bear it, her heart trembling, addresses the king, “Pillaiyar is a young boy, while the Jains are innumerable and have surrounded Pillaiyar. Pillaiyar will cure your illness; let these Jains speak afterward.” The king replies, “Do not worry,” and tells the Jains, “You Arhats and this devotee of Shiva, please reveal your clear divine essence to me.” Pillaiyar then addresses Queen Mangaiyarkarasi, He sings the Thiru Pathigam, “Maani Neerveli.” In that hymn, he reassures her, “Do not fear me as a child. With the Lord of Aalavaai standing, I am not weak before these ignoble ones.” Furthermore, addressing the persistently wailing Jains and Pillaiyar, who sat calmly, the king says, “You should individually attempt to cure my fever. Whoever cures my fever most quickly will be considered victorious in the debate.” Immediately, the Jains choose the king’s left side and attempt to cure his fever according to their customs, chanting mantras.

“They chant mantras and stroke him with peacock feathers. However, the king’s fever intensified. The king then looks at Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan, wishing him to make an effort to cure the disease on the king’s right side.

“At that moment, Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan sings the Thiru Neetru Pathigam (Hymn of Sacred Ash), beginning with “Manthiramavathu Neeru” (The mantra is sacred ash), declaring that the sacred ash of Thiru Aalavayaan will dispel the fever on the king’s right side, acting as both mantra and medicine. Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan then takes the sacred ash with his own sacred hands and anoints the king’s right side with it. The fever immediately subsided, and the king’s right side cooled down like a pond. The heat from the right side gathered on the left side, and the disease intensified like fire. On the left side, the Jains trembled. The fever on the king’s left side, which was their chosen side, increased and scorched the Jains themselves.

“Therefore, they moved away from the king and left. The Jains, unable to bear the fever, then heard the king declare, “At the same time, on one side, I feel as if I am in a cruel hell; on the left side, where the Jains claimed to cure, I feel a terrible hell.

“At the same time, on the right side, where Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan applied the sacred ash with his divine hands, I feel heavenly bliss. In my present form, I feel the nature of both sides.” Amazed, he tells the Jains, “You have lost. Leave me and go.” He then pleads with Pillaiyar, “Please bless me so that this disease is completely cured.” Pillaiyar completes the hymn and anoints the king’s left side with sacred ash, and the fever on the left side also completely disappears. The Pandya king is fully saved. Queen Mangaiyarkarasi and the great minister Kulachirai Nayanaar bow at Pillaiyar’s feet, saying that the king has attained a state beyond rebirth.

“The king, with folded hands above his head, states, “I have been saved by seeking the feet of Gnanasambandar, before the shameless Jains, and my disease is cured.” Let us continue to reflect on the condensed sacred history of Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan. Let us contemplate Thiruchitrambalam.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Five Hundred Forty-Seven, Vampara Varivandu Charukkam, authored by Sekkilar Swamigal. The sacred history of Thiru Gnanasambandha Nayanaar. The Jains realize that all their magical arts have been defeated by Pillaiyar’s words. Pillaiyar tells the Jains, “Speak the truth of your scriptures.” Fearing defeat in a logical debate, the Jains tell Pillaiyar, “Let us not engage in logical debate. Let us engage in debates that can be seen with the eyes, that are evident.” Hearing this, the king asks derisively, “Do you not know that my disease was cured by Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan?

“What debate do you need now? What debate are you going to do?” To this, the Jains say, they say, “Let’s have a fire debate.” The Jains state, “We and Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan will write the truths of our respective scriptures on palm-leaf manuscripts and place them in fire. Whoever’s manuscript does not burn or char in the fire will be the winner.” Immediately, Pillaiyar says, “If this is a debate, it must be conducted before the king.” The king then sets up the fire. Pillaiyar, with his sacred hands, takes a manuscript from his collection of sacred texts, which he preaches as the true nature of Shiva, along with sacred ash. The hymn on that particular manuscript was the Thiru Pathigam of Thirunallaaru, beginning with “Bhogamartha Poonmulaiyaal.” He takes that manuscript, declaring, “This is the sacred name of the Lord. Even if it is put into fire, nothing will happen to it.” He then sings the Thiru Pathigam, “Thalirilav Valaruli,” in praise, and places the manuscript into the fire for the kings and the assembly to witness.

“Pillaiyar offered the leaf into the fire, making the Lord, who holds Uma on His left side and is an Eight-Formed One, the subject. Because of this, the leaf remained fresh and green; the fire could do nothing to it.

“After this, the Jains, doubting whether their leaf containing the tenets of their religion would survive or burn, placed it into the fire. The Jains’ leaf burned like cotton in the fire. To everyone’s astonishment, Pillaiyar retrieved the leaf he had placed. It was fresher and greener than before. He showed it to the king and the assembly.

“Then he re-inserted the leaf into the sacred texts. The king looked at it with wonder.

“Then he told the Jains, “Show me the leaf you put in the fire.” The Jains searched for the leaf they had put in the fire.

“At that time, the heat was intense, so the king poured water to extinguish the fire. Only charcoal remained. The king, laughing, said, “You were unable to cure my disease then and lost.

“Now, you have also lost in this fire debate.” The Jains say, “Let’s have another debate.” The Jains say, “Let’s have another debate.” The king asks, “What other debate is there?” They say, “We will write the doctrines of our respective religions on palm leaves and cast them into a flowing river. If the leaf remains there without being carried away by the current, that leaf is the winner.” They challenge him to a water debate. Pillaiyar accepts it and says, “So be it.” At this point, the great minister Kulachirai Nayanaar comes forward and says, “Let us decide now what those who lose this debate should do.” The Jains, angered and envious of the minister, declare through their own mouths, “If we lose this debate, then the king will impale us on a stake.” Hearing this, the king forgot all their actions and, in anger, said, “You have spoken thus; now, come, let’s put the leaves in the water.” Pillaiyar descends from his jeweled seat and proceeds in his palanquin. The king rides on his horse. The Jains also come.

“As Pillaiyar proceeded through the streets of Madurai city, all the people of Madurai praised him. They discussed among themselves in many ways about the past events and what would follow from them, praising Pillaiyar and the glory of Saivism. The people of Madurai and the sacred emblems proclaimed Pillaiyar’s glories in various ways. With the king and queen following behind and the Jains coming as a separate group, Pillaiyar arrived at the banks of the Vaigai river.

“There, the river water flowed very swiftly. He tells them to cast their leaves concerning their religions. The Jains, who are empty like chaff in grain, write down their religious tenets, “Asti Nasti” (Existence-Nonexistence), and despite seeing the swiftness of the water, out of eagerness, they cast their leaf into the Vaigai River. The river quickly carried the leaf away. Seeing their leaf being swiftly carried away and disappearing, the Jains scattered in dismay and trembled, realizing their end had come. Nevertheless, hiding their fear, they say, “Let’s see what happens if you also cast your leaf into this water.” The king then looks towards Pillaiyar’s divine indication.

“He sang the Thiru Paasuram for the destruction of other religions. The king of the Pandya country, blessed with the sacred ash applied by Pillaiyar’s divine hand, had his past evil karmas removed, attained equanimity in karma, and achieved the ability to know the Lord.

“Therefore, for the king to understand this, Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan sang the Thiru Paasuram Pathigam, beginning with “Vaazhgaanthanar” (He who lives as a lord). In this Thiru Pathigam, he illustrates the universal truths of the Vedas, Sivagamas, Puranas, and Itihasas, teaching the world that the worldly Vedic rules and righteous path are indeed the Saivite path. Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan wrote on the leaf, If the leaf goes against the current, then knowledge is love for the Lord, and pronouncing this command, he finished writing on the leaf. He then casts the leaf into the Vaigai River with his sacred hands. Just as the minds of great ascetics go against the current of rebirth, the leaf cut through the waters of the Vaigai River and went against the direction of the river’s flow, showing that this is the true essence. In that hymn, he prayed for the king’s prosperity, and just as Anapayan Chola’s righteous scepter was exalted, the hunch of the Pandya king, the ruler of the south, straightened at that very moment.

“Seeing the leaf travel against the current of the Vaigai River, the celestials showered flowers, and all the Jains stood in fear. To retrieve that leaf, Kuthir Kulachirai Nayanaar, goes riding a horse. Pillaiyar sings for the leaf to stay at a place called Thiru Edagam. The leaf stays at the site of Thiru Edagam. The great minister Kulachirai Nayanaar takes the leaf, places it on his head, comes to the king, bows to Pillaiyar, and shows it to everyone. A shout of “Hara Hara” arose there.

“Immediately, the king said, “The Jains have now lost.

“Moreover, they previously offended Pillaiyar, and they set fire to the sacred monastery where Pillaiyar was staying.

“Therefore, it is righteous to impale them on the stake,” and the king commanded the minister. Pillaiyar also heard this. The king’s command to punish them for committing the terrible act of setting fire to the monastery where Saivites resided is Pillaiyar’s view was that it was appropriate.

“Therefore, Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan did not overturn the king’s order. According to the king’s command, the eight thousand Jain gurus of the eight great hills who had set fire to Pillaiyar’s monastery were impaled on the stake. Those stakes shone as pillars of victory, proclaiming the glory of Saivism and the fame of Pillaiyar.

“After that, Pillaiyar gave sacred ash to the king. The king also humbly accepted and completely applied the sacred ash. Seeing this, the people of Madurai also adorned themselves with the pure sacred ash. Everywhere, Vedic justice prevailed. The expanded radiance of the sacred white ash purified all directions. At that very moment, the darkness of Jainism vanished.

“Thus, giving life to the king Giving life to the king, showing him the true path, and removing Jainism, Pillaiyar’s truth, which he used to uplift the world, spread and flourished. The sacred path of Saivism prevailed, Vedic sacrifices and rains occurred without fail. By chanting Shiva’s name, this world was freed from the suffering of rebirth. With the king, queen, and minister accompanying him, Pillaiyar proceeded to praise the Lord of Thiru Aalavaai. The people of Pandya Nadu, who are of the Kanniya country, attained the fruit of having eyes to witness this. Entering the temple, with tears streaming down their faces and hands clasped, Pillaiyar prayed to the Lord, singing the Thiru Pathigam “Veedaal Aalavaai” (O Lord of Aalavaai, who granted salvation), saying, “O True One, who can bestow fearlessness upon this humble servant!” The king also praised the Lord, saying, “O Lord, you have bestowed this gracious Pillaiyar upon me to redeem me from the illusion of the Jains and take me into your grace.”

“After praising and worshipping, he sent the king and queen back to the palace, and Pillaiyar, after praising the Lord, resided in the monastery. The Pandya king, Queen Mangaiyarkarasi, and Minister Kulachirai Nayanaar worshipped and praised Pillaiyar’s feet daily. Pillaiyar, with deep devotion, sang hymns in praise of the Lord enshrined in Aalavaai, his heart melting with love. During this period, Sivapatha Hrudayar in Seerkazhi thought of Pillaiyar, whom he had received through his penance. Memories of Pillaiyar overwhelmed Sivapatha Hrudayar. He worshipped Thoni Appar and set off towards the Pandya country, worshipping the Lord in all the holy places along the way, and arrived in Madurai.

“Sivapatha Hrudayar went to Thiru Aalavaai, worshipped the Lord, and then went to the monastery where Pillaiyar was staying, which was nearby.

“The devotees inform Pillaiyar of Sivapatha Hrudayar’s arrival.

“Then, Pillaiyar, going before his father and bowing, as his father, who had followed the path of penance, came forward to bow to him, thinks of the lotus feet of the Divine Couple who, through his (Pillaiyar’s) connection, had cut off the bonds of rebirth when he appeared in Thoni at Seerkazhi. With folded hands and tears streaming down his eyes, he says, “O great ascetic, it was when I was in my unknowing childhood that the great Lord and my Divine Mother took me into their grace.” With this thought, he sings the Thiru Pathigam, “Mannil Nalla Vannam Vaazhalaam” (We can live well on earth). After feasting his father during those days, he also goes with the devotees to worship the Lord of Aalavaai and then departs from Madurai, intending to worship other holy places.

“At that moment, the king and queen their bodies softened, their hearts melted, and tears flowed down their faces, they fell at Pillaiyar’s feet and worshipped him. At that moment, Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan blessed them, saying, “Come with me to worship other holy places in this country, so that you may not suffer separation from me.” After that, he worshipped the holy places of Thirupparankundram and Thiru Aappanur, then went to Thiruputtur and worshipped there, staying for a few days.

“Afterwards, he visited and worshipped all the Pandya country’s holy places, including Thiru Poovanam, Thiru Kaanapper (Kalaiyar Kovil), Thiru Chuzhiyal (Thiru Chuzhi), Thiru Kutralam, Thiru Kurumbala, and Thirunelveli. Pillaiyar then reached Thiru Rameswaram and worshipped the Lord in the temple established and worshipped by Lord Vishnu. The king, Queen Mangaiyarkarasi, and the minister accompanied him and worshipped there. Standing on that seashore, Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan praises and worships the holy places in Lanka, the island nation, where the Lord is enshrined: Thirukonamalai and Thirukketheeswaram.

“Then, from there, he bows and proceeds north, worshipping many holy places, including Thiru Aadaanai and Thiru Punavaayil, which are holy sites in the Pandya country. He praises and worships them, bestowing grace so that people may live well, experiencing the clarity of the Vedic path and the glory of the sacred ash everywhere. He then arrives at Manamelkudi, the capital of Minister Kulachirai Nayanaar, and stays there, honored by the king, queen, and Kulachirai, visiting and worshipping other holy places.

“Let us continue to reflect on the condensed sacred history of Thiru Gnanasambandha Nayanaar.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam Part 548, “Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam,” by Sekkizhar Swamigal, the history of ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar. While staying in Manamelkudi, the hometown of Kulachirai Nayanar in the Pandya kingdom, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman decided to journey to the Chozha kingdom. The King, the Queen, and the Minister, unable to bear separation from ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman, declared their intention to accompany him. To them, the Child Saint said, “Listen to me; remain here and foster the path of Shiva.” He spoke comforting words to alleviate their distress. Unable to refuse, they respectfully took their leave with unwavering friendship.

The Child Saint then departed from the Pandya kingdom, journeyed to the Chozha kingdom, and there, wherever his devotees received him, he visited various sacred places in the Chozha kingdom. He worshipped at shrines such as Thirukkalar and Thiru Pathalicharam, and then reached Mullivaikkarai. A massive flood raged in the river, preventing boatmen from operating their vessels; they had tied their boats at the landing and departed. The Child Saint, having arrived at that bank, beheld the shrine of Thirukollampoodhoor on the opposite bank. Desiring to visit and worship there, he untied all the bound boats and, with his devotees, boarded one. He then sang the devotional hymn “Kottame Kamizhum” and miraculously propelled the boats across the river to the other bank without any boatmen.

There, he worshipped the Lord at Thirukollampoodhoor. ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman praised the Lord. Desiring to worship the Lord of Thirunallar, who had been instrumental in his victory in the Anarvadam at Madurai, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman visited all the shrines along the way. He reached the Thirunallar temple, circumambulated it according to custom, and prayed to the Lord. With tears streaming down, he extolled the Lord with the hymn “Kannarivi Payanendru Padagamelladi.” He sang of the unique nature of the Lord who, in the debate with the Jains before the Pandya king’s assembly, had caused the leaf thrown into the fire to remain green, thus abiding as his inner support in Thiru Alavai. Such is the meaning of the Thirunallar hymn.

Afterwards, he stayed there for some time, then took leave and proceeded to worship at Thiruthelicheri. On the way, he arrived at Bodhimangai, a city of the Buddhists. ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman, known as Parasamaya Kolarivan, the slayer of other religions, was heralded by the blowing of trumpets as he entered the town. Hearing this, the Buddhists, unable to tolerate it, gathered under the leadership of Buddhanandhi. They confronted the group of devotees and angrily declared, “You may boast of these symbols of victory only after you have defeated us.” The devotees informed the Child Saint, who was approaching in his palanquin. The Child Saint graciously replied, “Let us engage in debate directly, without delay; we shall expose their false doctrines.” Meanwhile, a devotee among the sacred assembly, who was writing the Thirumurai, unable to bear the unrighteous actions of the Buddhists, uttered, “May the head of this Buddhist fall, for the five letters (Namasivaya) are the weapon against the enemies of karma, adorning the Lord with water.” Immediately, a thunderbolt struck Buddhanandhi’s head.

His body and head fell apart. The Buddhists fled in fear.

The devotees informed the Child Saint of this incident. He declared, “This is an act of Shiva’s grace; everyone, chant the name of Haran!” The chanting of Shiva’s name resounded to the heavens. The fearful Buddhists who had fled reassembled, bewildered, wondering if it was a trick or their Shaivite truth. They returned, led by a Buddhist named Sariputhan from among them. They requested a philosophical debate rather than one involving sorcery. The Child Saint agreed, dismounted from his palanquin, and ascended to the debate hall.

He invited the Buddhists to debate. They arrived with Sariputhan. The devotee who had cursed Buddhanandhi bowed before the Child Saint. He engaged in a scriptural debate with them. The debate revolved around their leader, the principles he upheld, and their definition of liberation. In this debate, the devotee demonstrated that the Buddhist doctrines were baseless, making them realize it.

He asserted that Shaivism alone is the true reality, and there is no other true reality, citing Vedic pronouncements and the conclusions of the Agamas, thus defeating the Buddhists in the debate. As the Child Saint’s compassionate gaze fell upon them, the Buddhists bowed and worshipped him. After explaining to them that all moving and unmoving beings are Shaivite, the Child Saint departed from there and journeyed to Thirukkadavoor to worship. He inquired where ThiruNavukkarasar Swamigal was staying.

The devotees replied that ThiruNavukkarasar Peruman was residing in Thirupoonduruthi, engaged in sacred service. Hearing this, he departed with a great desire to meet ThiruNavukkarasar Peruman. He worshipped at all the shrines along the way and arrived near Thirupoonduruthi. Hearing the news that ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman was coming to Thirupoonduruthi, Vakeesar came forth. He was overjoyed, considering it a fruit of his past good deeds to go and worship the Child Saint. He worshipped the Lord and then entered the throng of devotees in the Child Saint’s procession.

Without being seen by the Child Saint, he worshipped him and joined those carrying the palanquin, helping to bear it, his heart overflowing with joy. No one there recognized ThiruNavukkarasar Peruman.

At that moment, a divine intuition arose in the Child Saint’s mind, and he inquired, “Where is Appar now?” Hearing this, ThiruNavukkarasar Peruman replied, “Having performed unparalleled penance in the past, I am now blessed to carry your sacred feet.” Filled with awe, the Child Saint immediately descended from the palanquin and prostrated before him, asking why he had performed such an act. Vakeesar prostrated in return, asking, “How else should one serve ThiruGnanaSambandhar?” The Child Saint embraced him with great affection, and all the devotees cheered. The two great saints proceeded together to the temple, entered, and worshipped the Lord Poiyili Appar enshrined in the Thirupoonduruthi temple. They came before the sacred entrance.

Then, Vakeesa Peruman inquired about the Child Saint’s journeys and returns. He recounted all those events.

The King worshipped him and declared, “You have been a great fence for the flourishing crop of sacred service.” Vakeesa Peruman rejoiced upon hearing of how he had revived the Pandya king with sacred ash, bestowed affection upon the Queen and the Minister, and re-established the Vedic path. Vakeesar then spoke of his own journeys, having visited Thiru Ekambaram in the great Thondai kingdom. Hearing this, the Child Saint also resolved to visit and worship in the Thondai kingdom. Appar Peruman, hearing the news from ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar, resolved to go and worship the Lord at Thiru Alavai. Seerkazhi Peruman, GnanaSambandha Peruman, decided to go to Seerkazhi. He worshipped the Lord, took leave of Vakeesar, and departed.

He worshipped at Thiru Naitthanam and Thirupazhanam on the northern bank of the Cauvery, then arrived at Seerkazhi. Hearing the news that the Child Saint, having dispelled the darkness of Jainism and reinstated the sacred ash in the Pandya kingdom, was arriving, the Brahmins of Seerkazhi, chanting Vedas, came to receive him. ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman descended from his palanquin and, seeing the temple, folded his hands in worship. He respectfully entered the Seerkazhi temple, worshipped, and ascended to worship Ammai Appar at Thiru Thoni. With goosebumps all over his body, tears streaming, and his heart overflowing with joy, he bowed and sang the Thiruyamaga Thirupathigam in praise.

Afterwards, he came out, worshipped the temple, and on the way, with women offering praises, he bestowed gracious leave upon Thiru Neelakanda Panar, allowing him to reside within his sacred form, and then returned to his sacred abode, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman.

At that time, Bhagavati Ammaiyar, the mother of the Brahmin lineage, came and bowed at his feet. He also mentally worshipped the Mother’s feet in Thiru Thoni.

Then, he worshipped Thoniyappar, sang a hymn in praise, and departed. The Child Saint resolved to go to the auspicious Thondai kingdom to see and worship Kambar, who had been embraced by the Mother.

Now, ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar’s sixth pilgrimage is about to begin. This will be a pilgrimage to the Thondai country.

We will continue to contemplate the brief history of ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam Part 549, “Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam,” by Sekkizhar Swamigal, the history of ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar. ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman begins his sixth pilgrimage from Seerkazhi. This sixth pilgrimage is to the Thondai kingdom. He informed the devotees of Seerkazhi of his intention, worshipped Thoniyappar, and took leave to depart.

At that time, the Peruman’s father also prepared to accompany him. The Child Saint then bade farewell to his father and the devotees from Seerkazhi who had started with him, asking them to stay there, perform sacrifices, and worship Thoniyappar. ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman, worshipping at all the shrines along the way, arrived at Thillai. He worshipped Thirupuliyur and was blessed to witness the Lord’s ecstatic dance. Continuing, he worshipped at Thiru Thinnainagar, Thiru Manikuli, Thirupathiripuliyur, Thiru Vadugoor, Thiru Vakkara, Thiru Irumbaimakazham, and other shrines, finally reaching Thiru Athikai Veerattanam. ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman was graced with a vision of the Lord dancing, surrounded by bhoota ganas.

He sang the hymn “Kundai Kuralbhoodham” there. He then worshipped at Thiru Amathur, and visited Thiru Kovaloor and Thiru Arayaninallur. While circumambulating, he saw Thiruvannamalai in the distance, pointed out by his devotees, and went to worship it with great fervor, chanting “Poovar Malara,” He stayed at Thiruvannamalai for several days, worshipping the Lord.

Afterwards, he journeyed north, visiting many of the Lord’s shrines, crossing great mountains and forests, and arrived at the blessed Thondai kingdom. ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman reached the sacred site of Thiru Oothur, worshipped and praised the Lord, and settled there.

One day, a devotee came before the Child Saint, weeping, and informed ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman, “I cultivated palm trees for the service of the Lord, but all these palm trees grew to be male trees.

“Therefore, they did not bear fruit. Seeing this, the Jains mockingly say, ‘The palm trees you cultivate for your deity do not bear fruit!’ O Lord, only you can bless me,” he pleaded. Hearing the devotee’s plea to ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman, the Child Saint, filled with compassion, went to the temple and sang a hymn to the Lord. In the concluding verse of that hymn, in the Thirukkadaikappu, he sang of the truth, “Kurumbai aan panaiyin kulaivoothur” (male palm trees bearing clusters at Oothur). In accordance with that truth, all the male palm trees bore abundant clusters of unripe female palm fruit. All who witnessed this were astonished.

“Thus, having fulfilled the devotee’s wish, the Child Saint remained happily in that town. Seeing this, the Jains were perplexed and left that country. The Child Saint then asked what happened to those female palm trees that bore fruit in clusters. Due to the Child Saint’s divine words, those palm trees, released from their former attachment, were purified and, in time, attained Shivam.

“Afterwards, he worshipped and departed, visiting many shrines where the Lord resided, including Thiru Makaral and Thiru Kuranganilmuttam. The Child Saint then arrived near Thiru Kanchi. Learning of his arrival, the devotees of Kanchi, overjoyed, decorated the city and, with auspicious offerings, came to receive the Child Saint. As everyone rejoiced, he journeyed among them and reached Thiru Ekambaram.

“There, he worshipped the Lord with devotion, sang the hymn “Maraiyanai” in praise, and then came out and stayed in the monastery. He approached the great charitable Kamakottam and worshipped there. He consistently worshipped Thiru Ekambanar without fail. He sang hymns such as Thiruyamagam and Thiruvirakkural, and then worshipped at Thiru Kachi Nerikkarai, Thiru Kachi Anekathangavatham, Thiru Kachi Metrali, and other sacred places before departing. He then went to the southern bank of the Palar river, worshipped at Thiru Marperu and Thiru Vallam. From there, he worshipped Thiru Ilambaiyangottoor on the northern bank, visited Thiru Virkolam, Thiru Ooral, and other shrines, and then arrived near Thiruvalangadu.

“This sacred place is where my mother, Karaikkal Ammaiyar, worshipped by walking on her head, for all the world to see.

“Therefore, the Child Saint, hesitant to step on Thiruvalangadu, stayed in a side building outside Thiruvalangadu for that night. In the middle of the night, Thiruvalangadu Appar appeared in his dream and asked, “Have you forgotten to sing of me?” Immediately, he arose, having understood and worshipped. He praised the Lord’s compassion, his body trembling, and sang the hymn “Thuncha Varuvarum Thozhuvipparum,” composed in the Pazhapanjarappann tune, extolling the Lord. In that hymn, he glorified the story of Pazhayanoorar, who valued his word more than his life. In the morning, he related this incident to the devotees who had gathered, and with heartfelt devotion, he sang praises. From there, he worshipped and sang of Thiruppasur and Thiruvenpakkam, and then, remembering Thiru Kannappa Nayanar, he resolved to visit Thiru Kalatthi mountain.

“Therefore, he departed from there, crossing fertile lands and entering the dry forests. He worshipped at Thiru Karikkarai, where clouds gathered, and then journeyed through the mountainous terrain. As the throngs of devotees, like a sea, surrounded him, animals, hearing the loud trumpeting announcing the arrival of Thiru GnanaSambandhan, were unified in thought and gathered around. Journeying thus, he passed by the hunting grounds where Thiru Kannappa Nayanar’s sacred footwear had trodden, and other places revered by even the Devas, and approached Thiru Kalatthi.

“There, throngs of devotees, matted-haired sages, Kapalis, and various Shaivite ascetics gathered to welcome the Child Saint. The Child Saint descended from his palanquin, bowed, and inquired which of the mountains was Thiru Kalatthi mountain. When they pointed it out, he was overjoyed. He worshipped and sang the Thiruviragappan hymn, extolling Kannappar’s service, recounting how ‘celestials and asuras’ (Vaanavargal Thaanavargal). He reached the foothills of the mountain, worshipped the mountain as he ascended, circled the temple, and approached the sacred presence. He prostrated himself fully, joining his hands, and arose, as if seeing the fruit of worshipping the Lord, and there he saw Kannappa Nayanar.

“Then, with a joyful heart, he experienced the true form and the Lord who was established within that love, all at once. He arose, worshipped many times, was immersed in devotion, and then departed to stay there. He stayed for many days, worshipping the Lord at every appointed time, and was delighted to reside there. Since the custom of refined Tamil was not prevalent in the northern and western directions, he worshipped various shrines such as Thirukayilai, Thiru Kedaram, Thiru Gokarnam, Thiruparuppatham (Srisailam), and Thiru Indra Neela Paruppatham from his abode in Thiru Kalatthi. He sang hymns about them.

“Afterwards, he resolved to visit and worship Thiruvottiyur.
