With the Lord’s grace, he departed from that sacred city and set out towards Thiruvottiyur, singing the hymn “Enthaiyar Inaiyadi En Manathullave” and worshipping as he proceeded. He traveled along the northern bank of the Palar river, worshipping all the shrines he had previously visited, including Thiruverkadu and Thiruvalithayam, and then arrived at Thiruvottiyur.

“The devotees of that city prostrated and came to receive him. He, too, descended from his palanquin, prostrated, and sang the hymn “Vidayavan.” He entered the Thiruvottiyur temple, worshipped and praised in the customary way, and then joyfully resided in that city with the devotees.

“We will continue to contemplate the brief history of ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam Part 550, “Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam,” by Sekkizhar Swamigal, the history of ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar. In Mylapore, also known as Thiru Mylapuri in Chennai, lived a merchant named Sivanesar. He was extremely wealthy, deeply devoted to Shiva’s devotees, and highly virtuous.

At that time, he heard about the Child Saint’s incarnation in Seerkazhi, his attainment of divine wisdom, and his actions in destroying other religions. Hearing all this, Sivanesar developed an unceasing love for the sacred feet of ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar and greatly rejoiced in hearing about the miraculous deeds performed by ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar. Although Sivanesar was a great wealthy man, he had no children. Due to his devoted worship, delighting and pleasing the devotees of Lord Shiva, a rare daughter was born to him. As the girl child was like a flower, he named her Poombavai and lovingly raised her. When the girl child turned seven, Sivanesar proclaimed that the man who would marry her would be the sole heir to all his wealth.

During those days, the Child Saint traveled to the Pandya kingdom, cured the Pandya king’s fever, debated and defeated the Jains in fire and water, destroyed them, bestowed sacred ash upon the Pandya king, And heard all about the divine acts that spread Shaivism in the Pandya kingdom. Sivanesar prostrated and worshipped in the direction where the Child Saint was. Hearing all these divine acts of the Child Saint, Sivanesar joyfully announced to all his relatives and kin that he had given his daughter Poombavai, all his wealth, and himself to the Child Saint, the ruler of the Kali country.

One day, while Poombavai was plucking jasmine flowers, a snake bit her finger, leaving four teeth marks. The poison ascended to her head, and the girl fell unconscious. Physicians, astrologers, and experts in various arts like Garudan Vidhya All those skilled in their respective fields tried to save her, but the girl’s life departed. Sivanesar and his relatives were distressed.

However, since they had dedicated the girl child to the Child Saint, they resolved not to grieve. They cremated her body and collected the remaining ashes and bones in a pot. This pot was placed in a maiden’s chamber, and her companions were instructed to offer lamps, garlands, and other services daily. Sivanesar and his family maintained this practice. During these days, Sivanesar received the good news that the Child Saint was currently residing in Thiru Ottriyur. Sivanesar was overjoyed.

He gave gold and garments to those who brought the news. He arranged for a flowery canopy, a “Nadaikavanam,” from Thiru Mylapore to Thiru Ottriyur. He planted plantain and betel nut trees, and adorned the path with banners and garlands, decorating it like a divine realm. He, along with his devotees, set out to worship the Child Saint.

At the same time, the Child Saint, having worshipped in Thiruvottiyur, was approaching Thirumylapuri with a throng of devotees. Sivanesar, overjoyed, prostrated on the ground. The Child Saint descended from his palanquin, worshipped before the assembly of devotees, and arose. Hearing the accounts of Sivanesar the wealthy merchant, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman arrived at Thirumylapuri. Bearing in his heart the events that had befallen the merchant, and filled with compassion, he worshipped the sacred Kapaleeswaram of the Lord. ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar circumambulated the temple.

He went before the Lord, worshipped the God of Gods, Kapaleeswaram. He praised and immersed himself in devotion to the ambrosia of Kapaleeswaram, then came out of the temple. Stepping outside, he addressed Sivanesar the wealthy merchant, saying, “Bring the pot filled with your daughter’s bones from outside the temple walls.” Sivanesar then took the pot from the maiden’s chamber. Placed in a covered palanquin, surrounded by her companions, he brought it to the outer entrance of the temple. He then took the pot from the palanquin, placed it directly before him, and bowed. When ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar asked for the pot containing the bones, and Sivanesar, the wealthy merchant, brought it, the people of Mylapore gathered to see what would happen.

The Child Saint, contemplating the greatness of the Lord’s compassion, thought that in this world, by merely using the bones of the deceased, that life could be restored to a good path through the continuation of those bones. He then, calling out the girl’s name, Poombavai, declared that if the greatest benefit of those born into this world is to offer food to the devotees of Lord Shiva and to witness the Lord’s festivals with one’s own eyes, then, before all the people of this world, “Come forth!” He announced this, worshipped the Lord, and began to sing the hymn “Mattitta.” Within that hymn, the divine words “Podhiyo” (Arise!) acted like ambrosia, entering the bones in the pot, causing a form to coalesce within. The air that passed through the verses caused a body, growth, and radiance to fill and be contained within the pot. Before she arose, the Child Saint sang the tenth verse.

At that moment, a hand appeared outside the pot, the pot broke, and Poombavai arose like a lotus bud unfurling. That is, Poombavai, the girl, gained her form with the first verse sung by ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar. In the following eight verses, she grew to the same extent, appearing as she would have at twelve years of age. At the time of Poombavai’s demise, she was seven years old; now, five years had passed, making her twelve.

Thus, she emerged from the pot, fully grown as she would have been at twelve years. Seeing this, the Child Saint concluded the hymn with the “Thirukkadaikappu” (concluding verse), thus completing the hymn. Those who witnessed this miracle, the true devotees, chanted “Hara Hara!” The celestial beings showered flowers. The kings They joined their hands and prostrated themselves. Those of other religions were confused in mind and body, falling into disarray, wondering how this could happen. The beautiful form that had risen, from head to toe, with every limb perfectly adorned with the highest marks of beauty, shone.

Poombavai appeared, astonishing both heaven and earth, an embodiment of beauty. Brahma, who has an immeasurable lifespan, and who, at such an advanced age, had succumbed to lust and lost his good sense upon seeing the illusory beauty of Tilottama, whom he himself had created with his four faces, sank into desire.

However, here, the Child Saint, having completed sixteen years of age, When Poombavai, even more beautiful than Tilottama, came back to life, our Child Saint saw in her only the overflowing compassion of the Lord. The Child Saint did not see Poombavai; he saw only the overflowing compassion of the Lord. Seeing this, Sivanesar prostrated himself at the sacred feet of the Child Saint. Poombavai bowed to the Lord and then to the Child Saint. The Child Saint then addressed Sivanesar, saying, “Take our daughter and go to your home.” Sivanesar bowed to the Child Saint and requested, “Please marry my daughter, Poombavai.” The Child Saint refused, saying, “The daughter you had fell due to poison. This girl, however, has been reborn through the Lord’s compassion.

“Therefore, what you ask is not appropriate.” The Child Saint comforted the grieving merchant and his relatives, explaining the truth of the Vedas to clarify their minds. They, too, abandoned their desire. The Child Saint entered the temple, compassionately worshipped the Lord of Kapaleeswaram, who had bestowed his grace. Sivanesar, unwilling to give Poombavai’s heart to anyone else, brought her back to the maiden’s chamber. Poombavai also attained Shivam.

“The Child Saint stayed in that sacred city for some days. Taking leave from the inhabitants of that city, and assuaging Sivanesar’s sorrow with sweet words, he departed and reached Thiruvanmiyur.

“There, he worshipped the Lord, the medicine for birth and death, He praised Him with a hymn composed in question and answer format, and resided there happily for some days. From there, he proceeded to Thiru Idaichuram, worshipped the Lord, marveled at the color of His sacred form, and sang a hymn praising, “Ivar Vanamenna.” He then arrived at Thirukazhukunram, circumambulated the mountain, worshipped the Lord, and sang a hymn in praise, “Kadhal Seyya Kovil Kazhukunre.” Afterwards, he reached Thiru Achirupakkam, worshipped there, sang the hymn “Aatchi Kondaar,” and resided there happily.

“Then, his devotees welcomed him as he journeyed to other shrines, worshipping at Thiru Varishili, Thiruppuravarpankattoor, and other sacred places, finally arriving at Thillainagar.

“The Brahmins of Thillai and the sacred devotees welcomed him. He descended from his palanquin, and with great love and folded hands, he went and worshipped Thillai. He bowed at the northern entrance and worshipped the sacred streets. He proceeded, worshipped the Perambalam, bowed at the sacred Anukkathiruvayil, and reached the Ponnambalam. He worshipped the divine dance of the great dancer who transcends qualities, bowed at the Thirukazhitrupadi, and was immersed in boundless bliss, reaching a state beyond the shores of supreme joy. When it was not the appointed time, he went outside and worshipped at every auspicious hour, staying there.

“Hearing the news of the Child Saint’s arrival, Sivapathakirudhaiyar, Brahmins, and devotees from Seerkazhi arrived at Thillai. The Thillai Brahmins honored them. They joined the Child Saint, worshipped the Lord of Ambalam, and were joyful. The Child Saint took leave of Koothaperuman and set out towards Seerkazhi, worshipping at many shrines along the way. Seeing the city of Seerkazhi from a distance, he descended from his palanquin, worshipped, and began to sing the hymn “Vandar Kuzhal Arivai,” extolling the Lord, as if the palace was supported by the sky. He continued to sing the hymn “Vezhupuram.” As he approached the city and reached the outer shrine, he offered flowers, incense, and lamps, then sang the concluding hymn “Kalinaagar Sermin,” urging them to enter the city of Kali.

“He entered the sacred city, his love overflowing, and systematically circumambulated the temple, worshipped, and ascended to Thiru Thoni. He joined his hands before Ammai Appar, fell in prostration, and was immersed in devotion, experiencing great bliss. He sang many hymns in praise, received divine leave, and then returned to his sacred abode and resided there.

“We will continue to contemplate the brief history of ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam Part 561, “Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam,” by Sekkizhar Swamigal, the history of ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar. Sekkizhar Peruman sings of the Child Saint’s crying. The verse is: “His lotus eyes filled with tears, he rubbed them with his lotus hands, his beautiful, red, cherry-like mouth and coral lips trembled, and as the endless sound of the Vedas surged, all beings rejoiced, and the holy calf-like one cried.” Generally, when children cry, tears first well up in their eyes, then they rub their eyes with their hands, after which their lips tremble, and then they cry out with sound. These are the stages observed when a child cries. The same method Sekkizhar Peruman employs here in his song: “His lotus eyes filled with tears, he rubbed them with his lotus hands, his beautiful, red, cherry-like mouth and coral lips trembled.” The terms “lotus eyes,” “lotus hands,” and “flower-red-cherry-mouth” indicate that the Child Saint’s eyes, hands, and mouth were all beautiful like lotus flowers.

Why did he cry? The Child Saint cried so that the sound of the Vedas would surge and all beings would rejoice. This crying is the means; the surging of Vedic sound and the rejoicing of all beings are the benefits. The benefit here means enabling these beings to attain the qualification for Shivam. That is why it is indicated here as “all beings rejoicing.” This means that just as a Guru purifies a disciple through his gaze, by placing his sacred hands on the disciple’s head, and by imparting instruction, these references to “lotus eyes,” “lotus hands,” and “lotus mouth” even in song, refer to the lotus flower.

This is like the “Thiruvalar Thamarai” (sacred blooming lotus) mentioned in Thirukovaiyar.

Therefore, because the Child Saint cried, the sound of the Vedas surged, and because of this, beings rejoiced.

Thus, the Child Saint’s crying was the means, and the surging of Vedic sound and the rejoicing of beings was the benefit. “Surging of Vedic sound” means the spread of Thevarams, which are the essence of the Vedas, In this world. Mahadheva Sivagnana Munivar Peruman further explains this by saying, “Tamil Vedas spread throughout the lands, causing all to sing.” Such a Child Saint is like the calf of righteousness. He is in the youthful form of righteousness. The righteousness referred to here is the good fortune of experiencing Shiva without forgetting Him. The Child Saint appeared as if that goodness itself had taken a form.

Why did the Child Saint cry thus? He cried looking at the Thonipuram peak in Seerkazhi. Sekkizhar Peruman sings, “His body trembled, tears fell, he cried looking elsewhere; did he cry remembering his past association (with Shiva), or was it the state of childhood? He cried looking at the Thiru Thoni peak of the red-bodied, white-ash-smeared Lord, calling out ‘Amme Appa!’” The Child Saint cried, with tears falling upon his sacred body, looking at the surrounding areas. Sekkizhar Peruman sings, “We do not know if the Child Saint cried remembering his former state, his past association, or if it was due to his current state of childhood.” There could be two reasons why the Child Saint cried, calling out “Amme Appa!” One is that the Child Saint realized his past association; the other is the state of childhood he was currently in.

We cannot know which of these two reasons caused him to cry, says Sekkizhar Peruman. He implies that we should infer and understand it through our own estimation. This is an excellent tradition of the Guru. When it is said that he cried because he realized his past association, “past association” refers to the Lord, Shiva. Realizing it means experiencing that realization outwardly.

Here, the Child Saint has two associations: that of Shiva and that of Sivapathakiruthaiyar at present. Sekkizhar Peruman sings that perhaps the Child Saint cried because he contained within himself that divine association, his past association with Shiva. His father having descended into the sacred waters, the Child Saint, instead of crying at the sight of his father, cried looking at the peak.

Therefore, it was his past association, realizing the Lord Shiva. He cried looking at the Thiru Thoni peak. In the Seerkazhi temple, the Brahmmapureeswarar temple, the peak that stands like a mountain, which is in the shape of a Thoni, that unique grand temple, he cried looking at the peak of the sanctum sanctorum, the Vimana. From the bank of the Brahmatheertham, he cried looking at the Thiru Thonipuram peak. “Peak” can mean Vimana.

At the same time, “peak” can refer to the letter “Si” (சி). The letter “Si” in the sacred Panchaksharam refers to Lord Shiva. The Child Saint cried, looking inwards at the sacred essence, Shiva, who resides in Thiru Thoni as the peak. The Agamas state that in the Sri Panchaksharam, the letter “Si” signifies Shiva, the letter “Va” signifies divine grace, and the letter “Ya” signifies the soul.

Therefore, the Child Saint cried, calling out “Amme Appa,” to the sacred essence, Lord Shiva, who resides in the Thiru Thoni temple as the peak. He places the Mother first, “Amme,” and the Father next, “Appa,” because the Mother is the one who introduces the child to the Father and unites the child with the Father. The Mother.

Therefore, he first sings of the Mother. Even in the scriptures, it is stated that it is divine grace that purifies souls and unites them with Lord Shiva. Even in Thiruvachagam, Manikkavasagar Peruman sang, “Ammaiye Appa Oppila Maniye,” placing the Mother first.

Therefore, although the great saint, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman, wished to see the Father, he cried, placing the Mother first, “Amme.” In the words “Amme Appa,” the first letter is ‘A’ (அ), and the second letters are ‘M’ (ம்) in “Amme” and ‘Pa’ (ப்ப) in “Appa.” The letter ‘A’ (அ), being the first letter, naturally emerges when we open our mouths. This letter ‘A’ (அ) and then the letters ‘P’ (ப்) and ‘M’ (ம்), which are formed when the lips close after opening the mouth, are the letters ‘Pa’ and ‘Ma’.

Therefore, these words “Amme Appa” are naturally the first words uttered by children. Gnana Shastras state that the Lord, mingled with the primordial pure Maya, creates this world with the support of Shakti.

Thus, Shakti and Shiva are the Mother and Father of the world, according to Shaiva Siddhanta. This is from Thiru Kayappakkam. Sivachettiyar’s commentary notes that since he called out and wept looking at the peak, both of them come. The peak is where the Lord resides. Sivagnana Siddhiyar states that the Mother and Father who create knowledge in all souls, and the Father with the Mother, come and bestow knowledge upon them. This knowledge will be beneficial to all souls.

Now we speak of how the Mother, who is divine grace, nurtures and prepares souls by providing them with bodies, instruments, worlds, and experiences. The Mother, being divine grace, prepares these souls and unites them with the Lord.

Thus, to those souls who have been united with the Lord, that is, those who have been granted moksha. To those souls who have attained the sixfold liberation, the Lord bestows His wealth, His property, which is Sivananda.

Therefore, He is the Father, and She is the Mother.

Thus, when Pillaiyar called out “Mother, Father” and wept, would the Lord remain silent?

The Lord manifests Himself. We shall reflect on this further. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 562, ‘Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam’, authored by Sekkizhar Swamigal, recounts the history of Thiru Gnana Sambandha Nayanar. Pillaiyar, looking towards the peak of Thonipuram, weeps.

At that moment, Lord Shiva, who was enshrined in Thiru Thoni, emerges to bestow His grace upon Pillaiyar. The verse states: “Thiruthoni veetrirundharul nokkal munnilamai thiruthondu munniyavarkku arul purivan pon malai valliyum thamum porudaimeel ezhundharuli chenniyilam pirai thikazha sezhumpoykai marunganaindhaar.” This means that to bestow grace upon Pillaiyar, who remembered his former state of sacred service, the Lord manifested Himself with His divine gaze, along with the golden mountain goddess, Uma, seated on His bull, with the young crescent moon shining on His head, near the rich pond.

The Lord manifests Himself to fulfill His divine gaze.

The Lord manifests Himself to fulfill His divine gaze. Pillaiyar called out, “Mother, Father!” Accordingly, the Lord, along with Uma, the mountain goddess, adorned with the crescent moon, appears on His bull, in that divine form. He manifests near the Brahma Tirtha pond. The next verse states: “Thirumarai nool vedhiyarkkum theviyarkkum thaam kodutha perugu vara ninainthothaan tham perumai kazhal penum oru neriyil varugnanam koduppathanukku udanirundha arumaraiyaal udaiyavalai aliththarula arul seivaar.” Did He remember the great boons He had granted to Sivapadahridhayar and Bhagavati Ammaiyar, and the sacred scriptures? To bestow the unique knowledge that comes from following the path of worshipping His feet, He bestows grace with the Lady of the rare Vedas, Parvati. This refers to the birth of this child.

The Lord gave birth to Pillaiyar.

The Lord brought forth Pillaiyar for the refutation of other religions and the flourishing of Shaivism. Is it to fulfill these boons that the Lord appears here with the Goddess? If grace is to be bestowed upon the weeping Pillaiyar, then the presence of Parvati, the Lady of the Vedas, and the Lord Himself would suffice.

But now, the Lord not only manifests but also intends to give Gnanaponakam (food of wisdom). This also serves to fulfill the boon given to Sivapadahridhayar and Bhagavati Ammaiyar. How so? By giving Gnanaponakam, it will manifest as Tamil Vedas, the Devaram verses, leading to the eradication of other religions and the creation of Shaivism. This knowledge will be the cause for all future events.

Therefore, the Lord, having thus conceived, manifests to bestow grace. Pillaiyar is one who never forgets the holy feet of the Lord.

Therefore, to bestow the knowledge that comes from diligently following the path of worshipping the Lord’s feet, the Lord manifests with the Goddess.

Thus, it is also conveyed here that even divine knowledge does not come on its own as a result of worshipping the holy feet; it comes only if the Lord bestows it, a truth affirmed by the sastras. For this purpose, the Lord manifests with Parvati, the Lady of the sacred Vedas. The Vedas themselves are the general form of the Lord, and the Goddess is the primal one who governs the knowledge enshrined within those Vedas. She, the Goddess, is the embodiment of the Vedas, the primal source of knowledge. The Vedas are knowledge, so the Goddess, as the primal source of knowledge, is capable of bestowing it. As the Goddess bestows this knowledge upon Pillaiyar, Pillaiyar will offer those words of knowledge as the sacred verses of Devaram.

Now, the next verse: “Azhukindra pillaiyar thamai nokki arutkarunai ezhukindra thiruvulla iraiyavar thaam evvulakum thozhukindra malai kodiyai paarthu aruli thunai mulaigal pozhukindra paal adisil pon vallathu vootu enna.” This means the Lord, whose heart swells with compassion, looks at the mountain creeper, Uma, worshipped by all worlds, and commands her, “Nourish him with the milk flowing from your twin breasts in a golden bowl.” This is the next verse. The Lord’s heart is filled with divine compassion. The heart in which divine grace arises is a heart filled with compassion. Grace and compassion are one and the same. In Sanskrit, ‘karuna’ and in Tamil, ‘arul’ are two words that convey the same meaning. Sekkizhar uses both ‘arul’ to explain the greatness of Lord Shiva’s grace in Tamil usage and ‘karuna’ to explain it in Sanskrit usage.

He uses both terms to emphasize the Lord’s immense grace.

Therefore, the Lord’s heart is a heart filled with divine compassion, a heart that is completely an embodiment of grace. Only grace occurs in that heart, nothing else.

Therefore, a heart where divine compassion arises. The Lord’s heart is the birthplace of grace. That grace itself is Ambikai. The grace that exists when souls are bound in the state of Petha (bondage), entangled in worldly attachments, is known as Marakkarunai (material grace). In the state of Mukti (liberation), the grace that exists in the form of Parashakti is Arakkarunai (divine grace).

Here, the compassionate heart of the Lord that arose when Pillaiyar wept is Arakkarunai, which exists in the form of Parashakti in the state of Mukti.

Thus, the Lord, whose heart is filled with arising divine compassion, looks with grace upon Uma Devi, the mountain creeper worshipped by all worlds. ‘Malai Kodi’ refers to Parvati Ammaiyar. She is the mountain creeper worshipped by all worlds. There is no living being, in any form, that does not desire to attain power and wisdom. There are no living beings that do not desire to attain the power and wisdom they yearn for. Ambikai is she who accepts this desire for power and wisdom as their worship and bestows compassion.

Therefore, she is the Mountain Creeper worshipped by all worlds, meaning all living beings.

Thus, the Lord looks upon Parvati Ammaiyar and says, “Thunai mulaigal pozhukindra paal adisil pon vallaththu vootu.” He instructs Parvati Ammaiyar, “Collect the milk-nectar flowing from your two sacred breasts in a golden bowl and feed it to this child.” The twin breasts of the Goddess are indispensable aids for souls to grow in knowledge and attain salvation. The two breasts of the Goddess represent Para Gnanam and Apara Gnanam. The milk flowing from them is the milk-nectar of knowledge.

The Lord instructs, “Take it in a golden bowl and feed it to the child.” The sacred breast of Uma Ammaiyar is not to be directly consumed by mouth but is to be collected and fed by her. That is why the Divine Mother is known by the Sanskrit name “Apeetha Kuchamba” and in Tamil as “Unnamulai” (She whose breasts are not directly consumed). It is for this reason, that it cannot be consumed directly but must be collected and fed by her, that this is said.

The Lord did not say to feed him milk directly, but rather to collect it in a golden bowl and feed it. In the Skanda Purana, in the Saravanappadalam, it is stated that Kaveri takes Lord Murugan, her beloved son, from Saravana Poigai, embraces him, collects the milk flowing from her breast in a golden bowl, and feeds him. The verse is, “Kongaiyil pozhi paal eethilaathathōr kurumaṇi vaḷḷam meethu yēttru kaathal maamakarkku anpinaal aruththinaal Kavuri.” Just as a mother breastfeeds her child according to its maturity, so too is knowledge, guided by the Mother of the World, Gnana Valli, bestowed by the Lord’s command, according to the maturity of souls. If not fed by the Mother. Just as a child unfed by its mother cannot obtain milk, souls cannot acquire knowledge on their own; it must be fed to them. This is the meaning.

Thus, as the Lord commanded, the next verses are: “Aranam ulakelum eendraruli anaiththinukkum kaaranamay valam perugu karunai thiruvativana seer anangu Shivaperuman aruluthalum sendru anainthu vaarinangu thirumulai ponvallaththuk karantharuli ennarriya sivagyanaththu innamutham kulaiththaruli unnadisil enavootta umaiyammai ethirnokkum kanmalar neer thudaiththaruli kaiyil ponkinnam aliththu annalai angu azhukai theerththu angananaar arul porindhaar.” This refers to how the Lord bestows His grace. The next two verses describe how, as Lord Shiva commanded to offer the milk-nectar in a golden bowl, the Mother collected the milk from her sacred breast in a golden bowl and offered it. She is the one who gave birth to the Vedas and all seven worlds. ‘Aranam’ refers to the collection of texts like the Vedas and other scriptures. She gave birth to that knowledge for the souls. She is the one who gave birth to the seven worlds. The ‘seven worlds’ refers to the collection of seven universes, and similarly, the collection of souls born in the seven types of births.

The phrase ‘gave birth’ here means to bring souls bound in the state of ‘kevala’ (primal state) into the ‘sakala’ state (state of activity) by awakening their consciousness and guiding them.

Thus, the Mother is the one who gave birth to the Vedas and all seven worlds. She is the cause of everything.

Here, ‘cause’ acts as an instrumental cause, meaning she serves as an auxiliary cause to the efficient cause, the Lord, providing bodies, instruments, worlds, and experiences from Maya. Through this, she enables souls to experience and exhaust their karmic fruits, thereby leading them to salvation.

Thus, she is the cause of everything. She is the embodiment of flourishing grace. ‘Valam’ refers to the wealth of enjoyment (bhoga) and liberation (moksha). Her very form is the grace that leads to the attainment of enjoyment and liberation. Such is the glorious goddess, the Mother. She, the Mother, who brings forth the Aranas (Vedas), and the seven worlds, and who is the embodiment of grace, does all this for the sake of these souls. This concept is elaborately explained in the words of Tayumanavar Swamigal, who states: “Aivagai enum bhoothamaadhiyai vaguththu athanul achcharachchara bedhamaana yaavaiyum vaguththu nal arivaiyum vaguththu maraiyaathi noolaiyum vaguththu.” Such a Mother, whose very form is grace, upon the command of Lord Shiva, goes to Pillaiyar and collects milk from her sacred breast in a golden bowl.

The Great Goddess, having thus collected it, mixes the sweet nectar of immeasurable divine knowledge with the milk. She wiped the tears from the lotus-like eyes of Pillaiyar, who was looking at her, and offered the golden bowl to his hand, asking him to partake of the milk-nectar.

Thus, Lord Shiva, who is Angananar, put an end to Pillaiyar’s weeping and bestowed his grace. Our reflection on this continues. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 563, ‘Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam’, authored by Sekkizhar Swamigal, recounts the history of Thiru Gnana Sambandha Nayanar. Uma Ammaiyar, the Great Goddess, mixed the sweet nectar of immeasurable divine knowledge with milk, wiped the tears from the lotus-like eyes of Pillaiyar who was looking at her, and offered the golden bowl to his hand, asking him to partake of the milk-nectar.

Thus, Lord Shiva, who is Angananar, put an end to Pillaiyar’s weeping and bestowed his grace. The mixing by the Goddess refers to the sweet nectar of immeasurable divine knowledge. We saw earlier that the two, Para Gnanam and Apara Gnanam, These Para Gnanam and Apara Gnanam serve like adjuncts. Shiva Gnanam is superior to them, like medicine mixed in an adjunct.

Therefore, to indicate Shiva Gnanam, which is superior to these Para and Apara Gnanam, Sekkizhar Peruman uses the term ‘ennariya Shivagnanam’ (immeasurable Shiva Gnanam) in this sacred verse. Shiva Gnana Siddhiyar states that knowledge like the Vedas, Shastras, Smritis, Puranas, arts, and all forms of manifest speech, even up to the ultimate sound, are ‘Pasa Gnanam’ (knowledge of bonds), and that Shiva Gnanam is distinct from these. Shiva Gnanam is also referred to as ‘Tiruvadi Gnanam’ (knowledge of the sacred feet) and ‘Oli Gnanam’ (knowledge of light). This Shiva Gnanam instructs both Para Gnanam and Apara Gnanam.

Therefore, the knowledge bestowed upon Pillaiyar by the Mother was of the nature of both Mother and Father. It is for this reason that the sacred verses of Devaram emanate from Pillaiyar’s holy mouth for the benefit of the world. We can understand this from the nature of the Devaram verses. For instance, the Panchakshara Tiruppathigam, which revealed the conclusions of the Vedas to the Vedic scholars; and the Namasivaya Tiruppathigam, which helped those of Sakti Nipada attain Shiva’s feet and helped them merge with Shiva; and also the fact that even palm trees were blessed to attain union with Shiva through the Lord’s words, and other such truths, are found in the Devaram verses that emanated from the Lord’s sacred mouth.

Therefore, what the Goddess mixed and gave him It is the sweet nectar of immeasurable divine knowledge. ‘Amudam’ here signifies that which can bestow immortality and freedom from rebirth. This sweet nectar of immeasurable divine knowledge is mixed with milk and fed to Pillaiyar. Before that, she wipes the tears flowing from his lotus-like eyes. Children tend to look at the giver’s face when offered milk or other things.

Similarly, Pillaiyar looks at the Mother who comes to feed him the milk-nectar in a golden bowl.

Thus, the Divine Mother first wipes the tears flowing from the lotus-like eyes of Pillaiyar, who was looking at her.

After that, she feeds him the milk-nectar, which is mixed with the sweet nectar of divine knowledge, in a golden bowl. All these actions are performed by the Mother according to the divine command of Lord Shiva. The implication here is that Lord Shiva is the one who inspires and directs everything. Although the Mother’s actions alleviated Pillaiyar’s weeping, all these are truly the actions of the Lord. Such a Lord is Anganan. ‘Anganan’ means one who possesses immense compassion for all living beings.

Thus, Pillaiyar, having consumed the milk-nectar given by the Mother, becomes Gnana Sambandar. Sekkizhar Peruman explains this in the following verse: “Yaavarkkum thanthai thaai enum avar.” Since they are the Father and Mother to all, they appeared themselves and bestowed it, thus he became Aludaiya Pillaiyar, and the unique, flawless Shiva Gnana, which is incomprehensible to all gods and sages, became connected to him, just as Shiva Shakti stands in ‘tadatmyam’ with Shiva. He became Shiva Gnana Sambandar, having attained the explanation of Shiva Tatatmyam Sambandha, absorbed within it. This is the meaning of this sacred verse. In this verse, the sacred names of Pillaiyar, such as Aludaiya Pillaiyar and Thiru Gnana Sambandar, Sekkizhar Peruman describes and explains the meanings of the sacred names Aludaiya Pillaiyar and Thiru Gnana Sambandar in this verse.

The Mother and Father are the father and mother to all. ‘Yavarkkum’ means to all beings. Even though it is stated in terms of higher beings, they are also the Mother and Father to lower beings. Referring to the Lord as Father and Mother is a conventional usage.

Thus, they, who are the Father and Mother to all beings, appeared in this form and bestowed the food of wisdom upon Pillaiyar. Although Shiva and Shakti are shown as two, their essence is one.

Therefore, as Uma Ammaiyar fed him, Lord Shiva bestowed his grace. Uma Ammaiyar and He thus appeared in their manifested forms, came forward, offered milk, bestowed knowledge, and claimed Pillaiyar as their own. This is how the Lord bestows grace upon the category of souls known as Pralayakalas. The scriptures divide souls into three categories: Sakalas, Pralayakalas, and Vijnanakalas. Sakalas are those who possess the three impurities: Anavam (ego), Kanmam (karma), and Mayai (illusion). Pralayakalas are those who possess only Anavam and Kanmam.

Vijnanakalas are those souls who possess only Anavam. Among these three types, Pralayakalas.

Thus, the scriptures state that the Lord will come in a manifested form to bestow grace. The Kandar Kali Venpa mentions, “Kanma malaththarkku malar kan moonrum thaazh sadaiyum van mazhuvum maanum udan maal vidai mel minnidaththu pootha pavalapporuppondru vaitthanaiya theiva vadivaahi muththa karuma mala kattaruththu kan arul seithu” (For those with karmic impurities, the Lord, with three lotus eyes, matted locks, a mighty axe, and a deer, appearing on a mighty bull in a divine form like a coral hill blossomed in a lightning flash, cuts off the ancient karmic bonds and bestows sight/grace). Shivagnana Siddhiyar states that for the first two categories of souls among these three, namely Pralayakalas and Vijnanakalas, the Lord, being Niradhara (without support) and beyond all, bestows grace through the descent of His Shakti, destroying their impurities. The ways in which the Lord bestows grace by appearing before them are also many. In a similar manner of bestowing grace, the Lord appeared in a manifested form with the Goddess on a white bull to Pillaiyar.

Thus, because he was claimed by the Lord, Pillaiyar becomes Aludaiya Pillaiyar. ‘Aludaiya’ means that which is owned by the Lord.

Therefore, Pillaiyar shines as Aludaiya Pillaiyar, the child claimed by the Lord. There is also an implication that Pillaiyar is of the nature of a guru, who claims souls and leads them to salvation. That is, the first meaning is Pillaiyar claimed by the Lord. The second meaning is that Pillaiyar is of the nature of claiming all souls as his own and leading other souls to salvation. Why is he called Pillaiyar? He is called Pillaiyar because he was given milk and knowledge by his mother and father, and his weeping ceased, thus acquiring the status of a child.

We can recall here that in the Puranas of Chandikeswara Nayanar, Chandikeswara Nayanar also acquired the status of a child and was called Sengalvar Pillaiyar. ‘Aludaiya’ here refers to the master-servant relationship, where one is claimed as a servant or slave. Thirugnanasambandar Peruman himself has sung this as an internal evidence in his Devaram verses: “Bothaiyaar ponkinnaththu adisil pollaathenadhu thaathaiyaaru munivar thaanena aandavan.” This is Sekkizhar Peruman’s explanation for the name Aludaiya Pillaiyar.

Similarly, Sekkizhar Peruman also explains the name Gnana Sambandar in this verse. Shiva Gnanam is a truth that is difficult for even the Devas and Munis to comprehend. Shiva Gnanam is knowledge bestowed through divine grace.

Therefore, it is extremely difficult for Devas, Munis, or anyone else to comprehend. Such a thing is Shiva Gnanam. It is flawless Shiva Gnanam, unparalleled and unique.

Therefore, it is flawless Shiva Gnanam, a Shiva Gnanam that is incomprehensible to Devas and Munis. Since the Goddess bestowed that Shiva Gnanam mixed with milk, Pillaiyar became Gnana Sambandar. Even in his previous state, he was Gnana Sambandar.

However, here that Gnana Sambandam manifests explicitly.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman sings that he became Sivagnana Sambandar. Sivagnana Sambandar means one who has a connection like that of Sivagnanam. What does Sivagnana Sambandam mean? It means a connection that is united with Sivagnanam. That is, Sivagnanam is Shiva Shakti. The connection between Shiva Paramporul and Shiva Shakti, where Shiva Shakti is united with Shiva Paramporul in a state of Tatatmyam, is Tatatmyam Sambandam.

What is Tatatmyam Sambandam? Madhava Sivagnana Swamigal states in Sivagnana Mapadiyam that Tatatmyam is a state where two things exist as one without separation in a certain way. Sivagnana Mapadiyam states that Tatatmyam is the quality of being entitled to exist in two ways without separation. Tatatmyam is the relationship between a quality and its possessor. This is an eternal and inseparable relationship. Tatatmyam Sambandam is called ‘one in two’ in Tamil.

Its explanations are elaborately discussed in the Sivagnana Bodham and Sivagnana Bodha Mapadiyam texts.

Therefore, here Pillaiyar, like Shiva Shakti, merged within it and attained the explanation of Advaita Sambandam, which is Shiva Tatatmyam. This complete understanding of this Sambandam is attained only in the Nirumala Thuriyaatheetha state. That is why Sekkizhar Peruman describes it as ‘therivariya’ (difficult to comprehend).

Thus, this Sambandam will be fully understood only in the Nirumala Thuriyaatheetha state. In the states below this, it is very difficult to understand all these explanations.

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman sings. At that transcendent state, when one is immersed in the ocean of supreme bliss, the knowing, knowledge, and knowable (Gnatru Gnana Sangalpa Gnanangal) and the knowledge of the arts (Kalaignana), which serve as means for contemplation, do not arise. Such is the state that Pillaiyar currently realized. If so, how did he realize it in that state? Pillaiyar is Aludaiya Pillaiyar, one who came into this world.

Therefore, he realized them for the sake of the people of this world. We can see this in Thiru Gnanasambandar Peruman’s hymn, beginning with “En ullam kavar kalvan” (The thief who stole my heart), where he describes the truth of that Advaita fusion of Shiva Ananda.

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman provides commentary on the sacred name Aludaiya Pillaiyar and his becoming Sivagnana Sambandar, which is Gnana Sambandar or Thiru Gnana Sambandar. We shall continue our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 564, ‘Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam’, authored by Sekkizhar Swamigal, recounts the history of Thiru Gnana Sambandha Nayanar. Sivagnana Sambandar became Aludaiya Pillaiyar. Sekkizhar Peruman describes how he attained knowledge in the next verse: “Sivanadiye sindhikkum thirupperugu sivagnanam pavamathanai aramaatrum paanghinil ongkiya gnanam uvamaiyilla kalagnanam unarvariya meignanam thava muthalvar sambandhar thaam unarnthaar annilaiyil.” This song is one of the crown jewels among the songs in the history of Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman. Sekkizhar Peruman sings in this song that Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman understood both Apara Gnanam and Para Gnanam. Sambandar, the foremost of ascetics, realized Kala Gnanam (knowledge of the arts), which is Apara Gnanam, and Meignananam (true knowledge), which is Para Gnanam.

In this verse, “Sivanadiye sindikkum thirupperugu sivagnanam” (the flourishing Shiva knowledge that meditates on Shiva’s feet) is an adjective for “uvamaiyilla kalaignanam” (unparalleled knowledge of the arts). “Pavathanai aramaatrum paanghinil ongkiya gnanam” (the exalted knowledge that completely removes karma) is an adjective for “unarvariya meignananam” (incomprehensible true knowledge). These are also referred to as Aparoksha Gnanam and Paroksha Gnanam. “Uvamaiyilla kalaignanam” refers to Apara Gnanam, and “unarvariya meignananam” refers to Para Gnanam. “Sivanadiye sindikkum thirupperugu sivagnanam” is an adjective for unparalleled knowledge of the arts. “Pavathanai aramaatrum paanghinil ongkiya gnanam” is an adjective for incomprehensible true knowledge.

For this verse, Kachiyappa Munivar has elaborated on this verse in the Thiruttanigai Puranam, in the chapter on receiving Agathiyar’s grace. In Shivaprakasam, Umapati Sivachariyar has stated in the Shivaprakasa Payiram: “Uyar gnanam irandaam maraa malar magala agalaadha mannu bodha thiruvarul ondru ondru athanai theliya pothum sivagamam endru ulagariya seppu noole” (Higher knowledge is twofold, that which removes enduring impurity and that which reveals eternal wisdom; one is divine grace, the other is the Sivagama that explains it for the world to know). The Paushkara Agama, in its Pati Padalam, states: “Sivasiya samavetaaya shaktir gyanathmikaamala shaivagyanam iti proktham shabdanthanumaamakam” (The pure, inherent knowledge-power of Shiva is called Shaiva Gnanam, which is conveyed by words and inference).

Thus, there are two types of knowledge: Para Gnanam and Apara Gnanam. Among them, Apara Gnanam is referred to here as ‘uvamaiyilla kalaignanam’ (unparalleled knowledge of the arts). Due to its characteristic of revealing tattva gnana (knowledge of principles), it surpasses other forms of knowledge of the arts. The Vedas and Agamas stand as exemplary foundations for all other knowledge of the arts.

Here, ‘kalaignanam’ signifies the Mukti Panchaksharam, but in a secondary sense, it refers to the Vedas, Sivagamas, and all other branches of knowledge that expanded from them. Such is the unparalleled knowledge of the arts, which is Apara Gnanam. It is the flourishing Shiva Gnanam that meditates on Shiva’s feet. It is the Shiva Gnanam that causes prosperity to grow. ‘Thiru’ means divine essence, which bestows Shiva-ness, liberation, and divine wealth. Panchaksharam means the Vedas and Sivagamas.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman realizes Apara Gnanam, which is the flourishing Shiva Gnanam that meditates on Shiva’s feet. At that moment, Sekkizhar Peruman sings that he attains Para Gnanam. He sings that he realized ‘unarvariya meignananam’ (incomprehensible true knowledge), which is the exalted knowledge that completely removes karma. This means that Para Gnanam is the knowledge that completely eradicates impurities.

Thus, even the karmic impurities that cause rebirth are completely destroyed in that state, and rebirth completely ceases.

Thus, the exalted knowledge that completely eradicates rebirth is Para Gnanam. It is also the knowledge that matures the root impurity of ignorance, which is the cause of rebirth. It is this knowledge that stands exalted in such clarity.

Thus, the exalted knowledge that completely eradicates rebirth is ‘unarvariya meignananam’ (incomprehensible true knowledge). That is Para Gnanam. It is unknown by Pasu Gnanam (knowledge of the individual soul) and Pasa Gnanam (knowledge of bonds), hence it is incomprehensible true knowledge. Those who attain that Para Gnanam will remain as that, their individual consciousness dissolved. This is incomprehensible knowledge, this Para Gnanam.

Therefore, Para Gnanam can only be realized if the Lord Himself, as the guru, reveals it; it cannot be realized through any other means. That is true knowledge.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman sings here that it is ‘unarvariya meignananam’ (incomprehensible true knowledge). The means to attain this Para Gnanam are ‘thelithal’ (clarity) and ‘nishtai kooduthal’ (meditation/abidance).

Therefore, ‘paangku’ (manner) here refers to clarity, and ‘unarvariya’ (incomprehensible) refers to meditation. These two are Para Gnanam.

Therefore, ‘bhavamathanai aramaatrum paangku’ (the manner that completely removes karma) is understood to lead to the destruction of bonds (pasa kshayam), and ‘unarvariya meignananam’ (incomprehensible true knowledge) is understood to lead to the attainment of Shiva (sivapperu).

Thus, Sambandar, the foremost of ascetics, realized both Para Gnanam and Apara Gnanam in that state. That state means the state of becoming Sivagnana Sambandar, having attained the experience of Sivananda and the pure Turiyaatita state upon consuming the food of wisdom, thereby becoming Sivagnana Sambandar. In that state, for the benefit of the world, both types of knowledge became manifest to him.

Therefore, Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman is not one who attained Apara and Para Gnanam in the sadhaka state like others. This is the implication here. Sambandar realized both Para Gnana and Apara Gnana because he is a ‘thava muthalvar’ (foremost ascetic).

Therefore, ‘thava muthalvar Sambandar thaam unarndhaar’ (Sambandar, the foremost ascetic, realized it) implies that ‘thava muthalvar’ indicates the reason why he realized it in that manner. It points to the reason for his manifestation as Thiru Gnana Sambandar at this time due to his past ascetic merit. We can recall here what we previously observed, that the term ‘thava muthalvar’ refers to one who never forgets the holy feet of the Lord. Such a one, possessing immense ascetic merit. Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman, therefore, the Lord, with three eyes, four arms, and a blue throat, along with other attributes, revealed his natural form, which performs the three actions, as a guru. The great penance of Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman, which was instrumental in the Lord, as the primordial being, revealing higher knowledge to the Pralayakalas, is explained through the word ‘thava muthal’. ‘Thavam muthal’ can also be taken as ‘first penance’, referring to the supreme merit of Shiva, standing at the sixteenth stage of ‘Sakthi Nipadham’ (descent of divine power), at the peak of intense maturity of the soul.

Such a ‘thava muthalvar’ (foremost ascetic) is Sambandar; therefore, he attained this state. The means to knowledge are listening, contemplating, clarifying, and abiding, which are four according to Sivagnana Siddhiyar. In Sanskrit, these are called Shravanam, Mananam, Nidhidhyasanam, and Nishta. Among these, the first two, listening and contemplating, belong to the Apara Gnanam category, and the latter two, clarifying and abiding, belong to the Para Gnanam category, as categorized by the Gnana Shastras. Why are these four divided into two like this? The first two, listening and contemplating, rely on scriptures, and thus are placed in the Apara Gnanam category.

The latter two, clarifying and abiding, occur due to divine grace, and thus are placed in the Para Gnanam category.

Therefore, knowledge obtained through the Vedas and Sivagamas is Apara Gnanam, and direct realization through divine grace is Para Gnanam.

Furthermore, among the four mentioned here, listening, clarifying, and contemplating are means to attain the knowledge that leads to liberation. One can learn by listening to instruction. One can also understand what has been heard by contemplating it through appropriate proofs. Having contemplated it thus, one can also understand it by clarifying it perfectly through Shiva Gnanam in one’s intellect. By this, one can destroy bonds, attain Nishta (abidance), and also experience Sivananda. Sri Madhava Shivagnana Munivar thus explains it to us.

Therefore, listening, clarifying, and contemplating—these three are gateways to attaining knowledge. Knowledge is a gateway to attaining liberation, which is implied here.

Therefore, knowledge is There is only one knowledge, but when categorized, it is two: Para (higher) and Apara (lower). The ways to attain it are four: listening, contemplating, clarifying, and abiding. It can also be five, in the form of Gnana Velvi (sacrifice of knowledge): studying and teaching sacred texts, making others listen to good principles, listening oneself, and contemplating flawless truths. This can also be eight, categorized as true Charya, Upaya Charya, true Kriya, Upaya Kriya, true Yoga, Upaya Yoga, true Gnana, and Upaya Gnana. These eight further expand into thirty-two, starting with Charyayil Charya. These are also explained as the ten దశకారியம் (Dasakaryam).

And in many other ways, knowledge expands. Even though all these exist, they are all subsumed within the two primary types of knowledge: Para and Apara. Sambandar, the foremost ascetic, realized such knowledge in that state. Generally, everyone would ask if Pillaiyar attained knowledge even without penance. To negate this, Sekkizhar Peruman uses the term ‘thava muthalvar Sambandar’ (Sambandar, the foremost ascetic) here.

Moreover, he describes the various classifications of the complete knowledge that he realized through this sacred verse.

Thus, Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman, the foremost ascetic who realized these two types of knowledge, arose. How did he arise? He arose, pulverizing the conclusions of other impure religions, each according to its understanding. He arose, pulverizing all the conclusions of other impure religions, which act according to their own understanding, without the awareness that the Lord is the one who directs all things, and without the knowledge that the true essence is the Lord and His devotees. Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman consumed the milk-nectar of wisdom, and thereby understood both types of knowledge. He was a foremost ascetic.

That very wisdom which entered him produced this sense of knowledge. That sense of knowledge that arose in Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman was of two types. This awakened state arose for the benefit of the world and its living beings. When this feeling arises in others, it benefits only them, but when it arose in Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, it arose for the benefit of the living beings of this world. The wisdom that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman embodied is of two kinds.

Therefore, that wisdom itself arose as two kinds of wisdom, as feeling and as knowledge. It is this wisdom that rises to shatter the impure conclusions of those of other religions into dust. The one who creates everything is Isan. Isan refers to Lord Shiva, the primal being, known as Pati. The Choodamani Nikandu states the truth that Isan and Bhagavan refer to Lord Shiva. Such an Isan alone is capable of creating everything; this understanding is essential.

For living beings, the two entities apart from Pati are Pasam and. Pasu.

Here, creation, in the context of Pasu (souls), means guiding those souls to be subject to the five functions such as creation. To create Pasam (bondage) means to activate the mala of Maya and render the mala of Anava powerless so that souls may experience the fruits of their actions.

Therefore, the understanding here is that God, Isan, is the creator of both Pasu and Pasam, and attaining this Isan is the ultimate goal. This is what the tenth sutra of Sivagnanabodham refers to as Pasakshayam (the destruction of bondage).

Thus, the wisdom gained by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman serves primarily to achieve Pasakshayam for these souls, and it is also intended to refute all other religions. That resolve is also conveyed here as the first type of benefit.

Now, the second benefit is that the fruits of this knowledge are manifested in the form of the Linga, the Guru, and the devotee, known as the Jangama. Among these, the Guru and Linga forms are the Lord’s forms. The Jangama is the devotee’s form. The understanding that these two are the only forms is the second type of benefit, signifying the attainment of Shiva and the removal of residual impurities. This conveys the conclusions of the eleventh and twelfth sutras of Sivagnanabodham.

Therefore, the two types of wisdom embodied by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman yield these two types of benefits. To summarize, the first benefit is the refutation of other religions, and the second is the establishment of Saivism. Lord Shiva, in His compassionate heart, desired that all beings in the world should attain salvation through these two benefits. He had Thirugnanasambandha Peruman born here and nourished him with the milk of wisdom, thereby elevating these souls.

Now, the child, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who partook of the milk of wisdom, is seated on the bank of Brahmateertham. Sivapatha Hirudayar, who went to bathe in the teertham for Akamarshanam, emerges.

Let us continue to reflect on the sacred history of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, part five hundred sixty-five, authored by Sekkizhar Swamigal, Vambara Varivandu Sarrkkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Sivapatha Hirudayar, having completed all his rituals, including Akamarshanam, comes out and looks at the child seated on the bank of the teertham.

The child appears immersed in supreme consciousness, shining with the unparalleled, singular light of Shiva’s wisdom, which is complete knowledge. This wisdom manifests as an outward light. Sivapatha Hirudayar looks at such a child and angrily asks, “Whose milk did you drink?” Milk is a food item that anyone can offer.

Here, however, Sivapatha Hirudayar becomes angry. Generally, one should not accept and consume food from just anyone, as it is not a good practice.

Moreover, milk, in particular, is not something to be received from just anyone. This is because the physical and qualitative traits of the mother would be present in that milk, and if it comes from someone else, those traits would transfer to the child consuming it.

Furthermore, due to the impurity of the vessel and many other reasons, it is not a good practice to accept and consume milk from just anyone, according to our custom. Especially for children, extreme caution must be exercised when giving milk and other initial. food items, otherwise, for children, that is, for children who drink milk given by others besides their mother, that milk can cause diseases and changes in disposition, among other things.

Therefore, one must be extremely cautious when receiving milk from others and giving it to a child. It is for these reasons that Sivapatha Hirudayar becomes angry. Not only that, many wicked people would wish harm upon a good child.

Therefore, this too contributed to Sivapatha Hirudayar’s anger and concern.

Thus, angered, Sivapatha Hirudayar further asks the child, “Show me the person who gave you this milk, allowing it to be defiled by their saliva,” and says, He took a small stick in his hand and raised it as if to strike. He held the stick and raised his hand as if to strike.

Here, ‘saliva’ refers to harm. He asks, “Show me the person who gave you this milk, mixing harm into it.” Why does he ask, “Show me the one who gave it to you?” Because if the item given might be harmful, he asks this in order to nullify that harm.

At that moment, the great little child stands on one leg, tears of overflowing joy streaming from his eyes, and points with one sacred finger of his raised hand towards the sky. The child. was a great little one. In form and age, he was small, but in nature, he was great.

Hence, the great little one.

At that time, in his father’s thoughts, he was considered a small child, but here there is also an indication that he possessed great glory that was then unknown to his father. From the sacred eyes of that great little child, tears of joy rained down. Tears poured from his eyes like rain due to joy. Just as it is said, ‘Is there a lock for love? The tears of the eager will proclaim it,’ here, tears of joy flow from the sacred eyes of the child. When asked, ‘Who gave you this milk?’, in response, the child.

The child raises one sacred finger of his sacred hand and points it upwards. He points it high above because, at the very moment the father questions the child, Thoniyappar, having fed the child milk, having assuaged his cries, continues to rise and bestow His vision upon the child. He descends from the heavens with Uma Devi on the bull, Rishabam. The father comes and asks the child this. That vision, however, is visible only to the child. Even though the Lord and the Goddess are in the sky, it is a sight not seen by Sivapatha Hirudayar.

The father, Sivapatha Hirudayar, could not see the Lord and the Goddess, but he only saw the mark of milk on the child’s lips. Sivapatha Hirudayar saw.

Therefore, he points upwards, raising the lower souls to the highest point.

The child raises his sacred hand to the highest point, intending to bestow grace upon the lower souls, bringing them to the supreme state.

How does Thirugnanasambandha Peruman begin this pathigam? He begins by taking the first letter of the boundless Vedas with its consonant. Sekkizhar Peruman sings that he begins by combining the first letter of the Vedas with a consonant. Those Vedas are referred to here with the epithet ‘boundless Vedas’. Boundless Vedas means that the Vedas are such that they discard all things by saying ‘Neti, Neti’ (not this, not this) and proceed without limit. These Vedas are revered as ‘unwritten scriptures’ because they cannot be measured, confined, or written down in their expansive nature.

They are transmitted through generations via oral tradition, through the ears, as instruction.

Therefore, they are called ‘Sruti’ in Sanskrit and ‘Othu’ in Tamil. Since they are not confined to written form but come as an oral tradition through recitation and instruction, they are called ‘Othu’ in Tamil. Since it comes through the ear, passed down through generations by way of oral instruction, it is called Sruti.

Thus, the four Vedas are boundless in nature. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman begins the pathigam by taking the first letter of such Vedas, combined with a consonant. Therefore, the Veda is an expansion of Pranava. So, the first letter of the Veda is the ‘O’ sound, the first letter of Pranava. This is a vowel. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sings this by combining it with a consonant. Sekkizhar Peruman states. That consonant is the letter ‘ith’.

When the pathigam begins with the letter ‘Tho’ as in “Thodudaiya Seviyan,” the ‘ith’ consonant is what Sekkizhar Peruman refers to here.

Therefore, the ‘ith’ consonant here. The consonant ‘ith’ here refers to this Thagaravidya. Thagaravidya is the true state of Sivashakti.

Furthermore, this ‘thagaram’ (த்) is the concluding letter of the Gayatri Mantras.

With this consonant ‘ith’, which possesses such distinctions, combined with ‘O’, the first letter of the Vedas. We saw that the four Vedas are ‘unwritten scriptures’.

Here, the Tevarams composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman are ‘written scriptures’. The Vedas describe the attributes of Brahman in an expansive manner that cannot be limited or confined. They are unwritten scriptures.

Here, the Tevaram, a written scripture composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, was able to limit and point out the Lord. This is indicated by Sekkizhar Peruman, who refers to the Vedas. Sekkizhar Peruman refers to the Vedas as boundless scriptures and the Tevarams composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as written scriptures. The wisdom of ‘thagaram’ is superior to life itself and elevates it.

Therefore, he sings by combining the ‘thagaram’, which brings forth this specialty, with ‘okkaram’. Even in Siva Agamas, the presiding deities and benefits associated with the matruka letters for ‘okkaram’ and ‘thakaram’ are mentioned.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composes this ‘written scripture’ in rich, grand Tamil. ‘Mallal’ means richness or abundance. It refers to the generosity or abundance that provides what is desired, as and when desired.

Here, Tamil possesses a similar quality.

Therefore, this is. It becomes ‘mallal nedum tamizh’ (rich, grand Tamil). This brought the special distinction of ‘nedum tamizh’ to Tamil. That is, Tamil has the glory of conveying the true philosophy of the world. How did this glory come to Tamil?

It is because the divine work called Iraiyanar Akapporul, composed by Lord Shiva, is in Tamil. Therefore, so that these souls might benefit by listening to, contemplating, and reciting the Tevaram pathigams, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed this pathigam in Tamil, so that the words of the people of this land might be excellent. Not only that, but sentient beings with six senses should benefit. Not only should they benefit, but all other beings, beyond those with six senses, should also greatly rejoice and attain bliss. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman blesses them in this way. How does he bless them? He begins by praising the sacred ear of the Lord, starting with “Thodudaiya Seviyan.” This is because, for the people of this land to receive ‘vasaga diksha’ (initiation through words) and for many souls to rejoice, his song must go to Lord Paramar (Shiva).

These pathigams must reach the sacred ear of the Lord.

Therefore, he begins by praising the sacred ear of the Lord.

Thus, the meaning and benefit of the Tevaram pathigams composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman are for the living beings of this world to be freed from suffering and attain joy.

Thus, it is understood that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed all these pathigams for the living beings of the world, and not for himself.

Therefore, for all these souls to chant the Tevaram pathigams that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman now begins, and for these sacred verses to reach the sacred ear of Lord Paramar, he begins by praising the ear of the Lord, saying “Thodudaiya Seviyan.” We can understand that the human souls of this land were blessed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s pathigams through his Panchakshara pathigams, Thiruneetru pathigam, Thirupassuram, Kolvaru pathigam, and other pathigams. All other beings. We can see that other beings also benefit, as mentioned in the Thiruvottur pathigam and other pathigams. In the Thiruvottur pathigam, we will soon see histories such as the male palm tree becoming a female palm tree without bearing fruit and then attaining Shiva. Through that, we can understand.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sings by praising the sacred ear, so that all beings may find rest and that the Tevaram pathigams may reach the sacred ear of the Lord.

The Lord has sacred limbs such as His sacred feet. Without mentioning them, he praises the sacred ear by saying, “Seviyan Thodudaiya Seviyan” (He with the ear and the ear-ornament), because the ‘thodu’ (ear-ornament) is an adornment worn by the Mother, who is the power of grace.

Therefore, the Mother. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman begins this pathigam by first praising the Mother. Sekkizhar Peruman then continues to explain how he composed it.

Boundless Vedas means that the Vedas, by eliminating all things with ‘neti, neti’ (not this, not this), are boundless and uncontained.

These Vedas are praised as unwritten scriptures, because these Vedas cannot be measured and written. They are boundless in nature and cannot be written. They are transmitted from generation to generation through oral instruction, through the ears.

Therefore, they are called ‘Shruti’ in Sanskrit and ‘Othu’ in Tamil. Because they are transmitted orally through instruction and not contained in written form, they are called ‘Othu’ in Tamil. Since it comes through the ear, passed down from generation to generation by instruction, it is called Shruti.

Thus, the four Vedas are boundless in nature. ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman begins the pathigam by combining the first letter of such Vedas with a consonant. The first letter of the Vedas is the primordial ‘Omkara’. When chanting the Vedas, it is customary to begin with ‘Om’ from the Pranava and end with ‘Om’ from the Pranava.

Therefore, the Veda is the expansion of the Pranava. Hence, the first letter of the Veda is ‘Omkara’, the first letter of the Pranava. This is a vowel. ThiruGnana Sambandha Peruman combines it with a consonant, as Sekkizhar Peruman states. That consonant is the consonant ‘Ith’. The pathigam ‘Thoduudaiya Seviyan’ begins with the letter ‘Tho’, and the consonant ‘Ith’ that appears there is what Sekkizhar Peruman refers to here.

Therefore, by combining the consonant ‘Ith’ with ‘O’, the first letter of the Vedas and Pranava, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman begins by singing ‘Tho’ as in ‘Thoduudaiya’. The consonant ‘Ith’ here refers to Thagara Vidya. Thagara Vidya is one of the thirty-two Vidyas mentioned in the Vedas. Just as there are Sat Vidya, Homa Vidya, Varuni Vidya, Thagara Vidya is also a Vidya mentioned in the Vedas.

Therefore, the ‘Ith’ here the consonant ‘Th’ here refers to this Thagara Vidya. Thagara Vidya is the true state of Shiva-Shakti.

Furthermore, this ‘Th’ is the concluding letter of the Gayatri Mantras.

Moreover, in the Vedas, the supreme reality, Brahman, is referred to as ‘Sat’. In the Chandogya and other Upanishads, the term used to denote Brahman is ‘Sat’, and its final letter is also this consonant ‘Th’. The Vayu Samhita states that the first letter ‘Sa’ in the word ‘Sat’ is the form of Shakti, and ‘Th’ is the form of Shiva. With such special qualities, the consonant ‘Th’ is combined with ‘O’, the first letter of the Vedas. ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman begins the pathigam ‘Thoduudaiya Seviyan’ by combining the ‘O’ (Omkara) to form ‘Tho’. Sekkizhar Peruman refers to this Tevaram pathigam, which ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman begins as ‘Thoduudaiya Seviyan’, as ‘Ezhuthum Marai’ (written Veda) here.

We saw that the four Vedas are ‘Ezhuthamarai’ (unwritten Vedas).

Here, the Tevarams composed by ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman are ‘Ezhuthum Marai’ (written Vedas). The Vedas describe the attributes of Brahman in an immeasurable and boundless way, they are ‘Ezhuthamarai’ (unwritten Vedas).

Here, the Tevaram composed by ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman, which is a ‘Ezhuthum Marai’ (written Veda), was able to point out and define the Lord, implying that Sekkizhar Peruman refers to the Vedas as ‘boundless scripture’ and the Tevarams composed by ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman as ‘written scripture’. The knowledge of ‘Thagara’ is superior to life itself and elevates life.

Therefore, to express that special quality, he combines ‘Thagara’ with ‘Omkara’ and sings. Even in the Shivagamas, the presiding deities and benefits of the Matrukavarnas corresponding to Omkara and Thakara are mentioned.

Thus, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman composed this ‘written scripture’ in ‘Mallal Nedum Tamil’. ‘Mallal’ means richness or abundance. It refers to the quality of being generous, providing whatever is needed, whenever it is needed.

Here, Tamil also possesses a similar quality.

Therefore, it is Mallal Nedum Tamil. This epithet ‘Nedum Tamil’ came to Tamil because it contained the Thirumuraigal, which serve as a measuring tool to ascertain Shiva, the ultimate reality. That is, Tamil has the greatness of explaining the true philosophy of the world. How did this come to Tamil? The sacred text ‘Iraiyanar Agapporul’, composed by Lord Shiva, is in Tamil. The Tevaram, Thiruvasagam, and other divine texts composed by Shiva through the Nayanmars, whose minds were Shiva-like, and the Jnana Sastras like Meikanda Sastras, were also composed in Tamil, having been blessed by the Lord.

Tamil has attained that divine quality.

Therefore, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman composes the Tevaram pathigam, the ‘Thoduudaiya Seviyan’ pathigam, in such ‘Mallal Nedum Tamil’. Through such Tamil, he bestows grace so that the people of this earth may excel in their understanding and benefit. ‘People of this earth’ here refers to sentient beings, because only such sentient beings benefit from the ‘Vasaga Diksha’ (initiation through words).

Therefore, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman composes this pathigam so that these beings may benefit by listening to, reflecting on, and reciting the Tevaram pathigams, so that the people of this earth may excel in their understanding. Not only that, sentient beings It is not just that they should benefit, but also that ‘all lives should rejoice’. ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman bestows grace so that other beings, besides the six-sensed humans, should also experience great joy and bliss. How does he bestow grace? He begins this pathigam by praising the Lord’s sacred ear, starting with ‘Thoduudaiya Seviyan’. This is because, for the people of this world to receive verbal initiation and for many lives to rejoice, his song should reach Paramanaar, Lord Shiva.

Since these pathigams should reach the sacred ear of the Lord, he begins by praising the Lord’s sacred ear.

Therefore, for the living beings of this world to be free from suffering and attain bliss, that is the purpose of the Tevaram pathigams composed by ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman. The meaning and benefit of the Tevaram pathigams are for the living beings of the world, not for ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman himself.

Therefore, it is understood that these living beings, by reciting the Tevaram pathigams that ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman is now beginning, should have these verses reach the sacred ears of the Supreme Lord. For this purpose, he begins by praising the Lord’s ear as ‘Thoduudaiya Seviyan’ (one with an earring). The fact that human beings on this earth were blessed by ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman’s pathigams can be known through pathigams like Panchatchara pathigams, Thiruneetrupathigam, Thiruppasuram, Kolattupathigam, etc. Many lives and other beings are benefiting, as can be known through pathigams like the Thiruvoathur pathigam. In the Thiruvoathur pathigam, we will see the history of a male palm tree becoming a female palm tree without a cluster and attaining Shiva, and other similar events. Through this, we can understand.

Therefore, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman praises the Lord’s ear so that all beings may find rest and that the Tevaram pathigams may reach the sacred ear of the Lord.

The Lord has sacred feet and other sacred limbs, but without mentioning all of them, he praises the ear as ‘Seviyan Thoduudaiya Seviyan’ because ‘thodu’ (earring) is an ornament worn by the divine Mother, Arulshakti.

Therefore, the Mother Ayai is first praised, and then ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman begins this pathigam. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to describe how he sang it.

We shall continue with our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 569, by Sekkizhar Swamigal, ‘Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam’, ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar Puranam. The second verse of the first pathigam, which begins with ‘Thoduudaiya Seviyan’, is as follows: (Mutral aamai ila nagamodu ena mulaikkompu avai poondhu vatral oadu kalanaa bali theerndhu enadhu ullam kavar kalvan katral kettal udaiyar periyar kazhal kaiyal thozhudhaertha petram oorndha piramapurameviya pemman ivan andre) “He, who wears the old tortoise shell, young snakes, and the boar’s tusk, and collects alms with a dry skull-bowl, is the thief who stole my heart. Is he not the Lord who resides in Bramapuram, riding the bull, worshipped by great sages learned in scriptures, with hands that touch his feet?” In this verse, the Lord’s attributes are identified through the ornaments he wears. ‘Mutral aamai’ means an ancient tortoise. It refers to the shell of the ancient tortoise, the Koorma avatar of Vishnu. ‘Ila nagam’ refers to Ananthan and other snakes that have an age of several Chatur Yugas. ‘Ena mulai kombu’ refers to the tusk worn by Vishnu in his Varaha avatar.

The Lord wears all of these as ornaments on his sacred chest. ‘Vattral oadu’ is the dried skull of Brahma.

The Lord carries it in his sacred hand as a begging bowl.

Thus, the Lord who seeks alms in Brahma’s skull is the thief who stole my heart. Such a Lord, who appears on the bull in a state of grace for those great sages learned in knowledge who worship his feet with their hands, is he not? ‘Katral kettal udaiyar’ refers to those who are proficient in spiritual knowledge and learning, and by implication includes meditation, clarity, and absorption. He is the Lord worshipped by such great ones.

Lord Shiva grants visions on the bull and resides in Bramapuram.

Now, the third verse: (Neeranda nimir punjadai mel or nila ven madhisoodi erparandha ina velvalai sora en ullam kavar kalvan oorparandha ulagin mudhalagiya oor idhu enna perparandha piramapurameviya pemman ivan andre) “He, who wears a crescent moon on his flowing, matted red hair filled with water, making the conch bangles slip from my hands, is the thief who stole my heart. Is he not the Lord who resides in Bramapuram, renowned as the first and foremost city in the world?” ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman is singing. This is a song in the akapporul (love poetry) genre. When the heroine suffers in thoughts of the hero, her body wastes away, and the bangles on her hands slip off – this is the scene in akapporul.

Here, all souls are heroines, and the Lord is the hero of these souls.

Thus, this song is set in the mood of heroine and hero. “This thief who stole my heart, he is the Lord who resides in Bramapuram.” This Bramapuram is a unique city that remained indestructible in this world during the great deluge. It is a unique city that was not destroyed even during the water deluge. That is why it also has the name Thonipuram.

Thus, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman composes this third verse. The fourth verse: (Venmagizhndha madhil eydhadhum anri vilangu thalaivo) On his head, rejoicing, he begged for alms, and came and stole my heart, the thief! Is he not the Lord who resides in Bramapuram, who, with a chest adorned with the revered serpent and blossoming konrai, joyfully holds the feminine in his chest?“ In this, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman sings about the destruction of the Three Cities (Thiripura Samharam) accomplished by the Lord. He was the one who held a single arrow to destroy the three walls that joyfully and proudly flew in the sky, but he burned them with his gentle smile without using that single arrow.

Thus, he was like one who aimed an arrow to burn those three walls. He is the thief who stole my heart. He is the one who joyfully holds Umaiyammai in the left part of his mountain-like chest. He is the Lord who resides in Bramapuram.

Now, the fifth verse: (Orumai penmai udaiyan sadaiyan vidai) He is one with a combined male and female form, with matted hair, riding a bull. The companions say, “He is so wonderful to describe,” and he is the thief who stole my heart. When the dark sea swelled and engulfed this world at the time of the great dissolution, he, the Lord who resided in Bramapuram, who was great and floated as a boat, is he not?” This is the meaning of this verse.

The Lord is one who granted the left side of his body to Umaiyammai in one sacred form. He has matted hair. He rides on a bull. The companions describe the beauty of the Lord in these ways. He is the thief who stole my heart, who came just as the companions described. He is the Lord who resided in Bramapuram, who was great and floated like a boat when the dark-colored sea swelled and engulfed this world during the great dissolution.

This is the meaning of this verse.

Now, the sixth verse: (Maraikkalandha oli paadalodu aadalaraagi mazhu aendhi iraikkalandha ina velvalai sora en ullam kavar kalvan karaikala) He, who, singing and dancing to the sound of the Vedas, holding an axe, came and stole my heart, making my shining white bangles slip. He, who resides in Bramapuram, wearing a crescent moon that shines light in the dense groves with tall trees and thick foliage. This is he.

Now, the seventh verse: (Sadaimuyangu punalan analan eriveesich sadhirvaidha udaimuyangum aravodu thandhanadhu ullam kavar kalvan kadanmuyangu kalisoozh kulir kaanal amponnam sirakannam pedaimuyangu piramapurameviya pemman ivan andre idhan porul) He who has the Ganga intertwined in his matted hair, fire in his sacred hand, and a serpent tightly bound over his garment, danced, showering flames, and came and stole my heart. Such a Lord resides in beautiful Bramapuram. That Bramapuram is surrounded by salt pans embracing the sea, possesses cool coastal groves, and is home to beautiful-winged swans that roam with their mates. Such a Bramapuram is where my Lord resides.

Now, the eighth verse: (Viyar ilangu varaivundhiya tholgalaiviram vilaiyaviththa uyar ilangai araiyan vali setru enadhu ullam kavar kalvan thuyar ilangum ulagil pala oozhigal thondrum pozhudhellam peyar ilangu piramapurameviya pemman ivan andre idhan porul Kailai malaiyai peyarthu thanadhu peru) He, who crushed the strength of the mountainous shoulders of Ravana, the illustrious king of Lanka, who lifted Mount Kailash to display his great valor, is the thief who stole my heart. He is the Lord who resides in Bramapuram, whose name shines forth, undestroyed, in this world of sorrow, through many eons whenever they appear. In the Tevaram pathigams of ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman, the eighth verses will always speak of Ravana and describe the pathigam in that way. The ninth verses will always praise the greatness of Shiva, whom Vishnu and Brahma could not find. The tenth verses will always condemn external religions like Buddhism and Jainism.

In the eleventh verses, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman will establish them as Thirukkadaikaappu (concluding verses). he will make it a Thirukkadaikaappu. This method is mostly followed in all the Thirukkadaikaappu pathigams composed by ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman. Sekkizhar Peruman explains the reason for this. Why does ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman sing about Ravana in the eighth verse of his pathigams? Sekkizhar Peruman explains this reason, saying, (Mannulagil vaazhvaargal pizhaithaalum vandhu adaiyil kannudalan perungarunai kai kollum ena kaatta ennamilaa val arakkan eduthu murindhu isaippada annal avarkku arul purindha aakkappaadu arul seidhaar endru) “Even if those who live on earth commit mistakes, if they come and seek refuge, the Lord with the eye on his forehead will embrace them with his great compassion.” To show this, the powerful, thoughtless demon Ravana lifted Mount Kailash, broke his body, and then sang. The noble Lord bestowed grace upon him.

This act of grace was expressed by ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman in the eighth verse of his pathigam.

Therefore, if beings who have committed mistakes truly realize their error, accept responsibility for their wrongdoings, and make a firm resolve not to repeat the mistake, and pray to the Lord with sincere devotion, the Lord will forgive and grant grace. To make us realize this, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman narrates the story of how Ravana’s arrogance was quelled, placing it in this eighth verse, as Sekkizhar Peruman shows us. Thirukkadaikaappu. This convention is followed in most of the Thirukkadaikaappu pathigams composed by ThiruGnanaSambaman. Sekkizhar Peruman explains the reason for this.
