Why does ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman sing about Ravana in the eighth verse of his pathigams?

Sekkizhar Peruman clarifies the reason: (Mannulagil vaazhvaargal pizhaithaalum vandhu adaiyil kannudalaan perungarunai kai kollum enak kaatta ennamilaa val arakkan eduthu murindhu isaippaada annal avarkku arul purindha aakkapaadu arul seidhaar endru) “Even if those who live on earth make mistakes, if they approach, the great compassion of the Lord with the eye on his forehead will embrace them.” To demonstrate this, the powerful, thoughtless demon lifted and crushed the mountain, then sang, and the Lord bestowed his grace upon him. Sekkizhar Peruman thus explains this reason. Even if beings living on this earth commit mistakes, if they surrender to him, Lord Shiva, who has an eye on his forehead, will, with his great compassion, forgive them and hold them by the hand. To show this, the thoughtless demon Ravana lifted Mount Kailash, broke his body, and then sang, and the glorious Lord bestowed grace upon him. ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman composed this in the eighth verse of his pathigam.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman shows us that ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman, to teach us that if beings who have committed mistakes truly realize their error, take responsibility for their wrongdoing, and make a firm resolve not to repeat the mistake, and pray to the Lord with sincere devotion, the Lord will forgive and bestow grace, places the story of Ravana’s arrogance being quelled in this eighth verse.

Now, the ninth sacred verse: (Thanudhal sei thirai kaaniya maaloodu thandhamaraianum neenudhal seyilayan nimirndhaan enadhu ullam kavar kalvan vaanudhal sei magalir mudhalagiya vaiyaththavaretha pezunudhal sei maapuram eviya pemman ivan andre idhan porul Thirumalum naanmuganum sivaperumanadhu thiruvadigalaiyum mudiyaiyum kaanbadharkaga panriyaagavum annamaagavum thedi seyalatru vizha annamalayaay nimirndhavan em peruman atthagaiya peruman en ullam kavargindra kalvanaga vilangugindran magalir ullitta ulagaththavargal anaivarum thudhika virumbudhalai seiyum piramapurameviya peruman ivan andre endru ivvaaru onbadhaavadhu thiruppaadal in porul amaigindradhu Thirugnanasambandha Perumal ivvaaru thanadhu) Throughout his pathigams, in the ninth verse of each pathigam, he has sung about the unique great quality of the Lord that Vishnu and Brahma could not find. Sekkizhar Peruman explains why ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman structured it this way. (Thozhuvaarkke aruluvadhu Sivaperuman ena thozhaar valuvaana manaththaale maalaaya maalayanum ezhivaagum karuvilangum paravaiyumai eydhaamai vizhuvaargal anjezhuthum thudhiythuyndhappadi viriththaar) Vishnu and Brahma sought the Lord. Although they knew that the Lord grants grace only to those who worship him, they, not worshipping our Lord, became deluded by a wrong mindset. Vishnu became a lowly boar and Brahma became Brahma, as an eagle, went up and down but could not find him and fell.

Later, they were saved by praising the five sacred letters. To explain this, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman structured this sacred history in the ninth verses of his pathigams. He reveals to us the truth that Lord Shiva grants grace only to those who worship him. If ‘granting grace’ means revealing the truth and helping the soul to quickly attain liberation, does it mean that Lord Shiva grants grace only to those who worship him and not to those who don’t? That is not the case. The greatly compassionate Lord gives the appropriate medicine to each soul according to its illness of ignorance, and liberates them.

Therefore, this too is the grace of the Lord. The former is known as ‘Arutkarunai’ (grace of compassion), and the latter as ‘Marakkarunai’ (grace of transformation). The Jnana Sastras state this: ‘Protecting those who cling, and being without malice, allowing devotees to do their own deeds and for others to complete their karma.’ Vishnu, who is in a high position, tries to see the Lord’s sacred feet by taking the lowly form of a boar. Brahma, who is in a high position, tries to see the Lord’s sacred crown by taking the lowly form of a swan and flying upwards. The degradation of taking the form of a swan, according to this sacred history, was that he lied and committed an offense. Both of them, after this, attained salvation by chanting the Lord’s sacred name, the five sacred letters.

In the previous verse, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman’s composition based on Ravana’s act was an instruction for those living on this earth. In this verse, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman’s composition based on the story of Vishnu and Brahma is an instruction for the devas (heavenly beings) to attain well-being.

Let us persist in our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 570, by Sekkizhar Swamigal, ‘Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam’, ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar Puranam. The tenth verse of the first pathigam is as follows: (Buddhrodu poriyil samanum purangura nerinillaa ottha solla ulagam bali theerndhenadhu ullam kavar kalvan mattha yaanai marugavuri porththadhor maayam idhu enna piththarpolum piramapurameviya pemman ivan andre) In this tenth verse, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman says that the Buddhists and Jains stray from the path laid out by the sages, propagating their own mistaken ideas, and that Shiva is the thief who stole his heart by going to all the worlds and receiving alms. He wonders if Shiva is not the Lord residing in Bramapuram, who, making a wild elephant tremble, flayed its hide and wore it, making it seem like a magical act, like a madman. making it confused and flaying its skin to wear, making it seem like a magical act, like a madman. Is he not the Lord residing in Bramapuram? ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman says this.

The Buddhists and Jains, due to their lack of good karma and merits, would speak ill of the Saiva religion and propagate their own erroneous ideas that they deemed appropriate for their intellect. In this tenth verse, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman condemns the Jains and Buddhists. This same pattern is found in most of ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman’s pathigams, meaning that the tenth verse contains a condemnation of the Jains and Buddhists. Why did ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman structure it this way? Sekkizhar Peruman explains why ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman structured it this way: (Vethakkaaranayavennbirai ser seyya sadai naathan neri arindhu uyyaar thamile nalam kollum bodhamilaa saman kaiyar putthar vazhi pazhiyaakkum edhame ena mozhindhaar engal piraan Sambandhar endru) Sekkizhar Peruman explains why ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman condemns the Jains and Buddhists, who are external religious practitioners, in the tenth verse of his pathigams.

Lord Shiva is the cause of the Vedas. ‘Vedhakaranar’ means he is the primordial composer of the Vedas. It also means that Shiva is the instrumental cause, as described by the Vedas. The Vedas praise Shiva as the instrumental cause of this world.

Thus, Lord Shiva, the cause of the Vedas, Those who do not know his path and do not attain salvation are external religionists. The Jains and Buddhists are among those external religious groups who wander without attaining the good fortune of clinging to Saivism and attaining salvation. They are those who do not consider the Vedas composed by the Lord as authoritative but praise what they have created and spoken with their own intellect.

Therefore, the paths they speak of, the paths they follow, are harmful paths that bring disgrace. What disgrace do they bring? The disgrace of betraying trust by misusing the intellect, which the Lord created for good, in wrong ways. Such is the path followed by Jains and Buddhists.

Thus, our Lord Sambandhar spoke. Sekkizhar Peruman sings that our Lord Sambandha Peruman, who is the revered Acharya of the Saiva faith, speaks thus.

Therefore, this verse explains the meaning of the tenth verse in ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman’s pathigams. The rejection of the evils of the external religions like Jainism and Buddhism, and the propagation of the glory of the sacred ash, these two are the objectives of Pillaiyar’s incarnation. All these objectives begin and manifest from this first pathigam composed by ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman. In it, the tenth verse is known as ‘Samanpaattu’ (the verse of equality). The great Acharya, who explained the sacred five letters and other Saiva tools in the preceding two verses, In this tenth verse, he emphasizes what is to be explained as ineffectual.

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman explains the tenth verse.

Now, the concluding verse of this pathigam, known as Thirukkadaikaappu, the eleventh verse: (Aruneriyamarai valla muniyagan poigai alar meya peruneriyap piramapurameviya pemman ivan thannai oruneriyamanam vathunargnanasambandhan urai seidha thiruneriyatamil vallavar tholvinai theerthal ezithame) The meaning is as follows: Brahma, who is proficient in the precious, world-giving Vedas, worshipped Lord Shiva at Bramapuram. Bramapuram is located on the bank of the Brahma Theertham, where wide lotus flowers bloom. Lord Shiva, who resides in such Bramapuram (Sirkazhi), is the Lord who leads souls to the path of liberation. For those who are skilled in this sacred Tamil path, which is a precious path, spoken by GnanaSambandhan, who understands such Lord Shiva with a mind of single-minded devotion, it is easy to remove all their ancient karma, their accumulated karma (sanchitha karma). This is the meaning of this concluding verse.

Thus, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman concludes this pathigam, which contains ten pathigams, by declaring the eleventh verse as Thirukkadaikaappu. lotus flowers have bloomed, that is Bramapuram. Such a Lord Shiva resides in Sirkazhi, which is Bramapuram. He is the Lord who leads souls on the path to liberation. It is easy for those who are skilled in this sacred Tamil, which is a precious path, spoken by GnanaSambandhan, who understands such a Lord Shiva with a single-minded devotion, to eliminate all their old karmas, which are accumulated karmas. This is the meaning of this concluding verse.

Thus, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman completes this pathigam, which has ten pathigams, by declaring the eleventh verse as Thirukkadaikaappu. Thirukkadaikaappu means that after completing a pathigam, The eleventh verse is the one that articulates his name and the benefit of the pathigam, imprinted with his seals, as a way to conclude and mark it. The eleventh verse is called Thirukkadaikaappu.

Therefore, in all the pathigams composed by ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman, the concluding verse is a Thirukkadaikaappu, and in it, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman has imprinted his name and the benefit of reciting the pathigam as a seal. ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman refers to the pathigam as ‘Thiruneriyathamizh’, which means Tamil that shows the path of Shiva.

Therefore, this name ‘Thiruneriyathamizh’ applies not only to this pathigam but also to other Saiva Thirumuraikal like Tevaram and Thiruvasagam. methods.

Thus, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman concludes, with his seal, that those who are able to recite this pathigam, composed by ThiruGnanaSambandhan, who understood Lord Shiva, the Lord residing in Bramapuram, with a single-minded devotion, will have their ancient karmas easily resolved.

Here, ‘resolving ancient karmas’ is stated by ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman as the benefit of the pathigam. ‘Ancient karma’ is also called ‘pazhavinai’ (old karma). It is referred to as ‘Sanchitha Karma’. This is the karma that remains to be experienced and exhausted. That is the old karma. ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman states that this accumulated karma (Sanchitham) will be resolved if this pathigam is recited.

Therefore, Sanchitha Karma If it is resolved, the karma that is the seed for future births will be gone.

Therefore, the Lord teaches that there will be no more births and that liberation is certain. Even though the removal of past karma (Sanchita Karma) is the benefit of this pathigam, it also means that Agamiyam (future karma) and Prarabdha Sedam (remaining Prarabdha karma) will also be resolved. It is also evident here that Pillaiyar incarnated as an Acharya to remove the suffering of birth from living beings and show them the path to liberation. In this first pathigam, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman points to the Lord saying, ‘Pemman Ivanandre’ (Is he not the Lord?). In his concluding pathigam, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman imparts the sacred five letters and shows the path to liberation.

Therefore, for the living beings who recite the Lord’s pathigams, for those souls, there is certainly no rebirth, but only liberation. Regarding this concept, the author of Thiruvichaippa has spoken of Pillaiyar’s nature as an Acharya in Thiruvichaippa, saying, ‘He cured all our binding karmic illness and rules over us, Sambandhan.’ ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman has similarly bestowed the benefits of the pathigam in other pathigams. We can also see the truth that these pathigams grant those benefits to the souls who recite them from then until now.

Thus, the meaning of the first pathigam composed by ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman is concluded. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing: “After completing the pathigam, and having sealed it with Thirukkadaikaappu, Pillaiyar, the master of Rig Vedic hymns, stood reverently, worshipping, and seeing the grace of the Lord’s divine compassion, all the celestials rejoiced greatly in the sky, shouting and showering fragrant flowers,” says Sekkizhar Peruman. Sekkizhar Peruman sings that Pillaiyar, the master of Rig Vedic hymns, who sang the complete pathigam and also composed the Thirukkadaikaappu, stood worshipping the Lord. ‘Irukku Mozhi’ means Rig Veda.

Here, it refers to all four Vedas, indicating the generality of the Vedas. Sekkizhar Peruman states this to show that Pillaiyar’s sacred words are the Vedas. Sekkizhar Peruman tells us that the Vedas, which are the Lord’s words, came from Pillaiyar’s sacred mouth.

Furthermore, ‘Irukku Mozhi’, understood as ‘Irukkum Mozhi’ (the existing word), also conveys the implication of a word that eternally exists without destruction. The term ‘Irukku Mozhi’ also implies that it is a word of grace that will make those who study this pathigam reside in Shivaloka, taking it as a causative verb (‘iruththum’).

Furthermore, Saiva elders state that ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman’s Tevarams are the essence of the Rig Veda. Sekkizhar Peruman also mentions this here as ‘Irukku Mozhi Pillaiyar’. The idea that Pillaiyar belonged to the Rig Vedic tradition is also subtly implied here. Even Arunagirinathar Peruman, in Thiruppugal, praises Pillaiyar’s sacred words in various ways as ‘Agama Veda Purana Nool’, ‘Shruti Thamizh Kavi’, ‘Aranaga Keetha Kavithai’, and ‘Upanishad Madhura Kavithai’.

Thus, after composing the first pathigam, he stands worshipping Lord Shiva. The child-saint stated that the celestials perceive the grace of Lord Shiva, who is the gracious lord. Although grace and compassion are one, here Lord Shiva, in His Ardhanarishwara form, bestows grace and compassion as two words that convey a single meaning. Though the words are two, their essence is one, and similarly, though Ardhanarishwara appears as two, their essence is one. To signify this, Sekkizhar Peruman uses the sacred name ‘Thiruvalan’ for the Lord in this verse. ‘Thiruvalan’ means the one who rules the prosperity of liberation; ‘Thiru’ here refers to the prosperity of liberation. This name is exclusive to Lord Shiva and great saints who have attained His nature.

Thus, the compassionate lord, Shiva, The celestials behold the grace of Lord Shiva. They gather in the sky, shouting with joy, showering divine, honey-laden flowers as a rain.

Our reflection now resumes. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Volume 571, by Sekkizhar Swamigal, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. As soon as Thirugnanasambandha Peruman recited his first pathigam, the Vedas themselves resounded. The light of the Vedas had diminished due to the external religions of Jainism and Buddhism.

Now, those very Vedas, through the child-saint’s words, would emerge as revealed scripture. From this pathigam onwards, the Kadai Kappu pathigams, as they issued from the child-saint’s lips, would clearly proliferate and grow, just as the formerly diminished Vedas now illuminated the world.

Thus, the Vedas themselves reverberated with a resounding sound. In the sky, the crowns of all the devas collided with each other, They shattered, and their gems scattered, falling to the earth like dew drops, covering the world. Crowds of ascetic sages, whose lives were always filled with truth and burgeoning peace, gathered like an ocean. Thoniyappar and Ammai, who had emerged from Thiruthoni to assuage the child-saint’s tears, now, after the child-saint had completed his pathigam, were again enshrined in Thiruthoni. Thoniyappar is compassionate, bestowing His two sacred feet as a sweet raft to devotees who approach Him with maturity and devotion, enabling them to cross the incomparable, powerful ocean of birth. Thoniyappar bestows His two feet, representing His gnana shakti (power of knowledge) and kriya shakti (power of action), upon the devotees gathered in Sirkazhi.

These feet serve as a raft, helping devotees cross the ocean of birth.

Thus, Thoniyappar enables devotees to reach His two raft-like feet through the pathigams composed by the child-saint.

Now, through the history of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, we will see the lives of those devotees who, by holding onto the Lord’s feet through the child-saint’s pathigams, crossed the ocean of birth.

The Lord Himself bestows the knowledge that enables devotees to grasp His sacred feet; only the Lord can grant it.

Thus, by revealing His sacred feet, The Lord and Lady, who bestowed grace, are again enshrined in the Thiruthoni temple. To soothe the child-saint’s tears, the Lord appeared, feeding him the milk of wisdom. When his father later approached in anger, the Lord, by the child-saint’s pointing and the singing of his pathigam, had revealed His divine form in the sky all that time, an act of great compassion. This manifestation was to bestow upon devotees the nature of His two feet as a raft. This is because the child-saint’s pathigams, which are his great spiritual teachings, possess the quality of a raft. Until the child-saint pointed Him out, the Lord and Lady, Thoniyappar and Ammai, who had manifested their divine form in the sky, returned to Thiruthonipuram, showing that they were the very essence of those pathigams.

The Lord and the Goddess Seeing them thus enshrined in Thiruthoni at the Sirkazhi temple, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, with ever-increasing love, entered the beautiful Thiruthoni temple from the bank of Brahmateertham, his mind, having entered through his eyes, remaining inseparable. From the bank of the pond, the child-saint saw the Lord, and due to his ever-increasing desire to continually unite with the Lord, as the Lord became enshrined in Thiruthoni, the child-saint also entered the Thiruthoni temple. The vision, having been granted in the form of Ardhanarishwara and through the feeding of the milk of wisdom, had imprinted itself in the child-saint’s heart. Captivated by this vision, the child-saint wished to see and worship again within the Thoni where Ardhanarishwara was enshrined, and so he proceeded to the Thiru The child-saint enters the Thoni temple. The child-saint’s father, Sivapadahridayar, performed immense austerities to become the child-saint’s father. He attained the blessing of being called ‘father’ by the child-saint.

Previously, he had raised a stick as if to strike him in anger, but from that state, the stick slipped from his hand, and he clapped his flower-like hands in joy and danced with bliss. Sivapadahridayar follows the child-saint, delighting in the sweet meaning of the ‘Thirunerith Thamizh’ (righteous Tamil) that the child-saint pointed out, having seen and heard it. He sees Lord Shiva and sees that Lord Shiva is enshrined in the Thoni, and follows Him. Like the child-saint, his father did not see Lord Shiva, Even though he had not directly seen Shiva, he perceived the signs of divine grace that occurred through the child-saint’s pathigam.

Therefore, with a heart overflowing with desire, he followed his son, who was walking ahead of him, believing it to be the grace of the Lord of Thonipuram. It is not proper to walk ahead of one who has received divine grace, so the father walked behind the child-saint who had received grace.

At that time, those who had seen what transpired, and those who, though not seeing, had heard, along with the Brahmanas wearing the sacred thread, wondered where else such a miraculous event had occurred. They gathered at the entrance of the Thiruthoni temple, where Lord Shiva, with his coral-red matted locks, was enshrined, their hair standing on end. They narrated this sacred history many times. Many people speak thus, and as they speak, they gather before the entrance of Thoniyappar’s temple. The child-saint, who had partaken of the nectar of wisdom, enters the Thiruthoni temple and stands before Thoniyappar and Periyanayaki Ammaiyar, before their sacred presence. He recites a pathigam expressing the sentiment, ‘Where is the Lord who owns me, along with Umadevi?’ and worships Him.

The pathigam recited by the child-saint now begins with ‘Naravanirai Vandarai,’ it is the 74th pathigam of the first Thirumurai, set to the Takkesi tune. This pathigam, which is one of the twelve names for Sirkazhi, bears the name ‘Puravam.’ On the bank of Brahmateertham, The Lord and Goddess emerged and bestowed grace, and then they were again enshrined in Thiruthoni.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composes this pathigam, centered on the idea that the Lord Shiva, who revealed Himself and took him as His own, is present here in this Thiruthoni temple with Uma. Thiruthoni is the shrine on the second floor of the Sirkazhi temple where Thoniyappar and Periyanayaki, the Lord and Lady, are enshrined.

Here, the Lord is enshrined with Uma, and Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composes this pathigam, alluding to this fact.

Therefore, throughout the verses of this pathigam, he concludes each verse with ‘Imaiyor Etha Uamaiyodu Iruntane’ (The celestials praise Him, residing with Uma), as a crown. He bestows this pathigam. This is the second pathigam to emerge from the child-saint’s sacred words. It is the first pathigam recited within the Thiruthoni temple. This pathigam has eleven verses. Its first and concluding verses are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. (Naravanirai vandarai tharkondrai nayanthu nayanathal suravan seirivankodiyon udalam podiya vizhiseythan puravam urai vanpathiya mathiyar puramoonru eriseytha iraivan aravan imaiyor etha umaiyodirunthane ponnar mada needum selva puravam pathiya minnar idaiyal umaiyallodum iruntha vimalanai than arvam sey thamilin virakan urraiththa tamilmalai pannal padiyada piri)

Thiruchitrambalam (Thiriyaparalokanthane).

Thus, the first and concluding verses of this pathigam are structured.

After the Lord accepted the child-saint as His own, the child-saint, having been thus accepted, experienced and praised the nature of servitude to the Lord throughout the verses of this pathigam. With love, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, whose sweet mouth exuded the fragrance of the nectar of wisdom, departs from the temple, accompanied by many Vedic Brahmins, to perform the sacred service of singing rich Tamil pathigams, imbued with melodious seven notes, as offerings to Lord Shiva, through the discipline and grace of servitude. Although Thirugnanasambandha Peruman departed from the temple, he was bound by servitude, He emerges without parting from our Lord, as if bound. This is the devotion Thirugnanasambandha Peruman held for the Lord’s feet. That very devotion, coupled with desire, manifests as the nectar of wisdom, as fragrant words of wisdom and love mixed, in the form of pathigams.

Moreover, these pathigams, like the Lord’s own words (the Vedas), are filled with the harmony of the seven musical notes. Without effort, they spontaneously gathered and harmonized in the child-saint’s words.

Thus, before the child-saint, who had received the Lord’s grace, and after he emerged from the temple, the devotees of Lord Shiva and the people of Thiruthonipuram gathered at the temple entrance and praised the child-saint. They came forward to praise the child-saint as he emerged from the temple, in the following manner: (Kaliyir thavame kauniayar thaname kalagnanath thalliya kadale athanida amuthe adiyar mun vazhiya vanthu immanmisai vanor thaninathan eyilisai mozhiyal than thiruarul perranai enbar marai valar thiruve vaithika nilaiye valar gnana poraiyanimukile pukaliyar pukale porponniththuraiparumaniye suruthiyin oliye veliye vanthu iraiyavan umaiyalludan arulthara eyithinai enbar punniyamuthalai punaimani arainanodu pothum kannirai kathire kalaivalar mathiye kavinmevum punniyal kathiyai paruvamathoru moovarudathe enniya porulai ninravar arulperranai enbar) Thus the devotees and the people of Sirkazhi praised the child-saint with these words. Sekkilap Peruman arranges these words of praise as verses.

Let us go on reflecting. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Volume 572, by Sekkilar Swamigal, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Brahmins, the people of Sirkazhi, and devotees of Shiva praise Thirugnanasambandha Peruman in many ways. They praise him as one who embodies the fruits of the penance of those residing in Sirkazhi. They say that the people of Sirkazhi received this blessing first, before anyone else in the world, to have him in their midst.

Therefore, they praise him as the fruit of the penance of the people of Sirkazhi. They praise him as ‘Kauniyar Thaname,’ meaning he is the treasure of the Kaundinya lineage, having been born into that gotra. They praise him as ‘Kalagnanath Aazhiya Kadale,’ meaning the ocean of artistic and spiritual knowledge. They praise him.

Here, ‘Kalagnanam’ refers to the compilation of aparajnanam (lower knowledge). This knowledge is extremely rare for others who have not received Shiva’s grace.

Thus, they praise him as one who emerged like nectar amidst this ‘Kalagnanam.’ Nectar removes aging and birth. The nectar mentioned here refers to the ineffable true knowledge, which is parajnanam (higher knowledge). He attained the fruit of aparajnanam, which was parajnanam, and beyond that, he attained sacred grace, and even beyond that, he attained it for the benefit of the world. Devotees of Shiva praise him in this sense. They bless him, saying that he incarnated on this earth for the devotees of Shiva to witness and live in truth, and that he received the combined grace of both Lord Shiva and Uma Devi. You have received the grace of both.

They bless him, saying that the child-saint appeared in a divine form before the devotees of Shiva, embodying the object of their meditation, and thus brought forth spiritual life for them. They also praise him as the manifestation of the combined grace of Lord Shiva and Uma Devi, the Shiva-Shakti form. Though the Lord and Lady are spoken of in plurality with their qualities, in essence, they are one. The child-saint incarnated as the grace of such a unified being. In accordance with the saying, ‘for the Vedic path to flourish,’ they praise him as the ‘Thiru’ (sacred one) who cultivates the Vedas. Through him, the Vedic order will now be established and endure.

Therefore, they praise him as ‘Vaidhika Nilaiye’ (the embodiment of Vedic principles). They praise him, saying that the surrounding cloud of Shiva-knowledge will now shower grace like rain. The place where the devas sought refuge was Puhali, also known as Sirkazhi.

Similarly, they praise the child-saint as a refuge for all. They praise him as ‘Kaveri Thuraiyil Vandha Maniye’ (the gem that came to the Kaveri ghat). Although the Kaveri is common to the entire Chola kingdom, the local history states that it came to the Chola kingdom with the specific intention of reaching Sirkazhi.

Therefore, they praise Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as ‘Ponnithurai Perumaniye’ (the great gem of the golden river). They praise him as ‘Punniya Muthale,’ meaning the source of merit. They praise him as ‘Kanneerai Kathire,’ meaning the full-eyed radiance that appears with an ornamental waist-belt. They praise him as ‘Kalai Valar Mathiye,’ meaning the growing moon of arts. The moon waxes and wanes, but he is said to possess ever-growing arts without diminishment. This also implies that he protects the Saivite crop with the nectar of arts.

They praise him as ‘Kavinmevum Punniyal Kathiye,’ meaning the beautiful path that embodies all melodies. That is, he is the sweetness to the music of the melodies. It means that all melodies, with their divisions of melodic structure and variations, will be elucidated in the child-saint’s words. The Vedas state that Shiva alone is to be meditated upon.

Accordingly, Shiva is the object of meditation for the knowledgeable. They praise him as the Lord who received the grace of such Shiva at the age of three, and who bestowed it upon us. They praise him as the Lord who received the grace of Shiva at the age of three and bestowed it upon us. The child-saint nurtured the Saivite faith in this world for sixteen years. This act of grace occurred in the child-saint’s third year.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman has structured this, implying that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman will elevate Saivism in the fourteen years from his third year until his sixteenth year, with the Sirkazhi Shiva devotees, people, and Brahmins praising him in these fourteen ways. Beginning with ‘Kaliyir Thavame Kauniyar Thaname,’ meaning he incarnated as the fruit of penance, Sekkizhar Peruman has woven into these verses references to the future events that will lead to liberation for souls. Sekkilar Peruman has woven into these verses all these praises and references to the future events that will lead to liberation for souls. Having offered such praises, the Brahmins, with their sacred words, and other devotees stand and praise the child-saint, adorning their heads with his sacred feet.

At that moment, Sivapadahridayar, filled with great joy, takes the divine child of Shiva-wisdom, the child-saint, and carries him on his shoulders. As the saying goes, ‘The touch of a child’s body brings joy.’ Until now, Sivapadahridayar found joy in holding the child-saint.

Now, he experienced immense bliss from the memory of touching the child-saint’s pure, wise, and divine form. Sivapadahridayar, the child-saint’s father, became worthy of the saying, ‘What good did his father do to beget him?’ Sivapadahridayar was already a person worthy of praise, and this came as a result of his unwavering devotion to Shiva’s feet.

Thus, with a growing crowd of distinguished Brahmins and devotees surrounding them, they joyfully toss their upper garments and shawls into the air, creating a wave of happiness. As a result, a beautiful flood of divine bliss surges through Sirkazhi, and like the rising and falling foam bubbles on its surface, the people joyfully dance, tossing their garments and clothes into the air.

The Brahmins of Sirkazhi gather on the terraces of their mansions, and the women, along with the Brahmins, offer auspicious blessings with sweet words. They stand and scatter fresh, cool flowers with fragrant petals and rice grains mixed with turmeric powder, They scatter cool flowers and rice grains mixed with fine powder. They welcome Thirugnanasambandha Peruman with praise. Turmeric-infused fragrant powder is called ‘Ponchunam.’ Scattering flowers, such ‘Ponchunam,’ and rice grains together is an auspicious ritual, mainly performed by women.

Thus, Brahmin women perform this. Others play auspicious musical instruments, and many other Brahmins chant Sama Vedas.

The Brahmins illuminate their verandas with beautiful lamps. They arrange rows of golden pots.

Thus, the townspeople, with growing wonder, great desire, and love in their hearts, praise and rejoice. Through the beautiful streets, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman circumambulates that city of Chanbai. The child-saint, whose sacred mouth still carried the fragrance of Umadevi’s milk, thus circumambulates the city of Chanbai and enters his sacred mansion.

At that time, conches sound, and divine drums (Devadundubhis) resound.

Thus, the child-saint, seated in his sacred mansion, with an unwavering love for the lotus feet of Lord Shiva enshrined in his heart on that night he was granted Shiva-wisdom, remains there.

Then, the next morning, even before sunrise, the child-saint reaches the Thiruthoniyappar temple. He approaches Thiruthoniyappar, who eternally resides in that sacred city of Thirukazhumalam without ever leaving it, The child-saint approaches. The child-saint sees and worships his father, Thoniyappar, and his mother, Periyanayaki Ammaiyar. The child-saint then worships and praises Lord Shiva, his divine father, and his divine mother, Periyanayaki Ammaiyar, who appeared to him and, through her breast, offered him the milk of wisdom—a profound wisdom difficult for anyone to comprehend—thus nourishing him. Having received their grace, the child-saint, with a desire to worship at Thirukolakka, begins his sacred pilgrimage towards Thirukolakka. This is the child-saint’s first pilgrimage.

We shall proceed with our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Volume 573, by Sekkilar Swamigal, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, after partaking of the milk of wisdom given by Uma Devi, sang the first pathigam, ‘Thozhudaiya Seviyan,’ and returned to his sacred mansion. The next morning, he stood before the shrine of Thoniyappar, enshrined in Thiruthoni at Sirkazhi, and worshipped Thoniyappar and Periyanayaki Ammaiyar. While he was worshipping, the thought arose in Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred heart that he should visit Thirukolakka, a sacred place near Sirkazhi.

Therefore, he set out from Sirkazhi, departing from the Sirkazhi temple, and proceeded towards Thirukolakka. This is the first pilgrimage undertaken by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. This is his first pilgrimage. In the sacred history of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, he would begin his pilgrimages from Sirkazhi, then return to Sirkazhi, and then again depart from Sirkazhi on another pilgrimage and return to Sirkazhi. This is the pattern of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s pilgrimages.

In this manner, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sets out from Sirkazhi towards Thirukolakka. We can reflect on some specific details related to the sacred place of Sirkazhi. This is the fourteenth sacred place on the northern bank of the Kaveri River. When Thirunavukkarasu Peruman was residing in Thiruchitrambalam, upon hearing of the child-saint’s greatness, he came to Sirkazhi to worship the child-saint and earned the blessing of his friendship. This is the greatness of this place. Thiruvarur Nambigal, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, out of reverence, did not step on the sacred ground of Sirkazhi, as it was the birthplace of the child-saint.

Instead, he circumambulated the town and worshipped from outside. When Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sang praises to the Lord from outside Sirkazhi, the Lord, enshrined within the Sirkazhi temple, appeared before him at his very location and bestowed grace. This is the sacred place where Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar came, worshipped the child-saint, played his pathigams on the Yazh, and was blessed to remain with him. This is the place where Gananatha Nayanar was born, trained devotees in various forms of service, created more devotees, and by ceaselessly praising and serving the feet of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar, attained liberation and the blessing of becoming a chief of the Ganas (Gananayakar). The shrine of Gananatha Nayanar is located as a separate temple to the west of Brahmateertham, in the outer prakara. In the sacred town of Sirkazhi, Lord Shiva is enshrined in three forms: as Brahmapuriswarar, a lingam; as Thoniyappar, a guru; and as Sattainathar, a jangama (moving image).

Sattainathar’s unique feature in this place is that he is enshrined with a beautiful form, wearing the skin of Narasimha, whom he severed after Narasimha killed Hiranyakashipu, thus bestowing boons. The weapon held by Sattainathar is the backbone of Vamana, whom he severed when Vamana became arrogant. Every Friday at midnight, special, disciplined worship is offered to Sattainathar in Sirkazhi. During the time of Vidurathan, Chandra, Murugavel, Adiseshan, Ketu, and other deities worshipped here and received blessings. The Kanda Puranam speaks of Indra, fearing Suran and other asuras, coming here to Puhali (Sirkazhi) for refuge and worshipping. The Kanda Puranam also speaks of the pleasure garden that Indra established for Shiva worship, and how, for that purpose, Lord Ganesha brought the Kaveri River here to Sirkazhi from Agastya’s kamandalam.

Therefore, the pleasure garden here is still known as Indranandavanam (Indra’s pleasure garden). In Brahmapuram, Lord Brahmapuriswarar and Goddess are enshrined. On the second floor, in Thiruthoni, are Lord Thoniyappar and Goddess Periyanayaki. On the pinnacle of Thiruthoni, Sattainathar is enshrined facing south.

Thus, the Lord is enshrined on three levels. The main water source (theertham) is Brahmateertham in the northeast inside the temple, and also There are many other sacred waters: Sulatheertham, Anandatheertham, Kaanitheertham, Rahutheertham, Vainavatheertham, Aazhitheertham, Sangatheertham, Sukratheertham, Parasara Theertham, Agathiyar Theertham, Gautama Theertham, Kazhumala Nadi, Pura Nadi, and many other theerthams. Among the temples that have received Thevaram pathigams, Sirkazhi is renowned for having the highest number, with seventy-one pathigams. The pathigams of the Three (Appar, Sundarar, Gnanasambandar), the Thiruvachagam composed by Manikkavachagar, the Thirukazhumala Mummanikkovai by Pattinathadigal in the Eleventh Thirumurai, and the works composed by Nambiyandar Nambigal about Aaludaiya Pillaiyar are all associated with this place. Many more local histories exist for this sacred place. We noted that Sirkazhi has twelve names.

There are individual temples in Sirkazhi corresponding to these twelve names. Among them, the Thiruthoni temple corresponding to Thonipuram The Thiruthoni temple corresponding to Thonipuram is prominent among these. One or two others are found as small, separate shrines in the western part of the outer prakara of the main temple. Sivakavimani Ayya has noted in his local history that renovating and rebuilding these other deities and temples, either individually or as a single temple complex, and continuing worship is a great act of Shiva-dharma. Sirkazhi is a sacred place with many such glories. The child-saint, having emerged from the Sirkazhi temple, begins his pilgrimage towards Thirukolakka.

Thirukolakka is the fifteenth sacred place situated on the northern bank of the Kaveri River in the Chola country. It is called Thiruthalamudaiyar Temple. The day after the child-saint partook of the nectar of wisdom, when he came here to worship, When the child-saint sang the pathigam ‘Madai Vazhai’ by clapping his hands, the Lord, seeing him create rhythm with his sacred hands, descended and bestowed upon him a beautiful golden cymbal inscribed with the five sacred letters (Panchakshara), and also gave it its sound.

Thereafter, the child-saint completed the pathigam with that sacred cymbal.

Sundaramoorthy Swamigal extols this divine act in his pathigam dedicated to this sacred place. The Lord’s name is Sapthapurishwarar, and the Goddess’s name is Osai Kodutha Nayaki (Goddess who gave sound). This sacred place is located southwest of Sirkazhi, on the bank of the Kaveri River. The Kaveri River flows here with an abundance of water, creating loud sounds and numerous waves. The river carries good water, showering honey-filled flowers and pearls. Bees swarm around these flowers.

Thirukolakka, a sacred place, has ponds with water for bathing. The child-saint proceeds to that temple. He circumambulates the temple of the Lord, who is the leader of the devas, and stands before the Lord’s sacred presence to begin singing a pathigam. The child-saint begins to sing praises to the Lord’s feet, which are difficult to attain even for the Vedas, despite all their efforts and fervent cries.

The Lord is the essence spoken of in the four Vedas, which are filled with truth and true meaning. The greatness and nature of the Lord are generally and specifically described in the Vedas. Shiva is the essence specifically described in the Vedas. The child-saint begins to sing in his pathigam about such a Lord, who bears a snake and the crescent moon on His matted locks, The child-saint begins to sing in his pathigam about the Lord who holds a snake and the crescent moon on his matted locks, and who has a throat containing poison. He begins the pathigam with ‘Madaiyil Vazhaikal Pay’ (where bananas spread in the fields) and utters it with his sacred voice. As he sings the pathigam, the child-saint claps his sacred hands to create rhythm, clapping both his hands.

He begins to sing and sings this pathigam, adjusting it appropriately with claps, stops, and lifts of his hands to suit the music of the pathigam. As the Lord saw the child-saint creating rhythm with his sacred hands, He felt compassion. He felt compassion for the child-saint who was creating rhythm with his sacred hands. Immediately, golden cymbals, engraved with the five sacred letters of Lord Shiva, the chief of the devas, appeared in the child-saint’s sacred hands through the Lord’s grace. (Kaiyadhanal oththarutthu paduthalum kandaruli karunai koorntha seyyasadai vanavartham anjezhuthum ezhuthiya narsempotthalm aiyyaravar thiruarulal eduththa padalukku isaintha alaval oththa vaiyamellam siruvar kaiththalaththu vandathanre) Thus, Peruman composes this verse. Even as he was singing the pathigam, beginning with ‘Madaiyil Vazhai Paaya,’ these golden cymbals appeared in the child-saint’s sacred hands. The child-saint’s hands, adorned with the sacred Panchakshara, The child-saint received the sacred Panchakshara engraved on his hands.

It was as if the Lord, by the appearance of the cymbals in his hands while he was still singing the pathigam, was telling him to stop clapping with his hands and instead sing the pathigam with a rhythmic instrument. The cymbals appeared in such a way that their arrival could not be seen.

Therefore, realizing through inference that this was a gift of divine grace, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman took those cymbals, inscribed with the sacred five letters, and placed them on his sacred head, as they were objects bestowed by divine grace. He bowed in reverence and continued to sing the pathigam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sang that pathigam with his melodious voice. He sang a rich Tamil pathigam with sweet music, allowing the seven musical notes to flourish through his melodious voice.

Sundaramoorthy Swamigal has praised this divine act in his pathigam. When Sundaramoorthy Swamigal visited the sacred site of Thirukolakka, he worshipped the Lord of that place and sang a pathigam. In the eighth verse of that pathigam, he praised the event of the Lord of Thirukolakka bestowing cymbals, saying, ‘For Gnanasambandhan, who spread Tamil with sweet music every day, the one who gave cymbals before the people of the world, and whose nature is to respond to his songs.’ Thirugnanasambandha Peruman continued to sing this pathigam before Lord Shiva, who wears ear ornaments, and completed it with the Kadai Kappu. He concludes it. Lord Shiva, desiring the music of the two Gandharvas, Ashvatharan and Kambalan, wears them as ear ornaments on his sacred ears, as they requested.

Similarly, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed this pathigam and concluded it with the Thirukkadaikkappu, implying that Lord Shiva’s ears, due to His love for music, would incline towards the child-saint’s music. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states the benefit of this pathigam in the Thirukkadaikkappu: (Valankol padal valla vaaimaiyar ulankol vinai poi ongi vazhvare). He says that those who recite this pathigam will be freed from attachments, attain Shiva-hood, and live prosperously. There is no other blessing a soul can attain greater than Shiva-hood. There is no greater blessing a soul can attain than that.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman enshrined that very blessing as the fruit of this pathigam in the Thirukkadaikkappu. This pathigam, dedicated to the sacred site of Thirukolakka, is the twenty-third pathigam in the first Thirumurai, set to the Takkaragam tune. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Madaiyil vazhaipaya madarar kudaiyum poikai kolakakavulan sadaiyum piraiyum sambar poochum kizh udaiyum konda uruvamen kolo nalangol kazi gnanasambandhan kulangol kolakavulanaiye valangol padalvalla vaaimaiyar ulankol vinai poi ongi vazhvare) Thiruchitrambalam.

Thus, the first and concluding verses of this pathigam are structured. In this pathigam, the child-saint wonderfully described the divine attributes of Lord Shiva individually and composed these verses. As Thirugnanasambandha Peruman completed this pathigam, the sound that emanated from his sacred cymbals reached such a height that the entire celestial world listened in awe. All the celestials, including Tumburu and Narada, who were skilled in melodic music and recitation, praised him and showered a rain of fragrant flowers, as if to descend upon the earthly realm. The truth of the measure of sound in this verse composed by the child-saint becomes the explanation of the true wisdom that shines within that measure of sound. The melody, rhythm, and meter align with the meaning of the song.

The Lord began to sing the pathigam, and while he was singing, the sacred cymbals The sacred cymbals appeared in his hands. With those sacred cymbals, he set the rhythm, sang this pathigam, and completed it with the Kadai Kappu. According to the local history of this sacred site, the Lord bestowed golden cymbals, and the Goddess blessed them with sound.

Therefore, the Lord is known as Sapthapurishwarar, and the Goddess as Osai Kodutha Nayaki (Goddess who gave sound) in this sacred place. Having thus sung and completed the pathigam, the child-saint proceeds to the sacred site of Sirkazhi.

We shall continue our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Volume 574, by Sekkilar Swamigal, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. The child-saint proceeds from Thirukolakka to the sacred site of Sirkazhi. Sivapadahridayar, unable to bear the child-saint walking with his tender feet, carries him on his shoulders to Sirkazhi. Surrounded by a crowd of devotees, they arrive at Sirkazhi and reach the Thiruthoni summit temple. The child-saint circumambulates that great temple and stands before the Lord to worship.

He reflects on the compassion of the Lord who gave him the golden cymbals.

Therefore, remembering that the Lord had given him golden cymbals when he recited the pathigam in the Takkaragam tune at Thirukolakka, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman resolves to sing a pathigam about Thoniyappar in the same Takkaragam tune. When he made this resolution, he began to sing the pathigam starting with ‘Poo Varkondrai’ (flowers and Kondrai). This pathigam is one of the structures (kattalai) belonging to the Takkaragam tune. There are many structural variations (kattalai bhedams) for a single tune.

Thus, he sings a pathigam about Thoniyappar in one of the eight structures prescribed for the Takkaragam tune. The structural rules for the tunes are extensively described in the Thirumurai Kanda Puranam.

Thus, eight pathigams are classified under one structure. This pathigam is one of them. For a tune, A special form combining inner peace, metric harmony, rhythmic variations, and lengthening and shortening of song verses is called a Kattaḷai.

Therefore, when he sang the pathigam “Vazhaipaya” at Thirukolakka, ThiruGnanasambandhar was blessed with the holy cymbal.

After that, he desired to sing the first pathigam, “Poovar Kondrai,” at Thiruthoni in the same Takkara tune and rhythmic structure. This pathigam is the first one sung by ThiruGnanasambandhar after receiving the cymbal. This pathigam is the twenty-fourth pathigam in the first Thirumurai. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam (பூவார் கொன்றை புரி புன் சடையீசா காவா என நின்றேத்தும் காளியார் மேவ - Lord, with a garland of Kondrai flowers and matted hair, Kāliyār praises you saying ‘protect us’). புறமூன்று அட்டார் அவர் போலாம் பாவாரின் சொற்பயிலும் பரமரே காரார் வயல் சூழ் காளிக்கோன் தனை சீரார் ஞானசம்பந்தன் சொன்ன பாறார் புகழப் பரவவல்லவர் ஏரார் வானத்து இனிதாவிருப்பரே Thiruchitrambalam.

Thus, the first and last verses of this pathigam are arranged. After singing the pathigam, worshipping the Lord with great devotion, Kāḷipillaiyār, like a cloud pregnant with perfect, undiminished wisdom, appears in the form of a child, so that all the inhabitants of Sirkazhi, surrounded by fields watered by the Kaveri, may attain great prosperity. The completeness of the wisdom Pillaiyār attained is perfect, being undiminished because there is no wisdom superior to his own. Pillaiyār, like a cloud pregnant with such wisdom, shines forth. That cloud pours forth wisdom as the divine words of the Vedas. The rain thus poured becomes the pathigams.

While Pillaiyār was thus seated in Sirkazhi, brahmins from the place called ThiruNanipalli came and gathered in Sirkazhi. They came with the desire to behold Pillaiyār. ThiruNanipalli is the sacred place where Pillaiyār’s mother, Bhagavathiammayār, was born. The town of ThiruNanipalli performed penance to have Bhagavathiammayār born there and received that blessing. ThiruNanipalli is the sacred place that received the divine connection of the mother being born there before Pillaiyār’s divine incarnation. The brahmins living in that place, meaning the relatives of Pillaiyār’s mother, came to Sirkazhi.

They came to witness the greatness of the divine wisdom with which Pillaiyār was endowed. With the desire to worship the sacred feet of ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān, they prostrated themselves at the Lord’s feet. Not only brahmins from ThiruNanipalli, but all the people of that town came and worshipped Pillaiyār’s feet.

In this way, the people of Sirkazhi performed various services, such as providing sacred food, to please the gathered devotees, brahmins, and others. Since the whole group of devotees gathered there, Sirkazhi became renowned as the divine Shiva’s Abode.

Thus, the devotees from ThiruNanipalli who had come there worshipped Pillaiyār. They then requested Pillaiyār to grace their town to worship the Shiva residing there. They pleaded that by Pillaiyār gracing their town, both they and their town would be saved by the fruits of their penance. As they made this request, ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān agreed. He then duly worshipped the feet of Shiva residing at Thiruthoni in Sirkazhi, took leave from the Lord, and set out to worship ThiruNanipalli and other sacred places. When departing from a sacred place, it is customary to take leave of the Lord’s grace.

It is a custom to seek divine permission when departing, a custom we see in many places in the Periya Puranam, and this is one such instance.

Therefore, when Pillaiyār departed from Sirkazhi, he sought permission from Thoniyappar and was about to go to ThiruNanipalli and other sacred places. Although they had requested him to visit ThiruNanipalli, it is customary to visit the places along the way when undertaking a pilgrimage.

Accordingly, Pillaiyār resolved to undertake a pilgrimage to ThiruNanipalli and other sacred places. Taking leave from Thoniyappar, he began his pilgrimage. This is Pillaiyār’s second pilgrimage.

We shall ponder further upon this. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 575, composed by Sekkizhar Swami, Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam, ThiruGnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. In response to the request of the brahmins of ThiruNanipalli, Pillaiyār begins his second pilgrimage towards ThiruNanipalli. No one could bear to see the tiny feet of Pillaiyār, who had partaken of the milk of wisdom, walk on the ground like the inner petals of a red lotus. Such loving people surrounded him. Even though no one could bear it, his greatly ascetic father, Sivapathahrithayār, unable to bear it himself, carried Pillaiyār on his shoulder.

And others also, from time to time, carried Pillaiyār on their shoulders. Even though his father and others carried him, Pillaiyār continuously bore the sacred feet of Shiva on his head and held that thought. As he journeyed towards ThiruNanipalli, Pillaiyār saw the sacred site of ThiruNanipalli in the distance. He asked his father, “Which place is this, appearing with sky-high flower gardens?” His father, filled with joy, replied, “This is ThiruNanipalli, filled with fields of water lilies.” While Pillaiyār was seated on Sivapathahrithayār’s shoulder, and ThiruNanipalli appeared in the distance, he asked, “Which place is this?” and Sivapathahrithayār replied, “This is ThiruNanipalli.” Seated on his father’s shoulders, Pillaiyār then composed the pathigam for the sacred site of ThiruNanipalli. This pathigam begins with “Kāraikal Kookai Mullai.” The pathigam for the sacred site of ThiruNanipalli is the eighty-fourth pathigam in the second Thirumurai.

This pathigam is notable for its excellent blend of scholarly and divine wisdom. Its subtlety is explained and praised in the treatise on wisdom, “Thirukazhitruppadiyar,” which states that it is not like other songs sung in the tunes of Paalai and Neythal. In the final verse of this pathigam, ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān declared with authority that all great troubles of those who remember ThiruNanipalli, where Shiva, who holds the Goddess in one part, permanently resides, will be destroyed. This pathigam, so endowed with greatness, is the second Thirumurai, eighty-fourth pathigam, composed in the tune of Piyanthaikandar. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. (காரைகள் கூகை முல்லை களவாகை ஈகை படர் தொடரி கள்ளி கவினி சூறைகள் பம்மி விம்மு சுடுகாடமர்ந்த சிவன்மேய சோலை நகர்தான் தேரைகளாரை சாய மிதி கொள்ள வாழை குதி கொள்ள வள்ளை துவள நாரைகள் ஆறல் வாரி வயன் மேதி வைகும் நனிப்பள்ளி போலும் நமர்காள் கடல்வரை யோத மல்கு கழி காணல் பாணல் கமல் காளி என்று கருத படு பொருள் ஆறு நாளும் உளதாக வைத்தபதியான ஞான முனிவன் இடுபறையொன்றவத்தவர் பியன் மேலிருந்தின் இசையாலுரைத்த பணுவல் நடுவிருள் ஆடும் எந்தை நனிப்பள்ளியுழ்க வினை கெடுதல் ஆணை நமதே - Friends, this place is like Nanipalli, where Shiva resides in a fragrant garden, filled with thorny bushes, owls, jasmine, thorny bushes, intertwined creepers, and beautiful cactus, with dense, overwhelming cremation grounds. Frogs stomp on snails, bananas leap, water hyacinths sway, herons catch fish, and buffaloes dwell in the fields.

The six meanings of the Vedas, considered by those who know, are ever present. The wise sage, who composed this musical work while seated on his father’s shoulder, as the drum beats one, says, ‘Our Lord, who dances in the midnight, in Nanipalli, it is our command that sins will be destroyed.’)

Thus, ThiruGnanasambandha Perumāl sang, transforming the land from a desert to a fertile region. Seated on his father’s shoulders, beholding ThiruNanipalli from a distance, he sang this pathigam. They then arrived at the entrance of the Shiva temple where Shiva resides in ThiruNanipalli. This sacred site was once a desert, and after Pillaiyār sang this pathigam, that desert became a coastal region, then a forest, and then an agricultural land. Nambiandar Nambigal greatly praises the nature of this pathigam, calling it a pathigam that transformed a desert into a coastal region, then a forest, and then an agricultural land. Nambiandar Nambigal, in many texts, and the treatise on wisdom, “Thirukazhitruppadiyar,” elaborate on and praise its subtlety.

Having completed the singing of this glorious pathigam, he reached the entrance of Shiva’s temple, entered, and with overflowing love, prostrated himself according to custom, praised the Lord, received abundant grace, and then emerged. Pillaiyār, the leader of the Kauniyar clan, was in the birthplace of his mother.

Therefore, his mother’s relatives, other brahmins, and the Shiva devotees of that place gathered around Pillaiyār, worshipped his feet, and praised him. Seeing the affection with which the brahmins praised him, Pillaiyār gladly stayed there. The name of the Lord at this sacred site of ThiruNanipalli is Natrunaiyappar, and the name of the Goddess is Parvathaputhri Malaiyan Madandai. The sacred tree is the Bilva, and the sacred water is the Swarna Theertham. When Pillaiyār arrived, this sacred place was a desert. Nambiandar Nambigal has recorded the glory of this sacred place, stating that it was a desert when Pillaiyār arrived, then transformed into a sandy coastal region (Neythal) after Pillaiyār sang the pathigam, then into a forest (Mullai), and subsequently into a fertile agricultural land (Marutham) with fields and surrounding areas.

This sacred place is blessed with pathigams from the three Thevaram composers: ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān, Appar Swamigal, and Sundaramurthy Swamigal. This is the forty-third sacred place on the south bank of the Kaveri. It is located northeast of Mayiladuthurai and is currently known as Punjai. The Mandapam called Nanipalli Kodi Vattam is beautifully situated in the temple’s circumambulatory path. Since an elephant came and worshipped the Lord at the main shrine, the sanctum sanctorum of this temple is very large and expansive.

Here, two Goddesses bless devotees with the names Parvatharājaputhri Malaiyan Madandai. This is the place where Shiva revealed his wedding form to both Ganesha and Agastya.

Therefore, the Goddess is seated on the right side of the Lord. In addition to this, the Lord, as Kalyanasundarar, resides with the Goddess in a separate shrine within the main sanctum. The Kaveri river flows here, turning from east to west. This is called Pasvamangini. To atone for the sin of knocking over Agastya’s கமண்டலம் (water pot) and spilling the water, Ganesha bathed in the temple tank here and worshipped the Lord. In most temples, Durga is seen standing on a buffalo’s head; however, in this temple, she is depicted holding a deer and a lion, in the posture of having slain Sumbha and Nisumbha.

The Lord appears as a Swayambhulingam. Such is the glory of the sacred site of ThiruNanipalli. While Pillaiyār was residing in ThiruNanipalli, Brahmins from the site called Thiruthalaichangadu came to see Pillaiyār. They wished to see Pillaiyār and requested him to visit their site, Thiruthalaichangadu.

Therefore, Pillaiyār departed from ThiruNanipalli and set out for Thiruthalaichangadu. We shall dwell further upon this. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 576, composed by Sekkizhar Swami, Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam, ThiruGnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān proceeds from ThiruNanipalli to the sacred site of Thiruthalaichangadu. Devotees beautifully adorn the sacred site of Thiruthalaichangadu. They plant areca and banana trees, hang flower garlands, and carry auspicious pots, decorating the streets in various ways to welcome ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān to Thiruthalaichangadu. All the brahmins in that place gather around, their minds overflowing with joy, chanting the Vedas loudly.

ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān proceeds to the Thiruthalaichangadu temple and enters that grand temple. He worships the Lord who shines forth as the meaning of the sacred Vedas. This temple, Thiruthalaichangadu, is a Mādakkōyil (temple built on an elevated platform). It is one of the seventy-eight Mādakkōyils built by Kochengat Chola Nayanar for Shiva. These are called Perunkoyils (great temples).

The Lord is seated on an elevated platform. To behold the Lord, one must climb steps. These steps are not directly in front of the sanctum but on either side. Kochengat Chola Nayanar built temples for the Lord as Mādakkōyils with steps on two sides, making it difficult for elephants to ascend.

So, this is one of the Mādakkōyils he built. This temple is designed in the shape of a Pranava (Om) conch, specifically a Valampuri Conch (a conch with a clockwise spiral). The circumambulatory paths spiral clockwise, like a Valampuri conch, with the sanctum sanctorum in the center, and above it, the Lord’s shrine. Just as a Valampuri conch always resounds with sound, so too does the Lord reside in this temple. Thiruthalaichangadu is the forty-fifth sacred place on the south bank of the Kaveri that has received Thevaram verses. One can reach this place from Mayiladuthurai by going to Aakur Mukutu and then proceeding on the road to Sirkazhi and Poompuhar.

The Lord’s name here is Sankaranyeswarar, Sangavanesvarar. The Goddess’s name is Soundaryanayaki. The sacred tree is the Purasa tree. The sacred water for this place is Sangutheertham and Kaveri Theertham.

Here, Mahavishnu worshipped Shiva. This is the place where Mahavishnu worshipped Shiva and received the conch named Panchajanyam. That is why the Lord’s temple is also designed in the shape of a Valampuri conch. The Lord’s name is also given for this very reason.

Thus, ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān, having arrived at Thiruthalaichangadu, composed a pathigam. It is the fifty-fifth pathigam in the second Thirumurai, composed in the Gandharam tune. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. (நலச்சங்க வெண்குழையும் தோடும் பெய்தோர் நால்வேதம் சொலச்சங்கையில்லாதீர் சுடுகாடலால் கருதாதீர் குளைச்செங்காய்பைங்கமுகின் குளிர்கள் சோலை குயில் ஆளும் தலைச்சங்கை கோயிலே கோயிலா தாழ்ந்தீரே நளிரும் புனற்காழி நல்ல ஞானசம்பந்தன் குளிரும் தலைச்சங்கை - You who have no doubt in the four Vedas, wearing a conch shell earring and a thodu, you who consider nothing but the cremation ground, you have worshipped the temple of Thalaichangai as your temple, where cool groves of coconut trees with red unripe fruits resonate with the calls of cuckoos. The good Gnanasambandhan of cool Kazhi, the cool Thalaichangai.) ஓங்கு கோயில் மேயானை ஒளிரும் பிரையானை உரைத்த பாடல் இவைவல்லார் மிளிரும் திரைசூழ்ந்த வையத்தார்க்கு மேலாரே Thiruchitrambalam.

Thus, after worshipping the Lord at Thiruthalaichangadu temple and singing a pathigam with great devotion, and as the brahmins surrounded and praised ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān, he came out of the temple and proceeded to the sacred site of Thiruvalamburam. He praised the Lord of Thiruvalamburam with a pathigam beginning with “Kodiyudai Mummathil” (three-walled fortress) and composed a pathigam. This sacred site called Thiruvalamburam is also known as Melapperumpallam. The Lord’s name is Valamburanathar, and the Goddess’s name is Vaduvagirkanni. The sacred tree is the Palmyra palm. The sacred waters for this place are Brahmateertham, Lakshmi Teertham, Swarna Teertham, and Pangayatheertham.

These are the sacred waters of this place. It is the forty-fourth sacred site on the south bank of the Kaveri that has received verses. It is said that Eranda Munivar descended into the Kaveri at Valanjuzhi and came ashore at this village.

Therefore, there is a temple for Eranda Munivar. The processional deity of Bikshatanar playing the veena is a very beautiful image. This is a Mādakkōyil. The presiding deity manifests as a Prithvi Lingam (earth lingam). A festival called Pattinathar’s Welcome Festival (Pattinatṭārai Mannar Varavēṟkum Aidika Vizhā) is held in this temple. An inscription from Vikrama Chola mentions this place as Rasaraja Valanattu Aakur Nattu Thalaichangattu Thiruvalamburam, the Lord as Valamburi Udaiyar, and the Goddess as Thadankannachiyar.

One can reach this place by traveling on the Mayiladuthurai-Poompuhar road, crossing the Kaveri river dam, and then going to Melaiyur via Sirkazhi-Kaveripoompattinam. Sekkizhar Perumān mentions that ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān sang the pathigam beginning with “Kodiyudai” at this sacred site. That pathigam is the one hundred and third pathigam in the third Thirumurai, composed in the Pazhampanjuram tune. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. (கொடியுடை மும்மதிலூடுருவ குனி வெஞ்சிலை தாங்கி இடிபட எய்த அமர்பிரான் அடியார் இசைந்தேத்த துடியிடையாழையோர் பாகமாக துதைந்தார் இடம்போலும் வடிவுடைமேதி வயல் படியும் வலம்புற நன்னகரே நல்லியல் நான்மறையோர் புகழித் தமிழ் ஞான சம்பந்தன் வல்லியன் தோலுடையாடையினான் வலம்புற நன்னகரை சொல்லிய பாடல்கள் பத்தும் சொல்லவல்லவர் தொல்வினை போய் செல்வன சேவடி சென்றணுகிச்சி - The good city of Valamburam is like the place where the Lord, who held a fierce bow and pierced the three forts to thunder and shoot, resides with a part of his body as his graceful consort, praised by his devotees. Beautiful buffaloes graze in the fields. Those who can recite these ten songs about the good city of Valamburam, spoken by the virtuous Brahmin Gnanasambandhan of Pukazhi, who wears a tiger skin as a garment, will shed their ancient karma and reach the sacred feet.)

சிவலோகம் சேர்வாரே Thiruchitrambalam.

Thus, ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān, having worshipped the sacred site of Thiruvalamburam, resolved to go to the sacred site of Thiruchaikaadu. He then worshipped the sacred site of Thiruppallavaneeswaram and reached Thiruchaikaadu. ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān praised the Lord of Thiruppallavaneeswaram with a pathigam. This pathigam is composed in a two-line meter. It is a pathigam that ends with the question, “Who knows?” Thiruppallavaneeswaram is the city also known as Kaveri Poompattinam and Poompuhar. The Lord’s name here is Pallavanesvarar, and the Goddess’s name is Soundaryanayaki.

The sacred trees include the Punnai tree, jasmine, and coral jasmine. Sacred trees are the Punnai tree, jasmine, and coral jasmine, among others. The sacred waters are Kaveri Theertham and Janavi Theertham. Opposite the temple is the Janavi Theertham, a sacred pond created by Agastya. This sacred site has two Thevaram pathigams composed by ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān. It is the birthplace of Pattinatthadigal.

It is also the sacred place where Iyarpaakai Nayanar was born and performed service to Shiva. Sekkizhar Perumān states that ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān composed pathigams with two-line verses. Sekkizhar Perumān refers to this as an Isai (musical) pathigam. This pathigam is the one hundred and twelfth pathigam in the third Thirumurai, composed in the Pazhampanjuram tune. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. (பரசுபாணியர் பாடல் வீணையர் - The Lord with the battle-axe, the one who sings and plays the veena). பட்டினத்துறை பல்லவநீச்சரத் தரசுபேணி நின்றார் இவர் தன்மை அறிவார் ஆர் வானமாழ்வதற்கு ஊனமொன்றில்லை மாதர் பல்லவணீச்சரத்தானை ஞானசம்பந்தன் அற்றமிழ் சொல்லவல்லவர் நல்லரே Thiruchitrambalam.

Similarly, the second pathigam composed by ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān is the sixty-fifth pathigam in the first Thirumurai, set to the Dhakecchi tune. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. (அடையார்தம் புறங்கள் மூன்றும் ஆர் அழலில் அழுந்த விடையார் மேனியராய்ச்சீரும் வித்தகர் மேயவிடம் கடையார் மாடம் நீடி எங்கு கங்குல் புறந்தடவ படையார்புரிசை பட்டினஞ்சேர் பல்லவணீச்சரமே பத்தரேத்தும் பட்டினத்து பல்லவநீச்சரத்து எம் அத்தன் தன்னை அணிகொள்காளி ஞானசம்பந்தன் சொல் சித்தஞ்சேறச் செப்பும் மாந்தர் தீவினை - The Lord, whose body is adorned with the bull, who caused the three forts of his enemies to be consumed by fire, the wise one who resides in a place where high-walled mansions reach out to touch the darkness everywhere, is Pallavaneeswaram, a fortified city. The people who devoutly praise our Father at Pallavaneeswaram in Pattinam and speak the words of Gnanasambandhan of Kali will have their evil karma). நோயிலராய் ஒத்தமைந்த உம்பர்வானில் உயர்வினொடு ஓங்குவரே Thiruchitrambalam.

Thus, ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān, having worshipped Thiruppallavaneeswaram, reached the sacred site of Thiruchaikaadu. At Thiruchaikaadu, the devotees joyfully welcomed ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān, and he graced that sacred place. He circumambulated the temple clockwise, entered through the sky-high entrance, and then approached the Lord, who was adorned with a garland of Kondrai flowers. He prostrated himself and praised Shiva, composing a pathigam beginning with “Man Puhar,” praising Shiva, who held the deer in his left hand, and melting everyone’s heart. ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān then joined his red hands above his head in worship. This pathigam is the forty-first pathigam in the second Thirumurai.

It is composed in the Seekamarappann tune. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. (மண்புகார் வான் புகவர் மணமிழையார் பசியாலும் கண் புகார் பிணியறியார் கற்றாறும் கேட்டாரும் வின் புகார் என வேண்டா வெண்மாட நெடுவீதி தன் புகார் சாய்க்காட்டு எம் தலைவன்தாள் சார்ந்தாரே நொம்பைந்து புடைத்தொல்கு நூபுரஞ்சேர் மெல்லடியார் அம்பந்தும் வரிக் கழலும் அரவஞ்சை பூங்காளிச் சம்பந்தன் தமிழ் பகர்ந்த சாய்க்காட்டு பத்தினையும் எம்பந்தம் எனக்கருதி ஏத்துவார்க்கு இடர்கெடுமே Thiruchitrambalam.) Those who have reached the feet of our Lord at Saikkaadu, also known as Puhar, will not return to this earthly world; they will enter the heavenly world. They will not lose their dignity, nor suffer from hunger or disease, nor will they need to lament. They will not desire to go to other heavens. This pathigam implies that those who worship the sacred feet of Shiva will not return to this earth, but will enter the heavenly realm. He asked, “What is the way to reach Shiva?” It is to constantly meditate on Shiva, worship Him with flowers, chant His names, and listen to His glories.

Therefore, offer flowers and worship His sacred lotus feet; reach Him. For His devotees, even heavens are insignificant.

Therefore, ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān composed this pathigam with the emphasis that those who think of Him will have no troubles. After singing this pathigam, ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān then sang another pathigam for the devotees to praise Him. This pathigam, beginning with “Nitthalam Niyamam Seithu,” is composed in the Indalappann tune. At the end of each verse of this pathigam, the word “Saikkaade” appears. This is the thirty-eighth pathigam in the second Thirumurai. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchi.

சிற்றம்பலம் நித்தலும் நியமும் செய்து நீர்மலர் தூவி சித்தம் ஒன்ற வல்லார்க்கு அருளும் சிவன் கோயில் மத்த யானையின் கோடும் வண்பீலியும் வாரி தத்து நீர் பொன்னி சாகரமேவும் சாய்க்காடே ஏனையோர் புகழ் தேத்திய எந்தைச் சாய்க்காட்டை ஞானசம்பந்தன் காளியர்கோன் நவில்்பத்தும் ஊனமின்றி உரை செய்ய வல்லவர் தாம் போய் வானநாடு இனிது ஆழ்வர் இம்மாநிலத்தோரே Thiruchitrambalam.

Thus, ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān composed this pathigam. This sacred site of Thiruchaikaadu is also known as Saayavanam. The Lord’s name is Saayavaneshvarar, Amudeshvarar. The Goddess’s name is Kuyilinum Nanmozhi Ammai. The sacred tree here is the Kōrai grass. The sacred waters are Kaveri, Iravatha Theertham, and Kadal Sangamathurai Theertham.

Since this place was a forest of Kōrai grass (Pañchaayi), it was named Saayavanam and Saikkaadu. It is also called Sai Oli because of the radiant gem of Adishesha. It is the place where Upamanyu Munivar and Iravatham worshipped and attained great blessings. It is also the place where Iyarpaakai Nayanar worshipped and attained liberation. This sacred place has received Thevaram verses from ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān and Thirunavukkarasu Perumān. It is one of the six places considered equal to Kashi.

There is a beautiful idol of Kumaran holding a bow. This is also one of the Mādakkōyils built by Kochchengachola Nayanar. The glories and history of this place have been extensively discussed in ancient Tamil literature. ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān departed from Sirkazhi, went directly to ThiruNanipalli, then to Thiruthalaichangadu, then to Thiruvalamburam, Thiruppallavaneeswaram, and Thiruchaikaadu, worshipped there, and then turned northeast. He now proceeds to the sacred site of Thiruvengadu.

We shall ponder further upon this. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 577, composed by Sekkizhar Swami. ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān proceeds to the sacred site of Thiruvengadu.

The devotees of Thiruvengadu, who serve Shiva adorned with Kondrai flowers, Vanni leaves, the Ganges, and the crescent moon, come before ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān and welcome him with great joy. In their boundless and immense happiness, unable to comprehend or express their exalted state, they welcome ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān, the king of Sirkazhi. Unlike the kings of this earthly world, who cannot fully govern even a small part of it, ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān governs the souls of this world with wisdom and guides them towards goodness.

Therefore, he is the great king of Sirkazhi.

The devotees of Thiruvengadu went to meet and worship ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān, the king who incarnated in Shanbai, also known as Sirkazhi, and rules this world. Pillaiyār, the master of the three Tamils, approached Shiva’s temple in Thiruvengadu and joyfully bowed before the temple tower.

Then, accompanied by devoted followers, he circumambulated the Lord’s temple. ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān arrived at Thiruvengadu with great desire and worshipped. He circumambulated the temple with the same overflowing love. What kind of joy is this? It is the joy that this world will be saved through the teachings of Meykandadeva Nayanar, who is destined to incarnate through the influence of ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān’s pathigam at Thiruvengadu after worshipping the Lord in this temple.

Thus, ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān worshipped at Thiruvengadu with immense love.

Thus, he worshipped and circumambulated the temple with the congregation of devotees. It is customary for those who desire worldly pleasures to circumambulate the temple clockwise, and for those who desire liberation to circumambulate counter-clockwise. Pillaiyār had no desires.

Therefore, to instruct and guide the people of this world, ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān circumambulated in both directions.

Similarly, we should observe the methods of worship shown by ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān.

Thus, worshipping the true essence, the Lord residing in the Thiruvengadu temple, he offered the ineffable pathigam, “Kan Kaattu Nuthalanum,” as a garland. In this pathigam, ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān sang about the three temple tanks at Thiruvengadu. Pillaiyār, who had partaken of the nectar of divine wisdom, sang about the three tanks of Thiruvengadu: Surya Theertham, Chandra Theertham, and Agni Theertham. Sekkizhar Perumān’s verse at this point states: “Meipporul Aayinārai Vengādu Mēvinārai Sepparum Pathikamālai Kan Kaattu Nūthan Mun Sērthi Muppuram Setrāar Pātham Sērum Mukkulamum Pādi Opparum Gnānam Undār Ulamakizhndu Ēthi Vāzhnthār” (He, who became the True Being, residing in Thiruvengadu, offered a garland of ineffable pathigams, beginning with “Kan Kaattu Nūthan,” and sang of the three tanks that reach the feet of the One who destroyed the three forts. He, who partook of incomparable wisdom, praised and lived with a joyful heart). In this verse, Sekkizhar Perumān sings of Shiva residing in Thiruvengadu.

Sekkizhar Perumān sings of Shiva as “Meipporuḷ Āyinārai” (the One who became the True Being). Meipporuḷ means Sat (existence, truth).

The Lord is that which cannot be known by mere perception or by any other means; He is the Sat which can only be known by divine wisdom. ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān begins the pathigam with “Kan Kaattum Nuthalānum” and praises that Lord. He sings of the three tanks that reach the feet of Shiva, who destroyed the three forts. In this pathigam, the phrase “Mukkula Nīr Tōyvinaiyār Avar Tammai Tōyāvām Tīvinaiyē” (those who bathe in the waters of the three tanks will not be touched by evil karma) is a key message of the pathigam. These three tanks are located within the temple.

Therefore, they are sacred waters associated with the Lord’s divine form, and thus, the souls who bathe in them. Also reach the feet of the Lord. The phrase “Muppuram Setrāar Pātham Sērum Mukkulam” (the three tanks that reach the feet of the One who destroyed the three forts) appears in this song. The word “Sērum” (reaches) here refers to the souls (Pasu) that reach the Lord. The phrase “Muppuram Setrāar Pātham” (the feet of the One who destroyed the three forts) refers to the Lord (Pathi) as the destination for the souls (Pasu) and the grace that enables them to reach it. “Mukkulam” (three tanks) here refers to the path by which these souls reach the Lord.

Thus, divine wisdom saves souls.

The Lord imparted that divine wisdom through the Siva Agamas, and Meykandadeva Nayanar, following the Siva Agamas, helped the souls of this world through his philosophical work, “SivaJnana Bodham.” The three tanks and this verse from ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān’s pathigam, which speaks of these tanks, were instrumental in bringing Meykandadeva Nayanar into this world. How so? Meykandadeva Nayanar’s father, who was childless, sought the help of his family guru. Their family guru, Sakalagama Panditar, sought divine guidance through the Thevaram scriptures. As he did so, this verse from ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān’s pathigam, which begins with “Peyadaiyā” and speaks of the three tanks, emerged from the sacred site of Thiruvengadu.

When the sacred thread was cast upon the Thevaram manuscript, this verse from this pathigam appeared. Sakalagama Panditar then explained it to the father. The father, accompanied by his wife, came to Thiruvengadu and bathed in the three tanks. They worshipped the Lord and received a boon. As a result, Meykandadeva Nayanar was born. At the age of two, he received instruction from Paranjothiyar and composed Sivajnana Bodham, a philosophical work confirming the meaning of the Siva Agamas, along with a commentary, and taught it to the world.

As a result, the souls of this world are blessed to reach Shiva’s feet. Sekkizhar Perumān’s divine words beautifully encapsulate all these later events by including the phrases “Muppuram Setrāar Pātham Sērum Mukkulamum Pādi” (singing of the three tanks that reach the feet of the One who destroyed the three forts) and “Meipporuḷānar” (the One who became the True Being) in this verse. ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān’s composition of this pathigam is an act of his singular great compassion.

Thus, by composing the Thiruvengadu pathigam, he proclaimed that praising Shiva is life. Praising Shiva is life-giving. Praising Shiva in this manner also leads to the prosperity of the world, declares ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān. This pathigam, Thiruvengadu pathigam, beginning with “Kan Kaattu Nuthalanum,” is uniquely significant as it simultaneously bestows the grace of ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān, the foremost among the Saiva Samaya Kuravarkal, and Sri Meykandadeva Nayanar, the foremost among the Santana Acharyas, upon the devotees of Shiva. This pathigam is the forty-eighth pathigam in the second Thirumurai and is composed in the Seekamaram tune. The first verse, the second verse which was instrumental in the birth of Sri Meykandadeva Nayanar, and the final verse are as follows.
