(கண்காட்டும் நுதலானும் கணல் காட்டும் கையானும் பெண்காட்டும் உருவானும் பிறை காட்டும் சடையானும் பண்காட்டும் இசையானும் பயிர்காட்டும் புயலானும் வெண்காட்டில் உறைவானும் விடை காட்டும் கொடியானே பேயடையா பிரிவைதும் பிள்ளையினொடு உள்ள நினைவு ஆயினவே வரம்பெறுவர் ஐயுற வேண்டா ஒன்றும் வேயனத்தோள் உமை பங்கன் வெண்காட்டு முக்குழநீர் தோய் வினையார் அவர் தம்மை தோயாவாம் தீவினையே தண் பொழில்சூழ் சண்பயர்கோண் தமிழ் ஞான சம்பந்தன் விண் பொலி வெண்பிரைச் சென்னி விகிர் தன் உரை வெண்காட்டை பண்பொலி செந்தமிழ் மாலை பாடிய பத்து இவை வல்லார் மண்பொலிய வாழ்ந்தவர் போய் வான் பொலியப் புகுவாரே Thiruchitrambalam.) The pathigam implies that one can attain a good worldly life and a liberated life free from karmic ties.

Thus, ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān, who composed this pathigam, also bestowed two more pathigams upon this sacred site. The second pathigam is the sixty-first pathigam in the second Thirumurai, composed in the Gandharam tune. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. (உண்டாய் நஞ்சை உமையோர் பங்கா என்று உல்கி தொண்டாய் திரியும் அடியார்த்தங்கள் துயரங்கள் அண்டா வண்ணம் அருப்பான் எந்தை ஊர்போலும் வெண்டாமறைமேல் கருவண்டியாழ் வெண்காடு விடையார் கொடியான் மேவியுறையும் வெண்காட்டை கடையார் மாடம் கலந்து தோன்றும் காளியான் நடையாரின் சொல் ஞானசம்பந்தன் தமிழ் வல்லார்க்கு அடையா வினைகள் - Our Father, who consumed poison and, as one part of Uma, granted grace to prevent the sorrows of his devotees from reaching them, resides in a town like Thiruvengadu, where black bees hum around white lotuses. Those who are skilled in the Tamil verses of Gnanasambandhan of Kaali, who appears with high mansions and lives at Thiruvengadu, where the bull-bannered Lord resides, will not have their karmas follow them.) அமரலோகம் ஆழ்வாரே Thiruchitrambalam.

Now, the third pathigam is the fifteenth pathigam in the third Thirumurai, composed in the Gandhara Panchamam tune. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. Such is the glory of Thiruvengadu, where Indra and Iravatham worshipped and were freed from their curses. These stories are praised in the pathigams. The Sthala Puranam states that when Shiva performed his cosmic dance of bliss, the drops of water that fell from his three eyes became the three sacred tanks at this site. These three sacred waters are known as Soma Theertham, Surya Theertham, and Agni Theertham, and are famously called the Mukkulam (three tanks). The Silappadikaram also praises this sacred site and the uniqueness of these waters, stating: “Kadalodu Kaveri Senrazaikkum Munril Madalavil Neythalangānār Thadamula Somakundam Suryakundam Sunai Mūlgi” (In the courtyard where the Kaveri meets the sea, in the fragrant Neythal region, there are Soma Kunda, Surya Kunda, and spring baths).

Surya Theertham is in the south, Chandra Theertham in the west, and Agni Theertham is in the north, opposite the Goddess’s temple. The Sthala Puranam states that the Devas, namely Surya, Chandra, and Agni, worshipped here and attained blessings. True to their names, these three waters have distinct temperature characteristics. The Surya Theertham is warm, and the Chandra Theertham is cool. The Agni Theertham has a sulfurous heat and its smoky touch. ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān has declared in his pathigam that those who regularly bathe in these waters and worship will receive their desired boons.

Similarly, as a result of this worship and the pathigam composed by Pillaiyār, Sri Meykandadeva Nayanar was born and became a foremost Saiva Siddhanta Acharya, a history known to all Saiva devotees. In this sacred place, Aghoramurthi is famously present and bestows abundant grace. He is Shiva’s Aghora form, a divine image of wisdom facing south. Opposite him is Kāḷi’s shrine. Special pujas are performed for Aghoramurthi every Sunday night, and the sixth day of the grand festival is particularly significant. This sacred place is glorified by the pathigams of the three poets.

In this sacred place, the Lord’s name is Svetharanyesvarar, Thiruvengatteesar. The Goddess’s name is Brahmavidya Nayaki. The sacred water is the Mukkulam. The sacred trees are the Banyan tree and the Kondrai tree. It is located southeast of Sirkazhi. One can reach this place from Mayiladuthurai and Kaveripoompattinam.

Manikavasaga Perumān has sung about this place in the Thiruvāsakam and Thirukkovaiyar, stating, “Virundhinagi Vengadu Adhanil” (as a guest in Thiruvengadu). Kapila Deva Nayanar, Parana Deva Nayanar, and Pattinathu Pillaiyār have also sung about this sacred place. Thiruvengadu is one of the six places considered equal to Kashi. In the Valmiki Ramayana, Thiruvengadu is referred to as Svetharanyam. Valmiki states that just as Svetha slew Yama in Svetharanya Kshetra, Rama also slew Khara and Dushana. This serves as proof of the antiquity of this sacred site.

Valmiki Munivar mentions this Svetharanya, or Thiruvengadu, in the Aranya Kanda of the Valmiki Ramayana. Sri Meykandadeva Nayanar was born as the son of Achuthakkalappalar. His child’s name was Svethavana Perumal, which is the name of the Lord of this place. A lullaby in this region explains the uniqueness of the three tanks of this place: “Sangu Mukam Ādi Saaya Vanam Paarthu Mukkulamum Ādi Mutthi Pera Vanthano” (Did he come to attain liberation by bathing in Sangu Mukam, seeing Saaya Vanam, and bathing in the Mukkulam?). When ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān visited this sacred site, where the entire village appeared as Shivalingams, the Goddess held ThiruGnanasambandha Perumān on her hip. The local legend is that she came and performed a puja.

In that very form, the Goddess Brahmavidya Nayaki Amman gives us an audience in the prakaram as Pillaiyidukki Amman. Thiruvengattu Nangai, the wife of Siruthonda Nayanar, and her companion Sandanangai were also from this town. These are all facts about this temple.

At that time, when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was residing in Sirkazhi, Thiruneelakantha Yazhpanar and his wife Mathanga Choolamani Ammaiyar arrived in Sirkazhi with their yazh to worship the feet of Pillaiyar. Musicians who sing verses are called Panars, and they would have a musical instrument called a yazh.

Therefore, Thiruneelakantha Yazhpanar would play music on the yazh, and Mathanga Choolamani Ammaiyar would sing songs suitable for that music.

Thus, Thiruneelakantha Yazhpanar, with his yazh, came to Sirkazhi to worship the feet of Pillaiyar. He arrived with Mathanga Choolamani Ammaiyar. Knowing that Thiruneelakantha Yazhpanar and Mathanga Choolamani Ammaiyar were coming to Sirkazhi, Pillaiyar, with great eagerness, went to the border of Sirkazhi to receive them and escorted them. The mansion where Thirugnanasambandha Peruman resided in Sirkazhi was located in the street of Brahmins, surrounded by Brahmins. Thiruneelakantha Yazhpanar, in that Brahmin-filled environment, cleared the way for them and, before they could worship Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman himself emerged from his mansion and welcomed them at the border of Sirkazhi. Upon seeing Aazhudaiya Pillaiyar, Thiruneelakantha Yazhpanar and Mathanga Choolamani Ammaiyar.

They worship the sacred feet that support those who reach them. They express their genuine praises from the heart and worship the feet of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Worshipping Pillaiyar is the life they had envisioned, a blessing attainable only through past penance and good fortune.

Therefore, they are immensely joyful upon realizing that their envisioned life of worshipping Pillaiyar has been fulfilled. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, seeing their boundless joy, says, “Sir, because you have arrived here with a happy heart, we have gained the assurance of that supreme truth.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman says this with a smile and takes them with him to Kazhumalam. They proceed towards the temple where Lord Shiva, enshrined in Thiruthoni, resides. He escorts Mathanga Choolamani Ammaiyar and Thiruneelakantha Yazhpanar to the front of the temple. Standing in the outer courtyard of the temple, he instructs them to worship Thoniyappar. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman commands them, “From here, create fitting music and play the yazh for your Lord.” He instructs them, “Play the yazh from here and sing devotional songs praising the Lord, do so for your Lord.” The Sivagamas, which prescribe the structure of temples, specify that certain classes of people may enter the temple only up to a certain point and stand to worship.

The social customs relating to caste and lineage, and so on, must be observed and protected as long as one has a connection to the body and the world. When one’s attachment to these diminishes, and these are abandoned, and a desire for liberation arises, then these connections to the body, worldly connections, caste, lineage, and social customs will automatically fall away without attachment. Aazhudaiya Pillaiyar was an Acharya who came to uplift beings by protecting and regulating both the Vedic and Saivite paths.

Therefore, he commanded Thiruneelakantha Yazhpanar, in accordance with the Sivagama rules regarding his musician lineage, to be seated in front of the temple, outside, and to play the yazh to delight the Lord. It should also be known that this did not diminish the Nayanar’s path of love.

Later, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, at Nallur Perumanam, without considering caste or lineage, led all those who came with a pure heart to the path of liberation, saying, ‘Gnana Meyneri than yaarkkum Namasivayach solam’ (The true path of wisdom for all is the Namasivaya mantra), making everyone present hear it, and proclaimed, ‘Enaamaam piravi theera yaavarum puguga’ (Let all enter to end their lowly birth).

Therefore, without considering lineage or status, Pillaiyar treats everyone equally and leads them to the gateway of liberation.

Thus, it is the divine rule for God to bestow grace according to time, place, and the maturity of souls. That is also the rule of the Agamas and the conduct of an Acharya.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, from the position of an Acharya, considers the respective time, place, and the maturity of souls. He thus bestows grace, considering their readiness. He commands, “Create the seven melodies for your Lord, so that he may be pleased.” This is an expression of affection and the special privilege he grants to Thiruneelakantha Yazhpanar and Mathanga Choolamani Ammaiyar, referring to Lord Shiva as their Lord. Immediately, Thiruneelakantha Yazhpanar and Mathanga Choolamani Ammaiyar worship Pillaiyar. Earlier, they had worshipped Pillaiyar with folded hands, having come with the intention of worshipping him.

Now, after Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has given this command, they worship him again. This signifies their acceptance of Pillaiyar’s role as an Acharya guiding them. He also commanded them to sing. They offered their respects for having been commanded to sing as well.

Thus, Thiruneelakantha Yazhpanar, having worshipped Pillaiyar, arranges the melodies and musical notes on the yazh in the appropriate manner, adjusting the strings to create the music, and plays the Lord’s verses on the yazh. Mathanga Choolamani Ammaiyar sings.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is pleased to hear Mathanga Choolamani Ammaiyar singing in harmony with him and playing the yazh. Even the Vedic scholars are amazed. The sound emanating from the yazh, combined with the voices of Thiruneelakantha Yazhpanar and Mathanga Choolamani Ammaiyar—that is, the sound of their combined singing—blends into one harmonious sound. Hearing this, Thoniyappar, residing in Thiruthoni inside the temple. Lord Periyanayaki Ammaiyar and Thiruneelakantha Yazhpanar and Mathanga Choolamani Ammaiyar come to the front of the temple where they are and bestow their grace.

Thus, the Lord himself comes there and listens attentively to the songs and music of both of them. Other musicians also listen to their songs and music and are amazed and praise them. Now, listening to the song sung by Thiruneelakantha Yazhpanar and Mathanga Choolamani Ammaiyar, those two birds, Kinnaram Midunam, residing in the moon. These two species of birds descend from there and stand amazed, listening to and experiencing the song and music of the two from the sky. Thus, after Thiruneelakantha Yazhpanar finished singing, playing the tune-filled yazh and singing in harmony with his voice, praising the feet of our Lord who is enshrined in Thiruthoni, possessing such unimaginable glory, Pillaiyar, the leader of Sirkazhi, takes them, arranges a place for them to stay, seats them there, and arranges a good feast.

During this time, the devotees present there sing the pathigams of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman with great devotion. Hearing the devotees reciting them. Thiruneelakantha Yazhpanar and Mathanga Choolamani Ammaiyar, hearing this, are deeply moved and filled with joy. Thiruneelakantha Yazhpanar, playing the pathigams blessed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman on his yazh, delighted all living beings. Thiruneelakantha Yazhpanar, who played the pathigam blessed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman with music on the yazh, worshipped Pillaiyar and, addressing Pillaiyar, requested, ‘I seek your command to play the music of these great pathigams, whose greatness is difficult to obtain, on the yazh.

Thus, when they made their request, Pillaiyar, with a happy heart, agreed, and they, considering it the Lord’s grace, with great desire, lovingly remain, playing Pillaiyar’s pathigams, which are garlands of Tamil verses, in the melodic style of the yazh, never parting. When the Lord bestows grace upon a soul, it is through two ways, as stated by the wisdom scriptures: by coming as an Acharya and by uniting with the community of devotees. This is the truth proclaimed by the Gnana Shastras regarding the two ways in which God bestows grace.

Thus, Thiruneelakantha Yazhpanar and Mathanga Choolamani Ammaiyar were blessed with this grace from the Lord. On the way to Thillai, where the Lord, who performs the dance in the deep night, is enshrined, they worship at the intermediate shrines and continue towards Thillai. Gnanasambandhar, the lamp of the Kauniya lineage, thus journeyed and reached the south bank of the Kollidam River. The Kollidam River carried with it rich clusters of flowers, in which bees were buzzing. It also brought along precious gems and sandalwood pieces. The Kollidam River flowed with many riches from the groves. The sea met the Kollidam River as it flowed thus. In such a situation, having crossed the sacred Kollidam River, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, along with the assembly of devotees, ascended to the north bank and resided there. With a large gathering of devotees and Brahmins surrounding him, and all beings, including the Devas, worshipping him, he reached the sacred boundary encircling Thillai, which bestows all desired boons upon them. Upon reaching the boundary of Thillai, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman prostrated himself on the ground. As Thirugnanasambandha, the auspicious young elephant calf, who brings prosperity to this refined world, approached Thillai, birds on both sides chirped and offered their blessings. As the red-faced lotuses gathered, the water ponds, with their blooming faces, welcomed Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. In the flower gardens, soft peacocks with their tails joyfully called out to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

A cool, fresh breeze welcomed Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Seeing Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who partook of the sweet nectar of Shiva’s wisdom, which Parvati Ammaiyar mixed, coming towards Thillai, the paddy fields in the vast fields, adorned with the beautiful, fine pollen of flowers, sprinkled it and welcomed him with beautiful faces. The fragrant betelnut trees near the fields, seeing Thirugnanasambandha. Seeing the dignified arrival of Peruman, they rejoice immensely and sway together on both sides, welcoming him. As Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who appeared to foster penance, approached, the sky, as if to welcome him and express its joy, spread a thin blue cloth above, like a canopy. The smoke from the yagnas performed in the common sacrificial halls on the boundary of Thillai rose to touch the sky, filling it.

These yagnas, commonly performed in sacrificial halls, are Shiva-related rituals. The homas performed in these yagnas bestow the nature of Shiva. Other yagnas yield worldly merits and lead to further births. These, however, bestow the highest benefit of Shivattva (the nature of Shiva) and prevent rebirth. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman thus proceeds along the path to Thillai, crossing the high fields of Marutha Nilam, where sugarcane, red paddy, and green betel nut trees are intermingled, at its boundary.

After that, he passes through beautiful Nandavanams (flower gardens). Outside are fields, then Nandavanams, and then the city of Thillai begins.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman passes through the area adjacent to the fields and the Nandavanams. He worships these Nandavanams as he passes, because. These Nandavanams are places where buds, tender flowers, sprouts, fruits, and roots all originate. These items are used for the Lord’s puja, hence they are called Thirunandavanams. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships these Thirunandavanams because they are the places where materials suitable for adorning the Lord’s body and for offering as sacred food directly to the Lord are produced. The souls born for the sake of Shiva’s virtues are destined to be born as plants in these Thirunandavanams.

Therefore, all Thirunandavanams are worthy of worship. We recall that in the earlier Purana of Thaduthatkondar, Sundaramurthi Swamigal, upon reaching Thiruchitrambalam, worshipped all the Thirunandavanams. We also recall here that in the legend of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman encountered all these Nandavanams when he came towards Thiruchitrambalam.

Thus, worshipping the Nandavanams, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrives at the south gate of the wall of Thillai city. Sirkazhi is a holy place south of Thiruchitrambalam, so it is natural for Thirugnanasambandha Peruman to arrive at Thiruchitrambalam. We have already learned that Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal arrived at Thiruchitrambalam through the west gate and Sundaramurthi Swamigal through the north gate. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman enters Thiruchitrambalam through the south gate. He entered through the south gate. The dancing Lord performs his divine dance facing south.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrives near the gate that is directly opposite that sacred front, on the south side. Among the four gates located in the four directions of Thiruchitrambalam, the south gate, situated in the southern direction, has the special distinction of directly facing the sacred Hall where the Lord performs his divine dance.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrives at the south gate of Thiruchitrambalam. Let us persist in our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam Part 581, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, composed by Sekkizhar Swamigal. To welcome Pillaiyar, who arrived at the south gate of the outer wall of Thiruthillai, the Thillai Brahmins gathered. The sound of the Vedas filled the air. Auspicious musical instruments resonated across the heavens. With holy water-filled Purna Kumbhams and auspicious lamps shining brightly, the Thillai Brahmins welcomed Pillaiyar.

Speaking auspicious words, they offered good wishes, saying, ‘May your arrival be auspicious,’ and offered blessings, welcoming Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and escorting him. The Thillai Brahmins, who were freed from evil, were blessed, just as the celestials live by blessing Pillaiyar. By blessing with auspicious words, the Thillai Brahmins were blessed. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman enters Thillai, the ancient city brimming with the wealth of Shiva, the wealth of liberation, through the south gate. He bows to the street of mansions, filled with rows of three thousand Brahmins’ houses, and proceeds, bowing, because it is the sacred street where the dancing Lord graciously appears and bestows his divine sight. In the mansions of those streets, Chandrakanta stones, large jewels, lamps, and other luminous objects cast a cool light, and the entire street is fragrant with the scent of Shiva.

Fragrances from incense and other aromatic items dedicated to Shiva waft through the air, making the sky and the street free from impurities. That sacred street shines, fragrant with the divine essence, because of the grace of Koothapiran (the dancing Lord) who processes there. Just as the luminous flame of Shiva, which blossoms in meditation, removes the heat of birth and brings the coolness of his sacred feet, those sacred streets shine coolly. Just as the minds of devotees are, free from the powerful bonds of anava (ego) and other impurities, attaining the state of Shiva through Sivayoga (union with Shiva), so too are those sacred streets. This greatness belongs to all four main streets, but the southern direction is directly in front of the dancing Koothapiran who dances facing south.

Therefore, the gatherings of devotees here are particularly special.

Thus, having circled and worshipped the streets, he reaches near the seven-tiered gopuram. Pillaiyar reaches near the gopuram. After prostrating before the gopuram and rising, he enters through the gopuram’s sacred entrance. He enters the courtyard. Adjacent to that courtyard is a row of mansions. Circling that golden mansion, he worships the towering, moon-crowned, elevated Perambalam (great hall), and proceeds further to reach the Thiru Anukkan entrance to the sacred presence of Koothaperuman, who performs the divine dance, continually praised by rare Vedas.

Here, the method of worshipping the temple is explained: Prostrating before the temple gopuram, prostrating before the sacred entrance, rising, entering through the gopuram’s entrance, entering the courtyard, circumambulating the mansion, worshipping the Perambalam, and then reaching the Thiru Anukkan entrance. This explains the method of temple worship. Nandi Peruman is the head and established leader of all the Sivaganapathis, and he is the prime guru of our guru lineage. At that Thiru Anukkan gate, with the Sivaganapathis led by Thiru Nandi Peruman standing in rows, and countless devotees, sages, Devas, and others standing behind the Sivaganapathis to worship, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, with immense eagerness in his heart, with his small red hands clasped above his head, and his eyes filled with joy, entered the Thiru Anukkan gate with melted devotion. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who is Kalai Pillaiyar, saw the Thiru Ambalam, which was the true knowledge granted to him by Annallar, and the great dance of bliss that arose from his full knowledge, with his own eyes. With an abundance of joy, he rose, worshipped, and praised the sacred dance.

He was a beacon of pure virtue, like a sacred sprout. He praised that the blissful Shiva experience, which arises perfectly from the understanding of purity, should be granted without hindrance, even to the extent of the five senses. He glorified this incomparable great compassion. He then sang this melodious pathigam, which he had composed earlier. The bones and soul within were melted and purified. He experienced the dance of the Lord of the heavens in the vast expanse, and partook of the nectar of his eyes. (kadal kali punniyak kozhundu anaivar potruvaar punidharaadiya poruppunharvin nerpera varum sivabhogathai oolvinri uruvin kan anaiyum aimpori aazhavinum ezhiyavara arulina yena potri inaiyil vanperum karunaiye yethimun edutha sorpathigathil punarum innisai paadinar aadinr polindhanar vizhimaari oozi mudhalvarkku urimai thozhil sirappaal vaazhi thiru thillai vaazh anthanarai mun vaith thezhisaiyum oonga eduththaar emai aazhum kaalzhaiyar tham kaavalanar katrangariyompi pannar pathigaththiruk kadai kaappu paravi unnaadum enpum uyirum karaindhu urukkum vinnayakan kooththu vettaveliyediththathu kannaar amudhu undhaar kaa)

Sekkilzhar Peruman, in four verses, describes Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s vision of the divine dance in Thillai with his sacred words. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman stands before Koothaperuman in Thillai and receives his darshan. He openly sees before his eyes the sacred Ambalam, which is the true knowledge granted to him by the Lord, and the unparalleled great divine dance, which is the bliss of Shiva arising from the Shiva-knowledge within him. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman receives all knowledge, which falls under Paragnanam and Aparagnanam.

Lord Shiva bestowed these two types of knowledge upon Pillaiyar.

Lord Shiva blessed Pillaiyar with that true knowledge. That true knowledge, which is the form of Parasakti, is the Ambalam.

Therefore, the knowledge within him and the Ambalam are one and the same; they are identical in both the cosmos and the individual. The dance performed therein is of two types: one is the Fivefold Action (Panchakritya) dance, and the other is the dance of bliss (Ananda Thiru Koothu). The Fivefold Action dance benefits souls in bondage, while the dance of bliss benefits liberated souls. For souls in the state of bondage (petham), the benefits are the conjunction of karma with its fruits. For liberated souls (muktas), the benefits are the blissful experience of Shiva, which is the ultimate among the ten stages of spiritual experience.

Therefore, the true knowledge granted to him by the Lord Annallar is manifested here as the sacred Ambalam.

Thus, Pillaiyar perceives with the same vision, both internally and externally, as one. The Ananda Thiru Koothu is the blissful experience of Shiva, arising from the fullness of true knowledge, experienced internally. Such a dance is indeed a great divine dance. Though knowledge and bliss are not visible to the external eye, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, as if they had manifested visibly, praises them with overflowing joy. If divine merit were a tree, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman would be its tender sprout, signifying excellence, youth, beauty, and essence. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, a sprout of such virtue, thus has this divine vision.

In Thillai, the soul, expanded and freed from impurities by the power of Shiva-Shakti, is experienced by the power of knowledge. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises, saying, “You have graciously enabled us to easily attain the bliss of Shiva (Shivabhogam) and the experience of divine joy (Shivananda) even through external senses, which are usually known only through inner perception. Shivabhogam is inherently an internal experience, understood and enjoyed through inner contemplation. You, the Lord of Dance, have mercifully made it accessible even through external vision, at the level of the senses.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman extols this as the Lord’s unparalleled and great compassion.

Therefore, the truth that merely seeing Thillai grants liberation arises from this compassion, which no one else can bestow.

Thus, the Shivabhogam, which is experienced internally, He praises the Lord of Dance, who graciously made the internal Shivabhogam accessible even through external senses, at the level of the five senses. He extols the Lord’s incomparable generosity and compassion in the pathigam (decade of verses) he composed. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, with tears of joy raining down, performs an ecstatic dance as he sings the pathigam. The pathigam begins with “Kattangkeriompi” and is dedicated to the Lord of Dance, the primal origin of eons. The Thillai Vazh Andhanargal (Brahmins of Thillai) are special, as they perform services belonging to the Lord.

Therefore, starting with the Thillai Vazh Andhanargal, he composed the pathigam “Kattangkeriompi”. He praises the primal one, the source of all creations, the leader of Shirkazhi, the supreme preceptor. The primal cause of the universe is Shiva, who, when all worlds dissolve into Him at the end of an eon, remains undestroyed and recreates the worlds and beings.

Therefore, He is the first of eons, the one who performs the five cosmic functions, including creation and destruction, through His dance of bliss. The Thillai Vazh Andhanargal are privileged to perform intimate service to such a Lord.

Therefore, beginning with them, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed the pathigam that starts with “Kattangkeriompi kaliyai varame settar vazh Thillai Chitrambalameya.” Having thus begun with “Kattangkeriompi” and completed the pathigam with its concluding verse, he praises the Lord, experiencing His gracious dance in the open space, consuming the nectar that filled his eyes, until his very bones and soul melted. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman experienced the melting divine dance of the Lord of the Devas in the open space, consuming the nectar that filled his eyes. He was one who cried out during his lifetime. This pathigam is set in the Kurinji tune. Sekkizhar Peruman speaks of the greatness of this pathigam, saying, “May the seven tunes flourish.” This pathigam, sung by Pillaiyar in the Kurinji tune, is special. The Kurinji tune has many distinctions; it is born from the chest.

Therefore, this Kurinji tune has many variations, such as Vyazha Kurinji, Mega Raga Kurinji, and Andali Kurinji.

Furthermore, this tune is composed in connection with inner feelings, signifying the intention of uniting with the Lord as the beloved.

Thus, this tune, in its various aspects, This Kurinji tune is uniquely special. We can recall here that the Thillai pathigam of Aludaiya Nambi is also set in the Kurinji tune. Pillaiyar composes this pathigam in this tune. The bone is the support that keeps this body, made of the seven dhatus, intact. Within this body, made of these seven dhatus, resides the soul. As indicated by the saying, “It is, it is not,” and the inference that the soul resides within the illusory machine of the body, the soul within this body is understood through inference.

Thus, the Lord performs His sacred dance in such a way that both the bones, which support this body, and the soul within this body melt. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman thus experienced the Lord’s divine dance in the open space, where the bones and soul melted, and consumed the nectar that filled his eyes and overflowed within him. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman consumed the nectar, immersed in the open space. “Immersing in the open space” refers to the state where the soul, having transcended all tattvas from prithvi (earth) to nada (sound), rests in the pure, transcendent state of Shiva-consciousness, devoid of its own action, immersed in Shivabhogam. This means that Pillaiyar, having transcended the inner senses, experienced and enjoyed the Shivabhogam, even perceiving it through his eyes, which are external senses. Such was Pillaiyar, who wept for a long time to attain the proper time for knowledge, and partook of the nectar of wisdom at Shirkazhi through his holy mouth.

Here, at Thillai, he also partook of that nectar through his eyes.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s vision of the Thillai divine dance, Sekkilappadiyaar explains the Lord’s pathigam within music. This pathigam, sung by the Lord, is the eightieth pathigam in the first Thirumurai, dedicated to the holy site of Thiruchitrambalam, located on the northern bank of the Kaveri River in Chola Nadu. It is set in the Kurinji tune. The first and concluding verses of that pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. “Kattangkkeriompi kaliyai varame settar vazh Thillai Chitrambalameya, Mutraa venthingal mudalvan padame pattra nindrarai pattra pavame. Gnalatthuyir Kaali Gnanachambandhan silatthar kolgai Chitrambalameya.

“Soolappadaiyanai sonna Tamil malai kolatthal padavallar nallare.” We shall continue our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 582, by Sekkizhar Swamigal, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. The Lord, whom neither Thirumal nor Brahma knew, dances His sacred dance in Thillai. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman stands before Him and worships Him at all times with pathigams, which are garlands of words. Standing before the Lord, Pillaiyar bows to the Lord of Dance’s gracious dance, sings pathigams, and consumes the nectar that fills his eyes. He remained there for a long time, unable to move away, composing many garlands of words, many pathigams.

Then, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman circumambulates the golden hall, the Ponnambalam, which is surrounded by countless floods of great Vedas, praising it. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman circumambulates the Ponnambalam. That Ponnambalam is praised by countless Vedas and possesses the greatness of being surrounded and worshipped by many groups of Vedic scholars. According to the reference that the Thiruchitrambalam (chitakasa) shines in the heart of the Vedas, that golden hall, the Thiruchitrambalam, is here the Thiruchitrambalam, and the Vedas surround and praise it. The pillars, windows, planks, and roof tiles of that golden hall are all structured to appear as various mantra components of the Vedas.

Here, he circumambulates and worships such a Ponnambalam. He prostrates on the ground in that outer court, rises, bows at the gate filled with divine beings, and worships the four streets that bestow great austerities. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships the four streets that bestow great austerities. No matter what kind of austerities are performed elsewhere, the fruits of all those austerities are bestowed by these four streets. This is because the Lord of Dance processes through these streets in His chariot, bestowing the ultimate benefit of liberation upon all who behold and worship Him.

Thus, these streets are special and grant the fruits of all austerities. Having thus circumambulated and worshipped the streets, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, fearing to stay in Thiruchitrambalam, goes to Thiruvetkalam, a site near Thiruchitrambalam, and stays there.

Thiruchitrambalam is the heart center of the Cosmic Being and the essence of the power of knowledge. Fearing to stay there, as it is the very essence of the power of knowledge, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman stays at Thiruvetkalam, near Thiruchitrambalam. He goes to Thiruvetkalam and there praises Shiva and sings a pathigam. This holy site of Thiruvetkalam is where Shiva appeared as a hunter and bestowed the Pasupatha Astra upon Arjuna. In that state, the Lord is enshrined here.

Therefore, the Lord’s name here is Pasupathesvarar. As sacrifices are performed here always, it bears the name Thiruvetkalam (place of sacrifice). The Goddess’s name is Sarkunambal, or Nallanayagi. The bamboo tree is the stala vriksha (sacred tree) here. The Nalar Theertham is the sacred tank here. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman stayed at this holy site.

He visits Sabhanayagar in Thillai daily.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having come to Thiruvetkalam, praises the Lord and sings a pathigam. This pathigam is the thirty-ninth pathigam in the first Thirumurai, set in the Takkaragam tune. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: “Andhamum adhiyum agiya annal Araral angyai amardhilangama Mandha muzhavam iyamba malaimagal kana nindradi Chandhamilangku naguthalai gangai thanmadhiyam mayale thadhumba Vendha venniru meippusum vetkalan nannagara Venniyanmadam vilangoli veedhi venkodi engum virindhilanga Nanniya seer valar Kali natsamil Gnanasambandhan pennin.” “Nallal oru bhagam amarndhu peniya Vetkalame mel mozhindha panniyal padal vallarkal pazhiyodu pavam ilare.” Thiruchitrambalam. The theme of this pathigam is as follows: The Lord of the beautiful city of Vetkalam, who smears sacred ash on His body, is the eternal Lord, the beginning and the end.

He desired alms, desired the bull as His mount, and was surrounded by many ganas. He became cold and heat, encompassing both earth and sky. He, the wealthy one, lovingly embraced the good woman (Parvati). These are some of the qualities with which He, seated with the good woman, bestows His grace, as described in this pathigam. Having sung this pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman stayed in Thiruvetkalam, going daily to Thiruchitrambalam, delighting in the sacred dance of the Lord residing in the Perambalam, and then returning to stay in Thiruvetkalam. Peruman stayed there for many days.

After that, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeded to the holy site of Thirkalippalai. He reached Thirkalippalai, where Shiva, holding a deer fawn in His sacred hand, is enshrined, and sang a pathigam filled with truth. Truth is that which is real and unfailing, and that which certainly yields its intended fruit. He composed such a truthful pathigam. That pathigam is the forty-fourth pathigam in the third Thirumurai, set in the Kaushikam tune. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam.

“Vendha kungiliyap pugai vimmame kandam nindrullavum Kazhippalaiyar andhamum mallavum ariyadathor sandhamalavar.” “Meviya Sandhame andhan Kaazhi arumarai Gnanasambandhan payppunal suz kazhippalaiyai sindhaiyal sonna senthamizh vallavar mundhi vanulagaadan muraiyame.” The theme of this pathigam is that the Lord of Thirkalippalai, who is adorned with calmness, is the master whose actions cannot be understood by anyone. Meditate on His feet and attain Him. If you attain and worship Him in this way, your karma will vanish. Having worshipped Balavannanathar and Vedanayaki Ammai at Thirkalippalai, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman then proceeded to the holy site of Shivapuri, also known as Thirunelvayil.

Here, the Lord’s name is Uchchinathesvarar, and the Goddess is Kanakkam. The gooseberry tree is the stala vriksha. Kanaga Theertham and Kirupa Samudram are the sacred tanks. This site is called Thiruchchi and is now known as Shivapuri. There is a stala puranam (legend of the site) called Shivapuri Manmiyam. Having arrived at this site, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises Shiva and sings a pathigam.

That pathigam is the twenty-sixth pathigam in the second Thirumurai, set in the Indalam tune. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: “Pudaiyinar pulli kal porundhiya madaiyinar mani neer Nelvayilar nadaiyil nalvirar kovanan nayandudaiyinar emadhuchchiyare Nen payangu Nelvayil Isanai Shanbai Gnanasambandhan sol ivai pan.” “Payankolap padavallavar vin payankollum vetkaiyalare.” The theme of this pathigam is that the Lord of Nelvayil is eternal. He is the beginning and the end. He resides within us (on our heads) and in the holy site of Shivapuri, which is called Uchchi (peak) and is worshipped by us.

This holy site is also very close to Thiruchitrambalam. Having worshipped these holy sites, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman returns to Thiruvetkalam and stays there, going to Thiruchitrambalam for darshan daily.

Our contemplation continues. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 583, by Sekkizhar Swamigal, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman stays in Thiruvetkalam and daily visits Thiruchitrambalam to witness the sacred dance of Ambalavanar. Adiyavargal (devotees), including Thiruneelakanta Yazhpanar, also witness the dance in the same manner. During these visits, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is astonished to see the great privilege of the Thillai Vazh Andhanargal, who are intimate servants of the sacred feet of the Lord dancing in the Thiruvambalam. The Thillai Vazh Andhanargal are very close to the divine form of the Lord who performs the dance of grace in Thillai, and they perform services such as touching the Lord’s form, performing ablutions, The Thillai Vazh Andhanargal are privileged to perform services such as anointing, adorning, and worshipping the Lord.

There are thousands of others, including the heads of monasteries, Brahmins, and external devotees, who serve the Lord. Among them, the Thillai Vazh Andhanargal alone have the privilege of serving the Lord intimately and closely. Such great fortune belongs only to the Thillai Vazh Andhanargal. This privilege has been inherited by the Thillai Vazh Andhanargal through generations, due to the excellence of their worship according to the Shaiva tradition (Shivagama) and the excellence of their Vedic conduct (Vaidika).

Therefore, when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman observed such a unique situation, which could not be found anywhere else, he felt a sense of pride and wonder. The Thillai Vazh Andhanargal steadfastly uphold Vedic conduct, such as studying the Vedas and performing sacrifices, and they excel in the Shivagama traditions. Seeing their intimacy and Vedic discipline, great affection arose in Pillaiyar’s heart for them. As he contemplated the boundless greatness of the Thillai Vazh Andhanargal, one day, as usual, while traveling from Thiruvetkalam to Thiruppuliyoor (Thiruchitrambalam), the Lord of Dance’s grace manifested. All three thousand Thillai Vazh Andhanargal appeared as Shivaganas (celestial attendants of Shiva) to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Pillaiyar, who had seen them appear as Shivaganas, who live by wearing sacred ash, not only saw this divine vision himself but also showed it to Thiruneelakanta Yazhpanar.

As soon as he saw the Thillai Vazh Andhanargal appear as ganas, Pillaiyar hurried to worship them. Before Pillaiyar could worship the Thillai Vazh Andhanargal, they worshipped Pillaiyar.

Thus, it was impossible to tell who worshipped first, as both Pillaiyar’s worship and the Thillai Vazh Andhanargal’s worship occurred simultaneously.

After this happened, Pillaiyar He circumambulates the streets of Thiruchitrambalam. With ever-increasing and overflowing desire manifest outwardly, Pillaiyar folds his small, red hands above his head and enters the gateway. His mind, detached from all else, merges with Shiva, and with a melting heart, he walks, offering worship. He had seen the Thillai Vazh Andhanargal as Shivaganas. In that state, his mind was firmly fixed on the Lord, and his heart melted because of the Lord’s gracious power, whereby the Lord Himself becomes the devotees.

Thus, he worshipped and entered the Perambalam, where the Lord performs His gracious dance. Standing before the Manickakkuthar (Lord of the Ruby Dance), at the bottom of the Thirukkazhitruppadi (sacred steps), he bowed down and rose. The Perambalam is full of knowledge and all-pervasive. Within it, the Manickakkuthar performs His sacred dance, animating and ruling it as the all-pervading reality. Before that Lord, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman prostrates and rises at the foot of the sacred steps. He then sings a pathigam with great longing, beginning with “Adinay naru neyyodu pal thayir.” In this pathigam, he describes how the Thillai Vazh Andhanargal appeared to him as ganas.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sang of the Thillai Vazh Andhanargal appearing as Shivaganas. That pathigam is the first pathigam in the third Thirumurai, set in the Gandhara Panchamam tune. In the third verse of this pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman describes how the Thillai Vazh Andhanargal appeared as Shivaganas. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: “Adinay naru neyyodu pal thayir Andhanar piriyadha Thiruchitrambalam Nadi nay idama narungondrai nayandhavane Padi nay maraiyodu palkithamum pal sadai pani kalkathir vendhingal Sudi nay arulay surunga yama tholvinaiye Naru poompozhil nanniya Kaliyul nan maraivalla Gnanasambandhan.” “Oorum in thamizhal uyarndhar urai Thillai thannul Eru thol pugazhendhu Chitrambalatthu Isanai isaiyal sonna pathu ivai kurumaru vallar uyarndharudum kuduvare.” Thiruchitrambalam.

In this pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, in the third verse, describes how the Thillai Vazh Andhanargal appeared as ganas. That verse is as follows: “Nilatthar kariya midarrar nalla netrime luttra kanninar pattru Soolatthar sudalaip podi niraniyar sadaiyar Silatthar thozhudhetthu Thiruchitrambalam serththalal kalal sevadi kaithozha kolatthayarulayuna karanam kuruthume.” In this verse, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman explains that The appearance of the Shivaganas, as described by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, is characterized by a blue neck, an eye on the forehead, and a trident. Although these features are not naturally present in the Thillai Vazh Andhanargal, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed this verse in the sense that, at that moment when the Lord revealed the Thillai Vazh Andhanargal as Shivaganas, they appeared with a blue neck (Nilakantha), a third eye on the forehead, and a trident.

Therefore, in this pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman teaches the world that the Thiruchitrambalam, which is worshipped by such Thillai Vazh Andhanargal, is where they offer prayers, and if one worships the Lord dancing within it, ancient karmas will be resolved.

In this manner, in this pathigam, with harmonious music, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman completes this pathigam with the concluding verse, praises the Lord, and becomes immersed in an eternal ocean of bliss. He takes leave of the Lord of Dance, with His long, matted locks, who dances before him, to receive His abundant grace. He circumambulates the Ponnambalam and reaches the outer courtyard of the temple. Pillaiyar bows in the outer courtyard, receives divine grace, and then, after reverently bowing at the beautiful, jeweled gateway, he emerges from the temple. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman passes through each gateway, from the Thiruvannukkan gateway onwards, bowing and taking leave, and finally bows at the outermost gateway, receiving the Lord’s gracious permission. Pillaiyar departs.

At that time, Thiruneelakanta Yazhpanar, who had the privilege of always accompanying Pillaiyar, bows at Pillaiyar’s feet. He requests Thirugnanasambandha Peruman to visit the unique holy sites along the banks of the Niva River, starting with Thiruerukaththampuliyur, his native place. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman agrees to the divine wish.

Therefore, from Thillai, he embarks on a pilgrimage to all the holy sites along the Niva River. Let us go on contemplating. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 584, by Sekkizhar Swamigal, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. As soon as he emerged from the Thillai temple, Thiruneelakanta Yazhpanar requested Pillaiyar to visit Thiruerukaththampuliyur, his birthplace. He also requested him to visit all the holy sites along the Niva River. Moving west from Thillai along the banks of the Niva River, the first holy site is Thiruerukaththampuliyur. Several holy sites are situated in that region along the Niva River.

The Niva River is currently known as Vadavellaru, but in the Thevarams and Thirumurais, it is referred to as the Niva River. Generally, villages located on river banks are highly esteemed, and holy sites on the banks of sacred rivers become especially sacred.

Therefore, it is our tradition to classify pilgrimages along river banks. This is why our elders have categorized and demonstrated holy sites as those on the northern bank and those on the southern bank of the Kaveri.

Similarly, here on the banks of the Niva River, holy sites like Thirukoodalaiyaatrur are situated. Continuing west along this bank for a long distance, on its southern bank lies the holy site of Irukkuvelur, the birthplace of Kanampulla Nayanar. This place is currently known as Belur in Salem district.

Therefore, Thiruneelakanta Yazhpanar first invites Pillaiyar to his village. Just as the Brahmins of Thirunanippalli worshipped Pillaiyar and took him to their village, Thiruneelakanta Yazhpanar requests Pillaiyar to visit his village. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman accepts this request. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman had set out from Shirkazhi due to his great love and devotion to the Lord dancing in Thillai.

After this worship was completed, instead of returning to Shirkazhi, he agreed to Thiruneelakanta Yazhpanar’s request and undertook a pilgrimage to all the holy sites along the Niva River. This was Pillaiyar’s fourth pilgrimage, where his sole activity was to see and worship Shiva in various holy sites. The request made by Yazhpanar is the reason for Pillaiyar’s upcoming fourth pilgrimage. It is during this pilgrimage that the Lord bestows the pearl palanquin upon Pillaiyar at the holy site of Thirunelvayil Arathurai.

Therefore, Thiruneelakanta Yazhpanar’s request to visit Thiruerukaththampuliyur and other holy sites along the Niva River was an indication of divine grace expressed through Thiruneelakanta Yazhpanar.

Thus, Pillaiyar undertakes a pilgrimage to visit all the holy sites along the Niva River. This Niva River is known as Vadavellaru. This river is formed by the confluence of several tributaries. It is a river flowing in northern Tamil Nadu. Rivers like Kanaari River and Ezhumur River, which originate from Kolli Hills (in Salem district) and Pachchaimalai (between Tiruchirappalli and Salem), as well as numerous streams flowing from Kalvarayan Hills, now known as Vashista Nadi (flowing through Attur, Aragalur, Chinnasalem), and rivers like Mayura Nadi, Thirumanimuththaru, Thenaru, which flow from Kalvarayan Hills and their slopes, all merge to form the Vadavellaru. The Thirumanimuththaru mentioned above is the Manimuththaru flowing through Vriddachalam.

Thus, the aforementioned rivers, impounded in numerous dams, canals, and tanks, flow down as clear and abundant water. The Vadavellaru, formed by the confluence of many rivers, flows with waves.

Furthermore, this river, originating from mountains with Shiva temples like Kollikulir Arappalli, flows through holy sites like Thirunelvayil Arathurai and Pennagadam before joining the sea, making its waters sacred. While the waters of some rivers can cause illness to those who bathe or drink them, the Niva River, unlike them, only brings well-being. It marks the northern boundary of Thillai and the border between the middle and Chola countries. This river joins the sea near Parangipettai. This river bank hosts several holy sites, including seven ghats ending with ‘thurai’ such as Vashishtaturai and Arathurai. The holy site of Thirukoodalaiyaatrur is located where the Manimuththaru joins.

Thus, Pillaiyar, departing from Thillai, undertook this pilgrimage westward along the Niva River, observing its course. During this pilgrimage, his father, Sivapada Hrudayar, along with his retinue and devout ascetics, accompanied Pillaiyar. Thiruneelakanta Yazhpanar, who held his lyre in his beautiful hand, came with his wife, Matangachoodamani Ammaiyar.

Thus, departing from Thillai, They reach the vicinity of Thiruerukaththampuliyur. Crossing large tanks and fields, Pillaiyar and others arrive near Thiruerukaththampuliyur. As soon as they approach Thiruerukaththampuliyur, Thiruneelakanta Yazhpanar comes forward, bows, and requests, “This place is my native place.” He bows with the intention that Pillaiyar should come inside, worship the Lord, and purify them. Looking at Thiruneelakanta Yazhpanar, who was bowing, Pillaiyar graciously says, “Oh, revered one, this place has performed immense austerities in the past for you to be born here.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman thus spoke with distinction. This place has housed and worshipped the Lord for a long time. Because of such worship, this place was blessed to have a devotee, who is superior among all devotees, born here.

The penance performed by the people of this place benefited this place. This is the meaning of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s statement. This means that the greatness of this devotee’s arrival surpasses the Lord’s presence in this place.

The devotees themselves are the places where the Lord’s grace shines, where the devotees see the Lord. This is the explanation. “To realize oneself, He gives His own form and resides within to know Himself.” This is from Sivagnanabotham.

Therefore, the Lord residing in this The Lord’s presence in this holy site is a general attribute; the greatness of the devotee’s birth there is a special attribute.

Thus, Pillaiyar, who came for the salvation of this world, spoke. While others’ births are for themselves, Pillaiyar’s divine incarnation was not for himself, but for the salvation of this world. Such a great Pillaiyar spoke thus. Having said this, he went to the Thiruerukaththampuliyur temple and there praised the Lord and sang a pathigam. That pathigam is the eighty-ninth pathigam in the first Thirumurai, set in the Kurinji tune. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: “Padaiyar tharubhootha pagadar uri porvai Udayan Umaiyodum udanaiyiduga.”

“Thangai sadaiyan Erukkaththampuliyur thakukkovil Vidaiyan adiyeththa mevavinai thane Eerar Erukkaththampuliyur uraiyanai Seerar thigal Kali thiruvar Sambandhan Ara arumthamizh malai ivai vallar Parar avaretttha pathivan uraiyare.” The theme of this pathigam is that if one worships the Lord of Thiruerukaththampuliyur, no karmas will afflict them, but instead, blessings will come, and we will attain the sacred feet of the Lord. This holy site of Thiruerukaththampuliyur is currently known as Rajendrapatinam. It is located near Vriddachalam. The Lord’s names are Nilakantesvarar and Swetha Arkavanesvarar. The Goddess’s names are Abeethakuchanamba.

Nayaki, Nilamalar Kanni, Nilotpalambal. The white calotropis is the stala vriksha here. Nilotpal Theertham, Kanda Theertham, Chengaluneer Theertham, and Nila Theertham are the sacred tanks. Vyagrapada and Rudrasanmar worshipped here. Because the white calotropis is the sacred tree, this place is called Erukaththampuliyur. The holy sites worshipped by the sage Vyagrapada are known by the name Puliyur.

This Erukaththampuliyur is one of them. Other Puliyur sites are Perumpatrap Puliyur (Thiruchitrambalam), Thiruppathirippuliyur, Omampuliyur, and Perumpuliyur. This site is known for Rudrasanmar’s worship of Shiva, which cured his muteness. To the east of this village, there is a Shiva temple. This is called Kilkottur Maniyambalam. This is a site sung about by Karuvur Devar in his Thiruvichaippa.

As we have seen before, this is the birthplace of Thiruneelakanta Yazhpanar. The marvelous forms of Thiruneelakanta Yazhpanar and Matangachoodamani Ammaiyar are enshrined here. There is a separate shrine for Thiruneelakanta Yazhpanar on the bank of the pond opposite the temple. Above Dakshinamurthy, in a small temple structure, Sattanathar grants darshan. These are some of the special features of the Thiruerukaththampuliyur site. Having worshipped and bowed at Thiruerukaththampuliyur, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman departed from this site and visited many other sites where Shiva and Uma Devi reside, worshipping them and singing exalted Tamil garlands of verses.

We shall proceed with our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 585, by Sekkizhar Swamigal, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman departs from Thiruerukaththampuliyur and embarks on a pilgrimage towards Vriddachalam. He travels towards Vriddachalam, also known as Thirumudhukundram, visiting many holy sites along the way. He continually offers worship as he travels towards Thirumudhukundram. The Thirumanimuththaru river flows through the holy site of Thiruvriddachalam.

That river, carrying precious gems, encircles Thirumudhukundram. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman travels towards Thirumudhukundram, composing and singing pathigams, which are garlands of words, that speak of reaching Thirumudhukundram. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed seven pathigams for Thirumudhukundram (Vriddachalam). Among them, the pathigam Sekkizhar Peruman refers to here begins with “Matthaavarai niruvik kadal.” This pathigam is dedicated to Thirumudhukundram. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed this pathigam while traveling towards Thirumudhukundram.

Therefore, all the verses in this pathigam conclude with “Mudhu kundru adaivome, Mudhu kundru adaivome” (We shall reach Thirumudhukundram). This event illustrates the fervor and determination one has for a holy site when undertaking a pilgrimage to it. This incident illustrates that it is natural for devotees, when undertaking a pilgrimage to a holy site, to continually sing and speak of its greatness.

Furthermore, in this pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has sung about the sacred Thirumanimuththaru river. He explains the etymology of its name, stating that it is called Manimuththaru because it carries gems from the mountain, washing them ashore. He sings about the Thirumanimuththaru river in the Thevara pathigam, saying, “Ozhirgugumam kondu muththaru vandhadi veezhtharru Mudhukundru adaivome.” Such a pathigam is the twelfth pathigam in the first Thirumurai, set in the Nattappadai tune. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: “Matthaavarai niruvi kadal kadaindhavidam unda Thotthararu mani neel mudi sudarvannana thidaham Kottar malar kulir chandhagil ozhira kungumam kondu Muttharu vandhadiveezhtharru Mudhukundru adaivome Mugilsertharru Mudhukundru adaiyanai migu thol seer Pugazhi nagar marai gnana sambandan urai seidha Nigarillana thamizh malaigal isaiyodu ivai pathum Bhagarum adiyavarkku idar pavam adaiyave.” Thiruchitrambalam. The theme of this pathigam is that we shall reach Thirumudhukundram, where the Manimuththaru, carrying gems, falls at the feet of the Lord and worships Him by circumambulating.

We have already contemplated the history of the Vriddachalam temple in the Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam, which we can recall here.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reaches Thirumudhukundram, singing pathigams. He now arrives at the Thirumudhukundram temple and circumambulates it.

At that time, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sings the special Thiruvirukural pathigam. In the method of temple worship, it is customary to first reach a holy site, circumambulate it, then enter the temple, circumambulate it again, and then proceed inside. Following this custom, while circumambulating the temple, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed the special Thiruvirukural pathigam. Irukural refers to the poetic structure where lines consist of two syllables, as found in this pathigam.

Therefore, the Lord mentions this pathigam, saying, ‘Praise it with துணை மலர்.’ துணை மலர் means two melodic lines, so it refers to lines composed of two beats. It also implies that this pathigam will assist those who learn it. We can also see how Thirugnanasambandhar, in the pathigam’s final verse, explained its benefit: ‘Those skilled in exposition will always prosper.’ This pathigam begins with ‘நின்று மலர்தூவி,’ which signifies offering flowers as well as verses resembling flowers. Thirugnanasambandhar, who circumambulates and worships Thirumudhukundram by offering flowers, also worships with vocal flowers, meaning praising with words. This is what is meant by ‘soll malar’ (word flower) in Tamil, referring to ‘Mantra Pushpam’ (flower of mantras). This pathigam is the ninety-third pathigam in the first Thirumurai, set to the tune of Kurinjipann.

Its specialty is that it is structured in the metrical form called Thiruvirukku Kural. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: (nindru malardhuuvi indru mudhukundraiy nanrum eettuviirkku endrum inbame nindru mudhukundraiy nanru sambandhan onrum urai vallar endrum uyarvare) Thiruchitrambalam. After composing this pathigam while circumambulating the temple, Thirugnanasambandhar enters the temple, stands before the Lord, and offers a cool Tamil garland of verses beginning with ‘Murasu adhirndhu ezhum,’ worshiping the Lord. Standing before the Lord in this manner, the pathigam offered, beginning with ‘Murasu adhirndhu ezhum,’ is set in Sadharipann. A unique feature of this pathigam is what is known as Thirumukkaal. Thirumukkaal refers to the metrical structure of the verses.

In each verse of this pathigam, the phrase ‘parasamar padaivudayir’ is placed at the end of the second line and again at the beginning of the third line. Because this phrase is interwoven, as in ‘parasamar padaivudayir umai paravuvaar,’ these verses appear to have three lines instead of four, like Viruthams, thus giving this verse the name Thirumukkaal. This pathigam, structured in this way, is the ninety-first pathigam in the third Thirumurai, set to Sadharipann. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: (murasu adhirndhezudharu mudhukundrameviya parasamar padaivudaiyire parasamar padaivudaiyir umai paravuvaar arasargal ulagil aavare muudiya solai suul mudhukundrathu eesanai naadiya gnanasambandhan naadiya gnanasambandhan sendhamizh paadiya avar pazhiyile) Thiruchitrambalam. Having offered this pathigam, Thirugnanasambandhar, due to his profound love for Viruthagiriswarar of Thirumudhukundram, stayed in that place for many days, offering pathigams and worshiping the Lord.

Additionally, four more pathigams offered by Thirugnanasambandhar exist. They are as follows: In total, we have discussed seven pathigams for this sacred place, and we have contemplated three of them.

Now, the fourth pathigam for this place is the fifty-third pathigam in the first Thirumurai, set to the tune of Pazhandhakkaraga. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: (devaraayum asuraraayum sidhdhar sezhu maraiserr navaraayum nannu paarum vin erikaal niirum mevaraaya virai malaron senganmaal eesan ennum muvaraaya mudhal oruvan meya mudhukundre moythu vaanorr palganangal vanangu mudhukundraiy pidhdharvedam perumai enum piramapurath thalaivan) The last two lines of the eleventh verse, which is the final verse of this pathigam, are not available to us.

Now, for this sacred place, the fifth pathigam offered by Thirugnanasambandhar is the one hundred and thirty-first pathigam in the first Thirumurai, set to the tune of Megaraga Kurinji. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: (meitthaaru suvaiyum eezhisaiyum en gunangalum virumbu naalvedaththaalum arivonna nadai theliya palinge pol arivaipaagam otthaaru samayangalukku oru thalaivan karudhum uurlavu thenniir muththaaru edhirudhara nitthilam vaarik kozhikkum mudhukundrame muzhangolinii muththaaru valanjcheyyum mudhukundrathu iraiyaim muuva pazhangkizhamai panniru per padaiththudaiya kazhumalame padhiyaa kondu thalankeri muundroombu thozhil thamizh gnanasambandhan samaiththa paadal vazhangum isai kuudum vagai paadum avar) (niidulagam aazhvardhame) Thiruchitrambalam.

Now, the sixth pathigam offered by Thirugnanasambandhar for the sacred place of Virudhachalam is the sixty-fourth pathigam in the second Thirumurai, set to the tune of Gandharapann. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: (devaasiriyom pizhaiyai poruppaay periyone aavaa endangadiyar thangatkkarul seyvaay ovaa uvari kolla uyarnthaa endreiththi muuva munivar vanangum koyil mudhukundre araiyaar kadal suuzh kaali sambandhan munivar vanangum koyil mudhukundraiy kuraiyaa panuval kuudi paada vallaargal piraiyaar sadayam perumaan kadalgal piriyare) Thiruchitrambalam.

Now, the seventh pathigam offered by Thirugnanasambandhar for the sacred place of Virudhachalam is in the third Thirumurai, the thirty-fourth pathigam, set to Kollipann.

(vannamaamalar kodu vaanavar vazhipada annalaar aayizhaiyaalodum amarvidam vinnin maa mazhai pozhindhu izhiya vellaruviseer thinnilaar puravani thirumudhukundrame thinninar puravani thirumudhukundraiy nanniyul gnanasambandhan sol enninaal iiraainthu maalaim இயலுமா panninaar paaduvaarkku illaiyaam paavame) Having worshiped Thirumudhukundram, Thirugnanasambandhar takes leave from Virudhagirisa Peruman and proceeds to the sacred place of Pennagadam. He prostrates before the feet of Lord Shiva, the incomparable supreme light who resides willingly within the temple of the sacred place known as Thungaanaimadam, where the sound of the revered Vedas resonates. He circumambulates the temple, prostrates before the Lord, rises, and offers a garland of sweet Tamil verses, a pathigam. In this sacred place, Thirugnanasambandhar notes that Brahmins constantly praise the Lord, and in every home, Vedas are studied, ensuring that the sound of Vedic chants continuously echoes. The sanctum sanctorum of this temple is structured like a Maadakoyil, resembling a sleeping elephant, thus forming the shape of a Pranava.

Accordingly, this place is renowned for the Vedas. Within this temple, Lord Shiva, as the singular supreme light, resides. As Shivagnanabodham states, ‘One is the Lord,’ a singular supreme light resides here. He is incomparable. The Lord, being peerless, resides there as the singular supreme light. He is beyond all living beings in the world.

Such a supreme light, Lord Shiva, resides here, and thus the Lord’s name is Sudarkozhundhisar. In that temple, where Lord Shiva resides as a singular supreme light, Thirugnanasambandhar approaches the Lord, bows down, and offers a pathigam to instruct the people of this world. Thirugnanasambandhar’s pathigam advises the people of the world: ‘If you wish to be free from harm, worship Thungaanaimadam.’ This pathigam offered by Thirugnanasambandhar for Thungaanaimadam temple, known as Pennagadam, is the fifty-ninth pathigam in the first Thirumurai, set to the tune of Pazhandhakkaraga. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: (odungum pini piravi kedu endu ivai udaiththaaya vazhkkai ozhiya thavam adangum idam karudhi nindreerellam adigal adi nizhal kizh aalaam vannam kidangum madhilum sulaaviyum kezhumanagaaldhorum maraiyin oli thodangum kadanthai thadangkoil ser thungaanaimadam thozhuminngale mannar muzhavadhirum maadaviidhi vayarkkazhi gnanasambandhan nalla pennagaththup perungkoil ser piraiyurinjjum thungaanaimadam eeyaan kannaar kazhal paravu paadal patthum karutthunara katraarumkettaarum poy vinnor ulagaththu mevivaazhum vidhiyedhuve) (aagum vinai maayume) Thiruchitrambalam. We have contemplated the local history of this sacred Thungaanaimadam temple in Thiruppennagadam within the biography of Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar.

We can recall that here as well. We shall go on deliberating. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Sekkizhar Swamigal’s Periya Puranam, Part 586, Vambara Varivandu Sarga. Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Sudarkozhundhisar, who resides in Thungaanaimadam, is worshipped by two groups: those who pray not to be reborn and those who have achieved the state of not being reborn, meaning those who have attained liberation. Those who wish to avoid rebirth worship Sudarkozhundhisar to prevent further births.

At the same time, those who have attained liberation and thus will not be reborn worship the Lord to avoid the taint of karmic residues.

Thus, Sudarkozhundhisar is worshipped by both types of devotees. Thirugnanasambandhar, having worshipped the Lord residing in Thungaanaimadam, receives his grace and decides to proceed to the sacred place of Thiruvarathurai. Previously, during his pilgrimages, Thirugnanasambandhar mostly traveled on the shoulders of Shivapadakiruthayar. Sometimes he walked, and at other times, Brahmins carried the child on their shoulders.

Now, after deciding to go to the sacred place of Thiruvarathurai, Thirugnanasambandhar avoids both his father’s shoulders and those of others. Instead, with both these great individuals walking by his side, Thirugnanasambandhar walks on foot towards the sacred place of Thirunelvaayil Arathurai. In this sacred place of Thirunelvaayil Arathurai, Lord Shiva has blessed Pillaiyar with a pearl palanquin, a pearl umbrella, and sacred trumpets.

Therefore, Pillaiyar walking towards Thirunelvaayil Arathurai is an initial indication of the divine event where the Lord will bestow a palanquin upon Pillaiyar, and he will ascend it to reach Thiruvarathurai. Thirugnanasambandhar proceeds very quickly, filled with intense desire, towards Thiruvarathurai of the Primal Lord. As Pillaiyar walks, his father, Adhiyar of Thiruvarathurai, also feels distressed. Due to walking for many hours on those intensely hot days, and because Thirugnanasambandhar’s feet are as tender as buds, his feet became slightly sore.

Here, the great Lord sings about Pillaiyar’s feet, implying that Pillaiyar himself was not at all distressed.

Therefore, Pillaiyar, without any fatigue, continues to proceed swiftly. As if all the Vedas had taken form, Thirugnanasambandhar hurries to worship the Lord of Thirunelvaayil Arathurai. As if all the Vedas and other arts had taken form, as if a crescent moon of sixteen arts had gathered to form a full moon, and as if that very moon had descended to earth, Kaali Pillaiyar arrives there. He approaches Thiruvarathurai, where the Lord who bears the Ganga resides. Thirugnanasambandhar, though devoid of worldly attachments, is a child-like figure radiant with divine light, due to his devotion to the Lord. As Shivagnanabodham states, ‘The form and the temple are worshipped as a fortress,’ worshipping in a temple is ordained for Jivanmuktas who have shed attachments.

This is ordained for Jivanmuktas to prevent the taint of residual karmic impressions when their intellect, desires, and actions occasionally extend outwards into the world. However, here, Pillaiyar is in a state of purity, free from any impurities such as residual karmic impressions.

Therefore, even though he is devoid of other attachments, he goes to worship the Lord of Thiruvarathurai with the desire to do so. Such a Pillaiyar, who is the embodiment of divine light, goes to worship the Lord of Thiruvarathurai. He goes, worshipping the Lord of Thiruvarathurai. The jewel of the Vedic lineage, Pillaiyar, who came to dispel the darkness of this vast world, bows low before the feet of his father, Lord Shiva, whose red matted hair holds the great nectar that wells up in his mind, and then rises and proceeds. The implication here is that the darkness of this world will be dispelled by the radiance of the sacred ash from the pearl palanquin that Pillaiyar is about to receive.

Therefore, Pillaiyar, who came to dispel darkness, proceeds quickly towards Thiruvarathurai, where the Lord resides. He proceeds, worshipping, bowing low and rising.

Thus, it is implied that every devotee should perform these acts of worship and devotion during pilgrimages. As he continues his pilgrimage, the village of Maranpadi appears.

At that time, Thirugnanasambandhar’s companions, become tired and distressed. Pillaiyar feels no fatigue or distress, but his companions, having walked a long distance and being exposed to the heat, are exhausted and weary. Pillaiyar arrives at the village of Maranpadi, constantly chanting the glorious Sri Panchaksharam, the five-letter sacred mantra. Pillaiyar took birth for the salvation of the world.

Therefore, the sun, seeing the fatigue caused by the long walk and the heat to Thirugnanasambandhar’s companions, fears. So, it withdraws its countless rays and sets in the western sea, and night falls.

Thus, on that night, Pillaiyar stays in the village of Maranpadi with the devotees who surrounded him, those great ascetics.

The devotees surrounding Pillaiyar are those who praise him; they are those who, through their penance directed towards Lord Shiva, have gained Pillaiyar’s company and, through that association, have triumphed over harm. As all these devotees accompanying Pillaiyar stay there, Pillaiyar resides in Maranpadi that night. To alleviate Pillaiyar’s distress, Lord Shiva residing in Thiruvarathurai decides to act. What distress has befallen Pillaiyar? As we previously saw, Pillaiyar was not distressed by his feet becoming sore.

However, because his companions were fatigued due to the long walk and the heat, Pillaiyar had to stay in Maranpadi that night, unable to reach Thiruvarathurai as he wished. This distress, which the Lord here refers to as Pillaiyar’s mental distress and travel weariness, is what the Lord decides to alleviate. Lord Shiva, who resides in Thiruvarathurai, resolves to remove that distress, because is it not the Lord who willingly bears and relieves the burdens of those who come to Him?

Therefore, to remove Pillaiyar’s travel weariness, and to prevent such weariness from occurring again, the Lord of Thirunelvaayil Arathurai resolved. Our deliberation continues. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Sekkizhar Swamigal’s Periya Puranam, Part 586, Vambara Varivandu Sarga. Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Sudarkozhundhisar, who resides in Thungaanaimadam, is worshipped by two groups: those who pray not to be reborn and those who have achieved the state of not being reborn, meaning those who have attained liberation. Those who wish to avoid rebirth worship Sudarkozhundhisar to prevent further births.

At the same time, those who have attained liberation and thus will not be reborn worship the Lord to avoid the taint of karmic residues.

Thus, Sudarkozhundhisar is worshipped by both types of devotees. Thirugnanasambandhar, having worshipped the Lord residing in Thungaanaimadam, receives his grace and decides to proceed to the sacred place of Thiruvarathurai. Previously, during his pilgrimages, Thirugnanasambandhar mostly traveled on the shoulders of Shivapadakiruthayar. Sometimes he walked, and at other times, Brahmins carried the child on their shoulders.

Now, after deciding to go to the sacred place of Thiruvarathurai, Thirugnanasambandhar avoids both his father’s shoulders and those of others. Instead, with both these great individuals walking by his side, Thirugnanasambandhar walks on foot towards the sacred place of Thirunelvaayil Arathurai. In this sacred place of Thirunelvaayil Arathurai, Lord Shiva has blessed Pillaiyar with a pearl palanquin, a pearl umbrella, and sacred trumpets.

Therefore, Pillaiyar walking towards Thirunelvaayil Arathurai is an initial indication of the divine event where the Lord will bestow a palanquin upon Pillaiyar, and he will ascend it to reach Thiruvarathurai. Thirugnanasambandhar proceeds very quickly, filled with intense desire, towards Thiruvarathurai of the Primal Lord. As Pillaiyar walks, his father, Adhiyar of Thiruvarathurai, also feels distressed. Due to walking for many hours on those intensely hot days, and because Thirugnanasambandhar’s feet are as tender as buds, his feet became slightly sore.

Here, the great Lord sings about Pillaiyar’s feet, implying that Pillaiyar himself was not at all distressed.

Therefore, Pillaiyar, without any fatigue, continues to proceed swiftly. As if all the Vedas had taken form, Thirugnanasambandhar hurries to worship the Lord of Thirunelvaayil Arathurai. As if all the Vedas and other arts had taken form, as if a crescent moon of sixteen arts had gathered to form a full moon, and as if that very moon had descended to earth, Kaali Pillaiyar arrives there. He approaches Thiruvarathurai, where the Lord who bears the Ganga resides. Thirugnanasambandhar, though devoid of worldly attachments, is a child-like figure radiant with divine light, due to his devotion to the Lord. As Shivagnanabodham states, ‘The form and the temple are worshipped as a fortress,’ worshipping in a temple is ordained for Jivanmuktas who have shed attachments.

This is ordained for Jivanmuktas to prevent the taint of residual karmic impressions when their intellect, desires, and actions occasionally extend outwards into the world. However, here, Pillaiyar is in a state of purity, free from any impurities such as residual karmic impressions.

Therefore, even though he is devoid of other attachments, he goes to worship the Lord of Thiruvarathurai with the desire to do so. Such a Pillaiyar, who is the embodiment of divine light, goes to worship the Lord of Thiruvarathurai. He goes, worshipping the Lord of Thiruvarathurai. The jewel of the Vedic lineage, Pillaiyar, who came to dispel the darkness of this vast world, bows low before the feet of his father, Lord Shiva, whose red matted hair holds the great nectar that wells up in his mind, and then rises and proceeds. The implication here is that the darkness of this world will be dispelled by the radiance of the sacred ash from the pearl palanquin that Pillaiyar is about to receive.

Therefore, Pillaiyar, who came to dispel darkness, proceeds quickly towards Thiruvarathurai, where the Lord resides. He proceeds, worshipping, bowing low and rising.

Thus, it is implied that every devotee should perform these acts of worship and devotion during pilgrimages. As he continues his pilgrimage, the village of Maranpadi appears.

At that time, Thirugnanasambandhar’s companions, become tired and distressed. Pillaiyar feels no fatigue or distress, but his companions, having walked a long distance and being exposed to the heat, are exhausted and weary. Pillaiyar arrives at the village of Maranpadi, constantly chanting the glorious Sri Panchaksharam, the five-letter sacred mantra. Pillaiyar took birth for the salvation of the world.

Therefore, the sun, seeing the fatigue caused by the long walk and the heat to Thirugnanasambandhar’s companions, fears. So, it withdraws its countless rays and sets in the western sea, and night falls.

Thus, on that night, Pillaiyar stays in the village of Maranpadi with the devotees who surrounded him, those great ascetics.

The devotees surrounding Pillaiyar are those who praise him; they are those who, through their penance directed towards Lord Shiva, have gained Pillaiyar’s company and, through that association, have triumphed over harm. As all these devotees accompanying Pillaiyar stay there, Pillaiyar resides in Maranpadi that night. To alleviate Pillaiyar’s distress, Lord Shiva residing in Thiruvarathurai decides to act. What distress has befallen Pillaiyar? As we previously saw, Pillaiyar was not distressed by his feet becoming sore.

However, because his companions were fatigued due to the long walk and the heat, Pillaiyar had to stay in Maranpadi that night, unable to reach Thiruvarathurai as he wished. This distress, which the Lord here refers to as Pillaiyar’s mental distress and travel weariness, is what the Lord decides to alleviate. Lord Shiva, who resides in Thiruvarathurai, resolves to remove that distress, because is it not the Lord who willingly bears and relieves the burdens of those who come to Him?

Therefore, to remove Pillaiyar’s travel weariness, and to prevent such weariness from occurring again, the Lord of Thirunelvaayil Arathurai resolved. We shall proceed with our deliberation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Sekkizhar Swamigal’s Periya Puranam, Part 589, Vambara Varivandu Sarga. Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandhar ascended the brilliant pearl palanquin.

The devotees, immersed in divine grace, chanted ‘Hara Hara.’ The Vedas themselves resonated, drums thundered, the heavens showered flowers, conchs blared, horns sounded, and the various branches of the Vedas also resounded. Relatives rejoiced. The pearl palanquin, bound by the grace of the Lord who is the life of life, shone brightly with its abundant pearls. The white umbrella, raised above, also shone brightly. This Thus, Thirugnanasambandhar shines with the light of sacred ash on a pearl palanquin that emanates white rays. It is as if the moon, rising from the milky ocean, appears on the pearl palanquin.

Numerous devotees, Brahmins, and others approach, their hearts overflowing with joy, their flower-like hands clasped above their heads, dancing as if possessed. Overwhelmed by immeasurable happiness, they are submerged in the flood of tears pouring from their eyes. The trumpet, called ‘Ekkalam,’ granted by Shiva, is adorned with the beauty of red gold and white pearls. It was given by Shiva, the leader of Shaivism and the four Vedas. Such a trumpet, called ‘Ekkalam’ ...the trumpet proclaims, ‘Thirugnanasambandhar has arrived!’ It trumpets that Thirugnanasambandhar has come to uplift all seven worlds, the four Vedas, and those of profound penance.
