The trumpet and other instruments like the ‘thari’ do not merely produce music like other instruments; they are designed to amplify the praises and propagate the true glories of Thirugnanasambandhar with magnified sound.

Now, the venerable Sekkizhar describes the messages that the beloved devotees proclaim through this trumpet. They trumpet, ‘Thirugnanasambandhar has arrived so that all seven worlds and the Vedas may be saved.’ The salvation of the Vedas refers to ...the Vedas, which were the divine word of God but inaccessible to all, became universally beneficial when they emerged as Tamil Vedas through the divine utterance of Pillaiyar.

Thus, it is trumpeted that Thirugnanasambandhar has arrived for the salvation of the Vedas. The trumpet also proclaims that Thirugnanasambandhar has arrived so that all ascetics may realize their penance and attain liberation. The great roars of mighty ascetics resound there. Devotees proclaim that the child who was nourished with the nectar of wisdom from the overflowing breast of the Divine Mother, who is the embodiment of wisdom, has arrived through the sacred trumpet that Shiva, who burned the three cities, graciously destroyed. They sing true glories.

Here, the name ‘Balaravaayan’ refers to Thirugnanasambandhar. ‘Palaraamai’ signifies the ever-flowing, abundant Shiva-wisdom, like milk, in the form of Thevaram music.

Therefore, the name ‘Balaravaayan’ is given to Thirugnanasambandhar.

Furthermore, devotees sing true glories using that trumpet, praising Thirugnanasambandhar as the one who, without studying, inherently understood the great Vedas and all the arts derived from them, a master of the three Tamils. Surrounded by crowds of devotees, Thirugnanasambandhar thus arrives at Thiruvaratthurai. Shiva bestows wealth, knowledge, and enjoyment upon those who worship him. Wealth is distinct from knowledge.

Here, wealth refers to something other than gold and the like ...the instrumental knowledge to perceive true reality. Knowledge here means Shiva-wisdom. Enjoyment, once knowledge is attained, is Shiva-bhoga, which is the final of the ten actions.

Thus, Shiva is the one who bestows wealth, knowledge, and enjoyment upon those who worship him. Such a Shiva is enshrined in Thirunelvayil Aratthurai. Thirugnanasambandhar arrives at this temple even before entering. Upon seeing the gopuram (temple tower) gateway and the gopuram from a distance, the rule is to bow to them.

Accordingly, as soon as he perceives the Thirunelvayil Aratthurai gopuram from afar, Thirugnanasambandhar descends from his palanquin and bows to the gopuram and its gateway. The gopuram is a sthula lingam, a manifest form of Shiva.

Therefore, bowing to the gopuram and rising, with increasing desire and joy in his heart, Thirugnanasambandhar proceeds ahead and enters the Thiruvaratthurai temple. Thirugnanasambandhar clasped his flower-like hands on his head. Pillaiyar danced, his body drenched by flowing tears. Remembering the grace of the Lord who has long resided lovingly in Thiruvaratthurai, Pillaiyar sang a pathigam in seven melodies. This pathigam, composed by Pillaiyar, is currently unavailable to us. Praising and completing such a pathigam with seven melodies, Pillaiyar stood in worship and ...received Shiva’s grace and stayed in that sacred place for a few days.

Thirugnanasambandhar, the child who received divine grace so that all in every direction might attain Shiva-wisdom and be saved, resided there with his unwavering devotees in Thirunelvayil Aratthurai. During those days, he visited and worshipped sacred places like Thirunelvennai, where Shiva is enshrined. Pillaiyar, the leader of Sirkazhi, worshipped all such shrines and returned to Thiruvaratthurai, where he stayed. The nearby shrines that Thirugnanasambandhar visited and worshipped include Thirunelvennai and other such sacred places. Of these, only the pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandhar for Thirunelvennai is available to us. This sacred place, Thirunelvennai, is now known as Neivena.

It is located in Tamil Nadu, on the Ulundurpettai-Thirukkoilur road, near Elavanasurkottai, next to Eraiyur village. From there, the road to Vadakurumbur leads to this place called Neivena. The Lord’s names here are Sorna Kadeswarar, Vennaiyappar, Nelvennai Nathar. The Goddess’s names are Piragan Nayaki, Neelamalar Kanni. Though the Sthala Vriksham (sacred tree) is mentioned as the Punnai tree, that tree is currently not there. The Bilva tree serves as the Sthala Vriksham.

The Pennai River is the sacred water source. This is a place where the four sons of Brahma—Sanakar, Sanandanar, Sanathanar, and Sanatkumara—worshipped and attained blessings. Daily, devotees perform external oil abhishekham to the Lord and conduct worship. Appar Peruman has enshrined this place as a ‘vaippu thalam’ (a place mentioned in his hymns) in his pathigam.

Here, Thirugnanasambandhar, who arrived from Thirunelvayil Aratthurai, composed a pathigam. It is the ninety-sixth pathigam in the third Thirumurai, set in Sadari pann. The songs of this pathigam are composed in the Thirumukkal poetic meter. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. ‘Solvanam iduvathu sollai nilamalku thol pugazh Nelvenai Eesanai nalamalku Gnanasambandhan nalamalku Gnanasambandhan sendhamizh sol.’ ‘They are free from suffering.’ Thiruchitrambalam. ‘O Lord residing in Nelvennai, those who praise and worship you daily will be free from fear and karma, free from blame, and possess fame, fortune, and virtue.’ This is the summary of this pathigam. Sekkizhar Peruman sings that Thirugnanasambandhar thus worshipped and visited places like Thirunelvennai. It is possible that these places include Thiruvellai Nallur, Thiruvidaiyaru, and other nearby shrines.

However, the pathigams composed by Pillaiyar for these shrines are not available to us. While Thirugnanasambandhar was staying at the Thirunelvayil Aratthurai shrine, the Lord who resides in Thiruththani in Sirkazhi and the Goddess Thirunilai Nayaki appeared in his heart, filling and entering his being. They manifested in his consciousness.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandhar, with his heart melting, wished to go to the beautiful Sirkazhi. So, he bowed to the Lord of Thiruvaratthurai, received His immense divine grace and permission, and with the beautiful feet of Shiva, who fills the heart with blissful dance and takes possession, held upon his head, Thirugnanasambandhar ascended the luminous pearl palanquin. The Lord’s feet are the embodiment of divine grace. They are beautiful, shining and pervasive, as the Lord’s grace manifests exceptionally in the pure consciousness of those freed from the three impurities. These are the anklets of the dancing Lord. Thirugnanasambandhar places the sacred feet of the dancing Lord on his head and ascends the palanquin.

Pillaiyar, having left Sirkazhi to worship Thiruthillai, worships Thiruthillai. At the request of Thiruneelakanta Panar, he travels along the Nivai River bank, worshipping shrines such as Thiru Erukaththampaliyur.

At this time, realizing that many days have passed since he saw Thoniyappar, who bestowed wisdom’s nectar upon him, his heart melts, and he resolves to return to Sirkazhi. Although tradition dictates that he should return to Sirkazhi via the same route he took to Thirunelvayil Aratthurai after worshipping Thiruthillai ...Thirugnanasambandhar, driven by an intense desire to see the Lord of Sirkazhi, quickly takes a different path.

Therefore, remembering and praising the feet of the Lord who performs the great divine dance in Thillai, he places them on his head and ascends the palanquin, continuing his pilgrimage. Although Thirugnanasambandhar mounted the palanquin, he did not view it as a mere vehicle, but as the divine grace of the Lord. Instead of being carried by that grace, he embraced the perception that he himself was carrying the ocean of grace that bestowed it, placing it upon his head. Thirugnanasambandhar arose, taking it as his duty to uplift souls by bearing divine grace upon his head and making Shiva’s greatness known to the world. This is symbolized by Pillaiyar ascending the palanquin.

Thus, Pillaiyar continues his pilgrimage towards his native place, Sirkazhi. Let us go on pondering. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam by Sekkizhar Swamigal, Part 590, Vampira Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandhar departs from Thirunelvayil Aratthurai towards Sirkazhi. He ascends the pearl palanquin granted by the Lord and begins his journey. Sekkizhar Peruman composes the verse: ‘The Vedas roared, the strong Tamil hymns echoed, the horns blared, the conches trumpeted, the trumpets sounded in order, the drums boomed, and the sound of praise resonated.’ As soon as Thirugnanasambandhar ascended the pearl palanquin and set off, the Vedas roared, the powerful Tamil hymns resonated, the sounds of horns rang out, the conches trumpeted, and the trumpets ...in an orderly manner, blew, proclaiming the true glories of Thirugnanasambandhar. Various musical instruments sounded, and large drums boomed.

Above all these, the sound of devotees praising Thirugnanasambandhar resonated, surpassing all other sounds. The chanting of ‘Harahara’ resounded above the music of all instruments.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandhar continued his pilgrimage, proceeding towards Sirkazhi.

Therefore, people in the villages along the way welcomed Thirugnanasambandhar. On both sides, they adorned the path with flags, beautiful cloths, canopies, temporary arches, banana and betel nut trees, and dense garlands. They welcomed him by arranging lamps and overflowing pots in rows. In all the places where devotees and the public welcomed Thirugnanasambandhar, he visited the temples of Shiva, composed glorious Tamil pathigams, bowed to Shiva’s feet, and continued his journey. The exact shrines that Thirugnanasambandhar visited and worshipped after departing from Thirunelvayil Aratthurai are unknown to us, and the pathigams related to these shrines are also unavailable. Since there are Shiva temples in places like Ezhumbur (a vaippu thalam), Valikandapuram, Thuraimangalam, and Ariyalur, Thirugnanasambandhar must have visited these shrines, because Pillaiyar is next expected to visit ...Thirupazhuvur.

Therefore, the shrines from Thirunelvayil Aratthurai to Thirupazhuvur must be located in the current Perambalur and Trichy regions.

Thus, after visiting many shrines, Pillaiyar arrives at Thirupazhuvur. Thirupazhuvur is the place where Shiva joyfully flayed the elephant demon. Pillaiyar, upon reaching this sacred place, bowed to the beautiful gopuram of the Lord’s temple, entered the temple, circumambulated the long vimana, and then, standing before the Lord, bowed to Shiva’s lotus-like feet and composed a pathigam. In this Thirupazhuvur, Brahmins from the Malaiyala Desam (Kerala) resided and performed countless excellent services to Shiva.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandhar has praised these Malaiyala Brahmins and their greatness in the pathigam for this sacred place. The phrases that Thirugnanasambandhar used to praise the Malaiyala Brahmins in the pathigam are as follows: ‘Manna-in misai aadi malaiyaalar thozhuthu eeththi pannan oli-konda payilkinra Pazhuvure’ in the fourth verse of this pathigam, and ‘Vedha mozhi solli maraiyaalar iraivanthan padhamavai eeththa’ in the fifth verse, and ‘Ontrum iru moontrum oru naangum unarvaazhkan manrinil irunthu udan magizhndha’ in the ninth verse, and the Brahmins of the mountain ...’He praised’ in the eleventh verse, Pillaiyar has thus composed. Such a pathigam is the thirty-fourth pathigam of the second Thirumurai, set in Indalappann. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. ‘Muttan migu muvilai nal velan viri nul an aththan emaiy aludaiya annal idam enbar maiththalai perum pozhilin vasamathu veesa pattharu sitthar payilkinra Pazhuvure.’ ‘The Brahmins, the Malayalis, praise the Lord of Pazhuvur, who is surrounded by devotees and filled with devotion. Gnanasambandhan, who understood profound wisdom, having recited these ten verses, will be praised by those who live in heaven.’ Thiruchitrambalam. This pathigam is a unique pathigam called Thiruvirakam.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandhar worshipped this shrine. This place of worship, Thirupazhuvur, is located in the Chola country, and it is the fifty-fifth shrine on the north bank of the Kaveri River. This shrine is situated northwest of Thiruvaiyaru. One can reach this place from Ariyalur, Thiruvaiyaru, Thanjavur, and Trichy. Pazhuvur is divided into two parts: Melapazhuvur and Keelapazhuvur. Among these, the shrine for which Thirugnanasambandhar composed a pathigam is Keelapazhuvur.

Melapazhuvur has a temple called Maravaneeswaram. The Lord’s names here are Vadamoolanathar, Yogavaneswarar, Alanthuraiyar. The Goddess’s name is Arunthavanayaki. The Kaveri and Brahma Theertham are the sacred waters. This shrine is named Pazhuvur because it has the Banyan tree as its Sthala Vriksham. ‘Pazhu’ means Banyan tree.

The place is called Yogavanam because the Goddess performed penance there. It is said that Parasurama attained Shiva’s grace here after performing penance to absolve himself of the sin of killing his mother at his father’s command. The place where the valorous act of Gajasaṁharam (slaying the elephant demon) occurred is commonly referred to as Veeraṭṭam Vazhuvur, which is located near Mayiladuthurai.

However, that Vazhuvur is a ‘vaippu thalam’ (a place mentioned in hymns but not necessarily having a specific hymn). This Pazhuvur has a pathigam by Thirugnanasambandhar. In that pathigam, in the sixth verse, ‘Mavayar anru urisai mainthanidam enbar,’ Thirugnanasambandhar has described the historical event of the Lord flaying the elephant. Sekkizhar Peruman also, when referring to this place, mentions the elephant flaying incident by saying ‘panai nedunkai marittha’ ’...thavar magizh perumpazhuvur.’ These are all worthy of contemplation. Having composed the pathigam, Thirugnanasambandhar received gracious leave from the Lord and, accompanied by all, proceeded to Thiruvijayamangai, a sacred place where Shiva lovingly resides. In Thiruvijayamangai, a village where Brahmins live, he circumambulated and worshipped the unparalleled temple of Shiva.

Standing before the Lord, he bowed and composed a pathigam. In that pathigam, Thirugnanasambandhar praised and hymned in his pure Tamil pathigam the history of cows and Kamadhenu worshipping the Lord at this shrine of Thiruvijayamangai. In the second verse of the pathigam for this shrine, Pillaiyar has thus described ‘Godhanam vazhipada’ (the worship by cows).

Thus, the pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandhar for Thiruvijayamangai is the seventeenth pathigam of the third Thirumurai, set in Ganthara Panchamam pann. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. ‘Maruvamar kuzhalumai pangarin vaarsadai aravamar kolgaiyam adigal koyilaam kuravamar surapunai kongu vengaygal viraviya pozhilani visayamangaiye. Vinnvar thozhudazhu visayamangaiyai nanniya pugazhiyul gnanasambandhan panniya sendhamizh patthum vallavar punniyar sivagathi puguthal thinname.’ Thiruchitrambalam. This shrine, Thiruvijayamangai, is the forty-seventh shrine on the north bank of the Kaveri River in the Chola country. This shrine is located a short distance from Thiruvaikkavur. The Lord’s name is Vijayanathar.

The Goddess’s name is Mangalambikai. Arjuna Theertham is located here. It is called Vijayamangai because Arjuna, also known as Vijaya, worshipped here. This shrine was worshipped by Devas, Kamadhenu cow herds, and a white bull. In the Moolavar (main deity) Shiv Lingam, there is a mark like a scratch from Arjuna’s arrow. Appar Peruman has mentioned Vijayamangai in Kurunthogai as Govandha Puttur on the Kollidam bank.

Govandha Puttur is on the north bank of Kollidam, and this Vijayamangai is on the south bank.

Therefore, these two were considered and referred to as a single town. Hence, the town’s name is considered Govandha Puttur, and the temple’s name is Vijayamangai. The name came about because a cow poured milk over a Shiva Lingam and worshipped it. The stucco figure depicting the cow’s worship is located in the west corridor of the temple. Govandha Puttur is now known as Gokkarandha Puttur. Having worshipped Thiruvijayamangai, Thirugnanasambandhar departed from there and reached Thiruaikkavur, where he composed a pathigam.

Thiru Vaikkavur is the name of the place, but it is popularly known as Vaikkavur. It is the forty-eighth shrine on the north bank of the Kaveri. It can be reached from Kumbakonam, near Swamimalai, by going to Nagukudi and then to Thiruaikkavur. The Lord’s name is Vilvavaneswarar. The Goddess’s name is Sarvajanarakshaki, Valaikkai Nayaki. The Bilva tree is the Sthala Vriksham.

Yama Theertham is the sacred water source. This is the miraculous place where, on a Sivaratri night, a hunter, fearing a tiger, climbed a Bilva tree and stayed awake all night, plucking and dropping Bilva leaves. In the morning, the Lord appeared and blessed him.

Here, one can see Nandi Peruman not facing the Lord but turned towards the entrance, facing east. This is related to the history of this place. This story is connected to the incident of the hunter: it is said that Nandi and the Dvarapalakas prevented Yama from catching the hunter, and Nandi turned to stop Yama. Because of this, it is said that there are no Dvarapalakas or Navagrahas in this temple. This place also has another name, Vilva Vanam. At the inner gopuram gateway, the story of the hunter is depicted as a stucco sculpture.

In this temple, the face of Murugan’s peacock is turned in a different direction. Opposite Durga, there are two Chandeswara idols. The main deity is a Swayambhu Murti.

Here, on Sivaratri, in the fourth jamam (watch of the night), a ritual procession takes place where the Lord appears to the hunter and his wife. The Sthala Puranam (history of the place), called Vaikkavur Puranam, was composed by Velaiyadeesikar. Thirugnanasambandhar, who visited this sacred place, composed a pathigam. It is the seventy-first pathigam of the third Thirumurai, set in Sadari pann. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. ‘Koazhai midaraaka kavi koaluvaka isai koodum vagaiyall Ezahai adiyaar avargal yavai sonna sol ma’. ...he delighted, is the abode of the Lord.

In Vaikkavur, where young coconut palms and mature areca nuts fall, scattering their full bunches, and plantains drop ripe fruits, making the fields muddy.

The Lord with three eyes, who wholly possesses us, and the Lord of Thiruvaiyaru, the enemy who destroyed the three cities. Those who master these ten Tamil verses composed by Gnanasambandhan will attain Rudrahood and live in the heavenly world, never separated from great glory.

Having thus worshipped Thiruvaiyavur, Thirugnanasambandhar proceeds to the sacred place called Thirupurambayam.

We shall continue pondering. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam by Sekkizhar Swamigal, Part 591, Vampira Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandhar arrives at the sacred place called Thirupurambayam. This is located northwest of Kumbakonam in Tamil Nadu. The Lord’s name is Sakshinatheswarar, Punnaivananathar. The Goddess’s name is Karumpadu Sollammai, Ikshuvanhi.

The Sthala Vriksham is the Punnai tree. Brahma Theertham, Sapthasagara Theertham, Manniyaru, Kollidam are the sacred waters. This place is named Purambayam because even during the great deluge, the floodwaters were stopped and remained outside the village, preventing them from entering. The Vinayagar of this place is called Pralayam Katha Vinayagar. His idol is made of shells and conches. Annually, on Chaturthi in the month of Avani, ...one ‘aadam’ (a measure) of honey abhishekham is performed, and all that honey is absorbed into his form.

This temple is located on the north bank of the Manniyar River. There are also Sthala Purana (local history) and Ula texts, as well as works like Purambaya Malai and Karumpumai Malai. This temple is under the spiritual authority of the Madurai Adheenam.

The Lord of this place is named Sakshinathar because he went to Madurai and testified for a merchant woman. The Vanni tree, well, and kitchen (madappalli) are located within the precincts of the Sokkanathar Temple at Thiruaalavai in Madurai. When a merchant woman, having abandoned her parents, came and stayed with her lover whom she was to marry, a snake bit the merchant, and he died. For the sake of the woman, the Lord appeared as a Siddhar, cured the poison, and arranged their marriage.

Later, when a case arose regarding that marriage ...the Lord testified as the Vanni tree, the well, and a Lingam. This is the history of the place. A play related to this Vanni incident was performed and enacted until recently. The detailed account can be found in the Sixty-Fourth Thiruvilaiyadal of the Thiruvilaiyadal Puranam, in the chapter titled ‘Vanniyum Kinjarum Lingamum Azhaiththa Padalam.’ The Lord imparted righteousness to the four sages, including Sanakar, at this place. It is also said that the Lord appeared to a devotee who daily brought firewood to the temple and granted him liberation.

Additionally, Varuna, King Harithuvan of Magadha, King Dronar of Vindhya mountains, King of Himalayas, Vishwamithra, and Sugriva worshipped the Lord of this place and received their desired boons. Thirugnanasambandhar, who visited this sacred place, has composed a pathigam. In this pathigam, he has given instructions about Shiva’s virtues, praising the ways in which the Lord shows mercy to living beings. Thirugnanasambandhar has taught moral principles. Sekkizhar Peruman has also referred to this as ‘arantharu kolgaiyar’ (those who bestow dharma). Such a uniquely significant pathigam is set in the Thiruvirakam meter.

This pathigam, set in Indalappann, is the thirtieth pathigam of the second Thirumurai. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: ‘Marampaya malainthavar madhil parisaruthanai nirampasumai semmaiyodu isainthunathu nirmaithirampayanu therinthunaru naalvarkku arampayan uraitthanai purampayam amarnthoy.’ ‘The dark-fruited clamoring waves of the sea brought forth pearls, and the Lord of Kazhumalam, the Tamil-speaking Gnana, who resides in the buzzing Purambayam, will unite with those who are skilled in Tamil, dispelling great illnesses.’ Thiruchitrambalam.

Thus, having worshipped Thirupurambayam, Thirugnanasambandhar visited many other shrines along the way and reached Thirucheingalur. The shrines that Thirugnanasambandhar visited along the way are believed to be Thiruvialur, Thirundhu Thevankudi, and others. There are individual pathigams composed by Thirugnanasambandhar for Thiruvialur and Thirundhu Thevankudi. Of these, Thiruvialur is located as the forty-third shrine on the north bank of the Kaveri. The Kaveri river makes the land fertile. It is known as Vadai Thiruvisanur.

Thevanayanar, who composed Thiruvontiyar, the first of the Meykandar Sastras, resided at this shrine. It is located a short distance to the east of Thirupurambayam. This shrine is located northwest of Thiruvidaimaruthur. This shrine is now popularly known as Thiruvisanallur. The Lord’s names are Yogananadeeswarar, Purathaneeswarar, Vilvaaranyeswarar. The Goddess’s names are Santhanayaki, Soundarya Nayaki.

The Bilva tree and the peepal tree are the Sthala Vrikshams. Jatayu Theertham is located here. In Chola-era inscriptions, this place is referred to as ‘Vada Karai Rajendra Simha Chola Valanattu Manni Nattu Brahmadeyamana Veppathur Chola Marthanda Chaturvedi Mangalam,’ and the Lord’s name is noted as ‘Thiruvisanallur Theva Pattakarar Shiva Yoginathar.’ Inscriptions from the time of Rajendra Chola mention the king’s donation of land to the temple and his queen’s gift of gold ornaments for the deity and a silver kavacham for abhishekham. Thirugnanasambandhar composed a pathigam for this shrine. Appar Peruman has referred to this shrine as a ‘vaippu thalam’ (a place mentioned in hymns) in his Thiruththandagam. The pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandhar for this shrine is the thirteenth pathigam of the first Thirumurai, set in Nattapada pann.

The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. ‘Kuravankamizh veruvarunkidam virinir viyalure vilangum piraichchadaimeluudai vikiathan viyalurai thalangondathor pugazhit thagu Thamizh gnanasambandhan thuzhangil Thamizh paravi thozhum’. Devotees who praise him will always shine with that glory and will possess the high heavens.

Having thus worshipped Thiruvisanallur, Thirugnanasambandhar proceeds to the sacred place called Thirundhu Thevankudi and composes a pathigam. Thirundhu Thevankudi is the forty-second shrine on the north bank of the Kaveri in the Chola country. It is a place where a crab worshipped and attained blessings. The form of a crab can be seen on the Shiv Lingam. Devotees say that if pure milk from a caracal cow is abundantly offered, a golden crab can be seen emerging from within the Lingam.

This place can be reached from Mayiladuthurai and Kumbakonam. This shrine is also known as Nandangoyil. The Lord’s name is Karkadakeswarar. The Goddess’s names are Arumarundammai, Apurva Nayaki, Periyanangai. The Sthala Vriksham is the Agil tree. Pangaya Theertham and the Kaveri River are the sacred waters.

As we have already seen, even today, if ten kalams of milk from a Karambu cow are offered, a golden crab-like vision is seen at the top of the Lingam. The Thevaram line, ‘Thenum vandum isai paadum Thevankudi,’ means ‘Thevankudi where bees and beetles sing music.’ Accordingly, the buzzing sound of bees can be heard in the temple. Thirugnanasambandhar, who visited this sacred place, composed a pathigam. That pathigam is the twenty-fifth pathigam of the third Thirumurai, set in Kolli pann. This pathigam carries the message that the sacred ash, rudraksha, medicine, mantras, and merits, which are the forms of the God of gods in Thirundhu Thevankudi, are both the means and the benefits. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. ‘Marunthu vendil ivai manthirangal ivai’.

These are the merits sought with understanding. The forms of the Lord, worshipped by great ascetics, are the very essence of the God of gods in Thirundhu Thevankudi. Those who are skilled in the ten verses of Tamil, composed by Gnanasambandhan from the prosperous town of Kandhar, with its mansions and groves, will be free from sin.

Having thus worshipped Thirundhu Thevankudi, Thirugnanasambandhar reaches the sacred place called Thirucheingalur.

Let us keep pondering. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam by Sekkizhar Swamigal, Part 592, Vampira Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandhar arrives at the sacred place of Thiruchengalur. Thiruchengalur is the place where Chandeswara Nayanar was born and attained liberation. Because Chandeswara Nayanar is the divine son of the Lord, it is customary in Saivism to refer to Chandeswara Nayanar as Chengalur Pillaiyar. Thirugnanasambandhar, on the other hand, is Kalippillaiyar.

Therefore, Kalippillaiyar arrives at the sacred place where Chengalur Pillaiyar was born.

The Lord is glorious for adorning his matted locks with a pure Konrai garland. Bearing in mind that this is the sacred place where Chandeesa Pillaiyar was born, Thirugnanasambandhar descends from his pearl palanquin and reverently bows towards the shrine. Descending from the palanquin, he bows in reverence towards the place and arrives at this shrine.

The Brahmins of Thiruchengalur, learning of his arrival at their sacred place, welcome Pillaiyar with great joy. They were overjoyed, as if their own Chandeesa Pillaiyar had returned to their sacred place of Thiruchengalur.

The Brahmins of that place welcomed him with immense joy, as if Chandeesa Pillaiyar had returned from the Sivapuri he had attained through worship. They rejoice that Pillaiyar, the benevolent one, is coming. They praise Pillaiyar’s magnanimity for coming and bestowing grace without expecting anything in return. Chandeeswarar Nayanar, also known as Cheyalur Pillaiyar, attained the Lord at a young age, having completed his Upanayanam and studied the Vedas. Pillaiyar, too, upon completing his current pilgrimage and returning to Sirkazhi, is about to perform his Upanayanam ceremony.

Therefore, seeing Pillaiyar arrive at the same age that Chandeeswarar Nayanar was when he resided in Thiruchengalur, and also because both are considered divine sons of Shiva, ...the Brahmins of that town welcome him with overflowing hearts. They welcome Thirugnanasambandhar by sprinkling him with water brought from holy rivers like Kaveri and purified with sacred mantras, which grants merit. More than this holy water, the Brahmins’ tears fell like rain, and in the joy of that experience, they invite him and proceed to the Thiruchengalur Shiva temple. Pillaiyar, the leader of Sirkazhi, also circumambulates and worships that temple with great devotion. Joining his hands above his head in reverence, ...this Thiruchengalur temple is a temple that forever shines in the minds of Shiva’s devotees. This is because it is absolutely essential for all devotees to remember this temple and Chandeswara Nayanar along with their Shiva puja, in order to receive the benefits of their Shiva worship.

Therefore, the Thiruchengalur temple is a temple that always shines in the minds of devotees who perform Shiva puja.

Thus, Pillaiyar, the leader of Sirkazhi, circumambulated and worshipped that temple with great love, joined his hands above his head, entered the temple, and bowed before the Lord. In the heart of Thirugnanasambandhar, immense love for the Lord of Thiruchengalur temple overflows. Even greater love for Chandeesa Pillaiyar also overflows. Thirugnanasambandhar composes a pathigam to praise the grace of the Lord of Thiruchengalur. Chandeesa Pillaiyar, who was born in this place, threw a stick to punish his father, and it became an axe. The grace of the Lord transformed the stick into an axe.

The grace of the Lord bestowed liberation upon those who threw it.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandhar composes the pathigam, praising this grace of the Lord, mentioning that Chandeesa Pillaiyar, who cut off his father’s leg, received the reward for his sin. The grace here is specifically lauded because it was bestowed on those who committed a Shiva offence for which there is no atonement. According to the saying, ‘Even the Lord’s punishment is His grace.’ Thirugnanasambandhar sings of such grace in this pathigam. Throughout this pathigam, he has specifically used the word ‘adaintha’ (attained/reached). This pathigam is set in Palandakkaraagam. In this, Thirugnanasambandhar has graciously instructed, ‘Cheyyadaintha Chengaluril selvan seerparavi’ (Praising the glory of the prosperous one in Chengalur which is filled with fields).

He has presented various benefits of attaining this sacred place, thereby benefiting souls. Through this pathigam, Thirugnanasambandhar has blessed. Such a special pathigam is the forty-eighth pathigam of the first Thirumurai, set in Palandakkaragam. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. ‘Nooladaintha kolgaiyale nunnadi kooduvatharku maaladaintha naalvarku ketka nalkiya nalla aratthai aaladaintha nizhalil mevi arumarai sonnathenne seladaintha than kazhaniseyalvanir paravidaintha than vayalchoozh Thonipurath thalaivan sayadaintha gnanamalku sambandhan innurai vagaiyadayaintha padavallavar vanulukazh avar.’ Thiruchitrambalam. In this sacred place called Thiruchengalur, the Lord’s name is Satyagirisevarar, Amma. We have pondered upon the historical significance of this holy site, where Ambal Sahadevi Ammai resides, in the legend of Chandi-nayanar.

After residing for a few days at this glorious site, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds to offer his prayers at the holy site of Thiruppanandal. Having thus bowed down and offered a garland of verses there, he then reaches the holy site called Thiruppandhanainallur, which is nearby.

There, he visits the temple of Shiva Peruman and offers a pathigam in praise of the Lord. This holy site of Thiruppandhanainallur is located northeast of Thiruppanandal, on the southern bank of the Kollidam river. This town is where Ammaiyar’s ball landed, hence it is known as Pandhu Anaivallur. This gave the pathigam its name. It is currently known as Pandhanallur. The Lord’s name is Pasupatheeswarar, and the Goddess’s name is Venu Bhujambikai, Kaambana Thozhiyamai.

The Sthala Viruksham is the Konrai tree. The Theerthams are Pasu Theertham and Surya Theertham. Uma Devi wished to play with a ball, and the Lord helped her by providing four Vedas as balls. Uma Devi was playing with great delight. Thinking not to interrupt her, the Sun remained without setting. When the Devas noticed the change in the cosmic order, they complained to the Lord, who then came to that place.

Uma Ammai continued to play, not even noticing the Lord.

The Lord then kicked the ball Uma Devi was playing with His sacred foot. Uma, unable to find the ball, came to the Lord and bowed, and the Goddess was asked to become a cow, and that The Lord decreed that He would be enshrined under the Konrai tree at this holy site of Thiruppandhanainallur, where the ball had fallen, and that she should go there and worship.

Accordingly, Uma Devi transformed into a cow, called Thirumal as a cowherd, and came from the Kanva Muni’s ashram. During those days, Uma Ammaiyar worshipped the Lord’s form, which was in the form of an anthill, by showering it with milk. Thirumal, who had come as a cowherd, daily provided milk for Kanva Muni’s abhishekam.

One day, finding no milk from the cow for the puja, he became enraged and followed the cow. Seeing it showering milk on an anthill, he angrily struck the cow with his hand. The cow then jumped, and one of its hooves landed on the anthill. Through the touch of the Lord’s form, Uma Devi regained her true form and received the Lord’s grace. Since she came as a cow’s consort, The Lord’s name became Pasupathinathar because the ball He kicked landed here, thus the village was named Pandhanainallur. One can see the imprint of a cow’s hoof on the head of the Moolavar’s form.

This is the place where the King Kaampili’s son regained his sight. This holy site has many names such as Thengailai, Kovoor, Konraivanam, Vishnu Puti, Indra Puti, Kanvarasramam, Valinagar, Bhanupuri, Aavoor, Kandukapuri. The entrance to the Lord’s shrine is named after Thirugnanasambandhar. The Moolavar is enshrined in an anthill, so the Abhishekam is performed with a covering. The Goddess is in a posture of penance, so Aiyanar and Kaali stand guard on both sides. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who graced this glorious holy site, composed a pathigam.

That pathigam is the one hundred and twenty-first pathigam in the third Thirumurai, That pathigam is the Puranirmmai pannil amaintha Thiruppathigam. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam (Idarinār kūṟṟai poṭi ceytār matilai ivai colli ulakēḻu tētta kaṭariṉār āvār kāṟṟuḷḷārāvār kātalitturaidaru kōyil koṭiraṉār yātun kuṟaivilār tām pōy kōpaṇaṅkoṇṭu kūttāṭum paṭiraṉār pōlum paṉtaṉai nallūr niṉṟa em pacupatiyārē kallicai pūṇa kalaiyoli ōvā kaḻumala mutupati taṉṉil nallicaiyāḻaṉ pullicai kēḷā naccamizh ñāṉacampantaṉ pallicai pakuvāyp paṭutalai ēnti mēviya paṉtaṉai nallūr colliya pāṭal pattum vallal avar mēl tolvī cūḻakilāvē Thiruchitrambalam) The Lord is like the sea, forest, and mountains of the world. His presence is beyond human comprehension. Whatever anyone says is a praise of Him. That Lord is our Pasupathi, who stands in Pandhanainallur. He is so because He is the Lord of all living beings, who are like cows.

Thus is the meaning of this pathigam. We shall go on pondering.

The meaning of this pathigam is thus.

Our pondering continues. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, part five hundred and ninety-three, authored by Sekkizhar Swamigal, the chapter of Vambara Varivandu, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, departing from Thiruppandhanainallur, arrives at the holy site of Thiruvomampuliyur. Thiruvomampuliyur is a town where righteous Brahmins, who study the great Vedas that remove evils, flourish.

The Brahmins of Thiruvomampuliyur are those who eliminate the sorrows of Kali Yuga by following the path of the Vedas and nurturing the three sacred fires. Thiruvomampuliyur is a site where Brahmins who perform sacrifices according to learned scriptures reside. It is the thirty-first holy site on the northern bank of the Kaveri River in the Chola Kingdom, located on the northern bank of the Kollidam River. Brahmins It is known for the special practice of performing homams, hence the name Omampuliyur for this holy site. One can reach this holy site from Thiruchitrambalam and Kattumannargudi. The Lord’s names are Pranava Vyakarapurishwarar, Thuyaram Theerthanathar, Pranapurishwarar.

The Goddess’s name is Pushpalathambigai, Poongodinayaki. The Sthala Viruksham is the Ilandhai tree. The Theerthams are Kollidam and Gauri Theertham. This is the place where Vyagrapadha Muni worshipped, hence it is called Puliyur. Since Brahmins perform the homams mentioned in the Vedas here, the name Omam Puliyur came to this holy site. This is the place where the Lord, as Dakshinamurthy, taught the meaning of Pranava to Uma Devi.

The Moolavar The Swayambhu Murti stands on a square pedestal with a tall Bana. An inscription from the time of Kulothunga III mentions this site as Vadakarai Virudaraja Bhayankara Valanattu Merkanattu Bramadeyam Omampuliyur, also known as Ulgalantha Chola Chaturvedamangalam, and the Lord’s name as Vadathalivudaiyar. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who graced this holy site, composed a pathigam. That pathigam is the one hundred and twenty-second pathigam in the third Thirumurai, composed in the Puranirmmai pann. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam (Poongodi madavaal umaiyoru paagam poridharu sadai mudi adigal veenginir nattam aadum em vigitar viruppadum uraividam vinavil thengazhi pozhilil sezhumaalar) (கோதி செறிதரு வண்டிசை பாடும் ஓங்கிய புகழார் ஓமமாம் புலியூர் உடையவர் வடதளி அதுவே விளைதரு வயலுள் வெயில் செறி பவளும் மேதிகள் மேய் புலத்திடறி ஒளிதர மல்கும் ஓமமாம் புலியூர் உடையவர் வடதளி அரணை களிதரு நிவப்பிற் காண்டகு செல்வ காளியுள் ஞானசம்பந்தன் அளிதரு பாடல் பத்தும் வல்லார்கள் அமரலோகத்து இருப்பாரே திருச்சிற்றம்பலம்) The essence of this pathigam is that if one asks where the Lord, who owns all beings, resides, it is in Omampuliyur.

Thus, after worshipping the sacred feet of Shiva Peruman, who is enshrined in the Vadathali temple in Omampuliyur, he departs from there and reaches the site of Thiruvalkizhiputhur. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrives. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who reaches that special temple, worships the sacred feet of the Lord and delights in seeing Him, then sings devotional verses praised by the world. Sekkizhar Peruman has referred to them as ‘Pathigams praised by the world’.

However, only two of the pathigams composed by Pillaiyar are available to us.

Therefore, it is understood through Sekkizhar Peruman’s words that there might be many more pathigams. This holy site of Thiruvalkizhiputhur is currently known as Thiruvalapputhur. It is located a short distance north of Nidoor, on the Mayiladuthurai-Chidambaram road. The Lord’s names are Manikavannar, Ratnapurishwarar. The Goddess’s name is Vandamar Poonguzhali. Brahma Kundalambal.

The Vagai tree is the Sthala Viruksham. Brahma Theertham. Thirumal established and worshipped this Manikka Lingam. The Lord, wishing to grace Arjuna, caused Vasuki to hide Arjuna’s sword where he had kept it concealed. Arjuna, seeking the sword, worshipped the Lord and Vasuki, and thus obtained the sword. The place where Vasuki resided was an anthill, hence the name Vazhozhiputtur.

In Sanskrit, this holy site is known as Arathanapuram. A bee worshipped the Lord at this holy site. Durga worshipped Shiva Peruman at this holy site.

Therefore, the temple’s history states that the Durga in the niche is worshipped with rituals as a boon she received by praying to the Lord of this holy site. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who visited this holy site, composed two pathigams. The first pathigam is the fortieth pathigam in the first Thirumurai, composed in the Thakkaragam pann. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam (Poṭiyuṭai mārpiṉar pōrviṭaiyēṟi pūta kaṇam poṭaicūḻa koṭiyuṭaiyūr tiriṉta aiyaṅkoṇṭu pala pala kūṟi vaṭivuṭai vāḻneṭuṅkaṇṇumai pākam āyavaṉ vāḷkkoḻipputtūr kaṭikamizh māmalariṭṭu karaimiṭaṟṟāṉ aṭi kāṇpōm kalluyar mākkaṭal niṉṟu muḻaṅkum karai poru kāḷiya mūtūr nalluyar nāṉ maṟai nāviṉ naṟṟamizh ñāṉa campantaṉ valluyar cūlamum veṇmazhu vāḻum vallavaṉ vāḷkkoḻipputtūr colliya pāṭalkal vallār tuyar keṭutal) (எளிதாமே திருச்சிற்றம்பலம்) The second pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for this holy site is the ninety-fourth pathigam in the second Thirumurai, composed in the Piyandhai Gandharam pann. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam (Shaakkai āyiram uṭaiyār cāmamum ōtuvatutaiyār īkaiyār kaṭai nōkki iṟappatum palapala uṭaiyār tōkai māmaiyilaṇaiyai tuṭiyiṭai pākamum uṭaiyār vākai nuṇṭuḷi vīcum vāḷkkoḻiputtūruḷārē nalaṅkoḷ pūmpoḻil kāḷi naṟṟamizh ñāṉacampantaṉ valaṅkoḷ veṇmazhuvaṉ vāḷkkoḻiputtūruḷāṉai ilaṅku veṇpiraiyāṉai ēttiya tamizh ivai vallār nalaṅkoḷ cintaiyarāki naṉṉeṟi eytuvar tāmē thiruchithra)

Sambalam. Having thus worshipped at Thiruvalkizhiputhur, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman departs from here and arrives at the holy site of Thirukkadambur, also known as Kadambai Karakkoil. This holy site, now called Melakadambur, is the thirty-fourth holy site on the northern bank of the Kaveri. It can be reached from Thiruchitrambalam via Kattumannargudi, from the holy site of Eyilur. This is a holy site praised by Appar Swamigal in Thirukkurunthogai as Kadambai Thirukkarakkoil. The legend of this holy site states that Indra, who worshipped here, wished to take it to his world.

He dug deep into the underworld, but seeing that the Shiva Lingam extended even further, he became afraid, restored it to its original state, worshipped it, and received a boon for amrita to be produced. Though it had a place in Kadambur, This holy site is praised in Thiruvachagam. Very close by is the Vaipu Sthalam called Kadambur Ilangkoil.

Here, the Lord’s name is Amirthakadeswarar. The Goddess’s name is Jothimin Ammai, Vidyut Jothinayagi. The Sthala Viruksham is the Kadamba tree. The Theertham is Sakthi Theertham, Sakthi Kulam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who visited this holy site, composed a pathigam. That pathigam is the sixty-eighth pathigam in the second Thirumurai, composed in the Gandharam pann.

The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam (Vāṉamar tiṅkaḷum nīrum maruviya vārcaṭaiyāṉai tēṉamar koṉṟaiyiṉāṉai tēvar tozhuppaṭuvāṉai kāṇamaram piṇai pulki kalaip payilum kaṭampūril tāṉamar koḷkaiyiṉāṉai tāḻa tozha vīṭeḷitāmē viṭai navila) (கொடியானை வெண்கொடி சேர் நெடுமாடம் கடைநவிளும் கடம்பூரில் காதலனை கடற்காழி நடைநவில் ஞானசம்பந்தன் நன்மையாலேத்திய பத்தும் படைநவில் பாடல் பயில்வார் பழியொடு பாவமிலாரே திருச்சிற்றம்பலம்) Thus, having worshipped the Lord in Kadambur, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman departs from there and arrives at the site of Thirunariyur.

We shall dwell further on this. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, part five hundred and ninety-four, authored by Sekkizhar Swamigal, the chapter of Vambara Varivandu, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrives at the holy site of Thirunaraiyur. Thirunaraiyur is the thirty-third holy site on the northern bank of the Kaveri in the Chola country. This site is named so because a stork (narai) worshipped here and attained blessings. This is the holy site where Pollapillaiyar is enshrined as a Swayambhu Murthi.

By worshipping Him and through His grace, Nambiyandar Nambi discovered and revealed the Thevara Thirumuraigal. He also composed the Thiruthondar Thiruvandhadhi, which served as the source for the Thiruthondar Puranam, known as Periya Puranam. The Lord’s name is Soundaranathar. The Goddess’s name is Thiripura Sundari. Karunya Theertham serves as the Theertham. This holy site is located on the road from Thiruchitrambalam to Kattumannar Koil.

This holy site is situated. Peruman refers to this holy site as Nalanthigal Naraiyur. In the pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for this holy site, he sings about it as ‘Nalandaangu Thempunal Soozhthigal Mamuduvil Thirunaraiyur Nan Nalanongu Thirunaraiyur Nalan’. Peruman has sung about this holy site in the past, present, and future tenses as ‘Nalandaangu Naraiyur’ and ‘Nalan Oongu Naraiyur’. As a result of Pillaiyar’s sacred words, some time later, Nambiyandar Nambigal, who received the grace of Pollapillaiyar at this holy site and was instrumental in revealing the Thevara Thirumuraigal and providing the Thiruthondar Thiruvandhadhi as a source for the Thiruthondar Puranam, was born. The good fortune is indicated here.

At this holy site, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed pathigams fragrant with Shiva’s essence. Currently, three such pathigams, which are like garlands of Shiva’s essence, are available.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman resided at the holy site of Thirunaraiyur with great devotion, composing these rare Tamil pathigams. As we have seen, there are a total of three such pathigams. The first pathigam is the second pathigam in the third Thirumurai, composed in the Pazhampanjiram pann. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam (Kāmpinai veṉṟa meṉ tōzhi pākam kalantāṉ nalaṅtāṅku tēmpuṉal cūḻttikaḷ māmaṭuvil tirunārayūr mēya pū) (புனல் சேர்புறி புன்சடையான் புலியின் உரி தோல்மேல் பாம்பினை வீக்கிய பண்டரங்கன் பாதம் பணிவோமே தன்மதி தாழ் பொழில் சூழ் புகழி தமிழ்ஞான சம்பந்தன் ஒன்மதிசேர் சடையான் உறையும் திருநாரையோர்தன்மேல் பண்மதியால் சொன்ன பாடல்பத்தும் பயின்றார் வினை போகி மண்மதியாது போய் வான் புகுவர் வானோர் எதிர்கொள்ளவே திருச்சிற்றம்பலம்) Now, the second pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for this holy site is the one hundred and seventh pathigam in the third Thirumurai, composed in the Pazhampanjuram pann. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam (Kaṭaliṭai veṅkaṭu nañcamuṇṭa kaṭavuḷ viṭa ēṟi uṭaliṭaiyoṭi pūcavallāṉ umaiyōṭoru pākaṉ aṭaliṭaiyiṟ cilai tāṅki eyta ammāṉ aṭiyārmēl naṭala)

(வினைத்தொகை தீர்த்துகந்தானிடம் நாரையூர்தானே பாடியலும் திரை சூழ் புகழி திருஞானசம்பந்தன் சேடியலும் புகழோங்கு செம்மை திருநாரையூரான் மேர் பாடிய தண்டமி மாலை பத்தும் பரவி திரிந்தாக வாடிய சிந்தையினார்க்கு நீங்கும் அவலக்கடல்தானே திருச்சிற்றம்பலம்) Now, the third pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for this holy site is the eighty-sixth pathigam in the second Thirumurai, composed in the Piyandhai Gandharam pann. Sekkizhar Peruman refers to this pathigam as ‘Arunthamil Thiruppathigam’. This pathigam begins with ‘Uraiyinil vantha paavam’. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has explained in every verse of this pathigam the benefits of worshipping the Lord of Thirunaraiyur, such as the removal of sins committed through words, diseases, and harms caused by actions, and the growth of penance and love.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to this as an ‘Arunthamil Pathigam’. If one worships the Lord of Thirunaraiyur, all those will be removed, and penance and devotion will grow, bringing good. This is what Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has explained in every verse of this pathigam.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to this as an Arunthamil Pathigam. The benefit of this pathigam is the removal of both pleasures and sorrows. This is the special significance of this pathigam dedicated to this holy site. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam (Uraiyinil vantha paavam uṇar nōykaḷum ceyarīṅku kuṟṟa mulakil varaiyināmai ceyta avai tīrum vaṇṇa mikavētti nitta niṉaimiṉ varaicilaiyākavaṉṟu matiṉ mūṉṟeṟintu vaḷar kaṅkuṇaṅ kai veṟuva) (திரையொலி நஞ்சமுண்ட சிவன்மேய செல்வத்திருநாரையூர் கைத்தொழவே எரியொடு வண்ணமாய உருவானை எந்தை பெருமானை உள்கி நினையார் திரிபுரமன்று செற்ற சிவன்மேய செல்வ திருநாரையூர் கைத்தொழுவான் பொறுப்புனல் சூழ்ந்த காளி மறைஞான பந்த நுரை மாலை பத்து மொழிவார் திருவளர் செம்மையாகியருள்பேருமிக்கதுளதென்பர் செம்மையினரே திருச்சிற்றம்பலம்) Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having worshipped the Lord in Thirunaraiyur, then visited nearby holy sites such as Thirukkurugukka and others, and arrived at the holy site of Thirukkaruppariyallur. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worshipped Shiva Peruman in Thirukkaruppariyallur and sang a pure Tamil pathigam.

This Thirukkaruppariyallur, where Sirkazhi Pillaiyar sang, is the twenty-seventh site on the northern bank of the Kaveri in the Chola country. It is referred to. We have already pondered upon the history of this holy site in the Puranam of Thiru Navukkarasu Peruman. The pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for this holy site is the thirty-first pathigam in the second Thirumurai. This pathigam is thus composed. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam (Suṟṟamuṭu paṟṟavai tuyakkaravaruttu kuṟṟamil kuṇattiṉoṭu kūṭum aṭiyārkaḷ maṟṟavarai vāṉavartam vāṉulakamēṟṟu kaṟṟavaṉ iruppatu karuppariyallūrē nalaṅtaru puṉar pukaḻi ñāṉacampantaṉ kalantavar karuppariyaṉmēya kaṭavuḷlai palantaru tamizhkizhvi pattum ivai kaṟṟu valantarum avarkku viṉai vāṭal eḷitāmē Thiruchitrambalam) The meaning of this pathigam is the praise of Shiva Peruman.

The glory of this holy site is Karuppariyal, meaning that this is a place where the birth, referred to as ‘karu’, of those who reach Shiva Peruman here will be removed. Hence, Karuppariyallur is a befitting name for this holy site.

Therefore, the special feature of this pathigam is that it sings the praises of the Lord, describing its nature. The pathigam’s benefit is stated in the verse ‘Kalanthavar Karuppariyal’, and the poet, who is also a teacher, has thus composed this pathigam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has praised the qualities of the devotees in this pathigam. In the tenth verse of this pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has mentioned the Lord of this holy site as ‘Kuṟṟamariyātha Perumān’, meaning ‘The Lord who knows no fault’, which is the sacred name of the Lord of this holy site, Kuṟṟam Poruthanathar. In the tenth verse, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has also sung about the temple structure of this holy site as Kokudi Koil. This pathigam and this holy site possess such glories.

Having thus worshipped at Thirukkaruppariyallur, he also worships the nearby holy sites. The nearby holy sites are considered to be Thiruppungur, Thiruppullirukku Velur, known as Vaidheeswaran Koil, and Thirukkondal, among others.

Thus, Pillaiyar, the benevolent who appeared by the merit of this earthly world, worshipped many such holy sites and then proceeded to Thirubrahmapuram, also known as Sirkazhi. There, the devotees, followers, and Brahmins give Pillaiyar a grand and enthusiastic welcome. They greet him.

We shall go on pondering. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, part five hundred and ninety-five, authored by Sekkizhar Peruman, the chapter of Vambara Varivandu, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Pillaiyar was born as a result of the penance performed by this earthly world. It is said that even celestial beings come down to earth to worship.

Accordingly, all those in the upper and lower worlds must come to this earthly world to perform penance to attain Shiva Peruman. This earthly world is of immense benefit in attaining Shiva Peruman. Since Pillaiyar guides and helps beings attain the fruit of their penance, Sekkizhar Peruman praises him as the fruit of this earthly world’s penance. Sekkizhar Peruman praises him as the fruit of this earthly world’s penance.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was born as a generous benefactor, who bestows countless benefits upon everyone, curing the disease of birth. Such a great soul, having completed his fourth pilgrimage, arrives at Thirubrahmapuram, Sirkazhi, with the sacred blessings bestowed by the Lord, namely the pearl palanquin, pearl umbrella, and sacred insignias. He reaches Sirkazhi, also known as Thirubrahmapuram, where the Lord resides, a region in the Chola country filled with paddy fields, plantain trees, and areca nut trees, all intertwined. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the Pillaiyar of Sirkazhi, Brahmapuram is the name of Sirkazhi. Sekkizhar Peruman states that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman came to Thirubrahmapuram under that sacred name, which was the name of the first pathigam composed by Pillaiyar when he attained gnana. This is because when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman came to Sirkazhi, he composed the Panchakshara pathigam.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman sings about him using the name of the holy site as it was in the first pathigam. Hearing the news of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s arrival, all the learned Brahmins living in Brahmapuram, filled with great love and overflowing joy in their hearts, went forth to greet and worship Pillaiyar. They worship the sacred feet of Thiru Thonipuram Nayakar and Periya Nayaki Ammaiyar. They proceed to welcome Pillaiyar. Thiru Thonipurar Thoniyappar is the one who bestowed Pillaiyar.

Now, Thiru Thoniyappar is also the one who bestowed the palanquin.

Therefore, the devotees depart after worshipping Thoniyappar and Periya Nayaki Ammaiyar.

Here, our divine Sekkizhar Peruman demonstrates the practice of worshipping the Lord to gain the worthiness to worship devotees, before actually going to worship them.

Thus, the Brahmins of that holy site proceed, filling all the streets with the sound of the Vedas. They arrange thick mango leaves, arches, plantain trees, and other such decorations in rows. They arrange golden pots, lamps, oil lamps, incense, flags, and other such items in rows. They arrange them in rows and perform all the rituals necessary to welcome Pillaiyar. They also place fragrant Purna Kumbhams decorated with sacred grass and Pipal leaves. Purna Kumbhams can be pots filled with holy water or Purna Kumbhams arranged purely for decoration.

They welcome him bearing both types of Purna Kumbhams. They sprinkle fragrant yellow powder and fresh flowers. They also sprinkle puffed rice. The people of Sirkazhi saw Pillaiyar, the benevolent who had partaken of the milk-nectar mixed with divine wisdom by Uma Ammaiyar on the sacred Vembur mound, resplendent in a beautiful pearl palanquin under a magnificent pearl umbrella. As soon as they saw Pillaiyar in the pearl palanquin, they immediately raised their hands. They immediately raised their hands above their heads, their eyes overflowing with joy, their hearts filled with love, and the devotees and Brahmins surrounded Pillaiyar, praising him with an indescribable outpouring of happiness.

The sound of their praises filled the eight directions. They expressed their joy by throwing their upper garments into the air. In accordance with the saying, “Grant me the grace to be amidst your devotees,” they experienced the benefit of being with the assembly of devotees.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the leader of Sirkazhi, entered the holy city of Brahmapuram. Devotees and Brahmins gathered at the city’s boundary to greet him.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman entered the city with them. He proceeds through the beautiful streets of Sirkazhi, which are adorned with tall, beautiful mansions that seem to touch the moon. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds through the sacred street of Sirkazhi. Virtuous women, who follow the divine path of the Vedas, chant auspicious greetings. They surround him on both sides and offer auspicious greetings.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman enters Sirkazhi, reaches the temple where Thiru Thoniyappar is enshrined, bows before the great Gopuram, enters the temple, circumambulates it, and worships Periya Nayaki Ammaiyar and Thoniyappar, who bestowed the divine food of wisdom upon Pillaiyar. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman then sings Tamil Vedic pathigams.

At that time, through Thiru Thoniyappar’s grace, he had previously received the golden cymbals.

Now, he receives the palanquin, umbrella, and insignias. He received the golden cymbals in Thirukkolakka. He received the pearl palanquin, pearl umbrella, and sacred insignias at the holy site of Thirunelvaayil Arathurai.

However, Pillaiyar’s view is that no matter where they were received, they are all Thoniyappar’s grace, bestowed by Thoniyappar. To highlight this, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who composed the Vedas in Tamil that the Lord had revealed, now sings pathigams about Thoniyappar. Sivakavimani notes that we cannot identify which of the pathigams composed by Peruman at this time belong to the holy site of Sirkazhi.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises the great compassionate grace of the Lord by singing such praising pathigams. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s lotus-like eyes shed tears of joy, his hands clasped above his head, he bows down, rises, and emerges from the temple. As Sirkazhi Pillaiyar proceeds, Thiruneelakanta Yazhpanar, who is always inseparable from Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, follows him. Seeing this, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman blesses Thiruneelakanta Yazhpanar and his wife to go to their home. We should remember that the first time Thiruneelakanta Yazhpanar and his wife came, he had arranged a home for them.

Therefore, after blessing them to reside in that home, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds to his own residence. As Pillaiyar arrives at his residence, the Brahmins The Brahmins praise Pillaiyar’s sacred feet. As their leader, Sirkazhi Pillaiyar, returns to his residence, women greet him, carrying auspicious items including lamps, in accordance with tradition, the Ashtamangalas, or sacred eight auspicious symbols. Bhagavati Ammaiyar, Pillaiyar’s mother, comes forward carrying sacred ash. Both her lineage and the lineage she married into, which are rooted in Saivism, are known for their devotion to sacred ash, as are Pillaiyar’s parents, who embody profound love for it.

Therefore, both Pillaiyar’s mother’s lineage and his father’s lineage are rooted in the tradition of sacred ash. Both lineages adhere to the tradition of sacred ash.

Therefore, both Pillaiyar’s father and mother were well-versed in Shiva rituals and understood the truth of sacred ash.

Thus, Pillaiyar’s mother, knowing that there is no greater auspiciousness or protection than sacred ash, lived by this truth.

Therefore, Pillaiyar’s mother greets him, holding and applying sacred ash. The sacred mother greets Pillaiyar not as her son but as a devotee blessed by Shiva Peruman’s grace, holding sacred ash. During the time Pillaiyar resided in his prosperous, spacious residence, he daily went to worship Thoniyappar, who is enshrined on the sacred Thoni, and composed many pathigams, praising him with great joy. We cannot identify which of the pathigams composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman at this time belong to Sirkazhi. Among the pathigams available for Sirkazhi, four were composed by Thiru Navukkarasu Peruman and Sundaramoorthy Swamigal. Excluding these, there are sixty-seven pathigams by Pillaiyar that belong to Sirkazhi.

Among these sixty-seven pathigams, we have already seen how Sivakavimani interpreted some of them as Sirkazhi pathigams based on time, place, and context.

Furthermore, Sivakavimani Ayya also provides interpretations for future Sirkazhi pathigams.

Therefore, it is possible to consider that all the other pathigams, apart from those mentioned, were composed during this period. It is considered that these were composed during this period, because this period is when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman resided in Sirkazhi for a very long time. It is possible that Pillaiyar stayed in Sirkazhi for several years during this time, because after this, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman undertakes his fifth pilgrimage to establish Saivism in the Pandiya country and then returns. He undertakes a pilgrimage to Thondai Nadu and attains the Lord in marriage.

Therefore, this period is when Pillaiyar’s Upanayanam took place and when he resided in Sirkazhi for many years.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed various pathigams during this period. Man, we will continue to ponder. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, part five hundred and ninety-six, authored by Sekkizhar Swamigal, the chapter of Vambara Varivandu, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman resides in Sirkazhi. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who incarnated as a Gnana Acharyar to reveal to the world the Thevara truth that “all days without speech are days unborn,” continued to worship Thoniyappar and Periya Nayaki Ammaiyar and compose pathigams during his stay in Sirkazhi, in accordance with the sacred words that he would always humbly mingle with devotees.

At this time, the age for Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s Upanayanam arrived. The Upanayanam, a special ceremony for the first three varnas, starting with Brahmins, must take place at the age of seven. This ceremony involves placing the panchashikkai, adorning the deerskin and the three-stranded sacred thread, imparting the Brahma mantra, and initiating the child into the first ashrama of celibacy. ‘Upa’ means ‘to approach’, and ‘Nayanam’ means ‘to lead’. It signifies a ceremony performed to enable one to approach or attain God. It also means opening the eye of wisdom through mantra initiation. Shiva is Brahman.

One who knows Shiva One who knows Shiva must bear His symbols and act accordingly.

Thus, the symbols of celibacy, such as deerskin, a waist cord made of munja grass, and the panchashikkai, are worn. Spiritual texts state that children who undergo the Upanayanam ceremony should have the panchashikkai, symbolizing the five-faced Shiva.

Furthermore, taking ‘Nayanam’ in the word ‘Upanayanam’ to mean ‘eye’, the third eye, which comes after the existing two eyes, also refers to Upanayanam. The other two eyes are transverse, meaning they are horizontal.

However, this third eye is vertical, looking upwards. The eye looks upwards. This is called Virupaksha. ‘Vi’ means ‘different’, ‘Virupa’ means ‘different form’, and ‘Aksha’ means ‘eye’.

Therefore, unlike the other two eyes, which are transverse, this eye is different and looks upwards. Hence, it is called Virupaksha. This eye is opened by Brahma Gnana and is known as Shiva Peruman’s eye of fire, the third eye. Virupaksha is a name of Shiva Peruman.

Therefore, this third eye is not transverse like the eyes of other worldly beings but stands upright. Shiva Peruman protects the world by having the Sun and Moon as His right and left eyes, creating day and night. Finally, the third eye And Shiva destroys with one spark. The Vedas declare that only you are a brahmin.

Therefore, the ceremony that bestows Shiva Jnana, which is Brahma Jnana, is considered Upanayana. This is a Vedic injunction. It is a very important ceremony that should not be scorned as a meaningless ritual. The general rule is that after this ceremony, a student will study the Vedas and then attain Shiva Jnana when maturity occurs.

However, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was one who realized world-transcending Shiva Jnana. He had attained the experience of Shiva, which is beyond animal and illusory knowledge, as self-realization. Others would study the Vedas after this ceremony, mature, and then receive Shiva Jnana.

But Pillaiyar, though he had already attained world-transcending Pati Jnana, still wore the deerskin and sacred thread because it was a Vedic ritual. Sekkizhar Peruman explains this by saying that though Pillaiyar had already realized Shiva Jnana, the ancient Vedic ritual was performed by the Vedic scholars, and he wore the deerskin and sacred thread. Even for the enlightened, as long as external actions exist, these are considered necessary.

Therefore, according to that rule, Pillaiyar also wore the three-stranded sacred thread and the deerskin. When one is devoid of external perception, loses oneself, and is immersed in the experience of Shiva, rituals are not necessary. Even though this was Pillaiyar’s state, Pillaiyar accepted the Upanayana ceremony according to the Vedic rule. Sri Meykanda Devanayanar, who bestowed Shivagnanabodham, offered a mangala vazhthu (auspicious greeting) at the beginning of the book Shivagnanabodham. Generally, a mangala vazhthu is offered so that the undertaken work may be completed successfully and without obstacles. Sri Meykanda Devanayanar is in a high state of understanding wakefulness beyond the ordinary.

Therefore, no obstacles would occur to him. Nevertheless, Sri Meykanda Devanayanar composed the mangala vazhthu at the beginning of the Shivagnanabodham because, as wise persons, they were preserving the tradition And to instruct his disciples. Sri Madhava Shivagnana Munivar explains that he thus composed the mangala vazhthu.

Similarly, here, Pillaiyar, having attained world-transcending Shiva Jnana, is in a state of being immersed in the experience of Shiva, having lost himself, devoid of external perception. In that state, such rituals are not necessary for Pillaiyar. Nevertheless, Pillaiyar accepts the Upanayana ceremony because, as sages have said, he performs this to preserve the tradition of the wise and because Pillaiyar is in the position of an Acharya to inform the world.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman wears the three-stranded sacred thread and the deerskin. He accepts it. The skin is the skin of a black antelope. The thread is the three-stranded sacred thread. Along with this, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman assumes these divine forms, including the five Shikais, the staff, and the munji grass waist-cord. These are all the symbols of a Brahmachari.

The thread is the three-stranded sacred thread. This three-stranded thread is adorned with the skin of a black antelope. The skin of a black antelope, made to be two inches in size, is attached to that three-stranded thread. This Krishnasinam is for purity, and the munji grass waist-cord is worn to control Prana and Apana.

In addition, the கமண்டலம் (kamandalam), a vessel, and the Panchasikai, among other These are symbols of Shiva.

Therefore, according to the rule that one who seeks Shiva must bear his symbols, these Brahmacharis, who are about to undertake Gurukulavasam, will wear these symbols.

Thus, Pillaiyar also bears these sacred symbols and blesses the people of the world. We shall continue our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 597, Vampara Varivandacchu Sargam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, composed by Sekkizhar Swamigal. According to worldly custom, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, accepting the Upanayana ceremony, appears with the three-stranded sacred thread and deerskin. Sekkizhar Peruman sings: (oru pirappum eyddamai udayar tammai ulagiyalpin upanayana muraimaiyagum irupirappin nilaimaiyinnai sadangu katti eydduvikkum maraimunivar edire nindru varuttin marai nankum tanddom endru mandirangal mozhiyndavarkku maduravakkal poruppa odhinar pugazhivanda punniyanar enniyiranda punida vedam endru) Sekkizhar Peruman structures this verse. He, who is free from all births, according to the worldly custom, undergoes the Upanayana ceremony, which grants the status of a twice-born. Standing before the Rishis who, having performed severe austerities, declared, “We have given you the four Vedas,” the holy one from Puhali, full of infinite sacred knowledge, responded with sweet words.

Sekkizhar Peruman thus composes the sacred verses. Jnanasambandha Peruman is of a nature that does not undergo any birth; he is not born in any birth as a result of karma. Pillaiyar, through his divine verses, expressed, “You made me a peacock that never forgets and showed me how to be born on this earth.” Pillaiyar, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, on the occasion of his sacred marriage, took everyone who came with him to attain liberation. Such is the greatness of Pillaiyar; would he undergo birth due to karma? Absolutely not.

Therefore, Pillaiyar is of a nature that does not undergo any birth as a result of karma. Sekkizhar Peruman sings that he is one who is free from all births. For such a Pillaiyar, in this world, others In their usual custom, these Brahmins perform the Upanayana ceremony for Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, thereby showing the state of being twice-born through the appropriate rituals. The state of being twice-born refers to the birth from the mother’s womb and the birth that follows receiving Upanayana, which reveals Shiva-ness. Generally, for these twice-born, the gross body remains one, but because the subtle state changes, they are said to have two births.

However, here, Sekkizhar Peruman beautifully states that these Brahmins showed such a state of being twice-born to Pillaiyar, who had no birth. Being born from the mother’s womb in one life. And then the second birth comes from Upanayana, and the third birth from initiation, making three types of births, as mentioned in sacred texts. These three births are progressively higher than each other. The phrase (Deeksha Janma Thrutheeyam) indicates this.

Thus, for Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who has no birth, they perform the Upanayana ceremonies, which signify the state of being twice-born. In doing so, they tell Thirugnanasambandha Peruman that they have given him the four Vedas. They intend to teach him all the Vedas, and for that, they first initiate him with the Pranava, the primeval sound.

Here, it is customary for the Veda to begin with Pranava.

Therefore, they utter mantras beginning with Om. This is the moment during the Upanayana ceremony that authorizes the Brahmachari to learn the Vedas.

So, starting with Om, they will initiate him and then continue to teach the Vedas. Starting with Om, they will teach the Brahma mantras, including the Gayatri Samhita mantra. This is a part of Upanayana. The Brahmachari will begin to learn the primary Vedas and other ancillary texts. The Gayatri mantra is also taught. Haradatta Shivacharyar has described in the Sloka Panchakam that Shiva Peruman himself is the meaning of the Gayatri mantra.

In the book Sloka Panchakam, (Gayatri Vallabhaditvat) is stated by Haradatta Shivacharyar, which Madhava Shivagnana Munivar translated as ‘being the meaning of the exalted Gayatri,’ and explained as ‘Sloka Panchaka Vishayam.’ Pandit Easwaramoorthy Pillai has written a commentary on this. The meaning is that Shiva Peruman is the essential meaning of the Gayatri mantra, which is the supreme among mantras. The Gayatri mantra is (Tat Savitur Varenyam Bhargo Devasya Dhimahi Dhiyo Yo Nah Prachodayat). Its interpretation is, ‘We meditate on the effulgence of that divine Sun, Bharga, who guides our intellects.’ This means there is a deity in the Sun whose name is Bharga. We should meditate on that deity Bharga, this is its meaning. Due to this, the deity with the name Bharga is called Bhargadeva.

This means that Bharga is the object of worship in the Gayatri mantra. This name Bharga belongs to Shiva Peruman. Bharga is a conventional name for Shiva Peruman. ‘Bha’ means one who illuminates the worlds. ‘Ra’ means one who brings joy to all beings. ‘Ga’ means one who controls and manifests all beings.

Therefore, Shiva Peruman is blessed with the name Bharga.

Thus, the word Bharga also explains Shiva Peruman’s yoga.

Therefore, the name Bharga is both yogic and conventional for Shiva Peruman. Sanskrit lexicons also state that the name Bharga is a name of Shiva. Bharga Bhargan means one who prevents the growth of future births, i.e., one who cuts off birth. The truth conveyed here is that Shiva’s powers are inherent in all other deities, enabling them to perform their respective functions. This is known by the fact that the names indicating the feminine gender for all masculine deity names refer to Umama. Bhairavi, Brahmi, Vaishnavi, Narayani, and others all refer to Umama.

Therefore, this moment of Upanayana is when the Brahmachari is established in the state of realizing Shiva-ness, having received initiation into Pranava mantra, Gayatri mantra, Samhita mantra, and other mantras. It is the moment of Upanayana.

Thus, they speak, ‘We have given the four Vedas’ to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. In response to these Brahmins who spoke thus and began to chant mantras with ‘Om,’ Thirugnanasambandha Peruman recites all the Vedas to them. The Vedas are infinite and expand immeasurably.

However, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman had already realized all these Vedas through previous austerities.

Therefore, after performing the Upanayana for Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and presenting the four Vedas to the Brahmins, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman recites all these Vedas.

The Brahmins are astonished to witness this. Sekkizhar Peruman, in his sacred words, states that they were amazed by the one who recited a thousand Vedas and expounded the ancient ancillary sciences, appearing as if a thousand crores of suns had blossomed, and whose greatness was due to the grace of the Supreme Light. The learned Vedic scholars, full of love and wonder, praised the young Kaundinya. They worshipped him as a manifestation of their meditative object and were enlightened, dispelling their doubts after hearing the Vedas they had mastered.

Here, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman recites countless Vedas to the Brahmins standing before him, along with their six ancillary sciences such as Shiksha and Vyakaranam. He also recites other arts such as Tarkam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman recites the Vedas which have a thousand branches; here, a thousand means ‘many.’ (Ananthavai Vedaka) is the saying. Hearing Thirugnanasambandha Peruman recite such infinite Vedas, their ancillaries, and other artistic texts, the Vedic scholars rejoice and praise Pillaiyar with wonder. They praise him with love and wonder, contemplating the greatness of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who, like countless suns gathered together and radiating their rays, was a effulgence of light who received the grace of the Lord. For these Brahmins had only attained Kala Jnana, which is worldly knowledge, without realizing Shiva Jnana.

Sekkizhar Peruman, in his sacred words, states: (Shruti aayiram odhi angamaana tol kalaigal edutthuiyambum thonthalarai paruthi aayiram kodi virinthaal enna paranjothi arulpetra paanmai menmai karuthi aadharavodu viyapputra etthum kalaimaraiyor kavuniyanar tammai kan mun varuthiyaana porul endru irainchi thamun valla maraikkettu ayyan thirndhu vazhndar endru) He describes how the Brahmins, considering the supreme glory of the Kaundinya child, who appeared as if millions of suns had risen, having received the grace of the Supreme Light, revered him with deep admiration and wonder. They prostrated before him, considering him the object of their meditation, and, having heard the Vedas from him, their doubts were dispelled, and they lived a blissful life. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, besides reciting countless Vedas to the Brahmins standing before him, also recited the six angas (ancillary sciences) such as Shiksha and Vyakarana. He also recited other arts like Tarkam. The Vedas have a thousand shakhas (branches); here, a thousand means numerous. The saying is, (ananthavai vedaka).

Hearing Thirugnanasambandha Peruman recite such boundless Vedas, their angas, and other literary works, all the Vedic scholars joyfully praise Pillaiyar with wonder. They praise him with love and wonder, contemplating the excellence of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who, having received the grace of the Lord, shone forth as a radiant light, as if countless suns had gathered and spread their rays. This is because these Brahmins had attained only worldly knowledge, which is a knowledge of attachment, without having attained Shiva Jnana.

However, before these Brahmins, as the supreme light transcending all other lights, as Paranjothi, The Brahmins, who had attained only worldly knowledge (pasa jnana) without realizing Shiva jnana, now perceive Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as a radiant manifestation of Shiva jnana, having received the grace of Shiva Peruman, who is the Supreme Light. They then bow to Pillaiyar, believing that he has appeared here as a result of their meditative practices, having chanted mantras according to the rules and contemplated them. According to the saying, (Uruvenath thavamame), the deity corresponding to a mantra, when chanted and contemplated according to the rules, manifests itself.

Accordingly, the Brahmins, having meditated on the meaning of the mantras for a long time, now see Pillaiyar manifest before their eyes. They perceive Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as a radiant manifestation of Shiva Jnana, having received the grace of Shiva Peruman, who is the Supreme Light.

Therefore, they bow to Pillaiyar, believing that he has appeared here as a result of their meditative practices, having chanted mantras according to the rules and contemplated them. According to the saying, (Uruvenath thavamame), the deity corresponding to a mantra, when chanted and contemplated according to the rules, manifests itself.

Accordingly, the Brahmins, having meditated on the meaning of the mantras for a long time, now see Pillaiyar manifest before their eyes.

Therefore, all those Brahmins praise and worship Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Although they were skilled in all the Vedas, those Brahmins had many doubts. Now that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the object of their meditation, has appeared before them and revealed all the Vedas, they asked Pillaiyar about their previously held doubts, cleared them, and became enlightened.

Thus, all those Brahmins who had previously suffered with doubts, lacking a good life, are now enlightened, free from all doubts, and have attained a great life that they had never experienced before. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman further imparts divine teachings to these joyful Brahmins.

Our contemplation continues. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 598, Vampara Varivandu Serkum Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, composed by Sekkizhar Swamigal. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who had recited all the Vedas and arts to the Brahmins standing before him, removes all their doubts and enlightens their minds with teachings. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman teaches that the cause for the manifestation of all mantras is the sacred five letters of Shiva Peruman, the Sri Panchaksharam. Sekkizhar Peruman composes this verse, explaining that having revealed all the mantras and removed the mental confusion and doubts that arose from the Vedic rituals and injunctions, he taught all the Brahmins clearly. The ancient primordial mantra All mantras originate from the five letters of the Lord, which is the primeval source.

The mantra chanted at dusk is the five letters.

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman composed the Thirupathigam of the Five Letters. After explaining all the mantras within the Vedas to those Brahmins, he also dispelled all the doubts that had arisen in their minds from the Vedic rituals and sacrificial ceremonies. He then taught them, in a clear manner, that the primary cause for the manifestation of all mantras is the Sri Panchaksharam of Shiva Peruman.
