He thus expounds the Thirupathigam of Sri Panchaksharam, which begins with the phrase, ‘The mantra chanted at dusk is the five letters.’ Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composes the Sri Panchakshara Thiruppathigam. That Thiruppathigam begins with (Thunjalum Thunjsalilladha Poladhinum) and is known as the Panchakshara Thiruppathigam, which holds a special place as a part of daily recitation for Saivites. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman now imparts this teaching.

In the Vedas, mantras are categorized into three sections: Mantras, Brahmanas, and Brahmana Seshas. In that part, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, in the section that follows the mantras, describes the rituals and Vedic ceremonies, such as sacrifices, performed using the previously mentioned mantras. These are in the form of injunctions like ‘Perform Agnihotram.’ Following this, in the section called Brahmana Sesha, there are sentences known as Arthavada. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman recites all these to the Brahmins. Having said this, he teaches that the source of all such mantras is the Thiruvainthezhuttu (Five Sacred Letters). He teaches that the Sri Panchaksharam is the primordial mantra.

The term ‘Adhi Mantram’ can mean ‘the mantra of the Origin,’ ‘the primordial mantra,’ or ‘the mantra dear to the Origin.’ Thus, he teaches that the Sri Panchaksharam is the primordial mantra, because it is this Panchaksharam that arises before creation. This holy mantra of Panchakshara. In creation, the first mantras to emerge from Kudila are those in the form of Nada, Bindu, etc. All mantras originate from the subtle Panchakshara, such as the syllable ‘A’. Whether it is Panchakshara, Pranava, Prasada, or Ajapa, these are all variations of Nada and Bindu.

Therefore, they are not different; they are all one.

Thus, the prime source of all manifestation is Sri Panchakshara. Akaram, Ukaram, Makaram, Bindu, and Nadam are the five kalas (energies). These five letters govern the five principles: soul, mind, intellect, consciousness, and ego. The combination of these five letters is Pranava. When all these are united as a whole, They are called Pranava, and when separated, they exist as these five letters, controlling the soul and other things. That is, from Pranava, Varna (syllable), Pada (word), and Mantra (incantation) arise in order.

Varna means letter.

Therefore, Pranava is the root cause of the entire world of sound. That Pranava also manifests as the subtle Panchakshara. Shivagamas state which letters arise from the Akara, Ukara, Makara, Nada, and Bindu kalas among the fifty-one letters.

Therefore, it is understood that the subtle Panchakshara is Pranava. Among mantras, Ajapa is considered supreme. The subtle Panchakshara that controls the faculties transforms into Ajapa. It controls the breath, letting it in and out. It also activates the inner faculties. Since the breath moves in and out alternately, that is, being activated by Pranava, by the Ajapa mantra, thoughts and forgetfulness alternate for living beings.

Therefore, the subtle Panchaksharam itself operates everything, existing as the gross Panchaksharam, Ajapa, Prasada, and Pranava. That is why Thirugnanasambandha Peruman thus explains Sri Panchaksharam as the origin of all. In this Panchakshara Thiruppathigam, in the second verse, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman teaches this as (Mantra Nanmaraiyagi).

Therefore, the Sri Panchaksharam is the source of the four Vedas, which were created as mantras.

Furthermore, in the section of the Vedas called mantras, The Sri Panchaksharam is also present. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman teaches that the Sri Panchaksharam is also in the heart of the Veda, and thus he composes the Sri Panchakshara Thiruppathigam, stating that the mantra chanted at dusk is the Thiruvainthezhuthu (the sacred five letters). The dusk period is called Devayamam. All mantras and their presiding deities appear with clarity during this time. For Brahmins who maintain the fire, this dusk period is special.

Therefore, in the second verse of this Panchakshara Thiruppathigam, he places this and teaches the virtuous Vedic scholars who maintain the sacred fire that (anthiyul mandiram anjezhutthume), meaning, the mantra to be chanted at dusk is the five letters.

Thus, before him, the Vedic Thirugnanasambandha Peruman thus reveals the Sri Panchakshara Thiruppathigam to the Srauthikas, who are Saivite Vedic scholars. Pillaiyar composed two Thiruvainthezhuthu pathigams (decades of verses on the five letters). One is this Sri Panchakshara Thiruppathigam, which he is now revealing. The other is the pathigam beginning with (Kadhalagi), which Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sang at Thirunallur Perumanam during his sacred wedding. It is called Namachivaya Thiruppathigam. The Thiruppathigam he is now revealing is called Sri Panchakshara Thiruppathigam.

This glorious and special Thiruppathigam is the 22nd pathigam in the third Thirumurai, set to the tune of Gandhara Panjamam. That Thiruppathigam is as follows: Thiruchitrambalam (Thunjalum Thunjsalilladha Poladhinum nenjsaga naindhu ninemiyum naadarum vanjsagamattadi vazhtha vandha kootranja) (udhaiththana vanjezhuththume mandira naanmaraiaagi vaanavar sindhaiyu nindravar thammai aazhvana sendhozhaloambiya semmaivedhiyar kandhiyunmandiram anjezhuththume ooniluyirppaiki yonsudar jnanavilakkinaietri nanbul thenai vazhithira thethuvaarkidaraanakkeeduppena vanjezhuththume nallavar theeyarenadhu natchinar sellal keda sivamutthikattuvak kkolla namanramatkkondu pomidath thallalkeduppanavanjaalutthume kongalarvan madhanvaali aindagthangullaboodhamum anja vaimpozhiRrangkaravin padam anjundammudaiangai ilaiviral anjezhuththume thummalirumarodarnthapozhdhinum vemmai naragam vilaindapozhdhinum immai vinaiyadar theydhum pozhdhinum mammai) (thunai anjezhutthume veedu pirappai aruththu mettinar peedai keduppana pinnai naadoru maadu koduppana mannu maa nadamaadiyugappana vanjezhutthume vandamaroothi madandai penaana pandaiya ravanan paadiyuyndana thondargal kondu thuthitthap pin avar kandamalippana vanjezhutthume karuvana naanmugan kaanaatharkkonna seeruvana chevadi sevvi naadorum peruvana pesip pitarum piththarkk karuvana mavanavanjaalutthume putthar saman kazhukkaaiyar poykkozhai sitthatthavargalezindhu therina vitthaga neeranivar vinaippagai kaththiramaavavanjaalutthume natramizh jnanasambandha naanmarai katravan kaliyar mannanaanniya vattramin maalai iraindhum anjezhutthutrana vallavar rombaraavar)

Since this Thiruppathigam concludes each verse with (anjezhutthume anjezhutthume) like a crown, it is named Sri Panchakshara Thiruppathigam. When Pillaiyar thus imparted his divine teaching, the Brahmins accepted his words with reverence, rejoiced, and were enlightened. Pillaiyar himself, having ascended the divine boat, went to worship the Lord, offered praises with truthful music, held the Lord’s lotus feet in his mind, and, contemplating the Lord’s sacred feet, emerged from the temple.

At that time, while he was blissfully with his devotees, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, who was residing in Thiruchitrambalam, heard about all the divine deeds of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman: how Umadevi and Shiva Peruman appeared on the bull, to remove his crying, and how he drank the boundless milk of wisdom offered by Umama in a golden bowl. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, having heard all these divine deeds of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, felt a great love to worship Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and thus set out from Thiruchitrambalam to Thirkazhi. This is the first meeting between Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal, which is about to take place. We had already contemplated this same historical event in the puranam of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, focusing on Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s history.

Now, in the history of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, we are going to contemplate the same sections, focusing on Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s history. Let us go on contemplating. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 599, Vampara Varivandu Sarcam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, composed by Sekkizhar Swamigal. Periya Nayaki Ammaiyar, who resides in Thonipuram, Thirkazhi, is Umadevi, whose delicate fingers play with balls. Ball-playing was a game women played in ancient times, making it a common trait for women.

Therefore, Periya Nayaki Ammaiyar has delicate fingers that play with balls. Periya Nayaki Ammaiyar is the divine power of the Lord. She releases the worlds, which are like balls, from herself and then makes them return to her. Sekkizhar Peruman sings about Periya Nayaki Ammaiyar, referring to her as the one with fingers that play with balls, to indicate her playful nature. Sekkizhar Peruman sings about Periya Nayaki Ammaiyar as the one with fingers that play with balls, indicating her playful nature. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is blessed with the greatness of having been fed the milk of wisdom, which encompasses all knowledge and transcends all others.

Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, who resides in Thiruchitrambalam, hears this divine news from the devotees. Having heard this, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, with great love to worship Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, arrives in Thirkazhi. This is the first meeting between Thirunavukkarasu Peruman and Pillaiyar, which is about to take place. (Vaakkin peruviral mannar vandu anaindhar enak ketta pookkamal vaasaththadanjchoozh pugazhip perunthagayaarum aakkiya nalvin perendru uLaththodu meyythi erkkum peruviruppodum edhirkoLa eydhumbOzhdhil sindhaiyidaiyaara anbum thirumEnithannil asaivum kandhai mikaiyaang karutthum kaiyuzhavaara padaiyum vandhezhigaNNIr mazhaiyum vadivilpolithirunIrum anthamilaa thiruvEdaththarasum edhirvandhu anaiya kandakavuniyak kandrum karuththipparavumeykkaththaruvedaa nerE thondriyadhendru thozhudhE anndarum pottra vanindhangarasum edhirvandhirainja mandiyavaarvam peruga maduramoLiyarul seythaar endru) Sekkizhar Peruman composes three verses at this point, describing how the King, a great master of words, arrived, and the venerable one from Puhali, surrounded by fragrant flower gardens, knowing that good deeds had brought a great reward, went to receive him with great eagerness. Seeing the King, who embodied endless devotion in his heart, trembling in his sacred body, thinking a patched cloth was excessive, holding a weeding tool in his hand, with tears flowing like rain, and radiant sacred ash adorning his form, the young Kaundinya, with inner devotion, worshipped him, thinking that the true form of devotion had appeared before him. As the gods praised and the King bowed in return, boundless devotion surged, and he spoke sweet words.

Sekkizhar Peruman thus describes the sacred event of the first meeting between the two great spiritual leaders, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman and Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Sekkizhar Peruman describes in one verse how Thirunavukkarasu Peruman came to worship Pillaiyar after hearing of his greatness. Sekkizhar Peruman had previously elaborated on this event, the arrival of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman in Thirkazhi, in the Puranam of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. He described seeing the King (Thirunavukkarasu) in one verse in the Puranam of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman.

Here, in the Puranam of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, he elaborates on it in three verses.

Thus, the extent of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s eagerness to meet and worship Pillaiyar Sekkizhar Peruman conveys that Pillaiyar also had the same eagerness and love to meet and worship Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. Sekkizhar Peruman conveys Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s inner thoughts through those three verses in his Puranam, and now, through these three verses, he conveys Pillaiyar’s inner thoughts. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, the king of great words, just as he heard about the grace of Pillaiyar becoming Thirugnanasambandar, Pillaiyar also heard about the grace of Marul Neekkiyar becoming Thirunavukkarasu.

Therefore, to meet and worship Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, the great master of words, arrived. Upon hearing that he had arrived, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, accompanied by his devotees, arrived at the boundary of Thirkazhi to greet Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. Generally, when Pillaiyar travels, his assembly of devotees, Brahmins, and attendants accompany him.

Now, when Pillaiyar arrived at the boundary of Thirkazhi to meet and worship Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, he left the Brahmins and attendants and went to receive Thirunavukkarasu Peruman with his assembly of devotees. The nature of sitting blissfully with devotees is still present. This nature is to sit with devotees on both sides.

Therefore, Pillaiyar, with his assembly of devotees, greets Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. Sekkizhar Peruman depicts in this verse, like a painting, how Thirunavukkarasu Peruman appeared to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s divine eyes. This is the 270th verse in Thirugnanasambandha Peruman Puranam. (Sinthaiyidaiyaara anbum thirumEnithannil asaivum kandhai mikaiyaam karutthum kai uzhavaara padaiyum vandhezhigaNNIr mazhaiyum vadivilpolithirunIrum anthamilaa thiruvEdaththarasum edhirvandhu anaiya endru) Sekkizhar Peruman depicts, like a painting, the divine form of grace that Thirunavukkarasu Peruman embodied. The scene we see here is the one Pillaiyar witnessed before him.

Similarly, Sekkizhar Peruman had previously depicted Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s divine form like a painting in two other places. In Thirupadhirippuliyur, when Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, after being rescued, arrived in Thiruvadhigai, Sekkizhar Peruman described the divine appearance seen by the devotees as (Thooyaven neeru thudhaindha ponmeni) in verse 1405. In verse 1490, Sekkizhar Peruman, describing the historical state of the King who performed services and sang in the sacred street of Thiruvarur, depicted it as (Maarbaara pozhi kaNNir), as his own statement, like a painting.

Here, what Pillaiyar sees is the inner manifestation of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, the boundless love.

Therefore, beginning with (Sinthaiyidaiyaara anbum), Sekkizhar Peruman portrays Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s divine form here. Sri Madhava Shivagnana Munivar, understanding this meaning and its greatness, in the Kanchi Puranam, composed a eulogy for Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, saying, (Idayara perunbum mazhaivaram inaiveliyum uzhavara thin padaiyara thirukkaramum shivaperuman thiruvadike pathiththa nenjum nadaiyara perunthuravum vakkisap perunthagai than gnana padal thodayara sevvaiyum sivaveda polivazhagum thuthiththu vazhvam endru). ‘Boundless love, eyes raining tears, hands holding the weeding tool, a heart fixed on Shiva Peruman’s sacred feet, immense renunciation, the wisdom of the great master of words, a sweet mouth that sings songs, and the beautiful radiance of Shiva’s attire—we praise and live by these.’ Boundless love is love that continues ceaselessly through all time. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman possessed such boundless love. (Thirumenithannil asaivum) Sekkizhar Peruman sings ‘trembling in the sacred body’ because this trembling in the sacred body is a manifestation of abundant love. It is an expression of abundant love.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman sings (Thirumeni thannil asaivum), meaning ‘trembling in the sacred body.’ He then sings (Kandhai mikaiyaam karutthum), meaning ‘the thought that even a patched cloth is excessive.’ Kandhai refers to a single piece of upper garment. ‘Kandhai mikaiyaam karuththu’ implies the ultimate mental state of renunciation, where even that single cloth is deemed unnecessary.

Next, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman holds a weeding tool in his sacred hand. He sings of it as (Kai Uzhavara Padaiyum).

Then comes (Vandhu izhi kaNNir mazhaiyum), meaning ‘the rain of tears that flows down.’ Thirunavukkarasu Peruman possesses boundless love in his heart. The rain of tears expresses that boundless love in his heart.

Thus, due to abundant love, the tears flow like rain, and the radiant sacred ash adorns his form. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s sacred body is adorned. The sacred ash, which he started wearing without interruption from the day Thilagavathiyar consecrated him, shines brightly on Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s sacred body. Such a timeless divine form of the King appears before him. This is the divine form of the Lord, hence an immortal divine form. As stated in Shivagnanabodham, (Than unara vendi thanathu uruvai thaan koduthu than unara thannul irutthalal than unaru nesathar thampal nigazhum thadhineybol), meaning, ‘to realize Himself, He gives His form and dwells within to be realized, like ghee from curd among those who love Him.’ Such is the boundless divine form of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman.

Such a divine form appeared directly before them, and seeing it, The young Kaundinya Pillaiyar also bows and worships, considering that the form of a devotee, which is the abode of true overflowing love in his heart, has appeared directly before him. Pillaiyar, holding the view that the form of a devotee is like a Shiva temple, worships it as Paramaswaran. When it says ‘the divine form appeared directly,’ it means that all the characteristics of a divine form became manifest and appeared as an embodiment before Pillaiyar’s eyes.

Therefore, Pillaiyar does not see Thirunavukkarasu Peruman as merely the form of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, but as the embodiment of the state of a devotee.

Thus, he arrives bowing. To make others, including the celestials, understand and attain salvation, Pillaiyar, from the position of an Acharya, makes them realize the greatness of the divine form. Pillaiyar thus comes bowing. Pillaiyar welcomes Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, who possesses great fame, and accompanies him, speaking sweet words. He takes him inside the sacred place of Thirkazhi. The first thing to do upon arriving at a sacred place is to worship the Lord of that place.

This was the decision of these two great souls and also the Saivite tradition. When Shivapadahrudayar went to see Pillaiyar in Thiruvalai, he first went to the temple to worship and only then inquired about Pillaiyar’s residence and went to meet him. This can also be recalled here.

Therefore, Pillaiyar leads him inside the sacred place of Thirkazhi. He leads Thirunavukkarasu Peruman with great eagerness to the Thiruthonipuram temple. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman also goes with Pillaiyar with overflowing eagerness. Having had the opportunity to meet and worship Pillaiyar as he had wished, and also to worship the Lord who granted wisdom to Pillaiyar, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman proceeds to the temple with that love. Pillaiyar also worships Thiruthoniyappar and makes Thirunavukkarasu Peruman worship as well. Pillaiyar considered meeting Thirunavukkarasu Peruman a great blessing obtained through divine grace.

Therefore, after receiving divine permission from Thoniyappar, he leads Thirunavukkarasu Peruman to his sacred residence. He provides accommodation for Thirunavukkarasu Peruman with the surrounding devotees. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman offers incomparable sacred food. This sacred food is prepared for the peerless Thirunavukkarasar Peruman, thus it also becomes incomparable sacred food.

In this way, great love and friendship flourished more and more there. This love, which both great individuals had for the Lord, fostered their friendship. As love and friendship thus shone ever brighter, they worshipped the Lord and, being immersed in the experience of spiritual wisdom that resulted, they remained joyful, singing pathigams in praise of the Lord, which were garlands of words that rose from their hearts.

In this way, they worshipped and praised the Lord for having brought them together, and sang pathigams. The two great individuals remained together for several days.

Then, Thirunavukkarasar Peruman, having received divine grace, wished to visit and worship the Lord in other temples. He obtained the consent of the esteemed child of Sirkazhi, who wore the three sacred threads on his beautiful chest, and then departed from that joyous and intimate friendship, with the intention of reuniting later.

Thus, Thirunavukkarasar Peruman departed from that inseparable friendship. The quote, “Joyful meetings lead to separation,” from the poets’ tradition, is exemplified by this event, as pointed out by Mathava Sivagnana Munivar. The idea of meeting again at the time of their separation arose in the hearts of both, and for this reason, Later, in Thiruppugalur, these two great individuals meet unexpectedly. The meaning here is that even though their physical forms separated, their bond of friendship did not. We can also recall the Thiruppoonduruthi event here.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman comes to the border of Sirkazhi and bids farewell to the unique Thirunavukkarasar Peruman.

Then Thirugnanasambandha Peruman returns to Sirkazhi and remains there. We will continue to contemplate in Sirkazhi. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Six Hundred, Vambara Varivandu Sarkkam, by Sekkizhar Swamigal. Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, after bidding farewell to Thirunavukkarasar Peruman, arrived at the town of Sirkazhi and worshipped the Lord residing in Thirthony, singing beautiful Tamil verses. He remained there. This period was when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman resided in Sirkazhi for a long time.

Therefore, every day, he would go before Thirthonyappar and offer numerous Tamil pathigams, which were garlands of Tamil composed in various poetic forms. He offered pathigams that were garlands of classical Tamil, composed in varied poetic forms: “senthamizh maalai vigarpa seyyutkalan mozhimatrum vantha sor seer maalai matrum.” He sang alliteration, repetition, rhyme, and unique verses such as “Yamakak Kavithai,” “Ekapaatham,” “Thiruvirukku Kural,” “Ezhukootrirukkai,” “Eeradi,” “Eeradi Vaippu,” “Naaladi Mel Vaippu,” “Mudugam,” “Ragam,” “Chakkaram,” and other varied compositions, just as Sekkizhar Peruman enumerates the pathigams composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, stating that “Gnanasambandhar sang the exalted Kaaliyar of the world, comprehending all things as the fundamental literature for the pathigams, which are said to be such varied compositions.” The pathigams thus composed as classical Tamil garlands include the pathigam named “Thirumozhi Matru,” the pathigam named “Vazhimozhi Thiruviraga pathigam,” the pathigam named “Thiru Ekapaatha pathigam,” the pathigam named “Irukku Kural pathigam,” the pathigam named “Ezhukootrirukkai pathigam,” the pathigam named “Eeradi pathigam,” “Eeradi” The pathigam titled “Adi Mel Vaippu,” the pathigam titled “Naaladi Mel Vaippu,” the pathigams composed in the accelerated rhythm known as “Thiruviragam,” the pathigam titled “Thiruchakkaramatru,” the pathigam titled “Aadhi Vigarpa Mukkali,” the pathigam titled “Thiruthalacchathi,” the pathigam titled “Aavin Paichal” or “Gomuthiri pathigam,” and the pathigam titled “Palpeyarpathu pathigam” — these are all referred to as Miraikkavigal. Miraikkavigal are pathigams where words and rhythm intertwine, creating many variations in sound. Miraikkavi means to cause distress.

These pathigams are structured such that readers must diligently apply their minds, analyze, and extract the meaning, hence their name Miraikkavi. For these varied compositions, the fundamental For those who desire fundamental grammatical rules, these pathigams composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman serve as foundational literature.

Therefore, before this, there was no literature for such varied compositions, and these pathigams composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman stand as the original literature. Tamil learners can consider these as the literary examples for their respective varied compositions.

Thus, we can contemplate the pathigams composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, one after another.

First, “Thirumozhi Matru.” This pathigam, “Thirumozhi Matru,” is the 117th pathigam in the first Thirumurai, set in the musical mode of Vyazhakurinji. It is a Miraikkavi, a varied poetic form where the words can be rearranged to derive meaning. This pathigam, “Mozhi Matru,” is one of the ways to understand meaning, where words must be separated and rearranged, either to the front or back, to grasp the meaning. This pathigam is structured in this manner. For example, in the first verse of this pathigam, the first line states, “Kaadathu anikalam kar aravampathi.” This should be understood by rearranging the words as “Kaadathu pathi” (forest is his abode) and “Kararavam anikalam” (dark snake is his ornament). This entire pathigam is structured in this way.

The verses of this pathigam, with their words separated and meanings, are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. (Kaadathu anikalam kar aravampathi kaalathanil Thoadathu anuguvar sundara kaathinil thoochilambar) He wears (ve) on his body and gives bows and arrows to the hunters. (peedu adhu mani maada piramapurathu arare) This means the Lord of Piramapuram makes the forest his abode, wears serpents as ornaments, wears earrings in his beautiful ears, anklets on his feet, and assuming the form of a hunter, bestows Pasupathiram upon the hunters. (kaadathu pathi anikalam kar aravum kalathanil thoochilambar sundarak kaathinil thoadathu anikuvar) This should be separated and combined to derive the meaning. Now for the second verse: (kattraich chadaiyathu kankanam munkaiyil thingal kangai pattithu muppuram paarppadaithon thalai suttathu pandu ettithu paambai aninthathu kootrai ezhil vilangum vettri silaimathil venupurathu engal vethiyare) The sage of Venupuram’s matted hair He wore the moon and the Ganga in his matted hair, a serpent as a bracelet on his wrist, and burned the head of Brahma, who saw the three cities. In the first verse, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman refers to Piramapuram, one of the twelve sacred names of Sirkazhi. In the second verse, he uses the name Venupuram.

Similarly, in all twelve verses of this pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has incorporated the twelve names. Now for the third verse: (koovilam kaiyathu pericha sadai mudi koottathathu thoo vilangum podi poondathu poosittru thutthi nagam ezhil vilangum nuthal aanaiyum paagam urithanar in ilam solai pugazhiyul meviya punniyare) The meaning of this is that the Lord, who resides in Pugazhi, also known as Sirkazhi, is a virtuous one who wears vilvam in his dense matted hair and holds a drum (peri) in his hand. He is one who smears himself with pure sacred ash, wears a cobra adorned with markings, holds a bow-like forehead (representing Uma) in one half of his body, and flayed an elephant. Now for the fourth verse: (urithathu paambai udalmisaiyittathu or aanakalittrai erithathu or aamaiyai inpura poondathu muppurathai seruthathu soolathai enthittru thakkanai velvi palnool virithavar vazhtharu venguruvil veetrirunthavare) The meaning of this is that the Lord, who resides in Venguru, also known as Sirkazhi, where scholars who have learned and expounded many texts reside, is one who flayed a unique and excellent elephant, wore a snake on his body, burned the three cities, joyfully adorned himself with a tortoise shell, raged against Daksha in the sacrifice, and held a trident in his hand. Now for the fifth verse: (kottuvar akku arai aarpathu thakkai kurunthazhaiyena ettuvai tham kalappu ilar inbugazh enbu ulavin mattu varum thazhal sooduvar maththahamum enthuvai vanthottu varum kodithonipurathu urai sundarare) The meaning of this is that the Lord Sundarar, who resides in Thonipuram, also known as Sirkazhi, which has tall banners reaching the sky, is one who plays the drum called Thakkai, ties conch beads around his waist, does not associate with short-stemmed ghost-dwarf forms, earns sweet praise, wears sweet-smelling thazhal and thorn-apple flowers, and holds fire. Now for the sixth verse: (saatthuvar paasam thadakkaiyil enthuvai kovanam tham kooththavar katchukkulavinindru aadu)

He wears a crane feather, holds many weapons, and a host of ghosts dance with him. The virtuous Lord, who resides in Poontharai, which is worshipped by blooming flowers, is one who wears a loincloth, holds a noose in his long hand, performs his unique dance, dances with a waistband, wears a crane feather, and performed a dance with many weapons, which are hosts of ghosts. He is exceedingly beautiful. Now for the seventh verse: (kaalathu gangai kattraich sadaiyullal kazhal silambu maalathu enthal mazhu adhu paagam valar kozhungottu aalathu oorvar adalthu iruppar animani neer selathu kanniyor pangai sirappuram meyyavaray idhu) The meaning of this is that Lord Shiva, who resides in Sirapuram, also known as Sirkazhi, has Uma Devi with beautiful blue sapphire eyes, which resemble fish, as one half of his body. He wears anklets on his feet, holds the Ganga in his matted hair, has Thirumal as his other half, holds a battle axe, resides under a banyan tree with lush branches, and rides a powerful bull.

Now for the eighth verse: (neruppu uru velvidai meniyar eruvar nettriyin kan maruppu uruvan kannar thaathaiyai kaattuvar ma murugan viruppuru paambukku mey thanthaiyar viral mathavar vazh poruppuru maligai then puravaththu ani punniyare) The meaning of this is that the virtuous Lord, who adds beauty to Puravam, also known as Sirkazhi, where brave and greatly ascetic sages live in mountain-like mansions, He has a body red like fire, rides on a white bull, has an eye on his forehead, is the father of Ganesha who has a tusk, and is the true father of Murugan, who loves serpents. He gives a place to serpents on his body and wears them. Now for the ninth verse: (ilangai thalaivanai enthittu irunthathu iralai il naal kalangiya kootru uyir pettra maani kumai pettra kalamkizhar munthaiyin aaduvar kottuvar kaattakatthu salam kilar vazh vayal shanpaiyul meviya thaththuvare) The meaning of this is that the Lord, who resides in Sanpai, also known as Sirkazhi, which has water-filled fields, is one who subdued Ravana, the king of Lanka, He held a deer in his hand, crushed the agitated Yama, and granted new life to Markandeya, whose lifespan had ended. He plays the drum called monthai, a leather instrument, and dances in the cremation ground. Now for the tenth verse: (adiyai kandilan thaamaraion mal mudi kandilan kodi aniyum puli eru uganthu eruvar thol uduppar pidi aniyum nadaiyal verppu iruppathu or kooru udaiyar kadi aniyum pozhil kaliyulmeya karaikantare) The meaning of this is that Lord Shiva, who resides in Karai Kandam, also known as Sirkazhi, which is surrounded by fragrant groves, could not be seen by Thirumal’s feet, nor could Brahma, who sits on a lotus flower, see the Lord’s crown.

The Lord who bears the tiger as his emblem He joyfully rides the bull which is on his flag, wears a tiger skin, and has Uma, whose gait resembles the beautiful walk of a female elephant, as one part of his body. His abode is Mount Kailash. Now for the eleventh verse: (kaiyathu venkozhai kaathathu soolam amanar butthar eithuvar thammai adiyavar eithar or enakkombu meyththigal kovanam poopathu odupathu methakaiya koyththalar poompozhil kochchaiyul meviya kotravare) The meaning of this is that Lord Shiva, the victor who resides in Kochai, also known as Sirkazhi, which is surrounded by beautiful groves of blooming flowers that are plucked, holds a trident in his hand and a white earring in his ear. Jainas and Buddhists cannot attain him; only his devotees can. He wears a boar’s tusk on his body and a loincloth. Now for the twelfth verse: (kalvuyar inchi kazhumalamaya kadavul thannai nal urai gnanasambandhan gnanaththamil nanku unara sollidal kettal vallor thollai vaanavarthangalodum selguvar seer arulal peralam sivalokam athe) The meaning of this is that those who are able to speak and listen, understanding well the spiritual Tamil composed by Gnanasambandhan in good words about Lord Shiva, who resides in the temple in Kazhumalam, also known as Sirkazhi, which has high walls, will go with the ancient celestials to the celestial world and then attain Sivalokam through his grace.

Thus is the meaning of this pathigam called “Thirumozhi Matru.” We shall proceed with our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Six Hundred and One, Vambara Varivandacharukkam, by Sekkizhar Swamigal. Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. We contemplated the pathigam “Thirumozhi Matru.” Next is the pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, called “Thirumalai Matru.” “Maalai” means sequence, and “Matru” means change.

Therefore, “Maalai Matru” is a type of poem where reading it from front to back, or from back to front, yields the same result. For example, the word “Vikkadakavi.” If you read it in the usual way, “Vikkadakavi,” you can also read it from the end as “Vikkadakavi.” It can be read as “Vikkadakavi.” Similarly, the phrase “Thodu aadu tho.” If read from the beginning, it can be read as “Thodu aadu tho.” If read backwards from the last letter, it will also be “Thodu aadu tho.” Words and phrases of this type are called palindromes in English. The word is a palindrome.

Thus, “Thodu aadu tho” is a phrase that is a palindrome.

In this manner, all eleven verses in this pathigam, “Thirumalai Matru,” composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, are structured so that they read the same way regardless of direction. In these eleven verses, if we take any one verse, whether read from the beginning in the usual manner or read backward starting from the last letter, it will be the same. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has structured all eleven verses in this pathigam in this way. In this genre, this pathigam by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is a pioneer for literature composed in the “Thirumalai Matru” style.

Similarly, it is known that Mathava Sivagnana Munivar composed such verses in the Kanchipuranam and Mahavidwan Meenakshi Sundaram Pillai in the Thirunagaikkaroonam Puranam. The pathigam “Thirumalai Matru” is also called Miraikkavi. This pathigam is structured such that one must exert considerable mental effort to properly separate the words and find their meaning.

Therefore, the beauty of this pathigam lies in its palindrome structure. Even in this pathigam, the consistent placement of events found in Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s pathigams, such as Ravana’s Kailash event, the story of Thirumal and Brahma searching for the Lord’s feet and crown, and the condemnations of Jainism and Buddhism, are present.

Now, let us contemplate the meaning of this pathigam, drawing upon the explanations provided by Pulavar Kanthasamy Pillai. This pathigam is the 117th pathigam of the third Thirumurai, belonging to the sacred site of Sirkazhi.

Now, the verses of this pathigam and their meanings: Thiruchitrambalam. First verse: (Yaama maani yaamaama yaazhikaama kanaa kanaa ka) (Ma kaliya maamaayaa nee maamaayaa) This is the first verse. As we have seen, this verse reads the same whether read forwards or backward.

Now, we can separate the words and read it as follows: (Yaam aamaa nee aam aam maayaazhi kaama kaan nagaa kanaa kaama kaaliyaa maa maayaa nee maa maayaa). This can be parsed. The meaning of these words is: If we, as souls, are God, does that fit? If you are God, then yes, it is entirely fitting. Oh, player of the great lyre (Yazhi), Oh, charming one whom all desire, Oh, serpent-adorned one whom all can see, Oh, destroyer of desire (Kama) so that he had no limbs, Oh, resident of Kali (Sirkazhi), Oh, great magician who also comes as Vishnu, the husband of Lakshmi, may you release us from the great illusion, the impurity of Maya.

Thus, we should separate the words and find the meaning of this verse. Its summary is: If we, as souls, are God, does that Does it fit? If you are the peerless God, it is entirely fitting. Oh, player of the great Yazh instrument, Oh, charming one desired by all! Oh, bearer of serpents whom all can see, demonstrating the truth that even enemies, if they align with Shiva, lose their enmity and become friends! Oh, one who made Kama bodiless, so that his limbs were unseen!

Oh, resident of Sirkazhi! Oh, one who also appears as Vishnu, the husband of Lakshmi! May you release us from the impurities of Maya! Now for the second verse: (Ya kaayaazhi kaayaa kaa thaayaaraara thaayaayaa yaayaa thaaraa raayaa thaa kaayaa kaaliyaa kaayaa) This can be separated as (Ya kaa yaazhi kaayaa kaathaa yaar aar aathaai aayaay aayaa thaaraar aayaa thaaga). Oh, Kaa! Oh, Yazhi!

Oh, Kaaya! Oh, Kaathaa! Oh, Yaar! Oh, Aar! Oh, Aathaai! Oh, Aaya!

Oh, Thaaraar! Oh, Aaya! Oh, Thaga! Oh, Aaya! Oh, Kali! Oh, Kaa!

This should be separated. The meaning of these words is as follows: (Yagaa) Oh, embodiment of sacrifice! (Yazhi) Oh, player of the Yazh! (Kaayaa) Oh, one who assumes a physical form to bless devotees! (Kaathaa) Oh, destroyer! (Yaar aar) Oh, one who is the mother of all beings! (Aathaai) Oh, one who became a mother! (Aayaa) Oh, one who is inscrutable, whose garland of flowers is made of Bones! (Thaaga) Oh, one who has a host of yearning female ascetics! (Kaaliyaa) Oh, one who protects us from all sufferings! (Kaa) Protect us! Oh, Kaa! The meaning of this summary is as follows: Oh, embodiment of sacrifice! Oh, player of the Yazh! Oh, one who assumes a physical form to bless devotees!

Oh, destroyer! Oh, mother of all beings! Oh, one who is adorned with a garland of Aththi flowers! Oh, one who made the women ascetics of Dharukavanam yearn for him! Oh, one who resides in Sirkazhi! Protect us from all suffering!

Now for the third verse: (Thavaa moovaa thaasaa kaa leenaathaa nee yaamaamaa maamaa yaani thaanaazhi kaasaa thavaa moovaa thaa) This can be separated as follows: (Thavaa moovaa thaasaa kaaleenaathaa nee yaama yaani thaana aazhi kaasaa tha vaa). Oh, Kaa! Oh, Kali’s lord! Oh, Nee! Oh, Yaam! Oh, Amani!

Oh, Thaana! Oh, Azhi! Oh, Kasa! Oh, Thava! Oh, Moovatha! The meaning of these words is as follows: (Thavaa) Oh, imperishable one! (Moovaa) Oh, ageless one, eternally youthful! (Thaasaa) Oh, one who is attainable through the ten spiritual deeds! (Kalinathaa) Oh, Lord of Sirkazhi! (Nee) You are the Lord who dances in the midnight when all fear to roam! (Maa) Oh, majestic one! (Maa) Oh, one who rides on Iravatham (elephant)! (Yaani) Oh, you, who ride on the elephant! (Thaanaazhi) Oh, one who is like an ocean in generosity! (Saa) Oh, protect us from death! (Kaasaa) Oh, one whose light is like a gem! (Thaa) Oh, giver of all desired boons! (Vaa) Come before me!

Oh, movatha! The meaning of these words is as follows: (Thavaa) Oh, imperishable one! (Moovaa) Oh, ageless, eternally youthful one! (Thaasaa) Oh, the one attainable through the ten spiritual deeds! (Kaaleenathaa) Oh, Lord of Sirkazhi! (Nee) You are the Lord who dances in the midnight when all fear to roam! (Maa) Oh, majestic one! (Maa) Oh, one who rides on Iravatham (elephant)! (Yaani) Oh, you, who rides on the elephant! (Thaanaazhi) Oh, one who is like an ocean in generosity! (Saa) Oh, protect us from death! (Kaasaa) Oh, one whose light is like a gem! (Thaa) Oh, giver of all desired boons! (Vaa) Come before me! (Moo) Oh, ancient one who appeared before all! Oh, primeval being who is the form of the five elements, starting with air! The summary of this is as follows: Oh, imperishable, ageless one! Oh, one who is attainable through the ten spiritual deeds! Oh, chief of Sirkazhi!

Oh, Lord who dances in the cremation ground at midnight, when all others fear to approach! Oh, majestic one! Oh, one who rides upon the elephant Iravatham! Oh, one who is like an ocean in generosity! Protect us from death! Oh, jewel-like radiant one!

Grant us the boons we desire! Appear before us! Oh, ancient one! Oh, embodiment of the five elements, starting with air! Now for the fourth verse: (Neevaavaayaa kaayaali kaavaavaano vaaraame meraavaano vaavaa kaali yaakaay) Oh, yaa vaavaa nee!

This can be parsed as follows: (Nee vaa vaayaa kaa yaazhi kaa vaa vaa no vaaraame meraa vaan no vaavaa kaaliyaa kaayaa vaa vaa nee) The meaning of these words is as follows: (Nee vaa) Oh, eternal truth that never changes! (Vaayaa) Oh, truth! (Kaa) Oh, bearer of the Yazh! (Yaazhi) Oh, bearer of the Yazh! (Kaa vaa) Come and protect us from the cruel cycle of birth and death! (No vaaraame) Oh, protector! (Meraa vaan) Oh, one who lifted Mount Meru to prevent the gods from suffering! (No vaavaa) Oh, one who lifted Mount Meru to prevent the gods from suffering! (Kaaliyaa) Oh, resident of Sirkazhi! (Kaayaa) Oh, embodiment of the sky! Oh, vaavaa nee! You come quickly! The summary of this is as follows: Oh, unchanging, true essence! Oh, bearer of the lyre! Come and protect us so that the cruel suffering of birth does not befall us!

Oh, one who held Mount Meru as a bow and destroyed the three cities so that the gods in heaven would not suffer! Oh, one who resides in Sirkazhi! Oh, embodiment of the sky! Please come quickly and grant your grace! Now for the fifth verse: (Yaakkalameyaakkaaliyaa methaavithaayaavithaavi thamaayaazhi kaayaame laagayaa) Its parsing is as follows: (Yaa kaalaa meyaa kaaliyaa methaavi thaai aavi veeyaathaa vi kinaru mathiya paravaigal me than arugil vanthu vizhum padi yaazhi vaasippavane yaam mel aagu aayaa). Oh, meyaazhi kaayaame laagayaa!

The meaning of these words is as follows: (Yaa) Oh, one worshipped by all! (Kalaa) Oh, one who is the form of time! (Meyaa) Oh, one who pervades everything like oil in sesame seeds! (Methaavi) Oh, supreme intellect! (Thaai aavi) Oh, mother and life of all beings! (Veeyaathaa) Oh, eternal one! (Vi) Oh, one who plays the Yazh so that birds like parrots fall near him! (Yazhi) Oh, player of the Yazh! (Yaam) We are above; (Aagu) what is happening to us; (Aayaa) do not search for it; (Kaa) protect us! The summary of this is as follows: Oh, one who is the creator of time for all things! Oh, one who permeates all things, inside and out, like oil in sesame seeds! Oh, we are above; (Aagu) what is happening to us; (Aayaa) do not search for it; (Kaa) protect us! The summary of this is as follows: Oh, one who is the creator of time for all things! Oh, one who permeates all things, inside and out, like oil in sesame seeds!

Oh, one who resides in Sirkazhi! Oh, supreme intellect! Oh, mother and life of all beings! Oh, eternal one! Oh, player of the Yazh so that birds like parrots, which produce sweet sounds, fall near him! Protect us from what is happening to us, which we cannot comprehend!

Now for the sixth verse: (Melaa pogaa metheli kaalaa lekaa laanaaye enaalaa kaalelaa kaali theme kaaleme) Its parsing is as follows: (Mele pogaame margandeyarmin) Oh, you became the very Death of Death when Yama tried to approach Markandeya, and your fierce roar made him retreat! Oh, you, who were the Guru for the four sages like Sanaka, under the Banyan tree! Oh, Goddess of Kali! Oh, you, who ride on a cloud-like Vishnu as your vehicle! Will we become like Vishnu, one of your many ganas?

The summary of this is as follows: Oh, you who reprimanded Yama with a harsh voice when he came to take Markandeya’s life! Oh, you who kicked him with your sacred foot and became the Death of that Death! Oh, you who, as Shiva-Guru, taught the truth to the four sages, Sanaka and others, under the Banyan tree and helped them attain spiritual wisdom! Oh, one who resides in Sirkazhi! Oh, supreme being who rode on a cloud as your vehicle! Will we become one of your divine retinue?

Now for the seventh verse: (Nee ya maani eyaa maa thave lee kaathane netha nee ka lee vethaa maayaa e nee maayaa nee) This can be parsed as follows: (Nee ya maani eyaa maatha ezhikaathane nethaani kaali vethaa maayaa e nee maay aani) The meaning of these words is as follows: (Nee ya) Oh, one who has Uma Devi, who never leaves you! (Maani) Oh, Uma Devi! (Eyaa) Oh, unique mother! (Maa tha) Oh, mother! (Ezhi) Oh, embodiment of the seven musical notes! (Kaathane) You protect me powerfully! Oh, one who protects me! (Natha) Oh, one who has a loving heart as his abode! (Nee) Oh, one who is the embodiment of the Vedas, residing in Sirkazhi! (Kali Vedha) Oh, resident of Sirkazhi! (Maayaa) Oh, illusionist! (E Nee) Oh, you, who kill the sufferings that come to kill us! (Maai Aani) You kill them, don’t you? The summary of this is as follows: Oh, one who has Uma Devi, who never leaves you! Oh, unique mother! Oh, embodiment of the seven musical notes! May you yourself come and protect us powerfully!

Oh, one whose abode is a loving heart! Oh, one who resides in Sirkazhi and has bestowed the Vedas and embodies their inner meaning! Will you not kill the sufferings that come to kill us? Now for the eighth verse: (Nenavaraavizhaiyasaliye vegathaleriyalayuulika kaliyulaayarulethaka) Its parsing is as follows: (Ne anavar aa vizha ya aasai izhiye vega athal eri azhaaya uli ka kaliyulaay aru izhavu ethu ahkave ezhisai yaazhaavane) The meaning of these words is as follows: (Ne anavar) Oh, one whose devotees are like cows that fall unconscious in their love for your feet! (Aa vizha) Oh, one who unties the great rope of desire that binds them! (Ya aasai izhiye) Oh, one who unties the great rope of desire that binds them! (Inni vegathaleriyalayuulika) This is separated as (Vegam athar eri aloy oli ka). And dividing it as (Vegam vilangukalil vegamay odavalla manin athal tholai anintha eri azhagane azhaaya uli thunbangal emmai soozhntha idaththu ka kappatruvayaga kaliyulaay ari lethakave sirakazhiyil ullavane arulethakave enpathanai aru izhavu ethu akave endru piriththu etham kuttram izhavu sirumaitthanmai aru etham mannikkatharku ariya kuttramgal endru piriththu elisai iravanane elisai paadiya iravananum allava perum pizhaiyum mannikka pettru thiruvarulukku paaththiramayinaan enave sirumaiyal seytha pizhaigalai mannikkavum endru uyirkal venduvathaga amaigindrathu ini ithan pozippurai iraivarin thiruvadigalil peranbu seluththum adiyavaraam pasukkal thanvayamattru kidakka kattriya aasai endru sollappadum perunkayittrai than karunaiyinal avizththu arulavarai).

Now, its summary: Oh, one who unties the great rope of desire, which binds the devotees who love the Lord’s feet, like cows that fall unconscious in their love for your feet, with his compassion! Oh, one who wears the skin of a deer that can run swiftly! Oh, supremely beautiful one! Protect us when hardships attack us! Even if we commit grave sins out of our insignificance, do not consider them great sins, but small ones, and forgive us! Oh, Ravana, who was skilled in the seven musical notes, committed a great sin out of pride, but you forgave him, did you not?

Therefore, please forgive the sins we commit out of our insignificance! Now for the ninth verse: (Kale mele kani kali kale male me poo poomele mali kani kale mele ka) This can be parsed as follows: (Kale mele kan nee kali kale male mepoo poomel ey male kali kan). Oh, Ee! Oh, Kale! Oh, Mele! Oh, Kaa!

The meaning of these words is as follows: (Kale) Oh, one who is mixed everywhere like the wind! (Male) Oh, one who causes illusion in everything! (Male) means confusion. (Me) Oh, excellent one! (Poo) Oh, bloomed flower! (Poomele) Oh, one who sits on a lotus flower! (Ey Male) Oh, Vishnu! (Kali) Oh, Kali! (Kan) Oh, one who could not be seen by Brahma and Vishnu! (Nee) You are the one who removed them! (Kali) Oh, fierce one! (Kan) Oh, one who has a fierce eye! (Ka) Grant your feet! The summary of this is as follows: Oh, one who is mixed everywhere like the wind! Oh, one who causes confusion in all beings through the power of illusion, and then grants grace! Oh, fierce one, whose feet and crown could not be found by Brahma, who sits on the best lotus flower, and Vishnu! Oh, one who resides in Sirkazhi! Cast your gracious glance upon us!

Grant us your feet! Now for the tenth verse: (Veriyum menava kaliyoy ene nine madalo karathe therakalodamane nine ezhikavanameyurive) This can be parsed as follows: (Veri manam en perumai navam puthumai kaliyay ene thunpaththaiyum neezh nem mikka anbhaiyum adu muraiye ozhithalum al allikkolluthalumaagiya seykal okarathu e yogigaludaiya seykaye therakodu). Oh, you whose fragrance, greatness, and newness are in Kali! Oh, you who eliminate suffering and bestow great love! This is the act of yogis! You think of the words of the Buddhists and the Jains, and you associate with them!

Oh, you, who protect us from entering those paths! This is your right! The meaning of these words is as follows: (Veri manam) Oh, fragrant one! (En) Oh, greatness! (Navam) Oh, newness! (Kaliyay) Oh, one who removes suffering! (Ene) Oh, one who removes suffering! (Neezh Nem) Oh, great love! (Mikha Anbaiyum) Oh, great love! (Adu) Oh, one who removes! (Muraiye) Oh, in order! (Ozhithalum) Oh, removing! (Al) Oh, giving! (Allikkolluthalumakiya) Oh, and receiving! (Seykai) Oh, action! (Okarathu E) Oh, this is the action of yogis! (Yogigaludaiya) Oh, of yogis! (Seykaye) Oh, action! (Therakodu) And with the teachings of the Buddhists, also remembering the teachings of the Jains. Oh, one who refrains from associating with them! Oh, one who protects us from entering those paths!

This is your right! The summary of this is as follows: Oh, one who resides in Sirkazhi, where fragrance, divine essence, greatness, and newness mingle! Oh, one who removes sufferings and bestows great grace! This is the action of Shiva-yogis, who are those immersed in inner penance. Oh, one who refrains from thinking about and associating with the words of Buddhists and Jains! The ability to protect us from entering such external religious paths truly belongs to your sacred feet!

Now for the eleventh and final verse, which contains the fruits of this pathigam. (Ner kazhaamidhayasali thaaye naniye nani layulika kaliyula ninaiye ninaiye thaliyasaiya thamizhagarane) This can be parsed as follows: (Ner akazh aam ithaya aasu azhi thaai el nan neeye nan neel aay olika kaliyulaan innaiye ninaiye thazh isaiyazha thamizh akarane) The meaning of these words is as follows: (Ner akazh aam) Oh, one who digs up and casts away righteousness! (Ithaya aasu) Oh, mental impurities such as lust, anger, and delusion! (Azhi) Oh, destroyer of these three impurities! (Thaai el nan neeye) Oh, you alone are worthy of accepting the role of mother to all the worlds! (Nal) Oh, good! (Nee) Oh, you! (Neel) Oh, great! Oh, one who is exceedingly good! (Aay olika) Protect us when we are weak! (Tamilakaran) Oh, Thirugnanasambandha, whose body is Tamil! (Kaliyulanin) Oh, Lord of Sirkazhi! (Naye) Oh, these songs that melt the hearts of listeners! (Ninaive) Oh, contemplate and sing! (Thazh) Oh, decrease! (Isaiyazha) Oh, and it will not be lacking! The meaning of this is as follows: Oh, one who is capable of destroying the three impurities of lust, anger, and delusion that arise in the heart, which undermine righteousness and cause suffering to all! Oh, unique one, you alone are worthy of accepting the role of mother to all the worlds! Oh, greatest in doing good!

Protect us when we are weak!

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who is the abode of fragrant Tamil, praised Lord Shiva in this pathigam called “Thirumalai Matru.” Those who recite and listen to this pathigam, which melts the hearts of those who sing and hear it, will not suffer any hardship.

Thus are the verses and meaning of this pathigam, “Thirumalai Matru.” We will continue to contemplate other pathigams. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Six Hundred and Two, Vambara Varivandu Sarkkam, by Sekkizhar Swamigal. Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. The next pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman in Sirkazhi is “Thiru Vazhimozhi Thiruviragam.” In the pathigam “Thirumozhi Matru” that we first saw, there are twelve verses. In it, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has sung, incorporating the twelve names of Sirkazhi.

Similarly, in the upcoming pathigams such as “Thiru Vazhimozhi Thiruviragam,” “Ekapaatham,” “Yamakak Kavithai,” “Irukku Kural,” “Eeradi,” “Eeradi Mel Vaippu,” “Naaladi Mel Vaippu,” “Chakkaramatru,” and others, we can see that twelve verses are composed, and the twelve names of Sirkazhi are incorporated in them.

In this way, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has composed this pathigam called “Thiru Vazhimozhi Thiruviragam.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has composed it. This is the unique feature of this pathigam.

Therefore, this pathigam is named “Vazhimozhi Pathigam” because it illustrates the history of the twelve names of Sirkazhi. It is called “Ragam” because it has a very fast rhythmic structure. In each verse of this pathigam, and in each line, all the words are repeated, and the words are repeated. This path of rhyme, structured in a poetic meter, can be seen in the various names of Sirkazhi mentioned in the verses.

Therefore, this pathigam is referred to as ‘Vazhimozhi’ (path of words). For example, the first name, Brahmapuram, is set in the first verse, with words like ‘surarulagu narargal payil’ (divine world, people live) and ‘purameriya varamarula’ (grant boons for burning cities), creating a rhyme scheme with ‘Brahmam’. This means that the second letter of the first word in each line of every verse aligns with the second letter of the respective Sirkazhi name. This beauty can be observed here. This pathigam, composed in Sadhari Pann, is the sixty-seventh pathigam of the third Thirumurai.

Now, the verses and meanings of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. The first verse: ‘Surarulagu narargal payirarani thala muranazhiya varanamathin mu purameriya viravu vagai saravisai kol karamudaya paramanidamam varamarula varanmuraiyin nirai nirai kol varusuruthi siravuraiyinar bramanuyaril kol saranavinai paravavalar bramapurame’. In this verse, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has graced us by using ‘Brahmapurame’ as the concluding word, which is the first of the twelve sacred names of the Sirkazhi shrine, Brahmapuram. Its gist is as follows: When the flying forts with strong walls tormented the celestial world where celestials reside and this earthly world where humans live, causing their might to diminish, the three cities It is said that Lord Shiva, who possesses the power to swiftly launch an arrow that burns and reduces them to ashes, is seated there. This shrine is called Brahmapuram because Brahma, after chanting the Upanishadic discourses, which are the head of the Vedas where all swaras are arranged in order, and extolling the great fame of Shiva with grace, surrendered and prayed to Shiva’s lotus feet to receive boons. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has revealed the history of why this shrine received the name Brahmapuram, that it came from Brahma’s worship, in the concluding line.

Now, the second verse: ‘Thanumigu vanisai kodanuvaiyar penumathu kanum alavir konunuthanee nayani konil pidi mani mathu nanum vagaye ezhu kari punazhiya vaniyal kon’. Venuvinai Eni nagar kaniravi kananadu Venupurame. In this second verse, Venupuram, the second name of Sirkazhi, is set. This place is called Venupuram because of the history where Indra, fearing Surapadman, hid here among the bamboos and worshipped Lord Shiva. Venu means bamboo.

Therefore, this history is sung in the second verse. The meaning of this verse is as follows: Lord Shiva, whom the celestials who worship him with love, and Gajamukasura, who suffered and feared, worshipped, took the form of a powerful male elephant. When Umadevi, with a curved forehead and long eyes, took the form of a flawless female elephant, Lord Shiva, to destroy Gajamukasura, who wielded power and caused harm, Lord Shiva, worthy of the greatness of creating the powerful and beautiful Lord Ganesha, resides in this sacred abode of Sirkazhi.

Here, Indra, the chief of the celestials, fearing Surapadman, lived in hiding. He worshipped Lord Shiva while concealed among the bamboos in this bamboo-filled region. Due to this history, this place is named Venupuram.

Now, the third verse: ‘Pagalo lisai nagamaniyaye mukaimalarai nigazh saranamagavu munivar kagalamali sakalakalai migavuraisai mugamudaya pagavanidamaam pagaigalaiyum vagaiyilaru mugaviraiyai migavarula nigarilimaiyor pugavulagu pugazhaveli rigazhaniga lalarperugu pugazhi nagare’. Its meaning is as follows: Lord Shiva possesses a graceful gaze, having graciously expounded all arts to the sages like Sanaka, who took refuge at his sacred feet, which are like the sun shining on a mountain and a blooming red lotus. Such is the Lord Shiva who resides here. This sacred place, Thirupugazhi, is renowned for its beauty, where peerless celestials take refuge, and is where Lord Muruga, with six faces, was graced to eradicate hostile demons. This place was named Pugazhi because celestials attained fame here. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has enshrined this history in this third verse with the name Pugazhi.

Now, the fourth verse: ‘Anganmathi Gangai nadhi vengana nara vangali rangumizhali tungamalar tangusadai angini karemgalirai tangumidamaam vengathirvizhangulaga mengum ethir pongeri pulangal kalaivo’. Lord Shiva, our Lord, adorns his fiery matted locks with a beautiful-petalled Konrai flower. This place, where he resides, is named Venguru. If people in this world want to overcome the suffering caused by the actions of the mind and other internal organs, which vex them greatly rather than leading them on the right path, they must worship him. This place is where Brihaspati, the celestial guru, worshipped Lord Shiva and attained fame.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reveals the history of how this place came to be known as Venguru.

Now, the fifth verse: ‘Aniyalbhu kana vanaviyal peni ethir banamalai ser thuni’. Venusilai peniyara nanivijayan paniyamar punavarul manubirama niyamidame ni murayir paniyulala miga vaninmal thoni nigar thonipurame. The meaning of this verse is: Lord Shiva, in order to show Parvati the valor of Arjuna, took the form of a hunter in the forest and started a battle against him. When Arjuna’s mountain-like arrows and the quiver containing them were exhausted, and his bowstring was broken, Lord Shiva, who carried a bow made of curved bamboo, then engaged in a wrestling match with Arjuna, who, out of shame, used his hands to fight.

Lord Shiva then blessed him.

Lord Shiva is the embodiment of the Pramanas (Vedas). This place is where he resides. In the course of time, during the great deluge, when the entire world was submerged in the waters of the flood, This place, which floated like a boat in that great flood, is the sacred place known as Thonipuram.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has enshrined the history of how this place came to be called Thonipuram, along with the name Thonipuram.

Now, the sixth verse: ‘Niramaya parabara puratana paravu sivarakavarulendriravum ethirayathu paraninaipurana namaradhipathiyam aramichirathalairayara parayanan varakigutharaymozhivirayapathye’. Its meaning: Lord is Niramaan, free from illness, the supreme being above all things, the most ancient, Shiva who is praised and meditated upon day and night as Paravu Shiva, the Lord of all celestials, The place where he resides with grace is this sacred place of Sirkazhi, called Poontharai. When the beautiful earth, stolen by Hiranyaksha, lay in the ocean, Vishnu emerged from the milky ocean, took the form of a white boar, killed Hiranyaksha, and lifted the earth on his tusk, saving it.

At that time, to atone for the sin of harming Hiranyaksha, Vishnu worshipped Lord Shiva here. This sacred place, Poontharai, is where Vishnu in the form of a boar worshipped.

Thus, the name of this place, Poontharai, and its history have been graced by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

Now, the seventh verse: ‘Aranaiyuru muranbalar maranam vara viranamathil aramalippadai karambisiru viraganavar karananuyar paranerigulkaranathidamam paravamuthuviravidhal porulamaru maravaiyarisiramariyava’. Siramarana saranamavai paravavirukagamar Sirapuramathe. Its meaning is as follows: Lord Shiva is the adept who wielded weapons with his hands to cause the death of many due to the demons of the three cities. He is the one who controls the activities of those who surrender to him. He is the supreme one, superior to all, and possesses the sacred hand that imparts teachings. The place where he resides with grace is this sacred place of Sirkazhi called Sirapuram.

During the churning of the ocean for ambrosia, when the serpent came in the line of celestials to drink the ambrosia, Vishnu severed its head. That head then surrendered to Lord Shiva and praised him, thereby obtaining the blessing of being revered as two planets in the planetary system. This sacred place of Sirkazhi, called Sirapuram, is where this occurred.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has graced us with the name Sirapuram and its history.

Now, the eighth verse: ‘Aramazhivu peravulaguru puyavan viralazhiya niruvi viran mamaraiyinolimurai muralsai piraiyan uravarumiraivanidamang kuraiyin miga nirai thayolimariyaramar niraiyomuraiyoduvarum puravanethir nirainilavudal’. Lord Shiva, who, when Ravana’s power waned, placed his great toe on him, caused him to realize his error, and then, when Ravana praised the Lord with Samagana, granted him a long life and radiant well-being. The place where he resides is this Sirkazhi. This is Puravam. Emperor Sibi, who cut off his own flesh to match the weight of a pigeon but it was not enough, and then ascended the scale himself to make the weight equal, worshipped Lord Shiva here to regain his flawless body, and Lord Shiva blessed him. This sacred place, Puravam, is where Agni, who came as a pigeon and caused this, worshipped Lord Shiva to atone for his sin.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has graced us with the name Puravam and the history of how the fire god, in the form of a pigeon, worshipped here.

Now, the ninth verse: ‘Venpayila manbagiri vanbirama nen periya panpadai konmal kanbariyam monbazhiya nunporulgal tan pugazhkol kandaniidamam manbariyam monbazhi’. Nunpusagar punpayila vinpadaravasei mozhi panbamuni kanpalisai panbugalai Sanbai nagare. The meaning of this verse is: This sacred place called Sanbai is where Lord Shiva, who is a subtle entity unseen by Brahma who flew in the sky as a swan and by Vishnu who went beneath the earth as a boar, resides. When the iron pestle turned into Sanbai grass, and the Yadava princes struck each other with them and ascended to the celestial world, Lord Krishna, having insulted Durvasa Muni and incurred a curse for his kin, worshipped Lord Shiva here to absolve the curse and heal the wounds caused by the Sanbai grass.

Thus, this sacred place of Sirkazhi was named Sanbai. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has graced us with the name Sanbai and its history in this verse.

Now, the tenth verse: ‘Pazhiyurai velanigar pazhamannar suzhumudalaazharunara ezhinisai yazhin mozhi ezaiyaval vazhumiraithaluumidama kizhisai kon melulagil vazararasu suzharasu vazaravaranu kalisaiyil kalisaiyavelulagil uzhivavalar kali nagare’. Its meaning is: Jains and Buddhists do not recognize the Lord. This city of Sirkazhi, known as Kali, is where Lord Shiva, accompanied by Uma Devi, whose voice is like the seven musical notes and the sweetness of the Yazh, resides. Kali, who engaged in a dance competition with the Lord and lost, worshipped Lord Shiva here to be free from her fault. The shrine thus established. This city of Sirkazhi is called Kali.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has graced us with the history of the name Sirkazhi and the name Sirkazhi in this tenth verse.

Now, the eleventh verse: ‘Nacharavu kachana vasai sumathi yuchiyin milaisorukaiyan meysiramanasulagi nichamidu pichaiyamar pichanidamam machamatha nachi mathamachirumiyai seithavachaviratha kochaimura vachalpani yachuramida kochai nagare’. Its meaning: Lord Shiva, who binds a snake as a belt, wears the moon on his head, carries a skull of Brahma in one hand, and desires the alms given daily in this world as a madman, resides in this sacred place of Sirkazhi, which is called Kochchavayam. Machagandhi. Sage Parashara worshipped Lord Shiva here to atone for his indiscretion of engaging in sexual activity with a fish-scented maiden in the middle of the river.

Therefore, this sacred name Kochchavayam and its history are graced by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for Sirkazhi.

Now, the twelfth verse: ‘Ozhugalaridhalikaliyil ozhiyulagu pazhi perugu valiyai ninaiya muzhududalil ezhumayirkadalavu muniguzhipinodu gezhuvu sivanai thozhuthulagil izhugumala mazhiyum vagai kazhumurai kazhumalanagar pazhuthilai ezhuthumozhi tamilviragan vazhimozhi kanmozhi thagayave’. Its meaning: In this Kali Yuga, where good conduct is rare, lamenting the increasing wickedness in this world, the sage Romaroma, whose whole body had hair, along with his group, stayed in this sacred place of Sirkazhi and worshipped Lord Shiva. By doing so, the impurities that bind one to worldly desires were removed, and they received divine knowledge.

Hence, this place is named Kazhumalam. Lord Shiva, the Lord who makes the faults of those who worship this shrine cease, and Gnanasambandhan, the Tamil expert whose words are revered as written Vedas, has revealed these ‘Vazhi Mozhi Thiru Viraga Pasurams’. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman advises that by chanting these Thiru Viraga Pasurams, one can benefit.

Thus, the twelfth name of the Sirkazhi shrine, Kazhumalam, and its history, are sung in these Thiru Viraga Pasurams.

In this way, this rare and unique pathigam is structured. We will continue to contemplate other pathigams. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, Part Six Hundred and Three, by Sekkizhar Swamigal, the chapter on Vambara Varivandu, the biography of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. The next pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is the Thiru Ekapadam pathigam, which comes under the category of ‘Mirai Kavi’. They speak of a type of poetic structure called Yamakam. If the same letter or the same word repeatedly appears in a poem and conveys different meanings, it is called Yamakam. In Tamil, it is called Madakku Ani.

Here, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has composed a special type of Yamakam called Thiru Ekapadam. In Yamakam, one or more syllables are repeated in each line.

However, in this Thiru Ekapadam pathigam, The same line appears four times, and each time it conveys a different meaning. For example, the first verse of this pathigam, ‘Brahmapurathurai Pemman Emman’, is the same line repeated four times as four lines in this poem: ‘Brahmapurathurai Pemman Emman, Brahmapurathurai Pemman Emman, Brahmapurathurai Pemman Emman, Brahmapurathurai Pemman Emman’. Even though the same line appears four times, it is structured to convey different meanings in each of the four lines. This pathigam is a unique pathigam of this kind and is considered a type of Chithrakavi. Ekam means one, Padam means line. This Thiru Ekapada pathigam is a poem where a single line is repeated four times, conveying different meanings.

The verses are structured in such a way that unless Thirugnanasambandha Peruman himself reappears to explain the meaning, or unless one can definitively state the meaning of these verses, it is a pathigam whose meaning cannot be clearly stated. Sirkazhi Kannudaiya Vallalar, a great person who lived accepting Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as his spiritual guru, has provided an interpretation of the inner thoughts of this pathigam. The philosophical work ‘Ozhivil Odukkam’ written by Sirkazhi Kannudaiya Vallalar is very famous. Such a great person, Sirkazhi Kannudaiya Vallalar, has given a commentary on this Thiru Ekapada pathigam. Based on that commentary, Sivakavimaniyar has provided notes for the verses of this pathigam. The one hundred and twenty-seventh of the first Thirumurai.

The Thiru Ekapada pathigam is structured as the seventy-seventh Thirubramapura pathigam.

Now, the verses of this pathigam and their meanings: Thiruchitrambalam. The first verse: ‘Brahmapurathurai Pemman Emman, Brahmapurathurai Pemman Emman, Brahmapurathurai Pemman Emman, Brahmapurathurai Pemman Emman’. As we have already seen, the single line ‘Brahmapurathurai Pemman Emman’ appears four times to form a verse.

However, it should be interpreted by dividing it as follows: The first line ‘Brahmapurathurai Pemman Emman’ should be divided as ‘Brahmam Purathurai Pemman Emman’, the second line as ‘Brahmapurathu Urai Pem Man Em An’, the third line as ‘Brahmam Purathu Urai Pem An Emman’, And the fourth line as ‘Brahmapurathurai Pemman Emman’ and interpreted accordingly. In this interpretation, the first line ‘Brahmam Purathurai Pemman Emman’ means: Our Lord is the one who marvels at and is greatly proud of the complete knowledge of Parashakti, having perceived Parashakti as the embodiment of knowledge. The second line, ‘Brahmapurathu Urai Pem Man Em An’, should be divided and interpreted as: ‘Brahmapuram’ means the celestial world, ‘Urai’ means residing, ‘Pem’ means greatly desired, ‘Man’ means a woman with a deer-like gait, referring to the Ganges, ‘Em’ means our, ‘An’ means life.

Therefore, the meaning is: He, who holds the Ganges, a woman with a deer-like gait, residing in the celestial world, with great desire in his matted locks, is like our very life. The Lord, who holds that deer-like Ganges woman in his matted locks with great affection, is like my very life.

Now, the third line, ‘Brahmam Purathu Urai Pem An Emman’, should be divided and interpreted as: ‘Brahmam’ means Brahmanhood, ‘Puram’ means body, ‘Urai’ means thinking, ‘Pem’ means desire, ‘An’ means not being contained, and ‘Emman’ means one who is like me. Taking these meanings, it means: He is the one who came to be like me, wishing to leave me in liberation in the form of Brahman. The fourth line, ‘Brahmapurathurai Pemman Emman’, should be interpreted as: The Lord who resides in the glorious Sirkazhi called Brahmapuram is my Lord.

Now, the second verse: ‘Vindalar Pozhil Ani Venu Purathu Aran’. Vindalar Pozhil Ani Venu Purathu Aran, Vindalar Pozhil Ani Venu Purathu Aran, Vindalar Pozhil Ani Venu Purathu Aran. This should be divided and interpreted as follows: The first line should be divided as ‘Vindu Alar Pozhil Anivu En Nupuram Tharan’. ‘Vindu’ means mountain, ‘Alar’ means sound, ‘Pozhil’ means a world full of beautiful groves, ‘Anivu’ means encompassing, ‘En’ means glorious, ‘Nupuram’ means anklet. Interpreting this, it means: Lord Shiva wears an anklet that is as glorious as encompassing the eight great mountains of the world and emits a sound as boisterous as containing all noisy worlds within itself.

Now, the second line, ‘Vindu Alar Pozhil Ani Venu Purathu Aran’, And interpreting it as: ‘Vindu’ means Vishnu, ‘Alar’ means slander, ‘Pozhil’ means shade of groves, ‘Ani’ means approaching and standing near, ‘Nindru’ means standing close, ‘Venu’ means desired, ‘Purathu’ means the three cities, ‘Arakkarkalai’ means demons, ‘Erittha’ means burned, ‘Aran’ means Shiva. Interpreting this as: When the demons of the three cities, influenced by the teachings of Vishnu who appeared as Buddha, abandoned the Vedic path and lived by slandering Shiva, the Lord burned them. Such is Lord Shiva.

Now, the third line, ‘Vindalar Pozhil Anivu Enu Puratharan’, should be divided and interpreted as: ‘Vindalar’ refers to the celestials living in the upper world, ‘Pozhil’ refers to the celestial wish-fulfilling tree groves, ‘Anivu’ refers to adorning, ‘Enu’ refers to considering glorious, ‘Puratharan’ refers to Indra, the lord of the celestials. And interpreting it to mean that Sirkazhi is the place where Indra resides, proudly adorning the celestial flowers showered by the celestials of the upper world.

Now, the fourth line, ‘Vindu Alar Pozhil Ani Venupuratharan’, should be divided as ‘Vindu’ means petals unfurling, ‘Alar’ means blooming, ‘Pozhil’ means groves, ‘Ani’ means beautifying, ‘Venupurathu Aran’ means Lord Shiva residing in Sirkazhi called Venupuram.

Now, the third verse: ‘Pundarikathavan Meviya Pugaliye, Pundarikathavan Meviya Pugaliye, Pundarikathavan Meviya Pugaliye, Pundarikathavan Meviya Pugaliye’. This should be parsed as ‘Pundarikathavan Meviya Pugaliye’, ‘Pundarikam Thavan Meviya Pugali E’, ‘Pundarikam Thavan Me Viyam Pugali E’, ‘Pundarikathavan Meviya Pugaliye’. The line ‘Pundarikathavan Meviya Pugaliye’ is divided as ‘Pundarikam’ meaning lotus of the heart, ‘Pundarikathavan’ meaning residing in my lotus of the heart, ‘Meviya’ meaning fixed without return, ‘Pugali’ meaning refuge. Interpreting this, it means that if we always meditate on the Lord and enthrone him in our minds, he will be an excellent refuge for us, leading us to the world of liberation without return. The second line, ‘Pundarikam’ refers to the one who wears sacred ash in three lines, ‘Thavan’ means one with great glory, ‘Meviya’ means spoken, ‘Pugazhuthal’ means praising. ‘E’ is an expletive.

Therefore, its meaning is: The Lord, who wears sacred ash in three lines, is worthy of all the praise conveyed by the words in the verses I have spoken here.

Now, the third line, ‘Pundarikam’ refers to the tiger, ‘Thavam’ refers to the sage. Pundarikam Thavam Pulikal Munivar Me Kuthu Viyan Pon Po pothu Kali Katravan, interpreted as: Lord Shiva is the one who danced in the golden hall of Thillai Chuttrambalam, for the viewing of Vyaghrapada, the sage known as Pulikal Munivar.

Now, the fourth line, ‘Pundarikathavan Meviya Pugaliye’, interpreted as: Brahmadeva, who has the lotus flower as his seat, worshipped in Pugazhi, the sacred place called Pugali.

Now, the fourth verse: ‘Vilangozhi Thigazh Tharu Venguru Mevinan, Vilangozhi Thigazh Tharu Venguru Mevinan, Vilangozhi Thigazh Tharu Venguru Mevinan, Vilangozhi Thigazh Tharu Venguru Mevinan’. In this, the first line, ‘Vilam Kozhi Thee Kal Tharu Engu Uru Me’. Dividing it as ‘Vinun’ (means to divide) and interpreting it as: ‘Vilam’ means wood apple, ‘Kozhi’ means calf, ‘Thiru’ means stone, ‘Kal’ means stone. ‘Eri’ means thrown and destroyed. This refers to Krishna, who used a calf as a missile to destroy the wood apple tree and the demons who were in the form of the calf and the wood apple tree in Gokulam. ‘Engu’ means where, ‘Uru Mevinan’ means where he has his form. Taking ‘Engu’ to mean ‘left side’, it means the Lord who has Vishnu on his left side. The meaning of this line is: The Lord who has Vishnu on his left side, Vishnu being Krishna who used a calf as a stone missile to destroy the wood apple tree, and destroyed the demons who stood in the form of the calf and the wood apple tree in Gokulam.

In the second line, ‘Vilang Olithi Kal Tharu’. Interpreting it as: ‘Vilang’ with a space in between means ‘bright’, ‘Oli’ means ‘light’, ‘Thee’ means ‘fire’, ‘Kal Tharu’ means ‘falling with great fear’, ‘Engu’ means ‘resounding’, ‘Urumu Evinan’ means ‘one who comes as thunder and rules the world’.

Now, for the third line, ‘Vil Angu Olithu Igazh Tharu Em Guru Mevinan’, dividing it and interpreting it as: ‘Vil’ means ‘departing’, ‘Angu’ means ‘there’, ‘Olithu’ means ‘bright’, ‘Igazh Tharu Em’ means ‘even in me, the lowly’, ‘Guru Mevinan’ means ‘mingled as a Guru’. There, departing from that place, he mingled with me, the lowly, as a Guru, and bestowed the nectar of divine wisdom.

Now, for the fourth line, Interpreting it as ‘Oli Thigal Tharu Vengurum Mevinan’ means: He resides in the sacred place of Venguru, which shines with radiant light. Sirkazhi Kannudaiya Vallalar has interpreted this line as narrating the history of Lord Shiva’s grace to Dharmaraja.

Now, the fifth verse: ‘Sudarmani Maligai Thonipurathavan, Sudarmani Maligai Thonipurathavan, Sudarmani Maligai Thonipurathavan, Sudarmani Maligai Thonipurathavan’. The lines in this can be interpreted as follows: The first line, divided as ‘Sudar Im Mani Ali Kai Thoni Purathu Avan’, and interpreted as: ‘Sudar’ means heat, ‘Im’ means this, ‘Mani’ means burial ground, ‘Ali’ means ruler, ‘Purathu Avan’ means destroyer of the three cities. ‘Kai Thoni’ means a thumbai flower, a symbol of victory.

Thus, it means: He is the one who rules over this hot burial ground, destroyed the three cities, and wears the thumbai flower, a symbol of victory. And interpreting it to mean: The one who wears the thumbai flower, which shines brightly and is a symbol of victory. The second line, ‘Sudarmani’ means a brightly shining jewel, ‘Sudarmani Mali’ means one who has a great desire to uplift souls, ‘Kai Thol’ means a trunk, ‘Thuthikkaiudaiya Yanai’ means an elephant. ‘Nipurathavan’ means one who destroyed it without form, who destroyed it beyond recognition. The third line, ‘Sudar’ means sun, ‘Mani’ means jewel, ‘Kazhuvi Mali’ means one who has washed away dirt, ‘Kettavan’ means one who has destroyed, ‘Kai Thoni’ means raft, ‘Purathavan’ means one who protects. Interpreting it to mean: He is the one who creates the primal sound (Pranava) in the ears, like a raft, to help souls caught in the ocean of birth and death, which washes away the stains of the sun. The fourth line, ‘Sudarmani Maligai Thonipurathavan’, should be interpreted as: He who resides in Thonipuram, Sirkazhi, which is filled with mansions adorned with shining jewels.

Now, the sixth. Thirupadal: ‘Pusurar Ser Poontharai Avan Ponnadi, Pusurar Ser Poontharai Avan Ponnadi, Pusurar Ser Poontharai Avan Ponnadi, Pusurar Ser Poontharai Avan Ponnadi’. This can be divided and interpreted as follows: The first line, divided as ‘Pu Surar Ser Pu Tharayan Pon Adi’, and interpreted as: ‘Pu’ means on earth, ‘Surar’ means celestials, ‘Adi’ means mirror, ‘Pu’ means navel lotus, ‘Tharayan’ means one who holds, ‘Pon’ means splendor. Interpreting it as: Lord Shiva stands as a mirror, reflecting both humans on earth and celestials in the upper world, as well as Brahma, and Vishnu who created Brahma from his navel lotus.

Now, the second line, ‘Pusurar Ser Pu Tharayan Pon Nadi’, and interpreted as: ‘Pusu’. Surar means divine beings, who, though living on earth, are considered celestials due to their freedom from impurities. ‘Ser’ means congregation, ‘Pu’ means splendor, ‘Tharayan’ means attained, ‘Avan’ means God, ‘Pon’ means gold-like, ‘Nadi’ means dancer. Interpreting this, it means: Lord Shiva is the one who performs an excellent, gold-like beautiful dance, to bring joy and splendor to the congregation of divine beings who are free from impurities.

Now, the third line, ‘Pusu Urar Serbu Untharai Yavan Pon Adi’, should be divided and interpreted as: ‘Pusu’ means sacred ash smeared, ‘Urar’ means one whose chest, ‘Serbu’ means completely removing, ‘Untharai’ means pushing away, ‘Yavan’ means whoever. The meaning of this, interpreted as: The state of being the fundamental source for divine beings who have smeared sacred ash on their chests and have cast aside the bonds of good and evil, escaping the cycle of birth and death and renouncing worldly life, is the eternal Lord Shiva.

Now, for the fourth line, ‘Pusurar Ponnadi’, and interpreting it as: I desire that the golden feet of the Lord, who resides in Sirkazhi, which is worshipped by the congregation of such beings, should embrace me.

Thus, six verses. Are structured.

We will continue to contemplate the meanings of the other six verses. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, Part Six Hundred and Four, by Sekkizhar Swamigal, the chapter on Vambara Varivandu, the biography of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. We are contemplating the verses and meanings of the Thiru Ekapadam pathigam.

In this context, the seventh verse: ‘Seruku Vayppu Udaiyan Sirapuram Ennil, Seruku Vayppu Udaiyan Sirapuram Ennil, Seruku Vayppu Udaiyan Sirapuram Ennil, Seruku Vayppu Udaiyan Sirapuram Ennil’.
