Here, the Lord’s names are Kannayiramudaiyar, Kannayiranathar, Sahasranetresvarar. The Goddess’s names are Muruguvalar Kodhai, Sugantha Kundalambikai. The sacred pool is Indra Theertham. This is the place where Vishnu worshipped Shiva during the Vamana avatar.

Therefore, it was called Gurumanikkudi. It is currently known as Gurumankudi. Devendran, afflicted by Gautama Muni’s curse, came to this place and performed penance. As a result, the thousand yonis on his body transformed into a thousand eyes.

Hence, the Lord here is named Kannayiranathar. The main deity is a Swayambhu Lingam, and true to the name, the Lord’s body is filled with eye-like depressions. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who visited this sacred place, blessed a Pathigam. It is the one hundred and first Pathigam of the first Thirumurai, set in Kurinji tune. The first and last verses of this Pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam! “Thannar thingatpongaravanthal punalsudi pennanaaya perarulalan priyaatha kannar koyil kaithozhuvorkku idar paavam nannavaagu nalvinaiyaaya nanugum.

“Kamarukan Kannaar Koiluulanai, surrounded by a sea of flower-filled groves, is the famed city of the golden mansions. Thiru Gnanasambandan, who spoke of ancient truths, said that those who master these ten soulful songs (paadal pathu) will be free from blame.

“Thus, after worshipping at Thirukkannanaar Koil, Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman visits nearby temples such as Thirukadaimudi, Thirukattuppalli, and Thirunangur.

“After these visits, he sings Tamil garlands of Thevaram Pathigams and continues his pilgrimage westward along the northern bank of the Kaveri. In this journey, Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman arrives at Thirupullirukkuvelur, also known as Vaithiswaran Koil.

“We shall carry on our contemplation.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Sekkizhar Swamigal’s Periya Puranam, Volume 612, Vambara Vari Vanda Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrives at Thirupullirukkuvelur, also known as Vaithiswaran Koil. This place is currently very famous under the name Vaithiswaran Koil. In this temple, Pul (Jatayu), Irukku (Rig Veda), Vel (Lord Murugan), and Ur (Surya, the Sun God)—these four worshipped Shiva, hence the name Pul-Irukku-Vel-Ur, Thirupullirukkuvelur. Because Jatayu worshipped, it is also called Jatayupuri.

Because the Vedas worshipped, it is called Vedapuri. Because Skanda worshipped, it is called Skandapuri. Because Surya worshipped, it is called Parithipuri. Because Angarakan worshipped, it is called Angarakapuram. And because Ambikai worshipped, it is called Ambikapuram. This temple has various names.

Besides these, it is also known by many other names such as Vinai Theerthan Koil, Thaiyal Nayaki Koil, Vaithiswaran Koil, and so on. The Lord’s sacred name is Vaithiyanathar, and the Goddess’s sacred name is Thaiyal Nayaki. The sacred tree is the Neem, and the sacred pond is Siddhamirtha Theertham. This is a place where the Lord blesses as a doctor, Vaithiyanathar. Lord Murugan blesses with the name Selvamuthukumaraswami. The Siddhamirtha Theertham of this temple has the power to cure diseases.

They offer Nethrapidi Sandhanam (sandal paste) and Thiruchanthurundai as prasadam. Consuming this cures all kinds of diseases. This is the sacred place where Vaithiyanathaperuman, the physician who cures the disease of birth, blesses with Thaiyal Nayaki Ambha. With a pot of oil and Amrita Sanjeevi (divine elixir) in her hands, and the earth from the base of the Vilvam tree, Shiva manifests here as Vaithiyanatha Peruman. This sacred temple is known to cure forty-four thousand four hundred and forty-eight diseases. This temple is under the compassionate governance of the Dharmapuram Aadheenam of the Thirukkailaya Paramparai.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who arrived here, blessed us with the Pathigam “Kallarntha Poongondrai.” Sekkizhar Peruman states this history thus: “The Lord of Pullirukkuvelur, whose love for the temple multiplied, the Lord with four broad shoulders and three eyes, accepted the worship of the two eagle kings and adorned the temple with sweet verses.” Reaching the temple where Shiva, with four mighty shoulders and three eyes, is enshrined in Thirupullirukkuvelur, There, with immense devotion, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships and blesses us with a Pathigam. In this Pathigam, he praises and extols the greatness of the worship performed by the eagle kings, Sampathi and Jatayu, for the Lord. Thirupullirukkuvelur is the sacred name of the place. Sekkizhar Peruman refers to it here as Pullirukkum Thiruvelloor. He has added the honorific ‘Thiru’ before the name of Murugaperuman, Vel. Sekkizhar Peruman states this to highlight the special worship performed by Murugaperuman, the ‘Sevvel’.

The first verse of this Pathigam begins with “Thallaaya Sampathi Sadayu enbar thamiruvur pullanaar karaiyidam Pullirukkuvelure.” Pillaiyar has extensively praised the special blessings received by the two eagle kings, Sampathi and Jatayu, who worshipped at this temple. He has stated in this Pathigam, “Yosanai poy pookonarnthu angu oru nallum ozhiyamay poosanai seythu inithirunthan” (He went a yojana, brought flowers, and worshipped continuously every day with joy) and “pathiyinal vazhipattu palakaalam thavam seythu puththiyonru vaithirunthan” (He worshipped with devotion, performed penance for a long time, and kept a focused mind). This Pathigam narrates the history of how Sampathi, the eagle king, maintained a Nandavanam (flower garden) in Kaveri Poombattinam, travelled from Kaveri Poombattinam to Vaithiswaran Koil, and worshipped Shiva daily with flowers from his garden. The distance from Vaithiswaran Koil to Kaveri Poombattinam is one yojana, which is referred to by Thiru. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman says, “Yosanai poy pookonarnthu angu oru nallum ozhiyamay poosanai seythu inithirunthan” (He went a yojana, brought flowers, and worshipped continuously every day with joy).

The benefit of this Pathigam is that those who worship at this place will be freed from the disease of birth that comes due to karma and will attain happiness. Such a Pathigam is the forty-third Pathigam of the second Thirumurai, set in Seekamarappaan tune. The first and last verses of this Pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam! “Kallarntha poongondrai mathamathang kathirmadhiyam ullarntha sadai mudiyam perumaanar uraiyumidam thallaaya sampathi sadayenbar thamiruvur pullanaar karaiyidam pullirukkuvelure.” “Sediyaya udal theerppan theevinai kor marunthavan podiyadi kadimai seytha pullirukkuvelurai kadiyarantha” The words of Kali Kavuniyan Sambandan, who is known for his firm resolve, will lead to a rebirth-free life for those who chant them without fail.

Jatayu and Sampathi were the sons of Surya. They flew up to the sun’s sphere, their wings scorched, and then fell. They later worshipped Shiva at this place and regained their wings and fame. This is a local legend. Manimekalai also mentions this: “Sampathivanam, where Sampathi lost his vast wings due to the intense heat of the sun.” In the eighth verse of the Pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sings about the Lord’s grace towards Ravana.

In this Pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman also includes the Ramayana reference in the eighth verse that mentions Ravana, stating that when Ravana was carrying Sita away, Jatayu fought with him to prevent him from proceeding further. “The place where the Lord with the dark neck, who bestows heaven without earth to the devotees who sing harmonious tunes, resides is the home of countless gods. He is the one who fought and destroyed the powerful, the Lord of Pullirukkuvelur.” This is the eighth verse, which contains the Ramayana reference. In the eleventh verse, which states the benefits of the Pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman explains the name Vaithiyanathar, the Lord of this temple, as “Sediyaya udal theerppan theevinai kor marunthavan” (He who cures the body’s ailments and is medicine for evil deeds). This brings to mind the verse “Manthiramum thanthiramum marunthumagi theeraa noy theertharula vallaan” (He who is mantra, tantra, and medicine, capable of curing incurable diseases) from Thiruthantagam. In the Vedas, the term ‘Bhisak’ also refers to Shiva.

This sacred place serves as another testament to the fact that He is Bhavaroga Vaithiyanatha Swamy. The temple history states that Rama performed the last rites for Jatayu, who had helped him, at this very spot. This is also the place where Angarakan’s leprosy was cured, thus it is known as a place worshipped by Mars.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, after bidding farewell to the Lord of Vaithiswaran Koil, proceeds to Thirunindriyur, a place that stands eternal. With great devotion, he worships the glorious sacred feet of the Lord and blesses us with a rich Pathigam. Thirunindriyur is a town located on the road from Vaithiswaran Koil to Mayiladuthurai. The Lord’s names are Mahalakshmi Sar, Lakshmipureeswarar. The Goddess’s name is Loganayaki Lakshmi Theertham. Thirunanniyur is currently the popular name.

The sacred tree is the Vilva tree. In ancient times, this was one of the Maada temples built by Kochchengachozhanayanar. There is a Lingam worshipped by Parasurama. The main deity is a Swayambhu Murti. The Pathigam blessed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who came to this temple, is the eighteenth Pathigam of the first Thirumurai, set in Nattapada tune. The first and last verses of this Pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam!

“Soolam padai sunnappodi santhan sudu neeru paalam madhi pavalachchadai mudimeelathu pandai kaalan vali kaalin nodu pogi kadi kamazhum neelam malarpoigai ninruyurin nilaiyorgay.” “Kunramathu eduthan udal tholum nerivaga ninrangoru viralaluru vaithan nintriyurai nanraar tharu pugazhil tamil gnanam mighubhandha” The perfect fame of Thirugnanasambandha, whose Tamil words from the glorious Pugazhi are flawless.

The message of this Pathigam is that the heart will not know anything other than the pure Lord of Nindriyur, and devotees who serve His feet will always be free from fear, sin, destruction, disease, and other evils. Departing from Thirunindriyur, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds to the sacred town of Thiruneedur. He blesses a Pathigam here. The Pathigam blessed for this temple is not available to us. From there, he departs and reaches the sacred town of Thirupunkur.

We have contemplated the special features of Thirupunkur in the Thirunaalaipovaar Puranam.

The Lord is Sivalokanathar, and the Goddess is Sokkanayaki, Soundaryanayaki. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who arrived at this temple, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman blessed us with a Pathigam. It is the twenty-seventh Pathigam of the first Thirumurai, set in Thakkaraga tune. The first and last verses of this Pathigam are as follows: ! “Munthi nintra vinaigal avai poga sinthai nenje sivanar thirupunkur anthamilla adigal avar polum kanthamalgu kamizh punsadaiaare.” “Maadamalgu mathil suzha kali man sedar selvar uraiyum thirupunkur naadavaalla gnanasambandan paadal pathum paravi vazhminae.” Thiruchitrambalam. The summary of this Pathigam is as follows: The infinite Lord, with matted locks, who placed the moon, who burnt the three cities, is Shiva.

Such is the divine nature of the Lord of Thirupunkur. He is the Lord who resides at our crown.

Thus, after worshipping at Thirupunkur, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman goes and worships many temples where the Lord joyfully resides in that vicinity. These temples are considered to be Thirukkaruppariyaloor, Thirukurugakka, Thiruvazhkolipuththur, and others. After worshipping at several such sacred places, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrives at Thiruppazhamanni.

There, he praises the Lord and blesses us with a Pathigam. However, that Pathigam is not available to us. Pazhamanni refers to an ancient tributary river. This sacred place is known as Izhuppappattu. The history heard at this place is that when the Lord consumed poison, the Goddess prevented it from going down by holding His throat with Her hand, thus the Lord showed His blue throat here. The Pathigam of Sundaramurthy Swamigal also mentions the Lord with the blue throat.

The Lord’s name is Neelakanthar, and the Goddess’s name is Amirthakaravalli. This temple can be reached a short distance west from Thiruvazhkolipuththur. After worshipping here, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman departs from here and goes to Thirukurukkai Veerattanam temple. He worships the Lord and blesses a Pathigam there. Thirukurukkai Veerattanam is one of the eight temples where the Lord performed heroic deeds. This is the place where the heroic act of burning Kamadeva took place.

A sage named Dheerghabahu, meaning one with long arms, desired to bathe the Lord with the waters of the celestial Ganga. When he raised his long arms, they shortened.

Therefore, This sacred place got the name Thirukurukkai, according to the local legend. The Thirumaraikkattu Sthala Puranam states that the assembly here is known as Kamanga Nasani Sabai and Shambhu Vinodha Sabai. In Thirukurukkai, the Kamadahana Murti, the Kadukkai tree, and the cremation ground in the southwest of the village are thought-provoking. Departing from Thirukurukkai, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reaches the temple called Thirumanniyur.

We shall proceed with our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Sekkizhar Swamigal’s Periya Puranam, Volume 613, Vambara Vari Vanda Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrives at the sacred site of Thirumanniyur. This is the twenty-second temple on the north bank of the Kaveri. It is currently known as Ponnoor. This is the place worshipped by Varunan.

This sacred site is located to the west of Thiruneedur, near Mayiladuthurai. Surya Bhagavan lost one arm due to a curse from Rathi Devi.

Later, to obtain relief from the curse, he came to Thirumanniyur and worshipped Shiva. By the grace of the Lord, Surya’s lost arm grew back. This is also one of the sacred sites worshipped by Agni Devar. Harichandra Maharaja, who suffered from white leprosy, came to this place and, as per the Lord’s command, On the auspicious day of Vaikasi Visakam, he offered curd rice and was cured of his illness. Varunan, the deity of the west, also worshipped here. All the Panchapandavas worshipped Easwaran here.

Agastya also worshipped. One Pathigam by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and two Pathigams by Thirunavukkarasar Peruman are available for this temple. The Lord’s name is Sri Abathsahayeswarar, and the Goddess’s name is Sri Piragunayaki. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who arrived here, blessed us with a Pathigam. It is a Pathigam set in Kurinji tune, with the special quality of Thiruvirukural. It is the ninety-sixth Pathigam of the first Thirumurai.

The first and last verses of this Pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam! “Manniyur irai senneyar pirai anneyur amar mannu sothiyae poontharai panthan aaintha paadalal” May you live long in this world, reaching the Lord in Anniyur, as sung in the well-researched verses of Poomtharai Pandan.

The Pathigam states that the Lord of Anniyur is the light of divine knowledge, the life of all beings; attain Him and live.

Thus, after worshipping at Thirumanniyur, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds to the sacred place of Thirumanancheri, where Shiva resides. He arrives at Thirumanancheri with his special devotees, worships the Lord there, and blesses us with a Pathigam.

The Lord of Thirumanancheri is the one who removes the bonds of beings. In Pandanainallur, Pillaiyar expounded on the fundamental principles of the Vedas. In Thirumanancheri, he enlightened the world about the Lord’s primal nature as the First. This sacred place of Thirumanancheri is now very famous. It is the twenty-fifth temple on the north bank of the Kaveri. It is referred to as Kizhe Thirumanancheri.

This is the sacred place where Manmatha worshipped and received blessings. There is a legend about two merchant women who agreed to arrange a marriage between their children. When one of them gave birth to a turtle, the other refused to give her daughter in marriage. The turtle then worshipped, gained a human form, and married the girl. The Lord’s name is Arulvallal Nadhar, Udhvaganatha Swamy, Kalyana Sundareswarar. The Goddess’s name is Kokilambal Mozhi Ammai.

The sacred pond is called Saptham Theertham.

Here, the Lord resides as Nitya Kalyana Sundara Peruman, the eternal bridegroom. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who came to this temple, blessed us with a Pathigam. It is the sixteenth Pathigam of the second Thirumurai. It is a Pathigam set in Indalapana tune. Its first and last verses are as follows: ! “Ayilrum ambathanaal puramundreithu kuyilrum menmoziyal oru kooragi mayilarum malgiya solai manamseri payilvaanai patri ninrarkku illai paavame.” “Kannaarum kaliyar kon karutharvitha thannar seer gnanasambandan tamil maalai mannaarum ma vayal suzhantha manamseri pannara paadal vallarkku illai paavame.” Thiruchitrambalam.

The summary of this Pathigam is that those who worship the Lord of Thirumanancheri will have their karma removed, no further karma will accrue to them, and they will attain only happiness.

Thus, after worshipping at Thirumanancheri, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds to Thiruedirkolpadi temple and blesses us with a Pathigam for the Lord there. The Pathigam blessed by Pillaiyar is not available to us. Thiruedirkolpadi is a temple associated with the history of Thirumanancheri. Since Iravatham worshipped here, the Lord is named Iravathesvarar. The Goddess’s name is Malarkozhal Nayaki. Sekkizhar Peruman extols the Lord of Thiruedirkolpadi as “Epporulm tharum Eesan ezhuntharuliyirukkum Ethirkolpadi Pathi” (The Lord who bestows all things, residing in Ethirkolpadi).

The Lord is the First Cause of the world, therefore He bestows His grace upon all beings. To instruct that the Lord’s grace provides all that beings desire, this reference is given. Sekkizhar Peruman refers to the Pathigams blessed here as unparalleled Pathigams.

However, due to our misfortune, those Pathigams are not available to us.

Thus, after worshipping at Thiruedirkolpadi, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reaches Thiruvellvikudi.

The Lord and Goddess, in a state of union, reside in the prosperous town of Thiruvellvikudi in their wedding attire. Thiruthuruthi and Thiruvellvikudi are two sacred places considered together.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has blessed a Pathigam connecting these two temples. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, adapting to the nature of the Lord who is visible in Thiruthuruthi during the day and resides in Thiruvellvikudi at night, sings a Pathigam in the form of a Tamil garland, uniting these two temples in a single Pathigam. Thuruthi means an island in a river. This is considered a very sacred area.

Thus, worshipping the Lord in a river is considered very sacred. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman blessed a Pathigam combining these two places, indicating that the Lord, who is openly manifest in Thiruthuruthi during the day, resides very specially in Thiruvellvikudi at night.

Similarly, Sundaramurthy Swamigal also sang about these two places together, saying, “Mooppathum illai” within a Pathigam in female raga, “Kaappathu Vellvikudi than Thuruthi engon” (My Lord, who protects Vellvikudi and Thuruthi). Thiruthuruthi is revered as the seventh distinct temple on the south bank of the Kaveri and is a sacred place sung by the Moovar Thevaram. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s Pathigam sings of the nature of the Lord who granted darshan to Uma Devi, residing in Thiruthuruthi during the day and Thiruvellvikudi at night. It is the ninetieth Pathigam of the third Thirumurai. It is a Pathigam set in Sadari tune. Its first and last verses are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam!

“Oongu meel olitharum oli punal Gangaiyai oru sadaimel thaanginaar idubali thalaikkalana konda am adigal paanginaal umaiyodum pakalidam pugaliidam paimbozhil suzha veengu neer thurthiyaar iravidaththu uraiyar velvikudiye.” “Vinnulaam viri pozhil virai manal thuruthi velvikudiyum onnulaam oli kalalaaduvaar arivaiyodu paaduvaar aaduvaar pazhiyile.” After visiting Thiruthuruthi and Thiruvellvikudi, Pillaiyar proceeds to Thirukodikkaa temple. Sekkizhar Peruman sings as follows: “He sang in his Tamil garland about the shining marriage attire of Vellvikudi, and the nature of the sacred Thuruthi overflowing with clear waters, and how the Lord with the crescent moon on His head went to Kodikka.” Sekkizhar Swamigal continues to sing: “He worshipped the Lord, the jewel among gods, who resides in Thirukodikkaa, adorned with Erukka, Kadazhi, and snakes, and with the tusks of a wild boar, and sang verses of praise.

“Then he went to Kanjanur to worship, a place that removes karmic impurities.” Having visited Vellvikudi, the twenty-third temple on the north bank of the Kaveri, and Thuruthi, the thirty-seventh temple on the south bank, as one single entity, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds to Thirukodikkaa. There, like a crown jewel for the gods, He blesses a Pathigam of praise, worshipping the Lord enshrined there, who is adorned with Erukku flowers and Konrai, and who wears the tusk of a wild boar. Thirukodikkaa is a place where three crore sages worshipped. We have contemplated this temple’s history in Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. The Lord’s name is Thirukodiswarar, and the Goddess’s name is Vadivammai. The sacred waters are Kaveri Theertham and Surunga Theertham.

“The Pathigam blessed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman at this temple is the ninety-ninth Pathigam of the second Thirumurai, set in Nattaraga tune. The first and last verses of this Pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam! “Indru nanru naalai nanru endru nintra ichaiyaal pontrugindra vaazhkaiyai pogavittu pothumin mintayangu sotiyan venmathi virippunal kondrai thuntu chenniyan kodikkaavu serminae konthani” The cool groves, adorned with blossoms, invite you to Kodikka. Thirugnanasambandan, the wise one from Pugali, who knows these ten songs, will remove your sins.

“In this Pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, highlighting the impermanence of life, guides people towards the Lord’s divine path. Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal’s Thevaram states, “All days not spent praising Kodikkavan will be wasted.” “Before your body wastes away, go to Thirukodikkaa.” These words from Aiyadigal Kadavarkon Nayanar’s Kshethiravenpa in the eleventh Thirumurai also convey the same sentiment.

“Thus, after worshipping at Thirukodikkaa, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrives at Kanjanur. Ruling in Thirukanjanur, Having seen and worshipped his Lord, he proceeds to Thirumanthurai and worships there. This Thirumanthurai temple is located very close between Kanjanur and Thirumangalakudi. There is another Thirumanthurai near Thiruanbil Alandurai, which is a temple sung in Thevaram. The Thirumanthurai mentioned here is one of the Vaipu Sthalams (places not sung in Thevaram but considered sacred).

“Thus, the Pathigams blessed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for Kanjanur and Thirumanthurai are not available to us. Thirukanjanur is a special place where Haradatta Sivachariya Swamigal incarnated and, being a great expounder of Saivism, established Saivism through many miracles. It is called Kanjanur because it is the city of Kamsa. That is, the town where Kamsa worshipped, hence the name Kanjanur. There is a story associated with this sacred place. A devotee in this village used to make a living by selling gourds.

“One day, only one gourd remained with him. He kept it aside, thinking it would be useful for seeds.

“At that moment, the Lord came to him as a guest and asked for food. The devotee was perplexed, not knowing what to do, because he was distressed, thinking that gourd curry was not suitable for guests.

“At that moment, the Lord, as an ethereal voice, said, “Half for seeds, half for curry.” So, he set aside half for seeds and made curry with the other half to offer. The history states that the Lord blessed the devotee who did this. There is also a history here of the Nandi eating grass. A Brahmin had accidentally dropped a bundle of grass, causing a cow calf to die. This resulted in him incurring the sin of killing a cow.

“The Brahmins ostracized the poor Brahmin. Not knowing what to do, he approached Haradatta Sivacharya. While appealing, he recited the Panchakshara mantra. Hearing this, Haradatta said that since he had recited the Shiva Panchakshara, the sin of killing the cow had been removed.

“The Brahmins did not accept this and demanded direct proof. Haradatta immediately called the Brahmin, asked him to bathe in the Kaveri, take a handful of grass, and said, “The Nandi is in the temple.” He gave the grass, and the Nandi is said to have eaten it. It is also said that because this Nandi ate the grass, its tongue is not sticking out here. Appar Swamigal’s blessed Pathigam is available for this temple. The sacred tree is the Palash tree, also known as Purasu.

“Thus, after worshipping at Kanjanur and Thirumanthurai, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds to the sacred place of Thiruvaiyaloor. We shall carry on our contemplation.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Sekkizhar Swamigal’s Periya Puranam, Volume 614, Vambara Vari Vanda Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrives at the sacred place of Thiruvaiyaloor. He worships the Lord of Thiruvaiyaloor, who rides on a bull, and blesses us with a sweet musical Tamil garland. Thiruvaiyaloor is currently known as Thiruvisanallur. The temple can be reached by travelling on the Thiruvidaimarudur-Vepathur road.

It is located very close to Kumbakonam. The Lord’s names are Yoganandeeswarar, Purathaneeswarar, Vilvaranyeeswarar. The Goddess’s names are Shanthanayaki, Soundaryanayaki. Jatayu Theertham serves as the sacred pool. People also call this town Thiruvisalur. Since there are many towns named Thiruvisalur in the Thanjavur region, this The place Bhandaravadai is also known as Thiruviasalur and Thiruvisanallur.

This sacred place is where Thiruvialur Uyyavandha Devanayanar, who sang Thiruvundhiyar, one of the treatises of Saiva Siddhanta, incarnated. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who graced this place, bestowed a pathigam, which is the thirteenth pathigam of the first Thirumurai, set to the tune of Nattapadai. Its first and concluding verses are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam (Kuravamgamil naru menkuzhal arivai aval veruva poruvengiri padavendradhan urivaiyudal anivon aravum malai punalum ilamadiyum nagudhalaiyum viravum sadai adigatkkidam virineer viyalure vilangum pirai sadai meludai vigirdhan viyalurai thalangondathorpugali thagu tamil gnanasambandhan thulangil).

When Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships the Lord at Thiruvisalur, the Lord directly reveals His gracious form to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. After worshipping Him and taking leave, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds to the sacred place called Thirundhu Thevankudi. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reaches the temple of the Lord, who is permanently enshrined in Thirundhu Thevankudi, a sacred place that helps beings to reform from the ocean of birth. With overflowing love, he goes and worships, and offers a rare Tamil garland of verses. The place name is Thevankudi, and “Thirundhu” is an adjective indicating reformation.

The name is referred to as Thirundhu Thevankudi, combined with Thevankudi. “Thirundhudhal” means causing beings to reform.

Here, Pillaiyar, who partook of the nectar of infinite wisdom, praises the Lord and bestows a pathigam. The nature of Siva’s forms and their ability to remove suffering from beings, bestow joy, and provide certainty, is the essence of the pathigam given by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for this place. It cannot be achieved by anything other than infinite wisdom.

Therefore, Pillaiyar, who partook of the nectar of infinite wisdom, bestows a pathigam implying that the Lord’s forms, which are sacred symbols, act as medicine and mantra. This form, ‘vedam’, also refers to. It also refers to the form of this year. Sivagnana Bodham states, “The form of those who are filled with love.” To realize oneself, He gives His form; residing within, He makes one realize oneself.

Therefore, Sivagnana Bodham praises this sacred form of the Lord as those who realize themselves with love.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman bestows a rare pathigam in Thirundhu Thevankudi, implying that the Lord’s sacred form acts as medicine and mantra, reforming living beings. Such a special pathigam is the twenty-fifth pathigam of the third Thirumurai, set to the tune of Kolli. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam (Marundhu vendil ivai manthirangal ivai purindhu ketkappadum punna). These are Thirundhu Thevankudi. The forms of the Lord, worshipped by the gods and revered ascetics, are these. The pathigam note for this pathigam is that the forms of the God of gods in Thirundhu Thevankudi are medicine and mantra, they dispel karma, and they show the path to liberation.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman begins this pathigam with the words “Marundhu vendil ivai manthirangal” (If you need medicine, these are the mantras), starting with the word “Marundhu” (medicine). The sacred name of the Goddess in this temple is Arumarundhu Ammai, or Apurva Nayaki.

Thus, Ammai. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman begins the pathigam for this sacred place by placing her sacred name first. This is the forty-second temple on the north bank of the Kaveri. It is a solitary temple amidst fields. A sacred pond surrounds the temple. Like the moat of Thirupugalur, it is like a moat on three sides.

This is a place where crabs worshipped, so the Lord’s name is Karkadakesvarar. A crab’s form is seen on the Lord’s sacred crown. Having worshipped Thirundhu Thevankudi, which is very close to Thiruvisalur, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman continues his pilgrimage. In this ancient town, surrounded by groves adorned with buds, he takes leave from the Lord’s grace and continues his pilgrimage. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, walking amidst the fields where growing. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman visits many temples of the Lord, who has a dark throat, amidst paddy, sugarcane, coconut, and areca palms, and worships them.

The places mentioned as being worshipped by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman in this way include Thirukottaiyur, Thiru Vijaymangai, Thirupurambayam, Thiruvaikavur, and others. After visiting all these places, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrived at Thiru Innampar. Shekizhar Peruman states: (Innampar mannum piranai irainji idaimadakaan pannun thamizh thodai malai paadal punaindhu paravi ponnang kadalinai potri purambondhu anaindhu pugundhar mannum thadangkarai ponni vada kurangadu thuraiyil). Sekizhar Peruman composed the verses here. Sekizhar Peruman refers to the pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman at Thiru Innampar as a garland of verses in Tamil composed in the Idaimadakku style. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises the Lord of Thiru Innampar with the pathigam called Thirumukkal, composed in the Idaimadakku poetic form.

That pathigam, which begins with “En Thisaikkum,” is the ninety-fifth pathigam of the third Thirumurai, set to the tune of Sadhari. Idaimadakku is a type where the second line in a four-line verse repeats as the third line. In such a type, since the second and third lines are identical in word and meaning, they are considered as one line, and thus, forming three. Since it consists of three lines, it is called Mukkal. This type of pathigam is composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman here as Thirumukkal. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam (En disaikkum pugazh innambar meviya vandisaikkum sadaiyeere vandisaikkum sadaiyeer umai vaazhthuvaar thondisaikkum thozhilaare yedamar pozhil aniyin nambar eesanai naadamar gnanasambandhan naadamar gnanasambandhanatramizh paadavallaar pazhiyile).

This sacred place, Thiru Innampar, is the forty-fifth temple on the north bank of the Kaveri. It is currently called Innambur. This is the place where the sun (Inan), Airavata, and Agasthya Muni worshipped the Lord. Inan Nambuvur has morphed into Innambar. The Lord’s names are Thondrisvarar and Ezhuttharinnathar.

The Goddesses’ names are Kondhar Poonguzhali and Nithya Kalyani. Two Ambikas bestow grace from separate shrines. Airavatha Theertham. Having worshipped Thiru Innampar in this way, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds to the sacred place of Vadakurangaadu Thurai.

Our contemplation continues. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 615, Vambara Varivandu Sarkkam, by Sekizhar Swamigal, on the history of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having completed his pilgrimage to Thiru Innampar and taken leave from the Lord’s grace, proceeds to the sacred place of Vadakurangaadu Thurai. Vadakurangaadu Thurai is the place where Vali worshipped the Lord and surrendered to Him. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises this history in his pathigam, making it known to the world, and circumambulates the temple, worshipping. There are two places called Vadakurangaadu Thurai and Thenkurangaadu Thurai.

Thenkurangaadu Thurai is now called Aaduthurai. This is the thirty-first temple on the south bank of the Kaveri. It is a place where Hanuman and Sugriva worshipped. Vadakurangaadu Thurai is the place where Vali worshipped. It is the forty-ninth temple on the north bank of the Kaveri. The Lord’s names are Dhayanidhiesvarar, Kulaivanangeesar, Valinathar, Chittilinganathar.

The Goddesses’ names are Jata Magudesvari and Azhagu Jadai Mudiyamai. When a pregnant woman, with a full pregnancy, walked this way, the fatigue of the walk afflicted her. To quench her thirst, the Lord bent down a bunch of coconuts, so the Lord’s name is Kulaivanangeesvarar. Because a sparrow worshipped the Lord here, the Lord is also named Chittilingesvarar. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who graced this place, bestowed a pathigam. It is the ninety-first pathigam of the third Thirumurai.

It is a pathigam set to the tune of Sadhari. In the sixth and eighth verses of this pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has sung about Vali’s worship of the Lord in this place. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam (Kongame kuravame kozhumalar punnaiye kogudhimullai vengaiye gnazhale vimmu paathirigalai viraviyangum onguma kaveri vadakkarai adai kurangaduthurai veengu neer sadaimudi adigalaar idamena virumbinare thalailang kaveri vadakkarai adai kurangaduthurai polila madhippodhi puridharu sadaimudi punniyanai kaliyaan arumarai gnanasambandhan karudhu paadal kozhaya valaippinum kooduvar needuvaanulagoodai thiruchitta).

Having completed his visit to Vadakurangaadu Thurai and visited the nearby temples like Thingalur, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrives at Thiruppazhanam. Entering the temple of Siva, who has three sacred eyes, enshrined in Thiruppazhanam, he stands and praises with a melted heart, sings a pathigam in Tamil, and stays there with great affection. The pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman in Thiruppazhanam is the sixty-seventh pathigam of the first Thirumurai, set to the tune of Thakkasi. Its first and concluding verses are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam (Vedhamodhi vennoozh poondu vellai yerudheri poothamsoozha poliya varuvaar puliyin uri tholaar naadhaavenaudan). They will worship the feet of the Lord, saying ‘akkaavena’ and ‘nambavenan,’ and remove the sins of those who live in Pazhanam. (Veymuththongi virai mun parakkum vezhupuran thannul naavuythanaiyath thiralaan mikka gnana sambandhan pesarkiniya paadal payilum perumaan pazhanaththai vaayir polindha maalai patthum vallaar nallaare).

The initial nature of the Lord, endowed with beautiful music and harmonious tunes, is spoken of in this pathigam. This pathigam contains the reference that the Lord is Param, Bhagavath, Paramesvaran, and He is the one residing in Pazhanam. We have already contemplated the history of Thiruppazhanam in the Purana of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. Having praised the Lord at Thiruppazhanam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman takes leave from Him and proceeds to Thiruvaiyaaru, which has lakes filled with blooming red lotus flowers. He reaches Thiruvaiyaaru, which has lakes filled with blooming red lotuses.

The devotees residing in Thiruvaiyaaru, which has rows of stately mansions, welcome Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. With hearts filled with eagerness, thinking that Pillaiyar, who appeared in Sirkazhi and partook of the nectar of wisdom for the salvation of the world, is coming, they adorn the beautiful ancient city, where dance and song are ceaseless, and welcome Pillaiyar with great joy. Pillaiyar also descends from his pearl palanquin, and surrounded by the gathered devotees, worships Thiruvaiyaaru. Thiruvaiyaaru is a sacred place where Nandi Peruman received the Lord’s grace. We have already contemplated the histories of this place, where Nandidevar performed penance and received grace. Sekizhar Peruman praises this sacred place in the forty-fifth verse of Periya Puranam, saying, “Nandi did penance and attained abundant grace.” When Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrives at such a sacred place, he worships the sacred place and bestows a pathigam even before entering it.

That pathigam begins with “Pulanainthum.” In this way, many pathigams have been bestowed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, worshipping and praising a sacred place from outside, even before approaching it. We can recall the histories of pathigams like “Aalavai aavadhum idhuve” and “Idaimarudhu eetho.” This pathigam, set to the tune of Megharaga Kurinji. It is the hundred and thirtieth pathigam of the first Thirumurai. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam (Pulanainthum porigalanggi nerimayanggi arivazhindhittai melundhi alamandha podhaaga anjelendra arul seyvaan amarum koyil valam vandha madavaargal nadamaada muzhavu adhira mazhaiyendru anji silamandhi alamandhu marameri mugil paarkkum thiruaiyaare annamali pozhil pudaisoozhaiyaatram perumaanai anthan kaali manniyar marainaanan valargnanasambandhan maruvu paadal innisaiyaal ivai patthum isaiyumgaal eesan adi yethuvaargal than nichaiyodu amarulagil thavaneri sendru eydhuvaar thaazhaadhanre).

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, with a heart filled with sacred thoughts, devoutly worships and praises this sacred place, Thiruvaiyaaru, with a melodic Tamil pathigam, stating that it is the place where the Lord bestows His grace saying, “Fear not” when the five senses are confused and the mind is bewildered. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who bestowed this pathigam from outside Thiruvaiyaaru, then enters Thiruvaiyaaru, passes through the beautiful streets, approaches the beautifully adorned gopuram of the temple where Siva, who is incomprehensible to Vishnu and Brahma, is permanently enshrined. He circumambulates the temple, prostrates before the Lord, rises, and praises Him with love.

At that time, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman bestows a garland of verses, the pathigam that begins with “Kodal Kongam Kulir Kuvilam.” (Kodal). Sekizhar Peruman states that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed and danced, with tears flowing from his eyes, the garland of pathigams known as “Kodal Kongam Kulir Kuvilam,” with a mind filled with the greatness of the Lord’s extended sacred dance, singing, “He is the Lord of Aiyaaru, who is skilled in dancing.” The history of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman bestowing this pathigam. This pathigam is the sixth pathigam of the second Thirumurai. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, with a heart overflowing with the grace of the Lord’s extended sacred dance, sings a pathigam with the essence, “He is the skilled dancer and the Lord of Aiyaaru,” and with joyful tears flowing incessantly from his eyes, filled with love and bliss, bestows this pathigam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman bestowed this pathigam, sang, and danced. Sekizhar Swamigal beautifully portrays the state of Pillaiyar’s heart when he bestowed this pathigam.

The first and concluding verses of this pathigam, set to the tune of Indalam, are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam (Kodal Kongam Kulir kuvilam malai kulaya seer Odhugangai oli venpirai soodum oruvanar Paadal veenai muzhavam kuzhal mondhai pannagave Yaadumaru vallanum aiyaaru udai aiyanay Pali thirindhuzhal pandangkan meya aiyaatrinai Kalikadandha kaiyaan kadarkaliyar kaavalan Oligol sambandhan on thamizh patthum vallargal poy Maligol vennidai manniya seer peruvaargale).

Having bestowed this pathigam and worshipped many times. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman emerged from the sacred temple and bestowed his grace there. During the days he stayed in that sacred place, established with the devotees who worshipped and rose, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman also visited nearby places like Perumbuliyur, sang Tamil garlands of verses, and returned to Thiruvaiyaaru, staying there with immense desire. The pathigam bestowed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, after visiting Thirupperumbuliyur from Thiruvaiyaaru and worshipping the Lord, is the sixty-seventh pathigam of the second Thirumurai, set to the tune of Gandharam. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam (Mannumor bhaagamudaiyaar malumor bhaagamudaiyaar Vinnu mor bhaagamudaiyaar vedhamudaiya vimalar Kannumor bhaagamudaiyaar gangai sadaiyir).

The Goddess is the one who holds a part, and He who embraced the river is the one who does not leave Thirupperumbuliyur. (Pirai valarum mudichenni perumbuliyur perumaanai nirai valarum pozhir kaali nachamizh gnanasambandhan maraivalarum thamizh maalai vallavar than thuyar neenggi nirai valar nenjinaraagi needu ulagathtthiruppaare).

This sacred place, Thirupperumbuliyur, is the fifty-third temple on the north bank of the Kaveri. It is located on the south bank of the Kollidam river. It is called Puliyur because Vyagrapadha Muni worshipped there. The Lord’s names are Priyanathar and Vyagrapurisvarar. The Goddess’s name is Soundaryanayaki.

This sacred place is very close to Thiruvaiyaaru. Having worshipped Thirupperumbuliyur, Pillaiyar returned to Thiruvaiyaaru and stayed for some days. From Thiruvaiyaaru, he took leave from the Lord’s grace and continued his pilgrimage towards the west. As he continued westward, he reached the sacred place called Thiruneytthanam, where he worshipped the Lord and composed rare Tamil garlands of verses. This sacred place, Thiruneytthanam, is also known as Thillaistanam. It is very close to Thiruvaiyaaru.

The Lord’s names are Neyyadiyappar and Kruthapurisvarar. The Goddess’s name is Balambigai. This is one of the Saptasthana temples of Thiruvaiyaaru. The pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who graced this place, is the fifteenth pathigam of the first Thirumurai, set to the tune of Nattapadai. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam (Maiyaadiya kandhan malaimagal bhaagamadhudaiyaan kaiyaadiya kedil kariyuri moodiya oruvan seyyaadiya kuvazhai malar nayanaththavalodu neyyaadiya perumaanida neyth). They said, “Neythanamenire. (Thalamalgiya punarkaali yutramizh gnanasambandhan nilamalgiya pugazhaanmigu neydhananai nigaril palamalgiya paadal ivai patthum miga vallaar silamalgiya selvan nadhi servar sivagathiye).

“Having worshipped Thirunaytthanam in this way, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman continues his pilgrimage to Thirumazhapadi.

“Let us go on contemplating.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 616, Vambara Varivandu Sarkkam, by Sekizhar Swamigal, on the history of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds to Thirumazhapadi. Thirumazhapadi is located very close to the northwest of Thiruvaiyaaru. The Lord’s names are Vairaththunnathar, Vajrastambesvarar, Vaidyanathar, and Mazhuvaadeesvarar. The Goddess’s name is Sundarambigai, or Azhagammai.

There are also Kollidam Theertham, Lakshmi Theertham, and Sivaganga Theertham. This is the place where Siva danced with the battle axe for Markandeya Muni, hence the name Mazhu Aadi, which became Thirumazhapadi. This is the place where Nandhidevar was married to Swayambikai Ammai. Purushamruga Rishi brought the Sivalinga from Brahmaloka here. When Brahma tried to move it again. When Brahma tried to move it again and failed, he exclaimed, “Is this a diamond pillar?” and so the Lord is known by the name Vairaththunnathar.

This is the sacred place where the Lord called out to Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, saying, “Did you forget to come to Mazhapadi?” when Sundaramoorthy Swamigal was passing by this place. The Thirukkalyana festival of Nandhi Peruman and Swayambikai Ambigai is celebrated annually with great splendor on Panguni Punarpoosam day. The Kollidam river flows from south to north in this place, flowing as Utharavahini. Siva holds a red fawn in His sacred hand. Such a Siva is enshrined in Thirumazhapadi. When Pillaiyar arrives at such a Thirumazhapadi, he bestows the pathigam that begins with “Angaiyar Azhal” from the boundary of Thirumazhapadi.

That pathigam is the forty-eighth pathigam of the third Thirumurai, set to the tune of Kausikam. The first and concluding verses of that pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam (Angaiyar azhalanna azhagaar sadai gangaiyaan kadavul idam meviya mangaiyaan uraiyum mazhapaadiyai thanggaiyaal thozhuvaar thagavaalare mandham undhu pozhil mazhapaadiyul endhai sandham inidhu kondu eththuvaan kadal kaaliyul gnanasambandha maalai vallaarkku illai paavame).

The pathigam note for this pathigam is that those who worship Thirumazhapadi are those who have performed penance. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who bestowed this pathigam at the boundary of Thirumazhapadi, approaches the sacred temple of the Lord, who is enshrined as a beautiful diamond pillar in Thirumazhapadi. He circumambulates the temple and prostrates at the Lord’s lotus-like sacred feet. Rising, he worships, dances, sings, and offers a pathigam with beautiful verses.

Thus, the pathigams now composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman are two pathigams. The first of them is the ninth pathigam of the second Thirumurai, set to the tune of Indalam. The verses of this pathigam are about the Lord who made the great mountain into a bow and shot an arrow at the three cities, the Lord who resides in Mazhapadi, adorned with fragrant konrai garlands mixed with humming bees. This is the sacred place. The concluding two lines of the eleventh verse are not available. This eleventh verse extends up to “maliyumaaligai soozh mazhapaadiyul vallalai kalisai maamadhil soozh kadarkalik kavuniyan.”

The second pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman inside Thirumazhapadi temple is the twenty-eighth pathigam of the third Thirumurai, set to the tune of Kolli. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam (Kaalaiyaar vandhinam kindaadiya kaarurum solaiyaar paingkili sorporul payilave velaiyaar vida mani vedhiyan virumbidam malaiyaar madhitthaval maamazhapadiye gnalatthaar aadhirai naazhinaan naadorum seelatthaan meviya thirumazhapadiyai gnalatthaan). Those who sing the beautiful words of Thirugnanasambandha, who is of great glory, will be free from faults.

Having worshipped the Lord in this way, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman stays in Thirumazhapadi for some days.

After that, he passes this place and worships the Lord at the sacred place called Thirukkanoor. It is located amidst paddy fields. On the way from Thiruvaiyaaru to Thirukkattupalli, a little distance past the Kaveri bridge, the temple is located amidst fields. The Lord’s names are Semmeninathar and Karumbesvarar. The Goddess’s name is Sivaloganayagi. Theertham is Kollidam.

About a hundred years ago, during a flood, the entire temple was submerged. When Thiru Subramania Iyer found only a sugarcane shoot growing on it, he tried to excavate it, and the temple was discovered.

Hence, the Lord is named Karumbesvarar. The vimanam is single-tiered and round. The Ambikai idol is a Salagrama Vighraham. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who graced this place, bestowed a pathigam. It is the seventy-third pathigam of the first Thirumurai, set to the tune of Thakkasi. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam (Vaanor sodhi mannu senni vanni punangkondrai thenaar podhu thanaar gangai thingalodu soodi maner nokki kandanguva malaiyaaduvaar kaanoor meya kannaar netthriyaanoor selvayre kazhudhu thunjum kanggulaadum kaanoor meyaanai pazhudhin gnanasambandhan sorpa).

He discovered the temple, and thus the Lord received the name Karumbesvarar. The Vimanam is single-tiered and circular. The Ambikai idol is a Salagrama Vighraham. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who graced this place, bestowed a pathigam. It is the seventy-third pathigam of the first Thirumurai, set to the tune of Thakkasi. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam (Vaanor sodhi mannu senni vanni punangkondrai thenaar podhu thanaar gangai thingalodu soodi maner nokki kandanguva malaiyaaduvaar kaanoor meya kannaar netthriyaanoor selvayre kazhudhu thunjum kanggulaadum kaanoor meyaanai pazhudhin gnanasambandhan sorpa).

Those who sing the ten verses, worship, praise, and weep with love, will have their sufferings removed.

Having worshipped Thirukkanoor, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds to Thiru Anbil Alanthurai, worships the Lord, and sings a beautiful Tamil pathigam composed of rich words. This sacred place, Anbil Alanthurai, is near Trichy. The Lord’s names are Satyabhagesvarar, Brahmapurisvarar, and Alanthuraiyar. The Goddess’s name is Soundaryanayagi. Theertham is Chandra Pushkarani, or Chandra Theertham.

The name of the village is Anbil. The name of the temple is Alanthu. The Vinayaka here is called Sevizaitha Vinayaka. This Vinayaka received this name because he listened attentively to the songs of Sambandar, who sang about the south bank of the Kollidam river. In this place, Paranthaka. This Vinayaka of this place, who previously listened to the chanting of Jaimini Samaveda by the hundred and eight Agnihotris settled by Paranthaka Chola, is also known as Samaganam Ketthavinayagar.

The sacred tree of this place is the banyan tree. The presiding deity is a Swayambhu Siva Linga with a square pedestal. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who graced this sacred place, bestowed a pathigam. It is the thirty-third pathigam of the first Thirumurai, set to the tune of Thakkaragam. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam (Moonrum eritththa iraivar pinaimaa mayilum kuyil ser madal annam anaiyum pozhil anbil aalantthurai yaare aravaarpurunal anbil aalantthurai thanmel karavadhavar kaaliyul gnanasambandhan paravaar thamizh patthisai). Those who can sing these Tamil verses will easily attain liberation in the heavenly abode.

When Sekizhar Swamigal refers to Thiruanbil Alanthurai, he calls it “Saiva Mudhal Maraiyor Anbil Alanthurai.” Sekizhar Swamigal refers to Anbil Alanthurai as the place where eminent Athisaivas reside. This means Anbil Alanthurai is a place where Athisaivas, who possess all good qualities and have controlled their senses, live. Having worshipped Anbil Alanthurai, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds to the sacred place called Vadakarai Manthurai, where the Lord is enshrined.

We shall proceed with our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 617, Vambara Varivandu Sarkkam, by Sekizhar Swamigal, on the history of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds to the sacred place called Vadakarai Manthurai on the north bank of the Kaveri. It is located northeast of Trichy, on the road to Lalgudi. It is the fifty-eighth temple on the north bank of the Kaveri. It is called Ambravanam.

It is a place where the Maruts also worshipped. The Lord’s names are Ambravaneswarar and Mrigandeesvarar. The Goddess’s names are Azhagammai and Balambigai. Theerthams are Ganapathi Vaikkal and Gayatri Nadi. The place is named Ambravanam, or Manthurai, because it has a mango tree as its sacred tree. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who graced this place.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman bestows a pathigam. It is the hundred and tenth pathigam of the second Thirumurai, set to the tune of Nattaragam. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam (Semponnaarththaruvenggaiyum gnazhalum serundhi shenbagam aanai kombum aaramum maadhavi surapunai kurunthalar pondhu ambun ner varu kaveri vadakkarai maandhurai urayindhra empiraan imaiyor thozhu painggazhal eththudhal seyvome varai valanggavar kaveri vadakkarai maandhurai urai vaanaai sirapuram padhiyudaiyavan kavuniyan sezhumarai nirainaanan aravaynum pani vallavan gnanasambandhan anporu maalai paravidum thozhil vallavar allalum paavamum ilardhaame).

Let us praise the Lord of Thiru Manthurai. We know nothing else but to worship Him. This pathigam conveys the message that those who do not contemplate Him will go to a bad path.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships the courtyard of Siva, who is enshrined in Thiru Manthurai, circumambulates the beautiful long temple, enters, prostrates before the deity, praises the state of the Lord, who is worshipped by the Sun, Moon, and celestial physicians, with a garland of verses, and leaves that place to worship many other sacred places where Siva is enshrined nearby. The sacred places visited by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman in this way are considered to be Lalgudi, Poovalur, Thirumangalam, and other places between Vadakarai Manthurai on the Kaveri and Thiruppacchilachiraman. The pathigams bestowed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman on these sacred places are not available to us due to our lack of merit.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having visited many such places, travels along the north bank of the Kaveri to worship the Lord at Thiruppacchilachiraman, a sacred place in Malanadu. Pachil is the name of this sacred place, and Achiraman is the name of the temple. This place is also known as Thiruvaasi. The Lord’s names are Matrari Varathar, Sameevaneswarar, and Brahmapurisvarar. The Goddess’s name is Balambikai. The Goddess is Balasoundari.

Theertham is Annamaam Poigai and Silambaaru. This is also called Panguniyaru and Amalaiyaaru. It is known as Pachilachiraman because it is Achiraman in the region of Pachil. It has morphed into Thiruvasiraman, and now the people here call this town Thiruvaasi. This is one of the places where Sundaramoorthy Swamigal received gold.

The Lord is enshrined in a forest surrounded by Vanni trees, hence the Lord’s name is Sameevaneswarar. Brahma worshipped the Lord here, hence the Lord is also named Brahmapurisvarar. The mandapam between the first gopuram and the second prakaram of this temple is called the Avudaiya Pillai Mandapam. In this mandapam. The sculptures depicting Thirugnanasambandha Peruman curing the daughter of Kollimazhavan are beautiful. In the Lord’s sanctum, there is a Snapan mandapam where Sundarar was given a gold purse.

The inscription of this sacred place refers to this spot as “Kizhikooththaruliya Thiruvazhasal.” The idol of Sundaramoorthy Swamigal here is depicted singing with cymbals in both hands. Inscriptions refer to the Lord’s name as Pachil Thiruvachiramatthu Perumanadigal. Rajaraja I, Sundarapandiyan I, Kulottunga I, and Krishnadevaraya carried out renovation works in this temple. About five hundred years ago, during the reign of Veerasamesvaran, the Hoysala king who ruled with Samayapuram as his capital, this temple received ten thousand Kalam of paddy, as recorded in an inscription. All these are the glories of Thiruppacchilachiraman. In this sacred place, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is about to perform a great miracle of grace.

Sekizhar Swamigal describes it in detail. We shall continue our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 618, Vambara Varivandu Sarkkam, by Sekizhar Swamigal, on the history of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has arrived at Thiruppacchilachiraman. In that city, a chieftain named Kollimazhavan rules. This land borders the Kolli hills. This land was a vassal state of the Chola empire.

The ruler of this city, Kollimazhavan, belonged to a lineage that traditionally served Siva. He had a beautiful young daughter, but she was afflicted with the disease called Muyalagan. Muyalagan is one of the major diseases. It is called Apasmara in Sanskrit. Those who suffer from this disease lie unconscious and experience seizures and many other difficulties. This disease is so severe that it makes one lose consciousness.

Such a disease afflicted the daughter of Kollimazhavan, causing him physical and mental distress. Kollimazhavan’s relatives also suffered greatly. As the saying goes, “The beauty of the wealthy is to support their flourishing family,” Kollimazhavan had a large family. Such a family stood by Kollimazhavan even when he was in distress.

Thus, Kollimazhavan is suffering with his relatives due to this disease that afflicted his daughter. Despite all efforts, Kollimazhavan’s daughter’s illness was not cured. Kollimazhavan’s lineage was one that had served Siva traditionally.

Therefore, Kollimazhavan, who was accustomed to living by holding onto Siva’s feet, brought his daughter before the Lord at Thiruppacchilachiraman temple to cure her of this suffering and laid her there. He laid her before the Lord’s shrine. Such courage and disposition come only to those who are steeped in the devotion of Siva, both from their mother’s and father’s lineage. When sick people are laid before the Lord, the Lord’s direct gaze falls upon them, and by the special power of the Lord’s direct gaze, diseases and other afflictions are dispelled. This is the conclusion. We see that the mischievous acts of minor deities with ethereal bodies are dispelled before the Lord’s temple in places like Thirualavai and Thiruchendur.

Therefore, Kollimazhavan brings his daughter before the Lord to cure her of the Apasmara disease.

At the same time, the sounding bells announce that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has approached the boundary of Thiruppacchilachiraman. Just as Mazhavan, who came by clinging to the Lord’s sacred feet, laid his daughter before the Lord, the Lord’s grace, which belongs to Pillaiyar. The mischief of small deities with ethereal bodies is dispelled before the Lord’s temple, as we see happening in places like Thirualavai and Thiruchendur.

Therefore, Kollimazhavan brought his daughter before the Lord to cure her of the Apasmara disease.

At the same time, the sound of trumpets announced that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman had approached the boundary of Thiruppachilachiraman. Just as Mazhavan, who had held onto the Lord’s sacred feet, placed his daughter before the Lord, the Lord’s grace, which belongs to Pillaiyar. The world will now clearly witness the truth that his arrival at that place at that time will bring about the removal of the disease and enable salvation. The sound of ‘Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is arriving’ echoes. In the temple, instruments play, announcing, ‘Thirugnanasambandan, the enlightened sage, has arrived.’ This echo of praise signifies that wisdom can alleviate all suffering and bestow joy. This praise, resounding for Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, was given by the Lord to resonate for the benefit of the world, to relieve its sorrows.

Kollimalavan, who was sighing in deep sorrow at that time, heard of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s arrival. Upon hearing the news, Kollimalavan immediately placed his daughter before the Lord and made preparations to receive Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Leaving his daughter in the care of the Lord, and letting go of his deep attachment to her, he rushed to make arrangements to welcome Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, driven by immense love for the grace-filled saint. Following the sacred traditions for welcoming a Shiva devotee and a guru, Kollimalavan made auspicious arrangements to receive Thirugnanasambandha Peruman from the temple. He adorned the streets with auspicious and magnificent archways, and placed beautiful, water-filled golden pots at every entrance. Kollimalavan adorned the entire city with golden pots, incense burners with lamps, and pearl canopies.

Despite Kollimalavan being a minor king under the Cholas, Sekkizhar Peruman praised him as a ‘Koman’ (lord) because of this deep devotion. As these arrangements were made and Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reached the boundary of Thiruppachil Achiramam, Kollimalavan also arrived there. Thinking, “I have received the great fortune of receiving Pillaiyar,” Kollimalavan’s eyes welled up with tears due to his ever-increasing love for Pillaiyar. He prostrated before the sacred pearl palanquin where Pillaiyar was seated.

Then, the benevolent Thirugnanasambandha Peruman addressed Kollimalavan, saying, “Arise.” Pillaiyar uttered the sacred words, ‘Arise.’ The inner meaning implies ‘Arise from the ocean of sorrow,’ and ‘Arise from the ocean of birth and reach the shore.’ He bestowed these sacred words, ‘Arise,’ upon Kollimalavan and his daughter collectively. Just as bees gently blow into a closed bud with their mouths to make it bloom, Pillaiyar’s sacred words, ‘Arise,’ caused Kollimalavan’s heart, shriveled by despair, and his daughter’s life, confined by illness, to blossom. As instructed by Pillaiyar, Kollimalavan arose and led Pillaiyar through the streets of Thiruppachil Achiramam. Auspicious musical instruments resonated. Even though the entire city and all its streets were adorned, the street through which Pillaiyar proceeded was a greatly blessed street.

This street was the eastern entrance to the town of Thiruppachil Achiramam.

Thus, proceeding through this street, Pillaiyar arrived near the temple tower. Upon reaching the temple tower, Pillaiyar dismounted from the beautiful pearl palanquin, paid respects at the beautiful temple entrance, entered the temple, circumambulated the Lord’s shrine, and as he was about to proceed to worship before Lord Shiva, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman observed a young girl lying unconscious on the ground. He crossed the auspicious, resounding, bell-laden streets, and as he was about to dismount from the pearl palanquin near the luminous temple tower of the Lord with the moon-adorned matted locks, he descended gracefully, paid respects at the beautiful entrance, and entered. As he circumambulated his Lord’s temple and was about to worship before the sacred presence, he saw a young maiden lying on the ground, having lost consciousness. He looked and asked, “What is this?” Kollimalavan, bowing in response, said, “This girl, my golden treasure, has been afflicted by the disease of Muyalakan, an incomparable ailment. I brought her to the Lord’s temple to be cured, and this is what has happened.” Sekkizhar Peruman composed these two beautiful verses.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman saw the maiden, like a young creeper, lying unconscious on the ground and asked, “What is this?” Upon hearing Peruman’s question, Kollimalavan came before Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, bowed, and said, “This girl, my treasure, has been afflicted by the disease called Muyalakan. As I was unable to cure it, I brought her before the Lord’s temple, and she lies here in this state.” Pillaiyar looked at the girl and mercifully asked, “What is this?” This mercy refers to the compassionate actions that were seen, observed, and then heard by Pillaiyar. As Thirugnanasambandha Peruman thus spoke mercifully, Kollimalavan humbly responded. He stood awaiting Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s gracious intention. He stood awaiting the divine will.

Sekkizhar Peruman composed the verse: “Hearing with grace the words spoken by Kollimalavan, and standing then, the Lord of Shanbai sang a Tamil pathigam that dispels intractable disease, prostrating before the Supreme Being residing in Pachil with matted red locks, saying, ‘Is it the greatness of the Lord with the jewel-adorned throat to make this maiden suffer and be confused?’” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman listened graciously to all that Kollimalavan said, pouring out his abundant compassion. Upon hearing Kollimalavan’s words, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman immediately stood there and, prostrating before Lord Shiva, who is seated in Thiruppachil Achiramam, sang a unique Tamil pathigam. He mercifully sang a garland of Tamil verses. Lord Shiva, who resides in Thiruppachil Achiramam, has red matted locks where snakes reside, and a throat where poison is contained. Pillaiyar mercifully sang a unique Tamil pathigam, asking, “Is it the greatness of our Lord to make this maiden, Kollimalavan’s daughter, suffer and be confused?” He sang a garland of Tamil verses that would cure the extremely difficult disease of Muyalakan. When Pillaiyar was going to worship the Lord, he saw this girl before the Lord’s presence and heard this news.

Therefore, without going further inside to worship the Lord, he sang the pathigam right there at that spot where he heard the news. From that very spot, he sang the pathigam without entering to worship in the customary way. Sekkizhar Peruman states that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sang the pathigam, asking, ‘Is it the greatness of the Lord with the jewel-adorned throat to make this maiden suffer and be confused?’ This marks the concluding line of the first verse of the pathigam he sang. This is also the central theme of this pathigam. The same idea is present in the concluding line of every verse throughout the entire pathigam. ‘Manikandar’ here refers to the name of the Lord of this temple. It signifies that the Lord, who protected the gods from the poison, will also protect this girl.

Thus, the pathigam mercifully sung by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is referred to by Sekkizhar Peruman here as ‘Thanivil pani thavirkkum pathiga thandamizh’ (a beautiful Tamil pathigam that removes intractable disease). This Muyalakan disease is incurable by any other means. Among the three types of diseases—sathiyam (curable), sathiya-asathiyam (partially curable), and asathiyam (incurable)—this Muyalakan disease belongs to the ‘asathiyam’ category. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman mercifully sings this beautiful Tamil pathigam that cures such a disease. That pathigam, which begins with ‘Thunivalar Thingal,’ is the forty-fourth pathigam of the First Thirumurai, dedicated to the Thiruppachil Achiramam temple, and is set to the ‘Thakkaraga’ tune. The pathigam is as follows: Thiruchitrambalam.

“The moon, bright and clear, shining and resplendent, encircled by the flaming matted hair. (Tunivalar Tingal tulangi vilanga sudarcchataisuttri mutittu panivalar kolgaiyar paridarnsoola varidavum palithervar anivalar kolamellam seythu pachilachiramathuraindra manivalar kantaroo mangaiyai vaada mayal seyvatho ivar maarbe kalaipunai manuri toludai aadai kanal sudar alivar kangal talaiyani senkannir taranimarrpartam adigal ivarenna alaippunal pumpolil suuldhamar pachilachiramathuraindra ilaippunaivelaroo velaiyai vaada idar seyvatho ivar eede venchudar aduvar tunjirun maalai venduduvor punbadu ven nul nanjadai kandar nanjidamaaga nannuvar nammai nayandu manchadaimaligai suulztharu pachilachiramathuraindra senchudarvannooro pai) “With a snake growing, they go begging for alms, surrounded by various beings. After adorning themselves beautifully, the Lord with the gem-adorned throat, residing in Thiruppachil Achiramam, does he cause this maiden to wither and become bewildered? Is this his glory?” “He wears a deer skin as an upper garment, his eyes are like fiery flames. He wears a skull as a head ornament, and his chest is adorned with garlands.

“The Lord who resides in Thiruppachil Achiramam, surrounded by gardens with flowing water, does he, with a leaf-adorned spear, cause this maiden to suffer and pine? Is this his nature?” “He dances with fierce fire, he desires the dark evening, he wears a white sacred thread.

“The Lord with the poison-throated neck, he approaches us, desiring our hearts as his dwelling.

“The Lord with the fiery red complexion, residing in Thiruppachil Achiramam, surrounded by mansions filled with clouds. (chitaichaiyvathoo ivar seere kanamalar konrai alangkil ilangkakkanaru thoomati kanni punamalar maalaiyanindhalagaya punitharkolaam ivarenna vanamali vinpolil suuztharu pachilachiramathuraindra manamali maintharoo mangaiyai vaada mayal seyvathoo ivar maambe maandhartam paru nei magizhndhadi valarcchadai mel punal vaithu mondhai muzhaakkuzhal taazamor veenai muthiravor vaaymuri paadi aanthai velicchiru puthatthar pachilachiramathuraindra saanthani maarbaroo taiyalai vaadaccathurseyvathoo ivar saarve neerumeypuusi niraichadattaazha netrikkannaalurrunokki aaradhichodi aada aravaatiyai virar kovanavaadai) “Does he defile? Is this his glory?” “He wears garlands of dense Konrai flowers, a crescent moon, and a garland of forest flowers, appearing beautiful. Is he a holy one?” The Lord, with fragrant youth, residing in Thiruppachil Achiramam, surrounded by cloud-laden gardens, does he cause this maiden to wither and become bewildered? Is this his greatness?” “He enjoys bathing with clarified butter, places water on his growing matted locks, plays the ‘mondhai’ drum, the flute, and a ripe veena, and sings a tune. The Lord, with small owls and ghosts, residing in Thiruppachil Achiramam, with a fragrant chest, does he play tricks to make this woman suffer?

“Is this his refuge?” “He smears sacred ash, his abundant matted locks hang down, he looks with his third eye, wears a garland of skulls, and dances. The Lord, wearing a serpent-loincloth. (paararu meniyar puthatthar pachilachiramathuraindra erathuveeriyar ezaiyai vaada idar seyvathoo ivareeDe pongila nagamoo regavadathodaamai vennul punaikonrai kongila maalai punaidhalagaya kulagarkolam ivarenna angilamangayor panginar pachilachiramathuraindra sangulivannaro taazkuzhal vaadaccathir seyvathovivar saarve evalathal visaiyarkkarul seythu iravanai eeDazhithu muvarilum mudhalay naduvay murthiyai anri mozhiyal yavargalum paravum ezhil pachilachiramathuraindra thevargalthevaro seyizhai vaadaccithai seyvathovivar serve melathu nanmugan eiyathathillai kizathu sevadi tannai nilathu vannanum eiyathathillai ena ivar nindradumallaal) “With a vast body, accompanied by ghosts, residing in Thiruppachil Achiramam, does the Lord, mounted on a bull, cause this innocent maiden to suffer? Is this his nature?” “With a shining serpent, a single sacred thread, a tortoise shell, white sacred thread, and a garland of young Konrai flowers, he is adorned beautifully. Is he a noble one?” The Lord, who has a young maiden as part of himself, residing in Thiruppachil Achiramam, with a conch-like hue, does he play tricks to make the long-haired woman suffer? Is this his refuge?” “He bestowed grace upon Arjuna by command, destroyed Ravana, and is the first, middle, and last among the three gods.

“Besides him, no one else is praised by words.

“The Lord of gods, residing in beautiful Thiruppachil Achiramam, does he destroy the adorned maiden? Is this his abode?” “Above, Brahma did not reach the crown; below, Vishnu did not reach the sacred feet. This is not the only place where he stands. (aalathumaamathitooypozhil pachilachiramathuraindra paalathu vannaroo painthodi vaadap pazhi seyvathoo ivar panbe nanodu kudiya sayinarenu nakuvaravar irupothum unodu kudiya udkunnagayal uraigal avaicolava vendam anodu penvadivayinar pachilachiramathuraindra punedummarbaroo puunkodivaadap punaiseyvathoo ivar porpe agamaliyanpodu tondar vanangaachiramathuraindra pugaimalimallai punaidhalagaya punitharkolam ivarenna nagamalithanpolil suuztharu kaali nattamil gnanasanbandan tagaimali tandamil konduivai etta saaragilavinai tane tiruccittrambalam ivvaru) “In Thiruppachil Achiramam, where large Banyan trees are adorned with jasmine flowers, does the Lord, with a milk-like hue, bring disrepute by causing this green-bangle-wearing maiden to suffer? Is this his character?” “Even if they are with knowledge, they will mock at all times. Do not heed those words spoken with inner contempt, intertwined with flesh.

“The Lord, who is both male and female, residing in Thiruppachil Achiramam, with a flower-adorned chest, does he adorn this flower-like creeper to suffer? Is this his glory?” “The pure one, adorned with fragrant garlands, residing in Achiramam where devotees worship with overflowing love, is he not beautiful?” Thus, the eminent Gnanasambandan of Kaazhi, surrounded by pleasant cool groves, with these exquisite Tamil verses, praised (the Lord), and karma will not cling.

“Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman mercifully sang the pathigam. Sekkizhar Peruman then composed two more verses: “As the Kaundiniya, who sang the Tamil Vedas of the pathigam, sealed it with the sacred final verse, the disease left the child-like, soft-spoken maiden, Kollimalavan’s daughter, who stood on the earth. She rose quickly and, like a golden creeper, gracefully approached her father. Seeing his daughter freed from the severe illness, Kollimalavan’s joy overflowed. His peerless daughter and he both fell at the feet of Pillaiyar, the chief of Seerkazhi. As the great Pillaiyar stood, he too, with a focused mind, worshipped the feet of the pure Lord with water-adorned matted locks.

“The devotees of the Lord rejoiced.” Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman mercifully sang the Tamil Vedic pathigam and concluded it with the sacred final verse. At that moment, the Muyalakan disease immediately left Kollimalavan’s daughter. As soon as the disease and unconsciousness left, the girl, who was lying down, regained consciousness and rose very quickly from the ground. Like a golden creeper, she gracefully walked and approached her father, Kollimalavan. Since she was an unmarried maiden, upon regaining consciousness and rising from her illness, she bashfully moved aside and came near her father. Kollimalavan was overjoyed to see his daughter, who was freed from the terrible disease of Muyalakan.

“His incomparable daughter and he both prostrated at the feet of Pillaiyar, the leader of Seerkazhi. As Kollimalavan and his daughter worshipped Pillaiyar’s feet. Pillaiyar worshipped the feet of the Lord. Through this, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman conveyed the truth that all reverence belongs to the Lord alone, and that all his actions are indeed the Lord’s actions.

“Therefore, Pillaiyar directed the worship offered to him towards the Lord. When Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was on his way to worship the Lord, this event occurred before the Lord’s presence. Now that Kollimalavan’s daughter had recovered from her illness and risen, Pillaiyar, with a focused mind, proceeded to worship the Lord, thinking it was time to seek the Lord’s darshan. As per the tenth sutra of Sivagnana Bodham, “He himself becomes one, becomes singular, and stands in service to the Lord,” Pillaiyar proceeded to worship the Lord with a focused mind. All the Lord’s devotees chanted Shiva’s name, making joyful sounds of ‘Harahara’. This was the manifestation of grace that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman performed in Thiruppachil Achiramam.

“Let us resume our reflection.”” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 619, by Sekkizhar Swamigal, ‘Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam’, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman mercifully cures the Muyalakan disease at Thiruppachil Achiramam temple. Due to this, the Muyalakan is not under the feet of Koothaperuman (Nataraja) in this temple. Instead, Muyalakan is seen standing near Koothaperuman, worshipping him.

However, there is a snake under Koothaperuman’s feet.

The Lord appears as Sarppa Nadanamurthy (dancing with a snake).

Thus, after worshipping the feet of the Lord, who is permanently enshrined in Thiruppachil Achiramam with Uma as one half, and with the grace of Lord Shiva, Pillaiyar, who was present there, further desired to visit more temples. Having received gracious permission from the Lord of Thiruppachil Achiramam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman visited and worshipped many sacred places where the Lord resides, praised their holy feet, and sang pathigams. Sivakavimaniyar opines that the temples thus visited by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman might include Thiruppulivalam, Thiruthudaiyur, and other such places. After visiting many such temples, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrived at Thiruppaingili. Paingili is a sacred place surrounded by groves where humming bees sing tunes.

There, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worshipped the Lord. Thiruppaingili temple is near Trichy. We have extensively discussed the history of this temple in the Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who came to such a temple, worshipped the Lord there and mercifully sang a pathigam. He sang this garland of Tamil verses, praised by the people of this world, and stayed in that place, delighted by his worship. The pathigam thus mercifully sung by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is the fourteenth pathigam of the Third Thirumurai, set to the tune of Gandhara Panchamam.

The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who worshipped at Thiruppaingili, then visited all the other temples where Lord Shiva is enshrined. These sacred places include Thiruthalaiyur, Thirunerkunram, Musiri, and other such temples. After worshipping at all these places, Pillaiyar reached the sacred hill called Thiru Ingoy Malai. In Thiru Ingoy Malai, reddish-eyed monkeys worship Lord Shiva. Devas come and praise the monkeys who worship Lord Shiva. Thiru Ingoy Malai is such a glorious place.

We can recall here what Sekkizhar Swamigal mentioned about Thiru Idaichuram in the 1090th verse: ‘Even Devas and Apsaras are born as peerless hunters and women to worship.’ This can also be seen in the work ‘Thiru Ingoy Malai Ezhupathu’ composed by Nakkeera Deva Nayanar. Thiru Ingoy Malai is such a glorious sacred mountain. This is the sixty-third and final temple on the northern bank of the Cauvery. People refer to it as Thiru Ingainatha Malai. The proverb, “Morning Kadambar, Noon Sokkar, Evening Thiru Ingoy Nathar,” is very popular in this region. Morning Kadambar refers to Kadambavaneswarar temple, Kadambavanathar, who is the second deity on the southern bank of the Cauvery.

Noon Sokkar refers to the Lord of Thiruvarpokki, the first deity on the southern bank of the Cauvery. Evening Thiru Ingoy Nathar refers to the Lord of Thiru Ingoy Malai, which is the sixty-third and final temple on the northern bank of the Cauvery. It is believed that by visiting these three temples as described above, one will receive good blessings. This has been a long-standing tradition in this region. This sacred place is blessed with the greatness of the work ‘Thiru Ingoy Malai Ezhupathu’ composed by Nakkeera Deva Nayanar. Thiru Ingoy Malai Ezhupathu is compiled in the eleventh Thirumurai by Nambiyandar Nambi.

When Sage Agastya came here to worship the Lord, seeing the large crowd of devotees, he regretted not having time to worship and transformed into a bee (ee) to worship the Lord. Hence, the place is named Eengoy Malai. The Lord’s name is Maragadachalar. The radiance of the emerald idol can still be seen today. The Goddess is Maragathavalliyar. One can reach this sacred place by crossing the vast Cauvery river north from Kadambavaneswarar temple in Kulithalai, on the way from Trichy to Erode.

Thiruvatpokki Malai, Kadambanthurai, and Thiru Ingoy Malai—these three sacred places are in the Somaskanda form. Since Ambikai worshipped here, it is also known as Sivasakti Malai. True to the name Maragathachaleswarar, the Lord’s idol shines in a brilliant green color. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who visited this sacred place, mercifully sang a pathigam.
