That pathigam is the seventieth pathigam of the First Thirumurai, set to the tune of Thakkasi. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Thenoththana menmozhi manpizhila thevi padamakaana theeravil eli kondaadum kadavul ulagethane theeral vandhu izhiyum saru ingoy malaiyare vilambar muzhavum ova verupuram thanthulazhaga pannaththu adigal ser anigal sambanda)

“With Uma, he is our Lord. He grants grace by removing all karmic impurities.” This is the central theme of this pathigam.

Thus, Pillaiyar worshipped the feet of the Lord and visited the surrounding hills adorned with dense groves, singing pathigams interwoven with melody and meaning. He then praised all the nearby sacred places of the Lord. He went to the western part of Kongu Nadu. Kongu Nadu is the land area in Tamil Nadu from Karur to Coimbatore. This Kongu Nadu is divided into three regions: Vadakongu (North Kongu), Thenkongu (South Kongu), and Melkongu (West Kongu). Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reaches the western part of Kongu Nadu.

Pillaiyar, the flame of true wisdom that eliminates the impurities of ego afflicting souls, now embarks on a sacred journey through Kongu Nadu. Let us continue our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 620, by Sekkizhar Swamigal, ‘Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam’, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrives in Kongu Nadu, located on the southern bank of the Cauvery. Thiruppaingili and Thiru Ingoymalai are temples on the northern bank of the Cauvery. The southern bank, opposite to that shore, forms the border of Kongu Nadu. The region from the Thalamalai mountain range to Kuzhithalai on the southern bank of the Cauvery was once the boundary of Kongu Nadu.

After visiting such temples, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrived at Thiruchengodu, known as Thiru Kodimada Sengunroor. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman visited all the ancient Shiva temples located between Thiru Kodimada Sengunroor and the Cauvery before arriving at Thiruchengodu. Thiruchengodu was a major city, one of the capital cities where kings resided. One can reach Thiruchengodu from cities like Salem, Erode, and Namakkal. The main deity here appears as Ardhanareeswarar. The name of Lord Murugan of this temple is Sengottu Velavar.

The name of the Goddess is Pagam Periyal. Deva Thirtham and Brahma Thirtham are the sacred ponds. This is a temple located on a hill. Since the hill is red, it is named Sengodu. It has several names such as Deiva Thirumalai, Nagamalai, Urasagiri. There are steps to climb the hill.

The sixtieth step is considered very special. It is said that if one takes an oath on this sixtieth step, it would be accepted even in a court of law by the local people. The temple history states that Kedara Gauri worshipped a Maragathalingam and received the left half of the Lord’s body. If viewed from Melamada Street, this hill resembles a snake, hence it is also called Nagachalam or Nagagiri. One can climb about 1200 steps to reach the temple on the hill. References to this temple can be found in Silappatikaram, Thevaram, Kandar Anubhuti, Kandar Alangaram, etc.

Sengottu Velavar has a beautiful standing idol. The main deity is a Swayambhu Murthy (self-manifested idol) made of white Pashanam (mineral), an undamaging idol that does not reflect light. It stands on a square pedestal, where the Lord appears as Ardhanareeswarar in a standing posture.

Thus, there is no Lingam here. The main deity is adorned with half a saree and half a dhoti, in the form of Ardhanareeswarar. The entire idol is made of white Pashanam. Cool water springs from beneath the holy feet, known as Deva Thirtham. In front of the main deity, there is a Maragathalingam and an idol of Bhringi Maharishi. The Adikesava Perumal shrine here was mangalashasanam (praised) by Nammalvar.

There is a Sthala Puranam (temple history) composed by Veera Kaviraja Panditar. Inscriptions from the periods of Rajaraja I, Sundarapandiyadevar, and Mysore Krishnaraja Udaiyar are found here. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrived at such a glorious temple. The common people and Shiva devotees residing in that sacred city were overjoyed and adorned the entire city. Before Pillaiyar entered the city, everyone gathered at the border, worshipped the Lord, praised him, and welcomed him. With their hands clasped above their heads, they welcomed Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrived before the temple of the Lord of Thiruchengodu. He entered the temple, prostrated before the Lord, rose, and mercifully sang a sweet, melodious Tamil pathigam so that the people of this world and the heavenly realms might benefit. That pathigam is the 107th pathigam of the First Thirumurai. It is a pathigam set to the tune of Viyalakurinji. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. (Venda venniyirivi nuligal marbin allaviralaal orubakam amarntharunthodi maadachenroor nindra arupaare alaimali than punal suulnda pugazhina) “The Lord’s form in this sacred place, Thiruchengodu, is Ardhanareeswarar, with the Goddess as half of his body.

“He is adorned with sacred ash, a primeval form of reality. Worshipping him is the true path, and it dispels karmic impurities.” This is the central theme of this pathigam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having thus worshipped the Lord in this place. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman stayed in this place for some days.

“Afterward, he visited and worshipped all the temples to the west, where the Lord desired to reside. The country to the west of Thiruchenkunroor is West Kongu Nadu. There are many Shiva temples in this West Kongu Nadu, some mentioned in the Thevarams and some not. These places include Perur, Avinasi, Kolli Kulir Arappalli, Mattur (also known as Sevur), Ezhur, Tholur, Thirumurugan Poondi, Kurakkathali, Kumarikongu, and others. References to these places can be found in works such as the Nayanmars’ Kshetra Kovai and other pathigams.

“Therefore, Sekkizhar Swamigal mentions that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman visited and worshipped all the temples in this region. There are seven Thevaram-sung temples in Kongu Nadu, and among them, Thirunana, also known as Bhavani, is the temple blessed with a pathigam in West Kongu.

“Thus, after visiting all these Kongu Nadu temples, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrived at Bhavani, known as Thirunana. Bhavani is the third of the seven Thevaram-sung temples in Kongu Nadu. It is believed that no harm will befall those who worship the Lord of this temple. It is such a sacred place. This town is named Nannavur or Thirunana. The Bhavani River and the Cauvery River meet at this temple, hence it is called Bhavani Koodal (confluence).

“The Sthala Virksham (sacred tree) is the Ilanthai tree, hence it is called Badarivanam. The Bhavani River is one of the tributaries of the Cauvery. In ancient Tamil texts of the Sangam period, this river is referred to as Vaani. We can compare this to the current practice of naming rivers as Mevani, Keavani, Siruvani. This temple is praised in Thiruppugazh as ‘Thiruvani Koodal Perumal’. This is a sacred place where Kubera, Viswamitra Muni, Parashara Muni, and others worshipped and attained fame.

“The confluence of the Bhavani River with the Cauvery is very special. The Amudha Nadi (nectar river) that emerges from the pit excavated by Parashara Muni, where he placed the pot of nectar, also joins here. Because it joins as a triple confluence, it is called Bhavani Mukkoodal, a sacred place with special waters.

“The Lord has a temple at such a confluence. Inside the temple, as mentioned in the eighth verse of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s pathigam, “Even Bhoomi Azhathan (Vishnu) worshipped and praised,” there is a separate shrine for Adikesava Perumal. Chettipalayam Vidvan Vasudeva Mudaliar, who lived about 180 years ago, composed the Sthala Puranam for this temple. The Bhavani Sthala Puranam contains 901 verses across eighteen chapters, starting from the introduction. This Sthala Puranam is a translation from Sanskrit. This temple is very close to Erode.

“One can also reach this temple from Salem, Karur, and Coimbatore. The Lord’s name is Sangamuganathar, and the Goddess’s name is Vedanayaki. Bhavani Mukkoodal, Bhavani, Cauvery, and Amudha Nadi are the sacred waters here. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who came to this sacred place, praised the Lord and mercifully sang a pathigam. That pathigam is the seventy-second pathigam of the Second Thirumurai, set to the Gandharam tune. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam.

“Poalum antha vaada”

“Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having visited Thirunana, Returned to Thiruchengodu and stayed there. We shall continue with our reflection.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 621, by Sekkizhar Swamigal, ‘Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam’, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Pillaiyar arrives at Thiru Kodimada Sengunroor, also known as Thiruchengodu. During those days, the early winter season arrived, and a cold fever spread throughout the region. Pillaiyar mercifully eradicated that disease from the country itself. Sekkizhar Peruman extensively describes this act of grace.

Sekkizhar Peruman beautifully explains how the winter season was like in Thiruchengodu during the days Pillaiyar stayed there. It was the early winter season. This season, when frost falls after the rainy season, is called the early winter season. It is a time when the sun is not very strong, a cold period after the rains.

Therefore, living beings yearn for the sun due to the cold. Even the mountains are extremely cold. Swarms of bees reject and avoid the flowers without enjoying them, as they cannot fly due to the cold. It is a time when frost falls, causing the tips of lotus flowers to wither. There are dewdrops on green tender leaves, like white beads on green emerald creepers. Dewdrops are present on all the tender leaves.

Even the hills are covered with frost, as if wrapped in a white blanket. The north wind blows. While the wind from the south is called ‘Thendral’ (pleasant breeze), the north wind signifies a wind coming from the north. It brings intense cold.

Therefore, they say that the ‘Thendral’ wind brings joy, and the north wind brings sorrow. The tender leaves in the groves are lush. Since there are no people to pluck them, and the birds that peck at them do not peck due to the cold, those tender leaves are thriving.

However, due to the severity of the cold, the tender leaves in the groves wither and reach a state of distress without flourishing. Due to the intensity, all creatures cannot fully extend their hands, so they stand for a short while, extending and then retracting them.

Similarly, in winter, the sun on the mountainside casts a dim light, then fades slowly, then casts a few rays again, in this manner. The houses in Thiruchengode are mansions, and pigeons reside in these mansions. Pigeons live in families like humans, and they are huddled in their nests within these mansions. A male pigeon is huddled with a female pigeon that has coral-colored feet. In the bird kingdom, the male is superior in beauty and attractiveness. It is nurtured by the female.

However, in the human race, the female is beautiful and attractive and is nurtured by the male. Such are the scenes in the houses of Thiruchengode due to winter. To ward off the cold, people fumigate. They grind turmeric and saffron, make it into a powder, put it on fire to produce smoke, and protect themselves from the cold. This smoke also has the quality of preventing the severity of fog and cold from affecting them. This is a truth stated in medical texts.

Similarly, they light a fire in a large iron pot with a wide mouth. Lord Thirugnanasambandha’s entourage stayed in Thiruchengode for many days during this winter to warm themselves. Many entourages would undertake pilgrimages with Lord Thirugnanasambandha. Lord Thirugnanasambandha came to Thiruchengode and then returned after visiting all the temples in the Kongu region, didn’t he? Until then, all these entourages stayed in Thiruchengode.

Therefore, during this winter, the entourage of Lord Thirugnanasambandha, who had been staying in Thiruchengode for a long time, was afflicted with a fever. This is a severe chill fever, which first brings cold and then fever. It is called mountain fever; it is the type of fever known as malaria that spreads there, throughout the region including Thiruchengode.

Therefore, Lord Thirugnanasambandha’s entourage is also affected. This significant chill fever spreads most extensively in the mountains and their forests. When Lord Pillaiyar was residing here in Thiruchengode, it was very widespread. The entourage approached Lord Pillaiyar and humbly reported this situation to him. They informed Lord Pillaiyar of their plight and worshipped him. Even if this land’s nature brings these ailments, they cannot affect us, declares Lord Thirugnanasambandha, and then he sings a pathigam in praise of Lord Shiva, who wears the crescent moon on his head.

Lord Sekkizhar here composes the verses. Lord Pillaiyar is a divine being dwelling in a pure transcendental state, so he will do nothing without the Lord’s grace.

Therefore, Lord Thirugnanasambandha prays for the grace of the Primal Lord. He proclaims that even if this chill fever is a natural phenomenon of this land, it will not affect us, the devotees of Lord Shiva. Just as poison does not affect a mantra-chanting sorcerer, similarly, fire cannot burn those who can perform Agnisthambanam (controlling fire).

Similarly, Lord Thirugnanasambandha states that even if this chill fever is a natural characteristic of this land, it will not affect the devotees of Lord Shiva. How is this so?

The devotees who are in servitude to Lord Shiva, before the power of that servitude, the inferior physical power of this land’s characteristic chill fever will be weakened, powerless, and inactive. As Sivagnanabodham states, ‘The unreal does not shine before the Real; all is naught before Truth,’ Lord Thirugnanasambandha declares that this chill fever will do nothing to us who possess the quality of servitude to the Lord. Having thus declared, he bestows a pathigam, saying, ‘For that action’. To this evil, what is the remedy? Previously, when poison was partaken by the Lord, he prevented it, and thus removed our suffering, thereby attaining victory, and by protecting his devotees from suffering everywhere, he was known as Thiruneelakandam, the one whose throat was not affected by poison.

Thus, Lord Thirugnanasambandha bestowed the pathigam that begins with ‘Avvinaiiku Ivvinaiyam’ (For that deed, this is the deed). This pathigam praises Lord Shiva’s Thiruneelakandam. It conveys the idea that it was Lord Shiva’s Thiruneelakandam that prevented the terrible poison he consumed and protected us from all suffering.

Therefore, in the first verse of the pathigam, he declares with an oath upon Thiruneelakandam, ‘Let no ill-doing come and touch us, by the grace of Thiruneelakandam.’ The blackness of Thiruneelakandam came from the Lord bearing the poison. It came from bearing the poison, which prevented it from spreading and causing suffering, stopping it from going beyond the throat—this is the Puranic history. Just as Thiruneelakandam protected the Devas then, so too today, Thiruneelakandam will protect us from great dangers, diseases, and sorrows. Thiruneelakandam possesses such a victory. Whenever great calamities strike, anywhere, at any time, it is Thiruneelakandam that protects us, the devotees of Lord Shiva, from such great dangers, great suffering, and great diseases. We are devotees of the Lord, therefore, ‘let no ill-doing come and touch us,’ Lord Thirugnanasambandha declares, taking an oath upon Thiruneelakandam.

This pathigam, ‘If you touch us, by Thiruneelakandam,’ recalls that oath. He swore an oath upon Thiruneelakandam, and that comes to our remembrance here.

Similarly, here too, Lord Thirugnanasambandha takes an oath upon Thiruneelakandam and bestows a pathigam. Although this is the Thirukodimaada Sengunrur, or Thiruchengode pathigam, it is also considered a general Thiruneelakandam pathigam. It is the one hundred and sixteenth pathigam of the First Thirumurai. The first and concluding verses of these pathigams are as follows: do acts of worship and praise the feet of our Lord. We are his devotees, let no evil deed come and touch us, by Thiruneelakandam. If one worships the feet of the Lord who is cherished in this birth, and if there be a next birth, then Thiru Gnanasambandhan, who is skilled and united with the entire world, will attain the feet of the immortals.

This is the inner meaning. Lord Thiru Gnanasambandhan declared that Thiruneelakandam protects the devotees from suffering, preventing it from reaching them, anywhere, at any time. This pathigam protects from all suffering caused by evil deeds. Lord Thirugnanasambandha gave a command that chill fever should not harm the devotees. A few years ago, when a new type of infectious disease spread across the country, all the devotees of the Lord recited this pathigam, ‘Avvinaiiku Ivvinaiyam,’ and were saved from that pandemic. This is a recent historical event, a moment that stood as another direct proof that Lord Thirugnanasambandha’s words, sung with an oath on the Lord, are indeed true. ‘Avvinaiiku Ivvinaiyam,’ meaning ‘For that deed, this is the deed’.

You know that saying: ‘Not seeking liberation is a flaw for you.’ ‘We, the devotees, perform actions with our hands and praise the feet of our Lord. Let no evil deed come and touch us, by Thiruneelakandam.’ This is the first verse. Lord Thirugnanasambandha addresses us by saying, ‘You know that saying, for that deed, this is the deed.’ He speaks to those who say that the experience of suffering for living beings comes from past deeds and cannot be avoided without experiencing it. He then states that there is a way to be protected from it. There is a way to find relief from the suffering that comes from past deeds, and that is through the sacred service rendered to the Lord through Charya, Kriya, Yoga, and so on. This is the only way to obtain salvation, which is to remove the Prarabdha, a portion of the accumulated karma.

This is the only path to salvation, which removes the suffering of prarabdha, a part of sanchita karma. Not thinking about and not performing such Shiva puja, which grants salvation, is indeed a fault. Not seeking that salvation is our fault.

Therefore, worship the feet of our Lord by performing Shiva puja through manual actions such as charya, kriya, and yoga. We are the Lord’s devotees, so prarabdha, which is the result of past actions, and agama, which arises from it, cannot touch us. Lord Thirugnanasambandha declares this in the first verse, taking an oath upon Thiruneelakandam.

After this declaration, Lord Sekkizhar continues to relate what happened: ‘Having thus graciously proclaimed the command with such clear intention, he then adorned it with the pure concluding verse of the pathigam.’ And Lord declares, ‘It did not just cease for those living in that beautiful city, but also for the entire country that was affected by that terrible affliction.’ Thus, Lord Thirugnanasambandha graciously bestowed the pathigam with such divine indication and command. He also adorned that pure pathigam with its concluding verse. As Lord Thirugnanasambandha declared, by the command of Thiruneelakandam, that these fevers would not affect the devotees, the chill fever ceased for all who lived in that city of Thiruchengode, as well as for those living in that region of the country. Since the command manifested through Lord Pillaiyar’s divine will, even today, those who regularly and disciplinedly recite this pathigam are relieved from diseases and other sufferings. This divine act took place in Thiruchengode. Sivakavimani Ayya further elaborates on this place.

This is the fourth of the seven praised temples in the Kongu region. This is the only temple located north of the Cauvery; the other Kongu temples are south of the Cauvery. The history of Brahma, Vishnu, Durga, and Murugan worshipping here is the history of this holy place. This is one of the mountains particularly sacred to Murugan, and it is praised in Thiruppugazh songs. Arunagirinathar sings about the grandeur of the beauty of Lord Murugan, known as Sengottu Velar, who resides in this place. He praises, ‘Did not that Brahma, who saw Sengodan, create four thousand eyes for me?’ Arunagirinathar laments, ‘That Brahma did not give me four thousand eyes to behold the beauty of Lord Murugan, Sengottu Velar, of this sacred place; he only gave me two eyes.’ Arunagirinathar sings that Brahma only gave him two eyes.

The ancient form, extensively discussed in Shaivism, Vedas, Agamas, and Puranas, as ‘Madharu Bagar’ (one who shares his body with a woman), i.e., Ardhanareeswarar, is the Moolavar deity in the sanctum sanctorum here. This temple is unique. There are many rare sacred springs on the mountain. Many wonders exist. Kaviraja Pandithar, son of Sankaracharya Ayyar, who sang Kasi Thala Puranam based on Bodhayana Sutra and Kashyapa Gotra, has sung the history of this place. Chithambala Upadhyayar has written a commentary on it.

The Parvata Khandam describes the glory of Ardhanareeswarar, the Kanda Khandam describes the glory of Lord Murugan, and the Teertha Khandam describes the glory of the springs found here.

Thus, this temple history has three sections. This history of the place was translated from a Sanskrit temple history. There is a peak there that grants boons such as progeny, known as Vandhya Bhashanam in Sanskrit. It is worshipped. Many springs like Naga Teertham and Shiva Teertham are present there.

Thus, Sivakavimani Ayya has provided these notes about this holy place. Our reflection now resumes. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam by Sekkizhar Swamigal, Part Six Hundred Twenty-Two, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Lord Thirugnanasambandha continues his pilgrimage from Thiruchengode. Having received gracious permission from the Lord at Thiruchengode, he worships many places of the Lord with the reddish matted hair. Lord Pillaiyar, adorned with a deer skin and the sacred thread, departs from Thiruchengode and proceeds to Thirupandikodumudi, a holy place on the banks of the Cauvery River. Lord Thirugnanasambandha worships the sacred feet of the Lord at Thirupandikodumudi, on the banks of the Cauvery, which flows abundantly without fail.

The prosperity that the Cauvery brings to the Chola kingdom is due to the generous offering of the western part of the Kongu kingdom. Beyond that, the Cauvery, which flows south to Thirupandikodumudi, now turns east and begins its journey to the Chola kingdom. The Cauvery River, which overflowed when Vinayaka tilted Agastya’s kamandalam to prevent Indira’s Nandavanam (sacred garden) in Sirkazhi from drying up, originates from the Kongu region.

Accordingly, the Vinayaka deity of Thirupandikodumudi is known as Kaveri Kanda Vinayaka. This holy place, Thirupandikodumudi, is situated on the south bank of the Cauvery. It is the sixth of the seven sacred temples praised in the Kongu region and is currently very popularly known as Kodumudi. History states that this is one of the peaks of the great Meru mountain. Brahma and Vishnu worshipped here. They are enshrined in separate temples here.

Brahma and Vishnu are still present in this temple, in a worshipping posture, remembering Lord Shiva. Not knowing this temple’s history, most people currently refer to this temple as the Thirumurthi Sannidhi, which is incorrect. We can find here the idea from Thiruvachagam: ‘Thinking of the three as one with our Lord, and proudly being called Devas in heaven and on earth, what a sin to wander!’ It is said that near this temple, Vinayaka, in the form of a crow, overturned Agastya’s kamandalam, causing the Cauvery to flow, and thus made Indira’s Nandavanam in Sirkazhi of the Chola country flourish. This history is discussed in the Kaveri Neengu Padalam of the Kanda Puranam.

Therefore, this holy place also bears the name Kaveri. This place is also known as Karaiyur.

Sundaramoorthy Swamigal referred to this holy place as ‘Karaiyur’ in his Thevaram. This place is praised in the ‘Rattaimani Maalai’ on Lord Shiva, composed by Kapila Deva Nayanar in the Eleventh Thirumurai.

Sundaramoorthy Swamigal visited the Lord here and sang the Panchakshara Pathigam with the sentiment that ‘even if I forget you, my tongue will not forget to chant your name mantra.’ This holy place has the distinction of having Thevaram verses sung by all three Acharayas. Some parts of the local history of this holy place were composed by Coimbatore Vidwan Kandasamy Mudaliar, and the greater part by Samakulam Venkataramanadasar, approximately one hundred and sixty years ago. Venkataramanadasar, who composed most of this local history, was originally a Vaishnava but received Saiva initiation. He became greatly devoted to Shaivism and spread it, earning the title ‘Kaliyuga Haradatta.’ The Lord’s name in this temple is Kodumudi Varadar, Kodumudi Natha, Magudeshwarar, Malaikkoluntheesar. The goddess’s names are Panmozhi Nayaki, Tripura Sundari, VadivuDai Nayaki. The sacred tanks are Kaveri Teertham, Brahma Teertham, Deva Teertham.

In the contest between Adisesha and Vayu over who was stronger, five gems from Mount Meru, which Adisesha had completely covered, scattered and fell as peaks. Among them, the diamond gem became this sacred place. It is the place where Lord Shiva granted Bharadwaja Muni a dance without Muyalagan. Lord Thirugnanasambandha, having come to such a significant holy place as Thirupandikodumudi, bestows a rich pathigam, beginning with ‘Pennamar Meniyinarum’. That pathigam. In this pathigam, there are allusions that state the Lord, who removes the enmity of karma and dispels the sorrow of those who remember and rise, resides in the body of his devotees.

Such is this pathigam, the sixty-ninth pathigam of the Second Thirumurai, set to the tune of Gandharam. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: ‘Kathammarum’. (Kadhamarum Padhalinarum Pandi Kodumudhiye Kalamalagu than Kadal choozhndha Kazhiyul Gnana Sambanthan Balamalagu ven Thalaiyendhi Pandi Kodumudi thannai Paadalgal PathaVeerndhu Nalamalagu Sindhaiya Ragha Nanney Thiruchitrambalam) The sacred notes of this pathigam are: ‘He, whose qualities are pleasing, the Lord of Kaveri thurai Pandikodumudi, destroys the karmic enmity of those who worship Him and removes the sorrow of those who remember and cry out to Him. He becomes enjoyment and bliss for those who praise Him, residing as the very embodiment of grace.’ Having thus worshipped at Thirupandikodumudi and many other holy places, Lord Thirugnanasambandha bowed and praised many peerless shrines such as Venjama Koodal. The Venjama Koodal mentioned here is the Thiruthalam of Karur Venjama Koodal, near Karur.

It is one of the seven praised temples in the Kongu region. However, the pathigam composed by Lord Thirugnanasambandha for this temple is not available to us due to our misfortune.

Thus, Lord Thirugnanasambandha, after bowing and worshipping at Karur Venjama Koodal, He goes to the Thiruanilai temple in Karur, also known as Karuvoor, worships Pasupatheeswarar, the Lord of Anilai, and sings a pathigam composed of rich Tamil words set to beautiful music. Sekkizhar describes this temple as the ‘Selvakaruvur Thiru Anilai Kovil,’ a temple rich in divine grace. It is also rich in material wealth. This refers to the Lord bestowing the power of creation upon Kamadhenu at this place. This history can be found in the Perur Puranam and the Karur Puranam. The Lord, known as Pasupatheeswarar, manifests his grace upon Kamadhenu and upon all living beings.

We have extensively discussed the Karur temple history in the Erypatha Nayanar Puranam. Lord Thirugnanasambandha reaches such a sacred Karuvoor Thiru Anilai temple and bestows a pathigam. That pathigam is the twenty-eighth pathigam of the Second Thirumurai, set to the tune of Indalam. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam (Thondalam Malaru Thoovi Undoor Aayathan Kandanaar Karuvooru AndarUl Eeyum Anbare Kandha Maarupolil) (Kazhi Gnana Santhan Cher Karuvooru Sonna Patthuvalla Sindhaiyil Thuyaraay Theervare Thiruchitrambalam). The pathigam’s summary note is ‘Karuvoor Anilaiyappar Arul Eeyum Anbar’ (The Lord of Anilai in Karuvoor, the giver of grace and love).

Thus, Lord Thirugnanasambandha, having praised and worshipped the Lord, concludes his Kongu region pilgrimage with the worship at Thirukaruvoor. Leaving that Kongu country, he will now visit the holy places along the Cauvery river.

Let us go on reflecting. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam by Sekkizhar Swamigal, Part Six Hundred Twenty-Three, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Lord Thirugnanasambandha, having worshipped at the Karur Thiru Anilai temple and concluded his pilgrimage in the Kongu region, is now about to visit the holy places along the banks of the Cauvery. The first such place he visits is Thiruvatpokki, also known as Rathnagiri. This place is called Manikkamalai (Jewel Mountain). It is the first of the holy places on the south bank of the Cauvery in the Chola country.

However, the pathigam composed by Lord Thirugnanasambandha for this place is not available to us. We have already discussed the history of Thiruvatpokki, or Rathnagiri, in the Puranam of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman.

Thus, Lord Thirugnanasambandha, having worshipped at Thiruvatpokki, visits many other places situated on long hills and in vast forests. He eagerly visits and worships all the temples where the Lord permanently resides.

Thus, the places Lord Thirugnanasambandha worshipped are between Thiruvatpokki, also known as Manikka Verpu, and Thiruparayathurai. Having thus visited, Lord Thirugnanasambandha proceeds to Thiruparayathurai. At Thiruparayathurai, he reaches the temple of the Lord with the third eye, and with a focused mind, he worships there and sings a flawless garland of Tamil words. Lord Pillaiyar, of the Kaundinya lineage, with tears flowing from his eyes, raised his hands above his head in anjali mudra (folded hands in reverence) and worshipped. Lord Thirugnanasambandha worships the Lord there with the intention of uniting with Him. Pillaiyar always desires to be one with the Lord.

With the intention that all living beings should unite with the Lord, he praises the Lord here with a united mind and bestows a pathigam. Thiruparayathurai is the third temple on the south bank of the Cauvery, surrounded by a type of tree called Parai. The Parai tree itself is the sacred tree of this place. We have discussed the history of Thiruparayathurai in the Puranam of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. Having worshipped at such a glorious holy place as Thiruparayathurai, Lord Thirugnanasambandha bestows a pathigam. That pathigam is the one hundred and thirty-fifth pathigam of the First Thirumurai, set to the beautiful tune of Megaraga Kurinji.

The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Neeru Servadho Meliyar Neeralai Koru Servadho Komaaru Serthalai Kaiyar Paraathurai Aaru See Anne Selvam Malviya Selvar Paraathurai Selva) (Melvan Gnana Sambandha Sentha Selva Matram Pazhum Paraththurai Adigal Neer Servadhor Meniyar Vedamodha Nindra Oruvanar Mudhaliya Thanmaigalal Ariyapadhubavar Avarai Nam Vaazhththuvome) The essence of this pathigam is that the Lord, who appears as one with water, who recites the Vedas, and is known by such divine qualities, should be praised by us.

Thus, having worshipped at Parayathurai and departed from that place, Lord Pillaiyar then visits many other temples such as Thiruvalandurai and Thiruchendurai, where deities come and worship, and arrives with joy. However, the pathigams for these temples, Thiruvalandurai and Thiruchendurai, are not available to us. Thiruvalandurai is located west of Thiruchirappalli, on the south bank of the Cauvery. The place currently known as Andanallur is Thiruvalandurai. The Shiva temple in this town is an ancient one. This temple was renovated during the time of the Chola kings, from Parantaka I to Rajaraja I, and later during the period of the later Pandyas.

There are inscriptions confirming this, in which this place is referred to as Anda Vananallur and Andu Vananallur, and the Shiva temple within it as Thiruvalandurai. The next place is Thiruchendurai. It is located west of Thiruchirappalli and very close to the east of Andanallur. Inscriptions from the time of Parantaka Chola I are found on the walls of this temple. There are also inscriptions from the later Cholas.

The Lord Shiva of this place is called Thiruchendurai Kattrali Parameswarar. The next holy place is called Poovalur. The place of Kamar (Manmatha) is called Poovalur. History states that Manmatha worshipped the Lord here.

Thus, it became Poovazhiyur and then, over time, Poovalur. There is a book called Poovalur Pattirruppathu Andhadhi, in which this place is referred to as Kamar Valampathi, Kamar Poompathi, Kamarur, and Kamarpathi.

Thus, having visited temples such as Thiruvalandurai, Lord Thirugnanasambandha reaches Thirukarkudi. Thirukarkudi is a place where the Lord resides on a mountain, shining like a golden shoot.

The Lord of Thirukarkudi’s great mountain is praised in Pillaiyar’s Thevaram. The Lord, who emerged spontaneously on the mountain, shines with divine grace and bestows abundant blessings with simplicity and purity. He is the divine Karpakam, as praised by Lord Arasu. This Thirukarkudi is a holy place that has the honor of being praised by all three Nayanars. Lord Pillaiyar speaks of the Lord’s natural grace. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman describes how the Lord is a vision for those who see him with their own eyes.

Sundaramoorthy Swamigal speaks of seeking refuge and asking the Lord to say ‘fear not’ to him, a devotee. We have discussed the history of Thirukarkudi in the Puranam of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. Lord Thirugnanasambandha, having come to such a glorious Thirukarkudi, bestows a pathigam. It is the forty-third pathigam of the First Thirumurai. This pathigam is set in the musical mode of Thakkaragam. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam (Vadanthigal men Moolai Palamathaga Mathithurai Thaarrigal Thunbham Mudum Em Kadanthavar Kadhaali Vani)

(Karkudi Maamalaiyare Kaamarvarpodu Soodum Karkudi Maamalaiyare Namaruvan Poogal Kali Nalanthigal Gnana Sambandhan Pamaru Senthamizh Maalai Paththivai Paadhavalla Pumalivanavar Porum Pumalivanavaro)

The Lord of Karkudi’s great mountain, who has transcended all sorrows and joys, lives with love among the Shaivites. With minds that bestow goodness, intertwined with the garland of names, he resides where devotees and Siddhas live with love, protecting them from all their troubles. These are the qualities described in this pathigam.

Thus, Lord Thirugnanasambandha, having worshipped at Thirukarkudi, proceeds to Thirumukkeeswaram, also known as Uraiyur. Thirumukkeeswaram, Uraiyur, is the fifth temple on the south bank of the Cauvery. It is currently very popularly known as Uraiyur. The sacred tree of the place is the Bilva tree, hence it is also called Vilvaranyam. A Chola king named Veeravaadiththan, while roaming, was defeated by a rooster, and the Lord revealed his abode, hence the place was named Kozhi (rooster). Utanga Muni, in a previous birth, was relieved of the sin of associating with a wife who had stolen Shiva’s property.

Kashyapa’s wife, Kadru, was relieved of the disease that came from her sin of deceiving her co-wife. Kadru’s son, Karkotakan, was relieved of his blindness, which he got due to his sin of deceiving his aunt, by worshipping the Lord of this place.

Here, Garuda received a boon from the Lord that whoever sees him or hears his voice would attain good fortune. A hunter, while stealing cattle, left an old cow that was obstructing him here, and as a result, he attained great blessing. When the Chola king Suravadithan wished to establish five Shiva lingams that he had brought from Nagaloka after marrying Nagaraja’s daughter Gandhimati, all of them merged with the Moolalingam here, making the Lord Panchavarneeswarar.

Therefore, the Lord’s name here is Panchavarneeswarar, the goddess is Gandhimathi, the sacred spring is Shiva Teertham, and the sacred tree is Vilvam. This holy place is located a short distance west of Thiruchirappalli. It is the place where the Lord appeared to Utanga Muni in five colors at five different times. It is the place where the Brahmin Vedashruti worshipped and was relieved of his ghostly form. This is the city where Pugalchola Nayanar was born and ruled. This is also one of the Madakkoils built by our Lord Kocchengat Chola Nayanar.

Lord Thirugnanasambandha, having come to this holy place, bestows a pathigam. It is the one hundred and twentieth pathigam of the Second Thirumurai, set to the musical mode of Sevvazhi. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchich Chantha ven Meeru Ena Oosi Vellam Sadai Vaiththa Kanthal Veeral Ezhaimodu Adi Karanam Ayndhu Kondangu Ariyee Meeyrindha (Aparavolo Vendhan Mukki Sarathu Adigal Seyyamalla Munmudi Mannar Mukki Sarathu Adi Selvar Aha Ninaim Padhi Seththi) (Sentha Nalla Vazh Ka Gnana Solla Vallam Umaiyodum Gangaiyodum Me Azhal Adal Mudhaliya Seygaihal Seyvanavellam Mookkeechcharathu Adigal Seyginra Meymaiye Mookkeechcharam Thennavanum) Kocchengat Chola, who was both a Southern and Chera king, built this elevated temple (Maadakkoil), and it is worthy of praise. This is the central theme of this pathigam.

We shall proceed with our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam by Sekkizhar Swamigal, Part Six Hundred Twenty-Four, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Lord Thirugnanasambandha, having bowed and worshipped at Thirumukkeeswaram, also known as Uraiyur, proceeds to the Thayu Manavar Swamy temple situated on the Thiruchirappalli hill. Thiruchirappalli is a place where waterfalls continuously cascade, bringing along precious gems and rubies.

There, he worships the brilliant light of the Lord residing on the hill. He bows at the sacred feet of the Lord who flayed the elephant and draped its skin, the one with the third eye, and filled with true joy and a cool heart, he bestows a glorious garland of Tamil words. The pathigam thus bestowed by Lord Thirugnanasambandha is the ninety-eighth pathigam of the First Thirumurai. It is the eighth pathigam, set to the tune of Kurinji. The pathigam begins with ‘Nandrudaiyanai Theeyathilanai’ (He who possesses goodness and no evil). The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam (Nandru Theeyathilai NagaiVallEru Ondrudaiyanai Umaioru Bhagam Udaiya Sentra Thiruvudaiya)

When I speak of the Lord of Sirapalli hill, my heart cools. In Kazhumoor, surrounded by the ocean and full of conches, where the Lord of Sirapalli resides, Thirugnanasambandha’s connection to Gowniyam flourishes.

The Lord of Sirapalli hill is blessed with purity that cannot be attained by others. He is our leader, our master. Who can truly comprehend his actions? There is no suffering for his devotees. Reaching his sacred abode is the key message of this pathigam. This pathigam begins with ‘Nandrudaiyanai Theeyathilanai’. ‘Nandrudaiyan’ and ‘Theeyathilan’ are the names of two sacred waters associated with the Thiruchirappalli temple.

These also signify the nature of the Lord and are named after sacred waters. The qualities of Lord Shiva are described in two ways by all Vedantic texts. One is His nature of being an eternal, boundless joy, which refers to the name ‘Nandrudaiyan’ and that sacred water. The other is the inherent absence of ‘mala’, which is the root cause of all suffering, and this is mentioned in this pathigam. The commentator in the Srikanta Bhashyam has explained that the qualities of Lord Shiva are described in two ways in all Vedantic texts. Both these qualities are here blessed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as ‘Nandrudaiyanai Theeyathilanai’.

Furthermore, ‘Theeyathilan’ signifies the eradication of karma, and ‘Nandrudaiyan’ denotes the attainment of Shiva. ‘Nandrudaiyan Theeyathilan’ thus represents two sacred waters and two names, indicating that the Lord removes the imperfections of beings and then bestows upon them the bliss of Shiva.

Therefore, ‘Theeyathilan’ refers to the divine Mother, and ‘Nandrudaiyan’ refers to the divine Father. This pathigam, with its subtle meanings, shines forth from its very essence. We have pondered upon the sacred history of Thiruchirappalli in the Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who praised and worshipped the Lord in such a Thiruchirappalli temple, then reached the temple of Thiru Anaikka, where the devas praised the Lord.

There, he worshipped the true essence of the Lord who appeared under the white Jamun tree, rose, and offered pathigams praising the Lord. Four-tusked white elephant. Thirugnanasambandha Pillai praises the Lord at Thiruanaikka by composing a pathigam, a garland of beautiful Tamil verses, that describes the elephant’s devotion to the Lord and the servitude of the glorious Kochchengat Chozha Nayanar. Lord Indra’s elephant, Airavata, has four tusks, as described here.

Here, the divine Mother molds the Lord with water, and the Lord appears as a mass of water. The poet Sekkizhar Peruman also describes this here.

Furthermore, the Lord’s devotee Kochchengat Chozha Nayanar. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises in his pathigam the devotion of the king who, having been a spider in a previous birth and worshipped the Lord, was then born as a king and built seventy-eight temples where elephants could not enter, serving the Lord. We have pondered all these historical accounts when discussing the Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam in the Thiruanaikka Sthala Puranam. The pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, incorporating all these divine events, is the twenty-third pathigam of the second Thirumurai. The first and concluding verses are as follows. Yazh kanava vizhavarum vennavalin meviam azhagayanum ayizhayazhavale vennaval amantoorai vedhiyanai vennaval amantoorai vedhiyanai kannar kamal kaliyar tham thalaivan pannodivai padiyathum valla vinnoavar eththa virumbuvare Thiruchitrambalam.

This pathigam, composed in the Akapporul style, speaks through the foster mother of a heroine whose mind is given to her lover, causing her distress. It aims to guide souls towards engaging in the great grace of the Lord, their divine spouse, and losing themselves in Him.

We shall continue our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 625, composed by Sekkizhar Swamigal, ‘Vambara Varivandu Serukkam’. When Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar arrived at Thiruanaikka, he composed a pathigam known as Koodachathukkam, which has a unique distinction. Sekkizhar Peruman sings about it as follows: ‘Naranan Nanmugan Kana Unmai Ven Naval Unmai Mahendiramum Seer Ani Needum Thirukkailai Selva Thiruvarur Meya Panpum Aranathu Utporul Ayinarai Yanaikkavin Kan Pugazhnthu Padi Yeraniyum Pozhil Suzhanda Shanbai Yenthalar Ellaiyil Inbamuttar’. This is a verse composed by Sekkizhar Swamigal.

Lord Shiva is the reality that neither Thirumal nor Brahma could perceive. Lord Shiva, the ultimate cause of dissolution, is the prime deity of the world, responsible for the appearance of Vishnu, the preserving deity, and Brahma, the creator deity, as elucidated in the first aphorism of Sivagnana Bodham. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reveals this nature of Lord Shiva, who is beyond the comprehension of both Vishnu and Brahma, in every verse of this pathigam. Sekkizhar Peruman refers to this as ‘Naranan Nanmugankana Unmai’. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises the greatness of Lord Shiva, who is present in four temples: Thirukkailai, Mahendiram, Thiruanaikka, and Thiruvarur, in this pathigam called Koodachathukkam. Thirukkailai is a temple where the glory of all other temples converges.

It is an eternal temple that will never perish. Thiruvarur is famous for the goddess of wealth, Thirumagal, having bestowed wealth there, and for the special presence of Selva Thyagesar.

Thus, it is known as Selva Thiruvarur. Mahendiram is the place where Lord Shiva revealed the Agamas, the true essence of reality. The Agamas reveal the nature of the three entities: Pati (Lord), Pasu (soul), and Pasam (bondage).

Therefore, Mahendiram is the place where Lord Shiva revealed these Agamas, which are the true essence of reality. It is said, ‘Mannu Mamalai Mahendiram Adanil Sonna Agamam Thottruvitthu Aruliyum’ (He revealed the Agamas on the great Mahendra mountain) and ‘Matravai Thammai Mahendirathu Iruntu Uttra Aimugangalal Panittharuliyum’ (He revealed them from Mahendiram through his five faces) in the Thiru. Some scholars say that Mahendiram, according to divine words, is a peak in the Himalayas. Others say that Mahendiram is a mountain in the southern sea that is now submerged. Researchers suggest in various ways that the Lord revealed the Agamas in both these places.

However, it is revealed through Thiruvichaippa that Mahendra mountain, where the Lord revealed the Agamas, is a mountain near Kailash. The next temple is Thiruanaikka. It is from this temple that this pathigam called Koodachathukkam was composed.

Therefore, in this pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman describes four temples: Thirukkailai, Thiruvarur, Mahendiram, and Thiruanaikka. In this pathigam, the Lord’s manifest grace in these four temples is praised.

Here, Thirukkailai represents Nodittan Malai, thus signifying cosmic dissolution. Thiruvarur is the temple where Putridam Konda Nadhar, Vanmeekanathar, resides, hence it represents the earth element and symbolizes creation. Thiruanaikka is where the Lord resides as a mass of clear water, thus symbolizing maintenance.

Therefore, Lord Shiva is enthroned here in the form of maintenance. This pathigam is thus composed as a ‘chathukkam’ (square) where these four temples converge, symbolizing the four states. This sacred. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed this pathigam while residing in the Thiruanaikka temple. Such a pathigam is the one hundred and ninth pathigam of the third Thirumurai, set to the tune of Pazhampanchuram. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam kana venbhu thiruk kannathuvelayan avar kaanbariya.

The next pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for Thiruanaikka temple is the pathigam that begins with ‘Venmathi’. It is the fifty-third pathigam of the third Thirumurai, set to the tune of Kausikam. The first and concluding verses of these pathigams are as follows. Enai kavilozhi devibhagam ayinan anaikavil annalai abayamaga vazhbar enai kaval vendu vakku ethum ethamilla ezhi uzhi vaiyathu uyirkal thottru vanono thaliyano kanakkila anaikavil annalai kali gnana. Sambandha karuthi sonnum elam. Having composed such pathigams, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the great one from Sirkazhi, attained limitless joy.

Singing itself is joy, and through such singing, Pillaiyar attained that supreme joy. Pillaiyar, by composing the special pathigam called Koodachathukkam in this temple, experiences such bliss. Koodachathukkam is a type of Chitrak. To sing about four temples within this one temple of Thiruanaikka is a special feature of Thiruanaikka.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having worshipped the Lord with folded hands, stayed for a few days at Thiruanaikka, enjoyed worshipping the Lord, received divine permission from Him, and then reached the temple of Thiruthavathurai. This Thiruthavathurai is currently known as Lalgudi. Upon reaching this temple, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worshipped Lord Shiva, stood up, and praised Him with a sweet Tamil garland of verses.

However, due to our lack of merit, that pathigam is not available to us.

Thus, having worshipped Lalgudi, also known as Thiruthavathurai, he visited nearby temples like Thirumangalam, Vadakarai, Manthurai, and others, praising all the temples where the Lord, bearing the bull banner, resides. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises all the temples, including Thiruppalthurai, Thiruverumbiyoor, and Mamalai, where the Lord resides. Thiruppalthurai is the fifty-ninth temple on the northern bank of the Cauvery. It is said that Markandeyar, distressed by the lack of milk for his Shiva puja, prayed to the Lord, and by His grace, milk flowed, hence the name Thiruppalthurai (Tirupatturai) for this temple. The deity is Thirumoolanathar, and the Goddess is Meganayagi Megalambikai. From Thiruverumbiyoor, travel a short distance north to Uthamasheri Palayam, and then another short distance north to reach this temple.

It can also be reached by going to Panaiyapuram on the way from Thiruanaikka to Kallanai and then from there to this temple. The Lord’s name is Adhimooleshwarar Adhimoolanathar, and the Goddess. Her name is Nithya Kalyani Megalambikai Meganayagi. The sacred water sources are the temple tank and the Kollidam River. This temple is currently known as Thiruppalthurai by the common people. It is believed that by worshipping the Goddess here with a melting heart, one can be blessed with progeny.

The main deity is a Swayambhu Lingam, a small murti. The assembly hall in the ardha mandapam, with its four pillars, is called Devasabai. In inscriptions, this temple is referred to as Thiruppatturai, a Brahmadeya of Uthamasivi Chathurvedi Mangala in Kollidam Thentkarai Nadu, and the Lord’s name as Thiruppatturai Mahadevar. An inscription from the time of Parantaka Chola I and Vikrama Chola indicates that Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s ashram was located near this temple. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who visited such a temple, composed a pathigam. It is the first Thirumurai.

The fifty-sixth pathigam, composed in the tune of Pazhanthakkaragam. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. Karkondrai kalantha moodiyanar seerar sinthai sela seitha paraviya paatru arar muthalvare bakthar manniya paathurai meya pathu nuru peyar anai bakthagnana. ‘Paathurai meviya paramar thampal en sinthai sela seythu en thanmai pokki ennai tham vannamakkikonar’ is the gist of this pathigam.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having worshipped Thiruppathurai and composed the pathigam, proceeds to Thiruverumbiyoor temple and composes a pathigam. However, the pathigam by Pillaiyar for Thiruverumbiyoor hill is not available. After receiving divine permission from the Lord at Thiruverumbiyoor, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reaches the Thirunedungalam temple.

Our reflections continue. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 626, composed by Sekkizhar Swamigal, ‘Vambara Varivandat Charkkam’. Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds to Thirunedungalam temple. Thirunedungalam is the eighth temple on the southern bank of the Cauvery, also known as Thirunattankulam. It is a sacred place where Vangiyachola worshipped and attained blessings.

This temple is praised in the Kshetra Venba of the eleventh Thirumurai. It can be reached by traveling a short distance on the road branching off from Thuvakkudi, on the road from Trichy to Thanjavur. The Lord’s name is Nithya Sundareshwarar Nedungalanathar. The Goddesses’ names are Mangalanayaki Oppilanayaki. The Bilva tree is the sacred tree. Agastya Theertham, Sundara.

Theertham are the sacred waters. The place where the Goddess, while performing penance, became frightened when the Lord appeared in disguise and caught her hand, and then she ran and hid, is called Olimathisollai. The bronze horse here has a peculiar structure. All the themes of the songs in the Nedungala pathigam are depicted as stucco sculptures on the front and back of the Rajagopuram. Two Vimanas are situated above the Moolasthanam, presenting a novel appearance. The form of Dakshinamurthy in this temple is marvelous.

He appears as Yoga Dakshinamurthy, seated in the Siddhasana pose, holding a deer and an axe in his upper hands, and displaying the Chin Mudra and a sacred ash casket in his lower hands, with the Yogapatta encircling his left leg. This temple is mentioned in inscriptions as Pandik. It is mentioned as Thirunedungalam in Ulasini Valanattu Vadavir Nadu, and the Lord’s name is Nedungalathu Mahadevar. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having arrived at Thirunedungalam, lovingly praised the Lord, Adimurthi, of this temple and composed a melodious pathigam, which is a humble prayer to the Lord. This pathigam is a supplication, asking the Lord to remove all sorrows that prevent one’s mind from going to Him with love and to shower grace. In this pathigam, beginning with ‘Kolgaiyinal Uyarntha Nirai Udayar Idargalaiyai’, in each verse, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman supplicates, saying ‘Idargalaiyai Nedungala Meyavane’ (Remove my sorrows, O Lord of Nedungalam).

This is for the devotees. It is a plea made by Pillaiyar out of compassion. Many devotees regularly recite this pathigam and benefit from it. Such a pathigam is the fifty-second pathigam of the first Thirumurai, set to the tune of Pazhanthakkaragam. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. Maravoodu tholodya vasadai pirai pinne yendru.

Ung needaya kutram orai kolgaiyile niraiyudaya eedalkalai nedungalam neyaveeda vallavaachadayaan neya.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having composed the pathigam, departed from Thirunedungalam and reached the temple of Thiruniyamam. This is a temple on the southern bank of the Cauvery. Pillaiyar, who never deviates from the disciplined path he has embraced, constantly praises the Lord. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having set an example for the world by visiting and worshipping temples and the sacred places in between, arrived at Thiruniyamam and composed a pathigam praising the Lord there. He then visited temples like Kadaiyakudi and subsequently arrived at Thirukkattupalli, also known as Melai Thirukkattupalli. Upon arriving at Thirukkattupalli, he approached the temple of the Lord with matted hair, circumambulated the courtyard, worshipped, fell prostrate, rose, and worshipped the Lord’s feet adorned with strong anklets.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was the child who was fed divine milk by the Lord.

Therefore, with a heart full of love, like a cow approaching its calf, he stood before the Lord with a luminous eye and praised Him, embracing the divine dance performed by the Lord within his mind, and composed the pathigam beginning with ‘Vaaru Mannum Mulai’. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed this pathigam. It is understood from the verses composed by Sekkizhar Peruman that this pathigam is endowed with the inner meaning of the greatness of the Lord’s divine dance. ‘Vaaru Mannum Mulai’ is the opening part of the pathigam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman remembers the Lord who appeared as the partner of the Goddess and bestowed grace upon him. In this pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises the Lord by referring to Him as the one who shares a part of the Goddess, the one who is the Lord of the Goddess, and the one who is a part of Uma. This pathigam is the twenty-ninth pathigam of the third Thirumurai.

It is set to the tune of Ollippann. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. Mangaiyor panginan ooru mannum unbathum ven thalaima suzhntha kattuppalli neeru mannarme porubhoonal pudaiya. Puravanan nagaru mannan arumarai avai valligul sambandhan sol karumani midattrinan karuthu kattuppalli paraviya tamil sollum.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having composed the pathigam, departed from Melai Thirukkattuppalli after receiving divine permission from the Lord and proceeded to the Thirualampozhil temple. He worships the Lord. The Thevara pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for this Thirualampozhil temple is not available to us. There is a traditional story passed down through generations about a miraculous event performed by the revered Pillaiyar at this temple. We have seen this when discussing the Thirualampozhil Sthala Puranam in the Thirunavukkarasu Peruman Puranam.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having worshipped Thirualampozhil, then proceeded to Thiruppunthuruthi temple, which is located on the rich banks of the Cauvery. Thiruppunthuruthi is the eleventh temple on the southern bank of the Cauvery. It is a sacred place where Indra, Kashyapa, and Chola kings worshipped and attained blessings. It is one of the Sapthasthana temples, including Thiruvaiyaru.

Here, the sacred bull statues moved aside for the revered Pillaiyar to worship from outside the gopuram. It is recorded in the temple’s history that the Rishabas moved aside. We have pondered upon the history of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, who resided for a long time in an ashram in this temple and composed many pathigams, and the subsequent meeting of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman and Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, in the Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam. We have also considered the sacred history of the meeting between Thirunavukkarasu Peruman and Thirugnanasambandha Peruman in the Thirugnana Peruman Puranam.

The Lord of this temple is Poyyiliar Adhi Purana Pushpavanathar, and the Goddess is Azhagarntha Nayaki. It is located a short distance west of Thirukkandiyur, on the road from Thanjavur to Thiruvaiyaru. The pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for this temple is not available to us.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having worshipped Thiruppunthuruthi, proceeded to worship all the nearby temples like Thirunaitthanam.

Then, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reached the temple of Veerattaneswarar in Thirukkandiyur. When Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrived at Thirukkandiyur, surrounded by throngs of devotees who had gathered from many temples out of overflowing love, he cast his divine gaze upon them. Standing before the Lord, he composed a pathigam in a manner that seemed to question the devotees, as if asking them to recount the glories of the Lord, making them the primary audience. Praising the Lord by making the devotees the primary audience and asking them about His glories is one of the ways to sing about the Lord. In Pillaiyar’s Thevarams, one can observe various ways of praising the Lord, such as addressing the Lord directly, addressing the world, or addressing specific individuals. Among these, the method seen here is a very excellent one.

He begins this pathigam with ‘Vinaivenan Ariyamaiyil’ (I asked out of ignorance). Pillaiyar emphasizes within the pathigam the method of delighting in hearing about the Lord’s power from the devotees. This is a unique feature of this pathigam.

Therefore, in this pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman portrays the greatness of the devotees and the greatness of the Lord as intertwined. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman blesses. We can see that the themes and ideas of the pathigam are arranged in such a way that he says, ‘I ask you out of ignorance; please tell me the answer. Tell me the truth. You are devotees, so please answer me. You are old devotees, so please reveal to me the Lord’s greatness and attributes.’ Thus, in this pathigam, which begins with ‘Vinaivenan’, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composes a Thirukkadai Kappu (concluding verse).

In it, he praises the Lord by recounting the divine deeds of Lord Shiva, who is difficult to comprehend, and by expressing his delight in hearing about them from the devotees. He, Pillaiyar, is a descendant of the Kowniyam clan from Sirkazhi. Such a pathigam is a question-and-answer pathigam, where he joyfully listens to the devotees. This is. It is the thirty-eighth pathigam of the third Thirumurai, set to the tune of Kollippann. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam.

Veenan ariyamaiyil urai seynal Kaveri karai meya kambiyoor veerattan tamaranar andam azhathan vananil vazhkai kondadi padi ivvai bali theerndha the. Karuthanai suzhum kandiyur veeratturai kalvanai thirumadiyurai thiruthigal kali gnanasambandan seppiya senthagum palarkalaga.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed this pathigam. We have reflected on the history of Thirukkandiyur temple in the Thirunavukkarasu Peruman Puranam.

Thus, Thirukkandiyur. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having worshipped and received divine permission from the Lord, then proceeded to Thiruchotruthurai.

We shall proceed with our reflections. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 627, composed by Sekkizhar Swamigal, ‘Vambara Varivandu Sarkkam’. Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds to Thiruchotruthurai temple. We have pondered upon the Sthala Puranam of Thiruchotruthurai in the Thirunavukkarasu Peruman Puranam. He approached the Thiruchotruthurai temple, composing a unique and beautiful garland of Tamil verses with focused devotion, with the intention of reaching Appar’s Thiruchotruthurai.

He arrived before the temple. The pathigam composed by Pillaiyar is the twenty-eighth pathigam of the first Thirumurai, set to the tune of Thakkaragam. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. Seppa nenje nerikol chitrinpan tuppanennatharulley thunaiyaga. Oppar Oppar Peruman Oli Vennattrar Soottrathurai Sendraivome. Anthan Soottrathuraiyam Adhiyai Sinthai Seymin Adiyeer Ayineer Santhampravu Gnanasambandan Vanthavaray Punaitthal Vazhipadey.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman circumambulated and worshipped the ancient and grand temple of Thiruchotruthurai, which houses the divine Lord. He bowed with immense love to the sacred feet of the Lord who consumed poison to alleviate the suffering of the devas. Having thus worshipped and praised the Lord, he stood up and sang a melodious Tamil pathigam, replete with sweet musical notes. He then resided in that sacred place for some time, received divine permission from the Lord, and accompanied by devotees, proceeded to the glorious Thiruvethikudi temple. Thiruvethikudi temple is renowned for being the place where the Lord, whose feet are worshipped by all, resides, as praised by Pillaiyar in his pathigam.

It is special as the place where the Lord, worshipped by everyone, dwells. In Appar Swamigal’s Thevaram verses, the Lord of this temple is referred to as ‘Ara Amuthan’ (the insatiable nectar). Thiruvethikudi temple also holds the distinction of being worshipped by the Vedas.

Hence, it is known as ‘Vedavethiyar Vethikudi’, a place special for its Vedic scholars. Having reached the temple of the Lord, where Vedic scholars reside and chant the Vedas, he praised and worshipped the auspicious lotus feet, stood up, and recited a pathigam in Tamil, whose music surpasses even the Vedas. The Lord’s feet are auspicious lotus feet. Auspiciousness here means the state of existing and flourishing by removing the bonds of the soul and bestowing Shiva’s grace. To shine means to embody that very nature. Divine grace is respectfully referred to as sacred feet.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed a pathigam praising such glorious lotus feet. It is noteworthy that Pillaiyar’s Thevarams, referred to as Tamil Vedas, surpass the Vedas in terms of music and meaning. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed a pathigam whose music transcends the Vedas. ‘Music transcending the Vedas’ implies music that is seven-noted, the source of all arts, and even greater than the Vedas. It is believed that the tune Sadari is equivalent to the high music of the Vedas. In the Thiruvilaiyadal Puranam. In the Thiruvilaiyadal story of selling firewood, the Vedic scholar sang in the Sadari tune.

Similarly, Sekkizhar Peruman’s verses indicate that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed a pathigam whose music, set to the Sadari tune, surpasses even the Vedas. Such a pathigam is the Thiruvethikudi pathigam, the seventy-eighth pathigam of the third Thirumurai, set to the Sadari tune. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows. Iruntha vedama vazhai veerai nara veezhai vazhai maduvil veru piriyathu velai ada vazha maarum vaya vethi koodiya kanthamali than pozhil nan madam edai kalivazha gnanam unarasa vanthanmali senthamizhin malai kodu vethi koodi aathi kazhale. Those who are capable of meditating are good people. If you attain this, that world is for you.

If you destroy evil, that is for sure. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman thus composed the pathigam in Thiruvethikudi. Thiruvethikudi is the fourteenth temple on the southern bank of the Cauvery, a place worshipped by the Vedas, Vedic scholars, and Vishnu. We have pondered upon the Sthala Puranam of this temple in the Thirunavukkarasu Peruman Puranam. Having worshipped the Lord in Thiruvedikudi and received His gracious farewell, Thirugnanasambandhar proceeds to the holy site called Thiruvenni.

There, upon reaching the Lord’s temple, with abundant love welling up from within, he praises the Lord’s feet and sings a pathigam (decade of verses) that overflows with praise. This place, Thiruvenni, is located a long distance southeast from Thiruvedikudi, with some other holy sites in between. Thiruvenni is the 102nd temple on the south bank of the Cauvery River. It is also known as Kovilvenni and Ikshupuri. ‘Ikshu’ means sugarcane. The Lord’s lingam, being a self-manifested form, exhibits characteristics resembling sugarcane pulp.

Hence, the Lord’s names are Venninathar and Vennikkarumbar. The name of the Goddess is Azhagiyanayaki / Soundaryanayaki. This holy site is also called Thiruvenniyur and Kovilvenni. It is located on the Thanjavur-Thiruvarur road, and is presently known as Kovilvenni. Surya Theertham and Chandra Theertham are the sacred waters here. The pathigam (decade of verses) composed by Thirugnanasambandhar upon arriving at this holy site of Thiruvenniyur is the 14th pathigam of the Second Thirumurai, set to the Indalam tune.

The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Uḍai thalaiyil veṇṇiyai alla. Uḷkāthaṉathumēvārūm sambanthaṉ thiruvārūm thigazh tharu veṇṇiyamandhāṉē. Those who worship the Lord of Veṇṇi, who is adorned with garlands, will have their karma cease. My heart will not contemplate anything else besides them. This is the central theme of this pathigam. This village, Veṇṇiyur, is mentioned in Sangam Tamil literature such as Akanaṉūṟu and Puranaṉūṟu.

“Ārkaḷiṉaraviṉ Veṇṇivāyil” in Akanaṉūṟu and “Kalikoḷ Yāṉar”. “Veṇṇippuṟanthalai” in Puranaṉūṟu, and “Veṇṇi thākkiya Karikālvaḷavaṉ” in Poruṇarāṟṟuppaṭai, demonstrate how this site is spoken of in ancient Tamil texts. Veṇṇikuyaththiyār, a female Sangam poet from the potter community, was also from this village. All these are notes from Sri N. Sivaprakasa Gurukkaḷaiyā. This holy site is a long distance southeast from Thiruvedikudi, with many holy sites in between.

After worshipping this, Thirugnanasambandhar proceeds to Thiruchakkarappalli, which is located far to the northwest and north of Thiruvedikudi, having worshipped many nearby temples.

Similarly, we will now examine the accounts of worship at Karukavur, Avalivanallur, Parutiniyamam, and Poovanur, which are close to Veṇṇi. Having thus worshipped Thiruvenniyur, Thirugnanasambandhar proceeds to Thiruchakkarappalli. Thirugnanasambandhar proceeds to Thiruchakkarappalli, traversing through fertile lands filled with dense groves and ponds, so abundant with lotus stems that they resemble a thorn-bush. Thiruchakkarappalli is the place where Shankara, who destroyed Daksha’s loveless yagna, resides.

There, the young Lord, leader of Tamil literature and music, arrives. Entering the temple of the Lord residing in Thiruchakkarappalli, with devotion, he worships the Lord’s feet, which resemble adorned flowers. He then sings a Tamil pathigam (decade of verses) filled with powerful words, encompassing the meanings of the four Vedas, praising the Lord whose waist is adorned with garlands of bones and conch beads, expressing intense love for Him. Thirugnanasambandhar then sings such a pathigam (decade of verses), which is the 37th pathigam of the Third Thirumurai, set to the Kolli tune. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam Paḍainār thōlarai. Kaṇṇuthal avanaḍi kazhumala senthamē.

The theme of this pathigam is that the Lord resides in Chakkarappalli. Thiruchakkarappalli is the seventeenth temple on the south bank of the Cauvery. The reason for this name is that the Chakravaka bird worshipped here. Because it was worshipped, this place received this name. Jayanta and other deities worshipped the Lord here and received blessings.

This is one of the seven sites highly praised in Sivarahasyam, Brahmakaivartha Puranam, and Linga Puranam. The seven holy sites thus sung are Thiruchakkarappalli, Arimangai, Sulamangai, Nandimangai, Pasupathimangai, Thazhaimangai, and Pullamangai. These are revered as Sapta Mangala Sthalams because they were worshipped by the seven Matrikas respectively: Brahmi, Mahesvari, Kaumari, Vaishnavi, Varahi, Mahesvari, and Chamundi. The temple history states that Nadasarma, along with his wife Anavithyadevi, regularly bathed in Devagatha Theertham, worshipped these seven sites, and received blessings. The reason for the Lord Vishnu worshipping and receiving the Chakra is also attributed to the name of this holy site. This is also the reason for the name of the holy site.

The Lord’s name is Chakravageeswarar, and the Goddess’s name is Devanayaki. The Cauvery Theertham and Kakkatheertham are the sacred waters. It is located in Ayyampettai on the Thanjavur-Kumbakonam road. On the temple wall, there is a depiction of the Chakravaka bird worshipping the Lord. The Goddess of this temple, named Devayaki, appeared as a young girl to Nadasarma and Anavithya, who had come on a pilgrimage from Kashi. The ‘Pedhai’ stage is the first of the seven stages of a woman’s life, and it refers to the form of a young girl.

The Goddess has her right foot slightly forward, indicating her readiness to quickly come to the aid of her devotees. During the Sankatahara Chathurthi in the month of Panguni, one can witness the miraculous sight of the sun worshipping these two deities. The eastern side of the sanctum sanctorum is built of black stone, and the western side vimana is made of stucco. Opposite the Goddess’s shrine, there is a Kungiliyam Kundam, which is believed to bestow mangalya (marital) benefits upon women and ward off the fear of Yama. In inscriptions, this village is referred to as Rajendra Chola Chathurvedimangalam, part of Vilannadu, in Kulothunga Chola Valanadu. On the Chithirai star day in the month of Panguni, Chakravageeswarar and Vedanayaki are carried in a flower palanquin from Chakkarappalli temple, followed by Nadasarma and Anavithyai in a vetiver palanquin.

These palanquins depart and return after visiting the other six sites among the Sapta Mangalas. Hence, this is known as the Sapthasthanam Palanquin Festival. These are the special features of the Thiruchakkarappalli holy site.

Our contemplation continues. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. We contemplated the pathigam (decade of verses) composed by Thirugnanasambandhar at the holy site of Thiruchakkarappalli, as described in Periya Puranam, Part 628, by Sekkizhar Swamigal, under the section ‘Vamparaa Varivandu Cherkkum Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam’. Thiruchakkarappalli was previously dilapidated and in a chaotic state due to Muslim invasions.

Later, Sri-la-Sri Ambalavana Desika Maha Sannidhanam of Thiruvavaduthurai, about a hundred years ago, restored and enhanced its glory. However, the same threats are starting to re-emerge at this site. It is the duty of the Saivite world to protect such magnificent holy sites from such foreign religions. Having worshipped the Lord in Thiruchakkarappalli and received His gracious farewell, Thirugnanasambandhar departs from the Lord’s Thiruchakkarappalli. He proceeds along the fields where beautiful water flows, reaching the holy site of Thiruppuḷḷamaṅgai, and then the temple known as Thiru Ālandurai. Puḷḷamaṅgai is the name of this holy site, and Ālandurai is the name of the temple.

With devoted love, Thirugnanasambandhar praises the golden feet of the Lord, who holds a deer in His hand and resides in the established temple, composing a pathigam (decade of verses) in Tamil. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Paraman piraman thōlum thīraḷ avar vāzhththaru pozhil sūzh Puḷamaṅgai Kālandīraḷ aṟacchāṭiya kaṭavuḷ iḍam karuvil Ālandūrai thozhuvār thammai aḍaiyā viṉai thāṉē Ponthin īḍai thēṉūriya pozhil sūzh Puḷamaṅgai. antha varu Ālandūrai yānai kandham mali kamal Kāzhiyuḷ kalaiñāṉa Santhan santham mali pāḍal Chōzhi pāḍaththavam āmē. Ēṟṟampaḷam Puḷamaṅgai Ālandurai iṟaivar amudhar pulai kalai vār iḷañāyiṟṟiṉ sōthi aṉṉār avaiyai meyththannōrum viṉai thīrvagai thozhumiṉ avarathu iḍam Ālandurai athuvē. This is the central theme of this pathigam. This holy site, Thiruppuḷḷamaṅgai Thiru Ālandurai, is the sixteenth temple on the south bank of the Cauvery. It is customary for this place to bear this name because the Lord graciously consumed poison here. Puḷḷamaṅgai is the name of the site, and Ālandurai is the name of the temple; hence, it is customary to refer to them together, as we can see in the pathigam.

We have seen that there is another site called Anbil Ālandurai; therefore, to differentiate, it is called Thiruppuḷḷamaṅgai Thiru Ālandurai. This site is also known as Veḷḷāḷa Pasupathi Koyil. In accordance with Puḷḷamaṅgai being the site where Brahma worshipped, eagles are permanently settled on the gopuram (temple tower) of this site. ‘Puḷ’ means eagle. Within this pathigam, it states, ‘Ponthin iḍai thēṉūriya pozhil sūzh’ (groves surrounded by honey flowing from hollows), and even today, beehives can be found in the hollows throughout this site. This is one of the Sapthasthanam sites, with Thiruchakkarappalli as the first. The Lord’s name is Alanthurainathar, and the Goddess’s name is Alliyankothai.

The Lord is also known as Brahmapureeswarar, Pasupatheeswarar, and Pasupathinathar. The sacred pond in front of the temple and the Cauvery River serve as theerthams. This village is now known as Pasupathi Koyil. The temple is situated on the bank of the Kudamurutti River. This is a water-front temple, distinguished by the Banyan tree as its sthalavruksham. This is a temple where Chamundi, one of the Saptha Mathas, worshipped.

It is believed that devotees who worship here are relieved from Naga Dosham, as Chamundi Devi performed Shiva Puja here with the eight Nagas. The temple history states that Jagadhambika also performed penance to receive the vision of Naga Abarana, and the Lord manifested in that form. The garbhagriha, which has a moat-like structure, has a black stone construction at the base and a stucco structure above. Beneath the vimana, the 108 dance poses of Shiva Puranam and scenes from Ramayana are exquisitely sculpted. In this temple, there is a Nandi in the center of the Navagrahas. The Mahishasuramardini form of Durga in this temple is unique.

Standing on a buffalo head under a black stone umbrella, holding weapons such as a conch, discus, sword, bow, mace, trident, and goad, with a deer and a lion on either side, and two warriors appearing to offer their severed heads and ripped thighs as blood sacrifice, Durga Ambika appears in a Thribangi posture, holding a bow in one hand and making a fearless gesture with her ring finger folded, with a quiver visible behind her back. This posture is unique. The Durgas in Thiru Nagapattinam, Thiru Pullamangai, and Thirunellikka temples. It is said that the Durgas in Paṭṭeeswaram and Thiruppuḷḷamaṅgai were sculpted by the same artisan, and all three are very powerful. The sculptures of the Bhoothaganas above the Ardha Mandapa, and the deities Subrahmanya, Rishabharoodar, and Ardhanareeswarar in the Vimana are exquisitely beautiful and unparalleled. In inscriptions, this temple is referred to as Alandurai Mahadevar Temple.

It stands as an example of Chola period sculpture. These are the special features of the Thiruppuḷḷamaṅgai Alandurai holy site. Having thus worshipped Thiruppuḷḷamaṅgai, Thirugnanasambandhar arrives at the holy site of Thiruchchelur, where the Lord resides, and worships Him. Thiruchchelur is one of the Thevara Vaippu Thalangal (places mentioned in Thevaram). We do not have a pathigam (decade of verses) composed by the young Lord from here. It is located a short distance south of Thiruppuḷḷamaṅgai Thiru Alandurai.

After worshipping Thiruchchelur, Thirugnanasambandhar proceeds to Thiruppalathurai. There, he sings a pathigam (decade of verses).

However, the pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandhar for this site is not available to us. We have already contemplated the special features of Thiruppalathurai in the Puranam of Thirunavukkarasar. The young Lord, chief of Sirkazhi, departs from Thiruppalathurai and proceeds to the holy site of Thirunallur. In Thirunallur, surrounded by beautiful fields, the people of Thirunallur, along with women, welcome the young Lord. The great sage of Sirkazhi, the young Lord, majestically arrived in a lustrous, pearl-adorned palanquin. Descending from the pearl palanquin, with the assembly of Vedic scholars going ahead and the devotees and attendants following him, Thirugnanasambandhar worshipped the gopuram (temple tower) of the Lord in Thirunallur and entered the temple.

Thirugnanasambandhar worshipped the gopuram, recognizing it as Shiva in its manifest form, before entering the temple. The rule and tradition of temple darshan, where one worships the gopuram first, is exemplified here by Thirugnanasambandhar. Just as the Sivagnanabodham, in its twelfth sutra, states that the temple itself should be worshipped as a fortress, the young Lord, considering the temple as Shiva Himself, worshipped it and entered. As the young Lord circumambulated the temple, which radiated light like the great Mount Kailash, tears of joy flowed profusely, drenching his entire body. He then ascended the multi-storied temple and worshipped the Lord, standing before Him and offering praise. Thirugnanasambandhar then sings a pathigam (decade of verses) full of praises before the Lord.

This pathigam, which begins with “Vaṇḍiriya,” is the Thirunallur pathigam (decade of verses), the 83rd pathigam of the Third Thirumurai, set to the Sadhari tune. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Koṇḍa paramanpathiya. Varai mēlaruvi muththam thiṇḍiraikaḷ mōtha viri pōthu kamaṭum thiru nallūrē thiraikaḷ karaiyum vaṟu poṉṉi nilavum thiru nallūr mēsutharu pāṇiyai nalandhirikaḷ sey thōṇipur nāthaṉ purai sey thamizh ñāṉa sambandhaṉ isai mālai mozhivār pōy virai sey. The theme of this pathigam is that Thirunallur is the place where the Lord pervades, so that all beings of the world may receive His great grace.

Thus, he offers a pathigam filled with words praising the Lord. Forgetting himself, he melts with the Lord’s presence within him. Overwhelmed with love, he comes out of the temple, with his mind melting, and lovingly resides in that holy place, Thirunallur, where the Lord pervades through the greatness of His great grace, so that all beings may receive His great grace. It is a steadfast place where people from all over the world come to receive great grace.
