The Thevara sacred sayings state that Shiva resides in Thirunallur, and that both Kailash in the north and Thirunallur in the south are His dwelling places. This is the holy site where Amarnithi Nayanar performed service and received grace.

This is the holy site where Thirunavukkarasar was granted initiation at the sacred feet by the Lord. We have contemplated the grace bestowed by the Lord upon Thirunavukkarasar in the Puranam of Thirunavukkarasar.

Furthermore, we have contemplated the special features of Thirunallur in the Puranam of Amarnithi Nayanar. Due to such great significance, Thirugnanasambandhar resided in this place for a few days. He sang many pathigams (decades of verses) with sweet melodies. Thirugnanasambandhar lovingly resided there, worshipped by all the Vedic scholars present in that holy site.

Thereafter, having received the grace of the Lord who performs the five-fold cosmic dance in Thirunallur, the young Lord departed from that grace-filled holy site and proceeded to Thirukkarugavur, worshipping all the nearby sites along the way. In Thirukkarugavur, a place fragrant with jasmine vines spreading over pavilions, the young Lord worshipped the feet of the Lord who granted the great Vedas with their melodies. The young Lord joyfully sang a rich Tamil pathigam (decade of verses) expressing the idea that the eternal Lord’s color is like that of fire. This holy site is referred to by Sekkizhar as a place full of jasmine-covered pavilions, as the jasmine plant is the sthalavruksham here. The period when the young Lord visited this place is indicated as the early spring, when jasmine flowers begin to bloom. The young Lord worshipped the feet of the Lord who granted the great Vedas, which are infinite in their melodies (Svaras), known as Chandas.

He then sang a pathigam (decade of verses) with the idea that the Lord’s color is like that of fire, such that it cleansed the minds of those who heard it and brought them joy. That pathigam, beginning with “Muththilaṅgum,” is the 46th pathigam of the Third Thirumurai, set to the Kaushika tune. The Thirukkarugavur pathigam (decade of verses). The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Muththilaṅgu muṟuvaḷ puñjavē maththiyāṉai maṟukūṟi vāṅkiya kaththai pōththa kaṭavuḷ Karugāpūriyam aththarvaṇṇam mazhaḷum azhaḷ vaṇṇamē kalavai uḷavum Karugāvū nilavu pāḍal kūḍa nīḷ kazhaḷ kuḷavu ñāṉa sambandhaṉ senthamuḷ solavallār varu tholviṉai thīrumē.

We have contemplated the glory of Thirukkarugavur in the Puranam of Thirunavukkarasar.

Thus, having sung the melodious pathigam (decade of verses) and worshipped Thirukkarugavur, Thirugnanasambandhar, the eloquent orator of Tamil, then worshipped many nearby sites. He then reaches Thiru Avalivanallur. Entering the temple of the Lord, who joyfully resides in that steadfast place, worshipped by even the celestials, the young Lord composes a pathigam that reveals the name ‘Thambarisudaiyar’ (One who possesses His own nature). ‘Thambarisudaimai’ means naturally being free from attachments, possessing infinite power, and having eight such qualities as His own. In this place, this name is specifically given to the Lord. Thirugnanasambandhar then proceeds to such a holy site as Thiru Avalivanallur.

Let us go on contemplating. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 629, by Sekkizhar Swamigal, ‘Vamparaa Varivandu Sarukkam’, ‘Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam’. Thirugnanasambandhar proceeds to the holy site of Thiru Avalivanallur. Thiru Avalivanallur is the 100th temple on the south bank of the Cauvery. In this place, the Lord’s name is Thamparisudaiyar / Sakshinathar, and the Goddess’s name is Soundaryavalli. The Theertham (sacred water) is Chandra Pushkarani, and the Pāthiri tree is the sthalavruksham.

The temple history of how this place came to be named ‘Aval Ival Nallur’ (She is the good one) is as follows: Of the two daughters of a priest who worshipped the Lord here, the husband of the elder daughter went on a pilgrimage. After he left, his wife’s form and color changed due to smallpox, and she lost her eyesight. Her younger sister reached marriageable age. The husband of the elder daughter, returning from pilgrimage, claimed that the younger of the two was his wife, and that he was being deceived by the elder, who had changed in form, color, and lost her eyesight due to smallpox.

The Lord appeared and gave evidence, showing that ‘this is your wife’. For this reason, the place was named ‘Aval Ival Nallur’.

The Lord then had the woman bathe in the sacred water, and she regained all her lost health. This is depicted on the backside of the Thirumoolattanar image. The name ‘Thamparisudaiyar’ is a specific reference in the pathigam. This place is indicated by Thirunavukkarasar’s pathigam as being associated with the grace bestowed upon Ravana. Thiruirumpoolai, which is a flower forest. This place, which is a Padiri forest, and Thiruarathai Perumbalai, which is a Sami forest, and Thirukollamboodur, which is a Vilva forest, are all located very uniquely, directly from west to east, close to each other.

This is a site worshipped by Varaha and Kashyapa. There are three Theerthams named after the sun, moon, and fire. It is said that visiting Thirukkarugavur, which is a jasmine forest, during Ushath Kalam (pre-dawn), Avalivanallur, which is a Padiri forest, during Kalasandhi (morning), Harithwaramangalam, which is a Vanni forest, during Uchchikkalam (noon), Alangodi Thiruirumpoolai, which is a flower forest, during Sayarakshai (evening), and Thirukollamboodur during Ardhajama (midnight) bestows great benefits.

Therefore, people have a tradition of visiting all five of these in a single day. These sites are known as Pancharanya Sthalams. Thirugnanasambandhar, who arrived at this site, composed a pathigam (decade of verses). It is the 82nd pathigam of the Third Thirumurai, which begins with “Koomperiya,” set to the Sadhari tune. In the first verse of this pathigam, the phrase “Thamparisinoḍu suḍunīru tharavandhu iḍavam ēṟi” indicates that the Lord’s name here is Thamparisudaiyar. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Kambariya sempoṉṉu kalvarai.

Perumān urai vathivaṉalūrē Āṉamozhiyāṉa thiraḷ ōr paravum Avazhivaṉalūrmēl pōṉamozhi naṉmozhikaḷ āya pugazh Thōṇipur ūraṉ Thōṇipur ūraṉ ñāṉamozhimālai pala nāḍu pugazh Ñāṉa sambandhaṉ pandhaṉ thāmē mozhi mālai pūkazh vār thuyarkaḷ thīyathiḻthē Thiruchitrambalam. Having thus worshipped Thiru Avalivanallur, Thirugnanasambandhar. then departs from there and reaches the holy site of Thirupparithiniyamam.

The Lord’s name is Paruthiyappar, and the Goddess’s name is Mangalanayaki. The Theertham (sacred water) is Surya Theertham.

This is one of the seven sites worshipped by the Sun God. The other sites are Thirukandiyur, Vedikudi, Kudandai Keezhkottam, Thelichery, Puravarpanankottur, and Nellika. This site also has the name Arasavanam. Thirugnanasambandhar, who arrived here, composed a pathigam (decade of verses). It is the 104th pathigam of the Third Thirumurai, set to the Pazhampanjuram tune. This pathigam (decade of verses).

The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam Veṇ koṇḍa thūmathi sūḍi nīḍu vithi thāḻa peṇ koṇḍa mārpiḻ veṇṇīr pūsi pēṇār pali thērkkum iḍam pōlum paṇ koṇḍam pāḍiyāḍum parithīṉiya. Mērē Kāndhaḷ parithīṉiya madhu thaiyalōrvāgam amarndhavaṉai thamizh ñāṉa sambandhaṉ poyyili mālai puṉaintha paththum aravi pugazhndhēththa aiyuṟavillai piṟappaṟuththaḷ avalam aḍaiyavē sutrampanam. Having thus worshipped Thirupparithiniyamam, Thirugnanasambandhar then reaches the Lord’s holy site of Thiruppoovanur. The pathigam (decade of verses) composed by Thirugnanasambandhar at Thiruppoovanur is not available to us. Thiruppoovanur is the 103rd temple on the south bank of the Cauvery. It is known as Pushpavanamm.

Sukha Rishi worshipped here. The Lord’s name is Pushpavanathar / Chathuranga Vallabeswarar, and the Goddess’s name is Karpagavalli / Rajarajeswari. At the ancient holy site, with a desire to worship the jewel-like Lord who graciously resides in the Pasupatheeswaram temple, he enters the temple and worships with abundant love, offering cool Tamil verses as garlands. Thirugnanasambandhar worships. Thiru Avoor is the name of the village, and Pasupatheeswaram is the name of the temple.

The pathigam (decade of verses) composed by Thirugnanasambandhar here begins with “Puṇṇiyar” and is the 8th pathigam of the First Thirumurai, set to the Nattappadai tune. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam Puṇṇiyar pūthīyaru pūthanāthaṉ endra kāthalāḷa irundha ūrāyar māḷigai māḍa vīthi sōlai sulāving. Paṇṇiyal pāḍal arātha Āvūr Pasupathichcharam pāḍuṇāvē Eṇḍi sey yum vaṇaṅgiya thum emparamāṉai eḻu koḷ Āvūr paṇḍuriyār silaṛ thoṇḍaru pōtṟum Pasupathīchcharaththu āthi thanmē kaṇḍal kaṇ miṇḍiya kāṇal kāḷi kavuṉiyaṉ ñāṉa sambandhaṉ soṉṉa kuṇḍiṉi thāyisai pāḍiyāḍi kūḍum. Thiru Avoor Pasupatheeswaram can be reached via Govindakudi on the Kumbakonam-Mannargudi road. The Lord’s name is Pasupatheeswarar / Asvaththanathar / Avoor Udaiyar, and the Goddess’s name is Mangalambikai / Pankajavalli. Brahma Theertham and Kamadhenu Theertham are among the sacred waters.

Avoor is the name of the village, and Pasupatheeswaram is the name of the temple. This is the place where Kamadhenu, cursed by Vasishta, came to earth on Brahma’s advice, worshipped here, and was relieved of her curse. The place where Kamadhenu arrived became Govindagudi. Our Lord Kochchenga Chola Nayanar consecrated the Madakoyil here. Manikoodam and Asvaththavanam are other names for this place. This village produced great scholars such as Avoor Kilar and Avoor Moolangilar.

In inscriptions, this place and its Lord are referred to as Pasupatheeswaramudaiyar of Avoor Kootram, belonging to Nitthavina. We will continue to contemplate the Valanadu. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 630, by Sekkizhar Swamigal, ‘Vamparaa Varivandu Sarukkam’, ‘Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam’. Having worshipped Thiru Avoor Pasupatheeswaram, Thirugnanasambandhar proceeds to the holy site of Thiruvalanjuzhi.

The devotees, who are the epitome of great penance residing in Thiruvalanjuzhi, gather and come forward to welcome the young Lord, the master of the three Tamils. At that moment, the young Lord descends from the pearl palanquin and walks towards them.

The devotees gathered around Thirugnanasambandhar like white clouds surrounding the moon in the sky. These devotees are those who have attained great penance and great love. They worshipped the Lord residing there by praising, singing, and dancing.

Therefore, such devotees welcome Thirugnanasambandhar and surround him. All those devotees prostrate themselves and then stand up. The young Lord, the great sage, holding his lotus-like hands in salutation, reaches the Lord’s temple in Thiruvalanjuzhi. He bows to the radiant golden gopuram (temple tower), rises, and enters the temple. He circumambulates the sacred courtyard of the Lord who burned the three cities of the enemies. With a melting heart and hands joined in anjali (salutation) above his head, the great young Lord prostrates himself before the feet of the Lord of Thiruvalanjuzhi, filled with overflowing love.

The young Lord, who partook of the nectar of wisdom, rises after prostrating before the Lord. Due to the deep love arising from this desire, he sings a pathigam (decade of verses) in which he addresses the Lord. He sings and praises the Lord with the beautiful neck resembling a blue lotus. This is the pathigam he composed. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: This is the pathigam (decade of verses) composed. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Nāṟu than thiruvimmi vaṇḍalām nasaiyāsai pāḍum vaḷañcozhi thoṇḍalām paravum sūḍaru pōl oḷi solīr paṇḍalām pali thēndhu ōli pāḍal payiṉṟathē vīḍum ñāṉamum vēṇḍuthirē virathaṅgaḷ.

Vaṇḍi ñāṉa āvadhum vaḷañcūzhi nāḍi ñāṉa sambandhaṉ koṇḍu isai pāḍum aḍisērvathu. Those who desire to reach the feet of the Lord will sing this pathigam (decade of verses) in Tamil with devotion. Those wise individuals who sing thus, the Lord. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states that reaching the feet of the Lord is certain, and the objective of this pathigam is to praise His glory by questioning the Lord. The glory of the Lord, who goes begging for alms and sustains His devotees, is sung throughout this pathigam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, offering sweet Tamil pathigams that can be cherished in the hearts of good people, bowed down, came out of the temple, and stayed in that holy place surrounded by the ever-flowing Kaveri River.

He daily worshipped the feet of the Lord with love and lived happily with the Lord’s devotees. Pillaiyar then composed two pathigams in this holy place. The first pathigam is the one hundred and sixth pathigam in the second Thirumurai, beginning with “Ennappuṇṇiyam”. The pathigam, beginning with “என்ன புண்ணியம் செய்தனை நெஞ்சமே இருங்கடல் வையத்து முன்னம் நீ பூரி நல்வினை முழு மணி தரங்கள் திருவழஞ்சோழி வாணனை வாயி ஆதரித்து எத்தியும் பாடியும்”, is set to the tune of Nattara. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: “O heart, what good deeds have you done in this vast ocean-like world, that you previously delighted in good deeds and offered fully radiant gems to the Lord of Thiruvalanjuzhi, praising Him with devotion and song.” “Worshiping the Lord, and hence, the medicine found in Valanjoli, the half-female Lord, which the brahmin of Vaigal, Gnanasambandha, sang as a Tamil garland, those who embrace and master it, even those who were delighted to hear it from the Chozhas, will have their suffering from past and future karma removed.”

The ultimate benefits for a soul are only two: worshipping Lord Shiva and being in the company of His devotees. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, from the state of self-realization, preached this pathigam, showing that these benefits arise from good deeds performed in the past. Sekkilar Peruman also informs us that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praised the feet of the Lord daily and rejoiced in the company of His devotees. It is only by the benefit of past Shiva-punya (merit) that one gets the privilege of worshipping Lord Shiva. This is mentioned in: Sivagnana Botham’s eighth sutra, using the word “thavaththil” (by penance). For this part of the sutra, it states that for these souls, liberation through penance will occur.

This is also supported by the example of those who performed penance attaining the world of penance.

Here, “punya” refers to Shiva-punya. “Nalvinai” (good deeds) refers to other good actions that indirectly lead to Shiva-punya. The hint here is that only by being with devotees will our strong karmic bonds be loosened.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman shows here how the service of Lord Shiva and the assembly of devotees are considered together. When one joins the assembly of devotees, the bonds of the three impurities, including anava malam, are completely shed, which is the idea of the twelfth sutra of Sivagnana Botham.

Therefore, it is through this that it is understood and explained that this earthly world is the place suitable for attaining liberation by performing such Shiva-punya. All other actions, except these two, multiply falsehood and disappear falsely. Only the worship of Lord Shiva and being in the company of Lord Shiva’s devotees are true actions. These are the preliminary stages of spiritual discipline.

Therefore, as preached in this pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman also lived happily with the devotees in Thiruvalanjuzhi, and Pillaiyar demonstrates and preaches the benefit of such joyful living with devotees here. Worshiping the Lord residing in Valanjuzhi, The second verse of this pathigam conveys the idea that all our strong karmic bonds were severed by being with devotees who perform such true actions. In the third verse, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises the sacred feet of the Lord. The sacred feet of the Lord, who is enshrined in Thiruvalanjuzhi, destroyed the three cities of the asuras, who were His enemies, by burning them. Those sacred feet lovingly protect the devotees. They are the sacred feet that appear to those who practice devotion.

They are the medicine and mantra for diseases such as unmattham. Unmattham means delusion. Thirukkural states that perceiving what is not real as real is delusion.

Therefore, the harsh action that obscures the eye of wisdom, is anava (ego). Such anava is a disease in the consciousness of beings. In the kevala state, it completely obscures the consciousness of beings. In the sakala state, the same anava malam creates delusion in the consciousness of beings. For this disease that affects the consciousness of beings, the feet of the Lord are the medicine and the mantra. Medicine is that which removes the disease.

Mantra is that which prevents the disease from recurring after it has been removed.

Thus, only the feet of the Lord serve as both medicine and mantra. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman bestows such a pathigam.

Now, the third pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman in Thiruvalanjuzhi begins with “Pallamathāya”. The pathigam, beginning with “Pallamathāya,” is the one hundred and sixth pathigam in the third Thirumurai, set to the tune of Pazhampanjaram. This pathigam also consists of divine discourses bestowed upon us by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. “The Lord, who rides the bull with delight, having overflowing compassion...” “Remember and worship Him with a melting heart, and diseases will not afflict you.

“This Tamil garland of thoughts, sung by Gnanasambandha, who is like a fertile field in the great city of Pazhanjuzhi, which is dear to me, will be sung by those on earth, and for them and their families” “It will be a great, eternal joy.

“” Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed the Thiruvalanjuzhi pathigams. We shall carry on our discussion. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Sekkizhar Swamigal’s Periya Puranam, Part 631, Vambara Varivanda Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is residing in Thiruvalanjuzhi.

At that time, the late spring season, or summer, arrives. The sun enters the zodiac sign of Gemini.

Therefore, the late spring season arrives, and there is intense heat. As a result, the clouds do not provide water, which even reduces the ocean’s bounty. The sun’s intensely hot rays are spread everywhere. The early spring passes, and the late spring season arrives. The heat from early spring intensifies. This season spans the months of Aani and Aadi.

This is called the late summer season, and it is the primary element of the desert region according to Tamil grammar. When Pillaiyar was seated in Thiruvalanjuzhi and proceeded to worship Thiru Pazhaiyarai, Thiru Aarai Metrali, and Thiruchatti Mutram, and then to Thiru Patteeswaram, it was during this same late summer season.

At that time, to alleviate the sun’s heat, the Lord graciously provided a cool pearl canopy.

Therefore, a traditional festival commemorating this event is still celebrated at Patteeswaram at the beginning of the month of Aani.

Thus, it is understood that this late summer season encompasses the months of Aani and Aadi. Previously, when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was in the Kongu region, severe winter conditions prevailed in Thiruchengodu. As Sekkizhar Peruman mentioned, he sang about all the events of that winter season, didn’t he?

Similarly, now Sekkizhar Peruman sings about all the characteristics of the summer season. During this summer season, people desire cool water and cool breezes. They wish to anoint their bodies with fragrant sandalwood. They long to sprinkle themselves with dew-laden fragrant flowers. Householders seek their life partners. They desire to wear various pearl necklaces and enjoy sweet foods and beverages.

In such a summer season, specifically the late summer season, the rivers filled with dark sand These temporary rivers dry up. In the rainy season, there is a flood there; in other seasons, these rivers have very little water. In this late summer season, the temporary rivers dry up. Herds of deer roam in search of water. During this hot season, mirages appear.

Therefore, believing the mirage to be real, herds of deer go to drink that water, but they are disappointed because there is no water there. There is a skylark bird called the Chathaka bird, which naturally feeds on raindrops.

Therefore, this Chathaka bird, the skylark, suffers from lack of food and wastes away during this hot season. Other birds try to fly with outstretched wings in search of food, but due to the heat of the sun, they are unable to spread their wings and fly. They retract their wings and go in search of cool places. People desire to be in the upper floors of tall buildings, near the moonlit terraces, and they stay there. They go to cool groves and reside there. They are on the banks of ponds filled with flowers.

The fragrance of flowers, the coolness of the water, and the touch of the gentle breeze that carries these elements provide coolness there. The humming of the bees also being present there makes the banks of ponds, flower gardens, and moonlit terraces suitable places for the summer season. People prefer these places and stay there. Peacocks shrink because peacocks are naturally delighted by clouds.

Therefore, in this hot season, peacocks shrink due to the absence of clouds. Bees feed on the nectar of flowers that bloom in the hot season and sing and dance. During the daytime in the hot season, the leaves of the trees in the groves are fully spread out. In such groves, cuckoos coo, plucking the tender shoots from the trees. All living beings sleep. The sun, with its radiant rays shining in the sky, does not reduce its hot rays, and the days belonging to the intensely hot late summer season are formed.

During these days of the late summer season, Pillaiyar, who appeared in Kalipathi, worships with great love and praises Lord Shiva at Thiruvalanjuzhi. He then lovingly proceeds with his devotees to Thiru Pazhaiyarai. When Pillaiyar departs from a place, it is customary to keep that holy place in mind, praise it, worship it, and then proceed.

Thus, Pillaiyar walks with his devotees. Currently, Pillaiyar does not travel in a palanquin but walks, desiring the great blessing of walking with his devotees. Pillaiyar, who is heading towards Pazhaiyarai, worships the Thiru Metrali temple along the way. Pillaiyar approaches Thiruchakthi Mutram, the sacred place where the mountain goddess with fragrant hair worshipped the Lord of fiery red hue, enshrined in Thiruppazhaiyarai Metrali, praising His feet with melting love. Thiruchakthi Mutram is named so because Shakti worshipped there and received blessings. Reaching Thiruchakthi Mutram, Pillaiyar reverently worships the beautiful feet that Thirumalavalliyar worshipped and offered archanai, filled with eagerness.

Pillaiyar, remembering the act of his mother, who fed him the nectar of wisdom, worshipping Lord Shiva, bows down there with immense enthusiasm.

The Lord enshrined there is the one who helps souls caught in the cycle of birth to cross over and reach salvation. He is the one who performs His first benevolence to souls. He praises the nature of that Lord who performs His first benevolence. Just as a compassionate person on top extends a hand to lift someone who has fallen into a pit, Lord Shiva, who is enshrined in Thiruchakthi Mutram, extends a hand to lift all souls that fall into the whirlpool of birth. The worship of Lord Shiva by Uma Devi, the daughter of the mountains, is for the sake of her children, the souls.

Therefore, Lord Shiva, as the father who bestows such a nature, is enshrined here in Thiruchakthi Mutram. Remembering such benevolence, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman lovingly praises the feet of the Lord there and sings.

Thus, bowing down and worshipping, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman resolves to worship the Lord of Thirupatteeswaram, which is nearby. Our discussion continues. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Sekkizhar Swamigal’s Periya Puranam, Part 632, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds from Thiruchakthi Mutram towards Thiruppatteeswaram with a retinue of devotees. It is the late summer season, bringing intense heat. The scorching heat of the late summer prevails there. During that hot time, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman walks with his devotees towards Thiruppatteeswaram temple.

At that moment, Shiva bhoothas, unseen by anyone, carry a pearl canopy. They hold the pearl canopy above Pillaiyar’s sacred head. Shiva bhoothas They cannot be seen by anyone. Those bhoothas, without anyone knowing, hold the pearl canopy above Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred head. The Shiva bhoothas said, “The Lord residing in Thiruppatteeswaram commanded us to come with this pearl canopy.” Only their voices were heard there; the Shiva bhoothas could not be seen. To alleviate the heat, the bhoothas brought this pearl canopy according to the Lord’s command.

They brought it and held it above Pillaiyar’s sacred head. Previously, the Lord had bestowed a pearl palanquin and insignias at Thirunelvaayil Arathurai.

Similarly, now He bestows a pearl canopy in the sky through the Shiva bhootha ganas. As soon as the voices of the Bhootha Ganas were heard, Seerkazhi Pillaiyar, thinking that this act was the grace of the Lord and would bring him joy, fell to the ground in reverence, his hairs standing on end. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman fell to the ground, saying, “This is the grace bestowed by the Lord, and I accept it.” He also worshipped the canopy, praising the manifestation of divine grace.

At that time, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s retinue held the four pillars of the canopy. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman walked inside the pearl canopy.

At that time, the devas from the sky showered flowers.

Thus, the pearl canopy also became a flower canopy. The groups of devotees chanted the name of Shiva, “Hara Hara,” in loud, high-pitched tones, filling all directions. The shadow of the white pearl canopy spread over Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred head.

At that time, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sat beneath the shadow of that pearl canopy, just as he would sit beneath the sacred feet of the Lord, the God of gods, in the sacred Thiru Ambalam. Sitting in the shadow of the pearl canopy bestowed by the Lord is equivalent to sitting in the shadow of the Lord’s sacred feet. The shadow of the canopy is a divine blessing; therefore, it is the shadow of His graceful feet. Just as he sat beneath the sacred feet that lift souls from the great abyss of birth, he sat beneath the pearl canopy. Pillaiyar, thus, walked on the ground with his devotees, under the pearl canopy. It was due to his desire for the great blessing of walking with his devotees that Pillaiyar did not travel in a palanquin but walked.

Upon reaching Thiruppatteeswaram, the devotees of Thiruppatteeswaram, with hearts full of love and overflowing with joy, came forward to welcome Pillaiyar. With radiant faces, the devotees gathered there. As the group of devotees from Thiruppatteeswaram joined the group of devotees accompanying Pillaiyar, amidst such loving devotees, Pillaiyar, with joy increasing in his loving heart, reached the Thiruppatteeswaram Peruman temple. Reaching the sacred entrance of the temple, he worshipped the entrance, entered, circumambulated the Lord’s temple, beheld the lotus feet of the Lord which even Thirumal could not see, bowed before the Lord, prostrated on the ground, rose, and praised the Lord with a pathigam in the form of a garland of words. The pathigam thus composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman before the Lord is the seventy-third pathigam of the third Thirumurai, set to the tune of Sadhari. The first and last verses of this pathigam are: “He who resides in Patteeswaram, within the ancient Pazhaiyarai, surrounded by beautiful mansions, is the Lord with a fierce, coiled serpent.

“He shows the path to liberation to those who seek Him and grants them the bliss of the Veena.

“The Lord of Patteeswaram, within the ancient Pazhaiyarai, filled with fragrant groves and mansions, adorned with matted locks...” Because the divine cow worshipped the Lord here, He is named Patteeswaran. Rama worshipped Lord Shiva here and was freed from the sin of Brahmahattya. This festival is celebrated grandly on Arkaḷi Amavasya. An ancient painting of Rama is in this temple. As Pillaiyar was approaching from a distance, Lord Patteeswarar in the temple moved all the Rishabha Devars (Nandis) aside and granted a direct vision to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

“Govinda Dikshitar and his consort, who performed many great services here, are enshrined in the temple. The Lord’s name is Patteeswaranathar, Thenupureeswarar. The Goddess’s name is Gnanaambikai, Palvalai Nayaki. The thirthams are Gnanathirtham and Kodi Thirtham. This holy place is located on the Kumbakonam-Aavur road. We saw that Pillaiyar journeyed from Thiruchakti Mutram to Thirupatteeswaram.

“Thiruchakti Mutram and Thirupatteeswaram are adjacent temples, with only one street separating the two temples. As the daughter of Kamadhenu, Patti, worshipped here, it is called Patteeswaram, and the Lord is known as Patteeswaranar. Since Ambigai performed penance here, it is called Devivanam. As we have already seen, the Lord moved aside all the Nandis here and granted a direct vision to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

“Accordingly, the Nandi devas here are positioned apart. It is said that when Rama returned after installing and worshipping Ramanathar in Rameswaram, he created the Kodi Thirtham here with the tip of his bow and worshipped. There is also a Ramalinga shrine and Kodi Thirtham here.

“Here, the presiding Ganesha is Anugnya Vinayagar, Mathavaarana Pillaiyar. The temple history states that Vishwamitra attained the title of Brahmarishi in this place. The Durga shrine here is very famous. The Durga enshrined here is a Chola period installation. On the first day of the Aani month, the festival of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman receiving the pearl canopy takes place. The history of this place is in Sanskrit.

“It has been translated into Tamil in a single style as Patteeswarar Manmiyam. These are all facts about Patteeswaram. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who is enshrined here, sings pathigams, praising the greatness of the Lord, and is immersed in the immense flood of joy that comes from it. Earlier, when Pillaiyar walked near Maranpadi, seeing that his lotus feet were slowly getting tired, the Lord of Thirunelvaayil Arathurai bestowed a pearl palanquin. Pillaiyar, astonished, praised it as the grace of the Lord of Arathurai. Here in Patteeswaram, during the late summer, even though the Lord had provided a pearl palanquin to alleviate the sun’s heat, the Lord, seeing Thirugnanasambandha Peruman walking out of his desire to walk with his devotees, bestowed a canopy to reduce the heat.

“Therefore, remembering the Lord’s gracious act, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praised the Lord and came out of the temple, filled with the boundless joy of such praise. From that holy place, after receiving gracious permission from the Lord, Pillaiyar proceeds to Thirupazhaiyarai Vadathazhi. Thirupatteeswaram and Pazhaiyarai Vadathazhi are adjacent temples. This Thirupazhai The Thiruppazhaiyarai Vadathazhi temple was occupied by Jains. The Jains concealed this place and made it their dwelling.

“After that, when Thirunavukkarasar Peruman visited here, he undertook a fast and revealed the temple where the Lord of Pazhaiyarai Vadathazhi was enshrined. This is the part we discussed in the Puranam of Thirunavukkarasar Peruman.

“Therefore, this temple, which was a Shiva temple when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worshipped it, later fell under the occupation of Jains after he left.

“Then, Thirunavukkarasar Peruman, who came later, removed that occupation and brought the temple back into prominence. We should connect these historical events in this way.

“There, in Thiruppazhaiyarai Vadathazhi, the Lord who stands as everything. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composes a pathigam, praising the Lord as “Epporulumai Nirkka.” The Lord stands as all things through His pervading nature, being all things, whether insentient or sentient. Even though He stands as all things through His pervading nature, by His own nature, He stands distinctly by definition. He is in union with them when He directs them.

“Thus, Pillaiyar composes a pathigam praising the Lord who stands as all things. However, we do not have the pathigam composed by Pillaiyar for this holy place. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who worshipped Thirupazhaiyarai Vadathazhi, proceeds to the holy place called Thiru Irumpoolai.

“We shall proceed with our discussion.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Sekkizhar Swamigal’s Periya Puranam, Part 633, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. From Pazhaiyarai Vadathazhi, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reaches Thiru Irumpoolai, a sacred place where Lord Shiva is enshrined. This holy place, Thiru Irumpoolai, is currently known as Alangudi. It is the sixty-eighth sacred place on the south bank of the Kaveri River. The plant called Poolai is the Sthala Vriksham (sacred tree) of this place, hence its name.

It is also known as Poolai Vanam. This is the place where Vishwamitra performed worship. The Lord’s names are Kasi Aranyeswarar, Apath Sahayar. The Goddess’s name is Elavaar Kuzhali. The thirthams are Kaveri and Amrita Pushkarani. Among the five Pancharanya Kshetras, This is the fourth sacred place.

Kashyaranyam is its Sanskrit name. Kalamega Pulavar has sung about this place and its Lord with a pun, saying, “If the Lord who resides in Alangudi is the one who consumed the poison, will not all the people of the world die?” The Vinayagar here is called Kalangamal Katha Ganapathi (Ganapathi who protected without fear) because he removed the danger that came upon the devas from Gajamukasura and protected them. Since Ambigai performed penance and married the Lord here, this place is called Thirumanamangalam. Thirumal, Brahma, Lakshmi, Sastha, the Ashtadikpalakas, Veerabhadrar, and Garuda, who came to witness this marriage, installed lingams in their own names and worshipped. Muchukunda Chakravarthi Swasanan also worshipped the Lord here. There is a traditional saying that when Sundaramurthy Swamigal came to this place, Lord Shiva appeared as a boatman in the Vettar River and blessed him.

This is a place where Dakshinamurthy Peruman is enshrined very resplendently. These are all the special features of the Thiru Irumpoolai temple, also known as Alangudi. To reach Thiru Irumpoolai, where Lord Shiva resides with pleasure, the devotees there erect canopies. They decorate these canopies with arches and, filled with great joy, welcome Pillaiyar. They hang large garlands from the canopies, arrange full pots in rows, and all the devotees praise and receive Pillaiyar. who composes rich Thevaram Tamil, the leader who speaks sweet words with a joyful face, upon seeing the beautiful group of devotees, descends from the pearl palanquin he was riding in. As the devotees who were waiting for him bowed to him, he also bowed to them.

Pillaiyar then reaches the temple where Lord Shiva is enshrined. He reaches the temple, bows, stands before the deity, and sings praises to the Lord with a melodious pathigam that expresses musical notes. Meru mountain is also called the golden mountain. It is an incomparable great mountain.

The Lord held it as a bow in His sacred hand and bent it, a mountain of great distinction. This mountain, which stands in the middle of all those worlds and is encircled by the sun, is a mountain that holds the distinction of being the leader of all mountains.

Thus, being endowed with incomparable greatness, that incomparable Meru mountain stands tall. Our Lord Shiva is so great that even that mighty Meru mountain becomes an atom before Him. An atom is the smallest of the small. Compared to the greatness of Lord Shiva, even the mighty Meru mountain becomes a very small atom. He is so great that He appears as a very large being, such that the atom becomes a world. The sacred utterance from Karuvurdevar’s ninth Thirumurai, Thiruisaippa, that comes to our mind is: “Aṇuvōraṇiyāmāka”

The Vedas praise the Lord as “Anoranīyāṇ mahatō mahīyāṇ” (smaller than the smallest, greater than the greatest). Though He is so immensely great, the Lord is extremely simple when there is love. When there is no love, the Lord is unapproachable and difficult to attain. He is like nectar to His devotees who experience Him. He is worshipped continuously by devotees through their minds, words, and deeds.

Therefore, the Lord is like nectar, enabling devotees to continuously immerse themselves in Shiva-Ananda. Pillaiyar, the brave Tamil poet, in a questioning manner towards the devotees, reveals these qualities of the Lord, singing a pathigam to elucidate the inner meaning of the rare Vedas. That pathigam is a pathigam that speaks the truth. Explaining the inner meaning of the Vedas, that Lord Shiva is the ultimate God, Lord Shiva is worthy of meditation, Lord Shiva possesses the eight qualities such as supreme grace and limitless power, and souls are subservient to Lord Shiva and worthy of salvation—all these meanings are set forth in his pathigam, the pathigams of Thiru Irumpoolai, also known as Alangudi. This pathigam is the thirty-sixth pathigam of the second Thirumurai, set to the tune of Indalappann. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: “This is the Lord of Irumpoolai, who is accompanied by the maiden and rides the bull, the one who consumed the dark ocean poison.

“This is the Lord of Irumpoolai, who is accompanied by the maiden and rides the bull, the one who consumed the dark ocean poison. He is the Lord of Irumpoolai. Those who master these ten verses sung by Gnanasambandha of Chanpai, rich in Tamil, will break free from their bonds and achieve liberation.” This pathigam is structured in such a way that the qualities of the Lord are heard through the greatness of His devotees. Each verse in this pathigam contains a question and its appropriate answer.

“Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, after worshipping Alangudi, visits holy places such as Thiru Arathai Perumpazhi. Thiru Arathai Perumpazhi, the ninety-ninth holy place on the south bank of the Kaveri, is called Haridwaramangalam. This is the place where Thirumal, in his Varaha avatar, worshipped Lord Shiva. The Sthala Puranam states that this is where Lord Shiva plucked and wore the tusk of that Varaha. It is said that there is a burrow dug by a pig in front of the Swami’s shrine. The name of the village also reinforces this.

“Hari refers to Thirumal, and Dwaram refers to a burrow.

“Therefore, this place is known as Haridwaramangalam, Thiru Arathai Perumpazhi. It is also called Samipanam. The Lord’s names are Padalavaradar and Padaleswarar. The Goddess’s name is Alangara Valli. The Thirtham is Brahma Thirtham. One can always see a large pit in front of the Moolavar.

“Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who visited this holy place, composed a pathigam. It is the thirtieth pathigam of the third Thirumurai, set to the tune of Kollippann. The first and last The verses are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. “The mad Lord, who wears a striped loincloth, has a bull with abundant eyes, and dances constantly in the cremation ground amidst loud roars, anointing himself with sacred ash, His temple is Arathai Perumpazhi. The mad Lord’s temple is Arathai Perumpazhi.” “The temple of the mad Lord, Arathai Perumpazhi.

“Those who are learned say that Thiruarathai Perumpazhi is the abode of Lord Shiva, the pure one. Those who master the sweet Tamil composed by Gnanasambandha of Seerkazhi for Perumpazhi will have no sins.” The world praises that Thiruarathai Perumpazhi is the abode of Lord Shiva, the pure one. The reference of the location is the pathigam as described in the third verse of the Peruman Sambandar Puranam: Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, after worshipping Thiru Arattai Perumpazhi, devoutly worshipped the sacred sites of Thirucherai, Thirunalloor, Thirukkudavayil, Thirunaraiyur, and Thenthirupputhur, composing many Tamil verses and abiding there joyfully. The sacred site that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman visited after departing from Thiru Arattai Perumpazhi is Thirucherai. We have already deliberated on the sthala puranam of Thirucherai in Thirunavukkarasu.

“Peruman Puranam. Pillaiyar, having arrived at this sacred site, graciously composed a pathigam. It is a special pathigam called Thiruviragam, set to the Sadhari tune, the eighty-sixth pathigam in the Third Thirumurai. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Muriyooru neeramalkeekil moolai maalai makal maadiri seytha viradinnoorum malarodu nadhi madhi) (Nakhathalai seriyooru sadai moodi adigal tham vaazhnakaru seraiye katra nanmaraipaiyil adiyavar adithozhu kavinooru sitraiyavalodu idam ena uraivathol serai maitamil poohaliyul ikazharu gnana sambandhana sotrakka ooramozhibavath) (Azhivelaru thooyar theerume) Thiruchitrambalam.

“The pathigam’s summary states that the Lord resides in Thirucherai, in the company of the exquisitely slender-waisted lady. Let us carry on our contemplation.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Volume 634, by Sekkizhar Swamigal, Vambaravari Vantu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, after graciously composing a pathigam at Thirucherai, received a blessed farewell from Thirucherai and proceeded to the sacred site of Thirunalloor Mayanam. Thirunalloor Mayanam is the ninety-sixth site on the southern bank of the Cauvery. It exists as two distinct sites: Nalloor and Nalloor Mayanam. Similar to Thirukkadavoor and Thirukkadavoor Mayanam, Nalloor and Nalloor Mayanam are structured.

Nalloor is a Maadakkoyil, and Nalloor Mayanam is the site where the Lord was worshipped by the four Vedas and where Apasthamba Rishi performed worship. The Lord’s names are Palasavananathar and Gnanaparameswarar. The Goddess’s names are Periyanayaki and Gnanaambikai. The sacred pond is Gnanatheertham. Kadavoor Mayanam, Kacchi Mayanam, Kaali Mayanam, and Nalloor Mayanam are the four Mayana sites, and Thirunalloor Mayanam is one of them. The Nalloor site, located nearby, is a Thevara Vaippu site.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, upon arriving at this site, graciously composed a pathigam that begins with “Paal oorumm malai paambum.” In accordance with this poetic utterance of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, even today we can see a large snake frequently crawling on the head of the Lord at this site. The pathigam thus composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is the forty-sixth pathigam in the Second Thirumurai, set to the Seekamaram tune. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchuttrambalam. (Paal oorumm malai paambum pani madheeyum mathamum meloorum senchadai ven noor maarpee naarmayanaththu nam) (Than adi neenthum maal oorumm sinthai vaanithu marupeerpe nyam pukazh kaantha naalu marai) (Neethu naaloor mayana eeseelam pukazha siranthu etthup pallaaarkku elum pookal panaththu inba iruppaare e) The pathigam’s summary states that for those who praise the Lord of Nalloor Mayanam, ancient karma will not surround them, sin will not cling to them, and joy will come to them.

Those who do not praise that Lord will not follow the ancient path and will not attain the good path. After worshipping Thirunalloor Mayanam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds to the sacred site of Thirukkudavayil. Thirukkudavayil is the ninety-fourth site on the southern bank of the Cauvery, and one of the Maadakkoyils. Because Shiva manifested through the mouth of a pot to the worshipping Sage Thrunabindhu and cured his leprosy, this site is named Kudavasal and Kudavayil. The sthala puranam states that Garuda worshipped here, brought Amrutham, and was freed from his curse and that of his mother. It is noteworthy that images of Garuda are found on the compound walls and mandapams.

When Aludaiya Pillaiyar visited, the pujas and festivities here were very prominent, as attested by Pillaiyar’s pathigams. This site can be easily reached from Kumbakonam and Thiruvarur. The Lord’s names are Koneswarar, Suryeswarar, and Brahganathar. The Goddess’s names are Periyanayaki. The sacred pond is Amirthateertham. This is a Maadakkoyil built by Emperor Kochchankachola Nayanar.

The Goddess’s temple is on level ground, while the Lord’s shrine is above, in the Maadakkoyil. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, upon arriving at this sacred site, graciously composed two pathigams. The first pathigam is the twenty-second pathigam in the Second Thirumurai, set to the Indalapann tune. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. (Thikazhum Thirumaalodu naan mukanum peruman adiyum peruman kooda vaayil manni nikazhum perungkoyil nilaaya) (Kudavaayil malineer kudavaayil thanil nedumaa perungkoil niraivane thadamaarpoohali thamizhaar veeragan thadamaarpoohali thamizhaar veeragan vadamaarththamil vallar nallavare etthambalam) The second pathigam graciously composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for the sacred site of Thirukkudavayil is the fifty-eighth pathigam in the Second Thirumurai, set to the Kandhara Pann tune. Pathigam.

The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Kalai vaazhum angkaiye kongai yaarum karungkoonthal alai vaazhum senchadai aravum piraiyum amarvetthe kulai vaazhai kamoham pon pavalam pazhukkum kudavaayil nilai vaazhum koyile koyilaka nintre nalirpook) (Thiraivalku kaazhi gnana sambandhan kulirpoongkudavaayil koyil meya komaana kulirpoo tamil maalai uraiththa paadal ivai vallarvaan thaanoliyath thagushivaana thiruppare) Thiruchitrambalam. The pathigam’s summary states that you, Lord, are the great one residing in the temple of Kudavayil, and you desired this very temple as your chosen abode. You stood. This is the pathigam’s concluding note. Let’s continue to contemplate. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Volume 635, by Sekkizhar Swamigal, Vambaravari Vantu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, after worshipping at Thirukkudavasal, arrives at Thirunaraiyur Siththeecharam. Thirunaraiyur Siththeecharam is the sixty-fourth site on the southern bank of the Cauvery. Thirunaraiyur is the name of the village, and Siththeeswaram is the name of the temple.

The Lord manifested here as a Siddharr to be worshipped by sages and Siddharrs. The Lord’s names are Siddhanatheswarar, Vedheswarar, and Nareswarar. The Goddess’s names are Azhagammai and Soundaryanayaki. The sacred ponds are Soolatheertham, Brahmateertham, and Thensitthi Theertham. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, upon arriving here, graciously composed three pathigams for this temple. The first pathigam The pathigam is the twenty-ninth pathigam of the First Thirumurai, set to the Thakkaraaka tune.

The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchittru Palikkondu annal maraiyore naraiyuril sentradai nenje meiththoolavum maraiyore naraiyuril siddhan sitthan The pathigam’s summary is: “Oh mind, go and reach the Lord’s Siththeeswaram in Naraiyur. Meditate on it, understand it, for it is spiritual practice, and that sacred site is the dwelling place of our Lord.” Therefore, this pathigam is understood to have been composed on the way to Thirunaraiyur Siththeeswaram.

Next, the second pathigam graciously composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for Thirunaraiyur Siththeecharam is the seventy-first pathigam in the First Thirumurai, set to the Thakechi tune. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Kapaalam enthu kaiyaalam) (Paadach sedharu manaiyin makizhvaithi sirakal vandu thenaar naraiyur siththichcharaththaare kuyilaarkola maathaveekal kulir poonjoora punnai seyyala poikai seru naraiyur siththi saraththaarai mayilaar solai soozhntha kaali malku sambandhan) The pathigam’s summary states that our Lord, the Lord of Siththeecharam, is rare even to the celestials. He will come to the minds of those who think of him, riding the bull, with anklets tinkling. This is our Lord of Naraiyur Siththeeswaram.

Next, the third pathigam graciously composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for Thirunaraiyur Siththeecharam is the eighty-seventh pathigam in the Second Thirumurai, set to the Piyanthai Kandhara Pann tune. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Neriyan aahum allan oru paalum me nee ariyanmunaaya ozhiyan neeriyal kaalum aaki niraivaanum aaki uruthi aaya nimalan aariyal pechcha peni ulagangal ettha nalkundu pandu sudalai) (Aa naariyorpaakam aaka nadam maadavalla naraiyurin amman avane enal ulaavi pothaam ethirmalku kaanthan munthi unara agnanam ulaavu sinthai adi vaithu ugandha naraiyurin nam) (Avanaam ilatha vannam isaiyal urai tamil maalai paththu ninaiyavar aana nilaavilum nindru vazhipaadu mika ve e thiruchi thalam) Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, after devoutly worshipping Thirunaraiyur Siththeecharam, arrives at the sacred site called Arisilkkarai Puththur, also known as Thenthirupputhur. This is currently called Azhagapuththur, located near Kumbakonam. The Lord’s names are Padikaasu Vaiththa Paramar and Swarnapureeswarar.

The Goddess’s names are Sivaambikai, Soundaryanayaki, and Azhagammai. The sacred pond is Arisil River. This temple was renovated by Emperor Kochchankachola Nayanar. It is the birthplace of Pugazhthunai Nayanar, and the site where the Lord granted coins to Pugazhthunai Nayanar. It is a sacred site praised by the three great saints. It has a west-facing shrine, and is the sixty-sixth site on the southern bank of the Cauvery.

This is a very ancient site, also known as Siruvizhipuththur. It is the site where Sage Unmaiyanandha worshipped and attained renown. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, upon arriving at this sacred site, graciously composed a pathigam. It is the sixty-third pathigam in the Second Thirumurai, set to the Kandhara Pann tune. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. (Minnurm sadai mel ilaven thigal vilangave thunnum kadal nanjerulthoy kandar thonmoozhu punalar alai kondru ponnum maniyum poruththan karai mel putthoore) The pathigam’s reference is: (Naravanga sambandha porikolravam poondanaantha puththoor mel serivan tamil seyrai puththoor enbathu iraivarthu moothoor avarthu naamam pothi naalthorum bramanarkal poovaalum neeraalum pottrum puththoor thiru arisilkkarai puththoore enbathu)

Thiruppathigam’s note.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, after reaching Thenthirupputhur and graciously composing a pathigam there, resided peacefully. While Pillaiyar was at Arisilkkarai Puththur, he had a strong desire to visit the sacred site of Sivapuram and worship the Lord’s feet.

So, he proceeded to Sivapuram. Thiruchivapuram is the sixty-seventh site on the southern bank of the Cauvery. This is the site where Mahavishnu, during the Swetavaraha Kalpa, rescued the world submerged in the ocean by lifting it on his tusk and then worshipped. It is also known as Shanbhagavanam, and even today, Champak trees are found in front of the temple. One can reach Sivapuram by taking a short branch road from Shakottai on the Kumbakonam-Thiruvarur highway. The Lord’s names are Sivagurunatha Swami, Shivapuri, Eswarar, Brahmapureeswarar, and Shivapuranathar.

The Goddess’s names are Ariyaambaal, Singaravalli, and Periyanayaki. Chandratheertham and Arisil River are the sacred waters. There is a belief in this village that a Shiva Lingam exists one foot below the earth everywhere. Because of this, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and others, instead of walking, performed Angapradakshinam (circumambulation by prostrating) and worshipped the Lord, then stood at a distance beyond the village boundary and sang praises to the Lord. The spot where Thirugnanasambandha Peruman thus sang is known as Swamigal Thurai. This is the site where Kubera worshipped Shiva.

Kuberapuram, Poohkailayam, and Shanbagaranyam are other names for this site. The main deity is a majestic, rather large Shiva Lingam. The Natarajar idol here is extremely beautiful. This idol was illegally transported to America, Later it was discovered and brought back to India through the great efforts of the Indian government and is now kept in a safe at the Thiruvarur Sivalayam. Currently, another Natarajar idol, along with Sivakami Ammai, is installed and worshipped. Among the four idols enshrined here, Paravaiyar is also present.

Directly opposite the east-facing temple is Chandratheertham. Upon entering past the five-tiered gopuram, one can see the shrine of Bhairava Moorthy facing south in the outer prakaram. He is a granter of boons. In the inner prakaram, when viewing the Goshtamurthis, one can see Vishnu in the form of a white boar worshipping near Dakshinamurthy in his graceful posture. These are some of the special features of Thiruchivapuram. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, upon arriving at this sacred site, graciously composed three pathigams.

The first pathigam The first pathigam is the twenty-first pathigam of the First Thirumurai, a Thiruviraga pathigam set to the Nattapadai tune. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. (Vazhi kanal poonal puvi kalai marai thiri konam amar nera thivam mali tharu muthaleeyaru thozha ninaivodu padumanan malarathu maruveeya sivanathu sivapooram) Those who meditate on Shivapuram will attain permanence in the rich earth. (Thikazh sivapooru nagar maruveeya sivanadi inai pani sirapooru nagar irai tamil veeraganathu nalam malivoru pathum navilpavaru nikazh kula nilai neerai thiru ooru nikarila kodai megu sayamagal pukazh puvi valar vazhi adimaiyin mikai punarthth) Shiva himself performs the actions of creation, preservation, and destruction for living beings. The paths to attain salvation are Chariyai, Kiriyai, Yogam, and Gnanam. The benefits for these paths are Salokam for Chariyai, Saamipyam for Kiriyai, Saarupyam for Yogam, and Saayujyam for Gnanam.

This pathigam describes in each verse that those who reach the Lord in Shivapuram will attain all glories, and the benefits appropriate to that verse are bestowed. In the final verse, the Thirukkadaikkappu, all these benefits are summarized and the pathigam’s overall benefit is stated. The benefits mentioned in those verses are the benefits of the worship described in those verses. In the Thirukkadaikkappu, The pathigam’s unique feature is its cumulative benefits.

Next, the second pathigam graciously composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for Thiru Sivapuram is the one hundred and twelfth pathigam of the First Thirumurai, set to the Vyazhakurinji tune. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. (In kooral isai kelung yaazh thankaram kaaviriyin thenkarai maruveeya sivapurame sivan urai tharu sivapura) Shiva will speak of Shivapuram.

Next, the third pathigam graciously composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for Thiruchivapuram is a Thiruviragam pathigam, the one hundred and twenty-fifth pathigam of the First Thirumurai, set to the Vyazhakurinji tune. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Mulai mali tharu theeru uruvamathudayavan silai malimathil pothi sivapura nagar thozha ilai nali veenai erumaiyum veedarkkedume punthiyarumarai navilli mgnanasam vandhanu thamizh kodu sivapura nagar urai enthayai urai seytha isai mozhi pavar veenai sinthai munnoora uyaru gathi peruvarkale)

The pathigam’s summary states that those who worship Shivapuram will certainly attain a higher state and their difficulties will cease.

Let us go on with our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Volume 636, by Sekkizhar Swamigal, Vambaravari Vantu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, departing from Thiruchivapuram, arrives at the sacred site of Thirukkudamookku. Thirukkudamookku is now known as Kumbakonam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrives at Thirukkudamookku, surrounded by groves full of honey-laden flowers. That is a place where many great Brahmins live.

What wealth do those Brahmins possess? They possess the wealth of righteousness that comes from the Vedas.

Furthermore, Kudamookku, or Kumbakonam, is a town where many Brahmins reside.

Therefore, that The wealthy Brahmins welcome Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, as described by Sekkizhar Peruman. Based on the majority, it should be understood that all devotees, including the Brahmins, welcomed Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. They welcome Thirugnanasambandha Peruman by chanting the Vedas, causing the sound of the Vedas to resonate. They welcome him as one would welcome a king. This method of welcoming a king is known as “Chakravarttiyupacharena” in Sanskrit, which describes how to welcome an emperor with proper honors. They welcome him accordingly.

As he approaches the sacred site of Thirukumbakonam, Thirukkudamookku, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, remembering the Lord enshrined in Kudamookku, graciously composes a pathigam with the theme, “He is the Lord of Kudamookku.” That pathigam is the fifty-ninth pathigam in the Third Thirumurai, set to the Panchamam tune. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Kura viri solai soozhntha kuzhagan kudamookkidamaa thigal chudi irunthavan emm iraiye ven kodi paadam ongu viralvengu nannagara nanbodu nindra seeraana thamizh gnana sambandhan nalla kann kudamookkamandha adi ser thamizh) The pathigam’s summary states that the Lord who joyfully resided in Kudamookku is our God. We have already contemplated the sthala puranam of Thirukkudamookku in Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar Puranam.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, after worshipping Adi Kumbeswarar and Mangalambikai Ammai in Thirukkudamookku and composing a pathigam, proceeds to the sacred site of Kudanthai Keezhkottam, accompanied and praised by a gathering of devotees and Brahmins. There, he praises the Lord and composes a pathigam. This site is called Keezhkottam because it is located in the eastern part of Kudamookku. Pillaiyar approaches from the eastern direction of Kudamookku.

Therefore, after entering the city, he visits and worships many temples in Kudamookku. Among such many temples, this temple is the first to be worshipped in terms of its arrangement.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships the Thirukkudamookku Keezhkottam temple, known as Kudanthai Keezhkottam. The pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for this site is not available to us. From here, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, receiving a gracious farewell from the Lord, proceeds to the sacred site of Thirukkaronam, accompanied by a multitude of devotees and praised by all the Brahmins. Sekkizhar Peruman states: He arrived and worshipped the divine being residing in Thirukkudamookku Keezhkottam with a joyous mind, then proceeded with his devotees. With Brahmins surrounding him and singing praises, he reached Karonam, surrounded by fragrant flower gardens. Sekkizhar Peruman then continues with the next verses, verses 408 and 409: “The temple where the sacred great waters, beginning with the Ganga, come to bathe in the Mahamaham.

“With hands adorned with pure flowers, they worshipped, circumambulated, and with eyes that gazed at the desire-inducing foreheads, they completed their worship.” Sekkizhar Peruman mentions that Thirukkaronam is a temple of great glory where all the sacred great waters, including the Ganga, come to bathe during the Mahamaham festival. Sekkizhar Peruman, through his verses, describes the significance of the Mahamaham festival that takes place in Thirukkudamookku.

“Here, we recall the verse by Thirunavukkarasu Peruman in Thiruttandagam: “Our Lord of Kudanthai Keezhkottam, surrounded by the waters of the Cauvery, Yamuna, Ganga, Saraswati, Pottamari Pushkarani, Southern Goviyodu, and Kumari.” This refers to the Mahamaham Teertham. The Mahamaham Teertham is glorious because it cleanses the sins of all beings who bathe in it. All seven great sacred rivers—the Cauvery, Ganga, and others—come here to cleanse their accumulated impurities by bathing in the Mahamaham Teertham and worshipping the Lord of Thirukkaronam. History says that this event happens once every twelve years as a grand festival during Maasi Makam. Devotees from all directions gather in large numbers to bathe in the sacred water.

“This sacred water, inherently pure, sanctifies those who bathe in it. It is called a great sacred water. There are many crores of sacred waters, and this one is among the most glorious. This special quality comes from its ability to wash away inner impurities. It is believed that the Ganga, Yamuna, Saraswati, Narmada, Cauvery, Kumari, and Godavari do not exist in a physical form but rather in a subtle spiritual form in the Mahamaham Teertham of Kudamookku. That is, the presiding deities of these rivers.

“Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds to worship the Lord who is like the rare black pupil of the eye, a rich nectar residing in Thirukkudandai Karonam, and the inner meaning of the four Vedas who burned the three cities of the enemies. He bows down, sings a melodious pathigam, and praises the Lord. The pathigam thus bestowed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is the seventy-second pathigam of the First Thirumurai, set in Takkesi tune. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: Neeraar Ondru endhi antha pulagan kooda mookkil kaaraar kandathu en thondai Kaaronae Kaaronarae karuvaar polil soozhnthu azhagaar selva Kaaronaththarai thiruvaar selva malku sendhai Thigazhoosambarvaar senjol malai vaare sutrambalam kudamookkil Kaaronaththar iraivar udalil adunoy avalam adaiyaavannamum kaalan adaiyaavannamum kaappaar enbathu iththiruppathigathin pathiga kurippu aagum. Thirukkudandai Karonam, this sacred site, is the twenty-eighth site on the south bank of the Kaveri. Kayaroganam is known as Karonam.

“It is said that the meaning of Kayaroganam is the Lord’s body (Thirumeni) was ascended by Shiva. This temple in Kumbakonam is located northeast of the Mahamaham sacred pond. The seven sacred mothers of the Ganges and other rivers are present here. The local history states that the deity, known as Kasi Viswanathar, invited these sacred mothers and, facing west, allowed them to bathe in the sacred pond directly before him.

“Similarly, the Abhimukeswarar temple, located on the east side of the Mahamaham sacred pond on the south side of this temple, is also known as Kudandai Karonam. The Lord’s name is Somanathar, and the Goddess is Thenaru Mozhi Ammai. Karonam is the site where the Lord united souls with himself during the time of the Great Dissolution. This site is called Karonam and Kaya Aroganam.

“In addition, it was named Karonam because the Goddess ascended the Lord’s body here. The pot of nectar placed here manifests as a Shiva lingam.

“Therefore, this site is called Sikkesam, where ‘Sikkam’ means pot.

“The Lord is also named Sikkesar at this site. It is also a local legend that Rama, to destroy Ravana, worshipped here seeking a portion of Rudra (Rudramsam), and upon receiving it in his body, the place came to be known as Kaya Aroganam.

“Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman bows down and offers a pathigam at Thirukaronam. We shall proceed with our contemplation.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 637, by Sekkizhar Swamigal, Vambara Varivandu Sarakkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, after worshipping the nectar-like Lord residing in Thirukkudandai Karonam, who is like the pupil of the eye, and bowing down, singing, and praising the melodious pathigam, pays homage to all other sacred sites and resides there happily with the devotees. The sites worshipped by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman include other temples in Thirukkudamookkil, and nearby sites such as Thirukkarukkudi, Thirukkottayur, and Thirukkalaiyanallur. Among these, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed a pathigam for Thirukkarukkudi. One pathigam is located.

Thirukkarukkudi is situated on the road from Kumbakonam to Mannargudi. The Lord’s names are Karukkudinathar, Brahmapureeswarar, Sarkunalinageswarar. The Goddess’s names are Advaitha Nayaki, Kalyana Nayaki, Sarvaalankara Nayaki. The sacred ponds are Yama Theertham and Kaveri. This site is currently known as Maruthandanallur. Since King Sargunan worshipped here and gained fame, the Lord of this site is named Sarguneswarar.

The history of Rameswaram is also told here, and a Lingam called Hanumath Lingam is located here. The Karuvai Vimanas are very tall, the Shiva Lingam is small, and the Avudaiyar is very low. These are notes about the site Maruthandanallur, also known as Thirukkarukkudi. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who resided here, bestowed a pathigam. It is the twenty-first pathigam of the Third Thirumurai. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. nanavilum kanavilum naalun thannoli ninaivilum enaku vandhu eydhum nirmalan kanai kadal vaiyagan thozhu karukkudi analeriyaadum em adigal kaanminae. kaanalil virai malar vimmu kaaliyaan vaanavan karukkudi maindhan thannoli aana meignanasambandhan solliya oonamil mozhi valaarku uyarum inbamae.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman visits many sites. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, a devotee who deeply cherished Lord Shiva in his thoughts, along with other devotees, visits all these sites. He reaches Thirunageswaram.

There, he worships Lord Shiva, who is seated like an incomparable golden mountain, having flayed the skin of a dark elephant and residing as the Lord with the eye on his forehead. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman bows down to that Lord and bestows a melodious pathigam of profound wisdom in sweet Tamil. The ultimate knowledge is Shivagnanam; there is no knowledge superior to it. Shivagnanam encompasses all other knowledge. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman bestows a pathigam filled with such profound wisdom in chaste Tamil upon the Lord of Thirunageswaram. The soil of Nageswaram town, This pathigam carries the precious message that praising Him as ‘Selva, Thalaiva, Arase, Thaye’ will completely destroy all karma.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman bestows this. The pathigams contain references such as ‘Those who are able to worship and praise the beautiful feet will attain beauty’ and ‘Those who are able to see with their eyes are truly blessed with sight.’ We have previously contemplated the local history of Thirunageswaram in the Puranam of Thirunavukkarasar Nayanar.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, after worshipping Thirunageswaram, bestowed two pathigams. Of these, the first pathigam is the one hundred and nineteenth pathigam of the Second Thirumurai, set in Chevvalli tune. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. Thalaikol sandhum agila. Mayil peeliym saadhiyin pazhamum undhi punal paay pazhangaaveri thenkarai nazhuviyil vaanor thozha nalguseer malku naageschuvaraththu azhagarpadham thozhuthu etha vallarkku azhagu aagumae. Kandamnaarum punal kaavery thenkarai kannudhal nandhi serumbathi naageschurathinmel gnananasambandhan naavil panuval ivai patthum vallargal poy endha eesan irukkum ulagu eydha vallargalae.

Now, the second pathigam bestowed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for Thirunageswaram is the twenty-fourth pathigam of the Second Thirumurai, set in Indalam tune. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. Ponner tharu meniyane puriyum minner sadaiyai virai kaaviriyin nannir vayal naageschuvar nagarin mannai Enavalvinai maaindharumae kalamar kadal soozhdharu kaaliyorkon thalamardharu sendhamizhin viragan nalamardharu nageschuraththu aranai sollan maaligal solla nalaa vinaiyae.

After worshipping the lotus-like feet of Lord Shiva, whom Adiseshan worshipped at Thirunageswaram, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman resided there. The local history of Adiseshan worshipping the Lord of Thirunageswaram is present there. Sekkizhar Peruman refers to this thus: Adiseshan is one of the eight principal Nagas. On one Sivaratri, he worshipped the Lord in four temples during four periods of the night. During the first period, he worshipped at Thiruvalanjuzhi, and during the second period, at Thirunageswaram.

During the third period, he worshipped at Thiruppambaram, and during the fourth period, at Thirunagai Karonam.

Thus, Adiseshan worshipped the Lord at these four sites during four periods respectively. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman bestowed pathigams praising such a Lord of Thirunageswaram, stating that worshipping him would destroy evil karma and eliminate suffering. We can also recall here that our great Puranic author, Sekkizhar Swamigal, revered the Lord of this site, the Lord of Thirunageswaram, as his personal deity of worship.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, after bowing down and worshipping Thirunageswaram, proceeded along the banks of the great Kaveri and entered the sacred site of Thiruvidaimarudur. We shall continue our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 639, by Sekkizhar Swamigal, Vambara Varivandu Sarakkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds to Thenkurangaaduthurai. This sacred site, Thenkurangaaduthurai, is the thirty-first site on the south bank of the Kaveri. It is currently known as Aaduthurai. This site received the name Thenkurangaaduthurai because Sugriva and Hanuman, the monkeys, worshipped here.

To the west of this site is an ancient temple called Maruthuvakkudi. The Lord’s name is Aabath Sahayeswarar. The Goddess’s names are Pavalakkodiyamman and Vandarkaru Menkuzhal Ammai. The sacred ponds are Deva Theertham and Sahaya Theertham. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who resided here, bestowed a pathigam. That pathigam is the thirty-fifth pathigam of the Second Thirumurai, set in Indalam tune.

The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: Paaridam sogurae parava kedumvinai paaridum po iravil puram kaattudai nindra arava sedai amna meya azhagai antha meya azhagaar puravar polil so purangaadu thora eravar surangaadu thoraia Nalla payu kaaliul gnana samban nalla payu kaaliul gnana samban kolle rudaiya kurangaadu kurai me nalla kaaliul yaana samba kolle rudaiyanga kurangaadu kurai mela tamil malai patthu pozhuthu. Tamil malai pathu porutha valla vaanavarodu vallavaruv vaanavarodu.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, after bowing down and worshipping at Thenkurangaaduthurai, proceeds to worship the temples of the Lord located near that site. These are believed to be sites like Saathanur. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman visits all these sacred sites. He then reaches Thiruvavaduthurai. Sekkizhar Swamigal states this as follows: “The noble sage of wisdom who came to relieve us of our impurities reached Thiruvavaduthurai,” as mentioned in the 417th verse. Sekkizhar Peruman states that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman came to relieve us of our impurities.

Impurity (malathuyar) refers to the ancient impurity of ego (aanavam) and the suffering of birth caused by it.

Thus, the noble sage of wisdom who came to relieve us of our impurities Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, that great one, reached Thiruvavaduthurai, as sung by Sekkizhar Peruman. It is at this sacred site of Thiruvavaduthurai that he received the inexhaustible purse (ulavakkizhi) to provide for his father’s sacrifices, and he blessed the Vedic sacrifices to proceed. Shiva sacrifices are performed for the world to be free from suffering and to attain salvation. “Having learned and performed sacrifices, they conquered Kali such that it would not come again,” is the sacred saying of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

Thus, he received the inexhaustible purse for performing Shiva sacrifices from the Lord of Thiruvavaduthurai and gave it to his father. The historical event of removing the world’s evil is about to take place here at Thiruvavaduthurai. Sekkizhar Peruman frames it as an introduction, stating, “The noble sage of wisdom who came to alleviate our suffering.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman incarnated to flourish the Vedic path and enlighten the glorious Saivite tradition.

Therefore, his divine incarnation occurred for this very reason, and there was no other purpose for Thirugnanasambandha Peruman to come into this world. We have contemplated the purpose of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s divine incarnation, from “for the world to be uplifted” to “for all sentient and insentient beings to merge with Shiva.” Such a Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who possesses the knowledge to remove our impurities, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who possessed the means of knowledge to bestow grace, is therefore a noble sage of wisdom. Such a Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds to Thiruvavaduthurai. The one residing there is Lord Shiva, the primordial deity, whom even the three gods, Brahma and others, find difficult to comprehend. He is residing in Thiruvavaduthurai. The three are Brahma, Vishnu, and Rudra.

Beyond these three and beyond their three functions, Lord Shiva is the Kartha (doer) who enables those who perform these three functions. The Vedas praise him as the fourth. The Vedas praise him as “Shivam Chaturtham” (Shiva is the fourth). The Thiruvasagam praises him as “Moozavar Konaai Nindra Mudhalvan” (The primeval Lord who stands as the king of the three). Virai Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred saying praises this as “The one primordial being who became the three: Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva.” Thiruvavaduthurai is the sacred site where such a primordial deity, the primal cause, Lord Shiva, resides. Thiruvavaduthurai is the sacred site where Thirumoolanaayanar received grace.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrives there. All the devotees come to greet Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman descends from his pearl palanquin and bows to those who came to greet him before they could bow to him. Before the devotees who came to greet him could attempt to bow to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, he bows to them. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, whose fame is widespread, born among the Brahmins of Seerkazhi to be contemplated as the very essence of the rare Vedas, proceeds to the temple of the Lord with a joyful heart. He worships the tall gopuram of Thiruvavaduthurai, enters, circumambulates the sacred enclosure known as Thirumaligai Pathi, and worships the Lord.

With profound love, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman bows down and rises before the primordial Lord who performs the great dance of grace and who resides as rich nectar within Thiruvavaduthurai, and bestows a pathigam of rare Tamil. Due to our lack of merit, the pathigam bestowed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman at this time is not available to us. With tears flowing like a waterfall due to his overflowing love, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who thus praised before the Lord with overflowing affection, then came out and, filled with joy, resided happily with the devotees in that sacred site of Thiruvavaduthurai. The minds of the devotees are free from sorrow, because future sorrows will become powerless before them; they are those who have attained the blessed state where sorrows have no effect on them. We contemplated in the Puranam of Thirunavukkarasar Peruman, “They bowed and departed, as there was no action to name the great one in a non-dual consciousness.” Such is the state of the devotees, a steadfast nature. And steadfastness, unwavering from that goal, is the nature of the devotees.

Their nature is not to be confused in their mental state; their consciousness does not wander elsewhere but is solely united with the feet of the Lord. The consciousness of the devotees is not affected by anything else. Such devotees are the great ones, embodying the definition of “great ones who perform difficult deeds.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman resides happily with such devotees in Thiruvavaduthurai. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman daily worships the Lord of Thiruvavaduthurai with those devotees. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, alone, goes to the temple to worship. The joy and benefit of worshipping with the devotees is immense, which is the truth stated by the scriptures of wisdom.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman shows us this here. Our contemplation continues. Thiruchitrambalam.
