Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 640, by Sekkizhar Swamigal, Vambara Varivandu Sarakkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman resides in the sacred site of Thiruvavaduthurai.

At this time, the season for performing sacrifices arrives. When Thirugnanasambandha Peruman embarked on his pilgrimage from Seerkazhi, his father, Sivapadahrudayar, requested to accompany him, and Thirugnanasambandha Peruman assented.

Accordingly, Sivapadahrudayar accompanied Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

Now, while residing in Thiruvavaduthurai, the appropriate time for performing sacrifices arrives. Arumukhatthambiran has explained that the Apastamba Sutra states that sacrifices should be performed during the Aavani and Purattasi monsoon seasons, either on a full moon or new moon day.

Therefore, the time for performing such sacrifices has arrived. These sacrifices are prescribed in the Vedas. In the Vedas, various deities such as Agni, Brahma, and Indra have prescribed rituals and sacrifices in general.

However, Shiva worship and sacrifices dedicated to Lord Shiva are particularly lauded and praised among the sacrifices.

Therefore, the Vedic Shiva sacrifices mentioned here are those prescribed in the Vedas. The time for performing such Shiva sacrifices has arrived. Such sacrifices are of three types: Nithyam (daily), Naimithikam (occasional), and Kamikam (optional, performed for specific desires). Among these, the Kamiyishtis are sacrifices that yield benefits in this life and the next. The benefit derived from sacrifices in this life is rain and other such things. The benefit derived from these sacrifices in the afterlife is heavenly pleasures.

Such sacrifices are called Kamiyeshti.

At the same time, for those whose powers have descended (Shakti Nipadars), there are different sacrifices prescribed in the Agamas.

Thus, as the time for performing sacrifices arrived, Sivapada Hrudayar stood before Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and requested the necessary materials for the sacrifices. The time for performing sacrifices had arrived.

Therefore, he needed to go to Seerkazhi to perform the sacrifices, and he needed the materials for them. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s father stood before him and made these requests. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the leader of Pugali, who was bound to guide all the Brahmins living in Pugali (Seerkazhi) according to Vedic injunctions, was about to provide the materials for the sacrifices to the Brahmins of Seerkazhi through his father. When Sivapada Hrudayar set out on his pilgrimage, he had expressed, “I wish to perform sacrifices that will bring joy in both worlds.” For this, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman also consented, and after Sivapadahrudayar accompanied him on his journey, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, recalling all these events, contemplated divine grace. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was one who surrendered all his actions to Shiva, believing them to be Shiva’s actions. “When our actions are known to be futile, and we are not, then His action is itself our action,” states Thiruundhiyar, and accordingly, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman rose, thinking, “Are not these things the sacred feet of my Lord?” “Anthamilla porul” means an endless substance, an indestructible substance.

Therefore, considering that the inexhaustible, imperishable things are the sacred feet of Lord Shiva, our Father, residing in Thiruavaduthurai, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arose from the monastery where he was staying and proceeded to the temple. Sekkizhar Peruman describes this in the following verses: ‘When the time arrived for performing the sacrifice during his stay there, the Father of the peerless Shanmukhars’ leader stood before him, asking for an invaluable object, which the leader heard.’ On hearing the father’s words, The leader, recalling what he had said on an earlier day, with grace in his mind, arose saying, ‘Are not the inexhaustible things the sacred feet of my Father in Thiruavaduthurai?’ Sekkizhar Peruman describes this in verses 422 and 423. What did Thirugnanasambandha Peruman do after arising? He went before the temple where the Lord of the Devas rejoices, stood there, and praised Him, singing the beautiful Tamil pathigam, expressing, ‘I have nothing else to give to those who ask for abundant wealth; I know nothing but Your feet.’ He praised Him with this composition, continuing the structure of the pathigam, which had two additional lines above the four standard lines. With overflowing love, he extolled the feet of the Lord and offered salutations with a devoted mind. These are verses 424 and 425.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who had departed from the monastery, arrived before the temple where the Lord of Lords joyfully resides. He reached the sacred altar of the Thiruavaduthurai temple. He sang a pathigam in beautiful Tamil, asking for the Lord’s great grace, stating, ‘I, Your servant, have nothing else to give to those who seek inexhaustible wealth, a never-diminishing fund. Your sacred feet are our only wealth. I know no other support than Your sacred feet.’ Thirugnanasambandha Peruman initiated the beautiful Tamil pathigam with the intention of seeking grace, stating that he had nothing else to offer to those who sought it, and thus meditated upon the Lord’s sacred feet. The words of Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, ‘My mind has contemplated Your sacred feet alone, without any other attachments,’ come to our remembrance.

Sekkizhar Swamigal describes Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s thought, expressed in the pathigam, ‘If I have nothing to give,’ as he contemplated and worshipped the Lord’s great grace, saying, ‘I have nothing else to give to those who ask.’ In accordance with the Thevaram’s sacred words, ‘Is that not Your sweet grace?’, he seeks the Lord’s sweet grace with the intent of obtaining wealth. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises the Lord and composes a beautiful Tamil pathigam, seeking wealth. He presents this rich Tamil pathigam in a structure called ‘Naladi Mel Vaippu,’ meaning ‘an addition of two lines over the four standard lines.’ This pathigam, beginning with ‘Idarinum Thalarinum’ (even in distress, even in weariness), is structured with two added lines over the standard four lines. Mostly, verses composed of four lines are called Virutham.

However, each verse of this pathigam is composed of four lines with an additional two lines appended in a varying style, bringing it to completion. Since two lines are added to the four standard lines, this is referred to as ‘Naladi Mel Vaippu.’ The Thiru Koodiyur pathigam ‘Kottamē Kamalūm’ was composed in the ‘Eeradi Mel Vaippu’ (two lines over two lines) style. The Thiru Aiyaru pathigam ‘Mādar Pirai Kaṇṇiyānai’ by Thirunavukkarasu Peruman was presented as a ‘Mel Vaippu.’ We can compare all these here. Sekkizhar Peruman refers to the two added lines as ‘Seer’ (meaning ‘lines of poetry’ or ‘metrical feet’), as they establish and conclude the meaning of the previous four lines, set to a different musical arrangement and rhythm. Although these four and two lines have a varying musical structure, this pathigam is arranged to be continuously sung to achieve the sweetness of the musical mode. With abundant love, he praises the Lord’s peerless sacred feet in his mind, composing the pathigam with his words and offering salutations.

He composes this pathigam, beginning with ‘Idarinum Thalarinum,’ as the fourth pathigam in the third Thirumurai, set to the tune of Kanthara Panchamam. This pathigam, composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman at Thiruavaduthurai, seeking the Lord’s great grace, is as follows: (Iḍariṉum taḷariṉum eṉatu iṭṭarum turaittuvāyum vārēṉum; Uḷaṇati āvatukurai iraṇe; Āvatukurai iraṇe; Naṉaviṉum kapaṉum kaṟai tamiḻum; Avaṟuvum taruvalum māṟā; Avaṟuvu vāyam terumē.) (Iḍarīyum taḷarīyum eṉatu iṭṭarum turaittuvāyum vārēṉum; Uḷaṇati āvatukurai iraṇe; Puṉalai terum kuṟai pōdā; Aḻal terum nuḻakē kaiya vaṇe; Iḍarīyum taḷarīyum eṉatu iṭṭarum turaittuvāyum vārēṉum; Uḷaṇati āvatukurai iraṇe; Puduvu.) (Kūṟiya tu tōṟēṉu mālaiyalar aṟṟātūṉai; Madhuvai ciṟai kalai oṉṟi eliyala muṉintavane; Iḍarīyum taḷarīyum eṉatu iṭṭarum turaittuvāyum vārēṉum; Uḷaṇati āvatukurai iraṇe; Kaiyatu vīraṉu talai muriyum; Ceytal aṭiyalār cintai ceyya toyyala.) (Kuḻāy cūṭarūṭai varaiya vaṇe; Iḍarīyum taḷarīyum eṉatu iṭṭarum turaittuvāyum vārēṉum; Uḷaṇati āvatukurai iraṇe; Kuyar pōṉṟi pērumurai enta ettāvit talaiyala; Kuṇṭa araitta caittha cantaram kōḻiyane cantaṟaṇe; Irum pō iṟaiyumāli vakunta macchuta.) (Athu unathu aruḷ āvaṭu kuṟaiyaṟaṇe; Veppoḍu vīra vīraṉappā uṇṭiyalum nuṭai poruvaṉai uruva appaṭiyala pitthavaṇe; Iru pō emai ārumaluvuṉra mayuḷ atu uṇati aruḷ āvaṭu kuṟaiyaṟaṇe; Perithal peruvariṉ.)

(Paraṇta cintai ceyya eṟuṇai maṇi muṭi tirāvaṇai āliṭpaṭavarai aṭaththavaṇe; Iru pō emai ārumāri vakuṇṭa macchu ēṇati ṇuḷ āvaṭu tuṇaiyaṟaṇe; Uṉilum pacippum ulakilum maṭai aṭainthathār uṟaiyātūṅka; Thaḷḷanum paṭiththavaḷ tavaṟai mēlum nalapaṟi mē āyavar.) (Iru pōyāḷum āntamaiyuḷḷa ēṇati rakuḷ āvaṭu puṟaiyaṟaṇe; Piņṭoṭu payaṅkiyō kiṟaiyum appaṭe aṟṟāvina puttāṇ cantarum puruṇṇūrai pattakaruḷ ceytu payiṉṟavaṇe; Iru pōyāḷum āntamaiyuḷḷa ētu uḷukila rakuḷ āvaṭu puṟaiyaṟaṇe.) (Iḷai nuḻai paṭai eṉalampi yāṉa campu coṉṉa; Niḷaimuṭai aruntaṟi vāḻai valla niḷaiyāyirōy tirunaḷarē; Viyanuḷakam niḷaiyāka muṉṉēṟuvar niḷaicci taikē niḷaiyila; Viḷaiyāy nalaru viyanuḷakam niḷaiyāka muṉṉēṟuvar niḷaicci tai niḷaiyila.) Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sang this pathigam, stating, ‘The Lord’s sacred feet are my only wealth; I know of no other wealth.’ In accordance with Thirugnanasambandha Pillaiyar’s desire, by the grace of the Lord who had previously bestowed grace, a Shiva-bhuta quickly came and placed an undiminishing purse of thousand pure gold coins on top of the sacred altar of the Thiruavaduthurai temple.

We shall proceed with our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 641, by Sekkizhar Swamigal, ‘Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam,’ Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. As Pillaiyar desired, Lord Shiva, who had previously bestowed grace, now also bestows grace as Pillaiyar desires. The desire of the Lord for Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is the Lord’s own desire.

The Lord has no desire for Himself. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s desire now becomes the Lord’s desire. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states this as ‘My word is His word.’ Therefore, to bestow grace as Thirugnanasambandha Peruman desired, one of the Shiva-bhuta ganas came and stood before the Thiruavaduthurai temple. It placed a purse containing a thousand pure gold coins on the sacred altar there. ‘Pure gold’ refers to gold of excellent purity, refined and precious. ‘Purse’ means a bundle.

Thus, a gold bundle was placed on the sacred altar of the Thiruavaduthurai temple. Even today, the images of the bhuta and Pillaiyar are depicted on the sacred altar of the Thiruavaduthurai temple. This event of Pillaiyar receiving the inexhaustible purse is celebrated on the fourth day of the Brahmotsavam. Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal praised this event by saying, ‘It is as if a thousand pure gold coins were given to the resident of Kazhumalam.’ The Shiva-bhuta that placed the inexhaustible purse on top of the sacred altar, stood there and addressed Pillaiyar with kind words, saying, ‘This purse contains gold, an inexhaustible treasure that will not diminish no matter how much is taken.

The Lord has bestowed this upon you.’ Thus, the Shiva-bhuta stood before Pillaiyar and spoke. Upon hearing the bhuta’s words and witnessing the grace revealed by them, Pillaiyar worshipped.

Lord Shiva is eternal, and therefore the wealth He bestows is also eternal, becoming an inexhaustible purse that does not diminish no matter how much is taken. That inexhaustible purse lies on the sacred altar, adorned with flowers. The flowers on that sacred altar are for the daily worship. are offered. The bhuta placed the inexhaustible purse upon those flowers. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman bowed, stood up, folded his hands in worship, took the gold purse from the sacred altar, placed it on his head, and praised the Lord. He said that since this is the Lord’s grace and wealth, it is proper to place it on his head, and he did so, praising and extolling Lord Shiva, the great Being confirmed by various scriptures.

He rejoiced and worshipped, saying that for Vedic sacrifices, it is indeed proper that the Vedas themselves provide the means. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman gave the gold purse to his father, who possessed a pure and truthful mind, and said: Following the injunctions of the great scriptures, and with Lord Shiva, the primal God with matted locks adorned with the Ganga, as the foremost, perform good Shiva-yagas so that all beings in this world may be freed from evil and attain happiness. All those Vedic Brahmins residing in Sirkazhi, perform that Shiva-yaga.

Thus spoke Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. The Vedas are the primary great scriptures, the source of all knowledge. Shiva is the one who gave these Vedas, the primal great scriptures.

Therefore, perform good sacrifices directed towards Lord Shiva as prescribed in such Vedas. Many sacrifices for various deities are prescribed in the Vedas.

Therefore, separating all these, he directs them to perform good sacrifices directed towards Lord Shiva alone. He says that even if sacrifices are performed for other deities, it is Lord Shiva who bestows grace through those deities.

Therefore, he advises to perform these sacrifices so that the world may be freed from its evils and attain benefits in this life and the next. He instructs all the Vedic Brahmins of Sirkazhi to perform this sacrifice. This indicates that all the Vedic Brahmins of Sirkazhi are pure-handed, disciplined in performing Vedic sacrifices for the happiness of this world. Having spoken all this and handed the gold purse to his father, his father, filled with great joy, set off towards Sirkazhi. Bidding farewell to his father, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman remained there, joyful and serene in his heart and outwardly. He remains there, joyfully and pleasantly seated at Thiruavaduthurai, worshipping with devotion.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is happy there because, with the wealth received by the grace of the Lord, his father and the Vedic Brahmins have worked to free this world from evil.

Thus, after residing there for some days, he remains seated, worshipping the Lord, who lovingly resides at Thiruavaduthurai, with abundant love in his heart. Sekkizhar Peruman describes this graceful event of Pillaiyar receiving the inexhaustible purse at Thiruavaduthurai.

Afterwards, Pillaiyar takes leave of the Lord from Thiruavaduthurai and proceeds to the sacred place called Thirukozhambam. He worships the Lord with matted locks adorned with konrai flowers at Thirukozhambam. Thirukozhambam is the thirty-fifth temple on the south bank of the Kaveri. It is now known as Kozhambiyam. This is the place where Chandan, a Vidyadhara cursed to become a cuckoo bird, worshipped the Lord and was freed from his curse. It is referred to as ‘Kuyil Payil Pozhil’ in Thirukurunthogai.

The Lord’s name is Kokileshwar, according to tradition. Kozhambanathar is another name.

Here, the Goddess’s name is Soundarya Nayaki. The Madhu Theertham is a sacred pond. The verse ‘Samarasoorapanmavai Thaditha’ speaks of the greatness of Lord Muruga here. This verse is greatly admired. It holds the distinction of being widely recited by many devotees. That sacred verse appears as the tenth song in the pathigam composed by Thirunavukkarasu Peruman for this temple.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who visited this temple, composed a pathigam. It is the thirteenth pathigam in the second Thirumurai, set to the Indalam tune. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thus, at Thirukozhambam, he sang a pathigam with pleasant music before the Lord. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman then proceeds to Thiruvaygal Maadakovil, where the Lord of Thiruvambalam joyfully resides. Vaygal is the name of the town, and Maadakovil refers to the temple built by our Lord Kochchengan Chola Nayanar. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worshipped the great Physician residing in the towering Maadakovil of Vaygal, falling at His feet with folded hands, rising, and praising Him with sweet Tamil garlands as tears streamed from his eyes like a waterfall.

The pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for Thiruvaygal Maadakovil is the eighteenth pathigam in the third Thirumurai, set to the Kanthara Panchamam tune. The first, second, and eleventh verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Tuḷamathi udai maṟi tōṉṟu kaiyinar iḷamathi aṭai entai yāriṭam uḷamathi uṭaiyavar vaikaḷ vāḻiya vaḷamathi taṭavya māṭak kōyile; Meyyakam mīḷum vētayarū mayakam malai makaḷōṭum vayaliṭam vaiyakam makizthara vaikaḷ vētiyai ceyya kavaḷar.) The pathigam indicates that the Maadakovil built by the red-eyed king in the western direction of Vaikal city is the abode of our Father. Vaikal Maadakovil. This great temple on the western side of the town of Vaygal, which is the 33rd temple on the south bank of the Kaveri, was sung by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. There is also a temple on the eastern side.

The Lord’s name is Vaygalnathar, and the Goddess’s name is Kombil Ilangodhai. This temple is near Aduthurai. Having worshipped at Vaygal Maadakovil, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds to the sacred place called Thiru Nallam, also known as Koneri Rajapuram.

We shall continue our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 642, by Sekkizhar Swamigal, ‘Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam,’ Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman departs from Thiruvaygal Maadakovil and proceeds to the sacred place called Thiru Nallam, also known as Koneri Rajapuram. Thiru Nallam is the 34th temple on the south bank of the Kaveri. It is now called Koneri Rajapuram and is located near Aduthurai. It is easily accessible from Kumbakonam.

The Lord’s names are Uma Maheswar, Bhoomeeswarar, and Bhoominathar. The Goddess’s names are Thega Soundari and Angavalanayaki. Brahma Theertham and Sakthi Theertham are the sacred ponds here.

The Lord here is said to have cured the leprosy of King Pururavas. It is said that chanting mantras in the presence of this Lord yields manifold benefits. This temple was renovated by Sembiyan Mahadevi, the wife of Gandaraditya Chola. In inscriptions, the Lord is referred to as Thiru Nallam Udaiyar. Inscriptional records also state that Kundavai Pirattiyar donated many gifts to this temple. The Sthalapuranam (temple chronicle) is in Sanskrit.

This temple has one pathigam composed by Appar Swamigal and one by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal has beautifully composed a Thirukurunthogai on the Lord of this sacred place, Thiru Nallam, saying: (Kolla-than Namanaar thamar vantha-kaal Illathaar seiyalavathu en Ezhai-kaal Nallathaan namai aaludaiyaan kazhal Sollathaan vallireththuyar theerume). Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal has beautifully composed this Thirukurunthogai on the Lord of this sacred place, Thirunallam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who visited this place, composed a pathigam. It is the 85th pathigam in the first Thirumurai, beginning with ‘Kallaal Nizhal Meya,’ set to the Kurinji tune. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman offered sweet Tamil garlands, bowing before the brilliant sacred feet of the Lord, the luminous jewel who long resided in Thirunallam.

Pillaiyar then praised and worshipped many of the Lord’s sacred temples, which were nearby. These are considered to be places like Sirukudi, Thirumiyachchur, Thirumiyachchur Ilangovil, Thiruppambaram, Thirukutthangudi, Thiruvazhuvur, and others. In this region, several branches of the Kaveri, such as Thenkovai Aru, Nanthalaru, Veerachozhan Aru, flowed in those days, enriching the land. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman visited and worshipped in such places. Among these, we have pathigams composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for Thiruchirukudi and Thiruvazhunthur. Thiruchirukudi is a sacred place where Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s Thevaram was sung.

It is a sacred place in Tamil Nadu, near Kumbakonam, close to Mayiladuthurai, after Peralam. You can reach Thiruchirukudi by crossing the Arisilaru bridge, taking a right turn onto the Kumbakonam-Nachiyar Kovil road, and then taking another right turn from Kadagampadi. The Lord’s names are Sukshmapureeswarar, Mangalanathar, and Sirukudiyisar. The Goddess’s names are Mangalanayaki and Mangalambikai. Theertham (sacred pond) is Mangala Theertham. It is said that the Goddess created and worshipped at Mangala Theertham by holding a handful of sand, and because the Goddess worshipped with a small handful (Sirupidi), Sirupidi became Sirukudi.

The presiding Ganesha is Mangala Vinayagar. In Sangam literature, Puhar This is the place where Pannan, one of the famous philanthropists lauded in Sangam literature, lived. The main deity is a Swayambhu (self-manifested) form with an indentation on the forehead and hand-held marks on both sides. The special icon of this temple is the Santhosha Alingana Murthy, which is very unique. The beauty of the Santhosha Alingana Murthy lies in the way the Goddess, pleased with Her worship, is embraced, with Her arm placed on Her shoulder. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, visiting such a special temple, composed a pathigam in the ‘Thirumukkal’ style.

It is the 97th pathigam in the third Thirumurai, set to the Sadhari tune. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Moḻi mathili ciṟukuṭi mē paṭamoḻi aṟavuṭaiyarē paṭamoḻi aṟavuṭaiyai umai paṇipavar aṭaivatū amarūlukatūvē; Namar pōlēḻa nī ciṟukuṭi mēṇamaru karam uṭaiyarē māṇamaru karam uṭaiyīr umai vāḻthiya ñāṉa campuṉa tamiḻē.) Having worshipped thus at Thiruchirukudi, the sixtieth temple on the south bank of the Kaveri, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman visited all the nearby temples and then proceeded to Thiruvazhunthur, which was praised by him as ‘Mannu Mamadam’ (a great, permanent monastery).

There, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises the great Being, the Lord, who joyfully resides there. Thiruvazhunthur is the thirty-eighth temple on the south bank of the Kaveri. It is now called Therazhunthur. It is said that this town got its name, Therazhunthur (where the chariot sank), because a chariot driven by King Urdhvathan, unaware that Agastya Muni was worshipping the Lord below, got stuck in the sky and could not proceed past this place. This is a place worshipped by the Dikpalakas, Vedas, Devas, and Sages. This sacred place is located on the Mayiladuthurai-Kumbakonam road.

The Lord’s names are Vedapureeswarar and Athyapakeswarar. The Goddess’s names are Soundaryambikai. Veda Theertham and Vedamritha Theertham are the sacred ponds. A beautiful story is told in the history of this sacred place. There was a thief named Karkasan. The king’s servants caught him and dragged him to the king.

It was a Monday. The Therazhunthur Vedapureeswarar Swamy Temple was decorated with oil lamps, and a deeparadhana (lamp offering) was underway.

At that time, the name ‘Hara Hara Hara Hara’ resonated everywhere. Upon hearing this name ‘Hara Hara’, Karkasan, the thief, became absorbed in the name ‘Hara Hara’ and attained a state of trance. Unaware of this, the servants greatly tortured Karkasan, causing his body to weaken. Messengers of Yama arrived with the noose of time to take his life.

But Shiva’s messengers also appeared there and came to take Karkasan. This was because, at the time of his death, Karkasan had meditated on Vedapureeswarar with the name ‘Hara Hara.’ Therefore, Shiva’s messengers told Yama’s messengers that Karkasan should be taken to Kailash, and they took him to Kailash.

Thus, it is considered highly auspicious to worship Therazhunthur Vedapureeswarar on a Monday. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who visited this sacred place, composed a pathigam. It is the twentieth pathigam in the second Thirumurai. It is the twentieth pathigam in the second Thirumurai, set to the Indalam tune. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Māṟu vallum icai pāṭa aḻum māṟu valli pāṭu ceyṟayō Peru ñāṉam ūṭai perumāṉā.) This pathigam expresses wonder at the Lord, saying, ‘Oh Lord, you eternally reside in the great monastery, where the Brahmins of Azhunthur perform worship.’ Our contemplation continues. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 643, by Sekkizhar Swamigal, ‘Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam,’ Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Pillaiyar, having left Thiruavaduthurai, the south bank of the Kaveri, travelled a long distance south and worshipped at places like Thirukozhambam, Thiruvaygal, Thirunallam, and Thiruvazhunthur. He then turned north again and reached the bank of the Kaveri. He arrived at Thiruthuruthi, a temple on the Kaveri bank, and praised the Lord ‘Sonnavaaru Arivar’ (He who knows as said). The Lord’s name at Thiruthuruthi is ‘Sonnavaaru Arivar.’ This name came about because the Lord Himself knew and proclaimed the Vedas for the benefit of beings, and because He Himself, as a Brahmachari, resided and recited the Vedas at this sacred place, according to its history.

After reciting the Vedas at Thiruthuruthi, he married the Goddess at Thiruvelvidi according to the prescribed rites, which is also part of its history. We have contemplated the special features of Thiruthuruthi in the Puranam of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. Pillaiyar, who arrived at Thiruthuruthi, composed a pathigam. Sekkizhar Swamigal refers to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s pathigam as ‘Varaithalai Pasum Pon enum Vandamil Pathigam Uraithu Meyyura Paninthu Ponthu’ (a pathigam of beautiful Tamil that speaks of pure gold from the mountains, which he recited, deeply bowed, and departed). This pathigam praises the Lord by questioning His divine qualities, expressing wonders like, ‘You have placed one woman in Your body, yet You remain a yogi in separation; what is this mystery?’ Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises the Lord with this pathigam, questioning His divine qualities. In the fifth verse of this pathigam, Pillaiyar says, ‘You made me, who cannot forget, infatuated and showed me how to be born on this earth.’ This pathigam is notable for Pillaiyar’s greatness in remembering and praising his previous state.

In the fifth verse of this pathigam, Pillaiyar says, ‘Tell me how to renounce; O Lord of Thiruthuruthi, You made me, who cannot forget Your sacred feet, infatuated and showed me how to be born on this earth.’ This pathigam is the 98th pathigam in the second Thirumurai, This pathigam is composed. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Varaittalaip paṟum poṉoṭu aruṅkalāṉkaḷ iṟaittalaittū malārntu koṇṭu ilaṅkā uraittalaittū pōḻinta uṇarttumāṟu vallamē kaṟṟu.) ThiruGnanasambandha, who became the full, complete ancient Tamil of the world, whose wealth was elevated by One, and who obtained complete salvation, came and bowed down thus, correcting the lack. Lord ThiruGnanasambandha arrives at the holy site of ThiruMooaloor. With fervent desire, he praises the Lord enshrined in ThiruMooaloor with words of devotion, standing in adoration and approaching with eagerness to worship the Lord there. ThiruMooaloor is one of the temples mentioned in the Thevaram hymns.

This site is also lauded in Thirukovaiyar. It is situated on the southern bank of the Cauvery, east of Thiruthuruthi, on the way to Mayuram. This holy site is where Sri Namasivaya Moorthigal, who founded the Thiruvavaduthurai Adheenam monastery, which has fostered Saiva Siddhanta, was born. After worshipping the Lord at this significant ThiruMooaloor, Lord ThiruGnanasambandha arrives at Mayiladuthurai, a place of abundant groves. The wealthy Brahmins living in Mayiladuthurai, surrounded by dense groves, along with the devotees, come forward to welcome Lord ThiruGnanasambandha. Sekkizhar Peruman states: “He came to ThiruMayiladuthurai, surrounded by tanks and fragrant with flowers, the leader of Pukali, praised by the first leader of Mooaloor, with fervent love, celebrating Him.” Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing: “He rose with boundless joy, worshipped and entered the temple where the playful deer’s fawn is offered, met by wealthy Brahmins and devotees in Mayiladuthurai, rich with groves.” Thus, with inner joy and overflowing love, he melts and sings a pathigam in clear, sweet musical verses.

Lord ThiruGnanasambandha composed two pathigams at ThiruMayiladuthurai. The first pathigam is the seventieth pathigam in the Third Thirumurai, set to Sadari pan. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Aanappoogal Vedhiargal aagudhiyum medhu poovai pogi azhagooru solai veesai maasupada moosoo mayiladu kooraike dhinam tharu mayanam melam vaanamadhiyoru suzha mudukka ganam thozhu kabaal etti meega vaaithoru kaadhal maiya manam thanmazhi mara) This pathigam’s central theme is the devotee’s immersion in the boundless bliss of the Lord’s grace, with a deeply loving heart, recognizing Mayiladuthurai as the Lord’s ancient abode. The second pathigam sung by Lord ThiruGnanasambandha for ThiruMayiladuthurai is the thirty-eighth pathigam in the First Thirumurai, set to Thakkaragam pan. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Maamalaru kuravum paagallum sirangundriyul yaana sambaladu koorai melu)

The core message of this pathigam is that the Lord’s abode is Mayiladuthurai.

Thus, Lord ThiruGnanasambandha bows and worships ThiruMayiladuthurai. We have reflected on the history of ThiruMayiladuthurai in the purana of Thirunavukkarasu. From ThiruMayiladuthurai, Lord ThiruGnanasambandha proceeds to ThiruChemponpalli, a temple of the Lord. ThiruChemponpalli is known as Semponar Kovil. We have also considered the special features of this temple in the purana of Thirunavukkarasa Nayanar. Lord ThiruGnanasambandha, having arrived at ThiruChemponpalli, composes a pathigam.

It is the twenty-fifth pathigam of the First Thirumurai, set to Thakkaraga pan. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: The central theme of this pathigam is that sin and karma accrue to those who do not worship the Lord of ThiruChemponpalli.

Thus, Lord ThiruGnanasambandha, having worshipped ThiruChemponpalli, proceeds to ThiruVilnagar to convey that the joy of worshipping the Lord, when experienced alongside the joy of being with devotees, culminates in supreme bliss, which the world should realize for its salvation. This joy is enhanced by sharing it with devotees. ThiruVilnagar is the fortieth temple on the south bank of the Cauvery, located east of Mayiladuthurai. The Lord’s name is Thuraikattum Vallal Ujjivaneswarar, and the Goddess’s name is Veyiru Thozhiyamman. The sacred waters are Meignana Theertham and the Cauvery. When a Brahmin named Arulvitthagar was carrying a basket of flowers for the Lord, the river current swept him away.

The Lord guided him to the shore and graced him.

Therefore, the Lord of this temple is named Thuraikattum Vallal (the benevolent one who shows the way). This is also mentioned in the Thevaram pathigam of this temple. This is the temple where King Kapistan worshipped and was freed from the sin of Brahmicide. This temple is under the spiritual administration of the Dharmapuram Adheenam. Lord ThiruGnanasambandha, who arrived here, composed a pathigam. It is the seventy-eighth pathigam of the Second Thirumurai, set to Gandhara pan.

The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Pulirilam mazhai tamil polil pola neer malgu kaveri nalirilam pona vaarthoorai nangai gangaiyai nanrunithalirilam pori aravi meyyathu veera nagarathe men sirai vandhu yaazh moorai vigala thoorai mevaiya) The core message of this pathigam is that the Lord resides in ThiruVazhi Nagar, located on the banks of the Cauvery, where the good moon, first, and conch-like Tamil are spoken.

Our reflection shall continue. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 644, by Sekkizhar Swamigal, Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam, ThiruGnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Having completed his visit to ThiruVazhinagar, Pillaiyar proceeds to ThiruPariyalur. ThiruPariyalur is a place where the Primordial Lord, adorned with Konrai and Thumbai flowers in his red matted hair, is pleased to reside. This is one of the Lord’s Ashta Veerastanam temples. This temple is praised within its own pathigam as Veerattathane of ThiruPariyalur and ThiruPariyal Veerattathaan.

ThiruPariyal Veerattam is the forty-first temple on the southern bank of the Cauvery. It is currently known as Parasaloor. This is the site where the heroic act of Daksha Yaga Samharam (destruction of Daksha’s sacrifice) took place. It is one of the eight sites where the Lord performed heroic deeds. This place is named ThiruPariyalur because the Lord punished the sins of the Devas who participated in Daksha’s sacrifice, thereby plucking away their transgressions. In this temple, Veerabhadra Swami is enshrined, as is Daksha.

The Lord’s name is Veeratteswarar, and the Goddess is Ilankombaiyal. This temple is located east of ThiruVazhinagar, which is east of Mayiladuthurai. It is also very close to Sempanar Kovil.

The Lord also has the name Dakshapurishwarar. Uttaravedi Theertham, Sivagangai Theertham, and Chandra Pushkarani are the sacred waters. Within the sanctum wall, there is a sculpture of Daksha worshipping the Lingam. The Moolavar (presiding deity) is a large, self-manifested Swayambhumurthy, with a square Aavudaiyar and a changed Gomugam (spout). This temple does not have the nine Navagrahas; only Suryanar is present. Ardha Jama (midnight worship) is performed for Bhairava here.

In an inscription from the reign of Sundara Pandiyan, this temple is referred to as Pariyalur, which is Jeyankonda Chola Valanattu Veezha Nattu Rajanarayana Chaturvedi Mangalam, and the Lord’s name is mentioned as Thiru Veerattanudaiyar and Daksheshwaramudaiyar.

The Guru Maha Sannidanam of Thiruvavaduthurai Adheenam, Sri La Sri Velappadeika Swamigal, has composed a Sthala Puranam for this temple. Lord ThiruGnanasambandha, who visited this place, composed a pathigam. It is the one hundred and thirty-fourth pathigam of the First Thirumurai, set to Megharaga Kurinji pan. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Thanaiyadhum) (Raniyana Meerana poova poonai patt arun nera arun peerputth arun pilapu) The central theme of this pathigam is that the Lord, known by qualities such as being the Creator and the Establisher, is enshrined in Veerattathanam at ThiruPariyalur.

Having thus worshipped and praised ThiruPariyalur Veerattam, Lord ThiruGnanasambandha, with fervent love, reaches the seashore from there and proceeds to worship many of the Lord’s shrines along the way. Sekkizhar Peruman states that Pillaiyar’s journey will now proceed along the coastline instead of overland from ThiruPariyalur. From ThiruPariyalur, the coastline is about ten Nazhigai (roughly 4 hours walking distance) away to the east. Lord ThiruGnanasambandha worships all the shrines located here. These shrines are believed to be ThiruIdaikali, ThiruAlappur, and other similar places.

Thus, he worships these shrines and proceeds to visit the temples along the coastline. These shrines, including ThiruIdaikali and ThiruAlappur, are intermediate shrines. After worshipping them, he goes to visit the coastal temples. This temple is special because Lord Muruga is praised here. Lord Muruga is enshrined here in a standing posture, worshipping Lord Shiva. The Kuram tree is the sacred tree of this temple.

This temple is located a short distance west of ThiruAlappur. The next temple is ThiruAlappur, which is a Thevaram Vaipputhalam (a temple mentioned in Thevaram hymns).

Sundaramoorthy Swamigal has sung about this ThiruAlappur in the Oorthogai Thevaram as “Aarooratta Ayattu Amude Alappur Ammane.” This ThiruAlappur temple is situated east of Thillaiyadi and is near the seashore. Lord ThiruGnanasambandha, having visited ThiruIdaikazhi and ThiruAlappur, takes the road south from ThiruAlappur, which is the Tharangambadi Karaikal road, and reaches a village called Varichikudi. From there, he turns east and reaches the holy site of ThiruVettakkudi. With great joy, the devotees welcome him. Lord ThiruGnanasambandha goes and worships at ThiruVettakkudi. Lord ThiruGnanasambandha composes a pathigam for ThiruVettakkudi.

ThiruVettakkudi is the forty-ninth temple on the southern bank of the Cauvery. This is the place where the Lord appeared in the form of a hunter for Arjuna. It is said that every night, a sight resembling fire burning can be seen on the seashore east of the sanctum. This is mentioned in the pathigam as “He who rejoiced in the burning of fire.” The Lord’s name is ThiruMezhni Azhagar. The sacred waters are Deva Theertham and Azhagu Theertham. The area where the temple is located is called Koil Medu.

According to the purana, Goddess Uma Devi was born into a fishing community in this place. The hunter who came as the head In the second verse of this pathigam, Lord ThiruGnanasambandha has sung specifically about the burning fire, that is, the sight resembling fire burning every night on the seashore, in the second verse of this pathigam. He has sung in the second verse, “He who rejoiced in the burning fire is the Lord of ThiruVettakkudi.” The first, second, and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Thondiraitthu kozhu thiraindha kulangu kozhi neer kudarpbalam thiraigal konarum theriyum ThiruVettakkudiyare vaaitthu milar valaiyodu meen vaari payinru engum kaasinily konarndhu attum kaidhal sodhanikkana oyiravil keyodum kulankaattil purindha) (Eri kai magizhndha ThiruVettakkudiyare thirai seppaiyal udukka ThiruVettakkudiyare thalai kaali tamil yaana sambi vaippum unarndhe thalladukkil vaanavarodu uyarvaana iruppe uyarvaana)

The core message of this pathigam is that Lord Paranjothi Sivamoorthy, the God of gods, resides in ThiruVettakkudi.

Let us resume our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 645, by Sekkizhar Swamigal, Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam, ThiruGnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. From ThiruVettakkudi, Lord ThiruGnanasambandha proceeds along the seashore, reaching the great cities of the fertile Chola Nadu, and worships them with devotion. Pillaiyar, Lord ThiruGnanasambandha, with his coral-like mouth that expounds the paths to salvation for this world, made it known to the world that the principles of Jains and Buddhists are flawed, and guided people accordingly. Not only did he declare them flawed, but he also revealed the path to salvation for the world. Lord ThiruGnanasambandha, the religious leader, exemplified the Saiva path.

In all of Lord ThiruGnanasambandha’s pathigams, in the tenth verse, we can see the condemnation of Jains and Buddhists. Sekkizhar Peruman had previously shown us, “He said it was a fault, a wrong, the path of the Jains and Buddhists who lack understanding.” We can recall this here.

Therefore, not only did he state that the principles of Jainism and Buddhism were flawed, but he also showed that the path by which all souls could attain salvation was indeed the Saiva path. Such was Pillaiyar ThiruGnanasambandha. Pillaiyar, as mentioned above, worshipped all the shrines in Chola Nadu and reached the site of ThiruDharumapuram. At this ThiruDharumapuram, Lord ThiruGnanasambandha is about to perform a miraculous act of grace. He is going to sing a glorious Tamil pathigam that cannot be fully contained by the Yazh music. Such is the glory of the site called ThiruDharumapuram.

ThiruDharumapuram is the fifty-first temple on the southern bank of the Cauvery. This is the place where Dharma, one of the Pandavas, worshipped the Lord and received blessings. Brahma Deva also worshipped here. This is the birthplace of the mother of Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar. This holy site is famous for the history of Aludaiya Pillaiyar composing the Yazhmuri Pan pathigam when he arrived here. We are about to witness that sacred history.

The Lord of this holy site has a very beautiful emerald-like Lingam. The Lord’s names are Yazhmurinathar and Dharmapurishwarar. The Goddess’s names are Madhuramin Ammai and Thenamirthavalli. Dharma Theertham and Brahma Theertham are the sacred waters. Yama, the king of righteousness, worshipped the Lord here and received blessings to atone for his error of attempting to seize Markandeya’s life.

Therefore, this place is named Dharumapuram. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, in the first verse of the second pathigam, Pukka Thiruthandaka pathigam, of the Sixth Thirumurai, has sung about this holy site as a Vaipputhalam, stating “Dharumapuraththu Ullaar.” Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, in the first verse of the twelfth pathigam of the Seventh Thirumurai, has sung about this holy site as a Vaipputhalam, mentioning “Thakkaloor Dharumapuram.” Therefore, this holy site is mentioned in the Thirumuraikal with one pathigam by Lord ThiruGnanasambandha, and two verses as Vaipputhalams in the sacred utterances of Appar Swamigal and Sundaramoorthy Swamigal. Sekkizhar Peruman states that Lord ThiruGnanasambandha arrived at ThiruDharumapuram, surrounded by flag-adorned ramparts. Since Dharumapuram is the birthplace of the great panar’s mother, his relatives came to greet him, bowed at his feet, and offered praises. Seeing this, the great panar, filled with pride, said to them, “Pillaiyar has composed a precious pathigam that I am skilled at playing on the yazh.” This ThiruDharumapuram is the birthplace of Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar’s mother. Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar, accompanied by his wife Mathangachoolamani Ammaiyar and carrying his yazh, has been journeying with Pillaiyar to various shrines.

It is also well-known that Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar received the great blessing from Lord ThiruGnanasambandha to set all the pathigams composed by Pillaiyar to music with the accompaniment of his yazh. This ThiruDharumapuram is the birthplace of Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar’s mother.

Therefore, all of Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar’s relatives come forward to welcome Pillaiyar and Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar. Previously, when Lord ThiruGnanasambandha visited ThiruNanippalli, which is the birthplace of Lord ThiruGnanasambandha’s mother, we saw that all of her relatives came forward to welcome Pillaiyar.

Similarly, here, all of Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar’s relatives come forward to welcome him. Generally, wherever Lord ThiruGnanasambandha visits, devotees and Shiva devotees welcome Pillaiyar with reverence.

However, here, along with the devotees, Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar’s relatives also welcome him. There is a difference: the way of welcoming Lord ThiruGnanasambandha is distinct from the way relatives welcome him. The welcome by devotees and Shiva devotees is rooted in a higher spiritual connection, while the welcome by relatives is based on a bodily connection. This difference forms the basis for the sacred event that is about to unfold in ThiruDharumapuram, as Sekkizhar Peruman sets the stage. All of Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar’s relatives come forward, bow, and offer their praises. To them, Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar explains, “Lord ThiruGnanasambandha, Aludaiya Pillaiyar, has bestowed upon me the great blessing of being able to set his precious pathigams to the yazh and play them.” Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar explains this to all his relatives.

Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar, the great panar, speaks thus, with a joyful heart, imbued with the supreme blessing received through his connection to Pillaiyar’s feet. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman sings in the Thiruangamalai pathigam, “Will I remain proud, counted among the countless devotees of the Lord, going to His sacred feet, carrying a small deer?” It is with a similar joy, having received such a great blessing and the connection to Pillaiyar’s feet, that Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar speaks. Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar was directly present and witnessed the miraculous events of the precious pathigams composed by Lord ThiruGnanasambandha, such as the Thillai pathigam, the Nelvayil Arathurai pathigam, the Sirkazhi pathigams, the Sribandha pathigam, the Thirpachilachirama pathigam, the Thiruneelakanda pathigam, the Thirpatticharam pathigam, and the Thiruvavaduthurai pathigam. He received the great blessing of setting these pathigams to the yazh. He followed Pillaiyar as he sang, and he himself received the blessing of playing the musical melodies of the pathigams on the yazh. This great blessing was sought and obtained by Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar himself from Pillaiyar.

Thus, Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar explains the blessing he received to his relatives. All the relatives listen to him. When these relatives hear this, they say, “Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar is our relative, isn’t he?” So, with that pride, all the relatives say, “You play the pathigams composed by Pillaiyar on your yazh, ensuring that the inherent melody in those pathigams is perfectly measured. By playing Pillaiyar’s pathigams on the yazh in this manner, that music is growing for the benefit of the whole world.” The relatives request this of Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar. They praise Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar, saying that it is only because he performs on the instrument, carefully measuring the inherent melody of the pathigam, that it became a music that the world could appreciate. They praise Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar, saying that it is only through his playing on the yazh that the melodic beauty of the pathigam becomes effective, and thus the world understands the greatness of the pathigam.

They praise Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar. A pathigam has three parts: words, meaning, and melody. We can understand the words and meaning explicitly, but the third part, the melody, cannot be known unless it is played.

Therefore, all those relatives praise Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar, saying that it is Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar himself who presents these pathigams as music, with their ragam and thalam perfectly measured. Upon hearing this, Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar’s heart trembles. This is because, in truth, it is only by playing Pillaiyar’s pathigams that the yazh attains greatness. The statement that the pathigam is enhanced by the yazh’s music is a false one.

Therefore, upon hearing this falsehood, Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar’s heart trembles and flutters. The words spoken by his relatives are contrary to the truth, and moreover, they constitute an offense against Aludaiya Pillaiyar’s pathigam, and thus an offense against Shiva, which makes Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar’s mind tremble and flutter. He immediately falls at the feet of Pillaiyar, the leader of flourishing Sirkazhi, the King of Sirkazhi.

Here, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to Aludaiya Pillaiyar as the “King of flourishing Pukazhi.” Why does he refer to Pillaiyar as a king, as the King of Sirkazhi? Because only a king has the right and power to resolve offenses.

Therefore, he refers to him as king.

Thus, Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar, bowing at the feet of Lord ThiruGnanasambandha, makes a request. We shall continue to reflect on what this request was at the feet of Lord ThiruGnanasambandha. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 646, by Sekkizhar Swamigal, Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam, ThiruGnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar falls at the feet of Lord ThiruGnanasambandha and makes a request. Sekkizhar Swamigal composes this verse: “Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar said that the immeasurable music of the pathigams, beyond what instruments can convey, should be revealed by you, not only for these people but also to teach the truth to all in the world and guide them to salvation. If you compose a pathigam praised by many for its beauty, I will be able to show that its profound music cannot be contained by the yazh.” Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar requests Lord ThiruGnanasambandha to compose a pathigam whose immeasurable musical qualities cannot be contained by an instrument.

He asks Lord ThiruGnanasambandha to compose a pathigam whose music cannot be contained within the yazh, a pathigam rich in musical nuances. When he composes such a pathigam, Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar states, “I will show these relatives and others in the world, to dispel their ignorance, that the music of the pathigam you compose cannot be contained by the yazh.

“Therefore, please compose a pathigam, and let its music be such that it cannot be contained by the yazh.” Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar, the one who propagates the Vedic path, goes before the Lord and worships Him for the manifestation of His grace. Sekkizhar Peruman composes this verse: “He who fosters the Vedic path, bowed before the Lord, and to manifest the truth of the pathigam, to show that it cannot be contained by the efforts of music born from the throat and instruments according to the texts that teach music to the people of the world, he sang ‘Madhar Madapidi,’ and the celestial beings also worshipped and praised it.” Lord ThiruGnanasambandha worships the Lord and receives His grace. He then composes the pathigam beginning with “Madar Madapidi” as requested by Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar. He composes this pathigam in such a way that its music cannot be contained by the voices or instruments of worldly people. The Vedas, through the Gandharva Veda, elucidate the rules of music.

“According to these, music treatises describe different musical forms. Lord ThiruGnanasambandha composes the pathigam beginning with “Madar Madapidi” in a way that transcends all efforts of singing from the throat and playing instruments according to these musical rules. He was one of the celestial beings skilled in music. The Vidyadharas, witnessing a musical arrangement superior to their own, stand in praise of grace.

“We shall proceed with our contemplation.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Sekkizhar Swamigal’s Periya Puranam, Part 647, Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, starting with ‘Madhar Madappidi’, bestows a pathigam and seals it with the Thrukkadaikappu. When Thirugnanasambandha Peruman beautifully sang and composed the pathigam starting with ‘Vanpugazhi Vediyanar Madhar Madappidi’, and was about to conclude with the Thrukkadaikappu, Perumpananar, as before, took up his beloved Yazh instrument and began to play.

However, the overflowing music of that pathigam could not be contained within the strings of the Yazh. This is mentioned by Sekkizhar Peruman in his 448th verse. He states in his verses that by the grace of the Lord, the truth of the pathigam needed to be shown to the world, and for that, a pathigam was needed, as requested by Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar. A pathigam was bestowed to help him, and it manifested as a great grace upon him and the people of this world. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, with his abundant generosity in bestowing pathigams, concludes by sealing the Thrukkadaikappu. He sang the pathigam with great beauty.

This pathigam, in terms of its poetic beauty, the meaning of its words, its structure, its rhythm, its core message, and its essence, among all other aspects of composition, is presented as a supreme compilation. The unique quality of the tune, which was specifically chosen for this pathigam, is thus completed. This pathigam’s unique nature causes all scholars of music to overflow with thoughts. Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar attempts to play this pathigam on his Yazh instrument as usual.

However, the abundant music of this pathigam cannot be contained when played on the Yazh strings; it does not settle on the Yazh strings. It could not be contained. Though it cannot be contained now, Pillayar is about to grace it, and then this pathigam will somehow be contained within the musical instrument, which we are about to see.

Therefore, this musical pathigam could not be set even on the Yazh that Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar had practiced with for many days. That is why Sivakavimani Ayya notes that the tune of this pathigam could not be decided. In some editions, the tune of this pathigam is mentioned as Yazhmoori tune, but there is no such tune as Yazhmoori. In some editions, the tune of this pathigam is found as Megharaga Kurinji and Vyazha Kurinji.

Therefore, Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar realizes that he cannot set this pathigam on his Yazh.

Now, the next verse is as follows: Then, Thiruneelakanda Isai Perumpananar, abandoning it with intense fear and anxiety, fell at the feet of Pillayar, rose, and looking at him, said, “How can the music of this great pathigam, graced by the great ones, be contained within the Yazh? Isn’t it because I touched this instrument?” Thus realizing, he prepared to break the Yazh, saying, “This happened because of the Yazh with its taut strings.” But Pillayar stopped him and said, “Ayya, you have created this instrument to the extent of its musical capacity. Give it to me.” And taking it from him, the child, who is the embodiment of the good fortune of this earth, commanded him, as recounted by Sekkizhar Swamigal in verses 449 and 450. Seeing that the music of this pathigam could not be contained within the Yazh strings, Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar’s body trembled with fear. What was this fear? This pathigam was sung by divine grace, a kind of music that could not be contained by vocal efforts or musical instruments.

But Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar thought, “Will this pathigam be contained or not? I have tried anyway, and this is a transgression.” So fear came upon him. His sacred body trembled with fear. The sorrow that arose in his heart was an internal event, and the trembling in his sacred body caused by it was an external event.

Moreover, his immense love for Pillayar overflowed and combined with this, causing Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar’s sacred body to tremble and melt.

Therefore, seeking a solution for this transgression, Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar bowed and prostrated at the sacred feet of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. He thought, “This idea came to me only because of my attempt to play and touch the strings of this Yazh instrument. That is why this fault occurred.” He declared that this fault resulted from the Yazh with its tightly bound strings, and then raised it to break it. Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar, attempting to measure grace with doubt, perceived the Yazh as the cause of this evil.

Therefore, with the intention that if the instrument causing evil, and thus the cause itself, were destroyed, its effect would also cease, he raised the Yazh to smash it on the ground and break it. At that moment, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman called out to the panar, “Ayya.” “Ayya” means a person of eminence. Whenever Thirugnanasambandha Peruman refers to Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar, he refers to him as Ayya.

Therefore, ‘Ayya’ here does not denote a caste or lineage but signifies the greatness of his character. Addressing him as ‘Ayya’, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman says, “You have tried according to the rules of music with this musical instrument in your hand. This instrument is created by human effort. Through it, we cannot measure the extent of God’s grace.” In the purana of Anaayanayanar, we have seen the intricacies of how a flute is made according to musical rules.

Similarly, this Yazh instrument is also a creation of human effort, instruments created according to the rules prescribed by musicology. There are many types of Yazh: Periyazh, Makarayaazh, Sakodaiyaazh, Sengottu Yazh, which are the four main types. Besides these, there are also other types of Yazh. Among these, Periyazh has twenty-one strings, Makarayaazh has seventeen strings, Sakodaiyaazh has fourteen strings, and Sengottu Yazh has seven strings. Among these, Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar held the Sakotaiyaazh. Music treatises state that its various parts—kod, aani, patthar, and strings—are components of the Yazh.

These details, including the method of creating a Yazh, its components, and its types, are extensively found in texts such as Silappadikaram Arangettrukkathai (Chapter 26), Kaanal Vari Katturai (Chapter 34), and Seevaka Chintamani Gantharva Dhatthaiyar Ilambagam (Chapter 228), and their commentaries.

Therefore, musicology prescribes rules for creating instruments. According to these rules, people create instruments and play music.

Thus, we cannot set the measure of God’s grace with an instrument created by human effort. The extent of God’s grace cannot be contained within these instruments made by humans. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states that it cannot be set. Is he not the embodiment of the good fortune made by this world? He is the very form of the meritorious deeds performed by the people of this earth. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred form is like all merit taking a sacred form.

In Kanchi Puranam, Madhava Sivagnana Munivar quotes this idea, saying that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred form is the fruit of our good fortune.

Similarly, we have already seen in this purana that Pillayar incarnated in this world due to the good fortune of its inhabitants. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who thus bestowed grace, continues to do so. In the next verse, Sekkizhar Peruman expresses it as follows: “Ayya, why do you break this Yazh?” Is it possible for us to comprehend the greatness of the grace bestowed by the Lord, who has a matted lock alongside his consort, through this instrument that has come into our hands? Is it not customary to perform according to our ability for the people of the world to understand, within the limits of this instrument?“ This is the 451st verse. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman asks Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar, “Ayya, why are you breaking this Yazh?

Is it possible for us, through this instrument we possess, to comprehend the greatness of the grace bestowed by the Lord, who has matted locks and is united with Parashakthi, his divine consort? Can the greatness of God’s grace be contained within the limits of this instrument? No, it cannot.

Therefore, it is appropriate that you play the pathigam on this Yazh instrument, which we possess, according to our ability, in a way that the people of this world can understand, and within the scope of the Yazh instrument’s capacity.” Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman first explains to him why he should not break the Yazh. He states that there is no reason to break it.

Moreover, he says that the grace of the Lord, who is united with the Goddess, cannot be contained within this instrument.

Therefore, even though grace cannot be measured, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman says that it is proper to present this pathigam within the limits of this instrument, in a way that delights the people of this world and is appropriate to our nature. Even though grace is immeasurable, to venerate it, we can play it according to our nature. This is a common practice to reassure someone who knows nothing, and it is a long-standing tradition of the wise, as demonstrated by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. The Lord’s state as Ammaiappar (Mother-Father) is the state of bestowing grace upon the world. Thirukazhitruppadiyar states, “Know that the Lord and Goddess are the Mother and Father of the world.” Therefore, the Lord, remaining inseparably with his power, bestows grace upon this world. The greatness of that divine grace, and the grandeur of the sacred pathigams, are thus revealed through Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred words, allowing beings with lesser capacities to understand them to some extent, as outlined by musicology and nurtured by knowledge.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having thus spoken, continues to bestow grace. Sekkizhar Peruman then presents the next verse, the 452nd verse: “The greatness of music, immeasurable by thought, how can it be attained through action? You, with this Yazh, play and sing the sacred pathigam of the Lord as it has come to be, and hand it back.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman said this. Perumpananar bowed to the Yazh given by the king of Pugazhi, took it in his hands, and placed it on his head. This is the verse. In the previous verse, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman graciously instructed that playing within the limits of this instrument is proper.

In this verse, he provides the reason for that. Among the internal faculties (antakaranas), thought (chintai) is superior. Can the immeasurable grace, which is beyond the scope of thought, be contained within the limited activities of the inferior external faculties? He explains this reason: why divine grace is boundless. Musical endeavor manifests in two ways: through bodily efforts like ‘eduthal paduthal’ (ascending and descending notes) and through instrumental efforts like ‘vaarthal vadithal’ (shaping and refining sounds).

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman explains that the greatness of divine grace, which is beyond the scope of even the highest human internal faculties, cannot be contained or measured by these external musical efforts. Given this, if it cannot be contained by instrumental limits, what is to be done? This doubt arises, and Pillayar addresses it here. Pillaiyar takes the Yazh from Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar’s hands with his own sacred hand and examines it. The touch of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred hand falls upon the Yazh. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman touches it with due reverence.

Having done so, he says, “Play this Yazh,” and gives it back to Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar. Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar, taking the Yazh that had been touched and returned by Pillaiyar’s sacred hand, attempts to play it. He begins to play and somehow completes this pathigam. That Pillaiyar took it in his sacred hand, touched it, and then returned it, indicates that Pillaiyar performed the necessary sacraments for it. Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar took that Yazh, which had been touched by Pillaiyar’s sacred hand, and placed it on his head. He also accepted Pillaiyar’s command.

Using that very Yazh, within its musical limits, Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar somehow played the pathigam, thereby demonstrating that the greatness of divine grace is immeasurable. It is precisely because Pillaiyar thus touched it with his sacred hand that even today, we can somewhat grasp this pathigam with our instruments made of illusory components—our ears, mind, and so on—and thus, to some extent, perceive the greatness of divine grace. As divine grace thus manifested, Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar worships and praises the two lotus-like sacred feet of Aludaiya Pillaiyar. Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar’s relatives also worship and praise Aludaiya Pillaiyar’s sacred lotus feet. With them, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman gracefully resides in that sacred place.

We shall carry on our contemplation.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Sekkizhar Swamigal’s Periya Puranam, Part 648, Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is residing in Thirudharumapuram. Previously, the relatives of Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar, who had held misguided notions, witnessed the miracle of the Yazhmoori Pathigam, understood the greatness of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, bowed at his sacred feet, and received his grace. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman resided there for some time with the devotees. As the saying goes, ‘There is no other attachment but to you, my Lord,’ the devotees are those who cling only to the Lord’s attachment.

Therefore, having no other attachments, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman demonstrates how to live peacefully with devotees. Afterwards, he departed from Thirudharumapuram and, in the Chola country with its ponds and fields, visited and worshiped many great shrines, delighting in them.

At this time, it is believed that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman visited shrines such as Thirutakkalur. Having visited all these shrines, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrived at the sacred shrine of Thirunallar.

There, a gathering of the Lord’s devotees, with great affection, received Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and escorted him into the Thirunallar shrine. Upon entering the temple where the Lord resides, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worshiped the prosperous gopuram. He circumambulated the temple, which is abundant in divine grace, and then prostrated before the Lord. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman performed the darshan according to the prescribed rules within that opulent temple. Firstly, Ganesha, then Sivasuriyanar, and then the main shrine of the Lord—the Agamic texts describe the rules for Shiva temple darshan. He performed darshan according to these rules.

Sekkizhar Swamigal refers to the gopuram of Thirunallar as Thiruvallarkopuram, the temple as Selvakkoil, and the Lord’s presence as Thirumunbu. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman bows to the prosperous gopuram. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman circumambulates the temple, which is filled with abundant grace. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman bows down before the Lord and rises.

Thus, he demonstrates the tradition of worship. Pillaiyar, standing in the position of a preceptor before the Lord, worships the Lord, and his love deepens, causing him to melt. With that intense love, his heart melts, and his entire sacred body experiences horripilation (hair standing on end). Thirugnanasambandha Peruman stands upright with goosebumps. Horripilation is like the moisture at the base of a seed for it to sprout. The sprout that emerges from the moisture caused by horripilation is great love.

Just as one waters and nurtures a plant that has sprouted from internal moisture, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman stands there, melting, with tears flowing all over his body. He bestows the incomparable pathigam, ‘Pogam Aartha Poonmulaiyal’. This pathigam is referred to by Sekkizhar Peruman as ‘Poruvil Pathigam,’ meaning an unparalleled, unique pathigam. We will witness the unparalleled nature of this pathigam through the later events that will unfold in Thirualavai in Madurai.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman begins the pathigam ‘Pogam Aartha Poonmulaiyal’. Before this, in Thirudharumapuram, he had sung the pathigam ‘Madhar Madappidi,’ demonstrating how music could not be contained in the throat, voice, or Vedic musical efforts.

However, this pathigam he sings in a way that the Yazh’s music can be accommodated. The ability of music to be contained or not contained in an instrument is not due to human effort or the instrument’s design; it is determined by the divine intention of God’s grace. This truth about the pathigam is explained here.

Thus, the pathigam graced by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is the Thirunallatru Pathigam, which begins with ‘Pogam Aartha Poonmulaiyal,’ the 49th pathigam of the First Thirumurai. This pathigam is set in the Padhathakkaraga tune. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Uzhai thannodum baagam pai kaattru anna aagam aarththa Thol udai aadai meru meyadhe than poomerum thangiya thadaiyum aa Nalla malgu bi mal Gnanasambandham nalla panbu nalla etthu padal patthum evai vallu neengi manavarodum pooliyuurai Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman stood before the Lord and sang this pathigam.

Afterwards, he came out of the temple, stood near the flagpole, and instructed Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar to play the pathigam he had just sung again on the yazh. The Agamas state that the flagpole is the place where one stands and worships in a temple. The rules of temple darshan also state that namaskarams should be performed beyond the flagpole.

Accordingly, standing near the flagpole, he instructed Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar to play the pathigam that had already been sung before the Lord. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman gave the instruction to Yazhpanar. He is a child, isn’t he?

Therefore, the divine words of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman are words of divine wisdom. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman himself, using the golden cymbals bestowed by the Lord, sang that pathigam. The cymbals in Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred hands were given by Shiva’s grace, inscribed with the five sacred letters. Though they were golden cymbals, they produced sound. With such cymbals, he made the music of the pathigam perfectly metered and sang the pathigam. Following him, Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar, with his yazh strung with sweet, nectar-like, melodious strings, adjusted the tuning to make the musical arrangement very clear and sang the pathigam.

The whole world rejoiced greatly. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, with great joy in his heart, resided there with the devotees in Thirunallar.

Afterwards, having obtained grace from the Lord, who resides as a remedy in Thirunallar, the child, the crest jewel of Saivism, worshipped and praised many shrines in the Chola country, fertile with abundant waters of the Kaveri, which bestows many blessings. Hearing the news of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman thus visiting many shrines and arriving, Thiruneelanaka Nayanar, who lives in Thiruchathamangai, Nayanar, to welcome Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, requested him to come to Thiruchathamangai. Anticipating the arrival of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, he prepared auspicious archways, plantain and areca trees, kalasams, incense, lamps, and other items all along the path where Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was to come, and went forth to welcome him. He welcomed Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and escorted him to the Thiruchathamangai temple. Thirunallar is a shrine located on the eastern coast, near the seashore. Thiruchathamangai is an agricultural region, far inland from the coast in the Chola country.

Therefore, it is understood that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having visited all the intervening shrines, Peruman arrived at Thiruchathamangai. In Thiruchathamangai, the name of the temple is Ayavanthi. He worshipped the temple of the Lord, who lovingly resides in that Ayavanthi temple, circumambulated the temple, and bowed before the Lord. The child, a Brahmin who incarnated here due to the great penance performed by this entire earth, joined his sacred hands above his head in reverence and stood up.

Let us go on contemplating. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, Part 649, ‘Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam’, the Puranam of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar, composed by Sekkizhar Swamigal. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrived at the residence of Thiruneelanaka Nayanar in Thiruchathamangai. We have extensively contemplated these narratives that are now unfolding in the Puranam of Thiruneelanaka Nayanar. Sekkizhar Swamigal summarizes here the history that was extensively narrated there. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrived at the sacred place of Thiruchathamangai, performed darshan at the temple, but the pathigam sung by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman at that time is not available to us.

After completing the temple darshan, Thirugnanasambandha Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar also stayed with him. There, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reclined to rest. Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar and Mathangachoolamani Ammaiyar stayed that night near the sacrificial altar in the central part of Thiruneelanaka Nayanar’s residence, and the sacrificial fire rose clockwise. We have extensively contemplated this history in the Puranam of Thiruneelanaka Nayanar. Sekkizhar Swamigal describes it here in just two words, ‘Perumpanarum Thanga’ (the great bard also stayed). The next morning, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman went to the Ayavanthi temple in Thiruchathamangai and worshipped the Lord.

He shows us that the temple itself is a fortress to be worshipped. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman shows us that.

There, in the Ayavanthi temple, the flawless, rare nectar, the Lord, resides with the beautiful goddess who resembles a tender young creeper. Peruman is faultless, rare nectar. ‘Godu’ means fault. ‘Godu ila ar amudhu’ means the rare nectar Lord who eradicates our faults. Our fault is the impurity (malakutam) that causes birth and death.

The Lord who removes such faults resides as rare nectar. ‘Aarudhal’ means omnipresence. ‘Amudhu’ means that which removes death and bestows eternal bliss. This name, ‘Amudham,’ is applicable only to the Lord. Other things are called ‘Amudham’ calling them nectar is merely ceremonial. Such a Lord resides there with Uma Devi, who is like a tender, beautiful young creeper. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sings a pathigam in praise of such a Lord. This entire pathigam praises the Lord’s state of being united with the Mother, saying, “He is with the Kanniya (garlanded one)” and “He is with the beautiful lady with the creeper-like form.” Such a pathigam is a pathigam born of the meaning of the primordial Vedas.

It is a pathigam that explains the meanings of the Vedas. The meaning of the Vedas explains the ability of Lord Shiva to bless the world as the Mother and Father. Thirukkalippadiyar states, “Know that the Mother and Father are indeed the Mother and Father of the world.”

Thus, in this Thiruchathamangai Thirunayavanthi pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman includes and sings the greatness of Thiruneelanaka Nayanar, saying, “Neelanaka, who lives by righteousness.” In the eleventh Thirukkadaikappu verse, he has praised the greatness of Thiruneelanaka Nayanar, saying, (Mariyinaar malku Kaazhi Tamizh Gnana Sambandhan Mannum Nirayinaar Neelanakkan Nedu Maa Nagar endru thondar araiyum oor Saathamangai Ayavanthi mel aaindha pathum Muraimayaal eethavallaar imaiyorilum mundhuvare.) “Those who can properly sing these ten researched verses on Ayavanthi in Saathamangai, the city praised by devotees, where Tamizh Gnana Sambandhan of Kaazhi, filled with Brahmins, and Neelanakkan, full of integrity, reside, will surpass even the celestials.” This pathigam is the fifty-eighth pathigam of the third Thirumurai, set to the Panjamam tune. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Kambalam thirumalar kunrai maalai thilaikkum mathisalai vaiththeeru irumalar kanni thannodu udanaagum erppathondre perumalar solai megam purinjum perum saathamangai arumalar aadhi moorthy ayavanthi amarnthavane maraiyinaar malku thali Tamizh Gnana) (Nirayinaar Neelanakedumaana Araiyum Saathamangai Ayavam vimel Aayudha Bhakthoo muraiyamal ethavalla imaiyorilum imaiyorilum imaiyorilum Thiruneelaka Nayanar parava Ayavanthi amarntha Iraivare) The note of this pathigam is the question, “Please explain the meaning of your being united with the Mother,” in the form of worshipping the rare nectar with the tender creeper-like Mother. In this pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has given the sacred name of the Goddess of this shrine as ‘Irumalkanni’. The sacred names of the Goddess in this shrine are ‘Ubhaya Pushpa Vilochani’ and ‘Irumalkan Ammai’.

He has composed and sung it in the first verse of this pathigam as, “You who placed the garland of glorious Kondrai flowers on your head adorned with the moon, being united with ‘Irumalar Kanni’.” The sacred name of the Lord is Ayavantheeshwarar and Brahmapureeshwarar. We have contemplated the history of the Thiruchathamangai shrine in the Puranam of Thiruneelanaka Nayanar.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having visited and worshipped the Thiruchathamangai Ayavanthi temple, stayed there for a few days due to the loving friendship of Thiruneelanaka Nayanar.

After that, driven by the desire to worship other shrines of the Lord, he took leave from Thiruneelanaka Nayanar and Ayavantheeshwarar. Giving a joyful farewell to Thiruneelanaka Nayanar, the child set out to worship other shrines. Keeping the great friendship of Thiruneelanaka Nayanar joyfully in his heart, he went to many shrines associated with Lord Shiva, worshipped, praised, and sang. These shrines are considered to be Iraiyancheri and other such places. There is room to consider.

Thus, having worshipped many shrines, and accompanied by a gathering of the Lord’s devotees, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reached the sacred place of Thirunagai Kaaronam, where learned people reside. Thirunagai Kaaronam is currently known as Nagapattinam. The Peruman refers to it in this verse as ‘Kattravar Vazh Kadal Nagaikkaaronam’ (Sea Kaaronam of Nagai where learned people live). ‘Kattravar’ means those who have learned to worship the Lord with love. The Thirukkural states that the benefit of learning is to worship the sacred feet of the Lord, who is pure wisdom.

Accordingly, ‘Kattravar Vazhum Oor Kadal Nagaikkaaronam’ (Sea Kaaronam of Nagai, the village where learned people live) and ‘Kattravar Payilu Nagaikkaaronam’ (Nagaikkaaronam where learned people practice) in Thirunerisai, and ‘Kattraar Payil Kadal Nagaikkaaronam’ (Sea Kaaronam of Nagai where learned people reside) in Thiruviruttam, the greatness of Nagaikkaaronam have been bestowed.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships Kadal Nagai Kaaronam. However, the pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for this shrine is not available to us.

Thus, having worshipped Kadal Nagai Kaaronam, he left there, moved away from the seashore where backwater groves lined the sides, and praised many shrines of the Lord. These shrines are considered to be Thiruchikkal, Thirukannangudi, Thiruvaazhiyur, and other such sacred places. Having visited many such shrines, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reached the Thirukeezhvelur shrine. There is a pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for the Thiruchikkal shrine, which is known as one of the shrines on the way.

Similarly, Sekkizhar Peruman states that he went to Thirukeezhvelur and worshipped. Sekkizhar Peruman mentions. We also have the pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for that Keezhvelur shrine.

We will continue to contemplate these. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, Part 650, ‘Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam’, the Puranam of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar, composed by Sekkizhar Swamigal. Sekkizhar Swamigal states that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman departed from the Thirunagai Kaaronam shrine and visited the Keezhvelur shrine. Keezhvelur is the eighty-fourth shrine on the south bank of the Kaveri. It is named Keezhvelur because Murugaperuman, known as Vel, worshipped Lord Shiva there. It is extolled as a beautiful Maada Temple, a great temple, in the pathigam.

The vimanam is a large structure of black granite.

Similarly, there is another vimanam. It is a shrine worshipped by Agasthiyar, Indra, Kubera, and others. Murugaperuman The Mother guarded his penance from five directions, so she is enshrined in the first enclosure on the north side as Anjuwatta Nayaki, an aspect of Durga. Kubera has a separate temple. This is the sacred place where Agasthiyar Peruman worshipped the right sacred foot of Koothapiran. This shrine, known as Keevallur, is located on the Thiruvarur-Nagai road.

The Lord’s sacred name is Akshaya Lingeshwarar, Kediliyappar. The Goddess’s sacred name is Vanamulai Nayaki, Sundara Kujambal. The sacred tank is Saravanai Saravana Theertham. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who came to this shrine, composed a pathigam. It is the one hundred and fifth pathigam of the second Thirumurai, set to the Nattaraaga tune. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Sirrarangalum sadaiyinar veedinar milirutharum ara odum maraiyozhinaru karaiyul noolaviya ondrayam thaarinru pugazh meedhu veloor ulnoolaviya sindhaiyar venai odida veede)

(Kurulvaar pulal sadaiyudai kuzhave alaka maru keezh velu thirandamaa maraiyavar tozhu perum theer koyilam perumaana irunda medhil inam miga vayal malku pugali mal samba paada valla avar sivagathi peruvathu thidam aame) The note of this pathigam is that the ailments of those who meditate on the Lord of Thiru Keezhvelur will flee, and along with the ailments, their karmas will also flee.
