Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having worshipped Thiru Keezhvelur, visits the nearby shrines. These shrines are considered to be Thiruchikkal, Thirukannangudi, Thiruvaazhiyur, and others. Among these, the pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for the Thiruchikkal shrine is available to us. Thiruchikkal is the eighty-third shrine on the south bank of the Kaveri.

It is a shrine where Murugaperuman resides prominently under the name Singaravelar, so Chikkal Singaravelar is very famous. This is a Maada temple. The Kanda Sashti festival is celebrated grandly here. Sage Vasishta worshipped Lord Shiva here and obtained Kamadhenu. After Vasishta installed and worshipped the Lord’s idol with butter from Kamadhenu, the butter lingam of the Lord could not be removed, hence the name Chikkal (meaning ‘stuck’) for this shrine. The Lord’s sacred name is also Navaneetheshwarar, Vennai Piran.

In this shrine, Vishnu is enshrined as Navaneetha Perumal in the northern circumambulation path. is enshrined. Navaneetheshwarar or Navaneethanathar’s Tamil translation is Vennai Piran. The sacred name of the Mother is Vel Nedunganni, Sakthiyathaga. The sacred tanks are Ksheera Pushkarani, Gaya Theertham, Lakshmi Theertham. The sthalavruksham is the jasmine creeper. The history of the shrine states that this is the place where Murugaperuman received the spear from the Goddess to slay Sooran.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who came to this shrine, composed a pathigam. It is the eighth pathigam of the second Thirumurai, set to the Indalap pan tune. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Ulavum madhu maaligai thenulaavum malar solai mal theegal chikka venal velai vil nira vellai perumaan adi gnanamaaga ninave kandhamar polil kaalivul gnana sambandha senthal poompozil chikkal vellai perumaal) The note of this pathigam is that the karma of those who meditate on the sacred feet of Vennai Peruman in the Thiruchikkal shrine will be diminished. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman thus continues to visit shrines. Thiruthonda Nayanar, who resides in Thiruchenkattangudi, hears of the greatness of the child’s journey.

The moment he heard it, Thiruthonda Nayanar rushed there, his heart overflowing with love and joy. He welcomed the child and brought him into his shrine. The abundance of love Thiruthonda Nayanar had for devotees is evident here. Sekkizhar Peruman states this, saying, “Having heard of the greatness of the child, who attained abundant wisdom by worshipping the Lord in all the nearby shrines, Thiruthondar rushed from Thirumaruvu Chenkattangudi, his heart melting, and joyfully welcomed him into his city.” Sekkizhar Peruman further sings, along with Thiruthondar, He went to Chenkattangudi, and there, the fame of the devotee who established his reputation in all directions, who was fond of the friendship of Thiruthondar, and who saved the celestials by bearing the blue throat, arrived at Ganapateeswaram with the true devotees who renounced all worldly pleasures and subsisted on alms. Sekkizhar Swamigal continues to sing. The child, along with Thiruthonda Nayanar, went to Thiruchenkattangudi and desired his friendship.

Thiruthonda Nayanar is a great devotee who established his greatness in all eight directions. The fame of Thiruthonda Nayanar is such that it pervades all eight directions. He is unique in this world, having established and made his greatness prevail in all eight directions. Thiruthonda Nayanar was the one who made it so. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having formed a friendship with Thiruthonda Nayanar concerning the service Thiruthonda Nayanar was performing, desired that friendship and went to Thiruchenkattangudi. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worshipped the Lord of Thiruchenkattangudi with the true devotees who had renounced all worldly pleasures and subsisted on alms.

Sekkizhar Swamigal mentions the greatness of the devotees here by praising them as “true devotees who renounced all pleasures and subsisted on alms.” As Thirunavukkarasu Peruman sang in Thirukkurunthokai in Mayiladuthurai, “We have no desire to reside and see even the life of the celestials or the abode of the immortals, as long as we can adorn the feet of the devotees.” According to that, true devotees are those who have renounced all pleasures, including the celestial life. The sacred words of Thiruvasagam state, “I desire no pleasures, not even the joy of Indra.” Such are the true devotees. Sekkizhar Peruman sings about their true state of renunciation. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman thus has darshan of the Lord residing in the Ganapateeswaram temple in Thiruchenkattangudi with such true devotees.

The Lord residing in the Ganapateeswaram temple is the Lord who bore the blue throat and saved the celestials. He is the Lord who consumed poison and gave nectar so that the celestials could live.

Therefore, the Lord is of such a nature. It is also noted here that devotees who follow the sacred feet of the Lord similarly renounce worldly pleasures and subsist on alms. It is also worth noting here that the Lord of Ganapateeswaram later came as Uthrapathy and accepted alms in the form of a child. This indicates that the ways in which the Lord manifests himself can also be seen in his devotees. Having circumambulated the Ganapateeswaram temple, he prostrated at the sacred feet of the Lord, tears flowing from his eyes like a waterfall, bowed before the Lord, and stood up, joining his reddened hands in worship. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman then sang a pathigam, overflowing with praise for the Lord who graced him, the Lord whom Thiruthonda Nayanar worshipped.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sings and praises. We have two pathigams composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for Thiruchenkattangudi.

We shall proceed with our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, Part 651, ‘Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam’, the Puranam of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar, composed by Sekkizhar Swamigal. Sekkizhar Swamigal narrates that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worshipped at the Ganapateeswaram temple in Thiruchenkattangudi. Sekkizhar Swamigal sings the 470th verse, saying, “Having arrived there, he circumambulated the temple, fell at the feet of the serpent-adorned Lord, and with red tears flowing, he bowed before the Lord, stood up, and with joined red hands, he praised the greatness of their Lord, whom Thiruthondar worshipped, and singing a pathigam overflowing with music, he departed from that place in a specific manner.” Having entered the Ganapateeswaram temple and circumambulated it, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worshipped, prostrating at the sacred feet of the Lord. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, with his reddened eyes shedding tears like a waterfall, bowed before the Lord many times, stood up, and with his reddened hands joined above his head, worshipped the Lord, the great benefactor who had graced him. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sings this entire pathigam, which he is now composing, in praise of the Lord’s nature, who resided there to be worshipped by Thiruthonda Nayanar.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sings throughout the pathigam about the Lord’s nature of residing there so that Thiruthonda Nayanar could worship him, saying, “Sirthondan performed service,” and “He resided there to bestow grace upon Sirthondar.” We can see that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has dedicated the entire pathigam to Thiruthonda Nayanar. Such a pathigam is the first of the two pathigams composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for Thiruchenkattangudi. It is the sixty-third pathigam of the third Thirumurai, set to the Panchamam tune. The first, second, and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Thavira Chenkattam) (Vilaiyaadum perumaane ponnam poongali kaanal punar thunaiyoduudan paazhum annam kaalandril kaa agandrum poy varuve kallathu thol siru tholdal ganapathi saran meyathudaya)

(Sentham poongunal parandha Chenkattam kudi merani maarbiri thon avan venda antha adigalaye adipparuvul samba Tamil porththa por sondham kol samboorai porththa por sambalam Thiru) Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s praise of his great Lord Shiva, and the manner in which Shiva resided there to be worshipped by Thiruthondar, is the note of this pathigam.

Now, the second pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for the Thiruchenkattangudi shrine is the sixty-first pathigam of the first Thirumurai, set to the Pazhanthakkaragam tune. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Neyooramutta panisi endara mudhi al karai pul kanda thanavathi nooram thara) (Malar uvalai thadi pola paya Tamil thambam thirai illam poona padappi katta uda)

The Lord resides in the Ganapateeswaram temple within Chenkattangudi, so that devotees may constantly serve him without hindrance, and to bestow grace upon Siruthondar—this is the note of this pathigam.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed two pathigams. After composing them, the child came out of the temple and lovingly stayed in the residence of Siruthonda Nayanar, who was born in the lineage of the great generals and was like a battle-bull, his heart filled with joy for his great penance. Siruthonda Nayanar was endowed with the nature of great penance. Great penance involves service to devotees and service to the Lord. ‘Vaaythal’ means attaining the blessing of constant remembrance.

Thus, as the narrative of Siruthonda Nayanar unfolds, he resides in his sacred home. While thus residing, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman travels from Thiruchenkattangudi to the Thirumarugal shrine. he stays there joyfully. Siruthonda Nayanar is one who has attained great penance. Great penance is service to devotees and service to the Lord. ‘Vaaythal’ means to attain the blessing of being constantly remembered.

Thus, the sacred narrative of Siruthonda Nayanar is about to unfold. He resides in his sacred home. While thus seated, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds from Thiruchenkattangudi to the Thirumarugal shrine. In the shrine of Thirumarugal, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships and praises the sacred feet of Manikkavannar, who has a long matted hair where the crescent moon and a red-eyed snake reside. Sekkizhar Peruman’s verse describes how the child of Perumpugali, having arrived in the city of Thirumarugal, with the moon and the red-eyed snake residing in his long matted hair, worshipped and praised the feet of Manikkavannar, and with overflowing love and devotion in his heart, he offered a Tamil garland filled with clear music and stayed there. The shrine of Thirumarugal, to which Thirugnanasambandha Peruman travels from Thiruchenkattangudi, is where Lord Shiva resides with the sacred name Manikkavannar.

There, Sekkizhar Peruman praises the Lord residing there in this verse as the Lord with the long matted hair adorned with the moon and the red-eyed snake. Sekkizhar Peruman praises him in this verse as the Lord with the long matted hair adorned with the crescent moon and the red-eyed snake. The crescent moon on the Lord’s matted hair is an ambrosial vessel. The snake on his matted hair is poison. The divine act that is about to happen in the Thirumarugal shrine is the result of the narrative of immortality, where the snake’s poison was cured and death was averted. Sekkizhar Peruman thus presents it to us.

The Lord’s matted hair accommodates two contrasting elements: poison and nectar.

Therefore, it is praised as long matted hair. Even in the pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for this shrine, he begins by singing about the Lord’s matted hair as ‘Sadaiyanummal’ (the one with the matted hair). We can also recall that here.

Therefore, the child of Seerkazhi arrived at the city of Thirumarugal and offered a garland of Tamil verses. The pathigams composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for this shrine are not available to us at present. The pathigam ‘Sadaiya’ for this shrine was composed later during the historical events, which we will see next.

We shall continue our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, Part 652, ‘Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam’, the Puranam of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar, composed by Sekkizhar Swamigal. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman journeys from Thiruchenkattangudi to the Thirumarugal shrine.

At this time, a wonderful and deeply moving divine narrative is about to unfold in the Thirumarugal shrine through Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. As Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrives at the Thirumarugal shrine, he hears the sorrowful cry of a young woman from a monastery outside the temple. The young woman is lamenting for her intended husband. When a young man, a merchant, who was about to be married, was staying at that monastery, a snake bit him, and he lay there as if unconscious and lifeless. When Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrived at the temple, he saw this. He asked the woman why she was wailing to Lord Shiva.

The woman recounted her story. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, by composing a pathigam, dispelled the woman’s sorrow, revived the merchant, and made him rise. This is the time when such a grace occurred, and this passage describes that historical event. Kizhar Peruman extensively narrates this history for us. It is a well-known story to all devotees.

Additionally, the pathigam, ‘Vishamtirtha pathigam,’ composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman at this time, which begins with ‘Sadaiya Enumal Saranyenumal,’ is a pathigam whose miraculous grace is still manifested today, to the extent that there are no devotees unfamiliar with it. This is a wonderful historical account that serves as the reason for us to receive such a pathigam. This is a sacred history that reveals the truth that even when faced with insurmountable sorrow, one should not forget Shiva’s grace, and for those who do not forget Shiva’s grace, Shiva’s grace will extend a helping hand and console them. Such a sacred history has been elaborately sung by Isaikkizhar Peruman. Isaikkizhar Peruman describes this sacred history starting from the 473rd verse: “In those days, a merchant, becoming a pilgrim, and accompanied by a young maiden, slept at night in a monastery outside the temple of Ponnal Meru-chilaayar. When a lightning-white-fanged snake bit him, and the swift venom rapidly ascended to his head, he appeared to lose his life.

“Seeing his state, the slender young maiden, distraught, collapsed in grief.” This is the 473rd verse. At Thirumarugal temple, a merchant brings a young maiden with him. Next to Thirumarugal temple, there is a monastery for travelers to stay.

“In those days, monasteries for travelers were built next to temples. This was a good arrangement found in urban layouts in earlier times. This arrangement also supports the historical event.

“Similarly, because this monastery is located next to the temple, the woman cries towards the entrance of the temple. That sound falls on the ear of Pillaiyar when he comes to worship the Lord there.

“Therefore, the cause of all this is the monasteries built near temples for travelers to stay.

“Therefore, a man from the merchant class is staying and sleeping in that monastery with a young maiden. It is a rule of temple darshan not to sleep inside the temple.

“So, in the monastery built next to the temple for devotees to stay, the man from the merchant class and the maiden sleep.

“At that time, a snake comes and bites the merchant. As a result, the snake’s venom mixes with the merchant’s blood and spreads throughout his body. When we look at the historical section in Apputhi Adigal Nayanar’s Periyapuranam where Apputhi Adigal Nayanar’s son, Mootha Thirunavukkarasu, was bitten by a snake, we saw that the venom from the snakebite accelerated in stages, reaching the seventh stage, meaning the venom had reached the seventh tissue.

“Similarly, here too, the venom, mixing with the merchant’s blood and circulating throughout his body, reaches the state of the seventh stage. This body is composed of seven tissues.

“Therefore, the venom progresses through each tissue and reaches the seventh tissue. In such a state, he appears to be in a state where his life is about to depart. He lies there unconscious and insensate, as if his life is leaving him. The maiden, who came with the merchant, sees this. The two are not yet married. They have left their hometown and come to Thirumarugal precisely for marriage.

“But this tragic event occurs before their marriage. Sekkizhar Peruman composes the next verse, the 474th verse: “Even though a serpent bit him, she could not touch him, for no one else would give him a new life. She fell near the lion-like man and wailed like a wilting flower creeper, crying out that though the fierce venom raged, and neither the furious thunder nor the eagle could relieve it, it would not diminish. All night long, until the dawn, amidst the fragrant evening and morning,”. Peruman composes this verse, describing her prolonged lament. This is an excellent passage that clearly illustrates the chastity of the maiden.

“This man of the merchant class and this young maiden have both left their homes without their families’ knowledge. They have done so for the purpose of marriage.

“Therefore, they are not yet married. Their act of leaving home and coming here cannot be compared to the moral degradation we witness today. Their attempt to marry is based on a very high moral standard; they came here intending to marry. The reason why they came here without the knowledge of both their families will be revealed through the words of the woman herself when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman questions her later.

“Therefore, they are staying here, having left home based on a high dharma and ethical principles. At that moment, this tragic incident occurs.

“So, Sekkizhar Swamigal sings, ‘Even though a serpent bit him, she could not touch him.’ A snake is untouchable, yet it bit the man. This maiden has the right to touch that man of the merchant class, but now she cannot even touch him and cry. Because they are not yet married. In such an unmarried state, the snake bites him. An untouchable, forbidden snake bites him. And she is not yet married to that man.

“So, she cannot touch him and cry. She is entitled, but because she is not married, she currently has no right to touch him and cry. Divine Sekkizhar Peruman explains such a high culture and the chastity of that woman in these two phrases. We also see that this is the divine poetic beauty of the author.

“At that time, the woman cries, lamenting that there is no one to console her. Like a male lion, the merchant lies there. Unable to touch him and cry, she falls down next to him and wails. They have left home without anyone’s knowledge, so in this situation, she has no relatives to console her.

“At that time, hearing her lament, some sorcerers attempt various measures to remove the venom. These sorcerers, like Garuda, are generally enemies of snakes, just as thunder is. Our medical texts state that a snake’s venom is removed if it is struck by lightning or comes under Garuda’s gaze.

“Therefore, these venom-removing sorcerers are like thunder and Garuda. They are capable of removing any kind of poison. These sorcerers, deeply immersed in and knowing the mantra for thunder and the mantra that embodies the nature of Garuda, have attained siddhi through practice. Scriptures refer to this as Garudoham Bhavana. Sorcerers, having practiced the Garuda mantra for a long time and being in the state of Garudoham, if they look at snakebite victims with that Garuda-like gaze, the venom from the victims’ bodies will subside. This is the traditional medical doctrine of our country.

“Even in spiritual scriptures, this analogy is used for Shivoham Bhavana. Just as the sorcerer is in just as the sorcerer is in Garudoham Bhavana, similarly, our scriptures compare the soul’s journey to attain the nature of Shiva, the practice for becoming Shiva-like, known as Shivoham Bhavana, to Garudoham Bhavana. Our scriptures cite Garudoham Bhavana as an example for Shivoham Bhavana. “Just as fear is dispelled and great danger ceases simply by contemplating the form of Garuda,” states the Thirumantiram composed by Thirumoola Devanayanar, appearing in the ‘Darshanam’ section. This is the second example stanza for the ninth aphorism.

“Therefore, spiritual scriptures speak about this. What is this ‘Garudoham Bhavana’ mentioned? Sivakavimani Ayyavargal writes a commentary. Generally, all living beings such as birds, animals, and trees have presiding deities. There are mantras associated with these presiding deities. The soul has the nature of taking on the color of whatever it is attached to.

“The soul is like a crystal; it reflects exactly the nature of whatever it is associated with.

“Therefore, if the soul continuously meditates on and practices the mantras of these presiding deities, it will transform into the very form of that mantra, as stated by Agamas such as Sarvagyanottaram. Shri Madhava Sivagnana Munivar has also explained this in Sivagnana Mapadiyam.

“Thus, there are presiding deities for all living beings such as birds, animals, and trees. Generally, these are divided into Adhibhautikam, Adhidaivikam, and Adhyatmikam. For example, what is explained in Garudoham Bhavana is Garuda.

“Therefore, Garuda is of three types: Adhibhautika Garuda, Adhidaivika Garuda, and Adhyatmika Garuda. Each of these also has three types. As we saw earlier, every bird, every animal, every tree, etc., also falls into these three categories.

“Here, we take Garuda as an example.

“Therefore, there are three types of Garudas in this world: Adhibhautika Garuda, Adhidaivika Garuda, and Adhyatmika Garuda. The Garuda bird that we see in its gross form is the Adhibhautika Garuda. All such Garuda birds have a presiding deity.

“Therefore, that presiding deity will be in the form of a mantra. That mantra is called Adhidaivika Garuda. The mantrika will hold this mantra in his heart, meditate on it, contemplate it, and practice it. After such practice, he will apply that mantra, which is the Adhidaivika Garuda. When he applies it, it is Shiva’s power that grants the result to the application made by the mantrika, residing within that mantra, the Adhidaivika Garuda.

“Therefore, this Shiva power is called Adhyatmika Garuda. In Garudoham Bhavana, what the mantrika does is to meditate on the Adhidaivika Garuda, which is the Garuda in mantra form. He will meditate on it daily. Due to the practice he has diligently pursued every day, that very mantra-form will become himself, and the mantrika will shine with ananya bhavana (non-dual feeling). His consciousness will become completely absorbed in the Adhidaivika Garuda. This state of being absorbed in the Adhidaivika mantra-Garuda, with his consciousness completely under its sway, is called Garudoham Bhavana.

“In such a state, if the mantrika looks with that mantra-eye at the body that has been bitten by a snake, the snake’s venom will change and subside due to the mantra-gaze of the Adhidaivika Garuda. Shiva’s power, acting through that mantra, Shakti will provide that benefit. This is what the scriptures call Garudoham Bhavana.

“Therefore, it is understood that this is true and that it is not untrue.

“Here, even when these sorcerers attempted, standing in this Garudoham Bhavana, it did not provide a solution.

“Therefore, the maiden had no one to console her, no place to touch the merchant and cry, and even with the sorcerers’ efforts, the venom did not subside. So she laments, she faints, and seeing that all their efforts are in vain, she now turns to the Lord enshrined in the temple, which is visible straight ahead, and cries out in prayer.

“We shall continue our reflection.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 653, composed by Sekkizhar Swamigal, ‘Vambara Varivandu Serukkam’ (The Story of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar). The woman cries and wails. Sekkizhar Peruman describes this in the 475th verse: “Leaving my mother and father, I came with you as my refuge.

“Now, bitten by a serpent, you have left me, departing from life. What shall I do? There is no one to relieve this distress. O jewel of the merchant clan, renowned and steadfast, I too shall not live,” saying this and distraught in her mind, she, having no other recourse, saluted and wept towards the entrance of the temple of Him who wears the young crescent moon on His head.

“Thus, the verse is composed. The woman weeps, wailing to the merchant, “Leaving my mother and father, I came with you as my sole refuge, but bitten by a snake, you have left me, departing from life!” For those alive to thus call out and wail to the deceased is due to the intensity of their suffering. She laments, “I relied on you as my refuge and came with you; you have left me and gone!” She laments, “You have left me alive here and gone alone!” She weeps, “Why did you leave me here and not take my life with yours?” Moreover, she weeps, “Is there no one who can alleviate this kind of suffering?” As we saw earlier, even the most skilled sorcerers tried their best, but it was to no avail.

“So, she cries, thinking, “No human effort can relieve this sorrow; is there no one to remove this suffering?” She weeps, “Just as you have gone and will not live here, I too shall not live now.” Sekkizhar Peruman uses the word “endru” (saying) twice to emphasize her repeated lament. He indicates that she cries, lamenting in many such ways. “Fate can be overcome by intellect” is an old saying, but this woman, due to her past practices, realizes that for the helpless, God is the only refuge, and she meditates on Shiva’s grace. She weeps, seeking Shiva’s grace, facing the entrance of the temple where Lord Shiva resides. She meditates on Shiva’s grace and weeps towards the direction of the temple entrance.

“Here, the idea is conveyed that even when faced with insurmountable sorrow, one should not forget Shiva’s grace, and that for those who do not forget Shiva’s grace, Shiva’s grace will extend a helping hand and console them. She weeps towards the direction of the temple of Lord Shiva, who wears the young crescent moon. Shiva wears the young crescent moon. That crescent moon is an embodiment of nectar. It diminishes in phases until only one phase remains. Sekkizhar Peruman mentions “the temple of him who wears the young crescent moon” to imply that the Lord revived that moon, giving it life and enabling it to grow.

“Sekkizhar Peruman next describes in the following verse how the woman reverently weeps to Lord Shiva, the 476th verse: “O nectar who consumed the poison from the roaring ocean to save the assembly of devotees! O stainless one who wears the blue venomous serpent, whose form could not be seen by the red-eyed Vishnu and Brahma! O virtuous one who graciously restored life to Kama, reduced to ashes, at Rati’s plea! O Lord of Kavin Marugal, surrounded by fragrant flower gardens and groves! Protect me!” And also, “O Lord of Marugal, adorned with the growing crescent moon on your beautiful matted hair, whose red feet kicked and brought down the black-bodied Kala, the formidable, fierce-eyed Yama, who came raging to take the life of the young Brahmana Markandeya, causing his body to crumble! Grant your grace so that this fierce venom’s speed may subside and I may rise from this pit of suffering!” Sekkizhar Peruman thus composes two verses.

“The woman cries throughout the night. In a situation where human efforts, however much they tried, failed to alleviate the suffering, she considers the Lord to be her only refuge, capable of removing any sorrow, and cries towards the direction of the temple entrance. She cries, praising Lord Shiva. She calls out to Lord Shiva as “O nectar who consumed the poison from the roaring ocean to save the assembly of devotees!” This is the first thought that arises in the woman’s mind about Shiva’s nature when she, finding no other refuge in that state, remembers Shiva. The act of Shiva consuming poison and saving the immortals is the first deed that comes to her mind. She considers saving the devotees and, for that purpose, consuming great poison as acts of Shiva’s grace.

“The assembly of celestials, known as ‘imayavargal,’ was a large multitude. The Halahala poison arose from the great ocean, bringing distress to them. The Halahala poison arose from the great ocean, causing distress to them.

“Lord Shiva consumed all that poison and protected the multitude of celestials. There was a large gathering of celestials, and the poison was Halahala venom.

“Therefore, Lord Shiva, who consumed such a formidable poison and protected such a vast multitude, for him to protect this small woman and save us from the ordinary snake venom is an easy feat for you. With this implicit meaning, this verse is composed.

“Next, she cries out to Shiva, “O stainless one who wears the blue venomous serpent, whose form could not be seen by the red-eyed Vishnu and Brahma!” Shiva is the Lord who displays his divine form adorned with many snakes.

“Therefore, for you, who stands adorned with many snakes, it is very easy to remove the venom of this small snake. With this implicit meaning, the woman praises the Lord’s form adorned with snakes. The form that Vishnu and Brahma could not see, the Lord revealed in that way. In this second phrase, the woman sings about that too. The history of Brahma and Vishnu not being able to find the top and bottom of Shiva, who stood as a pillar of fire, is extensively discussed in all the Shiva Mahapuranam. This is the second idea that comes to the woman’s mind, suitable for her situation.

“This history is extensively discussed in all the Shiva Mahapuranam. Thirugnanasambandha Pillai has mostly praised this story in the ninth verse of his pathigams.

“Therefore, that history comes to this woman’s mind second, along with the divine form adorned with snakes, and she cries out thus.

“Next, the woman cries out to Shiva, praising the Lord as “O virtuous one who graciously restored life to Kama, reduced to ashes, at Rati’s plea!” This is the third thought that arose in the woman’s heart, most appropriately fitting her helpless situation. Regarding Shiva, Shiva burns Manmatha to ashes.

“Then, after a long time, at the plea of Rati, Manmatha’s wife, he graciously restores his life. This is this is what the woman recounts, lamenting. She says, “O Lord, who gave life back to Manmatha, who died long ago! This merchant has only just lost his life. In this situation, it is surely easy for you to re-infuse life into his body and protect me, who desired him as my husband, O virtuous one!” By calling him ‘Punniyan’ (virtuous one), she implies that Shiva is a benevolent giver who helps without expecting anything in return. She praises him in all these ways and then says, “O Lord of Kavin Marugal, surrounded by fragrant flower gardens and groves, protect me!” This Thirumarugal temple is a sacred place surrounded by flower gardens.

“This temple of Thirumarugal is surrounded by flower gardens. This place is suitable for us to marry, not for such a tragic event to occur, the woman cries, stating this. She laments, thinking that they had intended to marry at this sacred place, and it is indeed a suitable place for marriage. Sekkizhar Peruman here also implicitly hints at the marriage that Pillaiyar is about to perform through grace. This Thirumarugal, surrounded by flower gardens, is a very cool place. The implication is that it is a place where grace resides, dispelling the heat of sorrow and bringing coolness.

“Such a beautiful place, a place of beauty, should not become a place that destroys beauty, she praises, remembering the Lord. This is the meaning of the 476th verse.

“Now, the 477th verse describes how she cries. “O Lord, whose red sacred feet kicked and brought down the black-bodied Yama, who came raging to take the life of Markandeya, the young Brahmana who sought refuge in you! O Lord of beautiful Marugal, grant your grace so that this fierce venom’s speed may subside and I may rise from this pit of suffering!” Thus, the woman pleads to the Lord. The event of Lord’s grace bestowed upon Markandeya Maharishi The event of the Lord’s grace bestowed upon Markandeya Maharishi is the fourth thought that arose in the woman’s mind, suitable for her state. Although the three thoughts mentioned earlier are also appropriate, if the question arises whether the actions of Yama, who comes according to the law of time, can be averted, then that too is possible only by Lord Shiva. Even if this suffering occurred due to fate for the woman, the thought of this graceful event arises in her mind to convey that Lord Shiva alone has the power to change even fate.

“She entreats the Lord to protect them from Yama, just as He kicked Yama for the young Markandeya. she fervently pleads to the Lord. Her fervent pleading to the Lord is a tradition belonging to devotees.

“The Lord kicks Yama.

“First, he kicks him, and Yama dies.

“Then, he grants grace for him to revive. “Such a Lord, lift us too from this pit of suffering,” she pleads, seeking the grace of Lord Shiva. This sound, raised by the woman who thus contemplates and acts upon Shiva’s grace, reaches the ears of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who is coming to perform the Thirupalli Ezhuchi worship.

“Our reflection now resumes.

“She pleads to the Lord in this manner, which is a tradition for devotees.

“The Lord kicks Yama.

“First, he kicks him, and Yama dies.

“Then, he grants him grace to revive. “Such a Lord, lift us too from this pit of suffering,” she pleads, seeking the grace of Lord Shiva. This sound, raised by the woman who thus contemplates and acts upon Shiva’s grace, reaches the ears of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who is coming to perform the Thirupalli Ezhuchi worship.

“Let us go on reflecting.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 654, composed by Sekkizhar Swamigal, ‘Vambara Varivandu Serukkam’ (The Story of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar). The sound of the woman crying and praying to Lord Shiva reaches the ears of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Sekkizhar Peruman composes the 478th verse as follows: “In this manner, the voice of the distressed maiden, whose slender waist swayed like a tender creeper, praising Shiva’s grace and longing for it, arose. When that sound reached the truly luminous sacred ears of our Shanbai lord, who was approaching to worship, His heart was filled with increasing compassion. He arrived, surrounded by great ascetics, near the distressed woman who was like a swan.” This is the verse.

The maiden, whose slender waist swayed like a tender creeper, suffers, contemplating only Shiva’s grace. The sound of her praising and exalting Shiva reaches the ears of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. That sound, which had the nature of meditating upon and exalting Shiva’s grace, reached Pillaiyar’s truly luminous ears. This is because no other sounds would reach Pillaiyar’s ears; they were truly luminous and sacred ears.

Therefore, the sound of this woman praising Shiva’s grace reached the ears of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. refers to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s ear as a sacred ear. He describes it as a truly luminous sacred ear. This is because Pillaiyar’s ears, speech, and other instruments are all truly luminous, being forms of reality, and sacred.

Therefore, Peruman refers to them as sacred ears. In this verse, he also reveres Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as Andagaiyar, meaning one who is replete with manly qualities. The beauty of manliness is to show compassion to the helpless.

Therefore, he refers to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as Andagaiyar.

At that time, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was arriving for the Thirupalli Ezhuchi worship at Thirumarugal temple in the early morning. The sound of the woman, who had cried and wailed throughout the night, continued to praise and cry out to Shiva until dawn. This sound reaches the ears of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Upon hearing it, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s heart is filled with increasing compassion for the woman. His compassion arises to alleviate the suffering of those who contemplate and praise Shiva’s grace.

Thus, compassion progressively rises more and more in the heart of our Lord, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. He arrives for the early morning Thirupalli Ezhuchi worship, surrounded by great ascetics. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. The presence of great ascetics indicates the absence of suffering. Sekkizhar Peruman then composes the next verse, the 479th verse: “The Brahmana from Sirapuram went and stood, praising Shiva’s grace, and with a melting heart, he looked at the lamenting woman and said, ‘Do not fear! Tell me your great sorrow and your state.’ Then, placing her lotus-like hands above her head, with tears gushing forth, she fell at the sacred feet of the Lord of Veda Puram and recounted how they had come and what had befallen them.” This is that verse.

The Brahmana who appeared in Seerkazhi, Pillaiyar, goes near the woman and bestows his divine gaze upon her, who was contemplating only Lord Shiva’s grace and praising it. Hearing her lament, Pillaiyar approaches her and casts his compassionate gaze upon her. This is because the woman is praising and exalting Shiva’s grace. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman says to the woman, “Do not fear! Tell me your great sorrow and your state.” He grants her fearlessness. Granting fearlessness to anyone is an act that can only be performed by Shiva and his devotees who are Shiva-like in wisdom.

It is an act that only Shiva and his devotees, who are Shiva-like in knowledge, can accomplish, for they are omnipotent. That is why others adhere to their own limits. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman first grants reassurance, saying, “Do not fear,” and then asks about the history. Is it appropriate to grant reassurance and fearlessness to her before knowing the history behind her crying and the nature of her sorrow? Yes, for Shiva has the great power to alleviate any kind of suffering, no matter how severe.

Therefore, it is appropriate. Isn’t it the sacred verse of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, “When the five senses, confounded, lose their way, and intellect is destroyed, and life is restless, He, the one who dwells in the temple, says, ‘Do not fear,’ and grants grace”?

Therefore, first, he grants reassurance and fearlessness, saying, “Do not fear,” and then asks her to narrate her suffering. The woman then begins to recount her past history, the history leading up to her and the merchant arriving at this sacred place.

We shall proceed with our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, composed by Divyasekkizhar Peruman, ‘Vambara Varivandu Serukkam’ (The Story of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar). The woman begins to recount the past history to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. The 480th verse: “This is the son-in-law of my father Thaman, the lord of Vaipur, surrounded by fertile groves. Among his seven young, elephant-like daughters, this one, the eldest, was promised to him. Yet, after receiving much wealth from a stranger and giving her away, he gave away one by one, leaving me.

“Distraught and lamenting for him, how could I not act? Hiding from them, I came with him alone.” This is the verse. In this one verse, Sekkizhar Peruman has arranged for the woman to describe all the past events that occurred. The woman begins to narrate the story of why she came to this town with this merchant, along with the events that happened before. Southwest of Thirumarugal, beyond the Putthar forests and fertile groves, at some distance, lies a village called Vaippur. In Vaippur, there is a merchant named Thaman.

“This Thaman is the woman’s father. Thaman has seven daughters, including this woman. Among the seven daughters, this woman is the youngest, the seventh daughter. The merchant who lies unconscious and dead is Thaman’s son-in-law.

“So, Thaman promises to marry his eldest daughter to this merchant. However, after receiving a large sum of money from a very rich man, he marries the eldest daughter, whom he had promised to this merchant, to that rich man. He tells this merchant, “I will marry my second daughter to you.” While the merchant was thinking of marrying the second daughter, Thaman receives a large sum of money from another rich man and marries his second daughter to that other rich man. He pacifies his son-in-law, the merchant, by saying, “I will marry my third daughter to you.”

“In this manner, he marries off six daughters—three, four, five, six—to wealthy men, having received money.

“Now, only this woman remains, the one who is crying. She observes all these events unfold. She realizes how greedy her father, Thaman, is. The woman feels pity for the merchant, Thaman’s son-in-law. She also falls in love with him. She feels a need to put an end to the cruelty of her father, who keeps promising to give him six daughters but then deceives him by marrying them off to wealthy men.

“In these times, there is a custom of receiving money from the bride’s family for marriage. It seems that in those days, there was also the evil practice of giving a price for a woman. Both are evil practices. Such an evil practice seems to have existed in those days. Thaman is a merchant, so this indicates that he is a very greedy person.

“Therefore, this merchant, who is now lying unconscious here, is repeatedly disappointed and heartbroken, thinking that he will marry one of the six women he is entitled to.

“Therefore, this seventh woman, seeing all this deceptive history, feels pity and love for him and decides that she must marry him. thinking, they leave Vaippur without her father’s knowledge and arrive at Thirumarugal.

“That night, while staying in the monastery opposite Thirumarugal temple, he is bitten by a snake. She cries all night long. She cries towards the entrance of Thirumarugal Peruman’s temple.

“In this way, the woman narrates her past history to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Sekkizhar Peruman has beautifully presented all this history in a single verse, as if spoken by the woman. This verse has a poetic beauty that condenses a long, deceptive history into a few words.

“Moreover, this sorrowful The venerable Deivasekkizhar composed this verse in the same way one would speak in short sentences. The next verse, number four hundred and eighty-one, recounts: “When the serpent bit and killed him, it was as if my ship had capsized in the tumultuous ocean. You appeared as a relative and, by your grace, relieved all my sorrows.” Thus, the venerable Deivasekkizhar narrates that the merchant was bitten by a serpent and died. This verse recounts that the girl then began to sing to the Lord of Thirumarugal, by the grace of the King of Kazhi, whom the learned worship and praise, so that the venom of the serpent that had bitten him might be cured.

“Thus, this merchant died from a serpent bite. “I stand as if my ship has capsized in the middle of the ocean. I have no support on either side. I am in a state of utter helplessness, broken in the middle. Having come with this merchant from her birthplace, she has no support there either. This merchant also has no other relatives.

“Therefore, she says, she is in a state of helplessness, like a ship capsized at sea, without support in either place. She comes from a merchant tradition that engages in sea trade, and so she uses this simile so beautifully. Even in this situation, she recounts the story that came to pass, the suffering she endured, and the reasons for it. When relatives were present and offered comfort, my mind was changed, as if sorrow had been removed. Your words produced that very support for me. She tells Thirugnanasambandhar, “You have graced me by removing all my sorrows.” Pillaiyar, the leader of Kazhi, is the revered king of Thirukazhi, whom the learned worship and praise.

“Grace overflowed in the mind of Pillaiyar, the king of Seerkazhi.

“Therefore, Thirugnanasambandhar sings to the Lord of Thirumarugal, wishing good for the girl, to grant her well-being, and to cure the venom of the serpent that had bitten. The venerable Sekkizhar shows us in the four hundred and eighty-second verse how Pillaiyar bestowed that pathigam, the pathigam that cured the venom. That verse is as follows: “Sadaianai, all souls...” “The Mother of all beings, Shankara, the one with the moon-crested crown, the rider of the bull, the knower of the Vedas, adorned with sacred ash, the one with the weapon that burned the three cities of enemies, the one whom Brahma, who resides on the lotus, and Vishnu, who sleeps on the serpent couch, praise with their beautiful form – ‘Oh Lord, is it fitting that this bright-jeweled woman suffers such weakness because of you?’” Thus begins the song, as the venerable Sekkizhar states. Thirugnanasambandhar sings the pathigam. He sings about the one with braided hair, the one who is the mother of all beings, Shankara, the one with the moon-crested crown, the rider of the bull, the knower of the Vedas, adorned with sacred ash, the one with the weapon that burned the three cities of enemies, the one whom Brahma, who resides on the lotus.

“Brahma, who resides on a lotus, and Vishnu, who sleeps on a serpent couch, praise the Lord whose beautiful form is adorned with ornaments. Oh Lord, is it fitting for you to cause this suffering to this woman adorned with radiant jewels?

“Thus begins this verse. In this verse, starting with “Sadaianai,” the venerable Deivasekkizhar presents the nine qualities of the Lord, just as Pillaiyar presented them in the pathigam. Just as Pillaiyar praised and cried out in the pathigam, so too has the venerable Deivasekkizhar composed this verse, as it appears in the beginning.

“Now, the venom-curing pathigam bestowed by Thirugnanasambandhar. Thirugnanasambandhar’s venom-curing pathigam begins with “Sadaianai.” Thus, the venerable Deivasekkizhar begins this verse with “Sadaianai.” Similarly, we can see how it is composed with phrases like “Vidaiyaai enumaal piraiyaar sadaiyum udaiyaai sadai mel malarum piraiyondru udaiyaay iruvar theriyaador theeththiralaayanaimunthaay enumaal enthaay periya maraiyaar marugal magizhvaay mazhu vaaludaiyaay.” He sings starting with “Sadaianai.” Lord Shiva is the one with braided hair. For Bhagiratha, to revive his deceased ancestors, Lord Shiva gracefully received the Ganges in his braided hair and released it into this world.

“Therefore, he sings starting with “Sadaianai.” Next, He then sings, “Thayaanaanai,” meaning, He who has grace like a mother’s compassion. He sings, “Evvuyirkkum Thayaanaanai,” meaning, He who is the mother of all beings. Next comes “Sankaranai,” which means, He who bestows comfort and grace.

“Next, he sings “Sasikanda Mouliyaanai,” referring to how the moon was in a state of decline, approaching its demise.

“The Lord accepted that moon, saved it from death, and allowed it to grow again. This refers to the Lord’s grace, hence “Sasikanda Mouliyaanai.” Next, he sings “Vidaiyaanai.” “Vidai” means bull, which represents Dharma Nandi. This signifies the Lord’s grace, which acts according to righteousness.

“Next, he sings “Vethiyanai.” This means he is the one who bestowed the Vedas that expound upon all these qualities; he is the one who revealed the Vedas with his grace. Next comes “Vennitraanai.” This term signifies his grace in performing the great cosmic dissolution, dissolving all these worlds, and then recreating them. Next comes “Viravaathaar puram moonrum eriyachethra padaiyaanai,” meaning, the one with the weapon that burned the three cities of enemies.

“The Lord burned the three cities, which signifies his grace in removing the three impurities of souls and bestowing joy. Next comes “Nanmuganum Thirumaalum potri thuthikkum kolam udaiyavan,” meaning, the one whose form is praised and worshipped by Brahma and Vishnu. This refers to the grace where the Lord stands as the supreme being. Next comes “Udaiyaan” which means “possessor” or “Lord”.

“Here, the grace shown to beings by the Lord, who considers all beings as his possessions and all inanimate objects as his property, is indicated by the term “Udaiyaan.” The verses in this pathigam, such as “Udaiyaay thagumo ival un melive enthaay thagumo ival esarave,” are arranged by the venerable Sekkizhar as “Udaiyaane thagumo intha ol ilizhaal un melivu” in this verse. This verse, along with these compositions, is a verse composed by the venerable Deivasekkizhar. Just as in the histories of pathigams like ‘Piththa Pirai Soodi’ and ‘Kootraayina Vaaru’, When recounting their histories, the venerable Deivasekkizhar beautifully portrays them with their respective melodic structures, pathigam arrangements, and rhythms.

“Similarly, the venerable Deivasekkizhar now bestows this verse. This pathigam, the venom-curing pathigam, which Thirugnanasambandhar graciously composed for the Lord of Thirumarugal, is set to this musical mode. It is the eighteenth pathigam of the second Thirumurai. This pathigam is as follows: (yaay thagumaa ivalu thoongaaumaar sivane ezumaar munthaayanumaal muthalvaa vilumaa poovazhai uzhavum marugal ezunthaay thagumo ivaiyae saravae araiyaar kalalum alalvaayavum iraiyaar sadaiyum udaiyaayp periya maraiyaar marugal magizhvaay ivalai iraiyaar valai kondu ezuvanaaiyae) (polineer thadaiyil karunthaayulagam pazhi neer theervaay pazhiyil poogalai mazhi neer marugal magizhvaaykkivalai veli neermaiyaakkavum vendinaayae thunineelam vannam muyal thondriya mani neela kandam udaiyaay marugal kanineelavandiival thann azhileezhdhan ayalvaakkina palarum parava padu) (vaay sadai mea malarum peerai undu udaiyaay marugal pularum thaniyum puyila udai poonthu alarum padamo adiyaali valae valuverumaan alarvaya ezuvinaiyum pagalum maluvaaludaiya marugal perumaan kuzhuvaali velai uyaraaginaiyae ilangai iraivan vilangal eduppa pulanga viral)

“(thondrala balam kolmathil sool marugal thirumalanthai alaraakkina eriya sadaiyum adiyum erovaru theriyaathoththi thiral laar piriyar marugal arivalai ayarvaakkinaae arivil samoo azhar saakkiyalum neriyala seythar roolvaar mariya) (iyarnthu kaiyaay maruthal perumaanaar kooda nirai neekkinaai yey gnaanam varula maruthal perumaan uyar gnaanam unarnthu adi unputhalar iyal gnaana sambandhan paadal palliya gnaana muyala vilangum poongale yezham ivar) Thirugnanasambandhar bestows this pathigam. Each verse of this pathigam expresses the woman’s sorrow and the intention to remove it. Subsequently, Sekkizhar composes the four hundred and eighty-third verse: “The surging venom subsided, and he rose. The vast assembly of unique devotees erupted in joyous shouts.

“She cupped her hands above her head and, with reverence, bowed at the feet of the gracious Pillaiyar of Kazhi. So that the woman and the devoted merchant could live happily on this vast earth, the king of Pugazhi, where dark clouds gather over the beautiful gardens, arranged for their prosperous life.” This verse states that as soon as Thirugnanasambandhar finished the pathigam and concluded with the Thirukkappu, the merchant was immediately cured of the poison and stood up. The surrounding devotees rejoice. The girl clasps her hands above her head and bows at the sacred feet of the graceful Pillaiyar of Seerkazhi.

“The King of Seerkazhi arranges their marriage, so that the woman and the loving merchant, her beloved, may live happily in this world. He graciously arranges for them to begin their married life and live a great life. Thirugnanasambandhar performed the wedding ceremony right there, in front of him, and completed the marriage. For those married by the graceful gaze of Aludaiya Pillaiyar, that itself becomes a great life. This great The Lord refers to the woman as ‘Nangai’, which means ‘the best among women’. He refers to the merchant as ‘Nambi’, meaning ‘the best among men’.

“He uses the word ‘nayandha’, which means ‘who loved’. He mentions that they live happily on this earth, which is the fruit of marriage. By being married through the gracious gaze of Thirugnanasambandhar, they attained a joyful life. This joy encompasses both worldly and otherworldly happiness.

“Thus, the venerable Sekkizhar composes this narrative of the miraculous event that occurred in Thirumarugal. This pathigam bestowed by Thirugnanasambandhar consists of eleven verses. This part of the Puranas, which recounts the incident in Thirumarugal where the poison was removed, The part of the Purana that recounts the incident of bestowing the venom-curing pathigam in Thirumarugal also comprises eleven verses.

“Therefore, if maidens who are suffering without marriage recite with devotion and regularity for some time these eleven verses from this part of the Purana, and also this pathigam beginning with “Sadaiyaa enumal,” bestowed by Thirugnanasambandhar, they will visibly obtain auspicious good marriages. This is a truth we witness in many places, and it illustrates the greatness of Pillaiyar’s grace even today.

“Thus, the history of that miraculous grace that occurred in Thirumarugal, demonstrated by Thirugnanasambandhar, comes to an end. We shall continue our reflection.”” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, Part 656, Vampara Varivandu Sarga, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, composed by the venerable Deivasekkizhar. In Thirumarugal, Thirugnanasambandhar bids farewell to the merchant couple who were married there, allowing them to return to their hometown.

Afterwards, he resides with great pleasure in the sacred place of Thirumarugal. It is then that Siruthonda Nayanar comes to Thirumarugal and meets Thirugnanasambandhar. Siruthonda Nayanar is renowned for having overcome the strength of the powerful impurity of anava (ego). Such a great saint comes and meets Thirugnanasambandhar. Siruthonda Nayanar requests Thirugnanasambandhar to return to his own city, Thiruchengattangudi. Pillaiyar, whose heart was filled with a deep desire to return to Thiruchengattangudi, considered the divine will of the Lord.

To worship Him, he reached the Thirumarugal temple with his devotees. Pillaiyar entered the temple, prostrated, and offered praise. Inside the temple, he stood before the Lord and worshipped Him.

The Lord revealed His divine form to Thirugnanasambandhar. The Lord, whose braided hair shone with the surging waters of the Ganges and the crescent moon, like a red sky, was adorned with a crown of matted locks. His divine body, adorned with sacred ash, appeared green on one side. Pillaiyar contemplated and worshipped the Lord with the venom-darkened throat, who resided in the temple of Thirumarugal.

At that moment, the Lord, holding fire in His hand, showed His form in Ganapateeswaram, revealing it to Thirugnanasambandhar. When worshipping the Lord in the Thirumarugal temple, the Lord appeared as Ganapateeswarar, who resides in Thiruchengattangudi. We saw that one part of the Lord’s body appeared green, which signifies that He should be meditated upon and worshipped as the Lord with Uma as His half, endowed with grace. Green represents the Mother’s side, and it indicates the divine grace.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandhar meditated. This is how the Lord in Thirumarugal appears as Ammaiappar. He showed the scene in Ganapateeswaram. Thirugnanasambandhar perceives that the Lord shows him the scene of Ganapateeswaram in Thiruchengattangudi while in Thirumarugal.

Therefore, Pillaiyar realizes that going there again is a divine indication. The beloved and complete form in Thirumarugal appears to Thirugnanasambandhar as the glorious form of Ganapateeswarar, which is established and flourishing in Thiruchengattangudi. As this realization dawns upon him, his heart melts.

Consequently, his love overflows, and compassion, intending to enlighten the world, surges in Thirugnanasambandhar’s heart. Tears of joy stream from his eyes like a waterfall, and he bestows a pathigam beginning with “Angamum Vedamum.” This pathigam is in the form of questions and answers. Siruthondar requested him to go to Thiruchengattangudi, and when he went to worship the Lord in Thirumarugal to take leave for that purpose, When Thirugnanasambandhar visited the Lord in Thirumarugal to take leave for that purpose, the Lord revealed His beloved form of Ganapateeswaram there. This pathigam was composed in the form of questions and praises. This pathigam praised the indication that he was given leave to go to Ganapateeswaram as he wished.

Therefore, this pathigam applies to both Thirumarugal and Thiruchengattangudi. In every verse of this pathigam, Thirugnanasambandhar sings about Thiruchengattangudi, where wealth abounds and glory thrives, and about Ganapateeswaram, where the Lord dances with a fierce elephant skin at night, as if he saw it in Thirumarugal. In each verse of this pathigam, praising both Thirumarugal and Thiruchengattangudi, Thirugnanasambandhar has composed verses like “Ganapathi Eeswaram Kaamurave Marugal Nilaaviyamaintha Sollaay.” This pathigam is the sixth pathigam of the first Thirumurai, composed in the Nattappadai musical mode. The first, ninth, and eleventh verses of this pathigam are as follows: “Wealth...” (SeerkuL chengaaga nuL kangul vilang ari yezhu yadum ganapathi sooram kaamurave angamum maathiriyum naan moog aravanai manthirave thangal pothum naruthal magizhntha solla thamizhorgal paraviyathum seerkuL chengaara) (athanu thangammaiyae thamalum ganapathi sooram thaamooravelaai pongu kaali aana sambam thangum alanthigalum maalin mathe thaval maadam vaangu marugil matradhe mozhintha semuyalum thilaiththa kallul chengathanoo soozamballa)

Having bestowed this pathigam, Thirugnanasambandhar, according to the Lord’s divine command, journeyed from Thirumarugal to Thiruchengattangudi, worshipped the Lord Ganapathi and resided in that town for some days. After staying in Thiruchengattangudi for some days, worshipping and taking leave from the devotees, Thirugnanasambandhar departed from that ancient town and began his journey to worship at the sacred place called Poompugalur.

Our reflection now resumes. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, Part 657, Vampara Varivandu Sarga, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, composed by the venerable Deivasekkizhar. Thirugnanasambandhar continues his pilgrimage from Thiruchengattangudi, intending to visit the sacred place of Thirupugalur. Siruthonda Nayanar, whose eminence is enhanced by his virtues, accompanies Thirugnanasambandhar for a short distance with friendship.

Then, Siruthonda Nayanar takes leave from Thirugnanasambandhar and returns to his city, Thiruchengattangudi. Thirugnanasambandhar bids farewell to Siruthonda Nayanar, who accompanied him, and instructs him to remain in Thiruchengattangudi and continue his service.

Therefore, Siruthonda Nayanar also returns to his city, Thirugnanasambandhar. visits many sacred sites. Sivakavimani Ayya explains that these sacred sites include Thiruramanadeeswaram, Thirupanaiyur, and others. Among these, we have a pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandhar for the sacred site of Thiruramanadeeswaram. It is the one hundred and fifteenth pathigam of the first Thirumurai. This pathigam is set to the tune called Vyazakkurinchi. The first and final verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam.

“Among those with conch-like hands, he who seeks alms and whose fierce serpent dances, may the world flourish. Oh Thiruramanadeeswaram!

“” The eleventh verse of this pathigam is not available to us due to our lack of merit. Having visited all these places, The venerable Deivasekkizhar mentions that Thirugnanasambandhar, having visited all these sacred places, arrived at the flourishing and wealthy city of Pugalur. Thirugnanasambandhar reaches the city of Pugalur, also known as Poompugalur. Poompugalur is a city where abundant wealth flourishes throughout the world. It is mentioned in Pillaiyar’s Thevaram pathigam as “Pugazhum Selvam Malgum Pugalur,” meaning “Pugalur where wealth praised by the world abounds.” Deivasekkizhar also highlights this here. Poompugalur is a place of immense wealth.

“This wealth includes both material prosperity and spiritual grace. Poompugalur is a sacred place that abundantly offers both these forms of wealth. How abundant is the spiritual wealth there? Indeed, Thirugnanasambandhar, who resides here, stays for a long time in Thirumuganayanar’s ashram with his devotees. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, Thiruneelanaka Nayanar, Siruthonda Nayanar, and other Nayanmars all come and join him during the period when Thirugnanasambandhar is residing there.

“Therefore, Thirumuganayanar’s ashram is a sacred place blessed with spiritual wealth, where Thirugnanasambandhar, Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal, Thiruneelanaka Nayanar, Siruthonda Nayanar, and other Nayanmars converse. It is a sacred place where Thirunavukkarasu Peruman is about to merge with the Lord, possessing spiritual wealth. It is a sacred place where Sundaramurthy Swamigal received the spiritual wealth of transforming bricks into radiant gold. Thirumuganayanar performed the sacred service of offering flowers, and Poompugalur is the sacred place that received that spiritual wealth.

“Therefore, Sekkizhar Swamigal refers to this sacred place as “Paarin malinthu niraintha selvam payil Pugalur,” meaning “Pugalur, where abundant wealth flourishes throughout the world.” Thirugnanasambandhar reaches this sacred place of Poompugalur. Thirumuganayanar, along with the devotees residing in Thirupugalur, comes with intense devotion to the outskirts of the city to welcome Thirugnanasambandhar. He is referred to by the venerable Sekkizhar as “Semmai Muruganar,” which means “Muruganayanar who stands on the path of righteousness.” The path of righteousness is indeed the path of Shiva. This is This is also called the path of truth, the path of light, and the path of the Guru. Such a righteous Thirumuganayanar, along with the devotees of Pugalur, comes out of the city to welcome Thirugnanasambandhar. Thirumuganayanar leads Thirugnanasambandhar into the city.

“Thirugnanasambandhar reaches the temple of the sacred place. There, he worships the temple tower, which stands like a mountain. The temple tower of Poompugalur is compared to Mount Kailash, possessing unique glory and pre-eminence. It is a path to reach Lord Shiva.

“Therefore, the temple tower of Poompugalur is said to be equivalent to Mount Kailash. There, he circumambulates the outer courtyard of the Lord’s temple. Thirugnanasambandhar, the Lord who comprehended all knowledge without studying, is meant to have understood knowledge not by learning in this birth but by previous spiritual merit. As for Aludaiya Pillaiyar and others, to address the question of how knowledge arose without penance, it is emphasized here that one should perform prescribed actions, rituals, and yogas. We can see this in the first adhikaranam of Sivagnanabodham, where Srimadhavar Sivagnana Munivar explained, “Here, through penance, knowledge arises in this manner.” Therefore, all the profound true knowledge and incomparable artistic knowledge within Thirugnanasambandhar’s intellect were realized by him as Shiva revealed them. This is what we saw in the one thousand nine hundred and sixty-seventh verse: “Thus, the chief of penance, Sambandhar, realized it.” Therefore, Thirugnanasambandhar, the Lord who realized all this knowledge without studying, reached the temple of Lord Shiva, the foremost of the Vedas.

“He entered through the temple tower, which was like Mount Kailash, circumambulated the beautiful courtyard, and with a unified mind, entered the temple. The venerable Sekkizhar composes this verse, number four hundred and eighty-nine: “With the devotees of Thirupugalur and Semmai Muruganar coming with genuine joy to welcome him, the Chief of the Vedas reached his temple, entered through the magnificent tower, circumambulated the flourishing courtyard, and with a focused mind, entered.” This describes how he entered.

“Next, the four hundred and ninety-ninth verse. The venerable Sekkizhar composes this verse: “He entered, prostrated, rose, and with a melting heart, his devotion overflowing, tears streaming from his eyes like a waterfall, he adorned the Lord, the virtuous one residing in Poompugalur, with a garland of beautiful Tamil verses, sang in the seven melodies, and then, with Murugar, whose fame spread in all directions, leading the way, he entered his ashram.” This verse describes how Thirugnanasambandhar entered the temple, worshipped the Lord, prostrated, rose, and with a melting heart, his devotion overflowing, tears streaming from his eyes like a waterfall, he adorned the Lord, the virtuous one residing in Poompugalur, with a garland of beautiful Tamil verses. He worshipped the Lord there by singing the seven melodies. This describes the methods of worship Thirugnanasambandhar performed inside the temple, the state in which he worshipped the Lord by singing pathigams, and his state after coming out. Each of Thirugnanasambandhar’s actions, such as prostrating, rising, adorning, singing, and leaving, is thus indicated in this verse. He worshipped the Lord with his heart melting and love overflowing.

“Melting means melting like butter in fire. As love increased more and more, like milk boiling with increasing heat, his heart melted with love and overflowed. When it overflowed, As his heart melted and love overflowed within, tears streamed from Thirugnanasambandhar’s eyes like a waterfall. “Is there a bolt to contain love?” asks Thirukkural.

“Thus, Thirugnanasambandhar, while worshipping, bestowed a pathigam rich in meaning and beautiful in language before the Lord. Afterwards, he sang it in the Lord’s courtyard, accompanied by rhythm and Yazh music. That pathigam is set to the Sevvazhi musical mode. The first, second, and final verses of this pathigam are as follows: (bel puzhallai aada veravu sing paayum pookooththu thingal sodi thire purambo amba) (eri engal adi para naalum idaru gali melum inee vaazhum naalum aritheerththumaa) (eaththa vintha thingal pori sadaiyam pungaloore yea soozhntha ulam udai puyal theerumea eanthi aantha)

“(periya yea thoothalooththanu venta sal pudi poosa vidai poorthiyai yem yea anal laadali yaana sang pannaa) Having bestowed this pathigam, Thirugnanasambandhar, with Thirumuganayanar guiding him, proceeds to Thirumuganayanar’s ashram. It is our tradition to refer to the dwelling places and lodging places of devotees as ashrams.

“Here, Thirumuganayanar’s ashram is where Pillaiyar resides with his entourage. Thirumuganayanar’s ashram is blessed with the presence of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, Siruthonda Nayanar, Thiruneelanakka Nayanar, and other Nayanmars, and is renowned for having hosted a great Maheswara Puja. Thirugnanasambandhar journeys to such an ashram.

“Let us go on reflecting.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, Part 658, Vampara Varivandu Sarga, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, composed by the venerable Deivasekkizhar. During the time when Pillaiyar was residing at Thirumuganayanar’s ashram in Thirupugalur, a desire arose in Thirugnanasambandhar’s heart to worship the Lord at Thirupugalur Varthamaneeswaram and praise Him. With overflowing love, Thirugnanasambandhar praises the exalted service performed by Thirumuganayanar there and bestows a powerful Tamil pathigam, rich in exalted qualities. Thirupugalur Varthamaneeswaram is a separate shrine within the Agneeswarar temple in Thirupugalur.

There, Pillaiyar praises the sacred service of offering flowers, performed by Thirumuganayanar, in his own divine words, and bestows the Thirupugalur Varthamaneeswaram pathigam. That pathigam, the Thirupugalur Varthamaneeswaram pathigam, is the ninety-second pathigam of the second Thirumurai, composed in the Piyanthaikandharam musical mode. The first and final verses of this pathigam are as follows: Pugazhoor, where birds and their mates frolic in the shelters, praised by circles, is the abode of the Lord.

The Lord is adorned with flowers, surrounded by a surging river, and praised by Thiru Gnanasambandhar with glorious verses that are like the light of the moon. This pathigam’s note states that in every part of Thiru Pugazhoor, Lord Muruganayanar and the deity reside, graciously accepting offerings and other services performed three times a day without fail.

At that time, while Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was staying in Thiru Pugazhoor, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman arrived in Thiruvarur, worshipped the Lord who had settled in the anthill, praised Thiruvarur, and then, intending to worship in Thiru Pugazhoor, he came to Thiru Pugazhoor with a throng of devotees who had received the grace of the Lord. Sekizhar Peruman sings about this in the following verses: “On that auspicious day, the great king of words came and worshipped the Lord who had settled in the anthill, praised Thiruvarur with its golden walls, and resolved to worship in Thiru Pugazhoor, where the Lord dwells with the goddess bearing a tiny golden bracelet. He arrived there with the multitude of devotees who had received the grace of the king.” This verse states that Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, after worshipping in Thiru Peruvellur, Thiru Vilamar, and other sacred places, first worshipped in Thiruvarur and praised the Lord of Aroor there. While staying in Thiruvarur, he visited and worshipped in Thiruvalivalam, Thikkiizhvelur, Kanraappur, and other shrines, then returned to Thiruvarur. After witnessing the Thiruvathirai festival in Thiruvarur, he departed from there and arrived in Thiru Pugazhoor. With a desire to worship Lord Shiva, who shares half his body with the goddess adorned with a small golden bracelet, he proceeded to Thiru Pugazhoor with a gathering of devotees.

Sekizhar Peruman continues to sing the four hundred and ninety-third verse: “When Thirugnanasambandhar, the son of the Lord who shines on the bull, heard the good news that Thirunavukkarasu was arriving, his heart swelled with fervent love, and he hastened to meet him. With true devotees, he crossed the boundaries of Thiru Pugazhoor, surrounded by blooming lotus ponds and gardens.” This is the verse. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman hears the good news that Thirunavukkarasu Peruman is arriving in Thiru Pugazhoor. The news of the arrival of kings is indeed a great and beneficial message. It is a great blessing to gather a crowd of devotees, and even greater is the blessing of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s arrival.

This is its meaning. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman had always expected Thirunavukkarasu Peruman at his wedding, and the news of his arrival was indeed good news for Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. The passage from Thiruvachagam, “Arularivar Empran Aavare,” is called “Thiruvartthai.” We can recall here that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, due to having consumed the milk of wisdom, attained the status of Lord Shiva’s son. Such a Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, with his heart overflowing with intense love, crosses the city of Thiru Pugazhoor to quickly meet Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. He goes to the outskirts of the city, where there are paddy fields, past the city limits of Thiru Pugazhoor, which is special for its lotus ponds surrounding the temple.

This indicates the intensity of his love and the tradition of meeting Thirunavukkarasu Peruman.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrived at the place outside the city, the area surrounded by fields, which is the southern boundary of the city. Sekizhar Peruman then composed two verses. “There, after worshipping in Aroor, the king arrived, and the lion of the Brahmins, who came from Pugazhi with surging waters, gracefully approached. With their love, they bowed and worshipped each other, and as they joyfully inquired about each other’s auspicious well-being, the true Thirugnanasambandhar, looking at the king of words with affection, said, ‘We are greatly blessed to have you here. Tell us how you worshipped and were saved in Aroor.’ To this, the great ascetic replied with a garland of beautiful Tamil verses, describing the glory of the Thiruvathirai festival.” This is what Sekizhar Peruman composes. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the embodiment of truth, was there at the border of Poo Pugazhoor to welcome Thirunavukkarasu Peruman.

At the same time, Appar, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, arrived there.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, addressing Appar Peruman, says that they were greatly blessed to have him, Appar, come there. Pillaiyar and Arasukal greet each other with auspicious welcomes and converse.

After these two great personalities met and parted in Seerkazhi, this is now their second sacred meeting here. So, they meet in Seerkazhi. After meeting and parting, they both exchange accounts of the auspicious events of Lord Shiva’s grace that have occurred to them until now. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the embodiment of truth, tells Thirunavukkarasu Peruman that his arrival here is a great blessing obtained through divine grace. This indicates the grace of the Lord and the grace of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman asks Thirunavukkarasu Peruman about this great grace, inquiring, “How did you worship and achieve salvation?” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman asks about the experience of worshipping and enjoying Thiruvarur.

In response, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman bestows a pathigam in the form of a Tamil garland. He bestows a pathigam, explaining the special significance of the Thiruvathirai festival in Thiruvarur, making it a masterpiece. The glory of witnessing the Thiruvathirai festival in Thiruvarur is considered the best among all riches, as if it were the true wealth itself. Appar Peruman then bestows the Thiruvathirai pathigam.

Now, the next verse: “Upon hearing the truth spoken by Arasu, the king of Sirapuram, endowed with divine wisdom, developed an intense love in his heart to worship in Southern Thiruvarur. He went, worshipped, and then returned, saying, ‘I will rejoin you,’ and with that understanding, he swiftly departed,” says the verse. Upon hearing the way Thirunavukkarasu Peruman had responded with his pathigam, Pillaiyar, the leader of Seerkazhi, immediately developed a great desire in his heart to go and worship in Southern Thiruvarur. This is because the Thiruvathirai pathigam bestowed by Appar Peruman is a true sacred utterance; it is a mantra.

Therefore, upon hearing that pathigam, which speaks of Thiruvarur and the glory of the Thiruvathirai festival in Thiruvarur, Pillaiyar felt compelled to go and worship in Thiruvarur. So, Pillaiyar takes leave of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, saying, “I will return here after visiting Thiruvarur, just as I came to meet you now. You must remain in this sacred place until I return.” With these words, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman takes leave of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. Pillaiyar, who had come to meet and receive Arasukal, did not enter Thiru Pugazhoor with Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. From the very spot where he met and worshipped Thirunavukkarasu Peruman amidst the paddy fields on the outskirts of Thiru Pugazhoor, he took leave of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman and set off towards Thiruvarur. This was due to his profound love for the Lord of Thiruvarur.

The immense love that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman felt in his heart, which prompted him to leave even Appar Peruman, whom he had intended to accompany, and to depart immediately upon hearing the greatness of Thiruvarur, was truly remarkable. This highlights the greatness of the pathigam bestowed by Appar Peruman, the truth of practicing the five-letter mantra, and the greatness of Appar Swamigal. It also underscores the glory of the Thiruvathirai festival in Aroor.

Furthermore, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman also Thirunavukkarasu Peruman was delighted and readily accepted Pillaiyar’s desire to go and worship in Thiruvarur and return, rather than having Pillaiyar accompany him to Thiru Pugazhoor at that moment. This demonstrates the greatness of love.

Thus, taking leave of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman hastened towards Southern Thiruvarur. The area where the Lord’s flower temple is located in Thiruvarur is its southern part, hence he headed towards Southern Thiruvarur. Driven by the intensity of his love, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman traveled very quickly.

Moreover, the Thiruvathirai festival had just concluded.

Therefore, with an eagerness to see the holy city of Thiruvarur before the signs of the festival disappeared, and a desire to worship Lord Thiyagarajar before he returned to his original seat, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman hastened towards Thiruvarur, his desire intensifying. We shall proceed with our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Six Hundred and Fifty-Nine, Vampara Varivandu Sarrkkam, by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, on the life of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman enters Thiru Pugazhoor to worship. Pillaiyar, the chief of Seerkazhi, continues his pilgrimage towards Thiruvarur, keeping Thiruvarur in his thoughts.

However, he worships in the temples along the way. Following the custom that one should worship at the shrines along the way when embarking on a pilgrimage, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships at the temples he encounters. Among the temples he worshipped was Thiru Virkudi. “The great king of words, and the leader of Thoni Mootoor, followed by love, went to worship in Thiru Pugazhoor.

“The Lord of Pugazhi, with a focused mind, went to Virkudi Veerattam, worshipped the feet of the Lord with the bull, praised Him, and sang the four Vedas with many thousands of devotees.” This is a verse composed by Sekkizhar Peruman.

“Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman sings that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman went to Virkudi Veerattam and worshipped there. We have obtained a pathigam bestowed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for this holy shrine of Thiru Virkudi Veerattam. Thiru Virkudi Veerattam is the seventy-fourth sacred place on the southern bank of the Kaveri. It is one of the eight places where Lord Shiva’s heroic deeds took place. This is the place where Jalandharasuran was destroyed. The Swami’s temple is built on a hill, a Madakkovil.

“We can see the Utsava Murthi holding the blazing discus that split Jalandharasura in his hand. This temple is very close to Thiruvarur, located between Mayiladuthurai and Peralam. The Swami’s name is Veerattaneshwarar, and the Goddess’s name is Yelavarkuzhali Parimalanayaki. Chakratheertham and Sangu Theertham are the sacred waters. This is the place where Vishnu accepted Jalandharasura’s wife as Tulasi by Lord Shiva’s grace, hence the sacred tree here is said to be Tulasi. The Linga image worshipped by Vishnu is in a separate temple.

“These are some notes about this sacred place. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who visited this place, bestowed a pathigam. It is the one hundred and eighth pathigam in the Second Thirumurai, set to the tune of Nattaragam. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (VadikkuL meniyaru panamathiyinaru nadhiyinaru madhuvar kadikkuL kudaiyizhaL udaip puliyath paru vidaiya therum emma amarndhu veeram adiyil yethavallamai aruvilai adaiya ve) (Vilangale silaiyidam ena udaiyavaL pirgudi veeraththu kizhangku suvaiyai em peruma thanai ezhuthigal kazhal peni nalang koLvar kaliyuL yana samba pazhangkote isai mozhiyumil mozhitha kattathathu param mame mattathathu param mame) This pathigam’s note states that those who praise the glories of the Lord, who resides in Verkudi Veerattam, will not be afflicted by karma.

“Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who departed from Thiru Pugazhoor, worships at this shrine on his way to Thiruvarur, heading south. After worshipping and singing this pathigam, he continues his pilgrimage towards Thiruvarur, surrounded by thousands of devotees. Pillaiyar proceeds, meditating on the Lord of Thiruvarur and singing pathigams.
