Thirugnanasambandha Peruman journeys towards Thiruvarur, singing the Thiruvarur pathigam that begins with “Paadal Nanmarai.” Therefore, this pathigam, beginning with “Paadal Nanmarai,” was bestowed while meditating on the Lord of Thiruvarur on the way to Thiruvarur. It is the one hundred and fifth pathigam of the First Thirumurai, set to the tune of Viyalakurinji. This pathigam is one of the six pathigams bestowed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for the sacred place of Thiruvarur.

“The first, third, and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: “Surrounding bracelets.” (Konde kella dalan adhi am thane uLLamuri puganthe kuzhumi thuNdithye kallam kozhidu arravadhi puzhu ahparkke melagan kaNi) (Aroor adaivome e puzhal pugale thamizh yar sambantham thaLLa aLLi mabar pazhani avoor amarnthana vallatho ichai nadu ivai patthum vaykoLLuthal kettakumbam udaiparu e) The pathigam states that going to Thiruvarur, worshipping, and bowing are our duties, and we shall achieve them by praising Thiruvarur. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, singing this pathigam on his way to Thiruvarur, reaches the outskirts of the holy city.

“The Lord of Thiruvarur is worthy of song and displays a divine form that delights those who behold it. He performs the sacred dance during the night of Samharam. He is Aathiraiyan. Aathirai is an auspicious day for Lord Shiva. This Thiruvathirai festival is of great significance in Thiruvarur. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman has elaborated on its glories in his separate pathigam about the Thiruvathirai festival.

“That It is also said that Pillaiyar was prompted to worship in Thiruvarur simply by hearing that pathigam.

“Therefore, in accordance with this, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises the Lord as Aathiraiyan in the first verse of this pathigam.

“The Lord of Thiruvarur performs the sacred dance of the Thiruvathirai festival. In Thiruvarur, where humming bees musically resound in the groves, and the smoke from the furnaces rises to meet the clouds, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman declares that it is our duty to go morning and evening to worship the sacred feet of the Lord, who is the Supreme Being, adorned with ghee and curd. “Palodu Ney Thairum Payindradu” refers to the This is a special reference to the Thiruvathirai sacred anointing ceremony. Worshipping Him is the act we must perform. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has beautifully explained this state of journeying towards Thiruvarur in this pathigam. The lines serve as internal evidence supporting the idea that Pillaiyar travels swiftly due to the immense love in his heart to worship Thiruvarur, as sung by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, “Worship with a heart filled with desire.” In this pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states that by praising the sacred feet of the Lord of Thiruvarur, who holds a battle-axe, who has a dark throat, who wears a five-headed serpent around his waist, and who is adorned with tender Konrai flowers, sins will Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has stated that sins will be destroyed and good things will come daily.

“Therefore, if we worship the Lord of Thiruvarur, our sins will be annihilated, which signifies the destruction of attachments, and good things will come, which signifies the attainment of Shiva.

“Thus, both the destruction of attachments and the attainment of Shiva will come to beings if they worship the sacred feet of the Lord of Thiruvarur. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sings that attaining liberation from birth is easy by worshipping the Lord of Thiruvarur. “Veedu Pirappu” means freedom from birth. It means being released from the cycle of birth. If one goes to Thiruvarur, praises the Lord, and bows before him, one will be freed from birth and attain liberation. It is very easy to attain liberation and freedom from birth in this manner.

“The easiest means to this is to go to Thiruvarur, praise the Lord, and worship with folded hands. In the Thirukadaikkappu of this pathigam, he refers to the Lord of Thiruvarur as “Alli Malarkazhani Aroor Amarnthanai.” This refers to the special feature of Thiruvarur, which is the Sengazhuneer stream, one of the three areas measuring five acres that include the temple, pond, and stream.

“Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises the Lord of Thiruvarur throughout this pathigam and reaches the outskirts of the city of Thiruvarur. We shall continue our reflection.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Six Hundred and Sixty, Vampara Varivandu Sarrkkam, by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, on the life of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reaches the boundary of the city of Thiruvarur.

There, the city of Thiruvarur appears like a golden world, shining with great brilliance. Sekkizhar Peruman composes the four hundred and ninety-ninth verse: “The city of Thiruvarur, where lofty banners reach the sun’s orb in the sky, appears like a golden world. Seeing its radiant brilliance, the white-ashed Pillaiyar from Sanbai sings the Tamil musical pathigam, ‘Parukkai Yanai,’ as bees and wasps hum in the groves, and he reaches the boundary of that holy city.” Lofty red rays There is a sun mandala with high red rays in the sky, and long banners in the city of Thiruvarur extend as if to reach it. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sees the city of Thiruvarur shining like a golden world. Pillaiyar, adorned with pure white sacred ash like milk, beholds this sight of the city of Thiruvarur and sings the Tamil musical pathigam, ‘Parukkai Yanai.’ The city of Thiruvarur appears like a golden world, not merely the heavenly abode, because in the heavenly abode, gods experience various joys and sorrows. That life in the heavenly world can lead to rebirth.

Therefore, Thiyagesa Peruman, who stayed there for some days, Lord Thiyagesan, who had been residing there, came to Thiruvarur and delighted in the flower temple, remaining there without going elsewhere.

Therefore, all the celestials come here to praise and worship Lord Thiyagesan.

Thus, Thiruvarur is named the golden world. The heavenly world is a luminous sphere, but the city of Thiruvarur shines with an even greater brilliance, visible from a great distance. Pillaiyar, adorned with pure white sacred ash on his body, sees this light. He then bestows a pathigam. The rhythm of this pathigam is very fast, and its musical arrangement is conducive to singing and dancing. This music is called Thiru Viragam.

Singing and dancing this pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reaches the boundary of Thiruvarur. Such is this pathigam, the one hundred and first pathigam of the Second Thirumurai, set to the tune of Nattaragam, the Thiru Viragam pathigam. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Nithilam neera ke poruppaL tharukkoL solai poola needu mada maligai thoni arukkan maNdalaththu anaivum antha Aroothh enpathe vaLLi solai sotham needu maNNu veethi ponnuLai aLLi madu amarnthiru antha Aro) This pathigam describes and revels in the fact that Thiruvarur is indeed the city of Shiva.

Thus, Pillaiyar, immersed in this, scatters flowers, sings, and worships the city of Thiruvarur. Sekkizhar Peruman describes this in the five hundredth verse: “As if the surging flood of love from Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s heart poured upon the earth, his palanquin, a jeweled litter emanating cool radiance everywhere, descended. The Tamil adept, Pillaiyar, came down, scattered many flowers with his red hands, and praised the city of Thiruvarur by singing the Thiruvirukural pathigam, where his Lord reigns.” This is the verse composed by Sekkizhar Swamigal. The great flood of love that surged from Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s heart seemed to pour onto this earth. From his palanquin, a pearl litter radiating cool light, he descended. Pillaiyar, the Tamil adept, scattered many flowers with his red hands and praised the city of Thiruvarur, where his Lord reigns, by singing the Thiruvirukural pathigam.

Pillaiyar, having earlier seen the abundant light of Thiruvarur and sung a pathigam in praise, arrived at the boundary of Thiruvarur. There, he descended from his palanquin, scattered flowers, and worshipped the city, singing the Thiruvirukural pathigam. The fact that he worshipped the holy city of Thiruvarur by scattering flowers with his red hands is evident from the numerous references in the pathigam just mentioned, where Thirugnanasambandha Peruman himself speaks of scattering flowers of devotion, golden flowers, fragrant flowers, and red flowers.

Similarly, we can see that Pillaiyar worshipped Thiru Muthukundram by circling the city and scattering flowers. The pathigam for that shrine, which also speaks of standing and scattering flowers, is structured similarly. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman demonstrates to us that worshipping the presiding deity of a shrine, as well as the shrine itself, and praising its sacred names, is a supreme act of devotion.

Therefore, the pathigam that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman now sang, scattering flowers and worshipping the city of Thiruvarur, is the Thiruvirukural pathigam. This pathigam, a poetic form with a two-footed meter, is where Lord Thiyagaraja reigns as Veethi Vidangar.

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to it as the place where the Lord reigns. “Amarar Naadu Aaladhae Aroor Aanda Airavanamay” is a sacred utterance from the Thevaram. The pathigam thus bestowed is the ninety-first pathigam of the First Thirumurai, set to the Kurinji tune, the Thiruvirakku Kural pathigam. It begins with “Sitthan Theliveergal Atthan Aroorai Patthi Malarthoova Muththi Aagumae,” meaning, “Oh pure souls, scatter flowers of devotion upon the Lord of Thiruvarur, and liberation will be yours.” The first, second, fifth, and eleventh verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman scatters flowers, sings, and worships the city of Thiruvarur. All the devotees of the city of Thiruvarur, upon hearing the news of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s arrival, meet Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

Our reflection now resumes. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Six Hundred and Sixty-One, Vampara Varivandu Sarrkkam, by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, on the life of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who partook of incomparable wisdom-nectar, is met by the devotees of Thiruvarur, who go forth to worship him. Who can fully comprehend the radiant beauty of Thiruvarur, where the Lord eternally resides? No one can.

The devotees of such a glorious city of Thiruvarur go forth to meet Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. The greatness of the devotees of Thiruvarur is immeasurable. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sings a pathigam, asking the devotees who worship him, “Will my Lord accept me?” This is the glory of the devotees of the city of Thiruvarur. These devotees are blessed to be born in Thiruvarur, which grants liberation upon birth.

Sundaramoorthy Swamigal and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman similarly worshipped the devotees of the city of Thiruvarur, sought their permission, and asked if the Lord of Thiruvarur would embrace them, singing verses of praise.

The devotees residing in Thiruvarur The devotees welcome Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

Therefore, no one has fully comprehended the complete beauty of Thiruvarur, where such great devotees live; only a few have seen a part of it, says Sekkizhar Peruman. Sekkizhar Peruman now sings four verses describing the greatness and beauty of Thiruvarur. The streets of Thiruvarur are exquisitely decorated. Golden-like lime powder is sprinkled there. This lime powder is mixed with cool mire containing civet and musk. The mire, made of sandalwood paste, civet, musk, and lime powder, is found in the streets of Thiruvarur.

Thus, the mire is spread in the streets of the city of Thiruvarur, making the feet slip. Just like rain falling from the sky, honey rains down from the flowers. In Thiruvarur, banners wave on the sides of mansions, palaces, and halls. Women with beautiful hair also dance there. Banana trees, arches, and rows of areca nut trees are adorned there, presenting a forest-like scene. The verandas of the houses in Thiruvarur are colorful.

The light from the hanging bells mixes with the red color, darkening it. In the evening, lamps with bells are hung. These lamps shine with beautiful, long, bright flames. The shadow of large blue gems falls between these lamps in rows.

Therefore, the floral canopies on the verandas appear dark red. There are abundant flower ponds, roads, verandas, and squares in the city of Thiruvarur. There are stages where women dance. There are large places, special and desired even by the hosts of gods. In all these places, auspicious musical instruments resound like the sound of rain.

Thus, Thiruvarur is a holy city adorned with various types of magnificent decorations. In that Thiruvarur, full of flower gardens, by the grace of Lord Thiyagaraja, who reigns there, the community of devotees and other The people come out of the city and welcome Pillaiyar. Sekkizhar Swamigal states that the group of devotees and their attendants come out to welcome Pillaiyar by the grace of the ruler of Thiruvarur. By the grace of Lord Thiyagaraja, those devotees come out of the city to meet Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. The grace of Lord Thiyagaraja informs them from within, prompting them to welcome him. Sekkizhar Peruman has stated, “by grace they approached.” Therefore, this act of welcoming Thirugnanasambandha Peruman illustrates the truth that the devotees of Thiruvarur are those who surrender themselves to grace, without ego or attachment, and not merely by their own initiative.

That is why these devotees were blessed with the great fortune of welcoming and worshipping Pillaiyar, and with the honor of having Thirugnanasambandha Peruman address them and sing a pathigam inquiring about their well-being. Sekkizhar Peruman composes the five hundred and seventh verse: “The true devotees came there and worshipped Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, and he, the Lord of Sanbai, the adept of beautiful Tamil, also worshipped them in return, and began a pathigam, asking, ‘Will my Lord accept me?’” Thirugnanasambandhar, the master of Muthtamil and the leader of Sirkazhi, bowed in return and began the pathigam “Andhamai Ulaga Adiyaam.” With the thought, “Will my Lord accept me?” he sang this pathigam, addressing the devotees of Thiruvarur with the sentiment, “Will Lord Thyagaraja accept me?” This pathigam begins with “Adhiyum Aayinan,” and the Lord, within the pathigam, reveals that He is the beginning of the world and also its end.

Thus, God is the cause of cosmic dissolution, and having dissolved the world, He re-creates it within Himself. Pillaiyar reveals the nature of that God, who is the cause of rebirth, at the beginning of the pathigam. This pathigam is structured as if Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is asking the devotees of Thiruvarur, after bowing to them, “Will my Father in Thiruvarur accept me?” This pathigam is the forty-fifth pathigam of the Third Thirumurai, set in the Kausikappann tune. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows. Thiru Arandai thanai endru polum ko vandi pondrai madhiyodu koovilam senni vaiththa piraan thiraiyaaru kaaliul Gnanasambandhal vaadal valla pallu paadal valla thodarnthu sinthippom Thiruchitrambalam Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. As narrated by Deivasekkizhar Peruman in Periya Puranam, Part 662, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, in the story of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar: Pillaiyar, the master of wisdom, having sung the pathigam, enters the city of Thiruvarur. Whether one says ‘vithagam’ or ‘gnanam,’ they are one and the same. ‘Gnana vithagar’ refers to the supreme wisdom of Siva-gnanam. This signifies that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman stood at the pinnacle of wisdom within wisdom. Those who accompanied Pillaiyar and the devotees of Thiruvarur who came to receive him were true ascetics. Asceticism (thavam) is Siva Puja and adherence to the Siva path.

With such true ascetics, Pillaiyar, the master of wisdom, enters the city of Thiruvarur. The people of Thiruvarur. With good hearts, they scatter powdered flowers, puffed rice, and other offerings, bowing and worshipping Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

Thus, passing through all the city streets of Thiruvarur, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reaches the entrance of Siva Peruman’s temple. Deivasekkizhar Peruman composes the verse: “He bowed before the decorated entrance and entered; seeing the vast expanse of many long, radiant light-clusters that bore within themselves all greatness, he bowed his head and worshipped the Devaasiriyan, then rose.” The city of Thiruvarur is always adorned and radiant. The archway entrance in such a city is always beautifully decorated and shines brightly.

Furthermore, due to Pillaiyar’s arrival, it appears. Arches are erected there, and the entrance, the Thorana Vaayil, is adorned. He enters through that Thorana Vaayil. Before entering, he sees it, bows low in worship, and rises. Although Pillaiyar’s heart’s desire is to enter and worship the Lord, as soon as he enters the entrance before performing that act, the Devaasiriya Mandapam becomes visible, offering a divine sight. Before going inside to worship the Lord, Pillaiyar bows and rises, worshipping this Devaasiriya Mandapam.

We saw that Sundaramoorthy Swamigal also bowed and worshipped the Devaasiriyan Mandapam and then entered the temple’s inner courtyard through the Thirumoolattanam gate. When going to worship the Lord, one should not engage in any other activity in between. The rule here becomes an exception.

Therefore, it is essential in Thiruvarur that one must bow to the Devaasiriya Mandapam before worshipping the Lord, and our revered acharyas have demonstrated this to us. That Devaasiriya Mandapam is a hall filled with divine wisdom’s light. It is a sacred hall where devotees gather. Due to their fervent love for Siva, Siva’s devotees gather and shine there, making it a hall radiating divine wisdom’s light.

Furthermore, the light from the sacred ash of the devotees within that sacred hall causes it to always shine brightly. As per Sivagnana Siddhiyar’s verse, “Parame Paarthiruppar Padarthangal Paaraar” (They will only look at the Supreme, not at the material things). According to the divine words of the Siddhiyar, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman possessed the wisdom that perceived nothing but the awareness of Siva. Since this Devaasiriya Mandapam, this sacred hall, shines as a compilation of the Sivagnana light of the great individuals who stood on the path of Siva (the path of light), it becomes visible and shines in Pillaiyar’s sight.

Therefore, he bows to it and enters. Deivasekkizhar Peruman composes the next verse: “He circumambulated the surrounding sacred mansions, worshipped, bowed to the gopuram with overflowing love, joined his hands in worship, and before the Lord, who is difficult for the searching Vishnu and Brahma to comprehend, and who resides within the flourishing jeweled ant-hill, he prostrated himself on the ground many times.” This is the 510th verse. After worshipping the Devaasiriya Mandapam, he circumambulated and worshipped the sacred mansions surrounding it, and with abundant love, he bowed to the gopuram. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman bows with folded hands. This gopuram is the inner gopuram. The Thorana Vaayil mentioned earlier was at the outer gopuram.

Now, Peruman is worshipping the inner gopuram, which is called the Thirumaligai Vaayil Gopuram. We have contemplated the history in the “Thaduthatkonda Puranam” where Lord Thyagesa appeared before Sundaramurthy Nayanar at the entrance of this gopuram and initiated him into composing the Thiruthondathogai. Pillaiyar bows to such a gopuram. Inside the temple, the Lord, who is difficult for Vishnu and Brahma to comprehend, resides within a jeweled ant-hill. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman prostrates himself on the ground many times before that Lord. How does he worship?

Deivasekkizhar Peruman then describes: “He bowed down, trembled, and with his body covered in goosebumps, he danced and sang, worshipping the true reality, Siva Peruman, whom he had firmly understood in his intellect, and he prostrated himself with intense longing that swiftly arose in his pure mind.” Pillaiyar, the master of wisdom, bowed and fell to the ground, trembled, and his hair stood on end. With his entire body thus affected, he danced and sang, worshipping Siva Peruman, the supreme reality whom he had clearly perceived within his intellect and now perceived outwardly. Pillaiyar submerges himself in the intense longing that swiftly arises in his pure mind. He worships the Lord, perceiving outwardly the same ultimate reality that he experienced through deep contemplation, having clearly understood it in his mind and achieved absorption, without forgetting the grace that the Lord bestows from within. This is also the essence of the eleventh Sutra of Sivagnana Botham. Pillaiyar is one who always attains and experiences the Sivanantha Anubhoothi, the bliss of Siva’s feet.

We have already seen this described as “Thiruvadi Marava Paanmaiyor” (those who never forget the sacred feet). We can contemplate the idea here that just as he clearly perceived Siva Peruman within his intellect, he also perceived Him outwardly, and the Siva Bhoga (divine bliss) that comes directly through experience, without any obscuration, reaching the five senses, is easily bestowed.

Similarly, just as he worshipped Thiruvarur here, our Sekkizhar Peruman also showed us the scene of his worship in Thiruchitrambalam. As per the Thevara Thirukkurippu: “From Thiruvarur, where the divine lamp glows with the kollapon, he entered Thillai Thiruchitrambalam, where the lamps are held by bhootas.” We can also contemplate the subtlety here that these acts of worship and related events are similarly arranged in both Thillai and Aaroor. Sekkizhar Peruman continues in the next verse, describing what Pillaiyar, having worshipped thus, does next: “He sang a pathigam in rich Tamil, set to tune, before the Lord who made poison into nectar.

“Then, coming out of the mansion gate surrounded by clouds, he reached the sacred monastery of those who truly understood the Panchakshara.” This verse states that Pillaiyar, beginning a pathigam in powerful, rich Tamil, praised the Lord who turned poison into nectar.

“Then, reaching the gate of the cloud-enveloped mansion. Pillaiyar, who had realized the true meaning of the sacred Five Letters, arrived at and resided in the sacred monastery. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman offers a Tamil pathigam rich in beautiful words with musical accompaniment. Since Sekkizhar Peruman refers to it as “Senchol Vandhamil Thiruppathigam” (a pathigam of rich, beautiful Tamil), we can infer that this pathigam begins with the phrase “Senchol.” The pathigam composed by Pillaiyar at this time is not available to us. It was Pillaiyar’s custom to sing pathigams before the Lord. The unavailability of this precious pathigam, sung before the Lord of Puttidamkondanatha, is a failing of our Saiva world.

“Pillaiyar, who had realized the truth of the Five Letters, attained the true meaning in his consciousness by chanting the sacred Five Letters according to scriptural injunction. The “Anjezhuthu” (Five Letters) referred to here is the Mukthi Panchaksharam. The object attained by the Sri Panchaksharam is also the same. To understand the Anjezhuthu, to understand the sacred Five Letters, means to discard worldly attachments, acquire wisdom, and perceive the knowable reality. For the steadfastness of that perception, to understand and chant the sacred Five Letters that yield that fruit, as prescribed, as expounded in the Ninth Sutra of Sivagnana Botham and in the brief commentary of Sivagnana Botham, “Pindappozhuppil Aruliyapadi,” Pillaiyar attained the true meaning of this sacred Five Letters, the Mukthi Panchaksharam, in his consciousness. We can find the nature of these in the gnana sastras like “Unmai Vilakkam.” Thus, Pillaiyar, who had realized the true meaning of the Sri Panchaksharam, resides in the monastery in Thiruvarur.

“Now, the next verse composed by Sekkizhar Peruman is: “Having arrived there, he resided with pleasure, bowing to the sacred red feet of the Lord with a bull banner, who delights in the path of dharma, and whose sacred lotus feet are embraced by overflowing love, the Lord of Puttidamkondan, whom he worshipped regularly at all times.” Pillaiyar, who was residing happily in the monastery, worshipped the sacred red feet of Siva Peruman, who graciously resides in Thiruvarur Aaraneri, the temple embodying the path of dharma. Thiruvarur Aaraneri is a separate shrine located in the southeast of the grand Thiruvarur temple. It is the sacred place glorified by Naminandhi Adigal Nayanar, who lit lamps with water. This sacred place is praised by Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal for the greatness of Naminandhi Adigal Nayanar, who lit lamps with water. This sacred place possesses the greatness. Lord Vanmeeganathar, in the Thirumoolattanam of Thiruvarur, shines like a gem within an ant-hill, a manifestation of Siva’s light.

“Here, in Thiruvarur Aaraneri, He shines as the great gem, Lord Puttidamkondan, abundant with great vedas. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships there.

“Thus, during his stay in Thiruvarur, Pillaiyar visits and worships during all the designated prayer times.

“Now, the next verse composed by Sekkizhar Peruman states: “Worshipping the holy Lord who resides in the ant-hill, with ever-increasing love, he bowed and sang many pathigams of sweet music, and with the virtuous devotees, as his well-being flourished, he stayed in that other sacred city during those days, worshipping many sacred places where the Lord of the four Vedas, such as Thiruvilivalam, Thirukozhili, and others, resided, and with countless pathigams, he praised them. And to relieve their suffering, he returned to Thiruvarur to worship again.” These are verses 514 and 515 composed by Sekkizhar Peruman. Pillaiyar bows to the holy Lord who resides in the ant-hill, praising Him with overflowing love and singing many pathigams of sweet music. Many melodious pathigams were composed by Pillaiyar at this time, but they are not available to us.

“Thus, during the days he stayed in the sacred city of Thiruvarur with the virtuous devotees, Pillaiyar visited and worshipped many other nearby sacred places where the Lord resides, such as Thiruvilivalam and Thirukozhili. He sang countless pathigams and then returned to Thiruvarur to worship again. Sekkizhar Peruman mentions Thiruvilivalam and Thirukozhili, stating, “These and other shrines.” Therefore, it can be assumed that the other shrines might have included Thiruvemaperur, Thirukkaraikkudi, Thirusaattiyakkudi, Thirukantrapur, and similar places.

“Let us proceed with our contemplation.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. In Periya Puranam, Part 663, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, composed by Deivasekkizhar Peruman, the story of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar continues. We saw that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman visited the sacred places near Thiruvarur and then returned to Thiruvarur. It is believed that the places Thirugnanasambandha Peruman visited include Thiruvilivalam, Thirukozhili, Thiruvemaperur, Thirukkarayil, Thirusaattiyakkudi, Thirukantrapur, and others. Among these places, pathigams composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for Thiruvilivalam, Thirukozhili, and Thirukkarayil are available. The first of these, Thiruvilivalam, is the 121st shrine on the south bank of the Kaveri, renowned for having received verses from all three revered poets.

This sacred place is named so because Valiyan, a bird, worshipped here. This is a Maadakkoyil built by our Lord Kochchengachozha Nayanar. Like Thiruppugalur and Thirumundeeswaram, the temple is surrounded by a moat. Since the birth story of Ganapathi is praised in Pillaiyar’s pathigam, the Ganapathi shrine is significant. This sacred place is located on the Thiruvarur-Thiruthuraipoondi road. The Lord’s name is Manaththunainathar, also known as Hirudayakalamanatheswarar.

The names of the Goddess are Vaazhaiyan Kanni and Angayarkanni. The sacred bathing places are Karanar Gangai and Sankarateertham. Ekachakrapuram, Munnurrumangalam, etc., are other names for this sacred place. The famous verse “Pidiyadhan Oru Umai Kola” is from the pathigam composed for this sacred place. It is the fifth verse within this pathigam. A book called ‘Valivala Mummanikkovai,’ which glorifies this Lord and Goddess, has been published by Thamizh Thatha Thiru U.

V. Swaminatha Iyer. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who visited this sacred place, composed two pathigams. The first pathigam, containing the verse ‘Pidiyadhan Urumai,’ is the 123rd pathigam of the First Thirumurai, set in the Vyazhakkurinji tune. The first, fifth, and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows. (Me viya theer uruvudaiyaval pirai malar maayiya polil vali valam puraiyirai pidiyarul ooru umai pola miga kariyadhu vadi podu thanathadi balippadum maridar kadi vanapathi vara arulina meedhu kodai veerarpayil pazhivala muraiyarai manniya valivala nagar puraiyaraivanai elliyal kazhum)

The summary of this pathigam is that the Lord of Valivalam is the one whose sacred form is entwined with Uma, the one who blessed Ganapathi. After worshipping at Thiruvilivalam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeded to the sacred place of Thirukozhili, worshipped the Lord, and composed a pathigam. The sacred place of Thirukozhili is located on the Thiruvarur-Ettikkudi road. It is currently known as Thirukuvilai. The Lord’s names are Brahmapureeswarar, Kozhilinathar, and Kozhilinatheswarar. The Goddess’s name is Bram.

Ammarambigai and Vandamar Poonkuzhali. Brahmatheertham and the Mukthi Nadi, Chandranadi, are the sacred waters. This place is named Kozhili because the Lord bestowed His grace here, removing the flaws associated with the Navagrahas. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s statement is, “Kolaaya Neekkumavan Kozhili Emperuman” (He who removes afflictions is the Lord of Kozhili). The history is that Bhima, after slaying Bakasura, came here, worshipped the Lord, and was freed from his sin. This sacred place is renowned as the place where Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sang seeking help to transport a mountain of paddy.

This place is one of the seven Vidanga Sthalas. It is also called Avanividanga Sthalam, where the Lord performs the Piringa dance. This sacred place has many names: Brahma Thapovanam, Gathakaranyam (meaning Thertramaravanam), Pushpavanam, and Thenkilai. At the front gopuram. There are images of Bakasuran and Brahmahatthi. Between the shrines of the Lord and Goddess, there is a Siva Lingam worshipped by Agasthiyar.

The Lord appears as a Sivamurthi made of white sand.

Here, the Navagrahas face the south in unison. In the southwest corner of the temple, Sivaboga Vinayagar, who showed Sivaloka to King Hemakandan, bestows his grace. Nineteen inscriptions from the Chola and Pandiya periods have been found in this temple. In the inscriptions, the Lord’s name is referred to as Thirukozhili Udaiya Nayanar and Thyagesar, Avanividanga Thyagar. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed a pathigam for this sacred place. It is the pathigam that begins with “Naalaaya Pogaame Nanjaniyunj Kandanuukke.” It is the sixty-second pathigam of the First Thirumurai, set in the Pazhanthakkaraga tune.

The first, fifth, ninth, and eleventh verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Thambalam naalaaya polaayu eerai theeram koyum) (Panchamanath jo payasaiy tharunu namba panchaparthi thonjipam janavum kozhiyam peru thavi) (Aavi thani joaduku angiru aadharikkum naay navina nallumban koyilum poyil koliyam peruman nambanai nalladaiy naam muraiyma thendhirikkum kombanai yaar paadham kiyam perumaanake vam) The summary of the pathigam is that the Lord of Kozhili, who removes afflictions, bestowed the Pasupathastram with joy. After worshipping at Thirukozhili, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeded to the sacred place of Thirukkarayil and worshipped the Lord. Thirukkarayil is the 119th shrine on the south bank of the Kaveri.

It is also known as Thirukkarai Vaasal. It is one of the Saptha Vidanga Sthalas. The Indra Puja is still performed here on the full moon day of the Purattasi month. This is the sacred place where Musukundar received grace. On the northern bank of the tank, Kadukkai Pillaiyar is enshrined. The local legend is that a merchant, when asked to deliver a sack of nutmeg, claimed it was kadukkai (terminalia chebula), and by divine grace, it transformed into kadukkai.

Later, through the grace of Vinayagar, it reverted to nutmeg. This sacred place is located south of Thiruppunavaasal on the Thiruvarur-Thiruthuraipoondi road. The Lord’s name is Kannayiramudaiyar. The Goddess’s name is Kailasa Nayagi. Brahma Theertham, Sesha Theertham, and Indian Theerthams are the sacred waters. In this, one of the Saptha Vidanga Sthalas, Lord Thyagaraja is called Adhividangar, His throne is Veerasimhasanam, and His dance is Kukkuda Natanam.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman came here and composed a pathigam. It is the 15th pathigam of the Second Thirumurai. This pathigam is set in the Indhallam tune. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows.

(Neerani neer sadai vel or nirai kundrari thaarani thaamarai mel ayal thozhum seerani seer thigazhum thiru kaayam iladha ee indha seeriyaliyil thigazhum thirukkarayil) The summary of this pathigam is that for those who praise thus, past karmas will not persist. After worshipping at Thirukkarayil, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeded to Thiruvemaperur and worshipped. This sacred place is known as Thirumappattru. It is the sacred place of Naminandhi Adigal Nayanar.

However, the pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for this sacred place is not available to us. After worshipping at Thiruvemaperur, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman went to Thirusaattiyakkudi and worshipped. This is one of the Thiruvisaippa shrines, having received verses from Karuvoorthevar. The temple in this place is called Ezhirukkai. The fiery deity, the god of fever and heat-related illnesses, is worshipped here as a form of the Lord Himself. It is located southwest of Kezhvelur, on the road to Thiruvilivalam.

One must cross the Kaduvaayaru river, which is a short distance away. After worshipping at Thirusaattiyakkudi, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman went to Thirukantrapur and worshipped. The pathigam composed by Pillaiyar there is not available to us. Having worshipped all these shrines, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman returned to Thiruvarur.

Let us go on contemplating. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. In Periya Puranam, Part 664, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, composed by Deivasekkizhar Peruman, the story of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar continues. Pillaiyar visited all the shrines near Thiruvarur. Due to his overflowing love for Thiruvarur, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman returns to Thiruvarur again, desiring to worship and praise the Lord who resides in Puttidamkond. The 516th verse: “With overflowing love, Thirugnanasambandhar, the one with boundless wisdom, stayed there with the devotees whose lives embodied sacred ash, worshipping the Lord with the flowing matted hair, who resides in Puttidamkond.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s overflowing love for the Lord of Thiruvarur intensifies.

Deivasekkizhar Peruman refers to this as ‘Ooru Kadal’ (overflowing love). ‘Ooru Kadal’ means an abundance of love that springs forth continuously like a fountain, never ceasing. This is what the eleventh Sutra of Sivagnana Botham refers to as ‘Ayara Anbin’ (unwavering love). Srimath Maadhava Sivagnana Munivar explains this ‘Ayara Anbin’ as follows: He writes that if the soul, becoming one with the Lord, performs service to Him, and if it contemplates the Lord’s inseparable grace, then the desire that goes towards that object will overflow without restraint with each contemplation.

Thus, the great bliss that manifests as that very desire will be experienced. The Munivar writes: “Just as sexual pleasure, when experienced, yields more and more joy, similarly, the great joy of union continues to arise, ever new, like the expanding waist of a woman with braided hair.” This can be understood from the divine words. And as understood from the divine words that speak of that object, Srimath Maadhava Sivagnana Munivar has bestowed these commentaries. We can interpret all of these as applying to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman residing there with that overflowing love for the Lord of Thiruvarur.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, with overflowing love, worships the Lord with the flowing matted hair. How does he worship? He resides there with the devotees whose lives embody sacred ash. Devotees are those whose lives are founded on the truth of sacred ash as the ultimate reality. We can contemplate here the inner meanings of the stories of Nayanmars like Meypporul Nayanar, Enathinatha Nayanar, and Murthi Nayanar. With such devotees whose lives embody sacred ash.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, with boundless wisdom, resides in Thiruvarur and worships the Lord. “Eerila Thirugnanasambandhar” means Thirugnanasambandhar with boundless, imperishable wisdom. Just like Siva Peruman, Siva Gnanam is imperishable and eternal. Pillaiyar is the blessed one who attained it. He is the one who attained imperishable wisdom.

Therefore, he is “Eerila Thirugnanasambandhar.” “Thirugnanam” and “Sivagnanam” are one and the same. “Thirugnanam” means all-transcendent Siva Gnanam.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman resides there. Sekkizhar Peruman composes the next verse, the 517th verse: “During those days he stayed in that sacred place, after some time, desiring to meet Thirunavukkarasu, he would go to Thiruppugalur, and having received grace, he would visit the outlying areas of that city and bestow his grace.” Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman stayed in Thiruvarur for some days. Deivasekkizhar Peruman refers to these days as ‘Nammaiyil Vaikum Naal’ (days spent in goodness). ‘Nammai’ here signifies the good path, the Siva path.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman resided in Thiruvarur for some days on the good path, the Siva path. Sivagnana Botham’s eighth Sutra speaks of wisdom as the good path. Srimath Maadhava Sivagnana Munivar, commenting on it, states that among all good things, liberation is the greatest good. And since it is the best path to achieve liberation, wisdom is called the good path.

Also, because all paths to liberation proclaimed by various religions converge within it, making it the great path, it is called the good path, he explains.

Thus, after some days, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman desired to meet Thirunavukkarasu Peruman and join him. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman was a great soul who showed immense compassion towards the beings of this world. His verses, like Pasupathi Thiruviruttam, composed for the sake of devotees, clearly demonstrate the simplicity of his great compassion towards the living beings of this world. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman desires to meet that Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman recalls how he had gone to Southern Thiruvarur, worshipped, and then, at the boundary of Thiruppugalur, told Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, “I will come back and stay with you,” thus gaining his consent before coming to Thiruvarur.

Therefore, he now wishes to worship Thiruppugalur, where Thirunavukkarasu Peruman resides.

Now, the next verse: “Leaving Thiruvarur, looking towards the Lord, he stood there, and with a flawless heart, he sang the pathigam ‘Pavanamai Sodaiyai’ with folded red hands, saying, ‘O mind, do not fear, you know the way to salvation, do not forget to worship Siva’s Thiruvarur.’” This verse states that Thiruvarur is the greatest city on this earth.

Therefore, it is the most excellent city in the world. We have seen in the ninety-seventh verse that Thiruvarur is like a shining tilak on the forehead of the earth goddess. In the forty-third verse, we saw that it is like the heart-lotus of the earth maiden.

Therefore, having received divine permission from the Lord in such Thiruvarur, he comes out of Thiruvarur and stands facing it, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. The pathigam he composed while standing there facing Thiruvarur is a praise of that sacred city. As he takes leave from Thiruvarur and departs, unable to bear the separation, he composes this pathigam, consoling his mind, saying, “You can achieve salvation by worshipping outside Thiruvarur; do not be disheartened.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sings this pathigam with the sentiment, “O mind, do not spend your days in folly without meditating on the sacred feet of Siva Peruman; worship the Lord’s feet and attain salvation.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composes the pathigam with the idea: “O mind, do you not know the way to salvation? Do not forget to worship Siva Peruman’s Thiruvarur.” Saying this, with his red hands folded above his head, he sings the pathigam beginning with “Pavanamai Sodaiyai” outside the city of Thiruvarur, facing it. As Pillaiyar leaves Thiruvarur, due to the pain of separation, he comforts his mind and bestows this pathigam as a teaching to the world.

This pathigam, set in the Gandhara tune, is the seventy-ninth pathigam of the Second Thirumurai. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows. (Naayala pai a a sivanada vetai maala neenaaya gavanamaayppaay eerugandhu eeriyakaala kandha avanadhoor thozhudhu uyaam mayil kondu anjanu je pallithal ma) (Vendu kaali ooran nallave nallave solliya gnana elliyam pothi yaaduyam eesadaiye yethu paadal sollave vallava thirilaru pothe maiyagaththe amman) As Sekkizhar Peruman has shown, the theme of this pathigam is: “Worship Siva’s Thiruvarur without fail; this is the rare path to salvation.

“Therefore, O mind, do not fear about leaving Thiruvarur.” Kaazhiyar, the one who came to bestow grace, the Gowniar Pillaiyar, having worshipped Thiruvarur, the Lord whom Vishnu and Brahma could not reach, departs. He who wore the hide of the great elephant and worshipped Panaiyoor, having sung the pathigam in the divine and glorious musical style, stayed in that city and then departed, becoming the cause for countless others. He worshipped other sacred places and composed verses in rich Tamil. Everywhere, the gathering of true devotees came to meet him. The next two verses, 519 and 520, composed by Sekkizhar Peruman, describe Pillaiyar, after being born in Kalippathi, reverently bowing to the Lord’s Thiruvarur, which even Mahavishnu could not comprehend. He sets forth from Thiruvarur, venerating the many sacred places where the Lord, the cause of all creation, manifests himself, and composes a pathigam.

“This world is the cause of everything. Sekkizhar Peruman refers to the Lord as the ‘Akilakaranar,’ the ultimate cause of all. The meaning is that the Lord is the instrumental cause of this world, and that is Shiva. Shiva resides in other sacred places, which he now worships. These places are considered to be Thiru Kondiswaram, Thiru Ramanadheeswaram, and similar sites. After worshipping these sites, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships the Lord at Panaiyur.

“Thiruppanaiyur is the 73rd site on the south bank of the Kaveri. The sacred tree is the Palmyra tree, hence the name Thiruppanaiyur. This is the place where the Lord granted a vision of his divine dance to Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, known as Aludaiya Nambigal, giving him a forward vision.

“Sundaramoorthy Swamigal then sang, “He who is skilled in dance is indeed beautiful.” This sacred site is renowned for the special grace bestowed upon Parashara Maharishi, who worshipped here and attained blessings. The Vinayagar here is known as Thunaitha Pillaiyar, the Vinayagar who assisted Karikala Chozhan. One can reach Panaiyur by traveling on the Thiruvarur Peralam road, past Sannallur. The Lord’s names are Soundareswarar, Azhagiyanathar, Thaalavaneswarar. The Goddess’s names are Piraganayagi, Periyanayagi.

“The sacred waters are Parashara Theertham, Amirtha Pushkarani, and Thirumagal Theertham. This is the place where Parashara Maharishi and the Saptha Maharishis—Kaushikar, Kashyapar, Bharathwajar, Gauthmar, Agastiyar, Athri, and Pirugu—worshipped the Lord. Since the Palmyra tree is the sacred tree, this area is called Thaala Vanam, and the temple is called Thaala Vaneswaram.

“Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, at the request of Paravaiyar, received gold from the Lord of Thiruppugalur for the Panguni Uthiram festival in Thiruvarur. After praising himself and worshipping Thiruppugalur, he then thinks of Thiruppanaiyur and arrives there.

“At that time, the Lord appeared outside the village in a dancing posture.

“Sundaramoorthy Swamigal went forth, prostrated himself, worshipped, and received grace by singing a pathigam, “Arangaaduvallavar Azhagiyar.” Although it is a very small village, it is ancient. There are two Palmyra trees as sacred trees, which have existed for a long time. As these mature trees age, like banana trees, palmyra saplings spontaneously appear and grow at their base. Without being sown, like banana saplings, palmyra saplings spontaneously appear and grow. In this temple, the Somaskandar idol is uniquely depicted holding a fruit in his left hand. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who resided here, composed a pathigam.

“This is the 37th pathigam in the first Thirumurai, set to the tune of Thakkaragam. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Paravi poliyum Panaiyoore Paaraiyappa Panaiyor venaatha pathu ooril uyarvarevar Panaiyoore) The Lord’s abode is Panaiyur, which is the theme of this pathigam.

“Let us go on reflecting.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Volume 665, composed by Sekkizhar Peruman, Vampara Varivandu Sarrkkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, after worshipping Thiruppanaiyur, proceeds to Thiru Ramanadheeswaram and worships the Lord. Thiru Ramanadheeswaram is a temple located near Thiruchengattangudi, Nannilam, and Thiruppugalur. It is the 77th temple on the south bank of the Kaveri. The Lord’s name is Ramanadheeswarar, and the Goddess’s name is Karuvar Kuzhali Soolikaambal.

The sacred water is Rama Theertham, now known as Kannapuram. This is the place where Rama worshipped the Lord to cleanse himself of the sin of killing Ravana, hence it is called Ramanadhi Eeswaram or Ramanadheeswaram. When Rama came to this place, it is said that Nandi initially blocked his way, but the Goddess, out of compassion, intervened and appeared to him.

Afterwards, Rama bathed in the sacred water and worshipped. It is also said that Ramanandeeswaram evolved into Ramanadheeswaram. As evidence of this, in the Somaskandar deity of this temple, Nandidevar is depicted holding the Goddess’s hand. The main deity is a large form with a tall, broad base. The vimanam of the deity has a Vesara architectural style. Inscriptions record that Kulottunga Chozhan donated a land area named Shivapada Sekaramangalam for the temple’s rituals.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who visited this place, composed a pathigam. It is the 115th pathigam in the first Thirumurai. The 115th pathigam is set to the tune of Viyazhakurinchi. The first, second, and third verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Sangokkaiye thamidai) (Aadhadhodha Angangal paadalo Azhagal nallaval ramani soora velaiyile eravan aadhadhodha mazhai bodhi thadaiyavan mannu thulaiyathu vilangiya kozhi maargil ilaiyaval ramani soora membalam Vedangalil) The theme of this pathigam is that the Lord, referred to as ‘that one,’ resides in Ramanadheeswaram.

The eleventh verse of this pathigam, the Thirukkadaikkappu, is not fully available to us. Only the portion “Thenmalar Kondraiyon Mundamakkoonamandre” is available. That we have received even this much is a great blessing.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having worshipped many temples, proceeds towards Thiruppugalur. Upon hearing this news, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman and Muruga Nayanar go forth to welcome Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. The 521st verse states: “Navinukku Arasarum Nambi Seer Murugarum mattram” (Namassevukaithavar Thiruththondar aanavargal mun senru Seethappoovinil poli punar pugazhiyar pothagath thethir paninthe Mevamattram avarudan koodave vimalar koyilai adainthar) This verse describes Thirunavukkarasu Peruman and Muruga Nayanar going forth to welcome him. As per Pillaiyar’s wish, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman was residing in Pugalur, awaiting his arrival. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman had told him to wait in Thiruppugalur while he went to worship in Thiruvarur.

Accordingly, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman had been staying in Thiruppugalur for a long time, eagerly awaiting Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, keeping him in his thoughts. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman goes to the boundary of Thiruppugalur to welcome Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Thirumuruganayanar also accompanies him. Sekkizhar Peruman refers to him as ‘Nambi Seer Murugarum,’ meaning ‘Muruga Nayanar, the noble and honorable.’ ‘Nambi’ means an excellent man.

Here, the special quality of Thirumuruganayanar is his profound love, which led him to serve Thirunavukkarasu Peruman and Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, along with other devotees, in his hermitage at the same time for many days.

Thus, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman and Thirumuruganayanar, accompanied by devotees, welcome Pillaiyar, who is like a baby elephant. After welcoming him, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman goes to the Thiruppugalur temple with them and worships the Lord there. “The Lord of the Devas” (Koyil pukku anaivarum Seer nilaththuravanaangi paavarum thamizh isaippathigamum paadi mun paravuvar purambanainthe Thaavil seer Muruganar Thirumanaiyku eithi atthanith thondarthame Yaavaiyum kuraivarutthida amarntharuluvar inithin angu uraiyu naalil Neelanakkadigalum nigazh siruththondarum udananainthu eithu neermai Seelam meyththavargalum koodave kumpidum seikai nerinindru vaaimai Saala mik kuyar thiruththondin unmai thiranthannaiye theliya naadi Kaalamutthavargalodu alavalavi kalantharulinaar Kali Nador) Sekkizhar Peruman composes the next two verses. Everyone enters the temple of Lord Shiva, the master of the Devas, and prostrates themselves on the ground. They rise and worship.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal, Muruga Nayanar, and all the devotees go directly from the Thiruppugalur border into the temple and worship in this manner. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman then praises the Lord and composes a pathigam. He sings a pathigam filled with Tamil music. The pathigam composed by Pillaiyar before the Lord is not available to us now. After composing the pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman goes to Thirumuruga Nayanar’s house. Previously, Pillaiyar had stayed in Muruga Nayanar’s hermitage.

Subsequently, Muruga Nayanar again welcomed Pillaiyar, worshipped him, and residing in his home, attained great blessings. This exemplifies the excellence of serving devotees and the continuous emergence of virtue. During the days when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal were staying in Thirumuruga Nayanar’s hermitage, Thiruneelanakka Nayanar and Siruthonda Nayanar heard this news and came to join them. The history of Siruthonda Nayanar will unfold later; the history of Thiruneelanakka Nayanar we have already reflected upon. These two great personalities, upon hearing that Pillaiyar was staying there, came and joined them.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman resided with these true devotees. The greatness of these devotees lies in their unwavering adherence to service and truth. With such devotees, the greatness of the devotees and the ease of the Lord’s grace bestowed upon them, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman rejoices, having heard, reflected, and understood. The nature of devotees is to spend all their remaining time, apart from the time spent in worshipping the Lord, in the company of devotees. If Pillaiyar also demonstrated this, then it is an essential lesson for other humble devotees without needing to be stated explicitly. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman not only preaches but also exemplifies this.

Therefore, the immeasurable greatness of service is conveyed here. Let us continue to the next verse, the 524th verse: (Kumbidum kolkaiyil kuri kalanthu isai enum pathigam munnaana paadal tham perunthali) (Nilamai saal pathi perumai saalapara vilampi ompambaravatharkkuriya sorpillaiyar ulla meykkaathal koora Nambartham pathigalayina ena palavum mun nanniye thoza nayanthaar) Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composes a pathigam, extolling the glories of Thiruppugalur. ‘Kuri kalantha isai’ is the initial phrase of the pathigam. The greatness of this place is that it provides a good state of being to those who reach it. We can recall the future events in Thiruppugalur, such as the conclusion of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s history and portions of Sundaramoorthy Swamigal’s history, here.

Thus, the Lord residing in Thiruppugalur, who commands Agni, Varuna, Yaman, and other deities, is a great Lord. In this pathigam, he extols the glories of Thiruppugalur, where such a great Lord resides. This pathigam is the second pathigam in the first Thirumurai, set to the tune of Nattappadai. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Siththiram) (Idam poi malaiyum porikal antool kayai puyalarum pugazhu puttru vaazhum aravam marai yaatthavan melum pugazhu kattu nall avar thazhi uzhiyaazha Sambandha Tamil maalai patri endrum isai paadiya maanatha paraman adi sernthu kuraipaadu)

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who worshipped the Lord of Thiruppugalur and sang pathigams, now desires to go and worship in other places where the Lord resides. The next verse is: (Pulaalampu than punal pugaloor urai punithanaar aruLpetru Pillaiyaarudan Navinukku Arasarum pira pathi thoza sellvaar Vallalaar Sirutthondarum Neelanakkkarum valam pathikku ekka Ullam anborul Murugar angu ozhiyavum udanpada isaiviththaar) The next verse describes Thiruppugalur, a town surrounded by cool ponds where water birds always chirp. Having received gracious leave from the Lord residing in such a Thiruppugalur, Pillaiyar and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman set out to worship the Lord in other sacred places. The benevolent Siruthonda Nayanar and Thiruneelanakka Nayanar return to their respective places.

However, Thirumuruga Nayanar’s heart was unwilling to part with Pillaiyar and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, but he reluctantly agreed. He reluctantly found peace of mind. Muruga Nayanar’s overflowing love was the reason for his hospitality to Pillaiyar and the accompanying group of devotees. With such abundant love, Thirumuruga Nayanar bids farewell to Pillaiyar and Appar Peruman. Thirumuruga Nayanar remains in Thiruppugalur.

Now, Pillaiyar and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman will continue to visit many temples together and praise the Lord. From verse 2424 to verse 2515, Sekkizhar Peruman will describe the unique worship performed jointly by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman.

Now, the next verse: (Kannagan pugaloorinaiththozhu pombuluzhathinil kadarkaazhi Annalaarththirunaavinukku arasartham arukku vittu akalaathee Vannanaiththila sivikaiyum pinvara vazhikola urungaalai Ennil seer Thirunavinnukku arasarum mattra avarukku isaikkintraar Nayanar umakku azhiththaruL seitha innalankizh oLi mutthin Thooya yaanatthin misai ezhuntharuLuveer enralum sudarththigal Meiyava veiyavan aruLum ivvaaru enil virumbu thondargalodum poi athu enku neer angu yaan pinvarappovathu endru aruL seithaar) These are the next verses. As Pillaiyar proceeds after worshipping Thiruppugalur, he begins to walk beside Thirunavukkarasar. He walks beside him, not riding in his pearl palanquin. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman observes this. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, realizing that it would be inappropriate for him to ride in a palanquin while Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, who was granted a palanquin by the Lord, was walking, chooses to walk alongside Appar Peruman. Seeing this, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman expresses his thoughts to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, which differ from Pillaiyar’s initial sentiment.

Thirunavukkarasu Peruman says to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, “You should ascend and reside in this beautiful, luminous, pure pearl palanquin that the Lord has graciously bestowed upon you.” Thirunavukkarasu Peruman states that the Lord has graciously given him the palanquin. All actions performed by the Lord are considered grace.

However, unlike others, since the Lord himself bestowed the palanquin upon Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, Appar Peruman states that he should indeed ride in it. Upon hearing this, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman accepts, saying that if Appar Peruman’s intention and the Lord’s grace are such, he will comply. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman accepts Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s intention as the Lord’s divine will. He speaks, referring to it as divine grace.

Therefore, this is both Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s wish and the Lord’s divine will. Pillaiyar understands that the Lord’s divine will is also aligned with this. Pillaiyar has the ability to understand the Lord’s will, as we will see in the upcoming events in Pandi Nadu. Having accepted this, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman says to Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, “You go ahead; I will follow you.” We shall proceed with our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Volume 666, composed by Sekkizhar Peruman, Vampara Varivandu Sarrkkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman agrees to ride in the pearl palanquin. He then tells Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, “You go ahead; I will follow you.” Just as actions follow the path of knowledge, Pillaiyar expresses his desire for his journey to continue with Thirunavukkarasu Peruman leading the way and himself following. Pillaiyar’s wish for Thirunavukkarasu Peruman to go ahead shows that he considered Thirunavukkarasu Peruman to be his guide, and he positioned himself as one who would follow him, adhering to that tradition. To illustrate this, according to the twelfth sutra of Shivagnana Botham, which states, “Neyam malinthavar vedamum aalayam thaamum aran ena thozhume” (worshiping the form of the devotee, the temple, and the protection as sacred), Thirugnanasambandha Peruman exemplifies this by showing that when Thirunavukkarasu Peruman goes ahead with the devotees, he too will follow and worship in the same temples that Thirunavukkarasu Peruman visits.

This teaches the world to worship the forms of the Lord, his devotees, and the temple as a protective refuge. The divine words of Thevaram state, “Puguvār avar pin puguvoam” (we will enter after those who enter).

Therefore, the instruction here is to follow the devotees to the temple. This message is conveyed to the Shaivites by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

Thus, from this point until the Thiruvetharanyam temple, we see the pattern of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman leading and Thirugnanasambandha Peruman following him wherever they go to worship together. While Thirugnanasambandha Peruman adheres to this method of going to temples, we also see him joining Thirunavukkarasu Peruman in worship once inside the temple. Having received such instructions from Pillaiyar, the great ascetic king, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, says, “Very well, I will do as you have commanded.”

Therefore, from that day onwards, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman continues to follow this practice every day he travels with Pillaiyar. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman goes ahead with the holy assembly of devotees, and Thirugnanasambandha Peruman follows in the palanquin with his retinue and devotees. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman proceeds and reaches the Thiruvambar temple. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman also follows Thirunavukkarasu Peruman in the palanquin and enters the Thiruvambar temple. (Shanpai Mannarum thambiraan aruL vazhi nirpathu thalaichelvaarkku Panbu mempadu pani kathir nitthila sivikaiyil paninthu eri Vanperum pugaloorinaik kadanthu poi varum parisana) (Thinpereunthavar anainthathu engu endru poi Thiru Ambar nagar pukkar Ambar maanagar anainthu maakkaalaththil annallaar amarkintra Sempom maa mathil koyilai valankondu thirumunbu paninthu eththi Vambulaa malar thoovi mun paraviyee van thamizh isai maalai Umbar vaazha nanjundavar thammai paninthu urugum anpodu thazhnthar) These are the next two verses composed by Sekkizhar Swamigal. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman and Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reach the Thiruvambar temple.

Ambar is the name of the place, and Maakaalam is the name of the temple. They arrive there, scatter freshly bloomed flowers, offer incense and lamps, and worship the Lord Kaalakandeeswarar residing in Ambar Maakaalam by chanting a beautiful garland of Tamil music (pathigam). Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships Kaalakandeeswarar by recounting many glories, singing hymns, reciting names, and performing archana before the Lord. Pillaiyar praises the Lord by singing a pathigam. After worshipping the temple and the Lord, Pillaiyar comes out of the temple with Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal and stays happily in that sacred place with the devotees surrounding him.

Thus, as we saw earlier, on the journey to the temple, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman leads, and Pillaiyar follows him. However, when they enter the temple to worship, the verse indicates that he worships along with Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal.

Thus, they stayed in that sacred place for a few days, worshipping the Lord at all times of worship, such as the Thiru Palliyeluchi. Sekkizhar Peruman composes the next verse: (Poruvillaatha sorppulgu ponnira muthal pathigangaLaal pottri Thiruvinaarantha Kochchakanan an nager seitha koyilaich sernthu Marupu vaaimai van thamizh malarmaalai avvazhavanai sirappithu Perugu kaathalil paninthu mun paravinaar peniya unarvodum) During his stay there, Pillaiyar worshipped the Lord. He praises the Lord with many pathigams, beginning with the incomparable words of “Pulgu ponniram.” Sekkizhar Peruman mentions that he praises with pathigams like “Pulgu ponniram.” Accordingly, we have three pathigams composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for the Thiruvambar Maakaalam temple. The first pathigam, which begins with “Pulgu ponniram,” is what Sekkizhar Peruman refers to. This pathigam for the Thiruvambar Maakaalam temple is the 103rd pathigam in the second Thirumurai, set to the tune of Nattaragam.

The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Kol neram uri sadaiyila mudi polila mathi soodi pilaku ezhludai narumalaru kondraiyum pinai seithavar meiyu than thorai Arisilin vadakarai varukkuNaL maakam pagalum thozhum adaiyavarkku aruvinai adaiya veru thanmodu) (Aagiya suviyai erumaru peruman thaaru poom koyil thaaliyul gnanasambanthana tamil malai aaruviyum ketka vallaaraiyum kutttrangal kugave e) In Ambar Maakaalam, for devotees who worship with fresh flowers, sandalwood paste, and incense, their karmas will not accumulate, and they will attain prosperity in this world. For those who worship this sacred place of Ambar Maakaalam with their hands, the Lord himself will remove their suffering, illness, and worries. This is the theme of this pathigam. This pathigam was composed after worshipping the place of Ambarmakam.

The second pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for the Thiru Ambarmakam temple is the 83rd pathigam in the first Thirumurai, set to the tune of Kurinji. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Adaiyaar puram analvayilai madaiyaar punal ambu maathaaLa vidaiyaar podiyoodum thadaiyakala etthaaraa vinai thaane erum ner kolavongum thenu puram thannuL thirumaraiyaana sambanthana thenaar thirumaan madi) This pathigam describes the benefit of worshipping the Lord in this sacred place, having been composed after worshipping the Lord. Worshipping the Lord of Ambar Maakaalam will prevent the accumulation of karmas and bring joy. This pathigam advises us, both positively and negatively, that the shortcomings of those who do not praise this place will not be removed.

Now, the third pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for the Thiru Ambarmakam temple: The third pathigam is the 93rd pathigam in the third Thirumurai, set to the tune of Saathari. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Siththiram adiyo adigalil) (Iruppidam ambaru paapaal thaane sempom maamani politthu ezhuthiraivar poon arisil soozhntha ambar maalame koyilodu iruntha ponai thambi ne sambi naaL mozhipparukku illaiyaamine) This pathigam describes Ambar Maakaalam as the abode where the Lord resides with the Goddess, urging us to worship and attain it, thus praising the place from outside.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has composed three pathigams for Ambar Maakaalam. Thiru Ambar Maakaalam is the 55th temple on the south bank of the Kaveri, located near Thiruvarur and Poondottam, very close to Peralam. The Lord’s name is Kaalakandeeswarar or Mahakaleswarar, and the Goddess’s name is Bakshanaayagi. The sacred water is Maakkaala Theertham. This place is popularly known as Koyil Thirumaalam. It is located on the banks of the Arisil River, which Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has also mentioned in his pathigams.

This is the place where Maakaali worshipped the Lord to cleanse herself of the sin of killing the two demons, Amban and Ambasuran, hence its name Maakaalam. Accordingly, there is a separate Kali temple on the south circuit. This is the place where Somaseemaara Nayanar performed yagna. The Somaseemaara Nayanar Yagna festival is celebrated with great splendor in the month of Vaikasi, on the day of Ayilyam star. The Nandi here is in a human form. The local purana of Ambar.

The Sthala Puranam named ‘Ambar Puranam’ was composed by Mahavidwan Meenakshi Sundaram Pillai.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who worshipped the Ambar Maakaalam temple, also worships the Lord of the nearby Thiru Ambar Perunthirukoyil temple. Thiru Ambar Perunthirukoyil is the 54th temple on the south bank of the Kaveri. It is a Maadakkoyil (elevated temple) in Ambar, hence it is called Ambar Perunthirukoyil. ‘Perunthirukoyil’ refers to a Maadakkoyil. This is one of the temples built by Kochchengatchozha Nayanar. The idols of the Lord and Goddess are located behind the Moolalingam in the sanctum sanctorum. It is located very close to the east of the Ambar Maakaalam we saw earlier.

The Lord’s name here is Brahmapureeswarar, Brahmapurinathar. The Goddess’ name is Poonguzhal Nayagi, Sugandha Kundalambikai. The sacred waters are Brahma Theertham, Arisilaaru, Annamaam Poigai, Indra Theertham, and Sula Theertham. Today, this place is known as Ambar Ambal. It has other names like Makalapuram, Makalipuram, Punnagavanam, Brahmapuri, Nandarajapuram, Chanpakaranayam, and Marabori. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who visited this place, composed a pathigam.

It is the 19th pathigam in the third Thirumurai, set to the tune of Gandhara Panchamam. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Maadu veral singala puril chengalvan poy thevare azhagarai adithalai ambevi nizhal thizhal sedai pudi neela kandarai ultheerai ulaguyil kothuvenna tamil keelu veeraginathamil seyilaiye tamil keelu veeraginathamil seyilai) The Lord’s name is Maadu veral singala puril chengalvan poy thevare azhagarai adithalai ambevi nizhal thizhal sedai pudi neela kandarai ultheerai ulaguyil kothuvenna tamil keelu veeraginathamil seyilaiye tamil keelu veeraginathamil seyilai. The note for this pathigam is that devotees should come and worship the Lord, who is eternally united with the great Thiru Ambar temple built by King Kochaṅga Chola Nayanar. It is noteworthy that the Lord’s dance is described in the first seven verses of this pathigam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman thus worships Thiru Ambar Ma Kaalam and Thiru Ambar Perunthirukkovil, and sings pathigams.

During this time, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman desires to worship Thiru Kadavur. Let’s continue to reflect. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 667, ‘Vampara Varivanda Sarakkam’ by Daivasekkizhar Peruman. Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. After visiting the temples of Thiru Ambar Ma Kaalam and Thiru Ambar Perunthirukkovil, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman desires to go and worship at Thiru Kadavur, and visits other temples along the way. These other temples may include Peralam, Thiruthilai Pathimutham, Vazhuvur Veerattam, Thiruvidaikkazhi, etc. After visiting all these temples, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman and Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrive at Thiru Kadavur.

They circumambulate the cloister of the Veerattam temple, where the Lord resides. They circumambulate and worship the lotus feet of the Lord. The lotus feet of the Lord residing in Thiru Kadavur Veerattam are those adorned with a golden anklet that kicked and rolled the asura Kuttruvan. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships that Lord and sings a pathigam beginning with ‘Sadai Udaiyan’. By praising the Lord with such a pathigam, this world attains salvation. This pathigam, sung by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for Thiru Kadavur Thiru Veerattam, is the eighth pathigam in the third Thirumurai, set to the tune of Gandhara Panchamam.

The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (meyyAdalAm saRi Ova Udaiyudaiya maiyAzhnda uNkaN kumai kEzhvan kadaiyudai nal nEde mAdam Ogum kadavu tani idaiyudaiya nallum vIrattu aRa nalli vIra vEru tam kadavu rU aNi kANiya santami) The note for this pathigam is that the Lord known by various attributes such as ‘Sadai Udaiyan’ (one with matted hair) and ‘Kovanam Udai Udaiyan’ (one wearing a loincloth) is indeed Shiva, who resides in Thiru Kadavur Veerattam. We have already reflected on the history of Thiru Kadavur in the biography of Kungiliyakalaya Nayanar. Having thus worshipped, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman resided in Kungiliyakalaya Nayanar’s home.

There, he joyfully accepted the hospitality arranged by Kungiliyakalaya Nayanar with boundless love. He then worshipped the temple of Thiru Kadavur Thirumayanam and sang a pathigam. The pathigam sung by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for Thiru Kadavur Thirumayanam is the eightieth pathigam in the second Thirumurai, set to the tune of Gandharam. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (udai kariyadai ada Ur mayAnam amarunda vidai vERu avaRaiyum perumA adi vERu pOnil sUl adaRpUr paNNum mayAnam amarunda aravam perumA akalam maRiyal Agav) The note for this pathigam is that the Lord residing in Thiru Kadavur Thirumayanam is the one praised by various epithets such as ‘MaRaiyar’ (one with the Vedas) and ‘PiRaiyar’ (one with the crescent moon). Having thus worshipped at Thiru Kadavur Veerattam and Thiru Kadavur Thirumayanam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman stayed in that holy place for a few days.

During that time, he received the Lord’s grace to worship other temples where the Lord resides. Kungiliyakalaya Nayanar, the great Shiva devotee well-versed in the Vedas, also agreed. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman then departed from Thiru Kadavur to visit other holy places. Just as he desired to stay and worship in Thiru Kadavur, he also desired to visit and worship other holy places. The next holy place Thirugnanasambandha Peruman visited was Thiru Akkur. In Thiru Akkur, eminent brahmins reside; it is said that they are of such nature that they give to those who have nothing and are without means.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praised the brahmins of Thiru Akkur in the ninth verse of his pathigam, stating that they give without saying ‘there is nothing’. Thiru Akkur is a place where such special brahmins reside. The history of Sirappuli Nayanar, a renowned benefactor who was born in this place and attained blessings, also comes to mind here. In such a Thiru Akkur, the Lord manifests as Thanthonrinathar, the self-originated Lord, residing in a Madakkovil named Thanthonri Madam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman visited and worshipped there, and sang a pathigam composed of melodious Tamil verses. This pathigam is set to the very sweet tune of Sigamaram.

This garland of pathigams is rich in Tamil. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sings such a pathigam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sings this pathigam. This is the forty-second pathigam in the second Thirumurai, set to the tune of Sigamaram. The first, ninth, and eleventh verses of this pathigam are as follows: (tOl pudaiyuRa puy po mey kE Ettiya taṅka Ayu tAn tOnRi mAdamE E) (maiyA nAn muganu kANpaRiya tunmaikkAn tOtRam kEda pOy maiy sem taikiyam)

(tanmaikkU tOn pada amarnda tAn tONDi maNi) (madam sen kali nAda aRi kE sI Antam suna illa illai pAvamE) The note for this pathigam is that the ancient temple of Thanthonri Madam in Akkur, where worthy brahmins reside, is where the Lord entered and stayed. We have reflected on the history of Thiru Akkur in the Puranam of Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar. Having thus worshipped this holy place, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worshipped all other temples and then visited and praised Thiru Miyachur. Daivasekkizhar Peruman’s verse states: “Worshipping the Lord with red matted hair in Thanthonri Madam, in the city where worthy brahmins reside, he sang Tamil verses.

“After visiting many other temples, he went to Miyachur and praised the Lord who dances surrounded by a retinue of ganas.” “And then reached Thirupamburam,” this is the verse composed by Daivasekkizhar Peruman. The other temples worshipped by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman could be Thirusempanpalli, Thirupariyaloor, etc. Having worshipped all these holy places, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman went and worshipped at Thiru Miyachur. Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal went ahead, and Thirugnanasambandha Peruman followed behind, and both worshipped here. In Thiru Miyachur, there are two temples sung about: Thiru Miyachur temple and Thiru Miyachur Ilangkovil.

“Of these, Thiru Miyachur is the fifty-third temple on the southern bank of the Cauvery. It is a place where the sun worshipped the Lord and Goddess by placing them on an elephant.

“Therefore, the vimanam (tower) is in the Gajaprishta (elephant-back) style. The Mother, residing in a seated posture, grants darshan as Sundaranayaki with the name Santhanayaki. The Lord’s names include Meghanatha Swami, Muyarchinathar, and Thazhalar. The holy pond is Surya Pushkarani, and the sacred tree is Vilvam. It is located very close to Peralam. Within the same temple, adjacent to the sanctum sanctorum of Meghanatha Swami, on the northern circumambulatory path of Thiru Miyachur temple, is another revered temple known as Thiru Miyachur Ilangkovil.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 668, ‘Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam’ by Daivasekkizhar Peruman. Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrives at the Thiru Pampuram temple. This holy place, Pampuram, is located very close to Peralam on the Kumbakonam-Karaikal road. Other names for this holy place are Urakapuram and Sesha Puri. In this place, no one dies from snake bites. Even if a snake enters a house, it is said to normally leave without biting anyone. In this temple, the main deity and processional deity of Adiseshan are installed. Since it is a place worshipped by a snake, even today, at certain times, a snake is said to be seen moving about in the sanctum sanctorum. Even today, at certain times, the movement of snakes is said to occur.

On Sundays, Tuesdays, and Fridays, the fragrance of jasmine and screwpine is said to waft strongly within the temple. This implies that a snake is somewhere within the temple at those times. The pond created by Adiseshan with the help of Sittrambala Vinayagar to worship the Lord during Mahashivaratri is located on the northern street of the temple, known as Sittrambalakkuttai. Inscriptions from the periods of Rajaraja Chola, Rajendra Chola, Sundarapandiyan, and Serfoji Maharaja are found in this temple. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman enters the city and approaches the temple, chanting praises that those who remember, understand, praise, and reach Thiru Veezhimizhalai will have their karmas diminished and attain elevation. Sekkizhar Swamigal composes the next verse: “While the peerless king of speech (Thirunavukkarasu Peruman) was with him, he circumambulated the temple built in the heavens, and seeing the body of the Lord, which descended to earth for Brahma to praise, his mind was filled with wonder.” Pillaiyar sees that this vimana (temple tower) is the true form of the Viratpurusha. The Thiru Veezhimizhalai temple vimana is a vimana that descended from the heavens.

“Therefore, this temple is called the ‘temple that descended from the heavens’. This vimana is named ‘Vinnizhinda Vimanam’ (the vimana that descended from the heavens) because it was brought down from Devalokam and installed by Mahavishnu. The temple history states that it was installed and worshipped. There is no other temple with a vimana like the one at Thiru Veezhimizhalai. It is covered with five-metal sheets. Considering its special nature, devotees are trying to cover it with gold, as explained by Sivakavimani Ayya.

“Sekkizhar Peruman refers to such a vimana as ‘Puvizhiyum Undhiyan Potra Puvikku Izhinda Vimanam’ (the vimana that descended to earth for Vishnu to praise). Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships such a Thiru Veezhimizhalai temple. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships the Thiru Veezhimizhalai temple. Let’s continue to reflect.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 669, ‘Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam’ by Daivasekkizhar Peruman. Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman enters the Thiru Veezhimizhalai temple and prostrates himself before the Lord, his entire body touching the ground. Sekkizhar Peruman composes the verse: “Entering after circumambulating, he fell prostrate before the unique primal being who held the Ganga in his matted hair, his body touching the ground, his mind overflowing with immense love, and he sang with music.” The fact that the Lord holds the Ganga in his matted hair indicates his unique primal nature. His having matted hair signifies his primal nature.

For Bhagiratha, he held the Ganga and blessed the world.

Similarly, this beautiful verse contains hints of future events where he will prevent all the sorrows that are about to occur in this world through these two great devotees. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s mind is entirely filled with love for the Lord, and as this great love spreads throughout his mind, it overflows as music, manifesting as a pathigam. Sekkizhar Peruman composes the next verse: “Praising him, he began with ‘Sadaiyar Punal Udaiyan’ (He who possesses water in his matted hair), and singing a Tamil pathigam garland with sweet melodies, he remained immersed and endured in the flood of bliss beneath the beautiful sacred feet of the Lord adorned with sacred ash.” Sekkizhar Peruman composes the next verse: (Ananda veLLatthil nIchchazhagar sEvaDikkIzh ninRalaiyndu nIDinAr).

The Lord is the beautiful one adorned with sacred ash. The sacred ash on his divine body signifies that he is the great cause of cosmic dissolution. Sekkizhar Peruman also refers to him as ‘Azhagar’ (the beautiful one). ‘Azhagar’ implies that he is the primal one who recreates the worlds dissolved during the great cosmic dissolution.

Thus, beneath the sacred feet of the beautiful Lord adorned with sacred ash, Pillaiyar sings a pathigam, immersing himself in a flood of bliss, experiencing that Shiva-bliss beyond measure, and reveling in it.

At that time, he began with ‘Sadaiyar Punaludaiyan’ (He who has water in his matted hair). He bestowed a pathigam, offering a garland of pathigam Tamil verses, praising and extolling the Lord. Praising means glorifying the Lord, extolling means narrating all His glories, and singing means compiling all these into songs.
