Thus, he praises, extols, and sings the Tamil music of the pathigam. This pathigam is dedicated to Thiruvalimilai, and it is the eleventh pathigam in the First Thirumurai. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows; this pathigam is set to the tune of Nattappadai. (Pazhaiudaya pada Bhootha padai udaiya mada maan mElE poomai maathidam udaiya udaiya vidaiya kodiyidam mElum nILa mElum nILIya veeram thannai virai sE thAlil nagaru kalai yaana tham vantha thamizh pisaival solla) The Lord, who is known by characteristics such as being the one with matted locks and the one with water, resides in Thiruvalimilai. This is the main point of this pathigam.

The second verse of this pathigam, which is adorned with numbers from one to eight, is the song: (eeraai muthal onraai iru peNNAn kuNam moondraai maaraa maRai naan) (avai ainthaai aaraar suvai Ezhoosai ettu thisai thaanaai vERaai udanaan idam vIzhi mizalaiyae) is that second verse. It begins with ‘eeraai muthal onraai’. ‘eeraai’ means the cause of dissolution. ‘muthal onraai’ means the primal being who absorbs the world and souls into Himself and then brings them back into existence. ‘aai’ signifies that the Lord stands as the souls of the world. ‘vERaai’ indicates that even though the Lord is inextricably mixed with the souls of the world, He remains distinct from them. ‘udanaan’ means that even though the Lord is both one with and distinct from them, He is also with them. It also signifies the manner in which one becomes united with the Lord. These three states are what the second sutra of Sivagnana Botham describes as ‘avaiyEyAi thaanEyAi avaiyE thaanEyAi’. This state of the Lord being one with, united with, and distinct from the world and souls is a unique and great truth not discussed elsewhere except in Saiva Siddhanta.

Sri Meykanda Devar describes this state of the Lord, being one, united, and distinct, as ‘advaita kalappu’ (non-dual mixing). Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has bestowed this second verse upon us, with these truths, by structuring it as ‘eeraai muthal onraai vERaai udanaan’. This verse possesses the greatness of being called the lifeblood of Saivism. Such a highly significant second verse is found in this pathigam. Sivakavimani Ayya writes a commentary on it as follows: ‘Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, whose heart was filled with boundless love, melting within him, stood before the Lord, singing, dancing with joy before Him, praising Him, bowing down, and rising to perform the divine dance. With the sacred feet, which perform such a great dance of grace, lovingly held within his heart, he approaches the temple from outside, by its side.

Pillaiyar and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman thus come out of the temple and meet. As soon as they meet, outside the sacred wall of the temple, in a large mutt, Arasukal, the king of eloquent Tamil, takes residence. Along with Arasukal, devotees also come and reside there.

Later, Pillaiyar, the great Brahmin who arrived from Sirkali, approaches the temple tower and resides in a mutt to the north.

Thus, the king of eloquent speakers and Pillaiyar reside separately in mutts. These two mutts are currently located on the west and east sides of the northern mutt complex street of the temple. They are now built as small temples, and the idols of the respective Nayanmars are enshrined and worshipped in those mutts. After Arasukal and the devotees reached the mutt, Pillaiyar reached his mutt. This is noteworthy here. To emphasize that these two mutts possess incomparable unique greatness, Sekizhar Peruman refers to Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal’s mutt as ‘Or Maamadam’ (a great mutt) and the mutt where Thirugnanasambandha Peruman resided as a mutt. ‘Oppatra’ (incomparable) comes here in this context.

In what way did these mutts possess incomparable greatness? Because they became places where the great charity of feeding devotees with the vast gold received through the grace of the Lord took place for many days, these mutts became incomparable. In the mutt where Thirunavukkarasu Peruman resided, the sacred meal was conducted daily without fail, using the gold coin bestowed by the Lord.

However, in Pillaiyar’s mutt, the sacred meal was conducted with some delay.

Therefore, Daiva Sekizhar Peruman refers to the mutt where Thirunavukkarasu Peruman resided as a ‘Maamadam’ (great mutt) and the mutt where Thirugnanasambandha Peruman resided as a mutt. While these two great individuals were residing in these mutts during those days in Thiruvalimilai, they regularly participated in the daily pujas to the Lord and praised and worshipped Him. They remained at the Lord’s feet and thus participated in the pujas without fail. The Lord’s sacred feet signify the fullness of grace. Within the omnipresence of those sacred feet, they are absorbed omnipresently. This is a reference to the state where the sacred feet are considered the head.

This is a sign of grace, staying there without wavering. During those days, they regularly participated in all the prescribed daily pujas for the ‘Parartha Puja’ worship in the temple. Daily pujas, according to the Agamas of those temples, are conducted once, twice, thrice, four times, five times, or six times a day, as part of the ‘Parartha Puja’. The Sivagamas conclude that worshipping during such times is beneficial.

Therefore, Sekizhar Peruman informs us here that these two great individuals performed temple worship every day and every period.

Now, in the many months of a year, Sivakavimani Ayya writes in his commentary that the present-day Saivite world, which lacks the discipline of at least one proper worship session on one day out of the many days in a month, and one day out of the many months in a year, should recognize this and attain salvation. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who could resolve difficulties wherever he went, visited and worshipped the shrines during his stay in Thiruvalimilai. These shrines include Thiruppenuperunthurai and Thilathai Pathimuttam, which are located near Thiruvalimilai, within its boundaries. (Oongu punal pENu perunthurai) In the 549th verse, Daiva Sekizhar Peruman thus states: (pangaar thilathai pathimuttamum paNintha veengoLi neer vIzhi mizalaiyinil meendum aNainthu aangu inithu kumbittu amarndhu ozhugu an nALil) Pezhperunthurai is a fertile shrine due to the abundance of water in the Arasilaaru river. Perunthurai is a different shrine, Thirupperunthurai, where the Lord bestowed grace upon Thiruvathavooradigal, and it is located in the Pandya Nadu.

However, the shrine near Thiruvalimilai is called Pezhperunthurai. This shrine is located to the west of Thiruvalimilai.

Similarly, Thilathai Pathimuttam is located to the east of Thiruvalimilai. Thiruppezhu Perunthurai is the sixty-fourth shrine on the southern bank of the Cauvery. It is now known as Thiruppattathurai. Ammai, Murugar, Brahmadeva, and others worshipped the Lord there. The Lord’s sacred names are Sivanandar and Pranaveswarar. The Goddess is Mangalambikai, Malaiarasi.

The sacred water body is Mangala Theertham. It is located on the banks of the Arisil River. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who visited this shrine, bestowed a pathigam. It is the forty-second pathigam in the First Thirumurai, set to the tune of Thakkaragappann. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Sel) (peitha solli see thozhil pENiyO sella ammaa nOkkiya am thalir mENi aRivaiyO paakam amarndhu nalkiya koL pugazhE perum thuRai yaarE kadaiyaar vaaTam nangaL kizhavi kazhumaLOorum kalanthu naTa)

(perum ulakil thaamE ulakil thaamE sithiram vaLam naakam konRai muthaliyavaRai poondu seyyOr selvar moovurumaaki iruvarumaaki muthalvanumaai ninRa) The Lord, who is known by attributes such as being the form, the lord of the Devas, and our Lord, is Thiruppenuperunthuraiyar. This is the main point of the pathigam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having worshipped at Thiruppenuperunthurai, proceeds to worship at Thiruthilaithai Pathi. This shrine, Thilathai Pathi Mathimuttam, is the fifty-eighth shrine on the southern bank of the Cauvery. It is currently known as Thilathai Pathi and Sithalaipathi.

This is the place where Rama and Lakshmana performed Thilatharpanam for their father, hence it is called Thilathai Pathi. Since Chandra worshipped the Lord here and received blessings, it is also known as Mathimuttam. Performing water rituals for ancestors here brings great merit. The Lord’s sacred name is Mutthesar Mathimuthar. The Goddess is SorNavalli Porkodi Nayagi. The sacred water bodies are Devi Theertham, Brahma Theertham, Chakra Theertham, Vasishta Theertham, Arisilaaru, and Chandra Theertham.

This shrine is located very close to Peravaram. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who visited here, bestowed a pathigam. It is the one hundred and eighteenth pathigam in the Second Thirumurai, set to the tune of Sevvazhipann. The first and last verses of that pathigam are as follows: (Ooda kaaLai) (Eththidam kodi vilaba thilathaippathi paTikkul salaruma raNam thamizha mathi) (mum aaLa mathimudhthampa)

The Lord’s abode is Thilathaipathi Mathimuttam. This is the main point of the pathigam.

Our contemplation continues. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 670, Vampura Varivandu Sarukkam, composed by Daiva Sekizhar Peruman, on Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. Pillaiyar was residing in Thiruvalimilai during those days.

The Brahmins of Sirkali, their affection for Thirugnanasambandha Peruman growing, desired to have his darshan and came to Thiruvalimilai. Sekizhar Peruman sings about this: (sEnuyar maaTap pugazhiyaLLAr Thirugnanasambandha PiLLaiyArai kANum viruppil perugum aasai kaithi kaathal karai ikappa pUNum manathodu thONimEvam poruviTaiyAr malar paatham pOtri vELnu puRathai aganRu pOnthu vIzhi mizhalai) The 2448th verse states: (vandhu aNainthAr). Sirkali is a shrine with towering mansions reaching the sky.

The Brahmins of Sirkali desired to see Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. This desire grew into an aspiration, which intensified and reached the state of love. Sekizhar Peruman explains this as ‘kANum viruppil perugum aasai kaithi kaathal’. The thought of seeing Pillaiyar, whom they had been separated from for many days, first sprouted as a wish, then grew into an aspiration, and then it blossomed into love. With a heart full of such matured love, they set out to see Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. As they embarked, they worshipped Thoniyappar of Sirkali, who had bestowed wisdom upon Pillaiyar and taken him into his grace.

After worshipping and taking leave, they departed. It is at Thiruvalimilai that Thoniyappar would later grant visions to Pillaiyar in his dreams and waking state.

Therefore, those Brahmins, after taking leave from Thoniyappar, reached Thiruvalimilai. They had journeyed from Sirkali, worshipping at the various shrines along the way.

However, Sekizhar Peruman quickly narrates their journey without mentioning all those details, simply stating that they set out from Sirkali and reached Thiruvalimilai. This highlights the speed with which they travelled and the great love they held. Sekizhar Peruman thus conveys the urgency of their love.

Now, the next verse: (Uzhi muTivilum uyarndha veLLaththu Ongiya kALi uyarpathiyil vAzhi maRaiyavar thAngaleLAm vandhu marungu aNainthArkaL ena vIzhi mizhalaiyin vEthiyarkaL kEttu meigngnAnam uNDArAI munnA EzhIsai sUzh maRaiyOrAI eythi ethirkoNmuRaimayil koNDu pukkAr) This is the 559th verse. Sirkali is a shrine that floats unharmed even in the great floods that occur through the ages.

The Brahmins residing in such a Sirkali come and arrive near their abode, Thiruvalimilai.

The Brahmins of Thiruvalimilai hear this news. Generally, when great personalities visit a place, it was customary in those days to inform the residents of that place about such auspicious events beforehand. It is about this that we find instances of devotees gathering to welcome our Nayanmars wherever they went.

Similarly, the Brahmins of Vimalai hear the news that the Brahmins of Sirkali are arriving. These Brahmins of Thiruvalimilai hasten to welcome the Brahmins of Sirkali. Although other people in Thiruvalimilai had also heard this news, since Brahmins were considered suitable to properly welcome other Brahmins, the Brahmins of Thiruvalimilai welcomed the Brahmins of Sirkali in the appropriate manner. They chanted Vedas with auspicious pronouncements, welcomed them, bowed, and spoke words of goodness. These Brahmins of Sirkali are Brahmins who chant Vedas, specifically those residing in the sacred town of Sirkali, and furthermore, they are associated with Pillaiyar. They possess three great distinctions: their being Brahmins is special, their being Brahmins residing in Sirkali is even more special, and their having received grace through their close association with Pillaiyar is even more exceptional than the previous two.

Therefore, the manner in which they were welcomed was based on their association with Pillaiyar. It is a worldly custom to honor individuals not based on their personal status but based on the place from which they hail, even if they are from the government or a great holy place.

Therefore, these Brahmins were welcomed with great honor, not merely as Brahmins, nor just as Brahmins from Sirkali, but as Brahmins possessing the special connection of being associated with Pillaiyar. The next verse states: (shaNpAy thirumaRaiyOrgaL ellAm thambirAnArai paNintha pOnthu naNpil perugiya kaathal kUrndhu gnAnasambandhar maTaththil eythi paNpil perugum kaTumalaththAr PiLLaiyAr paatham paNintha pUNdE eNpetra thONi puRaththil emmODu ezhu tharuLa peRa vENdum enRAr). All those sacred Brahmins who came from Sirkali first entered the Thiruvalimilai shrine and worshipped the Lord residing inside the temple. Even though they came with a great desire to see Pillaiyar, they first worshipped the Lord in the prescribed manner and then proceeded to the mutt where Thirugnanasambandha Peruman resided.

Similarly, we can recall the historical event that will occur later, when Sivapatha Kiruthaiyar, who had been separated for many days, went to see Pillaiyar when he was staying in Madurai (Thiru Alavai). Sivapatha Kiruthaiyar first worshipped the Lord of Thiru Alavai and then went to Pillaiyar’s mutt. This is a history yet to unfold.

Thus, after worshipping the Lord, the Brahmins of Sirkali stood before Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and worshipped him.

At that time, they made a request to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. They implored Thirugnanasambandha Peruman to grant them the boon of coming with them.

The Brahmins, who came with the desire to see Pillaiyar, were so overwhelmed by their love for him that they were not content with just seeing him. They wished for Pillaiyar to return to Sirkali with them and pleaded with him to do so. They made this request out of an intense desire to always be with Pillaiyar without interruption. When he made his request, (eereel sivagnAna PiLLaiyArum nanRu ithu sAlavum thONimEvu naatha) The 553rd verse states: (kadal iNai nAm iRainja inRu kazhiththu mizhalai mEvu iRaivar aruL peRRu pOvathu enRai anRu pugazhi arumaRaiyOrkku aruL seythu avarkku mugam aLiththAr).

Thus, Pillaiyar hears their request to come with them to Sirkali and replies to them. He says, ‘This is very good, but we will worship the sacred feet of the Lord residing in Thiruthoni today, and tomorrow we will receive the grace of the Lord of Thiruvalimilai and depart.’ He grants them a favorable response. He is a child of boundless divine wisdom.

Therefore, he gives a favorable response, saying he will come with the Lord’s grace and permission from Thiruvalimilai. He says he will come with the grace of the Lord of Thiruvalimilai and with His consent. This is because Pillaiyar experiences the Lord’s grace both in dreams that night and in reality the next day.

Now, major events are about to unfold, starting with the later history of Pillaiyar in the Pandya kingdom.

Therefore, considering all these, a divine premonition arises in Pillaiyar’s heart through grace. That is why Pillaiyar, in response to the Brahmins’ request, neither immediately says he will come nor that he will not come. Instead, he says he will depart tomorrow after receiving divine grace. You have said that this action is very good.

However, he states that they will come after receiving the Lord’s grace. When great individuals respond to a request and grant a favorable reply, they typically include both an affirmation and a caveat. This is their custom. Pillaiyar, who had already sensed through divine grace that a manifestation of grace was imminent between the day the Sirkali Brahmins made their request and the following day, thus replied to the Brahmins. The next verse is the 554th verse: (mElpaTTa anthanar shaNpAy mEvum vEthiyarkku aayIru virundhu aLippa pArpaTTa sinthaiyarai மகிழ்ந்தu param poruL aayinArthamai paravum sIrpaTTa ellai inithu sella thiruththOni mEvya selvarthAmE kArpaTTa vaN kai kavuNiyarkku) The 554th verse states: (kaNaviDai munninRu aruL seiginRAr).

Thus, when Pillaiyar gave his reply, the Brahmins of Thiruvalimilai offered a fitting feast to the Brahmins of Sirkali. The auspicious times for worship passed pleasantly. After those times of worship, and after midnight had passed, before the dawn, in that intervening period, the Lord residing in Thiruthoni granted a vision to Pillaiyar. He appeared before him and bestowed grace. He appeared in his divine form, adorned with the Bull mount, Uma on his left, a blue throat, a crescent moon on his sacred crown, and other divine attributes, but without the deer and axe in his hands. He granted a vision to Pillaiyar, appearing before him as he was seated in Thiruthoni.

Sekizhar Peruman states: (kArpaTTa vaN kai kavuNiyarkku kaNaviDai munninRu aruL seiginRAr). Sekizhar Peruman praises Pillaiyar’s sacred hands as ‘kArpaTTa vaN kai’ to denote the nature of Pillaiyar’s grace. Generally, clouds are associated with generosity. Sekizhar Peruman says that Thoniyappar granted a vision to Pillaiyar, whose sacred hands bestowed immense grace, surpassing even the generosity of clouds. He appeared before him and bestowed grace.

Thus, Thoniyappar, after granting a divine vision, bestows grace. Sekizhar Peruman describes it in the 555th verse: (thOniyil nAm angiruntha vaNNam thU maRai vIzhi mizhalai thannuL sENuyar viNNinRu ezhintha intha sIrkoL vimAnaththu kAttuginROm pENumbadiyAl aRithitru enRu peyarthu aruL seiya perunthavangaL vENupuRaththavar vanthAr viravum pulakaththoTum uNarndhAr). Thoniyappar, after granting a divine vision, announces to Pillaiyar: ‘We will show you the same divine form here, in this glorious vimana that descended from the sky in the sacred Vedic abode of Thiruvalimilai, as we reside in Thiruthoni in Sirkali. See and worship it.’ Thoniyappar thus bestows grace upon Pillaiyar.

The Brahmins of Sirkali requested Pillaiyar to come with them to Sirkali (Thonipuram). In response to this, the Lord clarifies that even though He is referred to as being in Thiruthoni in Sirkali and in Thiruvalimilai separately, He is indeed one and the same, present everywhere. This omnipresent nature of the Lord is explained here by Sekizhar Peruman. ‘He is everywhere, without distinction,’ such as ‘here’ or ‘there’. This glory, filled with grace, is omnipresent, as Thayumanavar Swamigal’s divine words remind us.

Therefore, the Lord indicates that ‘we are one and the same in Thiruthoni in Sirkali and in Thiruvalimilai’. However, He not only reveals the form of Thiruvalimilai but also states that He will show the same divine form, as He is in Thiruthoni in Sirkali, within the vimana that descended from the sky in Thiruvalimilai.

There, in Sirkali, He bestowed the divine wisdom nectar, manifesting His words through Pillaiyar’s words for the welfare of the world. He will continue to do the same here and later in Thiru Alavai. Thoniyappar thus bestows grace upon Pillaiyar, saying: ‘Know this through this vision’. This reminds us of the thought of Pillaiyar, who was considered a great person who adopted childhood as his own, in Thiru Alavai, where he inquired about Thoniyappar and Periya Nayaki Ammaiyar, who had taken him into their grace.

Therefore, the Lord, with His omnipresent nature, also reveals the nature of souls, which can only perceive if the Lord shows them. ‘The sentient being that is informed is also He, and the sentient being that knows by itself is also He,’ as stated in the 11th verse of Sivagnana Siddhiyar. Souls are sentient beings that know when informed. The Lord, however, is a sentient being that knows by Himself.

Therefore, the Lord states here: ‘We are showing you; you shall see it,’ and Thoniyappar appears before Pillaiyar and bestows grace.

Thus, when the Lord bestowed grace, Pillaiyar, who was born due to the great penance of the people of Sirkali, with his body trembling with joy and his consciousness awakened, understood the divine indication of the Lord’s grace. That sacred time was the time for Thiruppalli Ezhuchi (awakening hymn). With an enlightened mind, Pillaiyar arose, amazed, and with his beautiful sacred hands clasped above his head, he bowed. He then entered the temple where the Lord, adorned with a garland of konrai flowers, joyfully resides in a celestial vimana.

There, he beheld the Lord holding a deer in his hand, in the same manner as he had previously worshipped Him on Thiruthoni in Sirkali, and thus saw the Lord in the celestial vimana of Thiruvalimilai. Thoniyappar bestows such a divine vision upon Pillaiyar. In that state, Pillaiyar sings a pathigam that expresses this greatness.

We shall proceed with our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 671, Vampura Varivandu Sarukkam, composed by Daiva Sekizhar Peruman, on Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. When Thoniyappar bestowed grace upon Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, saying that he would reveal the divine form of Thiruthonipuram in the celestial vimana of Thiruvalimilai, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, amazed, clasped his hands above his head and worshipped. Sekizhar Peruman describes this in his verse: (aRivutra sinthaiyarAi ezhunthE athisayiththu uchimEl angkai kUppi veRiyuRRa konRaiyinAr மகிழ்ந்த viNNiLi kOyilil senRu pukku maRiyuRRa kaiyaraith thONimEl mun vaNangumpadi angE kaNDu vAzhndhu kuRiyil perugum thiruppathigam kulaviya koLkaiyil pAdaginRAr) Sekizhar Peruman refers to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s mind as an awakened mind. The Lord’s revelation to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was not like an event occurring in a dream for ordinary souls like us, who are bound by the three malas (impurities).

This is because ordinary souls, who are bound by the three malas, experience the association and dissociation of the instruments of bondage, leading them to comprehend the transcendent.

Therefore, Pillaiyar, being a Jivanmukta (liberated soul) who understands the transcendent in his waking state, is not subject to states like sleep, unlike other beings.

Therefore, Sekizhar Peruman phrases it here as ‘aRivutra sinthaiyarAi ezhunthE’. We have also pondered this in the biography of Thirunilakanta Nayanar.

So, the Lord reveals this to Pillaiyar. Immediately after the revelation, it was the time for Thiruppalli Ezhuchi (awakening hymn) at dawn. In that state, Pillaiyar, filled with wonder at the Lord’s grace, clasped his hands above his head and immediately went to the Thiruvalimilai temple. It was dawn, the time for worship of Thiruppalli Ezhuchi.

So, he went to the temple there. In the Thiruvalimilai temple, the Lord, as Thoniyappar, revealed to Pillaiyar his divine form from Sirkali in the celestial vimana. The Lord’s divine form in Thiruthoni in Sirkali is one without holding a deer or an axe. Generally, the Lord holds a deer and an axe in His two upper hands.

However, the ancient Lord resides in Thiruthoni without them.

Therefore, He reveals his divine form there without the deer and axe. It is the form and identity of Thoniyappar. Having worshipped that form there, Pillaiyar experienced it here as well. (eri mazhuvODu izhaimAn kaiyinRi irunthapirAn ithu eNkOl sollaay mizhalai viNNiLi kOyil virumbiyathE). Within the temple, within the celestial vimana, With that divine intent, and to enlighten the world, as well as to question the Lord and praise His grace, and to instruct the world about His divine acts, Pillaiyar of Sirkali bestows a pathigam. In that state, Sekizhar Peruman narrates the next verse: (mai maRu pUngkuzhal enRu eduththu mAru il perunthiru thOni thanmEl kommAI mulaiyinAl kUda nITu kOlangkulAvum semmai tharu viNNiLintha kOyil thikazhnthapaDi ithu enkOL enRu meimmai viLangum thiruppathigam pADi மகிழ்ந்தar vEthavAyAr). Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is a Vethavayar (mouth of the Vedas).

He incarnated here in a Brahmin family.

Therefore, he is a mouthpiece for the revelation of the Vedas.

Therefore, he bestowed a pathigam that shines with truth, just like the Vedas. He began the pathigam with ‘mai maRu pUngkuzhal’. ‘Mai maRu pUngkuzhal’ is the beginning of the pathigam bestowed by Pillaiyar. With the incomparable great Thiruthoni, adorned with the youthful breasted Thirunilanayaki Ammaiyar, the grand divine form was manifested in the celestial vimana in Thiruvalimilai. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sang this pathigam as if questioning ‘what is this wonder?’ This greatly wondrous pathigam, bestowed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, unites Thiruppukali and Thiruvalimilai.

Therefore, the shrines of this pathigam are Sirkali (Thiruppukali) and Thiruvalimilai. Since each verse of this pathigam mentions both Sirkali (Pukali) and Thiruvalimilai, this pathigam is named after both these shrines.

Similarly, we can recall the historical accounts of pathigams like Thirumarugal, Thiruchengattangudi, Thirunallar, and Thiru Alavai.

Thus, the pathigam bestowed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, which begins with ‘mai maRu pUngkuzhal’, is the fourth pathigam in the First Thirumurai, set to the tune of Nattappadai. The first, ninth, and eleventh verses of this pathigam are as follows: As a cluster of fire, the mountainous people praised him, and he, the three-eyed one, whose fame never dimmed, spoke words. He desired to return to the mountain and live there with the dense thickets and poems. He who was seated with the blazing fire and held a deer in his hand—what did it mean when it was said that he held a deer in his blazing hand? The meaning of that was revealed in the fragrant, flower-filled gardens. He desired silver, desired to go, and said, “My lineage.” He praised the beautiful creeper, extolling its virtues, and beautifully sang the verses of Gnanasambandham, which spoke of the city where good deeds and fame flourished, and the children sang along with the elders.

This pathigam expresses the wonder of how Lord Shiva, who resides with the Mother Goddess in the Thoni, chose to manifest that form here within the Vimana for all to see. This is the pathigam’s introductory note. Having sung the radiant pathigam and concluded it with the Thirukadai Kappu, those who prostrate with folded hands, rising in a flood of bliss, approach the great Brahmins of Pukali, who are residing in the beautiful groves, and reveal to them the profound truth that has emerged from the depths of their hearts. The love that inspired him to travel to all the places where the great Lord Mukkat, residing in Piramapuram, with his consort, lovingly assumed various forms and worshipped them, now became profound. He then explained, “What I saw and cherished there, He has now graciously manifested here for me to witness.” With these words, he instructed them to proceed to the great city of Sirapuram. Sekkizhar Peruman then presents the next two verses, numbers 558 and 559.

Pillaiyar sings this pathigam, which is rich with meaningful words. Having sung the pathigam and concluded it with the Thirukadai Kappu, Pillaiyar folds his hands in reverence, prostrates, and rises. Overwhelmed by a flood of bliss, Pillaiyar emerges and graciously addresses the venerable Brahmins who had journeyed from Sirkazhi, revealing to them the true nature of grace, which had filled his heart as a divine message. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman addresses those Brahmins and states, “I harbored a deep desire to visit all the sacred places where the great Lord Mukkat, who graciously resides in Sirkazhi, the divine Piramapuram, with His consort, has manifested Himself, and to worship those beloved forms.” He continues, “The Lord, seeing this desire of mine, has graciously allowed me to witness here what He lovingly resided as in Thiruthoni.” Thus, he bestows his grace upon the Brahmins of Sirkazhi.

Therefore, Pillaiyar bids them farewell, saying, “You should proceed to Sirkazhi.” The desire I had to visit and worship Shiva in all the places where he resides, the Lord of Thiruthoni and the Goddess of Thiruthoni, has been granted. Thiruthoniyappar, who resides there, has accepted this and has graciously shown me His form here. He then says, “You called me to Sirkazhi, but I have already seen the Lord here.” He then dismisses the Sirkazhi Brahmins, saying, “You may now return to Sirkazhi.” Thus, when Pillaiyar graciously bestowed his blessings with kindness and compassion, the Brahmins, bowing respectfully, accepted Pillaiyar’s divine command. Even though it was contrary to their wishes and thoughts, they understood it as a divine indication and thus complied with the order. This situation illustrates how souls should conduct themselves, and that such conduct is the path to salvation, a truth revealed to us through the Brahmins of Sirkazhi.

The Brahmins of Sirkazhi held great affection for Pillaiyar, their hearts filled with profound love. This was not because Pillaiyar was born into their clan, but because during Pillaiyar’s Upanayanam, these very Brahmins of Sirkazhi had received divine teachings directly from Pillaiyar’s sacred lips. They recognized Pillaiyar’s greatness as their own, possessing a sense of belonging.

Therefore, they wished that Pillaiyar would never leave them and would always remain with them. However, contrary to their wishes, divine will intervened.

Therefore, accepting Pillaiyar’s command and bidding him a graceful farewell, the Brahmins depart from Thiruvezhimizhalai. Along their journey, they visit various sacred sites such as Thiruchirukudi, Thirumiyachchur, Thirumayiladuthurai, and Thiruppullirukkuvelur before reaching Sirkazhi.

There, in Sirkazhi, they observe the custom of worshipping Thiruthoniyappar with even greater devotion. They recognized Thiruthoniyappar as the one who had bestowed upon them Pillaiyar and his divine wisdom, and that it was He who had manifested himself in Thiruvezhimizhalai. Bearing this in mind, they observed the custom of worshipping Thiruthoniyappar with even greater reverence. As the Brahmins of Pukali thus took their leave, Pillaiyar, accompanied by Thiruvarasu Peruman, lovingly worshipped the sacred feet of the Lord residing in Thiruvezhimizhalai, surrounded by devotees, and sang a magnificent pathigam. He adorned it with a garland of Tamil verses, a pathigam, and with the abundant grace of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, their deep friendship flourished.

Thus, Pillaiyar resided in Thiruvezhimizhalai. In this situation, the sacred event of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, the two great religious leaders, receiving the Padikkasu in Thiruvezhimizhalai, is about to unfold. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to graciously narrate this to us. Let us also continue to contemplate it. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The great Purana, Part 672, “Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam,” of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar, composed by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman. Sekkizhar Peruman is about to elaborate on the sacred narrative of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman receiving the Padikkasu bestowed by the Lord in Thiruvezhimizhalai, within the Purana of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. During those days when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman were residing in Thiruvezhimizhalai, the heavens withheld their rains. The rivers did not swell with floods. When the sky failed over the land, and the rivers dried up, all earthly creatures suffered, their food depleted.

Seeing the great famine gripping the world, which prevented even the celestial beings from performing their special worship, they pondered. This verse states that in that era, rain failed on this earth; it was a drought.

Therefore, the rivers did not overflow with seasonal floods. Because the rain failed, the rivers did not swell, and thus, food production was impossible.

Consequently, all living beings on this earth suffered. Even the gods, including Indra, could not receive their due offerings. People could not perform the special pujas.

Here, “special” refers to a specific, occasional puja called Naimitthikam. Thirukkural states in the chapter “Glory of Rain”: “When the sky fails, special worship and regular pujas do not proceed, even for the celestials here.” Parimelazhagar, in his commentary on this, writes that if it does not rain on this earth, the festivals and pujas performed by people for the gods on this earth will not take place. The word “special” here refers to Naimitthika puja, and “puja” refers to Nitya puja. Naimitthika is performed to alleviate deficiencies in Nitya.

Therefore, Parimelazhagar interprets that if it does not rain, not only Naimitthika puja but also Nitya puja will not proceed. Accordingly, Sekkizhar Peruman also sings here, “Even the special worship for the celestials cannot be performed.” Thus, The great acharyas, both of them, observe the suffering of these beings. As great acharyas, they understand the distress that comes upon living beings and seek a solution. They contemplate, “Will sorrow befall even those who are devoted to the sacred ash of the three-eyed Lord on earth?” Their conviction is that sorrow will not come to devotees.

Therefore, “Will sorrow befall even those devoted to the sacred ash?” implies that sorrow will not come. Thirukkural states, “It is rare to remove mental anguish for anyone other than those who have taken refuge at the feet of the unequalled One.” Devotees are all those who have taken refuge at the sacred feet of Shiva, the unequalled One.

Therefore, “Will sorrow befall them?” implies that sorrow will not come to them. They are devoted to the sacred ash, which signifies their devotion to Shiva. That is the view of the great Acharyas here.

Now, Sekkizhar Peruman presents the next verse, the 563rd verse. (Vanagi Nilanaagi Analumagi Maruthumaai IruSudaraai Neerumagi Oonagi Uyiragi Unarvumagi Ulakankal Anaithumai Ulukku Appaal Aanatha Vativagi Nindrar Seiya Adi Paravi Andru Iravu Thuyilumpothu Kanada Kangalar Mizhalai Muthur Kathalithar Kanavil Anainthu Arulichcheivar endru aruliya Sekkizhar Peruman thodarnthu Ainoottru Arupathu Naankavathu Thiruppadalai Arulukinrar Ulaku Iyalpu Nikazhchiyal Anaintha Thiya Uru Pasi Noi Ummai Adaiyaathu Eninum Umbal Nilavu Siva Neri Sarnthor Thammai Vaattatu Neekkatharku Nitham Oror.) Sekkizhar Peruman graciously continues with the 564th verse, conveying that the Lord of Thiruvezhimizhalai, the Father, appeared in their dream and said, “Though the evil form of hunger, a disease born of the world’s natural course, does not affect you, to remove the suffering of those who follow the Siva path through you, we will grant you one coin daily.” (Kasu Neetum Ilaku Manippeetatthu Kunakku Merkkum Yam Alitthom Umakku Intha Kalam Theernthal Alakil Pukazir Thavirvathaakum Endre Arul Purinthaar Thiruvezhimizhalai Aiyar) Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman continuously narrates two verses. The first verse, which begins with “Vanagi Nilannagi,” states that Lord Shiva, who became the sky, earth, fire, air, the two luminaries of the sun and moon, water, flesh, soul, and consciousness, and all the worlds, and also stands beyond the worlds as an undiminished form, is praised.

That night, as Pillaiyar and Arasu were resting, they worshipped His reddish sacred feet. The meaning of this verse is that the Lord, who wears bones and dances in the forest as a Gankalar, and who lovingly resides in the ancient city of Thiruvezhimizhalai, graciously appeared in their dream and bestowed His blessings. In this verse, the Lord’s attributes as Vishwaroopi (all-pervading), Vishwa Antaryami (indwelling in all), and Vishwatheeta (transcending the universe) are praised. The special attribute of the Lord manifesting as the eight forms (Ashtamurtams) is lauded here. The eight forms attributed to the Lord—sky, earth, fire, wind, the two luminaries, and water—are celebrated here. The five elements, the sun, the moon, and souls constitute the Lord’s Ashtamurtams.

The Lord, being such, has become all the worlds, and all the worlds. This refers to all the universes and all the experiences. The body is called Yakka because it is created by the combination of the five elements. The act of placing the soul within this Yakka and other things is called creation.

Therefore, to denote this, Sekkizhar Peruman first described the Lord’s nature as becoming the elements like the sky. Having thus placed the soul in these worlds, and having created the body as a combination of the five elements, the Lord then causes the soul to experience pleasures and pains through the inner instruments like the Antahkarana.

Therefore, it is understood here that the Lord exists as the Ashtamurtams, as the worlds, and also as the one who causes souls to experience their experiences. It is stated in Thandakam: “You became the flesh, the soul, and the consciousness within it, and you are all else.” In Thiruvachakam: “You became the sky, the earth, the strength, the light, the flesh, and the soul.” In all these, the words “agi agi” (became, became) are used, as in “Vanagi Mannagi Valiyagi.” “Agi” are creative words.

The Lord activates these three types of illusions by means of the elements such as the sky. As the efficient cause, as stated in the second sutra of Sivagnanabodham, “Enreyayi Avaiye Thaneyayi,” the Lord’s state of being one with the souls, and being non-dual with them, is understood. The phrase “Uunar” indicates that the Lord, existing in this manner, is also beyond the world in an undiminished form. This refers to the Lord’s essential nature, which transcends all principles. Sivagnanabodham describes this state as “Thaney.” This is the nature of the Lord: to be mingled within those souls, to be the dwelling place for them to experience the fruits of their actions, to provide worlds and experiences for all beings to reap the benefits of their deeds, yet standing apart from all these and issuing commands. This is what Sekkizhar Peruman expresses as “ulagukku appal aanatha vadivagi.” Therefore, this world.

The Lord bestows upon these living beings the fruits of their karma, which they experience as hunger and disease.

Therefore, the rain falling in this world, living beings appeasing their hunger through it, the onset of disease, and the provision of remedies for those diseases—all these are bestowed by the Lord according to the karmic fruits of the living beings in this world.

Similarly, now, when rain does not fall and rivers do not swell with water, living beings suffer. However, the devotees of the Lord, the sacred ash-clad devotees, are those who stand firm in their service to the Lord. Sivagnanabodham, in its tenth sutra, states that for those who stand firm in service to the Lord, there is no strong karma from the illusion of impurity. Thiruvakku says, “Even if one stands in any body, there is no accumulated karma for those who serve the Lord.” The sacred saying also states that it is the duty of leaders to protect those who rely on them.

Therefore, with the conviction that no harm will befall the devotees who have taken refuge at the Lord’s sacred feet, these two great Acharya Perumakkal, contemplating whether sorrow would affect even devotees, repose that night, worshipping the Lord’s feet, believing that only the Lord’s feet can prevent sorrow. The Lord, who wears bones and assumes the form of a Gankalar, is the one who performs rebirth. He has lovingly chosen to reside here in Thiruvezhimizhalai.

Thus, the Lord, who performs rebirth and the act of protection, The Lord, who performs both rebirth and protection, graciously appears in the dreams of the great Acharyas. Sekkizhar Peruman narrates how this happens in the next verse. Even though this evil, hunger-like disease, which occurs due to the nature of this world, does not affect you, to alleviate the suffering of those devotees who follow the path of Shiva and have come to you, we will grant you one gold coin each day, both at the eastern and western altars. When this period of scarcity ends, it will be stopped, said the Lord of Thiruvezhimizhalai to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman.

Thus, the cycle of hunger, rain, and famine in this world is a natural occurrence. The Lord’s grace ensures that living beings experience the fruits of their actions in due time. Just as individual living beings experience the fruits of their actions, all living beings, influenced by the season, experience poverty, hunger, and disease collectively. We even observe that substances of the same type, like inert objects, appear and disappear together at certain times.

Therefore, these are all natural occurrences of the world. The collective suffering of many living beings due to time, such as poverty, hunger, and disease, is a result of evil karma.

However, these evils do not apply to our great Acharyas and Nayanmars, because These are all fruits of good and evil karma, which alternate. However, for our Nayanmars and great Acharyas, there is neither evil karma nor its fruits.

Therefore, as per the saying, “The path where He is all, and He alone, stands firm in His service,” just as these things do not affect our Nayanmars, they do not affect the devotees who have taken refuge in our Nayanmars. By taking refuge in our Nayanmars, those who have done so are the sacred devotees of the Lord and serve Him without deviation from their principles.

Therefore, they too stand firm in His service on the path where He is all and He alone, and thus, this distress does not affect them, this path. The Siva path comprises guru worship and Jangama worship. These are all mentioned in spiritual texts like the tenth sutra of Sivagnanabodham. These are things that need to be learned by properly studying under experienced spiritual teachers. Having said all this, the Lord states that he will give them one coin daily until this famine ends.

Here, “one coin each” should be understood as one coin for Pillaiyar and one coin for Thirunavukkarasu Peruman.

The Lord states that he will give it on the altar. He bestows this upon Pillaiyar at the eastern altar and upon Arasu at the western altar.

The Lord states that he will continue to give it until this period of suffering, caused by the evil of hunger and disease due to the nature of this world, comes to an end and these living beings have experienced their allotted karma.

Thus, when the Lord of Thiruvezhimizhalai graciously revealed this, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, filled with wonder at the Lord’s immense grace, circumambulated the temple of the Lord of Thiruvezhimizhalai with Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. By the grace of the Lord who is united with Uma, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman found a gold coin on the altar facing him.

We shall continue our contemplation of this. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The great Purana, Part 673, “Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam,” of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar, composed by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman. Just as Shiva revealed the message to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, he also revealed the same message to Thirunavukkarasu Peruman.

Therefore, marveling at the abundance of the Lord’s grace, both Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman proceed to the Thiruvezhimizhalai temple. There, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman finds a gold coin on the altar directly opposite the Lord, that is, on the eastern side, just as the Lord had promised.

Similarly, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman finds a gold coin on the altar on the western side of the temple, as graciously given by the Lord. Sekkizhar Peruman has elaborately narrated in Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s Purana the history of how Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, upon seeing it, used it to feed the devotees in his monastery. We are now going to examine the narratives in Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s history, which recount how Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, upon seeing this gold coin, praised the divine event. As soon as Pillaiyar saw the gold coin, he reverently picked it up. He picked it up with great love and reverence, stood with folded hands, and with immense joy overflowing, he sent out a proclamation, inviting all the Lord’s beloved devotees to come daily for a good feast. Sekkizhar Peruman narrates the next two verses: (Kku varuga endru theethil parai nikazhviththu sendra thondar thiru amuthu kari ney pal thayir endru inna ethumuraathu inithu unna ootti anggan iruthiratthu porunthavarum iruntha naalil navinukku venthar thirumattaththil thondar natkuru thiru amuthu seyya kandu sevukaithar arulpetra pillaiyar tham thirumattaththil amuthaakkuvarai nokki theevinaikku neer endrum adaivilaathir thiru amuthu kalaththaal aakki ingu mevu mikka adiyavarku azhiyaavannnam vilainthavaaru ennkalo vilampum endrar.) Pillaiyar takes the gold coin he found on the altar.

The coin found in the temple is meant to be taken and used only by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who has received divine grace, with his sacred hands. It is not rightful for anyone who has not received divine grace to seize or use that coin, and to signify this, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman takes the coin with his sacred hands. He praises the divine event.

Now, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has a proclamation made and the message delivered to the devotees. He makes a proclamation, inviting all devotees who are dear to Shiva and loved by him to come and partake of a good feast every day. This sacred message is being conveyed. The Lord, after all, had said, “to alleviate the suffering of those who follow the path of Shiva and have come to you.” Accordingly, this message is proclaimed. The duty of a leader to protect those who rely on them is mentioned here.

Therefore, to alleviate the suffering of those who have taken refuge in Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, a good feast is arranged for Shiva’s devotees in Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s monastery, using the gold coin that was graciously granted. Food items such as blessed rice, curries, ghee, milk, and curd are arranged there.

Here, “Thiru Amudhu” refers to cooked rice, which is the principal food item.

Therefore, it is our tradition to specially refer to it as “Thiru Amudhu.” Along with this blessed rice, curries, milk, tender coconut water, and other such items are also arranged. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman feeds all the great devotees the Thiru Amudhu without any fault. “Etham Uraatha Unavu” means food without any defect. Food prepared excellently, without any ingredient being in excess or insufficient in any food item. That food is prepared in such a way that it does not cause any harm, such as bodily discomfort. Such faultless food is served to the devotees with kind words and other courtesies.

“Oottuthal” means to feed with the same love that a mother would feed her child.

Therefore, the act of serving sacred food to these devotees is taking place in Pillaiyar’s monastery and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s monastery.

At that time, in Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s monastery, the serving of sacred food to the devotees is completed before noon. However, in Pillaiyar’s monastery, there is a slight delay in serving the food. A day is divided into two parts, and the middle part is called Uchippozhuthu (noon). It is also referred to as Nanpagal (midday). This time is considered appropriate for meals by our elders. Eating multiple times before noon is a bad habit.

Doing so can lead to a decline in health and a shortened lifespan. In Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s monastery, the sacred food is served to the devotees at the correct time, before noon. He asks, “You never resort to evil deeds, but what is the reason why we are unable to prepare and offer sacred food to the devotees who come here at the right time in our monastery?” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s attendants are of very high character and have great love for devotees.

Therefore, this delay in serving food was certainly not caused by them. Considering that the reason was definitely not them, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman then ponders. Peruman asks, “What is the other reason for this?” Such questioning is a polite way of speaking, and it is the tradition of great people.

Therefore, he asks his attendants, “This was not caused by you, so what are the other reasons?” To this, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s attendants reply, “The food preparers in the monastery will speak as the leader of the Brahmins commanded. We know nothing of this. When we go to purchase provisions for the sacred food with the coin we received from our Lord, the merchants in the market say that the coin has a defect and reduce its value. The great sage Vagisar accepts the coin he receives. This is a later development,” they say to Pillaiyar. His attendants replied to Pillaiyar, “When we go to buy provisions for preparing sacred food with the coin we receive from the Lord, the merchants in the market reduce the value of the coin, saying it is defective.

“They reduce the amount according to the defect.

“Therefore, there is a delay. We don’t know why this is happening, why they are doing this and not giving the full amount for the coin you give.

“But for the coin received by the great sage Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, they accept it with great willingness without saying anything of the sort.

“Therefore, this is the reason for the delay.” They also state that they do not know the reason for this. Even though both received coins from the Lord, they say they do not know the reason why these coins have two different characteristics. Because the merchants act this way, saying that the coin given by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is defective, and causing such delays, there is a great delay in buying rice and other provisions for preparing sacred food.

“Therefore, there is a delay in serving sacred food, they explain. Sekkizhar Peruman then composes the next verse. Thirugnanasambandhar listens to it and contemplates. The gold coin Shiva gave us. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman listens to his attendants’ reply and contemplates why the coin given by the Lord to him is defective, while the other coin is perfect and does not show any defect. He realizes that the great Thirunavukkarasar is always engaged in selfless service, a great and venerable sage.

“Therefore, the coin given by the Lord to him is flawless because it is a reward for his selfless service.

“Thus, the divine will of Shiva reveals this to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. The coin given by the Lord to Thirunavukkarasu Peruman is a reward for his service.

“Therefore, because it is given in exchange for that service, He grants that coin flawlessly. Hence, the quality of standing independently, without being influenced by others, is conveyed here. That is why Sekkizhar Peruman praises the Lord as “Periyon” (the Great One) in this verse.

“The Lord Himself takes the initiative to offer this Padikkasu (coin) to alleviate the suffering of the devotees who worship Pillaiyar and Arasu as followers of the Siva path. Even though he bestows it upon both, he grants this distinction between the two coins. By granting it impartially based on their respective states of devotion, the Lord is praised as “Periyon” by the Swamis in this verse.

“Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman contemplates. When the divine will thus revealed itself to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, he resolved in his heart that he must sing a pathigam to the Lord, pleading with Him to change the coin and grant him a flawless one. Sekkizhar Peruman composes this verse, saying that on that day, he entered the Lord’s temple, sang a pathigam asking Him to remove the defect from the coin, and then, having received the good coin as he wished, he went to the marketplace. When he showed it to the people, they said, “Oh, great ascetic, this coin is excellent. We will give you whatever you need.” From that day onwards, he fed the devotees their daily portion of sacred food with great enthusiasm.

“The next day, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman entered the temple of his Lord and, requesting the Lord to remove the defect from the flawed coin, sang a pathigam that implied, “Please grant a coin free from defect.” He began the pathigam by saying, “Grant us a coin free from defect.” He continues to sing the pathigam.

“Our contemplation continues.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The great Purana, Part 674, “Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam,” of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar, composed by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sang a pathigam asking the Lord to grant a coin free from defect. This pathigam is the 92nd pathigam in the First Thirumurai. It is a pathigam pertaining to the Thiruvezhimizhalai shrine, composed in the Kurinji tune. This pathigam is as follows.

(Muraivail Meelaiye Seereri Neerum Nizhalaiye Perum Marula Kaman Mem Nizhalaiyume Sataiyi Mani Koll Nirari Anikkul Vizhalai Panikondarunume E Mangai Panginee Thunga Melaiye Kangai Mutiy) (Thangai Thavir Mileiyye Arakkal Eri Thara Irakkam Eiythu Parakkum Izhalaiyir Karakkai Thavir Mileiyye Ayalu Matumay Muyalu Muthi Ner Iiyalum Nizhalaiye Payanam Maruppume Parikkul Thalaiyinar Arivatharkir Perukkul Nizhalaiye Thirivatharriyathe E Kali Manavar Vali Sambantham Velimilai Ver Thazhmozhikale Kali Managa Vali Sambantham Pili Milaiye Thazhmozhikale) This pathigam was sung to receive coins without depreciation. It was a minor event that occurred through the immense grace of the Lord.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed this pathigam in a short metric form.

Also, due to his eagerness and speed to complete this pathigam and then use the non-depreciating coins granted by the Lord for the day’s sacred food offerings, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman rendered this pathigam in this brief, concise meter.

Similarly, the implicit meaning of this pathigam is: “You will grant coins without depreciation.” The special feature of this pathigam is that the request, its implicit meaning, was quickly and concisely stated at the outset. Immediately after completing this pathigam, by the grace of the Lord, gold coins without depreciation or defect are received. They are good coins. Unlike the depreciated coins received until now, these are good, non-depreciating coins.

So, Pillaiyar gives them to his attendants, and his attendants take them to the market street, the bazaar, and offer them. Since these coins are good, unlike those brought on previous days, they are readily accepted by the shopkeepers in terms of weight, purity, and all other aspects.

Consequently, all the necessary provisions for preparing sacred food for Pillaiyar’s attendants are obtained very quickly.

Thus, the sacred food is prepared very quickly for the devotees there. On this day, at Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s monastery, sacred food is offered to the devotees at the precise time. Not only that, from this day forward, and for all the days to come, until this famine ends, good monsoons arrive, and prosperous days return, the Lord daily grants non-depreciating coins to Pillaiyar.

Therefore, at Pillaiyar’s monastery and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s monastery, sacred food is offered to the devotees at the precise time. Sekkizhar Peruman beautifully and concisely presented this entire history in a single verse, allowing us to understand it.

Now, the next verse: (Aruvilai perungkasum avaiye aaki amudhu seiya thondar alavirandhu pongivarum avargal ellarkkum vanthaarukkum magizhndhu unna in adisil maalaathaaga Thirumudi mel thingalodu Gangai soodum Sivaperuman arul seiya sirappin mikka perumai tharu Shanbai nagar vendhar Navukkarasar ivar perum sorru piranjaal eenthaar). With the coins that the Lord grants daily, all the rare and precious items are acquired, and the devotees, who are ever-increasing in number, can partake in the sacred food. For everyone who comes, there is an endless supply of sweet food to be eaten with joy, by the grace of Lord Shiva, who adorns his head with the moon and the Ganga. And the Lord, who wears the mango, grants grace. Sekkizhar Peruman describes this sacred service as an endlessly flourishing service, saying “malathaaka.” In every place where acts of Shiva Punya (meritorious deeds related to Shiva) performed by remembering the Lord are abundant, food grows due to divine grace. Such are events of divine grace; acts of Shiva Punya are described as immortal asceticism.

Therefore, the Lord grants his grace to make it flourish endlessly. The single coin that the Lord grants daily to Pillaiyar and Appar Peruman becomes a coin that procures all the necessary items for that day. The sacred food prepared with such items The sacred food prepared with such items grows abundantly throughout the day, increasing as the devotees arrive.

The Lord who grants such grace is he who adorns himself with the moon and the Ganga. The food prepared there grows like the moon. The multitude of devotees who come there swells like the Ganga. Sekkizhar Peruman metaphorically uses “adorned with the moon and the Ganga” to convey this, as noted by Thiru Vasu Sengalvaraya Pillai.

Thus, with the Lord’s grace, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the king of Shanbai, and Appar Peruman, the king of speech, bestow mountains of sacred food upon the devotees there.

Here, Sekkizhar Peruman addresses Sirkazhi Pillaiyar as the king of Shanbai and Appar Peruman as the king of speech, using the terms “vendhar” and “arasar” (both meaning king). Sekkizhar Peruman uses these terms, comparing their leadership to that of a king, because they offered sacred food using the coins given by the Lord. Providing unlimited and abundant food is something only kings can do.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman hails them as the king of Shanbai and the king of speech. This act of grace, where these two great acharyas received coins in Thiruvezhimizhalai and offered sacred food to devotees, has been praised in many divine scriptures.

Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, in the seventh verse of the forty-sixth pathigam of the seventh Thirumurai, the Thirunagaikkaroon pathigam, sings of this event of grace, saying: (Nesamudai adiyavargal varundhaamai arundha nirai maraiyor urai Veezhimizhalai thannil nitthal kaasu arulichcha).

Furthermore, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, in the eighth verse of the eighty-eighth pathigam of the seventh Thirumurai, the Thiruveezhimizhalai pathigam, also sang about this event of grace, saying: (irundhu neer thamizhodu isai ketkum ichaiyal kaasu nitthal nalgineer). In the twelfth verse of the Thiruvichaippa pathigam by Senthanar Peruman in the ninth Thirumurai, dedicated to Thiruveezhimizhalai, he sang of this event of grace: (Paadalangaara parsil kaasu aruli pazhutha senthamizh malar soodi needhalangaaraththu em perumakkal nenjinul niraindhu nindraanai).

Thus, many divine sayings praise this event of grace.

During this time, the period of poverty ends, and the time for rain to fall upon the world arrives. Sekkizhar Peruman composes the next verse: (Avanimisai mazhai pozhiya unavu malki anaithuyirum thuyar neengi arulinale buvanamelam poli veyudhum kaalam eydha purichadaiyar kadal pala naal potri vaiki thava munivar sol vendharodum kooda thambiran arul pettru thalaththin meedhu Sivan magizhum thaanangal vanangapoovar then Thiruvaanchiya moodhur sendru sernthaar). Sekkizhar Peruman composes the five hundred and seventy-second verse, stating that this period of poverty ends, and the time for rain to fall upon the world arrives. Until then, By the grace of Lord Shiva, Pillaiyar and Appar Peruman have been receiving daily coins and offering sacred food to the devotees. Sivakavimani Ayya states that this period could have lasted for one year.

The Lord himself, in his divine words, said, “Until this time of suffering due to famine ends, we will bestow it.” Such a time has now arrived. The time when rain falls upon this world and food supplies increase has arrived. Just as the period of famine arises due to the karma of living beings, so too does this rainy season arrive naturally. Time is a principle that determines the experience of karmic consequences for living beings by divine command.

Therefore, this period of time possesses a power that living beings cannot explain. However, so that the suffering of this period would not afflict and weaken the devotees, the Lord granted coins.

Similarly, to alleviate the hardship of that time, to end this period of famine, until the world flourished with rain and joy returned, and until that joyous time arrived, both great personalities worshipped the Lord, protected by the coins, so that the severity of the times would not affect them.

Therefore, even when the severity of the times arrives, causing living beings to experience the suffering of their past karma, divine grace alone is the support to prevent that severity from affecting them, to resolve that severity, And to transform that severity into goodness. This event from the sacred history illustrates this. Until this time arrived, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, who protected living beings with the Lord’s grace, now that the good rainy season has arrived and food supplies have increased, thereby naturally alleviating the suffering of living beings, both these great personalities obtain leave from the Lord of Thiruveezhimizhalai and proceed to worship the many places where the Lord has graced. On that pilgrimage, they reach the ancient city of Thiruvaanchiyam.

Now, in the next verse, both these great personalities, having worshipped at six places, Sekkizhar Peruman composes the five hundred and seventy-third verse: (Needu Thiruvaanchiyaththil amarntha mukkan neelamidatru arumaniyai vanangi potri padoli neer thalaiyalanngaadu maadu paramar peruvelurum panindhu paadi naadu pugazh thanichchaaththangkudiyil nanni nambar Thirukkara veeram nayanthu paadi thedu maraikku ariyaartham vilamar potri Thiruvaroor thozha ninaindhu sendru pukkar) this is the verse. It means, having worshipped and praised the precious gem-like Lord, who is seated in the eternally enduring Thiruvaanchiyam, possesses three eyes, and a blue throat, they sang at Thiruthalaiyalangaadu with its echoing waters, and then bowed and sang at the Lord’s Thiru Peruvelur nearby. They then reached the uniquely famous Thiruchchaththangudi, and afterwards, delightedly sang at the Lord’s Thirukkara Veeram. They lovingly sang about Thirukkaraveeram, then praised the Lord’s Thiruvalamar, and finally, intending to worship Thiruvarur, they arrived at Thiruvarur. These two great personalities, who resided in Thiruveezhimizhalai for a long time, embarked on a pilgrimage from there, quickly visiting and worshipping many cities. In keeping with this journey, Sekkizhar Peruman describes how these two great personalities visited and worshipped six sacred places in a single verse: Thiruvaanchiyam, Thirupperuvelur, Thiruchchaththangudi, Thirukkaraveeram, and Thiruvalamar.

We have already reflected on the special features of the primary place, Thiruvaanchiyam, in the Purana of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who arrived at Thiruvaanchiyam, Composed a pathigam. It is the seventh pathigam of the second Thirumurai, set to the tune Indhalam. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. (Indaiyaday idamaaga uganthathe e sendral koonrum polil sendru anaiyu theer vaangiyum nira theeraiyanai unarundhu adiyaththalaaga nanru kaali marai Gnanasambandha sel thamizh onrum ullam mooda) The summary of this pathigam is that the Lord forever resides in Thiruvaanchiyam, having chosen it as his beloved place.

Among the six sacred places mentioned above, the next is Thiruthalaiyalangaadu. Sekkizhar Peruman describes how water gently murmurs and flows there. This place is situated on the northern bank of the Chola Choodamani River.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman Mentions it this way. The pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for this place is, due to our lack of merit, not available to us. The third sacred place is Peruvelur. A pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for this place has been found.

We shall continue our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 675, by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, having departed from Thiruveezhimizhalai, visit places like Thiruvaanchiyam and Thiruthalaiyalangaadu, and then reach the sacred place of Thirupperuvelur. We have already reflected on the special features of this place in the Purana of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who arrived at this place, composed a pathigam. This pathigam, which begins with “Annawum Kazhukunru,” is the sixty-fourth pathigam of the third Thirumurai, set to the tune Panchamam.

The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Aayamalai avai vaazhvinnoru mannorum viyanthe arul seivaru thannaavarula karuththaan puram eriththa perumaan Peruvelur periya paimpon seermani vaari pazhavum serkkundhi anngon sei madappara) The summary of this pathigam is that Peruvelur is a place where the Lord, whose grace is praised by both celestial and earthly beings, resides permanently, manifesting many such divine qualities. After bowing and worshipping at Peruvelur, both great acharyas proceed to Thiruchchaththangudi. Thiruchchaththangudi is a Thevaram repository. The pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for this place is not available to us. Thiruchchaththangudi is situated a short distance southeast of Peruvelur, on the way to Thiruvarur.

After bowing and worshipping at this sacred place, they proceed to Thirukkaraveeram. Thirukkaraveeram is located a short distance north of Thiruchchaththangudi, on the road to Thiruvarur. Thiruchchaththangudi and Thirukkaraveeram are situated opposite each other on that road, to the south and north respectively. We learn from Sekkizhar Peruman that Pillaiyar traveled south from Peruvelur to Thiruchchaththangudi and then proceeded to Thirukkaraveeram. This place, Thirukkaraveeram, is the sixty-first sacred place on the southern bank of the Cauvery. It is also known as Karayapuram.

This place is where a donkey worshipped. Hence, the place is named Karaveeram (Karayapuram is also used). It is a place where Sage Gautama worshipped Lord Shiva and gained renown. If you ask for Karayapuram after Vadakandam on the Thiruvarur-Kumbakonam road, you can reach this temple. It is a small village but a large temple. The Lord’s name is Karaveereshwarar, and the Goddess’s name is Prathy Min Ammai.

The sacred waters are Anavaratha Theertham. Karaveeram refers to the golden oleander flower. This place was named Karaveeram because the oleander is its sacred tree. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who arrived at this place, composed a pathigam, the fifty-eighth pathigam of the first Thirumurai, which begins with “Ariyum Nam Vinai” and is set to the tune Pazhanthakka Ragam. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. (Ariyum Nambinai ullana sara varigul maagamani pol kandam kariyavan thigazhum karaveeraththu veedila pilambum karaveeraththu sedam me thamizh naadum Gnanasambandhan solli) From Thirukkaraveeram, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds to Thiruvilamar.

Thiruvilamar is the sixtieth sacred place on the southern bank of the Cauvery. It is located a short distance southeast of Thiruchchaththangudi, on the road to Thiruvarur. There is a place called Thiruvizhanagar near Thirumayiladuthurai, but it is different from the Thiruvilamar mentioned here. This place, Thiruvilamar, is where Sage Patanjali worshipped. That is why Due to this, the Lord is named Patanjali Manoharar. In the first verse of the pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the reference to Patanjali’s worship is present in “Aravinar.” The Goddess’s name is Madurabhashini or Yazhinum Menmozhiyal (one with a voice sweeter than the Yazh).

The sacred water is Agni Theertham. Appar Swamigal, in the seventh verse of the seventh pathigam of the sixth Thirumurai, his Kaappu Thiruththazhakam, has mentioned this place as a sacred site: (Thenneer punal Kedila Veerattomum Seerkazhi Vallam Thiruvediyum unnneeraar edagum oorar ambar uraiyur naraiyur arananallur vinnar vidaiyan vilamar).

Thus, they have sung about this sacred place.

In addition, in the sixth verse of the seventieth pathigam of the sixth Thirumurai, the Kshetra Kkovai Thiruththazhakam, they have sung about this sacred place. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, who sings: (Mannippadikarai vaalkozhipuththur vakkarai mandaaram vaaranaasi venni vilaththotti velvikudi) then places Vilamar next, followed by Viradapura Vetkalam, listing the sacred places in order.

Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, in the sixth verse of the forty-seventh pathigam of the seventh Thirumurai, sang about this sacred place: (Thangur pini nin adiyar mel agala arulaye vengur urai vai vilamar nagarai). Sekkizhar Peruman also, in the Periya Puranam, in the Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal Purana And in the Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, they have sung about this place. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who arrived at this place, composed a pathigam for this place, the eighty-eighth pathigam of the third Thirumurai, which begins with “Matthaga Mani Pera” and is set to the tune Sadari. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Kumail vitthagarai uraippathu viri polil pala nagaru vilamara venthagkal podiya needigala nilai marum veyirutharai sindhaiyuliray pEra urai seidha thamizh ivai keluvaya antha poongalil ulagamarum arumaraiyambandhana mozhivai urai seyum meenai paraiyume) The summary of this pathigam is that Vilamar is the dwelling place of Lord Shiva, the master of Uma.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, having visited Thiruvaanchiyam, Thiruthalaiyalangaadu, Thirupperuvelur, Thiruchchaththangudi, Thirukkaraveeram, and Thiruvilamar, finally reach Thiruvarur. Here we see the special occasion of both these great personalities going together to worship Thiruvarur. After worshipping Thiruvarur, both great personalities continue their pilgrimage. Sekkizhar Peruman describes it in the five hundred and seventy-fourth verse. He sings about which sacred places Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman visited to worship the Lord: (Nambar magizh Thiruvaroor vanangi pondu nalangol Thirukkarayil nanni eththi paimpunal men panai Thevur anaindhu potri Paramar Thirunellikkka panindhu paadi umbar piraan kaichinanamum paravi thengur ongu pugazh Thirukkollikkadu potri sempon mathil Kotturum vanangiyeththi Thirumali vendurai thozhuvaan sendru serndhaar).

Thus, the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, in a single verse, describes these two great acharyas visiting all these sacred places.

Lord Shiva After worshipping Thiruvarur, which Lord Shiva delights in, they proceeded to the auspicious place of Thirukkarayil and worshipped there.

Then, they reached and praised Thirudevur, which is surrounded by soft paddy fields with lush waters. They bowed and sang a pathigam at the sacred place of Thirunellikkka, where the Lord resides. They also praised Thirukkaichinnam, where Lord Shiva, the chief of the celestials, resides. They worshipped and praised Thengur and the highly renowned Thirukkollikkadu.

Furthermore, they worshipped Thirukkottur, with its golden ramparts, and then went to worship Thiruvendurai.

Thus, the divine Sekkizhar Peruman has blessed us with this verse. This is the second time Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is worshipping Thiruvarur. Earlier, in Thiruppugalur, upon hearing Thirunavukkarasu Peruman compose a pathigam about the glories of Thiruvarur, Pillaiyar worshipped Thiruvarur and returned to Thiruppugalur. That was his first pilgrimage to Thiruvarur.

Now, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is worshipping it for the second time, accompanying Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal. Afterwards, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships the sacred place of Thirukkarayil. Thirukkarayil is an auspicious place where Musukundha Chakravarthi brought and installed the Thiyagaraja Peruman from the celestial world.

Therefore, it is one of the Saptavidanga Sthalams. The Lord’s name is Kannayiram Udaiyar, and the Goddess’s name is Kailasanayaki. Theerthams include Brahma Theertham, Sesha Theertham, and Indra Theertham.

Our reflection now resumes. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 676, by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has composed a pathigam for Thirukkarayil. It is the fifteenth pathigam of the second Thirumurai, set to the tune Indhalam. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. (Neerane neelchadai melor nirai kondrai tharane thamarai mel ayan than thozhum seerane seerthigazhum Thirukkarayil urane enbavar unam izhadhare yeindha seer ezil thigazhum Thirukkarayil ayndha seeran adi eththi arul pettru payndha neer kaliyul Gnanasambandhan sol vayndhavaru ethth) Those who worship the Lord of Thirukkarayil will reign in the celestial world.

Having bowed and worshipped at Thirukkarayil, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds to worship at Thirudevur. Sekkizhar Peruman describes this as “paimpunal men panai devur anaindhu potri” (having reached and praised Thirudevur, with its lush waters and soft paddy fields). The unique feature of Thirudevur, situated on the banks of the Kaduvai River, which Thirunavukkarasu Peruman praised in his Thirukkurunthokai as “mamalar gandha neer kaduvai,” offers a delightful sight here. Sekkizhar Peruman sings “paimpunal men panai devur” because it has pleasant scenes, fragrant breezes that yield sweet fruits, and cool waters, bringing musical sweetness. Thirudevur is the eighty-fifth sacred place on the southern bank of the Cauvery.

This place is named Devur because the devas worshipped Lord Shiva and received initiation here. It is a place where Indra, Kubera, Brihaspati, and other devas, as well as rishis like Gautama Maharishi, worshipped. It is one of the Maadakkoyils, located near Keezhvelur. This place is situated on the road from Thiruvarur to Valivalam. The Lord’s names are Devapureeswarar and Devagurunathar. The Goddess’s names are Madurabhashini and Thenmozhi Ammai.

Theertham is Deva Theertham. The sacred tree is the banana. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has composed two pathigams for this sacred place. The first pathigam begins with “Pannilaviya” and is the eighty-second pathigam of the second Thirumurai, set to the tune Gandharam. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. (Pannilaviya mozhi Umaippangan Emperuman Vinnil vaanavar kon Vimalan Vidaiyurthi Thennilamathi thavazh tharu maligai Thevur Annal Sevadi adaindhanam allal onrilame Allalinri vinnazhvargal Kaliyarkku athipan Nalla senthamizh vallavan Gnanasambandhan Ellaiyil pugazh malkiya ezil valar Thevur Thollai nambanai solliya paththum vallare Thiruchitrambalam). The summary of this pathigam is that since we have attained the sacred feet of the Lord of Devur, there is no sorrow.

One of the special features of this pathigam is that it is the only pathigam composed in the Kalinilaithurai meter, which has five poetic feet.

Now, the second pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for Thirudevur is the seventy-fourth pathigam of the third Thirumurai, set to the tune Sadari. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. (Kaadu payil veedu mudaiyodu kalan moodu mudai aadai puliththol thedu baliy unathudai vedamigu vedhiyar thirundhu pathithan naadagamathaada mangai paada varikodal kaimarippalamar sedumigu beda enavoodi magizh maadamidai Thevur athuve thungamigu pongaravu thangu sadai nangaliraithu kuzhalar sengaiyalgkal mangaiyumai nangkaiyoru panganamar Thevur athanmel painkamala mannganigul thinpugali Gnanasambandha nuraisai sangamali senthamizhgal paththu) Those who master these ten Tamil songs will have no doubts.

The summary of this pathigam is that Devur is the purified abode of Lord Shiva, the Vediyar. Having bowed and worshipped at Devur, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman bows at Thirunellikkka, where Lord Shiva, the Supreme Being, resides, and sings a pathigam. Thirunellikkka is the one hundred and seventeenth sacred place on the southern bank of the Cauvery. The sacred tree is the gooseberry (nellimaram), hence the name Thirunellikkka. It is a place where Surya and Brahma worshipped Lord Shiva.

It faces west. As a symbol of their worship of Lord Shiva, even today, from the fourteenth day of the second half of the Aippasi month for seven days, Surya performs Surya Puja in the evening with his rays. You can see it. Thirunellikkka is located very close to Thiruvarur. The Lord’s name is Nellivananathar, and the Goddess’s name is Mangalanayaki. Theerthams include Brahma Theertham and Surya Theertham.

The sacred tree is the gooseberry. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who arrived at this place, composed a pathigam. It is the nineteenth pathigam of the second Thirumurai, set to the tune Indhalam. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Araththal uyir kaaval amardhu aruli maraththal mathil moonrudan maanpazhiththa thiraththal therivaithiya venthingal niraththan NellikkavuL nilayanavanai pugar ethum illatha puththezhulagin nikara nellikkavuL nilayanavanai nagaranala Gnanasambandhan sonna pagarva) Those who recite these verses will be free from sin.

Having bowed and worshipped at Thirunellikkka, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds to Thiruththhenkur and worships the Lord there. Thiruththhenkur is the one hundred and sixteenth sacred place on the southern bank of the Cauvery. It is a place where Lakshmi and the nine planets, starting with Surya, worshipped the Lord and received blessings. The nine Shiva Lingams worshipped by the Navagrahas are located on the temple walls. The Shiva Lingam worshipped by Lakshmi is situated opposite her.

The Lord’s temple is known as Velliyangunnru. It is located very close to Thirunellikkka. The Lord’s names are Rajatagireeswarar and Vellimalainathar. The Goddess’s name is Periyanayaki. Theertham is Sivaganga Theertham. This place is called Thengur after its sacred tree.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who arrived at this place, Composed a pathigam. It is the ninety-third pathigam of the second Thirumurai, set to the tune Piyanthaikandharam. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. (Puraisai valvinai theerkkum punniyar vinnnnavar potra karaisai mal kadal nanajai undavar karuththalar purangal iraiseythaar azhalvooti yuzhalpavar idubalikkku ezilser viraisai poompozil thengur velliyankunnru amardhare ventha neerththinar thengur velliyankunnru amardharai kandhamar pozil soozhntha kaliyul Gnanasambandhan sandhamayina paadal thandhamizh paththum vallarmael bandhamayina paavam paaruthal theruthal payane Thiruchitrambalam). Having bowed and worshipped at Thiruththhenkur, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds to Thirukkollikkaadu. Worshipping the Lord there.
