Sekkizhar Peruman refers to Thirukkollikkaadu as “Ongu Pugazh Thirukkollikkaadu” (highly renowned Thirukkollikkaadu).

Sekkizhar Peruman refers to it as “Ongu Pugazh Thirukkollikkaadu” based on the pathigam’s mention of “Kollikkadara” (the Lord of Kollikkaadu) as a highly renowned and faultless place. On the Thiruvarur-Thiruthuraipoondi road, after reaching Nellikkka and then Thengur, if you proceed on the road to Kollikkaadu, you will reach the village of Keeralaththoor, and a short distance further, the temple is situated on the roadside. The Lord’s name is Agneeswarar. The Goddess’s names are Mrithupada Nayaki and Panchin Melladi Ammai. It is the one hundred and fifteenth sacred place on the southern bank of the Cauvery. It is named Kollikkaadu because Agni, the fire god, worshipped here.

It faces west. The west-facing shrine is interpreted as a temple for the planet Saturn. In popular usage, it is currently called Kallikkadu. In the Thevaram of this place, the Lord’s act of flaying the elephant is mentioned, which is why people once called this temple “Kariyuriththa Nayanar Kovil.” This is the place where a Chola king was relieved from Saturn’s affliction. The main deity’s Shiva Lingam is slightly reddish in color. The Chola king, Tripuvana Chakravarthi, who was freed from Saturn’s affliction by the Lord’s grace, donated lands around the temple.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who arrived at this place, composed a pathigam. It is the sixteenth pathigam of the third Thirumurai, set to the tune Gandhara Panchamam. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. (Ninambadu sudalaiyin neeru poosi nindru inanguvar peiygalodu iduvar maanadam unangal vendalai thanil unbar aayinum gunam perithu udaiyar nankollikkadare natravan kaliyul Gnanasambandhan kuttramizh perum pugazh kollikkadara solltamizh innisai malai sorvinri katravar kalaladi kaanavalle Thiruchitrambalam). The summary of this pathigam is that our Kollikkadara possesses great qualities, thus praising the Lord’s divine attributes. Having worshipped at Thirukkollikkaadu, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds to Thirukkottur and worships the Lord there.

Sekkizhar Peruman refers to Thirukkottur as “Sempon Madil Kottur” (Kottur with golden ramparts). Karuvoor Devar composed a pathigam for Thirukkeezhkottur Maniambalam, stating: (Girithaval mugilin keezhththaval maat kezhu kambalai seyttur). Thirukeezhkottur Maniambalam is a temple belonging to another part of Thirukkottur. Karuvoor Devar thus composed a Thiruvichaippa pathigam for that temple. This place, Thirukkottur, is the one hundred and thirteenth sacred place on the southern bank of the Cauvery. Devas and Sage Kuccha worshipped here and received blessings.

The devas’ worship is mentioned in the third verse of the pathigam for this sacred place, and the sage’s worship in the fifth verse. The Lord’s shrine faces west, and the Goddess’s shrine faces east. This sacred place is located near Thiruthuraipoondi. The Lord’s names are Kozhundeeswarar and Sameevaneswarar. The Goddess’s name is Thennarmozhiyal. Theerthams include Amutha Mulliyaru, Sivaganga, Brahma Theertham, Indra Theertham, Siva Theertham, Viswakarma Theertham, Rambai Theertham, and Mandai Theertham, totaling nine theerthams.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who arrived at this place, composed a pathigam. It is the one hundred and ninth pathigam of the second Thirumurai, set to the tune Nattaragappannam. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. (Neelamartharu kandane netriyor kannane ottrai vidai soolamartharu kaiyane thundru paimpozhilgal soozhntha azhagaya kolamamalar manamgamal kottur narkozhundhe endru ezhuvaargal saala neezhdhalam athanida pugazh mika thanguvar pangale panthula virar pavalavay thenmozhi pavaiyodu uruvarum konthulamaalar viri pozhil kottur narkozhundhinai sezhumbavalam vandhulaviya kaliyul) Those who master the garland of Tamil songs composed by Gnanasambandhan, the pearl from Kali, praising the Lord of Kottur, rich with blooming lotus flowers, will achieve renown.

Having worshipped Thirukkottur, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds to Thiruvendurai and worships the Lord there. Thiruvendurai is the one hundred and twelfth sacred place on the southern bank of the Cauvery. It is a place where Bringi Muni, in the form of a beetle, passed through between the Lord and the Goddess, who are inseparable, and worshipped only the Lord according to his custom. It is said that the humming sound of the beetle can still be heard in the sanctum sanctorum. Vidyadharas and others have also worshipped the Lord here.

It is currently called Thiruvendurai. This sacred place is located on the road from Mannargudi to Veerakki. The Lord’s names are The Lord’s names are Madhuvaneeswarar, Piramareswarar, Piramapureeshar, Vendurainathar. The Goddess’s names are Sakthiyaayuthakshi, Vel Nedunganni, Piragadambaal. The Theerthams are Kaveri Theertham and Piramapureesha Theertham. In popular usage, it is called Vanduthurai.

The original image of Bikshadanar in the temple corridor is worth seeing and special. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who came to this place, composed a pathigam. It is the sixty-first pathigam of the Third Thirumurai, set to Panchama Pann. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Aathiyan aathirayan analaadiya aarazhagan paathiyor maathinodum payilum paramamaa paraman pothiyalum mudime punalodu aravampuna) (Vethiyin maathimayaal virumbum idam venduraiye thinnamarum purisa thiru vendurai meiyavanai thannamarum pozhil soozh tharu sanpayartham thalaivan ennamar palkalaiyaan isaignana sambandhan sonna pannamar paadalvallar vinaiyaayina pattarume) Thiruchitrambalam.

Let us resume our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 677, authored by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, titled ‘Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam’, is the biography of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. After worshipping and bowing at Thiru Vendurai, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman continues to visit various temples and proceeds to Thiru Maraikadu, also known as Vedaranyam. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman describes this in the 575th verse: ‘And there, having worshipped, praised, and joyfully sung at many places where the Lord, who is difficult for Vishnu and Brahma to reach, resides, the holy assembly of devotees arrived. The learned live in Thandalai Nizhneri, with golden walls embracing the path of dharma. He also went to other places where those who destroyed the sacrifices of the ignorant reside and praised them.’ That day, he reached Thirumaraikadu, and its surroundings, as described in the verse.

Having worshipped, praised, and joyfully sung at Thiru Vendurai, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman visits many places where Lord Shiva, who is difficult for Vishnu and Brahma to reach, resides, offering pathigams. These places are considered to be Kundriyoor, Thiruchittemam, Manali, and others.

Thus, having visited many places, he arrives at the temple of Thandalai Nizhneri and composes a pathigam there. Sekkizhar Peruman refers to Thandalai Nizhneri as ‘Thandalai Nizhneri where the learned live’. Ganammangala, located a short distance from Thandalai Nizhneri, is where Arivattaya Nayanar lived. Arivattaya Nayanar used to come from Ganammangalam to Thandalai Nizhneri daily for worship, as we have discussed in his biography. ‘Learned’ here refers to those who have learned to worship the good feet of the Lord, who is pure knowledge. This applies to Arivattaya Nayanar.

Moreover, Thandalai Nizhneri shines as a place full of many learned people who worship. The benefit of learning is to worship the good feet of the Lord, as stated in the Thirukkural: ‘What is the use of learning if one does not worship the good feet of the Lord of pure knowledge?’ This Thirukkural is found in the ‘Praise of God’.

Therefore, learning to worship the Lord is truly education. To worship the Lord means to act solely for the service of the Lord, understanding that other things are not important, and to engage only in the service of the Lord. Such people are truly learned. Thandalai Nizhneri is a place inhabited by such learned people, located a short distance from Thiruturaipoondi. It is currently known as Thandalaichery in popular usage. This temple is the 110th temple on the south bank of the Kaveri.

The Lord’s name is Sthiraputheeswarar, Nizhneri Nathar. The Goddess’s name is Gnanaambikai. The Theertham is Homaga Theertham. Bathing in front of the Gnanassiddhi Vinayagar temple is special. Kaveri is another Theertham. Vyagrapadar, Patanjali, and others have worshipped the Lord here.

The village name is Thandalai, and the temple name is Nizhneri. We have already discussed the story that Arivattaya Nayanar daily offered red rice, red greens, and raw mangoes to the Lord of this place. This temple is one of the Maadakoils built by Kochchengat Chozha Nayanar. When that Maadakoil later fell into disrepair, in later times, Devakottai Ram Aru Aru Ramanathan Chettiar built the present stone temple. The temple’s stone structures and Vimanas have stucco work. When entering after worshipping Vinayagar, sculptures above on both sides depict Arivattaya Nayanar and his wife offering rice and raw mangoes, the Lord’s hand appearing to stop the Nayanar, and the Lord appearing to the Nayanar and his wife as Rishabaroodar.

Arivattaya Nayanar’s Guru Puja is celebrated as a grand festival in the proper manner. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who came here, composed a pathigam. It is the fiftieth pathigam of the Third Thirumurai, set to Kausika. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: ‘Sadaiaarku idamagiya Thandalai Nizhneri kaanmine’ is the thematic summary of this pathigam. Thandalai Nizhneri. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having worshipped at Thandalai Nizhneri, proceeds to the temple of Thirukkalar and worships the Lord.

Thirukkalar is the 205th temple on the south bank of the Kaveri, known as Parijatha Vanam. It is a place where the Lord displayed his divine dance to Durvasa Muni. This deity is present in the temple. It is also a place worshipped by Parashar and other sages. The Murugaperuman shrine is very special. The Lord’s name is Kalar Mulai Nathar, Adaintharku Arul Nathar, Parijatheswarar.

The Goddess’s name is Amudavalli Azhageswari. This place is located on the Thiruturaipoondi-Mannargudi road. It is a temple in Kalar land, hence its name. There are eight Chola inscriptions, two Pandya inscriptions, and Vijayanagara royal inscriptions. At one time, four Vedic schools were established here for the four Vedas, where students studied all four Vedas. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who came to this holy place, composed a pathigam.

It is the fifty-first pathigam of the Second Thirumurai, set to Seekamara Pann. The first, tenth, and eleventh verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Adaimathi paaraniul ravanne adaintharku arulaaya baktharkal paattodum pala panikal pediya gunaththirantha paakki naarmaro naay thaman thera solliyaakkinu ravanne adaintharku arulaayum maada veethiyu nakar thavuniyam) (Thirukallarul nindra oruvane adaintharku arulaaye) Thus, this pathigam was a plea on behalf of the devotees. Having worshipped and bowed at Thirukallar, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman intends to go to Thirumaraikadu, visiting temples along the way such as Thirukkanamangalam, Thirumugathalai, Kalappal, Thirukkundralur, Thirukadikulam, Thiru Idumbavanam, Thiru Usaththanam, and Hattoor, and finally reaching Thiru Maraikadu, also known as Vedaranyam.

Let us press on with our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 678, authored by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, titled ‘Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam’, is the biography of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman arrive at the temple of Thirumaraikadu. According to their pilgrimage custom, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman first reaches the temple of Vedaranyam. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman was a venerable person who, with the help of grace, crossed the cruel desert of Jainism. A desert is very harsh to cross, difficult and arduous.

Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, with the help of grace, crossed the influence of Jainism, which was like such a desert.

Now, there is an appeal for Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who has come from Pandya country to the Vedaranyam temple, to cross the Jain desert in Pandya country. These two great figures arrive at this great and glorious temple of Vedaranyam. The people and devotees of Thirumaraikadu welcome these two great figures very grandly. They decorate the entire temple and welcome them as if celebrating a festival, with tall betel nut trees, plantain trees, full pots, lamps, and the playing of auspicious instruments like drums. The people of Thirumaraikadu, along with the devotees, rejoice. To welcome these two great figures, they first meet Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, who arrived first, and are greatly delighted.

After welcoming him and escorting Thirunavukkarasu Peruman into the town, they then welcome Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who is arriving. As Thirugnanasambandha Peruman approaches, the sounds of his auspicious symbols and other noises are heard by the people and devotees of that place. Upon hearing those sounds of praise, they feel as if they have seen Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, and with folded hands, they welcome him at the town’s boundary. From the beautiful pearl palanquin, Pillaiyar, the leader of Seerkazhi, descends, bows, and joyfully joins them to enter the temple of Thirumaraikadu. The 578th verse states: ‘When Pillaiyar, accompanied by the King of Words, entered the ancient town of Maruga of Thirumaraikadu, surrounded by clear jewel-like waters, the sound of ‘Hara Hara’ raised by the great ascetics, Vedic scholars, and others, spread boundlessly, filling the vast sky and all eight directions, suppressing the sound of the roaring sea, and reaching beyond the heavens to the land of the celestials.’ Pillaiyar, accompanied by Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, enters that ancient town of Thirumaraikadu. Thirumaraikadu is a holy place surrounded by clear, jewel-like waters.

These jewels refer to pearls. In Vedaranyam, there is a condition where pearls are produced in the sea. Such a pure, pearl-producing, jewel-like water surrounds Vedaranyam, making it a very ancient and glorious place.

There, great ascetics, Vedic scholars, and others raise the chant of ‘Hara Hara’ and welcome these two great acharyas inside.

Here, ‘Madhavargal’ refers to devotees of Shiva, ‘Maraiyavargal’ refers to Vedic scholars who study the Vedas, and ‘matrum’ refers to other worldly people. According to Sivagnana Siddhiyar Parapakkam, which states that Shivagamas are the scriptures to be studied, the path of Shivagama is the path to liberation.

Therefore, those who adhere to such a path of liberation, are referred to as ‘Madhavargal’ by Sekkizhar Peruman.

Furthermore, here in Vedaranyam, the great honor of opening the door that was closed and protected by the Vedas, and revealing Shiva to the world for the salvation of Shiva’s devotees, is about to happen.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman first sang about such ‘Madhavargal,’ then placed the ‘Maraiyavargal’ who follow the path of the Vedas and Shivagamas second, and then thirdly, he respectfully listed other worldly people who wish to follow the path of the devotees of the Vedas and Shivagamas for salvation. The sound of ‘Hara Hara’ raised by these three large groups fills the vast sky, fills all eight directions, rises above, suppresses the sound of the sea, and reaches beyond the heavens to the land of the celestial beings. and then reaches the world of Lord Shiva beyond that.

Now, Sekkizhar Peruman composes the next verse: ‘As devotees and townspeople hailed from both sides, they proceeded through the beautiful streets. They bowed before the majestic Gopuram in front of the grand mansion, entered, and advanced straight through the divine courtyard, where endless ascetics and sages gathered, to the golden, jeweled main entrance that the Vedas had closed and protected long ago.’ As the devotees and people of the town praised these two great acharyas from both sides, they arrived through the beautiful streets of Vedaranyam, bowed before the great Gopuram in front of the grand mansion, and entered. The devas and sages approached that divine courtyard, and after circling it clockwise, they went straight to the main entrance. The doors of this entrance were sealed by the Vedas many years ago when they worshipped Lord Shiva here in Vedaranyam and then left. They remain sealed in that state. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman reach there.

Peruman continues to sing. The doors that the six Vedas had sealed to protect them must now be opened. Because the devotees filled with love, who were sufficient for those Vedas, could not remove the seal, a new gateway was opened on one side from that day onwards for passage. Having heard this, the leader of the exalted Shanbai Thirumaraiyur stood in wonder and addressed Thirunavukkarasu: ‘O Appare, we must enter through the main entrance and worship the Lord of Vedavanam.

Therefore, you, with your strong Tamil verses embodying the true essence, should sing to remove the seal of this entrance.’ When the radiant King of Words agreed, saying, ‘If you command me in this manner, I will do it,’ and began to compose a pathigam, even after all ten verses of that pathigam were sung, the golden door of the venerable, exalted golden gate remained sealed. Thereupon, Vagisar, with a sorrowful heart, desired it to be opened during the lengthy closing verse. When he sang, the seal was removed, and the devotees of the Lord with dancing red feet, and the celestial beings, cheered, filling all the universes.

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman composes three consecutive verses. The doors of Vedaranyam were sealed and closed by the rare Vedas.

Therefore, those doors must be unsealed and opened. These doors were closed by the Vedas, so the Vedas themselves must come and open them again, or loving devotees who have the greatness to chant those Vedas must come and remove this seal.

But such loving devotees who have the greatness to chant the Vedas have not yet arrived there to attempt to remove the seal of the doors.

Therefore, from the day the Vedas worshipped and closed the doors, because the seal of these doors has not been removed, a different entrance has been created, and people have been entering the temple through that entrance to worship the Lord.

The devotees of that town present these historical accounts to these two great figures. This is the entrance sealed by the Vedas, so only those loving people who chant those Vedas can open it, is the meaning. An action closed by a Vedic mantra cannot be undone by anything other than a mantra following the same rule, or another Vedic mantra. Even in Agamas, there are prescribed mantras for sealing a door and for unsealing it again.

Therefore, those who have the power to effectively employ the mantras that can remove the seal, such powerful devotees, have not yet come here and attempted to open the door. The power of the Vedas is none other than Shiva’s Sakthi.

Therefore, composing and singing in a way that is equal to the Vedas is that Shiva Sakthi.

Similarly, only words that are recorded and come as Shiva’s utterance have that power.

Here, the indication is that there is power to open this door again.

Therefore, since the direct main entrance was locked by the Vedas, from that day onwards, a gate was made on one side of the northern outer wall of the temple, through which the priests and devotees would enter and worship. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman hears all these facts and is astonished. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman here marvels at the greatness of the Lord’s grace, as the Lord, whom he cannot go and see directly inside, manifests through another entrance.

There, the Lord’s grace reveals something to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. What it reveals is that the Vedas themselves, which the Lord had bestowed, were the ones that sealed the door with grace.

Similarly, the Tamil Vedas revealed through the words of loving devotees will now remove that seal, directly show Himself as Lord Shiva to the world, and then seal it again, thus manifesting both aspects of the Lord’s grace within the pure heart of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

The Lord within reveals this, and understanding it, Pillaiyar is filled with wonder. Let us proceed with our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 679, authored by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, titled ‘Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam’, is the biography of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman stands in astonishment after hearing the history of Vedaranyam.

Then, he addresses Appar Peruman: ‘Appare, we must open the main entrance and directly enter to worship the Lord of Thirumaraikadu.

Therefore, you, with your powerful Tamil verses embodying the true essence, should sing so that the seal of this entrance is removed,’ he said. Pillaiyar addresses Thirunavukkarasu Peruman as ‘Appare’. This is the name by which Pillaiyar first addressed Thirunavukkarasu Peruman when they met for the first time in Seerkazhi, considering him a spiritual father. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman is Appar.

Therefore, in this event concerning the Vedas, Pillaiyar addresses Thirunavukkarasu Peruman as ‘Appare’ and asks him to sing, implying that he is the one suitable to act first. Pillaiyar says that these doors, which are sealed in this main entrance, must open, and they must enter through this main entrance to behold the Lord. The ‘Abimugathu Thiruvayil’ is the direct main entrance facing the Lord.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman desires to go through the direct main entrance and worship the Lord, rather than entering through another gate like others. This reveals to us the depth of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s fervent devotion to the Lord. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s pathigam is a ‘meyporul van Tamil pathigam’ (a strong Tamil pathigam of true essence). Just as the Vedas possess the quality of ‘Sat’ (truth), so too do Appar Peruman’s words possess that quality. Appar Peruman’s pathigam has the benevolent quality of guiding the world directly. The nature of the Vedas, revealed by the Lord, is also present in Appar Peruman’s words.

Therefore, Appar Peruman’s pathigam is equal to the Vedas. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman says, ‘O Appare, sing a powerful Tamil garland of true meaning, which implies that it is the Lord’s own utterance.’ Hearing this, Appar Peruman accepts, saying, ‘If you command me in this manner, I will do it.’ Appar Peruman accepts Pillaiyar’s command as the Lord’s own divine decree. He is one who stands in the service of the Lord, doing nothing without Shiva’s grace.

Therefore, he accepts Pillaiyar’s grace as the Lord’s divine decree. It is noteworthy that while Pillaiyar lovingly called Thirunavukkarasu Peruman ‘Appare,’ his spiritual father, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman regarded Pillaiyar as the Lord himself.

Therefore, Pillaiyar’s command is Shiva’s command. and so he composes a pathigam. He composes the Thirukkurunthogai pathigam beginning with ‘Pannin Neru Mozhiyal.’ We can recall here that Sekkizhar Peruman elaborated on this in his Appar Peruman Puranam in the 1533rd verse: ‘Pannin Neru Mozhiyal’ (By words matching the melody) and began to sing. Sekkizhar Peruman, who extensively described this historical event of Appar Peruman composing a pathigam in Appar Peruman Puranam, now continues to compose very elaborately to suit this Thirugnanasambandha Peruman Puranam. ‘Even after all ten verses of that pathigam were sung, the golden door of the venerable, exalted golden gate remained sealed. Thereupon, Vagisar, with a sorrowful heart, desired it to be opened during the lengthy closing verse and stood up.’ Sekkizhar Peruman sings, ‘When the seal was removed, the devotees of the Lord with dancing red feet, and the celestial beings, cheered, filling all the universes.’ This divine event is described by Sekkizhar Peruman in four verses in Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s Puranam. All ten verses of the pathigam sung by Appar Peruman were completed. Even after their completion, the glorious golden door of the main entrance remained sealed.

Seeing this, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman felt sad and sang in the concluding verse, ‘Enneer Irakkam Ondril Eer’ (What compassion is this, where there is none?).

Then the seal was removed. As the door’s seal was removed, the ‘Hara Hara’ chant raised by the Lord’s devotees and celestial beings filled all the universes. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing: ‘At that very moment, seeing it, the King of Words looked at the King of Praise, and as he praised him, and the other praised him, they stood in a state of wonder and entered directly through the royal temple gate of the ruler of the beautiful Thirumaraikadu.’ As soon as the Lord’s door opened, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the King of Seerkazhi, praised Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman also praised Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. In a state of wonder, both our great Acharyas entered through the direct path to the Lord’s presence in Thirumaraikadu. In this verse, Sekkizhar Peruman describes both of them with the quality of ‘King’ – ‘King of Words’ and ‘King of Praise’.

Here, Thirunavukkarasu As the divine manifestations of opening and then closing the seal happened in the same way for both, Sekkizhar Peruman describes it thus. They enter the temple through that direct main entrance. The 584th verse states: ‘Upon entering the temple, with hands clasped above their heads, they saw their Lord, who is sweeter than a mother. Their eyes, like flowing waterfalls, streamed tears. Their bodies, pervading the earth, trembled and they swiftly fell.’ This verse by Sekkizhar Peruman illustrates how the two great figures worshipped the Lord upon entering the temple. The next verse also illustrates to us the state in which these two great figures worshipped the Lord.

As they enter through the direct entrance, their red hands are clasped above their heads. There, they saw their Lord, who is sweeter than a mother.

The Lord is better than a mother, sweeter than a mother. ‘He is a lover to Shankaran, who is better than a mother,’ says Thirukkurunthogai. ‘You are better than the mother who bore me,’ says the Thiruvaiyaru Thiruthandagam. ‘Devotees praise his feet as the leader better than a mother,’ says Pillaiyar’s Thevaram, Thirukonamalai, fifth verse.

Thus, both Pillaiyar’s words and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s words praise and illustrate that the Lord is sweeter than a mother. How is the Lord sweeter than a mother? For one, A mother gives happiness only in one birth. The Lord, however, bestows joy upon beings in all births, before birth and after birth. In each birth, a different mother comes. The Lord, without being like that, comes as a mother to all beings in all births.

A mother, due to her limited understanding, acts accordingly. That is, a mother, out of ignorance, might inflict suffering thinking it is joy.

But the Lord always bestows only joy. A mother might cause illness and birth. The Lord, however, removes illness and birth. Due to these and many other reasons, the Lord is sweeter than a mother.

Therefore, such a Lord, sweeter than a mother, These two great figures behold and are overwhelmed with joy. Tears, like a flowing waterfall, stream from their sacred eyes. That stream of tears flows incessantly and pervades their sacred bodies. In this world, as the Lord’s truth is manifest, in that state of flowing tears on their enduring sacred bodies, their sacred bodies touch the ground, then rise quickly, and again prostrate themselves. ‘Unable to gauge the extent of their love, immersed in a flood of bliss, with bones melting, they looked and worshipped, falling prostrate repeatedly. They could not even stand before the Lord, their words faltered as they praised him and sang pathigams of the Lord with shining matted locks,’. This is the next verse composed by Sekkizhar Peruman.

Unable to see the extent of their love, immersed in the flood of bliss, with their very bones melting, they look and again rise and fall before the Lord, prostrating themselves again and again. Unable to even stand before the Lord, their words falter as they praise the Lord with pathigams. Such was their swift action in worshipping the Lord that it was only their falling that was visible; their rising was unseen, so swiftly did they fall and worship repeatedly. Their love transcended all bounds. Unable to stand before the Lord, they fall to the ground. Their words falter.

These are all manifestations of intense love. In such a state, they praise the Lord’s glories in various ways through hymns and other means, and compose pathigams.

However, due to our lack of merit, the pathigams composed by these two great figures are not available to us now.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, having worshipped, exit the temple through the same entrance and reach the outer courtyard. Let us go on contemplating. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 680, authored by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, titled ‘Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam’, is the biography of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman emerge from the temple. Sekkizhar Peruman composes the next verse: ‘When they came outside, the King of Pukazhi looked at the King of Words and said, ‘Now that the sealed, jeweled door, which was once closed and then opened, remains open, you should sing for it to close again.’ He, who could overcome the deceptive wickedness of the malevolent Jain ascetics, said to the King of Seerkazhi, Pillaiyar, that the door that was closed is now unsealed. From now on, this opened door should be able to close and open again. All people, all devotees, should be able to pass through this main entrance and behold the Lord at all times.

Therefore, this opened door should also close again. And from now on, like other temples, this door should open and close as usual. For that purpose, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman requested Thirugnanasambandha Peruman to sing a pathigam to close this door again, which was already unsealed. Earlier, it was closed and remained closed.

Now, it has been unsealed by Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s pathigam. Just as it was closed and remained closed before, now that it has been unsealed, it should not remain unsealed but should be able to close and open again. For that purpose, you should sing. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman addresses Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. He sang to have the seal removed.

Now, even though his singing a pathigam again would have the power and strength to seal the doors again, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman asks him to sing for both opening and closing. Why? Because earlier, he had requested him to sing to remove the seal. And you had agreed, saying, ‘If you say so, I will do it,’ and Appar had sung to remove the seal.

Therefore, now he stands asking Thirugnanasambandha Peruman to do what needs to be done next.

Moreover, the doors were previously closed by the Vedas, the Vedas bestowed by the Lord. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is the one who consumed the direct ambrosia of Shiva’s knowledge, which is the inner meaning of those Vedas.

Therefore, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman believed that it was only right for Pillaiyar to reseal the doors. The 587th verse states: ‘Thus, when Thirunavukkarasu Peruman spoke, Pillaiyar, skilled in the rare Vedas, desired and sang a sweet Tamil pathigam beginning with ‘Chaduram Marai’ to the Lord with the white bull in Thirumaraikadu, and the doors on both sides closed, fulfilling the sealing.’ Thus, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman spoke, and Pillaiyar, skilled in the rare Vedas, earnestly and with desire, sang a sweet Tamil pathigam beginning with ‘Chaduram Marai’ to the Lord residing in Thirumaraikadu, who has a white bull. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman entreats the Lord in the pathigam, saying, ‘O Lord of Maraikadu, please seal the doors.’ Just as Thirunavukkarasu Peruman requested the Lord to open the doors, Pillaiyar also requested the Lord and sang these pathigams. This is the beginning of the pathigam sung by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. As soon as Thirugnanasambandha Peruman began to sing the pathigam, the doors, which had stood in two parts, This pathigam, which has been granted Thiru-Kaappu, is the Thiru-Pathigam of Thirumaraikkadu. It is the thirty-seventh pathigam of the second Thirumurai, set to the Indalappann tune.

This pathigam is as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. “Sathuram Maraithan thuthi seythuvanaungum madhuram pozhil soozh maraikkaatturai mainthaa idhu nan kiraivai tharuls seyga enakun gathavan thiru kaapu kollum karuththale sangkan tharalam avaithan karaikke trum vanngak kadal soozh maraikkaatturai mainthaa mangai umai paagamumaagavithan kol gangai sadaimeel adaivitha karuthe kuravang kurukka thigazh punnaigal gnaazhil maruvum pozhil soozh maraikkaatturai mainthaa siramum malarum thigal senchadaithan mel aravam madhiyodadaiviththal azhage padar semba.” “O Lord of Thiru Maraikkadu, surrounded by lush groves, your body is adorned with Uma on one side. What was your intention in consuming the poison from the ocean? The celestials and great sages worshipped you, O Lord of Thiru Maraikkadu, surrounded by honey-filled groves. Why did you remain in the form of a hunter, revered by others?

“For many ages, the Vedas praised your feet and worshipped you with flowers, O Thiru Maraikkadu! You took offerings from the seven worlds, but what was the purpose of consuming those offerings?” “O Lord residing in Thiru Maraikkadu, where the waves of the ocean crash upon the shore, those who circumambulate you receive blessings. What was your intention in burning Kama, who aimed his bow with Indra and Vishnu in fear, as you reside in Thiru Maraikkadu, surrounded by beautiful groves?” O Lord of Thiru Maraikkadu, where those who circumambulate on the shore praise you, you blessed Lanka’s ruler by pressing your toe. You are praised as king by crores of Rudras, O Lord of Thiru Maraikkadu, surrounded by honey-filled groves. Why do the celestial beings and the sages, who are unable to see you, question your actions?

“Why do you dwell in Thiru Maraikkadu, where the Vedas and many sacrifices praise you, and the waves flow? Why do the words of the Jains and Buddhists not affect you, and why do they not shower flowers upon you? Thirugnanasambandhan of Kaali Nagar, who made the Lord of Maraikkadu known, those who master these ten verses in the evening, will be worshipped by the world and attain heaven.

“O Lord of Thiru Maraikkadu, whose doors the four Vedas praise and worship, it is your will to keep the doors shut for me. The note for this pathigam is the request: “May you bestow your grace upon me by keeping the doors shut.” “Sathuram Marai” means the four Vedas. When Thirugnanasambandha Peruman began singing this pathigam, requesting the Lord to keep the doors that the Vedas had shut, the doors remained shut.

“Therefore, in this pathigam, the child-saint’s request is not found in the pathigam’s verses. Even after the Lord sang before the doors, they did not open.

“Therefore, when Thirunavukkarasu Peruman sang with a heavy heart in the eleventh verse, the doors then opened. This sacred event was found as internal evidence in many Thevaram pathigams regarding the opening and closing of the temple doors at Thirumaraikkadu. Sekkizhar Swamigal continues to sing.

“After this, seeing the doors close, both Shanbai Andagaiyar and the profound Tamil poet bowed.

“The devotees rejoiced, and a shower of flowers fell everywhere. The pathigam garland of the king of Puzhali, rich in Tamil, was completed and praised.

“From that day, in that sacred doorway, as if they were true Vedas, people entered and worshipped the Lord. Sekkizhar Peruman then composed two more verses, stating that the world, surrounded by the ocean, lived in prosperity, bowing to those of immeasurable greatness who established this custom. Thirugnanasambandha When the Lord sang the verse, seeing the doors close on both sides, the two great souls bowed.

“The devotees rejoiced. Divine flowers like Karpagam and Mandaram rained down. Celestial beings showered these flowers and worshipped from above. Since this divine event occurred in the very first verse of the pathigam sung by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, he then sang the remaining verses and concluded the pathigam with the Thiru-kadai Kaappu.

“Thus, the celestial beings and others praised him. From that day onwards, through that sacred entrance, people from all over the world went directly and worshipped the Lord. Just as the Vedas had previously gone directly to worship the Lord, so too from now on, people of the world began to worship the Lord through the direct entrance. In the future too, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman are those of boundless greatness who made it possible for this to happen. The world, surrounded by the ocean, attained prosperity by joining hands and worshipping these two great souls. The child-saint and the king’s words are like the Vedas bestowed by the Lord.

“By bowing to them, this world attained prosperity. The world, which attained prosperity by seeing the Lord directly at the sacred entrance, further attained great prosperity by bowing to those great ones who granted that prosperity.

“Here, “Vaiyam” refers to the living beings in this world. The great Vedas, resounding throughout the vast sky, and the five divine musical instruments called Pancha Nadham, resounded gloriously. The two great souls, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman and Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who had no other purpose than to uplift these beings, bowed to each other. “May the prosperous city celebrate” is the next verse. The rare Vedas and their subsidiary branches, all resounded gloriously in the vast sky. The five divine musical instruments, known as Pancha Nadham, resonated clearly.

“These two great souls, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman and Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who had no other purpose than to uplift these beings, bowed to each other. They also bowed to the Lord. The people of that city celebrated and entered the sacred monasteries with these great souls, whom they escorted in a procession around the city. These sacred monasteries are separate sacred monasteries established by the local people for these two great souls. Sekkizhar Peruman composes the next verse, stating: “The countless crores of Vedas that diligently perform their duties, and who remove evils from us, these two have established. How can one describe the greatness of those who praise the feet of the Lord, whose matted hair is adorned with the Ganga, and who stands as the embodiment of sound?” Sekkizhar Peruman refers to the Vedas as countless crores of Vedas.

“It is a tradition that the Vedas are infinite. “Anantavai Vedaka” is a famous saying. The Vedas are countless. If the Veda is considered a tree, just as there are countless branches, twigs, leaves, and sprouts in that tree, so too are the Vedas. Even though the Vedas are innumerable and vast, their primary meaning and purpose are one. Such Vedas had closed the sacred doors.

“Those doors, which were shut, hindered the worship of the Lord, both inside and outside. These two great souls removed those obstacles. These two great souls are capable of removing the obstacles, both internal and external, that hinder us, who are living beings, from worshipping the Lord. Who can measure and describe the greatness of these great ones who always praise the sacred feet of the Lord? No one can. The sacred form of the Lord is referred to as the form that embodies sound.

“This is Sekkizhar Peruman’s sacred word. Sound refers to the primal sound, the exceedingly subtle speech. “Thadayar” is the sacred word of Sekkizhar Peruman. “Nadham” here refers to the supremely subtle speech, the primal sound. There are four levels of speech: Para, Pasyanti, Madhyama, and Vaikhari. The supremely subtle speech, which is the cause of these four levels of speech, is called Nadham.

“The nature of the Lord, coming in the form of Nadham and Bindu to bestow grace, is described in the Sivagnana Siddhiyar and other Gnyana Sastras. “That which is not destroyed like a transient flame, but creates, that which is devoid of imperfection, that which is pure consciousness and bliss, that which is primordial and eternal, that which is without coming or going, without variation or transformation, that is the Purusha” – this is the twenty-third verse of the first Sutra of Sivagnana Siddhiyar. All this is explained here. Regarding that Nadham, the Lord manifests as Nadham and Bindu to bestow grace. Those great ones who praise such a Lord attain the nature of the Lord. All their faculties become Sivakaranams (faculties of Siva).

“The Lord makes them perform the actions that He Himself does, by dwelling within them. These are the conclusions stated in the Gnyana Sastras.

“Therefore, those great ones who praise Him, the Nadham-form, will have the Nadham-form Vedas, manifested by the Nadham-form Lord, appearing within them.

“Thus, they are capable of performing the actions of those Vedas through their own sacred words. All these references appear here, where the Lord is referred to as the one who stands in the form of Nadham, and these two great souls, who are such exalted beings, are referred to as those who praise the feet of such a Lord, as Sekkizhar Peruman has stated. Sekkizhar Peruman blesses us by speaking these words. Sekkizhar Peruman composes this verse, asking who is capable of describing the greatness of these two great souls, implying that no one can.

“Now, the next verse: “Those devotees who stood united in saying the same words that the Lord had previously uttered, they themselves are capable of arranging the divine grace that comes from their Lord.

“Therefore, the unity between the great Vedas and the true devotees is indeed very great.” This is the next verse, the five hundred and ninety-second verse. The collection of Vedas that the Lord had previously revealed, those devotees who stood united in consciousness, are capable of performing acts of grace similar to those of their Lord.

“Therefore, the unity between the great Vedas and the true devotees is indeed very great. Sekkizhar Peruman marvels and praises.

“The Lord spoken of by the Vedas is Siva. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the devotee who stood in unity with the Lord, stood with a unified consciousness with Him. In Sivagnanam, it means to be mingled in non-duality.

“Thus, the ability of Aludaiya Pillaiyar to be one with Siva is described in the Thevaram of Ilambaiyangottoor as “my words are His words.” Sekkizhar Peruman has stated it as “the endless, primordial, true scripture taken as a written scripture.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is capable of performing the work of the Vedas, which are the sacred words of Siva, through his own sacred words.

“Therefore, the action of his words of grace is glorious. The Vedas, by worshipping the Lord and encompassing Him within themselves, shut the sacred doors. This is the meaning of the Vedas shutting the sacred doors. The countless Vedas bestowed by the Lord, uniting and striving, shut the doors. If Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is the one who, through a single sacred verse within a single sacred poem, brought about this event, then there is no one else who can be compared or equaled to that true devotee.

“Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is capable of performing actions similar to the grace of the Lord. There is no one who can be placed on par with or above such true devotees. Sekkizhar Peruman composes this verse, expressing wonder at the unity between the great Vedas and the true devotees.

“Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman describes and blesses us with the sacred events of our revered masters, who caused the sacred doors, which the Vedas praised and which were shut in the temple of Siva, who resides in Vedavanam, also known as Thirumaraikkadu, to open and close again. Let us go on meditating.

“Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman blesses us by describing the sacred events of our venerable masters, who caused the sacred doors, which the Vedas praised and which were shut in the temple of Siva, who resides in Vedavanam, also known as Thirumaraikkadu, to open and close again. We shall continue our meditation.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 681, by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman is seated in the Thirumaraikkadu monastery, contemplating the Lord’s grace at Thirumaraikkadu and reflecting on the nature and greatness of that divine grace. As we discussed in the previous verse, he ponders all those meanings in his heart. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman understands that there is great unity between the Vedas and Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the devotee who speaks them with single-mindedness. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred words easily accomplish the actions of the Vedas.

For others like me, there is a great difference between us and the graceful actions of the Vedas. Without realizing that this was the will of our Lord Siva, I dared to open the sacred door that the Vedas had closed, an act connected to the Vedas. Not only that, but I will not even speak harshly of the Lord’s compassionate nature.

Thus, contemplating all these thoughts, with a sense of conviction, and remembering the nature and greatness of divine grace, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman falls into a light slumber.

At that time, Siva appears in the guise of a Saivite and instructs Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, saying, “Come to Thiruvaaimoor.” Thiruvaaimoor is a place very close to Vedharanyam. The Lord, without revealing His true form, comes in the guise of a Saivite and thus instructs Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. He enlightens Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. According to the principle of conduct stated in the twelfth Sutra of Sivagnanabodham, “The form and temple of those filled with love are a refuge,” and because the Lord commanded, “We are in Vaymoor, come there,” Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal, concluding that the one who came disguised as a Saivite was indeed the Lord, immediately proceeds quickly with folded hands. He asks, “Why did the Lord of Vaymoor ask me to come there?” singing a Thevaram pathigam, and understanding the sacred intention of the Lord’s command, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman quickly goes to the site of Thiruvaaimoor. When Thirunavukkarasu Peruman was in a light sleep, the Lord spoke thus.

After speaking, he went ahead. When Thirunavukkarasu Peruman woke up and regained full consciousness, he saw the same Saivite form that he had seen before. As the Lord, hidden in that Saivite form, walked quickly away, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, unable to see him, quickly followed. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, intensely longing to see the Lord who had come in a Saivite guise, followed Him, searching in all eight directions. The Saivite Lord appeared in the distance, but due to his eagerness to see Him up close, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman continued to follow, unable to see the same Lord. As Thirunavukkarasu Peruman went to that place, the Lord of Sirkazhi, The child-saint asks where Appar has gone.

The child-saint asks the good devotees in Appar Swamigal’s monastery. To this, the devotees say that Appar Swamigal has gone to Thiruvaaimoor.

The Lord had enlightened Appar in his sleep, saying, “Come to Thiruvaaimoor.” Appar Swamigal also follows. But he goes to Thiruvaaimoor. He sings, “Why did he leave the monastery at that time?” and goes, saying, “If this is the grace of my Lord, I too will go,” and sings a pathigam.

So, he sings the pathigam, “The Lord of Thiruvaaimoor went there, saying, ‘Come here, why?’” Because of his intense love, he left the monastery.

The devotees who were with him understood from that pathigam that Appar Swamigal was going to Thiruvaaimoor. They said that Appar Swamigal went because the Lord had called him by showing a sign to Thiruvaaimoor.

However, the reason for the Lord’s grace and the thoughts that arose in Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s heart before that event were unknown to those devotees.

Therefore, the child-saint, wondering why Appar Swamigal had gone and what the reason was, also went to Thiruvaaimoor. Having gone there, the child-saint reached the same place where Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal was.

At that time, the Lord revealed to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman the sacred dance with the Divine Mother.

The Lord instructs Appar Swamigal to come to Thiruvaaimoor and leads him to the border of Thiruvaaimoor. There, a golden temple appears, and the Lord enters it and disappears. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman is distressed, unable to see the Lord.

At that time, Aludaiya Pillaiyar arrives there.

Then, the king informs him that the Lord called him and has now disappeared. At that moment, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman also sees the Lord and the Divine Mother there. We have extensively discussed all these historical events as Sekkizhar Peruman has revealed them in the Puranam of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman.

Now, as the child-saint comes to the place where the king is, the Lord shows the child-saint the miraculous sacred dance with the Divine Mother.

At that time, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman recites a pathigam.

Now, Siva reveals the sacred dance with the Divine Mother. This is not the dance of grace that follows concealment in the five great dances; this sacred dance is an eternal reality that is always revealed to the Gnanis through profound knowledge. This pathigam, which begins with the word “arul” (grace), is the pathigam belonging to the sacred site of Thiruvaaimoor, the eighty-seventh pathigam of the third Thirumurai, set to the Nattaraaga Pann. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows. The following is Thiruchitrambalam. “Thaliral valarena umaip paada thaazham idavor kazhal veesi kilari la maniyara varai yaarthu aadum vedakkirimaiyaar vilari la mulaiyavar karul nalgi venn neer aninthor senniyin mel valarila madhiyomodu ivaraaneer vaaimoor adigal varuvaare thingalodu aruvarai polir solai thenalang kaanal thiruvaaiymoor angamodu arumarai oli paadal azhanira vannaththar tham adiparavi nangadam vinaigeda mozhiyavalla Gnanasambandhan thamil malai thangiya manaththinal thozhuthu ezhuvaar thamar neri ulagukkor thava nerive Thiruchitrambalam.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman narrates the graceful dance he witnessed, describing how the Lord with a charming demeanor dances, swinging one leg, adorned with a shining serpent-gem at his waist, bestowing grace upon the beautiful-breasted woman (Uma), and with a growing crescent moon on his white-ash-adorned head, as the Lord of Vaymoor comes.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman narrates the graceful dance that the Lord revealed to him, describing how the Lord of Vaymoor comes. In this pathigam, the child-saint also shows this sacred vision to the king.

Therefore, it is noted here that Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s pathigams for this place and the events of the miraculous golden temple were revealed on the way to Thiruvaaimoor, in that intermediate time and place. After witnessing the sacred dance and reciting the pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman went together to Thiruvaaimoor and worshipped the Lord of Thiruvaaimoor, reciting pathigams.

Now, the pathigams sung by these two great souls are not available to us.

Thus, they stayed in Thiruvaaimoor for a few days. These two great souls stayed for a while.

Afterwards, both of them returned together to Thirumaraikkadu. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman stayed together in Thirumaraikkadu and worshipped the sacred feet of the Lord.

At this time, three of the pathigams composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman are available to us. These are pathigams for the sacred site of Thirumaraikkadu. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed a total of four pathigams for the sacred site. We have already reflected on the pathigam beginning with “Sathuram Maraithan.” Therefore, the other three pathigams composed at this time are as follows. The second of the total four pathigams is the twenty-second pathigam of the first Thirumurai, set to the tune of Nattapadai. The first, seventh, and eleventh verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam.

“Silai thanai naduvidai niruvi yoor sinamali arava thoduvithu thalamali surarasu roli salasalak kadal kadai oli migu kolai mali vidamezha avvarudal kulaithara avvadu nugar pavanezhin malaimali madil pudai thazhuviya maraivanam amardharu paramane irunila nadhupunal idaimadi tharavezhi pugavezhi adhumigu peruveli inilavi tharaveli kedaviy nadai muzhuvathu kedaviruvargal udal poraiyoduthiri ezhiluru udaiyava ninamalar maruviya varupathamisai muran maraivanam amardharu paramane vasai” “Malarmaga nilaviya maraivanam amarpar amanai ninaib pasaiyodu migukalai palabayil pulavargal pugazh vazhi valardharu visaiyamar kazhumala nagarirai thamilviraganathurai iyalvalavisai mali thamizhoru pathum valarvar ulagini.” The third pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for the sacred site of Thirumaraikkadu is the ninety-first pathigam of the second Thirumurai, set to the tune of Piyandai Gandhara Pann. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: “Pongu venmanal kaanal porudal thiraithaval muththang kangul aarirul pozhum kali maraikkadu amarnthaar tham thingal soodinarenum thiripurameriththanarenum engumingal pranaar pugazhaladhu igazh pazhiyilarai mayulaam pozhil soozhntha maa” “Those who worship the Lord and recite these ten melodious Tamil verses composed by Gnanasambandhan of Kaali, who is surrounded by beautiful groves, will go and enter heaven with the faultless celestials. This is glory.” Thiruchitrambalam.

This pathigam speaks of the glory of the Lord, stating that Thirumaraikkadu is His abode, and describes the special features of the place. This pathigam was given to the people of the world, instructing them to go and worship there.

Now, the fourth pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for the sacred site of Thirumaraikkadu is the seventy-sixth pathigam of the third Thirumurai, which belongs to the Thiruviragam category, set to the Sadari Pann. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. “My Lord, who performs a great dance in the forest and collects alms from women, is said to reside in Vedavanam, where the mighty, stormy ocean casts forth pearls like mountain peaks, and where courtesans with bow-like eyebrows gather.” “Mandalamura wangadal valankezhuvu Kaali pathi mannu Kavuni venpodi neer aniyum Vedavanamevu Sivana in arulinal santhamevai thandamilin innisaiyena paravu paadal ulagil bandhan urai kondu mozhivaargal payilvaargal uyarvaan ulagame Thiruchitrambalam.” The note for this pathigam is that the Lord’s abode is Vedavanam.

Thus, these two great masters reside in Vedharanyam, also known as Thirumaraikkadu.

Now, Sekkizhar Peruman begins to narrate the preface to the sacred history of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s avatar, which is the journey to Pandya Nadu, where he would eradicate Jainism and establish Saivism, and the subsequent divine events. Let us persist in our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 682, by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. During the time when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman resided in Thirumaraikkadu, Jainism flourished in Pandya Nadu, and Saiva Vaidika tradition was suppressed. The divine event of the child-saint’s avatar, which includes the refutation of other religions, condemnation, and the exposition of Saivism, is now about to unfold. Sekkizhar Peruman begins to narrate it. This section is the central part of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s Puranam, spanning one thousand two hundred and fifty-six verses.

This section is contained in verses five hundred and ninety-nine and six hundred. Sekkizhar Peruman, following the narrative of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred life thus far, now begins the section where the child-saint’s avatar’s purpose is fulfilled in Pandya Nadu. Verses five hundred and ninety-nine and six hundred are as follows: While they were there, in Pandya Nadu, the land of the Southern King, where the true path was lost due to the accumulated karma, and Jainism flourished, causing turmoil before the rightful ways ceased, the Southern King, due to the karma he had accumulated, considered that path as the right one and remained firm in it. The established truth of Saiva Vaidika tradition, which is the good path, was abandoned and replaced by the evil path. These are the verses. While worshipping the Lord at Thirumaraikkadu, in Pandya Nadu, the evil consequences of accumulated karma led to the rise of Jainism.

The good ethical principles of Saivism were suppressed, causing everyone to be distressed. Never before had Jainism flourished like this, nor would it again. During this intermediate period, Jainism was flourishing there. This Pandya Nadu, at the time this history unfolds, During the period this narrative unfolds, Pandya Nadu was entirely under the control of the Pandya kings. The Cholas also ruled Pandya Nadu for some time.

But this was a period when the Pandya kings, as Southern rulers, governed the land.

At that time, Jainism had greatly flourished during this interim period. The Chola dynasty was always a lineage that followed Saivism without fail.

However, the Pandya lineage was associated with Jainism. During the intermediate period, Jainism flourished in this Pandya Nadu. The Chola dynasty, which came from the lineage that followed established Saivism, and whose land was enriched by the Ponni River, always remained steadfast in the Saiva tradition. In this Pandya Nadu, at this time, Jainism was flourishing. “We are servants who perform deeds and praise the Lord’s feet” is a saying from the Thevaram. The land of Pandya was in turmoil because the Saiva path, which includes the paths of Chariya, Kriya, Yoga, and Gnana, and the discipline of adhering to it, and the exposition of the glory of the sacred ashes, were not upheld, and Jainism flourished.

“Just as all seeds sown in a rainy season sprout at the same time and then wither away together in the dry season,” says a verse from Sivagnana Siddhiyar. Generally, in the rainy season or other seasons, the same type of seeds sprout and grow at the same time, remain for a short period, and then wither away together. We observe all these.

Similarly, most living beings in a country experience the same type of karmic results at the same time. The karma of those beings is collectively bestowed by the Lord at the same time, and such karmic results come to the beings worthy of experiencing them.

In the same way, in Pandya Nadu, most living beings at that time were influenced by the fruit of evil karma to follow Jainism, by the Lord’s will.

At that time, the Pandya king, also due to the fruits of his past evil karma, considered the Jain path as the true dharma and followed it. All good morals in the country declined, and evil morals increased.

Similarly, the Pandya king, the ruler of Pandya Nadu, due to the fruit of his past evil karma, was destined to align himself with Jainism. If there was past evil karma, the Lord would bestow the fruit of that evil karma accordingly. Due to the fruit of that evil karma, evil thoughts and subsequent evil actions would occur. If there was good karma, then due to the fruit of that good karma, good thoughts and subsequent good actions would similarly be brought about by the Lord – this truth is stated in the Gnyana Sastras. Although the Pandya king was born into the noble lineage of Saivism and a Saiva royal family, His conversion to Jainism during this period was due to the decree that he had to experience the fruits of his past evil karma. He adopted Jainism, believing it to be the path of righteousness.

Therefore, it is implied here that it was not truly the path of righteousness.

Thus, when Jainism flourished, the good path of enduring Saiva Vaidika tradition was lost and changed in Pandya Nadu. Saivism in Pandya Nadu is Vaidika Saivism, which is an eternal and imperishable form of Saivism. The truth that underlies the Vedic tradition is the Saiva path. The essence of the Veda is Saivism. Its truth is the path prescribed by the Siva Agamas and Vedas, which originated from the Lord’s sacred word “Sat.” Even though it is prescribed by both Saiva Agamas and the Vaidika Vedas, both Saiva Agamas and Vedas lead to the same conclusion.

Therefore, great souls celebrate Saivism by calling it Vaidika Saivism. Vaidika Saivism is praised by the exalted as “Azhagidhu Antho” (how beautiful it is!).

Thus, the Vaidika Saiva tradition, the good path, is an eternal good path.

The Lord is eternal and unchanging.

Similarly, His sacred words, the Vedas and Siva Agamas, are also eternal. Yet, in Pandya Nadu, at that time, due to the karmic experiences of those beings and the fruits of evil karma, Jainism flourished and Saivism was suppressed. To uplift this Vaidika Saiva good path, the child-saint incarnated. Sekkizhar Peruman has thus composed the introductory verse in the child-saint’s Puranam, stating, “May the Vedic path flourish, may the abundant Saiva tradition shine.” In accordance with this, through the sacred words of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the evil path of Jainism will be removed, and Saivism will flourish there.

Now, the evil path has spread. Because when that good path of Vaidika Saivism changed, it not only changed but also allowed the evil path to act like the good path in Pandya Nadu, thus Jainism flourished. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing: “The peerless sacred places in the Tamil land of the Northerners all became ruins and many Jain schools, like groups of darkness, surrounded by hair-peacocks and water-vessels in hand, filled with Jains.” This is the six hundred and first verse. Pandya Nadu is called Tamil Nadu. Generally, all countries where Tamil is spoken, such as Chola Nadu, Thondai Nadu, Nadu Nadu, Kongu Nadu, and so on, All those countries are also Tamil Nadu. Even though the name Tamil Nadu is a common name for all those countries, it is uniquely attributed to Pandya Nadu by scholars.

Although Tamil Nadu can be a descriptive name applicable to other countries, it is specifically reserved for Pandya Nadu as a proper noun with inherent meaning. In the one thousand five hundred and fifty-fourth verse, Sekkizhar Peruman sang that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s arrival in Pandya Nadu was an arrival in Tamil Nadu. Because Lord Siva, the supreme deity, presided over the Sangam and nurtured Tamil, and because Agastya, the Tamil sage, still resides in the Podhigai mountains, and for many other reasons, Tamil Nadu refers specifically to Pandya Nadu. In such a Tamil Nadu, all the Saivite holy places were in ruins, meaning they became places with Jain ruins and schools. All the Saivite holy places in Tamil Nadu became desolate, turning into Jain monuments and schools. The glorious places in Pandya Nadu, such as Thiruppoovanam, Thirunelveli, and Thirukutralam, were filled with Jain monuments and schools.

“Paazhikal” refers to temples built by Jains for worship. “Palli” refers to places where Jain gurus gathered for study and resided.

In addition, There are also separate places for Jain gurus to reside in the monasteries. Generally, Paazhi and Palli are names given to our Saivite temples. These names have been in use since ancient times. We can still see Saivite shrines like Arathai Perumpali and Sembhon Palli.

However, Jainism, which emerged later, adopted these terms, Paazhi and Palli, for its own places and made it a custom. There, in those Paazhis, Jains gathered like groups of darkness. In their hands, peacock feathers shone like groups of darkness. In their hands, they held a Kamandalam, a water pot. Jains generally used to sprinkle water from the pot they held in their hands, stroke with peacock feathers, and chant mantras; this was one of the customs of Jain gurus. Not only that, but they also used peacock feathers to gently brush aside small creatures like ants from their path so as not to harm them.

Such Jains swarmed in the Paazhis and Pallis. Just as flies swarm around beehives, people also swarmed in these Paazhis and Pallis because the king was a Jain follower.

Therefore, people also followed the king and embraced Jainism.

Moreover, the teachings of Jains were based on non-violence as a superficial principle.

Therefore, those Captivated by the deceitful charm of those beautiful, superficial teachings, people became Jain followers and thronged to the Jain monasteries and schools.

Thus, while Jain gurus resided in monasteries and schools, Jain followers roamed everywhere, carrying peacock feathers, bamboo mats, and triple parasols. The triple parasol held by Jains is a symbol of their deity. It is made of gold, gems, and pearls, with a single staff. It is customary for Jains to mark their bodies with this symbol, like the emblem of their deity, on their chest, forehead, shoulders, and other places. These triple parasols of the Aragu deity are The Jains claim their beliefs are eternal bliss and encompass everything. They wander around carrying peacock feathers, water pots, mats, and umbrellas.

These Jains cling to the doctrines they found in their external religion, considering them the ultimate truth, and are content within those boundaries. They remain unresponsive even when they know a superior Saivite path exists, which is contrary to their own. Though Jainism had spread like darkness everywhere, two great people shone as the brilliant lamps of Saivism: one was our empress, Mangaiyarkkarasiyar, and the other was our lord, Kulachirai Nayanar. These two great individuals cherished and protected the Saivite path there. For the well-being of the Pandya king, who was a southerner, and to ensure his salvation, Queen Mangaiyarkkarasiyar, the auspicious daughter of the Cholas, and Kulachiraiyar, the great minister, shone as the brilliant Saivite lamps and served as pillars of support for the Saivite path.

Let us dwell further on this. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periyapuranam, Part Six Hundred Eighty-Three, by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, titled ‘Vambarav Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam’. The esteemed daughter born to the Chola king in the Chola country was the Pandya Queen Mangaiyarkkarasiyar. She was indeed the daughter born to the Cholas for the salvation of the Pandyas. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman himself, in his sacred words, has exalted our empress, the Pandya Queen, in a pathigam, referring to her as ‘Ammaiyar Mangaiyarkkarasi Valavarkon Pavai’. In the Pandya country, while the Pandya king, the husband of the Pandya Queen, was leaning towards Jainism, the Pandya Queen remained steadfast.

She steadfastly followed the Saivite path. Kulachirai Nayanar Peruman, the minister of the Pandya king, also stood firm in the Saivite path.

Thus, while the Pandya king leaned towards Jainism, the Pandya Queen and Kulachirai Nayanar Peruman stood firmly in the Saivite path. Saivism found its support only in these two individuals in the Pandya country. The Pandya king mentioned here will henceforth be revered as one of the Nayanmars, Nedumara Nayanar, through the grace of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Sekkizhar Peruman has depicted the situation of the Pandya country and the state of Saivism at that time, placing these three great individuals within a single verse. Sekkizhar Peruman stated this in the six hundred third verse: (Varrisilai Thennavan than Uytharku valavarkoman thiru uyirtharulum selvap pandimadeviyarum kuraikazhal amaichanaram kulachirayarum enum iruvartham pangum anri Saivam angu eythataga) meaning, apart from the Pandya Queen, the fortunate daughter born to the Chola king for the salvation of the southern king with the strong bow, and Kulachiraiyar, the minister with the ankleted feet, Saivism did not flourish anywhere else there.

Thus, Saivism was firmly established only in the Pandya Queen and Kulachirai Nayanar; it did not reach other places. Although it is stated that Saivism existed only in these two, the Pandya Queen and the great minister Kulachirai Nayanar, they sent some envoys to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. These envoys were also devoted to the Saivite path.

Later, when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman visited and worshipped the Lord of Thiruvalavai, the devotees serving him welcomed him with reverence. They too were followers of Saivism in the Pandya country at that time.

Therefore, even though Saivism existed among some individuals, the great people who served as protectors of Saivism were the Pandya Queen Mahadevi and the great minister Kulachirai Nayanar. That is why Peruman states that Saivism did not flourish anywhere else except with these two. Saivism had no other place to find support; it depended solely on these two in the good land of Pandya. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing: (Angavar thangal angann arumperal Tamil Nadu utra theenginukku alavuthetra sindaiyil parivukonde ongiiya Saiva vaaymai ozhukkathil nindra tanmai poongazhal sezhiyin munbu pulappadaa vagai kondu vaythar enbathu adutha thiruppadal) meaning, the next verse states that these two great individuals, Queen Mangaiyarkkarasi, and the great minister Kulachirai Nayanar, deeply distressed by the immense harm that befell this rare Tamil country, nurtured the lofty truth of Saivite conduct in their hearts, keeping it hidden from the king. The harm that befell the rare Tamil country, the Pandya land, refers to the decline of Saivite conduct and the widespread prevalence of Jainism. Tamil and Saivism are intricately linked; if it is Tamil, it is Saivism, and if it is Saivism, it is Tamil, both being inseparably intertwined and signifying special connections.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman does not say that it is a harm that befell the Saivite country, but rather refers to it as a harm that befell the Tamil country.

Thus, whether it is the Saivite country, the Tamil country, or the Pandya country, it all refers to the same meaning here. Some modern researchers, unaware of all these distinctions, distortedly claim that the superiority of Jainism is the superiority of Tamil. Sekkizhar Peruman here emphasizes that the glory of Tamil lies in guiding people towards a path of devotion.

Lord Siva as Iraiyanar, Lord Muruga as Kumaravelar, Agathiyar, and many other divine poets flourished Tamil in this land. This means that the greatness of Tamil lies in the supremacy of Saivism, not in the supremacy of Jainism. That is why Sekkizhar Peruman refers to the harm that befell Saivism as the harm that befell the Tamil country. As the Saivite country, the Pandya land, was thus afflicted, Queen Mangaiyarkkarasi and Kulachirai Nayanar contemplated in their hearts about when this suffering would end and how to find a solution. Even though the desire for Jainism to disappear and Saivism to return was a policy contrary to the king’s command and opinion, they felt obliged to ensure the flourishing of Saivism in this country and to protect it. Queen Pandi and Kulachirai Nayanar firmly upheld the true conduct of Saivism.

They maintained their Saivite path without the king’s knowledge. If these two individuals upheld the Saivite path in this manner, it was for the benefit of this country. This is because the command of God is enshrined in the Vedas and Sivagamas, and the essence of these scriptures is that all living beings should adhere to the true conduct of Saivism.

Therefore, it is also the king’s duty to guide the people towards the true Saivite conduct, which is the ultimate teaching of the Vedas and Sivagamas revealed by God. However, the king here practices a different religion.

Therefore, in this situation, while the king’s command is aligned with the Jain religion, these two great individuals adhere to the true Saivite path, contrary to the king’s command, but without his knowledge. This is because God’s command is superior to the king’s command and is worthy of being followed.

Therefore, even though the government had changed and stood on a different path, the Queen, Pandi, and the minister, Kulachirai Nayanar, followed the Vedic Saivite path, which is a higher command than that of the king. It is true that they followed the Saivite path in this way. If righteousness is not upheld and if one does not follow the king, then righteousness will not prevail in this world. The world cannot function without the king’s command. It is the minister’s duty to enforce the king’s command.

Furthermore, following the husband’s path is the essence of chastity. The world should be shown that following the husband’s path is indeed the essence of chastity. Those in leadership positions, such as the king and queen of a country, must exemplify these virtues to their people. It is also the duty of the queen, Pandi, to do so.

Therefore, they had the responsibility to practice Saivism discreetly, without the king’s knowledge, for the sake of the country’s worldly order under the king’s rule. This was for the sake of the worldly order.

At the same time, for the sake of guiding the souls in this country away from the harm of Jainism and towards Vedic Saivism, their adherence to Saivite conduct was necessary there. Even though the king’s religion was different, the welfare of the souls in the country lay in Saivite conduct, and thus they had to stand firm.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman has presented all these nuances very subtly. These two individuals, having themselves stood firm in the Saivite path, were now about to send envoys to Pillaiyar to ensure others also embraced it.

Thus, their unwavering commitment to Vedic Saivism and their fervent desire for all souls to attain salvation by following Vedic Saivism are evident here.

Now, Sekkizhar Peruman composes the next verse: (Innneri ozhugugindraar ezulagugazhi venthar) (Vaitika vaaymai Saiva sen neri vilakkugindrar thirumaraikkadu serntha nannilai kanni nattu nalvinai payathal kettar) Thus, in this situation where Queen Mangaiyarkkarasi and Kulachirai Nayanar were present, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman resided at Thirumaraikkadu, illuminating the pure path of Saivism in this world. These two great individuals heard of this situation. The Pandya Queen and Kulachirai Nayanar Peruman heard this news. It is due to the good fortune of the Pandya country that they heard and learned of this. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is the great one who came to save the seven worlds.

He is the great one who came to illuminate the true path of Vedic Saivism. If it is said that he came here, it means that he incarnated here. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman had no personal reason to come to this world. He incarnated here solely for the benefit of the souls of this world. The two sacred feet of the Lord are Jnana (knowledge) and Kriya (action). Thirugnanasambandha Peruman incarnated as an Acharya (spiritual teacher) so that devotees could embrace these two sacred feet and attain the Lord’s sacred feet.

Until now, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman had undertaken pilgrimages to various countries like Chola Nadu, Nadu Nadu, Kongu Nadu, composed pathigams, and performed many miraculous acts of grace, thereby bringing salvation to these lands. Pillaiyar is now about to go and save the Pandya country, and also to establish all worlds in the path of sacred ash for their salvation.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to Pillaiyar here as the glorious king who came to save the seven worlds. The Pandya Queen and Kulachirai Nayanar hear the news that Pillaiyar is illuminating the Saivite path in Thirumaraikkadu. Their hearing of this news signifies that the time has come for the good penance previously performed by the Pandya country to bear fruit.

Therefore, they hear this news. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing about how overjoyed they were upon hearing this news: (Kettappozhuthe sindai kilarnthezhu magizhchi ponga narpozuthu alarnda senthamarai nagaimugatharaaki vatpadai amaichanarum mangaiyarkkarasiyarum serpadu pulathaarenum sendradi panindharotar) meaning, upon hearing the news, immense joy surged in the hearts of Kulachirai Nayanar and Queen Mangaiyarkkarasi, and their faces bloomed like red lotuses freshly opened. The arrival of Pillaiyar, who is like the sun, is about to happen. Due to the arrival of Pillaiyar, who is like the sun, the faces of these two bloomed like red lotuses. Although Thirumaraikkadu is a long distance from the Pandya country, these two great individuals felt as if they had personally gone to Thirumaraikkadu and worshipped Pillaiyar’s sacred feet. They placed their minds there and worshipped the sacred feet; only their bodies remained here.

Sekkizhar Peruman then composes the next verse: (Kadhalal mikkor thangal kai thozhu karuthinale pothavil pugazhi kavalanar seyya pathangal panimin endru parisanamaakkal thammai maathavam sruthi seytha mamaraikkattil vittar) meaning, Queen Pandi and Kulachirai Nayanar, who had immense love for Pillaiyar, sent their servants, their retinues, to Thirumaraikkadu with the intention that they themselves should meet and worship Pillaiyar. They instructed them, “Go to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred feet and worship him.” They had previously worshipped Pillaiyar in their minds, but now they desired to meet and worship him in person.

Therefore, considering it as if they themselves were going to meet, worship, and submit their plea, they commanded their retinue to go there. They sent them with instructions to go there, prostrate at Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s feet, and submit their plea. That plea was a request to remove the harm that had befallen their country. These envoys were intelligent messengers.

Therefore, they fully understood the subtle message conveyed by the queen and the minister. They were blessed with the good fortune of worshipping Pillaiyar and submitting their plea.

Thus, even without the queen and the minister explicitly stating it, they understood their inner thoughts. They were capable of acting according to the task assigned to them. That is why Sekkizhar Peruman refers to them as ‘intelligent individuals’ in the next verse.

Now, accepting the command of the queen and the great minister, these envoys set off towards Thirumaraikkadu in the Chola country. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to narrate this.

Let us go on pondering. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periyapuranam, Part Six Hundred Eighty-Four, by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, titled ‘Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam’. Sekkizhar Peruman describes how the Pandya Queen and Minister Kulachirai Nayanar sent intelligent envoys to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. He states: (Angavar vida mun pontha arivudai manthar angann neengi van Tamilnattu ellai pirpada neriyin ekii gnangark neer nadum kadu nathigalum kadanthu vandhu thengamizh kaithai neythal thiru maraikkadu sernthar enbathu aru nuru ettavathu thiruppadal) This is the six hundred eighth verse.

Thus, those envoys who were sent were intelligent individuals. They were highly intelligent, and also It is also worth noting that they were fit to undertake this great task of bringing salvation to the Pandya country.
