They departed from there, meaning they left Madurai, the capital city of the Pandya country, Thirualavai, crossed the rich Tamil country’s border—here Tamil country refers to the Pandya country, a fertile Tamil land. The fertility of Tamil lies in its generous ability to guide those who study it to the path of God, bestowing upon them the three benefits of this world, the next, and the hereafter. Crossing the border of such a Tamil country, the Pandya land, these envoys entered the Chola country. This route is considered to pass through Melur, Thirupputtur, Aranthangi, and Athiveeraramapattinam, located northeast of Madurai.

The route by which Aludaiya Pillaiyar came to Madurai was from Thirukkodungunram, also known as Piramalai. This is another route. This route comes from the north towards Madurai and is a bit longer. As they crossed the Pandya country, they reached the Chola country, which is known as Neer Nadu (watery country). The regions of the Pandya country, with their many forests, small rivers, and tributaries, all flow into the eastern sea. It is mentioned here that these envoys crossed all these.

The names of places like Anappair Melpanaikadu, Maravakkadu, Thiru Idumbavanam, and Thirumaraikkadu reflect the nature of this region. The small rivers flowing here include the Mutha River, Thenaru, Pamparu, Thenvellaru, and Agniaru.

Thus, crossing the Pandya country and the intervening fertile plains of the Chola country (Neer Nadu), the envoys reached Thirumaraikkadu. The fragrance of screwpine flowers seemed to welcome them, wafting for a long distance in Thirumaraikkadu. Thirumaraikkadu is a coastal area, referred to as Neythal Nilam (coastal region). Having crossed the fertile plains of the Chola country, which is a watery land with abundant paddy fields, these envoys reached Thirumaraikkadu, a sacred place located in the eastern coastal region. Sekkizhar Peruman sings: (Thirumaraikkadu nanni sirapura nagaril vantha arumarai pillaiyar tham amarnthu inithu arulum selva perumadatthu anaiya vandhu perugiya viruppil thangal varum murai tanmayellam vayil kavalarukku sonnar) Having reached Thirumaraikkadu, they approached the great mansion where Thirugnanasambandha Peruman resided and bestowed his grace. The mansion where Thirugnanasambandha Peruman resided is a great mansion of wealth.

It is a mansion where Thirugnanasambandha Peruman lovingly resided. It is a great mansion where Thirugnanasambandha Peruman graciously resided, bestowing sattbhavana (pure thoughts), which includes all initiations, for the welfare of this world. Since Peruman graciously resided there, Since he gracefully resided there, it became a great mansion of wealth that bestows liberation from worldly bonds (pasakshayam) and the supreme state of Shiva (Sivapperu). It was no ordinary mansion; it was a great mansion, meaning a mansion endowed with greatness. Its greatness lay in being a place where assemblies of devotees gathered. This mansion gained the distinction of being a place where Pillaiyar resided for many days after the miraculous event of the sacred door of Thirumaraikkadu opening and closing again.

This sacred mansion is of great significance as it is the starting point for Pillaiyar’s journey to the Pandya country, where his Avatar’s purpose of refuting other religions (parasamyana nirakaripum) and illuminating Saivism (Saivasamay vilakkam) would take place.

Therefore, this sacred mansion becomes equal to the sacred mansion where Pillaiyar resided in Thirualavai, Madurai. The envoys arrived at the exterior of that great mansion. With great devotion, they explained the reason for their visit to the doorkeepers of Pillaiyar’s sacred mansion. These envoys, out of immense devotion to Queen Pandi and the minister, conveyed their purpose to the doorkeepers of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred mansion. It is the doorkeepers who have the right to enter the sacred mansion and inform Pillaiyar appropriately in his presence.

Therefore, the envoys conveyed this matter to the doorkeepers. Peruman then composes the next verse: (Matra avar sendru pukku valavarkon magalar thennan kotravan theviyarum kulachirayarumeva porkazhal paniyavanthom ena silar puraththu vandhu sottranar enru potri thozhudu vinnapam seythar) This verse describes how the doorkeepers of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred mansion went inside and submitted this news to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman in the form of a plea. The doorkeepers themselves had the right to enter the sacred mansion and announce any news. They stood before Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and submitted their plea, saying, “Oh Lord, outside our sacred mansion, the envoys sent by the daughter of the Chola king, the Queen of the Pandya king, and Kulachirai Nayanar, say that they have come to worship your golden feet.” Thus, the doorkeepers submitted their plea to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. When speaking about Queen Mangaiyarkkarasi, they first refer to her as the daughter of the Cholas and the Mahadevi (great queen) of the Pandya king, placing the Cholas first. They mention the Pandyas next.

Pillaiyar also belonged to the Chola country, and Queen Mangaiyarkkarasi was also the daughter of the Chola king in the Chola country.

Therefore, the doorkeepers first mention the connection between them, emphasizing the rights and uniqueness of this country, and then refer to her as the Pandya Queen, mentioning her connection to the Pandya country second. When Manikkavasaga Peruman, also known as Thiruvathavur Adigal, resided in a hermitage in Thillaiyambathi and Lord Shiva desired to obtain and write Thiruvachagam, he appeared as a Brahmin. When he came, he announced that his country was the Pandya country to Manikkavasaga Peruman. Manikkavasagar Peruman was also from the Pandya country.

Therefore, by announcing that he too was from the Pandya country, he created a connection based on their native land, fostering closeness. This incident comes to our mind here. These doorkeepers first mentioned the Chola country connection between Pillaiyar and Queen Mangaiyarkkarasi. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman himself, in his sacred pathigam, first refers to Mangaiyarkkarasi as ‘Mangaiyarkkarasi Valavarkon Pavai Varivalai Kaimadamani Pangayachelvi Pandimadevi’, meaning the daughter of the Chola king, and then as Pandi Mahadevi, the queen of the Pandya country, thus following this order.

Thus, the doorkeepers stood before Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, submitting their plea. Sekkizhar Peruman composes the next verse: (Pugazhi kavalar tham kettu poruvila arul mun kura agamalarndhu avargal thammai azhaiyum endru arulicheyya nagaumuch sevvii nokki natrava manthar kuva thagavudai manthar pukku thalaiyinal vanangi nindrar) Hearing what the doorkeepers said, Pillaiyar, the leader of Sirkazhi, was filled with divine grace. This incomparable grace overflowed within him. This divine grace was already kindled by the Lord from within even before they arrived and submitted their plea. When they submitted their plea, that grace surged and overflowed. This grace is instrumental in the flourishing of the sacred ash path and the removal of the opposing religions that hindered it.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to it as ‘incomparable grace’. With this divine grace overflowing, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman graciously spoke, commanding, “Call them here.” Seeing the special radiance of Pillaiyar’s joyful face, the good and devoted individuals, the servants, went outside and invited the envoys to come. These invited servants were intimate devotees of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. They were endowed with the merit of serving Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as intimate devotees, and also the merit of being present and assisting at the beginning of the divine grace event that was about to unfold in the Pandya country. Such devoted servants went outside the sacred mansion and invited the envoys to come inside. The intelligent envoys from the Pandya country also entered the sacred mansion.

How much merit did these envoys possess? They possessed great qualities of intelligence, love, and other virtues, making them worthy envoys to remove the great harm that had befallen the entire Pandya country, which was the Saivite path. Such worthy envoys entered the sacred mansion, and before Pillaiyar, they prostrated themselves on the ground, bowing their heads, and then rose to their feet. Addressing those who stood there, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman graciously spoke. He composes the next verse: (Nindravardhammai nokki nigaril seer Champaivendhar mantalanguzhaliiyaram maniyar thamakkum manakunrenan nindra meimai Kulachirayar thmakkum nandrithan vinavikuri narpatham potruvarkal enbathu padal) meaning, the verse describes how Pillaiyar, the king of Sirkazhi, addressed the envoys who stood before him after bowing, and graciously inquired about the well-being of Mangaiyarkkarasi Ammaiyar, whose fragrant hair was adorned with flowers, and Kulachirai Nayanar, whose truth stood like a mountain. It was Pillaiyar’s divine will to inquire about the welfare of the people of the Pandya country.

He first asked if Ammaiyar and Kulachirai Nayanar were well. Because these envoys were sent by them.

Furthermore, the well-being of Queen Mangaiyarkkarasi and Kulachirai Nayanar was to be the cause of future good for the Pandya country and its king.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman graciously inquired about the well-being of the Pandya Queen and Kulachirai Nayanar. Sekkizhar Peruman refers to Kulachirai Nayanar as ‘Kulachiraiyar, whose truth stood like a mountain of honor.’ Kulachirai Nayanar was unwavering in his adherence to the Saivite path, no matter what obstacles arose, and he protected his conduct.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman compares his unwavering adherence to the path of conduct to a mountain. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman thus inquired, and the envoys who had come to convey the message replied. Peruman composes the next verse: (Kanni nattu amanar thammal kattazhindhu ilindhu thangal mannavanum avargal mayathu azhundha mahadeviyarum konnavil kulachirayarum kudi innilai pugazhivendarku iyampum endru irainjivittar enbathu thiruppadal) The envoys stated, they pleaded, saying, “The Kanni country, the Pandya land, has been ruined and debased by the Jains. Our king is also submerged in their illusion. Seeing this, the Pandya Queen and Kulachirai Nayanar were greatly saddened and distressed. They told us to go to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the king of Sirkazhi, and convey this situation to him, and to worship and plead with you.”

The envoys conveyed this message. Hearing what they said, all the devotees of Lord Shiva who were surrounding Thirugnanasambandha Peruman submitted a plea at Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred feet. They pleaded that he should defeat the Jains and make the Vedic path flourish everywhere, and that he should also make the king wear the sacred ash, thereby establishing Saivism in the Pandya country.

The devotees of Lord Shiva who were there submitted this plea at Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred feet. We shall continue pondering. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periyapuranam, Part Six Hundred Eighty-Five, by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, titled ‘Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam’. All the devotees of Shiva who were seated with Thirugnanasambandha Peruman in the sacred mansion were full of love, as ‘love is Shiva’.

Therefore, when these envoys came and spoke about the prevalence of Jainism and the suppression of Saivism in the Pandya country, they were heartbroken to hear about the suffering that had befallen Saivism and the Pandya country. These devotees were interested in the flourishing of Saivism, the divine path.

Therefore, all of them submitted a plea to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. They pleaded that he should show compassion as requested by the people of the Pandya country. Our Lord, Lord Shiva, They implored him to defeat the Jains who did not worship the sacred feet, to make the Saivite path, which is the path described in the Vedas, flourish everywhere, to make the Pandya king embrace the sacred ash and transform him into a Saivite king, and to guide the Pandya king and his people to the path of God’s grace. They pleaded with Pillaiyar to make all practices in the Pandya country flourish as Saivite practices. Peruman then composes the next verse: (Matra avarkku arul purindhu pillaiyarum vakkesa munivarudan kuda sendru petram uyarthavar patham panindhu ponthu periya thirukkooupurathul irundhu thennadutru sei) (Pandimadeviyarum urimai amaicharum uraithuvitta varthai sottrani mannavarukku pugazhi mannar solli ezhuntharulutharkuth thuninthapodhu arasar arulicheygindrar pillaiy antha amankaiyar vanjanikkor avathiyillai urai seyvathu ulathu urukol thanum theeya ezhuntharula udanpaduvathu onnathu enna parasuvathu nam peruman kadalgal endral pazhudhu anaiyathu ena pagarnthu paramar seiya virai sey mal thal potri pugazhivendhar veyurutholiyai eduthu vilambinarre enpathu aduthu amekindra irandu thiruppadalgal) Thus, the envoys requested.

The following two verses describe this. After giving his grace to them, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, accompanied by Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, went and worshipped the sacred feet of the Lord in Vedharanyam (Thirumaraikkadu). They then came out and sat in the great Gopuram in front of the Lord.

At that time, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman conveyed to Thirunavukkarasu Peruman the message that the Pandya Queen and Minister Kulachiraiyar had sent to him about the state of the Pandya country.

Thus, he stated that he had decided to go to the Pandya country as per their request. Hearing this, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman replied, “My son, there is no limit to the deceitful acts of the Jains.

“Moreover, at present, the planetary positions are also unfavorable; they are evil.

“Therefore, it would not be right for me to agree to your going there.” Thirunavukkarasu Peruman spoke. Pillaiyar, the leader of Sirkazhi, replied, “When we consider that we worship the sacred feet of the Lord, no harm will befall us. If we worship the sacred feet of our Lord, no harm will come to us.” Saying this, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed the pathigam ‘Veyuru Tholipaangan’ (the one with the bamboo-like shoulder), which begins with these words. This is the essence of these two verses. The envoys from the Pandya country made their plea.

“Thirugnanasambandha Peruman bestowed his grace upon the envoys from the Pandya country and the devotees who were present and worshipped there.

“Later, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman went from the sacred mansion to the Thirumaraikkadu temple, also known as Vedharanyam. Before telling Thirunavukkarasu Peruman the news from the Pandya country, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman went with Thirunavukkarasu Peruman to worship the Lord and receive his grace, and also to inform Thirunavukkarasu Peruman about it. After worshipping the Lord, they came out and went to one of the great Gopurams located in the courtyard directly in front of the Lord. Generally, within a temple, there is praise, glorification, and singing of the Lord. The rule for visiting Shiva temples is that only essential discussions should take place, and no other conversations are permitted.

“However, Thirugnanasambandhar wished to discuss all these matters concerning the Pandya country with ThiruNavukkarasu Peruman before the Lord.

“Therefore, without speaking inside or immediately outside the temple, they met beneath the great gopuram between the two areas. There, Pillaiyar recounted all the historical events to ThiruNavukkarasu Peruman, explaining that he intended to travel to the Pandya country for these reasons. Upon hearing this, ThiruNavukkarasu Peruman addressed Thirugnanasambandhar, saying, “Pillai!” Thirugnanasambandhar always considered Appar Peruman as his spiritual father, addressing him as “Appare” from the very beginning.

“Therefore, from the position of a protective father ensuring no harm would come to Pillaiyar, ThiruNavukkarasu Peruman spoke, saying, “The Jains are extremely deceitful. Their treachery knows no bounds. Even the positions of the nine planets are currently unfavorable and are in a harmful state.

“Therefore, it would not be advisable for you to proceed to the Pandya country under these circumstances.” Upon hearing this, Thirugnanasambandhar replied, “If we praise the feet of our Lord, no harm will befall us.” He declared, saying and asserting this, and then blessed a pathigam that begins with “Veyuru Thozhippangan.” This pathigam, known as Kolaru pathigam, is so wonderfully divine that there are no people unfamiliar with it. The theme of this pathigam is “If we praise the feet of our Lord, no harm will befall us,” which is also its crowning statement.

“Thus, through this pathigam, Thirugnanasambandhar not only answered ThiruNavukkarasu Peruman’s objection but also praised the supreme Lord, ensuring His support. This Kolaru pathigam is truly remarkable. It holds great significance. Those who regularly recite it will find their misfortunes dispelled. Travelers who remember this pathigam before embarking on a journey will complete it successfully and without harm, a truth still evident today. This pathigam is included in the “Agathiyar Thevara Thirattu.” Each of its verses describes the Lord’s inseparable presence with the Mother and the benefits thereof.

“Thirugnanasambandhar, beginning with “Veyuru Thozhi Pangan,” starts by praising the Mother, stating that the Lord has Umaiyammaiyar, whose shoulders resemble bamboo, on His left side. Thirugnanasambandhar’s beginning by praising the Mother also signifies the essence of the Thiru Alavai temple. This pathigam is the eighty-fifth pathigam in the Second Thirumurai, set to the tune of Piyanthaikandarap. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. On the fourteenth day of the month, at dawn, The two months, Jupiter and Saturn, along with the serpent planets, will surely bring good things; good things will happen to devotees where there are sweet-smelling rice fields, jasmine, and abundant gold. The divine sage, the ascetic born in Piranmapuram, where the Vedas originated, has sung a garland of words so that the planets and days do not cause harm to devotees.

“Those who recite these verses will rule the heavens; this is our command.

“Thus, Thirugnanasambandhar composed this pathigam. Let us continue to ponder the explanation of the verses of this pathigam.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam by Deivasekkizhar Peruman, Volume 686, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandhar composed the Kolaru pathigam. This pathigam is the eighty-fifth pathigam in the Second Thirumurai, set to the tune of Piyanthaikandaram. This pathigam is also included in the Agathiyar Thevara Thirattu. Kayappakkam Sadasiva Chettiyar has written commentaries for the pathigams compiled in the Agathiyar Thevara Thirattu.

Kayappakkam Sadasiva Chettiyar taught Periya Puranam to Sivakavimani C.K. Subramania Mudaliar, the commentator of Periya Puranam. Kayappakkam Sadasiva Chettiyar attained divine grace by performing Shiva Puja in strict accordance with Agamic principles and by ceaselessly reciting and understanding the twelve Thirumurais many times. He was skilled in delivering discourses on Periya Puranam. This great personality stayed in Coimbatore for four years, teaching and explaining Periya Puranam. Sivakavimani Ayya, who received direct instruction from this venerable master, took notes at that time.

These notes later proved to be of immense help to Sivakavimani Ayya in publishing a comprehensive commentary on Periya Puranam.

Therefore, we can reflect a little on the explanation of the verses of this pathigam by combining the explanations written by Kayappakkam Sadasiva Chettiyar, the guru of our Periya Puranam commentator Sivakavimani Ayya, and the insightful commentary provided by Sivakavimani Ayya. The first verse of this pathigam is as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. “Veyuru Thozhi Pangan Vidamunda Kandhan miga nalla veenai thadavi Maasaru Thingal Gangai mudimel anindhu en ullamE pugundha adhanal Gnayiru Thingal Sevvai Pudhan Vyazhan Velli Sani Pambu irandum udanE Aasaru nalla nalla avai nalla nalla Adiyar avarkku migavE.” This is the first verse. Thirugnanasambandhar composed this pathigam, beginning with Umaiyammaiyar, calling the Lord “Veyuru Thozhi Pangan,” meaning the Lord who has Umaiyammaiyar, whose shoulders resemble bamboo, on His left side.

Additionally, Thirugnanasambandhar sang in each verse about the Lord residing with the Mother. He said that because the Lord, who has Umaiyammaiyar with bamboo-like shoulders on His left side and whose throat is adorned with the poison He drank, gently plays the excellent veena, and wears the flawless moon and the Ganga on His head, entered my heart—meaning, because He took residence in my heart—the Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, and the two serpent planets, Rahu and Ketu, Thirugnanasambandhar declares that these planets will cause no harm to devotees and will instead be benevolent towards them. When ThiruNavukkarasu Peruman raised the objection to Thirugnanasambandhar that the days and planets were not in a favorable state, Thirugnanasambandhar composed this pathigam as a reply.

Therefore, in the very first verse, Thirugnanasambandhar, using the nine planets and seven days, declares that they will only bring good things to devotees. It is because of this declaration that this pathigam came to be known as Kolaru pathigam, signifying that the days and planets are subservient to the Lord’s command. How can they be good to devotees? Our Nayanmars are all those who have transcended the senses and sought refuge in the feet of Shiva, thereby severing the cycle of birth and death. All the Thirutthondar Nayanmars are capable of experiencing the immaculate turiyatita state even in a waking state. Understanding this requires direct instruction from wise teachers; their meanings must be learned and comprehended from a guru.

Therefore, the Thirutthondar Nayanmars stand in such a state. They have no actions of their own but are solely agents of Shiva’s will. They are capable of doing everything, in accordance with the saying, “He creates for His devotees.” Therefore, if even the foremost deities seek the commands of these Thirutthondar, then what can these ordinary days and planets do to the Thirutthondar? This is the underlying meaning. In this verse, Thirugnanasambandhar concisely included the seven days, starting with “Gnayiru Thingal,” and the nine planets, demonstrating his divine poetic skill. That these great and extensive powers of the planets and days were subdued and made to serve is a testament to Thirugnanasambandhar’s grace.

The harm caused by these planets will cease for devotees. If it means that the harm caused by these will cease for devotees, what does it imply? It means that even the harms caused by them will turn into benefits. This is because, according to the Satkaryavada (the theory of pre-existence of effect in cause) accepted by Saivism, existing things have no destruction.

Therefore, the harms caused by these planets and days will transform into benefits. For the planets and days themselves, harm will also cease.

Moreover, unlike for others, they will bring only good benefits to devotees; this is its meaning. This also contains the subtlety of the upcoming historical events. “Aasu Arudhal” (removal of blemish) refers to the incident in Madurai when the Jains set fire to the monastery where Thirugnanasambandhar resided, but it did not affect him at all.

Therefore, the phrase “Aasu Arudhal” implicitly contains this historical outcome. Next comes “Nallana Agum” (will become good). In Madurai, the Jains are defeated in the three debates – Suravadam (fever debate), Analvadam (fire debate), and Punalvadam (water debate) – and Saivism triumphs.

Thus, “Nallana Adhal” (becoming good) encompasses this historical reference. With the removal of Jainism, the Pandya king and the people of the Pandya country embraced the sacred path of Saivism and applied holy ash.

Therefore, Saivism is about to gain three great devotees: the Pandya queen, the minister, and the king. This verse implicitly conveys all these historical events. This verse states that the Lord plays an excellent veena. This phrase refers to the Lord creating the world by producing sound through the veena.

Therefore, the Lord playing the veena signifies creation. The fourth Thirumurai, 112th pathigam, seventh verse, composed by ThiruNavukkarasu Peruman, states: “When the vast oceans overflow and the universe perishes, when Brahma too departs and his body is submerged, and the dark-colored Vishnu’s body is also gone, our Lord, holding the skull, plays an excellent veena, standing on the ocean.” Therefore, the meaning here is that the Lord plays the sound of the veena to bring about the re-creation of the world after dissolution. It is a Saiva tradition to state that during dissolution, the Lord plays the veena, signifying the first manifestation of Pure Maya as sound, to bring forth the world that had merged within Him.

Therefore, just as “veena thadavi” (playing the veena) signifies re-creation after dissolution, here it also implies the dissolution of opposing religions, specifically the removal of Jain impurities, and the re-creation of Saivism. It is mentioned here that all these events occur due to the Lord’s grace. This is based on the state of losing one’s ego. Sekkizhar Peruman has explained this very idea to us by saying, “If we worship the feet of our Lord, no harm will befall us.”

Therefore, the days and planets are good for the Thirutthondar, the devotees of Shiva, and thus they are also good for themselves; this is the implicit meaning.

Astrology texts generally specify which days, or rather, constellations, should be avoided for travel. There is an astrology text called “Jyotisha Graha Chintamani” which contains a verse under the heading “Kooda Naal” (inauspicious days): “Aathirai Parani Karthikai Ayilyam Muppooram Kettai Theethuru Visakam Sothi Chittirai Magam Eeraarum Maathanam Kondaar Thaaraar Vazhinadai Pattaar Meelaar Paaythanil Patuththaar Theraar.” Sivakavimani Ayya has cited this verse from “Jyotisha Graha Chintamani” under the heading “Kooda Naal” in his commentary here.

Therefore, in this verse, the numbers nine, one, seven, eighteen, and six appear. These are numerical references to the inauspicious days or constellations for travel. Bharani, Karthigai, Thiruvaathirai, Ayilyam, Magam, Pooram, Chithirai, Swathi, Visakam, Kettai, Pooradam, Poorattathi are considered inauspicious constellations for travel. The verse mentions nine, one, and so on. Generally, counting starts from Ashwini, but there is also a tradition of starting from Krithikai. If we count Krithikai as one, then nine refers to the Pooram constellation, one to Krithikai, seven to Ayilyam, and eighteen to Pooradam.

Therefore, these four constellations correspond to nine, one, seven, and eighteen. The number six then refers to the days that accompany it, meaning the remaining constellations not previously mentioned, such as Magam, Kettai, Bharani, Swathi, Visakam, Aathirai, and Chithirai. This signifies the twelve inauspicious days we have already discussed. There is another way to denote these constellations. According to Kayappakkam Sadasiva Chettiyar’s commentary, nine refers to the Ayilya constellation, ten to Magam, sixteen to Visakam, eighteen to Kettai, and six to Thiruvaathirai. “Udanaya Naalkal” (accompanying days) refers to the other seven days, totaling these twelve constellations.

There are various ways of counting them. However, Thirugnanasambandhar’s divine word states that all such days will bring only good to devotees.

There is another historical event associated with this pathigam and our nation, India. It is a contemporary history. In August 1947, according to the English calendar, legal arrangements were underway to grant India independence.

At that time, Governor-General Mountbatten called Jawaharlal Nehru and asked how India would symbolically receive its independence. Nehru was confused about what symbol to use to receive independence. Nehru sought advice from the elder statesman C. Rajagopalachari. Rajarishi Chakravarti Rajagopalachari explained how the tradition of assuming governmental responsibility and how a new king takes office was observed in India, especially in Tamil Nadu. The Rajaguru would present the Sceptre to the newly appointed king, thereby signifying the transfer of power.

Therefore, we should similarly receive a Sceptre from the British through one of our gurus, which would symbolize the transfer of power from the British to us, he advised. Nehru agreed. Time was short. Rajagopalachari contacted the Thiruvavaduthurai Adheenam, one of the ancient Saiva Adheenams in Tamil Nadu, belonging to the Thirukailaya Paramparai Sri Meykanda Devanayanar Santhanam, and conveyed this news. This message was submitted to the then Gurumaha Sannidhanam.

At that time, Sri-la-Sri Ambalavana Desika Paramacharyar Swamigal was ruling as the twentieth Gurumaha Sannidhanam of Thiruvavaduthurai Adheenam. Rajaji requested them to perform the auspicious ceremonies for the transfer of power in India.

At that moment, the Gurumaha Sannidhanam was suffering from a severe fever but agreed to perform the event. The Adheenam instructed Chennai UMID Pangaru Chettiar Jewellery, which was famous at the time, to make a silver Sceptre plated with gold, engraved with Saiva symbols. The Sceptre was prepared. The Gurumaha Sannidhanam summoned Sri Math Kumaraswami Thambiran, who was then the junior pontiff (Thambiran Swamigal) of the Adheenam, handed him the Sceptre, and commanded him, along with the Oduvars and the renowned Nadaswaram artist Thiruvavaduthurai Rajarathinam Pillai, to proceed to Delhi.

At that time, the Oduvamurthigal submitted a request to Sri-la-Sri Gurumaha Sannidhanam of Thiruvavaduthurai, asking which pathigam should be recited entirely when receiving the Sceptre during the transfer of power. In response, the Thiruvavaduthurai Gurumaha Sannidhanam commanded that the Kolaru pathigam, beginning with “Veyuru Thozhi Pangan,” should be recited in its entirety. He commanded that the entire pathigam beginning with “Veyuru Thozhi Pangan,” known as Kolaru pathigam, should be recited. Thirugnanasambandhar’s divine word states that if this pathigam is recited, the planets in the sky will always bring good to us.

Therefore, he ordered that this pathigam be recited. In a private airplane arranged by the wise C. Rajagopalachari, the Thiruvavaduthurai Thambiran Swamigal, the Oduvamurthigal, and Thiruvavaduthurai Rajarathinam Pillai all traveled to Delhi. On August 15, 1947, at midnight, as India awaited the golden moment of liberation from slavery, the Thiruvavaduthurai junior pontiff, Thambiran Swamigal, received the Sceptre from Mountbatten, which had been blessed and sent by the Thiruvavaduthurai Adheenam Gurumaha Sannidhanam. The junior pontiff of Thiruvavaduthurai Adheenam, Thambiran Swamigal, received the scepter from Mountbatten. The Oduvamurthigal purified the scepter with holy water and then fully recited the Kolaru Thevaram pathigam, which begins with “Veyuru Thozhi Pangan Vidamunda Kandhan.” As he finished reciting the last line of the eleventh verse, “Adiyaragal vaanila arasaazhvar aanai namathe” (Our devotees will rule the heavens, this is our command), Sri Thambiran Swamigal handed the scepter to Nehru.

This event took place with the accompanying music of the Nadaswara Chakravarti Thiruvavaduthurai Rajarathinam Pillai. A black and white photograph of this event still exists in the Thiruvavaduthurai Adheenam monastery. The photograph is dated August 15, 1947, and shows Nehru holding the scepter, along with Sri-la-Sri Thambiran Swamigal of Thiruvavaduthurai Adheenam.

Therefore, it is a very important point that this pathigam, composed by Thirugnanasambandhar, was recited when India attained political independence.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandhar composed this pathigam both as a reply to ThiruNavukkarasu Peruman and as a means of seeking the grace of the Lord. From Thirumaraikadu, also known as Vedharanyam, Pillaiyar’s journey to the Pandya country is about to begin.

“These are truly magnificent coastal landscapes. Even today, these areas with sand mountains and rain are worth seeing. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who incarnated in Sirkazhi, arrives at Thiruvagathiyanpalli, located in this area. He reaches Thiruvagathiyanpalli, the one hundred and twenty-sixth temple on the south bank of the Kaveri. This is the place where Agastya performed penance to witness the Lord’s marriage.

“Hence, it is known as Agathiyanpalli. An idol of Agastya Peruman is installed and worshipped in the temple. The Lord’s name is Agasteeswarar, and the Goddesses’ names are Bagampiriyal and Mangai Nayaki. Agastya Theertham, Agni Theertham, the ocean Theertham, Agni Pushkarani, and Yama Theertham are the sacred waters.

“The Lord faces east, and the Goddess faces west. This temple is located near Nagapattinam, south of Vedharanyam, and close to Kodiyakkarai. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who journeyed here, composed a pathigam. It is the seventy-sixth pathigam of the second Thirumurai. The pathigam is composed in Kantharappann. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam.

“Those whose minds sing praises of Agathiyanpalli, where our Lord danced, adorned with a garland of withered skulls, illuminating the deep darkness of the night with the lofty Kolliv Vilakku, will have no sin.” “The sins of those who are able to sing this garland of praises, composed by the Tamil Gnanasambandan of great fame, who flourishes with the world, regarding the Lord with the good weapon, who resides in Agathiyanpalli, surrounded by groves where great peacocks dwell, will vanish.”

“Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having bowed and worshipped at Agathiyanpalli, proceeds to Thirukkodi Kulagar, surrounded by sand dunes where clouds reside, with all the devotees accompanying him. This temple is near Vedharanyam. The pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman in worship of Thirukkodikkuzhagar is not available to us. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing: “Having worshipped Thirukkadikkulam, where the Lord with an eye on his forehead rejoices, and having praised the esteemed Thiruidumbavanam, he journeys on, worshipping other lands filled with joy and singing melodious Tamil praises.” This is the six hundred and twenty-third verse. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships Thirukkadikkulam, where the Lord with an eye on his forehead, rejoices. Thirukkadikkulam is the one hundred and ninth temple on the south bank of the Kaveri.

“The Lord’s name is Karpaganathar. Accordingly, this temple is known as Karpaganathar Temple, Karpaganar Temple, and Karpaganar Kulam, associated with the Lord’s name. Karpagavin. This name was given to the temple due to the story of Ganesha worshipping the Lord here and receiving a mango. This Ganesha idol is located outside the temple, in the southwest corner. The Goddess’s name is Soundariya Nayaki (Balasoundari).

“The Palmaram is the sacred tree. Vinayaka Theertham and Kadikkulam are the sacred waters.

“The Lord manifests as a self-manifested Lingam. In this temple, the main deity, Lord Shiva, manifests with eight-faced facets. It is considered auspicious to offer butter as a donation in this temple. The temple’s ancient history states that Rama worshipped Karpaga Vinayagar and Karpaganathar here before building the bridge across the Sethu Ocean.

“Accordingly, a Kodandarama temple is located near this temple. A Brahmin brought the ashes for his father’s obsequies. The temple’s ancient history states that the ashes turned into Konrai flowers upon arriving at this place. The demon Karthikajuran worshipped the Lord of this temple and received boons.

“Here, the Lord readily granted boons like a wish-fulfilling tree whenever he desired them.

“Therefore, he built a temple and worshipped there.

“Thus, the Lord of this temple is named Karpaganathar. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who journeyed here, composed a pathigam. It is the one hundred and fourth pathigam of the second Thirumurai, composed in Nattaraga Pann. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: “Those devotees who bow their heads and fall at the feet of Karpaga, who resides in Kadikkulam, surrounded by dense flower groves where he is adorned with a sacred thread of sacred ash on his body, a skin, and a tiger skin as a garment, and where anklets chime on his legs when he walks among the hills, will not be covered by past karma.” “Those who can sing these garlands of beautiful Tamil praises, filled with sweet fragrance, composed by Sambandhan, the King of glorious Tharangai, where wealth abounds, about the Lord who resides in Kadikkulam, where the sea with its waves comes and churns, will reside with the Lord.” Thiruchitrambalam.

“The note of this pathigam is that those who worship Karpaga, who resides in Kadikkulam, will not be affected by karma, and those who sing praises of him will become virtuous.

“Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having bowed and worshipped at Thirukkadikkulam, journeys to Thiruidumbavanam and worships the Lord there. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises the Lord who resides in that temple, using the refrain, “This is Idumbavanam.” Thiruidumbavanam is on the south bank of the Kaveri, the one hundredth and. The eighth temple. This is the temple where the demon Idumba worshipped and received boons. Kunrur, near Idumba’s capital, is mentioned along with it in the pathigam.

“Here, the white-colored White Vinayaka is worshipped prominently. The Lord’s bridal form can be seen behind the main deity, Moolattanathar. This is the place where the Lord appeared to Agastya. The Lord’s name is Sarkunanathar. The Goddess’s name is Mangalanayaki.

“The Lord is also known as Sarkuneswarar, Manakkolanathar, Kalyaneswarar, and Idumbavananeswarar. The Goddess is known as Mangalavalli and Kalyaneswari. Brahma Theertham, Agastya Theertham, Yama Theertham, Samaj Pushkarani, and Eka Theertham are the sacred waters. Since Bhima married Idumbai, the sister of Idumba. Vyasa Muni told the Pandavas that this temple, where the Lord blessed Idumbai, would henceforth be known as Idumbavanam. This is the story from the Puranas.

“The village of Idumba is Kunrur, which is next to this temple. This temple also has other names such as Vilvavanam, Sarkunesapuram, Mangalanayakipuram, and Manakkolanagar. It is one of the places for ancestral liberation.

“Therefore, this temple is very special for performing ancestral rites. Inscriptions state that Maratha kings made many endowments to this temple. This temple is located on the Muthupettai-Vedharanyam road. It can also be reached from Thiruthuraipoondi on the way to Thondiyakkadu. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who journeyed to this temple, composed a pathigam. It is the seventeenth pathigam of the first Thirumurai.

“The pathigam is composed in Nattappadai Pann. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: “This is Idumbavanam, the abode of the Lord, where ascetic sages of the lineage worship, and where young men, delighting with fragrant maidens, scatter flowers, and where wealth-filled conch shells rise from the sea, and where a demon, furious and strong, resides in the mountain.” “The sins of those who recite the verses spoken by the wise Sambandan from Kaliyur, who is rooted in the earth, about the Lord of Idumbavanam, where the mighty waves of the sea crash against the shore of the tall mansions of Kunrur, will vanish.” Thiruchitrambalam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman used “This is Idumbavanam, the abode of the Lord” as a refrain throughout the verses of this pathigam. From Idumbavanam, on his way to the Pandya country. Having visited temples such as Thillai Vilagam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrives at Thiruvusathanam.

“Sekkizhar Peruman then continues to sing: Sekkizhar Peruman composes two verses: “Having worshipped the feet of the Lord of the Devas at Thiruvusathanam, he sang a profound Tamil pathigam, praising him greatly, and with immense love, along with countless devotees who sever evil karma and attachments, he worshipped other temples and approached. Having crossed the dark, marshy tracts and the joyful coastal plains, he journeyed towards the southwest of the prosperous water-rich country, through paths filled with thriving fields of paddy, dense coconut groves, and close-growing areca palms.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman journeyed to Thiruvusathanam and composed a pathigam, specifically narrating the history of Thirumal worshipping the Lord at this site. Thiruvusathanam is the one hundred and seventh temple on the south bank of the Kaveri. This place is also known as Thirukkoilur. It is the place where Rama, Lakshmana, Jambavan, Sugriva, Hanuman, and others worshipped the Lord. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has sung about this in the first verse of the pathigam he composed for this temple.

“Since Sri Rama received mantra initiation here, the Lord is named Mantrapooriswarar. The name of this place also came from the same reason. Usavuthal means to inquire. Since Sri Rama received mantra initiation and inquired here, this place is named Thiruvusathanam. Since this place was a forest with many mango trees, it is also known as Soothavanam.

“The Lord is also known as Soothavaneswarar. The Shivlinga form is a white, self-manifested deity. This temple can be reached from Thanjavur, Thiruthuraipoondi, Vedharanyam, Mannargudi, Pattukkottai, and other towns. The Goddess’s name is Periya Nayaki (Brihan Nayaki). Theerthams are Hanuman Theertham, Markandeya Theertham, and Gautama Theertham. Currently, it is popularly known as Koilur.

“Since it is near Muthupettai, it is called Muthupettai Koilur. According to temple history, Rama received mantra initiation from the Lord in this temple before building the Sethu bridge.

“Also, because Rama inquired (usaviya) the Lord Shiva of this temple about the methods for building a bridge across the sea, this temple is named Usathanam. As evidence for this temple’s history, nearby villages include Rama Temple, Sambavan Stream, Hanuman Forest, Sugriva Pettai, and Thambi. Nallan Pattinam and other villages are located here.

“The Lord has shown the dance to Vishwamitra here. On the sanctum wall, Jvarahareshwarar appears with three faces and three feet. There are Lingams worshipped by Varuna, Rama, and Markandeya in the temple. There are inscriptions from the periods of Vikrama Chola, Kulothunga III, and Sundara Pandya. In the inscriptions, the Lord is referred to as Thiru Usathanamudaiya Nayanar and the Goddess as Periya Nachiyar. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who journeyed to this temple, composed a pathigam.

“It is the thirty-third pathigam of the third Thirumurai, composed in Kollipann. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: “Thambi, the one who slept in water, the long.” “Jambavan, Sugriva, and Hanuman worshipped our glorious Lord who consumed the dark poison and protected all, residing in Thiruvusathanam. Those who are skilled in the beautiful Tamil spoken by Sambandan, who understands the truth about Thiruvusathanam, where the water of the rivers turns and the fertile fields of Pugazhi are surrounded by the sea, will reach the good path without old age or decay.” Thiruchitrambalam.

“Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having bowed and worshipped at Thiruvusathanam, continues his pilgrimage towards the Pandya country. Sekkizhar Peruman elaborately describes this journey.

“We shall proceed with our contemplation.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Six Hundred Eighty-Nine, authored by Theivasekkizhar Peruman, Vambaravari Vandam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Purana. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman continues his journey from Thiruvusathanam. These are areas filled with marshlands located on the coast. From Thiruvusathanam, Pillaiyar travels towards the southwest of the Chola country. This area is the southern, coastal part of the Chola country.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman crosses these land areas, which are marshlands and coastal regions. The Chola country is a land where forests and barren lands were transformed into fertile agricultural regions. The Chola kings transformed this country into a water-rich land, an agricultural land. The great Chola kings performed many great deeds such as cutting down and clearing forests, leveling barren lands, digging canals, and settling people, thus transforming this water-rich Ponni country into a prosperous land. We can well understand these facts from inscriptions, historical records, and the names of countries, villages, rivers, and canals. Our revered teacher, Sekkizhar Peruman, during his ministerial tenure and the reign of Anabaya Chola, also performed many such deeds.

We can understand through true history that many great emperors like the subsequent Kulothunga Chola, Gangaikonda Chola, and Rajaraja also performed such great deeds.

Thus, the Chola country, also known as the Kaveri country, possessed refined excellences. From here, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman journeys towards the southwest. On both sides, there are vast fields of paddy, known as Salai, everywhere. All around, dense coconut trees grow with their bunches of nuts, and areca nut trees surround them. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman journeys through such a path in the agricultural land. Sekkizhar Peruman mentions “Tadamsali” in this verse, which is a type of paddy.

It is also called “Periya Chennel” (large red paddy). “Perunel” is another name for it. Thirunavukkarasar Peruman has sung about the types of paddy cultivated in this region in a pathigam: “The Lord of Arur, adorned with fertile fields, knows within his heart large red paddy, long bamboo paddy, fragrant paddy, and divine paddy.” The presence of paddy, coconut, and areca nuts all around is a characteristic of agricultural land. These fields appear as if the agricultural land itself is adorned with them as garments. In the previous verses, Sekkizhar Peruman described the richness and appearance of the coastal regions of the Chola country.

Now, he describes and presents to us the agricultural regions.

Similarly, he will now show us the pastoral regions.

Similarly, as Pillaiyar journeys to Madurai, also known as Thiru Alavai, through the historical narrative of the Purana, the poetic skill of Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman, who describes and displays the nature and wealth of these lands along the way, is truly commendable. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing: “Conches everywhere in the fields, paddy and sugarcane everywhere, fragrant lotus ponds everywhere, the shouts of farmers everywhere, and these joyful gatherings of flowers everywhere. Women bathing in the ponds, their body art washing away everywhere. Brahmins reciting Vedas everywhere in their monasteries, and devotees everywhere, and weddings everywhere in the homes, and continuous sounds of festivals everywhere in the good towns. Having crossed these water-rich lands, he passed through long desolate stretches with small bushes, dark groves of jasmine, and lands with strong fragrant soil. He journeyed through the barren lands of archers who love battle, and reached the glorious good Pandya country.”

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing three verses describing Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s journey across the coastal, agricultural, and pastoral lands of the Chola country, reaching the southern Pandya country. Sekkizhar Peruman, while describing the agricultural land, sings that there are fields filled with conches, and in those fields, there is paddy, and also sugarcane. He sings that conches are everywhere in the fields. He sings that paddy and sugarcane are cultivated there. “Kalai Karumbu” is a type of sugarcane. “Kalai” refers to a type of sugarcane that is thick and tall like bamboo.

Now, he sings “Kongu engu nirai kamalam.” “Kongu” means fragrance. The smaller fragrant flowers. There is the fragrance of other flowers, but more than that, there is the intense fragrance of the lotuses blooming in the ponds. Even if other flowers like water lilies and night lotuses are present in a pond, ponds are generally referred to as lotus ponds because of their prominence and special quality.

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman describes. With sugarcane groves and lotus ponds, farmers are engaged in agriculture there. They are making sounds and singing songs as they cultivate. This sound, although it might seem meaningless to those listening from afar, as one gets closer, all those sounds become meaningful songs. In this verse, Sekkizhar Peruman skillfully incorporates the staple foods of the agricultural land—paddy and sugarcane—and water from the cool, fragrant ponds, along with the farmers, the people of the agricultural land, and the lotus, the flower of the agricultural land, as the thematic elements. His poetic finesse in presenting all these constituent elements of the agricultural land, including the irrigation canals crucial for cultivation and the various types of cultivation, in a single verse, is truly admirable.

Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing that women are bathing in the ponds. These ponds are located near the village. The ponds mentioned earlier were located outside the village, amidst the fields in the agricultural land.

Therefore, in these ponds near the village, women are bathing. These are ponds used by the people. The ponds mentioned in the previous verse were used for agricultural work. In these ponds, which are near urban areas, women are bathing.

Therefore, the designs drawn on their bodies with red henna paste dissolve in the water, changing its color. In the open spaces in the outskirts of the towns, there are places where students learning the Vedas recite them. There are Vedic schools. There are sacrificial halls where yagnas are performed. There are Saivite monasteries. Vedic recitation places and teaching places are charitable institutions and places of dharma.

Therefore, the purushartha (goal of human life) of dharma is indicated here. Sekkizhar Peruman sings that there are sacrificial halls. Sacrificial halls are a cause for rain.

Thus, when it rains, the prosperity of the town increases.

Therefore, this indicates artha (wealth), the second purushartha. Women bathing in the ponds signify kama (desire), the third purushartha. There are devotees, which signifies the fourth purushartha.

Thus, in all these areas, the four purusharthas of dharma, artha, kama, and moksha flourish, as Sekkizhar Peruman sings. There are devotees, which refers to the fourth purushartha.

Thus, these regions are places where the four purusharthas of dharma, artha, kama, and moksha flourish, as Sekkizhar Peruman sings. These places, thus described, are currently considered to be the areas around Pudukkottai.

Therefore, the Peruman refers to them as “good towns,” because these towns are places that offer all four of the aforementioned purusharthas, the four aims of human life. As mentioned earlier, these areas extend to Pudukkottai and the present-day Karaikudi, known as Chettinad. As a result of the divine intention and sacred words of the guru, Sekkizhar Peruman’s blessings have led to these places becoming abodes where great acts of charity have continuously flourished, and where the Chettinad merchants in this region have established various Saivite charitable institutions everywhere. The Chettinad people who lived in this region, wherever they went in the world, established charitable institutions and temples, and even today, they continue to possess that quality of performing great deeds of righteousness.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman journeys across the water-rich agricultural land, then across the pastoral lands fragrant with jasmine buds, and through the lands inhabited by bow-wielding warriors, which are bordering on barren lands. The regions being described now are forest and forest-like areas, which are pastoral lands. These are not dense forests but small forested areas. These regions are inhabited by warriors who seek battle. These areas were sometimes under the control of great kings and at other times independent, functioning as separate small kingdoms.

Therefore, these areas were feudal states ruled by the local chieftains. These chieftains, known variously as Kongar, Maravar, and Kurumbar, often defied and fought against the great kings, causing trouble at various times, as we find in historical records. It was also customary for great kings to use these fortifications as border guards to prevent internal wars.

Therefore, the Maravars and other minor kings living in these areas would sometimes fight against the great kings and sometimes assist them in war. This region was under the rule of such minor kings, similar to what are called ‘warrior tribes’. Seeking battle is a characteristic of warriors, so Sekkizhar Peruman refers to it as the region where bow-wielding Maravars who seek battle reside. Even today, people in this region identify themselves as Maravars. We learn from many historical texts that they are the indigenous people of these lands. This region, unlike the water-rich Chola country with its vast irrigated fields, It is an area with small dry land parcels and small villages.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman journeys through these areas, inhabited by bow-wielding warriors who seek battle, and reaches the glorious, good southern Pandya country. We shall continue our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Six Hundred Ninety, authored by Theivasekkizhar Peruman, Vambara Vari Vandum, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Purana. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reaches the good southern Pandya country. In the Pandya country, the first temple Thirugnanasambandha Peruman visited on his pilgrimage was Thirukkodunkundram, also known as Piranmalai. Sekkizhar Peruman describes it as follows: “Having crossed many rivers flowing from fragrant flower-filled mountainsides, having ascended and descended many difficult paths where young deer bounded among thorny bushes, he reached Thirukkodunkundram, where the Lord with fragrant Konrai in his matted locks rejoices.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman crosses many rivers and enters the Pandya country. These rivers are those that carry heaps of flowers, carried by their waves, and deposit them on both banks.

These include the Thenvellarr, also known as the Swetha River, the Pamba River, and its many tributaries, and other rivers that flow in these regions. Identifying the fords to cross these rivers is extremely difficult.

Similarly, crossing them and ascending the other bank is also very difficult. However, Pillaiyar’s journey in these regions proceeds very quickly. Male deer are called ‘kalai’. This region is where such male deer, along with their female deer and fawns, leap and gather in herds. Having traversed such regions. He reaches the temple of Piranmalai, known as Thirukkodunkundram.

This Piranmalai is situated amidst many mountains. It is one of the fourteen temples in the Pandya country praised in song. It is a temple where the Lord resides with the name Kodunkundranathar. This is the first temple worshipped by Pillaiyar in the Pandya country. Sekkizhar Peruman sings: “Having worshipped the coral hill, the sacred hill, where the Lord who flayed the elephant skin resides delightfully in Kodunkundram, and having sung ancient Tamil praises, he crossed long mountains, dense forests, and prosperous lands, and reached the ancient city of Madurai, whose walls touch the moon.” In the six hundred and thirtieth verse, Peruman sings that Pillaiyar, having worshipped Kodunkundram, crossed mountains and forests. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrives at the sacred city of Madurai.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships Lord Shiva, who resides in Thirukkodunkundram, the coral hill, and sings pathigams.

Then, departing from there, he crosses long mountains, dense forests, and prosperous lands to reach Madurai. That is, he crosses long mountains, vast forests, and rich countries to reach Madurai. These places, referred to here as “long mountains,” are the Alagar Malai, Solai Malai, Sirumalai, and other mountainous regions. “Patkann” refers to the dense forests that follow these mountains. “Nirainadu” refers to the prosperous, agricultural regions with inhabitants, which follow those forests. The parts of the country.

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman sings about these three types of landscapes—the mountainous regions, the vast forests of the pastoral lands, and the agricultural lands—that lie between Thirukkodunkundram and Madurai. Even today, these regions retain the same characteristics and flourish. Having traversed these, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrives at the ancient city of Madurai. The walls of the great city of Madurai are tall and extended, reaching up to the moon. At the same time that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrives near this region of Madurai, bad dreams and ill omens appear to the Jains in Madurai.

At this point, Shekkizhar Peruman begins to describe the evil dreams and bad omens that occurred to the Jains in Madurai, when they came to settle in the eight great hills surrounding the city. He recounts that thousands of Jains had established their schools and lived in these eight hills, spreading their religion. The Jains resided in places like Anaipalamalai and other locations among these eight hills surrounding Madurai. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, in his sacred verses, refers to these Jains as ‘inferior ones.’ The Thiruvilaiyadal Puranam, in the chapter titled ‘The Elephant’s Arrow,’ lists these eight hills as Anjanam, Kavunjam, Govardhanam, Thirikoodam, Kanchi, Kunjarasaiyam, Hemakoodam, and Vindham. Paranjothiyar describes how these hills, still present around Madurai today as Nagamalai, Pasumalai, Panrimalai, and Yanaimalai, came to be. The Thiruvilaiyadal Puranam narrates how, due to actions contrary to Shiva’s path, various beings like cows, pigs, elephants, and serpents were sent to destroy Madurai.

However, the Lord protected Madurai by defeating them.

Thus, the serpent, the cow, the pig, and the elephant were all vanquished and fell as stone mountains around Madurai. The Thiruvilaiyadal Puranam states that these form the eight mountains surrounding Madurai. These events belong to ancient times. Just as these mountains were used by sages who opposed Shiva’s path, during the period of this sacred history, they served the Jains who were outside Shiva’s path. The Jains resided on these hills, seeking their own destruction. Sages in ancient times, opposing Shiva’s path, tried to harm Shaivism using these mountains.

Later, Jains resided on these mountains, and attempted to diminish Shaivism. However, both of them were destroyed, and Shaivism remained, firmly established. Even today, the descendants of those who came from foreign lands, representing external religions, occupy these mountains and continue to try to undermine the Vedic path.

Thus, evil dreams and bad omens appear to the Jains residing in these eight great hills around Madurai. Evil dreams occur in the dream state (svapna avastha), while omens are signals seen in the waking state (jagrat avastha). Both dreams and omens, indicate future events. It is true that dreams, caused by illness, past memories, and other factors, occur day and night.

However, do all such dreams indicate future events? Not necessarily. If it is the Lord’s will that future events, due to karma, be revealed beforehand, then such dreams and omens appear. These then become instruments that announce the results. Such evil dreams and bad omens occur to the Jains. In the places where Jains reside, in the caves where Jain gurus stay, and in the Ashoka trees and fortresses, owls, barn owls, and other evil birds fight among themselves, displaying these bad omens that are about to befall the Jains.

Owls and barn owls are types of birds that should not be seen or heard. These birds usually reside in crematories and deserts. They always indicate evil. Generally, the belief among us is that if a crow flies to the left, misfortune is imminent.

Similarly, owls and barn owls are birds that indicate evil events. Their eyes possess a high degree of fire (agni), thus they can see even in the dark of night, much like cats. These birds are inherently capable of foreseeing dark, death-related events and other impending misfortunes. They gather in Jain dwellings, fight among themselves, and reveal the impending destruction to the Jains. Jains carry peacock feathers and reed mats. These items, held in their hands, slip and fall to the ground on their own.

Their feet get entangled and they stumble. Their left eye twitches. Generally, a twitching left eye in men indicates a bad omen, and stumbling indicates a decrease in life energy in the body.

Therefore, a twitching left eye for men and a twitching right eye for women is considered inauspicious. This signifies an impending negative event. In men, the right side of the body is said to be strong, while the left side is less strong, being the feminine part. An eye twitch indicates a decrease in life energy.

Therefore, if an already weaker part further loses energy, it signifies destruction and impending sorrow. Even in the Ramayana, before Ravana came to the Parnasala, Sita’s right eye twitched, and in Ashokavana, while she was imprisoned, her left eye twitched.

Thus, such omens indicate future joys and sorrows. The Jains understand the destruction coming upon them, but they cannot comprehend its cause or how to avert it. Jain women become angry among themselves and cause disputes. Jain gurus also have differing opinions and harm each other, engaging in quarrels. They abandon the good qualities like patience prescribed in Jain scriptures, and their minds are filled with negative qualities like anger. The Jains, seeing these bad omens appearing everywhere they reside, communicate them among themselves.

The Jains residing outside Madurai, in places like Yanaimalai, and those within Madurai, all gather together in Madurai to report these evil dreams and bad omens to the Pandiya King. They go to meet the King of Madurai and tell him all the evil dreams they saw.

Let us go on reflecting. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, part six hundred ninety-one, authored by the divine sage Sekkizhar Peruman, from the Vambara Varivandu charukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. All the Jains in Madurai gather and go to the Pandiya King to recount the evil dreams and bad omens they experienced. They describe all the evil dreams they had. The Jains were well-versed in various arts and sciences, and thus they understood that these evil dreams would definitely bring them misfortune and suffering. The deity of the Jains is called Aruga Kadavul, who sits beneath an Ashoka tree.

They dreamt that the Aruga Kadavul, along with the Ashoka tree under which he sat, was uprooted and fell. The Jains dreamt that the Ashoka tree, which provided shade and a place to sit, fell upon the Aruga Kadavul. This signified that the Aruga Kadavul would be displaced, having no other place to reside, implying that Jainism would depart from the Pandiya kingdom.

Additionally, they dreamt that the Aruga devas, who hold the three umbrellas (mukkudai), rose, let their hands hang, and left the town. This indicated that the Jain deity, who had previously ruled there, was about to leave the place. This dream signified that the deity was moving very quickly to another place, as they dreamt. In that dream, everyone in the town saw the Jain deity leaving.

However, instead of following the deity, the townspeople rejoiced and remained in the town. Only the Jain deity left the town.

Therefore, this dream implies that Jainism would depart, and the people of Madurai and the Pandiya kingdom would embrace Shaivism, their ancient and former religion. This was conveyed to these Jains. There were also female ascetics in the Jain religion. Jain gurus would carry a water-pot (kundikai) filled with consecrated water. They dreamt that a Jain female ascetic broke the water-pot held by a Jain guru, tore the mat used by Jains, and ran away.

Therefore, this means that the Jains would abandon their religious affiliations and leave that place. They dreamt that Jain gurus came out of the caves where they resided, humiliated and disgraced, mounted on donkeys, and left the town. A donkey, therefore, symbolizes that Jain gurus would leave the town in defeat and disgrace, riding on donkeys, and they had these evil dreams.

Additionally, they dreamt that all the devotees of Shiva, who has an eye on his forehead and dances in the cremation ground, arrived in the Pandiya King’s city of Madurai. They dreamt that until now, they had conspired to prevent the devotees of Shiva, the God with the eye on his forehead, from entering Madurai, a place belonging to Shiva’s devotees.

Now, this situation had changed, and they saw in their dreams that they were being driven out, and Shiva’s devotees were returning to Madurai. They told this to the Pandiya King. They also said that they dreamt the Pandiya King was engulfed in a raging fire and then rose from it. This is a reference to the historical events where he suffered from fever and was later cured by the grace of Pillaiyar. The Jains dreamt all these things and reported them to the Pandiya King. The Jains, being well-versed in the arts and sciences, knew that these dreams would definitely bring them suffering and harm.

It was Shiva’s grace that announced these things beforehand. However, even though Shiva had forewarned the Jains of these misfortunes, they did not realize that these evils were the result of the harm they had inflicted upon Shaivism. If they had realized this, they could have sought and found a way to escape this evil.

But they did not do so and were ruined. What prevented them from doing so was their karma and the veil of their ego (aanavumalam). In the Kanda Puranam, Singamugan, Banukopan, and Iraniyan, all advise Surapadman. Murugaperuman, the God with six faces, himself directly reveals and instructs Surapadman.

But Surapadman does not listen to any of this and falls, along with his kinsmen. To be informed and to understand is the nature of a soul, but to act without understanding even after being informed is due to the strength of ego (aanavamala) and the state of karma, say the Gnana Sastras. These truths are conveyed here through these narratives. The Jains see some more things in their dreams. A very young calf comes and stomps on and disturbs the Jain assembly, causing all the Jains to scatter and run. Unable to stop it, afraid of it, and having no other place for refuge, no other shelter, they dreamt that the Jains climbed onto trees without shade, abandoning this earth.

This bull calf, a male calf, signifies a connection with Shiva. The male calf causing the Jains to flee in disarray is a sign of Pillaiyar’s arrival, symbolized by the young deer. Due to the actions of this calf, the Jains dreamt that they had no place to stand on earth and were climbing onto trees without shade.

Therefore, it means that they would no longer have any foothold on earth and would leave this earthly life. Trees without shade are a symbol of execution stakes (kalu maram). These dreams convey to the Jains the consequences of their debate with Pillaiyar, their defeat, their flight, and their eventual execution.

Thus, the Jains face such sorrows.

At the same time, good omens appear to the Empress Pandimadevi Mangaiyarkarasi Ammaiyar and the great Kulachirai Nayanar. Shekkizhar Peruman composes the six hundred forty-second and six hundred forty-third verses, stating that “In that state, to the Pandimadevi, a graceful woman of good Shaiva lineage, with swaying gait and broad hips resembling a coiled serpent, and to her true minister, auspicious omens appeared, bringing immense joy as a great premonition. When they experienced this heartfelt joy, they heard the words of those who came to announce the joyful news that the one who partook of the bright light of knowledge, who came to save the world, was arriving.” Shekkizhar Peruman composes the six hundred forty-second and six hundred forty-third verses. At the very moment when the Jains, convinced that the outcome of their dreams would surely bring them misfortune, felt sorrowful and even refrained from eating, wondering what to do, good omens appeared to Empress Mangaiyarkarasi and Kulachirai Nayanar. Empress Mangaiyarkarasi was a noble woman of good Shaiva lineage.

Shekkizhar Peruman beautifully praises her in the six hundred forty-second verse as “the Pandimadevi, a graceful woman of good Shaiva lineage, with swaying gait and broad hips resembling a coiled serpent.” The way Shekkizhar Peruman praises Ammaiyar in the six hundred forty-second verse shows the immense love he held for her sacred feet. Having spoken about Jainism, about the evil dreams and bad omens of the Jains, Shekkizhar Peruman is now about to speak of the glory of Shaivism. Out of this great joy, and for the Ammaiyar who was instrumental in it, he praises and glorifies her in this manner. It is very fitting to praise the help that caused the establishment of Shaivism to begin here, at this point, and it manifests in the divine words of the divine Shekkizhar Peruman. When praising Kulachirai Nayanar here, he praises him as a true minister.

A minister, Peruman, should ensure stability for the country and the government, without favoritism. Kulachirai Nayanar, the great one, provided such stability.

Therefore, Shekkizhar Peruman praises his truthfulness. Even if the king strayed from the path, Kulachirai Nayanar, as a minister, sought only truth and remained steadfast in the imperishable Shiva path. Shekkizhar Peruman refers to him as a true minister in this verse. To these two great individuals, good omens continue to appear. The good omens signifying that the previous state of dimness, where the glory of sacred ash was not recognized, would now be replaced by the establishment of sacred ash, rudraksha, and the panchakshara mantra, appeared to these two great individuals. Immeasurable These good omens show immense joy as a premonition.

While they were experiencing this joy within their hearts, and delighting in the good omens, the joyful news arrived to Empress Mangaiyarkarasi and Kulachirai Nayanar that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was approaching Madurai. Shekkizhar Peruman composes the six hundred forty-third verse: “When the great auspicious omens showing immense joy appeared, and their hearts rejoiced, they heard the words of those who came to announce the joyful news that the one who partook of the bright light of knowledge, who came to save the world, was arriving.” The term “bright light of knowledge” refers to Shiva Gnyanam. The knowledge that fosters light signifies the growth of Shiva’s essence within, as implied. Such is the flourishing knowledge, and Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who partook of it, is praised in this sacred verse as one who came to this world. “Ulagellam” (the entire world) is the first auspicious word given by the Lord for this Puranam, the Thiruthondar Puranam. The author has used it very beautifully in some places, and this is one of them.

In this important place, in this important sacred verse, the author praises Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, using the word “Ulagellam” given by the Lord, saying, “the one who partook of the bright light of knowledge for the entire world.” Thus, the messengers and those who came with Pillaiyar convey the good words that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is arriving, and hearing these joyful words, Empress Mangaiyarkarasi and Kulachirai Nayanar rejoiced more and more. Sivakavimani Ayya, who wrote the commentary on the Periya Puranam, has provided commentaries in seven parts. Of these, the fourth and fifth parts are extensive commentaries on the Puranam of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. With this sacred verse, Sivakavimani Ayya has concluded the fourth part of the Periya Puranam commentary.

Now, from the next sacred verse onwards, the fifth part of the Periya Puranam commentary is about to begin. Yesterday was the Guru Pooja day of Sekkizhar Peruman. We began our daily reflections on the Periya Puranam two years ago, on the day after Sekkizhar Peruman’s Guru Pooja. Today marks the completion of two years of continuous daily reflections on the Periya Puranam, and we are now continuing these reflections into the third year. Except for the period of Thiruvambavai Utsavam, we have continuously reflected on this work.

Similarly, we pray at the sacred feet of our Lord Sundaramurthy Swamigal, our Lord Nambiandar Nambigal, the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, and Sivakavimani Ayya, who commented on the Periya Puranam, that we may continue to reflect and complete this great Periya Puranam Yajna. We place this request at the sacred feet of our Lord Sundaramurthy Swamigal, our Lord Nambiandar Nambigal, the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, and Sivakavimani Ayya, who commented on the Periya Puranam.

We shall proceed with our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, part six hundred ninety-two, authored by the divine sage Sekkizhar Peruman, from the Vambara Varivandu charukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Hearing the news that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was approaching Madurai, Empress Mangaiyarkarasi and Kulachirai Nayanar rejoiced greatly. They generously bestowed upon those who brought this good news all that they desired and all that they themselves cherished. They gave lavishly, wishing that these bearers of good tidings should lack nothing. Both Pandimadevi and Kulachirai Nayanar stood in great joy, forgetting themselves.

Shekkizhar Peruman composes the verse: “Kulachirai, adorned with fragrant garlands, approached and bowed at the feet of Mangaiyarkarasi, and she said to him, ‘Our Lord, the one who partook of divine knowledge, is approaching. By his arrival here, we are saved. Go forth and welcome him with joy.’” Kulachirai Nayanar bows at the feet of Pandimadevi Mangaiyarkarasi. Addressing the minister Kulachirai Nayanar, who stands thus, Pandimadevi says, “Go forth to our Lord, the one who partook of the nectar of knowledge, and say that by his gracious arrival here, we are saved, and welcome Pillaiyar with joy.” This is what Pandimadevi says to Kulachirai Nayanar. Empress Mangaiyarasi refers to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as “Our Lord,” including the king and the minister, implying that he is the head of all. Ammaiyar’s wish on how to welcome Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is also revealed here, which we discern from her instructing the minister.

It is Ammaiyar’s wish that he be welcomed with the words, “We are saved.” Kulachirai Nayanar later elaborates on this extensively before Pillaiyar. When Pandimadevi said this, Kulachirai Nayanar, the great minister, bowed to Pandimadevi and quickly departed to welcome Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. This was the queen’s command, so he quickly departed from the palace, bowing and taking leave, to fulfill it. He hastened not only because it was the queen’s command, but also because he knew it would benefit the king. Although it wasn’t a direct royal decree, a minister’s duty is to act for the king’s good.

Thus, with such resolve and good intention, believing it would benefit both the king and the country, he hurried. He quickly traversed the many-storied streets of Madurai.

At the same time, Empress Mangaiyarkarasi departed from the palace to worship Thiru Alavai Sokkanathar. In the six hundred forty-seventh sacred verse, Shekkizhar Peruman sings: “Like a lotus-seated goddess, the queen, saying to her king that she wished to worship the Lord residing in Alavai, went with her attendants, making a solitary journey. She bowed to our Lord and stood, having received a good welcome.” Empress Mangaiyarkarasi shines like a lotus-seated goddess (Ambhuya malaral).

Here, the lotus refers to Umaiyamman, who is seated on the thousand-petaled lotus in the Dvadashantha great space. Umaiyamman, also known as Angaiyarkanni Ammai, is the first to worship Sokkanathar, who resides in Alavai.

Therefore, Empress Mangaiyarkarasi shines like Umaiyamman, who is seated on such a thousand-petaled lotus. She, the Empress Mangaiyarkarasi, informs the Pandiya King that she wishes to worship Sokkanathar, who resides in Alavai, and proceeds to the temple with her retinue. The king is not in agreement with this action. Empress Mangaiyarkarasi had been observing Shaiva practices subtly, unbeknownst to the king.

However, here it states that Pandimadevi informs the king that she is going to the Thiru Alavai temple. Although Jainism was prevalent in those days, and Shaivism was rare, Shaivism had not completely disappeared. The worship and services at the Thiru Alavai temple, dedicated to Madurai Sokkanathar, were carried out according to the circumstances of the time and were not entirely suppressed. There were many devotees in the Shiva temple, and while worship was not grand, it did occur, albeit rarely.

Therefore, the king did not entirely forbid or reject Pandimadevi’s occasional visits to the temple for worship and temple services. He did not issue a prohibition against such activities.

Thus, we must understand that Mangaiyarkarasi Perumatti informing the Pandiya King of her departure and going does not contradict the previously stated idea. Even though Pandimadevi said this, why did the king, as the ruler, not object but consent? That indicates his state of mind. As we saw earlier, Shiva’s grace contributed to this state of mind for the Pandiya King, ensuring that Shaivism was not completely destroyed.

Thus, the Pandimadevi, accompanied by her retinue of royal women, with security guards and other arrangements, reached the Thiru Alavai temple in a palanquin adorned with screens, and worshipped the Lord there. She offered thanks to Thiru Alavai Sokkanathar for granting Pillaiyar’s arrival in Madurai and praised him.

Now, Shekkizhar Peruman sings the sacred history of Pillaiyar’s arrival in Madurai: “Arriving in a beautiful pearl palanquin, he worships the Lord above. The lustrous white umbrella, like a crescent moon, casts its shade. Surrounded by a multitude of devotees adorned with radiant sacred ash, the one who partook of the nectar of divine knowledge, full of grace, approaches.” The six hundred forty-eighth sacred verse describes that the beautiful pearl palanquin, adorned with Shiva’s divine grace, carries him, and he worships Shiva. The pearl-white umbrella, like a moon casting its light, provides shade. A crowd of devotees, adorned with radiant sacred ash, surrounds him.

Thus, surrounded by these, Sambandar, who partook of the nectar of divine knowledge, full of grace, arrives in Madurai. Until now, the significance of sacred ash had been unrecognized in the Pandiya kingdom. This implies that the light of sacred ash is about to spread throughout the Pandiya kingdom. The light of sacred ash is an eternally spreading light; it does not diminish or perish, but is eternal. Pillaiyar comes to further enhance its radiance. Pillaiyar is one who partook of the nectar so that Shiva’s grace might flourish in the world.

If others were to partake of nectar, it would bring benefits only to them. But because Pillaiyar partook of nectar, it caused Shiva’s grace to flourish for everyone in the world.
