Thus, Pillaiyar, coming in that manner, approaches Madurai. While drums and other instruments sounded, Brahmin ascetics recited the sacred Vedas, and auspicious sounds of conches and trumpets resonated across the cardinal directions. A gentle breeze, scented with Tamil, came to welcome and serve Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and his assembly. As a fragrant Tamil breeze welcomed him from all directions, the countless sinful army of Jains, who had spread throughout the Pandiya kingdom due to their deceptive austerities, would be burnt and perish. Not only the earthly realm but also the celestial realm, through immense accumulated merit, would experience a resurgence of brilliance, as if an army of good deeds was advancing. The impurities of the Jains, which had accumulated in the minds of the people like dust, and their spiritual ignorance, were to be cleansed.

Just as the Ganges, with its shining purity, flowed into the virgin land of the Pandiyas, symbolizing the advent of pure Shaivism, the great darkness of the Jains, devoid of honor, that had spread across the fertile Tamil country, was to vanish. This was likened to the radiant jewel lamp of divine knowledge, illuminating all the worlds with its abundant light, rising to create a beautiful spectacle. As the merit of the King of the Pandiyas’ strong Tamil land, achieved through his austerities, manifested, and Shaivism flourished, many sacred instruments and trumpets played. The messengers announced, “The one who conquers other religions has arrived!” As Sambandhar, the great one, approached in this manner, the unparalleled golden unique large bell, sounding for the salvation of the world, reverberated. Its indescribable glory filled Kulachirai’s ears like nectar. Knowing this, he immediately prostrated himself on the ground, filled with immeasurable joy.

Thus, Shekkizhar Peruman has composed six verses describing Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s arrival in Madurai. We will continue to reflect on the meanings of these sacred verses. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, part six hundred ninety-three, authored by the divine sage Sekkizhar Peruman, from the Vambara Varivandu charukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. We saw that Shekkizhar Peruman describes Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s arrival in Madurai in six verses. The sound of various instruments like the Thundhubi resonates, but even louder than these instruments, the sound of the Vedas chanted by the Brahmins is heard. Auspicious sounds of conches, drums, and other instruments are heard. The Thendral (south wind), which is a fragrant Tamil breeze, welcomes and serves Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and his assembly.

The Thendral blowing in Madurai, in the Pandiya country, is not just any gentle breeze; it is a fragrant Tamil breeze. The greatness of the wind blowing here in Madurai, in the Pandiya country, is that it is imbued with Tamil. This is because Sage Agastya, who resides in the Pothigai mountains, fosters Tamil there. This Thendral breeze originates from those Pothigai mountains, the mountain of Tamil, from Sage Agastya, the Tamil sage. It flows through the Tamil land, the Pandiya kingdom, carrying the essence of Tamil. The subtle implication here is that this Thendral, imbued with Tamil, came to serve Thirugnanasambandar.

Thendral is a wind that blows from south to north.

Therefore, it surrounds Pillaiyar and the assembly of devotees accompanying him from all directions and serves them, welcoming them. The Thendral wind, blowing from the south to the north, truly welcomes those who come from the north to the south, towards Madurai. Peruman composes the next verse: “As the countless sinful army of Jains, who had spread throughout the Pandiya kingdom due to their deceptive austerities, would be burnt and perish, not only the earthly realm but also the celestial realm, through immense accumulated merit, would experience a resurgence of brilliance, as if an army of good deeds was advancing.” Jainism had spread throughout the Pandiya kingdom. Doing so was a deception. The Jain religion, which overtly preached non-violence, had in fact abandoned those virtues and spread throughout the Pandiya kingdom by deceitfully harming living beings through its ascetic practices. It was an army of sin.

To defeat this army of sin, an army of merit had to arise. The strength of the sins committed by the Jains was immeasurable and exceedingly powerful. To repel such great sinful power, only the collective immense merit accumulated by both the earthly and celestial realms could suffice.

Therefore, the great merit accumulated by both earth and heaven manifested as the resurgence of Pillaiyar’s arrival. With his arrival, Jainism would depart from the Pandiya kingdom, and not only the earthly realm but also the celestial realm would live in well-being. “May Brahmins live, may celestials live, may cattle live. May cool waters fall, may the king prosper. May all evil perish, may the name of Hara surround, may the world’s sorrows be dispelled.” In the first sacred verse of the Thiruppasuram, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s gracious command causes this auspicious rising.

Therefore, the present auspicious uprising of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is the reason for both the earthly and celestial realms to be freed from evil and live a joyful life. That the earth and heaven attain life is due to Pillaiyar’s gracious command. We can reflect on this in detail at the place where Shekkizhar Peruman himself acts as a commentator for Thiruppasuram.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s arrival in the Pandiya kingdom is a divine event, occurring due to the abundance of merit from the past austerities performed by all beings over many births. Due to the abundance of merit from the austerities performed by beings, the Lord Himself, as a guru, comes forward and tells the beings, ‘Until now, you have been under the sway of the five senses, growing and forgetting. Now you have become worthy of receiving the Lord’s supreme grace.’ He imparts teachings on the nature of the Lord, the path to attain Him, and so on. He then shows and guides them, saying, ‘Now, follow this path, attain Him, and achieve salvation.’ The Gnanasastram, Sivagnanabotham, in its eighth sutra, teaches this truth. According to that truth, not only the beings in the Pandiya kingdom, but all beings in this world, due to their past austerities, are graced by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who comes in the form of a guru. Pillaiyar imparts wisdom, dispelling the darkness of other religions (paasa neekam) and bestowing the grace of Shiva (Sivapettru) as an explanation of Shaivism to beings.

We can also understand this state of Pillaiyar’s arrival through the Nenju Vidu Thoothu composed by Umapathi Shivachariyar. (Vembum piraviyalai veezhamal veedu alitha Sambandha mamuni en Thambiran ambuviyor pottum thiruvadi vanon pavani vara kandu valvinaiyen enorum etthuthal kandu etthinen than ennai parthan pazhaiya vinai panchamala kotthaiyellam neethan ninaivu veru akkinan etthariya thonnuttru aruvar payil thokkil thuvakku arrutthan kannuru thenamudham kattinan vennirum vedamum poosaiyum.) He said it was true, he said it was false. He taught the inner meaning of the five letters of the Lord’s name to the world, which values wealth, life, and home. He said that liberation is the removal of the dirt and flaws that accumulate on the body, like rust and hair, without considering one’s lowliness, and that such is the pure nectar of truth. Do not fall into the trap of deceptive minds that claim this is the path to liberation. Do not believe the words of Brahmins who recite the ancient Vedas with eloquent words but do not understand their true meaning.

Do not associate with those who, despite wearing sacred ash and visiting Shiva temples, are inwardly impure and ignorant, and do not understand the true knowledge of Shiva. Do not associate with those who wear the garb of ascetics but lack true knowledge and devotion. Understand that to be born repeatedly is a long, arduous path. Srimat Umapati Sivachariar, one of the Santanacharyas in the Siddhanta scripture, states: “Those who slander Shiva are those who cast us down into darkness. O Sambandha, the great sage who rules us with your grace.” When we understand the inner meaning and true nature of these ideas, we can worship with insight. When we learn these spiritual scriptures and their truths directly from great spiritual teachers, Sekkizhar continues to sing that these Jains have dust-covered bodies, full of dirt due to their unhygienic practices like not bathing and lying on hard, dirty surfaces.

They are people with dirty bodies due to Jain religious practices such as not brushing their teeth. They are those who consider the wrong path as the right path and strive to spread it. If such great dirt of the Jains is to be washed away, water is needed.

Therefore, the Ganges, in the form of the arrival of Pillaiyar, flows in the Pandya kingdom to wash away the dirt of the Jain religion.

Now, if there is a huge dirt, a huge amount of water will be needed to wash it.

Therefore, Sekkizhar, who calls the Jains and the Jain religion as dirt, metaphorically describes the rise of Pillaiyar as the Ganges. “His entire body is surrounded by dust.” Sekkilār states in the 651st Thirupadal that just as the Ganges arrived in the Pandya kingdom with its bright white purity to cleanse the dirt of the Jains who were immersed in that path with their senses, so too did the rise of Pillaiyar occur there. This ‘Jain dirt’ refers to both internal and external impurity. Cleansing the external impurity is symbolized by whiteness, and cleansing the internal impurity is also depicted as the rise of the Ganges, which is full of whiteness. The Ganges is praised in many texts as being white.

The purity of the Ganges is evident. We can understand the nature of the Ganges by the fact that its water remains untainted for many days.

Similarly, the Ganges has the quality of purifying the things that join it and the living beings that immerse themselves in it. Western physical scientists who have tested and understood Ganges water are researching whether a certain life-giving essence in the Ganges water is the reason for its longevity.

But in reality, our scriptures state that the Ganges purifies inner dirt more than outer dirt. Just as the Ganges arrives in this maiden country of Pandya, so too does the rise of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman occur. It is found in many Sthala Puranas and Shastras that the Ganges arrives at various places at different times due to different reasons. In Periya Puranam, we have seen that the Ganges joins at Thirukudamookku in Kumbakonam during Mahamaham. We can recall the verses sung by Thirunavukkarasu Peruman in Thiruthāṇḍagam at Kudanthai Kizhkottam, where he lists all the sacred waters that arrive for Mahamaham, saying, “Our Lord is the dancer in Kudanthai Kizhkottam, surrounded by good Kaveri, pure Yamuna, Ganges, Saraswati, the golden lotus Pushkarani, and the waters of Goviyadu and Kumari, all sacred places.” Similarly, it is believed that the Ganges arrives at Paramānanda Kūpam in Thiruchitrambalam on the ninth day of the waxing moon in Aippasi. The truth that the sacred water taken from the Paramānanda Kūpam on that day remains unspoiled for a year is something we observe directly.

Similarly, even today, the truth that the Ganges arrives in the sacred tank called Paalkinaru in Thirukurugavur on Thai Amāvāsai is evident. The miracle of that water turning milky white is also occurring even today. The arrival and rise of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman are like the arrival of the Ganges River in the Pandya kingdom.

Let us resume our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, Part 694, by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, titled “Vambara Varivanda Chirakam Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam.” The land of Tamil Nadu, as its name suggests, should have sought the salvation-giving Tamil language.

However, instead of doing so, it was enveloped in the darkness of Jainism, which leads to sin. To dispel this darkness and bring forth light, Pillaiyar, like a peerless jewel-lamp of wisdom, came forth to do good. In each universe, external sources of light like the sun and moon dispel outer darkness.

But only the light of Shiva’s consciousness, which is wisdom, pervades all universes, dispelling inner darkness. It is the light that removes falsehood and reveals truth.

Therefore, Pillaiyar manifests as such a jewel-lamp, a lamp of wisdom. That wisdom, which is Shiva’s essence, exists pervasively and is not visible to the eyes.

However, this lamp of wisdom, Pillaiyar, appears visibly. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman manifests so that the fruits of the penance performed by the land of the Pandyas, this Tamil Nadu, may become evident. This Pandya land, which has until now suppressed its benefits, will now emerge and be enlightened through the penance performed by this land maiden. Saivism is about to flourish.

At that time, when Pillaiyar manifests. The sounds of “Parasamaia Kolari Vandhar” (He who came to conquer other religions) resound. As we have seen, Kulachchirai Nayanar is eagerly approaching to greet Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

At that moment, the sound of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s arrival is heard. Those reverberations reach the ears of Kulachchirai Nayanar. Sekkizhar Peruman continues, “The sound that arose and resounded, with indescribable greatness, filled Kulachchiraiyar’s ears like nectar.” Then, realizing this, he prostrated himself on the ground and was overcome with immeasurable joy. That was the essence of the sacred verse. This sound, with great intensity, proclaims Pillaiyar’s sacred name, announcing that he has come to save the world. The sound is so powerful that it can be heard even by those far away.

This sound, like nectar, fills the ears of Kulachchirai Nayanar, who possesses indescribable greatness. Kulachchirai Nayanar hears this sound. Kulachchirai Nayanar is at such a distance that the sound reaches his ears.

Therefore, even though he cannot see Pillaiyar’s retinue with his eyes, at the very moment he hears the sound, his entire mind is filled with thoughts of Pillaiyar and his retinue. He reaches out with his inner eye and, seeing it, immediately, upon hearing that sound, prostrates himself on the ground. The event of love overflowing upon hearing is praised as paramount devotion, belonging to the category of supreme love. Sekkizhar Peruman is about to describe in the next verse how Kulachchirai Nayanar bows down even when he sees Pillaiyar from a distance. The arrival of Pillaiyar, and the benefits derived from it, are inherent in all three periods of time. Thinking that the benefits of Pillaiyar’s arrival will be available to the Pandya kingdom in all three periods, Kulachchirai Nayanar immediately bows down to the ground.

Sekkizhar Peruman composes the next verse, the 655th verse: His hands, cupped in anjali, joined above his head. Approaching quickly, he saw the retinue of the Lord, whose throat is adorned with poison, resembling a sea of pure ascetics, and with profound devotion filling his heart, he went forth and prostrated himself on the long earth. The minister-leader of the Panchavars approached reverently and bowed before him. Upon hearing that sound, Kulachchirai Nayanar, who had prostrated himself on the ground, rose, and his hands, joined in anjali, quickly reached above his head. He swiftly moved towards the direction from which the sound came. His hands spontaneously joined above his head without any conscious effort.

Kulachchirai Nayanar sees from a distance the retinue of devotees, who shine like a sea of pure ascetics, accompanying the divine son of the Lord. Upon seeing that retinue from afar, Kulachchirai Nayanar prostrates himself again. Earlier, he had prostrated himself on the ground upon hearing the sound emanating from the retinue.

Now, he prostrates himself upon seeing the retinue with his eyes. Having seen the retinue with his eyes and prostrated himself, Kulachchirai Nayanar remains on the ground in that prostrated state. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing: “Many great ascetic devotees approached Kulachchiraiyar, who was prostrate on the ground, and bowed before him. Seeing that he would not rise from the ground, the devotees informed the Vaidika Sekarar (Thirugnanasambandha Peruman), who was worshipped by Brahma, that the minister of the southern king, Kulachchiraiyar, had arrived there with reverence. Hearing their words, his lotus-like face bloomed, and with a smile of radiant pearls.” He quickly approached them, took their lotus-like hands, and lifted them up.

While they stood in front with folded hands, the Benefactor, seeing them with abundant devotion, bestowed his sweet words. Sekkizhar Peruman then composed two continuous sacred verses. Kulachchiraiyar, who was prostrated on the ground, remained in that posture. The devoted servants, who were part of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s retinue and possessed such penance, bowed before Kulachchirai Nayanar. Kulachchirai Nayanar, however, remained prostrated before the retinue. Many devotees from Pillaiyar’s retinue came forward and bowed before Kulachchirai Nayanar.

Even then, Kulachchirai Nayanar remained on the ground, not rising.

The devotees convey this news to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who is the leader of the Vedics. He is on a pearl palanquin, so they convey this news to him. The members of the retinue convey to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s ears the news that Kulachchirai Nayanar, upon seeing them from a distance, prostrated himself on the ground and remains prostrate, not having risen. Pillaiyar, the chief of Sirkazhi, hears the words of the devotees. His lotus-like face blossoms. The blossoming of the face indicates the blossoming of the heart.

Therefore, as Pillaiyar’s heart blossoms, his face blossoms. His lotus-like face blossoms. Upon hearing this news, from the palanquin. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman quickly descends from the palanquin and goes to the place where Kulachchirai Nayanar is prostrate. Kulachchirai Nayanar should have come and prostrated himself near the palanquin where Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is seated.

However, he remains prostrate far away, having seen the retinue.

Therefore, Pillaiyar, the Guru, comes to the place where Kulachchirai Nayanar is. This is the result of the intensity of Kulachchirai Nayanar’s devotion. It was Kulachchirai Nayanar’s great love that made Pillaiyar come from ThiruMaraiKadu to the Pandya country and to Madurai.

Similarly, here, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman descends from the palanquin and comes to the place where Kulachchirai Nayanar is prostrated. The unwavering devotion of Kulachchirai Nayanar is evident as Pillaiyar himself goes to the place where Kulachchirai Nayanar is prostrated.

Similarly, we see this in the Puranam of Appoodhi Adigal Nayanar. On the day when Appoodhi Adigal Nayanar was worshipping Thirunavukkarasu Peruman as his Guru with all his heart, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman went to the house of Appoodhi Adigal Nayanar. This shows that Appoodhi Adigal Nayanar was always thinking of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman came to the place where he was prostrated and lifted him up by holding Kulachchirai Nayanar’s sacred hands with his own lotus-like hands. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman might have spoken these words.

But he remained prostrate, and the devotees announced his steadfastness.

Now, he also sees it.

Therefore, he realizes that if he were to say “Rise,” Kulachchirai Nayanar would certainly not rise. So, with his sacred lotus-like hands, he grasps Kulachchirai Nayanar’s hands and lifts him up. Sekkizhar Peruman composes in the poem, “He quickly went to them, embraced them, and lifted them up by their lotus-like hands.” The word “lifted up” is a mantra, a powerful word. The intensity of the minister’s devotion, his prostration, makes Thirugnanasambandha Peruman act in this way. He doesn’t say “Rise.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s grace comes to him not only as words but also as actions.

The intensity of Kulachchirai Nayanar’s devotion brought him the grace of being lifted up by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s hands. Kulachchirai Nayanar, instead of asking to be lifted up with his words, expresses his request through his prostration. In response, Pillaiyar, instead of saying “So be it” with his words, bestows his grace through his actions by lifting him up with his hands. Just as Kulachchirai Nayanar remains prostrate, the Pandya kingdom lies prostrate in the pit of other religions. Kulachchirai Nayanar’s prostration symbolizes the need for the Pandya kingdom to be lifted out of that state.

Now, when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman lifts Kulachchirai Nayanar with his sacred hands, it is an act of grace that lifts up the Pandya kingdom. The act of grace that lifts the Pandya kingdom from the pit of other religions has already happened through the act of lifting the minister. Everything that is to happen next is merely a continuation of this, a series of rituals, and this is revealed here by Pillaiyar’s divine action. The word “eduppa” (to lift) here, as Sekkizhar Peruman uses it, conveys profound meanings. The Sivagnana Siddhiyar Supakkam, in its second invocation, states that the word “eduthu” (having lifted) means to lift me in such a way that I am not born again in this cycle of existence. All these meanings related to the word “eduthu” (to lift).

We find them in these wisdom scriptures.

Therefore, when he takes Kulachchirai Nayanar, protecting him from the evil of other religions, it means that the Pandya kingdom has already risen above the influence of other religions. Kulachchirai Nayanar, who rose when Pillaiyar took his lotus-like hands, stands before Pillaiyar, worshipping him. He has received his act of grace, hasn’t he?

Similarly, he stands there, desiring to receive his gracious words. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the benevolent one who understands his intention, then expresses his sweet words. The opportune time for receiving the boon arrives. Due to his penance, Pillaiyar, whom he considered his Guru and worshipped, has come before him, lifted him with grace, and is now about to bestow his divine words. Let’s continue to reflect. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 695, by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, titled “Vambara Varivanda Chirakam Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam.” Kulachchirai Nayanar Peruman remains prostrated before Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, awaiting his divine words of grace. Sekkizhar Peruman then composes the next verse, the 658th verse, which contains Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred words: “To Mangaiyarkkarasi, the daughter of the Chola king, and to you, O noble-minded one, does our Lord’s divine grace abound with increasing goodness?” Upon hearing this, the minister, adorned with garlands of Vambalar, prostrates himself on the ground and worships his feet, explaining the nature of his great penance to those who cannot attain it. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman graciously asks Kulachchirai Nayanar, “To Mangaiyarkkarasi Ammaiyar, the daughter of the Chola king, and to you, a person of rectified mind, is the divine grace of our Lord Shiva abundantly flowing with goodness?” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman refers to Mangaiyarkkarasi Pirattiyar as the daughter of the Chola king. “Sempiyar” refers to the Chola kings. Pandi Madevi Mangaiyarkkarasi Perumatti was born as the daughter of the Chola king in the Chola country and married Nindraseer Nedumaran Nayanar, the king of the Pandya country.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman refers to Mangaiyarkkarasi by her Chola lineage as “Mangaiyarkkarasi, the daughter of the Chola king.” Our Empress Mangaiyarkkarasi Ammaiyar is one who follows the established path of Saivism and adheres to it without deviation, even amidst many obstacles. She is a great personality who strove to ensure that her country, the Pandya kingdom, flourished in Saivism. As a queen, she had the authority and right to issue commands. Despite all these qualifications, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman first mentioned her being the daughter of the Chola king and then inquired about Mangaiyarkkarasi Perumatti in this manner. In his Thiruppathigam, he also sang about Mangaiyarkkarasi, referring to her as “Mangaiyarkkarasi Valavarkon Pavai.” In this same manner of address, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman graciously asks, “Is the grace of our Lord abundantly flowing with goodness for Mangaiyarkkarasi and for you?” Sekkizhar Peruman renders Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred words as “Thiruvarul Perugu Nanmai Thaan Vaalithey.” “Vaalithey” means it proceeds well. The joys and sorrows that come to living beings are by the grace of the Lord.

Even when the Lord brings them, it is for the benefit of the living beings.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman indicates that the Lord’s grace “vaalithey” (proceeds well), meaning it proceeds pleasantly. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman recalls how the envoys of Mangaiyarkkarasi Pirattiyar and Kulachchirai Nayanar had met him earlier at ThiruMaraiKadu and explained the situation in the Pandya country. He reassures them with his compassionate words, saying, “Do not grieve.” He explains that the Lord’s grace has flourished well in the past, and it will continue to flourish. “The goodness we see today continues,” he says.

Thus, Pillaiyar’s divine words are clear and insightful. Upon hearing Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s gracious words, Kulachchirai Nayanar Peruman prostrates himself humbly before Pillaiyar. He replies with a most beautiful verse, the 659th verse, which is a glorious and profoundly meaningful verse that illuminates the administrative prowess of Kulachchirai Nayanar. This verse is memorized by most Shiva devotees. The verse is as follows: “The blameless past, the glory of the future, and the great fortune of having you here today – because of this, we are always blessed by your grace. The country, steeped in unrighteousness, and the good Tamil king have been uplifted, and have attained the glory of shining in the light of the sacred ash.” Thus speaks Kulachchirai Nayanar Peruman.

He says, “The blameless past, the glory of the future, and the great fortune of having you here today.” He speaks of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred arrival. Just as Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, in the previous verse, spoke of how the Lord’s grace had been evident in all three periods of time, and would continue to be so, and was now flourishing, and posed it as a question, so too does Kulachchirai Nayanar respond in this verse by affirming that divine grace supports them in all three periods. He states that the Lord’s grace brings goodness in all three periods, and the reason for this is Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s arrival in the present time. Kulachchirai Nayanar says that the great fortune of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s arrival in Madurai, the Pandya kingdom, today, is due to what. If it is due to the great penance, which was blameless in the past, that this blessing has come to fruition.

In the past, divine grace was abundant and brought that past penance to completion. That was the reason for Pillaiyar’s arrival here.

Now, with Pillaiyar’s arrival, divine grace flourishes well.

Thus, his arrival here now ensures that this blessing will bring the goodness of abundant divine grace in the future.

Therefore, Kulachchirai Nayanar states that the glory of the past, bringing blessings today, and the present blessing showing the glory of the future, indicate that in all three periods of time. Kulachchirai Nayanar replies that they are in a state where divine grace, in its increasing goodness, stands out. In response to Pillaiyar’s statement that divine grace abounds in all three periods and that goodness exists, Kulachchirai Nayanar states that the blessing of divine grace in all three periods flourishes specifically due to Pillaiyar’s arrival. He emphasizes that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has come as the embodiment of Lord Shiva’s grace, and that they are the possessors of such grace.

Additionally, in the previous verse, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman inquired about the well-being of the Queen and Kulachchirai Nayanar. However, in his own statement here, the King’s well-being and the nation’s well-being are also included. Kulachchirai Nayanar, even though Pillaiyar only inquired about the well-being of the two, also includes the well-being of the nation and the government. This is because Kulachchirai Nayanar is a person of high integrity who considers the well-being of the nation and the government as his own well-being. He replies accordingly. He also states that the nation, which was until now steeped in the unrighteous path of Jainism, will now shine with the light of the sacred ash.

The victory history that comes with the sacred ash Pathigam is hinted at here beforehand. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred words from Thevaram, “The sacred ash of the Lord, which destroys the Jains in debate with the Buddha, is true and firm,” also come to our mind here.

Now, the next sacred verse: “Upon hearing of the glory of your arrival, and having attained the unattainable blessing, Mangaiyarkkarasi also said, ‘Our life has arrived here.’ Therefore, she instructed, ‘Go forth and worship at his feet.’ Thus, having bowed and worshipped with overflowing joy, the minister of the king worshipped again.” This is the next sacred verse. Kulachchirai Nayanar further tells Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, “As soon as Mangaiyarkkarasi Ammaiyar heard of your glorious arrival here, she said, ‘Our life has arrived here.’ She also instructed me, ‘Go and meet Pillaiyar and worship at his sacred feet.’” Thus, he presents these words of Mangaiyarkkarasi Perumattiyar to Pillaiyar and stands worshipping. He emphasizes the Queen’s foresight in sending her minister to welcome Pillaiyar. This indicates that the welcome extended to Pillaiyar by Kulachchirai Nayanar is being done in an official capacity. By stating that this is the Queen’s command, Mangaiyarkkarasi refers to Pillaiyar as “our life has arrived.” Mangaiyarkkarasi Perumatti describes the one who bestows life as the embodiment of virtue itself. We can see this same idea in the upcoming verse, where she refers to him as the embodiment of wisdom.

They did not consider Pillaiyar to be merely a human form. Mangaiyarkkarasi Perumatti and Kulachchirai Nayanar perceived him as the embodiment of Shiva’s grace, the very form of their lives, and the embodiment of wisdom.

Thus, Kulachchirai Nayanar speaks and stands in reverence. The next sacred verse is: “At that time, speaking words of boundless grace, he bestowed his blessing, and as Madurai, surrounded by lofty walls, appeared, he looked at the great ascetic devotees and asked, ‘Where is our Lord’s Thiruaalavai temple?’ Then, the devoted worshipper, who bowed before him, pointed with his raised hands, which he had previously held in adoration, and said, ‘That is Thiruaalavai, where our Lord, who is adorned with bones and wears my unworthy service as an ornament, resides. It is surrounded by blossoming groves and lofty towers that reach the sky, adorned with long banners.” These are the next two beautiful sacred verses composed by Sekkizhar Peruman. Kulachchirai Nayanar, having offered these words of praise, falls at Pillaiyar’s feet and worships him.

At that moment, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman speaks further divine words with boundless compassion. Just then, as the boundaries of Madurai are reached, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sees Madurai, surrounded by its lofty walls on all four sides, appearing before his eyes. Pillaiyar is coming from the north towards the south.

Therefore, the place where Kulachchirai Nayanar greeted Pillaiyar is the northern boundary of Madurai. Pillaiyar and Kulachchirai Nayanar arrive at the point where the city of Madurai, its walls, and temple towers become visible to those coming from the north. From a distance, Madurai is visible to Pillaiyar’s eyes. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman graciously asks Kulachchirai Nayanar, “Where is our Lord’s Thiruaalavai temple?” He inquires where the Thiruaalavai temple is among the many temples and groves that appear amidst the city of Madurai.

Similarly, when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman visited Thirukkalaatthi, he asked, “Which of these mountains is Thirukkalaatthi mountain?” as there were many mountains surrounding it. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman thus graciously asks where the Thiruaalavai temple is in Madurai. Before Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who asked this question, the distinguished devotee Kulachchiraiyar bows down. He worships Pillaiyar’s sacred feet and, standing before Pillaiyar, points with his sacred hand. “There, where the tall banners flutter in the sky, and the towers appear, that is the Thiruaalavai temple where our Lord gracefully resides,” indicates Kulachchirai Nayanar. He points to the Lord who wears even bones as adornments, despite their lack of beauty.

He points out that this is Aalavai, where the Lord, who wears even my unworthy service as an ornament, resides. Kulachchirai Nayanar simultaneously describes its antiquity and greatness, stating that it is the temple where the Lord, who appeared and originated before everyone, setting the stages of the celestial worlds and other realms, resides; and it is the temple where the deities come to worship, ensuring the protection of their realms. Sekkizhar then composes the next verse: “The devotees, having shown it reverently, he saw it, and joining his lotus-like hands, he bowed to the ground with overflowing love, and rising, he sang a good pathigam that the world might praise, beginning with ‘Mangaiyarkkarasi,’ glorifying how the Lord accepted the services of both of them, saying, ‘This is Aalavai.’” This is the 663rd verse. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sees the Aalavai temple as the great devotee Kulachchirai Nayanar reverently points it out. He joins his two lotus-like sacred hands above his head, and with abundant love, prostrates himself on the ground, then rises. Upon seeing the tower, which is the form of the Lord’s lingam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman demonstrates the traditional custom of worshiping at that very spot where it is seen.

He bows down. Having bowed, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman begins the Thiruppathigam with “Mangaiyarkkarasi.” He composes each verse of the Thiruppathigam with the concluding phrase, “This is Aalavai.” In this Thiruppathigam, he sings a good Pathigam for the praise of the world, highlighting the special fact that the Lord accepted the service of Mangaiyarkkarasi Perumatti and Kulachchirai Nayanar, making it the central theme of the Pathigam. This Thiruppathigam belongs to the Thiruaalavai shrine in Madurai. It is the first Thiruppathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for Thiruaalavai. It is the 120th Thiruppathigam in the Third Thirumurai, set to the tune of Puranīrmai.

The first, second, and concluding verses of this Thiruppathigam are as follows. (Pangai-sī pāṇḍi-mā-dēvi paṇi-śeydu nāḷ-tōṟum parava poṅga-lūruvan bhūda-nāyaka nāḷ vēdamum poruḷ-gaḷum aruḷa aṅ-gēyē kal-loḍum āla-vayadu iduvē veṟṟavē aḍi-ya aḍi-miśai vēlum viruppa nēraḍiyum) (Koṟṟavan taṉakku mantiri-yā pula-cīṟai kuḷa-vil ētum oṟṟai-vil viḍaiyaṉ um vara talaivaṉ ulakil iyaṟkai-yai oḷindiṭṭu aṟṟavaṟku aṟṟa civaḷu āḷavai-yadu iduvē pal nalam pūṇa-rum pāṇḍi mā-dēvi pulacīṟai eṉum ivar paṇi) (An-nalam peru-cīr āḷavāy-i sam tiru-vaḍi yāka-vai pōṟṟi kaṇ nalam periya kāliyul yāṉa sambandam śemiḻ ivai koṇḍu in-nalam pāḍa vaḷḷavar mai-yōr ētta vīṟṟiruppavar iṉidē ētta vīṟṟiruppavar iṉidē ē) This sacred verse is one of the hymns that revived and protected the flourishing of Saivism in the world.

Let us continue our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, Part 696, by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, titled “Vambara Varivanda Chirakam Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sings a good Thiruppathigam that the world may praise, beginning with “Mangaiyarkkarasi.” This world is about to be saved by this Thiruppathigam.

Therefore, it becomes a good Pathigam. It becomes a Pathigam that brings us well-being. The Pandya kingdom, which was not praised due to the darkness of Jainism, will now be praised and flourish in the path of Shiva. This Thiruppathigam is a symbol of that. This Thiruppathigam, which begins with “Mangaiyarkkarasi Valavarkon Pavai,” tells of Pandi Madevi and Kulachchirai Nayanar’s worship. The pathigam notes that the Lord Alavai Sokkanatha Peruman, who graciously accepts the service of these two, resides sweetly with Angayarkanni in Thiru Alavai.

In the first verse, the greatness of the praise for the Goddess is expounded upon, and based on this, Sekkizhar Peruman constructs the Mangaiyarkarasi Ammaiyar Puranam, describing how Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praised her here. In this pathigam, the service of Queen Mangaiyarkarasi is praised in verses one, three, five, seven, and nine, and the service of Kulachirai Nayanar in verses two, four, six, eight, and ten. In the eleventh verse, the Thirukadaikkappu, both their services are praised, and it states that their service is that of the great Alavai Isan. The skill of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s pathigam lies in praising the Lord in this way. As a result of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s grace, the Pandya kingdom, Tamil Nadu, and Saivism have flourished from that day until now, and will continue to receive great benefits. Sekkizhar Peruman expands upon these details and the history of Kulachirai Nayanar in the Kulachirai Nayanar Puranam.

This pathigam is one of the great pathigams that revitalized and preserved the Saiva dharma in the world. It is the first pathigam sung by Pillaiyar in the Pandya kingdom, among the Sthala pathigams, after his arrival.

Similarly, it is also the first pathigam specifically for the Pandya kingdom, and particularly for Madurai. Only after Pillaiyar composed his pathigams did Thirunavukkarasar Swamigal arrive in the Pandya kingdom and compose his pathigams.

Similarly, after a short period, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, who was destined to incarnate, also came here and composed his pathigams.

Therefore, in that sense, this pathigam, Mangaiyarkarasi Valavarkon Pavai, is the first pathigam among the Sthala pathigams in the Pandya kingdom and also the first pathigam for Alavai. This pathigam is set to the tune Puraneermai pann. Puraneermai pann is one of the tunes sung during the day. They say that the equivalent raga in modern times is one that can be sung in the morning, a muhurtham before sunrise, called Bhupalam. This is also the time for Thirupalliyeluchi. Pillaiyar composed this pathigam in Puraneermai pann to indicate the coming of the dawn, where the evil darkness of Jainism that had spread and defamed the Pandya kingdom, would vanish.

Therefore, the indication we get here is that the time Pillaiyar arrived and sang was dawn. He begins with ‘Valavarkon Pavai,’ referring to Queen Mangaiyarkarasi as the daughter of the Chola king first, and then as the Pandi Mahadevi. This is because the Chola lineage is esteemed for its unwavering adherence to the Saiva faith.

Thus, he sang about her Chola heritage first, and then her status as Pandi Mahadevi. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman now composes the next verse. The pathigam sung by Sekkizhar Peruman describes how Pillaiyar, with devoted followers, came praising, approached the Thiru Alavai, where the Lord, difficult for even Brahma and Vishnu to find, rejoiced, bowed to the lofty, wealthy gopuram, and entered with great eagerness, circumambulating the temple. The next verse states that he entered the temple with the minister.

Thus, praising the Lord with pathigams, Pillaiyar arrives at the Thiru Alavai temple. He comes, singing and praising that this is Alavai, and beholding Thiru Alavai. The devoted followers all accompany Pillaiyar. These devotees are the faithful followers who always accompanied Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. It was they who, when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was staying at the hermitage in Thiruvedaranyam, delivered the message from the Pandya kingdom and requested Thirugnanasambandha Peruman to come to the Pandya kingdom, establish Saivism, remove Jainism, and anoint the king with sacred ash to make him a Saivite. These were the devotees, whom Peruman here refers to as virtuous devotees.

Kulachirai Nayanar comes forward to receive him in his official capacity. The people of Tamil Nadu were in a state where their minds were not inclined towards Saivism, as the land was filled with the monasteries and schools of the Jains. Only the Minister and the Queen Mangaiyarkarasi upheld Saivism there. The indication here is that some devotees, along with them, were unable to come and greet him.

Therefore, with the devotees who always accompanied him, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reaches the Thiru Alavai temple. He arrives near the lofty, wealthy gopuram. Earlier, when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was at the northern border of Madurai in the Pandya kingdom, he saw the gopuram peaks adorned with flags.

At that time, Kulachirai Nayanar pointed to the towering gopuram and showed him that it was Thiru Alavai. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman had previously bowed to the temple and the city identified by that gopuram.

Now, as he approaches the temple, the entire temple and gopuram are visible to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

Therefore, in accordance with tradition, he comes around the surrounding mansions near where the gopuram was erected, and then enters the sacred presence, having circumambulated the temple. He then enters the sacred presence, passing by the mansions located near where the Lord resides. He enters before the Lord. The dark night of Jainism enveloped the Pandya kingdom, and Thirugnanasambandha Peruman rises like a lamp of wisdom to dispel it. This signifies night. As Pillaiyar proceeds, the sound of the trumpets he plays falls like ambrosia into Kulachirai Nayanar’s ears.

It was then the early dawn, the time when night fades and day breaks, as described in Thiruvachagam: ‘Arunan has approached the direction of Indra, darkness has departed, and dawn has come.’ Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s pathigam, Puraneermai, was composed in that manner. Kulachirai Nayanar came forward to greet Pillaiyar, bowed to him, received his grace, and then Pillaiyar, by divine grace, composed the Thiru Alavai pathigam in the same Puraneermai pann and metrical structure. As he uttered it, Pillaiyar, along with his devotees and the minister, arrived at the Thiru Alavai temple. By then, the dawn had fully broken. Upon seeing the Lord of Thiru Alavai before him, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s command, ‘Neelama Midatru Alavaayilan Palathayinar Gnanam Aalvare,’ was about to be issued.

Thus, the darkness of Jainism had vanished, and Saivism flourished. Pillaiyar’s pathigam, guided by divine will, arose to endure through time.

In the same way, Sekkizhar Peruman’s verses also arose, conveying this divine will.

Now, the next verse describes him seeing the Lord, who, with a dark throat, resides sweetly in Alavai, and whose presence grants the eyes their purpose. With overflowing love, he bows, rises, and repeatedly falls prostrate on the ground. At Thiru Alavai, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman beholds the Lord, who, with a dark throat, graciously presides and lovingly resides there, seeing the sweet fruit of his eyes.

Here, he refers to the Lord of Alavai as ‘Aalum Anganar.’ This indicates that he is the Lord with a dark throat who rules and takes devotees into his grace. This implies that he had previously received grace, which bore fruit, and the compassionate glance relieved his suffering.

Now, as his karmas are completed and stand balanced, it is a state of receiving grace and being taken into his fold.

Therefore, Thirualavai’s Lord is referred to as ‘Aalum Anganar’. Seated on the Bull-mount, residing in Alavai, the Lord of the dark throat, to whom even the celestial beings bow in worship, is the one who bears the crescent moon on his head. Sekkizhar Peruman describes the Lord in this verse as having a dark throat, referring to his form where he consumed poison. The benefit gained by the eyes is that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who always sees the Lord with his eye of wisdom, now sees him with his physical eyes, and even those eyes are benefited. This indicates that just as he experienced the benefit of seeing, the people of Madurai, who had not seen the Lord until now, would also experience the benefit of seeing him. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman performs salutations according to custom to the Lord.

Even after bowing countless times, his mind is not at peace, and he bows and rises again and again. Sekkizhar Peruman describes this in the next verse: ‘With eight limbs, and five, he bowed countless times, with abundant love, his body bristled with joy, and tears flowed from his red eyes, adorning his divine form, praising the Lord of Pugali.’ The next verse describes how the Lord of Pugali, with eight limbs, or five, bowed countless times, his body bristling with love, tears flowing from his lotus-red eyes, and his glorious divine form adorned. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman performs countless Ashtanga and Panchanga salutations. Ashtanga salutation involves touching the ground with eight parts of the body, while Panchanga salutation involves touching the ground with five parts. Men should perform both Ashtanga and Panchanga salutations, while women are only to perform Panchanga salutations.

Thus, he repeatedly prostrates himself on the ground, bows, and rises. Pillaiyar’s entire body was covered in goosebumps, and tears flowed like a waterfall, soaking his divine form. In this state, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman shines with great beauty and the radiance of sacred ash. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman shines there with the brilliance of the sacred ash. He praises and worships the Lord in many ways. He then bestows the Thiruvirukkural pathigam, which begins with ‘Neelama Midatru Alavaayaan.’ Let us go on contemplating this. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 697, authored by Deivasekkizhar Peruman, Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, standing before Lord Somasundara at Thiru Alavai temple, composed the pathigam beginning with ‘Neelama Midatru Alavaayaan.’ Sekkizhar Peruman frames the verse as: (Neelama Midatru Alavaayaan ena nilavum moolamaghiya thiruvirakku kural mozhiyinthu seela mathava thiruththondar thammudhu thizhaithaar saalu menmayil thalaichchanga pulavanar thammun) ‘Declaring the root of the scripture, Neelama Midatru Alavaayaan, he associated with the virtuous and devout followers, excelling among the foremost scholars of the ancient Tamil Sangam.’ ‘Neelama Midatru Alavaayaan’ are the opening lines of the pathigam, and Sekkizhar Peruman refers to them as the ‘root of the scripture that prevails.’ The pathigam is in the ‘irukku kural’ poetic meter. This pathigam is small in size, with short lines, but it has the characteristic of conveying profound meaning. This pathigam is like a seed and its sprout. It contains the words that will lead to future events, suppressing them for now, and will later reveal those events.

In grammar, ‘adi’ refers to the lines that form the beginning of kuratpa and other poetic forms.

Similarly, in terms of meaning, this pathigam serves as a primary text, revealing the previously mentioned concepts. This pathigam, by divine grace, also contains hints of future events. Through this pathigam, we can understand that the Pandya king would embrace Saivism, as indicated by ‘Alavaayilan Palathayinar Gnanam Aalvare.’ This serves as proof. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman recites this before Lord Somasundara. Sekkizhar Peruman refers to it as ‘Thalaichchanga Pulavanar thammun.’ He calls Lord Sokkanatha of Thiru Alavai the leader of the Tamil Sangam poets. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and others were intent on referring to the Lord of Thiru Alavai as the leader of the Tamil Sangam poets.

Sekkizhar Peruman mentions this here. We saw in his puranam that Thirunavukkarasu Peruman also went to Madurai and worshipped the Lord as one who, in the scholarly Sangam, had researched Tamil and was a gracious Lord. This Lord is a poet. The note here is that he is the Lord who understands the greatness of Pillaiyar’s Tamil. Ancient Tamil texts refer to this Lord as the one with matted locks who burned the three cities. The pathigam delivered before the Lord in the ‘Thiruvirukural’ meter, in the Kurinji pann, is the second pathigam sung by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for Thiru Alavai.

It is the ninety-eighth pathigam in the first Thirumurai. This very beautiful pathigam consists of two-line verses, as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. Neelama Midatru Alavaayilan Pala. (Thayinar Gnanam Aalvare) The earth will be ruled. (Gnanam Elumam Alavaayilar Seelame Solir Kaalan Veetave) Speak of the virtues of Alavai’s Lord, so that Yama may be vanquished. (Alanilalar Alavaayilar Kalakalanaar Palathaminae) He who is under the banyan tree, the Lord of Alavai, the Destroyer of Kala, is our refuge. (Anthamil Pugal Enthai Alavay Banthiyarkazhal Sinthai Seimine) Meditate on the glorious feet of our father, the Lord of Alavai, whose fame is endless. (Aadal Etrinan Koodal Alavay Padiye Manam Naadi Vazhmine) Sing of the dancing Lord of Koodal Alavai, and seek him in your heart to live. (Annal Alavay Nanninan Thanai Enniye Thazha Thinnaminbame) By thinking of the Lord who approached Alavai, you will find firm joy. (Ampon Alavay Nambanarkazhal Nambi Vazhvar Thunbam Vidume) Those who trust in the golden feet of Alavai’s Lord will be free from sorrow. (Arakkanar Vazhi Nerukka Nalavay Uraikumul Tharkku Irakkammunmaye) There is compassion for those who speak of Alavai, even when the wicked harass the path. (Aruvanalavay Maruvinan Thanai Iruvar Eththininru Uruvamongume) The formless Lord who resides in Alavai, praised by two, stands tall. (Aranagamaam Seeran Alavay Theraman Chetr Veenan Enbare) They call him the hero who destroyed the Jains in the glorious Alavai, like a serpent. (Adigalalvay Padigal Sambandan Mudivilinthamizh) The endless Tamil of Sambandan, the Lord of Alavai’s verses.

The theme of this pathigam is to eradicate all evil in the Pandya kingdom, purify the Pandya king and his country with sacred ash, and lead them into the Saiva faith.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman concludes this pathigam with a sweet musical ending, the Thirukadaikappu. Besides this, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman also composed another pathigam at the same time, but due to our misfortune, that pathigam is not available to us. It ends with ‘Neelamadathu.’ Therefore, it is likely that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman must have composed another pathigam after this, for the purpose of further spiritual joy, but that pathigam is also not available to us.

Thus, having sung pathigams and praised the Lord’s grace. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman exits the temple. As he comes out, Queen Mangaiyarkarasi waits there to worship Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Queen Mangaiyarkarasi was already there when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman entered the Thiru Alavai temple.

However, she did not meet him then, as Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was heading directly to worship the Lord. She waited until Thirugnanasambandha Peruman had worshipped Lord Sokkanatha and emerged from the temple.

Now, as Thirugnanasambandha Peruman comes out, Queen Mangaiyarkarasi bows to him. We should also recall what happened earlier. Upon hearing the news that Pillaiyar had arrived near Madurai, the Queen sent Kulachirai Nayanar to welcome him, and she herself went to the Thiru Alavai temple to meet Pillaiyar, after telling her husband, the Pandya king, that she was going to the temple. The Queen arrived at the Thiru Alavai temple.

Later, Pillaiyar also entered Thiru Alavai. However, the Queen, who was waiting there to welcome Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, stepped aside when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman entered the temple. Pillaiyar, in his eagerness to worship the Lord, did not look elsewhere but went straight inside, worshipped the Lord, sang, received grace, and when he returned and reached the front of the temple, the Queen then came forward and bowed to him, welcoming him. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman could have been greeted by the Queen when he was entering the temple, but she did not do so. This was because Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was going inside with a great desire to worship the Lord. It would not have been appropriate to interrupt him and stand in the way to welcome him.

Moreover, it is not customary for those going to worship in a temple to focus on anything else.

Therefore, even if the Queen had been there, Pillaiyar would not have noticed her, and her welcome would have been futile. There is another reason as well. Pillaiyar would go straight in, worship his Lord, receive the grace of Lord Sokkanatha for his sake, and return. When Pillaiyar returned after worshipping the Lord, by then greeting him, she would receive Pillaiyar’s grace and also the grace of Lord Sokkanatha. For this reason too, the Queen had stepped aside. As Pillaiyar entered the Thiru Alavai temple, now as he comes out, Pillaiyar.

She waits, gazing at Pillaiyar, with eyes overflowing with tears of love. As Pillaiyar comes forward, Sekkizhar Peruman sings: (Vella Neerpothe Veeniyar Thamaitolum Viruppal Ulanaiththida Ethir Chellathu Oru Marungu Othungum Thellu Neer Vizhi Theriyaivar Chentru Munpu Eytha) ‘As he entered with the desire to worship the one with the white, water-laden matted hair, the maiden with clear, watery eyes stepped aside, not going forward to meet him, and then came before him.’ There, Queen Mangaiyarkarasi waits with eyes overflowing with tears of love. This arose from her maternal nature. Is there a lock for love? The tears of the loving reveal it, says Kural.

Accordingly, she waits there with eyes flowing with tears, an expression of love. Thirukkazhittruppadiyar’s fifty-fourth verse states: ‘The pure divine wisdom flowed from the breast that flowed for the child,’ referring to the flowing breast of the South Pandya Queen, whose mind was humble, and whose love was great. Thirukkazhitruppadiyar’s fifty-fourth verse states this. The eighth aphorism of Sivagnanabodam states: ‘The milk from the breast and the tears that weren’t there before flow from the jewel-like woman.’ The love a mother has for her child is an abstract love. The manifestation of that abstract love, which is formless, is the milk from the breast and tears. These two are the manifestations of a mother’s love for her child.

The milk and tears, which were absent before the child’s birth, appear upon seeing the child.

Therefore, the milk from the breast and tears are outward signs of a mother’s love for her child.

Therefore, both are forms of love. When there is a reason for love to manifest, it appears. When there is no reason for love to manifest, neither appears. Srimath Madhava Sivagnana Munivar explains all this in his Sivagnanabodam Maapaadiyam and Sirrutthai.

Here, Sekkizhar Peruman says that the Queen stood with tears, but he also implies the milk of the breast. Considering this idea, Sivaprakasa Swamigal also praised Queen Mangaiyarkarasi in Nalvar Nanmani Malai as ‘Komagale surantha arul kongai,’ meaning ‘Oh Princess, whose breasts flowed with grace.’ The Queen stands before Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, with her hands clasped above her head. As the Queen stands bowing, the minister Kulachirai bows at Pillaiyar’s feet and introduces her as Queen Mangaiyarkarasi, the daughter of the Chola king and the Pandi Mahadevi.

At this point, the Queen stands with her hands clasped above her head. As the minister speaks, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman quickly comes before the Queen. The next verse says: ‘The great queen of the South fell before the lotus feet of the calf of Siva, and the generous one, with great joy, lifted her with his sacred hand.’ Queen Mangaiyarkarasi, the great queen of the Pandya king, falls and bows before the reddish golden lotus feet of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who is like a calf of Siva. Pillaiyar, the benevolent one, with great joy and distinction, lifts the Queen with his sacred hands. Sekkizhar Peruman explains in a single verse that the Queen’s act of falling and Pillaiyar’s act of lifting occur simultaneously. The next verse is: ‘The virtuous woman of great penance, who rose bowing before the Gnanapongar, deemed her heart’s desire fulfilled, and with tears in her lotus-like eyes and a faltering voice, she said, ‘What penance have I and my husband performed?’’ The Queen, who had performed great penance and rose bowing before Pillaiyar, confirms that her heart’s desire, the establishment of Saivism and the restoration of the Pandya kingdom, has been fulfilled.

With tears welling in her lotus-like eyes and a faltering voice, she opens her coral-red mouth and says, ‘What penance have I and my husband performed to be blessed with your presence here?’ The Pandi Mahadevi opens her mouth and says, ‘What penance have I and my husband performed for your arrival here?’ The term ‘En Pathi’ here can refer to her husband, the Pandya king, or it can be taken to mean ‘city’ and ‘city dwellers,’ thus including the people of Madurai.

Therefore, she states that ‘I, my husband the Pandya king, and the people of this country have performed great penance for your arrival.’ The Pandi Mahadevi says that ‘we have not performed any great penance in this life, but if you have come for us, then we must have performed penance in the past.’ Thus speaks Queen Mangaiyarkarasi. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman responds to this.

Our contemplation of this continues. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Deivasekkizhar Peruman’s Periya Puranam, Part 698, Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. The Queen says to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, ‘We have performed great penance for your arrival.’ The next verse states: (Yazhin menmoziyar mozhiyinthu ethir kazhal vananga kaali vazhavanthu aruliya kavuniyar piranum suzhumaghiya parasamayaththidai thondu vazhu neermaiyir ummai kaanavanthaam enraar) ‘As the gentle-voiced one bowed before him, the Lord of the Kavuniyas, who had come to live in Kali Yuga, said, ‘I have come to see you, who embody service amidst the surrounding false religions.’ Here, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to the Pandi Mahadevi as ‘Yazhin Menmoziyar’ (one with a voice as sweet as a Yazh). The Queen’s words of welcome reach Pillaiyar’s sacred ears.

At this point, the state of Pillaiyar is described with this epithet. Generally, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, in Thirumaraikkadu Thevaram, referred to ‘Mozhi Mangai’ as having a voice that shames the Yazh, and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, in Thirumaraikkadu Thevaram, referred to Umadevi’s gracious words as having a voice more beautiful than the Yazh. They praised Umadevi as having words more beautiful than the Yazh.

Here, similarly, the words of Queen Mangaiyarkarasi reach Pillaiyar’s sacred ears. Thirunavukkarasar Peruman, in Thirumaraikadu Thevaram, also praised Umadevi’s gracious words as being more beautiful than a Yazh.

Here, similarly, the words of Queen Mangaiyarkarasi reach Pillaiyar’s sacred ears.

Therefore, the Queen’s request enters Pillaiyar’s sacred ears with the quality of a mother’s sweet words. Hence, in his reply, Pillaiyar states, ‘Tundu Vazhum Neermaiyir Ummai Kana Vandanam’ (I have come to see you, who embody steadfast devotion) and also refers to Pandi Mahadevi as ‘Pannin Ner Mozhiyan’ (one with words as melodious as a tune), thereby indicating the divine purpose of a child coming to see its mother in the pathigam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman addresses the Pandi Mahadevi, saying, ‘Even in this situation, surrounded by opposing faiths, you are steadfast in the path of devotion. I have come to see you.’ He says, ‘I have come to see you, who, even amidst this situation where false religions surround us, live steadfastly in the path of devotion.’ Jainism did not merely spread; it also aimed to harm Saivism. Even during a period when Saivism flourished, living well in the path of devotion is rare.

However, living in the path of devotion amidst the harsh environment of false religions is an extremely rare thing.

Furthermore, striving for others to prosper in that path, in addition to living it oneself, is an even rarer thing. Kulachirai Nayanar found all these qualities in Queen Mangaiyarkarasi. Kulachirai Nayanar states, ‘You, who strive for the flourishing of the righteous path even amidst such a hostile religious environment, I have come to see you.’ The analogy of a doctor visiting the sick comes to mind here. As Pillaiyar spoke, the Queen fell at his feet and bowed. Minister Kulachirai then described the sorrows that had befallen the country. In the previous verse, Pillaiyar’s words are not merely complimentary; they are truly blessings.

He speaks of ‘Tundu Vazhum Neermaiyir’ (one whose devotion thrives) in the present tense.

Therefore, he had already expressed his wish that their devout life should continue uninterrupted at all times. He has already given the assurance that his arrival here has occurred by the grace of the Lord for their sake, as he says, ‘I have come to see you.’ Moreover, by lifting them with his gracious hands when they fell at his feet, he indicated that their heart’s desire was fulfilled. It is common for words to precede actions and for actions to follow.

However, here, for Kulachirai Nayanar and them, Pillaiyar’s gracious words follow. This demonstrates the abundance of Pillaiyar’s grace. After Pillaiyar spoke words of grace, they bowed again in worship. The Saiva tradition teaches that those who receive sacred ash from acharyas should first bow, receive the sacred ash, apply it, and then bow again. This is taught to us here.

Therefore, those who first bowed at Pillaiyar’s feet, after Pillaiyar lifted them and spoke words of grace, bowed at Pillaiyar’s feet again. Bowing, they presented to Pillaiyar all the requests concerning the troubles that had befallen the country, how the darkness of Jainism had spread, the king had converted to Jainism, and the country was completely Jain, with the people’s minds not inclined towards Saivism, and asked him to alleviate all these conditions. All these requests, which the Queen Mangaiyarkarasi herself was now present for, and which had not been made when she went to welcome Thirugnanasambandha Peruman earlier. Minister Kulachirai makes his plea to Pillaiyar before the Thiru Alavai temple. After saying all this, he bids farewell to the Queen, who then goes to the palace. Pillaiyar comes out of the Thiru Alavai temple, surrounded by his true devotees.

Then, all those devotees who were engaged in service at the Thiru Alavai temple come near Pillaiyar and bow to him. They worship and praise Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, saying, ‘We have performed immense service for your graceful arrival here, like a full moon, to dispel the dark darkness of Jainism.’ These devotees who came and praised him were devotees engaged in service at the temple. The Queen and the Minister had already made this request to Pillaiyar. Nevertheless, the temple devotees approaching Pillaiyar again with welcome and requests demonstrates their intense devotion and their firm commitment to Saivism. They worship and praise Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as a full moon who has come to dispel the darkness of Jainism. The Pandya king also sees Pillaiyar in a similar way, as a rising moon, saying, ‘The moon that has risen from the sky to dispel the great darkness on earth is like the Gouniyar.’ When the Queen and the Minister see Pillaiyar now, they see him as that crescent moon.

Sekkizhar Peruman portrays Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as a soothing moon that removes the scorching heat of the devotees’ suffering. Sekkizhar Peruman describes Pillaiyar as one who came like a full moon to many places, and here too. The nature of the Lord is that he is like a cooling moon to his devotees, and like a fire to those who are not. The same applies to Pillaiyar.

Here, he graciously blesses all those devotees. As a result, all those devotees’ minds were filled with joy.

Then, Kulachirai Nayanar takes Pillaiyar to show him the monastery arranged for his stay. This monastery was built by Kulachirai Nayanar for Pillaiyar. This monastery, from that day until now, exists as the Madurai Aadheenam, known as Thirugnanasambandhar Aadheenam. This monastery is located on the South Avani Moola Street. In Paranjothi Munivar’s Thiruvilaiyadal Puranam, it is said that a great person like Vaakeesar invited Pillaiyar and his entourage to his monastery. In Perumpaththapuliyur Nambi’s Thiruvilaiyadal, it is referred to as Vaakeesa Swamy Madam.

According to the request of the Queen and the Minister, Kulachirai Nayanar himself arranged the monastery and other facilities for Pillaiyar. It is true that Kulachirai Nayanar himself built the monastery for Pillaiyar and his accompanying devotees to stay and receive hospitality through the grace of the Pandi Mahadevi.

Therefore, the monastery where Pillaiyar stayed on South Avani Moola Street still exists today. It is currently known as Sambandhar Aadheenam, serving as the Madurai Aadheenam.

We shall continue our contemplation of this. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Deivasekkizhar Peruman’s Periya Puranam, Part 699, Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman resides in the monastery built by Kulachirai Nayanar. Along with him, the devotees and his entourage are also staying in that monastery. Due to the great love of Queen Mangaiyarkarasi, and her grace, Kulachirai Nayanar arranges a feast for Pillaiyar and his companions. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is staying in that monastery, having been invited by the Queen.

Therefore, it becomes the duty of the royal family to welcome him, offer hospitality, and serve him. Such domestic duties of the royal family. Were incumbent upon Queen Mangaiyarkarasi, as the mistress of the house and life partner. Although Kulachirai Nayanar himself was capable of hosting and fulfilling all needs, since Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was staying here as a royal guest, the Queen commanded, and Kulachirai Nayanar undertook all the hospitality.

Therefore, the Pandi Mahadevi acts as the initiator, and Kulachirai Nayanar acts as the executor. All these actions arise from a state of profound love.

Thus, Peruman refers to it as ‘by the grace of Mangaiyarkarasi.’ The grace mentioned here means actions arising from an abundance of love, a heightened state of love. Hospitality is a duty of the ladies of the house and one of the special duties of women, all of which are conveyed here.

Thus, out of overflowing praise and intense love, the Queen acts in this manner. It is conveyed here that offering hospitality with love, friendship, and affection are essential qualities for those who host guests. In this great city of the Pandyas, the Jains see Pillaiyar, the leader of the great Vedas, arriving openly in broad daylight with his pure, virtuous devotees. The king himself was a follower of Jainism, yet Pillaiyar comes openly, without fear, like the sun. He comes there like a sun.

Therefore, just as darkness scatters and hides upon seeing the sun, the minds of the Jains are disturbed and afraid. The Jains, whose bodies and minds are dark, are disturbed and afraid. Just as ghosts that roam outside at night scatter and hide in one place upon seeing the sun, the Jains, who were like darkness roaming in the darkness of Jainism until now, scatter and hide in a corner upon seeing Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who is like the sun. The darkness in the hearts of the Jains refers to evil qualities such as falsehood, anger, deceit, and envy.

Therefore, Peruman refers to them as darkness. In that great monastery where Pillaiyar stayed, groups of devotees constantly gathered and recited pathigams. The sound of the pathigams, a great clamor, reached the ears of the Jains. In that monastery, devotees were gathered in separate groups, reciting pathigams throughout the monastery. They sang them with great love in the panns appropriate for the pathigams, thus singing in high pitch. The resulting great sound reached the ears of the Jains.

Sound waves, starting from their source, travel through the air as a medium, reaching the auditory senses of the listeners. This is how sound waves reach the ear. The eye perceives things by going to another place, but the ear and other senses perceive things that come to them where they are.

Therefore, it is customary to refer to the other senses as instruments that perceive things by stopping, and the eyes as instruments that perceive things by going. The eye is somewhat superior in sattva guna, while the other senses have less sattva guna.

Therefore, the other senses perceive only what comes to them, while the eye also perceives what it goes to.

Thus, the sounds of these Devara pathigams reach the ears of the Jains. They cannot tolerate it. If they hear anything about Saivism or see anything related to Saivism, they are disturbed. The Jain ascetics hold the belief of ‘Kandu Muttru’ (defilement by sight). These Jain ascetics, unable to endure hearing the true nature and degradation of their faith, which guides people towards the right path and uplifts them through these pathigams, are distressed. They conspire to inform the king, so they arrive at the palace.

They decide to report what they have seen and heard, and they inform the palace guards. The guards then announce to the king that a large group of ascetics has arrived. The king then orders them to be admitted. The king orders the guards to let them in. The guards go out and deliver the message to the Jain ascetics. Those Jains, accustomed to covering their bodies with mats, enter the palace with great trepidation.

As they enter, the king observes their deep distress. The king asks, “All of you have gathered here together; what is the reason for this?” The king asks this question upon seeing all of them with distressed faces and trembling hearts. In response, the ascetics say that an unspeakable evil has occurred. The implied meaning is that it is an evil that should neither be spoken nor heard. They state that an evil that cannot be spoken or heard has happened. Hearing this, the king asks, “Then...”

The Pandian king tells them, “Explain what has happened to you.” If the evil that has come upon them is unspeakable, the king asks them to explain the consequences they have faced because of it and to state its cause without actually speaking of the evil itself. The Jain ascetics, with expressions of deep distress, approach the king so that his affection for them may increase, and say, “O king, mighty warrior! They have arrived in your city of Madurai. By seeing them today, we have become ‘Kandu Muttru’ (defiled by sight).” Thus they speak.

Therefore, it is understood that in those days, the Jains had made it extremely rare to encounter Saivite Vedic scholars and Shiva devotees in Madurai, and to further establish that situation, they sought the king’s support to implement it. And that is how they implemented it, which we can understand here. The Jains claim they experienced ‘Kandu Muttru’ because they saw such Saivite Vedic scholars. ‘Kandu Muttru’ means defilement or impurity. If they see those adorned in Saivite Vedic attire, they consider it defilement and observe a full day’s fast to remove that defilement, performing expiatory rites. This is the custom of the Jains.

Similarly, if they hear any talk about Saivism, they consider it ‘Kettu Muttru’ (defilement by hearing) and observe a fast for the entire day. It was this practice of the Jains that later transformed into the concept of untouchability throughout the country. This is not merely a technical term within Jainism; they also burned and killed Saivites. The Jains committed murders. They did all these things under the guise of non-violence. We see this in the chronicles of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, and now in the chronicles of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and Naminandi Adigal Nayanar.

These Jains engaged in such heinous acts of murder and how they opposed the Vedic traditions, performing all these deeds to destroy Vedic practices. We can discern here the situation where Jainism flourished by captivating the king of the country, while Vedic traditions waned. With the aim of spreading their religion, they were hard-hearted enough to commit any crime, including murder. They hated the Saivite religion and Saivite Vedic scholars. They eliminated Vedic followers from villages. Even if one or two Vedic followers came into the village, they hated to see them.

With Jains like these present, they seethed with anger, unable to even tolerate the singing of religious songs by Saivites inside the monastery where Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was staying, considering it their own monastery. Jainism and Buddhism were committing such cruelties in those days. These religions arose in opposition to the Vedic religion that originated in India.

But today, two religions that originated outside India and are contrary to the Vedic religion are still engaged in these efforts. Even today, these two foreign religions undertake various efforts to spread their faith.

Moreover, they cannot tolerate the temple festivals and other events of the Vedic religions. We clearly see these foreign religions, even now, attempting to impose bans on them, prevent their occurrence, occupy the places of Vedic followers, and engage in conversions.

Thus, the actions that Jainism and Buddhism, which arose in India in opposition to the Vedic religion, performed in those days are now being carried out by two religions that originated outside India. When the king heard the news that Saivite Vedic scholars had entered the town, he too said, “Having heard this, I have become ‘Kettu Muttru’ (defiled by hearing).” It is shown here that the king was immersed and absorbed in the illusion of being pro-Jain. It was instilled in the king by the Jains that expelling and eliminating Saivism and other Vedic religions was a good dharma.

Therefore, the king becomes angry, taking offense at the presence of Saivite Vedic scholars here, disregarding his own command. He asks why the devotees of Lord Shiva, the three-eyed Peruman, have come to the city of Madurai. The king also asks who they are.

First, the king asks the reason for their arrival, then he asks who they are. To this, the Jains reply with the 685th verse, “The child of the Kauniyar clan from the Chola country, who received knowledge from Lord Shulapani, has arrived with his devotees, seated on a pearl palanquin, to defeat us in a debate.” Sekkilār Peruman presents this verse as the statement of the Jains.

Our contemplation continues. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Seven Hundred, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, composed by the divine Sekkilār Peruman. The Pandian king asks the Jains, “For what purpose have the devotees of Lord Shiva come to this city, and who are they?” To this, the Jains reply that a Brahmin boy, who received knowledge from Shiva in the holy site of Sirkazhi in the Chola country, has arrived with a group of devotees, riding on a pearl palanquin, to defeat them in a debate. The king asks why they have come and who they are. In response, they explain the country, village, name, and status of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the leader of the Shiva devotees who have arrived, and the purpose for which he has come.

Therefore, without just answering the questions asked, they state everything they know exactly as they know it. They say that a Brahmin boy has arrived, claiming to have received knowledge from Lord Shiva, who holds the trident. The Vedas state that the primordial Lord Shulapani is the master of all knowledge. Sekkilār Peruman places this reference in the words of the Jains. They say that a Brahmin boy has arrived here, claiming to have received knowledge from such a Lord Shulapani. They ask why he has come, and they unwittingly reveal the truth that is yet to happen in their words, saying that he has come to defeat them in a debate.

The truth that is yet to happen is revealed through their words. So, these Jains report all these matters to the king.

Thus, without just answering the king’s question, they say everything they know, without distinction between what was asked and what was not, what was needed and what was not, what was appropriate and what was not. This reveals the mental confusion and anger of the Jains, and they speak just as agitated people would. The king hears all this news. When the sacred name of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the benefactor of Sirkazhi, reached the king’s ears, Anger arises in him. The current state of the king is not one of neutrality, but one aligned with the Jains, in the delusion of Jainism.

Therefore, when the sacred name of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reached his ears, he became angry.

After this, when he suffered from fever, the Queen and the Minister mentioned the child’s sacred name. The child’s sacred name then became a mantra, alleviating his fatigue and restoring his ability to speak. That same sacred name of the child, now reaching the king’s ears, causes him to become angry, provoking his wrath. This is because, when madness takes over, Even milk tastes bitter. When that madness is cured, the same milk tastes sweet.

Therefore, until the karma is resolved and maturity is attained, divine grace acts as a power of concealment, hiding true knowledge and delivering the fruits of karma. When maturity is reached, the same power of concealment transforms into the power of grace, bringing joy—this is the truth stated by the scriptures of wisdom.

Similarly, the sacred name of the child here, like an enemy, tastes bitter to this king. Just as milk is sweet, he suffered from fever and when the queen and minister When they spoke the child’s sacred name, it cured his illness and gave him the strength to speak.

Once the Jains reported the news, the king asked them, “If that Vedic boy has come here, what should we do now?” This implies that the king respects Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. This is evident because he asks the Jains, “What should I do now?” Similarly, in the chronicle of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, we can draw a comparison here with the Pallava Jain king who, under the influence of the Jains, intended to torment Thirunavukkarasu Peruman in every way they suggested. We can see here, through such narratives, how powerful and deeply rooted Jainism was in those days, captivating even ruling monarchs and making them dance to its tunes, causing harm and evil to Saivism and Vedic religions. As soon as the king asked this, the Jains offer a most heinous response.

We shall go on reflecting. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Seven Hundred and One, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, composed by the divine Sekkilār Peruman. The king asks, “If that great Vedic boy has arrived here, what should we do now?” The Jains suggest, “Let us use a mantra to cause fire to appear in the monastery where that Vedic boy is staying. If we do that, he will leave this city.” The fire they speak of is a fire that can be created by a mantra. It would appear like fire, but it is not actual fire; it is meant to intimidate. This is what they call ‘Indrajal’ (magic).
