This is what the Jains tell the king. But in reality, the Jains’ intention was that if the fire created by the mantra failed to make the child leave the city, they would actually set a real fire. The Jains’ intention was that if the fire induced by the mantra failed to make the child leave the city, they would then actually set a real fire. The first attempt is to make it appear like fire through magical illusion. The second attempt is to invoke fire through mantra worship. If even that fails, their plan is to actually set a fire.

Hearing this, the king, finding no other way, says, “If this is the only thing to be done, then do so,” and sends them away. It is an act contrary to the principles of justice to banish or make a guest, an athithi (uninvited guest) as he is called, who has come to Madurai, leave the city. It is also wrong according to the rules of government.

Furthermore, setting fire to a monastery where people reside is against general law and even against the Jain religious texts that the king himself has embraced. The king, realizing all this, nevertheless says, “If there is no other way, and this is the only path, then do so.” Thus, the king, who considered falsehood as truth, went to his bedchamber with a mind full of worry, without speaking to anyone.

There, Queen Mangayarkkarasi arrives and finds the king completely silent. Mangayarkkarasi asks, “My beloved, who is the life of my life, what has happened to you? Before, you were always cheerful, but now your face is troubled. Please tell me what sorrow has befallen you.” Mangayarkkarasi asks him to tell her the sorrow that has befallen him. Mangayarkkarasi, seeing her husband thus grieved, addresses the Pandian king as her life’s beloved and speaks to him thus. ‘The woman who worships not any deity but her husband and arises’ (Thirukkural).

The divine scriptures state that for a chaste woman, her husband is her deity. To uphold this worldly life solely for the husband, and to end one’s life if harm befalls the husband, was a good practice established and followed by elders in our country in earlier times. In the Kanda Puranam, upon hearing that Surapadman had died, his wife Padmagoomala ended her life. In the chronicle of Karaikkal Ammaiyar, upon realizing that her husband had renounced her as his wife, she cast off her flesh and other bodily elements, adopting the form of a good ghost. These literary works are to be understood and cherished.

Here, Pandimadeviyar stands supreme in this conduct.

Therefore, all that Pandimadeviyar said were not mere pleasantries; they were words of truth. They were a noble ideal and a code of conduct. If Pandimadeviyar, being devout, is to bring the child here and make Saivism flourish in the Pandian country, would that not contradict the definition of chastity? It would not contradict it. would not contradict it, because chastity, according to the scriptures, means not deviating from one’s word. The word refers to the Vedas and Agamas spoken by the Lord, who is the life of all beings. To stand firm without deviating from their path is called chastity.

Here, the king completely turned away from these Vedas and Agamas. When he stood thus, Pandimadeviyar, by standing firm herself, dispelled the king’s delusion and guided him towards the good path, enabling him to attain spiritual benefit. Pandimadeviyar strove for the well-being of both the king and the country; therefore, it is a noble and highly chaste state.

Hence, if a husband is afflicted by madness, it is not chastity for the wife to also become mad. It is true chastity to liberate that husband from madness.

Therefore, in that sense, Pandimadeviyar’s current stance is of the highest order. She remarks, “Your heart is not as joyful as before.” Thus, it is understood that the domestic life of the king and queen was filled with love and immense joy. Even if they differed in their religious beliefs, their domestic life was very good. It is evident here that all of the Queen’s actions were driven by love.

Therefore, when the Queen asks why he is so joyless, the king replies, “O dear one with long, dark eyes, a boy from Sirkazhi, the prosperous land of the Chola king, has received Shiva’s grace and has come here to defeat the ascetics in debate.” The king replies to Pandimadevi, “O woman, a Brahmin boy, born in Sirkazhi in the Chola country, having received the grace of Shankaran, has come here to defeat the Jains in debate.” Even now, the truth of what is about to happen is revealed through the king’s words, without his knowledge.

We shall continue our reflection.

The king replies to Pandimadevi, “O woman, a Brahmin boy, born in Sirkazhi in the Chola country, having received the grace of Shankaran, has come here to defeat the Jains in debate.” Even now, the truth of what is about to happen is revealed through the king’s words, without his knowledge.

Our reflection shall continue. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Seven Hundred and Two, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, composed by the divine Sekkilār Peruman. When Pandimadeviyar asks why he is saddened, the king replies that someone has come from Sirkazhi, having received Shankaran’s grace, to defeat the Jains in debate. He adds that many devotees who apply sacred white ash have arrived, and seeing them caused ‘Kandu Muttru’ (defilement by sight) for the Jain ascetics, and hearing about it caused ‘Kettu Muttru’ (defilement by hearing) for him. This, the king says, is the reason for his distress. For those belonging to the Jain religion, sacred ash was merely white powder.

For them, sacred ash was simply white-colored powder, nothing more. They were unaware of the truths that sacred ash has the power to remove the impurities of those who wear it, and that is why it is called ‘Neeru’ (ash that cleanses).

Therefore, the king states that this is the cause of his mental distress. Hearing the king speak thus, Mangayarkkarasi also addresses the king, saying, “My king, if this is your state, then the Brahmin from Sirkazhi, in whom divinity shines, has already triumphed. Other deities will suffer, die, be born, and also perform karma, as the Sithiyar says.” Thus, referring to the principle that other deities, by the command of Shiva, dispense justice, and that Shiva is the eternal, imperishable deity, Mangayarkkarasi Perumattiyar speaks thus. Saying this, Mangayarkkarasi Ammaiyar becomes greatly delighted in her mind, thinking, “What is the nature of the leader of Sirkazhi’s coming to rule us?” She remains there with joy. Mangayarkkarasi Perumattiyar and the Minister both felt that the arrival of the Child was a great blessing for them, and that it happened for their salvation.

In this state, Mangayarkkarasi Perumattiyar, filled with great joy, comes out. At that moment, Kulachirai Nayanar arrives there. Mangayarkkarasi Perumattiyar informs Kulachirai Nayanar about the king’s state – how he was saddened, how she inquired about the reason, how he replied, and how she responded to him. Mangayarkkarasi Perumattiyar informs Kulachirai Nayanar about all these matters. These were all tasks performed by both for the sake of Saivism. She discusses this with Kulachirai Nayanar in accordance with the worldly and diplomatic principle that a minister should be aware of all ongoing events, and that one should strive to do good.

Hearing this, the minister clasps his hands above his head and says, “We have been blessed with the great fortune of the Child’s arrival here.” He agrees with the Queen’s words and expresses his joy.

Therefore, although the same thought brought joy to both, the minister, being skilled in statesmanship, does not stop there. He says, “We have been blessed to see and worship Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and his devotees, who are the devotees of the Lord.

“But we do not know what deceit these Jains are plotting.” The Queen Mother, hearing that, also becomes anxious and says, “These Jains are deceitful. They will perform despicable acts. If, due to their deceitful nature, any harm, rather than good, befalls our child, then our own life will leave us.” Thus, the Queen says here that if anything untoward happens to the Child due to the Jains’ plot, their own lives will depart before that. While their situation is such, what about the Jains? Those who hide behind the guise of ascetics and perform evil deeds cause fire to appear in the Child’s monastery through their mantras.

“There are mantras to invoke fire, and there are even great Shiva mantras. What the Jains did was to rely on the mantras of their own Jain religion and thus invoke fire. They are those who, disguised as ascetics, commit evil deeds. Through their mantras, they cause fire to enter the monastery where the Child resides. There are mantras to invoke fire, and there are even Shiva Mahamantras. The Jains used the mantras of their own Jain religion to invoke fire.

“The Child, however, is an incarnation who came to foster the Saivite path. They direct the fire to enter the monastery where he is staying. Sekkilār Peruman presents this verse: (adhimandhiram anjeluthu odhuvār nōkkum māthiraththinum maṟṟa) (adī māntiram anjeluttu ōtuvār nōkkum māttirattinum maṟṟa) (When those who chant the primal mantra, the five letters, merely glance in a direction, other mantras lose their power) (mandhira vidhi varumē pūthi sādhana madatthil thām punaintha sādhanakal sāthiyā vagai kantu aman kunṭarkal thaḷarntār) (the rules of other mantras come to naught. Seeing that their contrived efforts in the ash-adorned monastery failed, the Jain ascetics despaired). The holy five letters, the Panchaksharam, is the primordial mantra. It is the primal mantra; it is the mantra beloved by the Primal One.

“Even in the direction glanced at by those who chant such a primal mantra of the five letters, other mantras will cease to function and become ineffective. In such a situation, the fire sent by the Jains to the Child’s monastery, which is adorned with sacred ash, fails to produce the expected result and vanishes. Seeing this, the Jains become disheartened. They are discouraged, seeing that the fire they sent is ineffective and fails. The Jains fear that if the Pandian king learns of this news, he will no longer trust them, and their livelihood will be ruined. The Jains fear that if the king learns that their mantra was ineffective, he will no longer consider their religion, Jainism, to be superior, nor will he believe it.

“Jainism and Buddhism, and other religions, were established in India at one time in this manner. They would approach the king, bring him under their control, and employ various schemes to do so.

“In this way, they would captivate the king and propagate their religion, thereby securing their livelihood and wealth. All these events have occurred at various times in Tamil Nadu and other countries, and continue to do so even today. The Jains fear that if the king learns that their mantra was ineffective, he will no longer consider their religion, Jainism, to be superior, nor will he believe it. Jainism and Buddhism, and other religions, were established in India at one time in this manner. They would approach the king, bring him under their control, and employ various schemes to do so.

“In this way, they would captivate the king and propagate their religion, thereby securing their livelihood and wealth. All these events have occurred at various times in Tamil Nadu and other countries, and continue to do so even today. Similar to this, we see in the chronicle of Manickavasagar Peruman how these Buddhists spread in Sri Lanka, gaining the king’s support and livelihood, and came to Thillai to debate against Saivism. We can observe this in the Manickavasagar Puranam. Even in Sri Lanka, we can still see the spread of Buddhism today.

“Therefore, we see here the historical accounts of how Jainism and Buddhism spread in this country, seeking their livelihood, and thereby diminishing the glory of Saivism. The propagation of foreign religions like Christianity and Islam also continues in our country in a similar manner even today. One diminishes another to thrive; one diminishes another to thrive – this is not only a worldly state but also a religious state that we observe. We see this. This is the nature of humans bound by arrogance.

“Therefore, this world must understand these truths and behave accordingly. If it does, it can live well without conflict. If all religions abide by the principles stated by their respective faiths, it is good.

“But if they, abandoning that, decide to propagate their own religion, claiming it is superior, and intend to diminish other religions, then equilibrium will be ruined and conflict will arise. This is what we learn from all these historical narratives.

“We shall continue our reflection.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Seven Hundred and Three, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, composed by the divine Sekkilār Peruman. The Jains are filled with fear, realizing that the fire they invoked with mantras was powerless and could do nothing. Since the fire invoked by mantras did not yield the desired result, the Jains gather all the flammable materials and approach the monastery where Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and his devotees were residing. The materials they brought were easily combustible and fire-producing. They intend to carry out their intended act by bringing these to the sacred monastery.

This is the harm they intend to inflict upon the devotees who come to them.

Therefore, Sekkilār Peruman does not state it in his own words, but sings that they attempt to perform the act they had planned. The materials were like sulfur, fire-producing substances that contain fire within them and spontaneously ignite after some time. It is evident from this that the Jains were also proficient in such physical sciences. That monastery was a monastery for virtuous ascetics. ‘Anthan’ here means beautiful and cool. ‘Madhavar’ here refers to the group of devotees. The beautiful and cool compassion unique to the group of devotees is most excellent. As Thirumandiram states, ‘May the joy I received spread throughout the world,’ so live the group of devotees.

The Thevara states the same: ‘May the world be rid of suffering.’ The group of devotees lives. The Thevaram verse also states this: ‘May the whole world receive good and attain salvation.’ This is the compassion held by the devotees. Thiruvidai Marudhur Mummani Kovai states this: ‘The wealthy servants of God who look upon all living beings as their children.’ That monastery is where such great ascetics reside. We previously saw that Kulachirai Nayanar established this monastery for the Child to stay and reside. These Jains arrive outside this special monastery, carrying all those flammable materials. This monastery is well-guarded, so one cannot easily enter or approach it.

Therefore, they arrived near the outer wall, the Thiruchutru, of this monastery. Those deceivers, with their deceitful minds, are those who seek to thrive by deceiving others.

Here, the Jains have deceived the king. They intend to frighten the devotees and make them leave the city by attempting to set fire to them at the monastery. These Jains, therefore, were intent on harming the devotees and making them leave this city.

So, they placed combustible materials on the outer perimeter of the monastery and started a fire. They brought the fire-containing materials and created a fire on one part of the outer perimeter of the monastery. The flame began to rage. As soon as it started burning, They leave. The attendants of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, seeing the fire burning there, are filled with trepidation and distress. At night, a fire suddenly appeared there, so they are distressed and distraught.

These attendants have immeasurable love for the Child.

Therefore, they extinguish the fire, fearing that something untoward might happen to the Child. They destroy and remove the parts that caught fire and put it out. They clearly realize that the Jains were the ones who committed this improper act.

First, they see the fire. They prevent it from spreading further. They extinguish the fire.

Next, they discover who set the fire.

After this, the attendants convey this news to the Child. They convey these messages to the sacred ears of the Child. Hearing this, the Child’s divine words become the 702nd verse: (kazhumala padik kavuniyar karpaka kanrai thozhudhu nindru aman kundarsai theenginai sonna pozhudhu madhavar thuyilum itthirumada purambu pazhudhu seivatho pavigaal ena parindhu aruli) (When the attendants, standing and bowing to the Kalpaka sprout, the Kauniyar of Kazhumalam, reported the evil done by the Jain scoundrels, the Child, with compassion, said, ‘Do these wretches seek to harm the outside of this holy monastery where ascetics sleep?’). In this verse, the Child’s attendants, standing and bowing to the Child, who is like a Kalpaka sprout born in the Kauniyar clan in Sirkazhi, report the evil deeds of the lowly Jains. The Child is like a Kalpaka sprout. It is said that Kalpakam is a divine tree that grants wishes to those who desire them.

That is merely a complimentary saying; in truth, the Lord himself is the Kalpakam. ‘Kalpakam, I will not abandon you’ is a unique Thiruththāndagam.

Here, Sekkilār Peruman refers to the Child as a Kalpaka sprout. Just as the Lord shines as the Kalpakam, the Child also shines with the same quality.

Therefore, the Child becomes a Kalpaka sprout.

Here, the Child is about to engage in the act of granting appropriate benefits to various people, such as the Jains, the king, Pandimadeviyar, the minister, the temple’s devotees, and others, according to their wishes.

Therefore, Sekkilār Peruman extols the Child of Sirkazhi as a Kalpaka sprout at this point. The Jains are those who commit evil deeds.

Therefore, they reap the consequences of their evil deeds and ultimately face royal punishment, thereby escaping infernal punishment. The king, by the grace of the Child, endured the Jains’ wickedness.

Consequently, he is about to receive a terrible fever and then, by the sacred ash bestowed by the Child, he will regain his health.

Thus, the Child is capable of graciously bestowing appropriate benefits upon everyone, including the Jains and the king, according to their actions. This is about to happen now.

Therefore, Sekkilār Peruman extols the Child as a Kalpaka sprout at this point. When the attendants thus delivered the news, the first thought that arose in the Child’s divine heart was, “These Jains are committing an offense against the devotees!” Committing an offense against devotees is a great sin.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman exclaims, “O sinners!” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman says, “O sinners!” mentioning that these Jains set fire at night while the Shiva devotees, the ascetics, were sleeping. Generally, setting fire in a residential area is a major crime punishable by law even to this day. Setting fire to a house while people are sleeping is an even greater and more severe crime. More heinous than that is setting fire while devotees are sleeping.

Therefore, this is a great crime and a sin.

Thus, the word “O sinners!” comes from the divine lips of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Sekkilār Peruman also mentions that he spoke it with compassion. (madhavar thuyilum itthirumada purambu pazhudhu seivatho pavigaal ena parindhu aruli) (He said, ‘Do these wretches seek to harm the outside of this holy monastery where ascetics sleep?’), thus Sekkilār Peruman states. The Peruman mentions, “Do these wretches seek to harm the outside of this holy monastery where ascetics sleep?” Thus, even the Child’s response to the Jains was one of grace and compassion. This is because he first feels compassion for them, thinking, “These Jains have committed an offense against the Shiva devotees and have committed a sin for which there is no expiation, leading to a terrible hell.” The nature of those who have attained realization is explained in the twelfth sutra of ‘Sivañana Bodham,’ where it states that realized beings perceive all beings equally. This comes to mind here.

Thus, with compassion, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman further speaks divine words. The 703rd verse states: (en poruṭṭu avar seytha thīngku āyinum iṟaiyōn anparukku eythumō enru pinnaiyum achcham muṉpuṟa piṉpu muṉivuṟa muththamiḻ virakar maṇ ṉpurakkum mey muṟaivaḻu eṉa maṉam koṇṭār) (Even if it were harm done for my sake, would it befall the Lord’s devotees?

Even so, they committed an offense against these devotees. If they had done harm to him, it could be forgiven or prevented as a result of their ignorance.

But they have offended the devotees. Should this be left unaddressed so easily, or forgiven? The Child thinks it is not appropriate. He actually felt compassion for the Jains. He feared for the devotees.

First, Sambandha Peruman felt fear, then Thirugnanasambandha Peruman felt anger. The harm inflicted by the Jains fell upon the devotees, and he feared that some harm might befall them. This comes to mind here.

He wondered if they, those Jains, had committed such an offense against me out of ignorance; that could be excused or prevented.

First, Sambandha Peruman felt fear.

After that, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman felt anger. This anger was due to the harm inflicted by the Jains, which affected the devotees, and he feared that some harm might befall them. Pillaiyar’s mind was filled with fear, thinking, “They have committed offenses against the devotees; I must punish and purify them. These Samanars must be prevented from committing such offenses in the future.” This anger of Pillaiyar is a result of divine compassion, a divine attribute. It is not the arrogant anger that ordinary people like us harbor.

Therefore, just as the Lord’s anger becomes a blessing, so too is Pillaiyar’s anger a blessing.

Thus, Pillaiyar, filled with fear and anger, considered that the king’s rule of justice had weakened and justice had failed. A king must protect his subjects and those who come to his land from any harm. He must guard against the five fears that arise from thieves, enemies, and other beings, protecting those in his land and those who seek refuge in it from these five fears, and upholding righteousness. It is the king’s duty.

Here, through the pronouncement of this legal text, it is confirmed to us that the king himself is responsible for the evil committed by the Samanars.

Therefore, the king’s administration of justice has weakened here. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman perceives that this resulted from the king’s deviation from the path of justice. We also saw in the Purana of Murthi Nayanar the parts of history where the Vaduha Karnataka king, swayed by the Samanars, persecuted the devotees. We saw similar incidents in the historical accounts of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. We will also see it in the history of Thandiyadigal Nayanar.

Here, Pillaiyar understands that the Samanars themselves committed this evil act. Even though the Samanars are the primary cause of this evil, it was the king’s responsibility to prevent it. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman considers that the king’s deviation from his responsibility and justice becomes a contributing cause to this evil crime.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman determines in his sacred mind who is responsible for the offense committed against the devotees.

Thus, the fear, apprehension, and anger felt by Pillaiyar represent the state of great souls who decide with integrity in their hearts.

Therefore, even though they (Samanars) are truly the cause, the king’s failure to provide protection becomes a contributing factor. Hence, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman considers in his sacred mind that the punishment for this crime should first be meted out to the king. Let’s continue to contemplate. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, part seven hundred and four, of the Vambara Varivandu chapter, authored by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, the Purana of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. Although the reason for the offense committed against the devotees in the monastery was the Samanars, the king’s system of justice, which should have protected against such evil deeds, failed there, serving as a contributing factor. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, holding in his sacred mind that the punishment for this crime must first befall the king, composes a pathigam. Sekkizhar Peruman presents this in the next verse: (veyya thingu idu vendan merku enum vidhi muraiyal seyyane thiru alavaya enum thiruppathigam saivar vazh madaththu amanargal itta thee thazhu)

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman composes the verses: “This cruel crime is indeed the king’s fault, by the rule of justice.

“Therefore, may the fire set by the Samanars in the monastery where the devotees live, slowly go and befall the Pandya king,” commanded Thirugnanasambandha Peruman in the pathigam that begins with “Seyyane Thiru Alavayi.” Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, by the rule that “this severe evil rests upon the king,” makes this pronouncement. That is, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman makes this pronouncement based on the conclusion that the fault lies with the king’s system of protecting his land. The reasons for this are the king and the king’s minister, his advisory body.

“However, of these two, Kulachirai Nayanar’s ministerial skill is evident here, clearly showing that he is not the cause. We have seen how much love, devotion, and compassion he had for Pillaiyar, and how much affection and love he had for the country’s king.

“Therefore, of the two—king and minister—the minister is absolved here. From the causes of this crime, the minister is absolved here. Of these two, what remains is the king.

“Therefore, the king is the cause, the contributing cause. The king’s system of governance, which should have protected the justice of this world, failed here, and that is why this incident occurred. The worldly system of justice is the Lord’s decree. Although Pillaiyar, with his divine nature, realized that the king was responsible for this crime, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman decides that even according to worldly justice, the king is responsible. This demonstrates Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s integrity to us.

“Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman commands that the fire set by the Samanars should slowly go and befall the king. Sekkizhar Peruman thus publicly states the reason why Pillaiyar made such a pronouncement. Sekkizhar Peruman’s divine poetic excellence and his compassionate greatness in protecting the world from committing offenses against Pillaiyar are evident here. It is explained here that Pillaiyar resolved to find a solution for the offense committed against the devotees of Shiva, not for himself. Through Sekkizhar Peruman’s words, it is revealed that the Samanars initially tried to intimidate by showing fire like a magical illusion; that failed.

“Then they conjured fire, but that also became powerless before the devotees chanting the sacred Panchaksharam.

“Then they themselves brought fire and set a part of the monastery ablaze. This blaze, this flame, is one of the five elements. This is one of the Lord’s great sacred forms; this flame is one of the Lord’s eight forms. This flame is for the welfare of living beings, subject to the bodies, instruments, worlds, and enjoyments bestowed by the Lord.

“But the same flame, the same fire, was used here by the Samanars for evil.

“Therefore, Pillaiyar, resolving that this fire set by the Samanars in the monastery where the Saivites live should slowly go and befall the Pandya king, composes a pathigam.

“Here, Pillaiyar commands Agni, the god of fire. Agni is one of the gods who obey and serve the devotees.

“Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman commands Agni Dev. He commands that the fire set by the Samanars should slowly reach the Pandya king. Pillaiyar does not say, “Let the fire reach the Pandya king immediately,” but rather, “Let it slowly go and befall the Pandya king.” This is the clarity of compassion born from Pillaiyar’s anger and concern.

“Therefore, even in this severe punishment, we see the maturity of Pillaiyar’s divine pronouncement. The command “Let it go and befall the Pandya king” is a blessing that means, “May prosperity come.” Therefore, Pillaiyar’s intention is that through this punishment, born from his sacred heart, the king, the kingdom, and Saivism itself may prosper. This is expressed through the words of blessing.

“Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman commands the god of fire and then, remembering Alavay Peruman, composes a pathigam, which begins with “Seyyane Thiru Alavay.” In the first verse, he recites the first verse: (seyyane thiru alavay meviya aiyane anjal endru arul seya poyyaram amanar kozhuvunj sudar paiyave sendru pandiyarkku agave). The mention of commanding the god of fire to ‘befall the Pandya king’ is the central theme of this pathigam, which Sekkizhar Peruman has beautifully presented in this verse. The pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is dedicated to the sacred place of Thiru Alavay. The fifty-first pathigam of the third Thirumurai, set in Kausika tune. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Thiru Alavay Merul Amanaru Pandiyaruukka Velavay Adiyinal Veppam Melura Medhu) In every verse of this pathigam, one can find “anjal endru arul seiya” (grant protection without fear) and “amanar kozhuvum sudar pandiyarkku agave” (the fire set by the Samanars befalls the Pandya king).

“Through this, it is evident that Pillaiyar has enshrined the truth as internal evidence within this pathigam. In the first verse, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman mentions “koluvum sudar” (the blazing fire). Through this, it means that the Samanars, holding the burning embers in their hands, set the fire, and the action of the Samanars resulted in it afflicting the Pandya king.

“Therefore, since this evil resulted from the king’s weakened rule, Pillaiyar concluded that it was just for its effect to reach the king. And by saying “paiyave” (slowly), he commanded that the fire set by the Samanars should not immediately burn the Pandya king as fire, but rather slowly afflict him in the form of a fever. By saying “agave” (let it befall), it is an expression of compassion, and by saying “anjal endru arul seiya” (grant protection without fear), it indicates that he sang this pathigam to protect the devotees from any harm. All these historical aspects are enshrined in the verses of this pathigam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has enshrined and sung in the verses themselves. In the first verse, he addresses Lord Shiva as “Seyyane,” he addresses Alavay Sokkanathar as “Seyyane.” “Seyyane” means one with a body like fire.

“He has a body like fire, therefore, he is capable of protecting from fire. He addresses him as “Aiyane.” “Aiyan” here denotes the Lord’s status as the primordial one. Instead of going as fire, let the form of the fire change into a fever and slowly reach the Pandya king. Even that fever, even that affliction, quickly If it attacks, harm will occur.

“Therefore, Pillaiyar commands that it should go slowly so that such harm does not happen. We saw that in “agave,” “aga” is a word of blessing. In the second verse, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman addresses Lord Shiva, Alavay Sokkanathar, as “Siththane.” Here, it is hinted that the Lord performed divine sports as an all-powerful Siddhar in the Thiru Alavay temple in Madurai. Because of his nature as a Siddhar, he has the power to transform the fire set by the Samanars into a fever and inflict it upon the Pandya king. It is also hinted that he is capable of all other things. “Anjal” refers to fear.

“This fear arose for the sake of the devotees, out of concern that some harm might befall them. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman makes a plea to remove that fear. In the third verse, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises Alavay Sokkanathar as “Dhakkan velvi thagarthu arul Alavai sokkane” (Alavay Sokkanathar who destroyed Daksha’s sacrifice and showered grace). Just as Alavay Sokkanathar destroyed Daksha’s sacrifice and showed grace, he is capable of destroying the deceit and cruelty of the Samanars—this is the historical reference here. In the fourth verse, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises Alavay Sokkanathar Peruman as “Attamurthiyane” (Lord with eight forms), meaning that the Lord has eight forms, and fire is one of them. He is the one who has fire as one of his eight forms and is going to protect from the upcoming fire ordeal.

“Thus, the entire pathigam Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed and sang.

“Thus, as Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praised Lord Shiva, who dwells as medicine in Thiru Alavay, and composed a pathigam, by the grace of Alavay Lord, that intense fire, the heat of the fire, reached the Pandya king as a fever. That fire, known as fever, reached the Pandya king. At that very moment, we will continue to contemplate.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, part seven hundred and five, from the Vambara Varivandu chapter, composed by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, the Purana of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. We saw that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed a pathigam, praying to Alavay Sokkanathar Peruman. That pathigam was not motivated by evil thoughts such as enmity or hatred, but with the sole purpose that the king and the country should be reformed. In it, he praised Lord Shiva, who resides in Alavay as medicine. If a disease is to be cured, medicine must be administered internally.

Therefore, in this pathigam, he has enshrined Lord Shiva, who acts as the medicine of Thiru Alavay. This is indeed Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s grace. Is the king’s illness the Lord’s divine grace? Otherwise, to cause the ripening of the accumulated karma, to provide enjoyment, to stop the deluding power, to protect and bestow grace, and all other actions cannot be praised without grace, says the eighteenth verse of Sivaprakasam. Is it grace to cause someone to fall ill?

Here, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman blesses that the fire should slowly go and turn into a fever for the Pandya king. Does he make someone ill? What does medical science say? It says that the diseases that come into our body arise from the body’s natural tendency to remove the accumulated harm within us.

Therefore, it is a manifestation of the Lord’s grace. For living beings, Why do diseases come? Diseases come as a result of the sins committed by those living beings.

Thus, the Lord bestows disease and thereby resolves the sins already committed by those living beings.

That fire, which emerged and spread outwardly in various forms, retained its heat.

That fire, which remained subtle, reached the Pandya king with the same nature. That fever afflicted the Pandya king’s body. This happened at the very moment Pillaiyar commanded in his divine speech. The Samanars had set fire to the monastery where Gnana Pillaiyar, the son of Lord Shiva with the red sacred body, resided. That night is now fading. The sun rises over the eastern sea.

As morning arrives, the evil deed committed by those wicked Samanars the previous night is announced to Pandimadevi and Kulachirai Nayanar. Upon hearing the news, both the Queen and Kulachirai Nayanar are distraught. They think, “We invited Pillaiyar to this country where these evil people live. Is that why this offense befell Pillaiyar?

“Therefore, the atonement for this offense must be for us to take our own lives.” Both are confused. Those who came say that the Samanars set fire to Pillaiyar’s monastery, but it has been extinguished. Upon hearing the first part of this news, that the Samanars set fire to Pillaiyar’s monastery, Mangaiyarkkarasi Perumatti felt in her sacred heart, “We caused this; therefore, taking our own lives is the atonement for this.” Because the Queen’s love is of the highest degree, where milk spontaneously flows upon hearing Pillaiyar’s sacred words.

“Therefore, upon hearing that evil deed, upon hearing that evil news, the Queen became afraid and trembled for her life.

“Thus, upon hearing the first half of the news, Mangaiyarkkarasi Perumattiyar became distraught. Upon hearing this news, Mangaiyarkkarasi Perumattiyar and Kulachirai Nayanar recover from their agitation and become clear again.

“Thus, the same news, in two successive parts, is conveyed. Between the first and second parts of the news, the Queen became distraught.

“Then, upon hearing the second part, her agitation subsided, and she became somewhat clear, though still filled with increasing fear and trembling, they both grieved. While they were contemplating how the outcome of this evil committed by the Samanars would be, the next news arrives. The servants who are very close and guard the king very closely come and say that the king has a fever. To Mangaiyarkkarasi Perumattiyar and Kulachirai Nayanar, The Pandya Queen, the mistress, becomes agitated because her husband has a fever. She hurries to find a solution. This is a sin against Shiva, so Pandimadevi’s fear intensified due to doubt about how its resolution would be.

“The intensity of the fever burns the king, causing his body to tremble. Like a fire emitting heat, it quickly spreads both inside and outside the king’s body. Even those outside the palace where the king is located are affected by the fever. Due to this heat, the king’s body dries up and shrinks. The king’s body collapses. The consciousness, that sense of awareness, slowly leaves the king.

“That vital consciousness was set aside. Even those who stood close to the king could not bear the heat and stood far away from him. When diseases like smallpox or severe fever occur, they would lay the patients on tender banana plants.

Medical texts extensively describe types of diseases, methods to cure them, types of methods, and how diseases manifest. Medical science branches into many disciplines. As the Kural states, “Diagnose the disease, find its cause, discover the cure, and administer it effectively.” In this manner, experts in various arts implement the best treatments and medicines prescribed in those medical texts for this disease.

“They attempt to treat the king; they provide treatment. However, none of it proves effective. Instead, the fever continued to intensify for the king.

“Thus, the king has been afflicted with a very severe disease. The Samanars, upon hearing of the king’s condition, sigh and grieve. The Samanars suspect that this might be the result of their actions the previous night. Nevertheless, hiding their shame and humiliation, they approach the king. Upon hearing that the king had fallen ill, the queen was agitated, and the minister was afraid. They immediately arrive at the king’s side.

“These actions were born of their love. However, the Samanars, even though they heard the news earlier, arrive very slowly, at the very end. This highlights the deceitful nature of their hearts. They arrive, suspecting that the act they committed the previous night is manifesting in this way.

“Therefore, they suspected that what they did was an evil sin. The Samanars, however, did not believe that Pillaiyar was capable of causing such a consequence. Nevertheless, they suspected it because their act occurred the previous night, and at the same time, the king was afflicted with the fever.

“Thus, the Samanars suspect this due to the continuous occurrence and the related connection. The Samanars are adherents of a very confusing doctrine. They declare seven types of substances through the Anekantavada argument and do not provide a definitive conclusion regarding the nature of reality. The Samanars The Samanars, who are confused about their own principles, now come to the Pandya king and try to cure the disease. Medical texts state that those who attempt to cure a disease must understand the disease itself, its origin, and its cause.

“But here, the Samanars come and see that the king has a fever, yet they try to cure the disease without even realizing that its origin comes from their evil deed. The Samanars, with their Anekantavada, hold confusing principles; they try to cure the disease without knowing its origin and without even attempting to know it. The Samanars chant mantras in the name of their deity and perform what is called ‘mantra-treatment.’ They always carry a bunch of peacock feathers in their hands. When someone falls ill, they perform mantra-treatment with it. This is a tradition of Samanar gurus. They also carry a staff along with the peacock feathers.

“So, they took out the peacock feathers to rub on the Pandya king’s body, chanting their mantras with the staff and peacock feathers. At that very moment, it caught fire, scattering sparks and burning. Due to the intensity of the Pandya king’s fever, the peacock feathers also burned, and the staff caught fire and burned as well. The king’s fever was so severe. The Samanars, observing this, were extremely afraid. The Samanars sprinkle the water from the kundi they always carry on the Pandya king and repeatedly chant, “May Arihan protect you.” Arihan is the deity of the Samanar religion.

“As they sprinkled the water from the kundi, chanting the mantra, the water, like ghee poured on fire, greatly intensified the fever.

“Therefore, the Pandya king ordered them to leave immediately, saying, “None of you should be here; go at once.” At the same time, the king lost consciousness and fell into a state of oblivion. At that very moment, Pandimadevi addressed Kulachirai Nayanar, She says, “Is it not the evil committed by the Samanars the previous night against Pillaiyar, who was born in Sirkazhi and has graced us, that has ended in this manner?” Upon hearing this, the minister Kulachirai Nayanar humbly addresses the Queen, saying, “Certainly, it is the action of these Samanars, the offense committed against Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the beloved of the Lord, that has thus reached the king. If the Samanars try to cure this disease, it will only worsen.” Kulachirai Nayanar continues to contemplate.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, part seven hundred and six, from the Vambara Varivandu chapter, authored by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, the Purana of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. Pandimadevi, Mangaiyarkkarasi Ammaiyar, addresses Kulachirai Nayanar, who had taken on the responsibility of minister, saying, “Is it not the evil committed by the Samanars at night against Pillaiyar, who was born in Sirkazhi and has graced us, that has ended in this manner?” The verse states that Pandimadevi, filled with fear, asks the minister who had taken on the burden, “Has the evil committed by the Samanars at night against him who came from Pugazhi and graced us, ended in this way?” Pandimadevi is filled with fear. That duty is very great, very rare.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to it as the ‘burden of minister.’ Appar Swamigal’s Thevaram, in the pathigam dedicated to Arur Araneri, states that ‘those who are loved will also bear burdens.’ Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, born in Pugazhi, came here out of compassion for the Pandya kingdom, having graced Mangaiyarkkarasi Perumatti and Kulachirai Nayanar. The same evil is now about to befall the Samanars as well.

Similarly, if the Samanars, who are the root cause of this fever that has afflicted the king, come and attempt to cure it, it will only increase the disease, says the great minister.

Therefore, this is certainly a result of the offense committed by the Samanars against the devotees. Hence, the power to cure this disease resides only with the devotees of the Lord, the devotees of God.

Therefore, in the same way, the devotees of Shiva, who are the beloved of Lord Shiva, who previously destroyed the three cities, will go and eliminate the enemies.

Therefore, Pillaiyar Only one person can cure this fever and show compassion, says the great minister. After saying this, Mangaiyarkkarasi Perumatti and Kulachirai Nayanar stand before the king. They pay homage. Both sides bow before the king and say, “This fever has come because of the evil deed committed by the Samanars in Madurai against the benevolent one who came from Pugazhi. The grace of Pillaiyar is the solution to this.” (kayamum manamum masu kazhuvudal seyyar seyyum mayamum indha noyay valarpathe valar ven thingal meya veniyarpal gnanan pettravar virumbi nokkil theeya ippiniye andri piravi) These are the two verses Sekkizhar Peruman presents here.

Both sides stand humbly before the king.

Here, the two sides Sekkizhar Peruman refers to are the Queen and the minister. This term ‘both sides’ should be understood as referring to the Queen and the minister individually. The Queen’s ‘two sides’ refer to her duty to protect the Saiva faith and her duty to ward off the current evil.

Therefore, Pandimadevi is ‘two-sided.’ Similarly, Kulachirai Nayanar, who embodies both Saiva faith and ministerial authority, also represents these ‘two sides.’ Both of them stand before the king, humbly bowing. The king, however, is in a state of lost consciousness and awareness. Standing before him, Kulachirai Nayanar humbly explains to the king why this fever has come: it arose and intensified due to the harmful act committed by the Samanars upon seeing Pillaiyar, the benevolent one who came from Sirkazhi and arrived in Madurai. He resolved to grace and correct the king and the people of the country. These Samanars committed an improper act against Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Out of tradition not to speak evil, Kulachirai Nayanar refers to it as an “improper act.” Therefore, Kulachirai Nayanar says that Pillaiyar’s grace is the solution. Therefore, in accordance with the Kural beginning with “Diagnose the disease,” Kulachirai Nayanar, who is excellent in ministerial wisdom, thus declares. That moon, which was in a dying state, waning in its phases, was nurtured by the compassionate Lord.

So, the disease came from Ganesha’s cruel intention; it will be cured by Ganesha’s benevolent intention and also end rebirth, says Kulachirai Nayanar. (iru nokku ival un kan ullathu oru nokku noy nokku ontu annoy maruntu) is a verse from Thirukkural.

Similarly, this disease came from Ganesha’s cruel intention. The explanation here is that it will be cured by Ganesha’s benevolent, graceful intention. When Ganesha’s graceful intention falls upon someone, the impurities of the soul are removed, and the means to liberation are granted. Such is the power of Ganesha’s graceful intention. He is the ultimate Guru, so a mere glance from Him removes impurities and grants the means to liberation. This is what Kulachirai Nayanar says.

Then, Sekkizhar Peruman composes the next verses: “(Minavan seviyinodu mey unarvu alippor koora Gnanasambandar ennum nama mandiramum sella anapothu ayarvu thannai akanrida amana)”. He began to speak. At that time, didn’t the sacred name and mantra, Thirugnanasambandar, exist within their words? As soon as he heard that sacred name, the Pandyan’s weakness disappeared. When the sacred name Thirugnanasambandar reached the ears of the Pandyan king, who was in a state of unconsciousness and loss of speech, his weakness was removed. The king, having lost consciousness, was in a state of hidden thought and forgotten words.

Therefore, it was necessary to convey this message close to his ears.

Thus, Mangaiyarkarasi Perumatti and Kulachirai Nayanar conveyed it. This is also the method of a Guru initiating a mantra. Sekkizhar Peruman says, “(Nama mandiramum sella Gnanasambandar ennum nama mandiramum sella)”. According to the sacred words of Thevaram, “(Anchezuththin Namathan Kan)”, the sacred five-letter mantra, Panchatcharam, is the name of the Lord.

Here, Gnanasambandar is also a five-letter word. If you remove the silent letters from Gnanasambandar and count them, there are five letters.

Therefore, Gnanasambandar is also a five-letter word, and thus it is also a mantra.

This means it protects those who remember it. The definition of the word mantra in Sanskrit is stated as “(Mananath trayate iti mantra)” (that which protects one who contemplates it). Its meaning here is to protect those who remember it.

Here, the divine Sekkizhar Peruman explains the nature of this name, Gnanasambandar, becoming a mantra. From this point, the king begins to walk on the path of truth.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periyapuranam, Part 707, authored by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, “Vambara Varivandu Cherukkum Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam.” The next verse describes the Pandyan king addressing the Jains present there. The verse is: (Mannavan avarai nokki matra ivar seykaiyellam innavaru eydhu noykke ethuvayinana enru enni manniya Saiva neethi mamaraich chiruvar vanthal annavar arulal innoy akalume ariven enran.) The king looks at the Jains and, thinking in his mind that their actions were the cause of this disease, says to them, “If the boy, the great Vedic scholar of established Saiva tradition, comes here and this disease is cured by his grace, then I will be enlightened.” Thus says the king. The phrase “(Maniya Saiva Neethi Mamaraich Chiruvar)” in this verse is from the king’s speech. Jainism, which emerged in the middle, has now perished. Saivism, however, is a religion that has existed beyond measure, so ancient that it cannot be said when it originated.

Therefore, the phrase “(Maniya Saiva Neethi)” comes from the king’s own words.

Moreover, here he refers to Thirugnanasambandar in the plural as “(Mamaraich Chiruvar)” (children of the great Vedas). Previously, when he was swayed by the Jains, he referred to Ganesha in the singular as “(Mamaraich Maithan)” (son of the great Vedas).

But now, he refers to Thirugnanasambandar in the plural as “(Mamaraich Chiruvar)”. He refers to him in the plural as “(Mamaraich Chiruvar)”. Previously, the king’s state was as if his ego was non-dual with the Jains. The king, being under the influence of the Jains, was angered when he heard Ganesha’s name from their mouths. Being swayed by the Jains, Ganesha’s name, when uttered by them, angered the king and made him refer to him in the singular as “son”.

Here, the very name-mantra, Gnanasambandar, reaching the king’s ears through the words of Mangaiyarkarasi Perumatti and Kulachirai Nayanar, brought about true understanding and made him refer to Thirugnanasambandar as “(Maa Maraich Chiruvar)” in the plural.

Moreover, that very sacred name removed the mental delusion of the king, who had been enslaved by the words of the Jains, and gave him the wisdom to discern between good and evil.

Therefore, he tells the queen and Kulachirai Nayanar that if Thirugnanasambandar comes here and this disease is cured by his grace, he will attain clarity. He further states this in the next verse. The king’s mental delusion, which was subservient to all the words of the Jains, was dispelled, and he gained the wisdom to discern between good and evil.

Therefore, he tells the queen and Kulachirai Nayanar that if Thirugnanasambandar comes here and cures this disease by his grace, he will attain clarity. He further says, as the next verse states, (enru mun kuri pinnim yan utra pinaiyai theerthu venravar pakkam serven virakundel azhaiyum enna anravar uvakai pongi arwathal anaiyai nokki chenra neer vellam polum kathal vellathil selvar) which is the 723rd verse. The king, having spoken thus, further continues, addressing the minister and the queen, saying, “I will join the side of whoever cures this disease that has come upon me and triumphs.

“So, if there is a way to cure my disease, call him, call Thirugnanasambandar,” he tells the queen and the minister. The king first said, “If he comes and cures my disease by his grace, I will attain clarity,” in the first verse. That was a response to what the queen and the minister had said earlier.

“Here, the king says, “Call Thirugnanasambandar,” which is an order and command to Pandiyadevi and Kulachirai Nayanar. It is the duty of ministers to act without the king’s command to find a solution when the king is in a state of unconsciousness.

“Therefore, Kulachirai Nayanar could have brought Thirugnanasambandar then itself. However, Even though the king was in a state of diminished consciousness, he was previously strongly aligned with the Jains.

“Therefore, the king was in a state of both seeing and hearing with skepticism. So, the minister thought it was not right to bring Ganesha by himself at that time, and he spoke to the king face-to-face. As a result, the king regained some consciousness, and now, by the king’s own word, the order to bring Thirugnanasambandar is given.

“Moreover, the king says here, “I will join the side of the victor.” This indicates a mindset where he has abandoned his allegiance to the Jains and stands neutrally, without any bias.

“Therefore, the king is currently in a state of impartiality. The king’s mind is in a state of impartiality. The king asks, “If there is a way to bring that great Vedic scholar, bring him.” This is because the king had a doubt in his mind whether Thirugnanasambandar would come, as he was not someone who would come seeking royal wealth. If the king summons someone, who would come immediately? Only those who desire the king’s wealth or authority would come immediately upon being summoned.

“However, Thirugnanasambandar is beyond such things; he does not consider these matters important.

“Therefore, the king had doubts whether he would come when summoned. The king had doubts.

“Furthermore, he doubted if he would come among the Jains, who blasphemed Shiva. There were also doubts as the Jains had previously mistreated Ganesha. With so many doubts, the king ordered them to see if there was any way to bring Ganesha. Just as the king doubted, Ganesha, even after being summoned, did not go directly to the king but went to the Lord of Alavay, prayed to Him, understood His divine will, and only then appeared before the king.

“Therefore, when the king commanded Mangaiyarkarasi Perumatti and the minister to bring Ganesha, they received it with great joy. The two great individuals had, until that day and for a long time previously, longed and worried to bring this king and country to the path of Shiva. The queen and the minister experienced joy today. They felt joy because grace was about to manifest in the future and bring about good. The flood of their love and passion, which had been dammed up until then, flowed like a torrent when the dam broke. Just as naturally flowing water is dammed up and made to stagnate, so too did the king’s deviation from the path of Shiva obstruct the natural flow of Saiva dharma.

“Now that the king’s situation has changed, their love flows like a flood breaking a dam. The queen and Kulachirai Nayanar, having been grieved and saddened by the evil deeds committed by the wicked Jains in the monastery, quickly go with great eagerness to worship the noble feet of their leader, Ganesha, to dispel the sorrow in their hearts. Sekkizhar Peruman composes the next verse: (Mannavan idumbai theera matra avan pani merkonde anna men nadaiyinarrum animani sivikaiyeri minnidai madavar choozha verpadai amaichanarum mun anaintha eka sanpai muthalvanar madathai sarnthar.) To alleviate the king’s suffering, and taking up his work, the queen and the chief minister, who had previously been at odds with the king, now execute his command to summon Ganesha. To fulfill this command, the queen travels in a palanquin surrounded by women. The chief minister rides a horse and goes ahead of the palanquin. Traveling in a palanquin surrounded by women was a custom among noble families in those days.

“These customs are appropriate for the queen’s high status. The verse states that the queen travels in a palanquin surrounded by women. These are not only maidservants but also armed women guards and female attendants. The queen proceeds surrounded by them. The queen proceeds there. This is a royal command.

“According to the royal command, it would be enough for the minister to go to receive Ganesha. However, the queen also goes due to her overflowing love.

“Thus, both of them go to the monastery where Thirugnanasambandar is residing. The next verse says: (Thirumadam sarach chenru seyarik kanninar mun varupari ezunthu ninra amaichanar vanthapanmai sirapura pillaiyarkku vinnappam cheyveer ena parisanaththavarum pukku patham arinthu unarthukindrar.) After approaching the monastery, the chief minister, who came on horseback, dismounts and tells the attendants at Ganesha’s monastery, “We have come here. The minister tells the attendants, “Please convey our request to the Ganesha of Sirkazhi.” The attendants take this message and, standing before Ganesha, convey their request to him. They consider Ganesha’s presence to be like the presence of the Lord himself, and thus they make their request. They convey that the queen and the benevolent minister have arrived. When they inform him that the queen and the benevolent minister have come, the Lord says, “Bring them here.” They then return to summon them with great urgency.

“The attendants inform Ganesha that the queen and the benevolent minister, Kulachirai Nayanar, have arrived again. They, having arrived and welcomed Ganesha the previous day, also showed him the monastery and established him there.

“So, they have come again today.

“Therefore, the attendants inform Ganesha that these two have arrived again. As they convey this, Ganesha, the leader of Sirkazhi, graciously commands them to bring them immediately. The attendants then go with great eagerness to summon the queen and the chief minister. The queen and Kulachirai Nayanar enter the monastery. Upon entering, they behold Thirugnanasambandar and hear that wonderful verse. Sekkizhar Peruman then composes the next verse, which begins with “(Gnanathin thiruvuruvai)”.

“We shall proceed with our contemplation.”” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periyapuranam, Part 708, by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, “Vambara Varivandu Cherukkam Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam.” Mangaiyarkarasi Piratti and Kulachirai Nayanar enter the monastery where Ganesha resides and behold the divine form of Thirugnanasambandar. Sekkizhar Peruman composes a beautiful verse, the 728th verse, describing how they beheld him: (Gnanaththin thiruvuruvai vanaththin misaiyanri mannil valar mathikkozhunthai thenakka malarkkonrai senjadayar seertodukkum kanaththin ezhupirappai kankalippa kandarkal.) The queen and the minister beheld him. This verse portrays how the queen and the minister beheld Ganesha on that day, exactly as they perceived him in their minds. The queen and the minister had seen Ganesha both individually and together the day before. The state in which they saw him then was different, and Sekkizhar Peruman clearly shows in this verse that the state in which they see him now is different due to the events that have occurred in between and the various thoughts that have arisen in their minds concerning them.

Previously, the queen and Kulachirai Nayanar had a general vision; now they have a special vision. The special always encompasses the general and elaborates on it.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman sings extensively here.

Moreover, the state in which Mangaiyarkarasi Piratti and Kulachirai Nayanar behold Ganesha here is the very state in which Ganesha is about to appear before the king, cure his disease, and bestow knowledge upon him, after worshipping the Lord of Thiruvalavai and receiving His divine grace. In this state, Ganesha is about to appear before various people and Jains in Madurai, who will benefit according to their respective merits. He is about to grant a vision that will benefit them.

Furthermore, he is in the state of appearing as a Guru to save the king and the people of the country through the bestowal of knowledge.

Therefore, Mangaiyarkarasi Piratti and Kulachirai Nayanar behold him in this manner. Just as Sekkizhar Peruman describes Ganesha’s divine vision here, similarly, he describes the vision in which Ganesha will later bestow the true words of wisdom to all who attend the sacred wedding at Thirunallur Perumanam, granting them the ultimate liberation.

Here, Ganesha appears as a Jnana Desikar, bestowing “(Bhavana Diksha, Chakshu Diksha, Sparsha Diksha, Vachaka Diksha)” etc., upon the Pandyan king. The stories of Thirugnanasambandar making the Vaigai riverbed a Diksha mandapa, removing past karma, granting the ability to know the Primeval Lord, and placing His divine feet are yet to unfold. (Vinaikal oththu thulaiyana nirathalale) and (Alavayilan palathayinar Gnanamazhavare) are sacred verses from Thevaram which contain this idea. The great author of spiritual texts, in the Thirukkaliththuppadiyar, explains this concept by saying, (Manra pandiyan ketpa kizhakkum meijnanaththin atpalavarkku arul enpathai ariyee) in the Irupayirupattu. All these are spiritual teachings.

Therefore, the author Sekkizhar Peruman himself describes them there. We can also note Sekkizhar Peruman’s intention to change the poetic structure from the historical narrative style to the Narcheeradi Kochaga Kalippa from now on. The four phrases, from “(Gnanathin thiruvuru)” to “(Kanathin ezhupirappu)”, implicitly refer to the four paths of Saiva faith: Gnana (knowledge), Yoga (discipline), Kriya (action), and Charya (observance). In that way, the state in which Ganesha stands as a true guru, guiding the way to attain the Lord through these four paths, is explained here. Sivakavimani C.K.S. Aiya writes that the greatness of this verse, which contains so many rare references, should be heard and pondered upon from the mouth of an experienced guru.

Moreover, Sivakavimani Thirumaganar also delivers a wonderful commentary on this verse. The queen and the minister behold Ganesha, who is present in that state, as the embodiment of knowledge. “Embodiment of knowledge” means one who has a divine body formed by Shiva-knowledge. Thirugnanasambandar is a chief ascetic who realized true knowledge through consciousness, which is difficult to comprehend.

Therefore, while others perceive through worldly and illusory knowledge, Thirugnanasambandar, through divine knowledge, always remembers and beholds the feet of the Lord. He is one who has completely realized true knowledge, which is the fulfillment of those feet. This was explained in the context of the pathigam “(Veyuru Thozhippangan)”, and specifically through “(Thiruneeru Chemmay Thidame)” (the sacred ash is pure and steadfast) in that pathigam, by which the Buddhists’ arguments were destroyed, and also in many other places.

Thus, the timeless, all-knowing, divine true knowledge of Shiva is all-powerful.

Therefore, it is capable of removing all great obstacles and bringing salvation. This is indicated implicitly. Thirukkazhippadiyar states this: (Unarvariya kalangal chellatha kathaludan niruthi kalangal munrinaiyum kandu). We will see these qualities in the upcoming sacred history.

Next, after “(Gnanaththin Thiruvuruvinai)”, comes “(Nanmaraith Thaniththunaiyai)”. The queen and Kulachirai Nayanar beheld him as one who, with the help of Shiva-knowledge, restores the Vedic tradition and the Saiva path from the treachery of the Jains.

Next, thirdly, they saw him as (vanaththin misaiyanri mannil valar mathikkozhunthai) a growing crescent moon on earth, not just in the sky, as Thirugnanasambandar. There will be imperfections in the moon in the sky.

Here, Thirugnanasambandar is like a growing moon without any imperfections. The moon in the sky waxes and wanes; this moon, however, is always growing. The moon in the sky gives physical light; this moon, Thirugnanasambandar, gives the light of wisdom. The moon rises up to sixteen phases and then wanes.

Here, Thirugnanasambandar is one who shines with a fullness of sixteen phases, unchanging. The physical moon in the sky nourishes crops. This moon, Thirugnanasambandar, nourishes the Saiva crop. All this is implied as they behold him as (vanaththin misaiyanri mannil valar mathikkozhunthai) (a growing crescent moon on earth, not just in the sky). They perceive him there as the embodiment of Thirugnanasambandar as (Thenakka malarkkonrai senjadayar seertadukkum kanaththin ezhupirappai). Shiva always wears the Konrai garland and has matted hair adorned with Konrai flowers.

Matted hair is a special characteristic unique to Shiva, and so is the Konrai flower garland. They saw the seven births of song in the music that praises nothing but the glories of Shiva. The music that Thirugnanasambandar sings is beautiful. Song (kAnam) originates and expands from seven types of musical notes.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to it as the seven births of song. There are musical modes known as “(palai irulu kottha pan)” and so on. There are also other derivative musical forms that spring from them.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to the seven fundamental musical forms as “(Kanathin Ezhupirappu)”. Another musical tradition refers to these as Melakarta ragams and Janya ragams. Music (kAnam) is considered the Gandharva Veda, which is one of the four Upavedas. It brings joy to all deities. This Gandharva Veda, music, was used to sing about other deities and humans, and other beings, apart from Shiva. This music had longed to sing about Shiva and had been yearning for it.

Moreover, there was also penance.

Furthermore, after enduring seven births, these melodies finally found their fulfillment and purpose by being incorporated into the sacred pathigams that emerged from the divine words of Thirugnanasambandar, who was “(Konrayar adiyal peyna embiranar)” (our Lord who wears the Konrai flower and worships no other feet). The penance of those melodies, which longed to sing about Shiva, found its completion there.

Therefore, they beheld the seven births of song. They beheld all these things – the embodiment of knowledge, the unique support of the four Vedas, the growing crescent moon on earth, not just in the sky, and the seven births of song – with delight in their eyes. The queen and the minister (kannkalippa kandargal). “(Kazhiththal)” (delight) is a function of the soul’s consciousness. When the soul, through the external sensory organ of the eye and the mind, unites and perceives, a being experiences delight through that perception. The Sivagnanabodham, in its fifth sutra, explains that the five senses are perceived by the soul because the soul either unites with them to perceive, or they cannot function on their own.

Here, the delight experienced by the soul through the eye, a sensory organ, is referred to as “(kannin kazhippu)” (the eye’s delight) and “(kankalippa kandarkal)” (they saw with delight in their eyes).

Therefore, Sivakavimani Aiya summarizes the meaning of this wonderful verse as follows: “Just as a father and mother give birth to everyone, so too did Ganesha, who is the unrivaled, unique embodiment of Shiva-knowledge and who knows both artistic knowledge and subtle true knowledge, appear. They saw him as the very embodiment of that Shiva-knowledge. They saw that Shiva-knowledge as the unique support that protects the explanations of the scriptures bestowed by the Lord when they face obstacles. They saw Thirugnanasambandar as one who is like a crescent moon, born on earth, dispelling the burning heat of birth and radiating cool, wise light. They also understood that his graceful aid comes through his sacred words, which praise only the glories of the Lord with matted hair.

“Therefore, they comprehended that the seven births of song are embodied in Thirugnanasambandar’s divine form.

“Thus, Mangaiyarkarasi Perumatti and Kulachirai Nayanar perceived this with true understanding and experienced joy. The idea is that Thirugnanasambandar’s divine body, like tears and mother’s milk, is made of true knowledge, which is one of the qualities that cannot be grasped by superficial understanding. The bodies of others who have attained true grace, being illusory, are like a lamp in daylight; they are hidden within that graceful knowledge, becoming imperceptible.

“Therefore, Ganesha’s divine body is indeed made of knowledge. Sekkizhar Peruman has already described this as “Ganesha, who flows with great consciousness.” Thus, Mangaiyarkarasi Perumatti and Kulachirai Nayanar behold Ganesha, who is residing in the monastery. As they beheld him, tears flowed from their eyes like a stream, and they clasped their lotus-like hands together, prostrating themselves on the ground, touching his sacred feet, which were like lotus flowers. With faltering speech, trembling bodies, and troubled minds, they became oblivious to everything. They rolled on the ground, overwhelmed, and, like those who have fallen into the boundless ocean of sorrow and are clutching onto a shore to escape it, they clung to Ganesha’s lotus feet without letting go, due to their intense devotion, and lay there.

“We will continue to contemplate Thiruchitrambalam.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periyapuranam, Part 709, by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, “Vambara Varivandu Cherukkam Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam.” Mangaiyarkarasi Perumatti and Kulachirai Nayanar behold Thirugnanasambandar. This sight, which delighted their eyes, immediately brought to their hearts the thought of the grave injustice and harm the Jains had inflicted upon such a Ganesha. This thought immediately dispelled the delight they had experienced from the vision and, moreover, brought forth an ocean of anxiety and sorrow, manifold greater. As this sorrow welled up in their minds, tears flowed like a stream from their eyes. Both of them clasped their hands and prostrated themselves on the ground.

Their speech faltered. Their bodies trembled, and they rolled on the ground. These are all physical manifestations. First came delight, followed by sorrow due to memory. These changed, and a state of knowing nothing, other than those two states, came upon them.

Therefore, they rolled on the ground, overwhelmed. Like those who have fallen into the boundless ocean of sorrow and are clutching onto a shore to escape it, they clung to Thirugnanasambandar’s sacred feet without letting go, due to their intense devotion, and lay there. Ganesha, the noble one who came to Sirkazhi, raised those two who were clinging to his feet with his sacred hand and consoled them. Thirugnanasambandar is the one who came to dispel the interruption that occurred when the Vedic path was about to begin, causing the Vedas to flourish and thrive. He lifted both of them with his sacred hands. We saw how they lay as if immersed in an ocean of sorrow.

Thirugnanasambandar lifts them out of that ocean of sorrow with his sacred hands. Phrases like “(ennai ippavaththil sera vakaiyethuththu inithamudaiya yeduththa porpatham edukkum makathai)” refer to that act of lifting.

Similarly, this place, where Thirugnanasambandar lifts them with his sacred hands, is filled with grace. Having thus lifted them and bestowed upon them his compassionate gaze, he says to them. Ganesha graciously asks, “Has any harm come to you, who are blessed with grace?” Thirugnanasambandar says, “(Arumarai vazh poompugali annalar adipoonda iruvaraiyum thirukkayal eduththuth thethidavum therumanthu theliyadarthamai nokki sirapparuli thiruvudaiyeer ungal pal theengullatho ena vinava venjamanaar mun cheytha vanchanaikku miga azhinthe anjinom thirumenikku adathu enre athu theernthom vanchakar matravar cheytha theethozhil poy mannvanpal enjalila kodu veduppay ezha ninrathu ena thozhuthu veiyya thozhil aman kundar vilaikka varum veduppavar tham cheyyum mathi mayaikalal theeramai thippiniyan)”. (Mayalurum mannavan mun matravarai venrarulil emaathu uyirum avan uyirum ena uraiththarkal.) Sekkizhar Peruman composes three verses here. Thirugnanasambandar asked if any harm had come to them. In response, both of them say, “We were greatly distressed and afraid of the evil deeds previously committed by the cruel Jains.

“We then firmly believed that they could not harm your sacred body. But the evil deeds perpetrated by those deceivers did not end there; they manifested as an unbearable burning disease in the king.” Thus they spoke and worshipped him. The fear that the fire set by the Jains would harm Thirugnanasambandar subsided, replaced by a firm conviction. The fear that it might harm Ganesha passed, replaced by a firm conviction.

“But unexpectedly, that fierce heat reached the king. We feared it would come to Ganesha, but it lacked the power to do so; thus, it reached the king instead. The queen and Kulachirai Nayanar, having said that the burning disease caused by the vile actions of the evil Jains could not be cured by the illusory remedies of the Jains, pleaded with Thirugnanasambandar that if he would conquer the Jains in front of the king, who was afflicted by that burning disease, then their lives and the king’s life would be saved. They tried to cure the Jains who had committed evil deeds, but the disease did not subside; instead, it intensified, and the king lay bewildered within it. They request that Thirugnanasambandar must conquer those Jains in the king’s presence. If Thirugnanasambandar does not show such divine compassion, the king’s life will be lost, and before that, their own lives will also be lost.

“They explain the existing circumstances and the actions that need to be taken, and they plead with him. Their plea contains hints that their lives are bound together with the king’s, and that it is the Lord’s primary duty to protect them, and for that purpose, the king’s life must be protected.

“Furthermore, if harm is to come to the king’s life, then harm will come to our lives first.

“Therefore, in this situation, we await your divine action, they say, and request him to conquer the Jains. Conquering the Jains is one action, and then bestowing grace is the next action. Bestowing grace upon the king is the next action. Conquering the Jains implies the removal of bondage, and then bestowing grace implies the attainment of Shiva. Conquering the Jains happens by defeating them in debates (Suravadam), in trials by fire (Analavadam), and in trials by water (Punalavadam) in the king’s presence. Bestowing grace is explained by Thirugnanasambandar giving sacred ash (Thiruneeru) and taking the king under his protection, and by teaching him the sacred verses of the Shivagamas (Shivagama Mantropadesham).

“These historical events are yet to unfold.

“Thus, Mangaiyarkarasi Perumatti and Kulachirai Nayanar submit their plea. Thirugnanasambandar, having listened to their plea, graciously tells them, “Do not fear. I will, by the command of the Lord, defeat the senseless Jains today for all to see, so that you may rejoice, and I will make the Pandyan king wear the sacred ash.” Thus, Ganesha graciously speaks the next verse. Hearing this, they first bowed and their faces bloomed. (Azhunthum idar kadalidai ninru adiyomai eduththarula chezhuntharulach chivikaiyin mel thennadu cheyvaththal ezhuntharula perudaiyom en peram ena thozhutalum en). As ThiruGnanaSambandhar thus spoke the verses, the Queen and the Chief Minister, hearing him, bowed before him, their faces beaming with joy. They said, “You have arrived on this beautiful pearl palanquin as a result of the great penance performed by the southern country, in order to lift us from the ocean of suffering in which we were deeply submerged.

“Therefore, we have received a great blessing. What more could we not achieve? We can achieve anything!” Mangaiyarkarasi Ammaiyar and Kulachirai Nayanar then bowed in reverence.

“We shall carry on with this discussion.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Volume 710, written by Deivasekkizhar Peruman, the section on the buzzing streaked bees, the biography of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman declares that by the command of the Lord, he will defeat the Jainas in debate and bring the Pandiya King to the path of the sacred ash. Mangaiyarkarasi Pirattiyar and Kulachirai Nayanar rejoice, considering this a great blessing bestowed upon them. Sekkizhar Peruman composes the next verse: “Aavadhum azhivum ellaam avar seyal amanaraagum Paavakaarigalai nokkum pazhudhudan neenga vella Sevuyar kodiyinaardham thiruvullam ariven endru Poovalardh pozhil soozh Santhai puravalar podhuginraar.” (All that comes into being and all that perishes is His action. The protector of Santhai, surrounded by flower-filled groves, knowing the sacred will of the Lord with the bull banner, declares that he will conquer the sinful Jainas and remove the blemish.) All creation and destruction are the actions of Shiva.

The Vedas refer to Shiva with the word ‘Tat’, indicating Him. All creation and destruction are His actions.

Therefore, both the defeat of the Jainas, which is destruction, and the establishment of the Shaiva path in the Pandya country, which is creation, were desired by Mangaiyarasi Pirattiyar and Kulachirai Nayanar. These two actions, therefore, would not occur without the grace of Shiva. To emphasize this, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states, “All that comes into being and all that perishes is His action.” The Jainas are sinners, those who commit sins. Even looking at sinners is a blemish. If we see those who do not apply sacred ash, we are afraid. As stated in Thiruvachakam, “Even seeing evil people is evil.” Justice scriptures also state, “Seeing evil people is evil.” The Jainas held the principle, “Do not see, do not touch.” To remove the blemish that came from the king looking at these sinners, and to defeat the Jainas, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds to Thiruvalavai Temple, saying, “I know the sacred will of the all-powerful Shiva.” The evil of looking at sinners, debating with them, and then subsequently defeating and destroying them – all these actions must be performed.

Therefore, he ponders on the sacred will of Thiruvalavai Peruman. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman resolves that he must know and receive the grace and consent of Thiruvalavai Peruman before undertaking the evil of debating with the Jainas. To understand the sacred will of Thiruvalavai Peruman concerning engaging in debate, he addresses Thiruvalavai Peruman with the pathigam “Thiruvullamae” (Is it Your sacred will?).

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the generous one who took incarnation and came to this world, came to the Pandiya kingdom.
