He enters the temple with his hands joined above his head in worship. His eyes radiate joy. This is a sign of bliss as he approaches the Lord. The blooming of the eyes is an outward expression of inner joy.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman enters the Thiruvalavai temple. Deiva Sekkizhar Swamigal then composes the next verse: “Nokida vidhiyilaarai nokki yaan vaadhu seiya Theekanmal meniyaane thiruvullamae endraennil Baakkiya payanaay.” (O Lord with a fiery body, is it Your sacred will that I debate those who are not destined to be seen?) This is the 738th verse. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman stands before Thiruvalavai Sokkanatha Peruman and says, “O Lord with a body like fiery embers, O Lord with a body like fire, is it Your sacred will that I debate the Jainas, who are not destined to be seen?” Like the fruit of blessings, the child-like Balaraavayar, looking at the truth, sings a pathigam, a garland of rich Tamil verses.

The Lord has a body like fiery embers. Both ‘thee’ (fire) and ‘kanal’ (embers) refer to the same meaning.

Here, ‘theekkanal’ (fiery ember) denotes its intensity. Fire both cooks and protects through burning. Excessive fire takes lives, and the absence of fire also takes lives.

Therefore, here, fire has the power to both destroy and protect. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman addresses Sokkanatha Peruman as ‘Theekkanal Meniyane’ to signify that the Lord possesses a form capable of both destruction and protection. The burning fire is superior to the fire set by the Jainas and produces its effect.

Therefore, addressing the Lord as ‘Theekkanal Meniyane’, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman asks, “Is it Your sacred will that I debate with the Jainas, who are unworthy of being seen?” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states that the Jainas are unworthy of being seen or being seen by. They were not destined to receive the grace of Pillaiyar at that time. One should not look at the Jainas, nor should one debate with them.

Therefore, both these actions are explained in Shaiva scriptures. We have already seen the subtlety of the rule that one should not even look at wicked people. If one should not look at or debate, why does Pillaiyar attempt these actions here? Because, as Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal states, “For those with confused minds who debate, and for all those whom the poor call ‘gods,’ there is no other god but Mahadeva.” The truths of other religions are absorbed as parts and aspects within Shaiva dharma.

However, Shaiva dharma cannot be contained within anything else. When religions that held only a few doctrines arrogantly rose, claiming to know the whole truth, and deceived the people of this world, plunging them into the pit of other faiths, it became the duty of great elders, who guide the world, to stand by divine grace, debate, and reveal the true nature of those religions so that the world would not be deceived but saved.

Furthermore, when adherents of other religions seized and occupied our great treasures, the Shaiva temples and Shaiva principles, it also became our duty to reclaim and protect our heritage. All that Pillaiyar is about to perform falls within this framework. All external religions should remain within their boundaries. When they do not remain within their boundaries but rise up and begin to seize other religions, the Vedic religions, it becomes the duty of Pillaiyar and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman to protect the world from being deceived by such actions. Pillaiyar and Arasu performed these as acts of grace. Destroying any religion is a difference in maturity.

The true harmony of Shaivism is to find everything in its proper place, step by step, according to the difference in maturity. Without this, clinging to a few words and ideas and saying that everything is one, demonstrating harmony. Such a display of harmony is false harmony. These pseudo-explanations prevail due to a lack of proper instruction from teachers who truly understand Shaiva truths and a lack of adherence to experiential practice.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman appeals to Shiva, asking, “Is it Your sacred will to see the Jainas and defeat them in debate?” Whether it is the Lord’s sacred will can be understood by the concept in Shivagnana Bodham: “He stands as one, knowing and seeing, as if he himself is the Lord within the very truth of the Lord.” In that state, the Lord will grant grace so that people can understand. Without His grace, they do nothing, and the great souls who see only Shiva’s grace as their eye. The great souls who perceive only Shiva’s grace as their guide are capable of seeing everything encompassed within Shiva’s pervasiveness. This state is very difficult for others who do not abide in it to comprehend. The customs prevalent these days, such as understanding omens, casting lots, discerning intentions, and seeking flower oracles, are all practices that have evolved from the aforementioned truth, each according to their respective level. In a later part of this narrative, the event where Pillaiyar himself took up the Thirumurai with his sacred ash-stained hand and saw the divine manifestation written on the palm leaf of the Thirunallatru pathigam, is also based on this very concept.

Thus, the fruit of countless blessings, meaning the fruit of the countless penances performed by countless souls, is this: It is to receive Gnanasambandha Peruman.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Swamigal refers to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman in this verse as “Balaraavayar, the fruit of countless blessings.” Srimath Madhava Shivagnana Munivar also uses this same phrase, praising Sekkizhar Peruman as “Sekkizhar, who lives in Kunrai, the fruit of our blessings.” Such a Balaraavayar is Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. If we say Balaraavayar, it means that his sacred mouth, from which the fragrance of the milk of wisdom fed by the Divine Mother continuously emanates, gives rise to words of wisdom.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman uses the name Balaraavayar here to indicate that, by that divine wisdom, he perceived the sacred will of the Lord. Along with the Lord who was seated on the beautiful golden boat. We can recall the teacher’s explanation of this meaning in the 1995th verse: “The consort with golden bangles, whose sweet words are like the milk from her sacred breast, and whose mouth is like coral.” Realizing the significance and rarity of this name, later elders bestowed the name Balaraavayar upon their children. Our divine Sekkizhar Peruman’s younger brother also bore the name Balaraavayar. Such a Balaraavayar composes a pathigam, a garland of powerful Tamil verses. The richness of this powerful Tamil garland pathigam is its ability to guide souls to salvation by following the path of grace, standing firm in righteousness.

At this time, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sang two pathigams. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to explain how Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed those pathigams.

Therefore, after praying to the Lord with the first pathigam, “Is it Your sacred will to debate?” and realizing through divine grace that debating was indeed the Lord’s sacred will, Pillaiyar then prays to the Lord in the second pathigam, “Is it Your sacred will to win and destroy in debate?” Pillaiyar, who had resolved, “I will know the sacred will of the Lord with the bull banner to conquer and remove the blemish from those who look at sinners,” and then entered the Thiruvalavai temple to inquire, proceeds further only after the Lord’s sacred will has given consent.

Therefore, it is understood through this that the Lord’s sacred will indicates consent to Pillaiyar.

All those from other religions who doubt Pillaiyar’s compassion and the excellence of Shaivism should clearly understand this. Taking the verse, “Singing ‘Kaattumaa uri’ first, and then singing ‘Vedha Velvi’”, it is noteworthy that the pathigam ‘Kaattumaa uri’ signifies the rejection of other religions, and the pathigam beginning ‘Vedha Velvi’ signifies the creation of the path of sacred ash, both sought to understand the sacred will.

Here, a crucial point is to understand the state. These two—the destruction of bonds and the attainment of Shiva—are the core ideas of the tenth and eleventh sutras of Shivagnana Bodham, representing two different types of grace bestowed by the Lord upon souls. The two pathigams composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman are the fourth and fifth pathigams dedicated to the Thiruvalavai temple. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who bestowed these pathigams upon us, understanding the will of Thiruvalavai Sokkanatha Peruman, further addresses Thiruvalavai Peruman, saying, “O virtuous one, praised by the four Vedas! “Secondly, he addresses Him as Lord Shiva of Aalavai, which represents the Lord’s general characteristic as the inner essence of the five divine functions. When he sees Pillaiyar arrive, he raises his hands in worship and points to the pedestal next to his throne.

Thus, as grace settles, darkness gradually dissipates, and blessings arise in various places, as exemplified by this historical account. As soon as the king gives this command, Kulachirai Nayanar is overjoyed. Until now, Kulachirai Nayanar, on behalf of the king, had carried out the royal duty of welcoming guests as instructed by the Queen.

Now, the king himself agrees to welcome Pillaiyar and to arrange a pedestal for him and to send someone to receive him. Kulachirai Nayanar is exceedingly happy. Kulachirai Nayanar, with great joy, goes out from the palace to bring Pillaiyar. Kulachirai Nayanar goes very quickly to escort Pillaiyar into the palace.

Our reflection now resumes. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Seven Hundred Thirteen, authored by Thirudeva Sekkizhar Peruman, Vambaravarivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. As soon as Kulachirai Nayanar goes to welcome Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, all the Jainas surround the Pandya king. The Jainas, who consider the Aragu god under the Ashoka tree as their deity, approach the Pandya king and say, “Is this the way to establish our religion? How can you do this?” They say to the Pandya king, “This religion is the Jaina religion, and it is your religion. You must protect your religion; it is your duty.

“This religion is your possession, and protecting your possession is your duty.” They lay out this premise. Having said this, the Jainas further state, “You have invited him, that is, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, here. Let it be. He and we will try to cure your illness together in front of you. Even if your illness is cured by him, you must say that your illness was cured by the method we employed.” Thus, they speak to the king with great deceit. They are those who consider falsehood as truth.

“But the Pandya king does not agree. Until now, he had been subservient to the Jainas and had acted unilaterally in their favor. Now he does not agree to this deceit of the Jainas because The benefit of the penance previously performed by the Pandya king is now ripening and bringing good results.

“Therefore, he does not agree to the deceit of the Jainas. The scriptures state that the truth is that the fruit of penance manifests and becomes useful only when it ripens and comes to fruition; God will bring about the fruit of that penance.

“Accordingly, until now, the time for that penance to ripen and come to fruition had not arrived, so he was under the sway of the Jainas. Now is the time for the Pandya king’s previous penance to bear fruit.

“Therefore, the Pandya king does not now agree to the deceit of the Jainas. The Pandya king tells the Jainas, “You both try to cure this disease through your deities. I The Pandya king declares that he will not deviate from impartiality and speak deceitfully. When the king says this, the Jainas are very saddened and remain there.

“At the same time, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who is like the essence of the penance performed by the southern Tamil country, the Pandya kingdom, reaches the gate in front of the Pandya king’s palace, dismounts from his pearl palanquin, and enters. This is described in the seven hundred and fiftieth verse: (avan uraippa kundar ennangirundha ellai thenn thamizh naadu seythavakk kozhundu pOlvaar van thani pavana munnar vaayilul anaindhu maadu pon thigal tharala paththi sivikai ninru ezhundhu pukkaar) As Kulachirai Nayanar previously arrived, the queen, Kottravan Deviyar, also rose from her place and went. The next verse says that the king of the cool Tamil country saw the Kaundinya lord, who resembled the full moon with abundant arts, who had come to the earth to dispel the long darkness, standing in the sky. After informing the king, Kulachirai Nayanar arrives before Pillaiyar. The queen also comes inside the palace and descends from her palanquin. The Pandya king, the ruler of the cool Tamil country, sees Pillaiyar, the Kaundinya lord, who resembles the full moon with abundant arts, who has come to the earth to dispel the long darkness, as if from the sky.

“When Pillaiyar sets out from Thirualavai temple, the chief minister arrives with a large retinue of devotees before him. As they approach the palace, the minister separates from the crowd and quickly goes ahead, enters the palace, informs the king of Pillaiyar’s arrival, arranges a pedestal for Pillaiyar according to the king’s command, then leaves the palace again, receives Pillaiyar, brings Pillaiyar into the palace, and stands there. The queen also arrives there. The Pandya king, the ruler of his Tamil country, sees Pillaiyar coming. The Peruman mentions the inherent coolness that will cure his fever. He refers to the king as the ruler of his Tamil country, including the Pandya country, because of the coolness that the Podigai mountains bring to the Pandya country.

“The Pandya king sees Pillaiyar arriving like a full moon rising from the sky to dispel the long darkness, like the internal darkness of Jainism being dispelled, like a shining moon that neither waxes nor wanes in the ethereal sky. The Sekkizhar Peruman compares Thirugnanasambandha Peruman to the moon because he brings coolness with his divine arts and ambrosial arts. Since the sacred ash’s divine light shines everywhere when Pillaiyar arrives, it is compared to the white light of the moon. The Pandya king sees Pillaiyar arriving thus. Until the previous day, the king had been saying things like ‘see and touch’ and ‘hear and touch.’ Due to the benefit of his previous penance, this situation changes, and he sees Pillaiyar with great desire and love. Among the inner meanings, sight is the first thing that occurs.

“The king sees Pillaiyar. Sekkizhar Peruman describes what he did upon seeing him. The next verse states: (kanda appozhudhe vendhan kaiyedutthu eytha nokki than thunar mudiyin paangar thamaniya peedam kaatta vandhamizh viragar mevi adhan misai irundhaar maayai konda valla amanar ellaam kuripinul achcham kondaar) Immediately upon seeing Pillaiyar, the king raises his hands in worship and shows the elevated pedestal to Pillaiyar. The king, suffering from his illness, is unable to stand up and worship with folded hands, so he worships with folded hands from his seated position. He also points to the pedestal, indicating for Pillaiyar to be seated there. He points with his hand.

“The method of invoking the deity in Shiva puja involves actions such as Avahanam (invocation), Sthapanam (installation), and Sannirodanam (confinement), which are performed by showing specific mudras (hand gestures). We see a similar situation occurring here. When the king requested this, Pillaiyar graciously ascended and sat upon the elevated seat. The Jainas, whose religious principles included deceit and falsehood, felt fear within their hearts. They were afraid. The next verse is: (Chezhiyanum Pillaiyardham thirumeni kaanappetru vizhiyura nokkalaale vemmayinOy sirithu neengki azhivurum manam nernirkka anthanar vaazhvai nokki keluvuru pathi yaadhu enru viruppudan ketpOdhu)

“This is the seven hundred and fifty-third verse. The king saw Pillaiyar, and Pillaiyar’s gracious gaze also fell upon the king.

“Therefore, the king’s fever now recedes a little further. Earlier, when the name mantra entered the king’s ears, his exhaustion subsided slightly.

“At that time, the king expressed his joy, saying he would be happy if this illness was cured by the arrival of this young sage, and he would join their side.

“Later, when he was informed of Pillaiyar’s impending arrival, the illness receded a little further, to the extent that he ordered a pedestal to be placed next to his throne. He had also refrained from speaking deceitfully to the Jainas, which was another stage in the illness receding.

“Now, upon seeing Pillaiyar and receiving Pillaiyar’s divine gaze, his fever further recedes a little, and the king’s mind becomes clear. He looks at Pillaiyar with great desire and asks him, “What is your native place?” He gains the strength to ask this.

“Thus, it is explained here that the gradual relief from illness and the enlightenment of wisdom are attained by a soul through the grace of the Supreme Guru, Pillaiyar. Previously, the mind, which was disturbed and lost due to the severity of the illness, is now steady. With such a mind, he looks at Pillaiyar and asks, “Where is your village?” Is it not still a tradition to ask, “What is your village?” and begin conversation when welcoming a new person? When the king asked this, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman replied, (Ponni valandharu naattu punar pazhana purampanai) surrounding the beautiful town of Kazhumalam, which we consider our home. Thirugnanasambandhar, the child who has the excellent twelve names, thus sang a pathigam to the southern king, as described in the seven hundred and fifty-fourth verse. Pillaiyar replies, “Ponni Valandharu Nadu is the Chola country, my country.

“In the Chola country, irrigated by the Kaveri river, surrounded by fertile fields and wetlands, the child composed a pathigam, Thirukazhumalam, which is Sirkazhi, which we consider our home.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman replies, “Kazhumalam is the town we praise.” In the pathigam he just sang, “Kazhumalam is the town we praise,” is the concluding line of every verse. Kazhumalam is the town we praise. In each verse, this serves as a crown. Among the twelve sacred names of Sirkazhi, he mentions the other eleven sacred names and the twelfth name, Kazhumalam. In each verse of this pathigam, Pillaiyar thus blesses. Sekkizhar Peruman refers to this pathigam as a pathigam that embraces and praises the twelve names.

“This pathigam, which begins with Piramanur Velupuram, praises the twelve names of Sirkazhi in each verse. It is a pathigam set in the Gantharam tune and is in the style of Thiruchakkaramaatru. Piramapuram, Venupuram, Pugazhi, and so on are the twelve sacred names of Sirkazhi. In this pathigam, the first verse begins with Piramanur, and the second verse begins with the second name, Velupuram. The third verse begins with the third name, Pugali.

“In this way, each verse begins with one of those names, and Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has arranged the twelve names in the same order in each verse. This is a pathigam composed in the Thiruchakkaramaatru style, which is the seventieth pathigam in the Second Thirumurai. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thonipuram. (theraai ponnam sirappu sampai arulmal than kali kochchai vayam ullitta aathiyaai pannirandaai nindra theere kazhumalam naam paravum oore kaavimalaa pOraiyum kanna kazhumalathin peyarai naaLumbhaaviyasee pannirandum nalluzha) This pathigam was composed in the king’s palace to console him when he asked, “What is our village?” Although this pathigam belongs to Sirkazhi, it was composed in Madurai. Let’s continue our reflection.”” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Seven Hundred Fourteen, authored by Thirudeva Sekkizhar Peruman, Vambaravarivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Pillaiyar is seated on the golden pedestal.

At this time, the envious Jainas approach Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Hiding the fear in their hearts, their faces ablaze with anger like fire, and their eyes red like embers, they approach Pillaiyar. The hearts of the Jainas were filled with envy. The Thirukkural states that righteousness is formed by avoiding these four: envy, desire, anger, and harsh words.

At this point, the commentator Parimel Azhagar explains envy as not tolerating others’ prosperity.

Here, the envy among the Jainas is the desire to suppress Shaivism and to flourish themselves. They outwardly display their principles of non-violence, etc., but in reality, their mindset is to suppress Shaivism through deceit, falsehood, and other cunning means and to thrive themselves. This is the mindset of the Jainas, and this is called envy. Envy means jealousy. Because of this envy, the Jainas’ eyes turn red, and they utter many harsh words. From envy, desire arises.

When that desire is not fulfilled, anger arises. Due to that anger, harsh words are spoken. All these are interconnected and cause and effect each other, as Thiruvalluvar states in the Thirukkural about the four things: envy, desire, anger, and harsh words, which are integral to righteousness. We see this in these Jainas here. Their eyes red with envy, they utter many harsh words. If envy takes hold in one’s heart, it leaves no room for any other good qualities.

This evil quality of envy has the nature of completely taking over the heart.

Thus, the Jainas speak there. They possess both external and internal darkness. The internal darkness in their hearts consists of evil qualities like envy. All evil qualities arise from the quality of tamas, and the color of tamas is said to be dark. We can recall this here. Due to that envy, it is as if the fire of anger leaps out from their faces and eyes.

Generally, anger is referred to as fire because this anger will burn and consume those who are overtaken by it. Burning means that anger will torment those who are angry in many ways, both internally and externally.

Thus, the dark-skinned Jainas surround Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who shines like a red-gold light of Shiva knowledge. This is like clouds surrounding the rising sun in the morning. Since Sekkizhar Peruman refers to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as the sun here, we can understand that the previous Jaina darkness was like night, and when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, like the sun, rises, the surrounding Jaina darkness is dispelled. Just as the clouds surrounding the sun lose all their strength and cannot stand, so too the Jainas surrounding Thirugnanasambandha Peruman diminish before the light of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s Shiva knowledge in a little while. Generally, we refer to a dog barking as ‘kuraippathu.’ In the same way, the Jainas bark meaningless and very loud insults. Earlier, Sekkizhar Peruman referred to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as the sun.

Now, he describes the loud and meaningless harsh words uttered by the Jainas as dogs barking. The proverb “a dog barking at the sun” comes to mind here. Generally, those who lose in an argument make noise, speak evil words, and shout loudly. The Jainas, filled with envy, anger, and other evil qualities, shout loudly in this manner, without any thought for the Pandya king who is suffering, and without any regard for time or place. Pillaiyar, hearing them, says, “Speak properly, as is appropriate to your truth.” However, the foul-mouthed, frenzied Jainas leap up and, in a large group, surround and clamor and cry out. The young lady, seeing this, cannot bear it and trembles within.

She looks at the southern king and says, “It seems like the divine body is fragile. This gracious Pillaiyar, and these countless Jainas, O King, our Lord will surely dispel the delusion of your illness.

“Afterwards, these Jainas will be submerged. If they are strong, let them speak,” says Sekkizhar Swamigal, composing two verses here. Pillaiyar looks at the Jainas who are surrounding him and barking, and says, “You should speak in an orderly manner. Do not bark like this.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman says, “Speak as a religious debate should be conducted.” Pillaiyar says, “Let the debate proceed according to the rules.” Those who engage in religious debate should present their religious principles, the definition of God according to their religion, the principles of epistemology, what life means according to their religion, what liberation means, and so on, in a systematic and logical manner, with valid proofs. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states, “Explain all your truths and the meanings expressed in your religious texts.

“Do not shout like this.” Therefore, the Jainas surrounded Pillaiyar and challenged him to a debate and shouted. Pillaiyar tells them to speak in an orderly manner, according to the rules of debate, and not to shout or speak in a disorderly fashion. Nevertheless, those foul-mouthed, frenzied Jainas jump up. Many of them rise and surround him, panicking and crying out improperly. They engage in actions that do not conform to the rules of debate. Instead of entering the debate fairly as Pillaiyar instructed, they act improperly.

“Seeing this, Pandimadevi is unable to bear it and trembles within. The previous night, the Jainas had committed evil deeds in secret.

“Now, the same Jainas are misbehaving even when they meet Thirugnanasambandha Peruman in person.

“Therefore, Pandimadevi fears what might happen. The queen Mangaiyarkkarasi reaches a state where she cannot bear to see it, and her mind is filled with trepidation. This is also an outcome of her maternal quality of compassion. This gracious Pillaiyar is of a tender form, while these cruel Jainas come in a crowd and shout. These Jainas are capable of wicked deeds. Because of their strength in numbers and the burning anger of their envy, they will attempt to do anything they wish.

“This thought arises in Pandimadevi’s heart, and so Pandimadevi says to the king, “This Pillaiyar is a young boy, but the Jainas are innumerable, O King. Our Pillaiyar will cure the delusion of your fever.

“After that, these Jainas can debate if they are able.” Pandimadevi thus requests the king. Pillaiyar is of a tender form, The Jainas are in a group. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman will cure your illness.

“After that, the Jainas can debate. The Queen, with these four thoughts in her mind, speaks thus. The first thought among these four is about Pillaiyar’s divine form. This shows the motherly love and the profound love of Mangaiyarkkarasi Pandimadevi. When Pandimadevi speaks thus, the king replies to Pandimadevi, saying, (maaranum avaraai nokki varundal nee enru mattra veruvaadhu enkOl enmel veppu ozhitthu arughar neerum aaranich sadayinaarukku anbharaam ivaru ninggal theariya dheivatthanmai ennidath therippeer enraan) This is the seven hundred and fifty-ninth verse.

“The Pandya king replies. He calls the Queen, who was trembling inside, and first tells her, “Do not fear.” He tells her, “Do not be sad.” He says, “You need not grieve,” and then the Pandya king further says, “What other debate is needed? You, the Arhats, and this devotee of Shiva, who wears the Ganga in his matted hair – you both remove this fever from me.

“After that, you explain to me the true nature of your deities.” The Pandya king mentions them separately, not together.

“Therefore, the Pandya king tells them both to individually try to cure this disease and show the truth. This is also because of Pillaiyar’s gracious gaze, which further reduced the Pandya’s fever, allowing the king to speak this way.

“Here, he refers to Pillaiyar with great respect and high regard as “this devotee of Shiva who wears the Ganga in his matted hair.” He speaks this way, with his illness and delusion removed, because he heard Pillaiyar’s name mantra, saw Pillaiyar’s divine form, and received Pillaiyar’s gracious gaze.

“At the same time, when the king spoke thus, Pillaiyar looks at Pandimadevi and speaks words of grace, saying, “You need not grieve.” (Gnana aaramudhum undaar natsavuruvai nokki) (vizhiyinaay kel mattra ennai baalan enru nee nani anjavednda nilaiyilaa amanarkku enrum yaan ezhiyaan aleen enrumezhundirupathigam paadi pertiyaal arulic cheytha pillaiyaar thamakkum munnam surtru nindru alaitthal ovaa arugarkum thennar kOmaan itrai naaL ennai uttra piNiyai neer ikazhitththeerum tetrrana theerththaar vaadhil venranar enru seppa) These are two verses composed by Sekkizhar Peruman. Pillaiyar looks at Pandimadevi and says, “Do not be afraid,” and at this time, he also composes a pathigam. “O lady with eyes like a deer, listen. You need not greatly fear me, thinking I am a child. I am never weak before these transient Jainas,” he sang that pathigam with this sentiment.

“Let us go on reflecting.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Seven Hundred Fifteen, authored by Thirudeva Sekkizhar Peruman, Vambaravarivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, addressing Pandimadevi, says, “Do not be afraid. Do not think that I am a child and be afraid. Aalavai (Siva) is our protector, so I will not be weak before these Jainas.” He then composes a pathigam, beginning with “Maani Ner Vizhi Maadaraai.” “Maani Ner Vizhi Maadaraai” means “O queen with eyes like a frightened deer, listen, O great Queen, wife of the Pandya king. This child has pure, sweet words.

“Do not become anxious thinking that I am merely a child. Since Thirualavai is our protector, I will not be weak before these Jainas.” He thus composed the pathigam. Pillaiyar addresses the Pandimadevi as “Maani Ner Vizhi Maadaraai” in this pathigam. This is the only pathigam in which Pillaiyar addresses a specific individual directly. Such is the special nature of Pandimadevi. This pathigam is the sixth pathigam dedicated to Thirualavai, the thirty-ninth pathigam in the Third Thirumurai, set to the Kolli tune.

“The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (veli maadaraai vaLa vikkumaa perum devi ke paaLavayOru baala eevan enru nee paRi vedhi aaLai maamizhaiyaadhiyaaya idanggalaai pala azal chenarugeLi enallen thiru aaLavaai aruL nirkkave ekkara maN kaigaRu keLiye nallen thiru aaLavaai sokkaniyal uLLirukkave thuLangum mudhi) Thirugnanasambandha Peruman addresses Pandimadevi as “Maani Ner Vizhiyal” and begins this pathigam. “Maani Ner Vizhi” means eyes like a frightened deer. The queen, Mangaiyarkkarasi, trembles at the thought of what might happen to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s divine body and speaks to the Pandya king.

“At that time, she is trembling and has a frightened look in her eyes. It is to such a queen that Pillaiyar addresses and sings. He says that these Jainas are transient Jainas, meaning that they are confused, holding principles where something can be both false and true, unable to define their principles, wandering as confused individuals. He states, “I am not weak before them,” and thus composes this pathigam. (Maani ner vizhi maadaraai vazhudhikkum maa perundhevi keL paanalvaai oru baalan eengu ivan enru nee paRiv eydhidhel aanai maamalai aadhiyaaya idangaLil pala allal ser eanarkku eliyen alen thiru aalavaai araN nirkkave) This beautiful first verse is thus structured. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sings to the Queen and blesses her. “O great Queen, wife of the Pandya king, listen.

“Do not consider me easy, thinking I am a child with sweet, pure words. Thirualavai is our protector, so I am not weak before these lowly ones who cause much suffering in places like Anaimalai and other such places,” thus declares Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. We had previously seen that the Jainas had gathered in Anaialai and other mountains. We had seen that upon hearing of his arrival, Jainas from various parts of the Pandya kingdom gathered in large numbers in Madurai. There are eight hills surrounding Madurai: Elephant Hill, Pig Hill, Snake Hill, Cow Hill, etc. In each of these eight hills, a thousand Jainas, making a total of eight thousand, lived there, having established Jaina schools.

“They lived in caves and on rock beds in these hills. All of them, eight thousand Jainas living in these eight hills, came to Madurai. Throughout the pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman exposes the true nature of the Jainas. He explains how they lead their lives by holding false principles and outwardly displaying non-violence. He explains how they live by displaying non-violence outwardly. The language spoken by these Jainas was Prakrit, a corrupted form of Sanskrit.

“They did not even speak it properly. There are Vedic scholars who are proficient in Sanskrit and other languages, having thoroughly studied the Vedas, Agamas, and mantras. These Vedic scholars were ashamed when these Jainas spoke, distorting the Sanskrit language and using Prakrit, making a lot of noise. The Vedic scholars, who had thoroughly studied Sanskrit, the Vedas, Agamas, and mantras, were ashamed that these Jainas were distorting the language. These Jainas were accustomed to distorting all these languages and speaking with much clamor, as stated in the second verse. they are accustomed to distorting all these languages and speaking with much clamor, as stated in the second verse. In the third verse, he condemns the principles of the Jainas.

“The Jainas hold the principle of ‘asti-nasti’ (is-is not). If asked if God exists, the Jainas would say it cannot be definitively said that He does or does not, speaking in a confusing manner, unable to define their principles, wandering as confused individuals. They wander unclothed, making observers ashamed. In the third verse, it says that these Jainas roam around with names like Candrasena, Indrasena, Dharmasena, Gandhasena, Kanakasena. Whether it is Sanskrit or Southern language, Tamil, if one properly learns these two languages, the truth one will realize is that Shiva is the supreme God and Shaivism is the excellent religious path. This understanding will come to one.

“If one properly learns these North Indian and South Indian languages, one will realize this. But these Jainas, without properly learning these two languages, are unable to understand the Vedic path and the Shaiva path. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman explains in the fourth verse that these Jainas are blind-eyed and wander around. These Jainas compose books like Eliviruttam, Kiliviruttam, Nariviruttam, etc., and deceive people by claiming their contents are true. They outwardly portray themselves as doing many good deeds. They desire the wealth that comes from these deeds and accumulate riches.

“Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states in the fifth verse that he is not weak before such Jainas who seize wealth in this manner, and that our Aalavai Lord will always bless us. In the next verse, he mentions various types of Nandis, such as Kanakanandi, Pushpanandi, Bhavanandi, Kumanamasunakanandi, Kunakanandi, Divananandi, and states that these Jainas consider evil itself as penance. In the seventh verse, he says that these Jainas claim to have no attachments or relations but do not adhere to faultless moral conduct. They adhere to unjust paths. He states that he is not weak before such Jainas and Buddhists, because the Lord of Aalavai always protects us. In the eighth verse, he states that Ravana believed there was no one superior or equal to him, but Shiva destroyed Ravana’s arrogance.

“He sings that he is not weak before those Jainas who, without bowing to Shiva, practice false penance, carrying a water pot and peacock feathers, tucking a mat under their armpit, walking with fear and trepidation one after another, lest they harm any small creature, considering this their principle, because the Lord of Thirualavai protects him. In the ninth verse, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states that the Jainas are those who do not worship the sacred feet of Shiva, the holy one whom Brahma and Vishnu could not comprehend. They perform rituals for the deceased as if offering water to the dead. In the tenth verse, he states, “I am not easy for the Jains who pluck out their hair, subject their bodies to penance, causing suffering through false asceticism, and utter meaningless words, because the fortress of Thiruvalavay is my inner support.” He proclaims that Shiva is unknown to these Jains and Buddhists. Our leader, Shiva, has beautiful red feet. Abandoning His worship, they have embraced false asceticism, ignorant of the path taught by good texts, and not standing on that path.

“They speak like scholars but utter words of blame. “I am not easy for those Jains, for the fortress of Thiruvalavay stands within me,” he sings in the eleventh verse, which serves as the final verse.

“The Lord of Thiruvalavay, Sokka Natha, my Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who graciously declares, “Since the Lord of Thiruvalavay dwells in my heart, I am not easily swayed by the arrogant Jains,” states that those who recite this pathigam, graciously uttered by Gnanasambandhan, the Tamil Lord born in Thiruppukazhi in the presence of the Pandya king, will face no suffering.

“Thus, in the eleventh verse, he sets the palasruthi for this pathigam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman condemns the doctrines of the Jains and Buddhists in this pathigam. Both these paths stood against the Vaidika Sanatana Dharma, seeking to negate the Vaidika Dharma.

“Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed this pathigam. Pillaiyar incarnated to make the Vaidika path and the Vedic way flourish, and the Shaiva Sect to shine brightly, didn’t he?

“Therefore, he composed this pathigam. As soon as Pillaiyar composed the pathigam, the Pandya king began to speak. Addressing Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and the Jains, the Pandya king said, “Today, you two must individually try to cure this burning disease that has afflicted me. Whoever cures this disease will be victorious in the debate.” Pillaiyar is characterized by his connection to grace. He does nothing without His grace; being under the sway of grace, Shiva’s actions manifest as his own. This is the nature of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, Thiruvalava Didn’t Pillaiyar sing in the pathigam, “Though Arun stands, Sokka is within me”?

“Pillaiyar is such a person. The Pandya king speaks to him and the Jains. Upon hearing the king’s words, the Jains rush forward. They say to the Pandyas, “We will cure the disease in the left side of your body. Next, “Paravanamavathu Neeru” states that sacred ash embodies the essence of Parasakthi. ‘Paravanam’ means the color of the drum. ‘Para’ is a Sanskrit word referring to Parasakthi. In Tamil, ‘Parai’ is a name for Sivasakthi. This ‘Para’ being present means it is the form of Sivasakthi. “Pavamm Aruppathu Neer” means sacred ash removes sins. “Tharavanamavathu Neeru” follows, meaning sacred ash also embodies the color of the earth, ‘Thara’ being a name for the earth.

Next, “Thaththuvamavathu Neeru” states that sacred ash embodies the forms of principles. “Ara Vanangum Thirumeni Alavaayan Thiruneere” means that this is the sacred ash of Thiru Alavaayan, whose sacred form is worshipped by serpents, ‘Ara’ meaning snakes. In the ninth Thiruppadal, “Malodu Ayan Ariyaatha Vannamum Ullathu Neeru” means that sacred ash is an entity that even Brahma and Vishnu could not comprehend. “Melurai Dhevarhal Thangal Meyathu Vennpodi Neeru” signifies that sacred ash is also the white powder on the bodies of the celestials.

Next, “Yela Udambu Idarththeerkkum Inpam Tharuvathu Neeru” means that sacred ash removes bodily ailments and bestows joy. “Alamathu Undamidattril” This is the sacred ash of Thiru Alavaayan, who consumed poison. In the tenth Thiruppadal, “Kundikai Kaiyargalodu Sakkiyar Kootamum Kooda Kanndikai Pippathu Neeru Karutha Iniyathu Neeru” means that sacred ash bewilders even the Jain and Buddhist communities. It is delightful to contemplate. “En Dhisaipattta Porulaar Etthum Thakayathu Neeru” states that sacred ash is worthy of praise by the guardians of the eight directions, the Dikpalakas.

“Andatthavar Paninthu Etthum Alavaayan Thiruneeru Idhu Aakum” means that this is the sacred ash of Alavaay Chokkanathan, worshipped and adored by those holding high positions in the cosmos, ‘Andatthavar’ meaning those in charge of the cosmic realms. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman declares this.

Now, in the eleventh Thiruppadal, the final verse, “Aatral Adalvida Yerum Alavaayan Thiru Neetrai Por” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman concludes this pathigam with a benefit statement, saying that those who master these ten verses, which were sung to alleviate all diseases afflicting the body through sacred ash, will be good people. This is the sacred ash of Thiru Alavaayan, the Shiva who rides the victorious bull. Thirugnanasambandha, the Brahmin from Sirkazhi, states that those who can recite these ten verses from this pathigam, which he composed in worship, will be good people.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman explains the benefit of this pathigam.

Therefore, this sacred ash, by removing diseases of the body. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composes this pathigam, stating that it cures all diseases, including the disease of rebirth caused by the impurity of the soul. We have pondered the explanations of the verses of this sacred ash pathigam, composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, with the help of the commentaries of Kayappakkam Sadhasiva Chettiyar and Sivakavimani Ayya.

Let us continue to contemplate the sacred history. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periyapuranam, Part 718, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, by Deivachikilar Peruman. The Pandya king’s fever is cured by the grace of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Upon his recovery, the Pandya Mahadeviyar and Kulachirai Nayanar worship the lotus feet of the young saint, placing them on their heads. The verse states that the queen and Kulachirai rejoiced, saying, “We have achieved greatness today, we are truly born, and the king has attained liberation from rebirth.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman eradicated evil, here referring to the Pandya king’s fever, and its root cause, the king’s alignment with the Jains. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman simultaneously eradicated these three evils: the king’s alignment with Jainism, the evil influence of Jainism, and the evil karma from the king’s past actions.

Both Pandi Mahadevi and Kulachirai Nayanar prostrate themselves at Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred red feet. They worship him, declaring, “We have achieved greatness today, we are truly born.” They say, “Today we are truly born,” meaning, “Today we have reaped the benefits of our birth.” The Devaram sacred text states, “Days not spent in devotion are days not born.” According to this, all previous days, when they could not serve the king, the devotees, or Shiva, were as if they were not born.

Therefore, they declare, “Today we are born, and we have reaped the benefits of our birth.” They praise the king, saying, “The king has attained liberation from rebirth.”

Now, the Pandya king, free from all his fevers, attains supreme bliss and worships Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, raising his hands above his head. The king performs this act when he is healed and saved. The king’s state is thus explained.

After the fever was cured, the actions of the queen and the minister were first explained by Deivasekkilar Peruman.

Then, it is explained what the king did. This is because the happiness of Pandi Mahadevi and the great minister, who had earnestly prayed to the Lord for the welfare of the king and the country, and had suffered greatly. The joy of Pandi Mahadevi and the great minister surpassed the joy of the king who was cured of his fever and regained health.

Therefore, their joys were mentioned first. Just as when a sick child recovers, the mother’s joy upon seeing its well-being is felt before the child’s, we see this even in the natural order of the world.

Therefore, after first narrating the joy of Pandi Mahadevi and Kulachirai Nayanar, Sekkizhar Peruman then narrates the king’s actions. All of the king’s fevers, both those that came and went, and those that lingered in his left side, had subsided. The fever of delusion, which was the root cause of his bodily fever, also subsided. The fever of past severe karma, which was its cause, also subsided. These were all interconnected. These were the gross and subtle causes and effects.

Once all his fevers subsided, the Pandya king attained supreme bliss. The supreme bliss mentioned here refers to the bliss of liberation. This is because this very Pandya king will transform into Nindraseer Nedumaran, becoming one of the sixty-three Nayanmars, and as Nindraseer Nedumaran Nayanar, he will attain the state of a jivanmukta, liberated from rebirth and achieving supreme bliss. Sekkizhar Peruman alludes to this historical detail here. He states that the king attained supreme bliss. In reality, the removal of illness is a separate experience, and the experience of joy is separate.

Since illness obstructs the experience of joy, the removal of illness aids the enjoyment of bliss.

Therefore, the removal of illness is metaphorically referred to as having gained joy, even though the removal of illness is distinct from the attainment of joy. The Pandya king has now experienced the removal of illness. He will surely attain supreme bliss after receiving spiritual instruction from Thirugnanasambandha Peruman on the banks of the Vaigai. Sekkizhar Peruman confidently states here that the king attained supreme bliss. Srimad Madhava Sivagnana Munivar, in his Sivagnana Mapadiyam, explains that worldly pleasure, which is the experience of the mind deeply comprehending objects of enjoyment, is ‘sitrinpam’ (minor bliss), while deeply comprehending the manifestation of Shivathvam (Shiva’s nature) through spiritual wisdom is ‘perinpam’ (supreme bliss). He thus clarifies the distinction between ‘sitrinpam’ and ‘perinpam’.

Having shed all his fevers, the Pandya king. The Pandya king, with his hands clasped above his head, worships Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Earlier, we saw the Pandya king worshipping Thirugnanasambandha Peruman in his mind.

Now, having recovered, he worships with both hands raised. He says, “I have found peace by clinging to the feet of Gnanasambandha, who came to alleviate the severe illness before the Jains, who have no sense of honor.” Just as a furious elephant, freed from its bonds, charges forward, the Pandya king, who had been bound by the doctrines of the Jains, is now liberated from those shackles.

Now, the Pandya king comes forward directly and expresses the truth in this manner, causing all the Jains to fear. They feared when they saw that all the magical powers they possessed had completely lost their strength.

Now they ponder how to achieve victory and search for a way to succeed. Sekkizhar Peruman describes the thoughts of the Jains at that time in this Thiruppadal, saying, “Seeing the Saivite youth, through the victory of his words, and the fragrant garland of sweet words, remove the fever of that trickster, they thought among themselves that argument was useless.” The Jains witnessed that the fever of the Pandya king was completely cured by the Thiruppathigam of the Saivite youth, the young saint, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

Therefore, the Jains directly witnessed that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s pathigam, the garland of words, worked such miracles, curing the fever. Hence, they thought that they could not defeat Thirugnanasambandha Peruman through religious debate based on logic. ‘Tharkavatham’ means to establish one’s own position.

So, they realized the truth that they could no longer defeat Thirugnanasambandha Peruman through such debates.

Therefore, they thought to themselves, “Now we will try to win in fire and water.” Fire and water are both inanimate objects. The Jains believed they could control the inanimate power of fire and water with the spiritual power of their mantras. They mention both fire and water here. If they truly had faith in their religion and their mantras, they would have mentioned only one.

But here, they want to win in both fire and water. This shows that they doubted if they could win with fire alone.

So, they included water. This is because they had previously seen that the fire they had unleashed through their mantras on the Thirumadam where the young saint was staying had failed to harm him and had lost its strength.

Therefore, they had doubts about fire. But even after knowing that, they included fire in their plan. This is because the fire ordeal they were now planning, the ‘Analavatham,’ was not to be directed at the young saint, but rather they needed to demonstrate their ability to control the inanimate power of fire with their mantraic power. They also failed to realize the truth that the fire, which had previously not obeyed their command, became the fever and afflicted the Pandya king when the young saint commanded it. That is why they decided to combine fire and water, and to overcome by controlling the inanimate power of fire and water with their mantraic power through the two debates, ‘Analavatham’ (fire ordeal) and ‘Punalavatham’ (water ordeal). The Jains plan this.

While they are still contemplating, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman addresses them, saying, “You should speak about the truths of your religion.” Earlier, before the fever was cured, when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrived, the Jains, enraged, surrounded and belittled him. Even then, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman used these same words. Due to the commotion at that time, the debate did not take place.

Now, after the Pandya king’s fever is cured, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman suggests resuming the debate on religious truths from where it left off. Let us press on with our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periyapuranam, Part 719, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, by Deivasekkizhar Peruman. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman initially challenged the Jains to a doctrinal debate, asking them to present the truths of their religion.

However, the queen intervened, saying that if the Jains were truly capable, they should speak after the king’s illness was cured.

Thus, according to the king’s command, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman first undertook the task of curing the illness and succeeded.

Therefore, after his initial invitation was interrupted, the young saint now called upon the Jains again to continue the religious debate. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the supreme spiritual teacher, invited them to declare the truth that their religion could not stand before the true religion of Saivism, thereby guiding the world towards salvation. He issued this invitation so that the world might come to know this truth and attain liberation.

At that time, minor religions, with their limited doctrines and worship of minor deities, had confused the world by differing from Saivism, which recognizes Shiva, the primordial cause and ultimate deity, as the supreme God and the repository of all ultimate truths. This confusion led to a proliferation of falsehoods, a decline in Vedic practices, and a diminishing of Saivite principles, with the significance of sacred ash not being fully understood. To rectify this situation and to establish the true standing of all religions. It is the duty of the spiritual teacher to accurately inform and define them.

Therefore, the young saint undertook this task only after consulting with and receiving the permission of Lord Chokkanatha of Alavaay. For these reasons, the young saint invited the Jains to speak about the truths of their religion. In this world, Saivism, which embraces the tenets of many religions that appear to be contradictory, and thus shows these religions as progressive steps without conflicting with any of them, does not hate, oppose, or destroy any religion.

However, why are refutation of other doctrines and religious debates present here? They exist for self-preservation and to reveal the truth as it is. We must understand that the young saint’s invitation to the Jains for a religious debate was out of compassion to enlighten them, who were obstructing Saivism and confusing the world with their falsehoods, and to guide this world to salvation. The subsequent history of the Jains being executed on stakes falls under the category of royal justice, a form of punitive justice implemented by the king. There is no connection between the young saint’s invitation to a religious debate and the king’s subsequent implementation of that punitive justice system. The Jains refused the young saint’s invitation to a religious debate and chose a debate based on direct experience.

They agreed to conduct a debate based on direct experience, and if they lost, they would be impaled.

Thus, the Jains brought about their own destruction through their actions and words. This matter of royal justice will be explained in detail later when that historical event unfolds.

In this way, the young saint invites the Jains to engage in a debate by presenting the truths of their religion. In response, the Jains state that debating the truth of a doctrine is an auditory matter.

Therefore, a debate that can be seen with the eyes is better, and they agree to such a debate. The king replies to the Jains with a sarcastic remark, saying, “When my entire body was burning with fever, you could not even alleviate it slightly; you failed.

“So, what debate do you have left?” The king’s tone implies, “Why do you need a debate when you have already failed?” However, the Jains take this as an inquiry into what debate they wish to engage in and respond. They propose an ‘Analavatham’ (fire ordeal), where both parties write the tenets of their religion on a palm-leaf manuscript and place it in a blazing fire. The manuscript that remains unburnt will prove the truth of its religion. The Jains propose this fire ordeal to the king. The Pandya king attempts to respond. Before he can speak, the young saint begins to speak.

“The young saint tells the Jains, “The method you suggested is very good. You say that if the leaf placed in the fire remains unburnt, it will prove the truth of the religious tenets written on it. I accept this challenge. In the presence of the Pandya king, we will conduct the debate as you have suggested and decide the outcome. Come!” The young saint says this before the king can reply to the Jains.

“This is because the Jains had challenged them to a debate. If the king were to try to prevent them from doing so, it would not be fair. If the Jains were invited to a debate and then refused, it would also imply that those who refused were not victorious.

“Therefore, the young saint, realizing that the king now understood the truth and would not agree to the Jain’s debate, informed the Jains that he accepted the challenge before the king could reply. He did not stop at curing the fever in the Pandya king’s body, but rather, by showing all possible ways for the Jains to agree to a religious or magical debate. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, with the intention that the world would be freed from the illusion of Jainism, that the harm done to Saivism would vanish, and that the light of sacred ash would shine, offered his response before the king could reply to the Jains. He challenged the Jains to a debate according to their own principles. The verse states, “Before the king could speak, the young saint said, ‘It is good what you said; if the leaf placed in the fire wins, you said the truth of the matter is real; then come before the king with the strong trunked elephant.’” Thus, when the young saint spoke, the king ordered his attendants to create a fire in the royal court. The 779th verse states: “As the opposing Jains arrived in unequal numbers, at the command of the guardian of Sanbai, whose fame was incomparable, the king, whose vast army was beyond description, ordered his servants to prepare a burning fire in the royal assembly.” In this verse, Deivasekkizhar Peruman praises Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as “Oppil Vanpugazh Sanbayar,” meaning the incomparable glorious one from Sanbai.

“Even though the king initially refused, he eventually agreed to what the young saint said. Such was the incomparable glory of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. The term “Vanpugazh” (glorious fame) refers to his generosity, indicating that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, out of compassion for the Jains and the people of this world, bestowed grace without reservation.

“Thus, Deivasekkizhar Peruman praises Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as “Oppil Van Pugazh Sanbayar Kavalalar,” the guardian of Sanbai with incomparable glory. Accepting Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s words, the king commands that a good fire be made in the royal court. That court, just as the king reformed and understood the truth of Saivism, also reformed.

“Therefore, it was a reformed court, and a court that stood as a place for the world to witness and be reformed by this fire ordeal. It was customary for great matters to be decided before the king’s court.

“Accordingly, the king commanded his servants to make a good, hot fire in that royal court. The 780th verse describes: “The commanded men gathered firewood, arranged it, and lit the fire; the smoke rose, then vanished, and the fierce, burning fire god manifested his light; and the master of the three Tamils, seeking wisdom, arrived.” The men commanded by the king immediately brought cut firewood and arranged it in the royal court to create a fire. The fire began to burn, first releasing smoke, then emanating light.

“After the smoke dissipated, the fierce fire god revealed his light. The king had received the diksha of Thirugnanasambandha’s divine gaze, meditation, and touch, and had adorned sacred ash.

“Therefore, the king, having achieved the balance of good and bad karma, was destined to receive the fruits of his past penance.

“Thus, according to the pure thoughts of the king, the fire god appeared in that royal court. The young saint, the master of the three Tamils, approached the fire.

“Let us proceed with our contemplation.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periyapuranam, Part 720, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, by Deivasekkizhar Peruman. The young saint stands before the fire prepared by the Pandya king in the royal court. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing: “He praised the good arrangement of the melodious Thiruppathigams, which he had composed declaring that the Lord with the red-eyed bull is the only truth. He bowed, saying that our Lord is the Supreme Being, and with his hand, he took the manuscripts to his head and untied the protective cords.” This is the 781st verse. The Thiruppathigams composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman were written down on palm-leaf manuscripts and collected.

These are referred to as the ‘Thiruppathiga Nanmurai’ (good order of Thiruppathigams). It is recorded that Sambandha Charanalar, the maternal uncle of the young saint, was the one who wrote down and carried the palm-leaf manuscripts of the Thiruppathigams as they were composed.

Thus, all the Thiruppathigams composed by the young saint so far were written on palm-leaf manuscripts and carried by the young saint’s entourage. Sekkizhar Peruman here names this collection ‘Thiruppathiga Nanmurai’.

Here, ‘Thirumurai’ is the traditional name given to the collection of Thevaram hymns. It is the customary practice of Saivite scholars to refer to all twelve Saivite divine scriptures as ‘Thirumurai’. Referring to or calling other texts by the name ‘Thirumurai’ is an incorrect practice. It is also a tradition. Such a Thiruppathiga Nanmurai, composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and set to music by him, remains eternally youthful, new, and yields endless benefits, just as it did when he sang it. The Thiruppathigams within this Thiruppathiga Nanmurai are sacred verses revealed by the young saint, instructing the world to understand that Shiva, who possesses the red-eyed bull, is the ultimate truth.

These Thiruppathigams, composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, emphasize that Shiva is the sole primordial entity, the only truth, and nothing else holds such significance. They exemplify the principle of not praising anyone other than Shiva, thus enlightening the world with this profound truth. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships the Thirumurai manuscript containing these Thiruppathigams. He bows, stating that Shiva, our Lord, is the supreme God, the ultimate reality above all others. He then takes the Thirumurai manuscripts in his sacred hand and places them upon his sacred head.

After that, he unties the protective string of the palm-leaf manuscripts. Untying the string signifies his intention to open the manuscripts, and whichever leaf, whichever Thiruppathigam, appears is the one he will place in the fire.

Thus, the young saint unties the protective string on the manuscripts, preparing for the ordeal. This method of discerning the Lord’s will is called ‘Kairu Saatri Paarththal’ (reading by drawing lots). Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is the first to perform this. This practice has continued from that day until now, where devotees consult the Thirumurais by drawing lots. This tradition of ‘Kairu Saatri Paarththal’ is also found in the Kanda Puranam, Thiruvilaiyadal Puranam, and other texts. The belief is that whatever appears when the Thirumurais are consulted in this way reveals the Lord’s will to us.

Here, when the young saint consults the Thevaram Thirumurai by drawing lots. The pathigam that appears must remain unburnt when placed in the fire, demonstrating the true essence of Saivism. It must refute other religions and elucidate Saivite principles, thereby liberating this world.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman unties the protective cord on the Thirumurai manuscript containing the pathigams, seeking to understand the Lord’s will. Before the avatar of Sri Meykanda Deva Nayanar, his parents, on the command of their family guru, Arulnandi Sivachariyar, performed ‘Kairu Saarti Paarththal’ with the Thevaram Thirumurai of Aludaiya Pillaiyar.

At that time, the Thiruvengattu Pathigam appeared, specifically the second verse of the Thiruvengattu Thiruppathigam. The palm-leaf manuscript containing the verse, “Peyadaiyā Piriveydhum Pillaiyinuḍu Uḷḷa Ninai Ayinavē Varamberuvar Aiyura Vēṇḍā Eṉṟum Vēyaṉa Tōḻumai Paṅgaṉ Veṇkāṭṭu Mukkuḷḷa Nīr Tōy Viṉaiyār Avartaṉṉai Tōyāvām Tīviṉaiyē” (Devils will not approach, separation will occur, children will attain their wishes, no need to doubt; those who bathe in the three waters of Venkadu, where Shiva, who shares his body with Uma whose shoulders are like bamboos, resides, will not be touched by evil karma) appeared. As written in that verse, Sri Meykanda Deva Nayanar’s parents went to Thiruvengadu, prayed for a boon, bathed in the Agni Tirtham, and worshipped the Lord, receiving the boon of a child. That child was Sri Meykanda Deva Nayanar. He attained divine wisdom at the age of two, leading to the creation of the Sivagnanabodham, a sacred text that refuted other religions and established Saivism. This text became available to the Tamil world and became the cause for the world’s salvation.

That history, even its foundation, is this sacred practice of ‘Kairu Saatri Paarththal’ in the Thevaram Thirumurai. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was the first to demonstrate this during this fire ordeal. Sekkizhar Peruman describes it in the next verse: “When he himself opened the Thirumurai, which bestows the spoken truth, with his sacred ash-covered hand, it happened that the Thiruppathigam ‘Bhogamartha Poonmulaiyaal,’ praised by the Lord with four mighty shoulders and the virtuous one, appeared.” This is the next verse.

The Lord unties the cord of the Thirumurai, as the manuscript is called Thirumurai. ‘Thirumurai’ means a book that expounds truths that lead to the sacredness of liberation. The term ‘Thirumurai’ is conventionally and definitively applied to the twelve Saivite divine Tamil scriptures compiled from Aludaiya Pillaiyar’s Thevaram up to the Periyapuranam, also known as the Thiruthondar Puranam. This is the tradition of Saivite elders. Our divine Sekkizhar Peruman, by applying this tradition to the young saint’s Thevaram, initiates the usage of the term ‘Thirumurai’ here. The Thirumandiram’s verse, “Paadum Thirumurai Paarvathi,” serves as evidence that only the Lord’s compositions are called ‘Thirumurai’.

Therefore, based on this concept, Umapathi Sivachariyar explains that these collections, from the Thevaram to the Periyapuranam, which are the Lord’s own utterances, are named ‘Thirumurai’ and categorized as the twelve Thirumurais.

Therefore, it is customary not to use the name ‘Thirumurai’ for compositions by other souls. Such a Thirumurai, which contains the spoken truth, refers to the spoken form of Shiva, the ultimate reality, as conveyed by the Vedas and other scriptures, and by great sages.

Therefore, the meaning conveyed by this word is the ultimate truth. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman himself, with his sacred hand adorned with sacred ash, examines that Thirumurai, which conveys the spoken truth. He performs ‘Kairu Saatri Paarththal’ (drawing lots). Without allowing anyone else to do so, he himself takes the manuscript, places the protective string across the Thirumurai manuscripts with his sacred ash-adorned hand, and opens them to perform ‘Kairu Saatri Paarththal’. The Thiruppathigam that appeared was the Thirunallatru Thiruppathigam. It is the Thiruppathigam that praises ‘Annalaar Maruvu Nallatru’.

It is the Thiruppathigam that begins with ‘Bhogamartha Poonmulaiyaal’. That Thiruppathigam that begins with these words manifests there. When Thirugnanasambandha Peruman performs ‘Kairu Saatri Paarththal’ with his Thirumurai, the Thiruppathigam that appears is ‘Nallatru Potrum Thiruppathigam’, which means the Thiruppathigam that praises ‘Annalaar Maruvu Nallatru’. This is because this entire Thiruppathigam, composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, praises the holy site of Thirunallatru. The concluding phrase, “Nampemuman Meyathu Nallatru,” is embedded in every verse of this pathigam by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. “Nampemuman” is the first word of the first verse at the beginning of that pathigam.

Therefore, the first word of that pathigam that emerged in this manner. The word “Bhogamartha Poonmulaiyaal” reveals the divine will to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. The reason this leaf remained unburnt and fresh when placed in the fire is also attributed to the beginning of the verse, “Bhogamartha Poonmulaiyaal,” which refers to the sacred breasts of Ambikai. The sacred breasts of the Divine Mother are considered as knowledge, nectar, and givers of enjoyment to living beings. This is the significance of “Bhogamartha Poonmulaiyaal,” and it is the reason why the leaf remained unburnt and fresh in the fire. “Bhogamartha Poonmulaiyaal” refers to Uma Devi.

“Bhogam Artha” Poṇmulaiaḷ means a woman with ornamented breasts, referring to Umadevi. The first verse of that Thirunallar pathigam, “Bhogamārtha pūṇmulaiyāḷ taṉṉōṭum poṉ nakalam pāgamārtha paiṅkaṇ veḷḷēṟṟu aṇṇal paramēṭṭi āgamārtha tōḷuṭaiyan kōvaṇa āṭaiyiṉ mēl nāgamārtha nampaḷavāṉ mēyatu nallārē,” begins by placing the Goddess Ambika first. Umadevi, also known as Ambika, is the inseparable Abhinashakti of Lord Shiva. Just as the sun in the sky shines as a magnificent ball of light on its own, yet at the same time, it helps us see the objects of the world by mingling with the light of our eyes.

Similarly, the supreme being Shiva, untouched by anything, stands as self-luminous Shiva, and when that supreme being helps souls and stands by their side, it is called Shakti.

Therefore, Umadevi is eternally inseparable from Lord Shiva. This form of Ardhanareeswara, called Umaiyorubaga Murthy, is described in the sacred texts. The Vajasaneyi Samhita of the Yajur Veda praises this divine form as “Ahoratre paashve” (day and night are its sides). This mantra describes Lord Shiva, whose entire body is covered in sacred ash, as day, and the dark body of Umadevi as night. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states, “He possesses the quality of joining day and night” and “Our Lord is day and night.” Now, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman describes Ambika, who is the Abhinashakti of Lord Shiva, as “Bhogamārtha pūṇmulaiyāḷ” (she whose adorned breasts bestow enjoyment). In the Kanda Puranam, Umadevi’s breasts are referred to as “paramabodha neerathai” (the essence of supreme knowledge).

It is here explained that both forms of knowledge, Para (higher) and Apara (lower), are the breasts of Ambika, the universal Mother.

Therefore, “Bhogamārtha pūṇmulaiyāḷ” signifies the grace-bestowing Shakti, who nourishes souls with both Apara Gnanam (worldly knowledge) and Para Gnanam (divine knowledge). It is Lord Shiva who keeps such Umadevi on the left side of his beautiful body. He is the leader who has the bull Rishabam, with its green eyes and white color, as his vehicle. He is Parametti. Thiruppallandu says that something is “pandum endrum endrum ulla porul” (a thing that was, is, and always will be), and this applies to the ancient city of Madurai. In the streets of such an ancient Madurai, crowds of people surged. As பிள்ளையார் arrived in his pearl palanquin, followed by the king on horseback, and the queen behind him, and the minister on one side, and on the other side, eight thousand Jains, the street of Madurai city was resplendent.

Thus, the streets of Madurai city gleamed. Seeing Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arriving in his palanquin, all the people cheered and were filled with enthusiasm. பிள்ளையார் had cured the Madurai king’s fever and had won the fire debate. These two events had spread throughout Madurai city very quickly.

Therefore, a large crowd had gathered there, wishing to behold பிள்ளையார், who had performed these two acts of grace. Even though there was a large crowd, Sekkizhar Peruman sings that it was the women who were at the forefront to worship and behold Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. All these people, who had until now believed in the alien religion. The people, who had previously trusted the Jain religion, now, through the gracious acts of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, have abandoned their belief in that alien religion. Their previous allegiance to Saivism in Madurai has been restored, and they now stand worshiping and beholding பிள்ளையார். This is because the adherence to Jainism was a temporary phase for the people of Madurai.

Their inherent nature was Saivism.

Therefore, after a brief period of detachment, they quickly re-embraced it.

Thus, the people of Madurai, especially the women, came forward to behold Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

At that time, all the people praised Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Sekkizhar Peruman captures their praise in seven verses, which we will continue to reflect upon. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, Part 724, “Vambarav Varivandu Serukkam,” composed by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, describes the puranam of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrives in a pearl palanquin in the streets of Madurai city. All the people behold him and praise him. Some say, “Look at this Nayanar, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar, who cured the fever of the Pandya king and relieved our suffering.” Those who recognized Thirugnanasambandha Peruman told those who did not, “This is our leader, known by the name Gnanasambandhar; behold him.” There were some who had only heard the name Thirugnanasambandhar. Many people stood there who had never before seen the sacred form of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

Therefore, those who had already beheld Thirugnanasambandha Peruman introduced him to all those who were seeing him for the first time. பிள்ளையார் had arrived in Madurai the previous day.

At that time, only a few had beheld Thirugnanasambandha Peruman when he came to the temple, and later when he went from there to the monastery.

Then, that night, when the Jains’ evil deed caused the fever, and பிள்ளையார் entered the temple and then the palace for that reason, only a few beheld him.

At that time, the Jain religion was a dense darkness that deluded three types of people. In that state, very few beheld Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. The news that the fever was cured by பிள்ளையார்’s grace and the sacred ash, and that the palm-leaf manuscript placed by பிள்ளையார் in the fire remained unburnt, asserting the superiority of Saivism, and that the Jains were defeated in both these instances, and even after the king had ostracized them, they were coming for a third and final time to see the manuscript and be impaled – all this news spread throughout Madurai city like wildfire carried by the wind.

Therefore, a huge crowd of people had gathered to witness the glorious arrival of பிள்ளையார். Among these, as mentioned before. Only a few knew பிள்ளையார் by name and had seen his sacred form.

Now, they were introducing பிள்ளையார் to the many who had not seen him before. They explained his greatness, the pathigam he recited, the humiliation of the Jains he defeated, and other things.

In this way, those who had previously beheld Thirugnanasambandha Peruman were introducing him to the people who were now seeing him for the first time. As this happened, Sekkizhar Peruman presented all the praises that the people offered to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman in the following six verses. The verse begins, “Panarum kudhalai seiya pavalavay Pillaiyar thamm manaseer Thennadhu vazha vandhu annaindhar enbar” (Some say that பிள்ளையார், with a sweet, lisping, coral-like mouth, came to bless the great land of the South). Some say that பிள்ளையார், with a coral-like mouth uttering lisping words fragrant with milk, came here to bless the great and glorious Pandya kingdom.

Here, “manaseer nadu” refers to the Pandya kingdom. “Manaseer” means great glory. The Pandya kingdom is ancient, and the saying “Thenpandi nadu theli” (The southern Pandya land is clear) is a sacred utterance praised by great sages. The Pandya kingdom has the special glory of having the Lord, who is easily accessible to all beings, shining with immense grace and clarity. The glory praised by such great people, and the meaning of “manam” here, can be taken as greatness and the special quality of the Lord’s easy grace. This glorious Pandya kingdom, the land of the Southern King, came to thrive.

By its prosperity, they too gained benefit, and thus, everyone praised Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as the one who came to bless the Pandya kingdom. All the people spoke of how their Jain gurus had lost the fire debate to him. Some spoke of how they had seen with their own eyes that the sacred ash of Lord Shiva, with his matted locks, was the true reality. Some spoke of the beauty of பிள்ளையார் arriving in a palanquin made of pure gold, studded with brilliant pearls, saying, “What beauty!” Seeing this sight. Some said, “Our eyes have lived a full life seeing this.” Some said, “These Jain gurus are inherently evil; only evil came from them, and now we have seen it.” Some said, “The Supreme God is the Lord enshrined in the Thiruvalavai temple; rejoice in seeing him.” Some said, “To know the ancient Lord Shiva with three eyes is true wisdom.” Some said, “The Vedas and the sacred ash will spread everywhere and permeate all.” Some said, “The Lord in Thiruvalavai is Namban; go and see him.” Namban means one who is worthy of trust and refuge. This name, Namban, is attributive.

The name Nambi refers to Lord Shiva. The Thiruppathigam “Nambi” illustrates this. Others who trust and take refuge in lesser deities may obtain minor benefits from them, and such people do exist.

However, Shivagnana Siddhiyar states that other deities suffer, die, are born, and create further karma.

Similarly, the women of Madurai, seeing that the Arhat god, who had until now protected and benefited the Jains, was now abandoning them in the middle of a river, spoke thus: “The Lord of Thiruvalavai is Namban, worthy of trust and refuge.” They praised him, saying, “To know him is the ultimate wisdom, the wisdom of experience; he is the most ancient of all ancient things,” as the people understood and spoke. The people, looking at the Jains who were approaching on the other side, said, “Look how the faces of these Jains have withered!” Some spoke of how the cruel deceptions of the Jains had been destroyed. Some wondered about the change in the sharp-speared Pandya king’s allegiance to the Jain gurus. Some said, “The darkness of this cruel Jainism has departed, and now a new dawn has arrived for us all.” Some questioned, “Will those who lost in fire now win in water?” Some wondered, “Even if these Jains have hearts of iron, can they stand against this பிள்ளையார்?” Some said, “Look at the fate that awaits these Jains, who, abandoning subtle truths, only grasped coarse ones and were confined to that level.” The people say that these Jains understood only coarse matters. The Jains are those who only learned the texts that prescribe the virtues of animal dharma, but did not understand their subtle inner meaning.

The Jains do not understand sin and merit.

Therefore, these people say this. Their defeat has already been decided.

So, some say that Minister Kulachirayar has already prepared sharp impaling stakes for them. Some say that these Jains came to cast their palm-leaf manuscripts into the Vaigai River. Some wonder if a palm-leaf manuscript placed in flowing water will stop in one place without being carried away. Some speculated that பிள்ளையார், having attained supreme wisdom, could even stop those palm-leaf manuscripts. Some said, “ பிள்ளையார், whom the entire country can behold, will now arrive directly; just watch.” Generally, when an event takes place, people express such opinions.

Similarly, Sekkizhar Peruman beautifully illustrates how people were talking there. He states that பிள்ளையார் could stop the palm-leaf manuscript from flowing with the water.

Following this, another person said, “ பிள்ளையார் will arrive here shortly, and we will all see him win by stopping the manuscript in the flowing water. Look at that.” One person says, “See for yourself.” Some said, “Should the Jains be so bold as to agree that the losers must be impaled? The Jains should not have said that.” Some said, “This is befitting பிள்ளையார், who has demonstrated his gracious acts and possesses supreme grace.” Some said, “All the deeds that பிள்ளையார் has performed so far are beneficial to us.” The gracious act of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was performed with grace, untouched by negative qualities like anger. Even when the Jains set fire to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s monastery, he did not get angry at them. Instead, he graciously blessed that the fire should go to the king who had erred in his duty.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman possessed the grace to make the king experience his karma, cure his illness, and embrace him. Before entering the debate, he was endowed with the grace of entering the royal court only after inquiring about the divine will twice. Even there, when the king refused to give the Jains a place, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman intervened and graciously allowed the Jains to debate.

In this way, people praised the greatness of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s grace. Everyone who witnessed the Pandya king being freed from harm by the sacred ash would praise the power of Saivism.

Therefore, some urged everyone to embrace the Saivite path.

Thus, the people standing on both sides of the street spoke. There, a white umbrella with a beautiful golden handle, shining like lightning, cast its shadow from above, while பிள்ளையார், adorned in a palanquin studded with many gems, came to make the four Vedas prosper.
