He arrived to show the people of the Pandya kingdom the path of righteousness. As he thus arrived, many ceremonial instruments sounded.

We shall continue our reflection on this. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, Part 725, “Vambarav Varivandu Serukkam,” composed by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, describes the puranam of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. As Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeded through the streets of Madurai, ceremonial instruments sounded. The instruments praised the glories of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. The verse states, “Then thamizh vilangav vandha Thirukkalumala thon vandhan Manrullaar alitha gnana vattil vankaiyan vandhan Venru ulaga vaigaiyil velvan vandhan enru chinangal en thisai nerungiyenga.” (He who came from Thirukkalumalam to make beautiful Tamil shine has arrived. The strong-handed one who received the cup of wisdom given by those in the assembly has arrived.

He who will conquer in the Vaigai of the world has arrived, thus the ceremonial instruments resounded, filling all eight directions.) பிள்ளையார், who came from Thirukkalumalam to make beautiful Tamil shine, has arrived. The conch is still being played, heralding the arrival of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who came to illuminate southern Tamil. “Then” means beauty, so “Then Tamil” means beautiful Tamil. Beauty means to exist with eternal, unfading youth, and it also means that this Tamil, being full of knowledge, bestows an eternal and unchanging beauty leading to an affinity with Siva’s feet. This is extensively explained in the “Thiruthonda Thogai” which states “Then Tamil Payanai Ulla Thiruthonda Thogai Munpada”. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was born to spread Tamil.

The great Sekkizhar Peruman, describing Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s purpose of incarnation, states “Asaivil Sezhum Tamil Vazhake Ayal Vazhakin Thuraivalla” meaning, ‘whose unwavering rich Tamil path is adept in other traditions’. As he danced, he spoke. The conch sounds, announcing the arrival of Pillaiyar, who came to illuminate southern Tamil. The conch sounds, proclaiming the arrival of Pillaiyar, who received the golden bowl containing the Sivajgnana milk bestowed by Thillai Koothar, who dances in the assembly, and whose sacred hands grew with this grace. The conch sounds, heralding the arrival of Pillaiyar, who won the previous debates and will also win the upcoming debate by water in the Vaigai river.

Thus, the sound of these conches echoes intensely in all eight directions. The next verse is the 811th verse: “Pannmani Murasam Soozhndha Palliyam Iyamba Pinne Thennanum Theviyarum Udan Sella Thiran Sellum Pun Neri Amanar Veroor Pudai Vara Pugazhi Vendhar Manniya Vaigaiyatrrin Karaimisai Maruvandhar.” Sekkizhar Peruman, having sung about Pillaiyar’s sacred procession, now sings about the King and Queen’s procession. He also sings about the arrival of the Jain ascetics and then about Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s arrival on the banks of the Vaigai river. Pillaiyar goes ahead in a palanquin adorned with pearls, followed by the King.

The King makes his way through the street, so his musical instruments are played to mark his presence. Pillaiyar proceeds, followed by his retinue, and then the King and Queen join them. Until this point, that is, until the King’s illness was cured in the palace, the Queen and the minister had acted on their own initiative, without the King’s consent.

After that, the debate by fire took place, and now the debate by water is about to happen. Both of these debates, especially the debate by fire, occurred as a royal affair in the King’s court and presence. When royal affairs take place, the Queen must also be present.

Therefore, the Queen was present during the debate by fire in the palace court.

Similarly, now as the King comes to the banks of the Vaigai, the Queen also accompanies him. Here we can observe the tradition of the former day’s government, where royal affairs involved the King and Queen being together and acting in unison.

However, from the day the King adopted Jainism until he embraced Shaivism, it is not depicted that the King and Queen acted together. This is because the King stood apart on religious matters.

Now, both the Queen and the King are coming together.

Therefore, in these royal affairs concerning Shaivism, they are now both participating together. From today onwards, this is how it will unfold. As this sacred procession takes place, the Jains are also approaching on the other side of the street. Towards the banks of the Vaigai, during the fire debate in the King’s court, there were only a few Jain gurus.

But now, the debate by water is happening on the banks of the Vaigai.

Therefore, all eight thousand Jain ascetics are coming on one side of the Madurai street. As Pillaiyar proceeds with his devotees and retinue, the Jain ascetics, lacking the fortune to be associated with Pillaiyar and attain salvation, walk away on the other side. Pillaiyar thus makes his sacred procession through the holy street and arrives near the banks of the Vaigai river. This Vaigai river is sung by Sekkizhar Peruman as “Manniya Vaigai”. “Manniya” means permanent or established. “Mannudhal” means to be established.

It means to be established. This Vaigai river is a river established by fame, a river established by the merit of being associated with Siva. We learn from the Thiruvilayadal Puranam that the Ganga itself came as the Vaigai river at the command of the Lord for Kundotharan during the wedding of Meenakshiammayar. It was on the banks of this same Vaigai river that the Lord’s divine play of carrying soil took place. Appar Swamigal praises the Vaigai river in Thiruppoovan Thiruththāndagam, saying, “Aniyar Vaigai Thirukkottin Nindradhor Thiramum Thondrum” (The sight of the adorned Vaigai’s sacred bank will appear). Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrives on the banks of such a glorious and established Vaigai river.

The King looked at the rapidly flowing river water, and the next verse states: “Aatru Neer Kadugavodum Marungura Arasan Nokki Neetrani Thigazhdhameni Niraimadhi Pillaiyarum Vetrhoru Arugar Neerum Vithitha Edu Idgiraan Thotravard Tholaar Endru Munnura Thunindhu Ittargal”. Pillaiyar and others reached the banks of the Vaigai river, went along the sandy path of the river, and arrived at a spot where the river water flowed very rapidly.

At that moment, the King looked at Pillaiyar and the Jain ascetics and said, “Pillaiyar, whose body shines with the beauty of sacred ash like a full moon, and you Jain ascetics, who are of a different form, as you both have agreed, cast your respective palm-leaf manuscripts into the river.” The Pandyan King, having attained salvation through sacred ash, was captivated by Pillaiyar’s sacred form, which was resplendent with sacred ash, considering it a magnificent form. He (Pillaiyar) is full of divine wisdom.

Now, as he is about to impart spiritual instruction to the Pandyan King, he is full of perfect wisdom and possesses all the characteristics of a guru. It is to imply this that the Pandyan King refers to Pillaiyar as “Pillaiyar, whose sacred form shines with the beauty of sacred ash like a full moon.” At the same time, he refers to the Jain ascetics as those who have a form different from that sacred form of sacred ash.

Thus, the Pandyan King instructs Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and the Jain ascetics to cast their respective palm-leaf manuscripts into the river. He says, “One who loses will not always lose”. Following this worldly wisdom, the Jain ascetics decide to cast their palm-leaf manuscript into the floodwaters of the river first.

We shall proceed with our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, part 726, composed by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, from the Vambara Varivandach Charukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. In this water debate, the Jain ascetics first decide to write down their religious truth and cast that palm-leaf manuscript into the Vaigai river. Previously, in the fire debate, Pillaiyar first cast the palm-leaf manuscript containing the Pachaipathigam into the fire.

Now, the Jain ascetics decide that they should first write their Jain religious principles on a palm-leaf manuscript and cast it into the Vaigai river. The 714th verse states: “Paduporul Indri Nellil Pathadi Pol Ul Illaar Mei Adubavar Porulai Asthi Naatthi Endru Ezuthi Aatril Kadugiya Punalai Kandu Avavinaal Kaiyil Eduvidu Eduthalum Viraindhu Kondu Velai Mel Padarnthatandre.” This refers to those who are empty inside like chaff in rice, having no substantial meaning. They write “Asthi Naatthi” (existence and non-existence) concerning the true meaning, and seeing the swiftly flowing water in the river, they eagerly cast the palm-leaf manuscript from their hand. As soon as it is cast, it quickly drifts away into the distance. These Jain ascetics take a palm leaf and write their Jain religious principle, Asthi Nasthi, on it, then cast the leaf into the flowing waters of the Vaigai river. Asthi means ‘that which exists, is there’, and Nasthi means ‘that which does not exist, is not there’.

The principle of these Jain ascetics is that what they claim to be existent or real, they themselves immediately refute as non-existent.

Therefore, Asthi Nasthi is the core tenet of the Jain ascetics, and it forms a highly confusing philosophy.

Therefore, this religious principle, the Jain principle, is a doctrine whose inherent truth is lacking. It is a principle that resembles chaff in rice, meaning it has no substance. Like chaff in rice, which appears to be rice but is empty inside, their principles are of the same nature.

Furthermore, these Jain ascetics are those who declare the true essence to be false. They write the collection of principles found in Jain scriptures as “Asthi Naatthi” on a palm-leaf manuscript and cast it into the swiftly flowing waters of the river. They also observe it moving quickly along. Even after seeing this, they cast the palm-leaf manuscript into it. Previously, they cast the palm-leaf manuscript containing their principles into the burning fire. Not realizing that the fire would burn their palm-leaf manuscript, they cast it and lost.

Similarly here, Even seeing that the water (river) flows very rapidly, they, without realizing that it would carry their leaf away, cast their leaf into the Vaigai river with great greed. “Greed knows no shame” is a proverb. Not once, but twice, even after experiencing defeat, instead of accepting it and settling down, they continue to seek more and more defeat.

Thus, without shame, due to this greed, they are attempting this again. When they cast the palm-leaf manuscript, on which their principles were written, into the rapidly flowing waters of the Vaigai river with such greed, the floodwaters of the Vaigai river swiftly pull away the leaf written by the Jain ascetics and carry it away rapidly. The flood then performed its natural function. The next verse says: “Aaru Kondu Odum Ettai Thodarnthu Ethir Anaipaar Pola Theru Meyyunarvu Illathar Karaimisai Odi Sendrar Paarumepporul Mel Konda Pattigai Ettathu Angu Nooruvir Kadikku Munne Ponathu Nokki Kaanar.” The Jain ascetics, seeing their palm-leaf manuscript being carried away by the river, did not run along with the flood, but came to the river bank and ran along the bank. They came to the bank as if to go against the current and retrieve the leaf that was flowing with the river. Due to their confusion, they did not realize what they were doing and acted in this manner.

The mantra “Asthi Nasthi” will not stand before the truth.

Therefore, the river flood carried that leaf.

Therefore, they could not even see it. The next verse says: “Kanavum Eithaa Vannam Mel Sellum Edu Naanilaa Amanardham Vittu Pogadai Sendru Nindrar Thigaithaar Mannan Aanaiyil Valuvamaattathu Anjuvar Anaiya Meendar.” That palm leaf, which could not be reached by the Jain ascetics who ran on the bank, had gone so far that they could not even see it. These shameless Jains have now suffered defeat for the third time, culminating in three successive losses. They knowingly committed falsehood and deceit, and perhaps if they had gained clarity after one defeat, they could have sought good.

But instead of doing so, they lost repeatedly and also lost their honor.

Now, the palm-leaf manuscript on which they had written their Jain religious principles has left them stranded in mid-stream. “Abandoning those who trust in mid-stream” is a proverb. This proverb highlights the nature of ignoble people who are liars. Ignoble people will abandon those who trust them in mid-stream.

Similarly, The Jain ascetics trusted their principles, but the palm-leaf manuscript containing their false principles, contrary to their expectations, was not a true substance, so it flowed away in the middle of the river. The Jain ascetics had eagerly anticipated it, but contrary to their expectations, that great suffering befell them very quickly. The great suffering that comes from that disappointment had happened to them.

Therefore, as a result, they are in a state of confusion, thinking that as they had previously agreed, the king’s order would lead to their execution by impalement. They scatter and run in various directions. When they search for the palm-leaf manuscript but cannot find it, they return and stand beside the king. The next verse says: “Veroru Seyal Illaathar Veruvutru Nadungi Thampal Eeru Vandhu Eythitru Endre Mannavan Ethirvandhu Eythi Oorudai Nenjil Achcham Velipadum Ozhipaar Pondru Maarukonda Avarum Ittal Vandhadhu Kanddum Endraar.” Having no other recourse, the Jain ascetics were terrified and trembled. Three defeats, and now the prospect of being impaled, filled their hearts with fear.

But hiding all that fear, suppressing the fear that arose in their hearts from showing, they further speak to the King, saying that Pillaiyar should also cast his leaf, and then they will see what happens. The Jain ascetics think that now their leaf has been swept away by the flood and has not stayed, so their defeat is confirmed. Although defeat has occurred, they still need to conceal and manage this defeat.

Therefore, the Jain ascetics suggest that Pillaiyar should also be asked to cast his palm-leaf manuscript into the Vaigai flood. Perhaps it might also be carried away by the flood.

So, they think, let Pillaiyar also cast his palm-leaf manuscript into the flood, and only then they can determine their defeat. They have already decided in their minds that defeat and destruction are certain for them. Despite this, they concealed it all and spoke in this manner. When the Jain ascetics spoke thus, the King, who had renounced the Jain transgression and joined the path of removing Jain transgression, left the Jain ascetics and now looked at Thirugnanasambandha Peruman to ascertain his divine intent, who possessed the light of Siva’s wisdom. That Pandyan King knew that these Jain ascetics were impure both internally and externally. Their minds were tainted by evil qualities such as falsehood and deceit.

They did not cleanse their bodies, did not bathe, and lay in the sun. Due to these external actions, their outer bodies were also impure. They were deluded and suggested that Pillaiyar should also cast his leaf into the water, and then they could confirm victory. With this, the Pandyan King abandoned such Jain ascetics. He completely abandoned Jain allegiance in this situation at this time. As Sivagñana Siddhiyar states, “Arivilla Pinangalai Naam Inangil Pirappinilum Irappinilum Pinangiduvar Vidu Nee” (If we associate with ignorant corpses, we will quarrel in birth and death; leave them), this Jain allegiance and connection are completely removed.

Therefore, the King, abandoning Jain allegiance, looks at the radiant Pillaiyar. To understand Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s divine intent, the king looks at Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

We shall continue our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, part 727, composed by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, from the Vambara Varivandach Charukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. This is a beautiful verse composed by Sekkizhar Peruman, the 818th verse: “Maasu Ser Amanar Ellam Mathiyinil Mayangi Koora Aasilaa Neriyil Serndha Arasanum Avarai Vittu Thesudai Pillaiyartham Thirukkurippu Adhanai Nokki Paasuram Paadalutrar Parasamayangal Paara.” At this point, the Pandyan King completely abandons Jain allegiance. To understand Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s divine intent, the king looks at Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. The king who joined the blameless path. “Aasu” means blemish, so “Aasilaa” means without blemish.

The path he adopts is the path of Shiva. Since the king has joined this path of Shiva, he abandons the Jain faults. This path of Shiva is not only free from those faults but also eradicates the evil of rebirth.

Therefore, it is a flawless path. Having embraced the path of Shiva, the king observes the illustrious Pillaiyar, noting Pillaiyar’s sacred intention. Illustrious refers to the great light of Shiva’s wisdom, which is also the radiance of the sacred ash. The Jains were stained Jains; abandoning that, the king joined the flawless path of Shiva. He observes the illustrious Pillaiyar. Sekizhar Peruman, describing how such stained Jains abandoned the flawless path for the illustrious Pillaiyar, then composed this path of extinguishing external religions.

Sekizhar Peruman graciously presents to us a sequential and pleasing arrangement of these elements: the evil of external religions, the path that remedies it, the teacher who brings it forth, and the grace of Shiva that supports them from within. What is said here by Sekizhar Peruman indicates that the king is now ready to receive spiritual instruction. Sekizhar Peruman will explain this in the next two verses.

Thus, the king observes Pillaiyar’s sacred intention, seeking to understand it. Pillaiyar had already commanded the king to instruct the Jains to place their scrolls in the river. The question then arises: why is the king observing Pillaiyar’s sacred intention now? Previously, the command to place the scrolls was given because both parties had agreed to the debate. That was a process for conducting the debate as each party had agreed, an action taken by the king in his capacity.

However, in this debate, the Jains rushed ahead and confirmed their defeat.

Therefore, there is no longer a need for Pillaiyar to write a scroll, and the king now has the opportunity to declare the outcome of the debate, and can indeed do so. But these Jains are asking, hiding all their defeat, shame, and fear, that Pillaiyar should also place a scroll.

Therefore, even though the king believes the Jains were defeated and Pillaiyar was victorious, he stands neutral and, without announcing the decision, requests Pillaiyar’s sacred intention. If the king had simply said, ‘You too place a scroll.’ The king could have said this to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

But he did not say that; instead, he stands looking at Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred intention. Why is that, he asked? The king’s current state, having abandoned that evil Jain affiliation, is that of a mature disciple.

Therefore, having attained the state of a disciple, the king stands, having applied to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the acharya, awaiting his sacred intention.

Thus, the king’s state is that of a mature disciple. Sekizhar Peruman graciously sings about the nature of the king’s state in the coming verse, ‘unnaivalvinaithanjimudalanaiyum thunni nanvianaikalothu thulainana nirthalale,’ meaning ‘having shed past karmic burdens, knowing the Primeval Being, and with karmas balanced like scales.’ The king’s balance of two karmas. The teacher will now explain the state of karmic equivalence and mala paripagam there. It is for this reason that Pillaiyar is about to give spiritual instruction to the king. As Pillaiyar’s sacred intention is observed, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman then sings a sacred hymn. He sings the Thiruppasuram pathigam to vanquish external religions.

This Thiruppasuram pathigam, which begins with ‘Vazhga Andhanar,’ is sung by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman to eradicate external religions. ‘Paaruthal’ means destruction. So ‘Parasamyangal Paaruthal’ means the destruction of external religions.

Here, destruction means the eradication of the evils and delusions of external religions, and the rejection of their doctrines. It is explained to us here that this does not mean the destruction of religions themselves.

Therefore, the destruction of religions is not its meaning. This Thiruppasuram pathigam was composed so that the world might stand in the Vedic Saiva path, free from the evils and delusions of the doctrines of external religions. Before this, due to the pathigams and sacred acts, the inferior aspects of external religious doctrines remained unaddressed, not exemplified by scriptural debate.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed this pathigam, making those very aspects the focus. Parapaksha Nirakaranam means the refutation of opposing views. is extensively detailed in the Sivagamas, in Sivagnana Siddhiyar Parapaksha, and in the philosophical text called Sankalpa Nirakaranam.

Now, in this Thiruppasuram pathigam that Pillaiyar blesses, which begins with ‘Vazhga Andhanar,’ Pillaiyar has not only performed Parapaksha Nirakaranam but also established Saivaism and affirmed the true nature of Saivism (Saiva Sthapanam). Isn’t this Pillaiyar’s sacred purpose of incarnation? This Thiruppasuram pathigam, which begins with ‘Vazhga Andhanar,’ was composed to establish the sacred purpose of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s incarnation. This pathigam alone holds the special name ‘Thiruppasuram’. This greatly glorious Thiruppasuram pathigam is the fifty-fourth pathigam in the Third Thirumurai, set in the Kausikappann tune. That Thiruppasuram pathigam, Thirumukkichcharam, Uraiyur, from the sacred text of devotee Mahesh Ayyar, is as follows.

His sister, the one who rose in fiery splendor, the seven witnessed him, the dark one, whose life is in the forest, great sages who know his nature, who smeared sacred ash over their bodies. With their father and mother, they are free from karma, like joyful youths, who rule the colors. (Venda pol palavam vinaiyum kuruvamai endha thazh palavanangithalai nindrivai ketkath thakk ethukkalalum eduththa mozhiyalum mikku sodhikka venda sudavittulal engal sodhi mathukkinkal manam pattikka mikke iraiye vanthu sarminle adumenavum marum kurram muraiththu vedam padumenavum) (Allathuppavum neenga kedum pirappum arukum ena kettithayil nadum thirutharul nalladhu nattallak kadi serntha pothu malaran kai kondu nallapadi serntha pal kondu aatida tharai panru mudi serntha kalai ara vettida mukkan murththi adi serntha vallam arivar solak kettum andre veda mudalavanaga vilangi vaiyam ethappadamai ulakaththavaru) (Thal seyyappootha mudalvan mudale mudala pulil thoothal oli malai endre kali kovai sollep parali vattam pakaiyalil thattadi peraliyanaththidar kandarul seithal peni niralivittu yeri nenjidam kondavarkku poralinththa pugalum pugal uttrathal re malaya vanum maraivallanal muganum palayadevar pakalil amuthuttal peni kalayamu) (Kadanthaarkarithakkezunthayayalam ulladangu amarakku arul seiththe attranri antha mathurai thogaiyakkinaum thettrendru theivam theliyaarkkarai kolai ner pattinri pangu ethir viram panbu nokkil pettr eththapperuman perumanum andre nallargal pugazhi yana sambantha ellarkalum paravum eesanai eththu padal pallarkalum mathikka pasuram sonna paththum valla)

Sekizhar Peruman shows that this pathigam was Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s spiritual instruction, which explains the true essence of the Saiva path to mature souls. This pathigam consists of ten verses and has the unique quality of extracting and presenting the ideas from the culminating wisdom sections of the Sivagamas. It possesses the distinction of illustrating both the special and general aspects, known as Swaroopa and Thadasta. The first three verses of this pathigam are structured in one metrical form and rhythm, while the rest are in a different metrical form and rhythm, thus having two distinct sections. This Thiruppasuram pathigam alone possesses the distinction of being composed in two such styles. Among the pathigams composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, this Thiruppasuram pathigam is the only one arranged in two styles.

Our divine Sekizhar Peruman, the author of Periya Puranam, has provided an extensive commentary of twenty-two verses for this Thiruppasuram pathigam.

Now, Sekizhar Peruman himself acts as a commentator, graciously providing an extensive commentary of twenty-two verses for this Thiruppasuram pathigam.

Therefore, the divine teacher, This Thiruppasuram pathigam holds the distinction of being praised by the divine Sekizhar Peruman as the ultimate truth and having an elaborate commentary. This is the only pathigam that has the special name ‘Thiruppasuram.’ ‘Pasuram sonna patthum pasuram padalutrar,’ meaning ‘the ten verses that speak the truth, those who sang the truth,’ refers to this pathigam. This pathigam shines with two qualities: ‘Parapaksham’ (refuting other religions) and ‘Swapaksham’ (explaining the path of Shiva for knowing the Primeval Being), thus illuminating the path of Shiva. The special achievement of this Thiruppasuram pathigam is that it simultaneously fulfilled Sivapada Hrudayar’s wish, who had prayed for a child who could refute other religions and explain the Saiva path. It also fulfilled Pillaiyar’s sacred purpose of incarnation, which was the refutation of other religions and the establishment of Saivism. This Thiruppasuram pathigam possesses the unique distinction of having fulfilled both these aims simultaneously.

At the end of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred history, Sekizhar Peruman recounts and specifically praises the special quality of this Thiruppasuram pathigam, stating that just as he placed a leaf in the Vaigai river on that day for our salvation, this pathigam continues to bring life to souls forever. Arunanandi Sivachariyar praises this Thiruppasuram pathigam as divine wisdom.

Thus, this Thiruppasuram pathigam possesses innumerable and unfathomable special qualities. Let us continue to meditate upon it. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 728, composed by the divine Sekizhar Peruman, Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composes the Thiruppasuram pathigam to eradicate the evils and delusions of the so-called ‘other religions’ and to explain the definitive conclusions of Siddhanta.

Thus, Sekizhar Peruman frames this as ‘Parasamyangal Paara Pasuram Padalutrar’ (he sang the hymn to eradicate other religions).

Here, ‘other religions’ is used generally. What these ‘other religions’ mean is extensively explained in the Meykanda Shastras within Saiva Siddhanta. Saiva Siddhanta classifies all existing religions, apart from Siddhanta Saivaism, into four categories: Purappura Samayam (outermost), Purassamayam (outer), Akappura Samayam (inner-outer), and Akassamayam (innermost). For each category, there are six religions, totaling twenty-four. These are arranged in a hierarchical order, and their doctrines are refuted to establish the truths of Siddhanta in the Meykanda Shastras. Although ‘Parasamyangal Paara’ (to eradicate other religions) is stated generally here, the ‘other religions’ encompassed in this phrase refer to the three types of six religions each: Purappuram, Puram, and Akappuram, mentioned above.

The Akassamayaththavargal, meaning the inner religions, which are six in number besides the three types of six religions each (Purappuram, Puram, and Akappuram) mentioned above, are part of Saivism, and are thus embraced.

Therefore, the ‘Parasamyangal Paara’ sung by Sekizhar Peruman refers to the states of these three types of six religions each: Purappuram, Puram, and Akappuram. In this, he triumphs over Jainism in three debates—the Scroll Debate, the Fire Debate, and the Water Debate—to establish the supremacy of Saivism. The falsehood of Jainism is shown through the miraculous feats of victory in fire and water.

However, the inferior doctrines of Jainism remained unrefuted.

Therefore, it became necessary to refute them and the doctrines of other religions, and to establish the true nature of pure dualistic Saiva Siddhanta. That was also the philosophy behind the sacred incarnation of Aaludaiya Pillaiyar. The victory shown by miraculous events like the Scroll Debate, the Fire Debate, and the Water Debate is one thing. Apart from that, showing the superiority and inferiority of religious doctrines within religions and establishing the truths of Saivaism by refuting other religions logically and philosophically is another.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed this Thiruppasuram pathigam to refute other religions based on philosophical doctrines and to explain Saiva Sthapanam, the truths of Saivaism. We have seen that these ‘other religions’ are divided into four categories, with six religions in each, which Saiva Siddhanta refutes and transcends. Among the ‘Purachamayam’ (outer religions), which is mentioned as a group of three, The first category is Purappura Samayam. The religions in this Purappura Samayam are Lokayutham, Jainism, and the four types of Buddhism.

Thus, six religions are grouped in Purappura Samayam. In Purassamayam, six religions are grouped and refuted: Tarkam, Meemamsa, Ekanmavaatham, Sankyam, Yogam, and Panjaratram. In Akappura Samayam, six types of religions are arranged and their doctrines refuted: Maaviratham, Kaapalam, Bhairavam, Vamam, Aikyavada Saivam. In Akassamayam, from Paadaanavada Saivam to Sivaadvita Saivam, Paadaanavada Saivam, Bhedavada Saivam, Sivasamavada Saivam, Siva Sankaranthavada Saivam, Eeswara Avikaravada Saivam, and Sivaadvita Saivam are six religions grouped as Akassamayam and refuted. All these are generally classified into two: Aham (inner) and Puram (outer).

Then, Aham is further divided into Akassamayam and Akappura Samayam, and Puram is divided into Purassamayam and Purappura Samayam, making four categories as seen above. In each category, there are six religions. The Meykanda Shastras, which are fourteen Saiva religious texts, refute all these and establish the truth of Saiva Siddhanta. The six religions are Lokayutham and the four divisions within Buddhism: Maadhyamikam, Yogacharam, Sautranthikam, and Vaipashikam. These four Buddhist sects, along with Lokayutham, total six religions, which are categorized as Purappura Samayam, as classified by Srimath Maadhava Sivagnana Munivar in Sivagnana Maapaadiyam. He classifies them that way because these six religions do not accept the Vedas and Sivagamas as authoritative texts.

Therefore, he places them in the category of Purappura Samayas. Although they do not accept the four Vedas and Sivagamas as authoritative texts, they do have foundational texts of their own. These texts describe their conduct and doctrines.

Therefore, these are accepted as religions, and their doctrines are refuted as incorrect. The next category, Purassamayam, consists of six religions: Tarkam, Mimamsa, Ekanmavaadam, Sankyam, Yogam, and Panjaratram. These six religions are classified based on what they accept. are classified based on accepting the four Vedas as authoritative texts but not accepting the Sivagamas as authoritative texts. Saivism classifies them as Purassamayams. Although these six religions agree with the Vedas, there are differences in how they agree. The Tarkam adherents do not accept the concept of ‘that’ (Brahman).

Their doctrine, called ‘that’ or ‘this,’ is the second one. The Mimamsakas, also called Purva Mimamsakas, accept only the Karma Kanda, the first part of the Vedas. They do not accept the Jnana Kanda, the latter part of the Vedas. They only accept the Karma Kanda, the first part of the Vedas. They do not accept the Jnana Kanda, the latter part of the Vedas.

Similarly, the Ekanmavadhigal, who come next, are called Uttara Mimamsakas. They hold the doctrine that only Brahman exists. They accept the latter part of the Vedas, the Jnana Kanda, and do not give much authority to the Karma Kanda, the earlier part. The three religions that follow – Sankyam, Yogam, and Panjaratram – accept only the parts of the Vedas that suit their convenience and discard the rest. They also accept other texts, besides the Vedas, as true texts.

Therefore, these six religions in the Purassamayam, although generally accepting the Vedas as authoritative, only take a specific part that suits their doctrine as authoritative and do not accept the other parts. The next group, Akappura Samayathavargal, generally accepts both the Vedas and Sivagamas as authoritative texts. These Akappura Samayathavargal are the six religions: Pasupatham, Maaviratham, Kaapalam, Vaamam, Bhairavam, and Aikyavada Samayam. Among these, the first five accept special texts as authoritative. They follow practices forbidden by the Vedas as their own. Apart from these five, the Aikyavada Samayam (Aikyavada Saivites)

Saivites, they differ slightly from these, considering both the Veda and Sivagama as principal authoritative texts. In their code of conduct, they accept what is stated in both the Veda and Sivagama, following what is prescribed and abandoning what is forbidden.

However, these Aikyavada Saivites do not accept the important doctrine of ‘Anavamalam’ (primordial impurity) taught in Siddhanta Saivism. In that respect, they differ from Saiva Siddhanta.

Now, those belonging to Akassamayam are six sects, from Paadanavada Saivam to Sivaadvita Saivam. All these six sects worship Lord Shiva as the supreme reality. When they describe the nature of reality, they hold views similar to Saiva Siddhanta. They share similar views with Saiva Siddhanta, but they differ slightly from Saiva Siddhanta when explaining the ‘Swaroopa’ and ‘Thadasta Lakshanas’ (intrinsic and extrinsic characteristics) of objects.

Thus, we can understand the varying degrees of difference in doctrines among religions, from Lokayutha of Purappura Samayam to Sivaadvita Saivam of Akassamayam. The Sivaadvita Saivam in Akassamayam are those who attribute transformation to the efficient cause; hence, they are called efficient cause transformationists. Besides these six Akassamayam, there is also a pure Saivism that falls under Siddhanta Saivism.

Thus, Siddhanta Saivism classifies all religions based on their doctrines and, standing distinct from them, establishes its own truth of three realities. Saiva Siddhanta establishes the truth of these three realities: Pathi (God), Pasu (Soul), and Paasam (Bonds). We saw that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed this Thiruppasuram pathigam to refute other religions doctrinally and to establish Saivism. Sivakavimani Desikanar has written a commentary on how the truth of Jainism is refuted by valid reasoning. The doctrine of Jainism states that the Arhat is a Jiva (soul). It says that the Arhat has eternal and innate knowledge.

It also states that the Jiva is subject to contraction and expansion (Sankochavikasathannai). This is the second doctrine. The third doctrine is to describe the nature of a thing in many ways, saying ‘asti naasti’ (it is and it is not). saying ‘asti naasti’ (it is and it is not). The fourth doctrine is that this world was not created by anyone.

Thus, Jainism states these four important doctrines as its religious truths. Srimath Madhava Sivagnana Munivar explains Jainism in his commentary on Sivagnana Bodham, called Dravida Mahabhashyam, Sivagnana Mahabhashyam, or Sivagnana Mapaadiyam. This Jain religion is also known as Arhatam. It is now commonly called Jainism. Historians say it was founded by Vardhamana Mahavira.

But Jains do not accept that. According to them, twenty-three Thirthankaras lived for many years before Vardhamana Mahavira and propagated Jainism. The name Thirthankara refers to teachers who attained liberation by adhering to the Jain path. Vardhamana Mahavira is the twenty-fourth and last Thirthankara to appear. All objects in this world are divided into two categories: Jiva (living) and Ajiva (non-living). Among these, Jiva is conscious, and Ajiva is unconscious.

But both are indestructible; that is, they are beginningless and eternal. Jains again divide this Jiva into three: Anaadi Siddhan (eternally perfected), Mutthan (liberated), and Pethan (bound). Among these, Anaadi Siddhan is one who has never been born. They call him Arhat. From this, The name Arhatam came to this religion. Mutthan refers to those who were born into the world, followed the ethical path prescribed by Jainism, and then attained liberation.

Pethan refers to souls in a bound state. Jiva, as understood by Jains, can be considered the soul as described by other religions. What can be considered a unique doctrine of Jainism is that this soul adapts to the size of the body it inhabits, becoming either large or small. If that is the case, the soul in an elephant’s body should be large, and in an ant’s body, it should be small. According to their doctrine, it is measured.

Therefore, if the body is very large, it means the soul’s knowledge has developed. Such is their doctrine.

So, in the Jiva, which is the conscious division of the two categories, we saw these three divisions.

Now, in the category of Ajiva, they say there are four types: Purkalam, Akasam, Dharmam, and Adharmam. The word Purkalam means to join and become one, and to separate and become many.

Therefore, all physical objects, whether moving or non-moving, fall under the category of Purkalam. They say that many atoms together form a Purkala object. Let’s see how the four doctrines of Jainism are logically refuted. Firstly, the nature of the Arhat god is that he is free from faults like bondage, and like other liberated souls, he has acquired knowledge. This is because Jains say that if one adheres to dharma, no sin will come.

Therefore, the nature of this Arhat god, being free from faults like bondage, is like that of other liberated souls. Their own doctrine refutes this nature of their Arhat god. their own doctrine refutes the inherent nature of their Arhat god.

Therefore, the Arhat god’s innate infinite knowledge is refuted by themselves.

Secondly, their doctrine of Sankocha Vikasa Thannai (contraction and expansion), meaning that the Jiva has the nature to transform according to the size of the body, implies that the Jiva in an elephant’s body should be large and in an ant’s body, it should be small. If a limb is missing from a person’s body, the Jiva should decrease in that proportion. If that is the case, it would mean the Jiva undergoes transformation. If it expands like a lamp illuminating an entire house from one spot, it becomes a defect.

Therefore, the soul would become inanimate and also transient. So, their doctrine is incorrect.

Thirdly, those who hold the Asti Naasti (is and is not) doctrine, when asked if an object exists or not, they will say it exists and it does not exist, it is and it is not. Truth and non-existence, which are mutually contradictory like light and darkness, cannot coexist in a single object at the same time. To say so contradicts direct perception. If we take ‘it is and it is not,’ then during the time the sun exists, the meaning of ‘it does not exist’ should appear. During the time a snake exists, the fearlessness of ‘there is no snake’ should also appear.

But such things do not appear.

Therefore, their statement ‘asti naasti’ (it is and it is not) is inappropriate and is refuted.

Similarly, when asked if the soul exists before birth, some sects say it does, and some refute it by saying it does not. But in Jainism, without stating it firmly or clearly refuting it, they give seven types of answers to the same question. They will give seven types of answers: it exists, it does not exist, it exists and it does not exist, it cannot be described, it exists and cannot be described, it does not exist and cannot be described, it exists and does not exist and cannot be described.

Thus, they give such confusing and uncertain answers.

Therefore, their argument is called Anaikantavaatham, and they are called Anaikantavaadigal.

In this way, the Asti Naasti doctrine is refuted.

Now, their doctrine is that this world is eternal, so they say this world. Whatever has parts, whatever appears as manifold and insentient, whatever is an effect, is perishable. An effect implies it has been produced from a cause by an intelligent being. This world also has parts—he, she, it. It has the nature of appearing, existing, and perishing. It is insentient, and it is manifold.

Therefore, this world was caused by a Primeval Being. So, the Jain claim that this world is eternal and was not created by anyone is thus refuted by Saiva Siddhantins.

Thus, we have seen how the doctrines of Jainism are logically and authoritatively refuted in Saiva Siddhanta. Let us go on contemplating this. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 729, composed by the divine Sekizhar Peruman, Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed the Thiruppasuram pathigam to eradicate other religions and to establish Saivism. There are Jains present, and the Pandyan king, the southerner, is also there. By composing this Thiruppasuram pathigam, nothing will come of it for the Jains, because even if the sun is out, if one’s eyes are completely veiled, the sunlight is of no use.

Similarly, these Jains have their knowledge obscured.

Therefore, even though they will not understand the effect of this Thiruppasuram pathigam or the true path, if such Jains are present, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed this Thiruppasuram pathigam to inform the Pandyan king, and through him, to inform the living beings of this world, both to refute other religions and to explain the truth of Saiva Sthapanam.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sang the Thiruppasuram pathigam. The Pandyan king, the southerner, is touched by the sacred hands of Gnanasambandhar, the leader of Sirkazhi, and receives the sacred ash of Lord Shiva.

Therefore, just as a balanced scale demonstrates equality, this Pandyan king, having been freed from previous severe karma, attains the maturity to understand the Primeval Being. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Having been touched by sacred hands and having received the sacred ash, even though these Jains may not understand that worldly order is the order prescribed in the Vedas, and that the path to eternal liberation is the path of Shiva, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed this Thiruppasuram pathigam to make it known to the Pandyan king, and through him, to the world and its living beings, thereby benefiting them. The divine Sekizhar Peruman states in the 819th verse: ‘Thennavan Maran thanum Sivapura Thalaivar theendi ponnavil kondraiyarththam thiruneeru poosappetru munnai valvinaiyum neengi mudalvanai ariyum thanmai thunninan vinaikaloththu thulai ena nirthale.’ (The southerner Maran, touched by the leader of Sivapuram and having applied the sacred ash of the golden Kondrai-wearing Lord, shed his former severe karmas and attained the state of knowing the Primeval Being, with his karmas balanced like a scale.) The Pandyan king, touched by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, is about to be adorned with Lord Shiva’s sacred ash. Previously, to cure his fever, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman took sacred ash with his sacred hands and applied it to the king’s body, which we saw as a Sparsha Deekshai (initiation by touch).

Similarly, he is about to receive the sacred ash again. Previously, for his illness, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman performed the act of making him eligible for initiation.

After this, the Pandyan king is again about to receive the sacred ash from Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. That is the state of bestowing the sacred feet at the end of the initiation. The Pandyan king, thus adorned with sacred ash, shines there.

Consequently, all his past severe karmas are dispelled. We have already seen that due to the effects of his past evil actions, he had been leaning towards Jainism until then. This past evil karma refers to the ‘Prarabdha Karma’ (karma ready for fruition) accumulated in previous births by that body, which, taking the ‘Buddhi Tattvam’ (intellectual principle) as its support, manifests as ‘munnai’ (past), and is experienced. This is what is called ‘Valvinai’ (severe karma) here. Why is Prarabdha Karma called Valvinai? Because Prarabdha Karma cannot be easily eliminated.

It is so powerful that Prarabdha Karma exists even for Jivanmuktas (liberated souls), but for them, it only affects the physical body.

Thus, Prarabdha Karma is of indescribable power.

Here, how was his Prarabdha Karma so powerful? The Pandyan king was not a hereditary follower of Jainism. The Pandyan king was born into a Saiva family.

Moreover, he was married to a Saiva princess and had Kulachirai Nayanar as his chief minister. Even though he had such a loving Saiva affiliation, and even though the Pandyan country was an ancient holy land, as praised in Thiruvachakam, a Saiva holy land, he was deluded and leaned towards Jainism. That itself is the power of his Prarabdha Karma. In addition to leaning towards Jainism, he also helped harm Saivism. That too was due to the power of his Prarabdha Karma.

Thus, the Pandyan king is now free from both these ‘munnai’ (past) and ‘valvinai’ (severe karma), which are ‘Sanchita’ (accumulated) and ‘Prarabdha’ (fructifying) karmas. He has attained the state of ‘Iruvinai Oppu’ (equanimity towards karma). The Pandyan king attained the state of knowing the Primeval Being. Just as the beam of a balance scale remains neutral when equal weights are placed on both pans, the Pandyan king attains this karmic balance. Even when there are no objects on either pan, the balance beam remains neutral; similarly, the Pandyan king attains such karmic balance. As divine Sekizhar Peruman states, ‘Vinaikal otthal endru vinaikaloththu thulaiana nirthalale,’ meaning ‘with karmas balanced like a scale,’ this karmic balance is what is called Iruvinai Oppu in Saiva Siddhanta.

What is Iruvinai Oppu? It is the state of ripeness of the soul’s consciousness where, when joy comes as a result of good deeds, one does not get immersed in it, and when suffering comes as a result of evil deeds, one does not get immersed in that suffering. Instead, one considers both joy and suffering as coming by divine command and embraces them. The soul swallows it, viewing both pleasure and pain as divine commands. This is the mature state of the soul’s consciousness, called Iruvinai Oppu. This is a state of ripeness the soul attains through divine grace.

As Manikkavachaka Peruman sings in Thiruvachakam, ‘Unakkillathathor vittu mel vilaiyamal en vinai oththapin kanakillath thirukkolam nee vanthu kattinai kazhukkundrile’ (After my karma became balanced, so that no seed remains to sprout for you, you came and showed your immeasurable sacred form in Kazhukkundru), we can reflect on this here, where the Lord shows his sacred form after karma is balanced.

Therefore, having received Lord Shiva’s sacred ash from the sacred hands of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the Pandyan king is freed from past grievous karma and stands with Iruvinai Oppu, with karmas balanced like a scale. Consequently, he also attains the state of knowing the Primeval Being.

Thus, Sekizhar Peruman highlights three states. Sekizhar Peruman highlights three stages. These three are called Sakti Nipatham, Iruvinai Oppu, and Malaparipakam in Saiva Siddhanta. Even if ‘munnai valvinai’ (past severe karma) is taken to mean the evil karma he accumulated when he was a Jain, it is fitting. He stands free from such karma.

Thus, these stages are called Sakti Nipatham, Iruvinai Oppu, and Malaparipakam. ‘Nipatham’ means ‘fall’ or ‘descent.’ These are the Tapas (austerities) mentioned in Saiva Siddhanta: Chariyai, Kiriyai, Yogam, and Gnanam. Tapas manifests in various ways like this. Tapas manifests in various ways like this. For souls to mature in accordance with their penance, divine grace, Arulsakthi, will settle on their consciousness. Until this maturation, the divine power of obscuration, Thirodhana Sakthi, aided the impurity (malan) and propelled them forward. Due to the penance performed by these souls, the same Thirodhana Sakthi transforms into Arulsakthi to bring about their maturation and settles upon them.

Thirodhana Sakthi is the power of God; it is not distinct from Arulsakthi. It is the power of God that, when it stands by souls bound by impurities, is called Thirodhana Sakthi, and when those same souls are ready to be freed from impurities, the same Thirodhana Sakthi transforms into Arulsakthi and guides them. This is the truth proclaimed by Saiva Siddhanta.

Therefore, Madhava Sivajñāna Munivar describes Thirodhana Sakthi as ‘wooden compassion’ and Arulsakthi as ‘compassion’. The divine power of grace that settles upon souls is called Sakthini Padam. This Sakthini Padam and Malaparipakam occur simultaneously and their result is Iruvinai Oppu. This Sakthini Padam is of four types, based on the intensity of penance and the resulting maturation that souls must achieve. These four types of Sakthini Padam settle upon souls. The term Sakthini Padam means the ‘fall of Sakthi’.

Padam itself means ‘fall’, and Nipadham means ‘rapidly’ or ‘intensely’. When the previously unperceived Arulsakthi is perceived by souls, its impact creates profound effects.

Therefore, it is called ‘Sakthi Fall’ or Sakthini Padam. If a stone falls rapidly into a crowd, it causes those gathered to quickly disperse.

Similarly, when this Arulsakthi settles upon a soul, it makes that soul abandon worldly distractions like wife and children, and seek out a jñāna-guru.

Therefore, because it comes so rapidly, it is called Sakthi’s fall, Sakthini Padam.

Now, the second stage is Malaparipakam. Malaparipakam means souls aligning with the causes and co-causes for the diminution of their impurity. Malaparipakam means that the ignorance which completely shrouded the soul diminishes and reaches maturation. The alignment of impurity with the co-causes for its power to wane is called Malaparipakam. The benefits that arise from it are various.

Thus, good deeds (Siva puṇṇiyam) and pure instruments like the body serve as co-causes for the diminution of a soul’s impurity.

Here, the divine gaze and touch (sparsham) of Pillaiyar, embodying Siva puṇṇiyam, occur.

Therefore, the king obtains a pure body and other such instruments by these co-causes.

Thus, the stage of Malaparipakam comes to the king.

Now, regarding Iruvinai Oppu, some offer two types of answers to the question of what Iruvinai Oppu means. The first answer is that when the most elevated puṇṇiyam earned through performing sacrifices in many births, and conversely, the most heinous sins like Brahmahatti, both ripen simultaneously and yield their respective fruits, they cancel each other out.

Thus, the results of these two karmas perish. Some say this is Iruvinai Oppu.

However, it is not so. If exalted puṇṇiyam and terrible sin stood in opposition to each other and were destroyed, then other good and bad deeds would still yield their fruits.

Therefore, explaining it this way is not Iruvinai Oppu. This is not the meaning of Iruvinai Oppu.

Now, some others say that Iruvinai Oppu occurs when the good and bad deeds accumulated over many births are perfectly balanced, meaning not excessive good and minimal bad, or excessive bad and minimal good, but exactly half and half. This is not the meaning because a state where both are equal never comes. Even if they were to be equal, it would only destroy Karma Mala, and one cannot say that Anava Mala would be removed by it. Such a statement is also not appropriate.

Therefore, even if this Iruvinai Oppu were to occur as they describe, they would not attain liberation.

Thus, this is also inappropriate. These two theories are rejected in the Paushkara Agama. These two explanations for Iruvinai Oppu are rejected.

So, what does Saiva Siddhanta say Iruvinai Oppu means? It says that both puṇṇiyam and sin, like a golden chain and an iron chain, lead souls through births and deaths; both are binding. Understanding that both puṇṇiyam and sin are binding, and not desiring either of them but becoming averse to them, is the meaning of Iruvinai Oppu. This aversion occurs in the soul’s consciousness. Srimat Madhava Sivajñāna Munivar advises to understand this through subtle perception. The two types of karma are divided into Pasu Nallvinai (good deeds for the soul) and Pasu Theevinai (bad deeds for the soul), and Siva Nallvinai (good deeds for Siva) and Siva Theevinai (bad deeds for Siva).

Therefore, Iruvinai Oppu also has two types. What we have seen so far is the Iruvinai Oppu related to Pasu Nallvinai and Pasu Theevinai.

Similarly, the Iruvinai Oppu related to Siva Nallvinai and Siva Theevinai also leads to birth.

Similarly, Siva Nallvinai will also occur. Both Siva Nallvinai and Siva Theevinai must be balanced in the soul’s consciousness for this Iruvinai Oppu.

First, the Iruvinai Oppu arising from Pasu Nallvinai and Theevinai, as mentioned, occurs through maturation. This arises from Pasu Puṇṇiyam and common Siva Puṇṇiyam. This happens in the first Sakthini Padam, which is Mandataram, responsible for causing Malaparipakam. We saw that Sakthini Padam occurs in four types: Mandataram, Mandam, Theeviram, and Theevirataram. This first Mandataram occurs in this manner. The later-mentioned Iruvinai Oppu gradually ascends through other Sakthini Padams, eventually leading to jñānam.

These four types of Sakthini Padam are considered to be successively higher. This Sakthini Padam begins very slowly, then becomes slow, then intense, and then very intense. These four also expand into four each.

Thus, there are many types.

Therefore, it is clear that devotion (sariyai) and other penances are the cause of jñānam, and Mandataram and other Sakthini Padams are the cause of those penances. It is evident that the root cause of all these is the maturation of the soul’s consciousness. The maturation of the soul’s consciousness means the gradual enlightenment of the souls’ intellect. The reason for souls to gradually progress in consciousness, and to become enlightened, is the divine grace of the Primal Being (Mudhalvan), who remains inseparable from them even in their bound state (kevala nilai) and bestows grace. This is gleaned from this.

Thus, in the Siva Jñāna Māpadiyam, Srimat Madhava Sivajñāna Munivar has given a grand commentary on Sakthini Padam, Iruvinai Oppu, and Malaparipakam. Such the Pandya king attained these three stages due to the sacred ash of Lord Siva being placed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred hands.

We shall continue with our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, part seven hundred and thirty, Vambara Varivandu charukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, composed by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman. The sacred verses (thiruppasuram) by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman were delivered to impart divine instruction to the Pandya king. Presenting the Pandya king as the central figure, Thirugnanasambandha Pillaiyar graciously imparted divine instruction to the mature souls of this world. This is explained to us by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman. “The worldly Vedic order and the enduring true path, the Siva path, are not seen by the confused Jainas, but the celebrated southern king (Pandya) understands this truth.

“Thus, within the fragrant Kali, where primordial wisdom (adhi jñānam) blossoms, with divine words the great benefactor extended the sacred leaf (thiruvēdu) into the river, so that many may understand and attain salvation.” These are the eight hundred and twentieth and eight hundred and twenty-first verses. The Jainas will not understand the worldly Vedic order and the true Siva path. The worldly Vedic order refers to the Vedic path described in the Vedas. The true Siva path refers to the Saiva path, the Sivagama path. We must remember that Pillaiyar’s divine avatar was to allow the Vedic path to flourish and the Saiva domain to greatly shine. The Jainas are ignorant of these two aspects, which were the two great objectives of Pillaiyar’s divine avatar and are now being explained.

“This is where the world comes to be saved.

“Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman highlights the truth that the flourishing of the Vedic path and the prominence of the Saiva domain are the essence of the sacred verses (thiruppathigam). It is true that the Lord revealed the Vedas for the worldly people and the Agamas for mature souls who have attained Sakthini Padam. These Jainas do not follow the Vedic order, and therefore they do not follow the superior Saiva path either.

“Thus, they are external religionists (puṟaccamayi) who do not understand the truth of these.

“Therefore, this pathigam, revealed to teach these two paths, was not meant to instruct the Jainas. It was a jñāna-upadesha given to the Pandya king, who possessed a subtle maturity and the ability to know the Primal Being. It is true that this pathigam, delivered on the banks of the Vaigai, was intended to teach the king, in the presence of the Jainas, that the true substance is what can stand firm without being swept away by the current. The Jainas were also present there and heard the divine pronouncements of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman in this sacred verse (thiruppasuram) and pathigam.

“However, lacking maturity, the Jainas were unable to perceive its truth. But the Pandya king was in a state of maturity to understand the truth of this thiruppasuram and thiruppathigam.

“Therefore, Pillaiyar blessed him. The Jainas were in an immature state where they could not understand even when taught.

“Therefore, ignoring them all, Pillaiyar instructs the king with this pathigam. That it is not proper to teach jñānam to those who are immature, and that even if taught, they lack the ability to perceive it, is the truth we understand here. Thirugnanasambandha Pillaiyar is a generous benefactor whose divine words (thiruvaaku) make Siva jñānam blossom. Sekkizhar Peruman refers to Siva jñānam as Adhi Jñānam. Adhi Jñānam means the jñānam of the Primal Being, i.e., Siva’s jñānam. It can also be understood as the jñānam bestowed by the Primal Being, or as the primal jñānam itself, the supreme jñānam among all jñānam.

“Thus, this Adhi Jñānam, blossoming through Pillaiyar’s divine mouth, emanates like the fragrance of blooming flowers, spreading and permeating the entire world with the fragrance of Siva jñānam. Such a generous benefactor delivers this thiruppathigam and thiruppasuram, so that many may understand and attain salvation. Earlier, Sekkizhar Peruman explained that it was delivered for the king to understand.

“Now, Sekkizhar Peruman states that it is for the salvation of many. This is because, according to the saying, “The world, with its widespread lands, thrives through the king,” the people of this world, who follow the king, will understand by observing the king’s comprehension and follow him to attain salvation.

“Therefore, if one king is saved, many souls will be saved through him. So there is no need to save each soul individually.

“Therefore, for the sake of the well-praised southern king to understand, and through that method of instructing the highly mature king, for the souls of this world to understand this truth and attain salvation, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman delivers this thiruppasuram and thiruppathigam. He resolves in his sacred heart that many, and all the souls of this world, should be saved. This becomes his sankalpam. With this resolution in his sacred heart, he conceives and writes this pathigam on the sacred leaf. Before the guru’s instruction, his pure intention (sadbhavana) is greatly needed.

“Thus, with intention and sankalpam, he has these pathigams written on the sacred leaf by Sambandha Charanar. We have already seen that Sambandha Charanālayar used to write and compile all the pathigams composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman on sacred leaves.

“Therefore, when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman thus composed this thiruppasuram and thiruppathigam, Sambandha Charanālayar wrote it on a sacred leaf. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman then took that sacred leaf with his divine lotus-like hand and released it into the Vaigai river. Sekkizhar Peruman explains this historical event, stating that the leaf, instead of flowing with the river, went against the current, and from that day until now, it stands as a testament to truth for all souls in the world. From now on, in the twenty-two upcoming verses, Sekkizhar Peruman himself acts as a commentator, explaining this thiruppasuram and thiruppathigam by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, which begins with “Vazhga Andhanar.”

“Therefore, Sivakavimani Ayya has provided an explanation for this thiruppasuram and thiruppathigam based on the verses of the divine Sekkizhar Peruman. This thiruppasuram and thiruppathigam begins with “Vazhga Andhanar Vaanavar Aaninam.” Sekkizhar Peruman provides an elaborate commentary on this first line, “Vazhga Andhanar Vaanavar Aaninam,” in the eight hundred and twenty-second verse. That verse says: “May the Brahmins, celestials, and cattle prosper, so that the world may find joy through this truthful utterance, and the chanted sacrifices and primordial worship of Shankara may endure, O King.” When Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sings “Vazhga Andhanar Vaanavar Aaninam”, the meaning of this first line is a blessing for these three: Brahmins, celestials, and herds of cattle. This pathigam is praised by Sekkizhar Peruman as a truthful utterance.

“Therefore, the benefit of this truthful utterance, spoken by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as “May Brahmins, celestials, and herds of cattle prosper,” is for the souls of this world to be freed from suffering and attain joy.

“Therefore, for the sake of these worldly souls to be freed from suffering and attain joy, the Siva sacrifices accompanied by chants, and the primordial worship and other forms of worship that are primarily described in the Sivagamas for Lord Siva, may all endure. This is the meaning. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman explains in this verse that this is the explanation for the first line of the first verse of the thiruppasuram, “Vazhga Andhanar Vaanavar Aaninam.” If its benefit is for this world to be freed from suffering and attain joy, then “this world” refers to the living beings in this world. This is because it is the sentient beings who experience joy or sorrow.

“Therefore, its meaning is that Siva Puja should continually prevail so that these worldly souls may be freed from suffering and attain joy. Its meaning is that through such Siva Puja and Siva worship, they may be freed from suffering and attain joy. The Vedic mantras prescribed with chants, and the Vedic sacrifices containing mantras uttered with proper chants, may flourish. is the first meaning of this blessing. May the Siva Puja prescribed in the Siva Agamas flourish—this is its meaning. Those who perform these are the Andhanar (Brahmins). The Vaidikas (Vedic scholars) who perform Vedic sacrifices for the welfare of others, and the Sivavedis (Siva priests) who perform Agamic sacrifices, are the meaning of the term Andhanar.

“Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman blesses, saying, “Vazhga Andhanar,” meaning may the Vaidika Andhanar who perform Vedic sacrifices and the Sivavedi Andhanar who perform Sivagama sacrifices prosper. This is because these sacrifices are performed for the world to attain joy. They are also called Munivar, Andhanar, and so on. In the Periya Puranam too, Sivapathahrudaiyar, Naminandhi Adigal, Thiruneelanakkar, and others, including Pugazhthunai Nayanar, are praised. Their sacred lives are celebrated. We have extensively contemplated in the Thillai Vazh Andhanar Puranam on how the Thillai Vazh Andhanar perform Vedic sacrifices and Sivagama worship, described as “having learned well, they maintained the fire and prevented the Age of Kali.” We can understand this by considering those ideas.

“Thiruvalluvadeva says in Thirukkural, “Andhanar are virtuous ones who practice compassion towards all other living beings.” Thiruvalluvadeva Nayanar praises Andhanar as those who show compassion to all living beings. Such Andhanar, may they prosper, is the first blessing, “Vazhga Andhanar,” spoken by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. “Vaanavar” refers to Next, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman blesses the Devas. These Devas are entrusted by Shiva’s command to guide the people of this world onto the right path. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman blesses these celestials, who serve as instruments for Shiva, to prosper. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman blesses the cow herds, saying, “May the cattle thrive.” These cow herds provide essential ingredients for Shiva worship; they offer the cow dung, the primary component of Thiruneeru, a Shaiva sacrament.

“These cow herds provide the five ingredients for Panchagavya, used in the Thirumanjanam ritual during Shiva Puja.

“Additionally, they provide milk and other items necessary for Vedic sacrifices.

“Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman blesses, “May the cow herds thrive.” Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman blesses these three – the Brahmins, the celestials, and the cow herds – in the first line of the first verse of this pathigam.

“Now, the second line follows: “May cool waters fall, and may the king prosper.” In the next verse, the 823rd verse, Sekkizhar Peruman has given an commentary. We will continue to contemplate that.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The great Purana, Part 731, of Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, composed by Theivasekkizhar Peruman, recounts the life of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. Sekkizhar Peruman, who gave an elaborate commentary on the first line of the first verse of the pathigam, which begins with “Vazhga Andhanar Vanavar Aaninam,” now provides a detailed explanation for the second line, “Veezhga Thanpunal Vendhanum Onguga,” in the 823rd verse. That verse is: (Vezhvi nar payan veezh punalavathu, Naalum archanai nal uruppadhalal, Aalum mannanai vazhththiyathu, Archanai moolum matravai kaakkum muraimaiyal). This verse explains that the good outcome of sacrifices is falling water, and because daily worship is a good part of it, the ruling king is blessed for maintaining the proper order that protects all these things. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman blesses by saying, “May cool water fall.”

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman means, “May good, cool rain fall.” Why does he bless in this manner? As we saw earlier, Brahmins should thrive because they perform Vedic and Shaiva Agamic sacrifices. The celestials should thrive because they act as instruments for Shiva in delivering the benefits of these Vedic sacrifices. The cow herds should thrive because they provide the materials for Vedic sacrifices and Shaiva Agamic worship. We saw that the good outcome of such sacrifices is good rainfall.

Therefore, because the good outcome of sacrifices is falling water, and because daily worship is a good part of it, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman thus instructs. Hence, for the benefit of sacrifices, he instructs, “May the rain fall as a good benefit.” The rain that comes from sacrifices, that water, is a good component in Shaiva Agamic puja and worship. There are many benefits to sacrifices, and among the best of these benefits is rainfall. This is of greater significance than other benefits that arise from sacrifices, therefore it is called a good benefit. The sacrifices offered to Shankara become so. And the rain that comes from sacrifices, that water, is a very important component in Shaiva Agamic worship and Shiva Puja.

Flowers, incense, light, and ambrosia are also parts of Shaiva Puja, and among them, the best part is water. Water is an indispensable special element in Shiva’s worship.

Therefore, many sacred sayings have been composed about it. “For those who perform meritorious deeds, there are flowers and water” is a sacred saying from Thirumandhiram. “Your devotees who carry flowers and water” is a sacred saying from Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s Thevaram. “Using the pure good water of Kaveri” and “There are flowers and water to use” are sacred sayings from Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal’s Thevaram. “He brings rice and water to bathe” is a sacred saying from Sundaramoorthy Swamigal’s Thevaram. “If there is not enough, there are fresh leaves and water everywhere” is from the eleventh Thirumurai, Thirukkazhumala Mummani Kovai.

The verse from Puzhazhthunai Nayanar Puranam is: “Our Lord, I will not abandon him,” and it speaks of worshipping day and night with fragrant flowers and cool water.

Thus, throughout the Thirumurai, the saints have explained how water is an indispensable part of Shaiva Agamic worship and Shiva Puja. Even in Thirukkural, following the first chapter on the praise of God, Thiruvalluvar Deva Nayanar dedicates the second chapter to the glory of rain, emphasizing the importance of water and rain. In it, he states, “If the rain fails, even the special worship to the celestials will not take place on earth.” The eighth Thirukkural in the chapter on the glory of rain is, “If the rain ceases, the festivals and pujas that people perform for the celestials in this world will not happen,” thus states Thiruvalluvar Devanayanar. Parimelazhagar, in his commentary on this, says that “special worship” refers to occasional (naimittika) pujas, and “worship” refers to daily (nithya) pujas. He writes that the occasional puja is performed to rectify shortcomings in the daily puja, and therefore Thiruvalluvar refers to it with the word “special.” Thus, explains Parimelazhagar.

Therefore, rain, which possesses such significance, is a component of sacrifice. The benefit of sacrifice is a component of Shaiva Agamic worship, in Shiva Puja. In Shaiva Agamic Puja, water is indispensably required in all components such as Thirumanjanam, Arghyam, Padhyam, etc. Such Shiva worship should be performed every day, and at all appropriate times each day.

Therefore, the Vedic and Shaiva Agamic concept that rain is the result of sacrifice is nurtured here by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman: (Valarththi pukai naalum vinnal puyal kaattum Vezhi Mizhalaye) is Pillaiyar’s Thevaram. The smoke rising from the well-performed sacrifices always indicates rain in the sky, is its meaning.

Therefore, sacrifice The result is water, rain, and it also becomes a component of the sacrifice.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman blesses, “May cool water fall.” “Veezhga” is a special blessing that brings good fortune, specifically about rain.

Next, he blesses, “May the king prosper.” He blesses the ruling king because the king is bound by duty to ensure that all the aforementioned things happen without fail. This is why Thirugnanasambandha Peruman blesses the king. In the narratives of Periya Puranam, such as the stories of Eripattu Nayanar, Pugazhchozha Nayanar, Idangalinar Saritha Varalaru, and Manunithi Chozhar Saritham, it is explained how the king undertakes this duty to protect sacrifices and pujas. It has been explained how the king performs this duty of protecting the worship of the Lord. The duty of protecting worship rests with the ruling king. A country may have many religions; the king has the duty to act as a protector and refuge for adherents of each religion to perform their worship according to their respective faiths.

In particular, it is a primary duty of a king to ensure that the Vedic and Shaiva traditions, and the sacrifices, pujas, and worship prescribed within them, are carried out.

Thus, it becomes the king’s duty to protect this world by ensuring rainfall through the protection of divine worship. In the Thirumurai, there are many such sayings. “If the king errs in justice, then the rain will fail in the entire nation,” thus states the Thirukkural. And the Thirukkural also says, “In the land ruled by a righteous king, both rain and harvest abound.” Thus, Thiruvalluvar Devanayanar states this both positively and negatively. Thiruvalluvar Devanayanar also states in the Thirukkural, “Cows yield less milk, and virtuous scholars forget their texts, if the guardian king fails to protect.” This is the 560th Thirukkural. If the king who is supposed to protect fails to protect the lives of the people, then the milk from the cows in that kingdom will decrease, and the scholars living in that country will forget their texts, says Thiruvalluvar Devanayanar.

If the milk from cows decreases, it becomes difficult to provide the Havis needed for sacrifices. If sacrifices are not performed properly, it would be very difficult for the Brahmins to chant the mantras. If mantras and kalpas are not chanted, sacrifices will not take place.

Therefore, Thiruvalluvar Devanayanar explains that the righteous rule of a king protects all these, and that if there is a cruel government lacking such rule, all these evils will occur. He also states in the Thirukkurals: “The king’s scepter is the source of the Brahmins’ texts and righteousness,” and “Charity and penance will not endure in the vast world if the sky does not give.” The meaning of the Thirukkural “The king’s scepter is the source of the Brahmins’ texts and righteousness” is that the righteous rule exercised by the king is the foundation for the Vedas, which belong to the Brahmins, and for the dharma proclaimed by those Vedas. This is the meaning of the Thirukkural, “The king’s scepter is the source of the Brahmins’ texts and righteousness.” This is the 543rd Thirukkural.

Similarly, the Thirukkural also states, “Charity and penance will not endure in the vast world if the sky does not give.” Thiruvalluvar Devanayanar explains that if the sky fails and rain does not fall, then charity and penance will not take place in this world. Charity means joyfully giving possessions earned through righteous means to deserving individuals. Penance involves undertaking vows and reducing food intake, etc., to prevent the mind from following the senses.

Here, charity is largely performed by householders, and penance is practiced by ascetics. Thiruvalluvar Devanayanar states that neither of these will occur if the sky does not pour rain in this world.

Therefore, if sacrifices are to proceed correctly, if Brahmins are to thrive, if cow herds are to flourish, and if rain is to fall abundantly, then the king’s righteous scepter must function flawlessly. The responsibility and duty to protect all these rests with the king.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman places such a king in that sequential order.

Thus, Theivasekkizhar Peruman gives an elaborate commentary on the second line of the first verse of this pathigam.

Now, the third line is And what is its meaning? Sekkizhar Peruman expands on this in the 824th verse: (Azhga theeyathu endru oiththra ayal neri, Veezhga endradhu veru ellam Aran peyar, Soozhga endradhu tholluyir yavaiyum, Vazhi anjaliththu odhi valargave). Sekkizhar Peruman thus expands the commentary, stating that the intention is for all paths that are alien and contrary to the Vedic Agamas to lose their strength. This was spoken as “May evil drown,” or “May that which is evil sink.” Here, “that which is evil” refers to the collection of other religions apart from the Vedic and Agamic religions, which bring about misfortunes. These religions do not conform to the Vedas, nor do they adhere to Shiva’s sacraments like vibhuti and rudraksha.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states that these paths and religions, which are external to the Vedas and Agamas, should lose their strength. Even though these alien religions are numerous, they stand united in their blasphemy of Shiva and Shiva’s sacraments.

Therefore, all these must be rejected and cast aside. The beings of this world should attain salvation by following the Vedas and Agamas. For this, the power of these external religions must be removed, which is why he says, “May evil sink.” This should not be interpreted as meaning that the followers of those religions should be destroyed, but rather that their religious principles should become diluted.

Next, he blesses, “May the name of Aran pervade everything.” The name of Aran is the name of Shiva. Earlier, he said, “May alien paths fall,” which refers to the removal of evil. Its inner meaning is the removal of suffering. Sivagnanabodham refers to it as Pasakshayam in the tenth aphorism.

Now, when he blesses, “May the name of Aran pervade everything,” this indicates receiving good and obtaining joy, in addition to the previously mentioned removal of suffering. Freedom from suffering is not happiness. One must be free from suffering and also attain happiness.

Therefore, first, one must be free from suffering, which is Pasakshayam, as per the tenth aphorism of Sivagnanabodham. The idea of attaining happiness is the meaning of “May the name of Aran pervade everything.” This is called Shivapperu, or Shiva’s grace, and is the concept presented in the sixteenth aphorism of Sivagnanabodham. He instructs, “May the name of Aran pervade everything.” “Everything” here refers to all living beings, indicating the conscious universe. This is because conscious beings, as the conscious universe, Living beings possess the eligibility to attain liberation by chanting Shiva’s sacred name.

Therefore, “everything” means all living beings. All these living beings must attain salvation by chanting the name of Aran. The name of Aran is the sacred five-syllable mantra, Shri Panchaksharam, embodying Shiva’s sacred name. The Thevaram verse says: “Like the juice from sugarcane, the name of the five letters is sweet,” and “When I die, grant me the appearance of your sacred five letters, Lord Aiyararu.” When he states, “May the name of Aran pervade everything,” “pervade” means to meditate intensely. “Vazhi” is a blessing.

Therefore, the meaning of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s blessing, “May the name of Aran pervade everything,” is that beings should thrive by chanting these five letters. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman blesses, “May life flourish.” What does it mean for life to flourish? It means that the soul attains the state of Shiva and shines. The idea of flourishing means being freed from the cycle of birth and death, and then again birth and death, and attaining a state of fullness within Shiva-ness.

Therefore, “May evil sink” means the destruction of bonds, and thus Theivasekkizhar Peruman elaborates on all these concepts.

Now, the concluding part of the first verse is “And may the world be free of sorrow.” For this, Theivasekkizhar Peruman provides an explanation in a separate verse. We will continue to contemplate Theivasekkizhar Peruman. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 732, of Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, composed by Theivasekkizhar Peruman, recounts the life of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. In the first verse of the pathigam, which begins with “Vazhga Andhanar,” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman says, “May the world’s sorrow be dispelled.” Theivasekkizhar Peruman has given an explanation for this phrase, “May the world’s sorrow be dispelled,” in the 825th verse. In this 824th verse, Sekkizhar Peruman gave an explanation for the phrase “May the world’s sorrow be dispelled” by stating that Thirugnanasambandha first spoke of the nature of the world and the dispelling of its sorrow. The prose states that Gnanasambandhar said this. The benevolent wish of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is for the suffering of the world to cease.
