Its meaning is that the suffering of living beings, who dwell in this world and the next, should be removed. Suffering here refers to heavenly pain, indicating that both the state of supreme bliss and its absence are mentioned by Theivasekkizhar Peruman.

Therefore, to transform the suffering of beings living in the cycle of birth and rebirth, so they may attain the path of Shiva, which offers liberation from rebirth, ‘may suffering cease’. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, from the position of a divine teacher, bestows this language. This sacred pathigam of verses is the divine teaching of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, and the first verse serves as an auspicious blessing for this divine revelation. Theivasekkizhar Peruman concludes by explaining the meaning of this first verse, the Thiruppasuram, in these four verses, stating, ‘Thus spoke Gnanasambandhar.’ Similarly, when concluding the other eleven verses of the Thiruppasuram, Theivasekkizhar Peruman establishes the custom of mentioning Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred name, stating, ‘Thus he spoke.’ Therefore, this first verse of the Thiruppasuram begins with ‘Long live the’. May the celestials and cows flourish, may cool water fall, may the king prosper, may all evil sink, may the name of Arana surround, and may the suffering of the world cease. The meanings of this first verse, as elucidated by Theivasekkizhar Peruman, are as follows: The purpose of this pathigam of verses is for all beings in this world to be free from suffering and attain bliss.

For living beings to be free from suffering and attain bliss, sacrifices, anointing, and worship must take place. To ensure the continuation of such sacrifices and Agamic worship, the Brahmins and celestials who are instrumental in these practices May the herds of cattle, which are also part of these practices, flourish. And as a result of these sacrificial anointing and worship ceremonies, and as an integral part of them, may abundant rain fall. May the king who protects all these prosper. Through these, may all evils of other paths and external religions, which obstruct beings from attaining their rightful benefits, sink deep and cease to exist in their respective places. May all beings be surrounded by the name of Shiva.

This is the meaning of the first verse of this Thiruppasuram. In this, why are the Brahmins blessed first with ‘Long live’? Because these Brahmins perform sacrifices, anointing, and worship for Shiva not for themselves, but with the intention that all beings in this world should attain bliss. These Brahmins are those who conduct sacrifices, anointing, and worship for Shiva with the intention that all beings should attain happiness. They are compassionate towards all living beings. As Thiruvalluvadeva Nayanar states in Thirukkural, in the chapter on the greatness of renouncers, ‘Those who possess purity of heart towards all beings are called Brahmins.’ He reveals that those who practice perfect kindness and compassion towards all beings are known as Brahmins.

Parimelazhagar, in his commentary on this, writes that the term ‘Anthanar’ is a descriptive name.

Therefore, a descriptive name arises from a reason. Anyone who practices compassion towards all beings is called an ‘Anthanar.’ Its meaning is ‘therefore, for themselves’. They perform sacrifices, anointing, and worship for Shiva so that all may be happy.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman first blessed them, the Brahmins. Those who offer worship according to the rules established by Shiva are the celestials and gods.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman next blesses the celestials. Those who are praised first are the celestials who dwell, who are praised as living gods.

Thus, first blessing the Brahmins, who are the earthly gods living in this world, and then the celestials living in the celestial world, who accept and follow the rules established by Shiva, therefore, he next Blesses the herds of cows, as they provide excellent offerings and sacred ash for these sacrificial rituals.

Thirdly, he blesses the herds of cattle.

Then, he blesses the water, the rain, which is the result of the sacrificial rituals. And since the king bears the duty of protecting all these, he blesses the king thereafter. When all these are destroyed and cease to exist, the means to attain bliss is the name of Arana, the name of Shiva.

Therefore, the name of Haran surrounds. The benefit that comes from that means, namely the cessation of suffering, is placed thereafter. This is the order of arrangement that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman bestows. This first verse is placed in the first part of this Thiruppasuram. This Thiruppasuram is a message of divine instruction.

Therefore, this first verse serves as an auspicious blessing that precedes the divine instruction. Thirukkailayapathi Himself, having appeared as the Guru and having fed the divine nectar of knowledge, and having drunk it, Aludai Pillaiyar, the first of the Kailaya lineage, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, understood countless divine knowledge.

Here, the divine teacher is the bank of the Vaigai, the initiation hall, and the Pandya king is the ripened good disciple. The truth he instructs. The truth he taught is divine wisdom. The Lord, who stands as a cluster of knowledge, removes the cluster of flesh from good devotees; that too seems to be the ultimate truth. As per Thiruvannamalai Pillaiyar Thevaram, this Thiruppasuram shines as the divine wisdom bestowed by the Lord who stands as the cluster of knowledge, the ultimate truth that removes the cluster of flesh. It states that the Pandya king listened to the profound divine wisdom, and this serves as an auspicious blessing.

Generally, Tamil texts defining an auspicious blessing state that it can be one of three types: salutation, blessing, or explaining the nature of the subject. Tamil youths We can see it structured in the verse. ‘May the name of Arana surround all’ serves as a salutation. ‘Long live the Brahmins’ serves as a blessing.

Now, this Thiruppasuram, by clearly elucidating all the conclusions of the Sivagama Gnana Pada, is structured in the verse. How so? ‘The name of Arana’ appears and is established. ‘May suffering cease’ serves as the benefit. Thus, the name Haran, which signifies Shiva as the primordial being and the one responsible for dissolution, serves to illustrate the truth of the Lord and His characteristics. In the Srimat Raurava Agama, one of the twenty-eight Agamas revealed by Shiva, the Sivajnana Bodha is found in the Pachcha Vimochana Patala. In its first aphorism, it states, ‘Asmat Harah Prabhu,’ meaning Shiva, the deity who performs the act of dissolution, is the prime deity. In the first aphorism of Sivajnana Bodha, rendered in Tamil by Srimat Maikanda Devanayanar, it states, ‘The wise say that the end is the beginning,’ thereby indicating that this world has its beginning in the primordial cause of dissolution, who is the Lord. In accordance with this first aphorism, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, in this first verse which serves as an auspicious blessing, places the name ‘Haran’ and thereby reveals the truth of the Lord as the primordial cause of dissolution and His characteristics.

Now, ‘May all surround, and may the suffering of the world cease,’ this section describes the truth of the soul and its characteristics. Suffering refers to the impurity that causes sorrow.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reveals the truth and characteristics of the souls bound by impurity. By saying ‘evil and suffering,’ the truth and characteristics of that suffering, which is ‘pasa,’ are revealed. By Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

Therefore, just as the conclusions of Sivagama Jnana Pada reveal the truth and characteristics of the three entities—Pati (Lord), Pasu (soul), and Pasa (bondage)—so too does Thirugnanasambandha Peruman structure this first verse. By placing this first verse, which states that this Thiruppasuram itself is a Jnana Upadesa explaining the conclusions of Sivagama Jnana Pada, and by explaining the nature of the Thiruppasuram, this first verse, the Mangala Vazhthu, falls under the third category of the three types of blessings, namely ‘explaining the nature of the subject.’ Thus, Sivamani Peruman explains how the three types of blessings—salutation, blessing, and explaining the nature of the subject—are contained in this Mangala Vazhthu, the first verse. The Pillaiyar, that Theivasekkizhar Peruman, in the concluding section of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s Puranam, later states that this Thiruppasuram, which Pillaiyar composed in that present time, will continue to yield divine benefits in all future times, saying, ‘He placed the leaves in the Vaigai to bless us earlier.’ Therefore, we must understand this as a truly divine utterance. This is a divine teaching given by a divine teacher who attained true knowledge of God.

Similarly, Theivasekkizhar Peruman, a teacher who also received divine words from God, belongs to the Kailaya lineage and has expounded on this Thiruppasuram with great distinction and divine insight, as Sivakavimani Desikan states in his commentary.

Therefore, from 2720 to 2723, In these four verses, the great teacher elaborates on the first verse of the Thiruppasuram, ‘Long live the Brahmins.’ Theivasekkizhar Peruman’s commentary style is such that he separates each line of the Thiruppasuram, explains its meaning, and concludes each verse by stating, ‘Thus spoke Pillaiyar.’ When concluding the meaning of the twelve verses in the Thiruppasuram, he states, ‘Thus spoke Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, thus blessed Champai Andakaiyar, thus stated the king of Poonthurai, thus said the guardian of Champai, thus stated the king of Champai, thus said the learned, thus said Pillaiyar, thus said the one who knew without learning, thus said the one with a Vedic voice, thus said the king of Venguru who removed suffering, thus said the one who drank divine knowledge, the king of Champai. As Theivasekkizhar Peruman states in the prologue to the Thiruthondar Puranam, describing how this Thiruthondar Puranam removes internal darkness, ‘Just as the red-rayed sun removes the darkness of ignorance that resides in the minds of people, so too does this Puranam remove it.’ We can recall that here. In temples and monasteries, While chanting and worshipping with Thiruvempavai and Thiru Porchunnam from Thiruvachakam, there is a Saiva tradition of offering incense, lamps, and food offerings to Manivasaga Peruman with each verse. Thiruchitrambalam. We have examined Theivasekkizhar Peruman’s commentary on the first verse of the Thiruppasuram, from Periya Puranam, Volume 733, Vambara Varivandu Charukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. The second verse of the Thiruppasuram is as follows: ‘He who is of rare appearance, holding fire in his palm, delighting in the bull, black-throated, living in the forest, yet is great. Who knows his nature?’ This is the second verse. For the portion of this verse from ‘He who is of rare appearance, holding fire in his palm, delighting in the bull, black-throated, living in the forest,’ Theivasekkizhar Peruman provides commentary in verse 826. The 2724th verse in the sequence of Periya Puranam verses, which is verse 826, reads: ‘Being of rare appearance, He is unknowable by means of ordinary perception.

For those who perceive Him through true love, He spoke of the great and good signs that are real.’ Thus, Theivasekkizhar Peruman explains. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises Shiva in the beginning of this second verse. Theivasekkizhar Peruman states in the first line, ‘That Primordial Being.’ ‘That Primordial Being’ refers to the Primordial Being mentioned in the previous verse as ‘Aran’. That Primordial Being, referred to as ‘Aran’ in the previous verse, is described here in the second verse by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as ‘Ariya Kaatchiyar’ (one of rare perception). ‘Ariya Kaatchiyar’ means one who cannot be known or understood through mundane knowledge or the knowledge of the soul. ‘Ariya Kaatchiyar’ implies that Shiva cannot be comprehended by either the knowledge of the soul (pasu gnanam) or the knowledge of bondage (pasa gnanam). If someone is subject to perception, it means they are subject to experience. Anything subject to perception and experience is perishable; such things are also non-existent.

If something is unknowable by any means, it becomes a non-existent thing. However, without these two qualities, without these two categories, the Lord, who shines as the Pati (Lord) unknowable by both Pasa Gnanam (knowledge of bondage) and Pasu Gnanam (knowledge of the soul), such is the nature of that Lord, that primordial being, described here by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as ‘Ariya Kaatchiyar’ (one of rare perception). If something is knowable through evidence, then the universe knowable through evidence will be a perishable, non-existent thing.

But the Lord is not like that; He is praised as ‘Aprameyan’ (unknowable through evidence). If so, is the Lord unknowable by anything? If something is unknowable by anything, it is an empty thing. It is a substance.

Therefore, the Lord is the ultimate reality, Civacattu, possessing the nature of being both knowable and unknowable in certain ways, without being either entirely knowable or entirely unknowable. This is what the sixth aphorism of Civajnana Potam states regarding the characteristics of the Lord: ‘If conscious, it is not non-existent; if not conscious, it is not existent; other than these two, it is Civacattu,’ thus it is described in two ways in this world. This sixth aphorism states that the primordial being is not merely a being that is unknowable. He is Civacattu, possessing both the nature of being knowable in some ways and unknowable in others. Unknowable in one way. He is unknowable by Pasa Gnanam (knowledge of bondage) and Pasu Gnanam (knowledge of the soul).

If he is knowable in one way, it is only through Siva Gnanam (divine knowledge). This is because only through Siva Gnanam can he be known. Since objects known by Pasa Gnanam and Pasu Gnanam are inert, Shiva, who is not known by these two types of knowledge, is known only by Pati Gnanam.

Furthermore, objects known by Pasa Gnanam and Pasu Gnanam are impermanent, called ‘asat.’ Therefore, the Lord is beyond the reach of Pasu Gnanam and Pasa Gnanam, unknowable.

Thus, we praise the Lord as ‘Sat’ (existent) here. If he is unknowable by Pasu Gnanam and Pasa Gnanam, does that mean he is unknowable by any means? That is not the case. He is knowable to Pati Gnanam (knowledge of the Lord).

Therefore, we call it Civam.

Thus, this aphorism praises the Lord as Civacatu. Although Pati, Pasu, and Pasa are all eternal entities, among these three, Pati and Pasu are conscious entities, while Pasa is an inert entity. Pasu does not exist independently; it always depends on either Pasa or Pati.

Therefore, Pasa is called Jatasat, Pati is called Civacatu, and Pasu is called Jatasat.

Thus, the Lord exists as Chit Sat, unknowable by Pasu Gnanam and Pasa Gnanam, and knowable only by Pati Gnanam. This is a unique characteristic of the Lord, meaning. It is the intrinsic characteristic.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises the Lord here as ‘Ariya Kaatchiyar’ (one of rare perception). We saw that the Lord is unknowable by Pasa Gnanam (knowledge of bondage). Perception is of four types: sensory perception, mental perception, self-awareness perception, and yogic perception. Among these four, sensory perception, mental perception, and self-awareness perception, the Lord is not seen by these three types of perception, as Sivajnana Siddhiyar states that the Vedas, Shastras, Puranas, and various forms of knowledge—from gross to subtle, up to the ultimate sound—are all aspects of Pasa Gnanam.

Therefore, the Vedas and other scriptures cannot reveal the Lord.

Thus, the senses and mind and such. These are all products of Maya. They reveal only the elements below them, not the Lord beyond Maya.

Thus, it is understood that the Lord cannot be seen by three of the four types of perception that fall under Pasa Gnanam.

Now, the fourth type of perception is Yogic perception. In this Yogic perception, by means of Ashtanga Yoga Samadhi, such as Yama and Niyama, the obstructing malefic forces are partially destroyed, allowing the soul’s consciousness to perceive things at one place and time, and even across all three times. This is called Yogic perception, the fourth type of perception. Can the Lord be seen through this Yogic perception? Even in this yogic perception, the ego of the soul persists.

Therefore, the Lord is unknowable even to this yogic perception. So, how then does the Lord become visible? What is the state in which the Lord appears? The ninth aphorism of Civajnana Potam states, ‘The worldly eye cannot perceive the Lord; seek Him in the mind with the eye of knowledge.’ Accordingly, the Lord is accessible only to Pati Gnanam (knowledge of the Lord). Even in Pati Gnanam, the Lord can only be seen by souls if He reveals Himself. ‘Seek the supreme Lord who is difficult to see, with immense love in the heart,’ states the Civajnana Siddhiyar Thiruvirutham.

Similarly, other Meykanda Sastras, including Civajnana Siddhiyar and Civaprakasam, describe this, explaining how Pasa. We have seen that one cannot see the Lord.

Similarly, the ninth aphorism of Civajnana Potam describes how one can see the Lord through Patijananam. For this, Srimat Madhava Sivajnana Munivar has written a commentary in Sivajnana Mapashiyam. Saiva Siddhanta explains the stages of a soul’s spiritual development in ten steps, called Dasakariyam. All instruments for a soul are called Tattvas. That soul is called Atma. Shiva, the primal being, helps the soul achieve salvation, moksha.

The soul leaving the Tattvas and reaching the sacred feet of the Lord is called moksha or mukti. That is the greatest blessing a soul can receive. The soul attains this state in ten stages: Tattva Rupam, Tattva Darisanam, Tattva Sutthi, Anma Rupam, Anma Darisanam, Anma Sutthi, Siva Rupam, Siva Darisanam, Siva Yogam, and Siva Bhogam. It is not necessarily in this order; sometimes they occur simultaneously. The soul first realizes it is a distinct entity separate from the five senses. Starting from this, it attains these ten stages and eventually Siva Bhogam.

Generally, perception is of three types: illusory perception, dualistic perception, and clear perception. Seeing a rope in dim light and mistaking it for a snake is illusory perception; seeing one thing as another. This clear vision is also called flawless vision. For souls that have attained a very high level of maturity, these three can happen simultaneously upon hearing the divine words of the divine teacher. For those with less maturity, it will happen gradually: hearing, contemplating, and then understanding. As soon as Sivaruupana appears, it gives darisanam.

That darisanam brings about purity of the soul.

Therefore, by standing on the path of divine grace, and through Patijananam, one can see the Lord when He reveals Himself. By Pasujnanam and Pasa. The Lord, who is unknowable by knowledge, can only be seen by the eye of divine knowledge of that primordial being. How does one attain that Pati Gnanam? One must realize that the thirty-six Tattvas, from earth to sound, and their effects, are all bundles of bondage. One must understand that these are not eternal and are like mirages that disappear, and one must detach from them.

As one detaches, Pati Gnanam, like a cool shade that quenches the heat of the suffering of birth, will manifest. To ensure that the perception seen through this manifested Pati Gnanam remains stable, and to prevent the mind from unknowingly turning back towards the bundles of bondage due to long-standing habits, one must learn the Sri Panchaksharam according to rules. One must meditate.

Thus, the divine vision experienced through Pati Gnanam, that divine experience, will be in accordance with the tenth aphorism of Sivajnana Bodam, which states, ‘Being one and serving the Lord,’ and the eleventh aphorism, which states, ‘Seeing the mind and showing it.’ These are all topics discussed in the Jnana Pada of the Sivagamas. These revelations, found in the Meykanda Shastras which illustrate the Jnana Pada of Sivagamas, should be learned through the guidance of an experienced teacher.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states that the Lord is ‘Ariya Kaatchiyar’ (one of rare perception), being unknowable by Pasu Gnanam (knowledge of the soul) and Pasa Gnanam (knowledge of bondage). These are all These are states that cannot be revealed, states inaccessible even to Brahma and Vishnu.

Therefore, they are certainly unknowable to external religions such as Buddhism and Jainism.

Thus, the Lord is of rare perception, and the scriptures also state that He is accessible to Pati Gnanam (divine knowledge). Theivasekkizhar Peruman explains this by saying, ‘Though unknowable by ordinary perception, He spoke of the great and good signs that are real for those who perceive Him through true love.’ Even though He is inaccessible, He reveals Himself with auspicious signs to those who see Him with true love. We have seen the four types of Shakti Nipada. Among them, the state of attaining intense Shakti Nipada and Mala Paripakam is the state of devotees whose love has matured to see Him. The state of the devotees is where their love for the Lord has matured, and they perceive without even the thought ‘I see,’ but rather ‘He reveals, and I see.’ This is the state born of intense love. As we saw in the 777th verse of Periya Puranam, ‘Those who sought not to speak but to see with overflowing love.’ This is the state of the devotees.

Those who see Arana manifested within that love are devotees. Kannappa Nayanar, seeing Kalatthiyappar, remained seeing Him with that overflowing love. The 777th verse states: ‘Even munis and celestials, who performed severe austerities and dwelt in vast mountains, found Him difficult to see.

But Kannappa Nayanar, with overflowing and spontaneous love, saw Him directly and stood there, dispelling the deep darkness.’ This refers to that state. The state described here is one where the perceiver, the perceived, and the act of perception—the three distinct entities—do not appear as separate but merge into one. The Lord, for those devotees whose love is mature, reveals Himself with clear signs, making Himself visible. Through good Shiva qualities, good Shiva Yoga, good Shiva knowledge. The fifteenth verse of Thirukkazhiṛrupadiyar explains this: ‘If anyone loves with such strength that ‘I’ is destroyed, He will be found there, though He is Arana whom no one can see.’ Thus, the Jnana Sastra explains the state in which Arana, who is of rare perception, becomes visible. Appar Peruman states in his Thevaram, ‘Who indeed cannot see if He reveals Himself?’ And Appar Swamigal states in Thiruvachakam, ‘Only by His grace as the eye can one see His form, and that color, and that manner.’ These divine words explain that His vision is difficult to attain unless He reveals it.

To reveal Himself, that Arana The love and maturity that His devotees cultivate are the reasons. That maturity includes the qualities of Iruvinai Oppu (equanimity towards good and bad karma), Mala Paripakam (ripening of impurities), and Shakti Nipada (descent of divine grace) that we discussed earlier. To such mature and loving souls, the Lord will reveal true, great, and good signs. These signs are imperishable, having no superior, and encompass everything within themselves. If so, do all perceivable things and existent things, which have parts and are subject to the three cosmic functions, and thus perish, then come to pass? No, it is not like that.

The Lord’s graceful vision is not like that. To indicate that these gracious signs are not like that, Theivasekkizhar Peruman states, ‘True, great, and good signs.’ Truth implies imperishability. It signifies Sat (existence). ‘Great’ signifies Thatparam, meaning without a superior, encompassing everything within itself. ‘Good’ signifies that it bestows good results.

Therefore, the signs of the Lord—His holding fire in His palm, His riding the bull, and His blue throat—indicate His pervasive nature, supreme bliss, and supreme grace.

Thus, ‘Ariya Kaatchiyar’ (one of rare perception) signifies the Lord’s transcendent state, and His appearance with fire in His palm, riding the bull, and with a blue throat signifies His immanent state.

Therefore, even if the Lord is of rare perception to mundane knowledge, He is seen in these forms by those who perceive Him through divine knowledge. These are the signs. When Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sings ‘Thodudaiya Seviyan,’ he describes the Lord with signs, saying, ‘He who dwells in Brahmapuram.’ Theivasekkizhar Peruman explains those signs there. The signs mentioned here are ‘Angai Seyar Eriyār,’ which is structured in the Thiruppasuram like ‘Thodudaiya Seviyan.’ Just as ‘Thodudaiya Seviyan’ refers to a part of Shiva’s body and the object placed on it, ‘Angai Seviyar’ here refers to the Lord’s hand and the fire held in that hand. As Truth’s Revelation states, the fire held in the Lord’s hand signifies Samhara (dissolution). It also signifies how, after dissolution, the Lord, united with Shakti, bestows new creation.

Therefore, by explaining that the Lord is ‘Ariya Kaatchiyar’ (one of rare perception), beyond the grasp of Pasa Gnanam (knowledge of bondage), and then stating that the same Lord, with unceasing and overflowing love, reveals His signs to devotees, manifesting Himself and making Himself visible to souls through Pati Gnanam (divine knowledge), thus these signs. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman thus explains the transcendent (Nishkala) and immanent (Sakala) states of Shiva. Earlier, when showing the Lord to his father, and in the pathigam ‘Thodudaiya Seviyan,’ he also revealed the truth and characteristics of the Lord.

Here, Pillaiyar, who instructs the Pandya King on the characteristics of the Lord, similarly explains them. Based on this, Theivasekkizhar Peruman, in the beginning of his Puranam, Periya Puranam, also states, ‘He who is unknowable to the whole world.’ This means ‘unknowable to ordinary perception’. This refers to the Shiva whom Thirugnanasambandha Peruman here calls ‘Ariya Kaatchiyar’ (one of rare perception).

Similarly, in the first verse of Periya Puranam, Theivasekkizhar Peruman mentions ‘He whose matted hair holds the moon, who is of beautiful light, who dances in the cosmic hall.’ This refers to the immanent state of Shiva, whom Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises in this second verse as ‘Eriyar Eruvar Kariyār Vāzhkkaiyar’ (one who holds fire, rides a bull, is black-throated, and dwells in the forest).

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, in the first verse of his first pathigam, describes the characteristics of the Lord, and Theivasekkizhar Peruman incorporates this into the first verse of Periya Puranam. ‘That which is vast and unknowable to all beings, that substance which became manifest’ - thus begins the first verse of Thiruvunthiyar. “And gives of Himself” – thus begins the first verse of Thiruvunthiyar. “Like the letter ‘A’, the Lord, who is pure knowledge, fills everywhere, without equal” – thus is the first kural of Thiruvarutpayan. “Know that Ammayappar (Lord Shiva and Parvati) are the parents of the world. “All letters have ‘A’ as their first; so the world has the Primordial Lord as its first” – thus states the first kural of Thiruvalluvadeva Nayanar in Thirukkural. And further, “That which took a physical form, and that formless form which is beyond form, we saw both. When it became form and formless, we attained both forms. The three forms mentioned” And also, ‘He is the embodiment of compassion that came to destroy our dark karma,’ says the Sivajnana Siddhiyar Thiruvirutham. Such ideas from the Shastras and divine words are worth contemplating here.

All these are divine instructions, and we can also see the tradition of starting everything with the letter ‘A.’ Therefore, it is understood here that only those with love and proper maturity will see the Lord through Pati Gnanam when He reveals Himself, and others will not see Him.

Thus, for the second verse of the Thiruppasuram, ‘Ariya Kaatchiyar’ (one of rare perception), Theivasekkizhar Peruman wrote the commentary, ‘Though unknowable by ordinary perception, He spoke of the great and good signs that are real for those who perceive Him through true love,’ and Sivakavimani Peruman has thus elaborated on it. We will continue to contemplate the third verse of the Thiruppasuram. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. We have contemplated Theivasekkizhar Peruman’s explanation, given in verse 826, for the part of the second verse of the Thiruppasuram in Periya Puranam, Volume 734, Vambara Varivandu Charukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, which reads: ‘He who is of rare appearance, holding fire in his palm, delighting in the bull, black-throated, living in the forest.’ Now, the second verse also contains ‘yet is great; who knows his nature?’ For the part ‘yet is great,’ Theivasekkizhar Peruman provides commentary in verse 827. For the part ‘who knows his nature?’, he provides commentary in verse 828. As Divine Sekkizhar Peruman explains in the great Thiruvasuram verses, “He encompasses all expansive elements, numerous beings, and universes.” Even though the Lord is seen as having a fire in His hand, residing in the forest, and riding a bull, He is like that, even though He is mentioned in the great Thiruvasuram verses, if He is to appear, He will appear in that form to those with boundless love. Even so, He possesses immeasurable greatness within that form. His vast form encompasses the five elements, beginning with the sky, numerous beings, universes, and all other existing things.

He is of such greatness; He is the great, all-pervading form, and He appears in a divine form.

The Lord holds fire in His hand and rides a bull, not elephants or horses. He resides in the cremation ground. If one wonders whether these things detract from His supreme nature, it should be understood that these divine forms and appearances assumed by the Lord are merely His condescension for the sake of His devotees, and He is, in fact, the all-pervading, boundless form.

Therefore, even if He is so easily accessible, He is still great. As stated above, even though He possesses both intrinsic and incidental forms, His cosmic form is immense. Everything is contained within that cosmic form, and all objects are subsumed within His pervasiveness. He is not contained within anything, but extends boundlessly and is present everywhere. Although He graciously assumes the intrinsic and incidental states mentioned earlier for the sake of souls, He remains immeasurable even by the thoughts of those devotees who immerse themselves in His grace.

Therefore, He is great, encompassing the five expansive elements, all living beings, and the universes. All things are contained within His pervasiveness. This is what we worship as the Eight Forms. The Thiruvachagam states: “He stands conjoined in eight ways: earth, water, fire, life, the vast sky, the moon, the sun, and the senses.” All other things are contained and structured within His great form. He pervades everything, transcends everything, supports everything, and contains everything. They call it the cosmic form.

Lord Murugan revealed this cosmic form in two places.

First, He revealed the cosmic form for Indra and other devas to witness. This appears in the Kandha Puranam, Utpatti Kandam, Thiruvilaiyattu Padalam. The second instance is in the Yuddha Kandam, Surapadman Vadai Padalam, where he displays that cosmic form, that great form, for Surapadman. In the Kandha Puranam, in the Utpatti Kandam, Thiruvilaiyattu Padalam, the eighty-ninth verse describes it thus: “His feet extend to the earth and the netherworld, His mighty shoulders fill the heavens, His boundless head encompasses all. His eyes, full of grace, are the very life of Easana.” The cosmic form revealed by Lord Murugan includes the eight directions, fourteen types of worlds, eight mountains, seven oceans, the outer ocean, the Chakravazha Mountain, and all other objects, collections of universes, all living things, and all non-living things, taking on the forms of Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva. Lord Murugan, Kumarakkadavul, assumed this divine form, known as Parameshwara Rupam or Vishwarupam.

All the lower worlds, including the earth, are His sacred feet. The boundaries of the directions are His noble arms. All the upper worlds are His heads. The three great lights—the sun, moon, and fire—are His eyes. The entire space between the earth and the heavens is His sacred body. The melodious Vedas are His beautiful mouths.

All intelligence is His ears. Brahma and Vishnu are on His right and left sides. Uma Devi is His thoughtful mind. Lord Shiva, who performs the five cosmic functions, is His soul.

Thus, Lord Murugan reveals His cosmic form to the devas in the Utpatti Kandam.

Similarly, in the Yuddha Kandam, He reveals His cosmic form to Surapadman. In the Yuddha Kandam, Surapadman Vadai Padalam, from the four hundred twenty-second to the seventh verses, Kachiyappa Sivachariyar explains that great form. He states that the crying oceans, worlds, directions, universes, devas, and all other beings reside within the form of the six-faced benevolent Lord, and nowhere else.

There, He assumes a truly wondrous and magnificent cosmic form. All things and all beings exist within His sacred body. To clarify the truth that there is no other place, He assumes a form that makes visible what cannot be seen, demonstrating that everything originates from Him. Even though we know that everything originates from our God, Lord Subramanya, these things appear separate to our sight, and we cannot perceive them directly.

However, great sages demand penance to realize this. The very desire to see this form, that intense yearning, will not arise within us unless He grants it. We cannot create it ourselves. That divine form is wondrous, manifold, and a light that transcends words and concepts. It is a form that can melt bones and flesh into one. It is the one being that was, is, and will be.

Lord Murugan revealed that very vision to Surapadman there. Surapadman gained the privilege of seeing with his eyes that divine form which is beyond thought. Kachiyappa Sivachariyar describes it wondrously in his verses. In that cosmic form, that great divine form of Lord Murugan, on the beautiful, nail-tipped sacred fingers of His sacred feet, all the thunderbolts, stars, and planets in the sky reside. On the ankle above those wondrous sacred feet, Varuna, the king of the great waters, Oman and Niruthi reside. On the rounded calves above the sacred feet reside the sages and divine objects like Chinthamani.

On the knee, which is formed into the shape of the Janu, reside the Vidyadharas, and other hosts like Garudas, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and Kimpurushas. On the thigh, Indra and his son Jayanta. On the upper part of the thigh, Yama and his minister Kala. At the rear of the very powerful waist, on one side stand the asuras, and on the other side all the devas. In the loins of that waist reside the Nagas. At the tip of the sacred organ resides the divine nectar.

In the sacred stomach reside the beings that take birth as embryos. On the chest reside many arts. In the sacred thread, which has three strands, resides wisdom. In the hairs above that sacred body reside all the universes. In the beautiful sacred hands are the pleasures enjoyed by all in this world. In the repository of His mighty shoulders, the red-eyed Thirumal and Brahma are carried on each shoulder.

On the soft, petal-like fingers are the virtuous divine women. Agni is in the sacred neck. In the incomparable pearl-like sacred mouth are the Vedas. Between the teeth are the letters from ‘A’ onwards. On the sacred tongue are the Paramay Vedas of the Agamas. In the good sacred lips are the sciences of Manu.

Vayu Bhagavan resides in the nose. In the compassionate sacred eyes are the moon and the sun. In the sacred ears are the directions. On the sacred forehead is the root letter of the mantra known as Kudilai. In the sacred head is the supreme soul, Shiva, all in their proper order. Lord Arumugan is depicted as revealing His wondrous, boundless, immeasurable, and unknowable ancient form, which has existed eternally, everywhere, and unchangeably.

This cosmic form revealed by Lord Murugan is explained in the Kandha Puranam. The fifth verse of Thirukazhitruppadiyar states, “Where are the Agamas? Where are the six religions? Where are the yogas? Where is knowledge? If He had not come with His gracious form to rule?” Thirukazhitruppadiyar asks, “Who knows that great form?” This explains the meaning of “He is great,” questioning who can truly comprehend and describe that great form.

Thirukazhitruppadiyar specifically recites this. This is how the explanation for ‘He is great’ is established.

Now, regarding the phrase ‘who knows His nature,’ which concludes the second verse of the Thiruvasuram, Divine Sekkizhar Peruman offers an explanation in the eight hundred and twenty-eighth verse. He states: ‘Who knows His nature?’ means ‘who can comprehend His great nature, which no one can reach?’ Thus, the leader of Shanbai, who is surrounded by love, praised Him. This is the verse by Divine Sekkizhar Peruman. When Thirugnanasambandha Peruman asks, ‘Who knows His nature?’ he means that He possesses a great nature that is beyond the reach of anyone’s comprehension, as praised by Appillaiyar, the leader of Shanbai. If one asks, “Who knows His nature?” it means no one knows it. The Thiruvachagam states this: “The Lord whose nature is unknowable to others.” Even those who perceive Him with appropriate, elevated love can only see some signs that God reveals; they cannot fully comprehend His nature.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states this.

First, he said, “He is of rare vision,” then he said, “He is seen through burning signs.” After that, he spoke of His great state, which is not contained within these. If one asks whether His state ends with these, and then questions, “Who truly knows His nature?” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman concludes by emphatically stating that His nature cannot be known by anyone. The statement by Divine Sekkizhar Peruman, “He possesses great qualities that are difficult to attain,” brings to mind the verse “He is unknowable to the world, even to those who feel and know.” In this way, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises and extols the nature of God. He is enveloped in love, constantly and firmly meditating on God with profound devotion.

Thus, he praised Him. Sekkizhar Peruman, in his commentary on the second verse, states that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sung thus, indicating that he had fully attained God’s divine wisdom and remained steadfast in it, possessing heroic qualities. Divine Sekkizhar Peruman provides commentary on the second verse of this Thiruvasuram in three verses. The summary of that second verse is as follows: The second verse, “Ariya Kaatchiyar” (He is of rare vision), reveals the truth about the Lord and describes His characteristics. The intrinsic and incidental characteristics were discussed. By describing Him as “Ariya Kaatchiyar,” it is shown that the Lord’s existence is real, as characteristics are only attributed to existing realities.

“Eriyar” refers to the fire in His hand, signifying the act of destruction.

Therefore, it was explained, as the first sutra of Sivagnanabodham states, that the primordial being who performs the destruction is indeed the first cause of the world.

Furthermore, by saying “He rides the bull” and “He has a dark throat,” indicating His ride on a bull and His blue throat, it is implied that He is also the one who sustains. These signify His immense power and boundless grace. The idea of the second sutra of Sivagnanabodham, “He Himself is all of them,” is derived from His greatness. “Ariya Kaatchiyar” means He is unknowable by any means, even by the Vedas or Brahma. As Sivagnana Siddhiyar states, “By grace, one can know Shiva through the Agamas, and by meditating on Shiva with wisdom, one can live, removing all confusion,” it is explained that to those with true, elevated, profound love, He will grant His divine vision with His sacred symbols. Even though He is thus easily accessible to those with love, He is of cosmic form and all-pervading.

Everything is pervaded by Him within His pervasiveness, as stated next. If so, would His nature be completely exhausted? No, His nature cannot be fully described by anyone, as it is stated. In conclusion, in this second verse, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman expounds upon the reality and characteristics of the Lord.

We will continue to ponder the third verse. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. We have reflected on the commentary by Divine Sekkizhar Peruman in the Great Puranam, Volume 734, Vambara Varivandu Sarkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, on the first two verses of the Thiruvasura Pathigam.

Now, the third verse of the Thiruvasura Pathigam is as follows: (Ventha Saambal Viraiyena Poosiyē / Thanthaiyaar Udhayilar Thammayē / Sinthiya Ezhuvār Vinai Theerparāl / Endhaiyār Avar Evvagaiyaār Kolō). This third verse says that God smears burnt ash as fragrant paste; He has neither father nor mother; He removes the karma of those who meditate on Him without interruption. What are the qualities of such a Father God? This is the meaning of this verse. For this, Divine Sekkizhar Peruman offers a commentary. In this third verse, on the first line, “Ventha Saambal Viraiyena Poosiyē,” Divine Sekkizhar Peruman offers a commentary in the eight hundred and twenty-ninth verse.

The section of the Thiruvasuram that mentions “burnt ash” and “all non-luminous things” is referred to by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman in the third verse, first line of the pathigam, as “Ventha Saambal Viraiyena Poosiyē,” meaning that Lord Shiva, in His imperishable eternal divine light, sees all other luminous objects, which originate in the process of creation and are reduced to ash in the process of destruction. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sings about the way the Lord adorns His body with that ash as beautiful sandalwood paste, as Divine Sekkizhar Peruman explains. “Ventha Saambal Viraiyena Poosiyē” is part of the pathigam.

Therefore, it speaks of Lord Shiva’s role in sustaining the world during the great dissolution, the Mahasamharam. “Ventha Saambal” refers to the ash that results from burning. He smears that burnt ash as a fragrant paste, meaning He applies it as a mixed sandalwood paste. The Thevaram scripture refers to it as “Chunnarvin Chandana Chaandhu” (a mixed sandalwood paste). During the Mahasamharam, everything except the Lord is destroyed, dissolved, and turns into ash. This ash has no other place to rest, so it remains eternally on the imperishable sacred body of the Lord.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sings that the Lord applies this burnt ash as a mixed paste. There are many Shiva dharmas, among which Shiva puja is supreme. Among the rituals performed in the puja, five are pre-eminent: abhishekam, fragrance, lamp, archanai, and nivedanam. Among these, fragrance (virai) is of two types: lepana and sugandha. Lepana is the dense application of Malayaka sandalwood paste, mixed with rosewater, green camphor, saffron, gorojanai, musk, and kasturi, all over the Lord’s sacred body. This is called lepana, a part of virai.

The second part is sugandha. This sugandha involves stringing together seven items—jasmine, double jasmine, gardenia, malligai, rosewater, marukkozhundhu, and vetiver—to adorn the Lord’s form until it is completely covered, as stated in the Agamas.

Therefore, among the five observances of Shiva puja, virai, in the sense of lepana, refers to applying the mixed paste to the Lord. The virai mentioned here means that during the Mahasamharam, when everything except the Lord is destroyed, dissolved, and turned into ash, the Lord bears it on His sacred body.

Thus, it is stated that the Lord has applied that burnt ash as a mixed paste, meaning that during the Mahasamharam, everything except Shiva’s light merges and is extinguished. The divine light of Shiva is said to be endless because it is imperishable. The third part of the first sutra of Sivagnanabodham elaborates on this, proving that the one who performs the destruction is indeed the primordial being. All things other than Shiva, created during creation and annihilated during annihilation, remain extinct. This annihilation is known as Mahasamharam, the great annihilation. Annihilation is generally of five types.

There are five kalais, and each of these five kalais has its own Tattvas and Bhuvanas. Shiva is the Lord who annihilates these five types of kalais.

Therefore, he is praised as the cause of Mahasamharam. Hence, it is said that during annihilation, when everything else subsides, he smears the remaining sacred ash on his Thirumeni. This refers to Mahasamharam. Samharam means destruction or subsidence. Samhara Karanam means one who subdues everything. The universe is subject to the three functions of creation, preservation, and annihilation.

The deities performing these respective functions are praised and referred to as their cause. However, only one who subdues everything and remains stable is capable of creating them again. Saiva Siddhanta explains in great detail how worlds, which had such a primordial annihilator as their origin, are created by God and then annihilated again. Saiva Siddhanta states that there are many other worlds like the one we see, and universes containing those worlds, and Bhuvanas containing those universes, all exist. Saiva Siddhanta generally speaks of these as five kalais: Nivirthi Kalai, Pratishta Kalai, Vidya Kalai, Shanti Kalai, and Shantiyatheetha Kalai. Within these five kalais, thirty-six Tattvas are contained in each kalai.

Siddhanta states that there are so many Bhuvanas in each of these thirty-six Tattvas. It elaborates on how many universes are in each Bhuvana.

Therefore, all these worlds, universes, and Bhuvanas are encompassed within the five kalais, and their creation, preservation, and annihilation are brought about by God. All these are created by God from the real substance called Maya, and when it is time for them to subside, they are absorbed by God into that very Maya. That Maya is of three types: Suddha Maya, Asuddha Maya, and Prakruti Maya. The worlds in the two kalais, Shantiyatheetha Kalai and Shanti Kalai, originate from Suddha Maya. Their annihilation is directly performed by Shiva.

Now, the worlds in Vidya Kalai, which is in the middle, will be annihilated by Adhikara Moorthies (deities with authority) acting under Shiva’s command. The kalais below that, Pratishta Kalai and Nivirthi Kalai, and the worlds contained within them, are not directly annihilated by Shiva himself. Deities who have received authority from Shiva will annihilate the worlds in these two kalais.

Thus, Saiva Siddhanta describes the worlds existing in these five kalais.

Here, ‘kalai’ means ‘part’ or ‘division’. In Nivirthi Kalai, only the Prithvi Tattva exists. Brahma is its presiding deity. He has four Vyuhas: Hiranyagarbha, Virat Purusha, Kala, and Purusha. Although he has the authority to perform the five functions in Nivirthi Kalai, creation is his primary duty. This is called Prithvi Mandala.

Now, Pratishta Kalai comprises twenty-three Tattvas, from Appu Tattva to Prakruti Guna Tattva. Vishnu is its presiding deity. He has four Vyuhas: Vasudeva, Aniruddha, Pradyumna, and Sankarshana. Although he has the authority to perform the five functions in Pratishta Kalai, His primary function is preservation. This is called Appu Mandala.

Now, Vidya Kalai comprises the seven Vidya Tattvas, from Purusha to Maya. This is the third kalai. Rudra is its presiding deity. He has four Vyuhas: Shiva, Aran, Mrudan, and Bhava. Although this Rudra performs the five functions in Vidya Kalai, annihilation is his primary function. This is Agni Mandala.

Now, Shanti Kalai comprises the three Tattvas: Sadashiva or Sadakhya. Maheshwara is its presiding deity. He has four Vyuhas: Isha, Vishweshwara, Parameshwara, and Sarveshwara. Although he performs the five functions in Shanti Kalai, his primary function is Tirodhana. His primary function is Tirodhana.

Now, Shantiyatheetha Kalai, the fifth kalai, comprises the Bindu Tattva and Nada Tattva among the thirty-six Tattvas. Sadashiva is its presiding deity. Brahma, Vishnu, Rudra, and Maheshwara, who are the presiding deities of the previously mentioned four kalais (Nivirthi, etc.), are his Vyuhas. Although he is the presiding deity of the five functions in Shantiyatheetha Kalai, his primary function is Anugraha (grace).

Thus, all these aspects within these five kalais are explained in Saiva Siddhanta. The Supreme Being, the primordial God, referred to as Shiva, Paramashiva, and Mahārudra in Saiva Siddhanta, is the Ultimate Reality. The Rudra mentioned as one of the Trimurtis (Brahma, Vishnu, Rudra) is not the Supreme Being worshipped by Saivites. He governs and directs all these. The primordial God, Shiva, is the one. This Rudra, the one among the Trimurtis, is called Guna Rudra.

The worlds that emerged from Prakruti Maya are endowed with the three qualities: Satvik, Rajas, and Tamas.

Therefore, in the two kalais, Nivirthi Kalai and Pratishta Kalai, this Guna Tattva exists. In the worlds within Vidya Kalai, Shanti Kalai, and Shantiyatheetha Kalai, which are beyond these two kalais, these three qualities do not operate.

Therefore, those in them will not possess these three qualities. This Rudra is empowered to annihilate the worlds that possess these three qualities, that is, the worlds belonging to Nivirthi and Pratishta.

Therefore, he is named Guna Rudra. This Guna Rudra is one of the Trimurtis, Brahma, Vishnu, and Rudra. This Rudra is the one. All those who annihilate the worlds in the Vidya Kalai, Pratishta Kalai, and Nivirthi Kalai among the five kalais mentioned above, do so by receiving authority from Shiva. Shiva himself does not directly perform these annihilations. He is the one who performs the Mahasamharam.

Therefore, the primordial God, the Lord spoken of in Saiva Siddhanta, referred to by the names Shiva, Paramashiva, and Mahārudra, is the Supreme Being. This great Lord, Shiva, is the unique Supreme Being who annihilates the three kalais that are beyond the Guna Tattvas and then creates them again.

Therefore, Saivism praises him as Mahasamhara Karanam or Sarvasamhara Karanam. We can find many quotations from the Thirumurais proving that Shiva is the peerless Lord, superior to the Trimurtis. That Paramashiva has three states: Layam, Bhogam, and Adhikaram. These three states are not different in their substance; they are merely different states of the same substance. Shiva and Shakti are Layam, Sadashiva is Bhogam, and Maheswara and Suddha Vidya are Adhikaram. The forms that Shiva assumes in these three states are Aruvam, Aruvuruvam, and Uruvam.

Therefore, Shiva Paramaporul is Paramashiva, who annihilates all the worlds in these five kalais and then creates them again. We praise him as Mahārudra.

Thus, he, who performs the Mahasamharam, which is the ultimate annihilation that encompasses the annihilations occurring in the kalais and annihilates all five kalais, is the primordial God. When performing Mahasamharam, When performing Mahasamharam, everything except him is annihilated and reduced to ash. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman declares, “He smears the well-burnt ash as perfume on his Thirumeni,” because there is no other base for that ash on his sacred body. This smearing of this ash, this Vibhuti, signifies rebirth. Just as a farmer takes a portion of the harvested paddy to prepare for the next season, here, smearing this ash as a paste, as a mixture, indicates that rebirth is about to happen.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states, “He smeared the well-burnt ash as perfume”. To that line spoken by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, “He smeared the well-burnt ash as perfume,” Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman has provided this commentary.

Let us resume our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. We have reflected on the commentary provided by Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman in the Periya Puranam, Part 736, Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, for the line “Venthasambal Virai Ena Poosiye” from the third verse of the Thiruppasura Pathigam. The next section in this is “Thandhaiyaru Thayilar”. Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman provides the commentary for this section in the 830th verse. “Thandhaiyaru Thayilar” means that the Lord, who smears the well-burnt ash as fragrant powder, has neither father nor mother. This is its meaning.

In that 830th verse, Sekkizhar Peruman comments as follows: The Periya Purana verse states: “He has neither father nor mother, and establishing all things here, when they perish, He, the enshrined light, submerges them and then bestows them again, hence our Lord has no birth.” What does this signify when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman says that the Lord has neither father nor mother? As we saw in the previous verse, the Lord submerges and holds everything within Himself during the Mahasamharam. This refers to that rebirth, where He himself creates everything that He had submerged. This statement, “He has neither father nor mother,” refers to the rebirth that the Lord bestows. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman structures it by starting with “smeared as perfume” and then immediately following with “He has neither father nor mother.” During that Mahasamharam, he submerged all the Bhuvanas and the lords of the Bhuvanas within the five kalais there. Having subdued them, the Lord then performs rebirth.

Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman states this as “having subdued all these, then bestows them.” “Submerged in impurity” means that this world, having been submerged in Shiva, is created again, i.e., reborn. This is because the Anava Mala (primordial impurity) of the souls still exists. Since the Anava Mala of those souls still persists and has not left them, the Lord creates again to remove that Anava Mala. The Anava Mala, referred to as Sahaja Mala, is the reason why these worlds, having been absorbed into God, are created again for the removal of that inherent impurity, the Anava Mala.

Thus states the first Sutra of Sivagnana Bodham.

Here, the truth and characteristic of Shiva, the primordial one who performs Mahasamharam, accepting both annihilation and recreation, are established. Is it not a challenge to write the true meaning and cast the leaf into the Vaigai river?

Accordingly, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sets out the truth explained in Sivagnana Bodham, regarding the annihilation or lack of creation, in each section of this Thiruppasuram. A question arises: if it says that the souls’ Anava Mala has not been removed, and therefore the Lord creates again, then why should there be annihilation, and why then rebirth? Annihilation is performed to allow these souls, who have toiled, to rest from their weariness.

The Lord absorbs them all within himself for this purpose.

After that, he performs creation again.

Therefore, this Lord who does this is our leader. Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman writes commentary on this section saying that He has no birth. In the previous section, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proved that the Lord has no end, because He is the end of all others, and He himself has no end. We contemplated this in the previous verse.

Here, stating that the Lord has no father or mother means that the Lord has no birth.

The Lord is one who originates from nothing, and nothing originates from Him or is absorbed into Him.

Therefore, He is without birth or death, which is proven here. Saying that He has no father or mother indicates that father and mother are the place of origin.

Therefore, the Lord being without father and mother means that He originated from nothing and has no birth. He is our leader, that is, the leader of us souls, says Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman.

Now, the next part of this third verse, following “Thandhaiyaru Thayilar” (He has neither father nor mother), is “Thammaiye Ezhuvaar Vinai Theerpparaal” (He will remove the karmas of those who rise by Him). What is its meaning? It means that the Lord removes the karmas of those who contemplate Him ceaselessly. For this section, Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman provides commentary in the 831st verse: “Thammaiye Sindhiya Enum Thanmai” (The nature of contemplating Him alone). It means He will remove the powerful darkness of false dual karmas for those who think of Him. What is the meaning and explanation when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states that the Lord removes the dual karmas of those who contemplate Him ceaselessly?

It means that those who recognize Shiva as the true being and the truly shining light, and ceaselessly contemplate Shiva, will have the darkness of Mala, which causes the continuation of dual karmas, removed in this very life. Those who ceaselessly worship Shiva alone Only Shiva, considering Him as the true reality and worshipping Him, will rise. Rise from what? From the pit of rebirth. They will rise from the state of Kevila, where they had been submerged, to the state of Sagala.

Then, from the Sagala state, they will rise to the Suddha state. Who are they? Those who deeply and ceaselessly recognize the Lord as the imperishable, truly shining mass of light will rise from the pit of rebirth. “Since there is no other, they will attain the feet of righteousness,” states the eighth sutra of Sivagnana Bodham. Those who contemplate Shiva as the truly shining light will thus attain the feet of righteousness. That God shines as the true light, signifies that He shines as Paranjothi, as Swayamjothi, and as Alahil Jothi.

Thiruvachagam praises this as “Jothi! Sudare! Soozholi Vilakke!” (Oh Light! Oh Radiance! Oh surrounding lamp of light!).

The Lord is Paranjothi, meaning He is beyond all lights, with no light superior to Him.

Therefore, He is Paranjothi. He is also Swayamjothi, meaning He shines by Himself, not illuminated by anything else. Because He is immeasurable, He is praised as Alahil Jothi. Because He stands boundless, we praise the Lord as Jothi. Such a great Lord, looking at the Lord, He is both indivisible and, when compared to other lights in the world, indivisible. We praise Him as ‘Sudare’ (radiance) because He gives light to and directs the sun and moon.

The Lord also dwells within other finite lights, so we praise Him as ‘Soozholi Vilakke’ (the surrounding lamp of light).

Thus, Manivachaga Peruman praises the Lord in Thiruvachagam as ‘Jothi! Sudare! Soozholi Vilakke!’ (Oh Light! Oh Radiance! Oh surrounding lamp of light!).

The Lord removes the darkness of mala for those who contemplate Him. Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman states this as “He removes the powerful darkness of false dual karmas.” “Iruvinai Poimai Val IruL” (false dual karma, powerful darkness) means the powerful darkness of good karma and bad karma. This is the first meaning. “Iruvinai Poimai Val IruL” We can interpret “Iruvinai Poymai Val Irul” as the falsehood of dual karmas and the powerful darkness of Anava (ego) as the second meaning. “Irulsear iruvinaiyum sera iraiyan porulsear pugazh purindhaar maattu” is a Thirukkural.

Here, we saw “Iruvinai Poymai” (falsehood of dual karmas), meaning that both good and bad karmas are falsehoods. Valluvar Perumagan illustrates this in the Thirukkural as “Irul ser iruvinaiyum” (dual karmas born of darkness). “Irul ser iruvinaiyum sera” means that the two karmas, good and bad, which arise from delusion, will not affect those who desire the true praise of God. This is the meaning of that Kural. Parimelazhagar, in his commentary, states that good karma, like bad karma, also leads to birth. Parimelazhagar explains that since karma is the cause of birth, the two types of karma, good and bad, will not cling to one, hence they are considered false, as even good karma contributes to birth.

God removes and dispatches such false dual karma from those who incessantly contemplate Him. The phrase ‘false, strong darkness of dual karma’ refers to good and bad karma. Saiva Siddhanta describes karma as one of the three impurities (mala): anava, karma, and maya. We saw that karma mala will be removed by God from the souls that worship Him.

Now, regarding ‘darkness,’ the term ‘strong darkness’ appears. If we take darkness to mean anava mala, then God reduces the strength and power of this anava mala in souls. It can be understood that He makes anava mala lose its power, because darkness always refers to anava mala in Saiva Siddhanta. It also obscures the fact that ‘strong darkness’ exists, that is, it conceals itself and other things. Such is the power of anava mala; it reveals nothing. It does not reveal itself.

Even so, it naturally coexists with the soul. Thiruarutpayan’s twenty-third verse, ‘It shows no object; darkness shows form; it shows no two objects,’ explains this. There are external darkness and internal darkness. Souls perceive external objects with the aid of the eye, which is an instrument. This external darkness obscures the eye, an instrument, but it cannot obscure the intellect, which is a quality of the soul.

Therefore, when external darkness comes, the soul perceives that darkness has arrived and sight is obstructed, because the intellect remains unclouded.

Thus, the soul becomes aware of the presence of external darkness. It becomes conscious of it.

Therefore, as soon as darkness falls, we take appropriate precautions. But more severe than this darkness is anava mala, which obscures our intellect, which perceives external and internal objects. Because of this anava mala, we are unable to perceive the existence of anava mala, or that anava mala is the cause of our suffering, or our true nature, or the existence of divine grace that can liberate us from this suffering. As a result, the soul remains ignorant of its own ignorance and takes errors for truth.

Therefore, as Umapati Sivachariar says, ‘It shows no object; darkness shows form; it shows no two objects.’ In Thiruarutpayan, he explains this in this couplet.

Therefore, God renders ineffective the power of anava mala, which obscures the intellect of those who incessantly contemplate Him, causing its power to recede and subside. We have seen karma and anava among these three impurities. Maya mala is also mentioned. It states that He removes the falsehood of dual karma and strong darkness.

Here, dual karma refers to karma, and darkness refers to anava. Of the three impurities, what remains is maya. This maya is explained in the thirtieth verse of Thiruarutpayan by Umapati Sivachariar as, ‘Maya is like a lamp until dawn, coming in the form of action.’ This maya is given by God to remove the soul’s delusion. It is a favor granted by God to remove delusion, but we refer to it metaphorically as mala. In eternity, anava mala, with its immense power and obscuring energy, completely conceals the soul’s pervasive intellect, making it impossible for the soul’s intellect to shine even slightly.

At that time, God bestows upon the soul a limited illumination called maya. Just as a lamp aids those in darkness until sunrise, God grants this maya to souls in that primordial state of singularity, like a lamp. From maya, and from its effects, He provides body, senses, worlds, and experiences. To grasp this maya, The soul, which is the object, divests itself of all its defects, that is, all its impurities, and attains perfect intellectual illumination, which is Sivagnana. This is the natural state of the soul.

Therefore, the association with maya is temporary. This is given by God’s grace according to the karma of each soul. God’s grace helps us to attain clear knowledge with this limited knowledge.

Therefore, maya is a favor given to remove delusion. When both are removed by God, maya also departs, says Sivakavimani Ayya.

Therefore, God makes souls ready by bringing about the equivalence of two karmas and the maturity of impurities, thereby removing them from the suffering caused by impurities. God causes the strength of anava mala to diminish.

Therefore, to remove anava mala, God creates the re-creation, known as srishti. God performs the function of sthiti to remove maya mala. To attain the maturity of karma mala, and to incessantly contemplate God, a spiritual practice has been taught by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. By incessantly contemplating thus, The benefit of the removal of many things is also bestowed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. It is stated that those who contemplate only Shiva as the ultimate reality. Through this, the truth and definition that God is one are attained here.

When souls are referred to as those who arise from contemplation, their existence and definition are also attained here. By stating that, the truth of mala (anava, karma, maya) and their definitions have been discussed. By saying, ‘those who arise, contemplating themselves as truly shining light,’ the spiritual practice has been bestowed. It has been instructed what spiritual practice we should adopt. By saying that He will remove the falsehood of strong darkness, the removal of mala, or the destruction of mala, has been indicated. All these characteristics mentioned in Sivagnana Bodham have been taught and bestowed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman in this section.

Let us go on contemplating.

The benefit of the removal of many things is also bestowed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. It is stated that those who contemplate only Shiva as the ultimate reality. Through this, the truth and definition that God is one are attained here. When souls are referred to as those who arise from contemplation, their existence and definition are also attained here. By stating that, the truth of mala (anava, karma, maya) and their definitions have been discussed.

By saying, ‘those who arise, contemplating themselves as truly shining light,’ the spiritual practice has been bestowed. It has been instructed what spiritual practice we should adopt. By saying that He will remove the falsehood of strong darkness, the removal of mala, or the destruction of mala, has been indicated. All these characteristics mentioned in Sivagnana Bodham have been taught and bestowed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman in this section.

Let us resume our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 737, authored by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, from the Vamparavarivandu Canto, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, the fourth line of the third verse of the Thiruppasuram is ‘Enthaiyar avar evvagaiyar kōlō.’ The meaning of this section is that our Father, who is referred to above as the Lord, cannot be described in any category. Sekkizhar Peruman explains this in the 832nd verse: ‘Enthaiyar avar evvagaiyar kōlō’ – in what category can the ancient one, who transcends all other categories, be spoken of, thus declared the King of Pūntarāy (Thirugnanasambandhar). The 832nd verse asks, ‘What is the meaning of the leader of Sirkazhi declaring, ‘In what category is my father?’ Sekkizhar Peruman explains that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman declares that the Lord cannot be described by any kind of speech or category in this world, because He appeared and initiated before all of them.

Therefore, in what category can He be placed? The meaning is that the vocabulary, the world of words, that describes other things besides Shiva, cannot describe Shiva, who is eternally liberated and perfect, with any word from the realm of speech. Srimat Madhava Sivagnanamuni quotes this passage, ‘Enthaiyar avar evvagaiyar kōlō,’ uttered by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, in his great commentary on the third adhikaranam of the first sutra of Sivagnana Bodham. In his commentary on the exemplary Venpa for the third adhikaranam of the first sutra, which begins with ‘Ondralaa ondral,’ Madhava Sivagnana Munivar quotes this section by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Of the three realities—Pati (God), Pasu (Soul), and Pasam (Bondage)—Pasam, which consists of anava, karma, and maya, is inert. Pati shines as a sentient being with innate knowledge.

The Pasus, which are in between, are able to comprehend only if God makes them understand.

Therefore, Sivagnana Bodham refers to these multitudes of Pasus as the manifest world with indicative consciousness, the sentient world with indicative consciousness. Shiva, the great dissolver, knows everything by himself and knows things as they are. This is his state.

Therefore, these multitudes of Pasus, who can only be known by an indicative consciousness, do not have independence. Only God, who knows everything by himself, has independence.

Therefore, the multitudes of Pasus, for whom Shiva is the great dissolver, can only know if God reveals it. Such a manifested world, the multitude of souls, is called the sentient world. Even within this, they divide the sentient world into two types: formless and with form. Among these two types of manifested worlds, there is one who is not one. He is the unique Supreme Being. By such a unique Supreme Being, bodies, instruments, worlds, and experiences are given to these souls; this is Srishti.

He maintains them and provides experiences; this is Sthiti. According to the law, once these experiences are provided and their time is fulfilled, these bodies, instruments, worlds, and experiences are withdrawn; this is Samhara.

Therefore, by that unique Supreme Being, these souls, which are the sentient manifestations of the two types—formless and with form—are created, sustained, and dissolved.

Therefore, that one God of Dissolution is the primordial God of the world. Even so, it is stated in the Vedas and Agamas that this sentient manifestation, the soul, once liberated, will stand equal to Shiva and become Shiva.

Therefore, do liberated souls become independent like God? Do liberated souls perform the fivefold functions like God? Even in the state of liberation, souls do not possess independence. They experience Shiva’s bliss only if God enlightens them and allows them to experience it.

Therefore, even in liberation, souls are subservient to God. Hence, it is established here that the Supreme Being, the God of Dissolution, is but one. If that is the case, what is the explanation for the Vedas and Agamas stating that the soul becomes Shiva in the state of liberation? Just as Shiva has no birth or death, similarly, liberated souls are not subject to birth and death. In that sense, the soul becomes Shiva, and this is its explanation.

Therefore, even in the state of liberation, the soul becoming Shiva does not imply that the soul becomes independent like God or performs the fivefold functions like God. The world, which is this material manifestation, is inert. The soul, which is a sentient manifestation, is bound by anava mala, which causes ignorance, and stands with indicative consciousness.

Therefore, to operate both this world and these souls, to activate this world and enlighten the soul, there must be a primordial God distinct from both the world and the soul.

Thus, such a primordial God is endowed with unsurpassed qualities such as perfect knowledge, limitless power, immense grace, and independence.

Therefore, in this capacity, This applies only to the one primordial God. If this definition also applies to the God described by other religions, then it will lead to the fault of excessive application (athivyapti). When defining a thing, the definition (lakshana) must be stated without the three errors of non-application (avyapti), excessive application (athivyapti), and impossibility (asambavam). If the definition given to a thing applies to other things as well, it will result in the fault of excessive application.

Therefore, it applies only to the one primordial God.

Therefore, the Lord with the characteristic of performing samhara, whom we have seen so far, will be the primordial being of the world, and not many who lack that characteristic. It is not valid.

Therefore, He alone is independent. Even in the state of liberation, the soul will remain subservient to Him and experience Shiva’s bliss as He bestows it.

Therefore, He who is not one of these two categories of sentient beings, the formless and the form-endowed, His attributes cannot be encompassed by words or meaning. Even if He assumes a form out of compassion, He is devoid of growth, transformation, and illusion.

Therefore, Shiva, who is eternally liberated and perfect, has no origin or end. He is not subject to any proofs. He cannot be spoken of in terms of any other object, nor can He be described by any other words.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman declares, ‘My Father, of what kind is He?’ That is why, even though the Vedas mention various deities like Indra, Vishnu, and Brahma, Sivagnana Siddhiyar explains the nature of the Supreme Being by saying, ‘Whichever deity you worship, as that deity, the Lord with the female half will come.’ This explains that the Lord, the great dissolver, is the primal one, and other beings exist by His command.

Thus, the primal one is the one who pervades and operates within everything, and is supremely important. The primal one is the one who contains everything within himself.

Therefore, He who contains everything cannot be described or known by anything that is contained within His pervasion. This is its meaning.

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman provides commentary on the concluding part of the third verse of this Thiruppasuram. Sekkizhar Peruman explains the meaning of this third verse, which begins with ‘Venthasaambal,’ in four verses, from 2727 to 2730. The meaning of this third verse is as follows: Our Lord is the great cause of dissolution, who, without perishing in dissolution, gathers everything within himself and then again creates them; He is the one who removes the falsehood of karma and the darkness from those who remember Him. He is the leader who pervades and operates within everything; all moving and unmoving things are contained within one of His aspects. This is the meaning of the third verse of this Thiruppasuram.

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman comments and concludes this section of commentary, stating that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the King of Poontarāy, thus declared.

Now, we will continue to contemplate the meaning of the fourth verse. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 738, authored by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, from the Vamparavarivandu Canto, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. The fourth verse of the Thiruppasuram is as follows: “Aatpaalavarkku arulum vannamum aadi maanbum kētpaan pugil alavillai kizhakkavēndaa kōtpaalanavum vinaiyum kurukaamai enta taatpaal vanangi thalai nindru ivai kētka takkaar.” For this verse, Sekkizhar Peruman provides commentary in two verses. In the 833rd verse, he comments on the first part of the hymn, up to “Aatpaalavarkku arulum vannamum aadi maanbum kētpaan pugil alavillai kizhakkavēndaa.” That 833rd verse is as follows: “Aadi aatpaal avarkku arul thiram naathan maatčimai kētka navizhungaal ōthum ellai ulappila aathalin yaathum aaraayčiyillaiyaam.” This is the verse spoken by Sekkizhar Swamigal. If one were to ask about the ways in which the Lord bestows grace upon His devoted servants, they are endless and expansive.

Likewise, if one were to inquire into the Lord’s greatness, it too would expand endlessly beyond description. None of this can be understood or known through any kind of research. The Thiruppasuram says, ‘Aatpaalavarkku arulum vannamum’ (the manner in which He bestows grace upon His servants). Sekkizhar Peruman interprets this as ‘Aadi aatpaal avarkku arulum thiram’ (the way in which the Primal One bestows grace upon His primal servants). ‘Aadi’ refers to the Primal One. Aatpaalavar means those who are fit to be servants. It means those who are worthy of being God’s servants, those who are mature.

Therefore, the way the Primal One, the Aadi, bestows grace upon His servants, the Aatpaalavar, cannot be described by anyone.

Furthermore, the Lord’s greatness, the Maatchimai of the Nadan, also cannot be described by anyone; it cannot be contained in words. However, if one humbly listens, being subservient to the Primal One’s grace, then we can see what God reveals.

But if one tries to understand through one’s own ego, through the soul’s assertiveness, through self-assertion, that is certainly impossible. The research conducted by those who investigate with soul-consciousness will yield no benefit. Saiva Siddhanta divides souls into three types: Vignanakalar, Pralayakalar, and Sakalar. This classification depends on how many impurities (malas) cling to these souls—anava, karma, and maya. Souls belonging to the Vignanakalar category have only anava mala. Those called Pralayakalar have both anava mala and karma mala.

Souls belonging to the third category, Sakalar, are bound by all three malas: anava, karma, and maya. Among these, for souls belonging to the Vignanakalar category, God, abiding within their intellect, enlightens them. These Vignanakalars are those who have transcended the bondage of Prakriti, which is composed of the three qualities, through the special knowledge revealed by Shiva. For them, the anava mala bondage is subtle. There are two types of Vignanakalars: those who are naturally Vignanakalars and those who have attained this state through stages of maturity. Next are the Pralayakalar.

These are those who, at the time of dissolution, have been freed from the arts through gradual maturity. They too are of two types: those who are naturally bound by gross anava mala from their very first birth, and those who have attained this state. For these Pralayakalar souls, God appears before them, showing His form with a deer, battle-axe, four arms, and blue throat, and bestows grace. For both these types of souls, Vignanakalar and Pralayakalar, God does not need any other form as a basis to bestow grace; He bestows grace in His own form.

Hence, this is called ‘niradaram’ (without support). For Vignanakalar, God enlightens them from within. For Pralayakalar, as mentioned earlier, He manifests His inherent form, which performs the three functions and is adorned with a deer, battle-axe, four arms, and a blue throat, as the form of the Guru, and standing before them, enlightens them through oral instruction. We saw that He thus enlightened Adudaiya Pillaiyar as if he were a Pralayakalar.

Now, the third category is Sakalar. These are those who have gross anava mala bondage; therefore, they are bound by all three malas. How does God bestow grace upon these Sakala souls? He comes with His natural form, which we discussed earlier, and using another pure soul, a human form, as a base, He enlightens them. That is the Guru’s form. Disguised in the human guise of the Guru, God stands hidden and bestows grace upon Sakala souls through instruction.

This is called ‘saadharam’ (with support). Even among these Sakalars, the Guru’s form in which God comes to take them into His fold varies depending on the nature and maturity of each soul. We see this in various Puranas and Jnana Sastras.

Therefore, what is understood from this is that God does not bestow grace equally on all beings. It is understood that He bestows grace individually upon each one.
