Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states that if we try to understand the manner in which the Primal One bestows grace upon souls and the greatness of the Primal One through our own soul-consciousness, it is certainly impossible.

Now, the second part of the fourth verse of Thiruppasuram is ‘kōṭpālanavum vaṇangi thalai nindru kētka takkaar.’ For this section, Sekkizhar Peruman provides commentary in the 834th verse. That verse is as follows: ‘Anna aadhalil aathiyaar thaazh adaindhu.’ To listen to the appropriate doctrines, and for the powerful former karmas to come to an end for those of that nature, thus said the protector of Shanpai (Thirugnanasambandha Peruman). Sekkizhar Peruman explains that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states in the above verse that if one attains the feet of such a Primal One, and listens to all these truths, then for those devotees who have attained such a nature, the residue of mala, the mala itself, and the ancient powerful karmas will come to an end. God will bestow grace upon those who surrender and listen, abiding in the pervasiveness of His feet.

But for those who attempt to research with their own ego, without surrendering to God’s feet, These qualities cannot be spoken of; they cannot be measured in words.

Therefore, one must attain God’s feet and listen, abiding in those feet. If one listens thus, God will enlighten them with that knowledge, says Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. To attain God’s feet and listen means to realize it through the knowledge of His feet. In Thiruvachagam’s Thiruvempavai, Manikkavasaga Peruman praises God’s grace, saying, ‘You protect us without ceasing, having liberated us in all ways of liberation through the sport of Your grace, which takes us into Your fold.’ He asks, ‘O Lord, I am ignorant. By Your grace, please enlighten me on the ways to attain liberation through Your sport of taking me into Your fold.’ Manikkavasagar Peruman asks. This is what it means to reach the sacred feet of God and listen submissively.

In Thiruvempavai, there is a song where women sing to God while bathing, a song that begins with ‘Moyyaar thadam poigai’. In it, the women pray to God, saying, ‘Ayya, you have saved us through all the ways of salvation in your sport of taking us into your fold. Please protect us from faltering.’ They pray, ‘O Lord, we are your hereditary servants. By praising your sacred feet repeatedly, we, your hereditary servants, have attained a good life. You, as the Lord, through your divine play of enslaving and protecting souls, enable all souls to attain salvation. We have already attained all such ways of salvation.’ We have reached the peak.

Now, protect us from failing, the women pray. God taking one into His fold is an action; bestowing grace is an action. God, who has accepted souls as His servants, makes them experience their karmas and gradually elevates them by bringing about the maturity of impurities. This gradually loosens the anava mala bondage in these souls. This is God’s grace. To make them experience, He has to activate the mala and obscure their intellect.

His act of concealment, one of His five divine functions, is praised. Such a soul, having matured from impurities, becomes eligible for liberation.

Thus, God prepares these souls. He grants moksha to souls, granting them the bliss of liberation. Manikkavasagar Peruman sings of this as the ‘sport of grace.’ Here, all these five actions are a sport for God, indicating that He performs them effortlessly. God’s grace is always and everywhere pervasive. Souls that are mature will praise and worship that grace and submit to it. Those who are immature, even though that grace is pervasive everywhere, gain nothing from it.

Therefore, for these souls to remove their mala bondage and receive grace, there are paths such as Chariya, Kriya, Yoga, and Gnana, which serve as steps. They must attain salvation by using all these paths as means in a gradual manner. Manikkavasagar Peruman composes the women’s prayer as, ‘O Lord, we undertake all these practices. On this journey towards the spiritual realm, protect us from getting exhausted and falling back into rebirth.’ This is the meaning of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s statement, ‘Aadhiyar thazh adaindhu inna ketka vE.’ It means that if one reaches God’s sacred feet and listens, God, with His divine knowledge, will enlighten these souls, and they will understand.

Similarly, when Thiruarur Peruman commanded Sundaramurthi Swamigal to sing about the devotees, Sundaramurthi Swamigal asked, ‘What shall I say to sing? How shall I praise? You Yourself must grant me the ability to sing.’ To this, God replied, ‘To relieve suffering and to save the world, with the sacred word that destroyed the Vedas, begin by saying, ‘I am a servant to the Brahmins of Thillai.’’ There, Sundaramurthi Swamigal attained God’s sacred feet and, submitting to Him, asked, and God thus bestowed grace.

Similarly, when Anapaya Cholan asked Sekkizhar Peruman, our divine author, to compose this Periya Puranam, the epic of the devotees, Sekkizhar Peruman agreed. He bowed before the Lord of the Dance in Thillai, placed his hands together on his head, and with a melting heart, prayed to the Lord of the Dance: ‘O Lord, bestow Your grace by giving me the first line to narrate the glory of Your devotees, so that I, Your servant, may speak.’ Thus, praying with the thought of divine grace, When Sekkizhar Peruman asked, the divine voice by grace said, ‘Ulagelam’ and gave the first line. This great light, which Thirugnanasambandha Peruman refers to as listening by attaining God’s sacred feet, understanding through His divine knowledge, serves as the literary example for that definition in all these historical accounts.

Therefore, if one abides in God’s sacred feet and listens, ‘Aatpaalavarkku arulum vannamum’ (the manner of His grace to His devotees) and the greatness of the Primal One who bestowed such grace, were realized and blessed by our Sundaramurthi Swamigal and Sekkizhar Peruman, as we can see from this sacred history.

Thus, if one abides in God’s sacred feet, ’ ஏற்ற கோட்பாலவும் முன்னை வல்வினையும் முடிவு எ.’ Thus, says Sekkizhar Peruman. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman says that the primal anava mala, which clings to souls inherently like rust to copper from eternity, and its remnant, the subtle mala, along with the primal karma, all will cease and be utterly removed. Sekkizhar Peruman explains that the primal mala and the primal karma will both come to an end and be completely removed. This means that one must first cling to God’s sacred feet and listen in submission, which is the fourth stage of knowledge, the state of deep meditation where one understands by abiding within the divine knowledge of the sacred feet, guided by it. This is the meaning of ‘attaining God’s feet and listening to what He says.’ This is the meaning of “enquire.” And for those devotees who have attained the fourth stage of knowledge, which is the state of deep meditation, where one attains the sacred feet of the Primal One and understands by abiding within the guidance of that divine knowledge of the sacred feet, for such individuals, the primal mala (anava) and the primal karma will all be removed, and they will forever revel in supreme bliss and divine ecstasy. This is the truth of it.

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman says in two verses for the fourth verse of Thiruppasuram that the ways in which the Primal One bestows grace upon those who have attained Him are limitless, and therefore, they are not subject to research. Instead, if one humbly listens by taking refuge in God’s sacred feet, for such listeners, the doctrines to be accepted and the powerful former karmas—that is, the anava mala called primal impurity, And its subtle impurity, along with the primal karma, will all come to an end. This is the meaning of that verse, says Sekkizhar Peruman, explaining that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the protector of Shanpai, thus declared.

Next, we will continue to contemplate the meaning of the fifth verse of Thiruppasuram. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 639, authored by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, from the Vamparavarivandu Canto, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. The fifth verse of the Thiruppasuram is as follows: “Ēthukkaḷaalum eḍuththa mozhiyaalum mikku sōthikka vēṇḍā suḍarviṭṭuḷḷan engaḷ sōthi mā thukkam nīngaḷozhivīr manampaṭṭi vaazhmīṉ sāthukkaḷ mikkiṉ iraiyē vandhu saarmīṉkaḷē.” For this verse, Sekkizhar Peruman provides commentary in four verses. For the first part of this hymn, up to “Ēthukkaḷaalum eḍuththa mozhiyaalum mikku sōthikka vēṇḍā,” Sekkizhar Peruman provides commentary in the 835th verse. That verse is as follows: “Mannaum ēthukkaḷaal enum.” The truth that there is no other comparison for Sankaran’s nature, such as ‘what kind of nature,’ cannot be measured by examples or such proofs.

This is the meaning. What does Thirugnanasambandha Peruman mean by saying, ‘There is no need to examine too much with reasons and words uttered’? It means that there is no other object that can be used as an example for God. The qualities and greatness of Sankaran, Shiva, that we have seen, cannot be measured by reasons, examples, or other similar proofs. God is incomparable. ‘It is difficult to change mental distress for those who do not attain the feet of the Incomparable One,’ says Thirukkural in its section on God’s praise. The divine scripture of Thevaram praises Shiva as ‘One without comparison.’ Thiruvachagam honors Shiva as ‘Oru Uvamai Illai’ (One without comparison).

Thiruarutpayan’s second couplet states, ‘Pērumaikkum nuṇmaikkum pēr aruṭkum pēṭṛiṉ arumaikkum oppinmayāṉ’ (He is incomparable in greatness, subtlety, immense grace, and the difficulty of attaining Him). In the first couplet of Thiruarutpayan, Srimat Umapati Sivachariar says, ‘Nigaril Irai’ (The Incomparable God). He then elaborates on this in the next couplet, explaining what benefit we derive from that exalted being. In the third couplet, he explains how God is incomparable. That couplet from Thiruarutpayan is the third one: ‘Pērumaikkum nuṇmaikkum pēr aruṭkum pēṭṛiṉ arumaikkum oppinmayāṉ.’ What is God’s greatness? It is God’s nature to contain all things within Himself pervasively, and to be greater than them, filling everything as a pervasive being.

This is God’s greatness. How is He subtle, atomic? He is present as the divine essence, intermingling most subtly within all things.

Likewise, He is immensely gracious towards all beings, possessing boundless great compassion for them.

Furthermore, He is an extremely rare object, difficult to realize and attain in all these glories and qualities.

Thus, in greatness, subtlety, immense grace, and the difficulty of attainment, God is the only being who is incomparable in any of these aspects. Pati, the Shiva Paramatma. He is the compassionate being who contains all things, that is, all inert and sentient objects, within His vast fullness, within His pervasiveness, so that all these billions of universes may reside and be protected. He is the compassionate being who sustains all these inert and living beings by subtly intermingling within each of them. He is also the object of immense grace, for He guides souls and experiences Himself for their experience. Thiruvachagam refers to this as ‘Kēḷil Param Karuṇai’ (flawless supreme grace), ‘Vaḷarkindra Karuṇai’ (ever-growing grace), ‘Kōdhil Param Karuṇai’ (perfect supreme grace), and ‘Ellaiyil Mākaruṇai Kaḍal’ (boundless ocean of supreme grace).

This knowledge is not attained in just one birth, but through worship performed over many births, one receives Guru-knowledge. The supreme being, the incomparable entity possessing the great wealth of liberation, is described by texts like Devaram, Thiruvasagam, Thiruvisaippa, and Gnanamirtham. These texts proclaim Him as both vast and subtle, difficult to perceive, both minute and immense. He is the one who is unknowable, the inner thought, the atom, the truth unknown to anyone, the great one who transcends everything. He is described as greater than the smallest particles in a sunbeam that enters the universe, as the one whose greatness encompasses the atom, and whose fame, though subtle, stands firm within the atom of the universe. Texts like Devaram, Thiruvasagam, Thiruvisaippa, and Gnanamirtham all extol these qualities of the Lord.

The Sivagamas describe these qualities as incomparable.

Therefore, the Lord is one for whom there is no equal. He is called Shankaran. Shankaran means one who brings joy, one who brings happiness. The Kanchipuranam explains the name Shankaran by saying that Shankaran is our Lord in bestowing joy, and Sambu (Shiva) dispels the suffering of illness. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states that such a Shiva cannot be known by any arguments or pronouncements. Among the pramanas (means of valid knowledge), there are ten important ones, and among those, three are most crucial: Pratyaksha Pramana (perception), Anumana Pramana (inference), and Agama Pramana (scriptural testimony).

The other seven are subsumed within these three. Throughout this Thiruvasagam, it is proven that the Lord cannot be known through these three main pramanas. We extensively discussed in the second thiruppadal (verse) of this Thiruvasagam, across those four verses, that the Lord cannot be known through Pratyaksha Pramana.

Here, in this thiruppadal, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states that He cannot be known or tested by arguments or pronouncements. The term ‘ethu’ here comes from the Sanskrit word ‘hetu’.

Thus, it refers to Anumana Pramana. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who previously stated that the Lord cannot be known through Pratyaksha Pramana, now states that the Lord cannot be measured and known through Anumana Pramana. Pramana means a measuring instrument. In Tamil, it is referred to as ‘alavai’. ‘Prama karanam pramanam’ is the definition of the word ‘pramana’. True knowledge, called yathartha jnana, is when the knower (pramatha) accurately knows the object to be known (prameyam) without doubt or error. Whatever is the special instrument for this true knowledge is called ‘alavai’ or ‘pramana’.

Therefore, ‘pramatha’ means the one who measures, ‘pramana’ means the instrument of measurement, ‘pramiti’ means the act of measuring, and ‘prameyam’ means that which is measured. These are all explained in the texts of epistemology and logic (tarkashastras). In the chapter on ‘alavai lakshana’ in Sivagnana Siddhiyar, these logical concepts are also explained.

Therefore, although there are ten types of pramanas, as we have already seen, there are three main ones: Pratyaksham (perception), Anumanam (inference), and Agamam (scripture). Among these, in this thiruppadal, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states that the Lord cannot be known through Anumana Pramana, which is also called ‘karuthal alavai’ (inferential measure). Anumana Pramana is of two types: Svaartha Anumanam (inference for oneself) and Paraartha Anumanam (inference for others). In the Svaartha Anumanam, there are four components, of which Hetu Prathyam is the first component.

Here, the ‘hetu’ (reason) is embedded.

Similarly, in Paraartha Anumanam (inference for others), there must be five components. These are Prathijna (the proposition), Hetu (the reason) is the second component. Hetu means the aforementioned Pratijna establishes the ‘sadhya’ (that which is to be proven) within it. This is the hetu. For example, the proposition (Pratijna) is “There is fire on this mountain.” Here, the mountain is the ‘paksha’ (subject), and fire is the ‘sadhya’. The hetu given for this is smoke.

Therefore, it is derived that wherever there is smoke, there is fire.

Thus, the two components, Pratijna and Hetu, are formed. The third component here is called Drishtanta (example). This means that the presence of fire is self-evident. How is this derived? We have already seen the co-existence of fire and smoke in the kitchen.

Therefore, the pre-existing knowledge that smoke cannot exist without fire is gained when we observe it in the kitchen. is proven through inference. The example shown thus is the third component, Drishtanta. Besides these, there are Upanyaya (application) as the fourth, and Nigamanam (conclusion) as the fifth, making a total of five components for this Paraartha Anumana.

Therefore, in Anumana Pramana, Hetu and Drishtanta are very important. These help to establish the Pratijna and serve as its cause.

Here, for our Lord, we cannot provide any Drishtanta. That is what we saw earlier: He is incomparable, without equal. Nor can a Hetu be provided.

Therefore, among these five important components, these two components, the Hetu and the Drishtanta, cannot prove, demonstrate, or know the Lord.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states, “Do not examine much with arguments and pronouncements.” Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who stated in the second thiruppadal of that Thiruvasagam that the Lord cannot be known by Pratyaksha Pramana, now states here that the Lord cannot be known by Anumana Pramana.

Similarly, in the seventh thiruppadal, he states that the Lord cannot be known even by Agama Pramana.

Thus, the Lord is ‘aprameya’ (unknowable by ordinary means). The truth that He can only be seen and known by souls through something called ‘Sivagnana’ is revealed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman in this Thiruvasagam at this point.

Now, this The next part in the fifth verse is “He shines forth, our light.” For this, Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman provides an explanation in the eight hundred and thirty-sixth verse. That verse is as follows: “To those who see, He is the manifest light shining forth, seen as an outer fire, and within, as an emerging light fueled by love.” This is the meaning, according to Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman’s explanation of “He shines forth, our light.” What is its meaning? Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sings, “He shines forth, our light.” The meaning is that the Lord appears as the light of fire outside, but to those who observe with profound love, He reveals Himself as an inner light, and to those who perceive through that light, He becomes the object of their experience. He is present outside as luminous objects. He is also the light that manifests within those who are deeply rooted in love and intensely perceive through the power of that love. ‘Angi’ refers to fire. This fire is considered to be one among the five elements.

Within the term ‘angi’, the sun, moon, and all other luminous objects can be included, because all external luminous objects are components of fire.

Therefore, it is our tradition to include all luminous objects that possess the luminous quality of fire and exist outside as part of fire. In this world, there are two kinds of darkness: external darkness and internal darkness. Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman explains in the preface that Sivagnana Botham is lauded as the text that dispels internal darkness, similar to how the sun dispels external darkness. He is the light. He is the light within the Lord, and He is the light outside the Lord. This is known from the Thiruvachakas of Devaram, which say, “He became water and fire that emits water,” and “He became the earth, fire, and water.” When He stands as an external light, those things that have a defined, partial manifestation, that can increase or decrease, that depend on something else for their illumination, and that can be seen by the external eye are contained within the outward appearance of light.

The external light, fire, requires fuel like wood or oil. But the inner light requires no such fuel and manifests within the mind solely due to love. That inner light is self-luminous, not contained within anything, and rises spontaneously without diminution.

Thus, Sivakavimani Ayya distinguishes between inner and outer light. This great light emerges when one immerses oneself in love, making it the foundation for perception. The Thiruvachakam says, “He will come forth if you churn with the churning staff of relationship and the rope of awareness.” If, as mentioned above, He cannot be known through pramanas, then to those who perceive intensely with love, He manifests as a radiant light within their hearts. “Maranai, Ayanai, Malal, Manathin, Vakkal, matrum, Kuraivila alavinalum kura onathaagi nindra Iraivanar kamalapadam” (He whose lotus feet cannot be described by the Vedas, by Brahma, by Vishnu, by mind, by speech, or by any measure). Arunanathi Sivacharya Perumakan, in the introduction to Sivagnana Siddhiyar, says that the Supreme Being, who is unknowable and unattainable, can be known through grace. He explains that to those who are immersed in and perceive through the intensity of love, He will reveal Himself through His grace, enabling them to see Him.

Arunanathi Sivacharya explains that Shiva can be seen and lived with, by realizing Him through Sivagnana within the mind, dispelling all delusions. Thirumooladevanayanar, in the 2944th verse of Thirumandiram, states that fools see with their physical eyes, but true joy is to see with the inner eye. This is what Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman mentioned in the first thiruppadal as ‘alagil sothiyan’ (limitless light). That inner light is the limitless Sivagnana light that manifests within the heart. The boundless and rising Sivajnana light. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman thus sings, “He shines forth, our light.” Our contemplation of this continues. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, Volume Seven Hundred and Forty, Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, composed by Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman. The third part of the fifth thiruppadal of Thiruppasura Thiruppathigam is “Ma thukkam neengal uruveer manam patti vazhmin” (You shall remove great sorrow and live with a steadfast mind). For this part, Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman provides an explanation in the eight hundred and thirty-seventh thiruppadal. That thiruppadal is as follows: “Ma thukkam neengal uruveer manam pattum enbadhu aadhi sudar jothiyai anbin agaththullaakki bodhitha nookutru oliyaamal porunthi vazhnthu pediththa bantha pirappin neri permine enradham” (You shall remove great sorrow and live with a steadfast mind; this means, by making the prime effulgent light within with love, by being steadfastly attached without deviation from the taught vision, and by living, you shall depart from the path of differentiated birth and bondage). Thirugnanasambandha Peruman thus states in the Thiruppasura Thiruppathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has declared in the Thiruppasura Thiruppathigam, “You shall remove great sorrow and live with a steadfast mind.” What does it mean?

It means you will be freed from the path of differentiated birth and bondage caused by anavam (ego), which has continuously obscured knowledge and separated you since primordial times. This is achieved by perceiving the primal effulgent light, the Shiva Paranjothi, within your soul through love, by performing internal worship with the holy five-syllable mantra (Panchaksharam), by perceiving it through the inner vision taught by a Gnanaachariyar (spiritual preceptor) through the path of divine grace, and by constantly abiding in Sivayoga, living a life of Sivagnana. That Shiva Paramporul (Supreme Being) must be made to shine forth clearly within us, and this is only possible through love. Perceiving that Shiva Paramporul in the knowledge of the soul, one must worship with the Panchaksharam. One must worship with the Panchakshara. This is called Antharyaga Puja (internal worship).

Sivagnana Siddhiyar states that this Antharyagam is proclaimed as a means to liberation, and it is also the purification of the soul. How should this be done? It must be in accordance with the experience taught and revealed by the Gnanaachariyar, the spiritual preceptor. One must abide in that vision of spiritual insight shown by the Gnanaachariyar, which leads to experience.

Thus, one must perceive through the inner vision, abiding by divine grace, and unite in Sivayoga. One must live a life of Sivagnana, continuously united in that Sivayoga. As it is said, “He taught through tapas, as the first Guru.” One must abide in what the Gnana Guru teaches through experience. One must abide in that.

Here, Pillaiyar (Thirugnanasambandhar) imparts spiritual instruction to all classes of souls. It is also understood here that the Prime Lord bestows grace upon all classes of beings, hidden within the form of a Guru. Theiva Sekkizhar Perumal structures the central idea as “Bodiththa nookkutru oliyaamal porundhi vazhnthu” (Attain the taught vision, abide without deviation, and live). This phrase has three parts: attaining the taught vision is the first part, abiding without deviation is the second part, and living is the third part. These three are arranged as three adhikarana (sections) in the ninth sutra of Sivagnana Botham. The ninth sutra of Sivagnana Botham has the meaning of instructing on the purification of the soul.

That ninth sutra is The physical eye, when blinded by illusion, does not perceive the Lord. Seek Him with the eye of wisdom in your mind. Remove the supportive attachment, and as illusion vanishes, the Lord’s shadow will remain, by the rule of the five-letter mantra. Meykandar Devanayanar explains this sutra as having three adhikarana (sections). “The physical eye, when blinded by illusion, does not perceive the Lord. Seek Him with the eye of wisdom in your mind” is the first adhikarana, which corresponds to “bodhitha nookkutru” (attain the taught vision) here.

“Remove the supportive attachment, and as illusion vanishes, the Lord’s shadow will remain” is the second adhikarana, which corresponds to the meaning of “oliyaamal porundhuthal” (abiding without deviation) in the Periya Puranam verse.

Now, the third part, “living,” corresponds to the third adhikarana of the ninth sutra, which is “vidhi ennum anjallu the” (by the rule of the five-letter mantra). To attain the taught vision means to perceive through Sivagnana (divine wisdom). This forms the first adhikarana. Its meaning is that the Supreme Being, who cannot be known by pasu gnanam (soul’s knowledge) and pasa gnanam (knowledge bound by illusion), can be known by Sivagnana.

The Lord is beyond speech and mind, unattainable by them, but attainable by Sivagnana. When it is said He is beyond speech and mind, ‘speech’ refers to pasa gnanam, and ‘mind’ refers to pasu gnanam. ‘Vak mana atheethan’ means one who transcends these, who is beyond both pasa gnanam and pasu gnanam. Nevertheless, He is knowable by Sivagnana.

Therefore, He is within the reach of Sivagnana. Pasa gnanam is the knowledge that arises in the soul through instruments made of these Tattvas and Tatvikas, or the knowledge of objects that the Lord reveals through these instruments of illusion. Pasu gnanam is the knowledge that arises in the soul through the assertion of the soul’s own consciousness, or the perverted knowledge where the soul mistakes its own knowledge for Sivagnana. Pathi gnanam is the knowledge that arises in the soul through the grace of the Lord, which is the knowledge directly revealed by the Lord. Unlike pasa gnanam, where the Lord reveals through instruments, Pathi gnanam is the knowledge that directly arises in the soul’s consciousness without reliance on instruments.

Therefore, the Prime Lord can only be known by this Pathi gnanam. Without this Pathi gnanam, the soul does not have the ability to see the Lord by any other means. Knowledge that occurs in the soul through these Tattva-Tatvika instruments, or the objective knowledge that the Lord imparts through these Pasa instruments. Pasu gnanam is the knowledge that occurs in the soul through the assertion of its own consciousness, a perverse knowledge where the soul mistakes Sivagnana for its own. Pati gnanam is the knowledge that occurs in the soul through the Lord’s grace. This is the knowledge that the Lord directly imparts.

Unlike Pasa gnanam, where the Lord imparts knowledge through instruments, Pati gnanam is the knowledge that arises directly in the soul’s consciousness.

Therefore, the Lord can only be known through this Pati gnanam. Without this Pati gnanam, the soul has no ability to see the Lord by any other means. the soul does not have the ability to see. For example, when an eye sees an object, the eye alone does not see; it sees when the soul enables it.

Similarly, the eye that sees an object does not see itself. Nor does it see the soul that controls it.

Therefore, the eye cannot see itself or the soul that enables it to see.

Similarly, the soul cannot know objects that are different from itself, nor can it know the Lord who controls it. If so, are the eye and the soul one? No, there is a difference between them. The eye is an inanimate object, devoid of consciousness, but the soul is a conscious entity. The soul is a conscious, sentient entity.

Therefore, the soul has the capacity to understand if the Lord reveals it. This is the difference.

Thus, the part where Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman says, “Bodhittha Nookkutru” (attain the taught vision), constitutes the first part or the first adhikarana of the ninth sutra. That is, one must see and experience the Lord with the Pati Gnanam, that experience of divine grace taught by the Gnanaachariyar, revealed through his teaching, that comes through spiritual experience.

Now, the second part, “oliyaamal” (without deviation), which is the second adhikarana, describes the means to attain Pati Gnanam, which we previously stated allows one to know and experience the Lord. This second adhikarana explains how to obtain that Pati Gnanam. A The nature of a crystal is to reflect the color of an object placed near it as its own. If the object near it is removed, the true color of the crystal appears; that is its true nature. Just as a crystal loses its own nature and takes on the color of an object near it, so too the soul is like that crystal. Until now, it was attached to the ephemeral objects of the world, becoming their essence and color.

Through pasu gnanam and pasa gnanam, the soul was thus attached to the world, becoming its essence and color. However, when it realizes that these instruments, worlds, tattvas, tatvikas, and creations of maya are all impermanent, and when pasu gnanam and pasa gnanam vanish—just as the true nature of a crystal appears when the object placed near it is removed—then the soul’s inherent Sivagnana fills it.

Thus, to realize that this world, which is ‘asath’ (unreal), is indeed ‘asath’ is the form of Sivagnana itself. Until now, the soul was in the heat of birth; the shade for that heat of birth is the Lord’s feet, the Lord’s grace, the Lord’s wisdom. Realizing this, to be comprehensively contained in the shade of His feet is what is new for the soul. To realize that this unreal world is unreal and then to be comprehensively contained in Sivagnana. is the way to attain Sivagnana. How does one perceive the ‘asath’ as ‘asath’? If one firmly grasps the truth taught by the Gnanaachariyar that all these manifested things that appear and decay are impermanent, and lives according to that, then the soul will experience through experience that all these are impermanent.

When one lives according to the path taught by the Gnanaachariyar, this soul realizes that worlds like Brahmaloka, Indraloka, Vishnuloka, and the objects and positions within them are not permanent. It then takes refuge at the feet of the Lord. Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman describes this steadfast adherence to the path taught by the Gnanaachariyar as “bodhitha nookkutru oliyaamal porundhuthal” (attaining the taught vision and abiding without deviation). Thirugnanasambandha Peruman says, “Maanam pattuveer” (You will hold on to the mind). What does it mean for this soul to realize that Brahmaloka, Indraloka, and other such realms are false and to detach from them? It means that when one realizes that all tattvas from Prithvi (earth) to Nadam (sound) are false and detaches from them, then the Lord will appear there as unceasing knowledge, never separating from this soul.

Pati Gnanam will appear there. The example verse of Sivagnana Botham illuminates this: “Will not the unique Prime Being, who stands as Nirgunan, Nirmalan, Nithyanandan, and Tatparan, appear as boundless knowledge, like a miracle, from the first syllable of the Vedas?” Here, the ‘asath’ (unreal) world is categorized into three types: Asuddha Prapancham (impure world), Suddha Prapancham (pure world), and Misra Prapancham (mixed world).

The Lord transcends these three worlds.

Therefore, Meykandar Devanayanar describes Him with three terms: Nirgunan (attributeless), Nirmalan (spotless), and Nithyanandan (eternally blissful). Prakriti is three-fold in nature, known and measured by living beings, and exists as the Asuddha Prapancham. Among these three gunas, Sattva is known as light, peace, and bliss. Rajas is perceived as activity, harshness, and sorrow. Tamas is understood as inertia, ignorance, and delusion. These are all aspects within this Prakriti Maya.

However, the Lord is not known in this way.

Therefore, Meykandar Devanayanar refers to Him with the word ‘Nirgunan’. Nirgunan means one who is without the Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas gunas, one who transcends these three gunas. It means He is beyond qualities, not that He has no qualities at all. This is the meaning of the word ‘Nirgunan’.

Next, Meykandar Devanayanar refers to Him as Nirmalan (spotless). Even if one transcends these three gunas, the state of being entangled with Anava Malam (ego impurity) and Kanma Malam (karma impurity) will still exist for souls. This is because crossing these worlds of Prakriti Tattvas applies to souls whose Maya Malam (delusion impurity) has been removed, but they will still have two impurities: Anava Malam and Kanma Malam. The effects of Anava Malam are sevenfold, and the effects of Kanma Malam are known as pleasure and pain. The Lord, however, transcends both these Mala (impurities) and Karma.

Therefore, He is referred to as Nirmalan here.

Thirdly, Meykandar Devanayanar refers to the Lord as Nithyanandan (eternally blissful). The third world is the Suddha Prapancham, which transcends both Karma and Maya. It has the nature of giving happiness.

However, the happiness that arises in the Suddha Prapancham is impermanent. Meykandar Devanayanar states that the Lord transcends even this Suddha Prapancham, hence the term Nithyanandan.

Therefore, when the Lord, who is Nirgunan, Nirmalan, and Nithyanandan, and who is Tatparan (supreme, having nothing above Him), is realized by the soul as transcending all these worlds from Prithvi (earth) to Nadam (sound) by perceiving them as ‘asath’ (unreal) and detaching from them, then the inherent Pati Gnanam, which was hidden until now, will manifest in the soul’s consciousness. This is called ‘arputham’ (wonder). It signifies an experience that was previously unknowable. Thirumooladevanayanar expresses this in Thiruvachakam as “Arputham ariyene” (I know not the wonder).

Therefore, the Lord, who is beyond the comprehension of the soul’s limited knowledge, now will appear as boundless knowledge, like a miracle. Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman refers to this state in the second part as “oliyaamal porundhuthal” (abiding without deviation).

Now, he mentions “vazhthal” (living), which is the third adhikarana of the ninth sutra. Until now, this soul realized the unreal Pasa as unreal and detached from it. When it detached, that Pati Gnanam was revealed by the Lord. It was stated that the soul should seek it through Sivoham Bhavana (meditation on identity with Shiva). If it has attained Pati Gnanam, does it need to do anything further? No, it does not.

Meykandar Devanayanar states in the third adhikarana that one should now recite the Sripanchakshara according to the rules. When the soul, having abandoned Pasa, perceives the Prime Lord as the object of knowledge with the eye of wisdom, the Sripanchakshara, the liberating Panchakshara, The teacher states that one should recite the five-letter mantra (Thiruvainthezhuthu) according to the rules. This is because this sacred five-letter mantra must be received from a Gnanaachariyar (spiritual preceptor).

Therefore, it is clear that only a Gnanaachariyar has the qualification to initiate it. Until now, this soul, having engaged in spiritual practices, and as a result of those practices, having detached from worldly bonds and sought the Lord with the eye of wisdom, has made the Sripanchakshara, which was taught by the Gnanaachariyar, its own. The teachers have extensively explained this Sripanchakshara in Meykanda Shastras such as Unmai Vilakkam, Sivaprakasam, Thiruvarutpayan, Kodikkavi, and Nenju Viduthuvathu. Why should the Sripanchakshara be recited even at this stage, when Pati Gnanam (divine knowledge) has blossomed? An example is given here: A worm born and raised on a neem tree, accustomed to eating its bitter leaves, a worm that has been accustomed to eating the bitter neem for a long time now gets the opportunity to approach sugarcane and drink its juice. Even after knowing the sweetness of the sugarcane and its juice, due to its long-standing habit, that worm might still desire the taste of the neem it previously enjoyed.

Similarly, souls who have been in the midst of this unreal world, performed spiritual practices, achieved success, discarded their long-accustomed pasagnanam (knowledge of illusion), attained patignanam (divine knowledge), and thereby reached the Lord, might still, due to their long-standing habits, develop a desire for this unreal world. To prevent such desires and to guide them, the recitation of Sripanchakshara according to the rules is indispensably necessary. The verse in Sivagnana Bodham for the third adhikarana of the ninth sutra states: “Having seen the Lord as one’s own fortress through the five letters, one should worship Him in the heart with folded hands, perform homa in the Kundalini, and there in the brow center, the Lord will be present as the remaining essence.” The example verse for the third adhikarana of the ninth sutra in Sivagnana Botham is “Anjalluthal Ullam Aran Udaimai Kandu Aranan Anjalluthal Archithu Idhayathil Anjalithal Kundaliyil Seythu Homam Kothandam Sanikkil Andanam Sedanam Angu.” The soul, now with the Sivagnana it has attained, should daily practice the meaning of the great dictum “Sivoham,” which the Acharya (teacher) imparts by meditating on “Sivoham” within oneself and instructing “Sivatvamasi.” If the disciple practices this Bhavana (contemplation) of “Sivoham,” then through the Lord who manifests in that Bhavana, the inherent common nature that has been associated with impurities, Maya, and Karma since primordial times will be abandoned. If one performs Sivoham Bhavana through the five-letter mantra, then this soul will always remain in a state of servitude to the Lord who manifests thus, with an overflowing sense of being a servant to the Master.

Therefore, the soul’s servitude to Shiva one must understand the soul’s servitude to Shiva by observing the method of reciting the Sripanchakshara. One should consider the heart within one’s body as the place for puja, the navel as the place for homa, and the brow center as the place for meditation. Just as external puja is called bahya puja, this internal puja is called ahatha puja or antaryagam. One should establish Shiva in the lotus of the heart, in the form of the five-letter mantra. Just as one offers flowers and eight types of flowers in external puja, in this internal puja, one should worship with eight types of flowers: non-violence, control of the five senses, patience, compassion, knowledge, true austerity, and love, along with the Sripanchakshara. The homa for this is also performed internally, with the navel serving as the homa kunda for the kundalini, and the fire kindled within it being the fire of gnana.

The sacrificial fire is the fire of knowledge, and the ghee poured into it is the nectar flowing from the bindu sthana in the brow center. The ladle and spoon used to pour the ghee are the Sushumna nadi, Ida nadi, and Pingala nadi.

After that, the method of meditation is done with the Sripanchakshara. In the brow center, the syllables ‘Sikaram’, ‘Yakaram’, and ‘Vakaram’ represent the Lord, the soul, and their existence respectively. One should meditate with Sivoham Bhavana. If one does so, that state itself implies servitude as its integral part.

Therefore, these two are integral parts of puja. Puja is the main action. When meditating, one should contemplate the great dictum ‘Tatvamasi’ in mind and perform it with the help of the five-letter mantra, as explained by Srimat Madhava Sivagnana Munivar in the Dravida Mahabhashyam. Srimat Madhava Sivagnana Munivar also instructs that ‘Sikaram’ should be meditated upon as representing ‘Tatpadha’ (that ultimate reality), ‘Yakaram’ as representing ‘Tvam padha’ (you), and ‘Vakaram’ as representing ‘Asipadha’ (are). This is Sivoham Bhavana.

Thus, we have seen how Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman’s explanation of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s words, “Manam patti vazhveer” (Live with a steadfast mind), as “Bodhittha nookkutru oliyaamal porundhi vazhnthu” (Attain the taught vision, abide without deviation, and live), aligns with the three adhikarana of the ninth sutra of Sivagnana Botham.

Therefore, the Prime Lord, who is unknowable by pasu gnanam (soul’s knowledge) and pasa gnanam (knowledge bound by illusion), can be known by the eye of His own gnanam (knowledge). The way to attain that Pati Gnanam (divine knowledge) is by examining the eye of one’s own consciousness, and by realizing that the aggregate of illusion (pasa kuttam) from Prithvi (earth) to Nadam (sound) is impermanent and detaching from it.

Then, Pati Gnanam will emerge and shine forth as a cool shade against the heat of the sorrow of birth. The meaning of this is that in order to prevent the vision of having seen the object of knowledge (jneyam) with that manifested Pati Gnanam from wavering, one must understand and constantly recite the Sripanchakshara (the five-letter mantra) which bestows that benefit, according to its prescribed rules. If one does so, then Thirugnanasambandha Peruman declares, “You will be freed from the path of birth arising from ego, you will remove great sorrow.” “Vazhmin” (live) means to live by aligning with Shiva. The soul is by nature such that it becomes the color of what it is attached to.

Therefore, once the bondage is removed, the soul has no support other than Shiva. So, after removing these intervening ‘pasu’ (soul’s nature) and ‘pasa’ (bondage), it is natural for the ‘pasu’ to cling to something. Since there is no other place to cling to, it clings to the Lord, taking refuge in Shiva. Such a Live such a life. This soul, when it sees itself as distinct from the senses, will attain the sacred feet of the Lord. In the eighth sutra, the means of knowledge such as hearing and contemplation, and the ways to achieve them, are explained.

The essence of the ninth sutra is thus embedded here in the words of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, as elucidated by Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman. And Sivakavimani Ayya has explained this by quoting from Sivagnana Botham, Sivagnana Siddhiyar, Sivagnana Mahabhashyam, and other texts of spiritual wisdom.

We shall proceed with our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, Volume Seven Hundred and Forty-One, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, composed by Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman. The section “Sadukkul mikkir iraye vandhu saarminhkalley” (O venerable sages, come and approach the Lord) from the fifth thiruppadal of Thiruppasuram. For this section, Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman provides an explanation in the eight hundred and thirty-eighth thiruppadal. Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman composes this thiruppadal, stating, “Here, the sages are those who, with profound love, praise the feet of the pure One, fulfilling all their desires; come, O devotees,” thus did the King of Shambai (Thirugnanasambandhar) declare. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proclaims, “Sadukkul mikkir iraye vandhu saarminhkalley” (O venerable sages, come and approach the Lord).

Shiva is by nature free from all bonds.

The Lord is naturally free from all bonds. His sacred feet are worshipped by devotees who hold Him in their hearts with love. Devotees are those who place all their desires upon the sacred feet of the Lord. Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman explains the meaning of this thiruppadal as follows: Pillaiyar, the leader of Shanbai, instructs: “Come and approach those who worship with such love.” The characteristic of sages is that they have completely surrendered themselves to the Lord and have no actions of their own. They are those who worship the pure One’s feet with love, fulfilling all their desires. This should be rephrased as “Poonda anbinil Vimalar thal potruveer” (You who worship the pure One’s feet with abiding love).

It is about devotees who live by worshipping the sacred feet of the Lord with unwavering love. In Thiruvachagam, in the “Kuzhaiththapattu,” the sixth verse, Manikkavasaga Peruman sings, “You know what is to be desired, You grant all that is desired. You are unknown to the desiring Brahma and Vishnu. You desired and took me into service. Whatever You graciously granted, that alone I desire. If there is any other way I desire, that too is not my desire.” This describes the state of such sages.

The very next verse in Kuzhaiththapattu also illustrates this: “Is there any obstacle for me today, my Lord of three eyes, with my skin? You do good or evil, am I the master of this?” Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman, in Periya Puranam, in the “Thirumalaichcherukkam” and “Thirukkootachchirappu” chapters, describes the glories of this community of devotees. As the sacred verse states, “Those who have transcended loss and gain, who regard iron and gold equally, whose unwavering devotion is only to worship with love, and who do not even desire liberation.” Such is the nature of devotees. The wealth that devotees possess is an imperishable wealth, a state of perpetual bliss, unified with the Lord’s nature at His sacred feet. This wealth is called Ishvaratvam or Aishvaryam. Karaikkal Ammaiyar sought this as “iravatha inba anbu” (unending blissful love) from the Lord.

Similarly, we can connect the meaning of Pillaiyar’s Devaram, “Is this the way You rule us? If there is nothing You give us, is that Your sweet grace?” from Thiruvavaduthurai Devaram, here.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states, “O venerable sages, come quickly and approach!” According to the tenth sutra of Sivagnana Botham, “He Himself became that path, standing as the one, serving the Lord, abandoning Maya and evil Karma.” Devotees are those who attain that state, transcend birth, and establish a life aligned with Shiva.

Furthermore, as Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman states, “They shine forth with the virtue of not desiring even liberation, but only worshipping with abiding love.” They are those whose nature is to worship continuously due to that love, standing united with the Lord, and through that union, adhering to Him inseparably. This is the Sivayogam mentioned in the previous aphorism. The soul, having clearly understood divine grace, does not stand separately but merges with it. The soul’s knowledge, absorbed in the divine knowledge of Shiva, stands in a state where its own identity does not appear; this is called Sivayogam. The maturation of this Sivoham Bhavana is explained in detail in the ninth aphorism. This maturation of Sivoham Bhavana is Sivayogam, which is also called Yoga in Gnanam (knowledge).

Those who have achieved this are these devotees. Their state is Pure Turiyam. They possess this love. Due to that love, they have the nature of continuously worshipping. This is the Sivayogam mentioned in the preceding aphorism. The soul, having clearly realized the divine grace, does not stand separately but merges with it.

The soul’s knowledge, immersed in the divine knowledge of Shiva, stands in such a way that its own separate existence does not appear. This state is called Sivayogam. The maturation of this Sivoham Bhavana was explained extensively in the ninth aphorism. This maturation of Sivoham Bhavana is Sivayogam. This is also called Gnana Yoga. Those who have attained this are these devotees.

Their state is Suddha Thuriyam (pure transcendent state). is the Pure Turiyam (the fourth state of consciousness, beyond waking, dreaming, and deep sleep). Thirugnanasambandha Peruman previously spoke of spiritual practice (sadhana) in the ninth aphorism. The benefits attained through such sadhana are two: liberation from bonds (pasa kayam) and attainment of Shiva (Sivapperu). These are the states of these sages, who have attained these two benefits. In the state of liberation (mukthi), the soul merges with the Prime Lord, where it is not seen as separate, but only the Prime Lord exists. The soul is absorbed within Him.

The seeker who is thus absorbed stands in the service of the Lord. The tenth sutra of Sivagnana Botham states this as “ekanagi nitral” (standing as one) and “irai pani nitral” (standing in the service of the Lord). If the soul’s knowledge stands separate from the object of knowledge, then the experience of enjoyment will not occur. When knowing or experiencing something, if the feeling “I am experiencing this” arises, then in that instance, the experiencer perceives himself through the “I,” and perceives the object of his experience. He realizes, “I am experiencing this.” Thus, these three occur.

Therefore, in this state, the knower perceives himself and the object of knowledge as separate. This is called ‘Triputi’ (the triad of knower, known, and knowing). The knower and his knowledge are called ‘gnanam’. The state where all three (knower, knowledge, and known) exist is called Triputi. As long as this Triputi gnanam (knowledge of the triad) exists, the full experience of bliss will not occur. One must experience without distinguishing between oneself, one’s knowledge, and the object of knowledge.

Enjoyment comes only when one is immersed in that object, forgetting oneself and one’s consciousness, and becoming one with it. The experience of Sivananda arises only when the soul’s consciousness does not stand separate from Shiva but merges and dissolves into that Shiva.

Therefore, if the soul desires to experience Sivananda, it must forget itself and its consciousness, be without the thought of ‘I,’ and immerse itself in that primordial substance, Shiva, experiencing and knowing only Shiva. This is the state of those whom the Lord calls ‘sadhus’ and ‘great ones.’ If they are so dedicated and engaged in the Lord’s service, even the impurity of ‘mala’ will not approach them.

Thus, the destruction of ‘pasa’ occurs there, and then the Shivabhogam, which is the attainment of Shiva, will happen. This is explained in the eleventh sutra of Sivagnanabodham. The state of being immersed in grace is called ‘Arulnilai.’ The state of being immersed in Shiva through grace is called ‘Anandanilai.’ First, the explanation of grace in Arulnilai is given; now comes the explanation of Anandanilai, which is the bliss-state. That is called Shivabhogam. By this nature, in the state of liberation, the soul, attached to Shiva, will stand as Shiva, without even a trace of its separate existence. It is like a crystal attached to a ruby, standing as the ruby.

However, the crystal does not become the ruby; it displays the quality of the ruby as its own quality.

Similarly, in liberation, the soul does not become Shiva itself; it receives and displays the quality of Shiva as its own.

Therefore, the soul stands as if it were Shiva.

Thus, in this section, the meaning of the tenth and eleventh sutras of Sivagnanabodham is explained by Deivasekkizhar.

Therefore, with these four verses, Deivasekkizhar bestows his commentary on the fifth Thiru-verse of the ThirupPasuram. The summary of its meaning is as follows: In the previous verse, ‘Adpalavarkku,’ he said that the Lord bestows grace upon His devotees, and His greatness, when heard by one with spiritual understanding and recounted by another, is immeasurable; one should listen to these, free from impurities and surrendered at the Lord’s feet. In this verse, he explains how to listen and understand, thus surrendered at the Lord’s feet. Do not test that primordial being with logic and examples. He always helps by standing as an outer light, illuminating objects, and by standing as an inner light that arises within when one is rooted in love, illuminating. If one serves Him constantly, becoming one with Him, as taught by the Guru, with the eye of wisdom, then the path of birth will cease, and everything will be attributed to Him.

Then the soul, released from the cycle of birth, will attain a life of Shivapath and experience it. This is the means described in the eighth and ninth sutras of Sivagnanabodham and the benefit described in the tenth and eleventh sutras, which are taught in this fifth Thiru-verse by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

Thus, Deivasekkizhar, who bestowed this commentary on this verse, has stated that this is how the Lord Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the king of Chanpai, revealed it, concluding this eight hundred and thirty-eighth verse. The first part of ThirupPasuram, consisting of five Thiru-verses, and their respective commentaries have thus been extensively explained by Deivasekkizhar.

Now, the second part of ThirupPasuram The second part begins. This second part contains seven Thiru-verses. For each of these seven Thiru-verses, Deivasekkizhar bestows a commentary in one verse within Periya Puranam.

We shall continue our contemplation of this. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. We have contemplated the commentary given by Deivasekkizhar on the five Thiruppadal out of the total twelve Thiruppadal in Periya Puranam, Volume Seven Hundred and Forty-Two, Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. This is the first part. The second part of ThirupPasuram is about to begin. The five parts we have already considered, those five Thiruppadal, explain the true nature of the three entities according to Saiva Siddhanta: Pati, Pasu, and Pasam. They also describe the means and the benefits, citing the conclusions of the Vedas and Sivagamas.

Now, the next five These verses illustrate the truths already stated by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman with examples from the Mahapuranas.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has presented this in two parts using two types of poetic structures and meters.

Similarly, Deivasekkizhar, who provides the commentary for this, also follows the same path and bestows it upon us. Deivasekkizhar, who provided a very extensive and lengthy commentary for the five verses in the first part, now gives a commentary for each of the subsequent seven verses, one verse for each.

Now, the sixth verse of ThirupPasuram is as follows: (aadum enavum arungootram udaitthu vedam paadum enavum pugazhalladhu paavam neenga kaedum pirappum marukkum ena kaettaeraaga) (Naadum thirathaarkku arulalladhu naattalaamae) is the sixth Thiru-verse of ThirupPasuram composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman refers to three acts of grace: the Lord dances, the Lord kicked Yama for Markandeya, and the Lord revealed the Vedas. He asks whether these acts of grace were performed by the Lord for fame, or to remove the evil deeds of these souls, or to destroy the path of their evil karma. If asked, it can be stated with certainty that these were done by the Lord for His devotees and for no other reason. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states that the immeasurable compassion the Lord has for souls is the reason for His divine actions.

Deivasekkizhar gives a commentary for this verse in a single verse, the eight hundred and thirty-ninth verse. That verse is as follows: (aadum ena varum thiruppaattil amaittha moonrum needum pugazho pirar thunbam neeththarkko endru thaedum unarveer ulagukku ivai seythathu eesar koodum karunai thiram enranar kolgai maelor) This verse means: “O those with a searching mind, who wonder if these three divine acts of the Lord – dancing, kicking the fierce Yama, and singing the Vedas – were done for lasting fame or to remove the suffering of others, the great ones declare that these were done by the Lord for the world out of His immense compassion.” Thus, Deivasekkizhar states that Pillaiyar (Thirugnanasambandha Peruman) explains that these are acts of the Lord’s great compassion for the souls of the world. Are these three acts of grace mentioned by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman done for the Lord’s fame? Doing something for fame means doing it for oneself.

But the Lord did not do it for fame; it was for the souls to be freed from sin and the cycle of birth and death, to attain liberation. It is the unparalleled compassion that the Lord, without any reason, has for these souls. The same message is explained in the thirty-sixth Thiru-verse of the first sutra of Sivagnana Siddhiyar. The fivefold actions, such as anugraham, are performed as a play, very easily, without effort, by mere will. Why? It is so that souls, bound by malas in their conditioned state, are released from their bondage, attain maturity through these karmas, and reach the feet of the Lord.

Thus, it is for the sake of the souls’ upliftment. Thirodhanam (concealment) and Anugraham (grace) – these five actions (panchakrithyam) are of three types: Sthula (gross), Sukshma (subtle), and Atisukshma (very subtle). Among these, Sthula Panchakrithyam refers to the creation and dissolution of this universe. This is an obvious one. When the creation and dissolution of the universe are spoken of, the intermediate state is called Pralaya.

After the Lord performs Mahasamharam (great dissolution), the next Sthula Panchakrithyam, or the next Prathama Srishti (first creation), Until that comes, the intervening period is called the Kevala state. What the Lord performs in that Kevala state is Sukshma Panchakrithyam.

Now, Atisukshma Panchakrithyam is when the soul, in the Jagrat (waking) state, stands in the center of the eyebrows, combines with its instruments, and perceives objects. In this state, the Lord, as the life of the life, resides within and constantly enlightens this soul. If He did not enlighten it, the soul would not gain knowledge. This method of the Lord enlightening the soul is called Atisukshma Panchakrithyam.

Thus, these three types of Panchakrithyam – Sthula Panchakrithyam, Sukshma Panchakrithyam, and Atisukshma Panchakrithyam – are called Oona Natana. It is called the Oona Natana performed by the Lord. Oona Natana means the dance performed by the Lord to remove the imperfections of souls. It means the dance performed by the Lord to remove the impurities of souls. All the sastraic texts, such as Unmai Vilakkam and Thiruvarutpayan, extensively describe this sacred dance, this Thiru Koothu.

In particular, the text Unmai Vilakkam explains this sacred dance of the Lord as Oona Natana, Gnana Natana, and Ananda Natana. As we have already seen, the Sthula, Sukshma, and Atisukshma five actions performed by the Lord are called Oona Natana. In this, the sacred form of the Lord of Dance, the sacred body of Srimath Nataraja Peruman, the Udukkai (drum) or Damarukam He holds, by producing sound, signifies the act of creation (Srishti).

The Lord of Dance’s abhaya thirukaram (hand granting protection) signifies the act of preservation (Sthithi). The fire held by the Lord signifies the act of dissolution (Samharam). The Lord, firmly placing one foot on Muyalagan, The foot He is firmly placing represents the act of concealment, known as Thirodhanam. The lifted left foot, raised high, signifies the act of bestowing grace, known as Anugraham. This dance of Shiva, thus, signifies that He is the primordial cause of the five actions. Unmai Vilakkam beautifully describes how the five actions are manifested in this dance.

The act of creation is providing countless souls with bodies suitable for them and enabling them to move in this world. The hand that shakes the Damarukam to produce sound signifies the creation of this world. He not only performs creation, but also protects these souls. He sustains them until the time comes for them to experience their karmic enjoyments. That is the act of preservation.

Similarly, souls with bodies, Souls associated with bodies experience immense joy and sorrow from those bodies, getting caught in the cycle of birth and death, and enduring great weariness. To alleviate this weariness, the Lord separates the souls from their bodies, allowing them to rest for a while. This is the act of dissolution. This too is done by the Lord for the benefit of the souls. The fire held in the Lord’s hand signifies this act of Samharam.

Now, Thirodhanam is when the Lord, instead of revealing Himself to the souls, shows them the world and allows them to experience worldly pleasures. This is done by the Lord to bring the souls to a state of maturity where they can know Him. The sacred foot of the Lord resting on Muyalagan signifies the act of concealment. Anugraham, or the act of bestowing grace, is to remove all bonds and grant supreme bliss to the souls. The lifted sacred foot of the Lord of Dance signifies uplifting souls from the cycle of birth and placing them under His sacred feet.

Similarly, the Lord performs Gnana Natana.

The Lord performs this sacred dance to bestow both bondage and liberation upon souls. Among these, the dance that bestows birth is Oona Natana.

Now, the dance that bestows liberation is Gnana Natana. The small drum (dudi damarukam) held in the Lord’s hand signifies shaking off and removing Maya from the soul’s consciousness. The hand holding fire signifies burning away the karma that follows the soul. The Lord’s firm foot signifies restraining the Anava mala. The Lord’s lifted foot signifies uplifting from the states of being caught in the cycle of birth and death and placing the soul in a state of grace. The curve of that lifted sacred foot and the outstretched hand that displays it, symbolizing the cessation of the ego of ‘I’ and ‘mine,’ and that sacred hand, It has the implication of immersing the soul in supreme bliss.

That sacred dance of the Lord is called Gnana Natana.

Similarly, there is Ananda Natana. This is the dance of Ananda (bliss) that continuously bestows supreme bliss upon mature souls in the Jivanmukta state, without interruption. The exalted sages, who stand in the ultimate state of Mouna, completely remove the afflictions of the three malas (impurities) and manifest in a state devoid of ego, experiencing the nectar of supreme bliss.

The Lord stands visible within Thiruchitrambalam there, dancing, so that they can drink it with their eyes. That is Ananda Natana. The sacred dance performed by Srimath Nataraja Peruman, who shines by taking His own grace as a visible form, is Ananda Natana. Aazhuda Pillaiyar witnessed and worshipped that Ananda Natana in Thiruchitrambalam, in Thillai, and was overjoyed.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman explains that this sacred dance performed by the Lord is for the sake of souls. Kicking the fierce Yama, saving Markandeya by kicking Yama, and then reviving Yama, is a story that is extensively described in all Puranas and is well known to all of us. Thaayumanavar praises this, saying, “If one considers the plight that befell Yama for Markandeya, what benefit is it to the devotees, O Paraparame?” Therefore, when the Lord kicked Yama for Markandeya, it was not for Markandeya himself, but so that we, the souls of this world, may understand its true nature, come to the Lord, and escape the cycle of birth and death to attain salvation.

Therefore, this too was performed out of immense compassion for the souls.

Now, the third act of grace is what Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states as ‘singing.’ During the Punar-utbhavam, or recreation, the Lord reveals and bestows the Vedas and Agamas during that creation. This is so that the souls of this world may understand them, follow that path, and attain salvation. (Kadan meezha nindru em irai nal veenai vaasikkumae) is from Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s Thevaram.

Therefore, even the Lord’s bestowal of the Vedas and Agamas is out of compassion, so that souls may understand and adhere to them to attain salvation.

Thus, it is for the sake of showing compassion to this world that the Lord performs His sacred dance, kicked Yama for Markandeya, and bestowed the Vedas and Agamas. All these are for this world to see, contemplate, understand, and attain salvation. That is the Lord’s immense compassionate power. The primordial Lord, being omniscient, understands all the suffering of the souls in this world. He possesses immense power.

Therefore, the Lord is capable of leading all these souls to liberation at once. Names like Shiva and Shankara also signify this.

The Lord is of great compassion, acting equally towards all souls without likes or dislikes, without attachment, and with a mental urge to instantly remove the suffering of others when seen.

Therefore, the characteristic of the primordial being is spoken of here as the Lord being capable of leading all souls to liberation at once. If so, why has He not brought all souls to liberation? It is because the malashaktis (impure energies), which are the imperfections of souls, bind these souls. Only when these malashaktis are removed will the souls attain liberation, which will be beneficial for them.

Therefore, the primordial being, through His will, performs the act of concealment, called ‘maraippu,’ through the malashaktis, bringing the souls to maturity, and then bestows liberation.

Therefore, this concealment is also an act of His compassion.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states that the Lord’s sacred dance, His kicking Yama for Markandeya, and His bestowal of the Vedas and Agamas are all due to His compassion for souls. We will continue to contemplate this in the sixth Thiru-verse. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Devotees of the Lord Chikkalar’s Periya Puranam, Part 743, Vambara Varivandach Chapter, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, the seventh verse of Thiruppaasura Thiruppathigam. In this verse, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman extols Chandikeswara Nayanar, and through him, he graciously imparts to us the truth and greatness of that Agamic tradition. The seventh verse is as follows: (Kadiserntha pothu malaraana kai kondu nalla padiserntha paal kondu angu aattida thaathai pandu mudiserntha kaalai ara vettida mukkanmoorthi adiserntha vannam arivaar solak kettum andre). This verse speaks of Chandikeswara Nayanar, who, with hands holding fragrant flowers, reverently performed the ritual anointing (Thirumanjanam) of a Shiva Lingam made of sand with good cow’s milk. His father, in anger, kicked over the vessels used for the anointing with his foot, obstructing the Shiva puja.

Chandikeswara Nayanar, enraged, took a nearby stick and threw it at the foot that caused the obstruction. Even though the stick turned into an axe and severed the foot, Lord Shiva, the three-eyed deity, bestowed upon his devotee, Chandikeswara Nayanar, the gift of his sacred feet. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states that these events were heard by wise devotees in those very days. For this verse, Lord Deivasekkilar provides a commentary in the 840th verse, which is as follows: (Karuthum kadiserntha ennum thiruppaattil Eesar maruvum perum poosai maruththavarkkOran muththi tharu thanmaiyathu aathal Chandeesar tham seykai thakkOr perithum solla kettanam enranar pillaiyaardham). This is the commentary provided by Deivasekkilar Peruman for the seventh verse of Thiruppaasuram, which begins with “Kadiserntha.” In that seventh verse of Thiruppaasuram, it is stated that killing those who destroy the great puja, which the Lord lovingly accepts and presides over, is not an evil act; it is a good act that bestows liberation. Deivasekkilar Peruman explains that the Pillaiyar (Thirugnanasambandha Peruman) states that they heard this from great elders who are worthy of recounting Chandikeswara’s story.

We have already contemplated Chandikeswara Nayanar Puranam, and therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman extols it here, emphasizing the importance of Shiva Agama puja. Killing someone who obstructs the Lord’s puja is not considered a sin of murder, unlike the five great sins (panchama patakas). Murder is listed as the first among them, but killing someone who obstructs the Lord’s puja is not a sin. If one does so, one will not face the hellish consequences of sin. Instead, it is a Shiva punyam, superior even to good deeds (punyas), and capable of granting liberation. We have read about this in Chandikeswara Nayanar Puranam and heard it from elders.

Those elders possessed the qualification to know and speak the truth. What is that qualification? It is the maturity to understand the divine grace that the Lord reveals and to express it. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states that we have heard such elders speak in this manner, haven’t we? In this verse, a distinction is made between Padi Punyam and Pasu Punyam. Even Padi Punyams.

Divided into good and bad Shiva deeds, as discussed in the section on the equivalence of the two actions (iruvinai oppu) in Maapadiyam, we have already considered this in this very Thiruppaasura Thiruppathigam.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states that we have heard these matters from elders who have the maturity to understand the divine grace revealed to them and to articulate it. These qualified elders who lived before the time of the Pillaiyar include Thirumoola Deva Nayanar and Manickavasaga Perumanar.

Additionally, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, who lived during the Pillaiyar’s time, also praised Chandikeswara Nayanar. Following them, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal also praised Chandikeswara Nayanar in his Thevaram. Chandikeswara Nayanar has been praised in the Thiruvichaippaa, Thiruppallandu, and the Eleventh Thirumurai, to the extent that there is no place where Chandikeswara Nayanar Puranam or Chandikeswara Nayanar’s sacred story is not spoken of, and no texts where he is not mentioned.

Furthermore, this truth is revered in Gnanashastras such as Thirukkazhitruppadiyar and Sivagnana Siddhiyar. We have deliberated at the conclusion of Chandikeswara Nayanar Puranam about which Thirumurais, temple Puranas, and texts his sacred story appears in. Chandikeswara Nayanar was thus revered by various great individuals. The Puranam that praises him is Chandikeswara Nayanar’s Thiruppuranam. The Gnanashastras explain that such an act, which might be considered a great sin, leads to liberation because it is born of love. The Periya Puranam, in its 1264th verse within the Chandikeswara Nayanar Puranam, beautifully explains this, stating that actions performed by devotees out of love are considered penance.

The Thiruvachagam, in Thiruthol Nokkam, praises Chandikeswara Nayanar by saying, “Is it not a great sin that has consumed you?” The Ninth Thirumurai, Thiruppallandu, glorifies him with, “To him who has offered a reward for sin, we sing Pallandu!” Thirukkazhitruppadiyar states, “Without considering it a sin or a blame, he severed his father, the Brahmin’s, two feet; see how Chandikeswara was rewarded for his action!” Therefore, this verse explains that puja performed according to the Shiva Agama tradition, if interrupted, should be resumed after removing the obstruction, as demonstrated by Chandikeswara Peruman. This verse elucidates. As Deivasekkilar Peruman sang about Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred purpose for his incarnation: “May the Vedic path flourish, may the great Saivite tradition shine, and may the lineage of beings prosper.” The meaning of “may the Vedic path flourish” was obtained in the previous verse. We saw in the preceding verse that the Lord bestowed the Vedas for the sake of humanity and for the salvation of living beings.

Therefore, through Chandikeswara Nayanar explaining the Shiva Agama puja in the previous verse, the second benefit of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred incarnate purpose, “may the great Saivite tradition shine,” is obtained.

Thus, this seventh verse concludes.

Now, the eighth verse, a verse where Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sings of the Maha Puranas. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who sang of the Vedas in the sixth verse and the Agamas in the seventh, now, in this eighth verse, sings of the Maha Puranas. The verse is as follows: (Veda muthalvan muthalaaga vilangi vaiyam edappadaamai ulagatthavar eththal seiyya pootha muthalvan muthale muthala polinda soothan olimalai enre kalikkovai solle). This Thiruppaasura verse means that Lord Shiva, who shines as the Primeval Lord of the Vedas, is the one whom the world should praise to avoid suffering. The eighteen Puranas, which were graciously composed by Sage Sutha, praising Lord Shiva, the Primeval Lord of all beings, are teachings that promote good conduct. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states this.

For this, Deivasekkilar Peruman provides a commentary in the 841st verse, which is as follows: (Veda muthalvan enum meith thiruppaattinil ner aathi ulagOr idar neengida etha aadum paatha muthalam pathinen puranangal enre othu enru urai seithanar yaavum othaathu unarnthar). The meaning of this verse is as follows: In the true sacred verse beginning with “Veda muthalvan,” the primeval deity referred to by the Vedas, which are the ultimate प्रमाण (proof), is Lord Shiva, who dances (performs the sacred dance) with sacred feet so that living beings in the world may be freed from their suffering and may know and praise the Lord. He alone is the primeval deity. The eighteen Puranas clearly explain this truth proclaimed by the Vedas. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who knew without studying, graciously stated, “Study them decisively.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who knew without studying, graciously instructed to study them.

The conclusion of the Vedas is that the Lord, to alleviate the suffering of the people of this world, has sacred feet that dance and are uplifted. The Maha Puranas also state the same. The Veda is a general text; it appears to address all deities with greetings, but it reveres Lord Shiva, the Primeval Lord who controls all those deities, as supreme within its Sri Rudram.

Similarly, among the eighteen Puranas, which are supplementary texts to the Vedas, the ten Puranas that primarily praise the supremacy of Lord Shiva are the Saiva Puranas. In the other eight Puranas, Vishnu, Brahma, Agni, and Surya, who perform their respective functions under the direction of Lord Shiva. They are mentioned as leaders in a complimentary manner. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman thus refers to the eighteen Puranas as “Soothan Oli Maalai” (the garland of hymns by Sutha Muni), stating that Lord Shiva is the Primeval Lord of all beings. The meaning of this is the eighteen Puranas composed by Sage Sutha. These eighteen Puranas are the Matsya, Kurma, Varaha, Vamana, Shiva Maha Purana, Linga Purana, Bhavishya, Skanda, Markandeya, and Brahmanda – these ten Puranas directly declare Lord Shiva as the Supreme God.

These are called Saiva Puranas. The Vishnu Purana, Bhagavata, Garuḍa, and Naradiya – these four speak about Vishnu. The Brahma Purana and Padma Purana – these two speak about Brahma. The Agneya Purana speaks about Agni, and the Brahmavaivarta Purana speaks about Surya. Although these other eight Puranas speak about Vishnu, Brahma, Surya, and Agni, they state that these deities perform their duties under Shiva’s command, just as servants act on a king’s orders. By directing them, Shiva himself performs those actions.

Therefore, it is understood through the sacred words of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman that studying the Puranas is essential for those who study the Vedas, to understand their meanings. It is explained that even if one has a good understanding of the four Vedas, if one does not thoroughly understand the Puranas, it is difficult to grasp the meanings of the Vedas properly. The number eighteen specifically refers to the Puranas. It also refers to the eighteen Vidyas. In one way, the Vedas are four, their angas (auxiliary sciences) are six, Mimamsa is one, Nyaya is one, Purana is one, Dharma Shastra is one; thus fourteen. Adding to these fourteen, the four Upavedas – Ayurveda, Dhanurveda, Gandharva Veda, and Shilpa – make eighteen Vidyas.

It is heard that Lord Shiva graciously created Brahma and taught him these Vidyas for the welfare of the people of this world, so they may study them step by step and attain salvation. It is true that he is the creator of the eighteen Vidyas. Some people scornfully say that all these Puranas are false and fabricated, and in doing so, they cause trouble to themselves and commit offenses, and they also trouble and cause suffering to the people of the world. It is customary to learn how to interpret these Puranas, considering their inherent nature, metaphors, similes, and arthavada (exaggeration for emphasis), by consulting experienced teachers, and then to study the Gnanashastras. We must also note that these historical narratives of the Puranas are also cited in the authentic Gnanashastras.

Thus, in this eighth verse, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has spoken about the eighteen Maha Puranas. In the sixth verse, he spoke about the Vedas, stating that the Lord graciously gave them. Through the sacred words of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who spoke about Chandikeswara Nayanar and the Agamas, the second part of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred incarnate purpose, “may the great Saivite tradition shine,” was obtained. In this section, through the phrase “Boothanaayagar Muthalae Muthalaali” (Lord of all beings, the Primeval Lord). The third benefit of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred incarnate purpose, “may the lineage of beings prosper,” is established here by the sacred words of this verse.

Thus, these eight verses conclude.

Now, let us continue to contemplate the other verses. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 744, Vambara Varivandu Chapter, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, the ninth verse of Thiruppaasura Thiruppathigam, as revealed by Deivasekkilar Peruman, is as follows: (Paaraazhi vattam pagaiyan nalintaatta vaadi peraazhiyathu idar kandu arul seithal peni neeraazhi vittetri nenju idam kondavarkku poraali eentha pugalum pugazhutrathu anre). In this verse, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman extols Lord Shiva by referring to the gracious event where Lord Shiva bestowed the discus (Chakrayudha) upon Thirumal. For this, Deivasekkilar Peruman provides a commentary in the 842nd verse, which is as follows: (Paavuttra paaraazhi vatta thiruppaattin unmai kaaval thozhilaan enum kannanum). Its truth, about the protection obtained by Kannan, who is the protector, is that by receiving the discus of grace from the supreme Lord, he attained glory, so said the Vedic speaker. This is the verse.

The truth of the verse beginning with “Paaraazhi vattam” in Thiruppaasura Thiruppathigam is that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sings about the history of Vishnu, who undertook the duty of protecting this world and obtained that protective duty. Deivasekkilar Peruman reveals that Thirumal, by receiving the discus and grace from Lord Shiva, who is the foremost of all, became the one who performs the act of protection. It is here conveyed that Vishnu performs his assigned duty of preservation (sthithi) by the command of Lord Shiva and with the help of the discus granted by Lord Shiva. The story of Thirumal obtaining the discus. Is discussed in the six Maha Puranas.
