Once, Indra, consumed by arrogance, went to Thirukayilayam.

Lord Shiva appeared before Indra in the form of a Boothagananayagar. Unaware of Shiva’s true identity, Indra, in his arrogance, hurled his Vajrayudha at him. It shattered into dust.

Lord Shiva then assumed a Rudra form, appearing angry. Sweat appeared on Lord Shiva’s divine body. Seeing this, Indra was frightened and bowed down. The Lord’s anger subsided, and he graciously released Indra. The anger that the Lord then held was cast into the ocean. It took the form of a demon and was raised by Varuna, growing up with the name Jalandhara.

Because Jalandharasura was born from Lord Shiva’s anger. He disrespected Vishnu, Brahma, and all other deities, ruling the world independently, surrounded by numerous demons. Vishnu fought him for many years but was defeated. Indra and the other deities, frightened, took refuge in Thirukayilayam. Jalandharasura, surrounded by his armies and filled with arrogance, came to Kayilai to fight Lord Shiva.

Lord Shiva then appeared before Jalandharasura in the form of an old sage and asked, “Where are you going?” He told Jalandharasura that if he had the strength to fight Lord Shiva, he should take this discus and place it on his head. With his toe, Lord Shiva drew a discus on the ground. That Jalandhara. He took the discus, placed it on his head, and it cut him in two, killing him. To obtain that discus, Thirumal performed penance for many years at Thiruvezhi Mizhalai, daily offering a thousand lotus flowers to the Lord.

One day, by the Lord’s grace, one flower was missing from the thousand lotus flowers. At that moment, Thirumal plucked out his own eye and offered it at the Lord’s sacred feet as the thousandth lotus.

Lord Shiva then appeared and graciously bestowed the Sudarshana discus upon Vishnu. Thirumal, with his discus, governs this world and performs the duty of protection. This is the story of Thirumal receiving the discus. Its detailed accounts can be found in the Skanda Purana and other Maha Puranas. This story has also been sung in many places in the Thirumurais by the great saints. The ninth verse of Pillaiyar Thevaram on Thiruvezhi Mizhalai says: “Oh Lord, who resides in the beautifully constructed Vimanam (temple tower), grant me the discus with which you severed the body of the great Jalandhara who performed severe penance.” Thirunerisai says: “Having smeared much sacred ash, and daily offering a thousand flowers, when one flower was missing one day, he offered his eye.

“The Lord who bestowed the discus upon him and who was brought down by him (Thirumal), resides in Thiruvezhi Mizhalai and grants grace.” Thiruthantakam says: “He is the clever one who split Jalandhara, who sought battle, with his discus.” Sundaramoorthy Swamigal’s Thevaram on Thirukalayanallur says: “He granted the bright discus that split Jalandhara, who was full of water, to the red-eyed Vishnu, who offered his lotus-like eye.” Thiruvachagam in Thiruchazhil says: “What a wonder that he granted the discus to the virtuous Narayana, who split the body of Jalandhara, full of water! When the virtuous Narayana offered his eye at the Lord’s feet, did the Lord not grant him the discus?” From these sacred words, it is understood that this narrative is explained as being Vedic-sanctioned. That is why Deivasekkilar Peruman, when referring to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman in this verse, calls him “Veda Vayar” (one whose mouth speaks the Vedas).

“Now, the tenth verse of Thiruppaasuram: (Maalaayavanum maraivallum paalaaya thevar pagaril amuthootthal peni kaalaaya munneer kadainthaarkku arithayezhuntha aalaalam undu angu amararkku arul seithathaame). These are the sacred words of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Thirumal and Brahma, who are skilled in the four Vedas. And many other deities desired to partake of the nectar that is beyond words. When they churned the ocean of milk, the Alakala poison arose, and Lord Shiva consumed it to protect and bestow grace upon the deities. This is its meaning.

“For this verse, Deivasekkilar Peruman provides a commentary in the 843rd verse. The verse is as follows: (Maalaayavan ena varum thiruppaattil Maalum tholaa marai naan muganum thodarvaam amarar elaavakai suttan nanjundu iravaamai kaattha melaam karunai thiram venguru venthar vaithaar). The verse starting with “Maalaayavanum” speaks of the supreme compassion shown by the King of Venguru (Thirugnanasambandha Peruman), who declared that Lord Shiva consumed the unbearable poison that arose, to save Thirumal, Brahma, who is skilled in the victorious Vedas, and the other deities who followed them, from death. In this verse, the divine Sekkizhar Peruman states that our leader from Sirkazhi, Pillaiyar, made us all aware of that triumphant song.

“The Lord drinking the poisonous timeless poison indicates His great grace and immense compassion. This is one of the eight divine qualities of the Lord. Although the Vedas and the Mahapurana, which elaborate on them, praise Vishnu, Brahma, and other deities in addition to Shiva, their essential message is that Shiva is the primordial being among all deities. This is elucidated to us through the narratives of the consumption of poison, as recounted in the Vedas and Puranas. The story of Shiva drinking the poison is as follows: Once, devas and asuras to obtain ambrosia and attain long life With Vishnu as the leader, Mandara mountain as the churning rod, and Vasuki as the rope, they churned the ocean of milk.

“At that time, due to immense suffering, Vasuki spewed venom. That potent and terrible poison arose, overflowing and burning them, blackening their bodies. They all cried out and ran to Shiva for help. He ordered Alalasundarar to bring the poison, minimizing its effect. Alalasundarar collected all the poisons and brought them, which Shiva then consumed. At the request of the devas, the Divine Mother, with her sacred hand, stopped the poison at the level of the Lord’s throat.

“On the Lord’s fiery red body, at His sacred neck, the poison remained, appearing slightly dark. Just as Shiva wears the crescent moon and bears the Ganga, His great The sacred blue throat symbolizes the triumph of His compassion and His primordial nature. This story is recounted in many Mahapurana. Thirukurunthogai asks, “Is there any deity who consumed the surging poison from the ocean? Tell me.” After the Lord consumed the poison, the devas and asuras drank the ambrosia that arose from the ocean of milk, lived long lives, and eventually, at the end of their predetermined lifespans, died and were reborn.

“However, our primordial Lord Shiva, even though He consumed the poison to protect others, remains eternal, which is explained here.

“Now, the eleventh verse of the Thiruvasuram is as follows: (Atrunri Anthan madhurai thogai aakinanum thetrunru theivam theliyar karai) That day, when the learned scholars, fearing the divine judgment, composed the Anthology of Madurai, if they, with clear minds, did not discern the divine truth and sought to remove their doubts by the riverbank (Kolai thenneer patrinri paangedhir viravum panbu nokkil petronru uyartha peruman perumanum anre) If they, without attachment, observed the nature of opposing the flow, then the Lord, who raised the bull, is indeed the Supreme Lord. This is the eleventh verse.

“Here, the praises of Shiva, as mentioned earlier in the narratives, along with the establishment of the Tamil Sangam in Madurai and the nurturing of Tamil by Shiva, are celebrated. The Thiruvilayadal Puranam reveres this, stating, “Even the Lord with the eye on His forehead presided over the Sangam.” Here, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman teaches that it is the duty of all beings in this world to show love towards such a Shiva. For this, the divine Sekkizhar Peruman explains in the eight hundred and forty-fourth verse. That verse is as follows: In the verse (Atranrindan), it states that the Sangam was established in the city of Koodal, (Therat thera eenargal ellaikitta edu neer edhirndhu sellil gnanan eesanpal anbe endranar gnanam undar) those wretched ones, who were deluded, placed their sacred writings in the water. If the leaf were to proceed against the current, then true knowledge is indeed love for the Lord, as those who possessed knowledge affirmed. This is the verse by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman.

“This is the concluding part of the pathigam. The twelfth verse that follows is the Thirukkadaikkappu.

“Therefore, this verse completes the pathigam. In this concluding verse of the pathigam, the Pandian king, who established three Sangams in Madurai, also known as Nanmadakoodal, to foster Tamil, instructed that the written leaf should go against the current of the water to mark the end of the debate with the Jains, who were base and unable to comprehend. That leaf must contain the true essence. That true essence is love for the Lord. So says Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, as narrated by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman. The Pandian kings established three Sangams and nurtured Tamil.

“Therefore, “the one who established the Sangam in Koodal city” is a common title for all Pandian kings. Such a Pandian king, to attain clarity and to bring an end to the arguments presented by the Jains, had a leaf that bore the true essence. When asked what that true essence was, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, in this verse, tells the king that true knowledge is love for the Lord, so that the king may understand.

“Therefore, the divine Sekkizhar Peruman concludes by stating that love directed towards Shiva is the ultimate truth, saying, “Knowledge is love for the Lord.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, in his verse, (Peruman Perumanum Anre) In this verse, he proclaims that the Lord, who bestows grace upon us as our master and primal being, is Shiva alone, and no one else.

“Therefore, the divine Sekkizhar Peruman highlights the message of this pathigam, stating that it is the duty of these souls to love Shiva. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is one who has attained wisdom; therefore, he concludes that Shiva’s wisdom is the essence, and all else is ignorance.

“Now, the twelfth verse of the Thiruvasuram pathigam, which serves as the Thirukkadaikkappu and phalashruti, is as follows: (Nallargal ser pugazhi gnana sambandha nalla ellargalum paravum eesanai eththu padal pallargalum madhikka pasuran sonna patthum vallargal vanor) (Ulagalavum vallarandre) This verse means that the ten verses composed by Gnanasambandhan, who was born in Sirkazhi, known as Pugazhi, where virtuous Shiva devotees reside, praising Shiva, who is revered by all good people, are sacred hymns that are respected by many. Those who are capable of reciting them will attain the power to rule the heavenly realms. For this verse, this Thirukkadaikkappu verse, the divine Sekkizhar Peruman provides an explanation in the eight hundred and forty-fifth verse. That verse is as follows: (Veriyar pozhil shanbayar vendhar meippasurathai kuriyeriya ellai arindhu kumbittan allen siriyen arivukku avar tham thiruppadham thandha neriyey siridhu yan ari neerman kumbittan anbal endru) The divine Sekkizhar Peruman recites this verse.

“Sirkazhi is a sacred place surrounded by fragrant groves, and our Pillaiyar is its lord. This pathigam is the sacred hymn that reveals the true essence, composed by him. I am not capable of understanding and appreciating the divine essence of that sacred hymn. Nevertheless, I have offered this explanation. Due to my limited understanding, I have humbly bowed down and worshipped, following the path illuminated by the sacred feet of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, to the extent of my limited knowledge and out of love, says the divine Sekkizhar Peruman. The Thirukkadaikkappu of the Thiruvasura pathigam concludes the pathigam and bestows its benefits.

“This verse, which emerged to indicate its journey of grace, also serves as a grand commentary by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman for this pathigam, concluding it and revealing its essence and benefit. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman states, “I am insignificant, and my knowledge is limited.

“Therefore, my intellect cannot reach and grasp the full scope of Pillaiyar’s divine grace. Hence, with reverence, I bow down here, understanding it to the best of my limited knowledge. Although his sacred feet possess the power and compassion to reveal everything, my vessel of knowledge, this intellect, is small, so it can only contain In accordance with its small capacity, I am expounding the essence and meaning of this Thiruvasura pathigam and worshipping it. I possess neither the ability, knowledge, nor wisdom to do so, yet out of love, I bow, praise, and worship in this manner,” says the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, thus completing his grand commentary on the Thiruvasura pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

“Now, let us continue to contemplate the sacred history of how Pillaiyar placed the palm leaf bearing this Thiruvasura pathigam in the Vaigai River, and it flowed against the current of the river.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Seven Hundred and Forty-Five, by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, in the section on Vambara Varivandu, the story of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. Long live Thirugnanasambandha Peruman! In the Thiruvasura pathigam that begins with “Andhanar,” the divine Sekkizhar Peruman revealed the truths of Saiva Siddhanta Shivagamas and their profound meanings. He wrote them on a palm leaf and placed it in the floodwaters of the Vaigai River in Madurai.

At this point, the divine Sekkizhar Peruman provided a detailed commentary on that Thiruvasuram.

Now, let us continue to contemplate how the leaf placed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the leaf on which the Thiruvasura pathigam was written, traveled against the flow of the river’s current. Peruman recites that sacred narrative. The Jains proposed a water debate, stating that one should write their religious truths and place them in flowing water. When placed, the leaf should not flow with the current but remain stationary.

However, here, the leaf written by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman not only remained stationary instead of flowing with the current but also swam against the current. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman recites the forty-sixth verse as follows: (Thiruvudai Pillaiyar tham thirukkaiyal itta edu maruparum piraviyattrin mathavar manam sendral pol poruppunal vaigai aatril edhirndhu neer kizhiththu pogum) (Iru nilathorukkelam idhu porul endru katti) This verse declares that this is the truth for all people on Earth. Pillaiyar possesses divine Saiva essence, and thus the divine Sekkizhar Peruman sings, “Thiruvudai Pillaiyar.” Thiru refers to the divine Saiva essence, the grace, and the liberation.

Here, by composing the Thiruvasuram and imparting divine knowledge, Pillaiyar eradicated other religions and fostered Saivism, bestowing Shiva-gnanam. Hence, the divine Sekkizhar Peruman sings, “the leaf placed by Thiruvudai Pillaiyar with His sacred hand.” The leaf placed by Pillaiyar, who possesses the Saiva essence, with his sacred hand, demonstrates that this is the true essence for all, in the Vaigai River with its abundant flowing water, by going against the current of the water. It moves upward, tearing through the middle of the water. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman offers a simile to explain how it moves: “The leaf travels as the minds of great ascetics go against the current in the river of birth.” He offers a wonderful simile. Birth is a continuous, uninterrupted cycle.

Therefore, the divine Sekkizhar Peruman refers to birth as a river. The second Sutra, third Adhikaranam of Shiva Gnana Bodham states that this birth continuously comes without interruption, fitting the karma of living beings. In this river of birth, how do the minds of great ascetics travel? They go against the current of that river of birth. Great ascetics are those who adhere to the path of Shiva, which includes Chariya, Kriya, Yoga, and Gnana. Adhering to the path of Shiva is considered asceticism.

All other practices are conducive to these to that extent and are metaphorically called asceticism. Anything other than this is considered futile. Only the path of Shiva has the power to enable living beings to ascend instead of traversing the path of birth.

Therefore, in this river of birth, the minds of great ascetics tend to go against the current. The minds of others, however, follow the senses, leading to repeated births and making it impossible to escape from the cycle of birth.

Thus, others’ The mind follows the senses and becomes the cause of birth. However, the minds of those who have performed great penance will bring these senses under their control.

Thus, they are capable of overcoming birth. We have contemplated in the twelve hundred and seventh verse that they are those who keep their five senses under control.

Therefore, just as the minds of great ascetics go against the current in the river of birth, the leaf also goes against the current. If it goes in the Vaigai River, it shows all who live that this is the imperishable truth. The Jains asked them to write down the truth of their religion. In accordance with that, this leaf travels, demonstrating that the Shiva Gnana, which expounds the three fundamental principles of Saiva Siddhanta, Is the imperishable truth. The Thiruvasuram composed by Pillaiyar revealed this truth. The leaf on which the Thiruvasuram was written also revealed the truth in the same way.

Pillaiyar is endowed with grace, so he will reveal the truth. On the very day he was bestowed with Shiva Gnana, he revealed the truth, proclaiming, “He is the Lord.” Therefore, it is natural for Thirugnanasambandha Peruman to reveal the truth. Even the leaf placed by his sacred hand reveals that truth. This is because it was placed by his sacred hand that it reveals the truth in this manner. That leaf reveals the truth to all beings from heaven to earth. The next sacred The verse, the eight hundred and forty-seventh verse, is as follows: (Empiran Sivane ella porulum endru ezhuthum ettil thampran arulal vendan thannai mun onga pada ambuya malaral marban anabayan ennum seertthi sembiyan sengol enna thennan koondhu nimirndhadandre) This verse means: “As Thirugnanasambandha Peruman wrote in the leaf, ‘Our Lord Shiva is all things,’ by the grace of the Lord, he sang for the king to flourish.

“The fame of Anapayan, whose chest bears the lotus flower, like the just rule of the Chola king, the Pandian king’s hump straightened.” In that leaf, he wrote, “Our Lord Shiva is all things.” This signifies the primordial nature of Shiva. It denotes the omnipresent nature, filling all objects, animate and inanimate. This signifies His all-pervading nature, filling all things. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman’s previous statement, “The Lord is the creator of all things,” also comes to our mind here. This is the grace of the primal being, the essence of the Thiruvasuram, and it highlights the overflowing compassion, a state placed at the heart of that Thiruvasura pathigam. In that pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sang for the king to flourish.

“He sang, “May the Brahmins, the celestials, and the cows live long, may abundant water fall, and may the king flourish.” In that first auspicious verse, the term “king” generally refers to all future rulers. “May the king flourish” signifies the flourishing of the king’s righteous rule. This Here, at this time, it specifically refers to the Pandian king. Although the word “king” generally refers to all succeeding monarchs, the first among those to be blessed is this king, this Pandian king.

“Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sang for the king to flourish. Until now, he had been associated with Jainism, but now, touched by Pillaiyar and adorned with holy ash, his past karma is removed, and he stands united in knowledge of the primal being. He has attained the state of Iruvinai Oppu, Malaparipakavam, and Shakti Nipadam. Having attained this state, the king now becomes worthy of receiving divine knowledge through this Thiruvasura pathigam.

“Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman bestows grace, saying, “May the king flourish.” This “may he flourish” Signifies the spiritual well-being and excellence of the king.

“Furthermore, by the power of that word, the king’s hump straightened, and his body became upright. This king, the consort of Queen Mangaiyarkarasi, who had been associated with Jainism in the Pandian kingdom, had his fever cured by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman through the debate on fever, and was then adorned with holy ash. Until then, he was known as the Humpbacked Pandian due to his physical deformity.

“Now, immediately upon the recitation of the Thiruvasuram, he becomes Nindra Seer Nedumaran, his hump straightened. Until now, he was called the Humpbacked Pandian due to his physical deformity.

“Now, his hump is straightened, and he becomes Nindra Seer Nedumaran.

“Moreover, he shines as Nindra Seer Nedumara Nayanar, one of the sixty-three Nayanmars, bestowing grace.

“Thus, the straightening of the Pandian king’s hump is a marvel of Pillaiyar’s graceful and truthful words. At the Thiruvoorthur temple, due to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s words, a male palm tree bore fruit; that narrative is yet to come.

“There, without even commanding, “Let the male palm bear fruit,” his divine and truthful words caused the male palm to bear fruit.

“Furthermore, in due course, souls attained special liberation by uniting with Shiva.

“Therefore, the blessings bestowed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, whose truthful and graceful words prevailed, The blessing, “May the king flourish,” bestowed upon the Pandian king, resulted in his hump straightening, and he became Nindra Seer Nedumaran. This is likened to the just rule of Anapaya Chola, who bears Lakshmi on his chest; just as Anapaya Chola’s scepter stands upright, so did the Pandian king stand upright as Nindra Seer Nedumaran. Anapaya Chola requested our divine Sekkizhar Peruman to compose the Periya Puranam, also known as Thiruthondar Puranam. Due to this request, we have received this sacred text of knowledge. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman praises such a distinguished Anapaya Chola in eleven places in the Periya Puranam, and this verse is one of those eleven. Anapaya Chola was known by many names, such as Kulothungan, Abayan, and Thiruneetru Chola.

“Even though he had many names, the author primarily uses the name Anapayar here. Just as the scepter of such an Anapaya Chola stands upright, so too did the Pandian king’s hump straighten and become erect. The straightening of the scepter signifies a good reign, a righteous rule.

“Therefore, here, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, by singing “May the king flourish,” transformed the hunchbacked Pandian into Nedumara Nayanar.

“Similarly, by narrating this story, the divine Sekkizhar Peruman blesses the righteousness of Anapaya Chola’s rule, and we rejoice in witnessing the appropriateness, suitability, and tranquility of this here.

“Now, the next verse is the eight hundred and forty-eighth verse. (Edu neer edhirndhu sellum pozhudhu imaiyorgalellam neediya vazhthil potri nimirndha poomar thoorndhar adiyal yanai mannan arputham eythi nindran padu ser amanar anji pathaippudan panindhu nindrar) This is the next verse. When the leaf placed by Pillaiyar flowed against the current in the Vaigai River, as mentioned earlier, all the celestials praised it with prolonged blessings and showered abundant flowers, covering the earth. The king with elephants, accustomed to dancing, stood amazed. The defeated Jains, terrified, stood bowing with trepidation. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman reveals to us the situation there.

“Let us press on with our contemplation.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Seven Hundred and Forty-Six, by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, in the section on Vambara Varivandu, the story of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. The leaf placed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is traveling against the current of the river, isn’t it? To follow and retrieve that leaf, Kulachirai Nayanar mounts a horse and rides swiftly like the wind, pursuing the leaf as it proceeds.

At that moment, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composes a pathigam, so that the leaf may come to rest, as the leaf, continuously moving against the flow of the water, needs to stop at one place. (Edagam Pillaiyar tham vanni endreduthu pada kudia neeril edu Kulachirayarum koodi kadu idamaga adum kannudhal kovil madu needu neer nada) (Aduvul pukku nindra edu edutthukondar) This is the eight hundred and fiftieth verse. Pillaiyar sang with a divine command for the leaf to stop. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sang, intending for this leaf to travel against the current of the river. It did indeed travel against the current. It is continuously traveling against the current without stopping anywhere.

Therefore, a command must be given for the leaf to stop, and a song must be sung. It is in this situation that Kulachirai Nayanar finds himself.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sings for the leaf to stop. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman mentions that the pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for the leaf to stop begins with “Vanni.” It is the pathigam for the sacred place called Thiruvedagam, a pathigam that begins with “Vanniyum Matthamum.” The leaf that traveled against the current of the Vaigai River, did it not? That leaf went through the water. Kulachirai Nayanar rode very fast on his horse along the bank of the Vaigai River, following that leaf.

At that time, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed a pathigam for the leaf to stop.

Then the leaf stopped at a certain place. That sacred place is called Thiruvedagam. This sacred place is on the bank of the Vaigai River, located northwest of Madurai.

Therefore, the Vaigai River originates from the mountains in the west, flows into the plains, and enters Madurai through villages like Thiruvedagam and Cholavandan. So, the leaf placed in Madurai was traveling against the river’s current. We saw that it traveled against the current. That path it took is the path where the Vaigai River flows abundantly. That area is located west-northwest of Madurai. The sacred place there is called Thiru Edagam.

The temple in that sacred place is situated on the northern bank of the Vaigai River. In that area, this leaf stops. Since Thirugnanasambandha Peruman commanded, “Let the leaf go and settle,” that leaf stops at this place, neither going further against the current nor flowing with it. Kulachirai Nayanar takes it with his sacred hands. Kulachirai Nayanar takes that leaf, places it on his head, bows down, and celebrates it. The place where that leaf stopped is called Thiru Edagam.

We have seen that this is the fourth of the fourteen Thevaram-sung temples in the Pandian kingdom. The Thevaram states, “Edagam, which is situated on the northern bank of the Vaigai.” Kulachiraiyar rode from Madurai along the bank of the Vaigai River towards the west at a very high speed and, by the command of Pillaiyar, retrieved the Thiruvasura leaf that had traveled against the current and stopped there. Pillaiyar’s pathigam for this temple must have been known as “From the banks of the Vaigai in Madurai, where the water debate with the Jains took place.” Accordingly, due to the divine grace, the event of the leaf going and settling further enhanced the significance of that name. We can understand from Thevaram verses like “Maniya maraiyavar vazhipada” and “Sedanur” that an ancient temple already existed in that place. And “Ezhaiyodu ezhil perum kolamar.” Since Thirugnanasambandha Peruman specifically mentioned “Vanni” in the pathigam that begins with “Vanniyum Matthamum,” this place is considered to have the special significance of Vanni. The name of the Lord is Edaganatheswarar, and the name of the Goddess is Umadeviyar, also known as Elavar Kuzhali and Sugandha Kundalambigai.

The sacred tank is Brahma Theertham, the Vaigai River. Brahma, Vishnu, Adisesha, Garuda, Vyasa, and Parashara have all worshipped here. Bathing in Brahma Theertham and worshipping the Lord is the unique greatness of this place, as it cures mental delusions. Festivals like Panguni Uthiram are celebrated grandly. The festival of the leaf going against the current is celebrated on the first day of the month of Aavani. This place is mentioned in inscriptions as Baganur Kothaththu Thiruvedagam And the name of the Lord as Thiruvedagamudaya Nayanar.

At such a place, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman commanded the leaf to stop, and the pathigam that begins with “Vanniyum Matthamum” is the thirty-second pathigam of the third Thirumurai, composed in Kollipenn. The first and concluding verses of that pathigam are as follows: (Kodu) (Maniya Maraiyavar Vazhipada Adiyar Innisai Padala Edagaththu Orvane Kodu Sanam Pagil Pondu Vaigai Neer Edu Sendru Anai Tharum Edagaththu Orvanai Nadu Thenpugazhiyum Gnana Sambhandan Padal Pathu) The pathigam indicates that the leaf, which went against the current of the Vaigai River by command, reached and settled at Edagam. We can also recall here that the divine Sekkizhar Peruman announced that the leaf would stop. The Thirukkadaikkappu of this pathigam, “Edu Sendru Anai Tharum Edagam,” is also arranged in the same manner.

This pathigam was composed and commanded by Pillaiyar while he was staying on the banks of the Vaigai River in Madurai.

Thus, when the leaf stopped there, Kulachirai Nayanar picked it up and, with immense joy, Dances with joy, placing it on his head. (Thalaimisai vaiththu kondu thangarun magizhchi ponga alaippunal karaiyil eri angu inidhamarndha meru silaiyudaiyavar thazh potri meendu sendru anaivar dhaivamaimalai magal kuzhaitha gnanam undavar thambal vandhar) This is the verse composed by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman. That leaf is a great symbol of knowledge, so Kulachirai Nayanar places it on his head, the most esteemed part of his body. Having taken the leaf and come ashore, Kulachirai Nayanar worships Shiva, who is enshrined there, the primal leader of this victory of knowledge, just as He burned the three cities.

Then Kulachirai Nayanar returns to Madurai. Kulachirai Nayanar arrives at the bank of the Vaigai River, where Pillaiyar was staying. (Matra avar Pillaiyar tham malaradi vanangi potri kotravan muthalai ullor kana mun konarndha edu patriya kaiyil endhi panbinal yarukkum katta atrarul petra thondar araoli ezhundhadandre) This is the eight hundred and fifty-second verse. Kulachirai Nayanar bows down and praises Pillaiyar’s lotus-like feet. This act was performed by Pillaiyar’s command.

Therefore, the king and others are the ones who need to see it.

Thus, the chief minister, Kulachirai Nayanar, displays the leaf he carried on his head, holding it in his hand, for the king and all others present to see. He shows it to everyone in the assembly, including the Jains and others, so that they may understand it according to their respective understanding. Seeing this, the king, who was the victor, had to declare the outcome of the debate.

So, he showed the leaf to everyone, including the king. The king and those present in the assembly, who were blessed devotees capable of perceiving the manifestation of divine grace within it, all chanted “Hara Hara, Hara Hara.” That sound arose spontaneously, not through effort. The sound “Hara Hara” arose instantly upon seeing the leaf. Those who chanted “Hara Hara” upon seeing that leaf were those who had severed all attachments, both worldly and otherworldly. They were the devotees of the Lord of Alavai, Chokkanatha Peruman, just as He was initially praised as Shiva who is for those who are detached. They chanted “Hara Hara.” Let us proceed with our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Seven Hundred and Forty-Seven, by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, in the section on Vambara Varivandu, the story of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. Kulachirai Nayanar shows the palm leaf of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s Thiruvasuram to the king and others.

The devotees raise the chant of “Hara Hara.” Now, the Jains are defeated in their debates.

Furthermore, they attempted murder by setting fire to the monastery where Pillaiyar and his devotees were staying.

Therefore, the Pandian king orders the minister Kulachirai Nayanar to impale the Jains. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman narrates that sacred history. (Mannavan Maran kandu mandhiriarrai nokki thunniya vadil otti thotra isamanar thangal munnamae Pillaiyar) (Anusithamutra seidhar konnunai kazhuvil etri murai seiga endru koora pugazhiyil vandha gnana pungavar adhanai kettum ikalilar eninum saivar irundhu vazh madathil theengu thagavila samanar seidha thanmaiyal salum endre migaiyila vendhan seigai vilakidhadhu irundha velai panbudai amaichanarum parulor ariyamaatral kanbudai pattu neenda kazhutharri niraiyil etra nanbudai madathu thee nadia kundrathu ennnayiravarum erinargal) These are three verses (eight hundred and fifty-four, eight hundred and fifty-five) composed by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman. The king, Maran, is mentioned here by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman. Although “Maran” is a general title for Pandian kings, here the divine Sekkizhar Peruman uses it to imply that this Pandian king has shed falsehood and found truth, transforming from a hunchbacked Pandian associated with Jainism to Nindra Seer Nedumaran Nayanar, who stands tall in the Saiva faith. He is now about to dispense justice.

Therefore, King Maran addresses Kulachirai Nayanar, the minister, saying that these Jains, who initiated and lost this debate, are liable for punishment as they themselves agreed.

Furthermore, they had previously committed many improprieties against Pillaiyar.

Therefore, the king orders the minister Kulachirai Nayanar, “Impale these Jains and administer justice according to the law.” The Jains had willingly accepted this debate. They failed to cure the king’s fever, lost the fire debate, and lost the water debate. They had previously told the king that if they lost the debate, they should be impaled. They agreed to this.

Thus, seeing their leaf float with the current and Pillaiyar’s leaf go against it, they were defeated. However, their defeat alone was not the reason for the king to administer justice by ordering their impalement. There was another significant reason. That was an unacceptable and improper act. They deceitfully set fire to the monastery where Pillaiyar and the Shiva devotees were staying, attempting to burn the devotees alive. They deceived the king and committed this act, this crime.

This crime is punishable by death.

Therefore, the king commanded that justice be carried out according to the law. This was an act of royal justice by the king, a judicial ruling. It was not merely a punishment for the Jains losing the debate. Even if they had only lost the debate, and even if they had agreed beforehand that they would be impaled, a judge would typically reduce the punishment and administer justice accordingly. It has always been the custom.

However, the king is administering this punishment as royal justice for the horrific act of terrorism committed by the Jains, which was far worse than merely losing the debate. Even if they had only lost the debate, and even if they had agreed beforehand that they would be impaled, if that were the only reason, lighter punishments such as exile instead of capital punishment like impalement could have been imposed.

But they did not just do that; that was not the only reason. They attempted to kill people by setting fire to a place where ordinary people were staying, an unjust act, an illegal act, a criminal act. They tried to set fire to a residential house and attempted to burn people to death. All these were done without any reason. These are the blasphemies committed against the Shiva devotees, which led the king to pronounce the death penalty by impalement. This punishment of impalement was a common form of punishment in ancient times.

Moreover, in Jain religious traditions, impaling oneself and ending one’s life when facing disgrace to their religion was also a custom.

Therefore, there is no fault of cruelty or harshness in the king’s administration of justice in this manner.

Furthermore, we must understand that the king did not act in this manner due to religious bias.

Therefore, Pillaiyar, the Shaivites, or any Shaiva religious affiliations have no responsibility or connection to this. We must clearly understand that only royal justice was exercised here. The ethical text Thirukkural states that a king punishing cruel people with death is akin to a farmer weeding out weeds from a field of good crops. This is the five hundred and fiftieth Thirukkural from the chapter on Righteous Rule (Sengonmai). It means that a king must protect worthy people in the country by punishing cruel people with the death penalty. It is like a farmer who removes all the weeds and protects the good crops.

Therefore, a king must protect worthy people by imposing the death penalty on cruel individuals and removing them.

Here, Parimelazhagar explains who these “cruel people” are in his commentary on the word “cruel.” Parimelazhagar explains that these include those who set fire to people’s dwelling places, those who administer poison, those who steal by means of instruments, thieves, attackers, those who cause shortages, and those who indulge in illicit affairs.

Thus, Parimelazhagar lists arsonists as the first among these evil-doers. He also states that northern scholars refer to these individuals as “adhatayis.” If these cruel people are not executed, righteous people in the country will suffer greatly and face many hardships.

Therefore, Parimelazhagar explains this act as a Kshatriya Dharma, a righteous duty of a king. Parimelazhagar explains that it is the duty of a king to punish evil-doers with death and protect the virtuous; this is a part of righteous governance and kingship, in his commentary on Thirukkural by Thiruvalluvar.

Therefore, we must realize that there is no injustice or mistake in the eight thousand murderers who plotted to kill thousands of people by arson receiving the death penalty. Sivakavimani Desikanar, in his commentary on this section, has very clearly explained various controversies that arose concerning this part. We can read and learn more from them.

Thus, the king seeks that royal justice and order. Gnana-Pungavar, the child who came to Sirkazhi, Pillaiyar, the chief among the wise, hears the king’s command. Although Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who is the wisest, possessed the wisdom to explain this royal decree leading to the death penalty, and the mental purity to carry it out, he did not explain it. This is because these Jainas had committed great offenses against the devotees of Shiva, and therefore, Pillaiyar remained silent so as not to overstep the bounds of justice set by the king. Kulachirai Nayanar, the great minister, received this as a royal command. He was a minister capable of ruling well and protecting the world.

He knew that an offense against Shiva is a heinous crime and that just as Daksha’s head was removed, that alone is punishment.

Also, if kings punish criminals here in this world, these criminals will not suffer hellish punishments, as various Smritis of our land declare. According to this, even if the king here does not punish them, they will suffer in hell. If they are to avoid such hellish suffering, they must accept the royal punishment here. That is the way for them to escape the pain of hell and be saved. The great minister was aware of all these principles.

Therefore, the great minister carries out this royal justice and its truths so that the world may see, understand, and follow the path of righteousness to be saved. There are many types of punishments. All punishments except the death penalty are intended to reform the criminal and those in the world who observe the judicial process. With the death penalty, the criminal is killed by royal command, so only those in this world who witness it are reformed. It is a truth stated in various legal texts that those who are executed by the king will be freed from the hellish punishment of God in the afterlife. The king also acts according to the grace of God.

If mortals on earth commit grave sins, he punishes them severely and justly.

Then, those who are pure will follow the path and will not join the assembly of the pure, which is the righteousness before righteousness. This is what the thirty-second verse of the second Sutra of Sivagnana Siddhiyar states about this truth.

Therefore, rows of stakes were erected there for the impalement of those eight thousand people. Kulachirai Nayanar implemented the king’s command there. Hearing Kulachirai Nayanar’s order, the Jainas were impaled on the stakes according to that command. The eight thousand Jain gurus were impaled here. These gurus lived in caves, with a thousand gurus in each of the eight hills surrounding Madurai, such as Anaimalai. These Jain gurus were impaled by the king’s order and due to their religious principles.

The general public, who were other Jain followers, were kept safe from any harm. This punishment applied only to those Jain gurus. We must understand that the people who followed Jainism were not subject to this punishment. We also see here that all these Jain followers later became Saivites and were saved. The eight thousand Jainas who lost the debate were impaled. The stakes on which they were impaled, which everyone witnessed, served as pillars of victory signifying the Jainas’ defeat in the debate.

They also stood as flagpoles, demonstrating to the world the truth that there is no God other than Shiva. They also served as pillars of victory, proclaiming the glory of Pillaiyar, revered by the world.

Thus sings Devasekhizhar Peruman in the 857th verse.

Then, the prosperous ones generously offered the sacred ash to the King. He bowed, received it, and applied it all over his body. When the King wore the sacred ash, all the residents of Madurai, who had stood trembling, also wore the sacred ash. This is the verse. Pillaiyar, the chief of Sirkazhi, bestowed sacred ash upon the Pandiyan king. The king bowed to Pillaiyar, accepted it, and applied it all over his body.

He applied the sacred ash according to the prescribed rules. Because the king wore the sacred ash, all the people living in his city of Madurai also applied that sacred ash.

Let us dwell further on this. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 748, authored by Devasekhizhar Peruman, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. The king and the other people of Madurai city received and wore the sacred ash given by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. When the king, having adorned his body with sacred ash, became pure and content, justice and Vedic justice prevailed everywhere. The world became pure as the widespread light of the sacred white ash cleansed it, and the darkness of Jainism vanished.

Thus, Devasekhizhar Peruman sings the 858th verse. Pillaiyar, having received the sacred ash as medicine for his body, applied it. He became pure and content. He completely anointed himself with the sacred ash as both armor and medicine. Earlier, when Marulneekkiyar, who was afflicted with colic disease bestowed by God, arrived from Jainism, his elder sister Thilagavathiyar, similarly, recited the holy five-letter mantra and instructed him, then gave him the sacred ash. The story of Marulneekkiyar humbly accepting the sacred ash, applying it extensively to his body, and being saved, thereby becoming Thirunavukkarasar Peruman, comes to our mind here.

We saw there, “When Thirunavukkarasar accepted the sacred ash given by Thilagavathiyar, great prosperity came.” Here, we see that by applying the sacred ash, one attains purity. The saying “Sacred ash is purity” is a statement from Thevaram. When he applied the sacred ash in that manner, the justice spoken of in the Vedas, that Vedic justice, becomes the king’s justice and order there. When the king became pure, worldly order also became pure. Parimelazhagar has explained that doing what Vedic texts prescribe and avoiding what they forbid is righteousness.

Thus, the justice prescribed in the Vedic texts flourished there. All the people of Madurai, seeing Pillaiyar give sacred ash to the king and the king wearing it, all the people of Madurai received sacred ash from the sacred hands of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and wore it.

Therefore, the widespread light of the white ash prevailed there, and the darkness of Jainism vanished. Just as we saw earlier, “for the destruction of the shameful darkness of Jainism, which spread throughout Tamil Nadu, defaming it,” similarly now, that Jain darkness vanished, and the light of the sacred ash spread in all directions. “He gave life to the Pandya king, showed the true path, removed the great flaw of Jainism, and saved the whole world. The truth of Gnanasambandhar, thriving in his wisdom, brought about the path of Shiva, adorned with fragrant Konrai blossoms.” This is the 859th verse. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was the one who gave life to the Pandiyan king, who was like a fisherman, and showed him the true path. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman saved him by showing the true path and removing Jainism.

Here, we see the principle of Thirukkural: “Understand the attachment and abandon it.” If Thirugnanasambandha Peruman showed the true path, it means he delivered the holy verses of spiritual wisdom with divine grace, and also gave sacred ash.

Thus, he showed the true path, and as a result, the flawed Jainism, which caused immense harm, was removed. The great harms caused by Jainism include disrespecting the Vedas, disrespecting Saivism, and disrespecting devotees, which are offenses against Shiva. These were the flaws and harms caused by Jainism. These were offenses against Shiva that had no atonement.

Therefore, Jainism, which had caused such immense harm, was removed, and its power subsided and diminished. He took control of the king and saved the whole world. By guiding one king to the right path, he brought the whole world to the path of righteousness.

Thus, by making the king stand on that path, he made the whole world It was achieved. In this verse, Devasekhizhar Peruman uses the mantra-like word “ulakellam” (the whole world). “Ulakellam” is the true word, the wisdom-word, that Koothapperuman first bestowed upon Devasekhizhar Peruman. It is the holy five-letter mantra. Devasekhizhar Peruman, who began to sing Periya Puranam with the holy mantra “ulakellam” bestowed by God, places this mantra-word at rare and significant points where divine grace is revealed. This is one such instance.

When Sundaramurthy Swamigal recited the Thirunamasivaya pathigam at Thirupandikodumudi temple, he also used the word “ulakellam” as a holy mantra there. When Pillaiyar was given the pearl palanquin by God at Thirunelvayil Arathurai, he recited the five-letter mantra and ascended the pearl palanquin for the salvation of the world. Devasekhizhar Peruman had placed this mantra, “ulakellam,” at that central point of Periya Puranam for the salvation of the world.

Similarly, he concludes the final verse of Periya Puranam with “ulakellam” as the concluding word. This place is one of those rare and great places, and it is a very special place.

Here, too, at the place where Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s divine purpose of incarnation is fulfilled, Devasekhizhar Peruman has placed the mantra “ulakellam” bestowed by God. The truth of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is that he was graced with divine wisdom.

Therefore, his words of wisdom were the command of Shiva’s grace, as if they were his own words. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the child of awe, Kotur Thevaram has stated this.

Thus, the wise true path of Thirugnanasambandhar flourished and prospered in the world. The holy path of Shiva, adorned with Konrai garlands, then occurred.

Therefore, the meaning here is that the truth of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and the holy path of Shiva are one. It flourished and prospered here, abundantly in all beings, both in kind and in number. The truth of “May the name of God pervade all, and may the world be free from suffering” was uttered in the first verse of the holy verses, and it happened there. The bees, having tasted the honey from the Konrai flowers worn by God, sing in the Sevvazhi tune as divine knowledge grows.

Similarly, Pillaiyar, having partaken of the elixir of divine knowledge, became absorbed in it and sang songs of wisdom. The true path, that spiritual wisdom he spoke of here, flourished.

Therefore, the path of the Lord transpired and occurred. Devasekhizhar Peruman, who began by recounting the history of the Pandiyan kingdom, stating that the stable Saivite truth and Vedic tradition had deviated and changed to a wrong path, now presents the successful conclusion of that history with divine poetic excellence.

Here, the benefit of Pillaiyar’s incarnation, who was born as a boon from Thoniyappar to Sivapada Hrudayar, who performed austerities and worshipped to obtain a child who would reject other religions and restore the sacred ash, is explained. This is explained by Devasekhizhar Peruman in two hundred and fifty-nine verses, from verse 2498 to verse 2757 of Periya Puranam, and from verse 600 to verse 859 in Pillaiyar Puranam. These two hundred This constitutes the lifeblood and inner meaning for the Puranam and for this Periya Puranam, which is the Thiruthondar Puranam.

Therefore, Devasekhizhar Peruman now continues to describe how the path of righteousness progressed as Gnanasambandhar’s truth flourished in the following verses. Devasekhizhar Peruman then composes the next verse, stating, “Even though the Brahmins perform sacrifices and the celestials grant blessings, and the world’s joy is boundless, by uttering the name of the one who kicked Yama, the suffering of birth in the boundless ocean of existence is removed.” In the previous verse, Devasekhizhar Peruman sang that as Gnanasambandhar’s truth flourished, the path of righteousness progressed.

Now, he begins to explain how that happened in the verses that follow. This section, starting with this verse, describes how the path of righteousness came into being through Thirugnanasambandha’s truth, reiterating what was previously stated in the verse: “As Brahmins perform sacrifices.” Its first benefit is “May the Brahmins live long.” He blessed the Brahmins, and as a result of that truth, for the happiness of the world, it engaged in chanting and Shiva sacrifices.

Therefore, “Brahmins perform sacrifices” is its first benefit. Next comes “celestials.” As he stated in the first verse of the Thiruppasuram as an auspicious blessing, according to that, for the world to be happy as a result of that truth, due to the sacrifices that cause happiness, the benefit of sacrifice is rain. According to that mantra, during sacrifices, Indra, Varuna, and other deities invoked by the respective mantras, obeying Shiva’s command, bestow rain seasonably without fail.

Thus, the actions of those celestials who provide rain according to Shiva’s command are exalted here.

Next, the benefit is that the Lord flourishes in the path of righteousness.

Here, “Lord” refers to the King. As blessed in the first verse of the Thiruppasuram, “May the King also flourish,” as a result of that truth, the King rules righteously according to the codes of conduct prescribed by the Vedic and Sivagama scriptures given by the Lord.

The King himself follows the ethical principles of the Vedic and Sivagama scriptures established by the Lord and also makes his realm follow that path.

Thus, the world began to prosper. The next benefit, as stated by Devasekhizhar Peruman here, is that worldly happiness is boundless. This worldly happiness and the transient pleasures derived from rain and its products are explained. The king’s righteous rule sustains these worldly pleasures.

Therefore, this worldly happiness also began to grow boundlessly. This is the next benefit. Although there is boundless joy, the ultimate benefit is the removal of the suffering of rebirth. Those who indulge in these worldly pleasures do not completely relinquish attachment, and therefore, their cycle of rebirth does not cease. Only by relinquishing attachment can rebirth be stopped. Legal texts speak of the body being superfluous for those who have cut off rebirth.

Therefore, the benefit mentioned earlier was that worldly happiness flourished boundlessly. Even so, the removal of this suffering of rebirth is the ultimate benefit; all others are lesser benefits. The suffering of birth is the supreme purpose. To ensure that worldly happiness does not lead to an increase in birth, that suffering of birth must be removed, and the only way to do so is by chanting the sacred name. “Even if the five senses are joyful, and children and family are delighted, and the mind is happy, if one does not forget the five-letter mantra from one’s mouth and directs one’s thoughts to You, O Lord, one will not lose that liberation. Is this not Your greatness?” Pattinatthadi’s thought from Thiruvidaimarudur Mummanikkovai is explained here.

Thus, the world enjoyed happiness.

At the same time, to prevent the increase in birth that comes from such happiness, and to remove the suffering of birth, the reason for which is the name of Hara Hara, the sacred name of God, resounded there. The Lord, who kicked Yama to save Markandeya, is the only one who can remove the suffering of death, which is the suffering of birth. His name, who kicked Yama, was proclaimed, meditated upon, and chanted everywhere. This is the benefit of the truth of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who said, “May the name of God pervade all.” Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is the Supreme Spiritual Teacher.

Thus, the blessing of wisdom, born of his righteous state of mind, which he pronounced as an auspicious blessing in the holy verses, “May the Brahmins live long, may the celestial kingdom prosper, may the cool water fall, may the king rule, may all evil perish, may the name of God pervade all,” The wisdom-filled blessing, born of his pure intention, entirely fulfilled its purpose, as we see here. Although happiness was not lacking, the world obtained freedom from the suffering of birth by chanting God’s name, which is the result of Pillaiyar’s truth. Wealth is also found among the wealthy.

Therefore, when wealth comes, worldly people fall into hell by not caring for God even a little. But here, due to the blessing of the wise teacher’s good intention, the people of Madurai obtained both wealth and, by chanting the name, freedom from the suffering of birth. This is the meaning of this verse sung by Devasekhizhar Peruman.

Let us go on pondering. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 749, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, authored by Devasekhizhar Peruman. We saw how this world was saved due to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s elimination of other religions and his elucidation of Saivism. Devasekhizhar Peruman now continues to sing the sacred history. “With Angaiyarkanni, the Lord resided in Aalavai. Bowing to His lotus-like feet, the King of Pugali arose and ascended the pearl palanquin.

“The Queen and the King also followed, praising Him.” This is the 861st verse. As soon as this divine event occurred, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, there in Madurai, declared that he would worship the lotus-like sacred feet of Lord Somasundarar, the benevolent Lord who resides in Thiruaalavai with Angaiyarkanni Ammai.

“So, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman rose from the banks of the Vaigai river, ascended the pearl palanquin, and proceeded to the Madurai temple. Mangayarkarasi Ammaiyar and Pandiyan King Nindrasir Nedumara Nayanar also followed him, praising Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. He declared, “I will worship the sacred feet of the Lord, who resides in Aalavai with Angaiyarkanni.” This was uttered by Pillaiyar with devotion. He said, “I am going to worship the sacred feet of the Lord.” Before going to the palace, Pillaiyar went directly from his hermitage to the Thiruaalavai temple, prostrated himself, and received the blessings of Lord Somasundarar by singing pathigams starting with “Veda Velvi” and “Katumana.” Then he proceeded to the palace and concluded the debate with the Jainas. All these debates were conducted according to the grace of Lord Somasundarar, and his actions were His actions.

“Therefore, after these debates were over, Pillaiyar, without going to the king’s palace or to his hermitage, went directly to the Thiruaalavai temple and declared, “I will worship that Lord.” He entered the Thirualavai temple to prostrate, as described in the pathigams starting with “Katumana” and “Veda Velvi,” and received the grace of Lord Somasundarar before proceeding to the palace to debate with the Jainas. All these debates were conducted under the guidance of Lord Somasundarar’s grace, and his actions were manifestations of His actions.

“Therefore, after these debates were concluded, Pillaiyar did not go to the king’s palace or back to his hermitage, but went directly to the Thirualavai temple to worship the Lord. This is praised as the nature of great souls, who, forgetting themselves, always remember God, as described in Koil Nanmani Malai: “Those who forget themselves and remember you.” Here, Pillaiyar’s state of mind, always worshipping God without forgetting Him, is revealed. In the debate, he vanquished the Buddhists and Jainas. The Lord, who rode the mighty bull, said earlier, “The sacred ash is perfect and firm.” He then declared, “Gnanasambandhan, having consoled the king and removed the fiery disease from his body, sang songs praising the sacred ash of Aalavayan.” He also declared, “Even if the mountain maiden’s beautiful breasts, which grew coolly, are fiery, they are not flawed.” He also uttered the sacred words: Even if Madurai gathers wealth, if the Karai river is held without attachment, and its nature is viewed impartially. Our good Lord, “What is this? Tell me,” he later praises and worships the Lord of Aalavai from Thirunallaru.

“Here, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman says, “I will worship the feet.” As Sivagnana Siddhiyar, ninth sutra, eleventh verse, says, “Meditate with wisdom, and then meditate here, praise outwardly, and worship.” To worship the Lord who was his inner companion and guide, out of gratitude, and to guide the world, Pillaiyar proceeds to the Thirualavai temple. From the banks of the Vaigai, he could have worshipped the Lord of Thirualavai, but Thirugnanasambandha Peruman did not do so. Although the Lord is omnipresent, in these two places—the devotee’s sacred form and the Shiva temple—He manifests clearly and permanently like ghee in curd, whereas in other places, He is unmanifest like ghee in milk. He can manifest brightly in some places and not in others. We see all this stated in the commentary on the twelfth sutra of Sivagnanabodham.

“Therefore, regarding the omnipresent God manifesting brightly in a Shiva temple, Pillaiyar proceeds directly from the banks of the Vaigai to the Thirualavai temple. Mangayarkarasi Ammaiyar and Pandiyan King Nindrasir Nedumaranar accompany him. We can see here that Devasekhizhar Peruman has placed Mangayarkarasi Ammaiyar first in his verses, out of respect. Devasekhizhar Peruman refers to the Lord of Thirualavai as “Annal” (Lord), quoting Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. “Annal” means one who is great. The greatness of the Lord of Thirualavai is that he consoled them not to fear, guided them, and accepted them as he was requested.

“Through this one act, he saved both the king and his entire country. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises this feat of the Lord as “Annal.” The devotees, experiencing immense joy beyond measure, praised the holy Pillaiyar and worshipped his feet. They saw the great benefactor who had come to save the world, and their eyes found their purpose. Kanninar Peruman composes the 862nd verse. All the devotees, whose greatness is beyond measure, rejoiced and praised Pillaiyar, who was the embodiment of Shiva’s good deeds. They worshipped Pillaiyar’s sacred feet and accompanied him.

“Just as the Lord’s greatness is beyond imagination, so too is the greatness of his devotees. The saying, “It is difficult to speak of the greatness of devotees,” comes to our mind here. All such devotees, praising Pillaiyar and worshipping his sacred feet, accompanied him. All these people were those who came with Pillaiyar’s holy retinue, those who served in the Madurai Aalavai temple, and those devotees from Madurai who, having understood the truth, had again worn the sacred ash. The assembled crowd there praised Pillaiyar. Pillaiyar is one who has no karma of his own that could lead to rebirth; he was born to save this world.

“He has no karma of his own. He came to save this world.

“Therefore, Devasekhizhar Peruman praises Pillaiyar as “Vallar” (benefactor) here. The people of Pandiya kingdom, who saw and rejoiced in Pillaiyar, attained the purpose of their eyes that day. Earlier, when Pillaiyar went to the Vaigai river for the debate, those who saw him proclaimed, “Our eyes have lived a full life.” At that time, before the water debate began, many people in the streets of Madurai who saw Pillaiyar spoke in various ways, according to their own level of understanding and maturity.

“Here, all the devotees praising Pillaiyar in this manner signifies the state of those who, having realized the truth, were immersed in his grace, accepted, and saved by wearing the sacred ash. Earlier, when Pillaiyar went for the water debate, only a part of the many who saw him praised him, saying their eyes had lived a full life.

“But now, all the people were touched by Pillaiyar, received the sacred ash, and realized the purpose of their eyes. Seeing the temple of Aalavai Annan from afar, Pillaiyar, with great devotion, bowed and went forward. Vishnu and Brahma praised him. Standing before the entrance of the Lord’s temple, where great ascetics resided, he dismounted from the palanquin and entered. This is the next holy verse. The 863rd verse.

“While returning from the banks of the Vaigai in the pearl palanquin to the Thirualavai temple, as soon as Pillaiyar saw the Lord’s temple in the distance, he descended from the palanquin. With utmost humility, he bowed and proceeded. Before the entrance of the Lord’s temple, where Vishnu and Brahma praise, and where virtuous devotees resided, he dismounted from the palanquin and entered the Thirualavai temple. Our Chempian’s daughter, the minister, and Gnanasambandar, having worshipped the lotus feet, entered with him. The leader of the saints, having circumambulated the holy temple, entered. This is the 864th verse.

“The Pandiyan king and Mangayarkarasiyar, the daughter of our Chola king, and Kulachirai Nayanar, the minister who guides the world to righteousness, entered the temple with Thirugnanasambandar, praising his red lotus-like feet. When referring to Mangayarkarasi Perumatti, Devasekhizhar Peruman uses the phrase “our Chempian’s daughter” with great affection. This is a special honor due to the growth of Saivism. Having composed this Puranam as desired by Anabaya Chola, being his minister, and considering the tradition of Rajaraja Chola who revealed the holy scriptures, and other such traditions, Devasekhizhar Peruman refers to Mangayarkarasi Perumatti with such endearment as “our Chempian’s daughter.” When beginning the Purana, he praises Mangayarkarasi Perumatti as “the sole queen among women, our goddess.” He also praises them as “those who spread the white sacred ash.” Thus, as they all praised Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and accompanied him, Pillaiyar, the leader of Sirkazhi, circumambulated the holy temple of the pure Lord and entered the temple. Generally, when entering a temple and within the temple, it is forbidden to think or praise anything other than Lord Shiva, according to the rules of Shiva temple worship.

“But here, the Pandiyan king, Mangayarkarasi Perumatti, and Kulachirai Nayanar are said to be praising Pillaiyar. Why is that? This arises from their gratitude towards their Lord and ancestral deity, Lord Somasundara of Aalavai, for having bestowed Pillaiyar and taken them as His own.

“Furthermore, there is a rule that one must worship the Acharya within the temple, and according to this rule, the actions of these three great individuals are perfectly fitting.

“Now, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman will continue to enter the temple, worship Lord Somasundara, and compose a pathigam. We shall continue pondering.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 750, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, authored by Devasekhizhar Peruman. Having entered the Thiruaalavai temple, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships Lord Somasundarar. “With hands raised above his head, tears of joy streaming from his eyes, his entire body bathed, he bowed to the Lord, the source of the Vedas, and praised him: ‘O Lord, O truthful one who can say to this servant, ‘Fear not,‘” he began to sing the Thiruppathigam “Veedalaalavai.” This is the 865th verse composed by Devasekhizhar Peruman. With both hands clasped above his head, and torrents of joyous tears flowing from both his eyes, drenching his entire body, he bowed and praised the Lord, the primeval source of the Vedas, saying, “O Lord, O Lord, the true being who can grant me refuge, saying, ‘Fear not,‘” thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sang the Thiruppathigam beginning with “Veedal Aalavai.” Devasekhizhar Peruman mentions, “His hands rose above his head.” His hands, without his effort, naturally rose and joined above his head. Tears flowed from his eyes, and that flood drenched his entire body.

Lord Aalavai Peruman resolved to vanquish those who slandered and wandered about, denouncing Vedic sacrifices.

Therefore, addressing Him as “Vedamudale” (Primeval Source of the Vedas), and also as “Aiyane” (O Lord, O Great One), he sang the Thevaram Thiruppathigam, saying, “Aiyane, grant me refuge, saying, ‘Fear not.’” He praises Him as “Meiyyane” (O Truthful One).

The Lord is the embodiment of truth.

Therefore, addressing Him as “Aiyane” and “Meiyyane,” he sings the Thiruppathigam beginning with “Veedal Aalavai.” This Thiruppathigam is the 52nd Thiruppathigam in the third Thirumurai, set to the tune of Kausigappann. The first, second, third, and eleventh verses of this Thiruppathigam are as follows: This Thiruppathigam is the third Thirumurai, the fifty-second Thiruppathigam, set in Kausikappann. The first, second, third, and eleventh verses of this Thiruppathigam are as follows: (Kadala Kapa) (Etti seyal thayagu Paakaiyalor Paagava) (Kotti seyal thal uththiya) (Kotti seyal thayaadalay) (Koodala vaayilay) (Etti seyal thurthiyaayirundhavaridhazh naye sutram nee gunangal koodalala vaayilay) (Sutri pranu nee thodarndhu ang Sodhini) (Katra noo karuthu nee aruttham ilvam illai) (Mutrum nee pugazhndhu mul nurai padhil mugam mane kulthayangiloli nalam kulirndha pul sadai pin thayangaaduvaay pinaga pirappini) (Kunrayam mudiyalaay koodala vaayilay) (Niyaadal kolum poruppudal pugazhiyaan panbinaal aay sollil maalai kol Aalavaayil al nali theeyatheera ezhuuvaargal thaiyaavar thevare theeyadi) The essence of the pathigam is that remembering your dance, performed for the salvation of humanity, is a sacred rule. In the sixth verse of this pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman refers to the Lord’s dance as “nin thayangi aadal.” This dance is the holy cosmic dance that Sivagnanis always witness, worship, and immerse themselves in the bliss of Shiva.

The five-fold cosmic dance, which encompasses the recreation of the world, etc., up to dissolution through grace, which is referred to as the five actions, is different. The “thayangi aadal” mentioned here is different. “Thayangiaadal” is the dance that Sivagnanis witness and revel in. This dance, described as “a single great dance of bliss arising from profound wisdom” and “the dance of bliss that arises in the true understanding of the possessed mind,” was enjoyed and realized by Aludaiya Pillaiyar and Thirumoolanaynar. Thirumooladeva Nayanar, in the section on Thirukkoothu Darisanam in the ninth tantra of Thirumantiram, has sung about this Sivananda Koothu under the headings Sundara Koothu, Porpathik Koothu, Porthillai Koothu, and Arputha Koothu, starting with “Everywhere, the divine body, everywhere, Shiva Shakti.” Thus, this pathigam is structured. Devasekhizhar Peruman then continues, “I have no other understanding.

“The beautiful form that fills everywhere, praised by the four Vedas, for the salvation of humanity, your act of performing the dance of grace, remembering it is my sacred duty.” Thus, Devasekhizhar Peruman narrates the history of singing this pathigam in these words. Devasekhizhar Peruman describes the history of this pathigam: “I have no other understanding or attachment. The beautiful form, filling everywhere, in Thiruchitrambalam, praised by the four Vedas, you perform the dance of grace for the salvation of humanity. To ceaselessly remember this is my sacred duty.” With this sentiment, the king of Poompugali sang this sweet Tamil pathigam.

“Thus, Devasekhizhar Peruman sings. Having entered and worshipped the Thirualavai temple, the blessed Pillaiyar sang the pathigam and praised the Lord. In this verse, Sekizhar Peruman explains that sentiment. In the next verse, he explains the sentiment with which the king praised the Lord.

“After that, Devasekhizhar Peruman successively sings about Pillaiyar going to his hermitage and the king going to his palace. In this pathigam, we see Devasekhizhar Peruman’s unique way of explaining the dance praised by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman in the sixth verse in a separate verse as a commentary. We can see here the beauty of Devasekhizhar Peruman’s commentary on that sixth verse. Devasekhizhar Peruman composes the next verse: “The king bowed and stood, saying, ‘O Lord residing in Thirualavai, I was deluded by the illusion of the Jainas and knew nothing of You. You granted me this grace, giving me Pillaiyar to cure my illness and take me as Your own.’” This is the Thiruppathigam. This pathigam describes how the Pandya king worships Lord Somasundara, as narrated by the great poet Sekkizhar.

“The Pandya king bows down, rises, and stands before the Lord enshrined in Thiruvalavai, praising him thus: “O Lord, I was deluded by the treachery of the Jains and knew nothing of your great grace. You, O Lord, cured my illness and took me into your fold, granting me the divine and gracious form of Aludaiya Pillaiyar.” The Pandya king prostrates himself on the ground, worshipping. The text notes that the Pandya king worshipped there, indicating that Lord Somasundara, the first ancestor of the Pandya lineage, protected this lineage from harm. This continues with a reference to the negative tendencies resulting from past actions, the consequent delusion, and the feverish illness that resulted. The Pandya king recalls all those events, remembering the immense grace the Lord bestowed upon him, manifesting as Pillaiyar and taking him into his service. The Pandya king worships, considering the gift of Pillaiyar as the Lord’s great grace.

“He prays with intense devotion, saying, “Instead of being angry at my evil deeds, you mercifully inflicted this illness upon me, then cured it, gave me instruction, and took me into your fold by anointing me with holy ash – all through your grace. Just as you have previously removed the troubles of my ancestors and taken them into your fold, so too have you taken me, O Lord.” We shall continue our reflection on this.

“Achchampalam” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, Part 751, by the great poet Sekkizhar, in the Vambara Varivandu Sarrkkam, narrates the life of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. As Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships Lord Somasundara in the Thiru Alavai temple, Mangaiyarkarasi Ammaiyar, the Pandya king, Kulachirai Nayanar, and all the other devotees are also worshipping there. This was a time when Pillaiyar’s fame successfully grew, highlighting the eminence of the devotees. Worshipping the Lord in the company of devotees is a great source of joy and blessing. The twelfth aphorism of Siva Jnana Bodham states that one should “abide with the loving.” The preface to Siva Jnana Siddhiyar says, “May we be with the devotees.” We must remember all these events.

This All the gracious events, such as the Jwaravadam, Analavadam, and Punalavadam, happened on that very day—that is, on a single day. When Pillaiyar set out from his monastery in the morning, the king was lying there with a severe fever. Pillaiyar, anticipating the debate with the Jains, went to debate them and, in order to defeat and destroy them, appealed to the Lord of Madurai Thiru Alavai. He then proceeded with the Lord’s clear intention. All these things happened. After all the debates were concluded, the removal of other religions and the flourishing of Saivism occurred.

Now, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman stands before the Lord. How the Lord’s Thiru Neelakandam, that sacred blue throat, warded off all the harm caused by the poison.

In the same way, he now restrains the venomous cruelties of the Jains from causing harm externally. Worshipping the feet of that Lord, he praises him with abundant grace and love. Having praised him thus, he moves away from there, moving away with difficulty, unable to part, filled with grace and love, and praising, he takes up residence in his monastery. The Pandya king is one of enduring glory. Previously, he was Koonpandya, and now he is Nindra Seer Nedumaran Nayanar. The honor he received, the distinction he attained, is that he is celebrated by the Saivite world as one of the sixty-three Nayanmars.

In the Thiruthondathogai, by our Lord Sundaramurthi Swamigal, He was praised as one of the devotees. Such was the great honor. That Pandya king and Mangaiyarkkarasi Perumatti are seated in Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s monastery and are worshipping Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Earlier, Pandi Mahadeviyar and the minister had come to the monastery for royal duties.

Now, the king and the queen have come along. They worship and sit at the feet of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman went directly into the Thiru Alavai temple, worshipped, and has now entered and settled in the monastery. After directly entering and worshipping inside the temple, unable to stop there, due to immense love, he continues to worship more and more.

Thus, with great With great devotion, while residing in that monastery, he sings a pathigam and worships. The pathigams composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for the sacred place of Madurai, known as Thiru Alavai, are of great excellence and are indeed wonderful pathigams. Among them, the pathigam beginning with “Mangaiyarkarasi” was composed when he first arrived in Madurai, as the Thiru Alavai temple became visible to his sacred eyes on the way near the city of Madurai, from outside the sacred city of Madurai. The second pathigam is “Neelama Midatru.” This pathigam was composed when he first saw the Lord in the Alavai temple and sang before the Lord. The pathigams beginning with “Kaatuma” and “Vedavelvi” were also composed. To know the Lord’s intention when departing from the monastery for the royal palace, after the king’s fever was cured and the Jain debate was won, these were composed before the temple.

The pathigam beginning with “Mani Nerveli” and the pathigam beginning with “Mandiramavathu Neeru” were composed in the king’s palace before the fever was cured. As mentioned here, “Alaneezhal” is a pathigam composed in the monastery at this moment. It is a pathigam structured in the Thiru Iyamagam style.

Thus, nine pathigams have been composed.

Now, while in Madurai, three pathigams were composed about other places. Among them, the Thiru Nallatru pathigam beginning with “Thalirilav Valaruli” was Sung before the king at the palace during the Analavadam. The pathigam beginning with “Bhogamartha” was composed. Two pathigams about Sirkazhi were composed from Madurai. Among them, the pathigam beginning with “Bramanur” was composed as an answer when the king asked, “What is your sacred place?” before his fever was cured in the royal palace.

Now, the pathigam “Mannil Nalla Vannam Vazhalam” is about to be composed. This pathigam was sung when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s father came to the monastery, remembering Thiruthoni Appar.

Thus, keeping the history of the pathigams in mind and contemplating them is beneficial. Regarding this, the author Siva Kavi Mani Desikan writes that Sekkizhar arranged and presented them at various places. The pathigam “Padagameladi” was composed in Thiru Nallatru.

Similarly, the pathigam “Veyur Thozhi Pangan,” though considered a general pathigam, was composed in Thirumaraikaadu, keeping Thiru Alavai in mind. We can see this connection.

Therefore, the pathigams related to Thiru Alavai are thus formed.

Now, the pathigam composed in the Thiru Iyamagam style, while in the monastery, worshipping Thiru Alavai Peruman, is explained by the great poet Sekkizhar in the 870th verse. Within the Thiru Iyamagam, Thiru Neelakanda The verse states: “He praised the grace bestowed upon Yazhpanar, conversed with him, and came to earth to dispel darkness, surrounded by truthful devotees, having seen the truth of devotion, and resided there blissfully.” This verse means that within the Thiru Iyamagam pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises the grace and compassion that the Lord bestowed upon Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar. Conversing with Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar, surrounded by many enlightened devotees, and seeing the enduring truth of devotion, Pillaiyar, delighted, descended to this earthly realm to dispel darkness and resided there blissfully. The pathigam thus composed begins with “Alaneezhal.” This pathigam is composed in the Thiru Iyamagam style. In this pathigam, a word or phrase, such as “irukkaiye irukkaiye,” is repeated twice in the middle of each line.

This is a type of poetic structure. In each line, a word, phrase, or phrases appear first in this manner. This poetic style is called Iyamagam or Madakku Santha Viyamagam, as the author previously referred to it, which we can recall. In this pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises the grace bestowed by the Lord of Thiru Alavai upon Thiruneelakanda Pananar. The section “Tharamuythathu Panarku Arulode” appears in the sixth verse of this pathigam. In it, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises how the Lord of Thiru Alavai.

Sokkanatha Peruman bestowed grace upon Thiruneelakanda Pananar. What is that story? Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar, from Thiru Erukathampuliyur, visited many holy places in the Chola country, worshipped, and then went to Thiru Alavai. From the entrance of Thiru Alavai, he played the Yazh.

At that time, the Lord of Thiru Alavai spoke to his devotees, saying, “Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar is playing the Yazh outside the temple. Bring him before me.” Thus, Sokkanatha Peruman graciously commanded the devotees.

The devotees did as commanded, and Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar, standing before the Lord, sang with great devotion. The Lord, hearing him, told his devotees to place a beautiful plank before the Yazh, saying that the Yazh played by Panar might be damaged by the cold ground.
