That is, the Lord graciously instructed his devotees to place a beautiful plank, explaining that if the Yazh, which Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar was playing, remained on the ground, it might be damaged by the coldness of the earth.

The devotees then placed the plank. Placing the Yazh on that plank, Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar played the Yazh and praised the Lord. This story is later narrated in detail in the Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Puranam by the great poet Sekkizhar, which we will see there.

Therefore, after this sacred event, Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar went to Thiruvarur, worshipped, and then came to Sirkazhi.

After that, he came to Sirkazhi, received Pillaiyar’s grace, and served with him until he was united with the Lord; that is the sacred history.

Thus, in the sixth verse of this Thiru Iyamagam pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman narrates the grace bestowed by the Lord of Thiru Alavai, Somasundara Peruman, upon Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar. Although this pathigam was composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar was with Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, playing the Yazh.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, recalling the grace bestowed by the Lord of Koodal, Madurai Sokkanatha Peruman, upon Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar even before, praised it here; that is the sacred history. The pathigam thus composed begins with “Alaneezhal.” This is the third pathigam. The 115th pathigam in the Thirumurai, composed in Pazhampancharam tune. The first verse of this pathigam, the sixth verse which narrates the grace bestowed by the Lord upon Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar Nayanar, and the eleventh verse are as follows.

(Neethagu boothane kodila mana may poothane aalumum ulla kalethane alavayurai allathane nakam medumoorume nadham mesumoo thakka poomanai sutra karude tharamuthu paadar karude) (Kannaval devi kani ye mella thondarkanani yetrin aaramuthum kannodume alavayarana umaiyodumeyana jnanigal thamuda veeragane yeru pal porul muthamizh veeragane aana kazhiyul jnana sambe alavayil meyana samba) This pathigam was sung in joy, expressing the grace bestowed by the Lord.

Our reflection now resumes. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, Part 752, by the great poet Sekkizhar, in the Vambara Varivandu Sarrkkam, narrates the life of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. While Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was residing in his monastery in Madurai, the Pandya king and the people of Madurai together removed all Jain symbols from the eight hills outside Madurai, where Jains, Jain gurus, Jain schools, and hermitages had been established. They purified and illuminated those places, making Saivite symbols shine there. They erected and decorated with Saivite symbols such as the Rishabha flag, trident, and Rishabha emblem. They ensured that Saivism flourished there.

During this time, the Pandya king, Mangaiyarkkarasi Perumatti, and Kulachirai Nayanar would daily visit the monastery where Thirugnanasambandha Peruman resided, bowing and praising his feet. Pillaiyar, the leader of Sirkazhi, continues to worship the feet of Lord Somasundara, who resides blissfully in Thiru Alavai, causing his entire being to melt with devotion. The Pandya king, Mangaiyarkkarasi Perumatti, and Kulachirai Nayanar rely on Pillaiyar’s feet. While these three great Nayanars rely on Pillaiyar’s feet, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman himself relies on the Lord’s sacred The feet were taken as his refuge.

Therefore, these three great Nayanmars—Nindra Seer Nedumaran Nayanar, the Pandya king; Mangaiyarkkarasi Ammaiyar; and Kulachirai Nayanar—accepted Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as their Guru and attained liberation through Guru worship. Among the types of worship mentioned in Saivism—Guru, Linga, Jangama worship—the Pandya king Nindra Seer Nedumaran Nayanar, Mangaiyarkkarasi, and Kulachirai Nayanar accepted Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as their Guru and attained liberation through Guru worship, thus shining among the sixty-three great Nayanmars. These three great personalities, meanwhile, attained liberation through Linga worship. The idea here is that the Lord bestowed grace upon those three great personalities, taking Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as the medium.

During this time, Sivapada Hiruthayar in Sirkazhi profoundly thought of Pillaiyar, his son, who was a Vaishnava Choodamani. Sekkizhar’s verse 873 states: “Staying in Sirkazhi, Sivapada Hiruthayar, through the penance he performed, remembered his son, the Vaishnava Choodamani, the great life of ascetics, and the great wealth that received the grace of the Lord with the dark throat, while he was in the flourishing Poompukali.” Sivapada Hiruthayar was a great ascetic. He had accumulated penance from previous births, and in this world, he had performed penance by worshipping Thoni Appar in Sirkazhi. Sivapada Hiruthayar, who had performed penance, thought very fondly of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, his son. His son, Pillaiyar, was the Vaishnava Choodamani, who had made the Vedic path flourish.

Furthermore, Pillaiyar embodied the great life of great ascetics, bringing prosperity to the Saiva faith. He was the great treasure who had received the grace of Lord Shiva with the dark throat.

Thus, he made the lineage of Bhutas flourish.

In this way, Sivapada Hiruthayar thought deeply about Pillaiyar, praising his son’s excellence. From the day he parted from Pillaiyar, he has been continuously thinking of him without interruption.

Now, the next verse is composed. The great poet Sekkizhar then composes the next verse: “He departed, saying, ‘I will know what happened to him who went to debate and defeat the disrespectful Jains who wronged the glorious Thirunavukkarasu, and to spread the sacred ash for the well-being of the Pandya king’s land.’” Sivapada Hiruthayar thought of the highly renowned Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. The disrespectful Jains were those who had wronged him. Pillaiyar had gone to debate and defeat them, and to spread the path of sacred ash for the prosperity of the Pandya kingdom.

Therefore, Sivapada Hiruthayar set out from Sirkazhi towards Madurai, saying, “I will learn of the virtues that occurred with Pillaiyar there.” Sivapada Hiruthayar heard from devotees about Pillaiyar defeating the Jains in debate. Sivapada Hiruthayar learns about the expansion of the path of sacred ash from the devotees.

Furthermore, Sivapada Hiruthayar had performed penance before Lord Shiva, wishing for a son to reject other religions. Sivapada Hiruthayar had requested a boon for the flourishing of the Saiva path and, for that, had requested and received a boon for a son. The avatar of Pillaiyar occurred because of these two boons.

Therefore, Sivapada Hiruthayar set out from Sirkazhi to meet Pillaiyar, with an overflowing love for him, desiring to learn all the virtues that Pillaiyar had manifested in Madurai, which were the fulfillment of those two boons he had sought and received. How did he set out? He worshipped Thoni Appar and Periya Nayaki Ammaiyar there, received their gracious permission, and then departed. The great poet Sekkizhar composes two verses at this point: “He bowed at the feet of the Lord residing in Thoni with the slender-waisted goddess, and then set forth from the blossoming Chanbai. Worshipping the numerous temples of the Lord on earth, he came to the rich land of the Pandya king with the sharp, long spear, and the great Brahmins, traveling through many prosperous towns, reached Thiru Madurai, the sacred city of the southern king, adorned with fragrant garlands, and humbly prostrated themselves with great devotion at the lotus feet of the unique Lord enshrined in Thiru Alavai.” Periya Nayaki Ammaiyar has a slender waist like a drum. Sivapada Hiruthayar worships the feet of Thoni Appar, the Lord residing in Thiru Thoni.

Sivapada Hiruthayar has the practice of worshipping Thoni Appar, who is enshrined in Thiru Thoni with the Goddess. He received Pillaiyar through the grace of Thoni Appar.

Therefore, he worships Thoni Appar and Periya Nayaki Ammaiyar and sets out from Sirkazhi. The land between Sirkazhi and the Pandya country is the Chola country. The Chola country is filled with countless Shiva temples. Compared to other countries, the Chola country has more Shiva temples.

Therefore, Sivapada Hiruthayar worships all the Shiva temples along the way and reaches Madurai. Those undertaking sacred journeys intend to travel. Without going directly to the temple, one should visit all the temples along the way; this is the custom for temple visits, which Sivapada Hiruthayar demonstrates to us here. Such a Sivapada Hiruthayar arrives in the great city of Madurai. The Pandya kings’ lineage is associated with traditions such as offering the spear, giving away the spear, and shooting the spear to dry up the sea. Sivapada Hiruthayar arrives in Thiru Madurai, where such Pandya kings rule.

Sivapada Hiruthayar, who has visited many Shiva temples until the Chola country border ends, and as soon as the Pandya country begins, there is the Maravar country in between. Leaving that, crossing it, and then until reaching Thiru Madurai in the Pandya country. There are some Shiva temples which he also worships before arriving in Madurai. It is mentioned by the great poet Sekkizhar that when Pillaiyar visited the Pandya country, the temple he visited along the way was Thirukodunkunram.

Therefore, Sivapada Hiruthayar visits these Shiva temples in the Pandya country, stays in the villages where Brahmins live, and continues his journey to reach Madurai. The Pandya kings wore neem garlands as their identifying garland. The neem garland possesses qualities such as sweetness, fragrance, and freshness. Sivapada Hiruthayar arrives at the Thiru Alavai temple in the Southern land of the Pandyas, who wear such neem garlands. Upon arriving in Thiru Madurai. Upon arriving, he immediately worships the feet of the unique Lord, enshrined in Thiru Alavai.

Lord Somasundara, enshrined in Thiru Alavai, is the unique Lord, the primordial God, the unparalleled God. He is the one who absorbs everyone into himself during the deluge and remains alone. To those who reach him, he will similarly bestow grace while remaining unique. Sivapada Hiruthayar worships the feet of such a glorious Somasundara. The feet, upon which gods and sages have scattered flowers, are worshipped by him with great enthusiasm. The great Brahmin, Sivapada Hiruthayar, is referred to as a great Brahmin by the great poet Sekkizhar.

Why? Because, despite his great eagerness to see his son, Pillaiyar, Sivapada Hiruthayar, who is coming, does not go straight to Madurai but comes worshipping the Lord in the temples along the way. Even upon arriving in Madurai, he does not go directly to meet his son, Pillaiyar, but first goes to the Thiru Alavai temple and worships the Lord with great devotion. After worshipping, he asks the devotees where Pillaiyar’s monastery is and then proceeds to the monastery.

Therefore, the great poet Sekkizhar praises him as a great Brahmin. Sivapada Hiruthayar has been separated from Pillaiyar for at least two years.

So, it has been two years since he separated from Pillaiyar, and therefore, his memory of him is intense. Nevertheless, Sivapada Hiruthayar, upon remembering him, does not go immediately.

First, he worshipped Thoni Appar, then worshipped all the Shiva temples along the way. Upon reaching Thiru Madurai, instead of going to Pillaiyar’s monastery, he went directly to the unique Lord enshrined in Thiru Alavai and worshipped his feet with great devotion. Only after that did he ask where the monastery was and went there. Even though he came with great affection for Pillaiyar and a desire to know his well-being, his eagerness and method of worshipping the Lord came first, and he maintained a disciplined life.

Therefore, the great poet Sekkizhar praises him as a great Brahmin. Sivapada Hiruthayar desired a child for his household life, but more than that, he performed penance primarily for the flourishing of Saivism, for the establishment of Saivism. We must remember that story here.

Therefore, for us ordinary people, who are deluded by worldly attachments like wife and children, mistaking them for the ultimate truth, if we reflect on this true household dharma and the true household discipline that Sivapada Hiruthayar embraced, and if we follow it, it will bring us well-being. Sivapada Hiruthayar, who had received wealth from Pillaiyar at Thiru Avaduthurai to perform Shiva sacrifices, left Pillaiyar with difficulty.

So, he went to Sirkazhi, taking wealth from Pillaiyar, primarily to ensure the flourishing of the Vedic path and the performance of Vedic and Shiva sacrifices. The fact that he left Pillaiyar means that he held the Saiva discipline dearer than his household dharma, clinging to it as his very life, that truth. We must remember that truth here. Such a great Brahmin, Sivapada Hiruthayar, worships the Lord Somasundara of Alavai with great devotion. What was that devotion? He had prayed to Thoni Appar in Sirkazhi, performed penance, and sought boons.

He had asked for a son who would reject other religions and establish Saivism, and Thoni Appar had granted the boon. The sacred purpose of Pillaiyar’s avatar was fulfilled here by Lord Somasundara, who is enshrined in Thiru Alavai.

Therefore, Thoni Appar granted the boon. Thiru Alavai Somasundara Peruman fulfilled it.

Therefore, Sivapada Hiruthayar, who came here thinking greatly of Pillaiyar, first worshipped Thoni Appar before setting out, and then, here in Madurai, he worshipped the same Thoni Appar in his mind, and then met Pillaiyar.

Thus, he worshipped with great devotion. Having worshipped the feet of Thiru Alavai Sokkanatha Peruman, he came out of the temple and asked the devotees there where Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s monastery was. Those devotees showed him Pillaiyar’s monastery, saying it was here.

Let us go on reflecting. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, Part 753, by the great poet Sekkizhar, in the Vambara Varivandu Sarrkkam, narrates the life of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. Sivapada Hiruthayar, having worshipped Lord Somasundara of Madurai Thiru Alavai, comes out of the temple. After coming out, he asks the Shiva devotees present there where Pillaiyar’s monastery is. There would have been many Shiva devotees inside the temple, but inside the temple, it is forbidden to speak of anything other than Shiva.

Therefore, out of respect for that tradition, after coming out of the temple, he asks the devotees outside where Pillaiyar’s monastery is. To this, the devotees replied, pointing to Pillaiyar’s monastery, “This is where Pillaiyar, the young lion of Sirkazhi, who opened our eyes and showed us the path of light, resides.” The Shiva devotees who said this explain that they were previously blind internally due to being in the Jain religion, and that through Pillaiyar’s grace, they gained knowledge and internal sight. This demonstrates the gratitude of the people of the Pandya country.

Thus, they showed him the beautiful lotus monastery where Pillaiyar resided. That monastery was like a lotus. The idea of the analogy we previously saw, “like the primeval child on the lotus,” is explained here. Where did we see this analogy? In the 1939th verse, when Pillaiyar took avatar and was in the cradle as a small child, the great poet Sekkizhar used the analogy “like the primeval child on the lotus.” Similarly, here, the great poet Sekkizhar praises Pillaiyar’s monastery as a beautiful lotus monastery. It is the place where Pillaiyar, who destroys false Saiva faith, resides.

Therefore, the monastery was called “Sengamalam.” That place is where groups of devotees of the sacred ash gather. By Pillaiyar’s act of prospering the sacred ash. That monastery is a place where groups of devotees of the sacred ash gather, understanding that their former attachments are destroyed and that this is their good attachment.

The devotees show him, saying, “This is such a monastery.” This is a nearby pointer, so the truth that the monastery is very close to the Thiru Alavai temple is also understood here.

Thus, Sivapada Hiruthayar, hearing what the devotees said, goes to the monastery. Those who saw Sivapada Hiruthayar there bowed at his feet and then conveyed the joyful news to Pillaiyar, who possessed unparalleled fame. Sekkizhar composes two verses here: “Hearing this, he went to the monastery. Appar had come. Those who saw him bowed at his feet. When they conveyed the joyful news to Pillaiyar, who had unparalleled fame, Pillaiyar, asking, “When did you arrive?” came forward to receive him.

“Sivapada Hiruthayar, who had worshipped earlier and gone ahead, bowed before him. Pillaiyar, in turn, worshipped his father, who had followed the path of penance. Seeing his lineage, Pillaiyar remembered the feet of Thoni Appar, who had resided in Thiru Thoni and severed worldly attachments.” Sivapada Hiruthayar goes to the monastery where Pillaiyar resides. Seeing him, the devotees and attendants there bow at his feet. They convey the news of his arrival to Pillaiyar. They convey that joyful news, bowing at Pillaiyar’s feet.

“At that moment, Pillaiyar comes forward, asking, “When did you arrive?” Sivapada Hiruthayar worshipped first and approached him. Pillaiyar also worshipped his father, who had followed the path of penance. Why? Because, seeing Sivapada Hiruthayar, Pillaiyar remembered the sacred feet of Thoni Appar, who had resided in Thiru Thoni in Sirkazhi with his divine consort, severing worldly attachments.

“Therefore, he worshipped him. When Sivapada Hiruthayar worshipped Pillaiyar, Pillaiyar, remembering his father’s lineage, worshipped Thoni Appar and Periya Nayaki Nachiyar, his father and mother residing in Thiru Thoni. Pillaiyar, who worshipped upon seeing Sivapada Hiruthayar, did not worship him as an earthly father, but rather, remembering Thoni Appar, who is the father and mother to all through his lineage, he worshipped. This is the state of great ones like Pillaiyar. That state is one where they only see the divine and not worldly things.

“Therefore, we can understand the subtlety that for them, the element that was hidden in the divine is the primordial being. The great poet Sekkizhar continues to narrate: “Before that ascetic, he joined his lotus-like hands and, calling him ‘O great ascetic,’ praised the Thiru pathigam over the glorious Pukali, saying, ‘The great benefactor who adopted me in my unknowing age was with the great goddess,’ beginning with ‘Mannil Nalla’ (Good on Earth).” With the great joy that arose in his heart and the deep love that filled him, his eyes flowed with tears. He questioned the Lord and composed a pathigam. The verses describe the Tamil master who wore a garland of beautiful red lotuses.

“Here, the great poet Sekkizhar narrates the sacred history of Pillaiyar composing the Thirukazhumala pathigam, “Mannil Nalla Vannam Vazhalam” (May we live well on Earth). Sivapada Hiruthayar was a great ascetic. The great poet Sekkizhar has repeatedly emphasized Sivapada Hiruthayar’s penance, highlighting its great virtue for us. This is why Pillaiyar also addresses Sivapada Hiruthayar as “O great ascetic.” The fulfillment of Sivapada Hiruthayar’s penance is now being received here in Madurai. With this understanding, Pillaiyar praises him here.

“Thus, before Sivapada Hiruthayar, the great ascetic, Pillaiyar joined his lotus-like hands and asked, “Was the great benefactor who adopted me in my unknowing age with the great goddess?” Even though Pillaiyar joined his hands before Sivapada Hiruthayar, he did so with the intention of worshipping Thoni Appar, asking, “O Lord, was Thoni Appar, the great benefactor who adopted me in my unknowing age, with our great Nayaki?” With this thought, he composed a pathigam. The theme of that pathigam is “The great benefactor who adopted me in my unknowing age was with the great goddess.” The verse indicates that the “unknowing age” refers to the tender age of a child without full awareness, or it can also mean the period when one did not know or worship the Lord.

“Thus, even though he was unknowing, he asks, “Was Thoni Appar, the great benefactor who remembered and adopted me, with our great goddess?” and then he composed the pathigam. This pathigam is structured in a way that inquires about the well-being of the Lord and the Goddess. This is a pathigam of fitting glory. It is a pathigam sung about Sirkazhi from Thiru Alavai. Beginning with “Mannil Nalla Vannam,” with the great joy that arose in his heart, and with the fullness of love, his eyes filled with tears. As tears flowed like a waterfall, Thooniyappar questioned his father about the sweet presence of the deity, and with a serene heart, the beautiful lotus garland-adorned Tamil child, the Pillaiyar, composed a pathigam.

“The pathigam composed by the Sirkazhi Pillaiyar begins with the lines: “Mannen Nallavannam Vazhalam Vaigalum Ennin Nalla Kathiku Yadumor Kuraivillai Kannin Nallagutharum Kadumala Valanagar Pennin Nallalodum Perunthagai Irundathe.” This pathigam is well-known and cherished by all Saivite devotees. In the second verse of this pathigam, he states: “Pothaiyar Porkinnathu Adisil Pollathu Ena Thathaiyar Munivura Than Ena” The Pillaiyar himself, through his divine utterance, provided internal evidence that Thooniyappar and Perunaiyaki Ammaiyar fed him milk rice in a golden bowl, saying, “Andavan Kadhaiyar Kulaiyinun Kazhumala Valanagar Pethaiyal Avalodum Perunthagai Irundathe.” Such is the greatness of this pathigam. This pathigam is the twenty-fourth pathigam in the third Thirumurai, set to the tune of Kollipann. The first, second, and eleventh verses of this pathigam are as follows: Nalla Kathikalai Kannil Nalla Tho Thudumala Vala Nagara Pillil Nallodu Perunthagai Irundathe Pothaiuchi Adisil Ulla Thuni Urai Thaane Nalla Kalaiye Nalla Mala Vala Nuy Appo Peru Karutha Thus, Sirkazhi Pillaiyar composed this pathigam. Our Saiva Siddhanta teacher, Vikramasingapuram Shanmugam Ayya, offered a wonderful explanation for the first verse of this pathigam in class.

“They would say that the concluding line of the first verse is “Pennin Nallalodum Perunthagai Irundathe.” They would raise the question, who is this “Pennin Nallal” (good woman) mentioned, and then provide the answer. In the Sri Panchaksharam, the letter ‘Shi’ represents Shiva, ‘Va’ represents grace, ‘Ya’ represents the soul, ‘Na’ represents concealment, and ‘Ma’ represents impurity.

“Thus, each letter in the Sri Panchaksharam represents these meanings. Among these, ‘Va’, ‘Ya’, ‘Na’, and ‘Ma’, which are distinct from ‘Shi’ (Shiva), are considered women. This is because these four are cherished by the Lord, hence they are women. That is, because the Lord cherishes grace, soul, concealment, and impurity, and because these four are cherished by the Lord, they are considered women. If He is omnipresent, they are pervaded by Him. Since He rules over these four women, He is male.

“Therefore, among these four women, who is the “Pennin Nallal” (good woman)? It is the letter ‘Va’ that comes after ‘Shi’; that is grace, the power of grace. This power of grace removes attachment, faults, and impurities from the soul, and unites the soul with the Lord Shiva.

“Hence, among these four women, the power of grace, represented by ‘Va’, becomes the “Pennin Nallal.” Our teacher would give such a beautiful explanation.

“Thus, Sirkazhi Pillaiyar, having sung this, concludes this pathigam by placing the Thirukkadikkappu. With great desire and distinction, he offered a feast to his father and remained there, filled with joy.

“At that moment, in the heart of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the thought arose through divine grace that he should visit and worship all the other holy places where the Lord resides, along with devotees who constantly perform service.

“Therefore, the Pillaiyar is now about to embark on a pilgrimage to the holy sites of the Pandya country. Our reflection on this continues.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, authored by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, Part 754, Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, residing in the math in Madurai, decides to undertake a pilgrimage with his devotees. Guided by divine grace to visit the various holy places where Shiva resides in the Pandya country, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman embarks on the pilgrimage.

First, he worships Somesundara Peruman in Madurai and begins his pilgrimage to the holy sites of the Pandya country. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman composes the 883rd verse as follows: “Alin Keezh Nalvarkku Andru” “Aram Uraitha Angananai Noolin Kan Porul Padi Noolarivarkku Eenthanai Kalam Petra Inithu Iraingi Kaittozhuthu Puram Pondhar Seelam Kol Thennavanum Theviyarum Udan Potha” – this is the verse. Somesundara God, the compassionate one, who expounded Dharma to the four under the banyan tree, is Shiva, who enlightened the four sages under the Kallala tree. Dharma, wealth, pleasure, and liberation – these four are considered the purusharthas (goals of human life) by the Vedas, signifying ultimate good for humanity. Shiva, seated under the Kallala tree, imparted knowledge to the four great sages: Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanatana, and Sanatkumara.

“Azhindha Sinthai Anthanalarkku Aram Porul Inbam Veedu Mozhintha Vayan Mukkan Aathi Meyathu Muzhukunre” – this is from the Pillaiyar’s Thevaram.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships the Madurai Somesundara God, who preached dharma and other principles to the four under the banyan tree. This Somesundara God is praised by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman here as “Noolin Kan Porul Padi Noolarivarkku Eenthanai” (one who composed the text of meaning and gave it to the learned). The word “Porul” here, where it says “Noolin Kan Porul Padi,” refers to the text of meaning. “Noolin Kan” means excelling in Tamil texts.

Therefore, “Noolin Kan Porul Padi” means that the Lord of Madurai, Chokkanatha, is the one who revealed the text of meaning that is highly spoken of in Tamil texts. Among the four grammatical categories – Ezhuthu (orthography), Sol (morphology), Porul (semantics), and Yappu (prosody) – Porul grammar is the most excellent. It is further divided into Agapporul (inner meaning) and Purapporul (outer meaning), with Agapporul being superior. That Agapporul also speaks of two types of meaning: the subtle meaning of Jnana Yoga and the worldly meaning. Among these two, the subtle meaning of Jnana Yoga is the most excellent.

Thus, the meaning here is that the Lord of Madurai, Chokkanatha, composed the Jnana Yoga Porul text, which is the best among all types of Porul texts. “Meimai Porulam Tamil Noolin Vilangu” “Vaimai Semmai Porulum Tharuvar Thiru Alavayil Emmai Pavam Theerppavar” – We have seen in detail how the divine Sekkizhar Peruman sang this in the 904th verse.

Therefore, the texts that stand as excellent Agapporul texts in this Jnana Yoga Porul tradition are Iraiyanar Agapporul and Thirukkovaiyar. Among these, the Agapporul text composed by the Lord, as the head of the Tamil Sangam in Madurai, Somesundara Peruman, is known as Iraiyanar Agapporul. This Porul grammar text was revealed by Somesundara Peruman to the Sangam poets and the Pandya king. The story of that divine composition of Iraiyanar Agapporul grammar is explained in the commentary on the first sutra of Iraiyanar Agapporul. The Pandya kings were the ones who established and nurtured Tamil by forming three types of Sangams: Thalaichangam (First Sangam), Idaichangam (Middle Sangam), and Kadaichangam (Last Sangam). The poets of the Thalaichangam included Agathiyanar, Thripuram Eritha Virisadai Kadavul, and Kunrerintha Murugavel.

The Sangam where they researched Tamil was Madurai, which was engulfed by the sea. Their text was Agathiyam. In the Idaichangam, poets like Agathiyanar and Tholkappiyanar were present. Their texts included Agathiyam, Tholkappiyam, and Mapuranam, among others. The city where they researched Tamil was Kapatapuram, which was then the capital of the Pandya country, but it was swallowed by the sea. In the Kadaichangam, poets like Sirumethaviyar, Sendhambuthanaar, Arivudaiyaranaar, and Nakkiranar, son of Kanakkayanaar, researched Tamil.

The works composed by them include Nedunthogai Nanuuru, Kurunthogai Nanuuru, Nattrinai, Purananuuru, Aingurunuru, Patirrupattu, and others. Their texts were Agathiyam and Tholkappiyam. There were forty-nine Pandya kings during the Kadaichangam period. Among them, Ugra Peruvezhuthi was the forty-ninth Pandya king. The Sangam where they researched Tamil was the present-day Madurai, also known as Uttara Madurai. During the reign of this last Pandya king, for twelve years, there was a drought.

Drought means famine.

During that time, when famine persisted for twelve years without rain, the Pandya king sent palm-leaf messages to all the poets in the Pandya country, asking them to go and live in other countries and return to this country when the drought ended and rain came. The poets, likewise, went to neighboring countries until the famine ended. After twelve years, when the famine ended, rain fell, and the country returned to normal, the Pandya king sent his people everywhere to bring all the poets back. The messengers of the Pandya king brought back all the poets. These poets were proficient in grammar. They reported to the king that they could not find anyone proficient in the grammar of meaning, no matter where they searched.

To this, the king said, “Ezhuthum Sollum Aarayvathu Porul Athikaramagathane. Porul Athikaram Namakku Kidaikkavillai Endral Ezhuthum Sollum Kidaithum Payanillai.” Thinking this, he lamented and prayed to Somesundara God of Aalavaai with devotion. Somesundara God revealed that He would alleviate the Pandya king’s sorrow.

The next day, in the Aalavaai temple in Madurai, a text on meaning, consisting of sixty sutras, titled Iraiyanar Kalaviyal, was found on a copper plate at the pedestal of the Chokkalingam.

The priests of Aalavaai informed the king of Madurai. The king of Madurai came to the temple and worshiped Aalavaai Chokkanatha Peruman with love, his sorrow at the lack of a text on meaning now gone. Declaring that this text on meaning was bestowed by our Lord, sensing his distress, he took the Iraiyanar Agapporul text, placed it on his head, and gratefully remembered Iraiyanar with heartfelt devotion. He then summoned the Sangam poets, requesting them to write commentaries on this text, saying, “This is the text on meaning revealed by our Iraiyanar; please write commentaries on it.” Consequently, the forty-nine poets of the Kadaichangam wrote commentaries on this text. From Nakkira Devanayanar onwards, all forty-nine poets wrote commentaries.

Now, the king and the poets faced the dilemma of which commentary to accept and which to reject. The king then performed penance, praying to Aalavaai Peruman to resolve this dilemma.

At that moment, an ethereal voice was heard. As the voice of the Lord, it spoke of a young boy named Uthirasanman, son of Uppoor Kudikkizhar, who lived in Uppoor, near Madurai. He was mute. The voice instructed them to recite all forty-nine commentaries before him, stating that the commentary which caused the boy Uthirasanman’s body to tremble and manifest profound emotion would be the correct one.

Furthermore, the voice revealed that the boy was no ordinary child, but Lord Kumara, born thus due to a curse. Following the Lord’s instruction, the Pandya king and the other poets went to Uppoor, to the house of Uppoorikudikizhar, and requested to meet Uthirasanman. After showing due respect to Uthirasanman, the Kadaichangam poets recited and explained all forty-nine commentaries on the sutras before him. As he listened to the other commentaries, Uthirasanman occasionally nodded his head and showed minor expressions.

However, when he heard the commentary of Nakkiranar, son of Madurai Kanakkayanar, at every word of that commentary, Uthirasanman shed tears and his body hairs bristled.

Thus, it was confirmed that the commentary by Nakkiradeva Nayanar was the true commentary.

Thus, the Iraiyanar Agapporul text, which deals with the grammar of meaning, was composed by the Lord of Madurai, Aalavaai Peruman. Its commentary was written by Nakkira Devanayanar, and it was heard by Kumara Swamy, Lord Muruga.

Therefore, the Lord of Madurai, Aalavaai Peruman, was the one who alleviated the sorrow caused by the lack of a text on the grammar of meaning in Tamil. That is why the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, encompassing this entire history, explained such a vast history in the single line, “Noolin Kan Porul Padi Noolarivarkku Eenthanai” (He who sang the meaning in texts and gave it to the learned). As we have seen before, among the four texts – Ezhuthu, Sol, Porul, and Yappu – Porul is the most excellent. Even within Porul, it is of two types: Agam and Puram. Among these, Agam is superior. Even that Agam is of two types: worldly usage and Jnana Yoga textual meaning.

Among these, the Jnana Yoga text is the most excellent, and our Aalavaai Peruman revealed it. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships such a Peruman, bows down, and then leaves the temple to begin his pilgrimage. The Pandya king, along with his queen Mangaiyarkkarasi Perumatti, accompany the Pillaiyar as he departs. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman now proceeds to sing about Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s pilgrimage to the Pandya country. “Thenilavu Pozhil Madurai Purathu Ponntha Thennavanar Theviyar Amaichar Sinthai Oon Negizhum Padalindangu Ozhugu Kannir Payndu Iziya Unarvu Indri Veezha Kande Yan Ummai Piriyadha Vannam Innattu Iraivar Pathi Ena Palavum Paniveer Endru Gnanam Unarvar Arula” “Avarum Potha Nambar Thirupparankundrai Nannare” – this is the 884th verse.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrives at the outskirts of Madurai, surrounded by groves with honey-laden flowers. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman departs from Thiru Aalavai, and the Pandya king and Queen Mangaiyarkkarasi Perumatti accompany him until he reaches the outskirts of Madurai. It is a custom to follow elders for at least sixteen feet when seeing them off, and similarly, to walk sixteen feet ahead to welcome them.

Accordingly, the king, queen, and minister, filled with devotion, accompany Thirugnanasambandha Peruman to the border of Madurai’s outskirts. When they reach the outskirts of Madurai, the three great persons the Pandya king, the queen, and the great minister, were very saddened at having to part from Thirugnanasambandha Pillaiyar. Their hearts melted, and their flowing tears fell continuously, causing them to lose consciousness and fall. The Pillaiyar, seeing this, said to them, “I will not part from you; worship the many abodes of the Lord in this country.” Thus spoke the Pillaiyar, who was enlightened with divine knowledge.

Therefore, these three great persons accompany the Pillaiyar as he goes to visit the holy sites of the Pandya country, filled with great joy.

Thus, with these three great persons accompanying him, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reaches Thirupparankundram, the abode of the Lord. The Pillaiyar intended that his visit throughout the Pandya country, accompanied by these three great persons, would ensure that the entire Pandya country would uphold the path of the Vedic scriptures and that the glory of the sacred ashes (Vibhuti) would greatly flourish.

Accordingly, the Pillaiyar, who was going to visit the holy sites of the Pandya country, first reached Thirupparankundram. He arrived there and worshiped the Lord. He offered a pathigam praising the Lord, Peruman, who resides on Parangiri, the Lord of Sathyagiri. Thirupparankundram is the third of the fourteen Thevaram-sung temples in the Pandya country. It is considered the foremost among Lord Muruga’s abodes. It is a place of great significance where Lord Muruga married Deivayanai Ammaiyar.

At that wedding, Shiva and Uma Ammaiyar were present and revealed themselves to the Devas and others, a glorious event. The festival depicting the wedding scene is still celebrated today. This is the place where Sundaramurthy Swamigal, known as Aludaiya Nambi, came from Thiru Aalavai, worshiped with the three Tamil monarchs, and composed a pathigam. In that pathigam, “Kothittaiyum Kovalam,” Sundaramurthy Swamigal sang, remembering the greatness of serving at the Lord’s feet, “Adikel Umakku Atsaaiya Anjumame” (I am afraid to serve you, oh Lord), thus achieving great fame. The temple seen on this hill is one of the rock-cut cave temples established by Mahendravarman I during the Pallava rule, approximately 1200 years ago. It is a special privilege to witness and rejoice in the divine form of the Lord and Lord Muruga’s wedding pose with Deivayanai Ammaiyar, adorned beautifully.

This is a holy place where Lord Muruga, the visible deity of Kali Yuga, bestows all desired worldly and other-worldly blessings upon those who seek and worship Him with His wedding attire, showing great compassion. This place clearly exemplifies the truth stated in Sivagnana Siddhiyar: “Bhogiya Irunthu Uyirkku Bhogathai Purithal” (Being a enjoyer, He provides enjoyment to beings). The Lord’s name is Parangirinathar, the Goddess’s name is Audai Nayaki. The sacred waters are Saravana Poikai, and on the hill, Kasi Theertham, Kanda Theertham. To such a Thirupparankundram holy place, there is a pathigam, the 100th pathigam of the first Thirumurai, set to the tune of Kurinjippann. The first, eighth, and eleventh verses of this pathigam are as follows: Vetdu Soodali Soodariy eri Yedu Kadam Solla Paniyilaye Oru Bagam Padalam May Nallaroo Param Kundra Maithagume Neethinathin Thoruupum Sithirparam Kundramakum Seyvan Endra Nitthazhu Thoomali Po Sambaiman Gnanam Akkai Tharam Kundrai Thodai Vali Padal Patthumpalla Poduvazhi Kadan Arul Perum Thaigore Thiruchitram Valam Sivanathu Idamakiya Parankundrai Thirupparankundratthai Sivan Therefore, the essence of this pathigam is that for those who praise and celebrate it, past karmas will not endure.

We shall proceed with our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, authored by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, Part 755, Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, after worshipping Thirupparankundram and composing a pathigam praising Parangirinathar, then continued. Sekkizhar Peruman states in the 885th verse: “Aranindar Thamai Vanangi Angu Potri Aniyappanur Anainthu Paninthu Padi Neelnanaintha Selvarpathy Piravum Serthu Nilavu Thiruppathigangal Nizhala Padi Seranintha Vayal Pazhana Kazhani Suzhntha Sirappurathu Vantharulum Selvar Sengan Eranintha Vel Kodiyar Thirupputthoorai Inithu Iraingi Sila Nal Angu Irunthar Andre” – this is the verse. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who praised the Lord adorned with the Ganges in his matted locks at Thirupparankundram, then reached the holy place called Thiru Aappanur and worshiped the Lord there, composing a pathigam. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman praises this holy place as “Ani Aappanur.” The phrase “Ani Aappanuranaai” is found in the pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

This Aappanur is located in Madurai, on the northern bank of the Vaigai River. It is the second among the Devaram-sung holy places in the Pandya country. It is also known as Thiruvaappudaiyar Kovil. It received this name because the Lord revealed himself at the spot of the Aappu (jackfruit) for a Pandya king. Like Kanraappur Naduthari, this place is named Aappanur.

Here, the images of Nadarajar and Sivakamasundari Ammaiyar are enshrined as stone idols. The Lord’s names are Aappanur Karanar, Aappudaiyar, Rishapuresar, Annavinothan. The Goddess’s name is Kuravangamizh Kuzhali. The sacred waters are Vaigai Theertham and Rishaba Theertham.

The Lord transformed the sand from the Vaigai river, placed in a furnace, into food, hence His name Annavinothan (the one who delights in food). The divine Sekkizhar Peruman has stated that Sundaramurthy Swamigal also visited and worshiped this holy place. This temple is located in Madurai city, next to the Meenakshi Amman Thiru Aalavai temple, on the northern bank of the Vaigai river. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, after visiting and worshipping this holy place, composed a pathigam. It is the 88th pathigam of the first Thirumurai, set to the tune of Kurinjippann. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thuram Mutrum Sadai Mudime Muthirayalam Piraya Otrum Padavum Athu Konduarai Kaninthan Settravil Siranai Thiru Yappanuramma Manam Udaiya Paare Ethan Puna Aniyappanur Meya The devotional note of the pathigam, and its concluding benefit, is that those who contemplate the Lord of Thiru Aappanur will be freed from the grip of karma.

Thus, the divine Sekkizhar Peruman mentions that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, after bowing and worshipping Thiru Aappanur, went on to worship other holy places.

Thus, the places worshipped by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman include Pazhamuthircholai and Thiru Vadhavoor, among others. After worshipping these other holy places, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrived at the holy place called Thirupputthoor. He stayed there for some time, praising the Lord and composing pathigams. Thirupputthoor, this holy place, was a major town with governmental connections in those days, as known from historical records. Thirupputthoor is one of the great holy places in the Pandya country. It is the sixth of the fourteen renowned places in the Pandya country.

This temple is called Sridhali because Lakshmi performed penance here. It is a blessed place where Bhairavar performed worship and sits facing east, like Skanda, between the Lord and the Goddess. We have extensively discussed the historical details of this temple in the Puranam of Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar. The Lord’s names are Sridhaleeswarar, Sridhalinathar, Thiruthalinathar. The Goddess’s name is Sivakamasundari. The sacred waters are Sridhali Theertham and Sivagangai Theertham.

We have received a pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for this temple. It is the twenty-sixth pathigam of the first Thirumurai, set to the tune of Thakkaragappann. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thangai Thangum Mudiyaruvar Polum Engal Uchi Uraiyum Eeraiyaaru Engal Uchi Uraiyum Eeraiyaaru Nalla Kelviyana Sambaiyum Theer Putthoor Sollal Padal Vallattha Mendrum Allal Theerum Avalam Adaiyave The essence of this pathigam is that our Lord resides in Thirupputthoor. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman then composes the next verse: “Patrartha Purangal Malaichilayala Sendru Paramanar Thirupputthoor Paninthu Ponthu Putrarum Panibunda Punithanartham Poovanatthai Pukku Iraingi Pugazhnthu Padi Katrargal Thozhuthu Ettum Kanapperum Kaitthozhuthu Tamil Padi Suzhiyil Potri Kutrala Kurumbula Kumbittu Etti Kootruthaitthar Nelveli Kuruginare” – this is the 886th verse. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, after bowing and worshipping Thirupputthoor, the abode of Paramanar who destroyed the triple cities of his enemies with a mountain bow, then reached the holy place called Thiru Poovanam, the abode of the sacred Lord who wears serpents from anthills, worshiped Him, and praised Him with a pathigam. This Thiru Poovanam is a holy place located very close to Madurai.

The Lord’s names are Pushpavaneswarar, Poovanathar. The Goddess’s name is Soundarya Nayaki, Min Anaiyal. The sacred water is Vaigai Theertham. This holy place in the Pandya country is blessed with pathigams sung by the three great saints. We have extensively discussed the history of this holy place in the Puranam of Appar Swamigal. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who visited here, composed two pathigams.

The first pathigam, of the first Thirumurai, is the 64th pathigam, set to the tune of Thakkesi. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. “Araiyunum Mamalarum Adaravarame Kuraiyar Mathiyam Soodi Madodai Muraiyara Mudiser Tharasum” “Thirayar Poliche Sethir Poovaname Thevaname Thimunar Purisai Madambovum Thera Poovanaththae Perunarn Mairya Thamizhar Utkar” “Kali Mazhagum Yana Sambandham Sonna Padal Patthuvadhu Vanida Vanidalam” – The essence of the pathigam is that the Lord’s abode is Then Thiruppoovanam.

Now, the second pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for this holy place is the 20th pathigam of the third Thirumurai, set to the tune of Kantharapanchamam. This pathigam is special because it is structured in the “Eeradi Mel Vaipu” style. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: “Mathamar Meniyanagi Vandodu Pothamar Pozhil Ani Poovanaththurai Vethanai Viravalar Aranam Mundru Eytha Nathanai Adithozha Nanmaiyagume Punniyar Thozhuthazhu Poovanaththurai Annanai Adithozhuthu Anthiyul Nanniya Arumarai Gnana Sambandhan Panniya Tamil Sola Paraiyum Pavame” Thiruchitrambalam.

We shall continue our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, authored by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, Part 756, Vampara Varivandu Serukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. After worshipping and praising Thiru Poovanam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman also bowed to Kanapperu, which is revered by the learned, as stated by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman. The place referred to by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman as Kanapperu, worshipped by the learned, is the holy place called Kalaiyar Kovil. “Katravargal Vizhungum Karpaka Kaniyee” (The wish-fulfilling fruit swallowed by the learned) is from Thiruvishaippa. Who are the learned?

They are those who forget themselves and remember the Lord. Such people are truly learned. Such learned individuals Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships in person at Thirukanapper. This sacred place, Thirukanapper, also known as Kalaiyar Kovil, is the tenth of the fourteen praised temples in the Pandya country. When Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, known as Aludaiya Nambigal, and Cheraman Perumal Nayanar worshipped at Thiruchuzhiyal and left, the Lord revealed to Nambigal that “We are in Kanapper.” In a dream at night, in the form of Kalaiyan, with a golden scepter in his red hand and a crescent on his head, showing a unique form that is found nowhere else, He declared, “We are in Kanapper.” This is how Deiva Sekkizhar Peruman describes it, and Sundaramoorthy Swamigal understands it and begins the pathigam “Thondar adithozhulum.” This sacred place, Thirukanapper, is where Nambigal sang “When will I, your servant, behold Kalaiyan of Kanapper, surrounded by dark fields?” and came to worship.

Since Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sang about Lord Shiva as “Kalai of Kanapper,” this place is also known as Kalaiyar Kovil. This sacred place is praised in a pathigam as the spot where Airavatam, cursed to become a wild elephant, came and performed prescribed worship to be freed from its curse. The history mentioned in Pillaiyar’s words, “worship,” can still be seen there today. The sight of the elephant bathing in the temple pond and that sacred pond being called “elephant pond” are still observed. Today, we can still see the fields here flourish with dark rice varieties, confirming the truth of Nambigal’s words, “Karu Vayal Choozh.” This sacred place is a temple where the Lord and the Goddess bestow grace in three shrines. This temple has three shrines: Somaswarar and Soundaranayagi Amman in the first shrine, Kalishwarar and Swarnavalli Amman in the second shrine, and Sundareswarar and Meenakshi Amman in the third shrine.

This place can be reached via the routes from Madurai to Rameswaram and from Trichy to Manamadurai. There are numerous sacred ponds here, including Gajapushkarani (Aanai Madu), Sivaganga Thirtham, Kali Thirtham, Vishnu Thirtham, Saraswathi Thirtham, Gowri Thirtham, Rudra Thirtham, and Lakshmi Thirtham, Sudarsana Thirtham. This is the place where Kali, after the slaying of Bandasura, came here, worshipped Kalishwarar, changed her dark form into Swarnavalli, and married the Lord. Airavatam, cursed by Nandi, came here, bathed in the Anaipadu pond, and was freed from its curse. This sacred place has a pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, beginning with “Pidiyalam,” and a pathigam by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, beginning with “Thondaradi Thozhilum.” Appar Swamigal has also sung about this place as a Vaipputhalam in various pathigams. Kapiladeva Nayanar praised this place in the Eleventh Thirumurai, Shiva Peruman Thiruanthathi.

The other names for this sacred place are Dakshina Kalipuram, Jothivanam, Mandaravanam, Mokshabradam, Agasthiyakshetram, Kantharam, Thavakistiharam, Devataruvanam, Bhooloka Kailayam, and Mahakalapuram. Among the three shrines here, Kalishwarar is the one praised in Thevaram. Related to these three shrines, there is a proverb prevalent in this region: “Kalai theda, Somar azhikka, Sokkar sukikka” (For Kalai to seek, for Somar to destroy, for Sokkar to be happy). This proverb is based on the names of the deities bestowing grace in the three shrines of this temple. If one climbs this gopuram and looks, the Madurai gopuram can be seen. There is also a kummi song in this region about Marudhu Pandi, who built this gopuram so that the Madurai gopuram would be visible.

The British, intending to arrest the Marudhu Pandiyars, declared that they would destroy this gopuram if the Marudhu Pandiyars did not surrender. The Marudhu Pandiyars, who were living hidden in the forest, came to this sacred temple, Kalaiyar Kovil, to protect its gopuram, disregarding their own lives, surrendered, and were sentenced to death by the British.

Thus, this sacred place is where the Marudhu Pandiyars made their sacrifice. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who graced this place, composed a pathigam, which is the twenty-sixth pathigam in the Third Thirumurai, set to the tune of Kollipann. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Perunthai malizhividhin bali badum kadiyuzha poombu kana pe annal nadiya adaisaram udaiya ro adiya kattukaththu adala kadappe pottukaththu ilavar) (Puthi kolum Kaliyaththu Sambaththu Kanappe annal adiye sharan avathu athanai karuthalum thozhuthalum karumam athanai gnana neer peithu malaral vazhipaduvor nanmai peruvor enbathu pathiga kurippu avathu ivvaru) The pathigam notes that realizing and worshipping the Lord of Kanapper is our duty. Those who worship with the water of wisdom and flowers will receive blessings.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, after worshipping at Pazhaiyar Kovil, composed Tamil songs and praised Thiruchuzhiyal, as described by Deiva Sekkizhar Peruman. According to that, he sang Tamil songs, reached the sacred place of Thiruchuzhiyal, praised the Lord there, and composed a pathigam. Thiruchuzhiyal is one of the fourteen praised temples in the Pandya country. The Thevaram composed by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal for this place is available. This sacred place is near Aruppukottai, close to Madurai. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who graced this place, composed a pathigam, but unfortunately, due to our misfortune, that pathigam is not available to us.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praised Thiruchuzhiyal, then worshipped at Kutralam and Kurumbala, and arrived at Nellai, where the Lord who kicked Death resides. Sivachai Kilar Peruman states in that verse.

Accordingly, after praising and worshipping Thiruchuzhiyal, he proceeded to Thirukutralam, worshipped the Kurumbala tree there, and composed pathigams. Thirukutralam is the thirteenth of the fourteen praised temples in the Pandya country. The Koothar Kovil here is a beautiful ancient temple, praised in Thevaram and Thiruvasagam. The Kurumbala temple is located on the northern bank near Kutralam falls. The sacred tree here is Kurumbala, hence the temple is named after it. Kurumbala is a type of jackfruit tree.

Koothar Kovil is located north of the Kurumbala temple, within the town, on the way to Chitra Sabhai. Thiruvasagam Thiruppulambal sings, “Oh Koothan residing in Kutralam, when my life departs, who else but you will be my kin?” Thirunavukkarasu Peruman says about this place in Thiru Ankamalai, “When life departs, who else is there for us but Koothan of Kutralam?” Thirunavukkarasu Peruman has sung about this temple in Thirukkodikka Thiruththandangam: “Behold Koothan residing in Kutralam.” Chitra Sabhai, one of the five great Sabhas, is located here. This Kurumbala temple was a Vaishnava place of worship called Thirumutram. When Agasthya Muni visited that place, the Vaishnavas prevented him from entering the village, denouncing Shiva and Shiva devotees. Agasthya Muni, to destroy their arrogance, assumed the guise of a Vaishnava devotee, entered the temple, and placed his hand on the head of the Vishnu deity inside.

He transformed it into a Lingam, a sacred history described in the Thirukutralam chapter of the Kandapuranam. Since then, that temple became a Shiva temple. The Lord’s name there is Koothar, the Goddess is Sivakami Amman, the Sabhai is Chitra Sabhai, and the pond is Chitra Nadi. Two pathigams are associated with this sacred place.

Now, at Kurumbala temple, the Lord’s name is Kurumbalanathar, the Goddess is Kuzhalvai Mozhi Ammai, and the sacred tree is Kurumbala. One pathigam. This sacred place, near Tenkasi, is now a very famous tourist destination due to the Kutralam falls. Nowadays, fashionable people mostly identify it as a place for summer vacation celebrations, where they playfully waste time on worldly pleasures. It is a place of natural beauty. There are eighty-six inscriptions from the Pandya and Chola periods.

Kutrala Sthala Puranam and Kutrala Kuravanji are beautiful literary works. We saw that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who graced this place, composed a pathigam for the Lord of Thirukutralam. That pathigam is the eleventh pathigam in the First Thirumurai, set to the tune of Kurinjipann. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Vega si ko ve ku ada malar kunte nakar podavi) (Var punal kamal at inai utram adaval nambal a patpum) This pathigam is addressed to the devotees, saying, “Our devotees, go and worship Kutralam, the beautiful city of our Lord, with cool showers and groves.” Now, the pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for Thirukurumbala is the seventy-first pathigam in the Second Thirumurai, set to the tune of Gandharapann.

The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Mathi soodi theli sadai karathu devi bhagam poruthi poruntha vedaththa kadurai thal purintha sen thidam vinavil elam Tamil cholai vanthu yazh seethamanur idum chol tham chara kurumbulave komba) (Poosolai kurumbula mel yetru allal namba nadi paravum nalvarai gnana samba inbaya padal ivai poovalla veerum ve keppala theevinigal poiyathum nalvinigal thalare) The note for this pathigam is that the Lord’s abode is Kurumbalavae.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, after worshipping at Kurumbala, proceeds to Thirunelveli, where the Lord who kicked Death resides, and worships there. Let us keep pondering. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 757, Vambaravai Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, composed by Deivasekkizhar Peruman. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, after bowing and worshipping Thirukutralam, proceeds to Thirunelveli, where Shiva, who kicked Death, resides. Thirunelveli is the fourteenth of the praised temples in the Pandya country. It is called Nelveli because the Lord protected the paddy (nel) that a devotee named Vedasarmar had arranged for the Lord’s offering from being swept away by a flood, by building a fence (veli) around it. He is also called Nellaiyappar, who fenced the paddy.

Since the Lord emerged from under a bamboo, it is also known as Venunavanam. This is the place where Vishnu, Brahma, and Agasthya Muni worshipped. The story of the Lord going to Tharukavanam for alms is said to have happened here. The form of Bhikshadana is installed and worshipped in the first circumambulation. This is the Tamira Sabhai among the Pancha Sabhas. The Lord’s names are Nellaiyappar, Venuvananadar, Veimunthanadar, Nelvelinadar, Shalivatisar, Venuvaneswarar.

The Goddess’s names are Kanthimathi Amman, Vadivudai Amman. The sacred tree is bamboo. The sacred pond is Pottramaraikulam, also known as Swarna Pushkarani, Karumarithirtham, Sindhu Poondurai. When a devotee named Ramakone, who had seen the entire Thamirabarani, was carrying a pot of milk, the Lord, in the form of a bamboo, tripped him, spilled the milk on himself, and then revealed himself by being cut. The mark of the cut is still visible on the top of the Lingam.

The Lord who appears to us now is said to be the twenty-first Avudaiyar, with twenty Avudaiyars beneath the earth. This deity is Mruthyunjaya Murthy. This temple has many names: Venunavanam, Nelveli, Nellore, Shalivati, Shalinagar, Brahma Virunthapuram, Tharukavanam. The temple has mandapams like the Swing Mandapam, Wedding Mandapam, Thousand-Pillared Mandapam, Vasantha Mandapam, Sangili Mandapam, Somavara Mandapam, Navagraha Mandapam, and Mahamandapams, all adorned with exquisite sculptures. The mark of a Lingam is seen on Vishnu’s chest. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who came to this sacred place, composed a pathigam, which is the ninety-second pathigam in the Third Thirumurai, set to the tune of Sadharippann.

The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Marunthavai desam marumalavai matrum arunthuyaru kedum nama nalla jame porunthu thura ontrai pon sori thara thure pai pu sirudesam pola Thirunalvelai siruvartha) (Selvarthal mamalla visai ayanavaru peruthuparai Thirueli selvar thanmai poruthu neerthadam maruga pugazhiyul yambatham solla aruthavil padiyavum) The pathigam notes that the names of the wealthy Lord of Thirunelveli are the medicine, the good path for the afterlife, and meditation. He is one who cannot be thought of as having a single nature, and he is one who enjoys dancing, among other qualities. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises the Lord, calling him the wealthy Lord of Thirunelveli.

The Lord possesses imperishable wealth, which is called Aishwaryam. In the ninth verse of this pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises the Lord, saying, “The Lord of Thirunelveli, rich with monthly and daily festivals.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises the Lord, saying, “The Lord of Thirunelveli, rich with monthly and daily festivals.” The sacred place of Thirunelveli is full of monthly festivals and daily festivals. Deivasekkizhar Peruman then composes the next verse: “The virtuous one, after worshipping Nellai and praising the Lord of matted hair in other sacred places, remained there happily, singing with love, and always praising the Lord with good words. He then proceeded to Thiruvirameswaram, established by the strong golden-bowed Rama, who went to destroy Lanka, which was a great sin to get rid of, which had pleased the celestials.” Deivasekkizhar Peruman composes the eight hundred and eighty-seventh verse. Shiva is the target of all good deeds.

Therefore, Deivasekkizhar Peruman praises him as Punniyanar (the Virtuous One). “Punniya Unnadikkae” is a saying from Thevaram. Just as he is virtuous, his devotees also attain Shivathvam (the state of Shiva) through abundant virtuous deeds of Shiva, and thus devotees are also called virtuous. We can recall here how Deivasekkizhar Peruman praised Kannappa Nayanar as “the one with incomparable wisdom, who is the essence of virtue.” Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, after worshipping Thirunelveli where the Virtuous One resides, visits other sacred places where Shiva resides. These sacred places are likely various temples in the Thirunelveli region, such as Thiruppudaimarudhur, Thiruvagastheeswaram, etc. After visiting all these sacred places, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reaches Thiruvirameswaram.

On his way, he also visits sacred places like Thiruchuzhiyal and Thiruutharakosamangai. Deivasekkizhar Peruman sings that Rama, holding a beautiful bow, reached Thirurameswaram, which he established to atone for the great sin of destroying Lanka and the mighty Ravana, who had pleased the celestials. Since it was established by Rama, it is called Rameswaram. This fact is stated in the two pathigams composed by Pillaiyar and in Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s Thirunerisai.

Thus, Pillaiyar reaches Rameswaram. Deivasekkizhar Peruman composes the next verse, the eight hundred and eighty-eighth verse: “He worshipped the temple worshipped by the red-eyed Vishnu, bowed before the deity, and then, accompanied by the Pandya king and Mangaiyarkkarasi, and the truthful minister Kulachchirai, surrounded by them. With an overflowing desire, he entered through the beautiful long gate, circumambulated, and bowed inside. With his lotus-like red hands folded, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman stood and sang a pathigam, which the king also praised.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reached Thiruvirameswaram, worshipped by Vishnu. He bowed before the deity and then entered the temple, accompanied by the Pandya king Nindra Seer Nedumara Nayanar, Queen Mangaiyarkkarasi, and the truthful Kulachchirai Nayanar, who were all surrounding and following him. He entered through the beautiful long gate with an increasing desire and reached the interior.

While the king worshipped and praised, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, with his lotus-like hands folded, stood and sang a pathigam. Deivasekkizhar Peruman then composed the following verse: “He sang about the Shiva worshipped by the red-eyed Vishnu at Sethu, bowed, and with love, stayed happily in that city. The Pandya Queen, praised for her spotless fame, and the truthful Kulachchirai, removing all deficiencies, continued to praise him. The Lord, their daily worshipped deity, resided happily on the cool seashore.” This verse states that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, after singing and worshipping Shiva, who was worshipped by Vishnu at Sethu (Thiruvirameswaram), resided happily in that sacred city with great affection. The Pandya king Nindra Seer Nedumara Nayanar, Mangaiyarkkarasi Ammaiyar, and Kulachchirai Nayanar provided Thirugnanasambandha Peruman with everything he needed without any deficiencies. While they praised Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, he, in turn, worshipped and praised the Lord Ramanathar daily, and Pillaiyar resided happily on the cool seashore.

The king arranged everything needed for Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and his entourage. Generally, the king’s duty falls under the category of dharma.

But here, the king arranged everything for the devotees, which falls under the category of the Lord. Just as in the first verse, the Pandya king, out of a desire to be saved from the great sin of associating with Jains and committing offenses against Shiva, praised Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, as mentioned here.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman resided in this sacred place and composed two pathigams for Thiruvirameswaram. Among them, the first pathigam begins with “Alaivazhar” and is the tenth pathigam in the Third Thirumurai, set to the tune of Gandharapanchamam. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Ilaivazhar thalaigal ving kanal rameswaram thalaivazhar kolal malaiye pakalvalave pathiyo thannai ikazhthaval ezhu koyu irame) The pathigam notes that the Lord of Thiruvirameswaram, the temple established and worshipped by Rama to atone for the sin of killing Ravana and destroying Lanka, is a manifestation of wisdom and virtue, showering grace.

Now, The second pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for this sacred place begins with “Thiriththaru Mamani.” It is the one hundred and first pathigam in the Third Thirumurai, set to the tune of Pazhampancharappann. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Chithiram vadum vadiruththa nilanka kana ira soorang meyathirppirai malka semala seyyum seyal theeviyai mavviya thennilankai araiya thiral vaatti eiya vechilai allal rameswara tharai) The pathigam notes that those who truly understand the good light and the faultless actions will worship it as the divine act of the Lord of Rameswaram, who dances with endless fire. This pathigam notes that the Lord’s actions are to destroy. This entire pathigam praises the Lord’s prowess, who dances with fire in the forest. The pathigam also mentions his quality of dancing with the Goddess.

Therefore, it is believed that this pathigam was composed on the Sethu shore. Thiruvirameswaram, praised as Rameswaram, is the eighth of the praised temples in the Pandya country. It gained this name because it was established and worshipped by Rama to remove the great sin of killing Ravana and destroying Lanka and its demons. The episodes of Ramacharithra and Rama worshipping a Lingam here to get rid of the sin are found in Thevaram pathigams.

Here, Hanuman, who went to Kasi to bring a Lingam for installation, was delayed. So, Mother Sita made a Lingam out of sand, and Rama installed it. Rama installed and worshipped the Lingam. This deity is known as Ramanathar.

Afterwards, the Lingam brought by Hanuman was installed to the north of the main deity, named Viswalingam, and Rama decreed that it should be worshipped first so that Hanuman would not be saddened. This place is one of the twelve Jyotirlinga sthalams. Vishnu, separated from Lakshmi, grew up as Gunanaidhi, a Pandya king. Lakshmi, in the form of a Brahmin, married him here, and Vishnu resides here as Sethumadhavar. The Sethu Puranam states that those who do not worship him will not receive the benefits of worshipping Ramanathar. The Sethu Puranam extensively discusses the history and greatness of the numerous sacred ponds in this region.

This place is called Sethukkarai because Rama built a bridge and crossed to Lanka to kill Ravana. This place is also called Dhanushkodi because Rama found water by piercing the earth with the tip of his bow on Sethu. Sethu refers to the seashore. The sacred pond, the city’s north side, has Gandhamadhana mountain. Rama’s footprints are imprinted there. The Lord’s name is Ramanathar, the Goddess is Parvathavardini, Malai Vazhar Kathali.

There are numerous sacred ponds such as Agni Thirtham, Rama Thirtham, Lakshmana Thirtham, Dhanushkodi, and others.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praised the Lord with pathigams in Rameswaram and stayed there for several days. Let us dwell further on this. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 758, Vambaravai Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, composed by Deivasekkizhar Peruman. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, residing in Rameswaram, worshipped the sacred places of Thirukonamalai and Thiruketheeswaram in Eezham, Sri Lanka, and composed pathigams for them. Deivasekkizhar Peruman explains this in the eight hundred and ninetieth verse as follows: “Residing happily in that city, and in Eezham, the island surrounded by the roaring sea, he joyfully worshipped Thirukonamalai, praising the Lord with red eyes and a young bull. He then praised and worshipped the sacred feet of the Lord of Thiruketheeswaram in Mathottam, adorned with a crescent moon, and obtained imperishable wealth with his devotees, filled with joy.” This verse describes how Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, while staying happily in Rameswaram, worshipped and praised the Lord with red eyes and a bull, who resides joyfully in Thirukonamalai, an island in Eezham surrounded by the roaring sea on all four sides.

This historical account of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composing a pathigam for Thirukonamalai in Sri Lanka is mentioned by Deivasekkizhar Peruman. Thirukonamalai is a Shiva temple in Eezham. It is also known as Thirukanamalai. The history states that during the argument between Adiseshan and Vayu about shaking and preserving the peaks of Mount Meru, three peaks fell due to Vayu’s power, and these three peaks became Thirukalathi, Thiruchirappalli, and Thirukonamalai.

Hence, these three sacred places are praised as Dakshina Kailayam. Thirukonamalai is also the place where Indra worshipped Shiva. Konam means bend, and Kuri refers to the peak. We find in Periya Puranam that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, from Rameswaram, sang about Thirukonamalai and Thiruketheeswaram. Some time ago, during an invasion by foreign rulers, the Dutch, who were of other religions, captured this city. They completely demolished this temple and cast it into the sea, turning the city into a military base.

However, the devotees, during those days, protected invaluable deities like Somasthar and Chandrasekar from the Dutch and preserved them in Thampalakam, a village about ten naligai away from Thirukonamalai. The hot springs, which are one of the wonders of the world, are all located in one place, but they have different temperature readings. It is said that Ravana created them by bathing to perform his mother’s obsequies. This city is still a military base, so worship takes place only on Mondays and Fridays, as noted by Sivakavimani Ayyar. They write that this sacred place is located in Sri Lanka, southeast of Jaffna, on the east coast. The Lord’s name is Koneswarar, the Goddess is Mathu Umaiyal, and the sacred pond is Mahasune.

This sacred place has a history of nearly three thousand two hundred and eighty-seven years. It also has the name Thirukkoodam. Those who facilitated the supply of sufficient ghee and wicks for lighting lamps for the Lord made wicks from lotus stem fibers. That village is still known as Thridhay. The pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, praising Thirukonamalai from Rameswaram, is the one hundred and twenty-third pathigam in the Third Thirumurai, set to the tune of Puranirmaippann. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: The pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, praising Thirukonamalai from Rameswaram, is the one hundred and twenty-third pathigam in the Third Thirumurai, set to the tune of Puranirmaippann.

The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: (Suttram nirai keezhampozhiyalum nimalar neerani theer mel magaluvo bhagama pulandhu vadivinaru kodiyani vidaiya karai kezhu samuthum karayil keezhavum palavarum kanmani varanru kuraikka) (Kadal vaaththila polikkum ponnama mazhai amaruntha kutram ila kadal suuzhntha konnama malai amaruntha kattru nar kelvi kaliyaru perumal karuththudai gnana sambandham aatrru semil thamizh malai) The Lord, who is pure, who has the daughter of the mountain as one half of his form, who bears the bull on his banner, is praised in many ways, and resides in Konamamalai, surrounded by the temple, the pond, and the sea. This is the summary of this pathigam.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who bestowed the pathigam in praise of Thirukonamalai, then worships Thiruketheeswaram temple and bestows a pathigam. The great Sekkizhar Peruman narrates this history, stating that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, thinking deeply of and revering the sacred feet of the Lord residing in Thiruketheeswaram, a place in Madhottum with tall mansions where the moon is adorned on its peak, joyfully remained there with devotees. Thiruketheeswaram is the name of the temple, and Madhottum is the name of that region. Ketheeswaram is also the name of the town. It is mentioned in the pathigam as Madhottum Ketheeswaram.

Therefore, we can understand that Madhottum is the name of the town and Ketheeswaram is the name of the temple, according to Nambi’s pathigams. This shrine is situated on the banks of the river Palavi, as described in the pathigam. The glory of Thiruketheeswaram is narrated in the Dakshina Kailasa Mahatmiyam. It is said that Adiseshan established one of the peaks he plucked from the great Meru mountain in this place.

Also, the sage Thuvatta came here, performed penance, and gained renown, leading the city to be named Maha Thuvattapuram. Over time, Maha Thuvattapuram evolved into its current name, Madhottum, according to historical accounts. Over ages, the river, city, and temple have all decayed, eroded, and been buried under mounds of earth. Some time ago, devotees discovered the remnants here, renovated the temple, found the original lingam, established it, and have been worshipping it. The water bodies here are abundant with crocodiles. The Lord’s

name is Ketheeswarar, and the Goddess is Gowri Ammai. The sacred tank is the Palavi River. This temple is located a short distance west of Kottai Mannar, which is twenty naligais from Thalaimannar in Sri Lanka. It was named Ketheeswaram because Ketu worshipped Shiva here. This pathigam, composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman while staying in Rameswaram, is the 107th pathigam of the Second Thirumurai, set to the tune of Nattarapam. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (பொழுது ஊழையில் சிற்றவல் பற்றி நல்முறைப்பதி எண்ணூ கருது கனை கடல் கடிதமிழ் ஒளிர்அளி மாட்டம் ஆ கருத்த மேதி சேரும் கைத்தொழ கடுவினை அடையாவே மாடுல மணமூற செ)

(கடலது ஒளிகவரு மாட்ட ஆடல் ஏறுடை அள்ள கேதீச்சரத்து அடிகளை அடிதாலி நாடுல இறைஞான சம்பந்தன் சொல் நவிழ பாமாலை ஏ பாடல பாடுவியோ பத்தால் பரததி பெறலமே) The summary of this pathigam is that by worshipping Thiruketheeswaram in Madhottum, the abode of Shiva, all karmic actions will cease, and no further afflictions will occur.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who sang praises of the Eela Nadu shrines while in Rameswaram, remained there with great joy in the company of devotees. As stated in the twelfth chapter of Sivagnana Botham, “Anbaru Mariyi,” being with devotees is a characteristic of those who have attained realization. Sekkizhar Peruman states here that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was joyful, indicating that it brings immense bliss, surpassing even the bliss of liberation. While in Rameswaram, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman visited the Eela Nadu shrines. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sang praises for both shrines in Eela Nadu. This was because, due to the Vedic injunction that one should not cross the sea between Rameswaram and Sri Lanka, he sang praises for both shrines in Eela Nadu while remaining in Rameswaram.

Let us meditate further. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, Part 759, by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, the section on Vambara Varivanda Charukkam, the puranam of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing the history of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman residing in Thiruviramechuram and singing pathigams. The 891st verse: “He worshipped that shrine and proceeded north. Entering and revering the temple where the Lord who holds fire in His beautiful hand resides, he worshipped many shrines and praised them. Crossing the boundary of the ocean where the waves clash, he arrived at Thiruvadanai, a place of indescribable fame.

“He offered garlands of beautiful Tamil verses and praised the incomparable Punavaiyil, the abode of Shiva, and worshipped it.

“Thus, the one who partook of knowledge for the world worshipped.” This verse describes Thirugnanasambandha Peruman traveling from Thiruvirameswaram. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is traveling north from Thiruvirameswaram. He enters and worships the temple where the Lord, holding fire in His beautiful hand, resides, and then proceeds, worshipping many shrines. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who mentally worshipped Thirukonamalai, Thiruketheeswaram, and other temples from Rameswaram, now enters the Thiruvirameswaram temple, bows down sincerely, receives the Lord’s gracious permission, and embarks on his journey northward. The places worshipped by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman in this journey are believed to be shrines such as Uppur and Thiruverriyur. Among these, Thiruverriyur is a Vaippu Thalam (a shrine mentioned in devotional hymns but without a full pathigam dedicated to it).

“Having worshipped many such shrines and crossed the boundaries where ocean waves surge, he reached Thiruvadanai, a place of indescribable fame. He reached the shrine called Thiruvaadanai, and there he worshipped the Lord by offering garlands of pure Tamil verses. Although Sekkizhar Peruman used the plural ‘garlands of pure Tamil verses,’ we currently only have one pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for this shrine. This shrine, Thiruvaadanai, is the ninth among the celebrated shrines in the Pandya kingdom. It is the place where Sage Bhirugu, cursed to have the head of a goat and the body of an elephant, came and worshipped, thus being freed from his curse.

“Therefore, this shrine is named Aadanaai (Aadu meaning goat, Aanai meaning elephant). History relates that Sage Durvasa cursed Sage Bhirugu for not showing him reverence when he visited.

“Thus, the name Aadanaai came about due to Sage Bhirugu worshipping here with a goat’s head and an elephant’s body. This name came about for that reason. In Sanskrit, it is called Aja Gaja Puram (Ajam meaning goat, Gajam meaning elephant). This form is always kept and worshipped in the temple. Since the sun worshipped by installing a blue gem as a Shiva lingam, the Lord is known as Adhi Ratneswarar, Adanai Nathar, and Aja Gajeswarar. The name of the Goddess is Ambaayiravalli or Snehavalli.

“The sacred water is Surya Theertham. The shrine of Thiruvaadanai is also mentioned in the Thiruvilaiyadal Puranam and Sethu Puranam. This shrine, like Sirkazhi, has twelve names: Parijathavanam, Vannivanam, Kurukkathivanam, Bilvavanam, Mukthipuram, Adhi Ratneswaram, Adanai, Markandeyapuram, Agastheeswaram, Padmapuram, Gomutheeswaram, and Vijayeswaram. The purana of this shrine was composed by Thiruvarur Saminatha Desikar. This shrine’s purana contains eleven chapters and five hundred fifty-seven verses. The sacred waters are Manimuthai River, Surya Pushkarani, Varuna Theertham, Markandeya Theertham, Agasthiya Theertham, and Ksheera Kundam.

“According to puranic history, those who worshipped the Lord here and attained blessings include Surya, Varuna’s son, Varuna, Markandeyar, Romasar, Vasishtar, Agasthiyar, Gouthamar, Kalavar, Bharathwajar, Sanakathi Nalvar, Annathwajan, Harichandran, Manu, Muchukundan, Athiveeran, Mandhatha, and Arjuna. The Ramanathapuram Samasthanam Devasthanam published this shrine’s purana about fifty-six years ago. At the end of that book, the entire Parijathavanam Gaja Mahatmyam from the Kshetra Kandam, Uttarabhagam of the Brahmakaivartha Mahapuranam in Sanskrit, has been translated into Tamil prose and published. This Mahatmyam includes chapters fifty to fifty-eight. The Tamil shrine purana is also structured according to the titles of these chapters.

“Therefore, the section of the Sanskrit purana has been included as evidence that this shrine purana was composed following the stories in that Mahapurana in Sanskrit. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who arrived at this shrine of Thiruvaadanai, bestowed a pathigam. It is the 112th pathigam of the Second Thirumurai, set to the tune of Nattarapam. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (முருகேறிய ஆதி ஆட போதினா புனைதே தூ தமைவாதிய வினை மாயுமே ஏடின மழி வெங்கடத்து நூறு ஆடூரை ஆட நாடி யம்ப) The summary of this pathigam is that for those who praise Thiruvaadanai, where the Primordial Lord resides, their afflictions will not bother them, and their past karmic actions, diseases, and ailments will vanish. This pathigam was sung in praise of the shrine, believing that by showering flowers and worshipping this town, afflictions would disappear.

“Similarly, we can recall pathigams sung in praise of shrines like Thiruvarur and Thirumuthukundram. The pathigams for Aaroor and Muthukundram mention showering flowers. The pathigams say “showering flowers on Muthukundram.” Similarly, this pathigam was sung by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, advocating the worship of the Thiruvaadanai shrine by showering flowers.
