“Therefore, there is room to believe that this pathigam was composed from outside the shrine. If so, since Sekkizhar Peruman sang “offered garlands of pure Tamil verses,” it is possible that there are still more pathigams fitting that description.

“Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having worshipped Thiruvaadanai, was described by Sekkizhar Peruman as having partaken of knowledge for the world when he went to Thiruppunavayil and praised and worshipped the Lord. When mentioning the Thiruppunavayil shrine, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to it as “peerless Punavaiyil” (Oppariya Punavasa). Sekkizhar Peruman refers to it as “peerless Punavaiyil” because this shrine is ancient and possesses extraordinary divine significance.

“Here, in the Thiruppunavayil temple, we can worship and experience all fourteen shrines of the Pandya kingdom. Sekkizhar Peruman extols this shrine as the “peerless Thiruppunavayil” due to its many distinctions and other unique qualities. This shrine, also known as Thiruppunavasal, is the seventh among the fourteen celebrated shrines in the Pandya kingdom. It is renowned as an ancient town, known as Viruthapuri.

“Sundaramoorthy Swamigal praised this shrine in his Thevaram, stating, “It is an ancient town where many devotees sing and dance.” All thirteen other ancient shrines in the Pandya kingdom are collectively present in this temple. Sivakavimani Aiyya writes that establishing separate temples for these deities, inscribing their respective names, and performing worship and renovations is a highly meritorious act of Shiva dharma. The Thiruvasagam mentions that the Pandya kingdom itself is an ancient land. As Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sang, “The owls hoot in Punavayile,” and “the dark fowl climb the anthill and crow in Punavayile.” In accordance with Sundaramoorthy Swamigal’s words, the hooting of owls, the crowing of fowls on anthills, the sounds of hunters, rocky hills, thorny bushes, barren lands, coastal forests, kalli trees with long branches, and the drums of hunting all remain visible and audible in this shrine even today. The truth of the words of our great sages is evident. The main lingam and avudaiyar are of enormous size.

“Regarding the tying of the sacred cloth (parivattam) for these, the saying “three cubits for one round and thirty cubits for one round” is prevalent here. The parivattam for such a huge Lingam and Avudaiyar is tied to measure three cubits for one round around the Lingam and thirty cubits for one round around the Avudaiyar. The vimana (temple tower) is also very large and beautifully constructed. Among the shrines in the Pandya kingdom, this one is known to be difficult to reach due to arduous paths. Worshipping here alone is said to bestow the benefits of worshipping all other shrines in the Pandya kingdom. The fact that Lakshmi and Brahma worshipped this shrine is known through its sacred waters.

“The Lord’s names are Pazhampathinathar, Viruthapureeswarar, and Mahalingeswarar. The Goddess’s names are Piragunayaki, Periyanayaki, and Karunai Nayaki. The sacred trees are Punnai and Konrai. The sacred waters are Lakshmi Theertham, Brahma Theertham, Indra Theertham, Chakra Theertham, Surya Theertham, Chandra Theertham, Pampaa Ru, Varuna Theertham, Kalyana Theertham, and Sivaganga, totaling ten sacred waters. Lord Ganesha came here to seek blessings to defeat Gajamukhasuran. He bathed in Sivaganga and received the grace of Pazhampathinathar.

“The Tripuras who realized their mistakes worshipped here. Angarakan, who learned about the greatness of this shrine through Narada, worshipped here and received blessings, thus obtaining a boon from Shiva that the prayers of those who worship on Tuesdays will be fulfilled, and Angarakan resides here. Brahma regained his power of creation at this shrine. Chandra was freed from Daksha’s curse at this shrine. When Yama’s messengers attempted to take Susilan and his wife, Shiva’s Ganas rescued them, and they attained liberation at this shrine. Agasthiyar witnessed Shiva’s wedding in this place.

“Ambika as Bhadrakali destroyed the demon Vyagrasuran here. Mahalakshmi received a boon from Bhairava to protect Vishnu and her marriage. Devendran created a sacred tank and worshipped here to absolve Sage Gouthama’s curse. Rama worshipped and received blessings here. All these historical events are elaborately recounted in the purana of this shrine. Since Kali resides in the rock-cut cave at the entrance of the unfinished tower (mottagopura vayil), and the deity is very fierce, this door is always kept closed.

“The purana of this shrine was composed by Thiruvarur Thiyagaraja Kavirayar. It is said that those who die in Kasi attain liberation, but Thiruppunavayil bestows Jeevan Mukti (liberation while living) by removing the sins of those who come and worship here, as stated in the Viruthapuri Mahatmiyam. The Viruthapuri Mahatmiyam is described in the Ekadasa Rudra Vaibhava Khandam of the Shiva Mahapurana. This shrine is also known by the names Indrapuram, Sathanandapuram, Vajradrumavanam, Vanamugam, Kaivalyapuram, and Viruthakasi. Among the shrines surrounding Thiruppunavayil, Thirthaandathanam is in the southeast, Paraiyathur in the northwest, Kalyana puram further northwest, Velimuthy in the west, and the shrine worshipped by Vasishtar in the north. The purana states that Viruthapureeswarar bestows grace in these places as well.

“The shrine’s purana states that Yama and his messengers will not enter the vicinity of Viruthapuri, and all who die here will attain Shivalokam. Five inscriptions from the period of the Pandya kings have been discovered at this shrine. In the inscriptions, the Lord is referred to as Thiruppunavasal Udaiya Nayanar. It also has other names such as Virathapathi, Virathakasi, Indrapuram, Brahmapuram, Vajravanam, Kaivalyagnanapuram, and Dakshina Thiruchitrambalam. This Lingamurthi is next in size only to the Brihadeeswarar in Thanjavur. Its height is nine feet, and its circumference is eight and a half feet.

“The Avudaiyar has a circumference of thirty-three feet, and the Gomukhi is three and a half feet long. In the Mahamandapam, to the south, Somaskandar, Nalvar, and Sekkizhar are seen. We learn from the puranas that on Vaikasi Punarpoosam, the flag is hoisted, on Swathi, the chariot festival takes place, and on Visagam, the Theerthavari (bathing ritual) occurs.

“Also, on Maasi Magam, the Panchamurthis come forth and perform the Theertham (sacred bath) in the Sharpanathi (Paampaaru). Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who arrived at this shrine, bestowed a pathigam. It is the eleventh pathigam of the Third Thirumurai, a pathigam set to the tune of Gandhara Panchamam. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (பேரைப் பள்ளியுள் பழிகள் போற்றும் அமரும் இடம்) (உணல் மாமூதி உணவாயிலே பொண்ணு தோடிய உமைப்பே உணவாயிலை கேட்டவர் துழுது ஏத்த நியஞான) The summary of this pathigam is that the Lord, praised for various qualities such as having a red matted lock and a white crescent moon, resides with the Goddess in the Punavaiyil, surrounded by punnai trees.

“Let us press on in meditation.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, Part 760, by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, the section on Vambara Varivanda Charukkam, the puranam of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships at the Thiruppunavayil temple and resides there for some days. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing the 892nd verse: “Having praised many joyful abodes of the three-eyed Lord in the Pandya kingdom, a land filled with shrines, and having established the path of Vedic scriptures and bestowed elevated liberation through the essence of sacred ash, he came to live in Kalinagar. Surrounded by many devotees of the Lord with the eye on his forehead, and with the moon-crowned king revering him, he came to Manamelkudi, the town of the minister.” This verse describes how Thirugnanasambandha Peruman visits many shrines near Thiruppunavaiyil in the Pandya kingdom. He visits many shrines near Thiruppunavayil in the Pandya kingdom.

This Pandya kingdom is renowned for the Lord and the Goddess ruling as king and queen. It is a land where the Supreme Lord Himself reigns as sovereign. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman visits many such shrines in the Pandya kingdom. These shrines are believed to include Oriyur and others. Oriyur is a Vaippu Thalam (a shrine mentioned in devotional hymns but without a full pathigam dedicated to it). Having worshipped these shrines, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman travels to Manamelkudi, the town of Kulachirai Nayanar.

From Thiruppunavayil, traveling along the coast, usually northeast by road, one reaches Manamelkudi. Further along the coast from here, traveling north, this road passes through Ammanichatram, Sethupava Chatram, Rajamadam, Athiveeraramapattinam, and extends up to Mannargudi. In earlier days, this was the main road used by pilgrims coming to Rameswaram from the northern kingdoms. It was along this path that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman traveled from the Pandya kingdom back to the Chola kingdom. In the Pandya kingdom, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman established the path of Vedic scriptures and the elevated status bestowed by the sacred ash. Sekkizhar Peruman describes the path of Vedic scriptures as the “ordained path of Vedic scriptures.” The Vedas contain prescriptive statements like “Sathyam Vadha Dharmam Chara” (Speak the truth, practice righteousness).

Such prescriptive statements are prevalent in the Vedas. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, by commanding everyone to adhere to the discipline and path laid out by the Vedas and the scriptures derived from them, greatly promoted the Vedic way. He also removed all obstacles caused by external religions that condemned Vedic sacrifices and did not follow Vedic principles.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman emphatically stressed the Vedic path.

Next, the significance of the sacred ash: this is the path of the Agamas, the Saivite path, where the Saivite path leads to the highest liberation. The most excellent support for this is the sacred ash itself. The Saivite path and the sacred ash are inextricably linked. The sacred ash, as a symbol of rejecting other religions and upholding the Vedic path, and promoting the flourishing Saivite way, which were the core objectives of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s divine incarnation, were all established and fulfilled here in the Pandya kingdom by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. These actions, which began in Madurai, were carried out throughout the Pandya kingdom. Having completed this, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, accompanied by all the devotees, arrived at Kulachirai Nayanar’s Manamelkudi.

Manamelkudi was, in earlier days, a part of the Pandya kingdom, a shrine on its border. It is near Aranthangi and is a town with a significant Muslim population. It can be reached about sixteen naligais southeast of Avudaiyar Koil. From Thiruppunavayil, it can be reached in about eight naligais northeast to Mimeesal, and from there, about seven naligais northeast. The Vellar River near Manamelkudi This Vellar river, also known as Swetha Nadi, served as the northern border of the Pandya kingdom in ancient times, separating and defining the boundaries between the Pandya and Chola kingdoms.

Therefore, this Manamelkudi was a shrine within the Pandya kingdom. It was to this Manamelkudi, the abode of our Kulachirai Nayanar, that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrived. He was accompanied by the Pandya king, Mangaiyarkarasi Pirattiyar, and Kulachirai Nayanar. Sekkizhar Peruman then composed the next verses: “While he joyfully resided in that city, he visited the many shrines surrounding it. He returned and joined with the permanent holy devotees. The king, Mangaiyarkarasi, and Kulachirai, with his sharp spear, together worshipped his mighty feet and praised him with supplications.

“During the days when the Chief of Sirapuram, who praises the feet of the Lord adorned with the crescent moon on His head, joyfully resided there, he resolved to return to the Chola kingdom, the land of the surging Kaveri. Mangaiyarkarasi, the king of the South, and the minister, unable to bear separation from his sacred feet, wished to accompany him. Seeing this, he said, ‘If you agree to what I say now, you will be upholding the path of Shiva.’ Thus, to those who were greatly distressed, he gave suitable advice to prevent their distress. Having visited and worshipped these temples where the Lord resides, he returned and joined the devotees in Manamelkudi.

“The Pandya king, Mangaiyarkarasi Ammaiyar, and Kulachiraiyar, together, bowed at the sacred feet of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and served him. There, the chief of Sirkazhi, the child-saint, praised the Lord’s sacred feet and resided joyfully. During those days of his residence, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman resolved to return to the Chola kingdom, the land of the surging Kaveri River. Having received the Lord’s divine hint, he resolved to return to the Ponni Nadu (Chola kingdom). Mangaiyarkarasi Pirattiyar, King Nindraseer Nedumaran Nayanar of Pandya, and Kulachirai Nayanar, unable to bear separation from Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred feet, looked to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, expressing their desire to accompany him. They looked to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having decided that leaving their kingdom and government to follow and live with the child-saint was the most certain benefit.

“We see this profound state of love in Mangaiyarkarasi Pirattiyar, the Pandya king, and Kulachirai Nayanar, who were determined to accompany the child-saint. As they looked at him, the child-saint replied, “Listen to my words and accept them as a command. Remain here and uphold the path of Shiva. Upholding the path of Shiva is the duty of governance and the path of love, and it is pleasing to my heart.

“Therefore, you three should remain in the Pandya kingdom and uphold the path of Shiva.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman graciously instructed them to uphold the path of Shiva in the Pandya kingdom, holding it firmly without wavering as they did before. Unable to stay without the child-saint, yet unable to disobey his command and accompany him, their grief at separation intensified, and the three great individuals stood greatly distressed. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman spoke suitable words to console them, preventing their distress. Fearing to disobey the command of the eminent Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, they reluctantly agreed to his return to the Chola kingdom and, taking leave, prostrated themselves at his sacred feet. They stood revering the child-saint, who had incarnated for the salvation of the world, with an unbreakable friendship.

“With an overflowing love that could never be separated in their hearts, they prostrated at the sacred feet of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and stood worshipping him. At that moment, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman took leave from them, praised the Lord who had consumed the deadly poison of Kalakala, and departed from that land, the Pandya kingdom, returning to his own land, the Chola kingdom. In the 896th verse, Sekkizhar Peruman begins to sing the divine history of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman entering the fertile land of Ponni Nadu (Chola kingdom) from the Pandya kingdom and commencing his pilgrimage there: “Having entered the flourishing land of Ponni, he went to every temple of the Lord adorned with serpent ornaments, accompanied by a multitude of eminent devotees, and worshipped with the devotees, while the inhabitants praised him. He worshipped the holy Kanni Madhil Thirukkalar, sang praises of Karaiyanindar’s sacred feet and the Suram (shrine) of his sacred feet, worshipped other shrines he had visited before, and reached the banks of Mullivai. This is how Sekkizhar Peruman begins to sing about Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s divine history. “Let us go on meditating.””” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, Part 761, by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, the section on Vambara Varivanda Charukkam, the puranam of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having entered the Chola kingdom, where the Kaveri river bestows fertility, worships at the Lord’s temples with the assembly of devotees. We saw that the town of Thirumanamelkudi was on the border of the Pandya kingdom. From there, crossing the Vellar River, located four naligais to the north, one can enter the Chola kingdom. This Vellar River, also known as Swetha Nadi, served as the boundary between the Pandya and Chola kingdoms in those days.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who undertook this journey, worshipped at temples with his unparalleled devotees. The unparalleled distinction of these devotees was the honor of accompanying the child-saint, and later, the distinction of attaining Shivaloka and liberation.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having crossed the Pandya kingdom and reached the border of the Chola kingdom, visits all the temples on the border. These temples include Thiruvusathanam and others. Having traveled thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reaches the shrine called Thirukkalar, which has fortified walls. The distinction of achieving Shiva Loka and liberation.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having crossed the Pandya kingdom and reached the border of the Chola kingdom, visits all the temples on the border. These temples include Thiruvusathanam and other such places. Having traveled thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reaches the shrine called Thirukkalar, which has fortified walls. This shrine, Thirukkalar, in the Kaveri region of the Chola kingdom, is where Lord Nataraja, who manifested Himself on the south bank of the Kaveri, revealed His form to Durvasa. It is a shrine worshipped by sages such as Parasara and Kalavar. The Subramanya shrine here is particularly prominent.

To reach this shrine, one can travel west from Thiruvarurpoodi, on the path to Kalappal, and then a short distance north from the Muthuppettai road junction. Traveling west from Thiruvarurpoodi, on the path to Kalappal, and then a short distance north from the Muthuppettai road junction, one can reach this shrine. The Lord’s names are Kallar Mulaivannathar and Parijathavaneswarar. The Goddess is Amirthavalli, also known as Ilangombam. The sacred tree is Parijatham. The sacred waters are Durvasa Theertham, Gnana Theertham, Brahma Theertham, and Rudra Theertham.

It was at this shrine that Murugapperuman imparted the Panchakshara mantra to sixty thousand sages and Durvasa.

Therefore, Murugapperuman grants blessings here in the form of a Guru, without Valli and Deivanai. At this shrine, Shiva revealed the Brahmataandava (Cosmic Dance) darshanam. The form of Nataraja performing the Brahmataandava and the form of Durvasa standing with folded hands are present here. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who arrived here, bestowed a pathigam. It is the fifty-first pathigam of the Second Thirumurai. The fifty-first pathigam, set to the tune of Seekamaram.

The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (நீருள்ளார் கயல் வாவி சூழ் பொழில் நீண்ட மாவையல் ஈண்டு மாமதில் தேறினார் மருகில் விழாமல்கு திருக்களருள் ஊருளார் இடு பிச்சை பேணும் ஒருவனே ஒளிர் செஞ்சடைமதி ஆற நின்றவனே அடைந்தார்கு அருளாயே இந்து வந்தழு மாட வீதி எழில் கொள் காளிநகர் கவுணியன் செந்து நேர் மொழியார் அவர் சேரும் திருக்களருள் அந்தியன்னதோர் மேனியானை அமர்த்தன் பெருமானை ஞானசம்பந்தன் சொல் இவை பத்தும் பாட தவமாமே) Thiruchitrambalam. Groves, fields, walls, streets, and mansions, full of festivals. The summary of this pathigam is that the Lord, who is first praised as the one who seeks alms in the glorious Thirukkalar, which is abundant with groves, fields, walls, streets, and mansions full of festivals, grants grace to those who approach him.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having worshipped Thirukkalar and received the Lord’s gracious permission, went to the shrine called Thiruppadalaicharam and bestowed a pathigam. Thiruppadalaicharam is the 104th shrine on the south bank of the Kaveri to be praised in the Thevaram. It is known as Pamanipaambani (serpent-adorned). This shrine is where Dhananjayan, a serpent and brother of Adiseshan, came from the netherworld through a fissure, worshipped, and attained blessings.

Therefore, it is named Padalaicharam (netherworld shrine) and Pambani (serpent-adorned). In Sanskrit, it is called Sarppapuram. The Lord’s divine names are Sarppapureeswarar and Naganathar. The Goddess is Amirthanayaki. The sacred water is Naga Theertham.

When the sage Sukala saw Kamadhenu, which he had raised, worshipping a Shiva Lingam by showering milk, he grew angry, fearing a decrease in his milk supply, and struck her. Kamadhenu, distressed by this, ran and worshipped, then collided with the Shiva Lingam as if to convey its plight, and fell into the Pasupathi Theertham in the northern street of this temple.

At that moment, the Lord appeared and brought the cow back to life. Because Kamadhenu struck it, the original deity is seen with three scars, appearing as three divisions. These three divisions are joined together with copper plates, and the Lord grants his divine vision. Dhananjayan, the serpent, worshipped the Lord here on the first day of Aippasi. Green grapes, mangoes, and mango juice are special offerings here. In the inscriptions from the time of Rajarajan, this shrine is referred to as Pambani Kutram, Pambani of Sutraveli Valanadu.

This shrine is very close to Mannargudi. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who arrived here, bestowed a pathigam. It is the 108th pathigam of the First Thirumurai, set to the tune of Vyazakkurinchi. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (மின்னியல் செஞ்சடை மேல் விளங்கும் மதி மத்தமொடு நல்ல பொன்னியல் கொன்றையினான் புனல் சூடி பொற்பமரும் அன்னம் அன நடையால் ஒரு பாகத்து அமர்ந்தருளி நாளும் பன்னிய பாடலினான் உரை கோயில் பாதாளே பன்மலர் வைகு பொழில் புடைசூழ்ந்த பாதாளை சேர பொன்னியன் மாடமல்கு புகலின் நகர் மன்னன் தன்) (இன்னிசை பத்தும் வல்லார் எழில் வானத்து இருப்பாரே) Thiruchitrambalam. The summary of this pathigam is that the Lord, known by many attributes such as having a crescent moon and fragrant konrai flowers on his bright matted locks, and a beautiful earring in his ear, resides in Padalaicharam, also known as Padalaicharam.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having worshipped Padalaicharam, went on to worship other shrines. Although these were shrines he had worshipped before, he did not bypass them but went and worshipped them again. This is also the practice of pilgrimage. The shrines visited by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman include Thiruppoovanur, Thiruvenniyur, Thiruvayppadi, and others. Having visited many such holy places, including Tharum Poomullai, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reached Mullivaikkari. Mullivaikkari is now a branch of the Cauvery River, known as Odambokki Aaru or Mulliyaaru.

Just as Kaduvaykkari, Pazhamanni, and Padikkari exist, so does Mullivaikkari.

Therefore, this place is also named Mullivaikkari because it is situated on the bank of this river. Nearby, on the north bank of this river, is the sacred place of Thirukollambuthur. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman thus arrives at the bank of this river. A great flood flows in that river. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman composes the eight hundred ninety-seventh verse: “Malai Valar Sandhanam Agilum Thekkum Undi Malar Pirangal Vanda Sumandu Pongi Alai Peru.” He composes this verse, describing how he saw it and stood on that bank.

The river is heavily flooded. Sandalwood, agarwood, teak, and other trees that grow on the mountain are being pushed and carried by the flood.

Therefore, this river, coming from the Kurinji region through the Mullai forest, carries the items native to Kurinji, such as agarwood and sandalwood, and items native to Mullai, such as flowers, and thus arrives in the Marutha country. Due to this heavy flooding, boats are tied at the river’s ghats. It is impossible to steer boats in such a flood.

Therefore, the boatmen, those who navigate the waters, have tied their boats to the bank and left. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman observes this from the bank. As he watches, the sacred place of Thirukollambuthur appears on the opposite bank. The sacred place of Thirukollambuthur, where the Lord of the Devas resides, appears on the opposite bank. With a desire to go and worship, and with no boatmen to ferry the boats, the Guardian of Shanbai, with great haste, untied a boat, put the Lord’s devotees in it, and with the power of his tongue. Standing on it, he praised our Lord, singing ‘Kottam.’ By the grace of the Lord who consumed poison to save the celestials, the boat moved on its own.

After reaching the opposite bank at Kollambuthur, the abode of the Lord with golden matted hair, the Child who received wisdom, along with his good devotees, disembarked from the boat and arrived joyfully before the temple entrance of the Lord, who loves fragrant konrai flowers.

Thus, the divine Sekkizhar Peruman sings of this miraculous divine event in the eight hundred ninety-eighth and eight hundred ninety-ninth verses. From this bank of the river, as Thirugnanasambandha Peruman looks, the sacred place of Thirukollambuthur appears on the opposite bank of the river. The depth and speed of the water, the direction of flow, And other factors that allow a boat to be properly navigated are not present, and there are no boatmen there; only a boat is tied.

But Thirugnanasambandha Peruman intends to go to Thirukollambuthur on the opposite bank and worship the Lord. When we are on a pilgrimage or traveling somewhere, as soon as a temple appears in our sight, we should go and worship there. Such a desire to worship arises only in those who have a mature state of mind, born from previous spiritual practice. It will appear only to them.

Sundaramoorthy Swamigal and Cheraman Perumal Nayanar, after worshipping Thirukandiyoor, saw Thiruvaiyaru appear on the north bank of the Cauvery River. With a melting body and a melting heart, they joined their hands above their heads and crossed the Cauvery, which flowed like a vast sea, to worship the sacred feet.

Sundaramoorthy Swamigal desired to worship the sacred feet of the Lord. With a melting heart, he composed a pathigam, asking the Lord of Thiruvaiyaru how he could cross this river to worship Him.

Similarly, Kannappa Nayanar, from this bank of the Ponmugali River, looking towards the Thirukalathi hill, was prompted by an inner feeling born of previous spiritual practice to go and worship there.

Therefore, the inner meaning of the perfected states of Sundaramoorthy Swamigal and Kannappa Nayanar is something we should reflect upon here.

Similarly, when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman saw the temple, the sacred place of Thirukollambuthur, on the other side of the river, he desired to go and worship it. In these three instances, the rivers of this world hinder the natural flow of devotion towards the Lord.

But because the river of love overflows in these three great individuals, the connection with the Lord happens there.

Therefore, when one sees a Shiva temple or a sacred form, the surge of love and devotion occurs only if there is spiritual maturity. Such a surge of love and devotion is a sign of their maturity. We can recall what Pazhudurai Adigal says: “A time will come when one sees one’s beloved and rejoices; only a small path to salvation is created.” Therefore, there were boats there, but no boatmen. So Thirugnanasambandha Peruman gathered all the devotees into the boat, and he himself boarded the boat, and standing on it, he composed a pathigam with the refrain “Nalkumaru Arul Nambane,” remembering Shiva, the Lord, who never abandons those who trust and seek refuge in Him at all times, and who is always there to help from within. He composed a pathigam, taking his tongue’s power as a staff, and standing on that boat, he praised Shiva, the Lord, beginning with ‘Kottame.’ This pathigam is set to the tune of Gandhara Panchamam, it is the third pathigam in the third Thirumurai, and it is structured as a ‘Eeradi Mel Vaipu’ (two-line refrain). The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam.

“Kottame Kamazhum Kollambuthur Nattam Adiya Nambanai Ulgu Sella Unduga Sindhaiyaar Tozha Nalkumaru Arul Nambane.” “Konrai Ser Sadaiyaan Kollambuthur Nandru Kaliyul Gnanasambandan Indru Sol Malai Kondu Ye.” And they will be with the celestials forever.

“Nambane Arul Nalkumaru” – thus Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises the divine grace and composes this pathigam. As soon as he sang the pathigam, by the divine grace of the Lord who consumed poison to save the Devas, the boat was propelled. The boat was guided to the Thirukollambuthur of Lord Shiva and brought to the opposite bank. Just as the Lord protected the celestials who sought refuge in Him from dying, transforming the deadly poison into a life-giving force, here too, the grace of the Lord’s compassion is manifested, altering the power of the water that pulls downwards. The boat travels on its own, without a boatman, and reaches the bank at Thirukollambuthur.

It cuts through the opposing current. Although the boat appears to move on its own outwardly, it was the power of divine grace that propelled it from within without being outwardly visible.

Thus, the boat reaches the Thirukollambuthur bank. From the south bank, the boat goes to the north bank where the Lord’s temple of Thirukollambuthur is situated. Upon reaching there, the Child who received wisdom, accompanied by his good devotees, disembarks from the boat to worship the Lord. He joyfully arrives before the entrance of the temple of the Lord who wears the Konrai flower. Thirukollambuthur is the hundred and thirteenth sacred place among the temples on the south bank of the Cauvery that are praised in verses. It is known as Vilvavanam and also Thirukalambur.

The story of the Child driving the boat without a boatman and reaching the bank here is mentioned in the sixth and seventh verses of the pathigam we saw above. This festival, commemorating the Child’s act of driving the boat, is celebrated annually. The Lord’s name is Vilva Vananathar, and the Goddess’s name is Soundarya Nayaki. The sacred tree is the Vilva tree. One can reach this sacred place by going a short distance from Koradacheri to Sellur and then a short distance west. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman thus arrives at the temple of Thirukollambuthur.

The divine Sekkizhar Peruman explains in this verse how Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worshipped Thirukollambuthur: “He worshipped the tall gopuram, entered it, and accompanied by incomparable devotees, he approached the brilliant temple, circumambulated it, and stood before the Lord with the crescent moon in his matted hair, bowing down and saying, ‘O Lord who gave me grace by enabling me to drive the boat on the river by myself! O Lord adorned with snakes! O three-eyed pure one who is covered with the skin of an elephant!’” Thus, he worshipped and praised the Lord. Bowing to the tall gopuram, he entered through the sacred doorway, and accompanied by unparalleled devotees, he drew near. He circumambulated the radiant temple, arrived, and stood before the Lord with matted hair adorned with the crescent moon, bowing down. He humbly praised and glorified, saying, “O Lord who bestowed grace upon me by enabling me to steer the boat across the river by myself!

“O Lord adorned with serpents! O three-eyed pure one who wore the skin of an elephant!” After Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed the pathigam, steered the boat in the river, and reached the temple, the special worship offered by the Child there is thus explained by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises the Lord, saying, “O Lord adorned with serpents! O Lord who flayed and wore the elephant!” These two acts symbolize the Lord’s power to remove great obstacles and to transform evil into good. The flaying of the elephant and other heroic deeds were performed by the Lord out of abundant compassion.

“Therefore, the Lord is the wondrous one who stood as an unseen helper in the midst of the river.

“Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships and praises before the temple, remembering this repeatedly.

“Similarly, when Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal, who floated on a stone by singing a pathigam in the midst of the ocean and reached the shore, entered Thirupathirippuliyoor, he stood before the Lord and began to praise, saying, “You are my mother and my father,” and praised, “You were an unseen helper to your devotees.” Similarly, this sacred history, praised by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman here, reminds us of that. In this situation, the pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is not available to us due to our lack of spiritual merit.

“Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who worshipped Thirukollambuthur, decided to go and worship Tharbharanyeswarar of Thirunallaaru, the hero of the pathigam that emerged victorious in the fiery debate against the Jains in Madurai in the Pandiya kingdom, by not being consumed by fire. Our reflection now resumes.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 762, by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. During the days when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was residing in Thirukollambuthur after worshipping the Lord there, he desired to go to Thirunallaaru and worship the Lord.

The Lord of Thirunallaaru is the hero of the pathigam that remained unburnt and brought victory in the great fiery debate, the Annal Vatham, against the Jains in the presence of the Pandiya king in Madurai.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman obtained divine permission from the Lord at Thirukollambuthur and set out on a pilgrimage towards Thirunallaaru. Unable to bear parting from the Lord of Thirukollambuthur, he received divine permission and departed from there. He visits all the sacred places on the way from Thirukollambuthur to Thirunallaaru. Many sacred places like Thirukudavayil, Thiruvanchiyam, Thiruvambar, and Thiruppugalur are situated along the way. He visits all these places and reaches Thirunallaaru.

There, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reaches the temple of the Lord, who is widely praised and protects the land. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman refers to the sacred place of Thirunallaaru as a place that is widely praised by all directions. Even today, we see that those afflicted by sorrow and suffering come from all directions to Thirunallaaru, seek blessings, and find relief from their woes.

Therefore, the divine Sekkizhar Peruman praises such a Thirunallaaru as a widely praised sacred place. He worships before the Lord who owns the land. The name of the Lord of Thirunallaaru, Tharbharanyeswarar, is ‘Naddudai Nayagar’ (Lord of the land). The divine Sekkizhar Peruman explains the sacred story of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worshipping the Lord of Thirunallaaru and singing a pathigam in the nine hundred and second verse: “With many devotees surrounding him, he descended from the pearl palanquin, bowed at the glorious sacred entrance of Thirunallaaru temple, and entered. He circumambulated the temple where the Lord with the crescent moon on his head is enshrined, entered with joy, and with lotus-like hands joined in reverence, he worshipped the benevolent Lord. With tears flowing from his eyes, he sang a pathigam beginning with ‘Paadaka Melladi.’” All the devotees surrounded him, and from that place, he descended from the pearl palanquin.

He bowed at the magnificent sacred entrance of Thirunallaaru temple and entered. He circumambulated the inner precincts of the temple where the Lord with the crescent moon on his head is enshrined, entered with joy, and worshipped with his lotus-like hands joined together. The worship performed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman here was due to his insatiable remembrance of the immense grace that helped him internally in the royal court at Thirualavai. In this pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composes a pathigam beginning with “Paadaka Melladi,” making the great grace of the Lord of Thirunallaaru who came and resided in Alavai the refrain of each verse. Here too, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman begins this pathigam by placing Ambika first, saying “Paadaka Melladi Paavaiyodum.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman begins this pathigam.

We saw that in the unburnt green pathigam, “Bhogamartha Poonmulaiyaal,” Ambika was placed first.

Similarly, we saw that in the pathigam “Thaliril Valaruli Umai,” which was composed before the king in Madurai with the written leaf placed before him, the Goddess Uma was placed first.

Similarly, here in Thirunallaaru, in this pathigam that links the Lord of Thirualavai and the Lord of Thirunallaaru, Ambika, the divine energy, is placed first, as “Paadaka Melladi Paavai.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed this pathigam.

The Lord of Thirunallaaru is the benevolent one who manifested himself and came from the Chola country to the Pandiya country.

Therefore, to remove the Jains and enlighten Saivism, The Child, who returned from the Pandiya kingdom to the Chola kingdom, remembered it there and worshipped at Thirunallaaru.

Thus, in this pathigam, he questions, “What is this, that our Lord of Nallaaru resided in Alavai?” This pathigam, therefore, serves as a common pathigam for two sacred places, Thirunallaaru and Thirualavai. It is a question-and-answer pathigam. It asks, “What is it that the Lord who was in Thirunallaaru came and resided in Thirualavai?” This pathigam is set to the tune of Nattappadai. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: “Paadaka Melladi Paavaiyodum Padu Pinakkadidam Patti Nindru Naadakam A.” “Nallaaru Udaiya Namberuman idhu enkol Sollay Sudaga Munkay Madandai Maargal Thunaivarudum Thozhu Ethi Vaazhtha Aadaga Madam Nerungu Koodal Alavayin Kan Amarndhavare.” “Anbudaiyaanai Aranai Koodal Alavay Meviyathu Enkol endru Nanponai Nadanai Nallaatranai Nayambera Potri Nalanguzhavum Ponpudai Suztharu Madakaali Poosuran Gnanasambandan Sonna Inbudai Padalgal Pattum Vallar Imayavar Ethi Irupparthame.” Thiruchitrambalam.

The divine Sekkizhar Peruman explains the summary of this pathigam in the nine hundred and third verse as follows: “In the debate conducted by the Jains before the Southern King, the leaf placed in the fire remained green, and you were my inner support, residing openly in Alavai, my wonder, my Lord!” Saying, “What is this wonder, my Lord?” he adorned it with Tamil verses, praised it, and resided there with his virtuous devotees. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman then departed from Thirunallaaru, having received divine permission from the Lord of Thirunallaaru, to worship other sacred places of enduring fame. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman states that previously, in the debate conducted by the Jains in the presence of the Pandiya king, the leaf placed in the fire turned green, and the Lord manifested himself in Thirualavai as an inner support within his heart. He praises the Lord’s compassion repeatedly by composing this pathigam of sweet Tamil verses, asking, “What is this wonder, my Lord, that you resided there with such affection?” After this, he came out of the temple and resided in Thirunallaaru, that sacred place, accompanied by his sweet and devoted followers.

At that time, other sacred places of enduring fame. Having received divine permission from the Lord of Thirunallaaru, he worshipped and departed from Thirunallaaru.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reached the sacred place called Thiruthalicheri. A special divine event was about to happen there. In Bodhimangai, near Thiruthalicheri, many Buddhists lived.

At that time, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman began to sing. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman composes the nine hundred and fourth verse: “As he reached Thiruthalicheri, rich in glory, and worshipped Lord Shiva, he approached Bodhimangai, where the unattainable Buddhists reside. When the Saivites learned of this, they gathered like a tumultuous crowd, sounding countless instruments, and proclaimed, ‘The victor over other religions has come!’” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrived at the sacred place called Thiruthalicheri, rich in glories, and there he praised Lord Shiva and composed a pathigam. Thiruthalicheri is the fiftieth sacred place among the temples on the south bank of the Cauvery that are praised in verses. It is currently known as Koyilpattu.

The sanctum faces west, and a Sun worship (Surya Puja) takes place in the month of Panguni. The special feature of this place, where Devas and sages come to worship, is praised in Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s pathigam. The Lord’s name is Parvathivarar, and the Goddess’s name is Sakthiyammai or Parvathiyammai. The sacred pools are Surya Pushkarani and Parvathi Theertham. This place now forms part of Karaikkal town. This temple is located at the other end of the street where the Maampazheswarar temple stands in Karaikkal.

The pathigam (decade of verses) composed by Thirugnanasambandhar for this temple is the third pathigam in the second Thirumurai, set to the tune Indhalapann. The first and final verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam (PoovaLarnthana kondu muppodhum Porkazhal thevar vandhu vanangum miku theLichcheriyeer Mevorum thozhilaLodu keLal pin vedanam paavakam kodu nindrathu polum numpaanmaiye). (DikkuLam pozhil suzh theLichcheriyin selvanai Mikka kaaliyul Gnanasambandhan viLambiya thakka paadalgal pathum vallargal thadamudiththokka vanavar suzha iruppavar solli). This means: “O Lord of Thelichcheri, where devas come to worship your golden feet three times a day with blooming flowers! It seems you stood with the profession of a hunter, chasing a boar. Those who are skilled in these ten suitable verses, composed by Gnanasambandhan of Kaali, about the Lord of Thelichcheri, surrounded by groves in all directions, will be surrounded by celestial beings with grand crowns.”

This pathigam, composed by Thirugnanasambandhar, praises the Lord’s greatness, such as His going after a boar with the Goddess as a hunter, begging for alms everywhere, and adorning His head with the Ganga. As Thirugnanasambandhar thus worshipped Thiruthalichcheri and continued his pilgrimage, he passed through the nearby village of Bodhimangai. It was a village populated by Buddhists. As Thirugnanasambandhar traveled in the pearl palanquin bestowed by the Lord, accompanied by devotees blowing the trumpets and conches, and beating drums, he proceeded through the village of Bodhimangai.

We shall go on reflecting. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, composed by Dhivasekkilar, Part Seven Hundred and Sixty-Three, Vampara Varivandu Charukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. As Thirugnanasambandhar, after worshipping Thiruthalichcheri, proceeded on his pilgrimage, he passed through the village of Bodhimangai. This village of Bodhimangai was predominantly inhabited by Buddhists. As Thirugnanasambandhar proceeded through that village, seated in the pearl palanquin granted by the Lord, Shiva devotees and attendants, sounding the trumpets, conches, and other instruments given by the Lord, proclaimed the glory of Thirugnanasambandhar. This act of the devotees, attendants, and the general public, including the villagers, is a customary occurrence during all of Thirugnanasambandhar’s processions.

Therefore, as he passed through Bodhimangai, as always, Shiva devotees, in a fervor, blew conches, trumpets, and many auspicious instruments, proclaiming the glory of Thirugnanasambandhar as ‘ParasamyakolaRivan.’ ‘ParasamyakolaRi’ is an epithet praising Thirugnanasambandhar. ‘KolaRi’ means lion. ‘ParasamyakolaRi’ means one who is like a lion to the mad elephants of other religions.

Thus, singing praises, they proceed, immersed in this atmosphere. People traveling through public thoroughfares have the right to speak and act innocently, according to their own will. This is called freedom in modern times. In such a situation, the Jains in that village, unable to tolerate the words of praise for Thirugnanasambandhar and the sounds of trumpets, conches, and drums, gather together. They gather as if to obstruct the blessed procession of Thirugnanasambandhar. Overwhelmed by jealousy in their hearts, they are deluded and report this news to their leader, Buddhanandhi, and others.

They speak with great anger. The malice that arose in their hearts, the jealousy called ‘azhukkaaru’, clouded their intellect.

Thus, they went to Buddhanandhi, one of the foremost among their Buddhists, and spoke to him. Buddhanandhi is a traditional name for eminent and renounced Buddhists. Due to jealousy, as the Thirukkural says, ‘Azhukkaaru ena oru paavi thiruchattru theeyozhi uyththuvidum’ (Jealousy, that sinner, will completely lead one to evil). They are deluded due to this jealousy. For Buddhists, delusion means perceiving one thing as another and becoming confused. The Thirukkural describes this as ‘Porul allavatrai porul enru unarum marul’ (the delusion of perceiving non-existent things as existent).

While these Buddhists were thus reporting to their leader, Buddhanandhi, Thirugnanasambandhar’s procession approached. At that moment, the shouts of the devotees and the surging sound of the conches, along with the joyful exclamations of the Shiva devotees, reached Buddhanandhi’s ears. It was as if a sharp spear, heated in fire, had been plunged into his ears. Buddhanandhi, gathering all his followers, came before Thirugnanasambandhar’s assembly. Buddhanandhi angrily declared, “You hail your leader as ‘Parasama KolaRi,’ the conqueror of other religions, and sound trumpets as a sign of victory. You can only say that after defeating me in a debate!” Earlier, Thirugnanasambandhar had defeated the Jains in Madurai, which constituted a victory over all other religions.

However, Buddhanandhi, ignoring this, foolishly demanded that he too be defeated in a debate. He speaks out of ignorance, insisting he must be defeated in a debate. As Buddhanandhi spoke, what did he do? He obstructed the devotees in Thirugnanasambandhar’s procession that was approaching. He silenced the sacred conches they were blowing, claiming that conches should not be sounded in this village. He tried to use violence against the devotees, taking away their instruments.

Thirugnanasambandhar is a peerless pure sage of wisdom. He is the embodiment of compassion, devoid of hatred and attachment. This purity signifies inner cleanliness. The previous debate with the Jains and the upcoming debate with the Buddhists are not born of hatred towards external religions, nor are they due to affection for Shaivites. The compassion that Thirugnanasambandhar possesses is the compassion to reveal the true state of existence to all beings in this world and save them.

Therefore, he is a peerless pure sage of wisdom. These conches, trumpets, and other instruments were given by the true Lord; they do not proclaim false praises, but rather speak of the genuine and meaningful glories of Thirugnanasambandhar, the peerless wise leader.

However, when these instruments are sounded while passing through a public street, these Buddhists, believing themselves to be numerous in this village, unite and try to exert force, saying that such sounding should not occur and removing the instruments held by the devotees. Witnessing this, the true Shaivites become angry. In Shaivism, its path has always been one of patience and compassion.

However, when its state is encroached upon and obstructed by other religions, Shaivism also possesses the valor to not shrink from removing those obstacles and impediments through disciplinary action.

Therefore, these true devotees, becoming angry, thought that if they tolerated these outrageous acts of the Buddhists, the Buddhists would use more force. So they went to the palanquin where Thirugnanasambandhar was seated and informed the young child (Thirugnanasambandhar) of what was happening.

Here, we must remember one thing: whenever Thirugnanasambandhar visited any temple, a large crowd would surround him, preceding and following him, and the procession would extend for a great distance.

Therefore, this incident, this act of violence perpetrated by the Buddhists, occurred among the devotees in the front row of the procession.

Therefore, these devotees, becoming angry, walked back a long distance to where the young child (Thirugnanasambandhar) was coming and reported what was happening. They also recounted the violence committed by the Buddhists and the statement by Buddhanandhi that the praise ‘Parasama KolaRi’ would only be true after he was defeated in a debate. Thirugnanasambandhar, with a serene mind, considered that if these Buddhists spoke thus on the path where he was coming without any intention of debate, it was also for the good. He decided that he would expose the falsehood of Buddhanandhi and the true nature of their false doctrines. Thirugnanasambandhar thus graciously spoke to the devotees.

Therefore, this debate was not sought by them; it intervened on their path.

Thus, it was due to divine grace, and Thirugnanasambandhar, implying that divine grace orchestrates everything for good, decided to debate with these Buddhists and expose the true nature of their doctrines. As this was happening, Sambandha Saranalayar Swamigal, who was accompanying Thirugnanasambandhar’s procession, was the young child’s maternal uncle. He was the one who, always present, collected and compiled all of the young child’s pathigams onto palm-leaf manuscripts. It is mentioned that those palm-leaf manuscripts containing the young child’s pathigams would always be carried with him. We already saw this during the fire debate. Sambandha Saranalayar witnessed the events unfolding here, the use of force and violence by the Buddhists.

Immediately, he consulted the palm-leaf manuscripts containing the pathigams composed by Thirugnanasambandhar by drawing a string through them. The verse that appeared when he consulted the manuscripts in this manner was the tenth verse of the Panchakshara Pathigam, which begins with “Thunjalum Thunjalillatha Polthinam.” That tenth verse states: (Buddhar saman kazhukaiyar poikolla chithavargal theLinthu therina viththaka neeranivara vinaipagaikku aththiramavavana anjezhuththumae). This is the tenth verse of the Panchakshara Pathigam. What does it mean? It means that Buddhists and Jains, the false words they utter are not held in the minds of the clear-minded ones who recite with conviction the Sri Panchakshara. The divine five letters (Sri Panchakshara) are capable of striking like an arrow and destroying enemies who come to wage war against those who wear the sacred ash, which possesses all powers.

It says, ‘Aththiramavathu anjezhuththumae,’ meaning ‘the weapon is the five letters.’ In that verse, it is stated that ‘Aththiramavathu anjezhuththumae’ refers to the weapon for those who come to wage war with enmity against the wearers of sacred ash. As soon as ‘Aththiramavathu anjezhuththumae’ appeared upon consulting the Thirumurais, Sambandha Saranalayar considered this utterance to be the command of Thirugnanasambandhar, and taking this divine word as a command, Sambandha Saranalayar used it as a weapon. Unable to tolerate the slandering of Shaivism, devotees, and the Vedas by the Buddhists, Sambandha Saranalayar consulted the pathigams composed by Thirugnanasambandhar. When this particular verse from this pathigam appeared, he took it as a command and wielded it as a weapon. He declared that Buddhanandhi’s head should be struck by lightning and roll down, that his head should be severed and fall to the ground by a lightning strike. Dhivasekkilar, in the nine hundred and ninth verse, describes this: “The irresistible, powerful mantra, like a lightning bolt, that destroys obstacles opposing the order of the Shaiva path of the bull-mounted Lord, uttered by the truthful word of the devotee, tore the body and head of the Buddhist who came to engage in verbal battle into separate pieces.”

When this happened, the crowd of Buddhists scattered in disarray, filled with fear. The verse composed by Dhivasekkilar, the nine hundred and ninth verse, describes this. The divine command of the Lord of Shaiva tradition, who bears the bull emblem, was thus brought forth to dispel obstacles. The utterance of that devotee, filled with devotion, acted like an irresistible and powerful Shiva-weapon, a thunderbolt, that destroys and removes impediments to Shiva worship from all three sides – above, below, and in the middle. At that very moment, it shattered Buddhanandhi’s body and head into separate pieces. The word of the devotee manifested there as a Shiva-weapon.

A Shiva-weapon, according to the Agamas, is an Astra Mantra that, when used during Shiva Puja, unfailingly removes obstacles that hinder the puja from the above, middle, and lower regions, like a lightning strike.

Therefore, it is stated in the Agamas that one should remove all obstacles with that Shiva-weapon mantra and then begin the puja.

In the same way, that very Shiva-weapon, through the word of the devotee, caused Buddhanandhi’s body and head to separate. It was as if lightning had struck. Seeing this, the crowd of Buddhists was thrown into disarray, fled, and became filled with fear. Dhivasekkilar then states in the next verse, the nine hundred and tenth, that the others, seeing Buddhanandhi, who had challenged them to a verbal battle, fall with his head and body severed, and witnessing the devotees’ victory through that very word-weapon, came to the conclusion that this was the inevitable divine decree that had removed the impending obstruction, and they all began to proclaim: “Aran!” (Shiva). The sound of that proclamation reached the heavens. The next verse, the nine hundred and tenth, is composed by Dhivasekkilar.

The mantra of the pathigam, ‘Aththiramavathu Ainthezhuththumae’ (The weapon is the five letters), contained the weapon of Shiva as described in that verse. It was by this weapon that he fell, wasn’t it? The Sankalpa Nirakaranam states this: “The God of Kaunia in Kaali, with the joyful words of the devotees who compose excellent pathigams of divine wisdom, caused the head of the arrogant Buddhist to roll, not by wielding a sharp sword.” This incident, where Buddhanandhi’s head was struck by lightning and severed by the word of the devotee, Sambandha Saranalayar, occurred in the front row of the young child’s procession. The young child’s palanquin, however, was still progressing far behind.

Therefore, the devotees swiftly went to the young child and reported this event that had occurred in front. Thirugnanasambandhar heard it. When he heard that the Buddhist had died unexpectedly by a lightning strike, he declared that it was an act of Shiva’s grace, an inevitable divine decree, and urged everyone to praise Shiva. Thirugnanasambandhar proclaimed that the removal of the obstruction that had come upon their path, without them seeking it, was Shiva’s divine will (niyathi), and therefore, he asked everyone to chant Shiva’s name.

At that moment, the devotees in the procession chanted Shiva’s name, “Hara Hara,” which then reached up to the heavens. Let us go on reflecting. Thiru Thiruchitrambalam. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, composed by Dhivasekkilar, Part Seven Hundred and Sixty-Four, Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Buddhanandhi’s head fell separately from his body as if struck by lightning. Seeing this, all the other Buddhists were astonished and gathered among themselves, confused as to whether this event was caused by deception or was a result of the true power of the Shaiva religion. Pondering this in their minds and discussing it among themselves, they came to Thirugnanasambandhar, led by their leader, Sariputthan. Sambandha Saranalayar’s divine utterance caused that event, which was an act of sorcery.

Therefore, to perform that sorcery, these Buddhists, led by Sariputthan, approached the assembly of Shiva devotees and asked, “This is the truth of our religion, and we wish to debate it. Please agree to this.” The young child, born like a lion in the holy city of Seerkazhi, heard this, deemed it beautiful in his divine heart, and with great joy, quickly descended from his pearl palanquin. He ascended the mandapam (hall) of an inn there and sat with the Shaivites. In ancient times, inns were built along the routes for pilgrims from the North to Rameswaram. Thirugnanasambandhar, accompanied by his devotees, sat in the mandapam of one such inn.

Then, having obtained the young child’s consent, the Shiva devotees approached the Buddhist crowd and said, “Our victorious leader from Shambai, the head of the Vedas, and the master of the three Tamils, Thirugnanasambandhar, joyfully invites you. Please come and present the truth of your religion.” The Shiva devotees made it clear to the Buddhists that the one who invites them is a revered figure who upholds Vedic principles and who will conquer them by establishing those Vedic truths through the three Tamils. The Buddhists also They arrive before the assembly hall of that inn. Sariputta also arrives there. Sambandha Saranalayar then praises the sacred feet of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the beautiful leader of Sirkazhi, receives his grace, and begins the debate. Sambandha Saranalayar asks Sariputta to speak and elaborate on the God, the leader of his religion, and the nature of liberation, which is the meaning of what that God proclaims.

Thus, the religious debate begins. In general, during a religious debate, there are said to be two excellent areas for determining victory or defeat: the God concept of that religion and its liberation concept.

Therefore, the two topics of the definition of God and the definition of liberation were considered the best parts for presenting the arguments of one’s religion and achieving victory or defeat in a religious debate. In this era, religious condemnation itself serves as a religious debate, which we also observe here.

Thus, Sambandha Saranalayar Swamigal, praising the sacred feet of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and beginning the religious debate, asks Sariputta, “What is the concept of God in your religion? What is the definition of liberation in your religion?” Sariputta replies. For Buddhists, there is one Adi Buddha, and including him, there are a total of twenty-four Buddhas. Of these, the twenty-fourth The last was Gautama Buddha, who is widely known.

So, when asked about the concept of God in Buddhism, Sariputta explains the concept of God related to the Adi Buddha. There are fourteen Saiva Siddhanta Shastras, and among them, there is a Shastra called Sivagnana Siddhiyar, a text composed and bestowed by Arulnandi Sivachariyar, one of the Saiva religious Santana Acharyas. This Sivagnana Siddhiyar has two sections: Subaksham and Parapaksham. Parapaksham contains sections that refute and reject other doctrines.

Here, in this section of our Periya Puranam, where the debate with the Buddhists occurs, Theivasekkizhar Peruman presents that debate in ten verses. Desikanar, Sivakavimani, who wrote a commentary on this, quotes all those sections from Sivagnana Siddhiyar Parapaksham that refute the Buddhists. There are four branches of Buddhism: Sautrantika, Vaibhashika, Madhyamika, and Yogachara. Arulnandi Sivachariyar has refuted and rejected all four of these in Sivagnana Siddhiyar Parapaksham. As we saw earlier, those who do not accept or reject our Vedas as authoritative refer to their scriptures as Pitaka texts. This Pitaka refers to the tradition of twenty-four Buddhas, including the Adi Buddha.

These are texts taught through the order of instruction, categorized into three types: Vinaya Pitaka, Sutra Pitaka, and Abhidharma Pitaka. These are also known as Tripitaka or Pitaka Thrayam. Pitaka means ‘basket.’ The Buddhist saying is that Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are three types of jewels. Next, they speak of the second as Vedana Skandha. This is the sensation arising from the contact between the sense organs and their objects. This sensation is of six types, corresponding to the five sense organs and the mind. Since each of these six types can be classified into three categories—kusala (wholesome), akusala (unwholesome), and kusala-akusala (mixed)—Vedana becomes eighteen types.

Thus, this Vedana Skandha is of eighteen types. The third, Samjna Skandha, is the knowledge required to identify and name objects using general and specific understanding, which arises from the six types of sensations associated with the six sense organs: body, mouth, eye, nose, ear, and mind. This skandha arises through the six sense organs.

Next, the fourth is Bhavana Skandha. This refers to the special maturation (paripaka vishesham) that the karmic instruments (karana) attain due to the differences in actions performed by the three instruments: mind, speech, and body. This skandha is said to be of fifty-two types and is also called Samskara Skandha. Fifth is Vijnana Skandha. The consciousness of sleeping beings, like a single agent, resides within conscious beings and is the consciousness principle that supports all their knowledge. This Vijnana Skandha is categorized into eighty-nine types based on the various types of thoughts, good and bad actions, which are its functions.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman While Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was staying in Thiru Kadavur, due to the memory of his previous visit to this temple with Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, and remembering how he stopped Thirunavukkarasu at Thirumaraikadu (Vedaranyam) to separate and proceed to the Pandya kingdom to establish Saivism there, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman inquired of the devotees, “In which city is Vagisa Mamunivar residing?” When the devotees in that city approached him, “Konnavilum kootruthaithar kuraikkazhalgal paninthu ethi manni amarndu uraiyunal Vagisa Mamunivar en nagaril ezhuntharulittu” (Vagisa Mamunivar is residing in my city, after reverently bowing to the feet of the One who kicked Yama, who causes fear).

The devotees then told him that the Lord was residing in Thirupunduruthi, a city surrounded by abundant waters, and was engaged in joyful service, and asked, “Engu” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s query to the devotees, asking, “In which city is Vagisa Mamunivar residing?”, prompts us to recall the historical event where Thirugnanasambandha Peruman bid farewell to Vagisa Munivar at Vedaranyam and departed, as narrated by Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman in verses 927 and 928, “Vakkeesar maaratha vannam vanangi arul seidhu vidai koduththu mannam kathalinal arumaiyura kalanthu neengi” (Vakkeesar, unchanging, bowed and received grace, and departed with love and difficulty). Therefore, the immense and incomparable desire to see the ruling Lord grows greatly in Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s heart. Therefore, this is now in Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s heart. So, receiving gracious permission from the Lord there, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman quickly proceeds towards Thirupunduruthi. Poovium Thadanjolai Pudaipparappu. The 930th verse states, “Unnal parakkum Kaveriyin thenkarai poi kannudhalaar magizhntha idam mevi inithu amarnthu irainchi viruppuru mey thondarodu Navarasar uzhaichai nagararasar nannuvar” (Going to the south bank of the Kaveri, where water spreads, and arriving at the place where the Lord with the eye on his forehead rejoices, he joyfully worships and, with beloved true devotees, approaches Navarasar, the ruler of that city). Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds along the south bank of the Kaveri, where large groves of flowering trees extend on either side as the water spreads. When the Kaveri overflows, the water rises and spreads into the groves on the banks, nourishing them, as we can always observe. Thirukadavur is a temple on the south bank of the Kaveri. From there, the young Lord proceeds along the south bank of the Kaveri towards Thirupunduruthi, a shrine located on the south bank of the Kaveri. When Vagisa Mamunivar, who was residing and serving in Thirupunduruthi, heard the great news of the young Lord, the gem among brahmins, approaching very close to Thirupunduruthi, he was filled with joy.

He thought, “Our going forth to welcome and worship the young Lord, who rules over us, is a benefit we receive as a result of the good deeds we performed in our previous births.” Thirunavukkarasu Peruman then blossomed with inner and outer joy. Let us persist in our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 767, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, composed by Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman. When Vagisa Mamunivar heard the great news of the young Lord approaching Thirupunduruthi, he was filled with inner and outer joy, thinking, “Our going forth to welcome and worship the young Lord, who rules over us, is a benefit we receive as a result of the good deeds we performed in our previous births.” As the great news of the Lord, the jewel among brahmins, arriving near Poonthuruthi reached Vagisa, his face bloomed, and his heart blossomed, thinking, “Meeting our master, by going forth to worship, is the fruit of past karma.”

Thus, Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman composed the 931st verse. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the king of Sirkazhi, is the crown jewel of brahmins. The Sanskrit term Siroratnam is rendered as Chudamani in Tamil. Vagisa Mamunivar heard the great news that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the crown jewel of brahmins, had arrived near Thirupunduruthi. Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman refers to this news as “peruvartthai” (great news). “Peruvartthai” means a word that brings great good.

Upon hearing it, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s face and heart blossomed, thinking, “Our going forth to welcome and worship the One who rules over us is the fruit of past karma.” His face blossomed, and his heart blossomed. This was the thought that arose in Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s heart. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman thought that receiving the blessing of the young Lord himself coming was rare to obtain except through the fruit of many good deeds performed in previous births. It is a truth found in the Sivagamas that the company of devotees and the grace of the Guru are obtained as a result of good deeds performed towards Lord Shiva. To experience this thought arising whenever devotees are seen is the way to salvation.

Here, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman praises Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as “Nandamai Aaludaiyavar” (He who rules over us). He considered the young Lord as the primal being who enslaved and adopted him, and this is also evident in the joy with which Navukkarasu Peruman later carried the young Lord’s palanquin. Navukkarasu Peruman would later say, “I have performed incomparable penance, and therefore, I have been blessed to carry your feet now and have been saved.” Therefore, it is understood here that he considered the young Lord as the primal being who enslaved and adopted him.

Thus, without waiting for the young Lord to arrive at Thirupunduruthi, and without delay, he resolved to go forth and worship him. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, realizing that the young Lord himself was coming here, was the fruit of good deeds performed in previous births, in this birth, and until now, before today. Upon realizing this, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s face blossomed, and his heart blossomed. Although inner joy causes outer joy, Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman places outer joy first and inner joy second due to the immediacy of the event. Even though they are presented in this order due to immediacy, it is also noted that both occurred simultaneously. What does Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, having resolved thus, do next?

Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman narrates in the 932nd verse: “Ethir sendru panivan ena ezhukindra peru viruppal nathi thangu sadaimudiyar narpathangal thozhuthu antha pathi nindru purappattu parasamayam sithaiththavarpaal muthirkinra perunthavaththor mun eytha vandhu anainthar” (With a great desire to go forth and worship, he bowed to the good feet of the Lord with a matted lock in which the river resides, and departing from that city, he approached the great ascetics who had destroyed other religions).

Therefore, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman understood that going forth to worship the young Lord was the fruit of past penance. He now resolves to fulfill that action and departs, bowing to the feet of the Lord of Thirupunduruthi. This is because he needs the grace of the Lord to go forth and worship the young Lord.

Therefore, to obtain it, he bows to the feet of Poiyiliyappar, the Lord residing in Thirupunduruthi, and departs. The place where Thirunavukkarasu Peruman departed from Thirupunduruthi and came out to welcome and worship the young Lord is a short distance outside the city of Thirupunduruthi. It is an agricultural area surrounded by fields on all four sides. The place where the young Lord and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman met is still known as Sambandarmedu. The area is a slight mound amidst surrounding fields. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman arrives at this spot.

He joins the assembly of devotees who are mature ascetics. The “mutirkindra perunthavaththor” (mature ascetics) are the group of true devotees accompanying the young Lord. Their mature penance, through association with the young Lord, ripened and became the great penance conducive to attaining the state of Shiva at Nallur Perumanam. Such is the penance of those devotees. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman thus joins them.

Now, the 933rd verse: “Thiruchinnam pani maara ketta naatthisaiyullor perukindra aarvaththaal Pillaiyar thammai soozhnthu” “Nerukkin idai avar kaanaa vagai nilaththu paninthu ullam urukki ezhum manam pongath thondarkuzhathudan anainthaar” (Amidst the press, so that he would not see, he bowed to the ground, his heart melting, and his mind overflowing with emotion, he joined the throng of devotees).

There, the sacred trumpets sounded the glories of the young Lord. Hearing the sound of those trumpets proclaiming the young Lord’s glories in various ways, many people from all directions were drawn and gathered, delighting in seeing the young Lord and crowding around him. There was a dense crowd of devotees there. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman entered amidst this throng of devotees. Without the young Lord seeing him, he bowed to the young Lord repeatedly, prostrating himself on the ground, his heart melting with love. That fervent heart arose, and with such a heart, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman joined the company of devotees.

Thirunavukkarasu Peruman bowed to the ground many times without the young Lord seeing him, because if the young Lord were to see him, he would not allow it.

Therefore, without him seeing, he bowed to the ground many times and joined the company of devotees.

Now, the 934th and 935th verses: “Vandhadaintha Vakkeesar vanpugazhi vazhventhar santhamani sivikaiyinai thangudavarudan thangi sinthai kalippura vanthar Thirugnanasambandar punthiyinil veronru nigazhthida mun pugazhkkinrar appartham engutrar ippozhuthu enru arul seyya seppariya pugazh Thirunavukkarasar seppuvaar” (Vakkeesar arrived and joined those who bore the beautiful gem-studded palanquin of the king who lives in great Pugazhi, and his mind rejoiced. Thirugnanasambandar’s mind was pre-occupied with something else, and he asked, “Where is Appar now?” The indescribably glorious Thirunavukkarasu replied). “I have performed incomparable penance, and therefore, I have been blessed to carry your feet now and have been saved,” he said. These are the two verses. Vagisa Peruman, who had joined the throng of devotees, then joyfully came along, joining those great individuals who were carrying the beautiful, gem-studded palanquin of the young Lord, the king who sustains the prosperous Sirkazhi. Although carrying a palanquin is generally considered demeaning, he considered it an invaluable great fortune and the fruit of immense penance.

Therefore, with a joyful heart, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman joined those carrying the palanquin and carried it himself. This should not be considered a righteous act. The truth of the saying, “A palanquin for those who bear, and a palanquin for those who ride,” is clearly demonstrated here, rejecting its falsity. As Thirunavukkarasu Peruman was carrying the palanquin, a unique emotion arose in Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s heart. Due to divine grace, he was Thirugnanasambandha.

Therefore, another event, another emotion, occurred in his mind. This was because his intention for this journey was to meet Appar Swamigal.

However, a divine indication arose in Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s heart that Appar Swamigal was not there but had come and joined him here, which prevented Thirugnanasambandha Peruman from continuing his journey. As soon as such a thought arose, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman asked the devotees around him, “Where is Appar Peruman now?” The vision that Appar Swamigal was not in the monastery at the shrine where he intended to meet him arose in Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s spiritual insight.

Therefore, he asked, “Where is Appar now?” The name “Appar” is the name by which Thirugnanasambandha Peruman first addressed Thirunavukkarasu Peruman when he first met him.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman asked, “Where is Appar now?” In Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s heart, it was revealed by divine grace that Appar Swamigal was not in the monastery at Thirupunduruthi. He understood that, but he did not see that Appar Swamigal was carrying the palanquin here. That is why the young Lord asks, “Where is Appar now?” Why is it that the young Lord, who sees that Appar Swamigal is not in the monastery, cannot see that he is here? This is because when Appar Swamigal joined the crowd, he prostrated himself many times on the ground and praised him.

Moreover, he was carrying the palanquin. All these happened without the young Lord seeing them, as Appar Peruman wished.

Therefore, the young Lord could not see Appar Peruman carrying the palanquin.

Thus, this happened without the young Lord seeing it. Sivakavimani Desiganar writes that this is the strength of Appar Peruman’s sacred service. When Thirugnanasambandha Peruman thus asked, “Where is Appar now?”, the indescribably glorious Thirunavukkarasu Peruman replied. By the meaning of what he said, his glory became indescribable. He was not only blessed with the excellence of the meaning he conveyed but also with the richness of the words he used.

Therefore, the indescribably glorious Thirunavukkarasu replied, “I performed unparalleled penance before, and as a result, I have now been blessed to carry your sacred feet and have been saved.” Thirunavukkarasu Peruman thus declared that directly carrying the young Lord’s feet with mind, word, and body was the result of unparalleled great penance. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman clearly states here the cause-and-effect relationship of this truth.

Therefore, he says, “I have performed such incomparable penance, and therefore, I have now been blessed to carry your feet and have been saved.” “Uyndan nyan” signifies attaining liberation. Liberation is defined in spiritual texts as reaching the sacred feet.

Therefore, here, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman states that carrying the young Lord’s feet itself is salvation and liberation.

Thus, we understand the efficacy of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, praised by Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman as the “indescribably glorious Thirunavukkarasu,” who was able to encompass all the truths stated in Sivagnana Bodham, chapters two, eight, nine, eleven, and twelve.

Now, the 936th verse: “Avvartthai kettanju avaniyin mel ezhuntharuli ivvaru seitharulittru ennaam enru irainchuthalum sevvaru mozhi navar Thriggnanasambandarkku evvaru seyya thaguvathu enru ethire irainchinar” (Hearing those words, he was afraid and descended from the palanquin to the ground, and bowed, asking, “What is this that you have done?” Appar Peruman, whose words are righteous, bowed in return, asking, “How should one act towards Thriggnanasambandha?”). As soon as he heard those sacred words of Appar Peruman, the young Lord, fearing, quickly descended from the palanquin. He bowed to Thirunavukkarasu Peruman with trepidation, asking, “What would happen if your Holiness did this?” He feared that it was inappropriate for him to be carried in the palanquin while Appar Peruman was carrying it. What was his fear? He feared that it was wrong to employ a great elder whom he considered Appar (father) to carry his palanquin, and that it was wrong for him to be carried in the palanquin while the elder carried it. He feared that it was improper for him to be carried in the palanquin while the elder carried it, and quickly descended from the palanquin and stood before the elder as a junior, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

He bowed to Appar Peruman with trepidation, asking, “What would happen if your Holiness did this?” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, with trembling voice, asked what would be the consequence if he performed an inappropriate action. The young Lord considered Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s action as described by the sacred voice. When Thirugnanasambandha Peruman thus bowed with trepidation, asking, “What would happen if your Holiness did this?”, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, the master of eloquent words, replied. He bowed before Thirugnanasambandha, asking, “How should one act towards Thirugnanasambandha?” For he is Thirugnanasambandha, is he not? What is more appropriate to do than to bow to such Sivajnana when it is attained?

Therefore, Appar Peruman understood this action according to the Kural saying, “The deed that ought to be done will fail if not done.” The fact that these two great individuals interpreted the same action differently reflects their state of humility, having embraced the Saiva faith.

Therefore, we must understand that their positions, based on their respective states, are not contradictory.

Now, Theivasekkizhar Peruman composes the next two verses: “Soozhnthum ninainthu aruku anaiyum thondarellam athu kandu thazhnthu nilam ura vanangi ezhunthu angai thalaikkuviththu vazhnthu manam kaluppinaray mattravarai vananga” “Petru aazhntha pirappu uyndhom enru andamellam ura aarthaar” (The devotees who gathered around and came near, seeing that, bowed to the ground, rose, clasped their hands above their heads, and with joyful hearts, having worshipped them, exclaimed, “We have escaped from the deep cycle of birth!” and shouted so that the whole world might hear). All the true devotees who had gathered around and come near these two great individuals, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, seeing that, bowed to the ground, rose, clasped their hands above their heads, and with joyful hearts, having been blessed to worship these two great individuals, exclaimed, “We have escaped from the deep ocean of birth!” and shouted so that the whole world might hear.

Now, the next verse, the 938th verse: “Thirugnanasambandhar Thirunavukkarasar thamai perugu aarvaththodum anainthu thazhiya pillu” “Maruvaaru malaradigal vanangi udan vandhu anainthaar poruvarum punal sadaivar magizhntha Thiruppunduruthi” (Thirugnanasambandhar embraced Thirunavukkarasar with growing affection, and Thirunavukkarasar, bowing to the incomparable lotus feet of Thirugnanasambandhar, arrived with him at Thirupunduruthi, where the Lord with the matted locks, bearing the Ganga, rejoices). Thirugnanasambandha embraced Thirunavukkarasar with ever-increasing affection. Thirunavukkarasar, bowing to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s incomparable lotus feet, arrived with the young Lord at Poonthuruthi. In this single verse, Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman has blessed us by weaving together the names of these two great individuals, Thirugnanasambandha and Thirunavukkarasar, as sacred mantras.
