In previous verses, the author mentioned these two separately, but in this 938th verse, where the two met.

The inner meaning of showing these two names together at this place where these two met is that the devotees who directly witnessed the divine radiance of the reunion of these two spiritual preceptors, as described earlier, cried out, “We have escaped from this deep cycle of birth by worshipping these two together!” In the same way, Theivasaikilar Peruman’s immense grace is evident in his desire to allow lesser devotees like myself, who come later, to experience and find salvation through this sacred vision. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman embraced Appar Peruman. The eagerness to meet him after many days of separation was now an eagerness to meet him unexpectedly in an unexpected place.

Therefore, with such overflowing eagerness, he embraced Appar Peruman. This is an emotional outpouring that occurs when there is intense love between two equals. While the young Lord embraced Appar Peruman, Appar Peruman bowed to the incomparable lotus feet of the young Lord. The phrase “maruvaaru malaradi” (incomparable lotus feet) can also be interpreted as the sacred feet of the Lord. The “maruvaaru malaradi” refers to the sacred feet not only in terms of color, softness, and other qualities but also in terms of the quality of performing deeds with a pure mind, thus referring to the sacred feet as a flower.

Thus, as Thirunavukkarasu Peruman bowed to the young Lord’s feet, the two great individuals arrived at Thirupunduruthi, where the Lord rejoices. This is referred to by Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman as “udan vandhu anainthaar” (arrived together). “Udan anainthar” points to the twelfth part, “Anbarodu Mariyi Enbodam.” The arrival of these two great individuals near the Thirupunduruthi temple illustrates the concept of the twelfth aphorism of Sivajnana Bodham, “Alayam thanum Arananathozhum” (The temple itself is the worship of Aranan).

Let us resume our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 768, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, composed by Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman arrive at the Thirupunduruthi temple. They proceed with the devotees to the Lord’s presence in the temple where He joyfully resides.

First, they bow to the gopuram and then enter, worshipping the Lord with the devotees. There, they worship the Lord, prostrating themselves inside the temple with melting hearts, and praising Him. As the young Lord approached the Thirupunduruthi temple, the local legend states that the Lord made all the Rishabhadevas (sacred bulls) in front of him move aside so that the young Lord could have a darshan from a distance. In accordance with that, even today, in the Thirupunduruthi temple, the Rishabhadevas are not directly in front of the Lord but are slightly to the side, which we can still see.

There, they worship and praise the Lord whose name is Poiyiliyappar, and then come out to the entrance of the temple. Theiva Sekkizhar Peruman composes the 941st verse: “Vakkin thani mannar vanpugazhi venthar thamai pokkum varavum vinava pugunthathu ellam thookkin Tamil virakar solliranthu gnana marai thekkum thiruvaayal seppi arul seithaar” (Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, the unparalleled king of words, inquires about the departure and return of the prosperous king of Sirkazhi, and Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the master of Tamil, speaks with his sacred mouth, which holds the wisdom beyond words, explaining all that has transpired). Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, the incomparable king of words, inquires about the king of the prosperous Sirkazhi. He inquires about his visit to the Pandya kingdom and his subsequent return to the Chola kingdom. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the master of Tamil, who is a rejecter of other religions, a proliferator of sacred ash, explains all the events, including the arguments of the Buddhists who had infiltrated, with his sacred mouth, which holds the wisdom beyond words. The words that come from Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred mouth are wisdom beyond linguistic expression.

It is Sivajnana, which perceives the ultimate reality through direct experience. His sacred mouth, which holds that wisdom, can reveal that inexpressible wisdom through scripture.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman narrates all those divine events obtained through the grace of Shiva, which is beyond words. “Kaaliyinil vantha kavuniyar tham poretrai” “Aazhimisai kal mithappil vanthaar adivanangi vaazhi thiruththondru ennum vaan payir thaan ongu tharku soozhum peru veli aanir ena thozhuthaar” (He bowed to the feet of the one who came upon a stone raft over the ocean, saying, “You are the great fence that protects the growing celestial crop called sacred service”). Thirugnanasambandha Peruman recounts to Thirunavukkarasu Peruman the events that occurred in the Pandya kingdom and his return to the Chola kingdom. Appar, hearing this, bows to the feet of the young Lord, who came across the ocean on a stone raft. He praises the young Lord, saying, “You are the great fence that protects the growing celestial crop called sacred service.” For a crop to grow, cultivation, fertilization, weeding, irrigation, and protection are five essential and indispensable elements.

However, above the other four, the most important is the fence, which acts as a guardian for the crop.

Thus, in the Kural, “Erinum nanral eriyiduthal kattapin neerinum nanru athan kaapu” (Better than watering a crop is to fence it after planting, better than water is its protection), Thiruvalluvar emphasizes the importance of protection as the fifth element.

Similarly, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman praises and worships the young Lord, saying that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is like a great fence that suitably protects the great crop of service, which is the sacred merit that leads to the divine, enabling it to flourish and grow. The young Lord also bowed before him and with overwhelming love praised the greatness of the glorious Mangaiyarkkarasi and the excellence of Kulachirai Nayanar’s service. “Ellaam mozhinthu angu uvandhirundhaar” (He spoke of everything and rejoiced there), states the 943rd verse. The young Lord also bowed to Thirunavukkarasu Peruman and, recounting the virtues of Mangaiyarkkarasi Ammaiyar and the excellence of the service of the minister Kulachirai Nayanar, rejoiced there. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman thus narrated the virtues of Mangaiyarkkarasi Ammaiyar and the minister Kulachirai Nayanar. This was for Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, who was engaged in service, to hear and rejoice.

Upon hearing about their devoted service, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman resolved to go from Thirupunduruthi to Tamil Nadu to meet them. “Thennarku uyirodu neerazhiththu” “Sengamalatthu anna manaiyarkku amicharkkum anbu aruli thunnu neri vaithikaththin thooneriyey aakkuthalaan mannu pugazh Vakkeesar kettru manam magizhnthar” (He gave life to the Southern King and also gave sacred ash, and bestowed his love upon Mangaiyarkkarasi, who was like a swan in a red lotus, and upon her minister, thereby establishing the true path of Vedic dharma, and the eternally glorious Vakkeesar heard this and rejoiced in his heart). Thirugnanasambandha Peruman gave life to the Pandya king and also bestowed sacred ash. He showered his grace upon Mangaiyarkkarasi, who was like a swan in a red lotus, and upon her minister. The bestowing of his grace upon them meant that he fulfilled their wishes by eliminating Jainism and establishing Saivism.

Vakkeesa Mamunivar heard all these historical accounts and rejoiced greatly in his heart. It was Vakkeesa Peruman’s state of mind to rejoice in seeing the advancement of the Saiva path and the flourishing of living beings in the world. We can see this in many places in his Thevara sacred utterances, especially the Tilaka. Ammaiyar had always cherished in her heart the joy of having been saved by receiving the sacred ash, recited with the five letters.

Therefore, we can understand Appar’s enthusiasm for the explanation of the Saiva path, which is a glorious and orderly way of life that includes requests and other acts for the sake of devotees, through his sacred words. Here we see that Appar Swamigal heard all these historical accounts and rejoiced in his heart.

However, this joy, this rejoicing, is not due to attachments and aversions caused by ego. Rather, it is the compassion and sorrow felt by Appar, the servant of the divine Lord, who sees all beings as one, upon witnessing their suffering, and the joy he experiences when those beings are saved. We must understand this. “Sollin peruventhar Thondai vala naadu eythi malku pugazh Kanchi Ekambaram ennum selvar kazhal paninthu sendrathu ellam sepputhalum pulgu nool maarparum poy potra manam porinthar” (When the great king of words arrived in Thondai Nadu and recounted all his travels, including bowing to the feet of the wealthy Lord Ekambaram of Kanchi, which is full of glory, the young Lord, who wears the sacred thread, also went and worshipped with a joyful heart). Until now, we saw that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman recounted to Thirunavukkarasu Peruman all the historical events from his separation at Vedaranyam to his visit to the Pandya kingdom and his return to Thirupunduruthi, and both rejoiced.

Now, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman shares with Thirugnanasambandha Peruman all the events from his departure from Vedaranyam, including his worship at Thondai Nadu. Thirunavukkarasu Peruman narrates to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman all the historical events of his journey, including bowing to the feet of Lord Ekambar, the wealthy Lord residing permanently in Thiru Ekambaram in Kanchipuram, which is part of the prosperous Thondai Nadu and is full of glory. As a result, the young Lord also resolved in his heart to go there and worship. We can recall here that the young Lord had previously gone to Thiruvarur when Vagisar spoke of its sacred wealth. We can also observe that both Thiruvarur and Kanchi are Prithvi Sthalams (earth elemental shrines), and therefore, both are equally suitable places for the awakening of grace. We can also recall that it was in these two shrines that Sundaramurthi Swamigal received his sight.

After worshipping the Lord, Appar, desiring to depart, went to the monastery that he himself had established and rested there peacefully.

Therefore, the place where these two great individuals shared their stories until now was the outer courtyard outside the temple. Having sat there and conversed with devotees on both sides, he rejoiced, then praised the Lord and took leave from the Lord in the temple, and proceeded to the monastery established by Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal. Just as Thirunavukkarasu Peruman composed many pathigams while residing in that monastery, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman also composed pathigams for the Thirupunduruthi shrine when he resided there. Thirupunduruthi is the eleventh shrine on the south bank of the Kaveri. It is a shrine worshipped by Indra, Kashyapa, the Chola king, and others. It is one of the Saptasthanam shrines, including Thiruvaiyaru.

Thirunavukkarasu Peruman resided here for a long time, establishing a monastery and performing sacred service. The Lord’s names are Poiyiliyappar, Pushpavananathar, Poiyili Adipuranan, and Sel. These and other sacred names are found in Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s pathigams. Ammaiyar is Azhagarnda Nayaki. We have contemplated all this sacred history in Thirunavukkarasu Peruman’s Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman thus composed sacred pathigams.

However, due to our lack of merit, the pathigams composed by the young Lord are not available to us. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman recounted his visit to the Pandya kingdom to Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman recounted his visit to Thondai Nadu to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

Now, both these great individuals desire to do the same again, and they resolve to go to the Pandya kingdom. Having learned about the glories of Thondai Nadu through the sacred words of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, the young Lord resolves to go and worship in Thondai Nadu.

Therefore, the great sage Vagisa, the ruler, The great desire to go and worship the feet of the Lord residing in the eternally stable Thiruvalavai grew intensely.

At the same time, the young Lord’s growing love to go to Sirkazhi also increased. Earlier, when he was in Vedaranyam, the ruler had wished to go to Thiruvalavai, but he did not go then due to the young Lord’s command. That desire is now deeply embedded in the ruler’s heart and is surging forth.

Moreover, the sacred words of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, describing the flourishing state of the Pandya kingdom, and this great desire, are clearly seen in the pathigams sung by Thirunavukkarasu Peruman for Thiruvalavai.

Thus, after worshipping the Lord residing peacefully in Thirupunduruthi inside the temple and coming out, the glorious young Lord, having taken leave from Thirunavukkarasu, whose heart was filled with joy, departed with countless devotees. This was the last time these two great spiritual teachers met. The young Lord, departing from Poonthuruthi with countless devotees, proceeded to Thiruneythanam, Thiruvaiyaru, and other shrines on the north bank of the Kaveri. “Maadu punal Ponni elinthu vadakaraiyil needu Thiruneythani paadu Tamil malaigalum saatthi paravippoy aadal purinthaar Thiruppallanam sendru anainthaar” (He went down to the waters of Ponni and, reaching the north bank, adorned with Tamil garlands of praise for Thiruneythanam, and departed, going to Thiruppallanam). This is the 949th verse. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having taken gracious leave from Appar Swamigal at Thirupunduruthi, He descended into the Kaveri and proceeded to the north bank of the river, worshipping at Thiruneythanam and Thiruvaiyaru.

Thiruneythanam and Thiruvaiyaru are two shrines located close to each other on the north bank of the Kaveri. After crossing the river, the young Lord worshipped Thiruneythanam on the opposite bank and then proceeded along that bank to worship Thiruvaiyaru, which is nearby to the east. There are temples on both sides of the Kaveri.

Therefore, we have previously seen in the Thirunavukkarasu Peruman Puranam that it is customary for pilgrims to visit and worship at both these shrines.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman visits and worships these four shrines, Thirupunduruthi, Thiruneythanam, Thiruvaiyaru, and Thirupazhanam, which are in a continuous line among the Saptasthanam shrines, and sings pathigams. At this moment, he sings devotional verses, garlands of exquisite Tamil. The pathigam that Pillaiyar graced for the holy place of Thiruviyaru is structured in Thiruviragam and set in Indhalappann. We have already deliberated on the two pathigams that Pillaiyar presented here for the first time. The pathigam that Pillaiyar graced at this time is the third pathigam for the holy place of Thiruviyaru, appearing as the thirty-second pathigam in the second Thirumurai. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam (Thiruththikkal malaichirumiyodum mikuthesar uruththikal ezhil kayilai verppil uraitharkke viruppudai athpathar irukkum idam orar maruththikal pozhirkulavu vanthiruvaiyare)

“Pasamaliyium pozhilkol vandiruvaiyatrul Isanai ezhir pugazhi mannavan meijnana Poosuran uraiththa thamizh paththum ivai vallar Nesamali baththaravar ninmalan adikke” The concluding verse of this pathigam states that the Lord’s abode is Thiruviyaru. Having thus paid homage to Thiruviyaru, Thirugnanasambandha Perumal proceeds to the holy place called Thiruppazhanam, where the Lord resides, and offers many pathigams in praise of the Lord. This holy place, Thiruppazhanam, like Thirunallam and Thiruviyaru, is a place where Pillaiyar came and worshipped a second time. Sekkizhar Peruman states that he stayed in other celebrated shrines as well.

Accordingly, Sekkizhar Peruman mentions Thiruppoonduruthi, Thirunallam, Thiruviyaru, and Thiruppazhanam among the Sapthasthana holy places, and then indicates that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worshipped the other three holy places. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman then departs from Thiruppazhanam towards Sirkazhi, taking the hint. Along the way, he visits holy places such as Vadakurangaaduthurai, Thirupullirukkuvelur, Thirukkudanthai, and Thiruppanandal, before arriving in Sirkazhi. Sekkizhar Peruman recounts this in the nine hundred and fiftieth verse: “Sengan vidaiyar Thirupallanam sernthu irainji Pongiya kathalin mun pothum pathippiravum thangippoy Sanpai nagar sarnthar thaniporuppin Mangai thirumulaippal undarulum vallalar.” We shall carry on our discussion. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, authored by Sekkizhar Peruman, Volume Seven Hundred and Sixty-Nine, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrives at the holy place of Sirkazhi. Upon hearing the news that Pillaiyar, who had eradicated Jainism in the Southern land and spread the sacred ash throughout the country, was coming, the great Vedic scholars in Sirkazhi, eagerly wishing to serve Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, chanted the Vedas and went to receive him. After a long time, nearly two years, since Pillaiyar had left Sirkazhi, when the Vedic scholars of Sirkazhi had previously approached Thirugnanasambandha Peruman in Thiruvezhimilalai and requested him to return to Sirkazhi, at that time Upon hearing the news that Pillaiyar was returning to Sirkazhi, the Vedic scholars, who had been eagerly awaiting his return, chanting the Vedas, went to receive him. They had previously received him in the same manner when he returned to Sirkazhi after receiving the pearl palanquin.

Now, as Thirugnanasambandha Peruman returns to Sirkazhi with victory, having fulfilled the purpose of his incarnation, the Vedic scholars again receive him chanting the Vedas. he sought the Lord’s grace and sent them away, saying it was not possible to come to Sirkazhi then, but he would come later.

Therefore, it was a time when these Vedic scholars longed for Pillaiyar to return to Sirkazhi, a time when they waited eagerly to serve him.

Now, upon hearing the news that Pillaiyar was coming to Sirkazhi, all the Vedic scholars gathered together and, just as they had done when he arrived in Sirkazhi after receiving the pearl palanquin, they received him chanting the Vedas.

Now, as Thirugnanasambandha Peruman returns to Sirkazhi, having fulfilled the purpose of his incarnation and victorious, the Vedas they receive him, chanting. The place where these Vedic scholars received him was in a far-flung suburban area of Sirkazhi. Driven by their devotion to Pillaiyar, they came all that way to receive him and escort him. As such great and wise Vedic scholars came to receive him, Pillaiyar, the leader of Sirkazhi, descended from his palanquin adorned with cool pearls and walked towards them. The temple of Thirutthoni, where he resides, then appeared. As it appeared, he clasped his hands, like freshly bloomed lotuses, and worshipped.

As he worshipped, he went near the temple, which floats like a boat through the ages. The great land there Sekkizhar Peruman composes the nine hundred and fifty-third verse: “Angam manilam thaturra vanangi pukku anjali mudiyera pongu kathalin pudai valam kondu mun paninthu potretthu Othi thunga neel perunthooniyam koyilai arulinal thozhutheri mangaiyoduudan veerthiruntha arulinar malarkadal panivutrar.” As soon as he reached the vicinity of the Sirkazhi temple, he prostrated himself, touching the ground with all eight limbs, performed Ashtanga Namaskaram, and entered the temple. With hands clasped in Anjali, he circumambulated the temple, worshipped before the Lord, and offered praises. He ascended the mountain, reverently worshipping the great, long Thirutthoni temple with divine grace, and offered his respects to the two who resided there with the Goddess. Having now traveled to many lands and situations, defeated the Jains in the Pandya kingdom, and spread the path of sacred ash, then defeated the Buddhists in Bodhimangai, rejected other religions, and returned to propagate the path of sacred ash there as well, remembering all this, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, with great devotion, melts and worships the sea of flowers there. This is the two thousand eight hundred and fifty-first verse.

Thus, he worships Thirutthoniappar. He composes a pathigam, which Sekkizhar Peruman presents in the next verse: “Murrum meiyellam pulakangal mukizhthezha munthu kan kazhi koora patrum ullam ullalai thezhum anandham pozhithara paninthu etthi otrumai servathu enum thiruviyamaka muvakaiyal edutheththi vetriyaka minavan avai ethir nathimisai varuga aran enbar.” This is the nine hundred and fifty-fourth verse. Following this is the nine hundred and fifty-fifth verse: “Seerin malkiya thiruppathigathinil thirukkadaikkappu etthi vaarin malkiya vanamulaiyudan manninarthamai potri arum innarul petru meendu anaibhavar angaiyal thozhuthethi erin malkiya koyil mun paninthu ponthu irainchinar manivayil en.” This verse fully describes how, with hairs standing on end throughout his sacred body, and his eyes overflowing with immense joy, the surging inner bliss, unable to be contained, caused him to bow down and praise. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman then praises the Thiruviyamagam pathigam, beginning with “Otrumai servathu,” with great joy. His desire to see and worship the Lord was a long-held wish in his heart.

The heart, which never forgot the Lord even in his absence, now, seeing him with overflowing joy, fully embraced him. The overflowing bliss, unable to be contained within, seemed to pour out through his eyes as tears.

Thirukazhumalam: Otrumai servathu meyyina unarvathu ninnarul meyyina etravark kayvathu kamane kanal veli kayvathu kamane atram maraipathum un paniye amararkal seivathum un paniye petru mukarnthathu kanthane biramapuraththai ukanthana ethila ma Thurai man avaiyathire Pathigamathezhunilai avaiyathire Varunadhiyeedaimisai marugaranne Vasaiyodumalar kedavarugaranne Karuthalisaimoolal tharummarule Kazhumalamarisaaimarule Maruviyamizh vira kanmozhie Vallavar tham mader thidamozhie Thiruchitrambalam suraba This pathigam was composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, remembering the divine acts that occurred during the debates, such as the fire debate and the leaf floating against the current in the river in the royal court of Madurai. Having added the Thirukkadai Kappu to this special pathigam, he praises Thoniyappar, who resides with the beautiful-breasted Great Goddess, receives abundant sweet grace, and then, clasping his hands, worships and praises before the temple, bowing at the beautiful entrance.

At that moment, his father, Sivapadahirthayar, also comes and worships him. The unparalleled Pillaiyar, like a rising bull among the people of Sirkazhi, then worships at the ancient walled entrance and proceeds. His hair adorned with blooming flowers, The women, with adorned hair, lovingly bless him with words echoing on both sides of the beautiful street. He walks through the street, bestowing grace upon those who came with love, and then arrives at the front of his mansion, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Upon seeing Pillaiyar, who had completed the great act of rejecting other religions and illuminating the path of sacred ash, returning to Sirkazhi, the women on both sides of the street bless him with auspicious words. At the time of Pillaiyar’s incarnation, all the residents of Sirkazhi felt a sense of auspiciousness.

When Pillaiyar returned to his mansion after consuming the divine wisdom nectar, and also when he returned to Sirkazhi from his journey after receiving the pearl palanquin, the chaste women of Sirkazhi welcomed him with auspicious blessings, just as they had before. We can recall all those events here. The women of Sirkazhi welcome Pillaiyar with auspicious blessings, considering him like their own young son.

Thus, Pillaiyar proceeds through the street where his mansion is located and arrives in front of it. There, a gathering of devotees and the people of Sirkazhi have assembled. He bids farewell to everyone and sends them off. He dismisses them to go to the mansion that was prepared for him, and then Thirugnanasambandha Peruman enters his own mansion. As he entered his mansion, Thirugnanasambandha His mother, Bhagavatiyar, who came from the noble lineage, comes and worships Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred feet.

At that moment, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, keeping in mind the sacred feet of the Great Goddess, the mother residing in Thirutthoni, bows in return. When Pillaiyar entered the mansion, the women received him with lamps, and his mother, Bhagavatiyar, came to that spot and worshipped Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred feet. It is not customary for a mother to cross the threshold of the mansion to welcome.

Therefore, when Pillaiyar entered the mansion, his mother, remaining within, worshipped Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred feet. Since Thirugnanasambandha Peruman had consumed the divine wisdom nectar and attained Shivathuvam, it is appropriate for his mother to worship his feet. This peace can also be seen in the method of initiation. Pillaiyar is a Jnana Guru, so he is worthy of worship by all. It is appropriate for his mother to worship Pillaiyar.

Therefore, based on that principle, Pillaiyar did not bow in return to his mother, demonstrating that it is not appropriate to bow back. When his mother worshipped his feet, Pillaiyar, remembering his divine mother, the Great Goddess residing in Thirutthoni, bowed in return.

Similarly, previously in Thiruvalavai, when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s father, Sivapadakirthiyar, worshipped Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, Pillaiyar, remembering his father’s connection, worshipped Thirutthoniappar, as we have seen. We can be delighted to see the same arrangement here as well.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman stays in Sirkazhi for some time, composing many pathigams and praising the Lord. We shall carry on our deliberation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, authored by Sekkizhar Peruman, Volume Seven Hundred and Seventy, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Pillaiyar, residing in the holy place of Sirkazhi, attends worship at the temple daily, without fail, during all the prescribed puja times. He performs worship at the temple directly during the puja times stipulated by the Shivagamas. The Shivagamas extensively discuss the timing of pujas, such as Thiruppalliyezhuchi, morning, midday, evening, and Ardha Jamam. Thirugnanasambandha Perumal regularly participates in these pujas and worships the Lord.

It is a rule prescribed for Shiva devotees to go and worship directly during all puja times. This is the rule of Shiva temple visitation, which is only possible for a few deeply devoted individuals in these times. Without this, spending days idly without performing temple worship even once a day, and leading a ruined life, has become a very common practice today. This is the cruelty of today’s world. While going to the temple for worship, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman also goes with the devotees who are united with him.

Thus, being united with devotees and being part of the assembly of devotees is considered a very essential and indispensable aspect in Shaiva scriptures. The twelfth sutra of Shivagnana Botham beautifully explains this by saying, “Anbarodu mari.” This is also the nature of Jivanmuktas, who are realized souls. This is also their inherent nature. To mingle with those devotees means to be true jnanis who love as tirelessly as oneself. It means they are Jivanmuktas who, with devotion, ceaselessly praised and embraced the sacred feet of the Primordial Lord. Their nature is to show the path for the world’s souls to attain liberation.

Pillaiyar demonstrated this by his actions.

Furthermore, the second adhikarana of the twelfth sutra contains a sub-thesis that states, “Unite with Shiva devotees.” This is to say that those who are not Shiva devotees will teach ignorance.

Therefore, one must be united with Shiva devotees. For Jivanmuktas who have shed the three impurities For Jivanmuktas, the impurities that have been shed should not cling again. It is emphasized that they should associate with Shiva devotees. If a doubt arises whether Jivanmuktas should only associate with Shiva devotees and not with others, the answer is that those who are not Shiva devotees will teach ignorance. A doubt may arise here: is it right for true jnanis, who have shed attachment and enmity, to have friendship with some and unfriendliness with others? That is, true jnanis are those who have shed attachment and enmity and see all beings equally.

Is it appropriate for such individuals to have friendship only with Shiva devotees and no friendship with non-Shiva devotees, as mentioned above? Some may raise an objection that it is not appropriate.

Therefore, Srimath Meykandar Deva Nayanar emphasizes associating with Shiva devotees by pointing out the flaws of non-Shiva devotees. Srimath Madhava Sivagnana Munivar explains this by saying that non-Shiva devotees, who are ignorant, will create perverse understanding, which is ignorance. In this category of non-Shiva devotees, there are also those who delve into the nature of God and conclude that God does not exist. They say that there is no God, but only vows are God.

Thus, these non-Shiva devotees, each adhering to their own religions, will claim their religions are superior.

Therefore, one should understand that they are creators of perverse understanding, the sage explains. Srimath Manikkavasaka Swamigal states this in the Thiruvasagam Pothri Thirukakaval: “Yanai muthala erumbu iraya Unamil yoniyin ulvinai pizhaithum Manuda pirappinul matha utharathu Enamil kirumi cheruvinil pizhaithum,” and so on, continuing to explain this, and then says, “Deivam enpathor sitham undaki Munivilathathor porulathu karuthalum Aru kodi mayasakkthikal veru veruththam mayaikal thodangina Athamanar ayalavar koodi Nathikam pesi natherumbu erinar Sutramenum tholpasukuzhangal Patthi azhaithu patharinir perugavum Virathame paramakavediyarum Sarathamakave sathiram kattinar,” and then Srimath Manikkavasaka Swamigal, referring to the debaters of various faiths, says, “Samayavathikal thatham mathangale amaivathaka aratri malainthanar.”

Therefore, these groups of non-Shiva devotees will create perverse understanding in various ways.

Thus, these non-Shiva devotees, who are ignorant, are more dreadful than the three impurities. Why? Because these three impurities are capable of teaching ignorance when the time for self-realization arises.

However, these non-Shiva devotees, even when the time for self-realization does not arise, make it arise and, through various means, instill perverse understanding.

Therefore, it is wise for those with such knowledge, who are true Jnanis, to fear them more than the impurities and shun them. This is what is appropriate for such enlightened Jnanis, thus dispelling this apprehension.

Thus spoke Madhava Sivajnana Munivar. That is why Sekkizhar Peruman, who sings the sacred history of great saints like Thirugnanasambandar Peruman, consistently states that they are always surrounded by devotees. He also shows us here that: “Neela mavidam thirumidatru adakkiya nimalarai nereithum kalamanavai anaiththinum paninthu udan kalanthu anbarkalodum sala nal kalankuraibavar thazhuvida kuzhai kampar kolam arthara kumpidum asai kondu ezhum kuripinar anar.” Sekkizhar Peruman composes the nine hundred and fifty-ninth verse.

At that time, while residing in Sirkazhi, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s heart rises with a divine aspiration to worship the unique form of the Lord, who, embraced by Kamakshi Amman in Kanchipuram, showed his body yielding to her embrace. The divine intent of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s heart rises with an aspiration to worship that sacred form and find fulfillment there. The history of the Goddess performing penance and embracing the Lord is especially associated with Thiru Ekambam. This sacred form helps all beings, both standing and moving, whose souls and bodies melt and unite in praise, to attain liberation. The sacred form that the Lord revealed, yielding his body when embraced by the Goddess, is such that to see it with full eagerness, with hands clasped in worship, and to meditate upon it, is indeed the ultimate benefit.

Therefore, that desire arises in Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s heart. Sekkizhar Peruman composes the nine hundred and sixtieth verse. Sekkizhar Peruman composes the two verses, nine hundred and sixty and nine hundred and sixty-one: “Thandagaththirunattinai chcharntthu vanthu embiran magizh koyil kandu potri nam panivathu enru anparukku arul seyvar kalam petru andarukku ariyavum perum thozhiyil irunthavar arul petru thondar soozhnthu udan purappada thodarnthu ezhum thathaiyarkku urai seyvar appar neer ini ingu ozhinthu arumarai angi vettu anpodum thuppu nerchadaiyar thamai paraviyee thozhudirum ena cholli meiperunthondar meelppavar thamakkellam vidai koduthu arulipoy oppillathavar thamai vazhiyidai paninthu urugum anpodu selvar.” Thandaka Thirunadu refers to the Thondai Nadu. The Thondai Nadu is the region where present-day Kanchipuram, Chennai, and Thirukalathi are located. It was formerly known as Thondai Nadu. The king who ruled during that period was Thundiran, so this region was also called Thundira Nadu.

It is also known as Thondai Nadu because Thondaiman ruled it, and Thandaka Nadu because King Thandakan ruled it.

Therefore, Pillaiyar instructs his devotees to worship in the Thondai Nadu, where Kanchipuram is located. Although he generally speaks of visiting temples in Thondai Nadu, he blesses the devotees who surround him with the main intention of visiting Kanchipuram to worship Ekambareswarar.

Thus, having blessed them there in Sirkazhi With Thoni as the Pranava, and that Pranava-form being incomprehensible even to the gods, even to the great Brahma among them, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having received the divine permission to go to Thondai Nadu after worshipping Thoniyappar, who is difficult for even the gods to know, begins his pilgrimage with the devotees who accompany him.

At that time, as Sivapadakirthayar comes forward, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman tells him: “Father, stay here as you are, kindle the fire as prescribed by the Vedas, perform sacrifices, and with love, worship the Lord with coral-like matted hair.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman says this. This is how he instructs Sivapadakirthayar, who had expressed his intention to follow him. Pillaiyar thus replies to him and sends him to stay in Sirkazhi itself. His father’s old age might have been one reason.

Additionally, Pillaiyar might have sent him back due to his disinclination towards the continuation of bodily attachments, focusing instead on his connection to the Lord and his devotees. He instructs his father to remain in Sirkazhi, perform Vedic sacrifices, and worship Lord Shiva, thereby reminding him of his two duties. We may recall here that Pillaiyar had previously received a thousand gold coins from the Lord of Thiruavathurai as an inexhaustible treasure for the people of Sirkazhi to perform sacrifices.

Therefore, he tells his father, Sivapadakirthiyar, to remain there, performing his prescribed duties of Vedic sacrifices and worshipping Lord Shiva. Saying this, he sets off to worship the temples of the unparalleled Lord Shiva, accompanied by his devotees. Giving leave to the great true devotees who would not accompany him but remain in Sirkazhi, he proceeds, worshipping the unparalleled Lord along the way with melting love, and begins his pilgrimage. Sekkizhar Peruman composes the nine hundred and sixty-second verse: “Selvam malkiya thillai moothoorinil thirunadam paninthu etthi pal perum thondar ethirkolla paramartham thiruththinai nagar padi alku thondarkal thirumanikkuliyinai anainthu etthi malku varsadaiyar thiruppathiri puliyurai vanthutrar.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, departing from Sirkazhi, on his way to Thondai Nadu, in the ancient and great city of Thillai In Thiruchitrambalam, he worships and praises the Lord’s divine dance. Many great devotees come to receive him, and he worships there. This is the second time Pillaiyar worshipped in Thillai.

Sekkizhar Peruman had described in great detail the history of his first worship in Thillai.

Therefore, taking it that he worshipped there in the same manner again, Sekkizhar Peruman briefly states that he worshipped these places along the way as he was proceeding to Thondai Nadu.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman visits Thillai, then Thiruththina Nagar, Thirumanikkuli, and Thiruppathiripuliyur. These places are all located along the path from Thillai northward towards Thondai Nadu. These three places are in the middle country.

Thus, Pillaiyar, having set out to worship in Thondai Nadu The first ten verses of this song, Sekkizhar Peruman sings about how he also worshipped the holy places in the middle country along the way. The holy places of Thondai Nadu, Thiruvakkarai and Thiru Irumbai Magazham, which came in his direct path, became places of worship along the way.

Thus, we have the pathigams composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for Thirumanikkuli, Thiruththinai Nagar, and Thiruppathiripuliyur. The Thevaram pathigam by Pillaiyar for Thiruththinai Nagar is not available. Thirumanikkuli, which Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worshipped after Thiruththinai Nagar, is the seventeenth holy place in the middle country. The deity is Manikkavarathar, and the Goddess is Manikkavalli. We have discussed the history of Thirumanikkuli in the Puranas that speak of ‘Thaduthatkonda.’ The pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for Thirumanikkuli The seventy-seventh pathigam of the third Thirumurai, set in Sadari pann. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam.

The third Thirumurai, Thirumanikkuli: Ponni porupparaiyan mangaiyoru pangal vanniyodu maththa malar vaiththa viral viththakar magizhndu therinthunarum sol. The Lord’s abode is Thirumanikkuli, known by attributes such as ‘Porupparain Mangaiyoru Pangal’ and ‘Nedumal Kuralanaki vazhipadu seiya ninra Sivalokan.’ This is the summary of the pathigam.

Our discussion continues. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, authored by Sekkizhar Peruman, Volume Seven Hundred and Seventy-One, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Having worshipped at Thiruththinainagar and Thirumanikkuli, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds to Thiruppathiripuliyur and praises the Lord there with a pathigam. We have deliberated on the special features of Thiruppathiripuliyur in the Purana of Thirunavukkarasar Peruman. The pathigam graced by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for Thiruppathiripuliyur is the ninety-first pathigam of the second [Thirumurai], set in Sevvalli pann. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: The note for this pathigam states that those who do not have the fortune to worship the Lord of Thiruppathiripuliyur will suffer, and by worshipping the Lord of Thiruppathiripuliyur, one will not approach evil, and past karma will be destroyed by not incurring evil.

Sekkizhar Peruman, in the nine hundred and sixty-third verse, sings the sacred history of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worshipping Thiruppathiripuliyur, Thiruvudukoor, and Thiruvakkarai, mentioning, “Kannimavanam kappu yena irunthavar kadalinai paninthu angu munnam ma mudakkan muyarku arul seytha vannamum mozhinthu etthi mannuvar pozhil Thiruvadukoorinai vanthu eythi vanangipoy pinnuvar sadaiyar Thiruvakkarai Pillaiyar anaivutrar.” Thiruppathiripuliyur is a place where the Goddess performed penance and received grace, hence its sacred name Kannivanam.

Similarly, in Kanchipuram, Kamakshi Amman performed penance, and Sekkizhar Peruman called that Ambika forest a sacred forest.

In the same way, Thiruppathiripuliyur shines as this Kannimavanam. In this holy place, a sage named Mungana Munivar, who was cursed to become a rabbit with a crippled leg, came and worshipped the Lord and was freed from his curse. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, in the first verse, graced this history by stating, “Munna nintra mudakkal muyarkku arul seythu.” Sekkizhar Peruman also refers to this by saying, “Kannimavanam kappu ena irunthavar kadalinai paninthu angu munna ma mudakkan muyarku arul seytha vannam.” Thus, after worshipping Thiruppathiripuliyur, Pillaiyar worships Thiruvudukoor, Thiruvakkarai, and other holy places. These are places located along the path to Kanchipuram in Thondai Nadu. Thiruvakkarai is one of the celebrated holy places in Thondai Nadu. It is located north of Thiruvudukoor.

Thiruvudukoor is the sixteenth holy place among the Thevaram-celebrated places in the middle country. It is called Vadukoor because Vadugu worshipped there. Vadugu refers to Bhairava. It is currently known as Andar Kovil. This temple can be reached by taking the branch road from Perumpakkam on the Tindivanam-Mailam-Vanur-Puducherry route, crossing Koliyanur and Valavanur, and entering the Puducherry state border for a short distance. The deity’s names are Vadugeeswarar, Vaduganathar, Vadukoorunathar.

The Goddess’s names are Thirupurasundari, Vaduvakeer Kanni. The sacred water bodies are Vamadeva Theertham and Pennaiyaru. Vadukoor, in later usage, became Andar Kovil and is now commonly referred to as Thiruandar Kovil. Vaduga Bhairavar, one of the Ashtabhairavas, worshipped Lord Shiva here to atone for killing the demon Mundakan.

Hence, it is called Vadukoor, meaning the place where Vaduga worshipped. Andavanar Kovil is the name of the temple, and the name of the temple became the name of the village. This temple is built in the Chola architectural style. The Swami Vimana is in the style of the Thanjavur temple. The temple is being renovated and maintained by the Department of Archaeological Survey. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who visited this holy place, composed a pathigam, which is the eighty-sixth pathigam of the first Thirumurai, set in Kurinji pann.

The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam He states that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman resided for some days in Thiruvakkarai, also known as Vakkarai. Thiruvakkarai is the thirty-second revered holy place in Thondai Nadu. It is named Vakkarai because the demon Vakrasuran worshipped there. Many signs of this demon’s existence are still visible. This holy place can be reached by taking a branch road from Perumpakkam on the Tindivanam-Mailam-Vanur-Puducherry route. The deity’s names here are Chandrasekareswarar and Chandramouleeswarar.

The Goddess’s names are Amirteswari and Vadivambikai. The sacred water bodies are Brahma Theertham, Chandra Theertham, and Surya Theertham. As we have already seen, it is named Vakkarai because the demon Vakrasuran worshipped there.

Moreover, Vakkarai, meaning a strong bank, There are many rock formations around the temple.

Thus, Vakkarai became Vakkarai. The temple legend states that Vakrasuran, a descendant of the sage Kundalini, ruled this region. To destroy him, Kali worshipped Lord Chandrasekhara, the deity of this place, fought Vakrasuran, and emerged victorious. Another temple legend also speaks of Lord Vishnu fighting and destroying Vakrasuran here. It is said that when he was destroyed, his blood would regenerate him, so when Vakrasuran’s sister, Thunmuki, came to fight, Kali, with her eight arms, defeated her. This is the place where Kali worshipped.

This pathigam by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman exists, and Appar Swamigal has sung about this place as a Vaippu Thalam (a place where saints have sung, but no pathigam is available), and Kapiladeva Nayanar has sung about this place in his Shiva Peruman Thiruvandhadhi. The temple is majestically situated on the banks of the Sankarabharani River, also known as Varaha Nadhi, with a grand rajagopuram. It is a very ancient place, possessing the wonder of trees turned to stone. Trees buried in the earth thousands of years ago appear today as stone trees, with the same appearance of bark and branches. To the left of the rajagopuram, Vakra Kaali is enshrined, and her image is exceedingly beautiful. Full moon day is special for the Amman.

There is a large Vakralingam worshipped by Vakran, a circular avudai on a square base. The Moolavar (presiding deity) in the sixth form has a beautiful image with three faces, a majestic appearance.

Thus, the Moolalingam Murthi appears as a Mukalingam. They say that from the first yuga, one face appeared at the end of each yuga, so now he appears with three faces. It is said that at the end of this current yuga, the fourth face will appear. Since the Moolalingam is a Mukalingam, bearing an iconic form, the Swami is praised by the name Chandrasekarar, one of the twenty-five forms of Shiva. Sahasralingam is installed. In the inner circumambulatory path, there is a shrine for Kundali Mamunivar, with a Shiva lingam above the muni’s samadhi.

For this, Dakshinamurthy and Thirumal Varadaraja Perumal serve as Koshtamurthams. In the Arthamandapam, Natarajar is seen in the pose of Kallamariyadum Thirukkolam. The raised sacred feet extend above the waist, which is a novel arrangement. This is referred to as the Vakradhana. Mandapam. Unlike other temples, here the Moolavar shrine, the flagstaff, and Nandi are not aligned in a straight line but are slightly offset.

These are some notes about the sacred site of Thiruvaraikkarai. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who was present here, composed a pathigam for this place. It is the sixtieth pathigam in the third Thirumurai, set to the tune of Panchamam. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows. The abode of the Lord is Thiruvaraikkarai, he is the perfect one who wanders, carrying alms in a white skull. This pathigam’s note is to meditate on the inner self.

Thus, after residing for some days at Thiruvaraikkarai, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman went to Thiru Irumai Maakaazham, worshipped the Lord, and returned to Thiruvaraikkarai. Afterwards, he proceeded to Thiruvathigai Veerattanam and praised the Lord. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman narrates this history in the next verse.

Let us continue our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Seven Hundred Seventy-Two, Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, composed by Divasekkizhar Peruman. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who resided for some days in Thiruvaraikkarai, also visited Thiru Irumbai Magazham and Thiru Arasili from there, worshipped the Lord, and composed pathigams. Thiru Irumbai Magazham is the thirty-second site in Thondai Nadu. The meaning of this place name is the temple called Magazham in Irumbai. It is called Magazham because Mahakalar worshipped there.

This village is located a short distance on the road from Thindivanam to Pondicherry, via Kilianur, reaching Thiruchitrambalam Koodaroadai, and then taking the road to Alangkuppam. The Swami’s name is Mahakaleswarar; the Amman’s name is Kuyilmozhi Nayaki, Madhurasundara Nayaki. The Theertham is Mahakala Theertham. Two asuras, Ambhan and Ambasuran, who had received boons from Shiva, desired to marry Parvati. Parvati took the form of Maha Kaali and killed them at Ambar, near Mayiladuthurai in the south. To atone for the sin thus incurred, Amman performed penance towards Shiva at this place and was freed from the sin.

Mahakala Maharishi, during his Shiva pilgrimage, installed and worshipped a lingam in Ujjain in the north and another lingam in Ambar Mahakal near Mayiladuthurai Poomthottam in the south. When he came to this place, he realized its greatness, installed a lingam here, and worshipped it. Since it was installed by Mahakala Maharishi, the Lord also acquired the name Mahakalanathar. The name of the place is called Irumbai. During the reign of Kulothunga Chozhan, a Siddhar named Kadveli Siddhar. Was performing penance here.

A famine occurred in the country. The king announced a reward for anyone who could explain the cause of the famine. Valli, a dancing girl in that village, decided to learn the reason from the Siddhar and came to the place where he was meditating. When the Siddhar, still in meditation, reached out his hand to eat a ripe banyan leaf, she placed food in his hand. After he ate it, he regained consciousness. She implored him to open his eyes and bring an end to the famine, ushering in prosperity.

Subsequently, good rains fell, and the people, freed from famine, held a festival for Shiva. When the Swami was being paraded in the temple festival, the dancing girl who had disturbed the Siddhar’s penance danced in front of him. While dancing, One of her anklets came loose and fell. Seeing it, Kadveli Siddhar put the anklet back on her foot. The people, witnessing this, mocked them. Unable to bear the ridicule of the immature people, the Siddhar prayed to the Lord, and the Lord’s image split into three parts.

The people were terrified and stunned to see the Shiva lingam crack. They fell at the Siddhar’s feet and begged for forgiveness for their mistake. Kadveli Siddhar, feeling merciful, sang another verse. As soon as he sang that verse, two of the three split parts joined together to form the Shiva lingam as before. Only one part fell outside. The place where it fell is a small village nearby, named Kazhuveli.

The king worshipped the Shiva lingam by covering it with a copper plate and making it one again. From that day until now, the Shiva lingam is seen joined with a copper plate. In front of the temple, there is a large Iluppai grove. Kulothunga Chozhan, the fourth king, donated twenty-seven veli of land to the temple and fifty veli of other lands. Vikrama Pandiyan also donated land to this temple and the Arasili temple.

The Lord enshrined in this temple is mentioned in inscriptions by the names Thiru Irumbai Udaiyar and Thiru Magazham Udaiya Nayanar. During the time of Jatavar Pandiyan, Iruncheri Azhagiya Manavazha Perumal built this temple with stone. This village was part of Mathur Nadu, within Jayamkonda Chozha Mandalam. These are notes about this sacred site. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who visited here, composed a pathigam. It is the one hundred and seventeenth pathigam in the second Thirumurai.

This pathigam is set to the tune of Sevvalli. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. Second Thirumurai. Irumbai Maagaanam. (Those who hold and have destroyed the three cities, whose fame has spread far and wide, are in Maakaalam. Where is our Lord? In the beautiful groves of Irumbai, surrounded by mad elephants.)

The Lord’s abode is the temple called Mahakalam within this sacred place of Irumbai. From here, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman also composes a pathigam for the nearby sacred site of Thiru Arasili. Thiru Arasili is the thirty-first site in Thondai Nadu. It is now known as Olungappattu.

The Lord is enshrined here, having the Arasamaram (peepal tree) as his abode. The Arasamaram is in front of the temple. The first worship is offered to the Arasamaram. This is a place worshipped by Vamadeva Munivar. The Swami’s names are Arasili Nather, Halalalsundarar, Ashvaththeswarar, Arasileeswarar. The Amman’s names are Periyanayaki, Azhagiya Ponnamai.

Theertham is Pennaiyaru Mahakala Theertham. Vamadeva Munivar, who visited many Shiva sites and worshipped Shiva, came here and rested for a while near an Arasamaram. The Munivar thought, ‘If I, just sitting under this cooling Arasamaram, feel so much comfort, how wonderful it would be if a temple for Shiva were built here!’ Shiva, knowing his thoughts, appeared as a Swayambu Lingam under the Arasamaram. The overjoyed Vamadeva Munivar bathed in the nearby Theertham and worshipped the Swami. Shiva appeared before him. This place is named Arasili because the Lord made the Arasamaram his home.

This temple was built by a Saluva dynasty king. The Moolavar is enshrined as a small idol in the form of a Swayambu Lingam. When the Salukya king Satyavratan ruled this region, he had immense devotion to Shiva. The king had no children, so he established a flower garden and worshipped Shiva in a nearby temple with daily pujas. For this purpose, he employed a servant to bring flowers from the garden every day.

One day, when the servant went to the garden, there were no flowers. He returned to the palace and reported that there were no flowers on the plants. This continued daily.

So, the suspicious king suspected that someone was plucking the flowers early in the morning and went to the garden the next day. He saw a deer eating the flowers. The king, enraged that the deer was eating the flowers reserved for Shiva puja, shot an arrow at the deer. The deer escaped. The guards chased it, and the deer hid inside a hollow in an Arasamaram. The guards reported this to the king, who then shot an arrow into the Arasamaram.

Blood emerged from it. The king, thinking the deer was hit by the arrow, went inside, but there was no deer. Instead, there was a Shiva lingam. Blood was profusely flowing from the head of the Shiva lingam. The king was shocked. He prayed to Shiva.

Shiva appeared before the king, revealed that he himself had appeared in the form of the deer, and also blessed the king with a child. Afterwards, that Saluva king built a temple at this place.

Therefore, the Swayambu Lingam Murthi, the Moolavar. Has a wound from an arrow on its head. During pujas, a turban is placed over the Shiva lingam. The Koshtamurthi Dakshinamurthy is beautifully arranged with a separate vimanam. Usually, Muyalakan faces right, but here he faces left, holding a serpent in his hand. Above him, Natarajar is seen in the Anandha Thandava pose as a small deity.

It is very special to witness Shiva’s Gnana Upadesa form below and his Thandava form above at the same time. The Vaikasi Visakam Brahmotsavam takes place for ten days in this temple. Inscriptions from Vikrama Chozha Devar and Kulothunga Chozha Devar are found here. During the sixth regnal year of Vikrama Chozha Devar, this village is referred to as Thiruvarasi in Peruvemburnadu, Vijayarajendra Chozha Valanadu, Oima Nadu, Jayamkonda Chozha Mandalam. This place was part of Oima Nadu, associated with the great benefactor and one of the leaders of the ten songs, Sirupanattuppadai. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who was present here, composed a pathigam.

It is the ninety-fifth pathigam in the second Thirumurai. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows. The Lord’s abode is Arasili. This is the gist of this pathigam.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having visited Thiru Irumbai Magazham and Thiru Arasili from Thiruvaraikkarai, then departed from Thiruvaraikkarai and proceeded towards the glorious Athigai Veerattanam. There, the true devotees came to meet and worship Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

Thus, he reached the city of Thiruvathigai. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman goes to the temple. Sekkizhar Peruman sings about this as, “Worshipping the Lord of Vakkare, and staying there, by his grace, he went to Irumbai Maaganam, the Lord with the ruddy body, bowed, and returned.

“Then, encountering the flourishing Athigai Veerattam, the gathered true devotees came to meet him, worshipped, rose, and reached it.” Sekkizhar Peruman further sings that “Before those who reached Veerattanam, where the primordial deity resides, the Bhootas sang and danced, revealing the sacred dance. The Vedic scholars, bowing with true understanding and overflowing with devotion, sang the flawless musical composition, ‘Gundaikkural Bhootham,’ and thus praised him with a pathigam set to music, worshipping there. With abundant love and joy, the eloquent speaker, the pure one, praised him. Departed, and the Lord with the flowing matted locks and benevolent gaze, residing happily in Thiru Amaathur, the child of the sacred Vedas who came from Sirapuram, reached there.

“Thus, Divasekkizhar Peruman narrates in verses 965 and 966. We shall continue with our reflection.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Seven Hundred Seventy-Three, Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, composed by Divasekkizhar Peruman. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrives at Thiruvathigai Veerattanam. Before entering the temple, the primal deity, Shiva, residing in the temple, reveals the sacred dance to the child, Thirugnanasambandha, with the Gana-bhootas singing.

Thus, even before entering the temple, Shiva reveals the sacred dance to the child along the way. This is called Etirkatchi (pre-revelation). Having witnessed and delighted in that sacred dance, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed a pathigam for the sacred site of Thiruvathigai Veerattanam, placing ‘Adum Veerattanathe’ (dancing at Veerattanam) as the crown jewel of the pathigam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed this pathigam, beginning with ‘Gundai Kural Bhootham,’ set to the tune of Kurinji. This pathigam is the forty-sixth pathigam in the first Thirumurai. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam.

First Thirumurai. Thiruvathigai Veerattanam. The pathigam states that (those who are) useless (remain) as support.

This pathigam was sung after witnessing the sacred dance of the Lord, who dances while the Bhootas sing, and then singing ‘Adum Veerattane’. We have extensively discussed the history of the sacred site of Thiruvathigai Veerattanam in the puranam of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. This is the place where the Tripura Samharam took place.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman mentions and sings about that history in the fourth verse, referring to the Lord as ‘Ennar Eyil Eythan Iraivan’ (the Lord who shot the innumerable forts).

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, after worshipping Thiruvathigai Veerattanam, received divine permission from the Lord and proceeded to the sacred sites of Thiru Amaathur and Thirukovalur, where he composed pathigams. Divasekkizhar Peruman narrates this in the ninety-seventh verse as follows: “Having arrived and with joyful devotion, he reached the glorious Thiru Amaathur. He praised the feet of the Lord who adorned himself with golden Konrai and Vanni flowers, and singing the pathigam beginning with ‘Kunra Vaar Silai,’ with fitting music, he worshipped with abundant joy and proceeded to the city of Thirukovalur.” Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, after bowing to Thiruvathigai Veerattanam, proceeded with joy and devotion to the sacred site called Thiru Amaathur.

There, he praised the sacred feet of the Lord, who appeared adorned with beautiful Konrai and Vanni flowers. He composed the pathigam beginning with ‘Kunra Vaar Silai.’ Divasekkizhar Peruman states that he sang with music. ‘Kulaviya isai’ (harmonious music) refers to the special characteristic that this pathigam and another pathigam composed for Thiru Amaathur are both set to the tune of Sikamaram. We have discussed the history of Thiru Amaathur in the puranam of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. Peruman showed this in that verse.

Thus, this first pathigam for the sacred site of Thiru Amaathur is the fiftieth pathigam in the second Thirumurai, set to the tune of Sikamaram. The first verse of this pathigam. The first and concluding verses are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. Second Thirumurai. Thiru Amaathur. (The mountain, the curved bow, the sharp arrow, how he won over the wind, the Vethiya, surrounded by grand mansions and towers, long and tall, wearing a garland of skulls, in the dark night, holding fire, the dancer, the deer.) The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows.

(Worshipping the Lord, whose waist is adorned with clothes, whose matted locks bear a crescent moon, and who has a swan in his hair, to see him is Thiru Amaathur. If one does not praise the golden anklets of the Lord, it is an empty life.

The Lord who dances in Thiru Amaathur, if there is no song about him in the surrounding groves, it is a sin.) Thiru Amaathur. Not praising the Lord’s stone. Pakkamum Pokkame. Eyes that do not see him and other senses do not achieve their purpose. We have no support other than the Lord’s devotees.

This is the main theme of this pathigam.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, after worshipping Thiru Amaathur, proceeds to Thirukovalur. Thirukovalur is the capital city where the kings of Chedi Nadu, a subdivision of Munaippadi Nadu, which is part of Nadu Nadu, reside.

Therefore, Divasekkizhar Peruman refers to it as Thirukovalur Nagar. The prefix ‘Thiru’ also indicates that it is a divine abode. In the Meipporul Nayanar Puranam, it is mentioned as ‘Needum Thirukovalur of Chedi Nannadu.’ We have discussed the glories of Thirukovalur in detail there. The ancient history from Pathittuppattu also reminds us that Malaiyaman Thirumudikkaari, a poet of the Sangam period and one of the Last Seven Benefactors, ruled Thirukovalur as his capital on the banks of the Pennai River in Malaiyam Nadu. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds to Thirukovalur and praises the Lord there. Thirukovalur is the place where Shiva destroyed Andhakasura.

It is one of the Ashta Veeraththanams. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composes a pathigam in praise of the Lord. It is the second pathigam. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam. Is the second pathigam. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are.

(O my heart, rise like the parrot now! The ancient progenitor of the umbrella-bearing king, Kulakan, is in Kovalur.

The Lord who rides the bull and is in Veerattanam. Thirugnanasambandhan, surrounded by the jungle where Kali roams, has spoken these words to remove sins, because they are pure.

Therefore, the old wisdom of Kovalur, when it is understood, will remove your suffering.) This pathigam is an admonition by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, emphasizing the impermanence of the body – old age, disease, and death – and the futility of worldly pursuits where people suffer. He declares that the way to overcome these is to seek refuge and worship at Thirukovalur. He states that the words spoken to remove sins are purifying, and he presents this as the fruit of the pathigam in the concluding verse. (When the armies and Yama come and cast their nooses, who will be there to intervene for us? Oh heart, arise and go!) (The ancient progenitor of the umbrella-bearing king, Pulakan, is in Kovalur.

The Lord who rides the bull and has the flag of the bull is in Veerattanam. Seek refuge there.) Thirugnanasambandha Peruman imparts this wisdom in the first verse. In any case, Yama’s arrival to take our lives is certain.

At that time, there is no other support than the Lord of Thirukovalur Veerattanam, who is the destroyer of time and the slayer of Andhakasura. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman explains the futility of worldly pursuits in the second and third verses, and the suffering of diseases in verses four to eight, and then imparts the way to escape from them. Among these, he mentions the worldly afflictions of the body and the egoistic afflictions of the soul, referring to sins. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman explains that who can stand between the coming Yama and the soul to protect it? None other than the Lord of Thirukovalur Veerattanam. He advises the misers who hoard wealth and do not share it with others to at least have a little compassion.

This is the inner meaning of this Thirukovalur pathigam. Thirukovalur is divided into two parts: Melur and Kilur. The Amman temple is separately located in Kilur. In Melur, there is a Vishnu temple called Thiruvikrama Perumal.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman bows and worships Thirukovalur Veerattanam. Let us persist in our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part Seven Hundred Seventy-Four, Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, composed by Divasekkizhar Peruman. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships the sacred city of Thirukovalur, sings a pathigam, and bows. Divasekkizhar Peruman composes the next verse, the ninety-eighth verse, as follows: “Worshipping and praising the sacred feet of the Lord, who resides in the vast Veerattanam of Koval, he reached Thiru Arai Ani Nallur, where the Lord delights in the five products of the cow, and praised him. He blessed the devotees, whose fame is widespread, with the understanding of the greatness of their devotion, expressed in flowing classical Tamil.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships and praises the sacred feet of the Lord, adorned with tinkling anklets, who is present in the Veeratta temple in Thirukovalur.

The Lord wears an anklet on his sacred feet.

The Lord wears a ‘kazhal’ ornament on his sacred feet.

The Lord wearing the ‘kazhal’ on his sacred feet is a symbol of his vow to grant salvation to all beings. It is a symbol that the Lord will destroy the ego-malady, which is the enemy of souls, and grant salvation to all beings. Worshipping and praising such sacred feet, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reaches the sacred site of Thiru Arai Ani Nallur, the abode of the Lord who delights in accepting the panchagavyam. We have extensively discussed panchagavyam, which is a sacred ablution that the Lord loves, in the Puranam of Arivattaya Nayanar.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reaches the sacred site of Arai Ani Nallur, where such a Lord resides. The sacred site of Thiru Arai Ani Nallur is located on the north bank of the Pennai River. Thirukovalur is on the south bank of the Pennai River, and opposite it, on the north bank, on a small hill, is Thiru Arai Ani Nallur. Thiru Arai Ani Nallur is the twelfth among the temples sung about in Nadu Nadu. It is also known as Araikkanda Nallur. The Swami is Arai Ani Natheeswarar, Athulyanatheeswarar, Oppilamaninathar.

The Amman is Arulnayaki, Azhagiya Ponnamai. Theertham is Pennaiyaru. Maha Vishnu, after asking for land from Bali Chakravarthi, performed Shiva worship at several places and received emancipation from curse at Arai Ani Nallur. The Pandavas, during their exile, came here and built this temple on a rock, leaving it as an adornment to this village. The temple history states that the temple was established only after Nilakanda Munivar first worshipped here. It states that Appar Swamigal has consecrated this place as a Vaippu Thalam.

As we saw above, this temple is situated on a small hillock. A sky-high gopuram stands outside the temple, amidst the rocks. Bhiman Kulam (Bhiman’s pond) is said to have been created by Bhiman with his mace. At the base of the rajagopuram, there are five cave temples. These are the rooms built by the Pancha Pandavas.

Here, a ten-day Brahmotsavam takes place in Vaikasi. There are many inscriptions. When walking around the hill, if you stop at one point, you can clearly see Thiruvannamalai. Divasekkizhar Peruman will continue to elaborate on this. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who was present here, composed a pathigam. He composed a pathigam with the essence that ‘those who worship Arai Ani Nallur with their hands are great and exalted people.’ Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed a pathigam, making the core idea that those who worship Arai Ani Nallur with their hands are great and exalted people.

Divasekkizhar Peruman refers to it as, ‘He blessed the devotees, whose fame is widespread, with the understanding of the greatness of their devotion.’ The pathigam thus composed is the seventy-seventh pathigam in the second Thirumurai, set to the tune of Kandharam. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. (The Lord with a high crown). (Singing, adorned with ashes from the cremation ground, those who worship Arai Ani Nallur with their hands. If they go to see the wilderness, the fierce jungle, the ancient town with many sins, Thirugnanasambandhan, with good qualities, speaks words without wavering. Those who bow to the three forms of Arai Ani Nallur.) This pathigam was composed to illuminate the excellence of the devotees’ love, who spread the glories of the Lord.

Divasekkizhar Peruman continues to state in the ninety-ninth verse: “Singing the glorious pathigam earlier, and circumambulating that Thiru Arai Ani Nallur, with the abundance of the Queen’s breasts, the devotees who filled the earth and the celestials who daily worship and praise, were shown by the devotees the Annamalai, abundant with groves.” Thus, singing the Thiru Arai Ani Nallur pathigam mentioned above, the child (Thirugnanasambandha Peruman) circumambulated the sacred hill of the Lord, who shares a part with the Mother, at Thiru Arai Ani Nallur. Since the Thiru Arai Ani Nallur temple is on a hill, the child walked around the hill. As he walked around, the devotees showed him the distant peak of Thiruvannamalai.

Thus, the devotees showed it, and Thirugnanasambandha Peruman saw the peak of Thiruvannamalai from the hill of Thiru Arai Ani Nallur. Divasekkizhar Peruman states this as: “The devotees, and the celestials who daily worship and praise, were shown by the devotees the Annamalai, abundant with groves.” Hari and Ayan, the great gods, despite burrowing into the earth and flying into the sky, respectively, could not find the Lord. When they stood exhausted, the Lord appeared as a blazing column of light, a Lingam, at Thiruvannamalai for them to see and worship. They, along with other celestials, come here daily to worship. The Mahadeva, the God of gods, whom even the celestials do not know, is enshrined here so that human devotees can come and worship daily. These devotees, along with the celestials, bow and praise the Lord of Thiruvannamalai.

The clouds embrace the groves, which are so abundant that they reach the cloud regions, growing tall and luxuriant.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sees the peak of Thiruvannamalai, which presents such a magnificent sight, as shown by the devotees. The actions of the devotees are to point out and describe the qualities of the Lord. This is evident here. We can recall that earlier, the child saw Thiru Nanippalli and Thiru Alavay. We can remember seeing the holy time. Arunachala Puranam praises it as the place where serpents, great sages, and the entire world, filled with those who praise and worship, gather, a fertile land that echoes the sound of the ocean.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman thus beholds the peak of Thiruvannamalai. Divasekkizhar Peruman composes the nine hundred and seventieth verse: “As Annamalai appeared, he drank it in with his eyes, bowed with his hands, and with overflowing love, he sang the pathigam beginning with ‘Unnamulaiyal,’ and proceeded with the devotees to reach the Thiruvannamalai of the Lord with cool matted locks.” Thus, Divasekkizhar Peruman composes the next verse. Thiruvannamalai is seen from there. From Thiru Arai Ani Nallur, the sight of Thiruvannamalai appears to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as the divine form of Shiva. The Lord, who stood as a blazing column of immense light, beyond the comprehension of Hari and Ayan, transcending sky and earth, took a diminished form as this mountain for the people of this earth to see. This is the history.

Therefore, when the child saw Thiruvannamalai from Thiru Arai Ani Nallur, it appeared to him as the very form of the Lord. While other people of the world see Thiruvannamalai as a mere heap of earth and stones, sages, due to its inherent nature, see it as the Lord himself.

But the child, Thirugnanasambandha, saw it as the Lord, not only by its nature but also by its form. He graciously saw it. (The great light that bloomed as fire, contracted above, and became a mountain, a wonder that spread throughout the world.) This is mentioned in Kanda Puranam, verse ninety-four, regarding the search for the head and feet.

Therefore, Thiruvannamalai appeared as the form of the Lord to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, and even today, devotees who circumambulate Thiruvannamalai see its various aspects as Ardhanareeswara, Umamaheswara, Somasakanda, and so on. To those who see it from the Thiruvarai Ani Nallur hill, it appears as the body of Shiva. This state is explained to us here by Divasekkizhar Peruman. That indescribable joy, experienced through vision, that pleasure gained through the mouth. That indescribable joy, experienced through the sense of sight, that pleasure gained through the mouth. As if having truly reached Thiruvannamalai, absorbed in that sacred vision with the Lord of Thiruvannamalai in an advaitic union, Thirugnanasambandhar’s sacred eyes beheld the divine sight.

With sacred hands clasped above his head in reverence, his mind journeyed to Thiruvannamalai to merge in advaita.

Now, Thirugnanasambandhar begins to sing the wondrous pathigam starting with “Unnamulai Umaiyalan” in his sacred voice. This pathigam, dedicated to the sacred site of Thiruvannamalai, is set to the Nattapadai tune. It is the tenth pathigam in the First Thirumurai. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Oruvan pennagiya Peruman malai thirumani thigazha mannaandhana aruvi theeval mazhai muzhavu adhirum Annamalai thozhuveenaivaluvanna arume vembundhiya kadhiro nozhi vilagum veedhi saral ambu mooya ilaithavan Annamalai.

Thus, the pathigam praises Thiruvannamalai, stating that all the karmic attachments of those who worship the mountain of Peruman, Annamalai, are completely removed. This pathigam, composed by Thirugnanasambandhar, begins by placing the Mother Goddess first with the words “Unnamulai Umaiyal.” It is customary to describe the two types of knowledge, Param and Aparam, as the breasts of the Ambika, which Lord Murugan also mentions as the ‘unfed breasts,’ to signify the Lord’s unique act of blessing the world. The first verse of this pathigam describes the states where Shiva and Shakthi, having taken a united form, later separate for bestowing grace. Thirugnanasambandhar, departing from Thiru Arayani Nallur, reaches Thiruvannamalai, where the Lord resides, holding the great flow of clear water in his matted locks. The term ‘thel neer’ (clear water) signifies that the water, being held and released in small quantities from the matted locks, appears clear. Interpreting ‘thel neer’ as ‘purifying water’ suggests that it removes defilement, dispels ignorance, and brings forth knowledge.

If ‘thelluthal’ is understood as clarifying or displacing, it also implies water that removes sorrow. If a single sorrow within the heart remains, The Thiruvasagam verse “Ullavellam thellum kazhalukke sendroothai Kothumbi” comes to our mind in this context. It is a purana that the Lord held and released the Ganga for Bhagiratha. The term “thel neer mudiyar” refers to Thiruvannamalai, whose peaks touch the water-laden cloud regions. We can recall Thirugnanasambandhar’s verse “Mannarnthana aruvith thiral” here.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandhar reaches Thiruvannamalai. The divine poet Peruman composes the nine hundred and seventy-first verse as follows: “Angal anaivar paninthu ezhundhu potrisai tham malai meedhu thanguviripil veetrirundhar thazh thamarigal tham mudimel pongum aarvaththodum punainthu pulagam malarntha thirumeni engumagi kan pozhiyum inba aruvi perukkinar” This is the verse.

Thus, the child-saint, approaching Annamalai, prostrates himself on the ground, rises, and praises. There, Thiruvannamalainathar, Arunachaleswarar, is eternally present. He bows his head at the lotus feet, prostrates fully, and places the lotus-like feet on his head. With overflowing love, his body bristling with goosebumps, tears of joy stream from his eyes like a cascade, due to the intensity of his great and blissful love. The divine poet Sekkizhar Peruman composes the nine hundred and seventy-second verse: “Aadhimurthi kazhal vanangi angal inithin amarunal poothanathar avar thammai puvaar malaral potrisaiyu kaathalal athirumalaiyil sila nal vaigikil kondra Vedagidar thiru” Aruliyar Kootththavar Thozhuthu Nindra Thalaaththi Vaazh Thiru Gnanasambandar Vaar malar kondu adiyaar thoduvar pugazhvar vanorgal muvar purangal eriththa muvarkku arul seithaar thuma mazhai nindru athiravaruvi thoruvin niraiyo aama pinai vandhu anaiyusaral anna malaiyare alladaravam iyangu saral.

Annamalai Nalla Padava Paduvan Kali Gnanasambandha Vadalaala Patthoo Kattu Vallor Vaananthe Thiruchchi. This pathigam beautifully and tastefully describes many aspects of the Kurinji region in Tamil. In such Thiruvannamalai, the Lord who resides there, the devotees, It is the note of the pathigam that the celestial beings also worship Him, that He shines brightly, bestows grace upon His devotees, and is the true embodiment of beneficial greatness. Thirugnanasambandhar, intending to visit and worship the temples including Ekambaranathar in Thondai Nadu, bows at the temples he encounters on his journey.

However, Thirugnanasambandhar stays at very few places before continuing his pilgrimage.

Thus, he stays for a few days in Thiruvannamalai, which reflects the great affection he had for Thiruvannamalai. We can recall here that Sekkizhar Peruman sings about his exceeding greatness in worshipping Thiruvannamalai. Thiruvannamalai is such a sacred site of great renown.

Thus, having worshipped Thiruvannamalai, Thirugnanasambandhar, heading towards Thondai Nadu, visits all the temples along the way. Sekkizhar Peruman composes the nine hundred and seventy-third verse as follows: “Angan Amaran Perumane Panindhu Ponthu Vadathisaiyil Senkan Vidayar Pathi Palavum Panindhu Pugazhich Chemmalaar Thunga Varaigal Kaan Palavum Kadanthu Thondai Thirunattil Thingal Mudiyar Inithu Amarum Thiru Ooththoorai Seruvutrar.” By the grace of the Lord who has the Goddess on His side, he takes leave from the Lord of Thiruvannamalai, having worshipped Him, and proceeds northwards, worshipping many of the Lord’s abodes. Many wondrous acts of grace are now to occur in Thondai Nadu. For that purpose, he receives gracious leave from the Lord of Thiruvannamalai, bows gracefully, and proceeds northward. Kanchipuram, located in Thondai Nadu, is to the north of Thiruvannamalai, hence he travels north. As he journeys, he praises and visits the temples of Thiru Thellaru, Thiruvenkundram, Purisai Nadu, Purisai, and other sacred sites.

Additionally, he traverses the scattered hills such as Senji Malai, Nedungundram, and Javadhu Malai, which lie between Nadu Nadu and Thondai Nadu. This region is a mix of forests and hills. Thirugnanasambandhar crosses this area. We can identify this region as having small hills and forests from place names like Palgundram, Ilankadu, Tindivanam, Pulivanam, and Puravar Panangattur.

Thus, worshipping all these sites, Thirugnanasambandhar reaches the sacred site of Thiruvoththoor. We shall proceed with our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Volume 775, composed by divine Sekkizhar Peruman, Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandhar, having worshipped many sites in Thondai Nadu, reaches the sacred site of Thiruvoththoor.

Here, the miracle of male palm trees turning into female palm trees is about to occur. Sekkizhar Peruman sings about this divine event. This sacred site, Thiruvoththoor, is the eighth among the revered temples in Thondai Nadu. ‘Oththu’ means Veda. The Veda is called ‘Oththu’ because it is recited and transmitted from generation to generation. This is the place where the Lord taught the Vedas to the celestials.

This is the sacred site where the Lord bestowed His divine presence upon the Vedas.

Therefore, this sacred site is named Thiruvoththoor. Divine Sekkizhar Peruman refers to this as Thiruvoththoor, where the Lord instructed the celestials and sages.
