In this place, ripe palm fruits are offered to the Lord. A devotee, intending to offer these fruits, cultivated palm trees. When he found that all of them were male palms and did not bear fruit, the Jains mocked him. The devotee then appealed to the child-saint, Thirugnanasambandhar, who prayed to the Lord and transformed them into female palms.

Additionally, the history of those palm trees attaining liberation in due course, due to the auspicious nature of the child-saint’s words, is narrated by Sekkizhar Peruman in this section of the child-saint’s purana. In memory of this sacred history, palm trees are consecrated and worshipped at this site. The sacred site of Thiru Oththoor is located southwest of Kanchipuram. It can be reached a short distance northwest from Achirupakkam. From Thirumagaral, this site can be reached southwest. The Lord’s sacred name is Vedapureeswarar, Vedanathar.

The Goddess’s sacred names are Balakujambikai, Ilamulai Nayaki. The well inside the temple and the Cheyyaru river are the sacred waters. Nandi faces the entrance, not the main deity. The temple legend states that Nandi stands guard, preventing anyone from entering while the Lord taught the Vedas to the celestials, to ensure no disturbance. This place is currently known as Cheyyaru, and is also referred to as Thiruvaththipuram and Thiruvaththoor. In the outer prakaram of the temple, there are palm trees, which are the sacred trees of the place.

Opposite the Goddess’s shrine, the traditional palm tree of the site, Thirugnanasambandhar, And the Shiva lingam are seen. These are the special features of the Thiruvoththoor temple. Sekkizhar Peruman begins to sing the wonderful sacred history of the male palm tree turning into a female palm tree and bearing fruit. The nine hundred and seventy-fourth verse: “Devar munivarkku oththu aliththaar Thiruvoththooril thiruththondar thaavil Shanbai Tamil viragar thaam angu anaiya kali sirandhu mevum kathali thoranangal vilakku niraiththu niraikudamum puvum poriyum ethirkondar.” The devotees living in Thiruvoththoor, where the Lord bestowed the Vedas upon the celestials and sages, were overjoyed upon seeing Thirugnanasambandhar arriving at Thiruvoththoor. They joyfully erected banana tree arches and lamps in rows, carrying auspicious items like full pots, flowers, and powders, and welcomed the child-saint with praises. “Shanbai venthar thanthazha sivikai nindru ezhintharuli nanbin mikka seeradaiyar suuzha nambar gopuram suuzh vin pinnaaka mun ongum viyan porposai valam kondu panbin needi paninthu ezhundhu paramar koyil ulladaiyar” This is the nine hundred and seventy-fifth verse.

The leader of Sirkazhi, the child-saint, descended from his cool pearl palanquin. Surrounded by devoted and distinguished devotees, he circumambulated the temple’s grand, beautiful ramparts that towered so high as to dwarf the sky. With increasing humility, he prostrated himself, rose, and entered the Lord’s temple. “Varanaththin uriporththa mainthar umaiyal manavalar aranaththin utporulaaththa” “Nindrar tham mun anainthu irainji naranarkum piramarkum nannarku ariya kazhal potrum karanaththin varum inba kannir pozhiya kai thozhudhar” This is the nine hundred and seventy-sixth verse. It means that, having approached and worshipped before the Lord, who is mighty enough to wear the skin of an elephant, the husband of Uma, and the inner meaning of the Vedas, tears of joy flowed from his eyes as he worshipped the feet that were difficult for Narayana and Brahma to attain, which is why he worshipped.

‘Maindhu’ means power. This indicates the Lord’s quality as the cause of dissolution.

Therefore, ‘uriporththa mainthar’ Signifies the Lord’s role as the cause of dissolution. “Umaiyal Manavalar” indicates His role as the cause of creation. “Aranaththin Utporulal Nindrar” signifies His attribute of bestowing knowledge upon beings in creation, according to their capacity, removing ignorance, and enabling them to attain salvation.

The Lord stands as the inner meaning of the Vedas, the inner meaning of the scriptures. We have contemplated this in detail in the Purana of Thiru Pasupathi Nayanar. The Vedas are a universal scripture for all mature beings, and therefore, they speak of all deities.

However, they prominently feature Shiva in their central and sacred core, within the Shri Rudram.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman does not say ‘meaning of the Vedas’ but ‘inner meaning of the Vedas.’ This place is where the celestials Where celestials taught the Vedas, that reference is also found here. The inner meaning of the Vedas encompasses dissolution (Samhara), and Umaiyal Manaval signifies creation (Srishti).

Therefore, all five cosmic functions are derived from this.

In this way, the Lord imparts secret knowledge to beings according to their nature, enabling them to perceive it and achieve salvation by following it. How are the wondrous deeds described in this historical account? Firstly, the reference to the Samhara state, where the impurities of the Jains’ mockery were removed and they were enlightened.

Secondly, the reference to the rebirth state where male palm trees bore undeveloped fruits. The liberation of the palm trees from their bonds and the attainment of Shivapeeru (the state of Shiva) signify the grace of Shiva, which is the inner meaning of Saivism. The reference to this occurring through the truth of the sacred pathigam, which is a Veda, is also found here. All these are defined in this history. “Pokku varavu puriya” (to understand coming and going) – we must recall here what Srimath Madhava Sivagnana Munivar said in his great commentary on the second Sutra of Sivagnana Botham, as elucidated by Sivakavimani Desikanar. Due to praising such a great Lord, the child-saint sheds tears of joy.

He sheds tears of joy as he worships. For most people in the world, tears of joy come due to the continuity of Maya’s actions.

But here, without that, due to the connection of praising the Lord, tears of joy flow from the child-saint. The ease and rarity of attaining the feet that were difficult for Ari and Ayan to reach, contemplating that, the child-saint’s Tears of joy well up. “Vazhuththaiyum kaanaa malaradi inaikal vazhuthutharku elithay” — the Thiruvasagam, “Potri Thiru Agaval,” praises this. “Thozhudhu vizhunthu paninthu ezhundhu sol malaikalal thuthi seythu muzhuthumanaar arul petru ponthu vaigiya mudhalvar thamai pozhuthuthorum pukku irainji potri seythu angu amarvar mun azhudhu vanangi oru thondar amanar thiraththu ondru arivippar” This is the nine hundred and seventy-seventh verse. As mentioned earlier, with hands clasped, he prostrated himself, rose, and praised with pathigams.

Having received the grace of the Lord who is all-encompassing, he came out of the temple and stayed there, entering to worship and praise the Lord at all times. Before him, an elderly devotee came, wept, bowed, and informed Thirugnanasambandhar about the nature of the Jains. “Angai anal etravarkkum panaikalanaivellam mangulura neendu anpanayay kayavaaga kanda amanar ingu neerittu akkuvan kayaththarku adaivu undo endru pongu nagai seythu eliththurithar arula vendum ena pugazh” This is the nine hundred and seventy-eighth verse. For the devotee, who held fire in his hand, that devotee, that elderly devotee, cultivated palm trees.

But even though those palm trees grew tall, reaching the cloud regions, they were male palms and did not bear fruit. Seeing this, the Jains mocked them. That devotee submitted this to Thirugnanasambandhar’s sacred feet. The devotee submitted to Thirugnanasambandhar’s sacred feet that although all the palm trees he had cultivated grew tall, they were all male and did not bear fruit. Seeing this, the Jains mocked him, saying, “Is there a way for the palm trees you cultivate here with water to bear fruit?” They laughed scornfully and spoke disparagingly. He pleaded that Thirugnanasambandhar should kindly bestow grace to make the palm trees bear fruit to remove that ignominy.

“Paramanartham thiruththondar panbu nokki parivu eydhi viravu kadalodum virainthu vimalar koyil pukkaruli aravu mathiyum anindhar thammai adivanangi iravu potri thiruppathigam isaiyil peruga eduththa virumbum enmai thirukkadaikkappu athanil vimalar arulale kurumbai anpanai eenum ennum vaimai kulavuthalal nerungum etru panaiyellam niraintha kulaikalay kurumbai” “Arumbu pennai aagida kandar ellam athisayithar” Thus Sekkizhar Peruman composes the nine hundred and seventy-ninth and nine hundred and eightieth verses. Thirugnanasambandhar observes the character of the devotee who stood pleading and notes the loftiness of his devotion. He feels compassion. That devotee had cultivated and protected the palm trees with the intention of accumulating stable offerings for the Lord’s worship. He is saddened to see them not bearing fruit.

Moreover, he could not tolerate the external religious sects, the Jains, criticizing the devotee’s devotion. “Panai vithaitthavan panai edaan” (He who plants a palm tree does not harvest it) is a proverb. Palm trees take a long time to grow.

Therefore, it is rare for someone who plants a palm tree to live long enough to reap its benefits. But here, this The devotee, unlike others, lived for a long time, showing great old age. The fact that he could not tolerate the Jains’ insulting words and tearfully appealed to Thirugnanasambandhar indicates how strongly he desired the flourishing of Saivism. He greatly desires to alleviate the sorrow of this great devotee and to clearly establish the truth of Saivism.

Therefore, to indicate that these Jains who insulted him would henceforth live free from enmity, Sekkizhar Peruman graciously sings. Thirugnanasambandhar with the great grace of the Lord, Filled with great desire, he hastened to the Lord’s temple, prostrated himself at the Lord’s feet, sought His grace, and began to sing the pathigam starting with “Poottheerthayyana” in a flowing melody. In the Thiru Kadaikappu (final verse) of that pathigam, the eleventh verse, Thirugnanasambandhar sings that, by the grace of the Lord, male palm trees will bear tender fruits. As soon as he completed singing the Thiru Kadaikappu, the grace of the pathigam immediately bore fruit. It was a miracle, a wonder. Everyone witnessed that wonder with their own eyes.

They were astonished. They also realized that the reason for this was the pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandhar.

Thus, the pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandhar, which caused the male palm trees to become female and bear fruit, is the fifty-fourth pathigam in the First Thirumurai, set to the Pazhantakkaraagam tune. The first, seventh, and eleventh verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. Konnadiye Thoongur Meya Oli Mazhu Vazhangai Kooththirum Gunangale. Thathar kondrai thayangu moodiyudai natha endru nalam pugazhnthu othatharularo Thiruvoththuru arul nalagume kurumbaiyan panai en kulai oththo arumbu kondrai adigalai perumbugaliul gnana samban sol virumbuvaar veenai veeda Thiruchitrambalam. This pathigam is a prayer for the devotee who lamented that the Jains mocked him, seeing that all the palm trees he cultivated for the Lord did not bear fruit, and requested grace, saying, “Arul Vendum” (Grace is needed), thus asking for his wish to be fulfilled. This pathigam, throughout, highlights the nature of devotees’ praise and the Lord’s grace upon them, illuminated by this historical account.

We can observe how the plea for grace and the historical narrative shine forth. Within the poetic structure of the pathigam, the verses, in their metrical arrangement, alternate between four and three feet, signifying the Lord’s grace and His presence in lives according to their maturity. Many other profound meanings are revealed in this pathigam. Sivakavimani Desikanar notes that those who know should seek and understand them. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing. “Sirin mannum thirukkadaikkappu yetri sivanar arul petru paarin needu anpanai mun kayththu pazhukkum panbinal nerum anbar tham karuththu nere mudiththu koduththu aruli arum thiruththondar potru angal inithu amarnthar sirappinal.” Thirugnanasambandhar, having completed the pathigam with the distinguished Thiru Kadaikappu, received the grace of Lord Shiva.

As a result, the long-standing male palm trees on earth bore fruit and ripened. He thus fulfilled the wishes of the devout devotees directly and joyfully resided there amidst the praises of the six devotees. Even before Thirugnanasambandhar finished singing the Thiru Kadaikappu, as a result, those palm trees bore tender female fruits, and everyone who saw it was astonished. The devotee who had pleaded, along with the other devotees who witnessed its fruit, Everyone praised him, and the child-saint happily resided there. “Thennattu Aman maasu aruththaar tham seygai kandu thikaiththa amanar annaattu athanai vittu akalvar silar tham kaiyil kundikaikal ennavaana mattra ivai endru thakarppar iraivan yeruyarththa ponnaarmenI purisadaiyanandre endru potrinAr” This is the nine hundred and eighty-second verse. Seeing this act of the child-saint, who had removed the blemish of the Jains in the southern country (Pandya Nadu), some Jains, astonished, left that country.

Others broke their water pots, which were symbolic of their faith, saying, “What is the use of these?” and realized that the prime deity was indeed the gold-bodied, matted-haired Lord who carries the bull as his emblem. They praised Him, saying, “Is He not the one?” Fearing that a fate similar to the impalement of Jains in the South might befall them here, some left the town. Others abandoned their Jain affiliation, understood Shiva as the supreme deity, embraced Saivism, and praised the Lord. They praised Thirugnanasambandhar. What happened to those female palm trees that bore fruit there?

Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing about this. Sekkizhar Peruman sings in the nine hundred and eighty-third verse what happened to those palm trees in due course: “Pillaiyartham thiru vaakil piraththalal aththalam munbulla pasam vittu akala oliya piravithanai ozhiththuk kollum neermei kalangal kazhiththu sivame koodinal.” “Vallalar matrum avar arulin vaimai koorin varambennam” Thus Sekkizhar Peruman graciously sings. These palm trees were born from the truthful sacred words of the child-saint. Being born from the child-saint’s sacred words means being spoken with grace through those words. Is not the command of grace, “male palm trees will bear tender fruits,” an instruction?

Such were the palm trees born from the child-saint’s sacred words.

Thus, being born from the child-saint’s sacred words, the karma that was the cause of their birth as palm trees, that sanchita karma, was removed. Just as iron drinks water at a glance, as described in the story of Vadavoorar’s initiation in the Thiruvilaiyadal Puranam, those palm trees The sanchita karma, like a seed caught in fire, turns to ash.

Therefore, the primal impurity, the anava mala, becomes powerless and ceases to exist. Henceforth, there are no more births. Sekkizhar Peruman graciously states this here as “oliya piravithanai ozhiththu” (eliminating unceasing births).

Thus, the sanchita karma is removed, and there are no more births. Prarabdha karma can only be exhausted through experience, so the Siddhanta asserts that the body will remain due to prarabdha.

Thus, the sacred words of the Acharya helped to exhaust the remaining prarabdha karma through experience until the body’s limit. That sacred word, the command “male palm trees will bear tender fruits,” as an instruction, The sacred word of Gnanasambandha Peruman, the spiritual teacher, was the command.

Therefore, by that command, the karma associated with the body was experienced and exhausted.

Thus, with the three karmas eradicated and the primal impurity, anava mala, rendered powerless, all those palm trees attained Shivapeeru (the state of Shiva). That Thirugnanasambandhar ensured no further accumulated karma (agamya karma) would arise, and that anava became powerless, happened due to the grace infused in Thirugnanasambandhar’s sacred words.

Therefore, those palm trees attained Shivapeeru. In due course, through Thirugnanasambandhar’s sacred words, this occurred due to the truthfulness of the Lord’s grace. Thirugnanasambandhar, the spiritual teacher, bestowed grace upon all those palm trees, which were one-sense beings born from the fruit of karma, by performing grace initiation (arul deekshai), making them experience their karma, rendering the anava mula mala powerless, And enabling them to attain the auspicious merit of offering fruit to the Lord, and in due course, in this very birth, to attain Shiva. This was due to the grace and truthfulness of Thirugnanasambandhar’s words as a spiritual teacher, and the Lord’s boundless grace. The acts of Umapathi Sivachariar in bestowing liberation upon the Mullichchedu (thorn bush) and Pettraan Sambaanaar come to our minds here. If we understand this sacred history wholeheartedly, then in the concluding part of Thirugnanasambandhar’s purana, the nature of Thirugnanasambandhar’s generosity in granting liberation to everyone who attended his wedding will be easily understood.

If so, can the true nature of the generous child-saint’s grace be confined to limits? Sekkizhar Peruman graciously presents this divine event to us, stating that it cannot.

We shall carry on our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Sekkizhar Peruman’s Periya Puranam, Volume 776, Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandhar Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandhar, having worshipped at Thiruvoththoor, continues his pilgrimage to sacred sites in Thondai Nadu. Sekkizhar Peruman graciously composes the nine hundred and eighty-fourth verse as follows: “Angan Amarar Perumanai Panindhu Ponthu Aadu Aravinudan Pongu Gangai Mudikaniar Mahizhum Pathigal Palavum Potri Mangai Pakar Amarnthu Arulum Vayan Magaralai Vanangi Poy Kongu Malar Neer Kuranganil Muttaththai Sendru Kuruginar.” This verse means that, having worshipped the Lord of Devas, he praised many places where the Lord, adorned with the dancing snake and the surging Ganga on his head, joyfully resides. Having worshipped Vayan Magaral, where the Lord with the Goddess on his side graciously resides, he proceeded to Kuranganil Muttaththu, filled with fragrant flowers and water, and reached there. Thirugnanasambandhar thus praises these sites.

These sites are believed to be places like Purisai Nadu, Purisai, Thiruvanbarththan Panangattur, Vilvalam, and others.

Thus, having praised many sites, Thirugnanasambandhar worships at Vayan Magaral, where the Lord with the Goddess resides. Vayal Magaral is a term used by Sekkizhar Peruman, adding the prefix ‘Vayal’ (field) to the sacred site of Thirumagaral. Thirugnanasambandhar himself mentions “Vinguvilai Kazhani” (fertile fields) and “Madaikkol Punalodu Vayal” (fields with water channels) in his pathigam, and Sekkizhar Peruman uses these phrases to describe the prosperity of the Thirumagaral sacred site.

Thus, the site praised by Thirugnanasambandhar, Thirumagaral, is the seventh among the revered temples in Thondai Nadu. Indra It is the site where Indra worshipped. The Shiva Lingam is a swayambhu murti, the color of an iguana. The history states that the Lord appeared as a golden iguana to Rajendra Chozhan. When he chased it, it ran and hid in an anthill, later emerging as a Shiva Lingam. Those desiring progeny perform Angapradakshinam (prostrating while circumambulating) as a special practice at this site.

This site can be reached via Kanchipuram, Uthiramerur, or Orirukkai. The Lord’s sacred names are Adaikkalam Katthanathar, Agastheeswarar, Thirumagaraleeswarar. The Goddess’s sacred names are Buvananayaki, Thirubuvananayaki. The sthala Vinayagar is Poyya Vinayagar. The sacred waters are Cheyyaru, Agni Thirtham. This is the site where two asuras, Magaran and Malaiyan, worshipped Lord Shiva.

Hence, the site is named Magaral. ‘Magaram’ means iguana. As we have already seen, the Lord appeared as a golden iguana to Rajendra Chozhan. When he Chased it, it ran and hid in an anthill, later emerging as a Shiva Lingam. Other sacred names for the Lord here include Magam Vazhvithavar, Udumbeesar, Paraththazhumbar, Putridam Kondar, Nilaiyittanathar, Mangalam Kaththevar, Parinthu Kaththevar. This is the site where Murugapperuman, riding a white elephant, appeared before Mahavishnu. There is a prevalent oral tradition associated with this site.

A jackfruit was sent daily from the jackfruit tree in this temple to King Rajendra Chozhan. It was offered to Natarajar on the way and then given as prasad to the king. Over time, the temple workers destroyed this tree. When the king learned that no jackfruit was coming, he sent men to investigate. He planned to punish them but ordered that the temple workers be taken out of the town and left at a place where the next day’s dawn would break. The place where they were taken and left is known as Vidimagaral, located between Thiruththani and Thiruvallur.

Salem Subbarayapillai, whose lower body became paralyzed, tried all kinds of medicine without success. He consulted the Thirumurai by drawing a lot and found this pathigam for this place. He came here, stayed, worshipped the Lord daily, recited the sthala pathigam, lived for some time, and by the grace of this Lord, fully recovered and returned. The Shiva Lingam resembles an iguana; it is a swayambhu murti. The aavudaiyar (pedestal) was built later. Monday darshan is considered special.

The pathigam by Thirugnanasambandhar for this sacred site has the special distinction of being a karma-removing pathigam. The temple vimana has a Gajaprushta (elephant-back) structure. In this temple, a rare idol of Murugan seated on an elephant is beautifully displayed. The Brahmotsavam takes place for ten days in the month of Maasi. During the time of the Chola kings, especially Kopperakesari Vanman, also known as Thirubuvanachakravarthi Kuloththunga Chola Devar, who had the Meykeerthi (historical eulogy) beginning with “Poomevi Valar Thirupponmaathu Punaranamevu Kalaimagal Nalamperithu Sirappa,” and during the time of Kopperakesari Third Kuloththunga Pandiyan, who had the Meykeerthi beginning with “Kadal Suuzhntha Parmannarum Seermatharum Adal Suuzhntha Pormatharum Amarnthu Vaazha,” and during the times of the Vijayanagara kings, Veeradeva Maharayar and Kampanna Udaiyar, as well as during the reign of the Telugu Chola king Vijayakanda Gopala Devan, There are inscriptions that have been destroyed.

The Lord is referred to in the inscriptions by names such as Aludaiyar Thiru Agastheeswaramudaiyar, Magaral Udai Nayanar, Thiru Agatheeswaramudaiyar Nayanar. This village was part of Magaral Nadu, within Eiyil Kottam of Jayamkonda Chola Mandalam. In the seventh year of Kochaidaiya Panman, who was Sundara Pandiya Devar, the ruler of all lands, new streets and a sacred kitchen (Thirumadai Vilagam) were constructed near the shrine of Agastheeswaramudaiyar Nayanar by Magaral Pattiyar. These are some of the unique features of the Thirumagaral sacred site. Thirugnanasambandhar, who arrived here, composed a pathigam, which is the seventy-second pathigam of the Third Thirumurai, set to the Sadari tune. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Vengu Vazhai Kazhani Maadai Siyar Paadal Vazhaiyaadal Aravam Mangulodu NeelkKodigal MaadamalI Veedhu Pozhil Matharuuzha Kongu Veedhi Kondraiyodu Gangai Valar Thingani Senkadaiya Senkan Veedai An Nallavarkal Theevinigal Theerum Udaney Kadai Kalleddu Maadamega.

Vengu Vazhai Kazhani Maadai Siyar Paadal Vazhaiyaadal Aravam Mangulodu NeelkKodigal MaadamalI Veedhu Pozhil Matharuuzha Kongu Veedhi Kondraiyodu Gangai Valar Thingani Senkadaiya Senkan Veedai An Nallavarkal Theevinigal Theerum Udaney Kadai Kalleddu Maadamega. Ongu Kamil Veerimali Kazhiyar Podaiyum Vazhyazh Paravi Aranaiyadi Koodu Sambandha Ooraiyul Punalodu Vayal Koodu Pozhil Matharulan Adiya Udaiya Tamil Patthum Oonarvaravarkal Tholvinigal Olzhuvum Oodaney Udaiya Tamil Patthum Oonarvaravarkal Tholvinigal Olzhuvum Oodaka. Those who join the feet of the Lord of Magaral, praised by attributes like “Senjadaiyinaan” (one with red matted locks) and “Senkan Vidai Annal” (the Lord with the red-eyed bull), will immediately be rid of their evil deeds. Throughout the pathigam, we can see references to the removal of karma. This is the gist of this pathigam.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandhar, having worshipped at Thirumagaral, proceeds to Kuranganil Muttaththu, filled with fragrant flowers and water, and worships the Lord. This sacred site, Kuranganil Muttaththu, has a pond, Kaakkai Madu, which serves as a sacred water body, created by a crow worshipping Lord Shiva and pecking with its beak.

Additionally, this site is rich in water bodies surrounding the temple.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to this site as “Kongu Malar Neer Kuranganil Muttaththu” (Kuranganil Muttaththu with fragrant flowers and water). “Kongu” means fragrance or essence. Thirukkuranganil Muttram is the sixth Paadal Petra Sthalam in Thondai Naadu. It is a place where Vali the monkey, a squirrel, and Muttram the crow worshipped the Lord.

Hence, the place is named Kurangu Anil Muttram (Monkey Squirrel Crow’s spot). Since Vali worshipped, the Lord’s name is Valeeswarar. The pond surrounding the temple is called Kaakkai Madu (Crow’s pond) because a crow made it with its beak. This signifies the crow’s worship of the Lord. Images of these three creatures - the monkey, the squirrel, and the crow - are etched and installed at the temple entrance and worshipped. This place is located a short distance south of Kanchipuram.

The Lord’s name is Valeeswarar, Koyyamalarnathar. The Goddess’s name is Iraiyar Valaiyammai. The Theertham (holy water) is Kaakkai Theertham, Vali Theertham. We saw that Vali worshipped the Lord here in the form of a monkey. Indra in the form of a squirrel and Yama in the form of a crow also worshipped the Lord here. Vali worshipped Lord Shiva by shaking the trees to gather flowers, rather than plucking them with his hands.

Because he worshipped with flowers obtained without plucking them, the Lord is named Koyyamalarnathar (Lord of Unplucked Flowers). The shrine faces west. The local people affectionately call the Goddess Ilaiyaal. A rock-cut cave temple is visible a short distance from the main temple. In inscriptions, this place is referred to as Kuranganil Muttram of Pallavapuram in Maamandur Pattram, Irugali Naadu, Kaaliyur Kottam.

The Lord is mentioned in inscriptions as Thirukkuranganil Muttram Udaiya Nayanaar and Koyyamalar Eeswara Devar. Among the local people, the name ‘Kolai’ (murder) for the place can be seen here. This temple has six inscriptions. They date back to the reigns of kings Koneerinmai Kondaann, Kulothungan, Rashtrakoota Kannaaradevan, and Krishnadevarayar. For the upkeep of this temple, Krishnadeva Maharaja donated the village of Pallavapuram to this temple in 1451. Rashtrakoota Kannaaradevan donated land for the Sribali pooja.

Sambuvarayar ordered Sethurayar to grant the village as Nithamam to Sakthi Mangalam. All these are historical facts from the inscriptions. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who visited this place, composed a pathigam. It is the thirty-first pathigam in the First Thirumurai, set to the Takkaraga Pann. The first and concluding verses of the pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. (Vizhneer mazhuvadi annal vilangum kazhu neer koolai mala kayal paayum kozhu neer vayal soozhnda kuranganil muttham thozhu neer maya theeduru thunbam ile). The Lord, who shines with a flowing axe, resides in Kuranganil Muttram, surrounded by fertile fields where fish leap among clean water plants.

Worshipers there will not experience sinful suffering. (Kallaar mathil kaaliyuL gnana sambandha kollaar mazhu vendhi kuranganil muttham sollaar thamil maalai sevikku iniyaaga vallaar kelaam piragai). The essence of this pathigam is that by worshipping Kuranganil Muttram, sins will be removed.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships Kuranganil Muttram.

Following this, the great poet Sevakkizhaar Peruman recites the 985th verse as follows: (Aadhi mudhalvar kuranganil mutthatthai anainthu paninthu etthi neethi vaazhum thiruththondar potra nigaril sanpayinil vedhamodu saiva neri vilanga vantha kavuniyanar maathor baaga). This verse means that the primordial Lord’s Thirukkuranganil Muttram was approached, worshipped, and praised. Thiruthondar (devotees) who live righteously praise him. The Lord, who has the Goddess as part of his form, came to the incomparable Seerkazhi to illuminate the Vedic and Saiva paths. Pillaiyaar, who was born as Kavuniar to spread the Saiva path along with the Vedic path in the incomparable Seerkazhi, approaches the walled city of Kanchi where Ekambavaanar, who has the Goddess as one part of his form, permanently resides. The history of the Goddess worshipping and embracing the Lord and receiving boons in this sacred place of Kanchi is briefly mentioned by the great poet Sevakkizhaar Peruman as “Maadhorbhaaga mannnum mathil soozh Kanchi” (The Lord with the Goddess, residing in the walled Kanchi).

Sevakkizhaar Peruman refers to it as “Mathil soozh Kanchi” (Walled Kanchi). This Thirukanchipuram is one of the seven great places that grant liberation, and it also became the capital of the Chola kings. Throughout the Thirukkurippu Thonda Nayanaar Puranam, we have reflected on many aspects of the history of Thirukanchipuram.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman approaches Kanchipuram.

Now, Sevakkizhaar Perumal continues to sing about Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s history of worshipping the Lord in Kanchipuram. Let us resume our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam Part 777, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, composed by the great Sevakkizhaar Peruman. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrives at Kacchi Thirupathi. Sevakkizhaar Peruman sings about it in the 986th verse: (Needu Kanchi vaanalru nilavum meymmai anbarum maadu shanpai vaLLalar vandhu anaindha voagaiyaal koodukindra inba ner kuLavu veedhi koolinar kaadu konda poogam vaazhai kaamar thoranangalal). The people residing in Kanchipuram and the devotees steadfast in the path of truth, both these groups, were filled with immense joy upon hearing the news that Pillaiyaar, the benevolent one from Seerkazhi, had arrived near Kanchipuram. Due to this joy, they decorated the city of Kanchipuram grandly.

They adorned the streets of Kanchipuram with dense areca nut trees and banana trees, beautiful decorative arches, and other embellishments. (Kodiniraithe veethiyil kola vedhigai puram kadigonmaalai moiththa pandhar gandha neer dhasumbudan madivil pon vilakku eduththu maadhaar maindhar malguvaar padhivizhakum anbarum parandha panpinil eennduvar) is the 987th verse. They tied rows of flags in the streets. On the beautiful platforms in the streets, they arranged altars, tied fragrant flower garlands densely, and under canopies, women and men gathered in abundance, holding golden lamps with pots filled with fragrant water. Maidens dancing, the sounds of singing devotees, and the melodies of Vedic hymns rose in a great crescendo, filling the air. All the great devotees, filled with immense joy, made joyful noises and gathered outside the ancient walls of Kanchipuram to worship Pillaiyaar. (AaLum munbu thondar vandhu saarthalum panbu neediyaana munbu ezhundhu irainju paanmai kandu enperukku mikka thondar anjaliththu eduththa sol manparakka veezhndhu ezhundhu vaanamutta aarth). Peruman arranges.

Here, when the devotees arrived before Pillaiyaar, the leader of Seerkazhi, Pillaiyaar, out of humility, dismounted from the pearl palanquin and prostrated. They raised shouts of reverence. They prostrated and rose many times, shouting up to the sky. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s devotion, seeing the assembly of devotees and the sacred attire as Shiva himself, is evident in his humble prostration. Seeing this, the great devotees prostrated themselves to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, chanting ‘Hara Hara’ and rising many times from the ground. As if to say ‘May the name of Hara surround everything’, the name of Hara resonated up to the heavens.

Pillaiyaar, the leader of Seerkazhi, with the radiant sacred ash adorning his body, and with devotees whose hearts were filled with love for Shiva, entered through the gate of the high walls of Kanchipuram. The crowd, eager to see Pillaiyaar, had gathered outside the walls of Kanchipuram, lined up, and worshipped Pillaiyaar with folded hands held above their heads. As it is said, ‘The pure are within, just like the sacred ash on the flawless gem-like body’, the devotees gathered there welcomed Pillaiyaar.

The devotees living in Kanchi lead Pillaiyaar into the city. (Viya nedum theruvinvoodu mikka thondar aarthe ezhak kayal nedungan maatharum kaadhal needu maandharum puyal pozhindhadhaam ena poovinodu potrchonnnam iyalumaaru vaazhththu eduththu irumarungum veesinar) is the 991st verse. As the multitude of devotees raised their cries in the wide, long streets of Kanchipuram, women with long, fish-like eyes and men filled with love, as if a cloud was raining, showered flowers and golden dust, offering blessings and scattering them on both sides. The great Sevakkizhaar Peruman sings, “Maatharum kaadhal needu maandharum” (women and men filled with love). This indicates that the people there, couples, came together and blessed, and showered flowers, and were on both sides of the street.

Now, Sevakkizhaar Peruman sings about the worship performed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman at Kacchi Thiru Ekambam. (Innavannam yaavarum inbam eydha eydhuvaar pinnu vaarsadai mudi piraan magizhndha koilgaL munnurap panindhu poi moivarai thirumagal mannu poosanai magizhndha mannar koil munninar) is the 992nd verse.

Thus, Pillaiyaar, making everyone happy, entered the streets of Kanchipuram and worshipped the many temples where the Lord rejoices in Kanchipuram. We previously noted that there are countless Shiva temples, a crore of Shiva temples, within the limits of Kanchi city.

The Lord rejoiced in many places. We saw in the Thirukkurippu Thonda Nayanaar Puranam that it was the boundary of that holy city.

Therefore, Pillaiyaar, who set out to worship at Thiru Ekambam, worships all the Shiva temples along the way. These temples are located on the path from the south wall of Kanchipuram to the Ekambareswarar temple, because Pillaiyaar entered from the southern boundary of Kanchipuram.

So, these are the temples on the way from there to the Ekambar temple, which are considered to be temples like Kacchapesam and others. There, the Thiru Ekamba temple is seen, where the Goddess, the daughter of the mountain king, came and worshipped the Lord under the mango tree in Kanchi, establishing righteousness and residing there, and the Lord rejoiced in her worship. Approaching the entrance of the Kambanaar temple, he folded his hands and, bowing before the towering gopuram, he entered. Surrounded by devotees in the golden mansions, Pillaiyaar, who came to save this world, worshipped. This is the 993rd verse by the great Sevakkizhaar Peruman. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, seeing the entrance of the Ekambavaanar temple, folded his hands and raised them above his head in worship.

He bowed before the sky-high gopuram. This gopuram is the south gopuram of the Thiru Ekambar temple, a very large and tall gopuram. After bowing to the gopuram and the entrance, he worshipped the inner part of the Ekambam temple, the Lord’s abode, and the area around the mango tree, within the sacred walls of the temple. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships all these, including the large circumambulatory path inside, next to the outer wall. It is known that in those days, like in Thiruthillai, many parts of the temple here were covered with gold.

Thus, after worshipping, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman comes before Thiru Ekambanathar. (Sempon malaikkodi thazhuvakkulaintharum thirumeni kambarai vanthu ethir vanangum kavuniyartham kaavalanaar pambutholil kannaruvu paayndhu mayirpulagam vara tham perugu manakkaadhal thalla nilamisai thaazhndhaar) is the 994th verse. Pillaiyaar, the protector of the Kavuniyas, who came to worship the Thiru Ekambaranathar, whose body is softened by the embrace of Kamakshi Amman, the golden creeper-like daughter of the mountain king, his overflowing devotion caused tears to flow like a waterfall from his eyes, and goosebumps to appear on his body. Driven by the surging love in his heart, he prostrated himself on the ground. We have extensively reflected on the sacred history of the Goddess embracing the Lord like a creeper clinging to a support, in the Thirukkurippu Thonda Nayanaar Puranam. Kanchipuram is a place filled with the power of the Goddess.

Therefore, the great poet Sevakkizhaar Peruman first refers to the Goddess, saying, “Kambar, whose divine form softened when embraced by the creeper.” He prostrated himself many times, then rose, his lotus-like hands folded, and with the beautiful, radiant words emanating from his lotus-like mouth, he began the pathigam, “Maraiyaan,” to elevate the world. His melting love, which could melt even bones, and the perfectly composed tune and rhythm, made him sing the pathigam. He bowed in humility, and with overflowing joy, he performed the dance of bliss. His heart melted and was moved. He raised his folded hands in reverence to his head. His entire body was covered in goosebumps.

Sevakkizhaar Peruman recites the 995th and 996th verses, saying that the Lord’s son, Pillaiyaar, bowed many times, who was unknowable to the two great deities who sought his beginning and end, having taken the forms of a boar and a swan. Following the temple darshan rule that prostrations should be done three, five, up to eleven times, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman prostrated countless times due to the intensity of his love. The lotus of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s hands folded, and the lotus of his face bloomed. The lotus of his hands folded, and the lotus of his face bloomed with grace, like the moonlight of the Goddess and the radiant light of Ekambanathar. The truth of Gnana Sastras, that lotuses bloom and bud before the sun (the Lord), comes to our mind here. With his thus blossomed face and mouth, Pillaiyaar began the pathigam starting with “Maraiyaan” for the salvation of the world.

He sang it in the Indhalappann, in Aadhithaalam, the first rhythm.

Thus, the pathigam graced by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for Kacchi Thiru Ekambam is the twelfth pathigam of the Second Thirumurai, set to Indhalappann. This pathigam was sung for us by Shiva Thiru Mahadevan, the Oduvar Moorthigal of Thirukkalukkundram Vedagireeswarar temple. This sweet pathigam is dedicated to Kacchi Ekambam. Praise to the feet of Swamy Thiru Thazhuvakuzhainthanathar. Praise to the feet of Devi Thiru Kamakshi Amman. This is the Thirukkadaikaappu composed by Thirugnanasambandha Moorthy Nayanar.

(Maraiyaanai maasilaan piradu aagiya penn irayaane er kol kachi thiru Ekathu urai vaarai alladhu ulgadhu enadhu ullamme). He is the Lord residing in Thiru Ekam, Kanchi, who is faultless and has a perfect form. My heart does not think of anyone else but Him. (E nocchiye vanni konrai madhikkuuvilum uchchiye punaithal vedam vidai oorthiyaan kachi ekambeiy karai kandani nachchiye thoduminnum melvinai ennaa uzhava mundhai kuzhal yaazholi seeraal paadal aadal sithaivu illadhor erarpungae ekambanai emmaan seraadhaa inbamaa). (Neri sere kundrekum nedhu ven maada kodi koodi poi min thekum moogilgal thoyum viyal kachiyul mantrekum malgu seeraal maliye kambam sendrekum sindhaiyar mel vinai seraave sadaiyaanai thalai kaiye paLi tharuvaartham kadaiya poyppu moonrum kondaarn kali kachiyul pudaiye pon malaruva kambakaraiye kamba udaiyaanai alladhu ulgaadhanadhulla). (Me mazhuvodu kol soozhappadai vallaarthova kezhuvaaloorimaiyar uchivamaiya vazhuvaame malgu seeraal valar ekkaa thozhuvare vizhumiyar melvinai thumnaave vinnullar maraigal vedham virithu odhuvaar kannular kadalil velvaarkari kaalanai nannuvar ezhil kolke kambathu annalaraadukindra alankarame thooiyaanai thooya aayam arai oothiya).

(Yaanai vaazhakkann vazhi vaattiya theeyaanai theedhil kachche thiru ekambai mevvaar en thalai melaare naagam pooneeradheeral narungonraar paagam penn baliyum erpar marai paaduvar ekambam meviyaadum iraiyiruvarkavan nalla ne pothiya pindiyaar endruvar poyynoolai vaadhiyam in amma ennum kachiyul aadhiyaar meviyaar). (Aadum thiru eka neetthiyum innum melvinai anthan poongachi ekkanai kanthan poongazi ooran kali kovaiyaal santhame paadavalla thamil gnana sambandhan sol paadiyaada kedum paavame enna kambai karaiyekol kachchi thiruvekambam udaiyaanai alladhu ulgadhu en ullamme avanai seraadhaar inbamaya annneri serare) is the thematic note of this pathigam.

Thus, Sevakkizhaar Peruman describes the profound devotion of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as he composes and completes the Thirukkadai Kaappu (concluding verse) of the pathigam, worshipping the Lord. Sevakkizhaar Peruman shows us that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sang this pathigam, prostrated, performed a dance of bliss filled with love, his heart melted, he folded his hands in reverence and raised them to his head, and his entire body was covered in goosebumps.

Let us continue our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam Part 778, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, composed by Sevakkizhaar Peruman. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, worshipping the Lord at Thiru Ekambam, composes a pathigam. Sevakkizhaar Peruman continues to sing. (Maruviya ezh_isai pozhiya manam pozhiyum per anbaal perugiya kann mazhai pozhiya perum pugazhai perunthagaiyaar urugi avan pullalai kuzhaindhavarai unarvinaar) is the 997th verse. As Thirugnanasambandha Peruman recited the pathigams set to the seven musical notes, his heart overflowed with love, and tears flowed like a heavy rain. The great personality from the glorious Seerkazhi, Pillaiyaar, with his heart melting and love stirring his inner self, praised Ekambavaanar, whose form softened when embraced by the Goddess.

With that spiritual realization, he came out of the temple.

The Lord softened His form when embraced by the Goddess. Because of this, all living beings, both soul and body, melted and merged, praising the Lord.

In this way, when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman performed worship, his heart melted with an abundance of love, and his eyes shed tears like rain. Love is not something visible; it is an abstract concept. The tears that flow from the eyes show that this invisible love is overflowing. You cannot see love. Those tears reveal the unseen love. “Is there a bolt to bar love?

“The tears of the loving reveal it,” says the Kural.

“Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, experiencing an overflow of spiritual emotion, delivered the pathigam and emerged from the temple. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who emerged from the temple with the accompanying devotees, then resided in the sacred monastery prepared for him, joyfully staying there with an unceasing, deep love for the Lord. This sacred monastery was already suitably prepared for Pillaiyaar’s arrival. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman stayed there with his devotees. (Purathanaindha thondarudan pondhu amaindha thirumadatttil pirarkkum peruvulagu uyya pettarulum pillaiyaar mara). (Tharpariya kaathaludan vandhu eythi magizhndhuraippar arapperrunchelvak kaamakkottam anaindhu irainjinaar) is the next verse. During those days, as he stayed in the monastery and joyfully beheld Ekambavaanar, he approached Kacchi Thirukkaamakkottam, where the Goddess, who fostered all virtues, resided, and worshipped Kamakshi Amman there.

“We discussed extensively in the Thiruthondar Puranam how Kamakshi Amman received boons from the Lord and resided here, fostering all virtues and protecting all beings with her grace.

“Therefore, Sevakkizhaar Peruman refers to the Thirukkamakkottam, where Kamakshi Amman resides, as ‘Arapperrunchelvak Kamakkottam’ (the temple of great virtuous wealth). This great wealth is the wealth of compassion she held for all living beings. Our Paramacharya, apart from Lord Shiva’s temple, no separate temple for worshipping the Almighty is mentioned anywhere else. Only here, in Kacchi Thirukkamakkottam, is it a unique Shakthi temple, where Kamakshi Amman resides, worshipped by our Paramacharyas. This is a special feature unique to Kacchi Thirukkamakkottam. Pillaiyaar was blessed to save the world, so he appeared to save the world.

“We will see this in the upcoming Eiyarkon Kalikkama Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman always worshipped the glorious light residing in Thiru Ekambam, with his heart melting at His feet, without fail. He also composed Thiruviyamagam and Thiruvirukural, which are filled with growing music. Sevakkizhaar Peruman recites the 999th verse, saying that Pillaiyaar composed garlands of pathigams. The pathigams composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman that are currently available are. We have already seen one pathigam by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

“Therefore, there are a total of four pathigams composed by Pillaiyaar for Kacchi Ekambam. Among these four pathigams, the one composed now is the second pathigam, composed in the style of Thiruviyamagam. This pathigam is set to the Pazhampancharam Pann and is the 114th pathigam of the Third Thirumurai. This pathigam is as follows: Praise to the feet of Swamy Thiru Ekambam, Thiru Ekambaranathar. Praise to the feet of Devi Thiru Kamakshi Amman. This is the Thirukkadaikaappu composed by Thirugnanasambandha Moorthy Nayanar.

“(Paayum veedai meloru baagane paavai meloru baagane thuyar veda thoo vaniyeri aayum nanporul nunporul aadhi ezha nee arum porul aadhi kaayavil). (Adhu kambameye kannuthal paramakkidam kambameye sadaiyanindhadhum vendhalai maalaiye thambudum vendhalai maalaiye pada ilam kaiyil soozhamam adhu enbathe paranthilangaiyil soozhamadhu enbathe kudai parappanabooda ganangale potri seitha ganangale kadaigal thoorum eerappadhummicchaiye kambam meviyiruppadhum icchaiye velluru kodu thumbai meelachchiye yeru munsela thumbai). (Meelachchiye alli neeradhu poosuvadhaagame aanamaasoonam moosuvadhaagame pulliyadai oodupadhu katthume pona oozhi oodupadhu ugalaththume kallulaa malar kambam iruppadhe kaanchi maanakar kambam iruppadhe muttralaamai anindha moodhalvareyaamai anindha moodhalvare pattrri valaravaattum parisare paalum neeyogandhaattum parisareya vatrralodu kalam pazhi thervadhe).
