(Kalodagil santham muruttiye vedam odagil santham muruttiye athira aaru varathu azhuvaththoda aanai thadaravo thazhuvaththode kadhirkoL poon mulai kambam iruppadhe kaanchi maanakar kambam iruppadhe panda kann eduththa balaththaye paayndhara kann neduththa balaththaye kondarakkiyathum kaal viralaiye koLarakkiyathum kaal viralaiye unduzhandrathu mundaththaliye udupadhikke idam).

“(Undu aththalayil kandam nanjje adakkenne kambame kadavuL needam kondathu kambame thooyiyaana soodar veedu sothiye suththamaana soodar vidu sothiye peniyodu pirama paravaiye piththanaana pirama paravaiye seninodu keezh oozhi thirinthume siththamodu keezhoozhi thirinthume kaananil uttrathu kambame kadavuL needam uttrathu kambameya oorudambinai). (Eru aagave unboruL theram eru aagave aarummi than karithu perithuume aatttaraiyarku arithu perithuume therrum ariyaadhu thegaippare siththamum ariyaa thoodhi kaippare kaa niramam narkoru kambame kadavuL needam kondathu kambame kanthammarpozil soottaru kambame kaathal seibavar theerththidu oogu ambame punthi seivadhu virumbi poogaliye poosooran than). The thematic note of this pathigam is the praise of the Lord’s glories in various melodious and rhythmic ways.

“Now, the third pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for Kacchi Thiru Ekambam is structured as Thiruvirukural. It is set to Kollipann, and it is the forty-first pathigam of the Third Thirumurai. This pathigam is as follows: Praise to the feet of Swamy Thiru Ekambam, Thiru Ekambaranathar. Praise to the feet of Devi Thiru Kamakshi Amman.

“This is the Thirukkadaikaappu composed by Thirugnanasambandha Moorthy Nayanar. (Tharuvaarkachchi thiru ekambaththu oruvaai maruvaavinai e madhiyin nadhiyekumbam vidhiyaal eththa pathiye kaliyarkachchi mali ekam baliyaal potra naliyaavinai e varamaarkachchi puram ekam parava e). (Piravaavinaiye padamaar kachchiyidam ekamba thudaiya enna adaiyaavinaiye nalamaar kachchi nilave kambam kuLa vaayeththa kalavaavinaiye kariyin uriyan thiru ekamban periya puramoonreri seithaane ilangai arasai thulangga oondrum nalanggol kamban ilanggu sarane maraiyon ariyum ariya analan neriye kambam kuriyal thozhume pariya theraru neriyil kachchi seri koL kambam kuruguvoome kocchai vendhan kachchi kambam mecchum sollai acchum pugazhe). The essence of this pathigam is that by praising Thiru Ekambam, sins will not afflict.

“Now, the fourth pathigam graced by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for Thiru Kacchi Ekambam is the 133rd pathigam of the First Thirumurai. It is set to the Meharaga Kurinji Pann. This pathigam is as follows: Praise to the feet of Swamy Thiru Ekambam, Thiru Ekambaranathar. Praise to the feet of Devi Thiru Ela Vaarkuzhali Amman. Nayanar. (Kuzhaliyum kadipodhil kachchi thannul antha mil gunaththaar avar potra anangginodu aadal koori endha meviya ekambam thozhuthetthudume varam thigazhum avanaru maanagar moonrudan maaindhaviya saram thurandhu eri seiththa thaazhai sanggaran meiyidam).

“(Porundha malligai konggu maathavi nalla kura maravam thirundhu paimpozhil kachchi ekambam seraiyidarkkedume vannavven podi poosum maarbil variyaravam punaithu pennamal theriyaadal peniya pinnagan meiyidam vinnamar nedumaadam oonggi vilanggiya kachchi thannul thinna maambodil soozhndha ekambam seraiyidarkkedume thoLUm noolum thuthaindha varai maarbil soodalai venn). The God who burned Yama with his foot and who is contemplated wears a garland and has the cool moon on his great ramparts in Kanchi. In the city of Kanchi, surrounded by beautiful fragrant groves, worshipping Ekambam will remove suffering. (Todani malar konrai serchchayam padal nan maraiyaka palkana peygal avai sozha vadal venthalaiyodal enthi magizhnthudan nadal puriya se) He who shot an arrow to bring down the three cities of the demons, whose body has a female half, who wears sacred threads and books, and who is in the great city of Kanchi with its lofty jewel-studded mansions, the lord of Ekambam, worshipping his feet will remove suffering. The one with the cool moon on his red matted hair, who lives on the left side, who sustains life and begs for alms with a skull in hand. Worshipping Ekambam in Kanchi, a city with extensive groves, will remove suffering for those who seek it.

“The great Lord, whom Brahma and Vishnu worship, whose matted hair is adorned with snakes, and who resides with the good Goddess, in the city of Kanchi, where there are no hidden deceitful hands, touching Ekambam will destroy powerful karma. Those who suffer from ailments and those who wear patched clothes. Those who desire to understand the sayings of the arrogant and who have seen Him destroy the three cities of the enemies with a single fierce arrow, seeing Ekambam in Kali Kanchi will remove their suffering. Those who worship Him, who is in Ekambam surrounded by groves in Kanchi, are extolled by Thiru Gnanasambandhan from the city of Kazhumalam, which has tall jewel-studded mansions, and those who can recite these ten verses will be praised gloriously and join the celestials. Those who join the celestials, whose fame is exalted, those who join the celestials. This pathigam’s note is that worshipping Thiru Ekambam will remove suffering.

“Let us continue to contemplate Thiruchitrambalam.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, part seven hundred seventy-nine, composed by Theivasekkizhar Peruman, the Vampara Varivandachcharukkam, Thiru Gnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman, residing in Kanchipuram, visits and worships at many temples. Theivasekkizhar Peruman continues to sing about this. The thousandth and thousand-first verses in Pillaiyar Puranam, and the two thousand eight hundred ninety-eighth and two thousand eight hundred ninety-ninth verses in Periya Puranam, are as follows: (Nīdu thiruppozhil Kanchi neri Karaikadu irainji soodu mathikanniyar thunai mel malarchchevadipadum adum avar inithu amarum anekathangavatham paravi madu thiruththanangal paninthu ethi vaigu nal enthisaiyum pottraisaikkum thirupathi matrum athan puraththu thondu) Happily proceeded, worshipping the Lord with the dark throat who swallowed poison, and other deities, with great devotion, and then returned happily.

These are the verses. Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman visits the temple of Thirukkachi Nerikkaraikkadu, which is surrounded by long, beautiful groves, and sings and dances, praising the flower-like feet of the Lord’s consort. Thirukkachi Neri Karaikkadu is the fifth celebrated temple among those in Thondai Nadu. It is located northeast of Veppankulam within Kanchipuram city. Because it is on the eastern edge of Kanchi city, it is called Kachi Neri Karaikkadu. Because it is in a dense Karaimaram forest and bestows spiritual attainment upon those who join there.

It is named Kachi Neri Karaikkadu. It also has the name Sathyavirathanam. The Kanchi Puranam sings about this place, saying that Sathyaviratham, with its dense Karaitharuvanam, bestows Siddhi upon those who attain it, and that its sacred name Thiruneri Karaikkadu will flourish. The Thirunerikkarai Padalam in Kanchi Puranam extensively details the history of this place. In the Brahma Kalpam, during the sixth Indra’s life, Indra, disgusted with life and having attained equivalence of good and bad karma, followed the advice of his guru Brihaspati, came here to Kachi Thiruneri Karaikkadu, worshipped the Lord, and attained liberation.

Hence, it is also called Indrapuram, and its sacred pond. Is also called by the same name. Budha, born to Chandra and Thara, worshipped here and attained the status of a planet.

Here, on Wednesdays, those who bathe and worship are granted liberation and desired boons by Shiva, and Budha also received this boon.

Therefore, bathing and worshipping in this pond on Wednesdays is highly meritorious. This place is now known as Thirukaleeswaran temple. The main deity is Sathyaviratheeswarar, also known as Karai Thirunathar, and the Goddess is Kamakshi Ammai. The sacred pond is Sathyaviratha Theertham. In inscriptions, the main deity is referred to as Thirukkaraikkadudaiyar. The Goddess is referred to as Karaikkudi Ammai.

In Kanchi Puranam, the deities of this place are referred to as Sathyasakthiyar, Sathyasodhagar, Sathyasankalpar, and Sathyakamar. Sacred names are mentioned.

From that day onwards, that environment is Indrapuram. Kanchipuram sings about the greatness of this place, asking who can truly describe its glory, stating that those who have once seen the Lord with matted hair will not go to Yama’s realm and will not be born again. The sacred name of the Lord of this place, Sathyaviratheswarar, gave Kanchipuram the name Sathyaviratha Kshetram. The Veppankulam here is called Indra Theertham. The Moolavar is a Swayambhumoorthi, a slightly elevated lingam, appearing in a light reddish-brown color.

Here, before the Dakshinamurthy Peruman, there are seven disciples. Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman, who visited this place, composed a pathigam. It is the sixty-fifth pathigam in the third Thirumurai. A pathigam composed in the Panjamam tune. Some texts suggest that this Panjamam tune can be somewhat compared to the Akiri raga of the present day. The pathigam composed by Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman is as follows: Thiru Kachi Nerikkaraikkadu, praise to the sacred feet of Swami Thiru Karai Thirunathar.

Praise to the sacred feet of Devi Thiru Kararu Kuzhali Ammai. Thiru Gnanasambandhar’s Thirukkadaikkappu.

(Am kaiyinil poranavum mazhuvu eranavum azhivu angu ethivan podi anivar poranavum mazhuvu angu ethivan podi anivar karanavum manimadam kadai navintra kalikatchi karanavum manimadam kadai navintra kalikatchi) (Niranavum malarpoigai niranave malarpoigai nerukkarai kattare niranave malarpoigai nerukkarai kattare nerukkarai kattare nerukkarikattare katchi nerukkarikattare karur mani idattr karikadar udai thalai kondu ururan bali kuzhalvakhuzhai ma) (Poriyathalar ururran bali kuzhalvar uzhaimanjil poriyiyathalar therorum nedhuvedhi sezhungkachi manakarvar tharum karorum pani mitattrar kari kadar udai thalai kondu uran bali kuzhalvayi ural baliguzhalvar uzhaimanjil muriyathalar therorum nedhuvethe sezhungkachi manakarvar) (Nerorum malarpoigai nerikkarai kattare puranindar podiyettai pulisadai mel illamathiyodu aranintharadaravum poondugantharpandinthar podiyattan mel enpinthar varai marpil neranithar kalikarai kattare pira navina senchadaigal pin thazha buthangal marai navintha pa) (Adalodu adalaray mazhu entha thirai navina vandinangal thingani vaitthe kathuvo thirai navina kalikathi nerikkarai kattare andraling keezhirunthe andraling keezh thanga aramburindha arulalar ontrathavin silaiyil poleravum nan pozhuvi ontrrajapuram ontrum ongeriyil venthaviyin)

(Kalika nerukkarai kattare panmalargal kondadi ki vanorgal panindhiranja nanmaiyil vallavunar nagar muntrum oru nodiyil bilmalaiyin nan kozhuve venkanaiyal azhitha nirmalanar kalika nerukkarai kattare kutti deival aravinodu punai konrai matha matham ettroliya alai punalodu illamathi) (E thiru pedaiyar oru bagam pennudaiya kannamarum netrriyanar kalikkatti nerukkarai kattare ezhu kadal suzhdhin neelangkai pomanai elvaraivadal suzhlin neelangaiye pomanai ezhil varaivar thazhviralal untriyatho thanmaiyinar nanmaiyinar al kidangum suzhvayalo athil kolgi azhagamarum neelmaruvin kalikka) (Pundanum ollikadal ne udaithalaiyil balikolva mandatham ezhum panivar variyaravo illama pundarum variruvar ariyama kongeeriya nindarum kalikarai kattare kundadi samanpaduvar urai thannai mey porkkum min thadi thiritharuvar urai panaigal meyyalla) (Arunkuzhala paraiyaga thorubaga kandarum kalikkachi nerukkarai kattaru kannarum kalikkachi nerikkarai kattare kannarungalikatchi nerukkarikattare kannarum kali katchi nerikarikatturum kannarum kalikkachi nerikkarikatturum pennarum thirumeni) (Anarum perumeni perumanathu vadivazhi thannarum pozhilthazhi tamil gnana sambandhal pannarum tamil valla pannarum tamil valla paraloka thiruparu thannarum pozhilthazhi tamil gnana sambandhan pannarum tamil valla paraloka thiruparu paraloka thiruparu) The Lord, the One who applies white ash, who wears deer skin, and is known by many such qualities, is the Lord of Kachi Neri Karaikkadu.

This is the main point of this pathigam. Having worshipped Thirukkachi Neri Karaikkadu, Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman then praises the temple of Thiru Anekatangavatham, where the Lord who performs the dance of grace joyfully resides. Thiru Anekatangavatham is the fourth celebrated temple among those in Thondai Nadu. Anekatam means elephant. This is the place where Vinayaka worshiped Shiva. This place was worshipped, hence the name Anekatangavatham.

There is also a Thiru Anekatangavatham in North India, which is currently called Gauri Kund and is near Kedaram.

Similarly, there is one here in Kanchi. This Anekatangavatham, therefore, to specify this place in Kanchi, is referred to as Kachi Anekatangavatham. Kubera and others worshipped here and attained fame.

Here, Ganesha came to Kanchi, installed a Lingam named Anegameeswarar, and worshipped, receiving boons to successfully complete the endeavors of those who remember him and to cause obstacles to the endeavors of those who do not.

Additionally, as granted by the Lord, he defeated the Asuras of Hiranyapuram, took Vallabai, their source of power, as his consort. And reigned, this is the history pertaining to this place. In the Kanchi Puranam, there is a chapter called Anekatangavatha Padalam, which describes the glory and sacred history of this place. The deity is Swami Anekatangavatheeswarar, and the Goddess is Kamakshi Ammai. This sacred place is located southwest of the Ekambareswarar Temple in Kanchi, a short distance west of Putheri Street, in a field. Kanchi Puranam sings the glory of this place, stating that those who worship Anekapeesana, where Vinayaka resides and performs worship, will be freed from the intense suffering of birth and will reside in the silver Kailash of their Lord.

Dhanu Theertham is the sacred pond associated with this place. Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman visited here and composed a pathigam, but due to our misfortune. That pathigam is not available to us. One pathigam composed by Sundaramurthi Swamigal after visiting this place has been found.

Thus, after worshipping Anekatangavatham, Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman visits and worships all the various sacred places in Kanchipuram where the Lord rejoices and composes pathigams. The sacred places worshipped by Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman within the city limits of Kanchipuram include Thiru Onakanthan Thali, Kachi Meettali, Thakkeesam, Kanneesam, Salantareesam, Sittheesam, Abirameesam, Adipatheesam, Iraneesam, Renukeeswaram, Kachapeesam, Surakareesam, Navagrahisam, Narasingeesam, Parasurameesam, Parasaresam, Balabathira Ramesam, Pandaveesam, Makkeesam, Manickandeeswaram, Mutheeswaram, Vairaveesam, Vaneesam, Viswaseeneesam, Veeraraghaveesam, Panathareeswaram and others. Are various sacred sites.

However, due to our misfortune, the pathigams composed by Pillaiyar for all these places are not available to us. Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman, after worshipping all the sacred places within the city limits of Kanchipuram, which are revered by people from all eight directions, then proceeds with the devotees to worship temples outside Kanchipuram. He worships various prominent places. Such places include those to the south of Amareesam and to the west of Kachi Karunam. Among these is the temple called Kachi Thirumettali. These one hundred eighteen places are those worshipped by the one hundred eighteen Rudras, including the world protectors like Rudras and Srikandars.

These one hundred and eighteen places are sacred sites. Among these is the temple known as Thirumettali. This Thirumettali temple is the second celebrated temple in Thondai Nadu. It is also referred to as Kachi Meettali and Kanchi Meettali. Thirumettali is the sacred name mentioned by Theivasekkilar Peruman. According to Kanchi Puranam, Lord Vishnu worshipped here to attain Sivasaaroopam, and by the power of listening to the pathigam composed by Aaludaiya Pillaiyar, he attained Shiva’s grace.

Having listened to this pathigam and being moved, Lord Vishnu transformed into a Sivalinga and is enshrined here under the name Odhurugieeswarar. This is one shrine; the main deity’s shrine is separate as another shrine. To the east of this temple, Aaludaiya Pillaiyar and Mutheesamoorthi, who listened to the song. Reside. Due to its connection with Pillaiyar, this part of Kanchi is currently known as Pillaiyar Palayam. Pillaiyar’s worship and song at Thirumettali are mentioned in the thousand and first verse of Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman’s Puranam, and the transformation of Thirumal into Sivasaaroopam after hearing his song is mentioned in the thousand and second verse of Kanchi Puranam, which is a significant concordance.

The Lord’s name is Ekambaram, and the temple is located there. The pathigam composed by Peruman is not available to us. For this place, one Thirunerisai pathigam sung by Appar Peruman and one pathigam composed by Sundaramurthi Swamigal, making a total of two pathigams, have been found. The sacred pond is Vishnu Theertham. Having visited many such places, Pillaiyar returns to Kanchipuram city and resides there.

We shall continue our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam, part seven hundred eighty, composed by Theivasekkizhar Peruman, the Vampara Varivandachcharukkam, Thiru Gnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman, having worshipped Kachi Meettali, then visits various temples in that area. In that sacred place, with great desire, he worships the Lord and then goes to the southern bank of the Thiru Nadhi, Baliyar, whose fame is indescribable. He joyfully worships the Lord with the dark throat on his chest in Thirumaperu and adorns Him with a garland of verses, as mentioned in the thousand and second verse, saying that he worshipped the Lord there with great fondness. He worships the sacred places where the Lord graciously resides.

There is a river called Baliyar, and going along its southern bank, he joyfully worships the Lord in Thirumalperu and offers pathigams there. Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman offers pathigams. We have contemplated the glories of Thirumalperu in Thiru Navukkarasu Peruman Puranam. Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman composed two pathigams for Thirumalperu. The first pathigam is the fifty-fifth pathigam in the first Thirumurai, composed in the Pazhandakkaraga tune. This pathigam is as follows: Thirukkadaikkappu composed by Sri Thiru Gnanasambandha Moorthy Nayanar.

(Mani kandare man uzhiyartharu nanjinai undu umai niru se thiru meniyaru seru servayal then thirumarperril marila mani kandare thoda mamalaru kondiru podu ummai adaiwaram adigal ena madaiyar nir malku manniyamarperu udaiyere umai ulgi) (E paiyarum aravam kodu aatiya kaiyan endru vananguvar maiya nanju undu mapperru irukkindra aiyanin adiyargale sala mamalar kondu saran endru melaiyargal virumbuvar malinar vazhipadu seytrru nillamar kanda ninnaiye marila maniye endru vanavar erave miga etthruvar kurane kulavum tha) (Theer marperrin nirane endru ninnaiye uraiyathar illai ontrum nin thanmaiyai paravatha illai nalkalum thiraiyalil then karai mapperru thiraiyarpaliyil then karai mapperru araiyane arul nalkide arasalikkum ara kan avan thannai urai kedutthu avan ulgida varam miguththayum mapperru adigalai paravida kedum) The two Devas, Brahma and Vishnu, searched for Him, but no one else could comprehend Him. Those who worship the Lord of Thirumalperu, whose feet are eternally radiant, will find their karmas removed. Those who wear patched clothes and wander, those who consume the food given to them by others, those who are considered base, their towns and seven countries will praise Him as the Lord of Thirumalperu.

Vishnu and Soma, who worship here, the soil and Vishnu. Worshipped Thirumalperu, the Lord with the jewel-like throat.

The elders will desire you, your devotees will desire you, the celestials will praise you. There is no one who does not praise you. Worshipping you will remove karma, this is the summary of this pathigam.

Now, the second pathigam composed by Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman for Thirumalperu is the one hundred and fourteenth pathigam in the first Thirumurai, composed in the Viyalakkurinji tune. This pathigam is as follows: Thirumalperu Swami, the Lord worshipped by Vishnu, Thiru. Praise to the sacred feet of Devi Thiru Karunai Nayaki Ammai. This is the Thirukkadaikkappu composed by Thiru Gnanasambandha Moorthi Nayanar. Thiruchutrambalam. He is the short one, the one who speaks sharply, He is great, He is both male and female. (Kurundhavan kurukavan kurmai avan perunthagai pennavan anum avan anum avan karundhadam malar kanni kadhal seyyum karundhadam malar kanni kadhal seyyum)

(Marundhavan valanagaru marpere karundhadam malar kanni kadhal seyyum marundhavan valanagaru marpere parani ven thalai kaiyil enthi verani pazhi kollum vetkaiyana nerani thumaiyoru bagam vaiththa marili valanagar marpere karuvudaiyar ulagangal veva seruvidaiyeri mun sendru nindru uruvudaiyar)

The Lord and Uma together are in the beautiful city of Thirumalperu. He wore a garland of skulls, killed the fierce Yama, and desired it. He is the Lord of Kailayam, the mountain where many arts are learned, the Lord of the beautiful city of Thirumalperu. He is the one with the sacred river, the one who is selfless, the one who protects ancient lives. He is the Lord with matted hair adorned with a skull, the Lord with a neck like a shell, the one who destroyed Kala. He is the Lord of the beautiful city of Thirumalperu.

He who holds a good woman as half of his body, who burned Kama with his eye, is worshipped by celestials, demons, sages, and kings in the good Thirumalperu. The rakshasa who lifted the flawless mountain, Ravana, sang Vedic hymns with righteousness. The primal Lord, our Lord, is in the beautiful city of Thirumalperu. He, with his lotus-like eyes and fragrant flowers, is on the beautiful, sweet-smelling flower-strewn path. (Aiyanal sevadi athanai ulga mayal seygai marpere kulithu na ammana kundarakkaru ennum kazhithu nan kazhaladi kanalurar mulaiththavan mathiyinodu aravam senni valaithavan vall nagaru marpere sambandhan padal seyytrrai santhamin tamilgal konde thavallar entha than kazhal) The place where the Lord resides, a prosperous city, is Thirumalperu.

This is the summary of this pathigam.

Now, Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman, after worshipping Thirumalperu, proceeds to the temple of Thiruvalam. Theivasekkizhar Peruman describes this as follows: Having received the grace of the Lord of Thirumalperu, he then went to Thiruvalam, bearing the feet that even Brahma and Vishnu could not comprehend, and adorned his Lord with a great garland of pathigams, as mentioned in the thousand and third verse. From the sacred place of Thirumalperu, having received the grace of the Lord, he then proceeded to the sacred place of Thiruvalam. He visits and worships the temple.

There, he praises the Lord and offers pathigams. Thiruvalam is the tenth temple in Thondai Nadu and is currently known as Thiruvalam. Because it is the place where the demon Theekali worshipped and attained salvation, it is also known as Theekali Valam. It is historically said that the nine planets worshipped the Lord here and attained blessings. It is also called Vilvaranya Kshetram. It is a very large temple.

The Lord’s name is Vallanathar, and the Goddess’s name is Vallambikai. The sacred ponds here are Gauri Theertham, Sivagangai, Neetva Nadi, and Vajratheertham. This is the place where the Lord appeared to King Janaka. The Nandi here faces east, and the main shrine of the Lord faces west. The Goddess also has the name Dhanu Mathyambal. Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman, who visited here, composed a pathigam.

It is the one hundred and thirteenth pathigam in the first Thirumurai, composed in the Viyalakkurinji tune. This pathigam is as follows: Thiruvalam Swami Thiru Vallanathar, praise to his sacred feet. Devi Thiru Vallambikai, praise to her sacred feet. Thirukkadaikkappu composed by Thiru Gnanasambandha Moorthi Nayanar. He who burned the three cities, who is the Ganga on his head, who revealed various Vedas, his sacred abode is Thiruvalam. He is the mother of the world, unequaled.

He is pure, adorned with a cool moon, he became what he is, pure and beyond even the sages. His distant abode is Thiruvalam. He who burned Kama into ashes in the past, he who embraced the elephant’s hide, he who severed Brahma’s head, his abode is Thiruvalam. Those who wish to join his flower-like feet, he who made the Goddess Lakshmi worship him, he who poured abundant rain on the world. His abode is Thiruvalam. He who appeared to his devotees to grant them joy, he who searches with his consort, he who made them search, his abode is Thiruvalam.

He who kicked Yama, who rose up and was afraid, he who destroyed Daksha’s sacrifice, his abode is Thiruvalam. The one who lifted the despised mountain. He who subdued the proud rakshasa with his foot, he whom the realized ones seek, he who made them seek, his radiant mountain abode is Thiruvalam. He is great, unknowable even by the wise, he became the essence of the sacred Vedas. He is beyond Brahma and Vishnu. His visible abode is Thiruvalam.

He who conquered the wandering, wretched Sakya and the Kunthriya, whose abode is described as such. He who conquered the wandering, wretched Sakya, making the five elements shine everywhere, his abode is Thiruvalam. Those who have learned, who have seen Thiruvalam, and who are able to sing the flawless pure Tamil verses of Gnanasambandha will attain his feet. He who burned the three cities, who revealed various Vedas, who is the mother of the world, who caused abundant rain for the world to thrive, who appeared to his devotees to grant them joy, who is great—such qualities describe the Lord whose abode is Thiruvalam. Thiruvallam is the concluding phrase of this pathigam.

Let us go on contemplating. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, part 781, authored by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, from the chapter “Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam.” Having bowed and worshipped at Thiruvallam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships the other nearby holy places. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman composes the next verse: “He worshipped the feet of the inaccessible Lord in the other holy places there, and moving further north of the Paliaaru river, he worshipped the holy places where the Lord resides. He worshipped at Ilambayangottoor and sang a pathigam to the Lord who rides the red-eyed bull.” This verse indicates that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worshipped the Lord’s feet in all the other holy places there, and then proceeded north of the Paliaaru river, worshipping the places where the Lord is enshrined. It is reasonable to consider these places to be Thirukkarapuram, Virinchipuram, Mahadevamaalai, Thikkaali, Vallimalai, and other such sacred sites. All these sites are located on the north side of the Paliaaru river.

However, unlike the Cauvery North Bank sites which are very close to the Cauvery, these sites are on the north side of the Paliaaru, situated in various inland areas. This Paliaaru river usually does not have a flowing watercourse; water emerges from springs, which the divine Sekkizhar Peruman describes as “pongupunal” (surging water). After worshipping all these places, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds to and worships at the sacred site called Thiru Ilambaiyangottoor. Thiru Ilambaiyangottoor is the thirteenth revered site among the celebrated temples in Thondai Nadu. This is the site where Rambai and others worshipped and attained blessings. The name “Arambayam Kottoor” was derived from Rambai’s worship, and it is now known as Ilambaiyangottoor.

This is a site worshipped by Chandra and the celestial maidens. One can reach this site from Chennai and Kanchipuram. The names of the Lord are Arambeswarar, Deivanayakeswarar, and Chandrasekarar. The names of the Goddess are Kanakakujambigai and Kodaithazhai Mulai Ammai. Malligai Theertham and Chandra Theertham are the sacred waters. During the destruction of the three cities (Thiripura Samharam), Lord Shiva led the army of gods, and thus, he is known as Deivanayakeswarar at this site.

The celestial women, on the advice of Brihaspati, worshipped Deivanayakeswarar here to preserve their beauty and received blessings. Dakshan, who had received a curse, bathed in the Mallika Pushkarani Theertham here and worshipped the Lord. When Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was passing this way, the Lord appeared as a young boy and then as an old man, blocking his path and revealing this temple.

The devotees who accompanied him did not understand this at first.

Later, the Lord came in the form of a white cow and nudged Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s palanquin to a halt. It is said that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, then marveling and understanding, identified the temple and worshipped there. This information is granted by the divine Sai. It is said that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman included this reference in the third verse of this pathigam. The third verse states, “Balanām virutthanām Pasupathi thānam” (He is a child, he is an old man, he is Pasupathi).

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has sung about these truths, how the Lord came as a young boy and an old man to guide him. The Sthala Purana also narrates this event. In popular usage, the place is called Elumiyan Kottoor. The presiding deity is a touch-me-not Sivalinga. The Sivalinga is pale red. The large Aavudaiyar (base of the lingam) is shaped like a lotus.

It is in the pathigam for this site that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman uses the phrase “My words are His words” and sings with grace. The Dakshinamurthi, a niche deity, is in a yogic posture, with his hand in the Chinmudra gesture held at his heart, which is a marvelous sight. Sun worship takes place in the months of Panguni and Aavani. Inscriptions mention Ilambaiyangottoor as part of the Kaantroor region within the Manavil Kottam, during the reign of Pandya Konerimen Konda Tribhuvana Chakravarthi Jataavarman Sundarapandiyan. During the reign of Tribhuvana Chakravarthi Tribhuvana Veera Devan, it is mentioned as Chathurvedi Mangalam Ilambaiyangottoor in the country of Kantroor. Sivakavimani Desikanar has written that this village is now populated by Christians.

If that was the situation about eighty years ago, one can imagine what it must be like now.

Therefore, because there are many Christians in this village, the archakas and others come from the nearby village of Koovam to perform worship. The pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for this site is a very rare pathigam. The tune (pann) set for this pathigam is also very rare. In this extremely rare pathigam, the young saint extols this site, revealing very rare truths and subtle insights of Saiva Siddhanta. Sivakavimani Ayya notes that many Nattukottai Chettiars, through collective effort, renovated this temple and conducted a Kumbabhishekam approximately seventy-five years ago. Only one daily puja is performed.

If we wish to worship the Lord, as mentioned above, it is advisable to come with the priest from the nearby village of Koovam and return with him. Thakkolam is another celebrated temple. One can reach this temple a short distance to the west of that site. The pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for this site consists of eight lines. It is structured as an “En Seer Viruttam,” a type of verse form. We can observe that each line contains eight syllables.

The pann (tune) for this pathigam is Kurinji. This pathigam is set in the Akapporul thurai (love poetry genre). The natural description of Thiru Ilambaiyangottoor is beautifully presented in this pathigam. In this pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for this site, we can see references to sacred places such as Siparpathamalai (Srisailam), Thiru Poonduruthi, Thirumaal Peru, Thirumaraikkadu, Thirunaithaanam, Thirunindriyur, Thirukazhippalai, Kachchi Ekambam, Thiruottriyur, and Thiru Annamalai. This pathigam is highly significant, showcasing many excellent truths of Saivism. It illustrates the omnipresent nature of the Lord.

The nature of the Lord accepting the words of the young saint as His own words, is emphatically shown in this verse. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, in this pathigam, states that the words of Pillaiyar are indeed the words of the Lord. Concepts such as the Lord causing loving devotees to lose their individual consciousness (Pasubotham) and become one with Him are embedded in these verses. This pathigam, with its great significance, set in the Kurinji pann, is found in the First Thirumurai. yinār paruppatham thurutthi māpēru māsilāsi maṟaikāṭunai thānam nīḷinān enathurai thanathuraiyāka nēraṇinthēru vanthēriya malan thalaiyinār maṭappiṇai thuṇaiyōṭum thūyila kāṇalam pēṭai pulvi kaṇamayilum iḻaiyinār payampōḻil iḷampayaṅkōṭṭu irukayāyppēṇiyeḻil koḷvathiyal vērumalar koṉṟaiyān niyumē (He, the Lord, whose words are mine, rides the beautiful bull, adorned with garlands of konrai flowers, where the young deer, with their mates, wander in the groves of Ilambaiyangottoor, a place of beautiful pools, where birds chirp and peacocks dance.) thēvarkaḷ thalai makan thirukkaḻippālai nirmalan enathurai thanathuraiyāka nīraṉiṉ thērukaththēriya nimalan karumalar kamalacuṇai nī malar kūvaḷai kathiḷ mūḷaiyuḷaiyavar mathimukaththuḷavum irumala thaṉ poykaiyil payampaṅkōṭṭum irukayāpēṇiyaṉ eḻil koḷvathiyal vēḷaṉam viruthaṉām pasupathi thāṉām paṇṭu veṅkōtṟu ūthai thaṭiyavarkku (The pure Lord of Thirukazhippalai, son of the gods, whose words are mine, the blemishless one who rides the chariot, where black lotuses bloom in ponds, and water lilies sprout, and those whose minds are troubled seek refuge. He, the child, the old man, the Pasupathi, who once struck down the fierce cold wind.) pālanām vērutthaṉām pasupathi thāṉām paṇṭu veṅkōtṟuthai thaṭiyavar karuḷum kāṭaṉām enathurai thanathuraiyāka kaṉal eṟiyaṅkaiyil ēnthiya kaṭavuḷ nīḷamalar cōṉai paṇṭu paṉ ceyya nīrmalar kūvaḷaikaḷ thāthu viṇṭōṅkum ēlam nāṟumpōḻil ēlam nāṟumpōḻil iḷampayaṅkōṭṭūr irukkaiyāyppēṇiya eḻil koḷvathiyal vēḷam (He is a child, an old man, He is Pasupathi Himself. He, the forest dweller, who once blessed those struck by the fierce, cold wind, whose words are my words, the God who held fire in His hand.

In the groves of Ilampaiyangottoor, where long blue flowers bloom, and water lilies release their pollen, and cardamom fragrances fill the air, He resides in beauty.) koḷḷār ucchiyār katchi ēkam kuḷam koḷvār ucchiyār katchi ēkampan oṭṟiyōr ūṟaiyum aṇṇāmalai aṉṉal viḷampōvān eṉa thūrai thaṉathuraiyāka veḷḷa nīṭai thāṅkiya vimalan kuḷam ūṟa kaḷai thūḷa malaikaḷum cīḷampa koḻum poṭi eḻuntheṅkum pū viḷam koḷḷa iḷampīrai thavaḷ pōḻil iḷampayaṅkōṭṭū iru kaiyāyppēṇiyaḻil uḷvathiyal vēṉu mayamuthamāy theyvamum thāṉāyththīyōṭu nīrōṭu (They who do not comprehend the peak of Kachchi Ekambam, the one who possesses Kachchi Ekambam, Otriyur and Annamalai, the Lord who is like a banner, whose words are mine, the blemishless one who holds the Ganga on his head. Where pools overflow, weeds are cleared, mountains crumble, and thick dust rises everywhere, and flowers bloom. In the groves of Ilampaiyangottoor, where young creepers spread, He resides, beautiful and divine, being Himself fire and water.) vāyuvām pēm enathurai variya kacai thuḻi tharumaithaṉ kāṇamāṉ vēṟu uṟa karuviralūpam kaṭuvaṉōṭukaḷum kal kaṭum cāral ēṉamāṉ oḻitharum iḷam mayakōṭṭūr iru kaiyāyppēṇi eṉḷvaṭkuḷ purikiṉṟa pakaiyallāl paḻi pirinthum villāṉ maṟṟō thaṉamillāṉ enathurai thanathuraiyāka thāṭaiyila mathi thāṅkiya thalaivaṉ guṇamella maruvikaḷ iru vicēr muttham poṉṉōṭu (The wind, the fierce, my words, the striped whip, the strong one. Where black-fingered monkeys and civets roam in the steep, rocky slopes, and boars reside in Ilambaiyangottoor. He, who is worshipped and protected, who has no enmity, who is free from blame, and has no other equal. My words are His words, the Lord who holds the crescent moon in his matted locks.

Where rivers flow with pearls, gold,) maṇi koḻunthīṇṭi vantheṅkum iṉamella aṭai vara iḷam payaṅkōṭṭu iru kaiyāyppēṇi eṉ eḻil koḷvathil vēruḷḷāṉ tīyuḷḷāṉ anthatthuḷḷāṉ iṉai pavar maṉaththuḷḷāṉ niththamāyiththum ūruḷāṉ enathurai thanathuraiyāka oṭṟai veḷḷōkam thēṟiya oruvaṉ pāruḷar pāṭalōṭāṭalāṭa paṉṉūraṇṭai vaḷḷiṉam pāṭum ēruḷam paimbōḻil iḷam payam pōṭṭu iru kaiyāyppēṇi eṉ eḻil koḷvathē vēruḷamā kaṭal varu thirai ilaṅkai vēnthaṉai thaṭakkaikaḷ (and jewels gather everywhere, and where groups of people gather. He resides beautifully in Ilambaiyangottoor, revered and protected. He is within the fire, within the end, within the minds of those who desire Him. He is eternal, and within the village. My words are His words, the one who is pure and unique. Where the people of the earth sing and dance, and the Vallinam sings at Pannoorandai.

In the verdant groves of Ilambaiyangottoor, He resides, beautiful and protected. The waves of the sea come, and the king of Lanka, with his mighty hands,) nūlakil āruḷam enathurai thanathuraiyāka āka muṟavaṉ thuḻi tharum maṉṉal vārūḷam nalla nakākkalum cāra vāraṇam moḻi tharum mallalam kāṇal ēruḷam poḻilaṉi iḷam payaṅkōṭṭu iru kaiyāyppē nīṇiyaṉ ēḻil koḷvathiyal vēḷar maṭai thāṅki naṉṉāṉ mukaṉ uṭaiyum kīḻaṭi mēl mūṭi thērnthilaikkillā uḷamaṭaiṉathurai thanathuraiyāka uḷḷaṭal aṅkaiyil ēnthiya oruvaṉ pala maḻaiyaṉa kaḻivala thuḷi cūṟa mācuṉam moḻi tharumaṇiyaṇi mālai (He who has a heart of love. My words are His words. The king who comes, churning. The good Naga, and the nearby elephants that speak. The groves of Ilambaiyangottoor, revered and protected.

He, the Lord, whose beautiful form is adorned with garlands of precious gems, where many rains fall, and strong winds blow, and snakes speak their wisdom. My words are His words, the one who holds destruction in his hand, who is unshakeable.) iḷa maḻai thavaḻ poḻil iḷampayaṅkōṭṭu iru kaiyāyppēṇi eṉḻil koḷvathiyal vēṟiñcaṉa kūraikaḷ uṭampiṉi uḻitharu camaṇarum cākkiya pēykaḷ perumcelvaṉ eṉa thūrai thaṉathu palikkal uṭal periyavar perumān karuñcuṉai mullai nan poṉṉaṭai vēḷimukavaṇṭoṭu thēṉi nam muṟalum irunūṉai malkiya iḷampayaṅkōṭṭu iru kaiyāyppēṇi eṉḻil koḷvathiyal vēnthaṉai kaṉai kaṭal kanthaṉai mallikaṉai kaṭaloḷ (In the groves of Ilambaiyangottoor, where gentle rain glides, He resides, beautiful and protected, even as Jain and Buddhist demons roam, wearing their ragged clothes. The great wealthy one, whose words are mine, the great Lord whose body is like a sacrificial stone. In the dark pools, where jasmine and good golden flowers are found, and bees and honeybees hum, and many rare plants grow in Ilambaiyangottoor, He resides, beautiful and protected, the king, the loud sea, Kandan, Mallikanai, the ocean’s light.)

Thus, this pathigam is structured. Having bowed and worshipped at Thiru Ilambaiyangottoor, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds to the sacred site called Thiru Virkolam, also known as Koovam, and worships the Lord there.

Let us resume our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, part 782, authored by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, from the chapter “Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam.” Having worshipped at Thiru Ilambaiyangottoor, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeded to the site called Thiru Virkolam. This place is currently known as Koovam. Koogam became Koovam over time.

Therefore, Koovam is the name of this site, and Virkolam is the name of the temple. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman extols this, stating: “Surrounded by many devotees, the Lord of Thirupukali, having worshipped Thiru Virkolam and sung a garland of verses about burning the cities, then reached Thakkolam and worshipped the Lord of Thiru Ooral.” This means that many devotees surrounded him as he worshipped at the site of Thiru Virkolam, where he sang He grants a grace-filled vision in the form of fire. To ensure that the merchant would suffer no harm in court, Pazhaiyanoor Neeli, through deceit, took the merchant’s life. In order to atone for their broken promise in that situation, they had pledged to give their own lives if any harm befell the merchant.

He composed this pathigam to fulfill that promise. We have discussed this story in detail in the Puranam of Thiru-kurippu Thonda Nayanar. In this story, it is emphasized that worldly justice must not be perverted. Having given their lives to uphold worldly justice, they attained liberation at the Lord’s sacred feet. For this reason, they are glorified in Pillaiyar’s divine words. Deivachchekiyalar states that this pathigam was composed in the style of ‘panchuram’, meaning ‘old style’.

Panchuram is one of the musical modes played on the Kurinji lute. The Kurinji lute is associated with the Kurinji thinai (a genre of Tamil poetry). In this old panchuram style, Thirugnanasambandhar composed this pathigam.

However, the currently prevalent melody is classified as Thakaragam. Previously, the old panchuram mentioned was played on the Kurinji lute, as described by Deivachchekiyalar, and the Kurinji lute is associated with the Kurinji thinai. The primary theme of the Kurinji thinai is midnight, and the secondary theme is union.

Therefore, the Lord appeared to Thirugnanasambandhar in a dream at midnight, which is the primary theme of the Kurinji thinai. The divine grace signifies union.

Thus, the old panchuram melody, which combines the primary and secondary themes of the Kurinji thinai, is explained as appropriate for this pathigam. In practice, this pathigam is sung in the Thakaragam melody. Sivakavi, in his commentary, raises questions about singing it in Thakaragam, which is associated with the desert land and the separation theme. He writes that singing it in Thakaragam is a subject for research. This song, expanded by the grace of the King, is by Gnanasambandan of Pazhaiyanoor. As the author has elaborately explained the meaning of the divine pathigam, we have already seen it. He sang the divine pathigam with great melody and devotion. When the darkness of night receded and morning arrived, the host of devotees gathered.

At that time, he recounted the divine grace bestowed by the Lord of Thiruvalavanatu in the evening, and sang the verses with a blooming heart, praising the Lord.

Then, he worshipped the Tiruppadi and set off for Tiruppasur. This is the 1011th verse composed by the great Deivachchekiyalar. After singing that divine pathigam, Thirugnanasambandhar After the long night ended and darkness gave way to daylight, the time of dawn arrived. The host of devotees gathered.

At that time, he recounted to the devotees all the grace that the Lord of Thiruvalangadu had bestowed upon him during the night, and sang the pathigam again, making the devotees’ hearts bloom. It is customary that even after seeing the Lord in a dream and singing praises, one should remain in divine contemplation rather than sleep. Pillaiyar, reflecting on the divine grace that the Lord had bestowed upon him by appearing in his dream, remained awake throughout the long night due to his eagerness. When darkness receded and dawn arrived, he recounted all that his Father had bestowed upon him to the devotees, and again, to the delight of the devotees and with a blooming heart, Thirugnanasambandhar sang that divine pathigam. After singing the pathigam, without entering Thiruvalankadu, but remaining outside, Thirugnanasambandhar worshipped the Tiruppadi, received the Lord’s permission, and proceeded to the nearby holy town of Tiruppasur.

We will continue to reflect on our Pillaiyar. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Great Puranam, Part 784, compiled by the great Deivachchekiyalar, Sarukkam of Vambara Varivandu, Puranam of Thiru Gnana Sambandha Nayanar. Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman proceeds from Thiruvalangadu to the holy town of Tiruppasur. Upon arriving at Tiruppasur, and being welcomed by the people of the prosperous town, he entered the temple of the ancient one, who holds Uma, the daughter of the mountain king, on his left side, and who has the sacred moolasthanam of bamboo. He circumambulated the temple, worshipped, and composed a pathigam beginning with ‘May the entire body...’. These are the words of the great Deivachchekiyalar, the 1012th verse.

He arrived at the holy town of Tiruppasur, where the people and devotees welcomed him. He entered the town and reached the temple.

There, he joyfully entered the temple of the Lord, the ancient one who holds Uma, the daughter of the mountain king, on his left, and who has his sacred moolasthanam of bamboo in Tiruppasur. He circumambulated the temple with devotion, entered, worshipped the Lord, prostrated himself many times, and then, with goosebumps all over his body, he composed a pathigam with musical accompaniment, starting with ‘May the entire body...’. This pathigam was sung by Thirugnanasambandhar. Tiruppasur is a place very close to Thiruvalangadu. Earlier, in the Puranam of Thiru Naavukkarasu Peruman, we discussed the history of Tiruppasur. In this place, the Lord emerged from beneath a bamboo.

Hence the name Tiruppasur. Thirugnanasambandhar, who praised the Lord there, composed a pathigam starting with ‘May the entire body...’. This pathigam is the sixty-first in the Second Thirumurai, composed in the Kanthara Pen melody. The pathigam is as follows: Praise to the Lord of Tiruppasur! Praise to the Goddess! O my Lord of Pasur, surrounded by the jasmine groves!

Your name is sung in praise. O Pasur, where the divine grace of the Lord, who possesses the serpent, is sung! You are the city where the Lord dwells. O Pasur, adorned with the crescent moon, you are the city where the Lord bestows grace upon those who worship him. O my Lord of Pasur, surrounded by the jasmine groves! Your name is sung in praise.

You are the city where the Lord dwells. O Pasur, adorned with the crescent moon, you are the city where the Lord bestows grace upon those who worship him. O Pasur, adorned with the crescent moon, you are the city where the Lord bestows grace upon those who worship him. O Pasur, where the Lord dwells!

You bestow grace upon those who worship him. O Pasur, the city of the Lord, where the divine grace is bestowed. O Pasur, where the Lord of Lanka, with his sharp sword, bestowed great glory upon those who spoke and acted with divine wisdom. O Pasur, surrounded by fertile fields and lakes. O Pasur, the city of the Lord, where the divine grace is bestowed. O Pasur, where the Lord of Lanka, with his sharp sword, bestowed great glory upon those who spoke and acted with divine wisdom. O Pasur, surrounded by fertile fields and lakes. The theme of this pathigam is the praise of the Lord, whose name is ‘Sinthaiyidaiyar’, meaning ‘He who resides in the heart’, with divine grace. The words ‘Idaiyar’, ‘Misaiyar’, ‘Sollar’ and others that appear in each stanza illustrate the Lord’s boundless grace, enabling devotees to chant these names and worship him. Thirugnanasambandhar praises the Lord in this manner in Tiruppasur.

Next, the great Deivachchekiyalar begins to narrate the history of Thirugnanasambandhar’s divine vision of Srikalahasti. After singing and praising with melodious pathigams, he worshipped and then stayed in that town. He then visited other places such as Thiruvenpaakkam and others, filled with overflowing love. He then proceeded to the mountain of Kalahasti, meditating on Veda Kannappan, the first devotee to be bathed with divine water, and went with great longing to worship. This is the 1013th verse. Having sung and praised the divine pathigam in Tiruppasur, he received the Lord’s permission and proceeded to other holy towns where the Lord resides, such as Thiruvenpaakkam.

Deivachchekiyalar mentions ‘Thiruvenpaakkam and other towns’, which are considered to be Thiruvenpaakkam, Thirkalil, and other holy places. He then proceeds to Thirkalil. Pillaiyar then visited Thirkalil and returned. He is also mentioned as having visited Thirkalil. It is said that ‘Thiruvenpaakkam and other towns’ refers to Thiruvenpaakkam. Thiruvenpaakkam is currently known as Thiruvilampathur.

The name of that town in inscriptions is Ulompogipuram.

Here, the Lord granted Sundaramurthi Swamigal a staff to lean on, saying, ‘I am here, go forth.’ Thus, the name of this holy town came to be Ulompogipuram, meaning ‘go forth’. Thiruvenpaakkam holy town was originally located in the area where the Poondi reservoir now exists. It is submerged in the water. The deities from here were moved to another location, and the holy town of Thiruvenpaakkam was established there. The original temple lies within the water. Thirugnanasambandhar visited this place and composed pathigams, but unfortunately, those pathigams are not available to us due to our shortcomings.

However, a pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandhar for the holy town of Thirkalil is available. This holy town of Thirkalil can be reached by going to Kannigaiper, known as Kannipputhur, on the Chennai-Periyapalayam road, and then traveling a short distance.

The Lord here is Sivanandheeswarar, and the Goddess is Anandhavalli. This place is also known as Thirkalil, Thirkallam, and Thirkandalam. It is a place worshipped by Agastya, where Lord Shiva appeared to Agastya as Somas Kandha. The sage Bhrigu worshipped Lord Shiva here with stones and flowers.

Lord Shiva appeared to him as Dakshinamurthy, with Shakti seated on his lap. The Vimana of the temple is of the Thungaanaimada type. The moolavar is a Lingam with a square avudaiyar. Lord Murugan is depicted with a rosary in his right hand and a water pot in his left. Thirugnanasambandhar, who visited this place, composed a pathigam in the Nootru Pen melody in the First Thirumurai. The pathigam is as follows.

O Lord of Kallil, residing on the roof of the mansion! You are the Lord who wears the crescent moon. You are the Lord who destroyed the three worlds. You are worshipped by the great ones. O Lord of Kallil, who is adorned with the crescent moon and the Ganga! Having sung a pathigam for the holy town of Thirkalil, Thirugnanasambandhar travels north towards Thirukkalahasti. He visits other towns and, filled with overflowing love, meditates on Veda Kannappan, the first devotee to be bathed with divine water. He then proceeds with great longing to worship the mountain of Kalahasti. This is how the great Deivachchekiyalar begins to narrate the divine vision of Thirugnanasambandhar at Thirukkalahasti.

In this verse, ‘the first devotee to be bathed with divine water’ is a special epithet that Deivachchekiyalar bestows upon Kannappa Nayanar. We can also see the full name of the Nayanar here. We can see here the extent of love that Pillaiyar had in his heart to have a vision of Kannappa Nayanar.

Thus, Deivachchekiyalar states that Thirugnanasambandhar’s pathigam at Thirukkalahasti refers to Kannappa Nayanar’s worship using his mouth as a vessel. Deivachchekiyalar takes this very idea and presents it here as ‘the first devotee to be bathed with divine water’. Kannappa Nayanar filled his mouth with the water of the Ponmugali river, making his mouth a sacred vessel, and performed the abhishakam to the Lord of Thirukkalahasti. We have discussed in detail in his Puranam how Kannappa Nayanar performed this act. Taking that love as a basis, Thirugnanasambandhar sang at Thirukkalahasti, and Deivachchekiyalar highlights this here. Kannappa Nayanar performed the abhishakam for the Lord, and the water from the Ponmugali river, along with the holy water of the Ganges, merged to form the sacred abhishakam.

Driven by such overflowing love, Thirugnanasambandhar went with great longing and joy to have a vision of Kannappa Nayanar. To worship Kannappa Nayanar Deivachchekiyalar states: ‘Meditating and to worship the mountain of Kalahasti’. The desire that arose in Thirugnanasambandhar’s heart was not primarily to worship the Lord residing in Thirukkalahasti, but rather to worship Kannappa Nayanar.

Thus, to worship Kannappa Nayanar, he needed to worship the Lord of Thirukkalahasti.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandhar went to see the mountain of Kalahasti. The Lord’s worship was the means, and the ultimate achievement was the worship of Kannappa Nayanar. This is how Pillaiyar’s mind worked, as subtly revealed by Deivachchekiyalar. As those who see the fruit of their devotion, they fell at the feet of the great devotee. Deivachchekiyalar is about to elaborate on this. Sambandhar travels to worship the mountain of Kalahasti, to worship Kannappa Nayanar.

Even as he says this, Deivachchekiyalar himself worships Kannappa Nayanar.

Thus, he beautifully phrases the sentence: ‘Meditating and to worship the mountain of Kalahasti’. We see this in the words of the great ones. Pillaiyar went with great joy, as Deivachchekiyalar sings. This is because the path from Tiruppasur to Kalahasti is a very arduous one. It is a very difficult path with mountains, forests, and small rivers. Deivachchekiyalar sings that Pillaiyar went with immense joy, realizing that one can only traverse such a path with great love.

Deivachchekiyalar praises Kannappa Nayanar so extensively here. Before this, Thiru Naavukkarasu Swamigal praised Kannappa Nayanar in his Puranam. Deivachchekiyalar had previously sung of Thiru Naavukkarasu Peruman’s journey to Thirukkalahasti. He sang: ‘Reaching the feet of Kannappar, the steadfast devotee standing before the jewel of the mountain peak, and prostrating, tears flowed down like a river, and they bowed with their heads resting on their hands’. This is the 1611th verse, where Thiru Naavukkarasu Peruman worshipped the holy feet of Thiru Kannappa Nayanar. After a long interval, the current verse, the 2911th, is encountered.

Therefore, after such a long gap, the opportunity to worship and praise the holy feet of Kannappa Nayanar has arisen for Deivachchekiyalar. Due to this immense love, he too worships, and he reveals Pillaiyar’s heartfelt devotion, compelling us to worship as well.

We shall continue with our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Great Puranam, Part 785, compiled by the great Deivachchekiyalar, Sarukkam of Vambara Varivandu, Puranam of Thiru Gnana Sambandha Nayanar. Deivachchekiyalar continues to sing of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s journey towards the mountain of Thirukkalahasti. With great love, surrounded by devotees, leaving behind the land of gentle rivers, he reached the dense forest and proceeded to the temple of the Lord, the supreme being with three eyes, holding a skull in his hand, and with a radiant body, located in the mist-covered Karaikkal. He worshipped and praised, stayed in the town, and rejoiced with the Bhutaganas. This is the 1014th verse.

Surrounded by a great multitude of devotees, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman Embarks on a journey. Crossing the regions north of the Paalaru river. This region north of the Paalaru river is where the Paalaru flows and enriches the land. Rivers in this region rarely flood, and during other times, springs abound beneath their beds.

Thus, these are all part of the Thondai Nadu region. He crosses those regions with gentle rivers that flow smoothly without strong currents, including the Paalaru. Thondai Nadu is a region with five types of land: Kurinji, Mullai, Marutham, Neithal, and Palai. Their characteristics have been discussed in detail in the Puranam of Thiru-kurippu Thonda Nayanar. These five types of land form distinct regions within Thondai Nadu, shining like separate kingdoms. The ‘land of gentle rivers’ that Deivachchekiyalar refers to now can be considered the region with a high proportion of Marutham land within Thondai Nadu.

Crossing those regions, he arrives at the area considered to be the border of the present-day Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh. This area also contains forests. It is the region referred to as Thirukkalahasti, known as Vadavengadam. These regions are characterized by a blend of Mullai and Kurinji. Meaning, a region where mountains and forests are intertwined. One can observe this well when traveling through this region.

Unlike the Western Ghats, the mountains are not continuous and dense.

Likewise, the forest areas are not like dense jungles. Mountains, hills, and forests are all intertwined there. It is a rugged terrain.

Thus, crossing the Marutham land, he enters the region where Mullai and Kurinji are mingled. Thirugnanasambandhar arrives there. The holy town of Thirukkarikkara is located there. It is the temple of the supreme Lord, who holds the divine mace and skull in his hands and has a radiant divine body with three divine eyes. It is known as Thirukkarikkara.

There, Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman entered the temple, worshipped and praised the Lord, and remained there, joyful in the company of devotees adorned with sacred ash. This sacred place, Thiru Karikkarai, is currently near Nagalapuram in the Chittoor district of Andhra Pradesh.

The Lord is Valeeswarar, the Mother is Maragathambal, and the Theertham is Nandi Theertham. This is the place where Hanuman worshipped Lord Shiva. It is situated on the banks of the Kari river, hence it is called Karikkarai. Currently, it is known as Ramagiri. Our Periya Puranam states that Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman and Thiru Navukkarasu Peruman visited and worshipped at this shrine. We saw this in the puranam of Thiru Navukkarasu Nayanar.

When Thiru Navukkarasu Peruman set forth towards Thirukalathi, he passed through Thiru Karikkarai. He worshipped and proceeded.

Therefore, in one of his pathigams, he lauded this place as a Vaipu Thalam. The name of this shrine appears in the pathigam “Kadangalour Thiru Karikkarai.” Sundaramoorthi Swamigal mentions this shrine in the third verse of the thirty-first pathigam of the Seventh Thirumurai.

However, when Hanuman was bringing a Shiva lingam from the North for Rama to consecrate it at Sethu, Bhairavar wished to keep it for himself and devised a plan. Accordingly, Hanuman felt thirsty. Thinking that the Shiva lingam should not be placed on the ground, he handed it to Bhairavar, who appeared as a small boy, and went to fetch water. Before Hanuman could drink water from the pond, the boy, claiming it was too heavy, placed the Shiva lingam on the ground. Angered, Hanuman struck the Shiva lingam with his sword and pulled hard, but it was in vain. The Shiva lingam only tilted slightly and could not be dislodged.

Hence, the Lord was consecrated right there. Since it was pulled by the tail, the Lord was named Valeeswarar. The Sthala Puranam states that the mountain formed when Hanuman angrily threw a mountain, which fell into the water body formerly known as Kalingamadu, destroying it and forming a mountain. Since the Shiva lingam brought for Rama’s worship was consecrated here, due to the ‘Rama’ and the disappearance of the water body to form a mountain, ‘Giri,’ these two words combined to form ‘Ramagiri,’ which became the reason for calling this place Ramagiri. This ancient and grand Shiva temple is revered as a Kala Bhairava temple. Water continuously flows from the mouth of the Nandi here, filling the Theertha pond and flowing as the Kari River.

Here, Kala Bhairavar is renowned for granting offspring. The Moolavar, Valeeswarar, is a Swayambhumoorthi, slightly tilted. There are marks on the divine form from being pulled by the sword. The temple’s structure dates back to the Pallava period, and later Cholas and Vijayanagara kings contributed to its renovations. When Virupaksha Raya of the Sangama dynasty attempted to build a gopuram, the work ceased due to a sudden invasion by Purushothama Gajapathi. Inscriptions inform us that Virarajendra Chozhan made donations to this temple on his way back after defeating the Chalukyas in battle.

This place is known through inscriptions as Thiru Karikkarai Pillaiyar of Naduvinmalai, Nindriyur Nadu, Kunravarthana Kottu, Jayamkonda Chola Mandalam. Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman, who visited here, sang about the Lord of this shrine with great joy, accompanied by devotees adorned with sacred ash. When mentioning the Lord of this shrine, Deivasekkizhar Peruman describes Him as the primal leader with a trident and skull in hand, a blazing form, and three eyes.

The Lord holding a trident in His hand signifies His wielding the trident to destroy the three impurities: anava, karma, and maya.

The Lord holds a skull in His sacred hand; it is a Bali Pathiram (alms bowl). Why does He hold it? It is to receive the soul’s consciousness of devotees. The meaning of the Bali Pathiram, the skull held by the Lord, is that He receives the devotees’ soul-consciousness as an offering and blesses them to attain His feet. Deivasekkizhar Peruman mentions in a forthcoming verse, “Paambusadai Thirumunivar Kapala Kaiyar Palavedas.” Therefore, the various sub-sects of Saivism, such as Pasupatham, Kapalikkam, Bhairavam, Maviratham, and Vamam, comprise various types of Saivites who hold tridents in their hands, carry skulls, and adopt various guises. The reference here is that such Saivites worship in this region of the country.

Deivasekkizhar Peruman sings about Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman, stating that he rejoiced with the Bhoothiyar (devotees adorned with sacred ash) in such a Karikkarai temple. Bhoothiyar means a gathering of devotees adorned with sacred ash, specifically those who have applied Vibhuthi.

Furthermore, ‘Bhoothi’ can also be interpreted as Anubhuthi, meaning those who experience Shiva’s bliss as their self-experience and are always immersed in it. Deivasekkizhar Peruman continues to sing, explaining that these devotees were those who accompanied Pillaiyar and those who were present at the site. The Lord, after worshipping at Thiru Karikkarai and receiving a divine farewell, continued his sacred journey. On both sides, there were countless huge mountains, from which many waterfalls flowed abundantly, carrying gems and gold, scattering droplets all around. The waterfalls, laden with gems and gold, spread their droplets all around. It was as if these mountains, which in ancient times had wings and could fly, were now attempting to fly again, flapping their wings, to avenge their past.

In ancient times, Indra had removed their wings with his Vajra, causing them to fall and remain grounded, losing their ability to fly.

Now, these great mountains, with their abundant waterfalls, appear as if the waterfalls are their wings.

Therefore, it seems as if these fallen mountains are once again trying to fly, seeking revenge on Indra. Deivasekkizhar Peruman vividly describes these scenes with divine poetic flair. As the crowds of ascetics gathered and scattered. In ancient times, Indra had, with his Vajra, clipped the wings of these mountains, causing them to fall. Those mountains, having lost their wings, lay fallen and remained stable.

Now, these great mountains, with their abundant waterfalls, appear as if the waterfalls are their wings.

Therefore, it seems as if these fallen mountains are once again trying to fly with these wings, seeking revenge on Indra. Deivasekkizhar Peruman describes these regions with divine poetic skill. The throng of ascetics pressed forward. As the flawless, unbounded sound of the sacred pearl-banner, like the ocean of sacred ash, rose in many waves, and the sounds proclaiming “Thiru Gnanasambandhan has come” filled the ears of the great crowds, uniting their minds in well-being, Deivasekkizhar Peruman continued to sing. The throngs of devotees accompanying Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman spread out. The sounds of music rose boundlessly.

As the Lord of Seerkazhi arrived, the crowd of devotees adorned with sacred ash swelled and overflowed. The sound of the sacred banners praising Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman, the chant proclaiming “Thiru Gnanasambandhan has come,” filled the ears of the devotees and naturally reached the ears of the five-sensed animals living in those forests, bringing them well-being. The sound proclaiming “Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman has come” was the chanting of Pillaiyar’s sacred mantra, which has the power to eliminate all evil.

Therefore, it reached the ears of the five-sensed animals in those forests. The sound of the sacred mantra reached the ears of the five-sensed animals, such as peacocks, snakes, deer, and tigers, which are usually hostile to each other, and also the ears of predatory animals like tigers that hunt and eat humans. This single sacred sound, the name of Pillaiyar, reached all these living beings, which were otherwise hostile, and removed their inherent animosity, bringing them well-being. We deliberated on this philosophy in detail in the puranam of Aanaya Nayanar.

Similarly, here too, Deivasekkizhar Peruman sings that Pillaiyar’s name-mantra acts in the same way. We shall proceed with our reflection.

The single sound of the mantra, reaching all these other beings who harbored enmity, naturally removed that animosity and brought about their well-being. We extensively pondered this philosophy in the puranam of Aanaya Nayanar.

Similarly, here too, Deivasekkizhar Peruman sings that Pillaiyar’s name-mantra acts in the same way. Our contemplation continues. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 786, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thiru Gnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, as bestowed by Deivasekkizhar Peruman. The verse, numbered 1017, states: The King of Sambai set forth towards Thirukalathi, a place of immeasurable greatness, where even the heavens and hidden cosmic truths praise the presence of Lord Shiva, where large trees and thickets, along with other celestial beings, worship and pray, surpassing countless shrines, towards the Thirukalathi mountain where Kannappar, born into the hunter tribe, revered by the world, left his footprints. The holy birth of Kannappa Deva Nayanar was in the hunter clan. That hunter clan is praised by the whole world. The Thirukalathi mountain is the holy mountain of Kannappa Deva Nayanar, where his feet, adorned with sandals, touched the ground as he hunted in the forests.

That region is the area where Kannappa Deva Nayanar hunted. The region where Kannappa Deva Nayanar hunted is where his sacred feet, wearing sandals, touched the ground. Manickavasagar Peruman also praised those sacred feet, touched by sandals, in Thiruvachagam as ‘Serupputra Seeradi.’ In the third verse of Thiruthol Nookam in Thiruvachagam, he praises Kannappa Deva Nayanar: ‘As if the worship done with material possessions were shining, the sacred feet touched by sandals, the mouth as a sacred vessel, the flesh-food offered with delight by the hunter, as his body shivered in love, how he attained grace, let us dance the Thol Nookam.’ This region has huge trees and mountains that touch the sky. It is a place of immense greatness, where even the Devas come to worship and praise, and it contains countless shrines. There are many places where great sages perform penance. Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman, passing through these regions, approaches very close to Thirukalathi mountain.

Deivasekkizhar Peruman composes the next verse, saying: As soon as the news spread that Pillaiyar, who partook of the nectar of wisdom mixed with the milk from the golden mountain goddess’s breast, was approaching Thirukalathi, the throng of devotees at Thirukalathi gathered and swelled. Sacred sages with matted locks. Saivites of various guises, such as Kapalikas holding skulls, Maviratha Saivites, Pasupatha Saivites, Kalamukha Saivites, and many other types of Saivites, as well as people of the hunter clan, ascetics, and residents of that place, all joyfully come forward to greet Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman. The next verse describes how, as the light of sacred ash glowed in all directions, making it seem as if Shiva’s abode had descended upon earth, the Veda-chanting Brahmins descended from the jewel-studded palanquin and bowed. The great throng of unwavering devotees worshipped and praised, filling the cosmos with shouts of ‘Hara.’ At that moment, the Tamil singer, whose devotion was manifest, asked, “Which of these mountains is Thirukalathi Thirumalai?” As all the devotees gathered there, the place appeared like Shiva’s abode. The region appeared as if Shiva’s abode itself had come to rest there.

At that moment, Pillaiyar descended from his beautiful pearl palanquin and bowed. The great throng of devotees who had come to meet Pillaiyar worshipped and praised him, chanting ‘Hara Hara Hara Hara’ loudly, filling the cosmos.

Then, Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman asked the devotees, “Among these mountains, which is Thirukalathi Thirumalai, the sacred mountain with many continuously appearing peaks, showing great devotion?” Just as Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman had asked where Thiru Alavai Temple was when he arrived in Madurai, He asked the same question here. The great ascetics who had arrived bowed down and, addressing him as the life of the Vedas and the crest jewel of Saivism, pointed to the mountain before them and said, “This appearing mountain is Thirukalathi mountain, where the Lord, worshiped by Kalan (serpent) and Hasti (elephant) who were at enmity with each other, resides with endless glory.” Deivasekkizhar Peruman then composes the next verse, stating that bowing down to the ground with folded hands and a heart full of joy, Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman would sing the Thiruvirakam in praise of the Devas and Danavas.

The devotees, bowing to Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman who had asked which mountain among these was Thirukalathi mountain, addressed him as the life of the Vedas and the greatest among Saivite leaders, and then pointed to the Thirukalathi mountain before them. In ancient times, the serpent Kalan and the elephant, due to their enmity, worshipped the Lord here. The mountain where the Lord resides, having been worshipped by them, is the glorious Thirukalathi mountain.

The devotees point to this Thirukalathi mountain, explaining that the sacred name Srikalahasti came into being because the spider Sri, the serpent Kalan, and the elephant Hasti worshipped there. We discussed this in detail in the puranam of Thirukannappa Deva Nayanar, specifically the history of Thirukalathi.

Therefore, they recount that history and point to it here. There is also another subtle hint here: the state in which the Lord resides specifically refers to the worship performed by Sivagochariar and Kannappa Deva Nayanar. As soon as the devotees pointed it out, Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman fell to the ground and worshipped the sacred mountain. Upon seeing Shiva’s sacred mountain, it is the tradition of great souls to prostrate themselves. He felt immense joy. Filled with such great joy, he sang a Thiruppathigam in the rapid rhythm of Thiruvirakam, beginning with ‘Vaanavargal Thaanavargal’ (celestials and demons).

Thus, while praising Thirukalathi mountain with that Thiruppathigam, Pillaiyar drew closer to Thirukalathi mountain. The Thiruppathigam sung by Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman for Thirukalathi mountain is the sixty-ninth Thiruppathigam of the Third Thirumurai, set to the tune of Sadhari Pann. It is a very beautiful Thiruppathigam. In this Thiruppathigam, Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman has greatly extolled and praised the devotion of Kannappa Deva Nayanar. Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman, in the next verse, sings about the devotion of Thiru Kannappar, praising it beautifully. Deivasekkizhar Peruman mentions this in the subsequent verse.

That verse, praising Kannappa Deva Nayanar, is the fourth verse in this pathigam: “Veyanai Thol Umai Or Bagamadhuvaaga Vidaiyeri Sadai Mel Thuuya Madhi Suudi Sudukattil Nadamaadi Malai Thannai Vinavil Vaai Kalasamaaga Vazhipaadu Cheyyum Vedan Malaraagu Nayan Kaay Kanaiyinal Idanthu Kalathi Malaiye.” In this verse, Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman praises the devotion of Kannappa Deva Nayanar. We can see our Othuva Murthigal, Mahadevanaiya, rendering this pathigam very movingly. We can witness it being sung. The Thiruppathigam is as follows: Praise be to the sacred feet of Thiru Kalathi Swamy, Thiru Kalathi Nathar. Praise be to the sacred feet of Devi Thiru Gnana Poonkothai Ammai. The sacred hymn of Thiru Kadaikkappu, composed by Sambandha Moorthy Nayanar, speaks of the Danavas for a moment, and then.

If you ask about the mountain where Shankara, whose matted locks are adorned with a blooming crescent, desired to reside, it is Kalathi mountain, where light-filled gems from the growing sprouts dispel the darkness of the night, as they scatter, causing the arrows of the elephant to scatter and the wild boar to rise in battle.
