That is the greatest fortune one can receive.

Sages say that the best adornment for that household life, which they deem as auspicious, is the boon of good children. This is the meaning of the verse. Worldly people think that household life is enhanced by wealth and abundance of riches. If there is plenty of money, they believe, household life can be conducted well.

But such a life is not glorious without children. Wealth may bring prosperity in this world, but the glory of married life truly lies in having children. Since Sivanēchar had no children, his married life lacked the auspiciousness of progeny, leading to despondency.

Therefore, to obtain such progeny, the blessing of children ...was sought through intense penance.

Here, penance means worship directed towards Lord Shiva, praying for children. We saw this in the story of Kannappa Dēvanāyanār, where his parents, in their old age, performed rituals seeking children and a successor to lead their hunter lineage, praying to Lord Muruga. We examined this in detail there. We also saw that Sivapādhakirudaiyar and Bhagavathi Ammaiyar performed penance before Thōniyappar, desiring children who would nurture Saivism and vanquish other faiths. Mahavishnu ...too, performed penance and worshipped Lord Shiva in Thiruvarur, and begot Manmatha as his son. In his Krishna avatar, we see in the Mahabharata and Devi Bhagavata that to obtain progeny for Jambavati, Mahavishnu received mantra initiation from Upamanyu Muni, performed severe penance, and a son was born to Krishna and Jambavati.

Similarly, here, Sivanēchar is performing penance towards Lord Shiva. This penance involves worshipping Shiva and Shiva’s devotees. Offering food to Shiva’s devotees and fulfilling their needs, knowing them specifically, is part of Shiva worship. ‘Worshipping the Lord and serving His devotees’ - these two alone bestow great benefit to souls, as stated in the Vedas. This is the inner meaning... ‘Those born on earth receive great benefit ...’ sings our noble Gnanasambandhar in his ThiruMylāppūr ThiruPathigam.

Therefore, both Shiva worship and the worship of Shiva’s devotees grant the three benefits of this life, the next life, and liberation. The story of Poompavai exemplifies this.

Accordingly, Sivanēchar performs worship to the Lord and to Shiva’s devotees. The worship offered to Shiva’s devotees is known as Mageshwara Puja. We have examined this in detail in the stories of Ilaiyankudi Māranāyanār, Kungiliyakkalaiya Nāyanār, Appōthi Adigal Nāyanār, and others. Sivanēchar performs these activities immensely. While he was thus engaged, a daughter was born to Sivanēchar’s wife. Sivanēchar’s wife’s womb was like a lotus ...and the maiden who emerged from it was like the lotus itself. ‘On an auspicious day, born under a propitious star, with excellent qualities, the merchant, rich in vast possessions, loaded his warehouses full, and distributed them to the delight of all, showering them in the marketplace, rejoicing in his heart.’ This is the 1041st ThiruPadal.

When this maiden was born, on that auspicious day, under that favorable star, to the well-being of all, she emerged. The great merchant Sivanēchar, loading immense wealth, distributed it throughout the world, to the joy of all. Without specifically designating ‘this for this person,’ he showered all the wealth like rain. ‘He who wears Ganga on His matted locks, with love for His devotees, performed boundless oblations of every kind; to the matchless Vedic scholars, He fulfilled all their desires, surpassing all other rewards.’ This is the 1042nd ThiruPadal. Sivanēchar, whose matted locks bear Ganga, with abundant love for Shiva’s devotees, performs all sorts of boundless worship. The boon Sivanēchar received through worshipping devotees is the progeny.

To express gratitude for that boon, he first performs worships for Shiva’s devotees. To the unparalleled Vedic scholars, he gives whatever they desire, rejoicing greatly. He initiated auspicious deeds according to the Süda Nallvinai, nurtured by Vedic injunctions ...flourishing with rituals and observances; in the fervor of devotion, they celebrated the wedding ceremony.’ This is the 1043rd ThiruPadal. As this maiden was born, they began to perform the auspicious rituals required after childbirth. Sekkizhar Perumān describes this in Tamil as ‘Sūtha Nalvinai’. In Sanskrit, it is called ‘prasavam’.

From the day the child is born, for ten days, they perform all the events prescribed by the Vedas. They perform all these rituals according to the Kupa Sutras, which are based on Vedic principles. They perform rituals according to astrology, based on the positions of planets during the birth hour ...which map the events of this life’s journey for a soul undergoing the cycle of birth. They perform the rituals accordingly. Recitations, charity, and fire sacrifices are performed according to the customs prescribed for newborns. The Sastras dictate what should be done during those ten days.

The rituals performed during these first ten days are prescribed for the first three varnas. On the sixth day, Vigna Shanti (pacification of obstacles); on the ninth day, Bali (offerings); on the tenth day, Annadhanam (feeding the needy) are mentioned in our Sastras. Having done all this, they celebrate a grand festival on the tenth day. Sivanēchar, then, for the naming ceremony of the maiden ...and as the maiden grew, Sekkizhar Perumān continues to narrate her story. Let us contemplate further. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Perumān Sekkizhar, in his Periya Puranam, Part 797, Vambara Varivanda Sarukkam, ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar Puranam. As soon as the maiden was born, everyone was joyful. The infant girl was named Poompavai. Everyone rejoiced greatly. ‘Beholding her limbs, her beauty, her grace, she appeared like a flower; hence, they named her Poompavai, renowned on earth.’ This is the 1044th ThiruPadal. As mentioned before, everyone rejoiced and was happy.

Not only on that day, but in the days to come, the story of this maiden ...by listening, contemplating, and reading, the world will benefit and be happy.

Therefore, everyone rejoiced greatly. As the maiden, embodying auspiciousness, was born, possessing all the beautiful features according to Samudrika Lakshanam, resembling Lakshmi seated on a lotus, the maiden was named Poompavai. There can be many reasons for naming a child. Among them, the excellent physical attributes of this maiden, perfectly aligned with Samudrika Lakshanam, and her divine appearance like Lakshmi, led to the name Poompavai. ...was bestowed. In the Puranam of Kannappa Dēvanāyanār, upon his birth, the child was so beautiful and radiant that he was named Thinnan.

This also comes to our mind here. Due to the sturdy build of Kannappa Nayanār’s body, he was named Thinnanaar.

Similarly, Poompavai appeared. ‘Shining on this earth.’ This means a reference connected to Poompavai’s story. The name given now, Poompavai, is a name that will endure in history. Even when her body turned to ash and Poompavai was to be reborn, in Pillaiyāru’s divine word ...the name Poompavai is proclaimed. Generally, names given to others exist as long as the body and soul are united. After leaving the body, the name also vanishes. ‘Removing the name, calling it a corpse,’ says Thirumoolar.

But for Poompavai, even after her body left her soul, and her bones and ashes were placed in a pot, the name remained. This means that due to her virtues, the divine name Poompavai was established on earth. ‘On every full moon day, performing auspicious ceremonies, increasing in splendor, with joyous prosperity...’ ...in the city, completing the year, and taking faltering steps with great radiance.’ This is the 1045th ThiruPadal. In this verse, Sekkizhar Perumān sings about Poompavai completing one year and beginning to walk with faltering steps. Poompavai’s parents perform the monthly auspicious rituals for her from the day she was born. There are rules that monthly rituals should be performed on her birth star each month, up until her first birthday. The rituals include tying a Raksha Bandhan in the first month, placing her in a cradle, and Anna Prasanam (first feeding of solid food) in the seventh month ...and other auspicious ceremonies.

These rituals, prescribed by Vedic laws, are performed to foster qualities like wealth, longevity, and vitality in the child. There are rituals performed by parents, and also rituals performed by relatives for the child’s well-being and growth.

However, Sekkizhar Perumān uses the phrase ‘Mankalam Puri’ to indicate that, through Pillaiyāru’s grace, this maiden possesses the highest auspiciousness of Shiva.

After the monthly rituals are performed and one year is completed, Poompavai begins to walk with faltering steps. Generally ...children begin to walk around one year of age, and Poompavai is now taking faltering steps. In Tamil literature, in the ‘Pillai Tamil’ genre, the first seven stages are usually sung within the first year. The first seven stages are common to both boys and girls. The three stages after the seventh are specifically for boys and girls.

Thus, singing about ten stages is a tradition in Tamil literature. The 1046th ThiruPadal follows: ‘Like a sprout of lightning, she walks, a growing tender shoot like a creeper, a luminous flame of jewels, she grows into youth...’ ...she reaches seven years of age.’ This is the ThiruPadal. Like a sprouting lightning, the maiden sways, bends, and moves. Like a lightning sprout, appearing first and then becoming complete, she grows like a lightning creeper. She grows like a tender branch of a golden creeper. She grows like an unfathomable luminous flame emanating from precious gems. ‘Sprout,’ ‘tender branch,’ ‘flame’ - these appear in the verse, indicating youth and growth.

Furthermore, these words (sprout, branch, flame) denote subtle movements. Accordingly, she walks with small movements. ...passing through these stages, the youthful maiden reaches seven years of age, like a swan. In the 1047th ThiruPadal, Sekkizhar Perumān narrates how Poompavai plays games like ‘Kazhal’, ‘Ammanai’, and ‘Pandhu’. ‘Like the first step of beauty, like a ceremonial lamp, she plays with young maidens, with ‘kazhal’, ‘ammanai’, ‘kandhukam’, and other childish games.’ This ThiruPadal states: Like the first stage of beauty, like a ceremonial lamp, Poompavai grows. She plays with maidens of her age, like festivals. ‘Pethai’ is the term used in Tamil literature for a girl of seven years.

Thus, she reaches seven years of age and plays with other ‘pethais’ of the same age. She plays with ‘kazhal’, ‘ammanai’, and ‘pandhu’. In these playful games, it is essential to sing devotional songs to the Lord. Poompavai plays thus. ‘Kazhal’ is a game played with ‘kallichikay’ seeds, which is rarely seen among young girls today. Besides ‘kazhal’, ‘ammanai’, and ‘pandhu’, they also play games like ‘Thōl Nōkkam’, ‘Poovalli’, and ‘Unthiyār’ ...and other games. Our Lord Manikkavāchakar Perumān has described ‘Thiru Thōl Nōkkam’, ‘Thirup Poovalli’, and ‘Thiru Unthiyār’ in his Thiruvasagam.

Thus, she grows beautifully, speaking softly like a parrot. Like a flock of parrots, she plays with groups of maidens. In the next ThiruPadal, the 1048th, Sekkizhar Perumān describes Poompavai playing games like ‘Sitril’, ‘Siruchōru’, and ‘Oosal’. ‘With golden bangles, she joins groups of young girls, building small houses and playing in the courtyard, pretending to cook small rice dishes, playing with lamps and swings...’ ...and growing up with joy.’ This is the ThiruPadal. With girls her age, she plays in the courtyard, building small houses. Poompavai pretends to cook rice in the sand. Along with that, she pretends to cook other dishes.

Pretending to cook rice in the sand is a game played with dancing. ‘Siru Sōru’ means not just rice, but also the accompanying dishes, which she pretends to make in the sand. Poompavai, having made rice and other food items in the sand house she built, invites other young girls and serves them food. These are pretend play games ...that develop in young girls the qualities of household duties from a young age.

Similarly, ‘Ammanai’ and bathing are also activities unique to girls, special sections in ‘Pillai Tamil’ literature.

Furthermore, Poompavai plays on the swing. She also plays other games like running and playing in the dust on the street. She also bathes.

Thus, Sekkizhar Perumān unfolds the story of Poompavai’s growth in his divine Tamil work ...Let us press on with our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Perumān Sekkizhar, in his Periya Puranam, Part 798, Vambara Varivanda Sarukkam, ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar Puranam. Perumān Sekkizhar continues his narrative. The 1049th ThiruPadal: ‘The father, seeing this tender branch grow with such virtue in this world, rejoiced with immense delight, thinking, ‘To gain her heart, I shall bestow upon her my endless, precious wealth,’ he declared.’ This is the ThiruPadal. Sivanēchar, Poompavai’s father, is greatly pleased to see Poompavai, like a tender, young branch, growing with excellent qualities. Seeing the excellence of his daughter’s virtues brings him joy and delight.

Dwelling on this further increases his happiness. He rejoices, thinking that there is no one in this world with virtues equal to hers. He declares, ‘To match these unparalleled virtues, I shall give my endless, precious wealth to the groom who marries her, making him its owner.’ The idea is that it is fitting to bestow unparalleled wealth to match unparalleled virtues. It is the custom for merchants to give immense wealth when marrying off their daughters. We contemplated this earlier in the Puranam of Karaikkal Ammaiyar.

Furthermore, Poompavai is Sivanēchar’s only daughter. He is a great merchant, so all his wealth ...naturally belongs to the one who marries Poompavai.

In this context, Sekkizhar Perumān says in this ThiruPadal, ‘He who marries her...’ implying that there is no one else in this world suitable for her. This is implicitly conveyed in Poompavai’s story. The true Lord of all beings is Lord Shiva, as stated in Saiva Siddhanta. It is hinted here that she will not attain a worldly groom through marriage. Rather, after being reborn through the grace of Pillaiyāru, she will attain union with Shiva. Sekkizhar Perumān makes this declaration.

Sivanēchar, then, Sekkizhar Perumān ...continues in the following verses, narrating this story. Verses 1050, 1051, 1052, and 1053 follow in sequence: ‘In the land of Pandi, renowned for its wisdom, the Lord who bestowed true knowledge arrived; he defeated the deceitful ascetics in debate, cured the king afflicted with fever, rescued those terrified by fire and water, and banished those who adhered to the wrong path. He embraced the holy ash, which wards off suffering, and established the might of the divine ash. He is known for all these deeds. Arriving there, those who sang praises to him, he gifted them immense wealth and clothing. The benevolent one, from Kaali Nadu, bowed his head, placing his hands on his crown, and stood up...’ ...rose, surrounded by his kin and followers, who listened. ‘To the rulers of Kaali Nadu, I offer my child Poompavai, whom I have raised, along with my wealth and even myself,’ he proclaimed.’ Thus, these ThiruPadals are composed.

During those times, when Sivanēchar was living, ThiruGnanaSambandhar Perumān visited the Pandi country, refuted Buddhism, and established Saivism. Sivanēchar heard about this. He heard that Pillaiyār went to the Pandi country, where ascetics were prevalent, defeated those base ascetics in debate, and then cured the Pandi king’s fever. He heard about the king’s suffering from fever and how it was removed from the Pandi king’s body ...He won the fire ordeal. He defeated the ascetics in the water ordeal. Subsequently, the ascetics were impaled.

Then, with great devotion, he administered the holy ash to the Pandi king, thereby glorifying the sacred ash ritual of Lord Shiva, who holds the mountain bow.

Here, ‘ritual’ refers to the three elements: holy ash, Rudraksha, and Panchakshara.

Thus, establishing these three, he established Saivism in the Pandi country. ThiruGnanaSambandhar Perumān. News of all this spread rapidly throughout the land.

Therefore, Shiva devotees traveling to Mylapore heard these divine stories and conveyed them to Sivanēchar. ...When those who came told him these stories, he generously gifted them immense wealth, rejoicing. Out of love for Pillaiyār, he bestowed great wealth upon devotees who came on pilgrimage and spoke of Pillaiyār’s divine deeds. Giving treasures and clothes to those who brought good news was a way of expressing the joy in their hearts. Hearing these divine stories, Sivanēchar turned towards the direction where ThiruGnanaSambandhar Perumān resided and worshipped him as if he had seen him in person. From ThiruMayilai, also known as Mylapore, the city of Sirkali is to the south.

Therefore, Sivanēchar bowed towards the south ...This is implied. Generally, the rule for worship is to face east or north.

However, here, the direction of Pillaiyār is south from Mylapore.

Therefore, bowing south, rather than east or north, becomes a special rule. Sivanēchar did this out of his great devotion to Pillaiyār. Not stopping there, he gathered all his relatives and made an announcement for all to hear: ‘I offer my daughter Poompavai, born to the Lord of Kaali Nadu, ThiruGnanaSambandhar Perumān, along with my wealth and even myself, as a servant.’ He announced this loudly and clearly for all relatives and kin to hear. ...’Sutram’ means those who surround us without leaving in times of joy and sorrow. They are called ‘sutram’ because they come from a single tree like many branches. They are also called ‘kilai’ (branch).

This is also known as ‘vamsavarusham’ (lineage).

Thus, Sivanēchar announced this to all his relatives. Why? Because Sivanēchar’s relatives were the rightful claimants to marry his daughter Poompavai. Since Sivanēchar had no son, Poompavai was the sole daughter to continue the lineage.

Therefore, some of his relatives might have expected to receive wealth along with the bride. Since Sivanēchar had no son, many relatives might have desired to claim his vast wealth ...To prevent this, he announced for all to hear: ‘ThiruGnanaSambandhar Perumān, the benevolent Lord of Kaali Nadu, is my guru, my kin, and my master who has claimed me. I give my daughter, my wealth, and myself to him.’ He declared this for all to hear. ‘Are they not my true relatives and kin? They are merely attachments of illusion,’ says a Thevaram verse. ‘True relatives are those who possess selfless love for Lord Shiva,’ says a Thevaram verse. ‘The true kin are Shiva’s devotees,’ says Thiruvilaiyadal Puranam.

Therefore, indeed, worldly relatives are not our true relatives; only Shiva’s devotees are. This is what Thevaram and other verses state. Accordingly ...Sivanēchar made this announcement here. ‘I offer my daughter, my wealth, and myself to ThiruGnanaSambandhar Perumān.’ ‘Did you not claim me wholly when you embraced me, O mountain-like One?’ comes to mind from the Thiruvasagam. ‘My life, body, and possessions are now dedicated to the Lord of Kaali Nadu. They have no connection whatsoever to you, my bodily kin,’ he informed his relatives, making this announcement. In this ThiruPadal, Sekkizhar Perumān refers to Sirkali as ‘Kathamaanthavar Vaazh Kaalinaadu’ (Kaali Nadu where learned people live). He states that Sirkali is the city where learned people live ...He calls Sirkali the city where learned people live.

Who are the learned? Those who have understood that worshipping Shiva and Shiva’s devotees is the ultimate purpose of life, and who follow that path. ‘What is the use of learning if one does not worship the feet of the wise Lord?’ asks Thirukkural.

Accordingly, Sekkizhar Perumān states that Kaali Nadu is the land where such learned people live, and Sirkali is such a place. Sekkizhar Perumān then composes the next ThiruPadal. The 1054th ThiruPadal: ‘With immense joy, he made this declaration. Thinking that only the virtuous and the wealthy Brahmins possess prosperity, he rejoiced.’ This ThiruPadal states: Sivanēchar makes this declaration with boundless joy. Such a statement can only be made from a state of immense happiness. ‘When joy overflows, faults do not appear, and destruction does not occur,’ is a saying.

Accordingly, extreme happiness, like extreme anger, disrupts the mind’s equilibrium, overwhelming the ability to discern what is appropriate, what is inappropriate, what one can do, and what one cannot do ...Sivanēchar, considering his lineage, his status, his capacity, and his principles, did not analyze whether Pillaiyār would accept this.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Perumān states, ‘He made this declaration with boundless joy.’ Sivanēchar, convinced that his daughter, like a divine flower, Poompavai, and all his vast wealth, belonged to Pillaiyār, the divine child born in the Brahmin’s abode in Sirkali, rejoiced in this thought. Let us proceed with our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Perumān Sekkizhar, in his Periya Puranam, Part 799, Vambara Varivanda Sarukkam, ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar Puranam. Sivanēchar was thus rejoicing. Sekkizhar Perumān continues his song. The 1055th ThiruPadal: ‘On auspicious days, in the maiden’s chamber, near the garden, to pick flowers, with her maidens, she went out. With her tender hands, she picked buds...’ This is the ThiruPadal. ‘Ananga’ means divine maiden.

Here, Poompavai is referred to as ‘Ananganar’. This divine maiden, Poompavai, is in the maiden’s chamber with her companions. The maiden’s chamber is a private place for unmarried girls, heavily guarded. In that maiden’s chamber, there is a pond filled with pure water like milk. Nearby is a flower garden. Poompavai, with her companions, goes to that garden to pick flowers that are in bloom.

The 1056th ThiruPadal follows: ‘Not by the act of a devotee’s love, but only by the grace of the Lord of Pugali, who holds treasures, can this be possible. This was the understanding. Like a young serpent with delicate teeth, a thorny serpent...’ ...This is the ThiruPadal. As Poompavai was picking flowers that were in bloom on the plant, a young snake with thorny teeth hid there and approached. Sekkizhar Perumān uses a simile to describe how the snake came there. Sivanēchar, out of immense love and great joy for ThiruGnanaSambandhar Perumān, offered his daughter.

However, this was from Sivanēchar’s perspective only; it was not truly applicable to Pillaiyār. This is due to destiny, fate, or karma. Sivanēchar made the announcement, but it was not destined to happen that way.

Therefore, it would not apply to Pillaiyār. To prevent this from happening as Sivanēchar announced, the snake appeared there. Destiny itself seemed to have taken the form of a snake. Like that young snake, it appeared. Sivanēchar’s desire would not truly materialize because destiny decreed otherwise.

Therefore, it would not apply to ThiruGnanaSambandhar Perumān. In the Puranam of Sundara Murti Swāmigal, in ThiruNattiaththanKudi, Kōppuli Nāyanār offered his two daughters, Vanappagai and Singadi, to Sundara Murti Swāmigal, requesting him to accept them. Sundara Murti Swāmigal accepted both daughters as his own ...This is what we will see later.

Similarly, Sundara Murti Swāmigal accepted Vanappagai and Singadi as his daughters.

Thus, Kōppuli Nāyanār’s wish at ThiruNattiaththanKudi did not materialize as intended.

Likewise, Sivanēchar, out of excessive enthusiasm, announced that he would give his daughter, but it was not destined to be fulfilled by ThiruGnanaSambandhar Perumān.

Therefore, to prevent this from happening as Sivanēchar announced, destiny itself took the form of a snake and appeared there. Near the jasmine and mullai trellis, a small snake appeared. The 1057th ThiruPadal follows: ‘Hidden among the Mayavan Madhavi trellis, it emerged. As she reached to pick the buds, it seized her tender fingers. The graceful maiden, with doe-like eyes, fragrant forehead, and thick, wavy hair, and lips like kovvai fruit...’ ...This is the ThiruPadal. The small snake appeared hidden among the jasmine and mullai creepers that spread over the trellis.

Poompavai was reaching to pick the new buds that were in bloom. The flowers and creepers that grow together are usually trained on trellises. Snakes are attracted to the fragrance of flowers and creepers.

Therefore, they tend to hide beneath them. It is customary not to place such plants too close to human dwellings and to maintain them with great caution. Plants should not be allowed to grow carelessly.

Thus, the small snake was hidden in the trellis. Poompavai came to pick the buds that were in bloom. Sekkizhar Perumān describes Poompavai’s appearance: ‘Her hands like flowers, her eyes like doe-like deer, her forehead fragrant, her hair thick and wavy, her lips like kovvai fruit, her fingers like buds.’ Sekkizhar Perumān thus depicts Poompavai’s appearance. ...Her hands are like flowers (‘malar chengai’). Her eyes are like doe-like deer (‘navvi val vizhi’); sharp and radiant eyes. Poompavai’s forehead is fragrant (‘narunudhal’), a sign of perfection.

Poompavai’s hair is thick and wavy (‘seri neri koonthal’). This is also considered a good sign. ‘Neri’ refers to slight waves in the hair. Poompavai’s lips are like kovvai fruit (‘kovvai vaai’). Her fingers are like buds (‘mugil viral’), meant for picking flowers. Sekkizhar Perumān thus highlights Poompavai’s eyes, forehead, and hair. These qualities, this perfection ...Sekkizhar Perumān sings thus to show how much Sivanēchar rejoiced and loved Poompavai, and how much sorrow he would soon experience.

This is called ‘Mugadharisanam’ (seeing the face).

Furthermore, what has been described so far in this ThiruPadal about Poompavai’s condition and appearance is a creation of Maya (illusion). However, this same Poompavai, through the grace of ThiruGnanaSambandhar Perumān and Lord Shiva, will be reborn as a pure creation of Shiva. This is a pure manifestation. The divine parts will blossom. Verses 2993 to 3007 narrate this in great detail ...because it is the embodiment of the Lord’s compassion, the embodiment of Pillaiyār’s compassion.

Here, it is a creation of Maya, hence Sekkizhar Perumān briefly describes it in this ThiruPadal. As she reached out her finger, like a bud, to pick flowers, that hidden young snake bit her. The 1058th ThiruPadal follows: ‘Having bitten with its four fangs, it released venom. Raising its hood, it danced. The deadly dark venom spread upwards. The maiden, wearing a pearl necklace, felt faint...’ ...as if plunged into fire.’ This is the ThiruPadal.

The small snake, hidden in the trellis of jasmine and mullai creepers, emerged. Poompavai was plucking the new buds that were in bloom. The vines are intertwined. It is common to train intertwined creepers on trellises. Snakes are attracted to the fragrance of flowers and creepers that grow beneath them.

Therefore, they should not be kept near human dwellings and should be maintained with great care. Plants should not be allowed to grow carelessly.

Thus, the small snake was hidden in the trellis. Poompavai came to pick the buds that were in bloom. Her eyes are like doe-like deer (‘navvi val vizhi’); sharp and radiant eyes. Poompavai’s forehead is fragrant (‘narunudhal’), a sign of perfection.

Poompavai’s hair is thick and wavy (‘seri neri koonthal’). This is also considered a good sign. ‘Neri’ refers to slight waves in the hair. Poompavai’s lips are like kovvai fruit (‘kovvai vaai’). Her fingers are like buds (‘mugil viral’), meant for picking flowers. Sekkizhar Perumān thus highlights Poompavai’s eyes, forehead, and hair. These qualities, this perfection ...Sekkizhar Perumān sings thus to show how much Sivanēchar rejoiced and loved Poompavai, and how much sorrow he would soon experience.

However, this same Poompavai, through the grace of ThiruGnanaSambandhar Perumān and Lord Shiva, will be reborn as a pure creation of Shiva. This is a pure manifestation. The divine parts will blossom. Verses 2993 to 3007 narrate this in great detail ...because it is the embodiment of the Lord’s compassion, the embodiment of Pillaiyār’s compassion.

Here, it is a creation of Maya, hence Sekkizhar Perumān briefly describes it in this ThiruPadal. As she reached out her finger, like a bud, to pick flowers, that hidden young snake bit her. The 1058th ThiruPadal follows: ‘Having bitten with its four fangs, it released venom. Raising its hood, it danced. The deadly dark venom spread upwards. The maiden, wearing a pearl necklace, felt faint...’ ...as if plunged into fire.’ This is the ThiruPadal.

The small snake, hidden in the trellis of jasmine and mullai creepers, emerged. Poompavai was plucking the new buds that were in bloom. The flowers and creepers that grow together are usually trained on trellises. Snakes are attracted to the fragrance of flowers and creepers.

Therefore, they tend to hide beneath them. It is customary not to place such plants too close to human dwellings and to maintain them with great caution. Plants should not be allowed to grow carelessly.

Thus, the small snake was hidden in the trellis. Poompavai came to pick the buds that were in bloom. Sekkizhar Perumān describes Poompavai’s appearance: ‘Her hands like flowers, her eyes like doe-like deer, her fragrant forehead, her thick and wavy hair, her lips like kovvai fruit, her fingers like buds.’ Sekkizhar Perumān thus depicts Poompavai’s appearance. This hymn describes the four venomous fangs of the snake, the venom sac containing poison. The fangs, originating from the venom sac at the base of the fangs, are hollow and tube-like. These four sharp fangs are called Kali, Kalathri, Yaman, and Yamaduthan.

The snake bites with these four fangs, piercing deeply into the bone. It bites deeply into the finger bone of Poompavai, releasing the poison. The bone is the innermost part, beyond the skin, muscles, tendons, and nerves. The bone is deep inside, and the snake bites that deep. We saw that the snake bit the finger of Poompavai. Beside that finger bone is a blood vessel.

Therefore, when the poison was released into it, it spread rapidly throughout the body with the speed of blood. It bit that deep for the poison to spread so quickly. It spits out the poison through the hollow in the fangs, which are like tubes, from the venom sac at their base, into the blood vessel and thus injects it. Not only that, it also spreads its hood and dances. This is what snakes do when they get angry. It’s a sign of their anger; at other times, their hood is contracted.

When snakes get a little angry ...they immediately raise their heads, spread their hoods, and dance. After dancing with its hood spread, the snake quickly moves to another place and disappears. The poison spreads rapidly throughout the body. Just as a thin flower garland thrown into a fire instantly burns and withers, the poison spread so quickly that Poompavai lost consciousness and fainted. Verses 1059 and 1060 are as follows: As she fell to the ground, her attendants, distressed, carried her into the built chamber. The merchant and his mind lost composure, their sorrow increasing.

Relatives and friends were distressed. Many great ones, skilled in dispelling poison, arrived. Many have arrived to remove the poison, employing strong mantras, meditation, and visualization. They consult individually and collectively. These two verses are presented. Poompavai, unconscious, bewildered, and weak, falls to the ground.

Her friends, startled and frightened, carry her into the chamber prepared for her. Sivanēsar’s speech and mind are lost, extreme sorrow overwhelming him. The relatives who arrived there, along with Sivanēsar, are distressed and weeping. Many great ones, skilled in the art of curing poison, have gathered there to dispel the deadly poison. The art of dispelling poison ...is known as Garuda Vidya, the art of curing snake venom through Garuda mantras. Many who are proficient in this Garuda Vidya gather there.

Among those who have arrived, the foremost try. They attempt through strong mantras, meditation, and visualization. ‘Strength’ means the power to yield firm results.

Therefore, a strong mantra is one that firmly yields results in dispelling snake venom. This is the Garuda mantra.

Next, meditation: understanding the deity presiding over the Garuda mantra.

Thirdly, visualization: the magician visualizing his soul as the deity of the mantra. This is called visualization. When the speed of the poison increased rapidly, to subdue it, the magician makes a fist with his four fingers, leaving only the thumb extended, and touches the body of the victim from the crown of the head to the site of the bite. This is called the fist posture.

Therefore, this great magician employs mantras, meditation, visualization, and the fist posture. The practice of visualizing the Garuda is also called Garudōkambāvanai. In Saiva Siddhanta, Garudōkambāvanai is cited as an example of Sivōkambāvanai. Sivōkambāvanai is the state where the soul, visualizing itself as Siva, becomes Siva. Garudōkambāvanai is cited as an example for this. Garudōkambāvanai means the following: There are three types of Garuda: Adi Bhautika Garuda, Adi Daivika Garuda, and Adhyatmika Garuda.

Similarly, every object has three types. The Garuda seen in this world, the bird, is called Adi Bhautika Garuda. The magician mentally perceives the mantra that presides over it as Adi Daivika Garuda. The manifestation of Siva-Sakti that yields results to the magician through that mantra is called Adhyatmika Garuda. In the context of Garuda Vidya, ‘Garuda’ refers to the Adi Daivika Garuda, the form of the mantra perceived in the magician’s mind, which is the presiding deity. Visualizing this Adi Daivika Garuda means ...daily practice.

Through the special practice of daily visualizing this Adi Daivika Garuda, the magician, by intensely visualizing that mantra form itself, makes his consciousness subject to it and stands firm. By standing firm and looking with the ‘mantra eye,’ that gaze transforms the speed of the poison. This is certain. This is called Garudabhavanai, Garudokambhavanai. Others belonging to different religions claim this is false.

However, it is true that it was practiced in our country until very recently. There are presiding deity mantras for all creatures, animals, and plants. The soul is like crystal. The soul acquires the nature of whatever it associates with or is subject to. This is the nature of the soul.

Therefore, the soul becomes the form of the mantras it visualizes, as stated in the Agamas like Sarvajñānotthara Agama. This has been explained in detail by the revered Madhava Sivajñāna Munivar in the second section of the ninth sutra of the Sivajñāna Māpāḍiyam.

Thus, this Garudōkambāvanai is practiced by the chief magician. Verse 1061 is as follows: ‘Medicines and countless repetitions, and the poison, stubbornly clinging, spreads its seven stages. Swelling powerfully, with large eyes, it rises above the tender day on the head, overcoming all the performed actions. It has not been dispelled.’ Along with the four aspects we saw earlier—mantra, meditation, visualization, and the fist posture—countless medicines are administered by the experts present.

However, the poison, clinging strongly, spreads systematically in its seven stages, ascending. The poison has ascended. The seven stages of poison spreading refer to its progression through each of the seven dhatus (tissues). We have discussed this in detail in the Puranam of Adiyargal Nayannar.

Thus, the poison reaches Poompavai, who is like a creeper, ascending upwards. It has overcome all the actions performed to dispel the poison and has not been subdued. Ascending thus, with no other recourse, Sivanēsa ...issues a proclamation: ‘Whoever among the people of this world can cure this poison, to them, I will give all my boundless wealth.’ Let us carry on our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The great Periya Puranam, compiled by Devasēkkhilar Peruman, volume eight hundred, Vambarārivandu Sarukkam (Chapter of Busy Bees), Tirugnana Sambandha Nayinar Puranam. We saw that expert magicians tried to remove the poison. Verses 1062 and 1063 are as follows, as composed by Devasēkkhilar Peruman: ‘Life’s various shelters intact, skilled practitioners of Garuda Vidya, recognizing fate, commanded.

At that moment, a great retinue, crying out, fell upon the maiden. Their hearts burned like the roaring sea. Sivanēsa, regaining composure, saw no remedy. He proclaimed to the world: ‘To those who remove this deadly poison, I will give endless riches.’ ’ This verse means that the magicians and physicians tried, but they saw no signs of life remaining in the body. Even those skilled in Garuda Vidya abandoned the task, saying, ‘It is fate.’ They could not cure her and declared it was due to destiny. The relatives cried out like the sea, falling upon Poompavai and weeping.

Their hearts were filled with intense sorrow. Sivanēsa, realizing that all those who tried had given up, saying it was fate, became immensely distressed.

Then, regaining some composure, he ordered a proclamation. It stated: ‘Whoever among the people of this world ...removes this deadly poison, to them, I will give all the boundless wealth gathered here.’ He announced this publicly. He had previously dedicated all his wealth to the Pillaiyar. Someone asked if it was appropriate to offer the wealth dedicated to the Pillaiyar to those who cure this poison. It is appropriate because, out of love, he is protecting Poompavai, who belongs to the Pillaiyar, and returning her to the Pillaiyar. This act of proclamation stems from that reason.

When love intensifies, all actions become appropriate. Verse 1064 is as follows: ‘For three days, the drum sounded. All noble rulers, including those in the court, responded.’ After Sivanēsa made the proclamation and conveyed the message, skilled experts came and tried for three days. This is because, for three days, the body’s tissues could be sustained without disintegration.

Therefore, the king and others tried. It is a custom of kings to summon and keep in their court the most skilled experts from all fields in their kingdom. By supporting them in their society and benefiting the country through them ...was the practice of kings in previous times. We see this in many texts, such as Iraiyanar Agapporul, historical accounts of the Sangam period, the history of Tiruvadavur Adigal, and the Tiruththondar Puranam, as well as in historical records and inscriptions of that era.

Therefore, the king mentioned here, in that period, could have been ruling the Tondai Nadu region, of which Mylapore was a part. The capital of Tondai Nadu was Kanchipuram, ruled by the Pallavas. The rulers at this time could have been Simhavishnu from the Pallava lineage, or his son Mahendravarman. Even the most skilled experts in the court of such a king tried, but their efforts were in vain.

Now, verse 1065 is as follows: ‘Seeing the suffering, Sivanēsa’s heart was lost.’ ‘He saw the leader of Kailasa, surrounded by abundant gardens, had arrived. He kept the body within the fire, saving it with love. He gathered the ashes, clear of mind.’ This is a verse. The greatly renowned Sivanēsa, seeing this, was distraught. He was not distressed by the death of his daughter Poompavai due to poison, but rather by his failure to protect Poompavai, who was entrusted to him by the Pillaiyar, as she was in his possession. He was distraught and confused.

Therefore, Sivanēsa decided. He could not hand over the body of Poompavai, who was in his possession as belonging to Tirugnana Sambandha Peruman, to Tirugnana Sambandha Peruman in its current state.

Therefore, he decided to preserve the body as best as possible and then hand it over to Tirugnana Sambandha Peruman. Is this course of action correct? When love is abundant, all actions are correct. As Tirunavukkarasu Peruman says in his Tiruttāndagam: ‘The Lord, who is never displeased, who always grants grace to His devotees, accepting their unseemly actions born of immense joy...’. The Thevaram states: ‘You entered me, saying I know nothing, and showed me good and evil.’ The Tiruppasuram says: ‘There is no end to the ways of grace for those who are devoted to you.’ Therefore, Sivanēsa decided to preserve Poompavai’s body by keeping it within fire and then hand it over to Tirugnana Sambandha ...Peruman. The body, composed of the five elements, when placed in fire, separates into its constituent elements and merges with them.

Only bones and ash remain.

Therefore, the entire body disintegrates, leaving only the bones and ash. As Pattinathu Adigal says, ‘Finally, burnt to a handful of ash.’ But must the body be handed over as just bones and ash?

In those days, bodies were preserved in oil and other substances. The body of Dasaratha was preserved in oil. There is also the practice of preserving the bodies of certain creatures like snakes in liquids.

Furthermore, the body ...was packed inside and outside with medicinal substances and preserved for a long time. This practice existed not only in India but also in Egypt. Why not use those methods? Must the body be burned and handed over as just bones and ash? Those methods would preserve it for some time. Even if the body maintained its form through those methods, sometimes it could become toxic and harm the body, or even lead to its decomposition.

Therefore, adopting such methods would not be pure; it would become impure.

Thus, this physical body ultimately remains as bones and ash. It can be preserved in various ways. This is an age-old practice in our country.

Furthermore, during the cosmic dissolution (pralaya), the world, destroyed by fire, turns to ash, disappears, and then reappears, being recreated by the Lord. Saiva Siddhanta states this. Sivanēsa, understanding this, decided to place Poompavai’s body in fire and preserve the remaining bones and ash. He intended to preserve it until the Pillaiyar arrived and then hand it over to him. Because he didn’t know when the Pillaiyar would arrive, he believed that the form that could be preserved purely until that day was the ash and bone form. Understanding this, he proceeded accordingly.

In medical texts, if a medicine needs to be preserved for a short period, it is made into ghee, lehyam, powder, or oil. But if the same medicine needs to last for a very long time, it is made into bhasmam (ash).

Therefore, instead of burying Poompavai’s body in earth or water, he placed it in fire and reduced it. The nature of fire is such that the large form of the body is contained within this small amount of ash.

Thus, he preserved it. Sivanēsa said, ‘Because I entrusted her to my Pillaiyar...’ ...therefore, there will be no suffering for us.’ Verse 1066 is as follows: ‘After the sorrow is gone, place the collected ash within the large pot.’ This verse means Sivanēsa thought, ‘Since I have said that I have given her to the Pillaiyar, there will be no more suffering for us.’ She has become his possession. There is a ritual in weddings where parents say they have given their daughter, making her the groom’s possession.

After that, her joys and sorrows become his. Sivanēsa, including his wife and relatives, said, ‘This is no longer my concern, and hence no more sorrow for us.’ ‘Do I have any impediment today? You will do good, you will err, am I...’ ...this line from Tiruvachagam comes to mind.

Therefore, it is his possession, and it is my duty to guard it properly and hand it over to the Pillaiyar. With this thought, Sivanēsa dispelled his sorrow. He carefully poured the bones and ash into a large, wide-mouthed earthenware pot. Not only did he place the bones and ash in the pot, but he also considered it as if Poompavai were still there and performed all the usual observances for Poompavai daily. In front of the maiden’s chamber, arranging a comfortable bed with gold and pearls, adorned with fine cloths, a soft mattress of down feathers, placed upon it ...garlands of aromatic flowers, with sandalwood paste and ceremonial bathing, daily preparations of milk rice and other suitable offerings for the day, everyone marveled. Verses 1067 and 1068 are composed by Devasēkkhilar Peruman: ‘Adorned with garlands, sandalwood paste, and ceremonial bathing, daily offerings of milk rice and other suitable provisions for the day were made, filling everyone with wonder.’ He placed the pot in the maiden’s chamber, just as Poompavai had been.

He arranged the pot, guarding it. Devasēkkhilar Peruman describes the observances Sivanēsa performed for the pot containing Poompavai’s bones and ash, treating it as Poompavai herself. Is this permissible? Is it right? Poompavai’s body was offered to the fire, and the bones and ash ...became the shrunken form of Poompavai.

However, Poompavai’s soul is an indestructible conscious entity, not affected by fire or anything else. Poompavai’s soul is the conscious entity called ‘chit.’ Therefore, if we visualize that conscious entity as being present there, it will indeed be there. This is the nature of goodness, this continuity with love, as the Pillaiyar will later demonstrate.

Thus, Sivanēsa unified the body and soul, visualizing them as one, and considered it the Pillaiyar’s possession.

Therefore, he treated it with the same honor and care as one would treat the Pillaiyar’s possession. He adorned the pot as Poompavai. Arranging the mattress with soft swan feathers, adorned with fragrant substances ...he placed the pot upon it, providing a suitable seat. He decorated the neck of the pot with various ornaments. The place where the pot was kept was decorated with canopies. Daily, garlands, sandalwood paste, and ceremonial bathing were performed without fail.

Milk rice was offered daily. A lamp was lit during the day. We can understand these as practices similar to the ‘Bhavana Abhishekam’ in Shiva Puja. A lamp was lit during the day. Lamps are needed by humans at night.

After the sun rises during the day, lamps are not needed. However, lamps are lit during the day in temples.

Similarly, lamps are lit during the day in the presence of elders. This is one type of observance. Incense and lamps were offered. These observances ...were performed daily, with fresh offerings made daily out of love. Everyone marveled at these.

During this time, Devasēkkhilar Peruman describes what happened next. Verse 1069: ‘The ruler of Shambai, near Tiruvotriyur, with virtuous devotees, humbly conveyed the joyous news to the great merchant. He said, ‘The news has arrived.’’ This is verse 1069. While these daily observances were being performed, the news arrived that the Pillaiyar, the head of Sirkali, had come to Tiruvotriyur. The news that he was staying in Tiruvotriyur with Shiva devotees was brought to Sivanēsa, who was there. The messengers who brought this good news ...had great affection for Sivanēsa and a sense of ownership.

Thus, they conveyed the auspicious news: ‘The Pillaiyar, along with devotees, has arrived in the great city of Tiruvotriyur, where the Lord resides as Padampakkanāthar.’ This is what the noble devotees told the great merchant Sivanēsa. Verse 1070 is as follows: ‘The messengers were honored with gifts of gold and silver, and with affection.’ Sivanēsa, upon hearing this good news, was overjoyed. He was immensely happy, beyond words. He declared that he would create a procession from Tirumayilapur to Tiruvotriyur, the abode of Shiva, a distance of about ten ‘naligais’ (approximately 4 hours). Along this entire path, he arranged for a covered passage, constructing canopies with cloth and flowers. This entire route was thus decorated.

He constructed a canopy, built a covering of cloth overhead, and provided everything necessary to offer shade from the sun, wind, and rain below this canopy.

Thus, from Tirumayilapur to Tiruvotriyur, a distance of ten ‘naligais’, he arranged for a covered pathway and floral decorations. He erected arches and planted areca nut and banana trees for decoration. These all demonstrate the depth of Sivanēsa’s love for the Pillaiyar. Verse 1071 is as follows: ‘Magnificent arches, bunches of areca nuts, bananas, and countless floral garlands were arranged beautifully. The city streets were adorned with splendor, making it seem as if the golden city of the gods had descended to earth.’ Magnificent arches, bunches of areca nuts, bananas, and countless floral garlands were arranged beautifully. The city streets were adorned with splendor, making it seem as if the golden city of the gods had descended to earth.

This path is believed to be the coastal route from Tirumayilapur to Tiruvotriyur. It is supported by many facts that the temple of Tirumayilapur was also located by the seashore in those days.

Let us go on with our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The great Periya Puranam, compiled by Devasēkkhilar Peruman, volume eight hundred and one, Vambarārivandu Sarukkam (Chapter of Busy Bees), Tirugnana Sambandha Nayanaar Puranam. Sivanēsa, thus decorating Tirumayilapur and the entire route from Tiruvotriyur to Tirumayilapur, composed verse 1072 as follows: ‘Having thus adorned the place and sent messengers to Otrryur, he would venerate the golden feet of the Tamil scholar arriving in that city. The great devotees of that city also accompanied him as he proceeded.’ Having adorned the place in various ways, Sivanēsa then set out from Tirumayilapur to Otrryur to behold the Pillaiyar, who is a scholar of Tamil. The great devotees living in Tirumayilapur also accompanied Sivanēsa, and they all proceeded towards Otrryur.

In the meantime, the Lord of Otrryur, the embodiment of the Vedas, having taken leave, set out from that city towards Kailasapuram, accompanied by a host of pure devotees. This path is described by Devasēkkhilar Peruman as the ‘sea-surrounded Kailasapuram.’ ‘Kayal’ means salt pans. This route is a coastal path, hence the presence of numerous salt pans. Salt is a commodity of trade found in coastal areas and ports. On such a path, filled with salt pans, Tirugnana Sambandha Peruman proceeded towards Tirumayilapur, accompanied by a troupe of pure devotees. Pure devotees are those whose inner and outer purity stems from their connection to Shiva.

As we saw in the chapter on the greatness of the congregation, they are pure within and without, like the water applied to the human body.

Thus, Tirugnana Sambandha Peruman proceeded southwards from Otrryur, located north of Tirumayilapur, towards Tirumayilapur.

At the same time, from Tirumayilapur, he proceeded northwards. At that moment, a group of devotees was visible in the distance. Sivanēsa, along with the great merchant and devotees, seeing the gathering of ascetics adorned with Vibhuti from afar, prostrated themselves in immense joy. This is verse 1074. Sivanēsa and the great devotees accompanying him see the gathering of ascetics, who wear Vibhuti, from a distance. Realizing that this congregation is the one accompanying Tirugnana Sambandha Peruman, the son of Shiva, they fall to the ground and worship.

It is our tradition and custom to fall and worship when we encounter divine beings, gurus, and elders. Even without seeing the Pillaiyar, they saw the congregation accompanying the Pillaiyar. Sensing that the Pillaiyar was also within this congregation, they worshiped them. Verse 1075: ‘Kālināḍar, descending from his radiant palanquin, was greeted by the devoted attendants. He rose and said, ‘Hail, great sage!’ Hearing the words of the merchant, the divine son arrived in the glorious city of Mayilapur, surrounded by the sea.’ The Pillaiyar, the head of Sirkali, descended from his radiant jeweled palanquin. He rose and greeted the countless great devotees surrounding him.

Tirugnana Sambandha Peruman was now very close to Tirumayilapur. That is why he descended from the palanquin and walked among the devotees.

At that moment, the devotees accompanying the Pillaiyar narrated the history of Poompavai to Tirugnana Sambandha Peruman, mentioning Sivanēsa’s devotion. By narrating these events, the devotees were demonstrating their compassion. The purpose was to introduce Sivanēsa to the Pillaiyar and to fulfill Sivanēsa’s heart’s desire. The history was conveyed to Tirugnana Sambandha Peruman so that the Pillaiyar would understand. The Pillaiyar heard all this and kept it in his heart. As we have seen in the events at Tirumaraikkadu and other places, it is customary for those who have reached the Pillaiyar’s feet to be guided and blessed by him.

We see this here as well. The events that occurred earlier were established in his heart. Delighted by Sivanēsa’s actions, which were meant to fulfill his purpose, and with a compassionate gaze that destroyed external opposing religions like Jainism and Buddhism, he rejoiced. Arriving at the Kapaleeswarar temple, where Shiva, with his flowing matted locks, resides, he worshipped the tall, radiant tower and entered. Circling the temple of the Lord, who has the Goddess as his consort, and worshipping, he joined his palms on his head and stood before the deity. These are verses 1076 and 1077.

Sivanēsa, the merchant, who had experienced these events, was acknowledged by the Pillaiyar in his heart.

Here, Devasēkkhilar Peruman refers to Sivanēsa as ‘Sivanēsa of joyful heart.’ This means that even though Poompavai had passed away, he said he was not distressed, hiding his sorrow. We are reminded of this here. The sorrow of losing his daughter had already vanished.

Now, the time had come for him to offer his daughter to the Pillaiyar, and he was immensely happy. Sivanēsa, who had been visualizing Poompavai as alive until now, and was about to present her, was overjoyed. We will soon witness Poompavai being resurrected by the great compassion of the Pillaiyar.

Thus, Sivanēsa ...is about to achieve his goal. With this in mind, he experienced great compassion. Tirugnana Sambandha Peruman, who came to destroy external religions like Jainism and Buddhism, embodying great compassion.

In those days, Buddhism and Jainism spread throughout Nadu Nadu, Chola Nadu, and Pandya Nadu, causing suffering.

Similarly, adherents of these religions had spread in Tondai Nadu. ‘Jainas and Sakyas’ here refers to their aggressive encroachment upon other religions and the harm they caused. The meaning is to destroy this. The suffering caused to Saivism by them is what Tirugnana Sambandha Peruman intended to eliminate. We must understand this well. In that era, for about three centuries, Jainism and Buddhism spread throughout Tamil Nadu, causing harm to Saivism and Vedic religions. We see this through historical records and the Purāṇams of Tirunavukkarasu Peruman, Taṇḍiyadigaḷ Nāyanār, Naminaṉtiyaḍigaḷ Nāyanār, and others.

The eighth tiruppadal is sung by Gnanasambandhar, extolling with profound devotion the nectar of ThiruKapeeswaram, the Lord of Lords, the husband of Pavaai, praising him with humble sincerity and heartfelt love. This is the essence of that tiruppadal, starting with ‘Devadhevane’. In this song, Pillaiyar glorifies and worships Lord Kapeeswarar, and the divine Sekkizhar beautifully explains this act.

He praises the Lord as ‘Devadhevane’, the Lord of Lords. The Great Lord consumed the immense poison that arose from the sea, intent on destroying the Devas, and thus protected the hosts of Devas without harm. By consuming the poison, the Lord revealed His supreme, ultimate nature and His supremacy to all. Such is the greatness of the Lord, who can revive this small revive this small form of Poombavai is not difficult. This is the underlying meaning. The intent behind ThiruGnanasambandhar praising Him as ‘Devadhevane’ is that He is the nectar of ThiruKapeeswaram.

If nectar bestows immortality, then in truth, the Lord Himself is nectar. The substance consumed by the Devas is called nectar only by convention. In reality, the Lord alone is the embodiment of nectar.

Therefore, by singing ‘Nectar of ThiruKapeeswaram’, it is implied that He has the power to bestow immortality and resurrect the dead. He sings ‘Husband of Pavaai’. He praises the Lord. ThiruGnanasambandhar, who keeps the Divine Shakti, the Goddess, as one half of His being, naturally has the compassion to bestow grace upon Pavaai. This is the implied meaning.

Thus he praises.

Therefore, the underlying meanings of ThiruGnanasambandhar praising Him as ‘Devadhevane’, ‘Nectar’, and ‘Husband of Pavaai’ are thus established. With such divine intent, Pillaiyar prostrated before Lord Kapeeswarar. After such praise, he composed a pathigam. Due to our shortcomings, the pathigam sung by ThiruGnanasambandhar during that time is not available to us. After composing the pathigam, he performed Panchanga Ashtanga Namaskaram, prostrating himself such that his body touched the ground in five and eight parts.

We shall continue our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. ThiruppuRaNam by DevaSekkizhar Perumaan, Part Eight Hundred Two. Vambaraa Varivanda Sarukkam. ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar Puranam. Praising and glorifying the Lord of ThiruKapeeswaram in front of Him with a pathigam. ThiruGnanasambandhar, through the next ten consecutive songs, DevaSekkizhar Perumaan reveals the upcoming divine events.

From the 1079th tiruppadal to the 1088th tiruppadal, ten tiruppadals in the Puranam of ThiruGnanasambandhar, from the 2977th to the 2986th song.

Thus, these ten tiruppadals are composed consecutively, like a single pathigam by DevaSekkizhar Perumaan. After those tiruppadals Thus praising, with true grace and overflowing devotion, bowing down, His ash-covered holy form, where the dense hair strands cover the worlds, having vanquished Yama, who approached the temple. He emerged from the temple and graced the merchant with His compassion. He commanded them to bring the pot filled with the bones of the great maiden, a fruit of severe penance, to the great temple, outside the main entrance, where the dancer performs. With immense joy, they bowed down to the earth, brought from their homes, from the Kannimaadam in the fragrant garden nearby, the pot filled with ashes and bones, and carried it placed in a jeweled palanquin. Accompanied by maidservants, they arrived at ThiruKapeeswaram.

They placed the jeweled palanquin in front of the tall gopuram. Placing the pot containing the maiden’s bones at His feet, they worshipped. Those who reside in this world, in the city of Mayilapur, of the Pugalikkavalar, and others living in various lands. Even those of dissenting faiths, gathered to witness this spectacle. Many gods and celestial beings descended from the heavens. Surrounded by a large gathering of devotees, the Lord of the ancient universe, approaching the gopuram entrance.

Inside the pot filled with bones was the ashes. Seeing this, the Lord, contemplating His boundless compassion, declared that the bones of the deceased in this world, when reunited, would bring forth goodness. With this intent, he proclaimed, ‘Call forth the one named Poombavai, whose form is partially present in these ashes. Those who have gained immense benefit by being born on this earth, who have fed the ascetics, and have seen their joyous festivals, will find solace.’ ‘Let them come forth,’ he commanded.

Then, worshiping the Lord with matted locks, he uttered, ‘Will you not come to the pathigam sung by Mattiitta?’ This divine word, like nectar, descended upon that part and it formed into a pot. Thus ends these ten tiruppadals. The first tiruppadal, the 1079th tiruppadal, begins with ‘Praise, with true grace and boundless devotion, bowing down, His ash-covered holy form, where the dense hair strands cover the worlds, having vanquished Yama, who approached the temple. He emerged from the temple and graced the merchant with His compassion.’ As mentioned before, glorifying the Lord of Kapeeswaram and receiving His true grace, with unceasing remembrance, they worshipped the Lord of Kapeeswaram. Receiving the essence of His true grace, they stood in worship. ‘True grace’ means unfailing grace. ‘Receiving the essence of grace’ means receiving the grace of Shiva for the accomplishment of His actions. Receiving grace from the Lord is the meaning.

It is not possible without Shiva’s true grace.

Therefore, with unceasing thought, Gnanasambandhar prayed to Shiva for grace, and receiving the essence of Shiva’s grace, he worshipped the Lord of Kapeeswaram, who vanquished Yama. ‘Vanquisher of Yama’ refers to the Lord who annihilated Kala, and who is about to resurrect Poombavai. To signify the necessity of overcoming death for this purpose, DevaSekkilzhar Perumaan describes Him here as the ‘Vanquisher of Yama’.

Thus, after worshipping the Lord of Kapeeswaram, the Vanquisher of Yama, outside His temple, ThiruGnanasambandhar emerged. His holy form, covered in sacred ash, was filled with the dense hair strands. Having kicked Yama and brought him under control, he emerged from the temple of the Lord, who performed His divine dance bestowing His divine grace upon the merchant. This is what ThiruGnanasambandhar commanded. The next tiruppadal begins: ‘With singular devotion, and the good understanding that leads to salvation, to be known by the world, with great effort, the pot filled with the bones of the great maiden, brought to the great temple, outside the main entrance, where the dancer performs, and commanded to be brought.’ This tiruppadal is ThiruGnanasambandhar’s divine utterance. He addresses Sivanesar. ‘With singular devotion’ means one who is deeply immersed in servitude to Shiva, with a mind that does not waver from this thought.

To be unwavering in this service, not deviating even slightly from the path of devotion. This is the meaning of ‘singular devotion’. Such was Sivanesar. The divine words also state, ‘Do not waver in your mind; constantly be united in thought. I have thought of only one thing, decided on only one thing, and held only one thing in my heart.’ In this context, ‘singular devotion’ means unwavering resolve, regardless of what comes. As Appar Swamigal says in his Thirukkuruthanthokai: ‘Even if mountains fall, if you stand firm without being shaken, the Lord Shiva will protect you from destruction.’ Addressing Sivanesar with such ‘singular devotion and good understanding’ ThiruGnanasambandhar declares to the world.

He tells Sivanesar, ‘As a fruit of your arduous penance, bring the pot filled with the bones of your daughter to the entrance of the great temple, where the Dancer performs amidst the great cremation grounds.’ ThiruGnanasambandhar commands this, making it known to the entire world. He proclaims this so that all people may understand the greatness of Sivanesar’s love and realize the truth, and be saved. ThiruGnanasambandhar says to Sivanesar, ‘You have relinquished attachment.

Therefore, even when this maiden passed away, you were not distressed, nor will you be overjoyed when she is resurrected. This divine act is not for me either because we will not be in a state to accept the resurrected maiden.

Therefore, this is not for me either.

Thus, so that all people in this world may understand the greatness of the Lord’s divine grace and be saved, and understand the depth of Sivanesar’s love and be saved, ThiruGnanasambandhar commands Sivanesar to bring the pot and place it in front of the gateway of the great temple. Referring to the temple, he mentions it as the ‘Great temple of the Lord who dances amidst the great cremation grounds.’ This cremation ground signifies the Maha Samharam (Great Dissolution), and the dance signifies resurrection.

Therefore, at this place, in accordance with this divine act, ThiruGnanasambandhar bestows grace In those days, ThiruGnanasambandhar’s temple was a magnificent structure that the sea waves would embrace as they washed ashore. The current Kapaleeswarar temple in Mylapore, Chennai, was built about three to four hundred years ago. We can discuss its historical details elsewhere.

Thus, he commands them to bring the pot and place it outside the main entrance of that great temple. ThiruGnanasambandhar instructs that the pot containing the burnt bones and ashes should not be brought inside the temple, considering it impure Thus, he commands them to bring it and place it directly outside the entrance. Upon hearing these divine words, Sivanesar rejoices. With immense joy, he bowed down to the earth, and went to his home. The Kannimaadam where Poombavai lived was near his home. As we saw earlier, it was in that Kannimaadam that he kept the pot filled with Poombavai’s bones and ashes, and worshipped it.

He makes arrangements to retrieve the pot from the bed where it was kept in that Kannimaadam, and bring it to the entrance outside the temple. ‘Placing it in a jeweled palanquin, and with maidservants surrounding him, they arrived at ThiruKapeeswaram. Placing the jeweled palanquin before the tall gopuram,’ the next tiruppadal states. He carefully places the pot in a jeweled palanquin, adorned with precious gems.

Then, he covers it with a curtain. In those days, it was customary for royalty and wealthy merchants, and other high-class individuals, to travel in covered palanquins.

Here, Sivanesar, having treated the pot containing Poombavai’s bones and ashes as if it were Poombavai herself, and bringing her as if she were alive, places the pot inside the covered palanquin. Accompanied by her friends, they bring it forth. Arriving at the vicinity of the temple of Lord ThiruKapeeswarar, the dancer, and as instructed by Pillaiyar, they alight the pot from the jeweled palanquin in front of the great gopuram. Before the Anganaalar (those who serve the Lord) the pot containing the maiden’s bones, placed at His feet, they worshipped. This is the 1083rd tiruppadal. ‘With deep devotion at the feet of Lord Shiva, the pot containing the maiden’s bones is placed. The Pugalikkavalar, residing in this world, will demonstrate the steadfast state for those who live here.’ This is the 1083rd tiruppadal.

Sivanesar, with the devotion rooted at the feet of Lord Shiva, places the pot containing the maiden’s bones directly in front of the entrance, worshipping ThiruGnanasambandhar. Puhali is the king of Sirkazhi. Puhali is the third name of Shiva names. The act performed by Sivanesar with singular devotion, which brought fame and grace, is attributed to Gnanasambandhar. This is indicated by DevaSekkilzhar Perumaan’s description of him as ‘Pugalikkavalar’. Such a Pugalikkavalar is about to reveal the steadfast state that is essential for the people living in this world.

The steadfast state for beings is to perform Shiva dharma and attain moksha.

Therefore, even the celestials residing in the heavens descend to this earth, perform Shiva puja, and perform Shiva dharma. ‘We spend our days in this earth, not returning to the heavens. What a waste. This earth is Shiva’s way of salvation,’ says Thiruvachagam, Thiruppalli Ezhuchi. Brahma, Indra, Vishnu, and other celestials constantly reside here. Just as the celestials wait in front of the Thevaasiriyap Mandapam in Thiruvarur, it is on this earth that one can perform Shiva dharma and attain moksha.

Therefore, even the celestials come here to perform Shiva dharma and Shiva puja. To demonstrate that performing Shiva dharma and attaining liberation from suffering, and reaching bliss, the bliss of Shiva, is the ultimate goal of life, ThiruGnanasambandhar is about to reveal it.

Our reflection shall continue.
