Let us resume our reflection. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. DevaSekkizhar Perumaan’s Periya Puranam, Part Eight Hundred Three. Vambaraa Varivanda Sarukkam. ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar Puranam. ThiruGnanasambandhar looks at the pot containing Poombavai. He reveals to the people of this world what the ultimate goal of life is.

DevaSekkilzhar Perumaan, in the 1084th tiruppadal, describes how, to witness the divine act that ThiruGnanasambandhar is about to perform, various people and Shiva devotees have gathered. ‘The residents of Mayilapur, and those living in other parts of the country, even those of dissenting faiths, gathered to witness this spectacle. Many gods and celestial beings descended from the heavens,’ is that tiruppadal.

At that time, there the residents of Mylapore arrive. DevaSekkilzhar Perumaan describes Mylapore as ‘Mayilapur with towering mansions.’ Along with them, people from other parts of the country, the Thondai region where Mylapore is located, also gather. These are the common people. These are people from the world who have come to witness the divine manifestation of Shiva’s grace and to worship Him, having dedicated themselves to Shiva. Next are the crowds from ‘dissenting faiths’. This refers to followers of religions other than Saiva Siddhanta.

There are various types of religions categorized as external, inner-external, and inner religions, with six sub-categories within each. Saiva Siddhanta is the supreme among them.

Therefore, the text mentions the arrival of people from ‘dissenting faiths.’ These individuals belong to the three categories of external religions: inner-external, external, and outer-external. Among them, there are many types of people. Some have come merely to witness the spectacle without any particular allegiance. Some have come with doubt. Some have come with the firm conviction that bones and ashes cannot turn into a woman, and have come with scorn.

Thus, people from other religious backgrounds have gathered. They have come to witness the Lord Shiva’s constant benevolence towards all beings, His supreme nature, meaning His supreme divinity towards all beings, and His supreme divinity. This is why they have gathered. These are the ones belonging to the three types of external religions who have forgotten the truth that all belong to Shiva as His eternal devotees, and instead, babble about other truths that contradict this one, claiming them as the truth. Although they differ among themselves in their doctrines, they are united in forgetting and denying Shiva.

Thus, they are all gathered together as ungrateful people of religion. Jains, Buddhists, and others belonging to other religions also come and join them.

Furthermore, the celestials also come and gather there. Great celestials like Vishnu, and other celestials. ‘Nedu devargal’ means great celestials like Vishnu. The text states that ‘Nedu devargal’ are those who live long through their lifespan, knowledge, and penance. Others include beings other than these celestials and people living on this earth, such as Nāgas and Asuras. The gathering of celestials in the heavens is very dense. They do not have a gross physical body like ours, made of the five elements.

Even though they possess subtle luminous bodies, a very large gathering of celestials stands very close to each other.

The Lord then composes the next divine song (Thiruppadal) as follows: Surrounded by the great congregation of devotees, the ancient Lord of the celestials arrives directly at the tower gate. With hair adorned with bees, [he sees] the earthen pot filled with bones. The divine Sekizhar states in this divine song how all others gathered. He says, ‘Surrounded by the great congregation of devotees,’ indicating that the devotees of Shiva gathered in large numbers. These devotees of Shiva are those who accompanied Pillaiyar, Thirugnanasambandhar. It is said that many others from the Thondai region, along with Sivanesar, lived with Thirugnanasambandhar from Thiru-ottiyur, and they gathered in large numbers, forming a great congregation of Shiva devotees.

This same grand gathering can be seen even today during the festival of Poombavaiyar. We can still witness the congregation of great Shaivite devotees during the festival procession of the sixty-three Nayanmars.

In this way, all gathered, and Thirugnanasambandhar arrives directly at the tower gate of the divine temple of Kapaleeshwar Peruman. The divine Sekizhar composes this: ‘With hair adorned with bees,’ meaning Poombavai, who had long hair where bees would reside. He then looks with grace upon the earthen pot filled with the bones of such Poombavai. The divine Sekizhar states the word ‘kandu’ (seeing) as used by Thirugnanasambandhar is not a mere physical sight as we perceive it. This ‘kandu’ refers to the divine gaze of grace. How did Thirugnanasambandhar see?

He perceived Poombavai in his divine heart, creating her. This is called ‘Nayanadeekshai’ (initiation through sight). Just as a sculptor sees the sculpture in the stone before carving it, Thirugnanasambandhar, in his divine heart, created Poombavai and then saw the earthen pot. Pillaiyar saw within the pot outside, the bones and ashes, and within them, the fully formed body of Poombavai, and within that, Poombavai with hair adorned with bees. Thirugnanasambandhar thus saw by creating her in his divine heart. This vision is a divine creation made with the intention ‘let these bones become this body.’ In the fullness of Shiva Jnana, which is beyond comprehension, Thirugnanasambandhar created the entire body of Poombavai upon this pile of bones and saw her.

Because he sang of Poombavai as ‘she with hair adorned with bees,’ it is understood that Thirugnanasambandhar saw Poombavai as if she were alive and with her body. How did he see this? The divine Sekizhar says: ‘He saw by contemplating the greatness of the Lord’s compassion.’ ‘Thampiran’ means Shiva. In seeing this, Thirugnanasambandhar did not see himself but rather saw the greatness of his Lord Shiva’s compassion. Within that divine compassion, he merged and attained the fullness of Shiva Jnana, and thus he saw.

Let us go on pondering. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The divine Sekizhar, in his great Puranam, volume eight-four, in the chapter ‘Vambara Varivandu,’ narrates the life of ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar. ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman, seeing the greatness of his Lord Shiva’s compassion, merged within it, attained the fullness of Shiva Jnana, and thus gazed with divine grace upon the earthen pot. With what intention did ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman gaze with divine grace? The divine Sekizhar explains this in the thousand and eighty-sixth divine song. The Pillaiyar looked at the pot and addressed it by name, ‘Poombavai.’ He also commanded, ‘Will you not go?’ The thousand and eighty-sixth divine song explains the reason for this.

The divine Sekizhar explains the inner meaning of that divine song, the essence of the pathigam, in the thousand and eighty-seventh divine song. The miraculous events that occur due to the chanting of that pathigam are explained by the divine Sekizhar in the following three divine songs. Among the divine songs thus composed, the thousand and eighty-sixth divine song is as follows: ‘To reinstate the bones of those who have died in this world, and by the grace of his divine sight, he addressed the body which had Poombavai’s name, saying...’ This divine song addresses the pot by saying, ‘Poombavai.’ The Pillaiyar declared the deceased’s body ...bones and ashes were her former body.

Therefore, connecting the bones within the pot, her entire body, and Poombavai who possessed that body, he called her by the name ‘Poombavai.’ Why did Pillaiyar call the pot containing the bones by the name ‘Poombavai’? It is because, for those who have lived in this world, the actions performed with their remaining parts, namely bones and ashes, all these good practices reach the body which is the continuation of the bones, and then reach the soul residing within that body. We witness this in this world.

Therefore, addressing the bones as Poombavai ...Thirugnanasambandhar calls her Poombavai. In this divine song, the divine Sekizhar writes, ‘those who have died in this world.’ ‘Those who have died’ literally means deceased individuals. If we separate it as ‘those who remain after death,’ it means those who exist with a subtle body after death. This is the meaning of rituals performed with the bones of the deceased. The act of placing the bones of the deceased in sacred rivers and performing rituals there, the benefit derived from that good deed, reaches the body that was the basis of those bones, the body to which they belonged. The soul that resided in that body receives it.

Similarly, the act of addressing the bones in the pot with divine grace and calling them by name, is for Poombavai.

Therefore, Pillaiyar thus gazed with divine grace and called her by the name ‘Poombavai.’ The subtle body is primary to the gross body. When the gross body perishes, the soul, belonging to the subtle body that is the cause of the gross body, benefits from the good deeds performed on the bones, which are the components of the gross body. This subtle body ...exists with the soul until the time of liberation (mukti). This is the truth affirmed by Shaiva Siddhanta. The extensive details of this are elaborated in the commentary of the second sutra, third adikarana of the Sivajnana Bodham, by Sri Mathava Sivajnana Muni.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman gazed with divine grace and called her by the name ‘Poombavai.’ After addressing her thus, he composed a pathigam. What is the meaning of that pathigam? The divine Sekizhar explains this in the thousand and eighty-seventh divine song. This divine song is memorized by all Shaivites: ‘Having taken birth in this world, the great fruit is to feed the devotees of the Lord with the crescent-moon adorned one. Seeing their joyful festival’s brilliance, and finding solace, say, ‘Come forth before the world,’ they declare.’ This divine song, a summary of the Shivasgamas, reveals what the ultimate purpose of birth is for all beings in the world, and it guides them to attain it. This divine song reveals the purpose of life for beings in the world and has the greatness of showing the way to attain it.

In the Puranam of Thiruneelanakka Nayanar, the divine Sekizhar showed the essence of the Vedas, which are described as the Vedas’ inner knowledge, the ‘seven hundred and thirty.’ The Vedas state that the truth is the worship of Shiva and the worship of Shiva’s devotees.

Therefore, among the Vedas and Agamas, which are the divine words of the Lord, the divine Sekizhar, who revealed the essence of the Vedas there, has extracted the inner essence of the Agamas in this divine song.

Furthermore, this divine song, which is spoken by the Lord through the Pillaiyar’s utterance, possesses the greatness of being the Lord’s divine word.

Additionally, this divine song highlights the truth of the pathigam within the Thiru-mayilappur pathigam, which begins with ‘Mattiṭṭa puṉṉaiyam kāṇal.’ This divine song also possesses the greatness of conveying the inner truth of this entire Puranam. The truths stated herein are two: feeding the devotees of the Lord Shiva, and finding solace by witnessing the brilliance of Shiva’s divine festivals. The divine Sekizhar expresses these truths. The divine Sekizhar states that these two truths should be contemplated by people, sincerely practiced in their lives, and followed, which will lead to salvation. This divine song begins with ‘Having taken birth in this world.’ ‘Having taken birth in this world’ means that beings, taking birth in this earthly realm as a consequence of their karma, are given this life by the Lord. The upper worlds are given as a result of the good karma performed by beings, to experience the fruits of those merits.

The lower worlds are given for beings to undergo the consequences of their immense evil deeds. Experiencing the fruits of good deeds in the upper worlds and the fruits of evil deeds in the lower worlds, beings are reborn here.

Thus, the upper and lower worlds become causes for rebirth in this earthly realm, rather than being the places where the cleansing of karma occurs. This earthly realm is the only place where the cleansing of karma happens and where one can perform Shiva deeds.

Therefore, to cleanse karma and attain liberation by destroying the cycle of birth, only this earthly realm is suitable, not the heavens or the lower worlds. This is what ...Sivajnana Siddhiyar states: ‘Is not the human birth meant for the five senses of mind, speech, and body to perform worship? Even beings from the heavens descend to this earth to worship the divine abode. Do the ignorant, engrossed in their flesh, not realize this?’ Therefore, to perform Shiva deeds, one must perform Shiva puja. To attain liberation by destroying the cycle of birth through Shiva puja, this earthly realm is the only place. Among this earthly realm, it is the land of Bharata.

Even more so, this southern direction, having performed great penance, is the land most suitable for performing great Shiva penance and Shiva puja, according to the Agamas, in the temples where the Lord resides.

Therefore, coming here, performing Shiva puja, cleansing karma, accumulating Shiva merit, and destroying the cycle of birth ...one can attain liberation. This earthly realm serves as the means for that.

Therefore, the divine Sekizhar states, ‘Having taken birth in this world.’ This means those who have come into this world, embodied as a consequence of karma, to experience and cleanse that karma, and have reached the stage of liberation. Having taken birth thus, what is the great fruit? The great fruit attained through good Shiva deeds performed in that birth, through Shiva puja, is liberation (mukti). The actions that serve as the means to achieve that liberation, performed in this earthly realm by souls who have come with that divine intention, are such that ‘we do not return here to the cycle of birth and karma,’ as the Thiruvasagam states.

Accordingly, for souls who have come to this earthly realm with the intention of attaining liberation, the practices that serve as means to attain liberation, and the determination to adhere to them, are two. They are: feeding the devotees of the Lord, and finding solace by witnessing the brilliance of their divine festivals. The first of these actions is feeding the devotees of the Lord. This is the great Maheswara puja performed for the devotees of Shiva. Sivajnana Bodham, in the twelfth sutra, states: ‘Consider the form of the devotee as Shiva himself and worship.’ Thus, one should worship the forms of Shiva devotees, recognizing them as Shiva himself, without any doubt. Among the acts of worshipping Shiva’s devotees, the most excellent component is offering divine food to Shiva’s devotees.

Therefore, the divine Sekizhar states, ‘feeding the devotees of the Lord.’ Even though it says ‘offering divine food to devotees,’ we should also include other forms of hospitality based on kinship. Providing clothes, gold, jewels, and other necessities to devotees should also be included here.

Thus, ‘feeding the devotees of the Lord’ (Maheswara puja) is stated as the first and most important of the two means to achieve liberation. In our Thiru-thondar Puranam, the Great Puranam, nineteen Nayanmars attained liberation through such Jangama worship. Among them, Emperuman Ilaiyankudi Maranayanar and Emperuman Siruthondar Nayanar are prominent examples who demonstrated Maheswara puja.

Thus, ‘feeding the devotees of the Lord’ is stated first.

The Lord Shiva himself, residing within the devotees to whom divine food is offered, accepts that ambrosia and bestows grace. Thirumooladeva Nayanar states in his hymn: ‘If one offers to the temple of the dancing Lord, it is not received by the Lord of the dancing temple. If one offers to the Lord of the dancing temple, it is received by the Lord of the pictured temple.’ Thirumooladeva Nayanar says: Therefore, offering divine food to devotees means offering it to the Lord Shiva himself, who resides within those devotees. The truth is obtained that it is offered to the Lord Shiva residing within them. The divine song states, ‘feeding the devotees of the Lord.’ This is understood by combining ‘feeding the Lord’ and ‘feeding the devotees,’ implying that both benefits are derived from offering divine food to devotees.

Similarly, ‘feeding the devotees of the Lord’ implies that if one cannot do it oneself, one should arrange for others to do it.

Thus, to signify that ‘feeding the devotees of the Lord’ is the first and most important of the two உறுதி (resolute practices for liberation), the divine Sekizhar states it first. This same idea is also the inner meaning of the first divine song in the pathigam sung by Thirumylai Sambandhar ...’Mattiṭṭa puṉṉaiyan kāṇal.’ The second benefit is ‘finding solace by witnessing the brilliance of their divine festivals.’ This is the second of the two resolute practices for liberation. This truth is obtained from the second divine song up to the tenth divine song in the Thiru-mayilappur pathigam.

Thus, those nine divine songs also contain truths that benefit the soul.

Similarly, their glories are described in nine divine songs. “After the tenth verse of the Thiruppathigam is completed, Poompavai’s bracelet-adorned hands emerge from the pot.

“Then, the entire pot breaks, and Poompavai rises, rising for all to behold. How does she rise? She rises as if the goddess Lakshmi is emerging from an unfurling lotus bud. The lotus is an analogy for the pot. The emergence of Lakshmi from an unfurling lotus petal is an analogy for Poompavai rising from the breaking pot. We saw this story earlier: when Poompavai was born to Shiva Nesar and his wife.

“We saw that Poompavai was born like a vine that emerged from the lotus-like womb of Shiva Nesar’s wife.

“Similarly, Divine Sekkizhar blesses the same idea again here. ‘The pot broke’ does not mean the pot was destroyed, but rather, like the unfurling of a flower petal, it expresses gentleness, a divine poetic skill blessed here by Divine Sekkizhar. She who rises from the unfurling lotus bud is Lakshmi. This Poompavai is the daughter who attained Shiva. We will see later that ‘Thenamar Kothai’ also attained Shiva.

“Likewise, this Poompavai, the daughter who came to attain Shiva. The lotus that everyone praises, the lotus that everyone worships, the lotus in the hearts of those who lovingly remember and praise. Just as the divine power emerges in every heart, Poompavai is emerging here. The thousand nine hundred and first divine verse, Divine Sekkizhar blesses as follows: “In the blessed verse, having gained form, in the next four verses, reaching the growth of twelve years, emerging in the blessed Samanpāṭṭiṉil, the desirous ones saw and unfolded the concluding verse.” The verse ‘Mattiṭṭa’ starts with the first verse, where the maiden attained form.

“Then, in the eight divine verses blessed thereafter, the form developed, gradually reaching the growth of twelve years. Poompavai, in the tenth. Divine verse, emerges from the pot when it breaks.

“After that, Thirugnanasambandhar blesses the eleventh divine verse, the concluding verse, and completes this Thiruppathigam.

“Thus, in this divine verse, Divine Sekkizhar systematically summarizes the events that occurred from the first verse, the consequences within the pot. How? Poompavai’s previous body was consumed by fire, losing its form and remaining only as bone and ash. By the divine grace of the Pillaiyar, that lifeless bone form, concentrated within the subtle body composed of material elements, became a fetal form suitable for receiving life. The bone and ash became a fetal form. The nectar of the divine word, ‘Pothiyo?’, infused life into it.

“Then, in the eight verses from the second to the ninth verse of the Pathigam, the full growth of that body is shown. That growth is a systematic growth, reaching completion at the age of twelve years. This growth occurred to Poompavai’s body.

“Therefore, Poompavai’s death by poison occurred at the age of seven, as we saw earlier. Five years have passed since then. During these five years, Shiva Nesar nurtured the pot containing Poompavai’s bones, treating it as Poompavai. This is what we gather. At the age of seven, when Poompavai was poisoned, at the same time, the Pillaiyar achieved victory over the Jains in Madurai, at Thiru Alavai.

“At that time, Thirugnanasambandhar would have been about ten years old. After falling victim to poison, Poompavai, having undergone five years of growth, appeared at the age of twelve. During this entire period, Shiva Nesar treated Poompavai as if she were alive. According to his thoughts, the growth occurred. Not only that, Shiva Nesar, who worships Thirugnanasambandhar, wanted to marry Poompavai to Thirugnanasambandhar. He had pledged, “I will give you Poompavai, born to me.” Even after Poompavai fell victim to poison, the head of Kazhuma, Thirugnanasambandhar, would return.

“He said, “I will keep Poompavai’s body intact by fire, collect the bones and ash, and hand them over to Thirugnanasambandhar.” He kept the pot, treating it as Poompavai, in the Kanni Madam, and nurtured it. He handed over the pot, as Poompavai, to the Pillaiyar when he arrived. Tamil grammar states that the age of marriage for women is twelve years. This same age of twelve years appears here.

“Therefore, by the divine compassion of Lord Shiva, when rebirth occurred in that body, with the growth of the intervening five years, she appeared. At the age of twelve, Poompavai arose as a maiden.

“Thus, performing a miracle, a divine miracle, through divine grace, Thirugnanasambandhar, who had conquered his desires, who had left desires behind, just as it is said, “You who have conquered the five senses,” acted without any desire. Divine Sekkizhar shows us this, praising Thirugnanasambandhar as one who has conquered his desires. He then blesses the eleventh divine verse, the concluding verse, which speaks of the benefits of the Pathigam and serves as a blessing. “Ten verses praising the beauty of the Tamil language, sung as Poompavai’s song.” This is the eleventh divine verse, the concluding verse. In this Thiruppathigam, Poompavai, who died at the age of seven, now arises fully developed at the age of twelve, in her maiden form, due to the divine grace of Thirugnanasambandhar and the divine compassion of Lord Shiva, the divine brother. Divine Sekkizhar blesses this further.

“Let us also Continue to reflect.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The divine Sekkizhar, in his Periya Puranam, Part 807, Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam, narrates the life of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. Poompavai arises as a twelve-year-old girl. Divine Sekkizhar blesses the next divine verse. “Beholding the divine maiden who thus arose, they exclaimed, ‘Behold this wonder!’ The devoted ones cried ‘Hara Hara!’ Their resounding voices reached the heavens.” This is the thousand nine hundred and second divine verse. Those who saw the divinely beautiful Poompavai who arose exclaimed, “Behold this wonder!

“Look at this well!” The people of the world stood in awe. The Shiva devotees, the Shiva devotees. All of them, seeing this as a manifestation of the great compassion of Lord Shiva, cried ‘Hara Hara!’ and praised Him. Their resounding cries reached the heavens, reaching the gods. We saw earlier that the gods gathered in the sky to witness this divine event.

“Therefore, the ‘Hara Hara!’ chants raised by the devotees reached them. The gods and sages, seeing the greatness of divine grace, showered flowers from divine trees like Mandhara. They exclaimed, “This is a result of our Lord Shiva’s compassion!” They joined their hands above their heads, bowed down, and fell prostrate. The people of the world, seeing the divine form of Poompavai, were greatly astonished. It was as if they had lost. Those of opposing faiths, seeing this, became like those who had lost.

“They were bewildered, not understanding how this happened, and stumbled and fell to the ground. The Jains and other non-believers, like this. Sivakavi Mani Desigan elaborates on this section. Divine Sekkizhar continues to bless the story of Poompavai. Simultaneously, he blesses the notes on the Thirumylai Thiruppathigam, the history of the temple, the festivals held there, and the legend of Poompavai’s festival. Sivakavi Mani Desigan has explained these in his commentary.

“Let us reflect on this and then continue to consider Poompavai’s story. This Thiruppathigam, starting with ‘Mattiṭṭa Puṉṉaiyam Kāṇal,’ which was blessed for the sacred place of Thirumylai, has its inner meaning and essence explained by Divine Sekkizhar in the divine verse ‘Mannil Piranthar Perumpayan.’ This Thiruppathigam is of great importance in teaching the foundation of Shaivism and the vital essence of life to the people of the world. Let everyone study this well, follow the path it shows, and attain the purpose of human life.

“Thus, may people realize and live righteously and be saved, says Sivakavi Mani Desigan. In the first verse of this Thiruppathigam, Thirugnanasambandhar blesses the greatness of serving food to devotees: ‘Having been born on this earth, the greatest benefit is to feed the devotees of the Lord who wears the moon on His crown.’ This is blessed by Thirugnanasambandhar in the first verse. ‘Maṭṭiṭṭa Puṉṉaiyam Kāṇal, Maṭamailai Kaṭṭiṭṭam Koṇṭāṉ Kapālīccaram Amarntha, Oṭṭiṭṭa Paṇpiṉ Uruṭṭira Palkaṇattārkku, Aṭṭiṭṭal Kāṇātē Pōtiyō Pūmpāvā’ is the first divine verse. ‘Maṭṭu’ meaning. Means mind. ‘Mattiṭṭa Puṉṉai’ means a mind full of Punṉai. Puṉṉai is the primary produce of the coastal region, the Neythal land. ‘Kāṇal’ means sandy shore, shrubbery, or grove.

“Therefore, the place is Thiru Mylapore, where mind-filled Punṉai trees surround the sandy shore, shrubbery, or grove. It is ‘Maṭamailai’. ‘Maṭam’ means beauty.

“So, it is a beautiful Mailai. ‘Kaṭṭiṭṭam koṇṭāṉ’ means ‘He made it His abode.’ He is the one who resides in Kapālīccaram. This ‘Kaṭṭu’ is also called Mailaikkaṭṭu. It is the place where the divine mother worshipped the Lord in the form of a peacock.

“Therefore, the Lord, as Kapālīśvara, resides there, graciously accepting the connection with the divine mother peacock. He joyfully resides there.

“The Lord resides there. In such a Mailai, in Kapālīccaram, Thirugnanasambandhar blesses, ‘O Poompavā! For the Uruṭṭira Palkaṇattār, who possess the ‘Oṭṭiṭṭa Paṇpu,’ do not miss it.’ Here, ‘Uruṭṭira Palkaṇattār’ refers to the devotees of Shiva. They possess the ‘Oṭṭiṭṭa Paṇpu,’ which means the inseparable union of two principles, Shiva and Sakti, a mixture of Advaita, as stated in the Sivagnana Bodham: ‘Advaita with Sivagnana.’ They are united with Lord Shiva in Advaita. They are great Maheswaras. For them, ambrosia must be served. ‘O Poompavai, come to serve these Maheswaras, perform Maheswara Puja.’.

“The Lord is joyfully residing there. In such a Mailai, in Kapālīccaram, Thirugnanasambandhar blesses, ‘O Poompavā! For the Uruṭṭira Palkaṇattār, who possess the ‘Oṭṭiṭṭa Paṇpu,’ do not miss it.’ Here, ‘Uruṭṭira Palkaṇattār’ refers to the devotees of Shiva. They possess the ‘Oṭṭiṭṭa Paṇpu,’ which means the inseparable union of two principles, Shiva and Sakti, a mixture of Advaita, as stated in the Sivagnana Bodham: ‘Advaita with Sivagnana.’ They are united with Lord Shiva in Advaita. They are great Maheswaras. For them, ambrosia must be served. ‘O Poompavai, come to serve these Maheswaras, perform Maheswara Puja.’ Praising Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman, he ordains, “Poethiyo Poombavai!” and grants the second verses.

“The essence of the verses from the second to the tenth is to find solace in witnessing the splendor of the divine festival with one’s own eyes.

“Therefore, in these verses from the second to the tenth, Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman has sequentially described the festivals celebrated in Thirumayilai. The second verse, as composed by Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman, is: “Maidens with eyes adorned with kohl, in the great city of Mayilai, he who resides in Kapaleeswaram with ashes smeared from the ash-producing hands, come, do not miss seeing the festival of Aippasi Onam and the feasting of the ascetics!” Thirumayilai is a city where maidens reside. The term ‘Padanallar’ here refers to ‘madamai’, one of the four virtues attributed to womanhood. Some interpret ‘madamai’ not as ignorance, but as acting as if ignorant, even when knowledgeable. Such maidens, with eyes adorned with kohl, are young women living in Thirumayilai. In that Thirumayilai, the Peruman resides in Kapaleeswaram.

“There, the Peruman is seated, smeared with ‘kaippayantha neeru’ – meaning, the sacred ash that unfailingly yields benefits. We can recall here the Thiruppathigam sung by Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman, titled ‘Neeru’. The festival of Onam in Aippasi is celebrated for the Peruman, who resides in Kapaleeswaram, smeared with this beneficial ash. The Aippasi Onam festival, according to local history, was a celebration in ancient times where the flag was hoisted on the sacred day of Thiruvonam in the month of Aippasi in Thirumayilai, and the sacred bath was taken on Krithigai. The local Puranas state that Sri Rama conducted a festival for the Peruman at Kapaleeswaram on the day of Aippasi Onam. We can infer that the devotees partaking in the sacred food during the Onam festival in the month of Aippasi was an essential part of the celebration.

“Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman commands Poombavai to come and witness this Aippasi Onam festival. The third verse begins: “Maidens wearing bangles, in the great city of Mayilai, in the prosperous streets, to see the festival of Thazhalakku Kapaleesvarathan...” ...on the day of Karthigai, come, do not miss seeing the festival of lights celebrated by the women with firm breasts!” Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman urges Poombavai to come and witness the celebration of lights, where women with firm breasts, adorned with bangles, celebrate the festival of lights by lighting lamps in the month of Karthigai, at the temple of Kapaleeswaram, which is vibrant in the great city of Mayilai, with its firm streets. Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman refers to the streets of Mayilappur as ‘Valamargu veethigal’ (prosperous streets) and ‘Vanmargu veethigal’ (strong streets). These were prosperous streets, and Mayilappur was a port city with a harbor, where ships docked, and trade flourished. In such a Mayilappur, the festival of lights is celebrated in the month of Karthigai.

“Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman refers to it as ‘Thol Karthigai Naal’ (ancient Karthigai day). The festival of Karthigai Vilakkeedu is very ancient and is mentioned in the Sivasagamas and Mahapuranas. The Perur Puranam, in the chapter on special poojas, mentions: “From the month of Karthigai, the day of Purnami, the feast is full.” This is the festival of lighting lamps, celebrated by lighting lamps. This is prescribed in the Sivasagamas. The Sivasagamas prescribe what abhishekam should be performed on each Purnami day of the month. In the book ‘Pushpavidhi’, Kamalainjana Prakasar, the guru of Dharumayadhina Guru, mentions ...in his text, the abhishekam to be performed each month.

“It is mentioned that a lamp should be worshipped on the Purnami day of Karthigai month. ‘For Chittirai, it is mulai kothu; for Vaikasi, sandalwood; for Aani, thirumul; for Adi, milk; for Avani, sugar; for Purattasi, adhirasam and other cakes; for Aippasi, rice; for Karthigai, lamp; for Margazhi, ghee; for Thai, honey; for Masi, ghee; for Panguni, curd,’ are explained in that verse. Accordingly, Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman invites you to come and witness this festival of lights celebrated in the month of Karthigai in Mayilappur.

“Now, the fourth verse: ‘Oordhirai velai ulavum uyar Mayilai, Koortharu velvallar kotrangol seridhanil, Kartharu...’ ...solai Kapaleeswaram amarnthan, Aadhirai naal kaanaathe poothiyo Poombavaay.’ This verse states: ‘O Poombavai, in the high city of Mayilai, where waves wash the shore, in the settlements of the fertile Nidal land that capture fish, where forests have grown due to the mountain’s bounty, come, do not miss seeing the festival celebrated on the day of Aadhirai at the temple of Kapaleeswaram.’ The day of Aadhirai is the festival celebrated in the month of Margazhi. Thirunavukkarasar Peruman has sung about the glory of Aadhirai, saying, ‘Athan Aaroor Aadhirai naal adhan vannam.’ In Thirumayilappur, on the day of Aadhirai in Margazhi, the consecration of Nataraja Peruman takes place in the early morning, followed by the procession to the chariot street. The procession returns to the temple, and the Peruman is covered with white cloth in the sixteen-pillar mandapam, and then proceeds in divine procession. This is known as the Sapthapathi festival. The Peruman circumambulates the sixteen-pillar mandapam seven times, with different musical instruments playing for each round. The Peruman then re-enters the temple.

“After that, at around nine in the morning, the Aardhra Darisanam and the divine street procession take place. Such is the grandeur of the Margazhi Thiruvadhirai festival.

“Now, the next verse, about the Thaipusam festival, which is unique to Mayilappur. Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman sings: ‘Maipusam ondra kann madanallar, Ma Mayilai, Kaippusa neerthan Kapaleeswaram amarnthan, Nei pusam on pulukka ner izhaiyaar kondaadum Thaipusam kaana...’ ...it is said. In the great city of Mayilai, where women with kohl-adorned eyes live, the Peruman residing in Kapaleeswaram has a Thaipusam festival in the month of Thai. In that festival, ‘Neippusam on pulukka’ – meaning, rice cooked with ghee – is offered and distributed to devotees. Such is the special nature of the Thaipusam festival. Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman invites Poombavai to come and witness this Thaipusam festival.

“The Purnami in the month of Thai, when the star Pushyam is prominent, is considered very auspicious. It is believed that Brihaspati, the guru of the gods, bathed in holy waters on this day. This Thaipusam festival ...is celebrated with great splendor at the Mahalingaswami temple in Thiruvidaimarudur. Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman states that this festival takes place in Thirumayilappur.

“Thus, this is a very ancient festival. At the Kapaleeswarar temple tank, on the Thaipusam Purnami day, the first day features the Chandrasekhara Peruman’s Theppotsavam (float festival), and the second and third days feature the Singaravelar Theppotsavam. This float festival circles the temple pond five times on the first day, seven times on the second, and nine times on the third. On all three days, people gather in large numbers to worship the Lord. The sight of camphor lit on betel leaves floating on the water is breathtaking. On these three days, the Peruman, after leaving the temple in the evening, circumambulates the streets and joins the float from the pandal located in the upper section.

“After the Theppotsavam is completed, the Peruman ...circumambulates the other streets and returns to the temple. Such is the glory of the Thaipusam festival.

“Now, the sixth verse: ‘Madalaarntha thengin Mayilaiyaar Maasi kadalaattu kandaan Kapaleeswaram amarnthan, Adal aaneru oorum adigal adiparavi nadamaadal kaanaathe poothiyo Poombavai.’ This verse says: ‘In Mayilai, with its tall palm trees, on the day of Maasi Magam, he witnessed the sea bath. The Peruman residing in Kapaleeswaram, with the bull vehicle, come, do not miss seeing the divine dance!’ Maadalaarntha thengin refers to the long fronds of coconut trees. In Mayilappur, which has abundant coconut trees, a sea bath festival is held on the day of Maasi Magam. Kapaleeswarar Peruman emerges in procession. Maasi Kadalaattu means the festival where Kapaleeswarar Peruman performs the sacred bath on the seashore on the day of Magam in the month of Maasi. Kadalaattu means bathing in the sea.

“In such a Maasi Kadalaattu festival ...Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman mentions the divine dance. Many people gather there, sing, and dance.

“Thus, it is a festival where songs and dances are intertwined with performances. In this Maasi Kadalaattu festival, when the Lord gives the sacred bath, everyone goes to the seashore and bathes in the ocean. Processional deities from nearby temples also come to the seashore. From Kapaleeswarar temple, Chandrasekhara Peruman, along with Astradevar, comes to the seashore, performs the sacred bath, and returns. Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman invites Poombavai to come and witness this Maasi Kadalaattu festival.

“Now, the next verse, about the Panguni Uthiram festival, a very significant festival for Kapaleeswarar. Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman sings the seventh verse ...’Mali vizha veethi madanallar Ma Mayilai, Kali vizha kandaan Kapaleeswaram amarnthan, Pali vizha paadal sai Panguni Uthira naal, Oli vizha kaanaathe poothiyo Poombavai.’ The verse states: ‘In Mayilappur, where festivals abound, maidens live. In the city where divine dances, which dispel the suffering of the people, are held, the Peruman resides in Kapaleeswaram. Come, do not miss seeing the grand festival of Panguni Uthiram, where offerings are made!’ The streets of Mayilappur are streets where festivals occur. The divine dance, known as ‘Kali’, dispels the suffering of the people. In that city of Mayilai, where festivals are abundant, the Peruman of Kapaleeswaram resides, dispelling suffering.

“There, the festival of offerings is celebrated with great fanfare on the day of Panguni Uthiram. Come and witness it, says Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman. Bali Vizha refers to a grand festival celebrated with Rudra Bali and Dik Bali. It is also called Brahmotsavam. It is a festival of sounds, where various instruments and melodies resonate. This is the Panguni Uthiram festival, the Brahmotsavam of Kapaleeswaram, celebrated for ten days.

“The final day is Panguni Uthiram. During the Brahmotsavam days, the processional deities take a street procession through the main streets. This procession is accompanied by bright lamps, Nadaswaram, Vedic chants, and Thirumurai Devaram chanting. Every year, preparations for the festival begin on the Krithigai star in the month of Panguni. The day before the Brahmotsavam begins, a grand abhishekam is performed throughout the temple, and a feast is held. Pujas are performed for the two village deities, and offerings are made.

“Pujas are performed for the chariots, and offerings are made. On that day, the Vinayagar puja begins, and to mark the commencement of the festival, Saneeswarar, along with Angaraka, proceeds to the Ridhymoolai for Mrutha Sangrahanam (collection of earth) and circumambulates the main streets. Kuththaadum Pillaiyar (dancing Pillaiyar) comes in procession on the Mushika vahana (mouse vehicle) at night. On the first day of Panguni Uthiram festival, in the morning, Kapaleeswarar, along with the Panchamurthies, proceeds to the Dhwajjarohana Mandapam for the hoisting of the flag.

“After the flag hoisting, the Panchamurthies, along with Astradevar, perform the Navashakti Bandhanam and then proceed to the Mandapam. At night, the Lord, adorned as if Uma Devi herself is worshipping him under the Punnnai tree in the form of a peacock, ascends the Punnnai tree. For the first ten days, during the morning and evening processions to the yagasalai, Deeparadhanai is performed. On the second day of the festival, in the morning, the Lord, on the Surya Vrutham, and Ambal ...ascend their vimanas, receive their mandagapadi in the Ishanya corner, and return to the temple. At night, the Lord on the Chandra Vrutham, and Ambal on the parrot vehicle, Murugan on the elephant vehicle, proceed. On the third day of the festival, at six in the morning, the Lord, on the silver Adhikara Nandhi, Ambal on the Gandharva vehicle, Murugan on the Purusha Gandharva vehicle, Vinayagar on the silver Mushika vahana, and Saneeswarar on the silver Rishaba vahana, proceed.

“During this festival, on the southern main street, near the temple tank, the divine event where Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman gave his divine milk occurs. Kapaleeswarar and Ambal, on the Simha vahana and Yazhi vahana respectively, proceed. At night, Kapaleeswarar circumambulates the streets on the Naga vahana, while Ambal on the Kamadhenu vahana and Murugan on a goat’s skin proceed. On the fifth day of the festival, in the morning, Kapaleeswarar, Karpagambikai, and Singaravelar ascend their vimanas, circumambulate the main streets, and proceed to the Mandagapadi at the Vaishya Mandapam opposite the east tower. After midday, they return to the temple. At night, Kapaleeswarar on the silver Rishaba vahana, Ambal on the golden Rishaba vahana, Murugan on the golden Mayura (peacock) vahana, silver Vinayagar and Saneeswarar on silver Mushika and silver Rishaba vahanas respectively, proceed.

“Nadaswaram music, Vedic chanting, and sweet Devaram music continue throughout the night. On the sixth day of the festival, in the morning, the Panchamurthies ascend five palanquins. In the evening, Kapaleeswarar and Karpagambal ascend the elephant vahana, and Singaravelar ascends the green peacock vahana. On the seventh day of the festival, in the morning, the Panchamurthies ascend seven chariots. In the evening, Kapaleeswarar, with magnificent floral decorations and a grand orchestra, returns to the temple from the chariot street. At night, the Panchamurthies ...take a street procession.

“The eighth day of the festival is the Poombavaiyar festival. Sivanessar and Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman proceed to the west main street, opposite the temple tank, for the divine bath. During the day, a grand abhishekam is performed for Sivanessar and Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman. At two in the afternoon, Sivanessar and Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman return to the temple, obtain permission from the Lord, and again proceed to the temple tank with Poombavai’s skeleton. Everyone witnesses this divine event. Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman sings the verses of this Thiruppathigam, beginning with ‘Mattitta,’ and transforms the skeleton into a maiden, conducting a mandagapadi.

“They then circumambulate the main streets and reach the sixteen-pillar mandapam.

“At that time, the divine event of Kapaleeswarar, along with the Panchamurthies and the 63 Nayanmars, bestowing darshan takes place.

“Then, circumambulating the streets and reaching the sixteen-pillar mandapam ...Deeparadhanai and the wondrous sight of the 63 Nayanmars in procession take place. At night, Chandrasekhara Peruman, on the horse vahana, performs the Pari Vettai (hunting) festival.

“After that, at around midnight, Kapaleeswarar, along with the Panchamurthies, takes a street procession. The ninth day of the festival features the Panchamurthies’ procession in the morning. At six in the evening, Bhikshatanar, accompanied by Muni Pathinis, emerges from the Saudala vimana. The encounter with Mohini on the west main street takes place. At night, the Panchamurthies take a street procession. The ritual of Shantisevai for Nataraja Peruman, the application of white paste, and the Sapthapathi festival take place.

“Then, the Theerthavari (sacred bath) is performed, followed by a street procession. The Theerthavari for the Panchamurthies is performed at the temple tank. In the evening, Kapaleeswarar, in the Punnai forest shrine, along with Karpagambal, who was cursed to be a peacock, worships the Lord ...and attains her original form after receiving darshan from Kapaleeswarar. She then reaches the Thirukalyana Mandapam, where the divine wedding takes place.

“Afterwards, Kapaleeswarar and Karpagambal, swinging on a flower swing, ascend the Thirukailaya vahana, the Ravaneswara vahana, and circumambulate the streets in a silent procession with flute music, without any musical ensemble.

“At that time, along with Astradevar, Navashakti Dhikbandhana Visarjanam is performed, and they reach the temple. They ascend the Dhwajjarohana Mandapam, where Dhwajavarohanam (flag lowering) takes place.

“The Lord and Karpagambal then join in the Kalyana Mandapam. The Saneeswarar street procession takes place. On the eleventh day of the festival, in the morning, Uma Maheshwarar darshan takes place in the Kalyana Mandapam, which is the Lord’s Thalal (awakening) scene. When the door to the chamber where the Lord resides is opened in the morning, auspicious items such as an elephant, a bull, dancing maidens, chamaras, a mirror, and a lamp are displayed, and puja is performed. In the evening, the Pandamhari festival takes place. The Lord, along with the Panchamurthies, proceeds to the chariot street for the festival.

“At that time, Ambal, experiencing delusion, returns to the temple and locks the door. This divine event occurs.

“The Lord summons Sundaramurthi Swamigal, and the delusion is performed three times. A pact is made between the Lord and the beloved, and after being appeased, Ambal circumambulates the Lord and enters the temple. This divine vision takes place.

“Thus, the Panguni festival, the Brahmotsavam of Kapaleeswarar temple, is celebrated with great splendor for eleven days. This is what Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman refers to when he sings, ‘Panguni Uthira naal oli vizha kaanaathe poothiyo Poombavai.’ Now, the eighth verse: ‘Thannaa arakkan thol saithukandha thaalinaar, Kannaar Mayilai Kapaleeswaram amarnthan, Pannaa pathinganangal tham attaminaal...’ ...Kannaara kaanaathe poothiyo Poombavai,’ he ordains. Pathinen Ganangal refers to the Shiva Ganas. In the month of Vaikasi, on the eighth day, a festival is celebrated as the worship of these Shiva Ganas. This festival, along with the Potrapu and Perunsaanthi mentioned in the upcoming verses, is no longer in practice in many places. They should be revived, as it is a great act of Shiva devotion.

“Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman says, ‘Do not miss seeing these with your own eyes.’ The divine work, ‘Deivachchekkizhar Peruman,’ highlights this as a general principle, saying, ‘Seeing the splendor of the divine festival with one’s own eyes brings solace.’ Now, the ninth verse: ‘Natamarai mel naanmuganun naarananum, mutraangu unarkilaamoorthi thiruvadiyai, Katraargal ethum Kapaleeswaram amarnthan, Pottrapu kaanaa...’ ...Uthsavathai Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman sings. Thambu refers to Thappu. Pon Thappu is called Ponunjal (golden swing). This festival is generally celebrated in the months of Aani and Adi. Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman sings, ‘Do not miss seeing such a Pottrapu.’ Now, the tenth verse: ‘Urinjaya vaazhkai amudaiyavarkum porkkum, Irukkum naattil amarnthan...’ The verse states: ‘He who resides in the land where those with a barren life, like the Ajivikas, and those who embrace nudity as their faith, like the Saivaites, and those who take pride in wearing clothes as their faith, like the Buddhists, babble whatever comes to their minds, the Peruman of Kapaleeswaram, surrounded by dark groves, has attained...’ This verse signifies the fully developed Poombavai emerging from the pot, extending her divine hands. ...This verse, according to Deivachchekkizhar Peruman, is ‘Samapattu.’ He ordains, ‘Come and witness the grand festival of Perunsaanthi for the Peruman of Kapaleeswaram, surrounded by dark groves, in this world where the Ajivikas, who embrace nudity as their penance, and the Buddhists, who consider wearing clothes as their penance, prattle whatever comes to their minds.’ The Perunsaanthi festival mentioned here is the Pavithrotsavam.

“The Somashambhu Paddhati describes this Pavithrotsavam in great detail. Some also interpret this as Kumbhabhishekam.

“Therefore, come and witness this Perunsaanthi, also known as Pavithrotsavam ...invites Poombavai, says Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman.

“Now, the eleventh verse, the conclusion: ‘Thirukkadai Kaappu. Kaanamar solai Kapaleeswaram amarnthan, Thenamar poombavai paattaaga, Senthamizhaal Gnanasambandha nalampugazhndha, Pathum vallar vaanasambandhathavarodum vaazhvaare.’ This is the verse. Those who recite these ten verses, sung by Gnanasambandhar in classical Tamil, praising the Lord residing in Kapaleeswaram, surrounded by fragrant groves, and dedicated to Poombavai, the maiden as sweet as honey, will attain salvation and live eternally with the Shiva Ganas. This is the Phalasruti (fruit of recitation) that Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman has composed in this eleventh verse.

“Thus, the essence of this Thiruppathigam has been somewhat ...contemplated with the commentary of Sivakavi Mani Desikar. Let us go on contemplating.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Deivasigizhar Peruman’s Periya Puranam, Part 808, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandhanayanar Puranam. Commentary on the Thirumayilai Thiruppathigam. Sivakavi Mani Ayya continues to provide special notes on Thirumayilai. Thirumayilappur is the twenty-fourth holy site in the Thondai Nadu. It is also called Thirumayilai.

Mayilappur is the name of the holy site. Kapaleswaram is the name of the temple.

Here, Uma Devi worshipped the Lord in the form of a peacock, hence the name Thirumayilai. This deity is worshipped in a separate shrine at the base of the Punnai tree in the outer prakaram of the temple. The Punnai tree is the sthalavriksham. It is said that Sri Rama worshipped here and obtained his name. Festivals were celebrated with splendor on Aippasi Onam, as stated in the Puranas. The Sthalapuranam states that this is mentioned in the second verse of the Thiruppathigam dedicated to this holy site.

Histories of worship by devas like Brahma are also narrated in the Sthalapuranam. Among the 63 Nayanmars, Vailar Nayanar, who was born in this holy site, attained the feet of the Lord by establishing a sand temple for the Lord within the Vayilar stone. This is found in the Maha Puranam.

Sundaramurthi Swamigal praises him in Thiruthondar Thogai, saying, ‘Thurai konda sembavalam irulakatrum sothi, Thon Mayilai Vailar adiyarkkum adiyen.’ His shrine is a separate temple facing north, opposite the Karpagambal shrine. We have been elaborating on the history of Aaludaiya Pillaiyar (Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman) transforming the skeleton into a maiden for Sivanessar. The divine form of Poombavai emerging from the pot and the divine form of Pillaiyar singing the Thiruppathigam are also housed in a separate temple ...in the outer prakaram, to the north of the west tower entrance, and is worshipped. Aaludaiya Arasargal, Thirunavukkarasar Peruman, also worshipped here, as discussed in the Puranam of Thirunavukkarasar Swamigal. This is the place where Thiruvalluvar Devanayanar was born and composed the Thirukkural. The Thiruvalluvar temple is located in the northeastern part of the city.

Swami Kapaleeswarar faces west, and Ambal Karpagambal faces south. The Theertham is Kapali Theertham. The Sthalapuranam of this holy site, titled Thirumayilai Sthalapuranam, was recently written by Mayilai Nathamuniyar. It describes not only Kapaleeswaram but also the shrines of Vellishwar, Vailishwar, Mundaganniyammai, Mallishwar, Karaneesar, Virupakshishar, and Theerthapaleeswarar in the surrounding area. In total, it contains eight hundred ...and six chapters. The Sthalapuranam for this site is also found in Sanskrit in the Shiva Mahapuranam, Kothirudra Samhita, in the Utkrushta Shivashetra Prakarana, as the Kapaleesthalamaahathmyam, consisting of eleven chapters.

In Tamil, the Sthalapuranam authored by Srimath Amruthalinga Thampiran Swamigal from the Mayilai branch of the Kundrakudi Madam in Thiruvannamalai, with commentary by Mahavidwan Kanchipuram Sabapathi Mudaliar, was published some time ago.

In addition, there are Puranams written by Purohitas like Mayilai Vasi Mudaliyar. Sivakavi Ayya has also included historical notes about Thirumayilai in his commentary. The historical notes written by Thiru CM Ramachandra Chettiar are as follows: The current temple was built about three hundred years ago. The old temple was on the seashore. The Europeans ...demolished it, built their churches, and erected a fort around it. While excavating to repair a church about forty years ago, many sculptures and stones were found.

Based on these, it can be inferred that the old temple existed in that place. The new temple was built at the current location using the stones from the demolished old temple.

At that time, not realizing the value of the inscriptions, they were haphazardly joined. There are about fifty such inscriptions in the Amman temple. There are none in the Swami temple. Some stones with inscriptions are laid at the entrance of the Kalyana Mandapam. Some of the stones removed during repairs have inscriptions. These have been recorded by the government between 1923 and 1925, under numbers 215 to 223.

In one Tamil inscription, it is mentioned that a donation was made for a lamp in the Nataraja shrine for the dancing deity. In another, the beginning ‘Thirumagal Pola’ by the chief minister Rajaraja ...is found. The third inscription mentions the name Poombavai. These inscriptions are from nine centuries ago.

Furthermore, it is understood that Sivanessar’s residence was on the seashore, and a jetty must have been built for loading goods from ships, with living quarters behind it. Places like Trincomalee in Eelam and Goa in Tuluvana Nadu were also occupied by the Portuguese and Dutch four hundred years ago, just as this Mayilai might have been occupied by foreigners who built churches and residences. Evidence for this can be seen in the buried inscriptions mentioned above. In the Chennai history by H. Leev ...it is known that from 1516 onwards, the Portuguese, Turks, French, Dutch, and others repeatedly captured this area and held it. According to that book, between the French and the Turks in 1672, a war took place.

During that time, a part of the French army hid in the Kapaleeswarar shrine.

Therefore, it can be assumed that the present Kapaleeswaram existed in 1672. In a map of Chennai city drawn in 1798, the Mayilai temple tank is shown. There is also a legend associated with this temple tank. Further details about the antiquity of Thirumayilai by Thiru Palasubramania Mudaliar are as follows: ‘Thurai konda sembavalam irulakatrum sothi, Thol Mayilai’ ...sang the great Nambi Aaroorar. The Greek geographer Ptolemy, who lived two thousand years ago, referred to ‘Malliar’ in his geography book as Mayilappur, as stated by the author in Vestiges of Old Madras, Volume 1, Chapter 23. It is said that Thiruvalluvar lived in Mayilai two thousand years ago, and his friend Elala Sengar was a merchant here.

An inscription from the eleventh century mentions that many Nadesis gathered in Mayilapil and made certain decisions. A trading port is where people from many nations gather.

Therefore, from Ptolemy’s time to the inscription period, Mayilappur was a port. This port also flourished during the Portuguese era. Between this port and the port of Chennai, located in the northern part of Chennai ...there was trade competition and fierce battles, as well explained in the book Vestiges of Old Madras, Volume 1. During the reign of the Pallava kings, Mayilaimai flourished, so Thirumangai Alvar, when referring to Thiruvallikkeni, mentions ‘Thenamar solai maada maamayilai thiruvallikkeni.’ An inscription from the time of King Kambavarma of the Pallava dynasty indicates that royal families resided in Mayilappur. Inscriptions also reveal that many merchants from Mayilaimai, who were residents, made donations for lamp offerings and Nanda lamps when they visited various holy sites. These merchants from Mayilaimai were wealthy and possessed the resources and good conduct to make such donations.

They had the wealth and merit to make donations wherever they went. Among such merchants, the most prominent was Sivanessar, the father of Poombavai. The name ‘Mayilapoo’ is found for this place. In the Thevaram of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, Mayilappur is mentioned in three places. In the sixth verse of the Thirumayilai Thirunthakam in Thiruoor, the line ‘Vadivuudaiya mangaiyum thaamum ellam varuvaarai ethirkandom Mayilappulle’ is a testament to Deivasigizhar Peruman’s statement that Thirunavukkarasar Swamigal went from Mayilappur to Thiruoor. In the sixth Thirumurai, second pathigam, first verse, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman sings, ‘Mangun madhithavizhum maadhaveedhi Mayilappil ullar,’ praising the beauty of Mayilappur’s streets.

In the sixth Thirumurai, seventh pathigam, twelfth verse, he states, ‘Mayilappil manninar manniye thum,’ considering Mayilappur as a protective site. In these three instances, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman mentions Mayilappur. The name Mayilappil is also found in some inscriptions. In other inscriptions, it is found as ‘Mayilaarbil.’ We can see the similarity in names with ‘Thalamai’ and ‘Malli Aarpa.’ We see names like Mayilai and Mayilappur in the Periya Puranam. Palasubramania Mudaliar writes: The old temple was located where the Santhome Cathedral now stands. It was a well-known temple until the time of Arunagirinathar Peruman, around 1050 AD.

Arunagirinathar Peruman sang about the Mayilappur temple being on the seashore in his Thiruppugazh. In 1516, Mayilappur came under the control of the Portuguese. Within a few years, they demolished the temple and built a fort and their place of worship. The current temple must have been built in the current location before 1672. In that year, during a war between the French and the Moors, a part of the French army hid in the present temple. This is also pointed out by him.

When the Santhome Cathedral was renovated about forty years ago, stones and inscriptions from the old Shiva temple were found during excavation. Among them are the inscriptions recorded by the government in 1923, referred to as ‘those inscriptions.’ The note also states that these inscriptions were found here. The note is titled ‘Found on stone excavated below the Cathedral at Santhome.’ Now, Sivakavi Mani Desikar, under the heading ‘Festivals and Vratas mentioned in the Poombavai Pathigam,’ writes as follows: In this Thiruppathigam ...nine verses describe festivals. Among these, Karthigai Vilakkeedu, Thiruvadhirai, Thaipusam, Maasi Kadalaattu, and Panguni Uthiram are celebrated throughout Tamil Nadu.

Therefore, they were special in Mayilappur and are still celebrated specially. The festival of Aippasi Onam, celebrated by Sri Rama, is described in the Sanskrit Puranam, Chapter 9, verses 32, 33, and 34. It clearly states that the festival begins with flag hoisting on Aippasi Onam and the sacred bath on Krithigai. The Tamil Puranam states that the festival was conducted by Sri Rama, with the tenth day being the sacred bath. Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman, praising the splendor with which the Aippasi Onam festival was celebrated in a pure manner by the best of ascetics, says, ‘Do not miss seeing the Aippasi Onam festival and the feasting of the ascetics!’ Ashtami day is one of the eight Shiva vratas. It is observed on the Ashtami of the Vaikasi month’s Shukla Paksha.

Full details about this Ashtami vrata are elaborated in the Upadesa Kandam, in the Shiva Vrata Mahimya Sarukkam, verses 307 to 315. It is also known that Ashtami, two days in each fortnight, Amavasai, Purnami, and Aadhirai, were observed as Panchaparva festivals in Shiva temples.

However, it is most appropriate to consider the Ashtami in Vaikasi as referred to by Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman.

Now, the Potrapu festival mentioned by Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman is the Ponunjal festival. In many Shiva temples in the month of Margazhi, a swing festival is celebrated for three, seven, or ten days. This is called Dolotsavam in Sanskrit. During this festival, the Peruman and Piratti are placed on a swing, and verses like Ponunjal and Thiruvambavai are recited.

Next, the Perunsaanthi mentioned refers to the Pavithrotsavam, a festival celebrated with great splendor, including Shiva Yagam, for three, five, or seven days from Avani Avittam. This festival is celebrated in all Shiva temples with sufficient income. In Mayilai, it is celebrated with great splendor for three days. It is essential to perform this Pavithrotsavam according to Agama rules to purify the defects that occur in daily and occasional pujas throughout the year, both accomplished and unaccomplished. Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman refers to this as Perunsaanthi. Some interpret Perunsaanthi as Kumbhabhishekam.

Thus conclude the commentaries. Let us resume our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Deivashekkilar Peruman’s Periya Puranam, Part 809, Vambara Vadivandru Srekkum Thirugnanasambandhanayanar Puranam. Poombavai emerges there as a twelve-year-old maiden. We saw how the Shiva devotees and everyone else rejoiced at this, and how the followers of other religions stumbled and fell.

Now, Deivashekkilar Peruman, from verse 2993 to 3006, in fourteen verses, describes the divine rebirth of Poombavai, the miraculous resurrection, and the aesthetic beauty of her limbs, with great detail. In verse 3007, it is said that Pillaiyar, seeing with a thousand faces, saw the boundless compassion of Shiva, the compassionate eye, as the river of compassion of Shiva. Deivashekkilar Peruman says ...that Pillaiyar saw the compassion of Shiva as the river of compassion.

Thus, Deivashekkilar Peruman shows us this divine vision of Poombavai, who was seen by Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman as the embodiment of Shiva’s grace. While many poets often describe women with their illusory bodies, focusing on sensuality, Deivashekkilar Peruman, who lived a life of great Shiva devotion and authored only the Periya Puranam, had a different nature and tradition. We see that in the Periya Puranam, when describing young girls and mature women, Deivashekkilar Peruman, according to the context of the story, appropriately conveys their adornments in a general manner. This is his tradition. Because describing the physical characteristics of unmarried maidens can arouse sensuality and harm purity. Describing married women in such a way becomes a sin, praising the appearance of other men’s wives.

Therefore, both these sins are often found in the poems of other poets who write secular literature. However, in the Periya Puranam, which tells the glory of the devotees of Shiva, this Puranam, which narrates the Shiva virtues, the Shiva dharma, and the abundance of Shiva’s grace, our Deivashekkilar Peruman has maintained the tradition of conveying them only in a general manner. We see that Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman sees Poombavai as the embodiment of Shiva’s grace, and Deivashekkilar Peruman, to show us this vision, has written thus. Regarding the previous birth of Poombavai ...we can recall Deivashekkilar Peruman’s tradition of mentioning Poombavai in one or two verses. Those are different.

However, the tradition of highlighting Poombavai in these fourteen verses is different. The body mentioned earlier, which was described in one or two verses from her previous birth, where she grew up to the age of seven, was created by Brahma according to Shiva’s will. That body was an illusory form bound by worldly attachments.

But the limbs of Poombavai being described now, this body that has been reborn, is a divine creation, an embodiment of Shiva’s command, untouched by worldly or illusory attachments, a sacred form that has been reborn. These show us the results of Shiva Peruman’s compassion.

Therefore, describing these amounts to praising the boundless compassion of Shiva Peruman.

Thus, Deivashekkilar Peruman says that Pillaiyar, as the compassionate eye Peruman, saw the river of Shiva’s compassion with a thousand faces, not like Brahma admiring the beauty of his creation.

Therefore, we must understand and contemplate the difference and significance between the previous ways of description and the current way. We must also remember that Deivashekkilar Peruman does not describe in this manner anywhere else. The literary beauty, such as the use of metaphors, found in these verses, is something to be learned from great scholars.

Therefore, unlike other Thiruppathigams, Sivakavi Mani Desikar has provided only a compilation and brief commentary for these verses. The fourteen Thiruppadals are as follows: The verse beginning with ‘Kanni than vanappu’ (thousand nine hundred and fifth verse) describes the divine vision of Poombavai’s tresses, as depicted by Deivashekkilar Peruman. ‘Kanni than vanappu thannai kangalal mudiya kaanaar, Munnura kandarkku ellam moigarum kuzhalin paaram, Manniya vadhana senthamarinil kariya vandu, Thuniya ozhunguthu kuzhal pol irundu thondra.’ In this verse, Deivashekkilar Peruman refers to Poombavai as ‘Kanni’ (maiden). Poombavai remains a maiden until now and will continue to be a maiden.

Therefore, to indicate that she will remain a maiden throughout her life, the compilation of these verses refers to her as ‘Kanni.’ The festival is celebrated with great splendor for eleven days. This is what Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman refers to when he sings, ‘Panguni Uthira naal oli vizha kaanaathe poothiyo Poombavai.’ Now, the eighth verse: ‘Thannaa arakkan thol saithukandha thaalinaar, Kannaar Mayilai Kapaleeswaram amarnthan, Pannaa pathinganangal tham attaminaal...’ Sezhilar Peruman begins. The maiden Poombavai stands as if she had arisen from a lotus that bloomed after a pot broke. They stand there unable to fully behold the beauty of the maiden Poombavai with their eyes. To those who had seen her only to the extent their eyes could encompass, the state that appeared was as if a swarm of dark bees closely gathered and circled around the dense, dark tresses of Poombavai, resembling a lotus flower.

Now, the divine Sezhilar Peruman describes her forehead. Adorned with fragrant garlands, her radiant forehead, which rivals the beauty of a lotus, appears as if a lightning strike of a curved rainbow, placed beneath the clouds to bestow beauty upon the creeper-like maiden, is emitting abundant radiance. When one beholds the radiance of the beautiful, fragrant forehead adorned with a tilak, worn by the creeper-like Poombavai, it appears as if a bright, luminous rainbow is placed beneath the clouds, showering beauty upon the creeper-like maiden.

Now, he describes the eyebrows of Poombavai. The slender creeper-like eyebrows are like two great bows that have arisen before the eyes, appearing as if one is the bow of Kama, the god of love, that arises in battle, and the other is a protective bow, as if they have appeared from the forehead of Lord Shiva, who burned Tripura, whose single eye of fire had turned them to ash, and who later granted grace, making him capable of receiving grace, and also a bow of Kama that arises in battle and a protective bow. They appear as if they have arisen, embodying the qualities of those two great bows.

Now, he describes her eyes. The beautiful, luminous eyes, red like polished gems, appear like two swift fish, their dark, slender forms mingled with reddish hues, swimming in the expanse of moonlight cast by the radiant moon-like face, as if to ward off the light.

Now, he describes Poombavai’s nose and mouth. The nose and coral-like mouth of the maiden, whose form is like a creeper that blooms with dew, appear to those who seek to behold their beauty in the intense radiance, as if the Kamarupi, the Indra Gopa beetle, has descended, its beautiful colors darkening to attract and capture the red, jewel-toned beetle. The maiden, whose form is like a creeper, with a nose and coral-like mouth, standing near each other and appearing with great radiance, appears to those who behold it as if the Kamarupi, the Indra Gopa beetle, a jewel-red insect, has descended to attract and capture the red beetle. The nose and coral mouth appear as if the Kamarupi has arrived.

Now, he describes Poombavai’s ears. The ears of the maiden, who resembles a young peacock and is adorned with fine ornaments, are adorned with dangling jewels. They appear like two victorious banners of Kama, the god of love, due to their graceful form, their rich ornamentation, and their dazzling beauty, which resembles the Makara emblem, and they shine with unparalleled grace. They appear like two victorious banners of Kama. They shine like two victorious banners of Kama, the god of love, due to their graceful form, their rich ornamentation, and their dazzling beauty, which resembles the Makara emblem, and they possess unparalleled grace.

Now, he describes Poombavai’s neck and face. The neck, adorned with luminous pearl necklaces, appears as if it is the great treasure of a conch shell, which gave rise to the lotus treasure, and the face atop it is luminous. These appear as an indication of the great grace bestowed by Lord Shiva, the blue-necked one, whose throat was dark with poison.

Now, he describes Poombavai’s hands. They appear as if she has arranged tender Kanthal flowers, which bloom like fire, and is gently pressing them together in a cluster. It appears as if it is a garland of victory made of flowers, or perhaps a garland of celestial red flowers. Looking closely, it seems as if the radiance of her body has overflowed on both sides. The hands appear thus, astonishingly.

Now, he describes Poombavai’s breasts. The full breasts on her chest, which are like pots of nectar, appear to be filled and brimming with the ambrosia of grace from the benevolent gaze of the Pillaiyar, the sage who removes the poison of the serpent, as if they are adorned with the nectar of grace. The breasts, swelling on her chest, appear as if they are pots of nectar, brimming with the ambrosia of grace from the benevolent gaze of the Pillaiyar, the sage who removes the poison of the serpent.

Now, he describes her navel and the line of hair. The line of hair extending upwards from the navel of the creeper-like Poombavai, adorned with a beautiful girdle, appears as if Kama, the hunter, is hidden in the navel and has raised a spear-like string of pearls to capture the chakravaka birds that are her breasts. It appears as if a spear-like string of pearls, held in straight hands, has been raised.

Now, he describes her private parts. The private parts of the maiden, whose tresses are like flowers and who is like nectar, adorned with golden ornaments, appear as if the great serpent Adisesha, who rules the serpent world, has spread its hood in fear of being bitten by the maiden, and is surrounded by a girdle of eight strings of red jewels, appearing beautiful and spread out. It appears as if the thighs of the creeper-like maiden, who resembles a peacock, are more beautiful than the legs of a young elephant and the tender stalk of a banana. The beauty of her slender knees, which are soft and full of grace, appears like a golden ball, shining brightly and overflowing.

Now, he describes her calves and ankles. The calves of the golden creeper-like maiden, whose tresses are like flowers, appear as beautiful as Kama’s quiver of arrows. The ankles, surpassing the beauty of a golden platter, shine brightly and are like a canvas for painters. The calves appear as beautiful as Kama’s quiver of arrows. The ankles, surpassing the beauty of a golden platter, shine brightly and are like a canvas for painters.

Now, he describes Poombavai’s feet. Her beautiful feet, like clusters of flowers blooming from the Kalpaka tree, radiating the brilliance of red coral and adorned with golden circles and diamond patterns, appear as if they are a divine vision. This earth and the heavens, and all other worlds, marvelously appear, making her the ornament of beauty.

Thus, in these fourteen verses, divine Sezhilar Peruman. reveals the divine beauty of Poombavai, who blossomed as a creation of Shiva. The twelfth verse concludes with ‘She stood as an ornament.’ We can combine all these verses and understand them. When the hymn was completed, Poombavai, who was twelve years old, arose from a pot filled with bones and ashes, like a maiden emerging from a lotus. Her beauty was so immense that it could not be fully perceived by the eyes at once; it was limited to what could be seen. The weight of her hair, like a swarm of bees circling her lotus-like face, appeared as if a rainbow was placed beneath the clouds. Her eyebrows, like creepers, appeared as if they were burned by Shiva’s forehead eye and then, like the bow of Kama arising in battle and a protective bow, they appeared.

They appeared like the bow of Kama that arises in battle and a protective bow, as if her eyes, like two swift fish, swam in the expanse of moonlight cast by the moon-like face. Her nose and coral-like mouth appeared as if the Kamarupi was descending to attract the Indra Gopa beetle. Her Makara-shaped ears appeared like Kama’s victorious banners. Her neck, surrounded by pearl necklaces, appeared like the great treasure of a conch shell, which gave rise to the lotus treasure, as a symbol of Shiva’s grace. Her hands appeared as if she had arranged tender Kanthal flowers in a garland of victory, or as if the radiance of her body had overflowed on both sides. Her breasts appeared like pots of nectar, filled with the ambrosia from the benevolent gaze of the Pillaiyar, who removes poison.

The line of hair extending upwards from her navel appeared as if Kama, the hunter, hidden in the navel, had raised a spear-like string of pearls to capture the chakravaka birds that are her breasts. It appears as if a spear-like string of pearls, held in straight hands, has been raised. Her golden private parts, adorned with ornaments, appear as if Adisesha has spread its hood in fear of being bitten, surrounded by a girdle of red jewels. Her thighs appear like the hands of a young elephant and the stalk of a banana. Her knees appear like golden balls. Her calves appear like Kama’s quiver of arrows.

Her ankles appear like a golden platter. Her feet appear like clusters of flowers blooming from the Kalpaka tree, radiating the brilliance of red coral and adorned with golden circles and diamond patterns. The three worlds marvelously appeared, making her the ornament of beauty. This is the essence of the fourteen verses.

Let us press on with our contemplation. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Great Puranam of divine Sezhilar, Part 810. The Chapter of the Swarming Varivandhu. The Puranam of ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar. Divine Sezhilar Peruman composes the 1109th verse. The concluding verse states: ‘The creator Brahma, who lived for countless years, beheld the beauty of the woman he created, Tilotama, with his four faces.

The glorious king, revered for sixteen years, saw her, who is better than even that, with a thousand faces of divine grace.’ This is the verse. Lord Brahma has a lifespan of countless years. He created the woman Tilotama and admired her beauty with his four faces. A woman even better than Tilotama.
