The first time, the nature of the Ambal and the great unique dance he witnessed, and how he beheld and worshipped it, was explained by the great teacher Deivasekhilar. The perfection of this third vision of the dance of eternal bliss is clearly explained here.

“Deivasekhilar. He continues to sing. The 1341st verse states: “Having attained that state and reveling in it, he circumambulated the golden Ambal and came out to the street adorned with golden mansions. Singing devotional verses with sweet music daily, he worshipped and resided there peacefully.” Having attained that state and immersed in the experience, he circumambulated the steadfast Thiruchitrambalam and came out to the street adorned with golden mansions, where he resided peacefully. During his stay, Thirugnanasambandhar, singing devotional verses daily, worshipped and lived peacefully.

“At this time, his father, Sivapatha Hridayar, and other Brahmins from Seerkazhi also came to Thiruchitrambalam to see Thirugnanasambandhar. We shall continue our contemplation.”” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Part 818, by Deivasekhilar. Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam. Thiru Gnana Sambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandhar is residing in Thillai.

At this time, Sivapatha Hridayar and other Brahmins from Seerkazhi, hearing the news that Pillaiyar is in Thillai, come to Thillai. Deivasekhilar composes the 1342nd verse as follows: “Sivapatha Hridayar, the father of Thirugnanasambandhar, and the Brahmins and ascetics of the glorious Seerkazhi, who are praised by the great Vishnu and Brahma, having heard that they have arrived in Perumpatra Puliyur, came and joined them. Sivapatha Hridayar, the father of Thirugnanasambandhar, is referred to by Deivasekhilar in this verse as Sivapa. tha Hridayar. The meaning is that Sivapatha Hridayar, who possesses the virtue of reforming the world, is the father. The world is reformed by him because he rejects heretical faiths and upholds Saivism and the glory of Thiruneeru (sacred ash) in its true form. This is the state of the world’s reformation.

“Sivapatha Hridayar performed penance, desiring a child, with two objectives: one, to enjoy marital bliss, and two, to reform the world by rejecting heretical faiths.

“Thus, he was blessed with Thirugnanasambandhar as his son.

“Thus, he became the father. We must remember that it was previously stated that he attained the title of father through great penance. Of the two intentions of Sivapatha Hridayar, the greater benefit was the reformation of the world, which he considered foremost.

“Therefore, he was instrumental in the divine incarnation of Thirugnanasambandhar.

“Thus, Thirugnanasambandhar, having incarnated and completed his pilgrimages to Pandiya Nadu and Thondai Nadu, and having achieved all those benefits, the world and all of Tamil Nadu now flourish in perfection. This is the history of Thirugnanasambandhar so far.

“Similarly, the marriage of Thirugnanasambandhar and his merging with the divine feet of the Lord. and becoming one with Him are the remaining histories. This is a duty that a father must fulfill for his son.

“Therefore, that history is yet to unfold. Deivasekhilar, encompassing all these ideas, refers to him as “Sivapatha Hridayar, the father of Thirugnanasambandhar,” bestowing an epithet upon him.

“Similarly, the Brahmins from Seerkazhi, who are also mentioned, are referred to by Deivasekhilar as “Pugalipusurar and Mathavar.” The meaning is that they are conducive to his growth. The Pusalir, the Brahmins residing in Pugalipuri (Seerkazhi), why are they referred to as “Pugunthiruvazhgalipusurar” by Deivasekhilar? They are the ones who possess the qualities befitting their union with the Lord at the time of Thirugnanasambandhar’s marriage.

“Therefore, they are the “Pugunthiruvazhgalipusurar.” Next are the “Mathavar,” who are the devotees of Shiva. Shiva puja itself is considered penance. Mathavam refers to excelling in the four paths of Saivism: Sariyai, Kriyai, Yoga, and Gnana. Those who adhere to these paths are considered “Mathavar,” the devotees of Shiva.

“Thus, Sivapatha Hridayar, the Brahmins of Seerkazhi, and the devotees of Shiva, having heard that the great Tamil scholar, Pillaiyar, has arrived in Perumpatra Puliyur (Thillai), are also coming to Thillai. Deivasekhilar refers to him as “Tamil Agarar.” “Agaram” means place.

“Therefore, “Tamil Agarar” means one who is the place of Tamil. Hearing that Pillaiyar, the Tamil Agarar, has arrived in Thillai, they too have arrived. Although they knew that Pillaiyar would soon return to Seerkazhi after visiting Thondai Nadu, they could not bear to be separated from him and came to receive him. This shows the unbreakable bond between the Brahmins of Seerkazhi and the devotees of Shiva with Thirugnanasambandhar. These same Brahmins had previously, when Thirugnanasambandhar visited Thiruvelimillai, sent Sivapatha Hridayar to Seerkazhi, requesting him to come to Seerkazhi. They were the ones who sent him to Thiru Alavai temple to see Pillaiyar.

“And now, due to the same unbreakable affection, the Brahmins of Seerkazhi and the devotees of Shiva have come to Thillai to worship Pillaiyar and to worship the Ambale Koothar (dancer) along with Pillaiyar. The 1343rd verse states: “Seeing him there, and with great affection, they worshipped the Lord of Thillai, the one with matted locks adorned with Konrai flowers.” Having seen them there, Thirugnanasambandhar, with a radiant face and sweet words, addresses them. Along with them, with unwavering affection. Thillai Brahmins, who have an insatiable desire, have also come to worship the Lord’s Thiruchitrambalam.

“Thus, when Thirugnanasambandhar comes to worship the Ambale Koothar in Thillai, his father Sivapatha Hridayar, the Brahmins of Seerkazhi, the devotees of Seerkazhi, and the Brahmins of Thillai all go together to the golden Ambalam, the Thiruchitrambalam, which is Gnanaakasam, to worship the feet of the dancer. They worship there.

“The Brahmins of South Pugali and the Brahmins of Thillai, praising the feet of the Lord who has enhanced the path of love, and receiving the grace of the dancer with golden matted locks, come to worship the one who resides in the blessed Thoni. Along with the divine attendants who dance, they worship the sacred threshold of the golden city and proceed to other sacred places where the bull-emblemed Lord resides, and finally reach the learned ones’ sacred Kazhumalam, which is Seerkazhi. This is stated in verses 1344 and 1345. Deivasekhilar says that the beautiful Brahmins of Seerkazhi and the Brahmins of Thillai praise the feet of the Lord, who has enhanced the path of love. Having taken leave of the dancer with matted locks, Thirugnanasambandhar now intends to worship the Lord residing in the divine Thoni in Seerkazhi. He will depart from Thillai, accompanied by a congregation of virtuous devotees, and worship the sacred threshold of Thillai, where the Lord performs His divine dance, and then proceed.

“Having proceeded thus, Thirugnanasambandhar visits all the sacred places where the Lord resides and heads towards the sacred city of Seerkazhi. The southern boundary of Thiruchitrambalam is the northern bank of the Kollidam river, which is the southern boundary of Thiruchitrambalam. Having worshipped it, he proceeds from Thillai to Seerkazhi. While traveling, he visits all the temples in between. There is a route to visit Thiru Naraiyur after leaving Thillai to go to Seerkazhi. If he does not visit Thiru Naraiyur, he will proceed directly from Thillai to Seerkazhi.

“There is also a route that passes through places like Thiru Mahendrapalli and Thiru Kurukavoor.

“Thus, Thirugnanasambandhar, while traveling from Thillai to Seerkazhi, visits all the temples and reaches the sacred city of Seerkazhi, which is praised by the learned. Seerkazhi. As the sacred city of Seerkazhi appears in the distance to Thirugnanasambandhar, he worships Seerkazhi and sings pathigams. Deivasekhilar describes this in the following three verses: 1346, 1347, and 1348. Having passed through many sacred places, and upon seeing the distant Seerkazhi, which is endowed with twelve names, he alights from his gem-like palanquin, welcomes it, and sings a pathigam on the prosperous city. The pathigam begins with “Vandar Kuzhal Arivai” and ends with “Minnum Sudar Maligai Vintanguvol.” He sings this melodious song and enters the ancient city.

“This is stated in the verses. Having passed through many sacred places, he reaches the outskirts of the sacred city of Seerkazhi. Upon seeing the external area, Thirugnanasambandhar sings pathigams on the sacred city of Seerkazhi, which possesses twelve names. Deivasekhilar says that in the first four verses of the pathigam, which speaks of the twelve names of Seerkazhi, it mentions Thirkkalam, Poontharai, Venuppuram, Puravam, and Kali. He sings two pathigams on the sacred city of Seerkazhi, which he beholds from outside. The pathigam beginning with “Vandar Kuzhal Arivai,” which has a steadfast melody, and the pathigam with the concept of “Vintanguvol,” meaning like it supports the sky, are sung.

“The pathigam beginning with “Vintanguvol” is sung with the concept that the mansions of Venuppuram are also like that. This sacred place is known as Venuppuram. The Lord, who came from the Venu lineage, hid himself in Venu, and after Indra gained fame, he protected him and then restored his dominion over the celestial world. This is the history of Thiruvezhuppuram, which is Seerkazhi. This pathigam speaks of the prosperity of the celestials. The next pathigam speaks of the prosperity of kings.

“It is stated that near the flourishing Purambanai, where the wind carries the fragrance of Punnnai flowers, fragrant with incense and lamps, he completes the pathigam by saying, “Chermin” (join), and enters the fortified ancient city. The pathigam concludes with “Chermin Kali Nagar” (Join the city of Kali).

“Thus, after passing through many sacred places, he reaches the outskirts of the sacred city of Seerkazhi. Upon seeing this external area, Thirugnanasambandhar, who is adorned with twelve names, descends from his palanquin and sings pathigams on the prosperous city of Seerkazhi. The pathigam “Pannirupēr Padaithatholvalai” speaks of the antiquity and prosperity of Seerkazhi. Deivasekhilar describes this. In the two pathigams sung by Pillaiyar here, namely “Vintanguvol” and “Nalangol Kazhi Sermine,” both are dedicated to the sacred city of Seerkazhi. The pathigam begins with the concept of “Vintanguvol,” as if supporting the sky.

“The next pathigam speaks of the prosperity of kings. At that time, Thirugnanasambandhar sings many devotional pathigams with melody. Unfortunately, due to our lack of devotion, we do not have access to the pathigams sung by Thirugnanasambandhar on this occasion. After singing these pathigams, his eyes overflowing with tears of joy, he received the abundant grace of the Lord adorned with serpents and came out. Accompanied by devotees, he proceeded to the great mansion of Pillaiyar, the noble one of Seerkazhi. Upon entering the mansion. He blessed the Brahmins and his extended family who bowed down to him.

He sat with his divine servants, and the 1352nd verse states: “He bestowed grace upon the Brahmins, and his extended family, who bowed down to him, and sat with his divine servants, experiencing unending bliss.” Thirugnanasambandhar, having entered his mansion, sends away the Brahmins who came to see him, granting them his grace. These Brahmins, hearing that Pillaiyar was in Thillai, went there, worshipped him, and then came to Seerkazhi to join Pillaiyar. He first sends them away with his blessings.

Next, his extended family, who have come to behold Thirugnanasambandhar and bow down to him, are also granted his grace. These relatives, from places like Seerkazhi and Thiru Nannippalli, surrounded Pillaiyar. Deivasekhilar refers to them as the “extended family” because they were blessed by Pillaiyar.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandhar sends away the Brahmins and the relatives, granting them his grace. However, the devotees of Shiva, who are always with Thirugnanasambandhar, are the great ones.

Therefore, after sending away the other two groups, Thirugnanasambandhar sits with the devotees of Shiva. The joy experienced by being with the devotees is the Sivānanda that transcends this world.

Therefore, Deivasekhilar refers to it as “unending bliss that grows.” “Unending” means continuously growing without limit. “Greatly increasing” means increasing more and more.

Thus, the nature of the great bliss of Sivānanda experienced in the company of devotees is described. On that day, when Thirugnanasambandhar was residing there, the devotees, including Thiru Muruganayanar, Thiru Neelanakkayanar, and others, who wished to worship the feet of the Lord of Kaalinaadu, came to Seerkazhi with a desire greater than the ocean, worshipped Thiru Thoni Puram, and approached Pillaiyar. This is described in the following verse, 1353, by Deivasekhilar. “The Lord of Kaali Naadu, along with Thiru Muruganayanar, Thiru Neelanakkayanar, and other devotees, surrounded by a large retinue, worshipped Thoni Puram and arrived with immense love, a love greater than the ocean.” The desire that brought them is a desire that grows greater than the ocean. As the Thirukkural states, “The help rendered by the selfless is greater than the ocean if its merit is considered.” The rejection of heretical faiths by Pillaiyar and the establishment of Thiruneeru’s glory, which he rendered selflessly, have a merit greater than the ocean.

Therefore, the devotees, worshipping Pillaiyar with great love, have come.

Thus, their desire has become greater than the ocean. Thiru Muruganayanar, Thiru Neelanakkayanar, and other devotees, along with their retinues, have arrived there. Thiru Neelanakkayanar and Thiru Muruganayanar are among the sixty-three Nayanmars. “The Lord of Kaali Naadu, along with Thiru Muruganayanar, Thiru Neelanakkayanar, and other devotees, surrounded by a large retinue, worshipped Thoni Puram and arrived with immense love, a love greater than the ocean.” The desire that brought them is a desire that grows greater than the ocean. When the devoted souls arrived there, mentioning their sacred names, the great God Deivachchegilar states that these and other Siva devotees gathered there.

Moreover, to Thiruneelanakka Nayanar, the great God Deivachchegilar bestows the special epithet ‘Vaazhi Thiruneelanakkar’. This is because the marriage of Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman is about to take place, and it was Thiruneelakka Nayanar who had the fortune to perform the wedding rituals and receive blessings.

Therefore, Deivachchegilar Peruman refers to him as ‘Vaazhi Thiruneelanakkar’. All of them, along with their relatives, come to Thiruthonipuram, worship the Lord of Thonipuram, and then come to worship Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman. All these individuals are destined to witness the marriage of Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman and receive the special grace of participating in it.

Therefore, they arrive with immense eagerness, greater than the ocean. They arrive with immense eagerness, greater than the ocean. The hint is that the state of entering into Siva-bhoga, the bliss of Siva-jnana that overflows limitlessly, is now very close.

Thus, Deivachchegilar Peruman states, ‘with eagerness swelling beyond the ocean’.

Next, in two verses, the 1154th and 1155th, they welcome those who have arrived, rejoice, and respectfully sit with the devotees of the king of S’anbhaya, whose glory is endless. They sing many pathigams in classical Tamil, filled with great joy. Those who have attained them through great penance, along with the noble Brahmins of the great lineage, thinking, ‘This is the right time for the union of the Graceful Jnana Leader,’ inform him and approach. These are two verses. Welcoming the true devotees like Thirumurugan, Thiruneelanakka Nayanar, and others who have arrived, and also the others, with great joy in His heart, the leader of S’irkaazhi, Pillaiyar, joyfully resides with those noble devotees, and with the grace of Periyanayagi Ammaiyar, the abode of beauty, who resides in Thiru-thoni, He sings many pathigams in classical Tamil to Thoniyappar.

Thus, the pathigams sung on this occasion are not available to us due to our lack of penance. With great joy, Sivapadagiruthayar and the relatives of Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman, the Brahmins of his great lineage, gather. Having performed great penance, as a result of which they were blessed with Pillaiyar, the father Sivapadagiruthayar, along with his relatives, gather. The master of Jnana, who is conducive to the flourishing of liberation, Pillaiyar, Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman, thinking, ‘This is the right time for his marriage,’ convey their thoughts to Pillaiyar by coming to the place where Pillaiyar resides. According to Tamil tradition, the appropriate age for marriage for men is sixteen years. This is evident in works like the commentary on Iraiyanar Akapporul and Tolkappiyam.

Thus, they come to the place where Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman resides to inform him that the time has come. Sivapadagiruthayar and his relatives, in the 1156th verse, ‘O ancient Vedic tradition’, ‘To be united with the embodiment of Jnana, they decided. To perform many Vedic sacrifices according to the flawless Vedic path, they requested to be granted a virgin.’ This is the verse.

After the Brahmacharya ashram, the Grihastha ashram follows for the three varnas including the Brahmins.

Therefore, the Vedic path states, ‘After Brahmacharya, live in the Grihastha ashram.’ A Brahmachari is entitled only to Samithadhanam, not to Aubasanam. In the Grihastha ashram, to perform daily rituals like Aubasanam and occasional sacrifices like Kruthu, one must marry a virgin.

Therefore, among the ashrams prescribed in the Vedas, they intended to marry Pillaiyar to one for the Grihastha ashram.

The Brahmins approached Pillaiyar and requested him to marry a virgin to perform the Vedic sacrifices prescribed in the Vedas. In this verse, Deivachchegilar Peruman mentions, ‘O ancient Vedic tradition, to be united with the embodiment of Jnana, they decided.’ At this point, the Brahmins thought that the Vedic disciplines should be applied to Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman as well.

However, Deivachchegilar Peruman emphasizes that these disciplines are for ordinary people, not for Pillaiyar, who possesses complete Siva-jnana, stating, ‘To be united with the embodiment of Jnana.’ Deivachchegilar Peruman continues.

Next, the 1157th verse, is the verse where Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman gives His reply. ‘Hearing their words, He who is the crest of great penance, having attained the state of freedom from the bonds of worldly attachments, and having received the grace of Him who raised the bull, did not agree, saying it is not suitable. Though it is not yet complete, it is not advisable,’ He replied. This verse is thus composed. Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman listens to all the words of the Brahmins. He is the crest of great penance. Great penance is the supreme penance performed for Lord Siva.

The crest of great penance means the fruit born at the culmination of that great penance, which is gentle, cool, beautiful, and fruitful. This is a metaphor for the peak of the crop of penance, the part of the plant that reaches its summit. This is compared to the peak of the crop of penance, the part of the plant that reaches its summit. Siva Puja performed for Siva is called penance.

Here, ‘great penance’ also implies the meaning that He is the fruit of the great penance performed by Sivapadagiruthayar. Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman, who has attained the state of freedom from the overwhelming attachments of worldly ties that surround Him, is described by Deivachchegilar Peruman as ‘having attained the state of freedom from the bonds of worldly attachments.’ The Tiruvachagam, in the Pottri Thiru-agaval, states, ‘The ancient herds of cattle called relatives rush about and cause distress.’ Even up to this point, Pillaiyar lived detached from the worldly attachments called relatives.

However, the state He has now attained is one of detachment from the surrounding relatives. A complete state of detachment. Pillaiyar, who has already attained the complete Siva-jnana, the form of divine grace, does not naturally fit into the stages of ashrams prescribed for ordinary people.

Therefore, the state of fulfillment in Siva-ananda is beyond all these, even the fourth stage of Shakti-nipatha. However, Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman has already attained the complete Siva-jnana, the form of divine grace, which is the ultimate conclusion.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman did not agree to this. ‘Though it is complete, it is not suitable.’ ‘Even if one practices virtue through fame, attains the virtues of ashramic renunciation, performs arduous penances, and learns many arts, and studies the Vedas, and clearly understands the essence of the Vedas taught in the Puranas, one will attain the path of Saivism. Through the paths of Saygai, Kriya, and Yoga, one will reach the feet of Siva through Jnana.’ This is stated in the eighth sutra of Sivagnana Siddhi, second adikarana. Sivakavimani Desikan quotes this at this point.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman, without agreeing to the words of the Brahmins who have come there, says, ‘Your words are indeed appropriate, but that state is not suitable for me; it does not fit me.’ He replies, ‘Your words are in accordance with the Vedas, which were spoken by the all-knowing First Being. However, I do not agree to them.’ This is a situation of ‘agreeing and disagreeing.’ The disciplines prescribed for ordinary people are not suitable or applicable to those who have attained the state of Shakti-nipatha and are Sages of Siva-jnana.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman refuses. He refuses now, but later He agrees and blesses it. The reason will be explained later. There is another hidden meaning to His statement, ‘Though it is complete, it is not suitable.’ This marriage will indeed take place later, but it will not be for the purpose of performing sacrifices and household rituals as you think. It will be a great marriage, a union with Siva, not a worldly marriage. This inner meaning is also implied here.

The Great Puranam by Deivachchegilar Peruman, Volume 820, Vambaravarivandu Sarukkam, Life of Thirugnanasambandhar Nayanar. ‘This marriage is not suitable for me,’ said Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman. In response, the Brahmins, in the 1158th verse, ‘O noble Brahmins, they then joined their hands and informed Him. You have upheld the Vedic tradition in this world.

Therefore, according to the proper procedure, it is requested that you consider performing a marriage in accordance with the Vedic path of righteous actions.’ This verse is thus composed.

The Brahmins who were present joined their hands and submitted their request to Pillaiyar’s sacred feet. Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman’s words did not satisfy them.

Therefore, without being content with Pillaiyar’s response, they proceeded to state their request again, beginning humbly with folded hands.

The Brahmins, joining their hands and bowing to Pillaiyar, informed Him: ‘You have upheld the Vedic tradition in this great world.

Therefore, in accordance with the Vedic path, we request that you consider performing a marriage in accordance with the righteous Vedic conduct, which includes the six duties.’ The Brahmins said, ‘Thiru Gnanasambandha Peruman, you have elevated the Vedic tradition that had declined. You have revitalized the Vedic discipline. Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman has incarnated to ensure the flourishing of the Vedic path.

Therefore, as one of the ways to uphold the Vedic tradition, marriage is one.

Thus, we request you to perform a marriage. You have removed the harm and transgressions caused by other religions to the Vedic path.

Now, you must also show us how to live according to the Vedic path. The Vedas have prescribed six duties for Brahmins. You should reveal to the world how to perform these six duties.’ ‘We request this,’ they pleaded. The six duties prescribed by the Vedas for Brahmins are: learning, teaching, performing sacrifices, officiating sacrifices, giving charity, and receiving charity. In Sanskrit, these are called Adhyayanam, Adhyapanam, Yajanam, Yajanam, Daanam, and Prathigraham. Adhyayanam is learning the Vedas.

Adhyapanam is teaching the Vedas. Yajanam is performing sacrifices oneself. Yajanam is officiating sacrifices for others. Daanam is giving charity to others. Prathigraham is receiving charity.

Thus, the Vedas prescribe these six duties for Brahmins.

Therefore, Brahmins are called Shat- karmata-nirata. In Tamil, the term for Shatkarmata-nirata is ‘Arutolilor.’ Tolkappiyam also refers to this as ‘Aruvagaippatta Parppana Pakkam.’ Nachchinarkiniyar, who commented on this, describes these duties in detail.

Therefore, they request Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman to demonstrate the manner in which these six duties prescribed by the Vedas are performed.

The Brahmins who are present say, ‘You, who have removed the weeds that hindered the Vedic path, should also perform the act that cultivates the Vedic crop.’ They submit this request at the sacred feet of Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman. As the Brahmins gathered there submitted their request, the next verse, the 1159th, ‘May the Vedic way of life, and the tradition of Vedic righteousness of the Brahmins, flourish. May the relatives be blessed. Having agreed, He whose crown bears the crescent moon, and who wears snakes, the Lord of Karai, is worshipped with a joyful heart.’ This verse is thus composed. To enable the Vedic way of life and the flourishing of righteousness derived from the Vedic tradition of the Brahmins, He blesses the relatives and agrees to their request. Previously, Pillaiyar had refused, stating that this marriage was not suitable for His state.

But now, He agrees. What is the reason? What reason did the Brahmins give first for Pillaiyar to get married? They said that Pillaiyar should perform many sacrifices, and therefore, He needed to marry a virgin. They made their request based on Pillaiyar’s unique nature.

However, Pillaiyar, standing in the state of supreme Jnana, felt that He was not obligated or bound to perform sacrifices for Himself.

Therefore, He refused at that time.

Now, for the second time, the Brahmins make their request differently. ‘We ask you, Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman, to get married. We are not asking for your sake. You have incarnated to uplift and elevate the Vedic traditions.

Therefore, from the perspective of your spiritual guidance, you should uphold the Vedic traditions and the six duties of the Vedic path, demonstrate them, and help the Vedic path to take root and flourish,’ they request.

Now, Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman agrees. This is not for His own sake, but for the flourishing of the Vedas and the discipline of the six duties of the Vedic Brahmins. ‘Let us undertake this,’ Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman agrees. Even after agreeing, during the wedding ceremony, the worldly life surrounded Him. ‘Even with her, who is inseparable from Him, He will merge with the eternal Siva.’ As such, driven by overflowing devotion, He performed the act of union with the divine.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman’s life story states. Even after agreeing to marry, Pillaiyar merges with Siva during the wedding. Why is this so? Deivachchegilar Peruman will explain this later in the verse.

Therefore, we can see it there. As Pillaiyar agreed, the Brahmins present worship the Lord. They believe that Pillaiyar’s agreement is the result of the Lord’s divine will and worship Him.

The Lord has the moon, the Ganges, the snake, and the blue throat. All these have contrary natures.

Therefore, the request of the relatives and Pillaiyar’s initial refusal followed by agreement are indicative that the historical events that will unfold hereafter will also be similar.

Thus, Deivachchegilar Peruman praises the Lord Siva in this verse. The praise of Lord Siva by Deivachchegilar Peruman in this verse.

Next, the 1160th verse: ‘Having received the consent with immense joy, they returned. They reached Kazhumulam, the city of flowers, and began the marriage ceremony for the glorious Pillaiyar, as promised.

The Brahmins and their father, who had received the grace of God, rejoiced with indescribable happiness, realizing it was the grace of the divine.’ This verse states that although Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman had attained transcendent Siva-jnana, He agreed to follow worldly customs. For this agreement, the Brahmins of S’irkaazhi and Sivapadagiruthayar, the father of Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman, received immeasurable blessings. They believed this to be the grace of the Lord and rejoiced with heartfelt happiness.

Next, two verses, 1161 and 1162: ‘The excellent Brahmins of unstained glory, in accordance with their noble lineage, and with the Lord’s great marriage, Nambiyandar Nambi of Tirupperumanam, the Lord of Kailasa, took His hand. It was fitting for His greatness. Thirugnanasambandhar, whose glory increases, will marry.

The devotees and the Brahmins will come with great affection. The esteemed daughter will speak. The father of Nallur, who resides in Thannpanai, is present.’ These two verses are about Pillaiyar agreeing.

Now, preparations for the wedding begin. Sivapada Hirudayar and the Brahmins of S’irkaazhi. Near S’irkaazhi is the holy place Tirupperumanallur, which is now called Aachchapurm. Nambandar Nambi, a great man, resides in Tirupperumanallur. He was born in a lineage of flawless Brahmins. Deivachchegilar Peruman refers to him as ‘Ethamil seer maraiyavar’ (Brahmins of flawless lineage).

Etham means blemish. Etham maraiyavar means Brahmins without blemish. This refers to the lineage of Brahmins. It is implied here that there are also blemished lineages among Brahmins. Some lineages of Brahmins might have been excluded due to certain curses.

However, he was born in a lineage of flawless Brahmins. Nambandar Nambi’s blessed daughter is a suitable bride for the leader of S’irkaazhi, Pillaiyar. They thought she was worthy of His greatness. Sivapadagiruthayar and the Brahmins of S’irkaazhi consider this. Ethamil seer maraiyavaril etra kulam means a lineage suitable for marriage, with appropriate gotras, pravaras, and sub-divisions, which are well-matched. Nambandar Nambi is the father of the bride of Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman.

They thought that Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman should take the hand of the daughter of Nambandar Nambi. They thought it was appropriate. ‘To take the hand’ means to marry. This is called Panigrahanam in Sanskrit. The great life of the wedding of Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman, filled with glory, will be celebrated by the devotees and the Brahmins, along with their large retinue. They go to Thannpanai Nallur, also called Tiruaachchapuram and Tirupperumanallur. The 1163rd verse: ‘The great devotees and the Brahmins together went to Tirupperumanallur, which resonates with glory in all directions.

Hearing this, the esteemed Nambandar Nambi, worshipping the sacred feet of Him with matted locks, rose up.’ Thus, with the devotees and the Brahmins accompanying Him, they reach Tirupperumanallur, where the greatness of the land resounds in all directions. Hearing of their arrival, Nambandar Nambi worships the sacred feet of Lord Siva and rises. He believes this to be the divine grace of Lord Siva. Nambandar Nambi, the great man, worships the Lord’s sacred feet. Nambandar Nambi, the great man, worships the Lord’s sacred feet.

Next, the 1164th verse: ‘With overwhelming joy, he welcomed them. With full pots and lamps adorning the decorations, and with a great retinue, he greeted them, saying, ‘I have attained all that is to be attained.’ This verse describes Nambandar Nambi, with unparalleled joy swelling within him, making excellent arrangements for their reception. He welcomes them with full pots and lamps, adorning the streets. He welcomes the devotees and the Brahmins who have come due to their connection with Pillaiyar. The scriptures state that one must attain the four purusharthas – dharma, artha, kama, and moksha – through a systematic path. Nambandar Nambi, with great joy, proclaims, ‘I have attained Moksha, the highest of all purusharthas, liberation from the cycle of birth and death.’ Nambandar Nambi proclaims, ‘I have attained Moksha, the highest of all purusharthas, liberation from the cycle of birth and death.’ Let us go on contemplating. Thiruchitrambalam.

Nambandar Nambi makes excellent arrangements for the reception. The 1165th verse: ‘Welcoming them, they reached the splendid mansion and spoke many sweet words.

The Brahmins of S’anbai, who are superior to Chaturmukha, and the mature, wise devotees, described the situation.’ This verse states that Nambandar Nambi, after welcoming the devotees and the Brahmins of S’irkaazhi, led them to the mansion and offered them a warm welcome. He spoke many sweet words and provided hospitality, including feasts, according to custom. Sivapadagiruthayar, one of the Brahmins of S’irkaazhi, is a Brahmin superior to Brahma. He possesses virtues such as learning the Vedas and excelling in Vedic disciplines. Although Brahma, the Chaturmukha, creates many beings by reciting the Vedas, he too is subject to the cycle of birth.

However, Sivapadagiruthayar, through his penance, begot Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman alone, and thus attained liberation from the cycle of rebirth.

Therefore, Nambandar Nambi welcomes and honors Sivapadagiruthayar, a Brahmin superior to Chaturmukha Brahma. He also welcomes and honors the devotees and other Brahmins who are wise and knowledgeable.

At that time, the devotees and the other Brahmins describe the reason for their arrival. What they said is described in the 1166th verse: ‘To seek the hand of your unstained daughter, for the sake of the embodiment of Jnana, through the excellent discipline of penance, they said. The great happiness of receiving this noble lineage is a testament to your greatness.’ This verse states that the devotees and the Brahmins are here to seek the hand of your unstained daughter, for the sake of the embodiment of Jnana, through excellent penance. Those who negotiate marriages are usually very mature and wise individuals. They begin the conversation thus. They have come to ask for the bride.

It is customary to first describe the groom’s qualities. Following this tradition, the Brahmins say: ‘For the embodiment of Jnana.’ They speak of Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman, the groom. The name ‘Jnana Pothagar’ itself encompassed His lineage, family, status, character, and virtues throughout the land.

Therefore, they refer to Him simply as ‘Jnana Pothagar’ without any further epithets. ‘For such Thirugnanasambandhar, who possesses great penance and sweet discipline, we have come to seek the hand of your unstained daughter.’ After describing the groom’s qualities, they proceed to describe the bride’s qualities. Sivapadagiruthayar and others describe her as: ‘Your daughter, who possesses great penance and sweet discipline and unstained virtue.’ Upon hearing this, Nambandar Nambi says, ‘This honor of you coming here is due to the grace you have shown me, not because of my own merit.’ Nambandar Nambi, with great joy, says to Sivapadagiruthayar: ‘This honor of you coming to ask for my daughter in marriage is not because of our merit, but because of the grace you have bestowed upon me.’ Nambandar Nambi replies with joy. The 1167th verse states: ‘By your great penance, we offer our family’s jewel, the bride, to Him who has drunk the nectar of divine wisdom from the breast of the Mother who gave birth to the worlds. Come!’ he said, and sent them away with great joy. Nambandar Nambi says, ‘By your great penance’ – meaning, he says to Sivapadagiruthayar – ‘O Sivapadagiruthayar, by your great penance, we offer our family’s jewel, the bride, to Him who has drunk the nectar of divine wisdom from the breast of Mother Uma, who gave birth to the worlds. Come!’ he says with great joy.

Generally, parents decide to marry their daughter to a groom. They do so with the reason that the groom’s family will be elevated through this marriage. The Smritis state that by marrying their daughter into a good family, that family will be elevated.

But here, Nambandar Nambi says, ‘We offer her so that we may be saved; we give her for our salvation.’ This implies that as a result of this bestowal of the bride, Nambandar Nambi, his relatives, and indeed the whole world will be saved and attain liberation. With this inner meaning, Nambandar Nambi speaks thus. Having said this, he bids farewell to Sivapadagiruthayar, the devotees of Siva, and the Brahmins of S’irkaazhi, and sends them back to S’irkaazhi to attend to the necessary arrangements. Nambandar Nambi.

Next, the 1168th verse: ‘Having received the consent with great joy, they returned. Reaching Kazhumulam, the city of flowers, they began the marriage ceremony as promised to the glorious Pillaiyar.’ This verse states that Sivapadagiruthayar, having received Nambandar Nambi’s consent with great joy, returned to the holy city of S’irkaazhi. They explained everything that happened there to Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman.

Now, they begin the preparations for the wedding that will illuminate the world. The 1169th verse: ‘The auspicious wedding day and the auspicious hour were determined. Astrologers calculated the auspicious time and date. The auspicious wedding invitation was sent with great splendor.’ The astrologers determine the auspicious day for the wedding.

First, they fix the day.

Then, they calculate the auspicious hour. The auspicious hour is a good part of the day, also called Lagnam. A period of two and a half Nazhikas constitutes an hour, which is called Horai.

Thus, the auspicious day and hour are calculated by the ‘Ganita Mangala Noolavar’ (astrologers who calculate auspicious works). Ganita Mangala Noolavar means astrologers. Ganita means calculation, observing the positions and effects of planets. Nool means astrological text.

Therefore, Ganita Mangala Noolavar refers to astrologers. Deivachchegilar Peruman does not simply say ‘Noolavar’ but ‘Mangala Noolavar.’ This is because it is a day when all the devotees of Siva are about to unite with Him, the auspicious day.

Therefore, the text that describes this auspicious occasion is called ‘Mangala Nool.’ Generally, Ganita Noolavar means astrologer. Astrologers calculate the day and hour for auspicious events like weddings with the intention of bringing good to the world.

However, while these auspicious events occur as calculated, the name ‘Mangalam’ (auspiciousness) is merely a convention. True auspiciousness does not reside in them, as all worldly auspiciousness is temporary and will eventually turn inauspicious.

But here, the astrologers mentioned as ‘Ganita Mangala Noolavar’ by Deivachchegilar Peruman have calculated a day and hour that will lead all those attending the wedding to attain the eternal auspiciousness of Siva’s union.

Therefore, Deivachchegilar Peruman refers to them not just as ‘Ganita Noolavar’ but as ‘Ganita Mangala Noolavar.’ In his poetic work, Kambaramayanam, Kamban refers to the astrologers who calculated the day for Rama’s coronation as ‘Ganita Makkal’ (astrologers who calculate). He also calls that day ‘Mudipunai Kadigai Naal’ (the day of crowning).

Here, Deivachchegilar Peruman specifically refers to the astrologers who calculated this day, which will bring eternal auspiciousness and the state of Siva’s union to all who attend, as ‘Ganita Mangala Noolavar.’ They calculate and prepare the wedding invitation, send it to the bride’s family, and also deliver it to other relatives.

Thus, the auspicious day, which Lord Siva has ordained, is calculated and given by the Ganita Mangala Noolavar. This day is destined to be a day when all who attend the wedding will attain the feet of Siva and be liberated. The tradition is to perform the ritual of ‘Pālīkai’ (sowing seeds for sprouting) seven days before the wedding. This is a tradition and a scriptural rule. They sow the seeds for the Pālīkai. It is customary that the sprouting of these seeds in the Pālīkai will occur on the seventh day before the wedding.

This will be explained later.

Thus, the commencement of preparations for the wedding, by sowing the Pālīkai, is a tradition followed by our elders and prescribed by the scriptures. Let us proceed to discuss the wedding preparations.
