Thiruchitrambalam. The Great Puranam by Deivachchegilar Peruman, Volume 822, Vambaravarivandu Sarukkam, Life of Thirugnanasambandhar Nayanar. Preparations related to the wedding of Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman are underway in S’irkaazhi. The 1170th verse: ‘The prosperous city of Tiruppukali was adorned with rows of full pots, lamps, and Makara Toranas. Countless pearl garlands of immense light were hung everywhere, signifying great prosperity and splendor.’ The prosperous city of S’irkaazhi was decorated with lamps, Makara Toranas, and pearl garlands of immense light hung everywhere, signifying great prosperity and splendor.

The devotees of great penance, the people from nearby, and others, all gathered, and under the guidance of the esteemed elders, they carried the wedding invitation to Aachchapuram. The 1171st verse: ‘The devotees of great penance and the Brahmins, along with others nearby, gathered, and under the guidance of the esteemed elders, they carried the wedding invitation to Aachchapuram. The esteemed Nambandar Nambi, who is renowned for his virtue, welcomed them. As a result of the penance from previous lives, he will give his daughter as the bride to Pillaiyar and commence the wedding rituals.’ This verse describes that the devotees of great penance and the Brahmins, along with others nearby, gathered, and under the guidance of the esteemed elders, they carried the wedding invitation to Aachchapuram. The esteemed Nambandar Nambi, who is renowned for his virtue, welcomed them. As a result of the penance from previous lives, he will give his daughter as the bride to Pillaiyar and commence the wedding rituals.

Nambandar Nambi began to perform the wedding ceremonies, referred to as ‘Vaduva Vinai.’ Seeing this, the relatives of Thirugnanasambandhar Peruman in S’irkaazhi and the relatives of Nambandar Nambi rejoiced greatly. The 1172nd verse: ‘All the esteemed relatives gathered, and on the auspicious day, with the sound of auspicious drums and trumpets, they performed the ritual of sprinkling sacred water on the Pālīkai.’ This verse states that all the esteemed relatives gathered, and on the auspicious day, seven days before the wedding, they performed the ritual of sprinkling sacred water on the sprouts that had grown from the seeds sown for the Pālīkai. This is a tradition and a scriptural rule. This ritual is performed with auspicious music. Sowing the Pālīkai and the sprouting of the seeds are important parts of the wedding ceremony.

First, the sowing of the Pālīkai was mentioned.

Now, the sprouting of the seeds is described. In temple festivals, the ritual called ‘Ankurarpana’ (sowing seeds for sprouting) is a very important part. The Agamas also state this. In Sivālaya festivals, Ankurarpana is performed. In weddings, the growth, development, and abundance of these sprouts are considered a sign of the auspiciousness and success of the wedding.

Here, Deivachchegilar Peruman does not just say ‘sprouts’ but ‘sacred sprouts,’ indicating that this is a divine union. This signifies that the wedding is a divine union.

Next, the 1173rd verse: ‘The splendid mansions and halls were decorated with great beauty. The exquisite artwork was painted with skill. Auspicious designs were drawn on the walls of the celestial abode.’ This verse describes the splendid mansions and halls, filled with splendor, and the exquisite artwork painted with skill. The art of painting and drawing, executed with skill, was one of the auspicious decorations in ancient times. The art of painting was highly developed and renowned among the Tamil people for thousands of years.

Thus, illustrating with skill.

Thus, illustrating with skill. Sivakavimani Desiganar presents numerous examples of enlightenment in his commentaries. He also writes that the high level of art of painting that Tamils possessed in earlier times is now greatly diminishing, calling it a tragedy of time. Sivakavimani Desiganar further states: “Now, the one hundred and seventy-fourth Tiruppadal, [describing] long, standing pandals, overshadowed by marugu trees, replete with prosperity, high-reaching flag garlands, gem garlands interspersed, stately vedikas, rich sandal paste, and a grand canopy of pearls.” Thus, the Tiruppadal states that they set up long, standing pandals in rows along the long streets, and interspersed them with tall green flag garlands and gem garlands, and reached luminous platforms with rich sandal paste. They set up many grand canopies filled with lustrous pearls.

Now, the one hundred and seventy-fifth and one hundred and seventy-sixth Tiruppadals describe: “On the days starting from the wedding day, in front of every house, in every street, in every grand entrance, shining gem lamps, golden pots filled with auspicious water, clustered luminous garlands, and incense were offered. True devotees, Brahmins, and others celebrated the auspicious rituals with great splendor. From the day the bride’s breasts were filled, on all the following days, at every entrance, in every street, in the courtyards of mansions, and in every grand doorway, standing ...luminous gem lamps and golden pots filled with pure water were placed closely. Hearing the news of this wedding, true devotees from all over and others came to the great city of Sirkazhi, filled with joy for the auspicious wedding festivities, arriving daily. For all those who arrived, their lodging and needs were met. The Tiruppadal states: “With fragrant smoke from the Agil wood, smoke from the offerings in the sacred fire mingled, spreading a divine fragrance.”

“The sound of auspicious music resounds through the streets. The chanting of the four Vedas, louder than the roar of the ocean, prevails. With the rich smoke of fragrant Agil wood, the smoke from the sacred fire mingled, spreading a divine fragrance. The smoke of Agil and the smoke of offerings combine to create a fragrant atmosphere. The idea is that the smoke of Agil, by mixing with the smoke of the offerings, acquires a divine quality, as if its physical nature has changed.

“Now, the one hundred and seventy-eighth Tiruppadal states: “Those from all directions converge here with prosperity, and warehouses of various kinds abound, with great riches piled up like mountains...” ...overflowing with food, the sounds of feasting never cease.” Thus, the Tiruppadal states that people from all eight directions come together with their local resources. Those from each direction bring the unique products and specialty items of their region. This was a good tradition in Sirkazhi in earlier days. We saw in the Puranam of Thinnanar that when he held his bow festival, the hunters from the mountains brought gems and gold. Mountains of treasures are piled up there.

“Food is served to those who attended the wedding at all times. The sound of this never ceases. It is a good custom to eat without talking. They eat at these many feasts without talking. Yet, the sounds made by those serving them are abundant there.

“Now, the one hundred and seventy-ninth and one hundred and eightieth Tiruppadals state: “Cooks preparing pure, good ingredients according to the rules prescribed by the Vedic scriptures; those arranging the fragrant sandalwood paste; those offering incense made of a rich, new blend; those pounding fragrant camphor powder; those weaving garlands of flowers...” ...thus the Tiruppadals conclude. They prepare pure Vedic offerings according to the rules prescribed by the great Vedas and Vedic scriptures. Brahmins, great ascetics like Brahma, were there. Golden pots filled with sacred water, adorned with flowers, gleamed. Groups of people preparing rich sandalwood paste mixed with saffron arrived.

“Groups offering new fragrant incense blends arrived. Those pounding fragrant camphor powder arrived. The crowds of those weaving flower garlands were very large everywhere. The one hundred and eighty-first Tiruppadal states: “Diverse crafts...” ...filled the surroundings, and all the divine ornaments were arranged. As if the king of treasures, Kubera, had commanded it, the treasures accumulated here.

“Thus, people of various crafts from all sides meticulously perform the wedding preparations. The streets of the holy city of Sirkazhi are adorned with the beauty of the wedding. It is filled with splendor.

“Thus, the place shines as if Kubera himself had arranged all these treasures. This is the wedding of our Gnana Pillaiyar, therefore, Gnana Pillaiyar ...invites the world to His realm. This is a divine event, meant for the divine consciousness.

“Therefore, it is understood that the Lord himself commanded these arrangements. We shall continue our meditation.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam by Deivachilaiyar Peruman, Volume Eighty-two, Chapter of the Bee’s Pride: Puranam of ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar. Preparations for the wedding ceremony of ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman are underway. Currently, the sacred thread of protection (kappu nan) is being placed on ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman. Deivachilaiyar Peruman sings about it. The one hundred and eighty-second Tiruppadal states: “On the day before the auspicious day, the group of Brahmins and the devotees adorned with sacred ash adorned the incomparable Pillaiyar with the grace-filled sacred thread of protection.” The tradition is to place the thread of protection the day before the wedding.

This is called Rakshabandhanam. It is also called Rakshabandhanam. In fact, the rituals for the wedding ceremony begin with the placement of this sacred thread. Tying the sacred thread is done for both the bride and the groom.

After the sacred thread is properly placed, it is untied after all the wedding ceremonies are completed. From the time the sacred thread is placed until it is untied, it is understood that the groom and bride are under the special protection of Lord Shiva.

Furthermore, it is the tradition that during the time this sacred thread is worn, the groom and bride are considered to be Shiva and Shakti.

Therefore, it is also a custom to believe that the worldly attachments will not affect them. The one with the eye on his forehead, His sacred threads of protection ...is a Thevaram verse. On the day before the wedding day in the holy city of Sirkazhi, the crowd of Brahmins and the devotees adorned with sacred ash gathered to place the sacred thread of protection, blessed by Lord Shiva, on the incomparable Pillaiyar. The one hundred and eighty-third Tiruppadal states: “The rules of Vedic truth, shining with light, as they are chanted, will cause righteousness to flourish in the world. The long-married women performed circumambulations. The rules spoken by the Vedas will shine brightly because of this wedding ceremony.

“Righteousness in the world will also flourish. Thiru Gnana Sambandha ...Peruman’s wedding ceremony will cause the rules and practices prescribed by the Vedas as true words to shine brightly. Although these rituals have no benefit for Gnana Pillaiyar’s state, and such rituals are not necessary for His state, Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman accepts them to uphold the traditions and practices prescribed by the Vedas, thus revealing them. Earlier, at the beginning of the Puranam of Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman, we saw that the Upanayanam ceremony was performed for him, which was necessary for his state ...therefore, we saw that the Upanayanam and other ceremonies were merely nominal, existing only at the ritualistic level. We can apply the same understanding to the wedding ceremonies that are about to take place here. Sri Meykandar, who bestows the Sivagnana Bodham, first composes a protective verse.

“As an auspicious greeting, he composes the Ganapati protection. Sri Meykandar is one who experiences the transcendent in the waking state. Generally, those who begin to write a book ...do so to ensure that their endeavor proceeds well and is completed successfully, and that the book endures in the world, and that the students who read it understand the meaning correctly.

“Therefore, it is customary to sing a protective verse before starting a book. For Sri Meykandar, who experiences the transcendent in the waking state, obstacles and impediments are of no concern. Nevertheless, he offers an auspicious greeting when bestowing Sivagnana Bodham. This is to preserve the tradition of the elders. Even though he knows that no impediment will occur to his endeavor, he begins the book with an auspicious greeting. This is the tradition of the elders.

“Therefore, to preserve that tradition, he also acts likewise. Secondly ...the reason is to instruct the students. When starting a book, they instruct the students on how to begin. For these two reasons, Sri Meykandar offers an auspicious greeting when bestowing Sivagnana Bodham. Sri Madhava Sivagnana Muni explains this in his commentary on Sivagnana Bodham. He states: “Although he knew that no impediment would approach him, who experiences the transcendent in the waking state, he offered an auspicious greeting to the god of obstacles, Ganesha, to protect the tradition of the elders and to instruct the students.” Thus, Madhava Sivagnana Muni explains the auspicious greeting composed by Sri Meykandar in his Sivagnana Bodham.

“We recall here ...that the Upanayanam ceremony performed for Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman and the wedding ceremonies to be performed now are accepted by him to preserve the tradition of the elders and to instruct the world, even though he is in a state of experiencing the transcendent in the waking state. We understood earlier that the Pillaiyar, who descended to establish the Vedic way of life, agreed to marry to uphold that Vedic order.

“Therefore, even in His wedding ceremonies, He had to agree to the Vedic rituals to ensure that the Vedic way of life would flourish. If Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman had not accepted these ceremonies, the world itself might have become confused ...and the worldly way of life might have declined, abandoning Vedic rituals.

“Therefore, beloved devotees, Brahmins, beautiful women, and men gathered, taking the golden thread of protection and parading it around the city. Deivachilaiyar Peruman says that women and men participated, indicating that people would come as spectators and conduct these auspicious events. The one hundred and eighty-fourth Tiruppadal states: “After parading around the city and entering, they reached the hall adorned with nine gems, where the Vedic ritual of Samavartanam shone. They approached the fully bloomed, sacred flowers.” Thus, as previously mentioned, they carried the golden sacred thread of protection ...and entered the auspicious hall. They reached the hall adorned with nine gems, with pictures arranged beautifully. They brought the sacred thread of protection.

“Deivachilaiyar Peruman describes the auspicious event taking place there: “Samavartanam shines with the Vedic ritual.” Samavartanam is the completion of Vedic studies and the end of the Brahmacharya vow, followed by residing in each ashram. Staying in one ashram throughout life without change is called Naishthikam, which means adhering to discipline. Naishthikam is thus ...staying in one ashram. This state of unwavering devotion can only be achieved by a few. For others, when moving from one ashram to another, they first perform the rites that complete the previous ashram and then begin the new one. This is the Vedic tradition.

“The Vaidika rite performed when transitioning from the Brahmacharya ashram to the Grihastha ashram is called Samavartanam. Samavartanam means the right that leads to marriage. In this case, Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman, who at the age of three years had attained the state of complete Sivagnana illumination, is involved.

“Therefore, these ashram-related rules and rituals are merely ceremonial. The one hundred and eighty-fifth Tiruppadal states: “In a golden vessel, spread with red paddy, surrounded by long garlands, placed on either side, with auspicious water, a golden pot, fig leaves, darbha grass, and a long, luminous gem lamp shining brightly on the surface.” Thus, this Tiruppadal states: “They spread red paddy in a golden vessel and arrange long, fragrant garlands on both sides.” We already know from the Puranam of Azhathondar Nayyanar and other places that extremely excellent paddy is best. Establishing a pot of abundance on top of this spread of red paddy is a tradition. The spread of paddy serves as a base for the pot.

“Now, the one hundred and eighty-sixth and one hundred and eighty-seventh Tiruppadals describe: “With the sounds of auspicious music, the Vedic chants of ascetics, fragrant Tamil incense, sandalwood paste, flower garlands, and fine garments, the ascetics, resembling embodiments of merit, sat on a beautiful flower couch. With great love, they approached before the Pillaiyar, who resembled Brahma on a lotus, and the Brahmins, proficient in Vedic rituals, offered the sacred thread of protection to Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman’s hand.” Thus, Deivachilaiyar Peruman describes this in these two Tiruppadals. The auspicious sounds of the musical instruments, the Vedic chants of the ascetics, fragrant incense, sandalwood paste, beautiful garments, and flower garlands ... adorn the divine ascetics, who resembled embodiments of merit. Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman sat on a flower couch. With overflowing love, Brahmins, proficient in Vedic rituals and resembling Brahma on a lotus, approached. They placed the sacred thread of protection on Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman’s hand, who removes the bond of the two karmas that bind beings to birth in this world.

“The Brahmins are compared to Brahma here because of their skill in performing Vedic rituals. We can recall the history of Lord Brahma performing the wedding rituals for Goddess Deivayanai and Goddess Meenakshi. They are experts in the Vedas and their associated Kalpa Sutras. They tied the sacred thread on Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman’s hand. The Pillaiyar, who removes the bonds, will later decree that all beings should enter to be freed from the cycle of birth.

“Therefore, Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman, who eradicates worldly attachments ...had the sacred thread tied to His hand. In other weddings, tying the sacred thread is a ritual that leads to further entanglement in the cycle of birth.

“However, this wedding, where the sacred thread was tied to the Pillaiyar’s hand, not only prevented further entanglement in worldly karma but also served to liberate all beings in the universe. Although the sacred thread was tied to the Pillaiyar’s hand, and the act of tying is a physical act, it truly served to loosen the bonds and attachments of the beings of this world. This is the significance ...of this. The one hundred and eighty-eighth Tiruppadal states: “The people who witnessed this, the devotees with pure minds and faces, rejoiced, their thoughts and faces beaming. The great Vedic clans erupted in joyous celebration.” Thus, the people who witnessed the placement of the sacred thread on Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman’s hand, and the devotees who came to see the wedding, rejoiced, their thoughts and faces beaming. The great Vedic clans, filled with Vedic knowledge, proclaimed joyously.

“Let us meditate further.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam by Deivachilaiyar Peruman, Volume Eighty-two, Chapter of the Bee’s Pride: Puranam of ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar. The one hundred and eighty-ninth Tiruppadal states: “As the treasures of the night ended, and the dawn arrived, as if the sun of wisdom, dispelling the darkness of false doctrines and the deep ignorance of misguided paths, had arisen, so did the great light appear.” Thus, the day of the wedding of Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman, a divine event, has arrived. Deivachilaiyar Peruman describes in this Tiruppadal how this auspicious day dawned. From this Tiruppadal onwards, for seven Tiruppadals, the sun, the directions, and the five elements ...are described as having participated in the wedding of the Pillaiyar. In this Tiruppadal, Deivachilaiyar Peruman describes the sunrise.

In the next Tiruppadal, he describes how the directions are honored. Since all beings and the moon are illuminated by the radiant sun, the sun is understood to encompass beings and the moon.

Thus, in the following seven Tiruppadals, the eight forms of the Lord, who is embodied as earth, water, fire, air, and ether, are described. Manikkavasagar Peruman states in the Tiruvachagam: “He became one with the eight forms, encompassing earth, water, fire, air, the vast sky, and the moon, along with consciousness and the five senses.” These are all symbolically represented here. This wedding signifies that the Pillaiyar, along with those who stood with Him, entered into the fullness of the Lord’s grace and became one with Him. The eight forms, comprising the five elements, the sun, the moon, and consciousness, are symbolically represented.

Therefore, let us first look at the meaning of the one hundred and eighty-ninth Tiruppadal. We saw that the sacred thread was tied to Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman’s hand the day before the wedding. The night of that day has arrived.

Then, generous donations are given. The scriptures state that many donations should be given before embarking on a wedding. In accordance with this, many donations rained down that night before the wedding. That night ended, and the sun rose. How is this? When Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman descended to this world sixteen years ago, the darkness of various false doctrines was dispelled by His appearance, like the sun.

Similarly, this night ended, and the sun, the bringer of day, rose.

Now, the one hundred and ninetieth Tiruppadal states: “The small wings of the bees hummed in the groves of the Sembiyan city. The wedding of the worthy one of Sembiyan took place, with penance, ablutions, and purification from sin and darkness, adorning themselves with the radiant sun’s rays, the directions embraced.” This Tiruppadal describes how the directions appeared on the day of Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman’s wedding. This verse employs the figure of speech known as ‘tharkurippaetral ani’ (inferred meaning). That day was the day of the divine wedding, the day when the mind united with Lord Shiva, the bridegroom.

Therefore, that day had performed great penance. It had attained that grace for the Pillaiyar’s divine wedding to take place. Realizing this, what did the directions do? They cleansed themselves of their impurities and darkness, and adorned themselves with the sun’s radiant rays. The directions, as if performing ablutions, cleansed themselves of the darkness and sins that had settled upon them, and donned the sun’s rays. The words ‘masu’ (impurity) and ‘irul’ (darkness) appear in this Tiruppadal.

For the directions, ‘masu’ refers to darkness.

Therefore, within the directions, beings and the moon can be included. The inner darkness of beings, referred to as ‘aga irul’, and the outer darkness of the moon, referred to as ‘puraiya irul’, are dispelled as the directions adorned themselves with the sun’s rays. The previous verse discussed the sun. This Tiruppadal, mentioning the directions, encompasses beings and the moon.

Thus, the sun, the moon, and consciousness, three of the eight forms of the Lord, are described in these two Tiruppadals.

Now, the remaining five Tiruppadals will describe the glories of the five elements, which are the remaining components of the eight forms.

In this context, the one hundred and ninetieth Tiruppadal, ‘Parambu...’ ...from all parts of the world, bringing abundant treasures, and the people from the eight directions approaching, it is like showcasing the immeasurable benefits of the divine wedding of the unparalleled one. In this Tiruppadal, the world, the earth element, is described as shining with splendor. People from all eight directions of the world gather at the Sirkazhi temple, bringing their finest treasures. The convergence of people and their treasures is like the earth displaying its immeasurable benefits at the divine wedding of the unparalleled Pillaiyar. Each part of the earth possesses unique treasures. On this day, all these treasures from different regions of the earth were displayed at the Sirkazhi temple as if the earth itself had gathered all its bounty.

Thus, the earth received its due.

Now, the one hundred and ninety-first Tiruppadal ...’Ezhuchiyin muzhakku enna thunga venthirai surivalai aarpoadu soozhndhu pongu perozhi muzhakkudan ezhundhadhu punari’ (What is the roar of the celebration? The great ocean, surrounded by the sounds of waves and the white screen of its expanse, rose with a mighty roar.) This Tiruppada describes the water element, one of the five elements, and how the great ocean, its symbol, appeared. It is as if the life we have been blessed with has taken form. The auspicious wedding procession of the blessed Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman is accompanied by auspicious roars. The ocean rose with a mighty roar, surrounded by the sounds of waves. The wedding procession, which we now call the wedding procession, is referred to as the wedding celebration here.

It is customary for the groom, his relatives, and others to proceed in groups with auspicious music towards the bride’s home during this wedding procession. This is what is called the wedding celebration or wedding procession. The ocean’s waves rose with a mighty roar, just like the auspicious music.

Now, the one hundred and ninety-third Tiruppadal states: “As if the seven oceans, united in greatness, moved swiftly with the grand wedding festival, the sacrificial fire of the Brahmins began to rise, swirling in the sacred fire.” This Tiruppada vividly describes the nature of fire, the third of the five elements, in the context of Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman’s wedding. The wedding procession of Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman is very long and grand. It is as if the seven oceans have converged. ‘Azhakkar’ means ocean. ‘Azhakkar ezhu’ refers to the seven oceans: the ocean of salt water, the ocean of sugarcane juice, the ocean of ghee, the ocean of curd, the ocean of milk, the ocean of saltwater, and the ocean of fresh water. These are called the Sapta Sagara in Sanskrit. It is as if the seven oceans have merged, their waves surging, and the Pillaiyar’s wedding procession moved forward.

The Brahmins of Sirkazhi also wished to join the procession. As if they too would rise and move along with the fire that the Brahmins tend, the fire swirled and rose. The fire kept in the houses of Brahmins is always a perpetual flame, not extinguished. It is tended with ghee, wood, and chanting of mantras, and the Homa (sacrificial fire) is performed. The fire of these Brahmins, ready to participate in Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman’s wedding procession, rose and swirled swiftly. The rising and swirling of fire, along with a pleasant fragrance, are considered auspicious omens.

The Brahmins of Sirkazhi are steadfast and unwavering. Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman himself praised the Brahmins of Sirkazhi in His Thevaram Tiruppadigam, stating: “In the great city of Kazhumala, where the steadfast Brahmins dwell, who have not forgotten their duty, who are skilled in their craft, whose minds are pure, who are free from sin and attachment, and who possess strong, unwavering hands...” These Brahmins separately perform the sacrificial fire in their respective homes with ghee, wood, and chanting of mantras. Their fire eagerly rose and swirled to join Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman’s wedding procession.

Now, the one hundred and ninety-fourth Tiruppada states: “The wedding procession began with the soft scent of flowers, adorned with the pollen, with the divine bodies marked with sacred ash. It was adorned with the pollen of soft flowers, and the divine bodies marked with sacred ash.

“Thus, it was marred.” This verse describes how the wind, the fourth of the five elements, appeared at the wedding celebration.

“The devotees are participating in the wedding procession of the Pillaiyar. They are adorned with sacred ash and rudraksha beads. It is a rule that devotees, those who go to temples, and those who go to monasteries should wear sacred ash and rudraksha beads. Not wearing them when participating in the Lord’s festivals or temple worship has become a bad practice in recent times. The scripture ‘Nenju Viduthuvathu’ states: “Do not approach those who lack true knowledge and who defile the Lord’s grace with falsehood. Do not associate with the ignorant who reject the divine and wander about criticizing.

“Do not admire those who are foolishly arrogant and do not recognize the truth of birth.” Similarly, the wind thought, “I too should go with this gathering of devotees.” To go with the gathering of devotees, one must wear sacred ash. The wind, carrying the white pollen, set out. As it went, it encountered rows of bees. Taking them along, the wind set out. The wind carrying the pollen scattered from the flowers appeared as if it were wearing sacred ash. The wind carrying the rows of bees appeared as if it were wearing a garland of rudraksha beads.

“Thus, the wind also took on a divine appearance and joined the gathering of devotees.

“Now, the one hundred and ninety-fifth Tiruppada states: “From all eight directions, everyone came to the grand wedding procession, and the white clouds, like scattered fragments of brilliance, adorned the sky, resembling white silk flags.” This verse describes how the sky, known as ‘visumbu’, appeared during the wedding procession of the Pillaiyar. What service did the sky render? It filled itself with white clouds flying about. The sky appeared as if it were arranging rows of white silk flags. The white clouds are likened to white flags. The clouds, white and dense, moved about, resembling white flags.

“White flags are auspicious symbols and also symbols of victory. Such white flags adorned the wedding procession. This is the meaning of this Tiruppada.

“Thus, Deivachilaiyar Peruman shows how the eight forms of the Lord participated in the wedding procession. Let us press on in meditation.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam by Deivachilaiyar Peruman, Volume Eighty-two, Chapter of the Bee’s Pride: Puranam of ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar. The one hundred and ninety-sixth Tiruppada states: “All the auspicious things were revealed in the morning. The great Kauniyar Peruman, whose actions were complete, worshipped the first Lord on the sacred boat and proceeded with the divine grace in His mind.” In the preceding verses, we saw the magnificence of the wedding procession. The Lord, Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman, worshipped the Lord on the sacred boat, which is His origin, and proceeded with divine grace in His mind. Deivachilaiyar Peruman refers to him as the ‘Kauniyar Peruman whose actions were complete’.

The literal meaning is that he completed the daily duties of the morning. However, a deeper meaning can be derived: ‘Kauniyar Peruman whose actions were complete’ refers to the Peruman who, having completed the karmas that caused His birth in this world, and having refuted the false doctrines and embraced sacred ash through the Lord’s grace, had finished His mission. He worshipped Thiru Thoniyappar, who resides in Thonipuram, and the great Goddess Ammaiyar. That boat, located on the peak of Sirkazhi, is called the ‘Moolagiya Thoni’ (the original boat). This ‘Moolagiya Thoni’ represents the primordial Pranava mantra. The Vedas themselves, in the form of a boat, carry and support the Lord.

This is the history of Sirkazhi. The Lord, the primordial Being, resides on that ‘Moolagiya Thoni’. The ‘Moolamudhalvar’ (the first cause) here refers to Shiva, who acts as the efficient cause and encompasses all beings, performing the five cosmic functions. He is the supreme Lord. He worshipped this primordial Lord. Whenever Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman set out on a pilgrimage from Sirkazhi, He would worship Thoniyappar and take His leave.

This is a general form of worship.

Now, this worship is being performed ...in the same manner, as He bids farewell to Thoniyappar and proceeds to Thiru Perumanallur, also known as Aatralpuram.

Therefore, He takes leave from Thoniyappar.

Furthermore, this is the final time, and Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman will not return here. Hence, He worships Him specially. The one hundred and ninety-seventh Tiruppada states: “The Brahmins of KaaLi city, along with the assembled devotees and others, surrounded Him. The great Vedic hymns resounded. Worshiping the prosperous city, He ascended the radiant white palanquin.” Thus, the Brahmins of the great city of Sirkazhi, along with the assembled devotees and others, surrounded Him. The life-giving great Vedic hymns resounded.

They worshipped the prosperous Sirkazhi city and ascended the radiant white palanquin. The golden sacred thread, as mentioned before, was paraded around the city and brought into the auspicious hall. It was adorned with nine gems and beautiful pictures. They reached the auspicious hall. They brought the sacred thread of protection. Deivachilaiyar Peruman describes the auspicious event taking place there: “Samavartanam shines with the Vedic ritual.” Samavartanam is the completion of Vedic studies and the end of the Brahmacharya vow, followed by residing in each ashram.

Staying in one ashram throughout life without change is called Naishthikam, which means adhering to discipline. Naishthikam is thus ...staying in one ashram. This state of unwavering devotion can only be achieved by a few. For others, when moving from one ashram to another, they first perform the rites that complete the previous ashram and then begin the new one. This is the Vedic tradition. The Vaidika rite performed when transitioning from the Brahmacharya ashram to the Grihastha ashram is called Samavartanam.

Samavartanam means the right that leads to marriage. In this case, Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman, who at the age of three years had attained the state of complete Sivagnana illumination, is involved.

Therefore, these ashram-related rules and rituals are merely ceremonial. The one hundred and eighty-fifth Tiruppada states: “In a golden vessel, spread with red paddy, surrounded by long garlands, placed on either side, with auspicious water, a golden pot, fig leaves, darbha grass, and a long, luminous gem lamp shining brightly on the surface.” Thus, this Tiruppada states: “They spread red paddy in a golden vessel and arrange long, fragrant garlands on both sides.” We already know from the Puranam of Azhathondar Nayyanar and other places that extremely excellent paddy is best. Establishing a pot of abundance on top of this spread of red paddy is a tradition. The spread of paddy serves as a base for the pot.

Now, the one hundred and eighty-sixth and one hundred and eighty-seventh Tiruppadals describe: “With the sounds of auspicious music, the Vedic chants of ascetics, fragrant Tamil incense, sandalwood paste, flower garlands, and fine garments, the ascetics, resembling embodiments of merit, sat on a beautiful flower couch. With great love, they approached before the Pillaiyar, who resembled Brahma on a lotus, and the Brahmins, proficient in Vedic rituals, offered the sacred thread of protection to Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman’s hand.” Thus, Deivachilaiyar Peruman describes this in these two Tiruppadals. The auspicious sounds of the musical instruments, the Vedic chants of the ascetics, fragrant incense, sandalwood paste, beautiful garments, and flower garlands ...adorn the divine ascetics, who resembled embodiments of merit. Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman sat on a flower couch. With overflowing love, Brahmins, proficient in Vedic rituals and resembling Brahma on a lotus, approached. They placed the sacred thread of protection on Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman’s hand, who removes the bond of the two karmas that bind beings to birth in this world.

Emperor Thirugnanasambandhar ascended and was seated in the pearl palanquin. As he ascended, the Brahmins who accompanied him, the devotees who loved the child dearly, and others walked alongside out of affection. The attendants also followed. They too are destined to attain liberation in Thiru Perumanallur. We shall see them attaining salvation through divine grace.

Thus, surrounded by everyone, Emperor Thirugnanasambandhar worshipped the land of Seerkazhi. This was the final time he was departing from Seerkazhi. With that in mind, he worshipped the town of Seerkazhi and departed. Previously, when Emperor Thirugnanasambandhar came from Thillai to Seerkazhi, as the town of Seerkazhi appeared in the distance, he alighted from the palanquin and He came forward and sang a pathigam to the town, starting with ‘Vandaar Kuzhal Arivai’. Upon reaching the outer precincts, he worshipped the town with incense and lamps, and thus completed the pathigam, saying ‘Proceed to Kaalinaagar’. He then entered the town of Seerkazhi.

We saw there that his arrival in Seerkazhi was the final time.

Similarly, by worshipping the land of Seerkazhi now, it signifies that Emperor Thirugnanasambandhar would no longer come to Seerkazhi in a worldly manner. He has ascended. Just as he is the leader, the land he ruled is also worthy of worship, as taught by God Sekkizhar Peruman. He demonstrated this by showing the Emperor Thirugnanasambandhar worshipping the leader in one hymn and the land in another, in two hymns. After worshipping the town, Emperor Thirugnanasambandhar ascended the pearl palanquin, which shone with white light. We discussed in detail when he first ascended the palanquin, which was also called the ‘luminescent pearl palanquin’ and ‘white ash light’.

The act of ascending the palanquin, which began in Thiru Neilvaayil Arathurai when our Lord gifted him the pearl palanquin, continues to this day and reaches its conclusion here. To show this, Pillaiyar, our Lord, is described by God Sekkizhar with the epithet ‘luminescent white light’. In the 1198th hymn, ‘Those who ascend the vehicle, to be taken as a means of support, to be carried, to be fanned...’ ...approaching from the sky and earth with auspicious sounds. Emperor Thirugnanasambandhar, the benefactor of Seerkazhi, ascended and was seated in the pearl palanquin. All those around him ascended their respective vehicles. Those who needed to be nearby, such as the elderly, the infirm, and women, who could not walk, also boarded vehicles.

Similarly, others boarded vehicles for various reasons. Those who were supposed to be close to them also boarded vehicles.

Furthermore, those carrying goods also boarded vehicles. This is all due to the divine grace of the Lord. Those who owned palanquins, horses, and other vehicles also boarded them and proceeded. The ceremonial items like decorative hangings and fly-whisks, held aloft, can be seen to some extent even today in large temples and monastic institutions. Such hangings, velvet canopies, umbrellas, and fly-whisks, approaching from the sky and earth, accompanied by celestial music and auspicious sounds, resounded. The Emperor continued to sing about the procession of the wedding.

The hymn is ‘With conches, trumpets, drums, cymbals, pipes, and other percussion instruments, the Vedic chants of the Brahmins resounded with overwhelming sound, filling everywhere. A wedding procession has begun.’ The conches and trumpets were unparalleled. The great trumpets, cymbals, and pipes, along with other wind instruments, blended with the Vedic hymns of the Brahmins and resounded everywhere. The trumpets, cymbals, and drums mentioned here were gifted to Pillaiyar by the Lord. The conch is the most auspicious among all musical instruments, a divine instrument. Unlike other instruments made by humans, it emanates the Pranava sound continuously.

It is also in the form of Pranava.

Therefore, with the conch, and other instruments also resounding, the Brahmins chanted. They chanted along with the Vedic hymns.

Thus, the wedding procession, the groom proceeding with his retinue to the bride’s home, commenced. The hymn is ‘The sound of swarms of bees in the women’s coiled hair on one side, the sound of Vedic truths recited by the radiant Brahmins on another side, the sound of the flawless Veenai and Yazh on another side, and the melodious sounds of auspicious songs sung with praise on another side.’ The sound of swarms of bees in the women’s coiled hair resonated on one side. The Vedic truths, recited by the Brahmins with grace, resounded on another side. The sound of the flawless Veenai and Yazh resonated on one side. The melodious sounds of auspicious songs sung with praise resonated on another side. In this hymn, God Sekkizhar Peruman mentions the Veenai and Yazh.

The Veenai gives life to music. It is a type of Yazh from the Kurinji region. The Veenai is a different musical instrument from the Yazh. The Veenai can be divided into three types. The first is the ‘Vichitra’ Veenai, which has only one string and belongs to Saraswati, the goddess of knowledge. The second is named Veenai, which has seven strings and belongs to the goddess of wealth.

Therefore, God Sekkizhar Peruman refers to it as ‘Veenai Yazh’. The Veenai and Yazh are capable of giving life to music, while other musical instruments ...are for playing music. This is why Thiruvalluvar also mentions ‘The flute is sweet, the Yazh is sweet’. In a similar vein, the flute is a superior instrument. To explain this concept and their superiority, we are shown the history of the Lord holding a Veenai in his hand and Vishnu, his consort, holding a flute. ‘My Lord plays the Veenai beautifully.’ The sounds that occurred during the wedding procession were described.

Now, in the next hymn, the adornments of the wedding procession are described. The hymn is ‘White conch, sharp eyes, intense brilliance, radiating fly-whisks...’ ...adorned with colorful powders, filling everywhere.’ Numerous white banners filled the sky. Swarms of radiant fly-whisks were present. Adorned with gems, and with colorful powders, they filled everywhere.

Thus, this hymn concludes. Let us resume our contemplation. Trichyrambalam. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Trichyrambalam. Periya Puranam by God Sekkizhar Peruman, Volume 826, Vambara Varivandu Sargam, Thiru Gnana Sambandha Nayanar Puranam. The 1102nd hymn in Thiru Gnana Sambandha Nayanar Puranam. In this hymn, God Sekkizhar Peruman describes how the group of Brahmins, who followed Vedic traditions, participated in the wedding procession. The hymn is: ‘With crests, deer hides, and staffs, the preceptors proceed, carrying the smoke-emitting sacrificial fire. With fervent joy, they chant great pathigams, and the great ascetics, having conquered all enmity, proceed.’ In the wedding procession of Emperor Thirugnanasambandhar, along with the Brahmins adorned with five crests and wearing deer hides, young Vedic scholars, and their preceptors, they proceeded together.

The preceptors also went together as a group.

The Brahmins, carrying their sacrificial fires, proceeded with their wives. The sacrificial fire is the eternal flame maintained by Brahmins. Vedic law dictates that Brahmins living the householder’s life must daily tend a fire and perform sacrifices.

Therefore, they carried this fire with them. Since a sacrifice is performed with one’s wife, they carried both the sacrificial fire and their wives in this procession. This eternal flame ...initiated at the wedding sacrifice, was to be protected without extinguishing until death.

Next, the third group consists of those who recite the Emperor’s pathigams, appreciating their greatness, and the Vedic texts gifted by the Lord. Emperor Thirugnanasambandhar’s true words possess the same quality. Those who have directly seen and experienced this are the Brahmins studying Vedic texts, who are greatly delighted and recite the Emperor’s pathigams. The fourth group consists of the great ascetics, who have conquered the six vices: lust, anger, greed, attachment, ego, and envy.

Thus, God Sekkizhar Peruman describes how the group of Brahmins, following the Vedic path, participates in the wedding procession.

Now, in the next hymn, he will describe the procession of the Siva devotees who follow the path of Siucom. God Sekkizhar Peruman sings about how their gathering proceeds. The hymn is: ‘Six types of prominent Saivite traditions, immense vows, those who stand in the path of truth, those who have attained great penance, devotees who have come through the path of love with a pure heart, yogis who have attained the state of grace, proceed in groups.’ In this hymn, God Sekkizhar Peruman explains how the gatherings of Saivites participate in the wedding procession. Those who have followed the paths of conduct within the inner traditions, those who have attained great penance through their monastic appearance, participate. The six types of Saivism mentioned here by God Sekkizhar Peruman are referred to as inner traditions. These are the six types of Saivites: Padanavada Saivam, Vedavada Saivam, Sivasamavada Saivam, Sivasankaravada Saivam, Iswara Avikaravada Saivam, and Siva Advaita Saivam.

These belong to the inner traditions. Saivism is divided into four categories, with six types of Saivism in each category, totaling twenty-four types of Saivism presented hierarchically. The other three categories are the Lokayata, and the six types of Buddhism and Jainism, known as outer-inner traditions. The six types of Tarka, Mimamsa, Ekanmavada, Sankhya, Yoga, and Pancharatra are classified as outer traditions. These outer-inner traditions did not have the opportunity to witness the wedding of Emperor Thirugnanasambandhar. The outer traditions are not relevant here.

In the inner-outer traditions, we have Pasupatha Saivam, Mavradha Saivam, Kapala Saivam, Vama Saivam, Bhairava Saivam, and Aikya Vada. Although they agree with Saivism in some aspects, they differ from Saivism in their respective paths and conclusions. They do not accept the concepts of Ekam, Anekam, Karumam, and Mayartham in the same way as Siddhanta Saivites. As stated, they are considered ‘darkness’ to the outer traditions regarding these six substances.

Therefore, only the six types of inner Saivites are considered here. These explanations are clearly elaborated by Sri Madhava Sivagnana Muni in Sivagnana Mapadiyam. Grace concerning the inner tradition practitioners. These inner tradition practitioners, such as Padanavada Saivites, accept the six substances like Ekam, etc., which are also accepted by Siddhanta Saivam.

Therefore, they are qualified to understand the essence of the Siddhanta Saiva philosophy, which is explained through the principles of general and specific nature found in the Agamas. As stated in Sivaprakasam, Chapter 7, ‘They are light to the inner tradition practitioners.’ Therefore, these practitioners of inner traditions participate in the wedding procession of Pillaiyar. They accept the six substances described by Saiva Siddhantam. Although they may differ slightly, they have the maturity to accept the truth of Siddhanta when instructed.

Therefore, they ...participate in this procession alongside the Siddhanta Saivites. These practitioners of the inner traditions are the ones who receive the initiation of ‘Namasivaya’ from Pillaiyar at Perumanam, realizing the true path. When the gate of light is shown, they are destined to merge with the supreme divine light.

Therefore, all these Siva devotees of the inner traditions participate in the wedding procession. They are considered ‘parents’ by those who brought them forth, as mentioned by God Sekkizhar Peruman. This shows how close they are to the Siddhanta Saivites. In the Puranam of Manakkanchara Nayanar, Mavradiyar and ...in the Puranam of Siruthonda Nayanar, Vairavar were killed as Siva devotees. It is understood that those who are pure Saivites will easily grasp the essence and practice the Siddhanta philosophy by hearing this text. Because they are so close, it is understood that they were brought closer to Saiva Siddhantam.

God Sekkizhar Peruman will now describe the gathering of Siddhanta Saivites who come after them. The two lines, ‘Devotees who have come through the path of love with a pure heart, yogis who have attained the state of grace,’ from the second part, indicate that the Siddhanta Saivites participated in the wedding procession as Siva devotees. These are Siddhanta Saivites. Among them, the first ones to arrive are ...those referred to as ‘coming through the path of love with a pure heart’. They are at the stage of ‘knowledge’. Among the four stages described by Saiva Siddhantam - Kriya, Yoga, Gnana, and Charya - they are at the highest stage of knowledge.

The second stage is referred to as Yoga, meaning they are at the highest stage of Siva Yoga. The third stage is ‘Kriya’, where they worship by fixing their attention on a Lingam or an emblem. The term ‘Thondu’ (service) refers to those who are at the stage of ‘Charya’.

Thus, those in the four stages of Charya, Kriya, Yoga, and Gnana among the Siddhanta Saivites also participate. These four paths, the noble paths of Saivism, are explained by God Sekkizhar Peruman in the Puranam of Thirmoola Deva Nayanar as Gnana, Yoga, Kriya, and Charya. Sivagnana Siddhiyar states that these four are the good paths to reach Sankara within Siddhanta Saivam. These are all detailed in gnana texts like Sivagnana Siddhiyar.

Thus, after describing the Vedic path followers in the first hymn, and the Siucom path followers in this hymn, God Sekkizhar Peruman, in the next hymn, describes the celestial beings. The hymn is: ‘Vidyadharas, Yakshas, Siddhas, Kinnaras, crowded Devas, with dark-eyed beings...’ ...Apsaras, and those accompanying them, ascended their radiant aerial chariots with great eagerness and proceeded through the cloud-covered sky to witness the wedding. The people who participated in this wedding procession on Earth will attain liberation through the grace of Pillaiyar and reach the path of no return.

However, these celestial beings, not being worthy of that great boon, are content with merely witnessing the wedding ceremony. The hymn is: ‘Others, while these beings of the world are thronging and joining...’ ...witnessing the wonderful spectacle, their minds ascend like the reflection of a beautiful mind. How are the celestial beings proceeding in the sky? When the people of this world gather and participate in the wedding procession, the gathering of celestial beings appears like a shadow of the gathering of people participating in the wedding procession on Earth.

Thus, God Sekkizhar Peruman sings. Let us press on with our contemplation. Trichyrambalam. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Trichyrambalam. Periya Puranam by God Sekkizhar Peruman, Volume 827, Vambara Varivandu Sargam, Thiru Gnana Sambandha Nayanar Puranam. Emperor Thirugnanasambandhar departed from Seerkazhi and proceeded to Thiru Perumanallur. God Sekkizhar Peruman describes this in the next two hymns. The 1106th hymn: ‘The Lord who rules the kingdom of penance, casting his unique umbrella’s shade, He who can sever the bonds of worldly existence, with His feet in his heart, the King of Poondharai, who descended to bless the worlds, arrived at Nallur Thiru Perumanam, where Shiva resides.’ Emperor Thirugnanasambandhar proceeded in the wedding procession under the shade of the pearl umbrella. He who can sever the bonds of worldly existence ...holding the divine feet of the Lord, who can sever the bonds of worldly existence, in his heart, and who descended to bless all worlds, the King of Seerkazhi, Pillaiyar, arrived at Thiru Nallur Perumanam, the place Shiva loves to reside.

This is the meaning of this hymn. Emperor Thirugnanasambandhar was holding an unparalleled pearl umbrella. It is like holding an unparalleled umbrella to rule the kingdom of penance. Pillaiyar proceeded with the unique pearl umbrella held above him. According to the eighth sutra of Sivagnana Bodham, ‘He who is our first guru, and teaches through penance’, the souls, due to their past penance ...receive instruction from the all-powerful Supreme Being, who appears as a guru, and are blessed with the bliss of Sivap perum, the abode of Siva. This is what the eighth sutra of Sivagnana Bodham states.

Here, all the souls, due to their past penance, have Pillaiyar as their guru, and all those who have come to witness this wedding are witnessing it due to their past penance.

Thus, Emperor Thirugnanasambandhar proceeds, holding the unique umbrella, which is the ‘state of penance, lifted high’. Normally, a white umbrella is a symbol of kings.

However, in reality ...the true king is Shiva. The white umbrella, the crown of nine gems, and the throne are special symbols of kings. Considering their superiority, only the pearl umbrella is mentioned here. By extension, we should also include the crown of nine gems and the throne. The eighth sutra of Sivagnana Bodham, in the commentary by Sri Madhava Sivagnana Muni, states: ‘The primordial Lord, who is the cause of the universe, has a great white umbrella. He has a great radiant intelligence that knows all things equally.

He has a great throne that sustains every soul as its life. These are exclusively His own. Because He severs the impurities of the souls, He is called the primordial Lord, the King.’ Thus, the soul is metaphorically represented as a prince, who enjoys the supreme bliss of the Lord, which is entirely His own. This is explained by Sri Madhava Sivagnana Muni. As stated in the fifth sutra of Sivagnana Bodham, ‘received from the Lord, who is the sole refuge,’ the umbrella gifted by the Lord is held over Emperor Thirugnanasambandhar. Emperor Thirugnanasambandhar, as the guru, who unites all mature souls with the Lord’s divine feet, proceeds.

At that time, he always holds the Lord’s divine feet in his heart. An acharya, before initiating a mature disciple and guiding them on the right path, remembers the Lord and prays, ‘O Lord, look at this disciple’s maturity and grant me the grace to initiate them and guide them on the right path.’ This is the rule in the Siucom Agamas.

Accordingly, Emperor Thirugnanasambandhar, as the guru, always remembers the Lord’s divine feet in his heart while proceeding to witness this wedding. The 1107th hymn: ‘Those within the Perumanam temple, with increasing auspiciousness, towards the approaching wedding, to welcome and escort, entering the temple...’ ...of Ilankai continent, where the Lord resides. In this hymn, he describes Emperor Thirugnanasambandhar directly entering the Thiru Perumanam temple. In worldly customs, it is customary for the relatives of the groom to come forward and escort him to the wedding venue.

However, here, before the bride’s family can come forward to welcome Pillaiyar, who is arriving for the wedding, the devotees of the Thiru Perumanam Siva temple have already gone forth with special honors to welcome and escort Pillaiyar. With them ...Pillaiyar directly entered the temple where Shiva resides. Although Pillaiyar appeared to be getting married in the worldly sense, he actually came to Thiru Perumanam to merge with the Lord in divine union, the ultimate wedding. It is rare for those worldly people who go for worldly pursuits to proceed directly to the temple of the Lord instead of the wedding venue.

Therefore, the devotees of the Thiru Nallur Perumanam temple, with increasing auspiciousness, went to welcome Pillaiyar, the great soul from Seerkazhi, who was arriving for the wedding, and escorted him into the temple of the Lord. He who resides within the darkness of the ocean’s poison ...the Lord with the dark hue.

Here, darkness refers to the darkness of impurity. In this wedding, through Pillaiyar, those who come to seek refuge will have their fundamental impurity, the ego, weakened and destroyed, leading to liberation. This state will be illuminated.

The Lord residing in the Thiru Perumanam temple is alluded to by God Sekkizhar Peruman.

The devotees of the Thiru Perumanam Siva temple, carrying the Lord’s umbrella and other auspicious items, went forth to welcome Pillaiyar. Auspiciousness is Siva. The auspiciousness that began with Pillaiyar’s arrival has increased manifold. In the way of the upcoming wedding, they went forth to welcome him. Worldly celebrations like weddings are ultimately impermanent and lead to inauspiciousness.

Therefore, calling worldly weddings auspicious is merely a matter of convention, not reality. This wedding, unlike the worldly wedding which perishes with the body, is the union of the soul with the Lord, Siva, the divine groom. That wedding is an eternal auspiciousness, which grows with experience and brings supreme bliss, unlike worldly weddings.

Thus, welcomed by the devotees, he entered the Thiru Perumanam temple. Emperor Thirugnanasambandhar.

Now, the 1108th hymn: ‘After worshipping the Lord, singing a pathigam of good meaning, receiving the grace of love and truth, the leader of the Kouniyas entered the wedding hall of the Brahmins...’ ...in a pavilion outside the temple.’ This hymn states that he entered a pavilion outside the temple. Emperor Thirugnanasambandhar, after entering the temple, worshipped the Lord and sang a pathigam of good meaning. We do not have the pathigam sung by Emperor Thirugnanasambandhar at Thiru Nallur Perumanam at this time, due to our lack of penance. Thus, as Emperor Thirugnanasambandhar came out of the temple, the Brahmins gathered and requested Emperor Thirugnanasambandhar to adorn himself in wedding attire. Now, the 1110th hymn: ‘With divine feet blooming like flowers, adorned with rows of pearls, with gem-studded anklets, with radiant necklaces of pearls strung on gold, and with dangling tassels...’ This hymn describes the adornment of Emperor Thirugnanasambandhar from feet to head, which will be elaborated in the next six hymns. The word ‘Mutthu’ (pearl) also means ‘to be freed’.

Liberation is derived from this meaning. Since Pillaiyar, as the guru who bestows liberation on everyone, stands as the groom, the ornaments he wears are also made of pearls. The types and qualities of pearls were explained by Sivakavi Mani Desiganar under the 492nd hymn of Viranminda Nayanar Puranam. We discussed this in detail there.

Now, the meaning of this hymn: the divine feet are adorned with blooming flowers, and above them, rows of pearls are worn, like radiating white light. Gem-studded anklets are placed on the divine feet. Tassels, like the fringes of a pearl necklace, are adorned. The part above the ankle is called ‘Paradu’. The tassel is called ‘Kuncham’. The phrase ‘Mutthu Thamam Pirangiya Thongal’ means a cluster of pearl necklaces gathered as tassels.

Thus, ornaments are adorned on the shins of Emperor Thirugnanasambandhar’s divine feet.

It is made of large pearls strung on gold threads.

Now, a lustrous pearl necklace, radiating light, is worn on the expansive garment, beautifully adorning the waist. This is referred to as the ‘pin kachcham’ garment. This garment has pearl embellishments along its border.

The divine ash is the ornament that gives beauty to all ornaments. Without divine ash, other ornaments become impure, worldly things that lead to suffering. ‘As the sacred ash does not adorn the forehead...’(Thiruvasagam). The blessings of the meditating sages and devotees, along with Vedic chants, rose higher and higher, spreading in all directions, and the world bloomed.
