Therefore, it is described as the waves of the Ganges. These waves entered the mountain, called the golden mountain, just as the Pillaiyar entered the mansion called Aadhi Bhoomi. This mansion belongs to Nambiyandar Nambi. He entered the mansion, which is called Aadhi Bhoomi. He is the one who, in the past, won the river debate by placing the palm leaf manuscript in the Vaigai River, writing the hymn ‘Vaazhka Andhanar’ (May Brahmins live). In that hymn, the lines ‘Aazhka theeyathu ellam aran naamame soozhga vaiyagavum thuyar theergave’ (May all evil sink, may only the name of God surround, may the world be free from suffering) show how he saved us, future generations.

The Pillaiyar uttered commands like ‘Aazhka’ (live), ‘Soozhga’ (surround), and ‘Theerga’ (be free) using the imperative mood.

Therefore, this hymn, which bestows life not only at that time but for all future generations, is significant. Because he placed the palm leaf manuscript in the river, we are alive today, and future generations will also live. The phrase ‘to live for us’ means ‘to grant life’. The victory in the river debate and the subsequent eradication of opposing ideologies led to the establishment and growth of the Saiva faith, bringing us life. That is the significance here.

Thus, the Pillaiyar, who grants us life, entered the mansion called Aadhi Bhoomi. He is destined to grant great bliss and liberation to all who have come to the temple, which is the city of Shiva, known as Aadhi Bhoomi. One should understand this as the Lord’s grace, which was bestowed upon us by placing the palm leaf in the river in the past. ‘Aadhi Bhoomi’ also means the city of Shiva. Verse 1231: ‘Incense smoke diffused, fragrant flowers adorned the canopy, on the flower-strewn seat, with tassels, the groom, adorned with pearl necklaces, smiled. Surrounded by virtuous Brahmins, he sat there.’ This verse describes the scene as the groom, Pillaiyar, sat on the flower-strewn seat in the mansion called Aadhi Bhoomi. Incense smoke diffused, a canopy adorned with jewels shone above, maidens sang praises, and Brahmins chanted Vedic hymns.

As soon as the groom took his seat, the first ritual was performed. The next ritual will be described in the following verse. Sekkizhar continues. Verse 1232: ‘The bride’s father, a sage who received the bride, along with his virtuous wife, who performed great penance, joyfully washed the groom’s feet. They brought pure milk and water with affection.’ This verse refers to Nambiyandar Nambi, the father of the bride, who is a sage who received the bride. Sekkizhar describes him as a sage.

We saw earlier that in verse 1059, Sekkizhar referred to the groom’s father, Shivapadakirthiyayar.

Similarly, here, Nambiyandar Nambi, the bride’s father, is referred to as a sage. Nambiyandar Nambi and his virtuous wife, who have performed great penance, have attained the boon of having a daughter who is destined to become the Pillaiyar’s consort. Without such great penance, it would not be possible to have such a daughter.

Therefore, Nambiyandar Nambi’s wife also performed great penance to beget this daughter. If Nambiyandar Nambi’s wife had not performed such great penance, Nambiyandar Nambi would not have had the privilege of giving his daughter in marriage today.

Thus, Nambiyandar Nambi received such great honor. His wife performed such penance. Although they had a daughter, the right to give her in marriage belongs to the father.

Therefore, Sekkizhar first mentions Nambiyandar Nambi and then his wife. Nambiyandar Nambi and his wife, with great joy, washed the Pillaiyar’s feet. They were honored to give their daughter to the Pillaiyar, a fact that filled them with pride. This act was not merely a duty but also an expression of their right.

Therefore, they brought pure milk and water to wash the divine feet of Thirugnanasambandhar. With great joy, they washed the divine feet. They were blessed to touch, wash, and worship the divine feet, and they were filled with immense happiness. They imprinted the divine feet in their hearts. Since the Pillaiyar’s body is immaculate, washing his feet is not essential.

However, to show their detachment and devotion, they washed the Pillaiyar’s feet, as explained by the sage Sivakavi Mani Desikar. He interpreted the act as the parents of the bride treating the groom as Lord Shiva and washing his feet with cow’s milk, which is one of the wedding rituals. The Kandapuranam, in the chapter on the divine wedding, verse 39, states: ‘The celestial beings descended, accompanied by divine maidens, and washed the feet of the supreme being with milk and water.’ Similarly, in the Kandapuranam, chapter on the divine wedding of Deivanai, verse 206, it is stated: ‘Indrani, receiving the auspicious occasion, brought forth milk from a new cow and filled a vessel with it, and performed the ritual with reverence.’ In all these instances, the Lord established this ritual for the world. It signifies that in auspicious rituals, one should consider the bride as Shakti and the groom as Shiva, and both should see themselves in this manner. These are truths that reveal that the goal of auspicious rituals performed by Saivites is to attain the divine state of Shiva. These are the teachings of the Shaiva Shastras, and we see that they are perfectly embodied in the Pillaiyar.

We are about to witness how the Pillaiyar’s divine feet guided the world to liberation. Nambiyandar Nambi and his wife, in order to show the world that these divine feet are worthy of worship and lead to liberation, performed this act. The divine feet of the Pillaiyar are always in the hearts of devotees. They are worshipped with flowers by the people of this world. They are worthy of poetic composition by scholars. ‘The golden feet of the sage are divine.’ Nambiyandar Nambi later reveals this.

Now, he is showing it. Verse 1233: ‘Arriving before him, and with the merit of their past penance, Nambiyandar Nambi and the bride, with their mind fixed on the divine feet of Gnana Ponaar, poured water from the golden vessel.’ Thus, after taking pure water and cow’s milk, they arrived before the Pillaiyar. Nambiyandar Nambi, whose merit from past penance is overflowing, and his wife, poured water from the golden vessel, meditating on the divine feet of the Pillaiyar, whom they considered as Shiva with matted hair. This is the meaning of this verse.

Following this, verse 1234 states: ‘After sprinkling the pure water over their heads, they cleared the auspicious water within the house and outside. They poured it into their bellies with great joy.’ As stated in verse 1233, Nambiyandar Nambi, having performed great penance in the past, and now having the boon of giving his daughter in marriage, and anticipating the imminent attainment of bliss and liberation for himself and others, washed the Pillaiyar’s feet. By washing the Pillaiyar’s feet, the wedding ritual took place, and it also served as the worship of the Guru. As a result of this Guru worship, they attained liberation.

Thus, the merit of their past penance increased, as mentioned by Sekkizhar. ‘Kanthavar Kuzhalinar’, meaning Nambiyandar Nambi’s wife with long, fragrant hair. The fragrance is natural in the hair of virtuous women.

Therefore, Sekkizhar refers to her not by her name but as ‘Kanthavar Kuzhal’ (fragrant-haired). It is a rule to treat the groom as Shiva during wedding rituals.

Therefore, considering him as Shiva, Nambiyandar Nambi’s wife poured water from the golden vessel. It is customary for the mother of the bride to wash the groom’s feet with milk and water.

Here, not only was he the groom, but he was also being worshipped as the Guru.

Therefore, Nambiyandar Nambi’s wife poured the water from the vessel, and Nambiyandar Nambi himself performed this ritual. Verse 1234 describes how Sekkizhar states that he performed it with great affection. He sprinkled the extremely pure water on his head. This was the pure water used to wash the Gnana Ponaar’s feet.

Therefore, after sprinkling this holy water on his head, the most important part of the body, which sustains life, is the head. He first sprinkled it on his head, and then on the inside and outside of the mansion, which is the place where the body lives. As a result, the place was filled, completed, and adorned. After sprinkling the holy water inside and outside the mansion, they joyfully drank it, considering it as the source of life in their bellies. The relatives, experiencing great delight, also sprinkled it on themselves. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Great Puranam by Sekkizhar, Part 831, chapter ‘Vambara Varivandu’, Puranam of Thirugnanasambandhanayanar. The foot-washing ceremony performed for the groom is also considered Guru worship. This holy water is sprinkled throughout the pavilion. All the relatives cherish it with great devotion. Verse 1235: ‘The Pillaiyar, who has attained overflowing wisdom, received the flower-like hand holding the vessel of auspicious water.

He proclaimed his lineage and declared, ‘I have given my precious daughter to the Pillaiyar.’’ This verse refers to Thirugnanasambandhar as the Pillaiyar who has attained overflowing wisdom. ‘Overflowing wisdom’ here refers to divine wisdom, which has the power to dispel the inner darkness of primal ignorance.

Therefore, it is called overflowing wisdom.

Furthermore, because it has no superior light, this divine wisdom is indeed overflowing. The Pillaiyar, who has made this divine wisdom, like nectar, available to us, received the vessel of auspicious water in his lotus-like hand. Nambiyandar Nambi, holding the auspicious water in the vessel, poured it, declaring, ‘I have given my daughter.’ It is customary to pour water while giving away the daughter, signifying the ‘Kanyadhanam’ in Sanskrit. While pouring the water, Nambiyandar Nambi ...stated his lineage and family, and declared, ‘I have given my daughter, whom I cherished as a precious treasure, to the Pillaiyar.’ Thus, Sekkizhar describes Nambiyandar Nambi’s daughter as ‘Arunidhi Paavaiyar’, meaning one adorned with precious ornaments. This refers to a ‘Sallankruta Kannikadhanam’. The tradition of Krita Yuga, which was to place a young maiden, whose waist was slender like the rays of the sun, and give her hand in marriage before she was ripe, is narrated in the Thiruvilayadal Puranam.

Nambandhar Nambigal, referred to as Arunitipavaiyar, his daughter whose name is given as Stotra Purnambigai in the Tala Puranam of Tirunallur Peruman, is stated to have performed the Kanyadhanam, dedicating this maiden, this young girl, to Pillaiyar (Ganesha). ‘I have given this maiden, this young girl, whom I received, to Pillaiyar,’ thus states Nambandhar Nambigal.

Now, the thirty-sixth Tiruppadal: ‘Nattavakkanniyar Kai Gnanasambandhar Chengai Patriyudaiya Panpil Pazhuthil Narpozuthu Nanna Pettravar Udan Pirandhaar Peru.’ This refers to the act of escorting the bride to the groom and the people surrounding them, bowing and offering praise. This is from the Tiruppadal. Nambandhar Nambigal announces that he is performing the Kanyadhanam. As soon as this is announced, the auspicious moment for the wedding ceremony, Panigrahanam, arrives. This Panigraha Muhurtham, as it is called in Sanskrit, is referred to as ‘Narpozuthu, free from blemish, suitable for Gnanasambandhar to take the maiden’s hand’ by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman. The ceremony of Thiru Mangalya Dharanam, tying the sacred marital thread, began later.

In earlier times, the Koda (giving away the bride) was performed by those who were accustomed to it, along with the Vedic ceremony called Velvi (fire ritual). Later came the act of holding hands, called Panigrahanam, and the adorning with garlands. That is, exchanging garlands and circumambulating the sacred fire were the initial rituals, some say. It is also said that references to wearing the Thiru Mangalyam are first found in the Matsya Purana.

However, the Thiruvilayadal Puranam, in its wedding chapter, the one hundred and eighty-fifth verse, states thus: ‘Sutru naan maraigal aarppuriyam sangam engu katra naan mugaththon velvi chadangu nool karaintha atraal utra Mangalaathi muzhuthu ulagu yandran sengkai patrina patriyilaarkke vidu arul paramayogi.’ In this, Lord Shiva, appearing as Somasundara Kadavul, during the wedding of Meenakshi Amman, and Brahma performing the Vedic ceremony. He placed the auspicious thread on Meenakshi Amman’s neck and held her hand. So goes the verse.

Similarly, in the Kanda Puranam, in the chapter on the wedding of Deivayanai Amman, the two hundred and forty-seventh Tiruppadal states: ‘Sengkmalathu iraichinthaiyin aatri angaiyin enthida aanda kai konda mangala naanai manikkazhum aarththu nangai mudikkor narunthodai suzhan.’ This verse describes how Lord Muruga tied the auspicious thread around Deivayanai Amman’s neck.

Therefore, for those who argue otherwise, the Thiruvilayadal Puranam (wedding of Meenakshi Amman) and the Kanda Puranam (wedding chapter of Deivayanai Amman) provide a beautiful and fitting answer.

Thus, now arrives the Panigraha Muhurtham. Just as we look for an auspicious time for Thiru Mangalya Dharanam, it is our custom to look for an auspicious time, a Muhurtham, for Panigrahanam as well. That moment, according to astrological texts, is a good time, a Nammumurtham, free from flaws. This is referred to as ‘Narpozuthu’ by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman. ‘Pazhuthu’ means flaw, and ‘Nalpozuthu’ means a good Muhurtham, free from defects.

Moreover, ‘Pazhuthayil Pozuthu’ means the time that causes the removal of the impurity of the souls. This signifies that in this wedding, all souls are destined to be cleansed of their impurities and attain liberation. At that auspicious time, during the Panigraha Muhurtham, having received the bride. The parents and siblings of the bride bring her into the groom’s presence. It is also customary to seat the bride on the groom’s right side. Here too, Stotra Purnambigai Amman is brought forward by her parents and siblings, surrounded by companions resembling deer, and presented before the groom, Pillaiyar.

The divine Sekkizhar Peruman mentions ‘Pettravarum Udan Pirandhaar,’ meaning parents and siblings.

Therefore, Stotra Purnambigai Amman is brought by her parents and siblings to be presented before Pillaiyar.

Thus, through this verse, we learn that Pillaiyar has siblings.

Now, the thirty-seventh Tiruppadal: ‘Ekamam Siva Meygnanam Isainthavar Valappaal Eythi.’ ‘Nagamor Panapper Alkun Natrava Kolundhu Anaarai Magamar Sodhimalka Manni Veetriruntha Vellai Megamodu Isaiyum Minnu Kodiyena Vilanga Vaithaar.’ This is the Tiruppadal. Pillaiyar is one who has attained ‘Ekamam Siva Meygnanam’ – the singular, true knowledge of Shiva. This true, unchanging, eternal knowledge is Sivagnanam. We can recall from the beginning of this Puranam the descriptions of this as ‘Perumaikkazhil Peenum Or Neriyil Varignanam’ (knowledge in a path that leads to great glory) and ‘Ennariya Sivagnanam’ (unfathomable Sivagnanam).

Thus, the benefit of the knowledge that Pillaiyar attained is now reaching its fulfillment. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman concludes this by stating, ‘Ekamam.’ ‘Siva Meygnanam Isainthavar’ (one who has attained true knowledge of Shiva) is how Pillaiyar is described here. This is the place where the state of knowledge attained by Pillaiyar is discussed. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman states this here, signifying that the fruit of that knowledge is about to be attained. Pillaiyar, who has attained that true knowledge of Shiva, has made it his very form. Pillaiyar has indeed partaken of the nectar of Sivagnanam.

The bride is seated to the right of such a Pillaiyar. That divine vision appears like a lightning streak in white clouds. It is customary for the bride to be seated on the groom’s right side until the wedding rituals are completed and the circumambulation of the fire is done.

After that, she moves to the left. The scriptures state that a woman, after observing vows and penance, obtains a suitable groom. This is what the scriptures say.

Therefore, after the fire ritual, the bride should join the groom’s left side. That is, it is the rule to seat the bride on the groom’s left side. The left side is the side meant for femininity. The stories of Uma Amman’s penance and other legends explain this concept. The fact that Amman also took her place on the left side is also part of this.

Therefore, the bride is referred to here as ‘Natrava Kolundhu Anaar’ (a tender shoot of great penance). She is seated to the right of the divine Sambandhar Peruman. How does that divine vision appear? It shines like a lightning streak in white clouds. It is natural for lightning to appear in clouds. The proverb states, ‘After lightning comes rain.’ ‘Lightning indicates the clouds, clouds indicate rain’ is the meaning.

Here, it signifies that a rain of divine knowledge is about to fall, leading to the bliss of liberation, the divine enjoyment of Shiva. This simile is used here. Our texts state that white clouds, more encompassing than dark clouds, yield great benefit. Pillaiyar is seated here like a white cloud. The whiteness of his sacred ash, the brilliance of the pearl ornaments he wears, and his radiant effulgence as a flame of knowledge – all contribute to his appearance like a white cloud. The Amman seated to his right resembles a streak of lightning, clinging to that cloud.

Now, the thirty-eighth Tiruppadal: ‘Punitha Meykolam Needu Pugaliyaar Vendhar Thammai.’ ‘Kunichilai Puruvam Men Poongombu Annaar Udaney Kooda Nanmiga Kandapozhuthil Nalla Mangalangaal Koori Manitharum Thevaraanar Kan Imaiyathu Vazhthi.’ This is the Tiruppadal. When the divine Sekkizhar Peruman saw the venerable Pillaiyar, the king of Pugali, with his pure, divine form, accompanied by the bride resembling a delicate flowering creeper with eyebrows like a bent bow, with great affection, those present there offered auspicious blessings and gazed at that divine vision without blinking. As the humans present there gazed at that divine vision without blinking, they appeared like gods. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman praises the bride of Pillaiyar here as ‘Kunichilai Puruvam Men Poongombu’ (a delicate flowering creeper with eyebrows like a bent bow). The bow’s curve indicates its usefulness; the greater the curve, the more beneficial it is.

Here, the curved state of the Amman’s eyes and eyebrows signifies her ability to bestow the benefit of liberation upon everyone through her compassionate gaze. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman implicitly conveys this. This divine vision is the first auspicious sight of the couple seated together. This is the first time that divine Sambandhar Peruman appears with his consort.

Therefore, it is a good tradition to bless such a divine vision upon seeing it. Those who witnessed this divine vision here were so captivated that they gazed without blinking and offered blessings. Those who bless the divine beings elevate themselves through that blessing. They bless the divine beings for that very purpose. ‘To bestow life upon oneself by blessing the divine, and for the celestials to bow to you, desiring to be praised,’ as stated by our Lord Manikkavachakar Peruman in the Thiruvachagam.

Therefore, those who saw and blessed Pillaiyar and his consort here attained life through their blessings. By having the opportunity to see and bless Pillaiyar and his consort in this way, they are destined to attain eternal Shiva. In ordinary worldly weddings, the blessings offered are merely formalities.

But here, the auspicious words spoken to bless Pillaiyar and his consort were genuine, not mere formalities. All those blessings are destined to culminate in eternal, unperishable divine auspiciousness.

Therefore, the divine Sekkizhar Peruman describes them as ‘good auspiciousness.’ Let us continue contemplating. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. The Periya Puranam by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, Part 832, Vambara Varivandu Sargam, ThiruGnana Sambandha Nayanar Puranam, the one thousand two hundred and thirty-ninth Tiruppadal: ‘Bhakthiyil Kuyitrum Paimpon Pavala Kaal Pandhar Naappen Chiththira Vidhanathin Keezh Sezhunthiruneelakkar Muththamizh Viragar Munbu Mudhal Marai Muraiyinodu Meyththa Namberuman Paathamevum Ullaththal Seyya.’ This is the Tiruppadal. A pandal with a base of vermilion coral, adorned with gold, supported by pillars of green gold, and a central canopy decorated with paintings. Under this canopy, the auspicious wedding rituals are taking place. The noble Thiru Neelanakka Nayanar, acting as the teacher, performs the Vedic rituals for the Pillaiyar, who is a master of the three Tamil literatures, in the presence of the divine. He performs the essential Vedic rituals according to the prescribed method, with a heart devoted to the divine feet of our Lord.

Thiru Neelanakka Nayanar is well-versed in the four Vedas, as we saw in the one thousand eight hundred and thirty-ninth Tiruppadal: ‘Gnyalamikka Naanmari Porul Vilakkiya Nalathaar.’ Thiru Neelanakka Nayanar is officiating as the Purohit, the Vedic priest, at this wedding ceremony. The term Purohit means ‘one who performs welfare in front.’ Therefore, Thiru Neelanakka Nayanar, being well-versed in the four Vedas, officiates as the Purohit and performs the wedding rituals for Pillaiyar. He performs the wedding fire ritual. It is customary to perform the wedding ritual with the groom as the central figure.

Similarly, the ritual of offering rice flakes (Porikay) is performed before the bride. These are all prescribed in the Vedas. The Vedas state that Lord Shiva alone is the Supreme Reality (Sat). With his mind contemplating the divine feet of Lord Shiva, who is described as Sat by the Vedas, Thiru Neelanakka Nayanar performs the rituals. He is very pure, an expert in the Vedas, and highly virtuous. Nevertheless, if one undertakes actions with individual consciousness, they are subject to the three Gunas and may deviate from the proper course.

Therefore, performing these rituals with individual consciousness. Thiru Neelanakka Nayanar performs them with a mind devoted to the divine feet of the Lord. As it is said, ‘True devotees who perceive the Lord’s consciousness do not succumb to karma,’ he will complete the rituals smoothly, thinking of Lord Shiva. The Tiruppadal also states, ‘Ullaththarai’ (with a devoted heart). It is also fitting to say that he performs these duties with the thought that by doing this noble work, he will attain the grace of the divine feet. We can also see that Thiru Neelanakka Nayanar is destined to attain the grace of the divine feet.

Now, the next meaning: Pillaiyar does not cherish anything other than the divine feet of the Lord.

Therefore, it is a rule that his Vedic rituals must also be performed with the same devotion. This is about. Thiru Neelanakka Nayanar performs them by remembering the divine feet of the Lord. The Śivāgamas state that when performing rituals like Pujas, one must transform their sensory organs and mind into a divine form through appropriate mantras, Nyasa, and Bhava kriyas. Thiru Neelanakka Nayanar performs these actions with the thought of dedicating himself to the task of performing Pillaiyar’s wedding rituals. Another interpretation is that although these rituals are performed with Pillaiyar as the central figure, they are done with the understanding that they ultimately reach the Lord’s feet.

Furthermore, these rituals are destined to grant the attainment of Shiva, the ultimate state, to all those present at this wedding. With the intention of bestowing eternal divine auspiciousness. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman elaborates extensively on this point, stating that Thiru Neelanakka Nayanar performs these rituals with such devotion, meditating on the divine feet of Lord Shiva. It is also mentioned that most of this commentary is based on the notes of Thiru Kayapakkam Sadashiva Chettiyar. The commentator states: ‘Now, the one thousand two hundred and fortieth Tiruppadal: ‘Maraiyoli Pongki Ongga Mangala Vazhthu Malga Niraivazhai Chengai Patra.’ ‘Neriizhai Avar Mun Anthap Poraiyani Munnool Marbar Pugazhil Van Porikai Atti Iraivarai Yetum Velai Erivilam Kolla Vendi.’ This is the Tiruppadal.

The Brahmins and relatives gathered there chanted Vedic hymns. The women of the priestly class and others proclaimed auspicious blessings. For the maiden adorned with numerous bangles to hold the hand of the groom, Thiru Neelanakka Nayanar, before her, took handfuls of faultless white rice flakes, offered them as oblations into the sacred fire, and praised the Lord. Offering white rice flakes into the sacred fire before the bride, accompanied by appropriate mantras and visualizations, and praising the Lord. This is performed for Panigrahanam. There are many rules regarding how the new rice flakes should be prepared, starting with the requirement that they be crushed by chaste women in a new, clean clay pot in a pure environment.

The rice flakes prepared according to these rules are faultless and are the best offering for the oblations. It is customary to take these rice flakes and offer them into the fire with one’s hands, not with tools.

At this time, the mantras recited convey the request for the Lord’s grace, enabling the Lord to accept this ritual and bestow its appropriate benefits. After offering the rice flakes into the fire, the groom must hold the bride’s hand and circumambulate the sacred fire seven times. This is a very important part of the wedding rituals. It is customary for the wedding rituals to conclude with this.

Therefore, before doing so, Thiru Neelanakka Nayanar supplicates the Lord by offering rice flakes into the sacred fire.

Now, the one thousand two hundred and forty-first Tiruppadal: ‘Aruppu Menmullaiyinaarththam Animmalar Kaippidiththu Angu Or Padum Udaiya Pillaiyar ThiruUllam Thannil Viruppurum Angiyaavar Vidai Uyarththavare.’ This is the Tiruppadal. The divine Pillaiyar, who is twelve years old, holding the beautiful flower-like hand of. Stotra Purnambigai Amman, reflects within his divine heart. He contemplates the Vedic fire ritual that has been performed so far and is about to undertake the circumambulation of the fire. As he holds the Devi’s hand to proceed with the circumambulation, a thought arises in his divine heart through divine grace, a clarity emerges. Pillaiyar thinks within his divine heart, ‘The fire that is pleasing is none other than Lord Shiva, who bears the bull banner.’ He reflects this within his divine heart.

The divine Sambandhar Peruman sees the fire arising in this wedding ritual as the sacred fire. However, he realizes that Shiva Himself is the fire within that fire. This thought arises in his divine heart through divine grace. The Thevaram verse states, ‘Without fire, there is no form; without the bull, there is no ascent.’ Therefore, upon seeing the fire in the wedding ritual, the thought arises in the divine heart of divine Sambandhar Peruman that Shiva Himself is the fire. This is because fire is one of the eight forms of the Lord mentioned in the scriptures. Earth, water, fire, air, ether, sun, moon, and soul are the eight forms.

We find references to these in various places in the Thirumurai, including the Thiruvachagam.

Therefore, these eight are indeed the divine forms of the Lord. Among these eight, fire is the most significant. Earth and water are considered inferior to fire. Air and ether. Although they are the first two, they are not visible to the eyes. In the sun and moon, the Lord’s form is subtle and hidden, not openly visible.

However, fire has a special characteristic: the Lord’s form resides within the fire itself. As Rudra, the embodiment of fire, the Great Rudra, the Lord manifests in the form of fire. In that Great Rudra, He is the destroyer and also the creator, bringing about regeneration.

Therefore, among these eight, fire is the superior form. However, even within this fire, the Lord remains hidden like ghee in milk.

But the places where the Lord manifests brilliantly and openly are the Guru’s form. Shivalayam, and the divine attire of the devotee.

Therefore, upon seeing the fire in this wedding ritual, the thought arises in the divine heart of divine Sambandhar Peruman that the Lord, who has the fire as His form, is none other than Him. He decides to have the darshan of Lord Shiva, who resides within the Tirupperumanam temple. Divine grace instills this clarity in his heart.

The Lord is omnipresent. Such a Lord resides in the temple of Tirupperumanam, and this thought is instilled in the divine heart of divine Sambandhar Peruman.

The Lord is everywhere.

Therefore, even in the fire of this wedding ritual, nurtured by mantras, rituals, and visualizations. Pillaiyar, thinking that the Lord is the fire, is about to go to the Tirupperumanam temple. This is because the Lord exists everywhere as inert and conscious matter. While it is true that those with true perception can see Ishwara everywhere, both as inert and conscious, the Lord shines brightly in three forms: Guru, Lingam, and Jangamam, and less so in other places.

Therefore, worshipping the Lord’s divine form within the temple is of great significance. The Sivagnana Bodham, twelfth sutra, states: ‘Although the universe is divine, worship with love.’ Even though all inert and conscious things are the form of that divine being, worship where love blossoms. We see this concept articulated in the Mahabhashyam as a command: ‘O one who has attained that non-dual Siddhanta.’ Just as milk overflows from the cow’s udder, even though the entire body is filled with milk, the Lord does not manifest Himself outwardly except through the divine form in the temple.

Therefore, it is conveyed that the love that arises there will not blossom elsewhere. Even though the Lord manifests in this sacred fire of the wedding ritual, which has been invoked through mantras, those who lack the ability to perceive Him in the fire will only see Him if invoked by the mantra’s presence. Without the mantra’s presence, He remains hidden.

However, for those with true penance or wisdom, He always appears in all places. Pillaiyar, too, was in such a state of liberated consciousness (Jeevan Mukta).

Therefore, Pillaiyar’s incarnation here was for the sake of the worldly people who lack the penance to see the Lord everywhere.

Thus, realizing that Lord Shiva Himself resides in this wedding fire, Pillaiyar decides to go to the Tirupperumanam temple where that Lord resides. This is because the Lord has manifested here due to the invocation through the sankalpa for this wedding ritual. This is because the Lord has manifested here due to the invocation through the sankalpa for this wedding ritual.

After the wedding ritual is completed, He will withdraw His presence with Udyapana (retirement) rituals. However, in the temple, the Lord resides eternally, manifesting His presence.

“They are unable to find the Lord’s beginning and end, even after searching. Lord Siva, who bestowed the four Vedas, is the essence of those Vedas. So say the wise. That Lord resides permanently in the temple of Perumanam in the sacred place of Thiru Nallūr.

“Now, the meaning of the tenth verse is: O Jains and Buddhists, who lack the knowledge to realize the Lord, come! Do not argue and cling to the wrong path, but come and join the righteous path of Siddhanta Saivism. Come! Join the righteous path of Siddhanta Saivism.

“Lord Siva is the Lord of all beings. He resides in the temple of Perumanam in the sacred place of Thiru Nallūr and is the essence of the Vedas. Worship the sacred feet of such Lord Siva. By doing so, liberation is certain.

“Now, the eleventh verse is the concluding verse. Its meaning is as follows: Thiru Gnanasambandhan, who was born in the fragrant Sīrkāzhi, has bestowed this Tamil Thiruppathigam, which is capable of yielding great benefits, with the intention of merging with the sacred feet of Lord Siva, who resides in the temple of Perumanam in the sacred place of Thiru Perumanallur, where liberation is difficult to attain. For those who chant this Thiruppathigam with devotion, sins and flaws will be removed, the suffering of birth and death will cease, and they will attain the bliss of divine union. They will attain. Thiru Nallūr Perumanam, this sacred place, is the fifth in the Chola country on the northern bank of the Kaveri. During one kalpa, when Brahmā and other gods came to Sīrkāzhi, they learned of its greatness and called it Nallūr, hence this name.

“Nallūr is the name of the place, and Perumanam is the name of the temple. Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman bestowed this Thiruppathigam.

“Here, having commanded the Namachivaya Thiruppathigam, he made all who heard it eligible for liberation. This is the place where Pillaiyar’s consort resided.

“Hence, it is called Āchāzhpuram. It is located a short distance east of Kollidam, near Sīrkāzhi. It is also said to be a place with Āchā trees. The Lord’s name is Sivālōka Thyāgar, and the Goddess is Thiru Vennīrrumai. The sacred water is Panchāksara Theertham. There are eight sacred waters seen by sages in eight directions.

“This temple is well maintained by the Tharmapuram Adheenam of the Kailaya Paramparai. The wedding festival of Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman in Vaikāsi Mūlam and the divine forms of Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman with his consort are unique specialities of this place. These are the notes about the place Thiru Nallūr Perumanam.

“Let us proceed with our contemplation.” Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Volume Eighty-three, Chapter on the Buzzing Bees, by Devashekulār Peruman. The life of Thiru Gnanasambandhan Nayanar. Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman makes a plea for liberation to Sivālōka Thyāgar, the Lord of Thiru Nallūr Perumanam. Devashekulār Peruman bestows the next verse, number two thousand four hundred and forty-six: “Gods, with divine grace, you and Pūvai Annāl, and all who have come to this sacred wedding of yours, will come to us.” This verse reads: “The three worlds will then be filled with light, and the entire flame will become one.” Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman makes a plea for liberation.

The Lord, who is the leader of all gods, bestows grace. Thiru Gnanasambandha. Peruman is graced. How? He commanded: “You and your wife, Pūvai, and all who have come to your sacred wedding, come to us within this light.” Lord Siva, shining with His effulgence, rises as a Jōthirlinga, illuminating the three worlds. The Lord’s command is accepted.

The Lord’s plea in the Thiruppathigam, “O Lord, bestow your grace upon us,” is accepted. The gift of being united with our feet is thus bestowed. Is this not a sacred wedding? Unlike the minds of others in the world, it is a wedding that bestows the fruit of divine merit, not one that leads to worldly attachments. From Thiru Nīlanakka Nayanar onwards. All those who came to that wedding to attain liberation, the mind that unites them all in the bliss of liberation.

Therefore, “You and your wife, come to us within this light,” the Lord commanded, and rose as a complete, radiant flame, shining brightly like a great flame of divine wisdom. There, as it is said, “Light itself is the flame, the lamp of brilliance.” He stands as a pillar, supporting all things, shining brightly. The seventh verse: “Within the temple, the light overflows, the divine gateway is shown. The virtuous King of Pugazhi, illuminated by the light, praises the great radiant light.” Worship! He bestows the way for the world to be saved.

The Lord stands there as a great flame. That flame, encompassing the Āchāzhpuram temple within itself, becomes so vast that the temple is not visible, and only the flame is seen, rising and expanding.

Furthermore, He has created a divine gateway within that flame. So that everyone can merge into that flame through that divine gateway. He stands as that flame with the divine gateway. Although the Lord is everywhere, filled with divine wisdom, unless the Lord shows the way through Vedas and other scriptures, souls cannot understand and follow the righteous path.

Therefore, here, the Lord not only rises as a flame but also ...creates the gateway for souls with maturity to approach. Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman praises and worships the Lord as the great radiant light, which shines brightly. He bestows the way for the souls in this vast, dark world to be saved. Although Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman shows the Lord as a flame and the gateway to merge into that flame, it is not possible to know it as a gateway and the way to enter it, and to have the eligibility, without the guidance of a guru.

Therefore, Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman, the King of Pugazhi, shows the way to enter that flame to all the people there, to all those mature souls, and bestows grace. The meaning and underlying thought of the Thiruppathigam, “Kādalāgi Kasindhu” (Melting with love), is this. The entire temple is enveloped by the flame, making it invisible, and the flame rises. The divine gateway is visible. The gateway of the temple is merely a means. As it is said, “The temple itself is worshipped.” This divine gateway is none other than Lord Siva Himself, the ultimate reality.

The ways to enter the temple gateway are spoken of in Vedas, Agamas, and Puranas, but souls cannot know the way to enter the divine gateway of that great radiant flame, Lord Siva.

Therefore, He explains it.

Thus, before showing that gateway to souls and leading them to liberation, he worships and praises that great radiant light, Lord Siva. The guru, who guides souls with maturity to liberation, first ...meditates and praises Lord Siva, saying, “O Lord, grant me the grace to initiate and guide this mature disciple.” This is the rule of the Agama Sastras, which we can recall here.

Thus, worshipping the great radiant light, he shows the way for all the souls in this vast, dark world to be saved. Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman has shown the way for souls bound by the darkness of ignorance and ego, the fundamental impurities, to attain liberation. In the state of liberation, this darkness, this ego, loses all its strength.

Here, Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman appears as the guru. Through meditation, divine instruction, and other forms of initiation, Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman bestows grace upon the mature souls who have come to witness the wedding there. The two thousand four hundred and forty-eighth verse reads: “The path of true wisdom is the mantra Namachivaya for everyone.” He composed the Namachivaya Thiruppathigam, which is significant and pleasing, so that the celestial beings and the king could hear it, and all who have come to this wedding will have their miserable birth removed and enter. This verse is as follows. Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman, by composing the Namachivaya Thiruppathigam, which is a path of true wisdom, and which is significant and pleasing, bestows it so that the celestial beings and the king can hear it. He further declares: “All who have come to this wedding, enter this light to have your birth removed.”

Thus, he commands.

Therefore, in this verse, Devashekhilār Peruman explains that Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman bestowed the Namachivaya Thiruppathigam and, after bestowing it, commanded all who came to the wedding: “Enter this light to have your birth removed.” “Gnana Meineri” is the path to liberation, the path to salvation, which cannot be attained without divine wisdom. “Meineri” means the path to attain the true Lord. Such Gnana Meineri is the five-letter mantra, Namachivaya. It is the conclusion of all Gnana texts, for all people of all religions, of all levels of maturity, at all times and in all places. It is the conclusion. The word Namachivaya is the path of true wisdom.

Namachivaya refers to the five sacred letters, Panchāksaram. The essence of Panchāksaram, the five sacred letters, is for a soul to be freed from attachments and attain Siva.

Therefore, the meaning of the Thiruppathigam is to contemplate and realize the essence of Sri Panchāksaram while entering the divine gateway and attaining the Lord. Due to the greatness of divine grace, the merciful gaze of the guru, and the grace of meditation, the Namachivaya Thiruppathigam has yielded the fruit of Panchāksaram, which is the culmination. It means that liberation cannot be attained without wisdom, and that wisdom is the understanding and realization of the essence of the five-letter word, the five sacred letters. This is its meaning.

Therefore, Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman makes souls realize the path of wisdom through the teaching of Panchāksaram. That teaching of Panchāksaram is revealed as the words of Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman in the Namachivaya Thiruppathigam, which begins with “Kādalāgi Kasindhu.” As stated in the eighth sutra of Sivagnana Bodham, “The first guru, who reveals through penance, leads to the feet without anything else.” The entire meaning of the eighth sutra can be understood here. In accordance with this, the souls who came to Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman’s wedding are those who have performed penance in previous lives and have attained maturity. And they have attained the time when they are eligible for liberation.

The Lord makes Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman realize this.

Therefore, we must understand that Pillaiyar sang, “It is time to attain the shadow of the Lord’s feet,” and the Lord gave the command accordingly. As Sri Meykanda Devanāyanār has stated in the sutra, “Without showing the path of wisdom, which is the righteous path of performing Sariyā, Kriyā, and Yōga, liberation cannot be granted.” Sri Meykanda Devanāyanār elaborated on this sutra, explaining: “The path of true wisdom is Namachivaya for everyone.” He explained that the path of wisdom is the path that leads to liberation, which is considered the greatest good. “Wisdom is the righteous path.” “Righteous path” and “good path” have the same meaning. This is what Sri Madhava Sivagnana Muni has explained in the first adhikaranam of the commentary on the eighth sutra of Sivagnana Bodham.

Thus, Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman bestows the Namachivaya Thiruppathigam for the heavens and the earth to hear. “Heaven and earth” means celestial beings and kings.

Therefore, Devashekhilār Peruman says, “for celestial beings and kings to hear.” This indicates that this Namachivaya Thiruppathigam was composed in the Nishāda svara, the highest note.

Here, all who came to the wedding were mature and eligible for liberation.

Therefore, he bestowed it for them to hear. Generally, the instruction of a mantra should be given secretly, to the student alone, so that others do not try to listen. This rule does not apply here. This rule does not apply to the teaching that Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman is bestowing here. The souls who came to the wedding are eligible for liberation, and they are listening to this teaching, the Namachivaya Thiruppathigam, to attain liberation. Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman bestows this teaching, the Namachivaya Thiruppathigam, so that celestial beings can also hear it.

However, celestial beings do not attain liberation. They are not going to attain liberation because they are in higher worlds due to their abundant good karma. Those celestial beings, after exhausting their karma, will be born on this earth, perform divine merit, and attain wisdom, and only then will they be eligible for liberation in due course.

Thus, the scriptures say that they have not yet attained that stage.

Therefore, even if the celestial beings see this wedding from the heavens, they will not merge into this light and attain liberation. Devashekhilār Peruman has shown us this later.

Thus, Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman, who bestows the Namachivaya Thiruppathigam for the heavens and the earth to hear, appears as the guru in this situation, as stated in Sivagnana Bodham: “The first guru, who reveals through penance.”

Here, the soul, as a result of the special merits accumulated through past lives, has been guided by the indwelling Lord through the paths of Sariyā, Kriyā, and Yōga.

Now, to receive the path of wisdom, the Lord has appeared in the form of a guru. He bestows divine initiation and, looking at the mature soul, says: “You, as a prince, have been deluded and suffered, being subject to the five senses. You have forgotten your greatness.” “Your true nature is to experience divine bliss as a prince, a prince of Siva.” Realizing this truth, and with the Lord Himself appearing as the guru and revealing this truth, the soul, immediately upon realizing this truth, abandons the five senses, which are like hunters, and becomes inseparable from the great Lord, the king. He attains the sacred feet of the great Lord. In accordance with this, Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman, appearing in the form of a guru, bestows the teaching of the Namachivaya Thiruppathigam to the mature souls present there.

At that very moment, all the mature souls who gathered there attain the feet of grace. Such is the Thiruppathigam, the Namachivaya. Thiruppathigam, which begins with “Kādalāgi Kasindhu.” Let us continue to contemplate this Thiruppathigam and its meaning. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Periya Puranam, Volume Eighty-three, Chapter on the Buzzing Bees, by Devashekhilār Peruman. The life of Thiru Gnanasambandhar Nayanar. Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman bestows the Namachivaya Thiruppathigam, which begins with “Kādalāgi Kasindhu.” This Thiruppathigam is the forty-ninth Thiruppathigam in the third Tirumurai. It is a general Thiruppathigam composed in the Kausika tune. The Thiruppathigam is as follows: The concluding verse of the Thiruppathigam is “Kādal Āgi Kannīr Kādal Āgi” (Melting with love, tears of love).

When one melts with love, shedding tears, and chants, it elevates them to the right path. The right path is that which elevates; it is the essence of the four Vedas. The essence of the four Vedas is the Name of the Lord: Namasivaya. Namasivaya, Namasivaya. Those who believe, speak it with their tongues, and it blooms like fragrant flowers. It is the golden tilaka for all the world: The Name to believe in is Namasivaya.

Those who think of His grace, count with rudraksha beads in hand, become worthy. The Name of the naked One is Namasivaya. Even Yama’s messengers fear these words. The excellent Name When one thinks of the divine decree with love, and stands firm, it leads to bliss. Those who embrace it gain many virtues; those who lack them suffer diseases. The Name of the good ones is Namasivaya.

Even kings of the earth, bound by sins, will speak of Him. The Name is Namasivaya. If you seek to enter hell, uttering it a hundred times will help you escape. The Name of the Boon-Giver is Namasivaya. When the king of Lanka lifted Kailash, Sankara pressed it down with His toe. The one who cried out then, and was saved, his good path is the Name of excellence: Namasivaya.

Brahma, the teacher, and the enemy (Ravana) sought His feet. Those who are unable to see Him are lost. The Name is Namasivaya. Those who eat from a skull bowl, and those who speak falsehoods, will be rewarded by the great Lord who drank poison. Namasivaya. The Name of Nandi is Namasivaya.

Those who rejoice in the Tamil words of Gnanasambandhar, filled with love, can break the bonds of worldly attachment. Those who rejoice in the Tamil words of Gnanasambandhar, filled with love, can break the bonds of worldly attachment. The path to salvation revealed by Gnana is the Name of the Lord, the word Namasivaya. This pathigam proclaims it. “When one melts with love, shedding tears, and chants, it elevates them to the right path. The right path is that which elevates; it is the essence of the four Vedas: The Name of the Lord is Namasivaya.” This is the first verse.

It begins with “When one melts with love, shedding tears, and chants...” This verse explains how those who chant the mantra Namasivaya, the five sacred letters, should conduct themselves in mind, speech, and body to benefit. “Melting with love” indicates the state of mind of those who chant Namasivaya. “Shedding tears” shows the physical state of those chanting the mantra Namasivaya. “Chanting” refers to the state of speech.

Therefore, one must chant the mantra Namasivaya with love, melting and shedding tears. It is a Vedic mantra, and thus it must be chanted. Those who chant thus are led to the right path, the path of Siva. The path of Siva, or the right path, is the path from discipline to divine knowledge. To be led on this path of Siva means to be guided. The mantra Namasivaya leads one to the path of liberation.

The Name of God is declared as the ultimate reality in the four Vedas, at the beginning, middle, and end.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandhar proclaims, “It is the essence of the four Vedas.” The mantra Namasivaya, the Sri Panchakshara, being the essence of the four Vedas, is explained in texts like “Sadhurvetha Tatparya Sangraham” and “Siva Tattva Vivekam.” These texts have elaborated and proven it extensively. The Panchakshara, the Name of Siva, is the heart of the Vedas. The mantra that is the essence of the four Vedas is the Name of the Lord Siva: Namasivaya. Lord means God. He is the first, possessing eight divine qualities.

He is the Lord, and it is His duty to embrace all souls. His Name is the five sacred letters. As the juice of sugarcane is sweet, so is His Name. The Thevaram says, “His Name is Siva,” and “He is the Lord with a pure form.” Thus, the Name of the Lord is Namasivaya. Thirugnanasambandhar proclaimed, “Namasivaya.” The method of chanting the mantra Namasivaya, its benefits, and its origin have been explained. “Melting with love” indicates that upon hearing the Name, love overflows.

We can contemplate the full meaning of the Thevaram verse, “She heard His Name earlier.” “Melting” signifies the mind’s focus, the beginning. “Shedding tears” is a physical manifestation of the mind’s melting. Hearing the Name causes melting and tears, which imbue those who chant the mantra Namasivaya with the understanding of their Lord’s greatness, their own smallness, the grace of His Name, and His compassionate embrace, drawing them closer. Knowing these aspects – His imperishable grace, the strength of the darkness of bondage, and the supreme bliss He bestows – leads to melting and shedding tears while chanting Namasivaya. Chanting refers to reciting the mantra in the mind, softly, or aloud. Sivagnana Bodham states, “Reciting the five letters is the rule.” This concludes the meaning of the first verse.

Now, the second verse: “Those who believe, speak it with their tongues, and it blooms like fragrant flowers. It is the golden tilaka for all the world: The Name to believe in is Namasivaya.” This is the second verse. It refers to the devotees who take refuge in the sacred feet of Lord Siva. Those who believe in the five sacred letters will utter them with their tongues. Thirugnanasambandhar refers to those who believe and utter this Name. “He is the Believable One” is His Name, meaning He is worthy of belief.

Accordingly, the verse states, “The Name to believe in is Namasivaya.” He is the Believable One, worthy of trust. Thirugnanasambandhar calls those who believe in Him “Believers.” For one who is ill, there must be faith in the medicine and the doctor. If there is no faith in either, the illness is rarely cured.

Thus, those who take refuge in the sacred feet of Lord Siva will utter the five sacred letters with their tongues. For them, the mantra Namasivaya is as sweet as the honey in fragrant flowers. It is like pure gold and a shining tilaka for all the worlds. Divine bliss is a state beyond mind and speech, unattainable by words.

However, to enlighten the world, Thirugnanasambandhar reveals it through concepts understandable to them.

Now, the third verse: “Those who have great longing in their hearts, think of Him, and count with rudraksha beads in hand, become worthy. The Name of the naked One is Namasivaya.” When the heart melts with love and devotion to Lord Siva, thinking of Him ...it makes them worthy of being exalted above the gods. The Name of Lord Siva, Namasivaya, the five sacred letters, bestows this qualification. When chanting the Sri Panchakshara, it is customary to count with a rudraksha mala in hand. Those who remember the Name Namasivaya in this manner – meaning those who visualize the form within the mantra – become qualified for liberation. It is the Name of the naked Lord Siva, Namasivaya, that makes them worthy.

Now, the fourth verse. Even Yama’s messengers fear, those who can eloquently chant with sweet words. For those who remember the divine decree with love, He is the beloved, the one with the third eye. The Name is Namasivaya. For the devotees who meditate on and worship Lord Siva daily, He always does good. The Name of the Lord with the third eye on His forehead is Namasivaya, the Sri Panchakshara.

Those who can eloquently chant the five sacred letters with sweet words will be feared by Yama’s messengers. Not only that, but Yama’s messengers will also fear approaching those who associate with those who chant the Sri Panchakshara.

Therefore, the Name of Lord Siva, Namasivaya, grants those who chant the Sri Panchakshara according to the rules, freedom from birth and death. This is the Name of Namasivaya.

Now, the fifth verse: “Even if they are murderers, or lack many virtues, if they utter it, all evils will vanish. The Name of the good ones is Namasivaya.” This verse describes the accumulation of evil deeds. The next verse will describe how these sins turn into suffering, and the following verse will explain how they become the fruit of sin and lead to great hell. “Even if they are murderers...” In this verse, murder is the greatest of all evils. Even those who commit this greatest evil, the murder of a living being, and who lack good qualities and virtues, if they chant the Sri Panchakshara, the five sacred letters, due to some past merit ...they will be freed from all kinds of harm, as elders say. The greatest evil, murder, is mentioned first.

All other evils are included within it.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandhar first states, “Even if they are murderers.” Then he says, “Or lack many virtues.” Committing evil is a sin, and not doing good is also a sin.

Thus, after mentioning evil deeds first, Thirugnanasambandhar follows by saying, “Or lack many virtues.” Sivagnana Siddhiyar states: “Doing good for living beings is beneficial; not doing good is harmful.” Harmful means not doing good for living beings. Although they may be in such a state, if they chant the Sri Panchakshara, they will be freed from all evils, as the wise Sivajnanis say. The Name that Sivajnanis speak of is the Name of God, Namasivaya. This is the meaning.

Now, the sixth verse. “Even kings of the earth, bound by sins, will speak of Him. Their evil deeds will vanish, and wealth will increase. The Name of Nandi is Namasivaya.” ‘Mandaram’ means Mount Meru. Even if one has committed countless sins like Mount Meru, and is bound by attachments, if they chant the five sacred letters ...their evil deeds will be destroyed, and their wealth will increase. “Their evil deeds will vanish” means their wicked actions will cease.

This signifies the release from bondage. “Wealth will increase” means their prosperity will grow. This signifies attaining the state of Siva.

Therefore, the Name of Nandi, Namasivaya, removes suffering and brings joy. Nandi is a Name of God. It means one who makes sins perish. ‘Nandhu’ means to perish or diminish.

Now, the seventh verse: “Even if they seek to enter seven hells, if they utter it, they will reside with the Rudras. The Name of the Boon-Giver is Namasivaya.” Even if they are sinners destined for seven hells, if they chant the Sri Panchakshara with devotion, even if only by word of mouth, they will attain the privilege of residing with the Rudras. The Name of Lord Siva, Namasivaya, grants all the boons that devotees ask for. The Name of the Lord, ‘Varadan’ (Boon-Giver), is mentioned in this verse. The Thevaram says, “Perhaps He is the Boon-Giver with a bull’s horns.” Varadan means one who grants boons.

Now, the eighth verse: “When the king of Lanka lifted Kailash, Sankara pressed it down with His toe. The one who cried out then, and was saved, his good path is the Name of excellence: Namasivaya.” ‘Addukkal’ means mountain. When Ravana, the king of Lanka, tried to lift Mount Kailash, Sankara pressed it with the tip of His toe. As he cried out in pain under the mountain, the great Lord Siva, who naturally bestows liberation and does good, His Name is Namasivaya, the Sri Panchakshara. Thirugnanasambandhar always includes a verse about Ravana’s liberation by Siva in the eighth verse of his pathigams. We see this pattern here as well.

Similarly, in the ninth verse of his pathigams, Thirugnanasambandhar traditionally places a verse about Brahma and Vishnu searching for the Lord. In that vein, the ninth verse is as follows: “Brahma, the teacher, and the enemy (Ravana) sought His feet. Those who are unable to see Him are lost. The Name is Namasivaya.” Brahma, dwelling in the lotus, and Vishnu, with lotus-like eyes, searched for the feet and head of the Supreme Lord Siva, the master of all. Unable to find them, they repented their efforts.

Later, gaining true knowledge, they chanted Namasivaya, the Sri Panchakshara. This is the meaning.

Now, the tenth verse. Thirugnanasambandhar traditionally refutes the Jains and Buddhists in the tenth verse of his pathigams.

Accordingly, the tenth verse is as follows: “Those who eat from a skull bowl, and those who use their hands as bowls, those who speak harsh words, are not blessed. The Name of the Poison-Drinker, who accepted nectar at the request of the gods, is Namasivaya.” Those who drink nectar at the gods’ request and hold the poison in their throats, Lord Siva, the Blue-Throated One, His Name is Namasivaya, the five sacred letters. The Buddhists, who have the custom of drinking kanji from a skull-shaped vessel, and the Jains, who eat food from their hands, are not the ones who are blessed.

Now, the eleventh verse. Thirugnanasambandhar traditionally concludes his pathigams with the eleventh verse, revealing the fruits of chanting the pathigam. In this vein, the eleventh verse serves as the concluding verse: “The Name of Nandi is Namasivaya. Those who rejoice in the Tamil words of Gnanasambandhar, filled with love, can break the bonds of worldly attachment.” ‘Santhai’ in this verse is the Tamil form of ‘Chandas’. ‘Chandas’ refers to the musical structure of the Vedas. ‘Chandas’ also generally refers to the Vedas. Thirugnanasambandhar’s pathigams are also considered Vedic pronouncements. Thirugnanasambandhar states in the eleventh verse of his first pathigam, “Thodu udaiya Sevian,” that the pathigams he composed are Vedic hymns.

He has composed numerous pathigams, and in this pathigam too, he concludes by stating that all his pathigams are Vedas. The five sacred letters are the essence of the Vedas and the pathigams. Thirugnanasambandhar conveys here that those who chant this pathigam, composed by Gnanasambandhar, who has the Name Nandi (Siva), with joy in their hearts, can break the bonds of worldly attachment. ‘Bandha Pasam’ means bondage and the impurities that cause it. ‘Arukkal’ means to sever. This is the fruit of this pathigam and the ultimate fruit of Saivism.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandhar concludes this pathigam. We shall continue pondering. Thiru Thiruchitrambalam. Thiruchitrambalam.

Chapter on ThiruGnanasambandhar Nayanar.

Thiruchitrambalam. Thirugnanasambandhar Peareumaal instructed the people gathered for the wedding to attain liberation from the cycle of birth. He declared at the Thiru-perumana-nallur temple, “Enter, all!” into the divine light of Siva that manifested above the temple. The great Lord Thirugnanasambandhar commanded, “Enter, all!” Verse 1249: “They who are immersed in the endless flood of births, suffering in the body’s cage of sorrow, lost in ignorance, enter the divine light by reaching the divine feet and ascending into the effulgent glow of Siva.” This verse describes their entry into the divine light. This birth is the continuous cycle of birth.

Therefore, Devasikhamani calls it the “flood of births.” The actions performed in one birth lead to many more births, and those actions in turn lead to countless thousands of further births. This is the continuous lineage of births. They are called the “flood of births” because they are endless. Drowning in this great flood of endless births, people become lost in ignorance within this body, which is a cage of sorrow. Just as a bird trapped in a cage cannot escape and remains confined within it, similarly, the soul, which should pervade everywhere, is confined and restricted within the body.

Therefore, Sivagnana Bodham calls the body “a cage of suffering.” Most people are trapped in this cage of suffering and become deluded. Delusion is the misapprehension of things – perceiving the unreal as real. It is thinking of something as something else, or thinking of the eternal Brahman as impermanent, or thinking of this transient world as eternal. This state of emotional confusion grips most people. The desire to escape this cage of suffering and attain liberation arises in very few, by the grace of God. Those who realize this body is suffering and wish to escape it will seek the way.

Sivagnana Bodham calls this the soul seeking the body of suffering. This delusion, where one thing is mistaken for another, is dispelled by the teaching of the Panchakshara and the compassionate gaze of the true spiritual teacher. The delusion of the people who came to the wedding was dispelled by the teaching of the Namasivaya pathigam, the Panchakshara, and the divine gaze (Sakshudikshai) of the true spiritual teacher, Thirugnanasambandhar. They were freed from their delusion simply by witnessing the wedding. “Becoming one with Him, serving Him, their impurities and sins vanish.” This is from the tenth sutra of Sivagnana Bodham. “Becoming one with Him and serving Him” refers to reaching the divine feet in the wedding.

This is because the Child (Thirugnanasambandhar) is full of divine knowledge. “They who are immersed in the endless flood of births, suffering in the body’s cage of sorrow, lost in ignorance, enter the divine light by reaching the divine feet...” Those drowning in the suffering of birth realize it is suffering and desire to reach God’s feet. Their delusion is dispelled, and divine consciousness arises. By attending the wedding and reaching the divine feet, they attained liberation. This signifies the purification from impurities and sins mentioned in the tenth sutra of Sivagnana Bodham. According to the ninth sutra of Sivagnana Bodham, “Bondage arises from illusion; the five letters are the rule.” By receiving initiation and teaching according to the rule, and due to the ripeness of their past karma, the power of the primal impurity, anava malam, was destroyed, and they attained liberation from birth.

Those who came to the wedding and witnessed it attained this. The three impurities lost their power, and the fruits of past karma, experienced in this life and remaining for future lives, were also removed by the initiation given by Thirugnanasambandhar.

Thus, freed from the cycle of birth, they entered the divine light. This shows the gradual progression of a soul towards liberation, like climbing steps. By the merit of past penance, one receives the grace and teaching of a Guru. Through the Guru’s teaching, one contemplates and worships the meaning of the mantra. By doing so, the three impurities lose their power. With the power of the three impurities diminished, and through unwavering love, one attains the state of never leaving the sacred feet of Lord Siva.

However, for all this to happen instantaneously and without any hindrance, the ripeness of the soul’s past karma and the intense descent of divine grace, along with the Guru’s grace and spiritual power, are necessary.

Therefore, all those who attended the wedding entered the gateway of divine light shown by the Child. Verse 1250: “Sírperugu Thiru Neelanakkar, Thiru Murugar, and the first devotees, along with their families, entered the divine light.” Following the previous verse, which stated that all who came to witness the wedding entered the divine light, Devasikhamani continues here. The great devotees like Thiru Neelanakkar Nayanar, Thiru Muruganar Nayanar, and the first devotees, along with the radiant Sivapada Irudhayar, Nambandar Nambi, the virtuous Thiru Neelakanta Perumpaana Nayanar, and others, entered the divine light with their families, surrounded by their relatives. These Nayanmars – Thiru Neelanakkar Nayanar, Thiru Muruganar Nayanar, and Thiru Neelakanta Yazhpaana Nayanar – merged into that divine light. Their stories are intertwined with that of Thirugnanasambandhar throughout the Puranam. These three great Nayanmars were praised by Sundaramurthy Swamigal in the Thiru Thondar Thogai pathigam, hence they are mentioned first by Devasikhamani.

In the story of Thirugnanasambandhar, other Nayanmars like Thiru Navukkarasu Perumaan, who is one of the Paramaacharyas, Siruthondar Nayanar, and Kungiliyakalaya Nayanar are not mentioned here. This implies that Thiru Navukkarasu Perumaan, Siruthondar Nayanar, and Kungiliyakalaya Nayanar had already attained the divine feet of God before this event. The groom’s father, Sivapadagirudayar, and the bride’s father, Nambandar Nambi, also entered the divine light and attained the divine feet. Others who came from various places to witness the wedding also merged into the divine light. Generally, relatives are bound by worldly connections.

However, here, these relatives remained until they attained the world of Siva. This indicates that the relatives who came to the wedding were souls ripe for liberation.

Moreover, in the Purana of Iyarpagai Nayanar, Ilaiyankudi Maaranaar Nayanar, Amarneedhi Nayanar, Siruthonda Nayanar, etc., we see the Nayanmars entering the divine world with their wives and children. Throughout the Periya Puranam, even those with strong familial ties like wives and children do not accompany them in worldly death.

But here, they attained the eternal blissful world of Siva without separation. This is demonstrated by Devasikhamani’s words, “Surrounded by their families, they entered.” Now, verse 1251: “Those who carried the jeweled palanquin, those who adorned themselves with pearls, those who performed auspicious rites, and the attendants who served, their minds freed from worldly bonds, attained liberation by merging into the divine light.” In the previous verse, Devasikhamani described how the devotees and the parents of the bride and groom who came to witness the wedding entered the divine light. In this verse, he describes those who attained liberation by performing various services for the great wedding of Thirugnanasambandhar. “Those who carried the jeweled palanquin” refers to those who carried the beautiful pearl palanquin and other royal insignia of Thirugnanasambandhar. They too merged into the divine light.

Next, “women adorned with pearl necklaces” refers to the women who decorated the bride and performed other decorations for the wedding. They all entered the divine light.

Next, “those who performed auspicious rites.” These are the eight auspicious symbols like lamps, full pots, mirrors, fly-whisks, trumpets, banners, and paired fish, which are specially mentioned in the Agamas for Lord Siva, and other auspicious items. Those who carried these also entered the divine light and attained liberation.

Next, “attendants.” These are the servants who performed various tasks, starting with cooking and other services for the wedding. They too entered the divine light and attained liberation. Devasikhamani states, “Their minds freed from worldly bonds, attained liberation by merging into the divine light.” Freed from the bonds of karma and the primal impurity, ‘pasam’, which is the root cause of attachment, they attained liberation. All the aforementioned individuals, filled with this liberating consciousness, attained the divine feet of the Child (Thirugnanasambandhar) and Lord Siva. When the bonds of ‘pasam’ were severed, only God’s presence remained. They merged into the divine light, embodying the truth of unity with God, having served the Child and the Goddess.

Thus, they attained the state of blissful unity with Siva. Let us keep pondering. Thiru Thiruchitrambalam. Thiruchitrambalam.

Thiruchitrambalam. Thiru Thiruchitrambalam. Devasikhamani, in the Periya Puranam, Part 838, Chapter on ThiruGnanasambandhar Nayanar, describes those who merged into the divine light of Siva at the wedding of Thirugnanasambandhar and Sri Sthotrapoornaambigai. Verse 1252: “The ascetics of the six sects, the devoted ascetics, the Vedic scholars, and those who came to worship, as well as others who came for divine grace, all entered the great divine light.” The ascetics of the six sects, who are internal sects of Saivism, also entered the light. They are classified as ‘agachayamis’. Their nature was observed earlier when the wedding procession of Thirugnanasambandhar left சீர்காழி, and people from the six sects joined. All these devout ascetics from the internal sects entered the divine light.

The Vedic scholars who chant the Vedas, the great ones adhering to the Vedic path in the four asramas, also entered the divine light. Next are those who came to worship. These are people who do not fit into the aforementioned three categories but came to worship. They joined the wedding celebration. This includes those who came from சீர்காழி and those who gathered at Thiru-perumana-nallur. They too merged into the divine light.

Next, Devasikhamani mentions “others who came for divine grace.” There was no apparent external reason for them to come, yet they attended the wedding. They too, along with others, entered the divine light and attained liberation. It was divine grace that brought them there. For the sole purpose of granting them liberation, the Lord brought them there. They all entered the great divine light. Devasikhamani calls it the “great divine light.” The Tiruvachakam says, “Unending great light, without beginning or end.” Earlier, Devasikhamani referred to it as “endless Siva’s feet.” The lords like Anandheesar are lords of muktis, but only Paramasivam is the ultimate.

He alone has no beginning or end, no other light greater than Himself. He is the embodiment of divine light. Even the lords of mukti merge into the ultimate Siva at the end of time.

Therefore, Lord Siva alone is the “great divine light.” All who stood there entered that great divine light and attained liberation. The Tala Puranam of Aazhpaala states that a woman who stood aside, unable to join due to some reason, was also called and entered the light.

Now, verse 1253, which describes the greatness of Thirugnanasambandhar and Sri Sthotrapoornaambigai merging into the divine light, appears as verse 3151 in Periya Puranam and verse 1253 in the Child’s Puranam. “Embracing the beloved, circumambulating, and arriving to remove evil, Thirugnanasambandhar, whose divine light grew radiant, entered into it and became one with it, his state of consciousness complete.” Devasikhamani states, “Embracing the beloved, circumambulating...” ‘Beloved’ here refers to the Goddess, the wife. In common worldly usage, the term ‘beloved’ is sometimes used for a wife due to worldly attachments.

However, the love mentioned here is not worldly attachment. It is impossible for such worldly love to exist in Thirugnanasambandhar. Thirugnanasambandhar demonstrates adherence to Vedic norms and worldly life. The wedding was like a divine play.

Therefore, Devasikhamani uses the worldly term ‘beloved’ here. Thirugnanasambandhar, by the command of divine grace, embraced the beloved and circumambulated the divine light. Generally, the principle of a soul attaining liberation is that after living a householder’s life with a wife and fulfilling the remaining karma of their births, they attain the state of Siva through divine merit.

However, for those who are completely free from attachment, like the great souls in this Puranam, attachment cannot even approach them.

Therefore, the Child (Thirugnanasambandhar) did not desire or reject the woman. The householder’s life, living with a wife, is prescribed in God’s scriptures for the welfare of humanity. It is meant to help shed attachments. We saw this earlier when Thirugnanasambandhar blessed the merchant’s daughter in the Thiruppathigam. All these apply to others.

But the Child was free from any attachment, pure, and liberated. Thiruchitrambalam.
